Calls have grown for the resumption of inquests into the Guildford pub bombings, as campaigners and families of victims press for answers to questions they say remain unresolved decades after the attacks.

The bombings took place on October 5, 1974, when the Horse and Groom and the Seven Stars pubs in Guildford, Surrey, were targeted by the Provisional Irish Republican Army. Five people were killed and dozens were injured in the attacks, which were carried out during a period of intense violence linked to the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

Four people were wrongly convicted in connection with the bombings and became widely known as the Guildford Four. Paul Hill, Gerry Conlon, Carole Richardson and Patrick Armstrong were sentenced to life imprisonment in 1975 on the basis of confessions and evidence later found to be unreliable or fabricated.

Their convictions were quashed by the Court of Appeal in 1989 after it emerged that police had withheld evidence and that confessions had been obtained through coercion. The case became one of the most significant miscarriages of justice in British legal history.

In the years that followed, the Maguire Seven, including members of Conlon's family and others who were convicted in relation to explosives, were also exonerated after their convictions were found to be unsafe.

Families of those killed have long expressed frustration with the pace at which the state has responded to their concerns. Many say they were not given adequate information about the investigation and the wider circumstances of the attacks.

Inquests into the deaths of the five victims were opened in the years after the bombings but were adjourned and did not proceed to full examination for a long period. Campaigners argue that this left families without a formal public accounting of what happened.

The original police investigation has itself been the subject of sustained criticism. Former officers and independent reviewers have examined how evidence was handled, how suspects were interviewed, and how information was shared within the force.

Legal experts have noted that the passage of time creates real obstacles to establishing the facts. Many witnesses have died, records may be incomplete or lost, and memories have faded.

Nonetheless, supporters of renewed inquests argue that the public interest in a full and transparent examination remains strong. They say that a formal hearing could clarify how the attacks were investigated and whether any further lines of inquiry were neglected.

Questions have also been raised about whether intelligence was available before the bombings and how it was acted upon. Campaigners want to know whether warnings were given, and whether security services or police had information that could have prevented the attacks.

Some families have asked for the release of documents held by government departments and security agencies. They argue that material relating to the investigation and to informants should be disclosed where national security concerns can be addressed without blanket secrecy.

Government officials have previously said that they take the concerns of victims seriously but must balance transparency against the need to protect sensitive information and ongoing operational matters. This balance remains a central point of contention in the current debate.

Legal representatives for the families have argued that the existing framework for inquests can be used to examine these matters, provided that the coroner is given the powers and resources needed to conduct a thorough investigation.

Surrey coroners have, in the past, been asked to consider how to proceed in cases involving historical deaths linked to the Troubles. Each case presents its own difficulties, and coroners must weigh procedural fairness, the rights of those who may be affected, and the practical limits of investigating events so long ago.

The Guildford bombings are part of a wider pattern of attacks during the 1970s that affected communities across Britain. Many of the victims and survivors have spoken publicly about the long-term physical and psychological effects of the attacks on their lives.

Survivors have described the trauma of the explosions, the loss of friends and colleagues, and the difficulty of rebuilding their lives while waiting for answers. Some say that the failure to resolve key questions has deepened their sense of injustice.

Community groups in Guildford have also called for remembrance and for an honest acknowledgement of what took place. Local leaders have spoken of the need to ensure that the town's history is recorded accurately and that the voices of those affected are heard.

Commemorations held in recent years have drawn crowds of residents, former police officers, relatives and journalists. Speakers have urged that the lessons of the miscarriages of justice be remembered alongside the grief of those bereaved.

The wrongful convictions of the Guildford Four and the Maguire Seven led to major reforms in the criminal justice system, including changes to how confessions are handled, how forensic evidence is disclosed, and how appeals are considered. Some campaigners argue that similar scrutiny should now be applied to the investigation itself.

Academic researchers have examined the case as a study in how public pressure, police culture and political priorities can shape investigations. Their work has contributed to ongoing debate about accountability and institutional memory.

Some commentators have argued that the case illustrates the importance of independent oversight, while others caution against reopening wounds without a clear purpose or a realistic prospect of substantial new findings.

Victims' advocates counter that the purpose of an inquest is not only to assign blame but to establish facts, to give families a voice, and to demonstrate that the justice system is willing to examine its own failures.

Politicians from several parties have raised the matter in Parliament, calling for clarity about the government's position and for a timetable for any further review. Some have asked whether a statutory inquiry might be more effective than a coroner's inquest in examining the wider questions.

Officials have said that any decision will be guided by legal advice and by the need to ensure that proceedings are fair to all those involved. They have also indicated that they will consider the practical resources required.

Families have welcomed the renewed attention but say that words must be followed by action. Many have spent decades seeking information, and they say that further delay compounds the original injury.

For some relatives, the central demand is simple: a full and public account of how their loved ones came to die, and a recognition that the investigation and its aftermath were not handled as they should have been.

Whether an inquest will resume, and in what form, remains uncertain. What is clear is that the question of unresolved answers continues to resonate in Guildford and beyond, nearly half a century after the bombings that changed so many lives.

This paper addresses the problem of learning optimal transport costs between two datasets when only partial, group-level correspondences are available rather than point-to-point matches. The authors frame the task as a neural learning problem, parameterizing the cost function with a network and training it so that the resulting transport plans respect known group-level alignments. The motivation is compelling, since in many applied settings, such as single-cell biology or population studies, individual correspondences are unavailable while coarse group labels are routinely measured. The introduction situates the work clearly within the optimal transport literature and identifies a genuine gap between fully supervised cost learning and purely unsupervised transport. The methodology is described with reasonable detail, including the loss formulation that combines an entropic transport objective with a group-consistency term. However, the derivation of the group-level constraint could be stated more rigorously, as it is not fully clear how the constraint behaves when group sizes are highly imbalanced. The experimental section evaluates the method on synthetic data and two real-world datasets, which is a sensible progression from controlled to realistic settings. The synthetic experiments convincingly show recovery of a ground-truth cost structure under varying amounts of group-level supervision. The real-data results are less convincing, as the baselines chosen are somewhat limited and do not include recent neural optimal transport solvers that could serve as stronger comparisons. Ablation studies on the regularization strength are informative, though the sensitivity analysis would benefit from reporting variance across random seeds. The paper would also be strengthened by a discussion of computational cost, since neural parameterization of the cost adds training overhead relative to fixed-cost transport. The related work section is thorough but occasionally repetitive, and some citations appear without a clear connection to the proposed approach. Figures are generally well designed, though the transport plan visualizations would be easier to interpret with clearer color scales and annotated group boundaries. The writing is clear overall, with a few passages in the methods section that would benefit from tighter notation consistency. The theoretical claims about identifiability of the cost function under partial supervision are stated but only sketched, and a fuller proof or a precise statement of assumptions would greatly improve confidence. The authors should clarify the conditions under which the learned cost is unique, since multiple cost functions may induce the same group-level marginals. Code availability is mentioned, which supports reproducibility, but the hyperparameter settings for the real-data experiments should be reported more completely. Overall, the paper makes a useful contribution at the intersection of optimal transport and weakly supervised learning. Its practical relevance is clear, and the core idea is promising. I recommend a major revision that addresses the theoretical assumptions, strengthens the baselines, and expands the reproducibility details before the work can be considered for publication.

Allowing students to use phones during lunch and free periods, under clear school rules, is a reasonable compromise between student freedom and academic focus. Phones are now a central part of how teenagers communicate with family, friends, and even emergency contacts, so a complete ban can feel unnecessary and frustrating. Lunch and free periods are times when students are not in class, so permitting phone use during these windows does not interrupt instruction. Students also need some downtime to rest their minds between lessons, and scrolling or messaging can be a simple way to recharge. Clear rules, such as phones staying in bags during class and being used only in designated areas, would help prevent misuse. Schools could also set consequences for violations, such as temporary confiscation, so students understand that the privilege depends on responsible behavior. Allowing phone use at these times can also teach self-regulation, a skill students will need in college and at work. Supervised, limited access may reduce the temptation to sneak phones into classrooms, since students would no longer feel they must hide their devices. Teachers would also be spared the constant task of enforcing a total ban throughout the day. Some worry that phones encourage bullying or distraction, and these concerns are valid, which is why rules must include clear expectations about respectful behavior online. Ultimately, trusting students with limited, well-defined freedom can build maturity and mutual respect between schools and the students they serve. A thoughtful policy that balances access with accountability is better than either a blanket ban or unlimited use.

Academic eligibility requirements for student athletes exist to keep education at the center of school sports. Most high school and college athletic associations require students to maintain a minimum grade point average, often 2.0 on a 4.0 scale, in order to compete. These standards send a clear message that athletic participation is a privilege earned through classroom effort rather than a substitute for it. Critics argue that such rules can unfairly punish students who struggle in a single subject or who come from schools with limited academic support. However, many schools respond to these concerns by providing tutoring, study halls, and mentoring programs that help athletes stay on track. Eligibility checks are typically reviewed each grading period, which gives students a regular chance to recover before losing their place on a team. Supporters also point out that the discipline required to balance practice schedules with homework can teach valuable time management skills. Coaches and teachers often work together to monitor progress, creating a support network around each athlete. Some educators believe that stricter requirements would encourage more students to take their coursework seriously from the start. Ultimately, the goal of academic eligibility rules is not to exclude students but to ensure that sports strengthen, rather than weaken, a student's overall education.

Innovative Sanitation Solutions and Global Efforts to Expand Access to Toilets

Access to safe toilets is one of the most basic yet most overlooked foundations of public health. Today, billions of people still lack safely managed sanitation, and the consequences include diarrheal disease, stunted growth in children, and the spread of intestinal parasites. Improving sanitation is therefore not only a matter of comfort or dignity but also a direct route to better health, education, and economic opportunity. Governments, international organizations, researchers, and communities have increasingly recognized this and have worked to expand access in many parts of the world. One major focus is the development of low-cost toilet designs suited to areas without reliable water or sewer systems. Pit latrines with improved ventilation and lining, urine-diverting dry toilets, and pour-flush designs that use only small amounts of water are examples of solutions that can be built locally. Another area of innovation is faecal sludge management, which addresses what happens after waste leaves a toilet. Many households rely on septic tanks or pits that need regular emptying, so trucks, treatment plants, and safe disposal systems are essential parts of a complete sanitation chain. Decentralized treatment units, some of which convert waste into fertilizer or energy, are being tested in several countries. Community-led total sanitation is a widely used approach that encourages villages to recognize open defecation as a shared problem and to build and maintain their own toilets without external subsidies. Its success depends on local participation, social motivation, and ongoing follow-up rather than simply distributing hardware. Public and school toilets are also important, since girls who lack private, clean facilities at school may miss classes during menstruation or drop out altogether. Sanitation programs that include hygiene education, handwashing stations, and menstrual health support tend to produce stronger and more lasting benefits. Many countries have set national targets, and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 6 calls for universal access to adequate and equitable sanitation and hygiene by 2030. Progress has been real but uneven, with rapid urban growth, weak institutions, and funding gaps slowing advances in many regions. Monitoring through household surveys and national reporting helps track coverage and identify where help is most needed. Financing remains a central challenge, and experts often recommend a mix of public funding, private investment, and microfinance loans that allow families to pay for toilets over time. Technology is also playing a growing role, with mobile apps for tracking emptying services, sensors that monitor toilet use, and digital payment systems that make services easier to access. Researchers continue to explore ways to recover nutrients and water from waste, which could make sanitation systems more sustainable and reduce pollution. Wastewater that is discharged untreated can contaminate rivers, groundwater, and coastal areas, so treatment is an essential part of any long-term strategy. Effective sanitation depends on combining appropriate technology with good governance, community engagement, and sustained investment. When these elements work together, the benefits extend well beyond the household, improving public health for entire neighborhoods and nations. Continued global cooperation will be needed to ensure that every person, regardless of where they live, can access a safe and dignified toilet.

Src-Mediated Inhibition of PP2A Modulates ERK Signaling and Neuroprotective Transcription Factors Following Cerebral Ischemia

Abstract

Cerebral ischemia triggers a cascade of molecular events that determine whether neurons survive or die, and kinase and phosphatase signaling networks are central to this outcome. Among these, the non-receptor tyrosine kinase Src and the serine/threonine phosphatase protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) have emerged as important regulators of neuronal stress responses. This study examines how Src-mediated inhibition of PP2A influences extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) signaling and the activity of neuroprotective transcription factors after ischemic injury. We propose that Src activation following ischemia phosphorylates specific tyrosine residues on the PP2A regulatory subunit, reducing holoenzyme activity and thereby sustaining ERK phosphorylation. Sustained ERK activity, in turn, promotes the nuclear accumulation and transcriptional activation of factors such as CREB, Nrf2, and NF-kB subunits that support neuronal survival. The findings are discussed in the context of therapeutic strategies targeting this signaling axis. We acknowledge that much of the mechanistic detail remains to be validated in vivo, and we identify key gaps for future investigation.

Introduction

Stroke remains a leading cause of death and long-term disability worldwide, and ischemic stroke accounts for the large majority of cases. The core pathology involves reduced cerebral blood flow, which deprives neurons of oxygen and glucose and initiates excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, calcium overload, and inflammation. Over the past several decades, numerous neuroprotective agents that performed well in preclinical models have failed in clinical trials, prompting renewed interest in the intracellular signaling pathways that govern neuronal fate after ischemia. Rather than targeting a single downstream event, many investigators now focus on upstream regulatory nodes that coordinate multiple protective and destructive responses simultaneously.

Protein kinases and phosphatases form a dynamic regulatory layer that controls the phosphorylation state of countless substrates. The balance between kinase and phosphatase activity determines signal amplitude and duration, and disruption of this balance is implicated in many neurological disorders. Protein phosphatase 2A is one of the most abundant serine/threonine phosphatases in the brain, existing as a family of holoenzymes assembled from a scaffolding subunit, a catalytic subunit, and one of several regulatory subunits. These regulatory subunits determine substrate specificity and subcellular localization. PP2A has been shown to dephosphorylate components of the mitogen-activated protein kinase cascade, including ERK, and therefore acts as a brake on proliferative and survival signaling.

Src is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that integrates signals from receptor tyrosine kinases, integrins, G protein-coupled receptors, and ion channels. Src activity is elevated in neurons and glia following ischemia and hypoxia, and pharmacological inhibition of Src has been reported to reduce infarct volume in several rodent models. Src is known to phosphorylate and modulate the activity of PP2A, although the precise sites and consequences vary by cellular context. A plausible model is that Src phosphorylation of PP2A regulatory subunits diminishes phosphatase activity toward ERK, allowing ERK to remain active for longer periods than would otherwise occur.

Extracellular signal-regulated kinase is a central effector of survival signaling in neurons. Transient ERK activation supports synaptic plasticity and cell survival, whereas sustained activation can, depending on context, either protect or promote death. The temporal pattern of ERK activity therefore appears to be critical, and the phosphatases that terminate ERK signaling are attractive candidates for controlling this pattern. We hypothesized that the Src-PP2A axis shapes ERK dynamics after ischemia in a manner that favors neuroprotection.

The downstream consequences of ERK activation include phosphorylation and activation of transcription factors that regulate genes involved in cell survival, antioxidant defense, and anti-inflammatory responses. Cyclic AMP response element-binding protein (CREB) is phosphorylated by ERK-activated kinases such as RSK and MSK, and phosphorylated CREB recruits coactivators to induce expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor and Bcl-2 family members. Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) controls antioxidant response element-dependent genes, including heme oxygenase-1 and components of glutathione synthesis, and ERK signaling has been reported to facilitate Nrf2 nuclear translocation. Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kB) plays a more ambiguous role, since its activation can be neuroprotective early after injury but detrimental when prolonged, and its regulation by ERK-dependent pathways remains an active area of study.

Despite these advances, several questions remain unresolved. It is not clear which Src phosphorylation sites on PP2A are relevant after ischemia, whether these modifications occur in neurons versus glia, or how the timing of Src activation relates to the reperfusion window. It is also uncertain whether the transcriptional outputs of sustained ERK signaling are uniformly beneficial. The present work was designed to address these gaps through a combination of mechanistic experiments in cultured neurons and in vivo models of transient middle cerebral artery occlusion.

Materials and Methods

Animals

Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats weighing 250 to 300 grams were housed under standard conditions with free access to food and water. All procedures were approved by the institutional animal care committee and conformed to national guidelines for the care of laboratory animals. Animals were randomly assigned to sham, ischemia-vehicle, and ischemia-drug groups, and investigators performing outcome assessments were blinded to group allocation.

Transient Focal Cerebral Ischemia

Transient focal ischemia was induced by intraluminal occlusion of the middle cerebral artery for 60 minutes, followed by reperfusion. Anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane, and body temperature was controlled throughout surgery. Regional cerebral blood flow was monitored by laser Doppler flowmetry to confirm occlusion and reperfusion. Sham animals underwent identical surgical procedures without filament insertion.

Pharmacological Treatments

The Src inhibitor PP2 and the selective PP2A inhibitor okadaic acid were used at concentrations previously shown to be effective in neural tissue. Drugs were administered intraperitoneally or intracerebroventricularly at defined time points relative to reperfusion. Vehicle controls received equivalent volumes of diluent. A MEK inhibitor, U0126, was used to confirm that observed effects depended on ERK activation.

Primary Neuronal Cultures and Oxygen-Glucose Deprivation

Primary cortical neurons were prepared from embryonic day 17 rat embryos and maintained in neurobasal medium supplemented with B27 for 12 to 14 days in vitro. Oxygen-glucose deprivation was performed by replacing culture medium with glucose-free balanced salt solution and placing cultures in a hypoxic chamber containing 95 percent nitrogen and 5 percent carbon dioxide for 90 minutes. Reoxygenation was achieved by returning cultures to normal medium and standard incubation conditions.

Immunoblotting and Immunoprecipitation

Protein lysates were prepared from cortical tissue and cultured neurons in buffer containing phosphatase and protease inhibitors. Equal amounts of protein were resolved by SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride membranes. Membranes were probed with antibodies against phospho-Src (Tyr416), total Src, the PP2A catalytic subunit, the PP2A regulatory subunit B55alpha, phospho-ERK1/2 (Thr202/Tyr204), total ERK1/2, phospho-CREB (Ser133), total CREB, and Nrf2. Immunoprecipitation of PP2A was performed using catalytic subunit antibodies, and co-immunoprecipitated Src was detected by immunoblotting. Phosphotyrosine status of B55alpha was assessed by immunoprecipitation followed by blotting with a pan-phosphotyrosine antibody.

PP2A Activity Assay

PP2A phosphatase activity was measured in immunoprecipitates using a malachite green-based assay with a phosphopeptide substrate. Activity was normalized to total PP2A protein determined by immunoblotting. Specificity was confirmed by parallel reactions containing okadaic acid.

Quantitative PCR

Total RNA was extracted from cortical tissue and cultured neurons, reverse transcribed, and subjected to quantitative PCR for Bdnf, Bcl2, Hmox1, Nqo1, and Tnf. Expression was calculated using the comparative threshold cycle method and normalized to Gapdh and Actb.

Immunohistochemistry and Infarct Measurement

Brains were sectioned coronally at 20 micrometers and stained with antibodies against phospho-CREB and Nrf2 for nuclear localization analysis. Infarct volume was assessed at 24 hours after reperfusion by 2,3,5-triphenyltetrazolium chloride staining, with correction for edema. Neurological deficits were scored using a standardized five-point scale.

Statistical Analysis

Data are presented as mean plus or minus standard error of the mean. Comparisons between two groups were made using two-tailed Student's t tests, and comparisons among multiple groups used one-way analysis of variance followed by Tukey's post hoc test. Non-normally distributed data were analyzed with nonparametric tests. A p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Sample sizes were determined by power analysis based on pilot data.

Results

Ischemia Increases Src Activation and Reduces PP2A Activity

Phosphorylation of Src at tyrosine 416, a marker of kinase activation, increased markedly in the ischemic cortex and peaked between 30 minutes and 2 hours after reperfusion. This increase was accompanied by a significant reduction in PP2A catalytic activity measured in immunoprecipitates, while total PP2A protein levels remained unchanged. Sham animals showed no comparable changes. In cultured neurons subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation and reoxygenation, a similar pattern emerged, with Src activation preceding the decline in PP2A activity.

Src Associates with and Phosphorylates the B55alpha Regulatory Subunit

Co-immunoprecipitation experiments revealed that Src physically associated with PP2A holoenzymes in ischemic tissue, and this association was enhanced after reperfusion. Immunoblotting with anti-phosphotyrosine antibodies showed increased tyrosine phosphorylation of B55alpha following ischemia, and this modification was blocked by pretreatment with PP2 but not by vehicle. These observations support the proposal that Src directly modifies the regulatory subunit and reduces the capacity of the holoenzyme to dephosphorylate its substrates.

Inhibition of Src Preserves PP2A Activity and Limits ERK Dephosphorylation

Administration of PP2 at the onset of reperfusion prevented the ischemia-induced decline in PP2A activity. In parallel, PP2 treatment shortened the duration of phospho-ERK elevation, with ERK phosphorylation returning toward baseline more rapidly than in vehicle-treated animals. Conversely, okadaic acid treatment mimicked the effect of Src activation by sustaining ERK phosphorylation and extending the time course of phospho-ERK elevation. These results indicate that PP2A normally limits ERK activity after ischemia and that Src suppresses this limitation.

ERK Activity Controls CREB and Nrf2 Activation

Phosphorylation of CREB at serine 133 increased after ischemia, and this increase was reduced by PP2 and enhanced by okadaic acid. The effects of okadaic acid on CREB phosphorylation were abolished by U0126, confirming that they depended on ERK signaling. Nuclear localization of Nrf2 was similarly increased after ischemia, and it was sensitive to the same pharmacological manipulations, suggesting that ERK-dependent signals support Nrf2 nuclear accumulation. Consistent with these findings, transcript levels of Bdnf, Bcl2, Hmox1, and Nqo1 were elevated after ischemia, and their induction was modulated in the expected directions by the Src and PP2A inhibitors.

Transcriptional Responses Are Dependent on Timing

Quantitative analysis revealed that early ERK activation, occurring within the first two hours after reperfusion, was associated with increased expression of neurotrophic and antioxidant genes. In contrast, prolonged ERK activity beyond six hours was associated with increased Tnf expression and elevated NF-kB nuclear signal, suggesting a shift toward a pro-inflammatory transcriptional profile. Okadaic acid treatment, which sustained ERK activity, produced a similar shift when administered late, but not when administered early, indicating that the timing of PP2A suppression determines whether downstream transcriptional outputs are protective or harmful.

Neuroprotective Outcomes

Animals treated with PP2 at reperfusion showed significantly smaller infarct volumes and improved neurological scores at 24 hours compared with vehicle-treated animals. Okadaic acid administered early after reperfusion did not significantly alter infarct volume but worsened neurological outcome when given late. Co-administration of U0126 abolished the protective effect of PP2, supporting the conclusion that the benefit of Src inhibition depends on preserved ERK signaling and not on an ERK-independent mechanism.

Discussion

This study supports a model in which ischemia-induced Src activation suppresses PP2A activity through tyrosine phosphorylation of the B55alpha regulatory subunit, thereby modulating ERK signaling dynamics. The principal finding is that the duration and timing of ERK activation, rather than its mere presence, determine whether downstream transcription factors promote neuronal survival or contribute to injury. Early ERK activation, which we find is facilitated by Src-mediated suppression of PP2A, appears to drive CREB and Nrf2 activity and support the expression of neurotrophic and antioxidant genes. When ERK activity is prolonged, the transcriptional program shifts toward inflammatory signaling involving NF-kB, which may account for the detrimental effects of late PP2A inhibition.

These results are consistent with prior work showing that ERK signaling is neuroprotective in some contexts and harmful in others, and they provide a mechanistic explanation for this apparent contradiction. The temporal window model proposed here suggests that therapeutic strategies should aim to enhance ERK activity transiently during the early reperfusion period rather than sustaining it indefinitely. Src inhibition may be well suited to this goal because it restores PP2A activity over time, allowing natural termination of ERK signaling once the acute phase has passed. This property may distinguish Src-targeted approaches from direct ERK activators, which could produce prolonged activation.

The link between Src and CREB activation is of particular interest because CREB is a convergence point for multiple survival pathways in neurons. Our data suggest that ERK-dependent phosphorylation of CREB contributes substantially to the neuroprotective effects of Src inhibition. Whether this effect involves direct phosphorylation by ERK-activated kinases or indirect mechanisms through calcium-dependent kinases remains to be determined. Similarly, the enhancement of Nrf2 nuclear localization by ERK signaling raises the possibility that Src-PP2A signaling coordinates antioxidant defense with transcriptional support for neuronal survival, an interpretation that merits further testing.

The role of NF-kB in our model deserves careful consideration. NF-kB activation contributes to early inflammatory responses that clear damaged tissue, but sustained activity can exacerbate injury. Our observation that prolonged ERK activity correlates with increased NF-kB nuclear signal and Tnf expression suggests that the Src-PP2A-ERK axis may influence the balance between these outcomes. However, we did not directly establish a causal link between ERK and NF-kB in our experiments, and this relationship should be examined using targeted genetic approaches.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the pharmacological agents used, including PP2 and okadaic acid, have off-target effects, and their selectivity in neural tissue is incompletely characterized. Although we included controls with U0126 and parallel PP2A activity assays, genetic approaches such as conditional knockdown or knock-in of nonphosphorylatable B55alpha mutants would provide stronger evidence. Second, our analyses were largely confined to the cortex, and the striatum and hippocampus may respond differently given their distinct cell populations and vulnerability profiles. Third, we examined a single ischemic duration and a single rodent strain, and extending these findings to other models and to female animals is necessary. Fourth, the transcriptional measurements were performed on bulk tissue, obscuring potential cell-type-specific responses in neurons, astrocytes, microglia, and endothelial cells.

Future studies should identify the precise tyrosine residues on B55alpha that are phosphorylated by Src and determine whether mutation of these sites alters ERK signaling and infarct outcome in vivo. Single-cell transcriptomic and spatial profiling would clarify which cell populations mediate the protective transcriptional responses. Time-resolved imaging of ERK activity using biosensors in living animals could further refine the temporal window model. Finally, the translational potential of Src inhibition must be weighed against the broad physiological roles of Src in platelets, endothelium, and immune cells, and combination strategies that limit systemic exposure may be necessary.

Conclusion

Src-mediated inhibition of PP2A after cerebral ischemia appears to prolong ERK signaling in a time-dependent manner, favoring the activation of CREB and Nrf2 and supporting neuronal survival during the early reperfusion period. Excessive or late ERK activation may instead promote inflammatory transcription through NF-kB and worsen outcome. These findings identify the Src-PP2A-ERK axis as a potential therapeutic target for ischemic stroke, with the caveat that its benefits depend critically on timing and that further mechanistic and translational work is required before clinical application can be considered.

Polyhouse Technology: An Introduction to Protected Crop Cultivation

A polyhouse is a protected structure covered with transparent or translucent polyethylene film that allows farmers to grow crops under controlled conditions. Polyhouses are widely used in horticulture to extend growing seasons, improve yields, and protect plants from adverse weather. This page explains the core components, common applications, key advantages, and the methods used to control the environment inside these structures.

Structural Components

The frame is the skeleton of the polyhouse and is typically made from galvanized steel pipes, although some low-cost structures use bamboo or wood. The frame must bear the weight of the cover, withstand wind loads, and support any additional equipment such as irrigation lines and fans. The cover is most often made of ultraviolet-stabilized polyethylene film, commonly between 100 and 200 microns thick, which transmits sunlight while retaining heat. Some growers use polycarbonate sheets or glass, which offer longer life and better light diffusion but at a higher cost.

Doors, vents, and side walls allow access and airflow. Roof vents or ridge vents release hot air, while side vents and exhaust fans provide cross-ventilation. Insect-proof nets are fitted over openings to block pests while still allowing air to pass through. The floor may be bare soil, gravel, or concrete, depending on drainage needs and the crop being grown.

Growing Systems

Polyhouses can house several growing systems. Soil-based beds remain the simplest and most common option. Raised beds improve drainage and make cultivation easier. Soilless systems, such as hydroponics, aeroponics, and grow bags filled with coir or perlite, deliver nutrients directly to roots and reduce soil-borne disease. Drip irrigation is usually paired with these systems to supply water and fertilizer efficiently.

Applications

Polyhouses are used to grow a wide range of crops. Vegetables such as tomatoes, cucumbers, capsicum, lettuce, and leafy greens are commonly produced in protected structures. Flowers, including roses, carnations, and gerberas, are grown for the cut-flower market. Seedling and nursery production benefits from the stable conditions, allowing uniform and disease-free young plants. Some growers also use polyhouses for herbs, strawberries, and high-value specialty crops.

Advantages

The main advantage of polyhouse cultivation is protection from unfavorable weather, including heavy rain, hail, strong winds, and extreme temperatures. Growers can produce crops outside their natural season, which often commands higher market prices. Yields per unit of area are generally higher because plant growth is more consistent and inputs are used more efficiently. Water use is reduced when drip irrigation is combined with the controlled environment, and pesticide use can be lowered because the structure limits pest entry. Product quality, including size, color, and shelf life, tends to be more uniform.

There are also limitations. Initial construction costs can be substantial, and the system requires skilled management, regular maintenance, and reliable power for fans and automated controls. Polyethylene covers degrade over time and must be replaced periodically.

Environmental Control

Managing the internal environment is central to polyhouse success. Temperature is regulated through ventilation, shading, and, where needed, heating or evaporative cooling. Pad-and-fan cooling systems draw outside air through wet pads, lowering the temperature inside the house during hot periods. Shade nets reduce light intensity and heat load during peak sunlight. In cold climates, heaters, thermal screens, and double-layer covers help retain warmth at night.

Humidity is another critical factor, since high humidity encourages fungal diseases. Ventilation, dehumidifiers, and careful irrigation scheduling help keep relative humidity within an appropriate range for the crop. Carbon dioxide enrichment can boost photosynthesis in sealed houses, while sensors monitor levels and adjust supply automatically. Light management, including supplemental lighting and shade control, ensures plants receive adequate photosynthetically active radiation.

Modern polyhouses increasingly use automated climate control systems. Sensors measure temperature, humidity, light, and soil moisture, and a controller adjusts vents, fans, shade, heaters, and irrigation in response. Such systems reduce labor, improve consistency, and allow growers to respond quickly to changing conditions.

Conclusion

Polyhouse technology offers a practical way to produce high-quality crops with greater reliability and efficiency. By understanding the structural components, suitable growing systems, and environmental control methods, growers can choose the right design for their crops and climate. Careful planning, ongoing monitoring, and regular maintenance are essential to achieving the full benefits of protected cultivation.

Online schooling offers a practical path for students who must juggle education with work, family duties, and limited access to transportation. For many young people, the traditional model of attending classes at a fixed campus during set hours simply does not fit their lives. Online learning changes that equation by bringing the classroom to wherever the student already is.

Consider a student who works part-time at a grocery store to help support a household. A rigid morning schedule at a physical school may force that student to choose between income and education. With online courses, many of which allow asynchronous participation, the student can review lectures late in the evening or complete assignments during a quiet break between shifts.

Family responsibilities present another significant barrier. Some students care for younger siblings, aging grandparents, or relatives with health needs. Online schooling allows these students to remain present at home while still making academic progress. They do not have to abandon their families to earn a diploma, nor abandon their studies to meet family obligations.

Transportation is often an overlooked obstacle. In rural areas, a school may be an hour away by bus, and some families own no car at all. Students in these situations can miss classes, arrive exhausted, or leave school entirely. Online learning removes the commute, along with its costs in money, time, and energy.

Critics sometimes argue that online schooling lacks the social connection and structure of in-person education. These concerns deserve attention, and well-designed programs address them through scheduled video sessions, discussion boards, and mentoring. Structure can also come from clear deadlines and regular check-ins with teachers.

Flexibility alone is not enough, however. Students need reliable internet access, a functional device, and a quiet place to study. Schools and communities can help by providing loaned laptops, subsidized connectivity, and spaces such as libraries where students can log in. Without these supports, the promise of online learning remains out of reach for the students who need it most.

Teachers also play an important role. They must design courses that respect students' varied schedules while still encouraging participation and accountability. When instructors respond promptly to questions and offer feedback that feels personal, students are more likely to stay engaged.

Online schooling does not suit every learner, and some students thrive best in person. Still, for those balancing work, family, and limited transportation, it can mean the difference between finishing school and dropping out. Education should adapt to the lives of students rather than forcing students to abandon their other responsibilities. Online learning, when supported properly, moves toward that goal. It recognizes that a student's worth and potential do not depend on the ability to travel to a building each morning. By widening the doors of education, online schooling gives more people the chance to build the futures they want.

Community-Centered Development: Meeting Human Needs Sustainably

Development is often measured by income, infrastructure, and economic output, but a growing body of thought asks a more basic question: what do people actually need in order to live well? This approach, often associated with the work of economist Manfred Max-Neef and others, starts from universal human needs rather than from a fixed list of goods or services. Human needs, in this view, are few, finite, and the same across cultures and across time. What changes from one society to another is the set of strategies people use to satisfy those needs. Understanding this distinction is the foundation of a community-centered approach.

The needs commonly identified in this framework include subsistence, protection, affection, understanding, participation, leisure, creation, identity, and freedom. Subsistence covers food, shelter, water, health care, and the physical basis of life. Protection includes safety, social security, and systems that shield people from harm. Affection refers to bonds of love, friendship, and care, while understanding concerns learning, analysis, and making sense of the world. Participation means having a voice and a role in decisions that affect one's life, and leisure refers to rest, play, and reflection. Creation includes imagination, skill, and the making of new things, identity is a sense of belonging and self-definition, and freedom is the capacity to choose.

A key insight is that needs are not hierarchical in the way often assumed. Traditional models present needs as a ladder, where basic survival must be satisfied before higher aspirations emerge. A needs-based approach instead treats all fundamental needs as simultaneously present and interrelated. A person without participation or identity is not less human for having enough food, and a community rich in affection may still lack adequate subsistence. Recognizing this interdependence helps planners avoid treating one dimension of well-being as a substitute for another.

Poverty, from this perspective, is best understood as the failure to satisfy fundamental needs rather than simply a shortage of money. Income is one means of meeting needs, but it is not the only one, and it can even undermine some needs when pursued at any cost. A community whose members are forced to migrate for work may see its affection and identity eroded, even as household incomes rise. This is why community-centered development pays close attention to the full range of human needs and the social fabric that supports them.

Sustainability enters the picture because the strategies used to satisfy needs have consequences for people and the planet. Some ways of meeting needs are destructive: they deplete resources, damage ecosystems, or create dependence that eventually fails. Others are regenerative and can be sustained for generations. The approach encourages communities to evaluate satisfiers, meaning the specific goods, services, practices, and institutions used to meet needs, according to whether they nourish or diminish the capacity to meet needs in the future.

Consider the need for subsistence in a rural village. One satisfier might be an industrial monoculture that produces large quantities of food for export but degrades soil and displaces local farmers. Another might be a diversified system of local agriculture, seed-saving, and cooperative marketing that feeds families while maintaining the land. Both satisfy subsistence in the short term, but only the second keeps the means of satisfaction intact over time. Evaluating satisfiers in this way makes trade-offs visible.

Sustainable satisfiers tend to share several characteristics. They are often local, drawing on resources, knowledge, and labor within the community. They tend to strengthen relationships rather than replace them, and they usually allow many needs to be met at once. A community kitchen, for example, may satisfy subsistence, affection, participation, and creation simultaneously. By contrast, a purely commercial service may meet one need efficiently while leaving others unaddressed.

Community-centered development places local people at the center of defining needs and choosing satisfiers. Outside experts can contribute knowledge, but the people who live with the consequences should guide decisions. This is not romantic localism; it reflects the practical reality that communities know their own conditions, histories, and resources, and that solutions imposed from outside often fail when they do not fit local life. Participatory processes such as community assemblies, local surveys, and collaborative planning help bring diverse voices into the discussion.

Participation is itself a fundamental need as well as a method. When people have genuine influence over the decisions that shape their surroundings, their sense of freedom, identity, and understanding grows. Development projects that exclude residents may deliver physical outputs while weakening the social capacity needed to sustain them. Involving the community from the beginning tends to produce more durable results and builds the skills that allow communities to respond to future challenges.

Local knowledge deserves particular respect. Many communities have developed sophisticated practices for managing water, forests, food, and health over generations. These practices often reflect deep understanding of local ecosystems and social relationships. Recognizing this knowledge does not mean rejecting useful innovations from elsewhere, but it does mean treating local expertise as a partner rather than an obstacle. The best outcomes often come from combining traditional understanding with new tools.

Economic systems play an important role in shaping which satisfiers are available. Markets can efficiently provide many goods, but they can also crowd out non-market ways of meeting needs, such as family care, volunteer work, and mutual aid. A community-centered approach does not reject markets but asks how they can serve human needs without displacing the relationships and institutions that give life meaning. Cooperatives, community land trusts, local currencies, and public services are examples of arrangements that can keep economic activity connected to community well-being.

The distinction between needs and satisfiers also helps clarify the problem of consumption. Modern societies often try to meet needs such as affection, identity, or leisure through the purchase of goods. A new product may promise belonging or status, but it rarely satisfies these needs fully, and the cycle of purchase and disappointment can drive environmental damage without deepening well-being. Recognizing that many needs are better met through relationships, shared activities, and meaningful work can reduce material demand while improving life quality.

Affection and understanding are needs that thrive in community settings. Families, neighborhoods, schools, and congregations all provide spaces where people give and receive care and learn from one another. Development strategies that strengthen these spaces, such as supporting neighborhood gatherings, intergenerational programs, and community education, can meet multiple needs at low material cost. These social infrastructures are often overlooked in conventional planning, yet they are central to resilience.

Creation and identity are also deeply tied to community life. People express their creativity through art, music, craftsmanship, storytelling, and the design of their own spaces. When communities have opportunities to create, they affirm their cultural identity and develop a sense of ownership over their environment. Supporting local artists, traditional crafts, and participatory design can therefore be a form of development in its own right.

Protection, the need for security and safety, requires attention to both physical and social dimensions. Physical protection includes safe housing, clean environments, and reliable infrastructure. Social protection includes networks of mutual support, fair institutions, and systems that cushion people against illness, unemployment, and disaster. Communities with strong social ties often recover more quickly from crises because people already know and trust one another.

Leisure, though sometimes treated as a luxury, is a genuine human need. Rest, play, celebration, and contemplation renew people physically and emotionally. Development that considers leisure may protect public parks, support festivals, and ensure that work schedules allow time for family and community life. Such provisions are inexpensive compared with many material goods yet contribute significantly to well-being.

Freedom, in this framework, is both a need and a condition for meeting other needs. It means having real options and the capacity to choose among them. Communities that lack freedom cannot easily shape their own futures, while individuals who lack it may be unable to pursue education, work, or relationships on their own terms. Community-centered development seeks to expand these options by distributing power more fairly and by removing barriers that concentrate control.

Measuring progress is a challenge for this approach. Indicators such as gross domestic product capture some aspects of economic activity but miss many dimensions of need satisfaction. Communities may develop their own indicators, tracking such things as access to clean water, participation in local decisions, the health of social networks, and the condition of local ecosystems. These measures can guide action and help communities see whether their strategies are truly working.

Education has a special role in this vision. Learning systems can equip people with understanding of their own needs and the satisfiers available to them, and they can teach skills for participation and collaboration. Community-based education, which draws on local knowledge and connects to local problems, tends to be especially effective. It also helps build the capacity for ongoing self-direction.

Health care illustrates the value of a needs-based perspective. Medical treatment addresses illness, but health depends on many factors, including clean water, nutritious food, safe housing, social connection, and meaningful work. Community health initiatives that address these determinants alongside clinical care tend to produce better results. They also engage residents as active contributors to their own well-being rather than passive recipients of services.

Environmental sustainability is not an add-on to this approach but part of its core. Because human needs depend on the natural world, damage to ecosystems ultimately undermines subsistence, protection, and other needs. Communities that protect their watersheds, maintain healthy soils, and conserve biodiversity are investing in their own long-term capacity to meet needs. Local stewardship often proves more effective than distant regulation because residents have a direct stake in the outcome.

Challenges remain. Community-centered development can struggle when communities are divided by conflicting interests, when local leaders are unaccountable, or when resources are too scarce to support ambitious plans. It can also be slow, because genuine participation takes time. Recognizing these limitations allows practitioners to design processes that are inclusive, transparent, and realistic, and to build the trust needed to address difficult questions.

Scaling up is another question. Local initiatives may succeed in one place but fail to spread, or they may be absorbed into larger institutions that dilute their original purpose. Some practitioners address this by building networks among communities, sharing lessons while respecting local differences. Others focus on changing policies and institutions so that supportive conditions exist more widely. Both paths require patience and careful attention to the principles of participation and sustainability.

Ultimately, a community-centered approach asks us to rethink what development is for. Its purpose is not simply to produce more goods or raise national income but to enable people to satisfy their fundamental needs in ways that are fair, meaningful, and lasting. By focusing on universal human needs, evaluating the satisfiers we choose, and placing communities at the center of decisions, this approach offers a path toward well-being that respects both people and the earth they depend on.

Marcus had spent three years learning to hide what he felt. On the track, he was all discipline, all clean lines and steady breath. Off it, the resentment he carried for Dylan Reyes had been building like pressure behind a dam.

It had started in their sophomore year, when the coach named Dylan captain over him. Marcus had trained harder, arrived earlier, and never missed a session, yet the armband went to the boy who laughed easily and never seemed to try.

Over time, the grudge hardened into something colder. Marcus told himself he was over it, but he replayed the moment in the locker room every night before he slept.

Then came the relay final at the regional meet. Dylan had dropped the baton on the final exchange, and the team lost by a fraction of a second. Afterward, the coach blamed Marcus for a slow first leg, and Dylan said nothing to defend him.

That was the night Marcus followed Dylan to the parking lot. The shouting started quickly, and words he had swallowed for years came pouring out. Dylan shoved him, and Marcus shoved back, harder than he meant to.

Dylan hit the concrete curb with a sound Marcus would never forget. For a long moment neither of them moved. Then Dylan's eyes fluttered and went still.

Marcus ran. He drove home with his hands shaking on the wheel and told his parents he had been sleeping all evening. The next morning, the school was buzzing with rumors of a hospital transfer and a head injury.

The police came to the school two days later. Marcus sat in the counselor's office and answered every question with a calm he did not feel. They believed the accident account he gave, and the case was ruled a fall.

Months passed. Marcus ran faster than ever, and the coach praised his discipline. He almost believed the secret was buried for good.

Then, in the spring, a letter arrived at the house with no return address. Inside was a photograph taken from the lot's security camera, showing two figures near the curb and one of them clearly his own jacket.

Marcus stared at the image until the paper blurred. Someone had seen everything, and they wanted him to know it. He folded the photograph and slid it into his bag, his heart pounding louder than any starting gun.

The next day, he walked into the principal's office without being called. His voice shook as he told the truth from beginning to end. The secret he had buried for months finally surfaced, and with it, the weight he had carried for so long began to lift.

Remote education has become a common part of modern schooling, and it offers several benefits that can support students' well-being, independence, and academic concentration. Although it is often criticized for isolating learners, a well-designed remote learning experience can give students more control over their time and environment, which in turn can make learning more meaningful and sustainable.

One of the most important advantages of remote education is the opportunity it provides for improved well-being. Many students spend long hours commuting to school, which can be tiring, expensive, and stressful. When learning takes place from home, students can save this time and use it for rest, exercise, or family activities. Being in a familiar environment can also reduce anxiety for students who feel overwhelmed by crowded hallways, loud classrooms, or social pressures. For students dealing with bullying, illness, or social discomfort, remote learning can offer a safer and calmer space in which to participate.

Remote education also encourages independence. Students who learn online must take responsibility for organizing their schedules, managing assignments, and tracking deadlines. Without a teacher standing nearby to remind them of every task, they learn to set goals, plan their work, and monitor their own progress. These skills are valuable far beyond the classroom, as they prepare students for university, careers, and everyday life, where self-direction is essential. Over time, students who practice these habits often develop greater confidence in their ability to handle challenges on their own.

Academic concentration can also benefit from remote learning. Many students find that they can focus more deeply when they control their surroundings. They can choose a quiet corner, adjust the lighting, or take short breaks when their attention begins to fade. Some learners who struggle with constant interruptions in a traditional classroom discover that they can work through material at their own pace, rewatching lessons or pausing to take notes. Digital tools such as recorded lectures, interactive exercises, and online libraries further support focused study by allowing students to revisit difficult concepts whenever they need to.

Of course, remote education is not without challenges. Students need reliable internet access, a suitable workspace, and guidance to avoid distractions from phones or social media. Teachers must design online lessons carefully to keep students engaged and to check in on their well-being. Schools and families therefore play an important role in helping students make the most of remote learning. With the right structure and support, however, the benefits can be significant.

In conclusion, remote education has the potential to improve students' well-being by reducing stress and giving them more time for rest. It can build independence by asking students to manage their own learning. It can also strengthen academic concentration by allowing students to create focused study environments that suit their needs. When combined with thoughtful teaching and community support, remote learning can be a valuable and effective option for many students.

Attending school in person offers students advantages that go beyond what a screen can provide. While online learning has expanded access to education, the classroom remains a uniquely effective environment for academic growth and for preparing students for the opportunities ahead. This essay examines why in-person schooling supports both academic success and future prospects.

The first advantage lies in the quality of direct interaction between students and teachers. A teacher in a physical classroom can read facial expressions, notice confusion, and adjust an explanation on the spot. Students who hesitate to ask questions in a large online meeting often feel more comfortable raising a hand in a familiar room. This immediate feedback helps students correct misunderstandings before they grow into serious gaps in knowledge.

Consistent routines also play a central role in academic achievement. Arriving at school at a set time, moving between classes, and working alongside peers create a structure that many students need to stay focused. Without that structure, the day can easily drift, and assignments can be pushed aside. The discipline built through regular attendance often carries over into college and the workplace.

Peer learning is another powerful benefit of in-person education. Students gain much from discussing ideas with classmates, debating interpretations of a text, and solving problems together at the same table. These exchanges sharpen reasoning and expose students to perspectives they might never encounter on their own. Group projects in a shared space tend to be more productive because collaboration happens naturally rather than through awkward digital coordination.

Access to school resources further strengthens the case for attending in person. Libraries, science laboratories, art studios, music rooms, and athletic facilities are often difficult to replicate at home. Hands-on work in a chemistry lab or a woodworking shop develops skills that a video demonstration cannot fully teach. Students who use these resources regularly build practical competence alongside theoretical knowledge.

School counselors and mentors are more accessible in person as well. A student struggling with course selection, personal stress, or career direction can drop by an office and speak with an adult who knows them. These relationships often lead to scholarship information, internship referrals, and letters of recommendation that open doors later. Such guidance is harder to provide when students are isolated behind a screen.

In-person schooling also builds social and emotional skills that employers and universities value. Students learn to manage conflict, work in diverse groups, communicate with people of different ages, and handle the ordinary pressures of a shared community. These abilities are developed through daily contact rather than through formal instruction alone. Many of the qualities that future employers describe as essential, such as teamwork and adaptability, grow from these experiences.

Extracurricular activities provide additional opportunities that depend on physical presence. Sports teams, debate clubs, theater productions, student government, and volunteer groups all contribute to a well-rounded profile. Participation in these activities builds leadership, time management, and a sense of belonging. Admissions officers and hiring managers often look for evidence of this kind of involvement.

Finally, attending school in person helps students develop a sense of belonging and identity. Feeling connected to a school community can increase motivation and reduce the isolation that sometimes undermines academic effort. Students who feel known and supported are more likely to persist through difficult courses and to pursue ambitious goals.

None of this means that online learning has no value. Flexible formats can serve students with particular needs, and technology can enhance instruction when used thoughtfully. However, for most students, the combination of direct teaching, peer collaboration, structured routines, rich resources, and personal mentorship makes in-person attendance the strongest foundation for academic success. Schools and families should therefore prioritize in-person learning while using technology as a supplement rather than a replacement. Doing so gives students the best chance to achieve their potential and to build the skills and relationships that will shape their futures.

Hi team, I wanted to share some examples of long-term electricity procurement auctions held in Europe and North America that may be useful for our planning. In the UK, the Contracts for Difference auction rounds have awarded long-term contracts to renewable generators, providing revenue stability for new projects. In France, the Commission de Régulation de l'Énergie has run periodic tenders for onshore wind and solar capacity with multi-year support arrangements. In the United States, several state utilities, such as those in New York and California, have conducted long-term renewable and capacity procurement solicitations through competitive bidding. Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator has also used long-term procurement processes to secure supply for its grid. I can pull together the auction design details and results for any of these if that would help our analysis. Please let me know which ones you would like me to prioritize.

This paper proposes an optimal transport-based framework for robust learning under label noise, and the central idea of aligning noisy label distributions with clean target distributions via a transport plan is well motivated and timely. The authors' emphasis on cost-metric design is a strength, as they systematically compare Euclidean, cosine, and learned feature-space costs and provide a clear rationale for why the choice of ground metric affects the robustness of the resulting transport plan. However, the theoretical justification for the chosen cost function is largely heuristic, and the manuscript would benefit from a formal analysis of how the metric interacts with the entropic regularization parameter and with the assumed noise transition matrix. The experimental section evaluates on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and a real-world web-noise benchmark, which is a reasonable selection, but the noise injection protocols are not fully specified, making it difficult to judge whether the reported gains reflect the method or the particular noise realization. On fairness of comparison, the baselines include several recent methods, yet the authors do not state whether all methods received the same backbone, data augmentation, training schedule, and hyperparameter search budget, and this omission is important given how sensitive noisy-label results are to these choices. The tuning procedure for the proposed method appears to use a validation set with clean labels, which would give the method an advantage unavailable to some baselines, and the authors should either report results under a noisy-only validation protocol or explicitly discuss this asymmetry. Ablation studies isolating the contribution of the cost-metric design from the transport formulation are included but limited to a single dataset, and extending them would strengthen the central claim. The reported standard deviations are computed over only three random seeds, which is insufficient to support the claimed improvements of less than one percentage point on several benchmarks. The related work section is thorough in covering optimal transport in domain adaptation but underrepresents recent robust loss and sample-selection methods that are the most direct competitors. The writing is generally clear, though several notational inconsistencies between the transport plan and the label-correction matrix should be resolved. Code availability is mentioned, which is commendable, but the release should include the exact noise generation scripts to enable reproduction. Overall, the paper offers a promising direction, but I recommend major revision to clarify the experimental protocol, strengthen the statistical reporting, and provide a more rigorous justification for the cost-metric choices before the claims can be fully accepted.

An optimistic outlook is more than a cheerful attitude; it is a way of interpreting the world that can shape how people pursue their goals and how they treat the people around them. Although optimism is sometimes dismissed as naive, research in psychology has linked a hopeful mindset with greater resilience, better health, and stronger social bonds. Understanding how this outlook supports both personal success and healthy relationships can help students see why it is worth cultivating.

The first benefit of optimism lies in how it affects motivation. A person who believes that effort will eventually produce results is more likely to keep trying after a setback. Consider a student who fails an exam. A pessimistic student may conclude that they are simply not capable and stop studying, while an optimistic student may treat the result as information about what to change. This difference in interpretation often determines who continues improving over time.

Optimism also helps people manage stress. Challenges such as heavy workloads, financial pressure, or personal loss are unavoidable, but the way a person frames them makes a significant difference. Optimists tend to focus on what they can control and to look for solutions rather than dwelling on what has gone wrong. This does not mean ignoring problems. Rather, it means approaching them with a sense that they can be addressed, which reduces the emotional toll and keeps energy available for constructive action.

In the workplace, an optimistic outlook can open doors. Employers often value people who remain calm under pressure, take initiative, and see opportunities where others see obstacles. An optimistic employee is more likely to volunteer for new projects, ask for feedback without feeling threatened, and recover from mistakes without losing confidence. Over the years, these habits can build a reputation for reliability and leadership.

Optimism plays an equally important role in relationships. People are naturally drawn to those who radiate hope and goodwill, and a positive attitude can make social interactions more enjoyable for everyone involved. An optimistic friend is someone others want to talk to, because they tend to listen generously, celebrate successes, and offer encouragement during difficult times. Such qualities create a sense of safety that allows friendships to deepen.

The way optimists interpret other people's behavior also strengthens their connections. When a friend forgets a birthday or a colleague makes a careless remark, an optimistic person is more likely to assume good intentions or at least consider alternative explanations before reacting with anger. This generosity prevents small misunderstandings from escalating into lasting conflict. In contrast, a habitually suspicious mindset can erode trust, even when no real wrong has occurred.

Optimism also supports empathy. Because optimists believe that people and situations can improve, they are often willing to invest in helping others grow. They may offer patient guidance to a struggling teammate or stay supportive of a sibling going through a hard period. This willingness to see potential in others encourages those people to rise to the expectations placed on them, creating a cycle of mutual encouragement.

It is important to recognize that optimism has limits when it becomes unrealistic. Someone who ignores warning signs, dismisses legitimate concerns, or refuses to prepare for foreseeable risks may end up worse off. The healthiest form of optimism is grounded in honesty. It accepts that difficulties exist while maintaining a belief in one's ability to meet them. This balanced approach allows people to plan carefully without losing hope.

Students can cultivate optimism through practical habits. Keeping a journal of small accomplishments can remind a person of their progress during discouraging periods. Reframing negative thoughts by asking what might be learned from a setback can shift attention toward growth. Surrounding oneself with supportive people also reinforces a hopeful perspective, since attitudes often spread through social circles.

Gratitude is another useful practice. Taking time each day to notice good experiences, however small, trains the mind to recognize positive aspects of life. Over time, this habit can make optimism feel less like an effort and more like a natural way of seeing the world. Many people find that expressing gratitude to others also strengthens their relationships, since appreciation tends to be returned.

Optimism does not guarantee success, and no mindset can erase every hardship. Talent, opportunity, and circumstance all play roles in what people achieve. However, an optimistic outlook improves the odds by keeping people engaged, resilient, and open to others. It shapes the choices they make and the way they treat those they care about.

In conclusion, an optimistic outlook supports personal success by fueling persistence, reducing the harmful effects of stress, and opening opportunities in work and study. It also strengthens relationships by encouraging trust, generosity, empathy, and mutual support. When balanced with realism, optimism becomes a practical resource rather than a wishful fantasy. For students preparing to build careers and communities, cultivating a hopeful yet grounded perspective may be one of the most valuable investments they can make in their future.

The river had been dying for as long as Mara could remember. Its water ran gray with runoff from the factories upstream, and the fish that once leapt beneath the bridge had long since vanished. Her grandmother used to say the river remembered when it was clean, and that it was waiting for someone to remember with it.

Mara did not believe in waiting. She believed in the cracked concrete of the riverbank, where she spent her mornings collecting bottles and plastic scraps that the current carried in. Most of the town saw her as a nuisance, a girl who wouldn't stop talking about pollution at the council meetings.

Across the water lived Tomas, whose family ran the largest of the plants. His father had built the town's jobs with his own hands, and to Tomas, the factory was not a monster but a promise kept to people who had almost nothing. When Mara and Tomas first met at the town hall, they shouted at each other until the chairman banged his gavel in frustration.

Neither of them was wrong, and that was the hardest part. Mara saw children coughing in the clinic and farmers whose wells had turned bitter. Tomas saw his neighbors losing their homes when the plant closed, and he saw his father's dignity rooted in that work. Each of them carried a truth the other could not easily hold.

For a long time they stayed on opposite banks, speaking only through the newspaper and the cold stares of the market. Then came the flood that spring, when the river rose higher than anyone had seen and swept through the lower streets. Mara was there with a boat and a rope, pulling a stranger from the current, and Tomas was there too, hauling sandbags until his hands bled.

They did not talk much that night. They simply worked side by side, and when a child was carried out of a flooded kitchen, both of them reached for her at the same moment. The child's mother wept, and neither Mara nor Tomas could say whose hands had saved her.

In the weeks that followed, the town gathered in the school gymnasium to rebuild. Mara brought her map of the contaminated wells, and Tomas brought the plant's engineering records. They argued over every line, but the arguing had changed. It had become a conversation between people who had seen each other's courage.

It was Tomas who first proposed the filtration project, though his father resisted it at first. It would cost money and time, and the plant would have to change its methods. Mara agreed to accept the compromise, and she agreed to help design the system that would clean the river at its source.

Progress was slow. Some residents still blamed Mara for the lost jobs, and some still blamed Tomas for the poisoned water. But Mara began teaching the younger children to test water with simple kits, and Tomas began bringing his engineers to the riverbank on weekends.

One autumn evening, Mara sat on the bridge with Tomas and watched a heron land in the shallows. It was the first bird they had seen there in years, and neither of them spoke for a long while. The water was still gray, but there was a faint silver in it where the light touched.

"My grandmother said the river was waiting," Mara said quietly.

Tomas smiled. "Maybe it was waiting for us to stop shouting."

They did not agree on everything, and they never would. But they had learned that caring for the same place could be a bridge between people who saw the world differently. The river did not heal overnight, and the town did not become perfect. Still, when the children of the valley came down to the water each morning, they came together, and in their laughter Mara heard the first real hope she had known in years.

The hospital corridor smelled of antiseptic and burnt coffee, the same as it had for twenty-six years of Daniel Reyes' working life, but tonight it felt like a foreign country. He had walked it a thousand times as a physician, greeting nurses by name, delivering bad news with a steady hand. Tonight he was only a husband waiting outside a room he could not enter.

Inside, Elena was sleeping after the sedative they had given her.
