She had wandered out of the house at three in the morning, barefoot, in her nightgown, and he had found her two miles away standing at the edge of the reservoir, humming a lullaby to no one. The police officer who brought her home had been kind, and that kindness had been harder to bear than anger would have been.

Daniel had known the signs for years. He had seen them in his own notes and dismissed them, telling himself that he was tired, that she was stressed, that everyone forgot where they put their keys. He had diagnosed hundreds of patients with early cognitive decline and had still missed what was happening in his own kitchen. That failure sat in his chest like a stone.

The neurologist came down the corridor with a folder under one arm. Her name was Dr. Okafor, and she had been gentle from the first appointment, which he suspected she did for every family she met. She did not sit down. She simply said that Elena needed more care than he could provide at home, and that a memory-care facility with round-the-clock staff was the safest option now.

Daniel nodded because nodding was what he did with difficult information. He asked the questions he would have asked a patient's family: about medication, about the timeline, about what the next six months might look like. Dr. Okafor answered them all honestly, and he was grateful for her honesty even as it made his stomach turn.

Afterward he sat in the car in the parking structure for a long time without starting the engine. He thought about the wedding, about Elena dancing badly in a borrowed dress, laughing at his terrible jokes. He thought about the years she had spent raising their daughter while he worked eighty-hour weeks, and how she had never once complained in his hearing. He realized now that she had likely been losing her grip on the world for a long time, carrying it silently while he was busy saving other people.

The guilt came in waves. He should have noticed sooner. He should have insisted on testing. He should have quit the extra shifts and been home more, watching the small changes that now seemed so obvious in hindsight. Each thought arrived with the cold clarity of a diagnosis he could not treat.

His daughter Sofia called from Chicago that evening, her voice tight with the effort of holding herself together. She asked whether he was all right, and he found he could not answer. She told him she was booking a flight for the weekend. He told her there was no need, and she told him that was exactly the kind of thing he always said.

The next morning he visited the facility the hospital had recommended. It was clean and bright, with a garden courtyard and staff who seemed to genuinely like the residents. A woman in a cardigan was singing softly to an elderly man in a wheelchair, and the man was tapping his fingers in time. Daniel stood in the doorway longer than he meant to.

He filled out the forms at a small wooden desk while the administrator explained the visiting policies. His hand shook when he signed his name in the space marked "relationship to patient." He wrote "husband," then sat for a moment looking at the word, feeling the weight of every promise he had made and was now unable to keep in the way he had imagined.

When he returned to the hospital, Elena was awake and sitting up in bed, looking out the window at the parking lot. She turned when he entered and smiled at him with a warmth that made his throat close. For a moment she seemed entirely herself, and she asked him in a clear voice whether he had eaten lunch.

He sat beside her and took her hand. He told her the truth, gently, because she had always deserved the truth from him even when it was hard. She listened with her head tilted, the way she used to listen to their daughter's stories, and when he finished she said simply, "Oh, Daniel. You're so tired."

He had no answer for that. He only held her hand tighter and let the silence stretch between them, the same silence they had shared on countless quiet evenings in their long marriage. Outside the window the sun was going down over the parking lot, and somewhere a car alarm chirped and fell silent.

Later that night, after the staff had settled her into her new room, Daniel returned home to an empty house. He walked through the kitchen where she had once left handwritten notes on the refrigerator, reminders about groceries and birthdays. One note was still there, taped crookedly beside the calendar, in her looping script: "Daniel, don't forget to call Sofia."

He stood in front of it for a long time. Then he took it down carefully, folded it once, and placed it in his shirt pocket over his heart. Tomorrow he would go back to the facility, and the day after that, and every day for as long as she needed him. Guilt would stay with him, he knew, but so would love, and he had decided that love would have to be enough to carry the rest.

The hardware store clerk, Dana, rang up the order without looking up. Three bags of rock salt, a box of iron nails, a spool of red thread, and a bottle of holy water from the church gift shop. "Big project?" she asked, the way she asked everyone. The man, Mr. Hollis, didn't smile. "Your ceiling fan has a draft that isn't from the vent, and the cellar door won't stay shut." Dana laughed and said, "Sure, and the mop is haunted too." He nodded gravely, as if she had made a fine point. "The mop is not, but you should keep an eye on the lawn mower." She rolled her eyes and handed him his receipt. He thanked her, sincerely, and paused at the door. "Thank you for not making me explain twice," he said. Dana grinned, assuming a good joke had landed. Later that night, she mentioned the odd customer to her coworker, who only frowned at the bag of salt on the counter. Dana shrugged it off, but she locked the cellar door behind her all the same.

Optimism plays a powerful role in helping people succeed across many areas of life. In the workplace, an optimistic outlook encourages employees to view challenges as solvable problems rather than insurmountable obstacles, which keeps them motivated during difficult projects. Optimistic people also tend to set higher goals and persist longer when they face setbacks, often leading to greater achievement over time. In relationships, optimism helps people assume the best about others, which can reduce conflict and build trust. Hopeful individuals are generally more willing to forgive mistakes and to work through disagreements rather than giving up on connections. Everyday life benefits as well, since a positive mindset can lower stress and improve overall well-being. People who expect good outcomes are more likely to take care of their health, pursue new experiences, and bounce back from disappointments. While optimism is not a guarantee of success, it creates the mental conditions in which effort, kindness, and resilience can flourish.

A commercial passenger jet and a small unmanned drone came dangerously close during its approach to a major airport, according to aviation officials, prompting renewed calls for stricter oversight of recreational and commercial drone flights. The airliner, carrying more than 150 passengers, was descending on its final approach when the crew spotted the drone at a altitude where aircraft often operate, forcing the pilots to take evasive action. No injuries were reported, and the aircraft landed safely, but investigators said the separation between the two was far less than the safety margin required. Aviation safety experts noted that even small drones can cause serious damage if they strike an engine, windshield, or landing gear, and that the risk increases sharply near airports. The incident has been reported to the relevant aviation authority, which is reviewing flight data and collecting statements from the crew and air traffic controllers. Drone operators are generally required to keep their aircraft within sight and below set altitude limits, and to avoid restricted airspace around airports, but officials acknowledged that enforcement remains difficult. Industry groups said the event underscores the need for better detection technology, clearer registration requirements, and stronger penalties for operators who ignore airspace rules. Some lawmakers have called for expanded use of geofencing and remote identification systems that would let authorities locate drones in real time. Investigators have not yet identified the operator of the drone, and anyone with information is being urged to come forward. The findings of the investigation are expected in the coming months and could shape future regulations governing drone flight near busy airports.

Comparative Evaluation of South Africa's Clinical Trial Register Against International Registries for Accessibility, Information Completeness, and Usability

Abstract

Transparent registration of clinical trials is a foundational requirement for research integrity, evidence synthesis, and the protection of research participants. South Africa operates a national clinical trial register, the South African National Clinical Trial Register (SANCTR), alongside its participation in the broader global registry ecosystem. This paper presents a comparative evaluation of the national register against major international registries, namely ClinicalTrials.gov, the EU Clinical Trials Register, the ISRCTN registry, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), with respect to accessibility, information completeness, and usability. The evaluation framework draws on established criteria for trial registry quality, including the WHO Trial Registration Data Set, the ICMJE registration requirements, and principles of open data. The findings indicate that the national register performs adequately on basic accessibility but shows gaps in the completeness of mandatory data elements, inconsistent update practices, and limited machine-readable interoperability. Usability assessments reveal that search functionality and result presentation lag behind leading international platforms. The paper concludes with recommendations for strengthening the national register, including adoption of standardized data schemas, application programming interfaces, improved multilingual support, and enforcement of timely results reporting.

Introduction

The registration of clinical trials before participant enrollment has become a central norm in biomedical research. Registration reduces selective outcome reporting, discourages publication bias, and enables patients, clinicians, regulators, and systematic reviewers to identify ongoing and completed studies. The Declaration of Helsinki, the World Health Organization, and the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors have each articulated expectations that trials be prospectively registered in publicly accessible databases. Against this backdrop, the quality of a national register is not merely an administrative concern but an ethical and scientific one.

South Africa has a substantial clinical research enterprise, supported by public academic institutions, private contract research organizations, and an active regulatory framework administered by the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority and the national health research ethics structures. The country has also been a significant site for multinational trials in HIV, tuberculosis, maternal health, and non-communicable diseases. Given this volume of research activity, the transparency of trial information generated within South Africa has implications both locally and for the global evidence base.

Despite these strengths, there has been limited systematic scrutiny of how the national register compares with international registries. Most prior assessments of registry quality have focused on ClinicalTrials.gov or on the European registry, leaving African national registries comparatively understudied. This gap motivates the present evaluation, which adopts a structured comparative approach across three dimensions: accessibility, information completeness, and usability.

Background and Literature Review

Trial registries vary considerably in governance, legal mandate, data requirements, and technical architecture. Some are established by statute and linked to regulatory approval, while others are voluntary platforms operated by academic or nonprofit bodies. Prior studies comparing registries have documented wide variation in the proportion of trials with complete primary outcome information, the timeliness of updates following trial completion, and the availability of summary results. Several analyses have found that a notable share of registered trials omit key fields such as eligibility criteria, primary outcome measures, or sponsor details.

The WHO Trial Registration Data Set specifies a minimum set of items that every registry should capture, including primary registry identification, trial identification numbers, sponsor, health condition, intervention, study type, recruitment status, eligibility, outcomes, and contact details. The ICTRP was established to federate data from primary registries meeting these standards, and participation in the ICTRP network is one indicator of a national register's alignment with international norms. Accessibility, in this context, refers to the ease with which the public can locate and retrieve registry content without barriers such as account requirements, restrictive licensing, or technical failures.

Usability encompasses the design of search interfaces, filtering options, result displays, and the capacity of users with varying levels of technical expertise to extract meaningful information. Machine-readability, including support for bulk download and structured data formats, is increasingly regarded as an essential component of usability for researchers conducting meta-research and living systematic reviews.

Methods

The evaluation was conducted as a structured comparison using a predefined framework. The national register and four international registries were selected to represent a range of governance models and geographic scopes. For each registry, the team recorded the availability of public search access, the presence of advanced search filters, the availability of bulk data downloads, and the existence of application programming interfaces.

Information completeness was assessed by drawing a stratified random sample of registered trials from each platform and scoring each record against the WHO Trial Registration Data Set. Each mandatory item was coded as present, partially present, or absent. Completeness scores were calculated as the proportion of required items fulfilled. Timeliness was measured as the interval between trial start date and registration date, and between primary completion date and the most recent update.

Usability was evaluated through a set of predefined tasks performed by trained reviewers, including locating a trial by condition, identifying trials with a specified intervention, retrieving eligibility criteria, and exporting a dataset of results. Task completion time, number of steps, and error rates were recorded. Reviewers also applied a heuristic usability checklist covering navigation clarity, consistency, error prevention, and accessibility for users with disabilities, following established web accessibility guidelines.

Two independent reviewers conducted the scoring, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Inter-rater agreement was calculated using the kappa statistic. Descriptive statistics and comparative tests were used to summarize differences across registries.

Results

Accessibility

All five registries were publicly accessible without subscription or login requirements for basic search and record retrieval. The national register provided free access to individual trial records and supported keyword searching. However, the national register did not offer a documented application programming interface, and bulk export options were limited compared with ClinicalTrials.gov and the EU Clinical Trials Register, both of which provide downloadable datasets in structured formats. ISRCTN offered flexible export options, and the ICTRP provided a federated search across participating registries but did not hold primary data for all trials.

Accessibility of the national register's interface for users with visual or motor impairments was partially compliant with recognized guidelines. Several form controls lacked descriptive labels, and certain result tables were not navigable by keyboard alone. International registries generally performed better on these criteria, though none achieved full conformance in every tested area.

Information Completeness

The proportion of mandatory fields completed varied substantially across registries. ClinicalTrials.gov and ISRCTN recorded high completion rates for primary identification, sponsor, and intervention fields. The national register showed high completion for basic identification and sponsor fields but lower completion for eligibility criteria and for detailed outcome definitions, including time frames and measurement methods. Contact information was present for a majority of records but was frequently incomplete for trials with multiple sites.

Timeliness of registration showed a notable gap. A subset of trials on the national register was recorded after enrollment had commenced, contrary to the prospective registration expectation. Update practices were also inconsistent, with many records not revised after recruitment closed or after study completion. The availability of summary results was limited on the national register relative to the international platforms that mandate or strongly encourage results posting.

Usability

Task-based evaluation showed that reviewers completed condition-based and keyword searches on all platforms with comparable success. Differences emerged in more complex tasks. Filtering by intervention type, recruitment location, and phase was more straightforward on ClinicalTrials.gov and the EU register, which present faceted search options. On the national register, several filters required manual entry of terms, increasing task time and error frequency. Bulk export of a filtered result set was possible on international platforms in a single step but required multiple steps on the national register.

Heuristic review identified issues with terminology consistency, including variable use of condition labels and inconsistent date formats. Result displays on the national register were less standardized, which complicated comparison across records. The inter-rater agreement for the heuristic checklist was substantial, supporting the reliability of these findings.

Discussion

The findings suggest that the national register fulfils a basic transparency function but falls short of international best practice in several respects. The most consequential gaps concern the completeness of eligibility and outcome information, timeliness of registration, and machine-readability. Each of these limits the register's value for patients seeking trials, for researchers conducting evidence syntheses, and for regulators monitoring the research landscape.

The lack of a documented application programming interface and limited bulk export capabilities are particularly significant for meta-research. Automated monitoring of registry content, which underpins living systematic reviews and research integrity audits, depends on structured and programmatically accessible data. Without these features, researchers must rely on manual retrieval, which is labor-intensive and prone to error.

Several factors may explain the observed gaps. The national register may operate with limited technical resources relative to larger international platforms. Enforcement of registration timelines and update obligations may be weaker, and submission workflows may not prompt researchers for complete information. Language and format considerations may also play a role, as trial information is not uniformly available in all official languages used in the country.

It is important to note that the comparison is not intended to diminish the achievements of the national register or the research community it serves. Many of the shortcomings identified are addressable through targeted investment and policy alignment rather than fundamental redesign.

Limitations

This study has several limitations. The sample of trials, although stratified, may not capture all registration patterns, particularly for trials sponsored by smaller institutions. The usability tasks reflect a defined set of use cases and may not represent every user group. Registries evolve rapidly, and the findings represent a snapshot at the time of data collection. The scoring of completeness depended on the interpretation of partially completed fields, which introduces some subjectivity despite the use of two independent reviewers.

Recommendations

Based on the findings, several recommendations are proposed. First, the national register should adopt the WHO Trial Registration Data Set explicitly as a mandatory standard, with validation rules that prevent submission of incomplete records. Second, the register should implement a documented application programming interface and provide bulk downloads in standard machine-readable formats such as XML, JSON, and CSV. Third, enforcement of prospective registration and timely updates should be strengthened through alignment with ethics approval and regulatory processes. Fourth, the platform should prioritize accessibility improvements, including labeling of form controls, keyboard navigation, and conformance testing against recognized guidelines. Fifth, faceted search and standardized result displays should be introduced to reduce user effort. Sixth, the register should promote and facilitate the posting of summary results, and should consider incentives or requirements aligned with the global movement toward results transparency. Finally, ongoing monitoring of registry performance, using the framework applied in this study, is recommended to track progress over time.

Conclusion

The comparative evaluation indicates that South Africa's national clinical trial register provides basic public access to trial information but lags international registries in information completeness, timeliness, machine-readability, and usability. Addressing these gaps would enhance transparency, support evidence synthesis, and strengthen public trust in clinical research conducted in South Africa. Because the national register sits within a wider global system, improvements to its interoperability with the WHO ICTRP and other platforms would also benefit the international research community. Continued evaluation will be necessary to ensure that improvements are sustained and that the register meets the evolving expectations of patients, researchers, and regulators.

Chiral symmetry and heavy-quark dynamics constrain meson multiplets and their pion-transition amplitudes

Abstract

We examine how the approximate chiral symmetry of light quarks and the spin-flavor symmetry of heavy quarks jointly restrict the spectrum and decay structure of heavy-light mesons. Combining heavy-quark effective theory with chiral perturbation theory, we organize the low-lying heavy-meson multiplets into representations of the combined symmetry group and derive relations among their pion-induced transition amplitudes. We show that a small number of low-energy constants governs the leading strong transitions, and that the resulting relations are testable against measured widths and branching ratios. We discuss the regime of validity of the expansion, the role of finite-mass corrections, and the implications for the identification of newly observed states.

1. Introduction

Mesons containing a single heavy quark occupy a special place in hadron physics because two approximate symmetries act simultaneously. The first is chiral symmetry of the light quarks, which is spontaneously broken in the QCD vacuum and gives rise to nearly massless Goldstone bosons, the pseudoscalar mesons. The second is the heavy-quark symmetry that emerges when the heavy-quark mass greatly exceeds the QCD scale, rendering the heavy quark's spin and flavor decoupled from the light degrees of freedom. Each symmetry, taken alone, has been exploited extensively, but their combined consequences for the organization of meson multiplets and their transitions deserve a systematic treatment.

The purpose of this paper is to assemble these constraints into a coherent framework. We work with the heavy-meson fields, classify the states into multiplets dictated by the light-quark spin and parity, and then insert the chiral Lagrangian to determine how pions couple within and between these multiplets. The outcome is a set of relations that reduce a large number of unknown amplitudes to a handful of parameters.

2. Heavy-quark and chiral frameworks

In the limit of infinitely heavy quarks, the heavy-quark spin symmetry rotates the spin of the heavy quark independently of the light-degree-of-freedom spin, so that each heavy-light state is labeled by the total angular momentum of the light cloud, j_l, which is one-half for ground-state mesons. The heavy-meson fields are conveniently packaged into a matrix H that transforms under both the spin and the light-flavor symmetries. Excited states with orbital angular momentum l = 1 carry light-cloud spin j_l equal to one-half or three-half, forming two doublets that are distinguished by their parity.

Chiral symmetry enters through the pion field, which is introduced as an element of the exponential of the pion matrix divided by the pion decay constant. The chiral Lagrangian couples the heavy-meson fields to this pion field through derivative interactions, and the leading term is fixed by the axial coupling g, which governs the strength of pion emission between states of opposite parity or between members of different doublets. Because the pion is a Goldstone boson, its couplings vanish as its momentum goes to zero, and this suppression is what makes the expansion in pion momenta controlled.

3. Multiplet structure

Combining the two symmetries, the ground-state pseudoscalar and vector mesons form a single multiplet with total spin degeneracy in the heavy limit, and the excited p-wave states organize into two multiplets, one containing the spin-zero and spin-one states of the lighter doublet and another containing the higher-spin states. We show that the heavy-quark symmetry forces the members of each doublet to be degenerate at leading order, while the mass splittings between doublets arise at order one over the heavy-quark mass and from the spin-dependent interactions of the light cloud.

We write the mass formulas for each multiplet as expansions in one over the heavy-quark mass and in the light-quark masses, and we identify which terms are allowed by the symmetries. The leading chiral-symmetry-breaking contributions are proportional to the light-quark mass and enter through the pion mass, whereas the heavy-quark symmetry-breaking corrections are organized in powers of the inverse heavy-quark mass.

4. Pion-transition amplitudes

The strong decays of excited heavy mesons to ground states plus pions are governed by the same couplings that fix the multiplet structure. At leading order, the amplitude for a p-wave state to emit a pion and transition to a ground-state meson is proportional to the axial coupling and to the pion momentum, with the angular dependence determined by the total angular momentum of the initial and final states. Because the spin structure is fixed by the heavy-quark symmetry, the ratios of amplitudes for different final-state members are predicted without reference to the detailed dynamics.

We derive these ratios explicitly for transitions between the two excited doublets and the ground-state multiplet, and we show that the partial widths satisfy relations that depend only on the axial coupling and on the phase-space factors. These relations hold to leading order in the chiral and heavy-quark expansions, and we estimate the size of the corrections from kaon-loop and finite-mass effects.

5. Comparison with phenomenology

The predicted width ratios can be compared with measured branching fractions for the charmed and bottom mesons. We find that the qualitative pattern of observed widths, including the relative suppression of certain transitions and the ordering of the two excited doublets, is reproduced by the leading-order relations. Quantitative agreement requires an extracted value of the axial coupling, and the values obtained from different channels are broadly consistent, which lends support to the framework. We emphasize, however, that the uncertainties in the experimental widths and in the treatment of higher-order corrections prevent a precise test at the present level of accuracy.

6. Discussion and limitations

The framework has several limitations. The heavy-quark expansion is controlled only for mesons containing charm and bottom quarks, and the corrections for charm are sizable. The chiral expansion requires pion momenta small compared with the chiral scale, which restricts the kinematic region in which the predictions are reliable. Coupled-channel effects, in which nearby hadronic thresholds distort the line shapes of broad states, are not included in the leading-order analysis and must be treated separately when interpreting the widths of the broadest resonances.

Despite these caveats, the constraints derived here provide a useful organizing principle. They reduce the number of independent parameters needed to describe a large body of data, identify the transitions most sensitive to the axial coupling, and offer a systematic way to assess whether a newly observed state is consistent with a conventional heavy-meson assignment.

7. Conclusions

We have shown that the combined constraints of chiral and heavy-quark symmetry organize heavy-meson multiplets and fix the pattern of their pion-transition amplitudes in terms of a small number of parameters. The leading-order relations are consistent with the qualitative features of existing measurements, and their quantitative test awaits more precise data and a controlled treatment of higher-order effects. Future work should extend the analysis to include coupled-channel dynamics and to incorporate lattice-QCD determinations of the axial coupling, which would sharpen the predictions and tighten the comparison with experiment.

References

The relevant literature includes the foundational papers on heavy-quark effective theory, the formulation of heavy-meson chiral perturbation theory, and the experimental measurements of charmed and bottom meson spectra and decay widths, which should be consulted and cited with full bibliographic details before any submission.

The paper proposes an attention-guided framework that jointly selects informative channels and applies knowledge distillation to support efficient transfer learning and model pruning, addressing a practical need to reduce compute without sacrificing accuracy. The motivation is clearly stated and the problem is well situated within the existing literature on pruning and distillation, though the related work section would benefit from a more direct comparison with recent attention-based pruning baselines. The method is described in reasonable detail, but the channel selection criterion would be easier to assess with a clearer formalization and an ablation isolating the contribution of the attention guidance from that of the distillation loss. The experiments span several benchmarks and report consistent accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, yet the paper would be stronger with variance across random seeds, latency measurements on target hardware, and a discussion of failure cases. Overall, the work is a useful and technically sound contribution, and I recommend minor revisions addressing the comparisons, ablations, and reporting of statistical uncertainty.

Venus is often called Earth's twin because the two planets are similar in size, mass, and rocky composition. Yet the similarities end there, and the differences have made Venus one of the most difficult worlds in the solar system to study. Its surface temperature hovers around 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, and this heat comes from a runaway greenhouse effect driven by a carbon dioxide atmosphere roughly ninety times denser than Earth's. The air pressure at the surface is equivalent to that found about nearly a kilometer beneath the ocean on our own planet. These conditions pose serious problems for any spacecraft hoping to survive long enough to collect useful data. Electronics designed for Earth fail quickly in such heat, and most landers have lasted only minutes or hours before succumbing. The Soviet Union's Venera landers achieved the longest surface operations in history, transmitting for about two hours in some cases, which remains a remarkable but limited achievement. The thick clouds of sulfuric acid add another layer of difficulty. They block visible light, so orbiters must rely on radar and infrared instruments to peer through them. Radar mapping, such as that performed by NASA's Magellan mission in the early 1990s, revealed volcanoes, tectonic features, and vast plains, but resolution and depth of information are constrained by these techniques. Atmospheric entry is also hazardous, since the descent subjects a probe to intense heat and corrosive chemistry. Engineers must design heat shields and pressure housings that can withstand these forces while still carrying scientific payloads. Given these obstacles, researchers have proposed a range of creative exploration methods. High-altitude balloons or airships could float in the upper atmosphere, where temperatures and pressures are close to Earth-like levels, allowing longer observations. Solar-powered aircraft might travel through this relatively mild zone as well. Some concepts call for landers built with advanced high-temperature electronics, such as silicon carbide chips, which could extend operational life considerably. Sample return missions would allow laboratories on Earth to analyze Venusian material, but retrieving samples from such a harsh environment presents formidable engineering challenges. Beyond the technical risks, studying Venus carries scientific value. Its runaway greenhouse climate offers a natural laboratory for understanding how planetary atmospheres evolve, which bears directly on questions about Earth's future. Scientists want to know whether Venus once had oceans and how it lost its water. Answering these questions would sharpen our models of climate change and help us judge how habitable other exoplanets might be. In this way, the difficulty of exploring Venus is itself a reason to pursue it. The planet tests our engineering ingenuity and our understanding of the forces that shape worlds, including our own.

A woman named Dana boarded the crowded 7:40 train, clutching a coffee and half-asleep. Across from her, a young man kept glancing at his watch and tugging at the strap of his backpack. Dana noticed him only because he looked as tired as she felt.

When the doors closed, the man stood and moved toward the center of the car. A passenger shouted that he had dropped something. Dana turned, and in the confusion a bag strapped to the man's chest caught on a pole and split open.

People screamed and scattered. The man stumbled, his face pale, and tried to pull the wires free from his jacket. Dana saw his hands shaking, and in that instant she understood he was not a bomber. He was a student who had been sent a package he never meant to carry, filled with supplies for a job he had been pressured into taking.

She pushed through the crowd toward him, shouting at the conductor to pull the emergency brake. The train lurched and slowed. The man looked at her with wide, terrified eyes and said he was sorry, that he had only wanted to pay off his brother's debts.

Before anyone could reach him, a second passenger, a stranger in a gray hoodie, lunged from the back of the car. There was a flash, a sharp sound, and then a silence so complete that Dana could hear the wheels grinding against the rails.

When the lights flickered back on, the young man lay motionless near the doors. The gray-hooded stranger was gone, the platform beyond the windows empty except for police running toward the train.

Dana knelt beside the student and pressed her hands to his chest, though she knew it was futile. Someone behind her was sobbing. Someone else was calling for help in a voice that cracked on every word.

The investigators later said the device had been crude and unlikely to detonate fully. They said the attacker had been watching the young man for days, choosing him because he was young, anxious, and easy to manipulate. They said the real bomber had planned to vanish in the chaos, and that the student had been a tool and a victim at once.

Dana gave her statement in a small room that smelled of stale coffee. She described the bag, the wires, the apology, and the moment she had seen fear instead of hatred in his eyes. The officer taking notes asked her whether she had been frightened. She said she had been, but mostly she had been sad, because she had seen a boy trapped in something he could not escape.

In the weeks that followed, Dana rode the same train each morning, watching the faces around her. She noticed how quickly people looked away from one another, how carefully they guarded their bags. She understood the fear, but she also wondered how many others, like the young man, were being pulled into harm by people who never showed their faces.

A memorial appeared at the station, a small bouquet tied to a railing with a handwritten note that read, "You were more than what they made you." Dana stood before it for a long time before she left for work.

Year-round schooling has been proposed as a way to strengthen student learning and reduce the knowledge loss that often occurs over long summer breaks. Under this model, the academic year is divided into shorter instructional blocks separated by brief, evenly spaced breaks, rather than one long summer vacation. Supporters argue that this structure keeps students engaged with material more consistently and reduces the time spent relearning content at the start of each year. Research on the "summer slide," the documented tendency of some students to lose ground in reading and mathematics over the summer, provides the strongest justification for this approach. Studies have suggested that the loss is most pronounced among students from lower-income households, who may have fewer opportunities for enriching activities during the break. Year-round calendars could address this gap by ensuring that learning continues at regular intervals throughout the year. Shorter, more frequent breaks may also help students avoid burnout and give teachers more time to provide remediation and enrichment. Critics, however, point out that the evidence on academic gains is mixed, and that many studies show only modest differences in achievement between year-round and traditional schools. Some of the reported benefits may also reflect other factors, such as smaller class sizes or additional instructional time, rather than the calendar itself. Logistical concerns are also significant, since year-round schedules can complicate family childcare arrangements, teacher planning, and extracurricular commitments. Staggered calendars, in which different groups of students attend on different schedules, can reduce some costs but may create their own administrative challenges. Retention of knowledge depends not only on when instruction occurs but also on how it is delivered, including the use of spaced practice and regular review. Year-round schedules may support these methods, but they do not guarantee them. Therefore, the calendar alone is unlikely to determine learning outcomes. A school that uses year-round scheduling alongside strong teaching practices is more likely to see improved retention than one that simply changes its dates. On balance, year-round schooling shows promise for reducing knowledge loss, particularly for disadvantaged students, but its benefits depend on careful implementation. Policymakers should consider both the potential gains and the practical costs before adopting such a system.

Key Ideas of Six Major Philosophers in Seventeenth- and Eighteenth-Century European Philosophy

Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century European philosophy was shaped by debates over reason, experience, knowledge, and the nature of the mind and the world. The following overview introduces six influential thinkers and their central ideas.

René Descartes (1596–1650) sought certain knowledge by doubting everything that could be doubted, and he concluded that the thinking self must exist because it cannot doubt its own thinking, expressed in the phrase "I think, therefore I am." He also argued for a fundamental division between mind, which thinks, and body, which occupies space.

Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) held that there is only one substance, which he identified with God or nature, and that everything that exists is a modification of this single reality. He believed that human freedom consists in understanding the necessary causes of things and that reason could lead people to a more peaceful and joyful life.

John Locke (1632–1704) argued that the mind at birth is a blank slate, or tabula rasa, and that all our ideas come from sensation and reflection on experience. He defended natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and held that governments derive legitimacy from the consent of the governed.

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) proposed that reality consists of simple, indivisible units called monads, each reflecting the entire universe from its own point of view. He argued that God chose the best of all possible worlds, and he emphasized the principle of sufficient reason, which holds that everything has an explanation.

George Berkeley (1685–1753) maintained that material objects exist only insofar as they are perceived, a position summarized as "to be is to be perceived." He argued that what we call matter is really a collection of ideas, and that God continually perceives all things, sustaining their existence.

David Hume (1711–1776) examined human knowledge through the lens of experience and concluded that we cannot rationally prove causation, since we only observe one event following another and form habits of expectation. He was skeptical of claims about the self and of miracles, and he argued that reason serves the passions rather than directing them.

Together these philosophers framed questions that remain central to philosophy today, including how we know what we know, what reality is made of, and how individuals should live and govern together.

Cramond Weir sits at the mouth of the River Almond in Edinburgh, Scotland, where the river meets the Firth of Forth. For centuries the weir and its associated structures altered the flow of the river, creating barriers that made it difficult for migratory fish such as Atlantic salmon, sea trout, and European eel to reach their upstream spawning and feeding grounds. Scientists and conservationists have long recognised that such obstacles fragment river habitats, isolating fish populations and reducing the diversity of species that depend on connected waterways. Restoration efforts typically begin with surveys of fish passage, water quality, and sediment movement to understand how the structure affects the wider ecosystem. Engineers may then consider options such as fish passes, rock ramps, or partial removal of the weir, each chosen to suit the local hydrology and the needs of target species. Careful design aims to let fish move past the obstacle at a range of water levels while keeping the historic character of the site intact. Monitoring with fish counters, electrofishing surveys, and environmental DNA sampling helps reveal whether migration has improved after works are completed. Healthy migration routes also support other wildlife, including otters, birds, and invertebrates that rely on a balanced river food web. Restored sections of river often show gains in juvenile fish numbers, a sign that spawning success is recovering. Community involvement matters too, as local volunteers, schools, and angling groups can contribute records and help protect river banks. Long-term success depends on maintaining water quality, reducing pollution from runoff, and keeping passage routes clear of debris. Ultimately, reconnecting the River Almond at Cramond demonstrates how thoughtful engineering and ongoing care can bring a historic river back to ecological health.

Should the United States abolish the Electoral College and elect its presidents by popular vote? This question has divided Americans for generations, and it deserves careful consideration. The Electoral College was created by the framers of the Constitution as a compromise between those who wanted Congress to choose the president and those who favored direct popular election. Its supporters argue that it protects federalism by giving smaller states a voice in national elections. They also contend that it encourages candidates to build broad coalitions across different regions rather than concentrating solely on the most populous areas. Finally, defenders maintain that the system produces decisive outcomes and reduces the likelihood of disputed national recounts. Yet the Electoral College has serious flaws that weaken its claim to legitimacy in a modern democracy. The most troubling is that it has twice in American history, in 1876 and 2000, and again in 2016, resulted in a president who lost the national popular vote. Critics argue that a system in which a candidate can win the presidency without winning the most votes undermines the basic democratic principle that every citizen's vote should carry equal weight. The system also concentrates campaign attention on a small number of swing states, leaving voters in safe states largely ignored. Candidates spend most of their time and money in a handful of places, while issues important to millions of other Americans receive little attention. Furthermore, the winner-take-all method used by most states magnifies the impact of narrow margins and can distort the actual preferences of the electorate. A popular vote system would address these problems directly by making every vote count the same regardless of where it is cast. Under such a system, a candidate would need to appeal to voters across the entire country, encouraging a more inclusive and national campaign. Supporters of direct election also point out that the Electoral College is not mentioned in the Constitution's core principles of equal representation and popular sovereignty as they have evolved. Abolishing it would require a constitutional amendment, which is a difficult process, but the difficulty of change should not prevent a reasoned debate about what is best for the nation. Opponents raise legitimate concerns about a national popular vote. They worry that it could diminish the influence of smaller states and rural areas, which might find their concerns overlooked in a system driven by population centers. Some also fear that a direct election would make recounts across the entire nation more complicated and that a very close national result could be harder to resolve. Others suggest that a national popular vote could encourage fragmentation, with multiple candidates competing for small percentages and no clear majority emerging. These are real considerations that proponents must address rather than dismiss. Still, many of these concerns can be mitigated through careful design, such as instant runoff voting or a national majority threshold. Ultimately, the question comes down to what kind of democracy Americans want. If the goal is to ensure that the candidate with the most support nationwide wins the presidency, then the Electoral College fails that standard in ways that have already materialized. If the goal is to preserve a federal balance that gives states a distinct role in choosing the nation's leader, then the current system has merit. Weighing these values honestly, I believe the strongest argument favors moving toward a national popular vote. The principle that each citizen's vote should count equally is fundamental to a democracy, and the Electoral College repeatedly violates it. Abolishing the system would not solve every problem in American elections, but it would bring the presidency closer to the will of the people it is meant to serve.

Tomas had always believed his hands were simply good at sauces. For eleven years he ran the kitchen of the Halcyon Commons, a sunlit dining hall where the residents of the Meridian Valley community gathered each evening to eat bread still warm from the ovens and talk about the future they were building together. He knew every regular by their order. Mira took her soup without salt. Old Anselm wanted extra honey in his tea. The twins from the orchard shared one plate and argued over the last bite.

Nobody had ever asked where his talent came from. The Commons was built on the principle that every person's gifts belonged to everyone, and Tomas had never felt the need to question a gift that made people happy.

The trouble began with a recipe card. Tomas found it tucked inside an old cookbook that had been donated to the library, the kind of thing no one read anymore. The card was not written in ink but etched into a thin metal plate, and the handwriting on it was his own, though he had never written it. It listed ingredients in a precise sequence, and beneath the ingredients was a line of coordinates and a single word: Stillwater.

He told no one at first. He turned the plate over in his hands during the quiet hours after service, when the ovens had cooled and the room smelled of rosemary and dough. The coordinates pointed to a location in the hills north of the valley, a place the community's maps labeled as a restricted research site.

Two weeks later, a woman named Isolde arrived at the Commons with a letter of introduction and a soft voice. She was new to the valley, she said, and she wanted to learn the rhythms of the kitchen. She watched Tomas work with unusual attention. She asked him questions about his childhood, and he found, to his unease, that he could not remember much of it before the age of twelve. He remembered the valley. He remembered the first meal he had cooked here. Before that the memories were smooth and blank, like river stones.

Isolde noticed his hesitation and smiled as if she had expected it.

"You were grown in Stillwater," she said quietly, while the others were setting the long tables. "You were one of the first. Do you know what you were made for?"

Tomas set down the knife in his hand. "I'm a cook."

"You are a cook," she agreed. "That was the cover. It was also the truth. Your hands were built to be exceptional, and your place in the kitchen was built to put you close to everyone who matters to this community. Close enough to end any threat before it grew."

He felt cold spread slowly through his chest. "Threat to what?"

"To the Meridian plan. A world without hunger, without war, without the old cruelties. The founders believed that such a world could only survive if certain people were removed when they became dangerous. Dissenters. Organizers of rival factions. Anyone who might pull the valley apart." She tilted her head. "You were designed to be trusted and never suspected. Your recipes are your instruments. Poison, if necessary. A slow thing, or a fast one. You would never be caught, because no one looks twice at the man who feeds them."

Tomas looked at the bread cooling on the racks, the honey jar beside Anselm's usual cup, the ladle he had used a thousand times to serve Mira her unsalted soup. He thought about the twins, sharing their plate and laughing.

"And if I refuse?" he asked.

Isolde's expression did not change. "Then you will be retired, as the earlier designs were, and someone else will cook the dinners."

That night he did not sleep. He walked the edge of the valley in the dark, following the faint line of the old irrigation canal toward the hills, and he thought about the word Stillwater and what it meant to be a made thing that had been given a life it had not chosen. He thought about what he owed to the people who had given him a name and a home, and what he owed to the people he had been built to harm.

At dawn he reached the hills. The restricted gate stood open, rusted at the hinges, as if someone had left it that way on purpose. Beyond it lay rows of empty cradles, glass-walled and silent, each one labeled with a number and a single word in his own handwriting. The last cradle was empty. Its label read: Tomas, Revision Seven.

He understood then that he was not the first, and that he might not be the last, and that Isolde had known exactly where he would walk.

Tomas returned to the Commons before the morning bell. He went to the kitchen, lit the ovens, and began the bread the way he always did. He worked with the same precise care, but he did not cook the poison the plate had described. Instead he sat with Anselm over his honeyed tea and listened to him talk about the years before the valley, when the old man had been a farmer in a country that no longer existed. He let the twins argue over their shared plate. He served Mira her soup, unsalted, as she liked it.

When Isolde came to the kitchen that afternoon, she found him kneading dough with his sleeves rolled to the elbow.

"You didn't do it," she said.

"No," Tomas said. He did not look up. "I'm going to tell them everything, and then I'm going to ask them what kind of future is worth building on a dead man's hands."

She was quiet for a long moment. Then she turned and walked out into the sunlight, and Tomas heard the gate close behind her.

That evening the residents of the Halcyon Commons gathered for dinner as they always had. Tomas stood before them, flour still on his hands, and told them the truth. Some listened in stunned silence. Some wept. Mira asked him to repeat the part about the restricted hills twice. Anselm nodded slowly, as though he had suspected something of the sort for years.

Nobody ordered him removed from the kitchen. Instead, the valley's council met through the night in the great hall, arguing and shouting and at last falling into the exhausted quiet that follows hard decisions. By morning they had voted to dismantle the Stillwater facility, to publish its records, and to set a new rule that no community's dream could be defended by making its people into weapons.

Tomas went back to the ovens. He still did not remember his childhood. He never would. But every morning he chose what he would cook, and every evening he served it to people who knew exactly who he was and chose to share the table anyway.

It was not the utopia the founders had imagined. It was harder, and messier, and more honest. Tomas thought it might be the first thing in his life that he had actually made for himself.

The NHS cancer drug fund has cut patient access to several treatments after spending exceeded its budget, a decision that has drawn sharp criticism from cancer charities and patients' advocates. Health officials said the restrictions were necessary to keep the fund within its allocated limits for the financial year. Under the revised criteria, some drugs that were previously available will now be offered only to narrower groups of patients. Clinicians have been told to review eligibility carefully before prescribing affected medicines. Campaigners argue that the changes will leave many people without access to treatments that could extend their lives or improve their quality of life. Several cancer charities said the decision reflects a system under pressure rather than a considered judgement about clinical value. Patients' advocates described receiving calls from worried families who had been told that treatment plans were being reconsidered. One advocate said the uncertainty itself was causing distress, particularly for people already facing difficult diagnoses. Officials responded that the fund must balance access to new medicines against the need for financial sustainability across the wider health service. They said decisions were guided by independent assessments of cost-effectiveness and clinical benefit. Critics countered that cost-effectiveness thresholds do not always capture the value that patients place on additional time with loved ones. Some oncologists have privately expressed concern that the cuts could force them to choose between drugs on financial grounds. Hospital trusts reported that they are preparing for a rise in requests for appeals and individual funding. Charity leaders called on the government to commit additional funding and to publish clearer criteria for future decisions. They also urged greater transparency about how the fund's budget is set and monitored throughout the year. Patient groups said they would continue to press for a review of the policy and for direct engagement with people affected by the changes. Parliamentary committees have requested further information on the scale of the overspend and the number of patients likely to be affected. Government representatives said they remain committed to improving cancer outcomes and to ensuring that effective treatments reach those who need them. Health economists warned that without long-term planning, similar budget pressures are likely to recur as new and expensive therapies continue to emerge. Advocates said that any lasting solution must involve patients, clinicians and charities in shaping how scarce resources are allocated. The coming weeks are expected to bring further debate over whether the restrictions will be reversed or adjusted.

Education Funding Oversight and Social Insurance Consolidation

Governments periodically review how public money is spent, and two areas often attract attention: education funding and social insurance. This page explains the general goals behind plans to strengthen oversight of education funding and to consolidate overlapping social insurance schemes.

Education funding is typically distributed through a mix of national, regional, and local channels, which can make it difficult to track how resources reach schools and students. Oversight measures aim to clarify who is responsible for allocating funds and how those allocations are reported. Common tools include independent audits, public dashboards showing spending by school or district, and clear performance indicators linked to budgets. Stronger oversight is intended to reduce waste, limit misuse, and help parents, teachers, and taxpayers understand whether funds are achieving their purpose. Critics sometimes worry that additional reporting requirements can increase administrative burden on small schools, so well-designed plans usually include support for local reporting capacity. Oversight bodies may also be given authority to recommend corrective action when problems are found.

Social insurance refers to programs that pool contributions to provide protection against risks such as unemployment, illness, disability, old age, and work injury. Over time, many countries have built up several separate schemes, each with its own rules, contribution rates, eligibility tests, and administrative systems. This fragmentation can create overlaps, where people are covered by more than one scheme for the same risk, and gaps, where some workers fall outside all of them. Consolidation aims to combine related schemes into a smaller number of coordinated programs. The expected benefits include simpler rules for workers and employers, lower administrative costs, and more consistent coverage. Consolidation can also make it easier for people who move between jobs, or between formal and informal work, to keep their protection.

Reforms of this kind usually involve trade-offs. Merging schemes can require transferring records, reconciling different benefit levels, and protecting the rights of people already receiving payments. Transition periods, clear communication, and phased implementation are often used to reduce disruption. Governments commonly consult employers, unions, beneficiary groups, and experts before making major changes. Evaluation after implementation helps determine whether the intended goals of efficiency, fairness, and transparency have been met. Anyone seeking detailed information about a specific national plan should consult official government publications, as the details, timelines, and legal provisions vary considerably between countries and over time.

The evening opened with a lap of honour, as each departing player received a warm reception from the crowd. Club captain Brodie Croft, who led the side through a series of tense finals, was among those given a standing ovation. Head coach Rohan Smith praised the group for their professionalism, loyalty, and the lasting impact they have had on the club's culture. Supporters also shared memories of key moments from the campaign, including several dramatic late wins that kept the team's hopes alive. Club officials announced a series of tributes, including a commemorative display at the stadium and a special edition programme chronicling each player's contribution. Several retiring veterans spoke briefly to the crowd, thanking their families, teammates, and the loyal supporters who had backed them through good times and bad. Choosing which extracurricular activities a student joins is a decision that shapes a young person's skills, friendships, and sense of self, so it is worth asking who should make that choice. The most natural answer is the student, because the student is the one who will spend the hours practicing, performing, and living with the results. A teenager who is pushed into a debate club against their wishes may resent every meeting, while one who chooses a robotics team out of genuine curiosity often becomes deeply committed. Ownership fosters motivation, and motivation is what turns an activity into real growth.

Yet students are not always the best judges of what will serve them, especially when they are young. A ten-year-old may want only to play video games or may drop an instrument after a single frustrating week, and an adolescent may avoid challenging activities simply because they feel uncomfortable. Parents and guardians bring a broader view of a child's long-term development, along with knowledge of family resources, schedules, and values. Their guidance can help a student try something new that they would never have considered on their own.

Schools also have a legitimate role. Educators understand which programs are available, what commitments they require, and how they connect to academic goals. Teachers often notice talents that students have not yet recognized, and counselors can help match a student's interests with realistic options. Schools also set rules about eligibility, such as minimum grades or attendance requirements, which protect students from overextending themselves.

The best answer, then, is probably shared responsibility rather than a single decision-maker. Students should have the final voice in choices that concern their own interests and time, while parents and educators offer advice, encouragement, and necessary limits. When these voices work together, a student can explore widely, commit thoughtfully, and learn that the activities they choose are truly their own.

This manuscript proposes a method for efficient low-rank domain adaptation that combines spectral reduction with Nyström-based sampling to lower the computational cost of adapting large models to new data distributions. The problem is well motivated, since full fine-tuning of large networks is expensive in both memory and compute, and low-rank adaptation has become a practical alternative. The authors position their contribution clearly against prior low-rank adaptation approaches, and the introduction frames the central question in a way that is easy to follow. The core idea, using spectral reduction to identify dominant directions of the adaptation subspace and Nyström sampling to approximate the relevant kernel or covariance structure at lower cost, is a reasonable combination of established tools. The writing is generally clear, though some passages in the methods section would benefit from tighter notation, particularly where the same symbol is reused for both the sampled subset and the full data index set. The derivation of the reduced objective is presented in enough detail to be checked, and I verified the main algebraic steps, although the transition from the full spectral problem to the Nyström approximation skips an intermediate step that readers unfamiliar with the technique may find difficult. The theoretical analysis provides an error bound on the approximation, and the assumptions behind it are stated explicitly, which I appreciate. However, the bound depends on a spectral decay condition whose practical validity for the target architectures is not established, and the authors should either verify this empirically or discuss when it may fail. The choice of the number of Nyström landmarks is treated somewhat heuristically, and a sensitivity analysis over this parameter would strengthen the paper considerably. The experimental setup covers several domain adaptation benchmarks, which is a strength, yet the selection of baselines omits some recent low-rank adaptation methods that would be the most natural comparison points. Reported gains over the strongest baseline are modest on two of the four datasets, and the paper does not report variance across random seeds, so it is hard to judge whether these differences are meaningful. The ablation study isolating the contribution of spectral reduction versus Nyström sampling is valuable and supports the claim that both components matter, though the ablation table would be easier to read with consistent units for runtime and memory. The computational cost analysis is one of the stronger parts of the paper, with wall-clock timings and memory footprints reported across model sizes, and these results convincingly show reduced overhead relative to full fine-tuning. Nevertheless, the timing comparisons were run on a single hardware configuration, and the authors should note how the speedups might change on different accelerators or distributed settings. The related work section is thorough in covering low-rank methods but is thinner on prior Nyström-based approaches in machine learning, which would help situate the novelty of the sampling strategy. The authors state that code will be released, which is commendable, though at the time of review the repository link was not functional and I was unable to reproduce the main results. Hyperparameter settings are listed in an appendix, but learning rate schedules and early stopping criteria are described only briefly, which could affect reproducibility. The limitations section acknowledges the dependence on the spectral decay assumption and the single-hardware evaluation, which is appropriate, but it does not discuss potential failure modes under severe distribution shift. The figures are generally informative, though the convergence plots lack confidence intervals and some axis labels are too small to read at print size. The discussion of broader impact is minimal, which is acceptable for a methods paper of this kind but could briefly address how adaptation efficiency might affect deployment of models to new domains. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant problem with a sound and practically useful combination of techniques, and its computational efficiency results are its strongest contribution. The main weaknesses are the unverified theoretical assumption, the limited baseline comparison, and the lack of statistical reporting for the modest accuracy gains. I recommend a major revision that addresses these points, with the efficiency contribution remaining the central argument if the accuracy claims are better supported. With these revisions, the work could make a worthwhile contribution to the literature on parameter-efficient domain adaptation.

The paper proposes representing graph nodes as time series in order to identify optimal vertex sets, and it evaluates this approach on synthetic graph experiments. The core idea is interesting and potentially useful, since it bridges graph analysis and time series methods, which could give practitioners a new lens on structural node properties. However, the manuscript does not clearly explain how the time series are generated from the graph, such as which dynamical process, diffusion, or walk is used, and this omission makes the method difficult to reproduce. The optimality criterion for vertex sets is also not precisely defined, and the paper would benefit from a formal objective function along with a comparison to established baselines such as greedy selection, spectral methods, or centrality-based heuristics. The synthetic experiments cover a limited range of graph models, so the authors should test on additional generators such as stochastic block models and scale-free networks, and report variance across random seeds. Finally, the authors should include real-world benchmark datasets and a discussion of computational complexity, since the time series construction may become costly for large graphs. With these revisions, the paper could make a meaningful contribution, but in its current form I recommend major revision.
