Under the current arrangements, motorists using the crossing face charges that many regional residents and freight operators have criticised as unfair. The government is now examining whether a reduction in the toll would bring meaningful relief to commuters and local economies on both sides of the border. Among the options under review is an overnight exemption, which would allow vehicles to cross without paying during set hours when traffic is light. Supporters argue such a measure could benefit night-shift workers, delivery drivers, and emergency services who often travel at unsocial hours. Critics, however, warn that exemptions could complicate enforcement and reduce revenue needed to maintain the structure. Traffic-management measures are also being considered as part of the wider package. These could include variable pricing, lane controls, and improved signage designed to spread demand more evenly throughout the day. Transport planners say better management of congestion could reduce delays at peak times and lower emissions in surrounding areas. Local councils in Gloucestershire and South Wales have welcomed the review but have called for clear timelines and firm commitments. Business groups have said that lower tolls would help reduce costs for companies that rely on the route to move goods between England and Wales. Environmental organisations have raised questions about whether cheaper crossings could encourage more car journeys, urging that any change be paired with investment in public transport. Motoring groups, by contrast, have largely supported the principle of lower charges, arguing that drivers have already paid considerably over the years. The government has indicated that it will consult with stakeholders before finalising any changes. Officials said public feedback would play a central role in shaping the final proposals. Technical assessments are also expected to examine the impact of different toll levels on traffic volumes and revenue. The outcome could set a precedent for how other tolled crossings across the country are managed in future. For now, drivers are advised to check official sources for updates as the review progresses.

Amnesty International has accused both Russian and Ukrainian forces of committing abuses against civilians in eastern Ukraine, as fighting and a major explosion unsettled the region during a fragile ceasefire.

The human rights organization said its researchers had documented cases in which both sides failed to protect civilians and, in some instances, appeared to deliberately target non-military areas. The group called on all parties to respect international humanitarian law and to allow independent investigators access to affected communities.

Residents in several towns described a night of sporadic gunfire and artillery rounds, despite the ceasefire agreement that was meant to halt major hostilities. Local officials said the violations had made it difficult for families to leave their homes or reach medical care.

Hours later, a powerful explosion rocked an industrial area, sending a plume of smoke over the surrounding neighborhoods. Emergency crews rushed to the scene, but officials had not yet determined the cause of the blast, and they cautioned against speculation until an investigation was complete.

Witnesses said windows were shattered in nearby apartment blocks and that some residents spent the night in basements. Hospitals in the area reported treating several people for minor injuries, including cuts from flying glass and smoke inhalation.

Ukrainian authorities condemned what they called continued Russian shelling and said their own forces were operating within the terms of the truce. They urged international partners to press Moscow to honor its commitments and to withdraw forces from contested areas.

Russian-backed officials in the occupied territories offered a different account, accusing Ukrainian units of firing on civilian neighborhoods. They said they had recorded their own casualties and promised a response, though they provided few details that could be independently verified.

Amnesty researchers said they had interviewed survivors, relatives of victims, and local health workers, and that they had cross-checked accounts against satellite imagery and video footage where available. The organization cautioned that access restrictions and active hostilities limited how much it could confirm.

The group's report cites specific incidents in which civilians were killed or injured, homes and schools were damaged, and humanitarian convoys were delayed. It said several of these incidents may amount to war crimes if further investigation confirms the findings.

Humanitarian agencies operating in the region warned that the instability was worsening conditions for displaced people, many of whom have already endured months of disruption to water, electricity, and heating. Aid workers said supplies were struggling to reach the most vulnerable communities.

Energy infrastructure remained a particular concern, as repair crews were unable to work safely in areas where shelling continued. Engineers said the damage in some districts would take weeks to fix even under calm conditions.

Diplomats from several Western countries expressed alarm at the reports and called for an immediate halt to all attacks on civilians. Some urged the United Nations to send a monitoring mission capable of verifying compliance with the ceasefire.

Ceasefire monitors said they had logged dozens of alleged violations over the previous week but that many remained unverified. They acknowledged that the agreement lacked a robust enforcement mechanism, leaving compliance largely dependent on the political will of the parties involved.

Analysts said the episode underscored how difficult it is to sustain a truce without clear mechanisms for reporting violations and resolving disputes. Some warned that repeated breaches could erode trust and make future negotiations even harder.

Ukrainian and Russian negotiators have not publicly commented on the Amnesty report in detail. Officials on both sides have, however, reiterated their stated commitment to the ceasefire while blaming the other for ongoing incidents.

Local residents expressed exhaustion and frustration, saying they had grown weary of promises that were not kept. Many said they simply wanted to live without fear of sudden shelling and to know whether their homes would still be standing the next morning.

In one village, a retired teacher said she had decided to stay despite the danger, because leaving would mean abandoning the home her family had occupied for generations. Her neighbors, she said, were making similar choices, relying on one another for food, water, and information.

Aid groups reported that the number of people seeking assistance had risen sharply in recent days, with clinics and shelters operating beyond capacity. Some organizations said they were rationing supplies while waiting for new deliveries to arrive.

The explosion's cause remained under investigation, with officials saying forensic teams would examine the site once it was safe to do so. They said the results would be shared publicly, though no timeline had been announced.

Amnesty called on governments to ensure that anyone responsible for abuses, regardless of affiliation, is held to account through credible and impartial legal processes. The organization said accountability was essential both for victims and for any lasting peace.

As the ceasefire entered its uncertain next phase, international observers said the coming days would be critical in determining whether the truce could be preserved or whether fighting would resume on a wider scale. For now, communities in the east remain on edge, waiting to see what the next night will bring.

The vessel was listed under a UN Security Council sanctions regime that bars certain shipments of Libyan petroleum deemed to have been exported without the approval of the internationally recognized government in Tripoli. Officials said the tanker had been loading crude at a port under the control of forces aligned with the eastern administration, which is based in Benghazi and led by a parliament and military command that rejects the authority of the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity. Diplomats familiar with the decision said the listing was intended to deter further unauthorized exports that have deprived the national oil company of revenue needed to pay salaries and fund public services. The eastern authorities have repeatedly defended their right to manage resources in territory under their control, arguing that revenues have been distributed unfairly and that the central government has failed to represent their interests. Libya has been divided between rival governments and armed factions since the 2011 uprising that toppled Muammar Gaddafi, and oil production and export infrastructure have frequently been used as leverage in the conflict. Energy analysts warned that sanctions against a single vessel could disrupt shipping schedules and raise insurance costs for other tankers operating in Libyan waters. Shipping agents said some buyers had already begun avoiding cargoes linked to the eastern export network, citing legal and reputational risks. The sanctions also authorize member states to inspect, seize, and redirect the vessel if it enters their ports or territorial waters. Libya's National Oil Corporation has previously called for the protection of oil facilities and urged all parties to refrain from actions that could further damage the economy. Representatives of the eastern administration did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the listing, though officials have previously rejected similar measures as politically motivated. UN envoys have urged both sides to resume negotiations on a unified budget, a single central bank framework, and national elections, saying that a lasting solution depends on a fair and transparent distribution of oil revenues. The latest measure underscores how the dispute over oil continues to shape Libya's political future, with the international community signaling that unauthorized exports will carry consequences.

The manuscript under review proposes a Bayesian filtering framework as a foundation for deriving adaptive gradient optimizers, with the stated goal of explaining why methods such as RMSProp and Adam work and of motivating principled extensions. The central idea is to treat the gradient of a loss function as a noisy observation of an unknown latent quantity, typically the true gradient or the local curvature, and to recover adaptive step sizes as posterior estimates under a state-space model. This is an appealing perspective, and the authors deserve credit for attempting to unify several heuristics under a single probabilistic interpretation. The paper is generally well organized, moving from background on stochastic optimization to the filtering model, then to derivations, and finally to experiments. The introduction positions the work clearly relative to prior probabilistic views of optimization, including variational and natural-gradient approaches, though the related work section could engage more directly with existing Bayesian interpretations of Adam. The motivation is sound: practitioners routinely tune adaptive methods with little theoretical guidance, and a derivation that explains the role of the second-moment estimate would be valuable. The authors state their modeling assumptions explicitly, which I appreciate, since much of the credibility of a Bayesian derivation rests on them. However, several of these assumptions are strong and deserve more justification. In particular, the choice of a random-walk or Gaussian transition model for the latent gradient is convenient but not obviously appropriate for the highly nonstationary gradient sequences seen in deep networks. The paper would benefit from a discussion of when this assumption breaks down and what the consequences are for the resulting update rule. The derivation of the Kalman-style update is mostly correct as far as I could follow, and the steps are presented at a reasonable level of detail. Still, the transition from the exact filtering recursion to the tractable approximation is compressed, and the reader is asked to accept several simplifications without a clear account of their approximation error. I would ask the authors to quantify or at least bound this error, or to provide a sensitivity analysis showing how the approximation affects the final update. The connection between the posterior variance and the familiar RMSProp denominator is one of the more interesting claims, and it is supported by a reasonable algebraic argument. Yet the correspondence is somewhat looser than the abstract suggests, since it holds only under a particular limit of the noise parameters. This should be stated plainly in the main text rather than deferred to the appendix. The treatment of bias correction in Adam is handled briefly, and I was not convinced that the Bayesian account provides a genuine explanation rather than a reparameterization of the same initialization effect. A clearer comparison here would strengthen the paper considerably. The experimental section evaluates the proposed optimizers on standard image classification and language modeling benchmarks against Adam, RMSProp, and SGD with momentum. The experiments are a welcome addition, and the inclusion of multiple random seeds is commendable. However, the reported improvements are often small and within the range of seed-to-seed variation, which weakens the claim that the new method is practically better. I recommend reporting confidence intervals or statistical tests and being more cautious in the language used to describe the gains. The hyperparameter search also appears to be less thorough for the baselines than for the proposed method, which could bias the comparison. The authors should describe the tuning budget and procedure for every method on an equal footing. The ablation study is useful for isolating the contribution of the filtering component, but it would be more informative if it varied the noise parameters over a wider range to show robustness. Figures are generally clear, although the learning-curve plots would be easier to interpret with a logarithmic loss axis and shaded variance bands. The related work discussion omits several recent papers on adaptive methods with theoretical convergence guarantees, and situating the contribution against these would help readers judge its novelty. The writing is mostly clear, though some notation is overloaded; the symbol used for the posterior mean is also used for a smoothing parameter in a later section, which caused confusion on first reading. A notation table would resolve this. There are also a few typographical errors and inconsistent capitalization of optimizer names that should be corrected before publication. The paper does not discuss computational overhead in detail, and since the filtering update adds state beyond the standard first and second moments, the memory and runtime costs should be reported. Reproducibility is partly addressed through a promised code release, which I strongly encourage the authors to deliver upon acceptance, along with the exact hyperparameter configurations used. In summary, the paper offers a thoughtful and potentially valuable probabilistic perspective on adaptive optimization, and its core idea merits publication interest. However, the strength of the theoretical claims exceeds what the approximations and experiments currently support. I recommend a major revision that addresses the approximation error, the rigor of the empirical comparison, the positioning relative to prior work, and the notation issues. With these changes the contribution could become a solid addition to the literature on the theory of adaptive gradient methods.

Uber has agreed to compensate drivers following allegations that the company made misleading claims about how much they could earn and about the costs of leasing vehicles through its platform. The settlement comes after drivers and regulators raised concerns that promotional materials painted an overly optimistic picture of take-home pay.

Under the agreement, eligible drivers who signed up based on the company's earnings projections will receive payments intended to offset losses they incurred. The compensation fund is designed to address the gap between what drivers were led to expect and what many actually earned after expenses.

Critics of the gig economy have long argued that ride-hailing platforms present headline figures that do not account for fuel, insurance, maintenance, depreciation, and other costs borne by drivers. Uber has disputed some of these characterizations in the past while also revising its disclosures over time.

The allegations centered on two main areas: the earnings potential advertised to prospective drivers, and the terms and true costs associated with vehicle leasing programs offered through partner companies. Drivers said these programs were marketed as affordable pathways to full-time income.

Lawyers representing the affected drivers said the settlement reflects a recognition that recruitment materials must be accurate and complete. They argued that drivers often made major financial commitments, such as signing multi-year leases, based on figures that did not reflect typical outcomes.

Uber stated that the settlement does not constitute an admission of wrongdoing. A company spokesperson said the business is committed to transparency and continues to update its tools to help drivers understand their potential earnings and expenses.

Regulators involved in the matter emphasized that clear and honest information is essential for workers evaluating whether to join a platform. They noted that misleading financial claims can have serious consequences for individuals who rely on driving income to meet household needs.

The payments will be distributed according to a formula that considers the period a driver was active on the platform and the documented vehicle lease obligations they carried. Drivers will be notified through the email addresses associated with their accounts.

Advocacy groups for gig workers welcomed the settlement but said it should be the beginning of broader reform. They called for standardized disclosures that show earnings after expenses, not just gross fares.

Industry observers said the case highlights the difficulty of accurately representing income for workers whose pay varies with demand, location, time of day, and local regulations. Some suggested that independent auditing of earnings claims could help restore trust.

The settlement also raises questions about how other companies in the sharing economy present financial opportunities to prospective workers. Analysts expect closer scrutiny of recruitment advertising across the sector.

Drivers who believe they were affected but have not received notice are encouraged to check the claims process details published by the settlement administrator. Deadlines for submitting claims will be listed in official notices.

Uber said it will also review its driver onboarding materials and make revisions where necessary. The company indicated that updated earnings information will include more detailed assumptions about expenses.

Labor economists note that many drivers work part-time or sporadically, which can complicate comparisons between advertised hourly rates and actual annual income. They recommend that platforms publish median earnings alongside averages to give a more realistic view.

The case also drew attention to the role of third-party leasing partners, which in some instances operated under separate contracts with drivers. Questions remain about how responsibility should be shared among companies in these arrangements.

Financial advisers encourage prospective drivers to calculate net earnings before committing to any vehicle lease, accounting for insurance, maintenance, fuel, and taxes. They also suggest reviewing lease terms carefully, including early termination penalties.

Some drivers said the settlement, while welcome, does not fully cover the financial strain they experienced. Several described months of unexpected expenses that left them in debt or forced them to sell vehicles at a loss.

The compensation total has not been publicly disclosed in full, though court filings indicate it is substantial. Administrators will verify claims before any payments are issued.

Uber's leadership has repeatedly said that most drivers value the flexibility of app-based work. The company argues that its platform provides income opportunities for people who might otherwise be excluded from traditional employment.

Supporters of the settlement said it sends a message that companies must be accountable for the statements they make to workers. They added that clear rules could benefit both drivers and platforms by reducing disputes.

Legal experts expect the case to be cited in future negotiations over driver classification and disclosure requirements. Several jurisdictions are already considering rules that would require transparent reporting of earnings data.

For many drivers, the most important outcome may be practical: receiving payment and gaining clearer information before making future financial decisions. Advocates say that clarity is the foundation of fair work.

The agreement must still receive final court approval before payments can begin. Once approved, the administrator is expected to publish a timeline for distribution and a contact line for questions.

Observers will be watching whether the settlement leads to lasting changes in how ride-hailing companies communicate with the people who power their networks. For now, drivers hope the agreement will mark a step toward more honest and transparent relationships with the platforms they depend on.

This manuscript proposes a generative adversarial network framework for partial multilabel learning, a setting in which each training instance is associated with a candidate label set that contains the true labels mixed with false positives. The problem is well motivated, since annotation noise in weakly supervised settings is common and existing disambiguation methods often rely on strong assumptions about the candidate label structure. The authors present the architecture clearly, describing how the generator and discriminator interact to recover plausible ground-truth label distributions from the noisy candidate sets. The training objective is reasonably explained, though the paper would benefit from a more explicit derivation of how the adversarial loss is combined with the classification loss and whether the two terms compete during optimization. The experimental section compares the proposed method against several established partial multilabel baselines on multiple benchmark datasets, which is a strength. However, the reported gains are often small, and the manuscript does not include variance across random seeds or statistical significance tests, so it is difficult to judge whether the improvements are robust. The ablation study is informative in isolation but omits a key component: removing the adversarial term entirely to show its specific contribution. Hyperparameter selection is described only briefly, and it is unclear whether the baselines were tuned with the same effort as the proposed method, which raises concerns about fairness of the comparison. The related work section covers the main lines of partial label and multilabel research but overlooks recent generative approaches to label noise, which would help position the contribution more precisely. The discussion of computational cost is missing, and given that GAN training is known to be unstable and expensive, readers would need training time and convergence behavior to assess practical value. The code and data processing details are not fully specified, limiting reproducibility, although the authors state that code will be released. Overall, the paper is a reasonable incremental contribution with a sound core idea, but it requires stronger statistical evidence, a fairer baseline comparison, and fuller implementation details before its performance claims can be considered convincing. I recommend a major revision.

Barnaby was a patched brown teddy bear who lived on the top shelf of a small blue bedroom in a house at the end of Willow Lane. Every night, when the lights went out, the shadows in the corners began to stir and whisper. They were the Gloam, a crowd of hungry monsters that fed on dreams and thin, sleepy imaginations. Barnaby had watched them creep closer for years, and he had decided long ago that he would not let them have the girl who slept beneath him.

Her name was Pip, and she was seven years old, with a gap in her front teeth and a habit of talking to the moon. She drew dragons on the back of her spelling homework and invented countries in the margins of her storybooks. Every drawing she made was a small light, and the Gloam hated light more than anything.

On the first night of the great battle, a shadow slid out from under the wardrobe with a sound like wet paper. It had too many elbows and a mouth that opened sideways. Barnaby leapt from the shelf, his button eyes gleaming, and landed squarely between the monster and the bed.

He had no sword, so he used the only weapon he had, which was the stubborn softness of a well-loved stuffed animal. He wrapped his arms around the creature's legs and held on until it toppled over the rug. Then he pressed his nose against its forehead and whispered the words Pip had taught him: "Once upon a time, there was a dragon who could not be frightened." The shadow shrieked, shrank, and dissolved into a puff of gray dust.

Barnaby dusted himself off and climbed back onto the bed just as Pip rolled over and sighed in her sleep. She had not even woken up.

The second night brought three of them. They came through the crack beneath the door, sliding over the floorboards in a crooked line. Barnaby stood at the foot of the bed with his stuffing puffed out to look twice as large. He reminded them, in his gruffest voice, that the girl beneath him was writing a story about a kingdom made of lemon cake, and that they were not invited.

One of the Gloam laughed, a hiss like a kettle. "Your stitches are fraying," it said. "You are only cloth and cotton. We are older than the first lullaby."

Barnaby did not argue. He simply held up the crayon drawing Pip had left on the nightstand, a picture of a yellow sun with a smiling face, and the Gloam recoiled. The light from that small drawing was enough to send them scurrying back under the door, and Barnaby slumped against the pillow, his left ear torn and his heart pounding like a drum.

Over the following weeks the battles grew fiercer. The Gloam learned to wait until Pip was almost asleep, then slip in through her half-dreams, whispering that her stories were silly and her drawings were ugly. Pip began to hesitate before she drew, and some nights she would fall asleep with her crayons still in her hand and no pictures finished at all.

Barnaby noticed the change in her, and it frightened him more than any monster ever had. A child without imagination was a child with no defenses, and he could not fight a war that lived inside her head. He realized then that the Gloam were not simply monsters under the bed. They were the doubt that crept into a young mind and told it that wonder was foolish.

So Barnaby changed his strategy. Instead of standing guard against the shadows, he began to fill the room with stories. He hid folded paper rockets inside Pip's drawers, scrawled tiny maps on the back of her cereal box, and tucked notes into her coat pockets that read, "Your imagination is the bravest thing you own."

On the night of the final confrontation, the Gloam came in a great dark tide, filling every corner and crowding the ceiling. Barnaby climbed onto the windowsill, where the moonlight fell in a silver stripe across the room. He faced them with his one good ear raised and his button eyes blazing.

"You have taken many things from this house," he said quietly, "but you will not take her wonder. Every time you come here, you make it stronger, because every time she fights you with a dragon, a song, or a made-up word, she grows braver. You are shadows. She is light, and she is learning to be brighter than you."

The Gloam roared and surged forward, but Pip stirred in her bed. Her eyes fluttered open, and she saw the bear standing in the moonlight. She smiled sleepily and reached for her crayon, drawing a wobbly rocket on the wall above her head. Then she whispered, "Go, Barnaby, I'll be okay," and the room filled with a warm, golden glow.

The Gloam shrieked and dissolved, one after another, until only a few wisps remained curling against the baseboards. Barnaby watched them fade and felt something inside him settle, like a stitch pulled tight at last.

Standing there, he made a vow to himself. This war would not last forever, he decided, for the Gloam were born from the absence of imagination, and a world full of children who dreamed could starve them out entirely. He would teach every child who needed him that their own minds were castles, and that no shadow could enter without their permission.

Pip yawned and pulled the blanket up to her chin. Barnaby climbed down from the windowsill and settled beside her pillow. Tomorrow there would be new drawings to protect and new stories to tell, but tonight, for the first time in a long while, the room was quiet and safe.

Summer coursework is a significant part of many students' academic lives, and yet the question of who should design it is rarely asked. Students often assume that because they are the ones doing the work, they should have a say in what that work looks like. However, summer coursework should be designed by teachers rather than students, because teachers possess the expertise, perspective, and accountability that a well-structured course requires.

The first reason is that teachers understand the subject. A student may know what they find interesting or difficult, but they rarely understand how the pieces of a discipline fit together. A teacher who has spent years studying and instructing a subject knows which concepts are foundational, which skills build on one another, and which misconceptions tend to derail learners. Without that knowledge, a course designed by students would likely be a collection of favorite topics rather than a coherent path toward mastery.

Second, teachers know how learning actually happens. Pedagogy is a field of study in its own right, and effective course design depends on sequencing material, pacing practice, and building in assessment that reveals whether understanding has taken hold. Students, however capable, are usually experiencing learning from the inside and cannot easily see the mechanisms that make it work. A teacher can judge how much review is needed after a long break and how to space difficult material so that it is retained.

Third, teachers are accountable for outcomes in a way students are not. When a teacher designs a course, they answer for whether it meets curriculum standards, prepares learners for the next grade, and aligns with the expectations of schools and examining bodies. This accountability creates a professional incentive to be rigorous and fair. A student-designed course, by contrast, might drift toward the easiest possible workload, since the person choosing the content also has the most to gain from lighter demands.

Fourth, a teacher can balance competing needs across a class. Summer coursework is usually taken by a diverse group of students with different strengths, gaps, and goals. A teacher can design activities that stretch advanced learners while supporting those who are behind, and can include multiple pathways to the same objective. Students designing the course would tend to optimize for their own preferences, which may not serve the whole group.

Some will argue that student input is valuable and that engagement improves when learners have a voice. This is a fair point, and teachers can certainly gather feedback, survey interests, and offer limited choices within a structured framework. But gathering input is different from handing over design authority. A menu of carefully vetted options, selected by a teacher, gives students meaningful agency while preserving the coherence and quality that only expert design can provide.

Another concern is that teacher-designed courses can feel rigid or disconnected from student life. This risk is real but manageable. A teacher who listens to students, revises courses based on results, and connects content to real-world applications can create courses that are both rigorous and relevant. The solution to a poorly designed course is better teacher training and better feedback loops, not a shift in who holds design responsibility.

It is also worth considering what summer is for. For many students, summer coursework is meant to close gaps, get ahead, or explore a subject more deeply. These goals require planning that looks beyond the immediate moment. A student focused on the next few weeks may not weigh the long-term value of a skill that feels tedious now. A teacher can make those tradeoffs deliberately, asking what a student will need in the autumn and building the summer around that need.

Finally, placing design in teachers' hands respects the purpose of education itself. Schooling is an institution built on the idea that trained adults guide young people toward knowledge they could not yet reach on their own. Summer coursework is no exception. Asking students to design their own curriculum would invert that relationship and undermine the reason the course exists in the first place.

Ultimately, the strongest case for teacher-designed summer coursework rests on expertise, pedagogical knowledge, accountability, and fairness across a whole class. Students deserve a voice in their education, and it is reasonable to seek their feedback and honor their interests. But the careful work of building a course that truly teaches should remain with the professionals trained to do it. Summer is a valuable opportunity, and it deserves to be used well, which means entrusting its design to those who know best how to make learning happen.

Subject: Methodology for Calculating NYISO Virtual Bidding Credit Requirements Using Historical Price Differences

Dear Team,

I am writing to outline a proposed methodology for estimating NYISO virtual bidding credit requirements using historical market price differences. The approach begins by collecting day-ahead and real-time locational-based marginal price data for each virtual bidding point of interest over a defined lookback period. For each trading hour, we would compute the price spread between the day-ahead and real-time markets, which represents the potential settlement exposure of a virtual position. These spreads would then be aggregated by location and position direction to build an empirical distribution of exposure outcomes. From this distribution, we would estimate a high-percentile loss figure, such as the 95th or 99th percentile, to represent the credit needed to cover adverse price movements. Position sizes and portfolio netting effects across correlated locations would be incorporated to reflect the true aggregate exposure. We would also apply a stress-testing overlay using extreme historical events to ensure the requirement captures tail risk. The resulting estimate would be compared against NYISO's posted collateral requirements to identify any shortfall or excess. Model inputs, including the lookback window and confidence level, should be documented and reviewed periodically as market conditions change. I recommend we validate this methodology against actual settlement data before adopting it for internal credit limits. Bank fees and overdraft charges have long been a source of frustration for consumers, and new comparisons show that the experience of paying for everyday banking varies considerably between Britain and other developed countries. Analysts who track current account charges say that the differences lie less in the headline cost of holding an account than in the penalties imposed when customers run short of money or fall behind on payments.

In Britain, the overdraft has traditionally been the main form of short-term borrowing for millions of current account holders. Banks have generally offered arranged overdrafts, which are agreed in advance up to a set limit, alongside unarranged overdrafts, which occur when a customer spends beyond what has been agreed. For many years unarranged overdraft charges were high, and campaigners argued that they hit the least well-off customers hardest.

Regulators intervened to change this picture. The Financial Conduct Authority introduced rules to make overdraft pricing clearer and to limit some of the most expensive practices. Many banks responded by scrapping or reducing unarranged overdraft fees, moving instead toward daily interest charges or fixed monthly fees that customers can see more easily before they borrow.

Consumer groups welcomed these changes but noted that the cost of borrowing through an overdraft can still be significant, particularly for people who rely on it regularly rather than as an occasional buffer. Some reports have found that customers who use overdrafts for long periods can pay more than they would through a personal loan or a credit union, even when the headline interest rate looks modest.

Account switching is another area where Britain has taken a distinct approach. The current account switch service allows customers to move their direct debits, standing orders and incoming payments to a new bank within a set timeframe, and the process is backed by a guarantee that payments will be redirected. Supporters say this has increased competition and made it easier for people to leave a bank that is charging them too much.

Switching data suggests, however, that many people still stay with their existing provider. Surveys have repeatedly found that a large share of account holders have never switched, often because they believe it is complicated or because they are unaware that better options exist. Some banks also offer loyalty benefits or incentive payments that make switching less attractive in the short term.

Other countries have taken different routes. In the United States, overdraft fees have historically been a major source of bank revenue, and a number of large institutions have faced pressure to reduce or eliminate them. Several American banks have introduced no-overdraft-fee policies or allowed customers a short grace period before charges apply, and some have moved to cap the number of fees that can be charged in a single day.

In much of continental Europe, the structure of retail banking is different. Many countries have strong legal limits on how banks can charge for basic accounts, and in some places a basic account with limited features is guaranteed to customers at low or no cost. Comparisons of this kind often show that European consumers pay less for routine services but may have fewer options for short-term credit through overdrafts.

Australia and Canada have also seen debate about overdraft charges and account switching. Regulators in both countries have examined whether fee structures are fair and whether customers can easily compare products. Measures have included requirements for clearer disclosure of fees and efforts to make account comparison tools more reliable.

Economists point out that comparing fees across countries is difficult. Some countries charge monthly account fees, others rely on transaction fees, and others depend on interest margins and cross-selling of other products. A bank that appears cheap for everyday use may recover its revenue through higher charges elsewhere, so consumers need to look at the full cost of their banking relationship.

Financial education groups advise customers to check their account terms carefully, set up balance alerts, and consider whether a fee-free overdraft buffer or a separate savings cushion would be more affordable over time. They also encourage people in financial difficulty to contact their bank early, since many lenders have support schemes that can reduce or pause charges.

For consumers in Britain, the main message from recent developments is that protections have improved but that the cost of short-term borrowing and the effort required to switch accounts still matter. For those comparing their options with banks in other countries, the lesson is that fee structures differ widely and that the cheapest-looking account is not always the least expensive in practice.

Looking ahead, observers expect regulators and banks to keep refining the rules around overdrafts, fees and switching. Greater use of digital banking tools and open banking data-sharing may make it easier for customers to compare accounts and move between providers, which could put further pressure on banks to keep charges transparent and competitive.

Manchester has stepped up its response to a sharp rise in incidents linked to Spice, the synthetic cannabinoid drug that has become a growing concern across the city's streets and public services. Local authorities, health workers and police say the drug's unpredictable effects are placing increasing strain on emergency services and hospitals. Ambulance crews report being called repeatedly to people who have collapsed, become agitated or shown signs of severe distress after using the substance. Hospital staff say they are treating patients with symptoms ranging from seizures and rapid heart rates to prolonged periods of confusion and psychosis. Health professionals warn that because Spice is manufactured in unregulated labs and often sprayed onto paper or plant material, the strength and composition of each dose can vary dramatically. Users, many of whom are already facing homelessness, mental health problems or addiction, are among those most at risk. Outreach teams working in the city centre say they are seeing more people in crisis on a daily basis, and some have called for expanded support services. Council representatives said a multi-agency approach is being developed, bringing together housing providers, drug treatment services, the NHS and the police. Plans under discussion include additional outreach workers, improved access to addiction treatment and more emergency shelter places for people at risk. Police have also increased patrols in areas where Spice use is most visible, and officers are working with health partners to direct vulnerable people toward support rather than solely toward enforcement. Public health experts emphasise that the response must address the underlying causes of drug use, including poverty, trauma and lack of stable accommodation. Some residents and business owners have expressed frustration at the visible impact of Spice use on their neighbourhoods, including littering, anti-social behaviour and concerns about safety. Local leaders acknowledge these concerns and say they are working to balance community safety with compassion for those affected. Campaigners argue that more long-term investment is needed, pointing to funding cuts in recent years that they say have weakened the city's ability to respond. The council has said it will review the effectiveness of the new measures over the coming months and report back on outcomes. Health officials are also urging anyone who knows someone using Spice to seek help early and to contact local services for advice. Experts note that there is still limited research into the long-term health effects of the drug, which adds to the difficulty of planning treatment. As the situation develops, officials say they will continue to monitor trends closely and adjust their approach as needed. For now, Manchester faces a complex challenge that will require sustained cooperation between public services, health providers and the communities most affected.

The manuscript proposes a neuron-reuse architecture in which individual neurons are shared across multiple layers or processing steps, aiming to reduce parameter count while preserving predictive performance. The motivation is clearly stated and well situated within the literature on parameter sharing, recurrent depth, and efficient model design. The experimental section compares the proposed model against standard feedforward and transformer baselines on several benchmarks, and the reported accuracy gains at matched parameter budgets are promising. However, the authors should specify whether baselines were tuned with the same effort and training budget, since differences in optimization can account for a substantial share of reported improvements. The ablation study is useful, but it would be strengthened by isolating the effect of reuse itself from related factors such as depth, width, and the choice of activation function. Wall-clock latency and memory measurements are absent, which is a significant gap given that the paper frames its contribution around practical value; parameter reduction does not necessarily translate into faster inference, especially when reused neurons require sequential computation. The discussion of scaling behavior is limited to models of modest size, and it remains unclear whether the advantages persist at the scales where efficiency concerns matter most. The theoretical justification for why neuron reuse should not degrade expressivity is sketched rather than proven, and a more formal treatment would add credibility. Reproducibility would benefit from released code, complete hyperparameter tables, and multiple random seeds with reported variance, since several reported differences are small relative to likely run-to-run noise. The related work section omits some recent efforts on weight-tied and looped architectures that address closely overlapping questions. The writing is generally clear, though the methods section would benefit from a precise mathematical description of how reused neurons receive gradients during training. Overall, the paper presents an interesting direction with encouraging early evidence, but the claims of practical value are not yet fully supported. I recommend a major revision addressing the baseline fairness, efficiency measurements, and reproducibility concerns before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Why Donald Trump Retained Strong Support Among Republican Voters Despite Controversy in the 2016 Race

Donald Trump's campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2016 defied many of the conventions that political analysts had long considered essential to winning primary contests. Throughout the race, he faced a steady stream of controversies, from inflammatory remarks about immigrants and women to disputes with fellow candidates and the press. Yet his support among Republican voters remained remarkably durable. Understanding why requires looking at a combination of political, cultural, economic, and psychological factors that shaped the electorate in that moment.

One of the most frequently cited explanations is the depth of dissatisfaction within the Republican base with the party establishment. Many primary voters felt that Washington politicians from both parties had failed to deliver on promises related to immigration, trade, and economic security. Trump positioned himself as an outsider who was unbeholden to donors and party elites, and this framing resonated with voters who felt ignored for years. For these voters, his willingness to break with party orthodoxy was a feature rather than a flaw.

Trump's message on trade and manufacturing also struck a chord in communities that had experienced job losses over the preceding decades. He promised to renegotiate or withdraw from trade agreements, to bring manufacturing jobs back to the United States, and to protect American workers from foreign competition. Many voters in states such as Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Michigan had seen factories close or relocate, and they responded to a candidate who spoke directly about those losses in blunt terms.

Immigration was another central pillar of his appeal. His proposal to build a wall along the southern border and to restrict immigration from certain countries became a defining element of his campaign. Supporters who prioritized border security and stricter enforcement viewed his commitment as a sign that he would act on an issue they had long considered neglected. Even critics acknowledged that the issue carried enormous emotional weight for a significant portion of the Republican electorate.

Cultural identity and a sense of displacement also played a role. Some voters, particularly those without college degrees and those living in rural or economically struggling areas, described feeling that their values, communities, and way of life were disregarded by elites in media, academia, and government. Trump's rhetoric, which was often combative toward those institutions, offered these voters a sense that someone was speaking on their behalf.

Analysts also pointed to the phenomenon sometimes described as partisan loyalty reinforced by media consumption. Many Republican voters relied on conservative talk radio, cable news, and social media sources that amplified Trump's messages and framed controversies as attacks by biased opponents. When a story about a candidate's remarks emerged, supporters often encountered counter-narratives that attributed the coverage to a hostile press, which tended to reduce its impact within their circles.

The phenomenon of perceived authenticity was another factor. Trump's style was unscripted, direct, and unconventional, and many voters said they valued that quality over polished political language. Some supporters argued that they preferred a candidate who said what he thought, even when his statements were offensive to others, because they saw this as more honest than the careful messaging of traditional politicians. This perception of candor allowed some voters to separate his manner of speaking from their assessment of his policy positions.

Supporters also frequently emphasized that they were voting for policy outcomes rather than personal conduct. Tax cuts, judicial appointments, regulatory reform, and a tougher stance on foreign adversaries were cited as reasons to back him, and many said they were willing to look past controversial statements to secure those goals. This transactional view allowed voters to evaluate him on a set of priorities that differed from the standards they applied to other public figures.

Strategic considerations within the Republican primary field also helped sustain his position. The crowded contest, with numerous candidates dividing the more conventional vote, allowed Trump to win substantial shares of delegates with pluralities rather than majorities. His ability to hold a loyal core of supporters while others competed for the remaining votes gave him a structural advantage that many observers underestimated.

Some Republicans who were initially skeptical came to view Trump as the most viable candidate to defeat the Democratic nominee. Concerns about electability can prompt voters to rally behind a candidate they might otherwise reject, particularly when they believe the alternatives are weaker. As the primaries progressed and Trump continued to win contests, many Republicans shifted toward the view that he represented the party's best chance in the general election.

Party leaders also faced a dilemma. Many elected officials and party figures had publicly criticized Trump early in the race, but as his support grew, they confronted the choice of opposing a candidate who commanded the loyalty of a large portion of primary voters or accommodating him. Some eventually endorsed him, citing unity and the importance of defeating the Democratic candidate, and these endorsements helped reassure hesitant voters that his candidacy was legitimate within the party.

Demographic patterns in the primary electorate also contributed to his strength. Polling during the primaries indicated that Trump performed especially well among white voters without college degrees, a group that had been trending toward the Republican Party for decades. His message was tailored to speak to the concerns of this constituency, and their turnout in primary states helped deliver him victories that others had not anticipated.

Critics argued that the durability of his support reflected a willingness among some Republicans to overlook behavior they would have condemned in other candidates. They contended that partisanship, fear of the opposing party, and the appeal of a disruptive outsider had led many voters to accept rhetoric that previously would have disqualified a candidate. These critics warned that normalizing such conduct could have lasting consequences for political discourse.

Supporters, by contrast, rejected the idea that their backing reflected a lack of principle. They maintained that they had weighed the candidate's flaws against his positions and concluded that his agenda justified their vote. For them, the controversies were distractions created by a media they viewed as unfair, and they remained focused on issues such as the economy, national security, and the direction of the country.

The role of grassroots enthusiasm should not be overlooked. Trump's rallies drew large crowds, and many attendees described a sense of energy and belonging that they had not felt in previous election cycles. This enthusiasm translated into volunteer activity, social media engagement, and turnout that strengthened his organization and reinforced the perception of momentum.

The experience of social networks also mattered. Many supporters encountered Trump's message through friends, family members, and local groups, and these personal connections reinforced their commitment. When people around them shared their enthusiasm, it became easier to maintain support despite negative coverage, as the community itself provided validation and reassurance.

Historical comparisons were frequently drawn, with some observers noting parallels to other populist movements in American politics. Figures such as Andrew Jackson and William Jennings Bryan had also built followings by challenging established elites and speaking to grievances of ordinary citizens. Whether such comparisons were apt remained a matter of debate, but they helped frame his candidacy for many commentators and voters.

Political scientists have also examined the role of identity-based attachment. Research on partisanship suggests that for many voters, party identification functions as a social identity, and loyalty to a leader who embodies that identity can outweigh disagreements on individual issues. In this view, Republican voters who saw Trump as representing their side in a broader cultural conflict were more likely to stand by him when controversies arose.

Economic anxiety was another theme that surfaced repeatedly in exit polls and interviews. Many voters expressed concern about stagnant wages, the cost of healthcare, and the stability of their communities. Trump's promises to address these issues, however general they sometimes were, gave supporters a sense of hope that the political system would respond to their needs.

The question of foreign policy also influenced some voters. His call for a more restrained approach to foreign military interventions, combined with a tougher posture on trade and security threats, appealed to those who felt that previous administrations had committed resources abroad without clear benefits at home. This stance cut across traditional lines within the Republican Party and attracted support from some who had previously aligned with more interventionist views.

Finally, the 2016 primary illustrated how quickly political norms can shift when a significant portion of the electorate believes the existing system has failed them. Trump's ability to retain strong support amid controversy reflected a convergence of grievances, personal loyalties, media dynamics, and strategic opportunities. Whether that support reflected a lasting realignment within the Republican Party or a more temporary response to the particular circumstances of that election remained an open question for analysts as the general election approached.

Cities across the world are beginning to rethink how people move through urban spaces, and one of the most promising changes is the shift away from private cars toward walking and public transportation. This transition offers a path toward cities that are healthier, cleaner, and more pleasant to live in. For decades, urban planning prioritized the automobile, building wide roads, sprawling parking lots, and suburbs that made driving a necessity. The consequences of that approach are now clear, and many communities are searching for alternatives.

The health benefits of walking and using public transit are among the most compelling reasons for change. People who walk to work or to the store incorporate physical activity into their daily routines without needing to set aside special time for exercise. Regular walking has been linked to lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, and obesity, as well as improved mental health. Public transportation supports this as well, since riders often walk to and from stations, adding exercise to their commute.

Cleaner air is another major advantage of this shift. Vehicle exhaust releases pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate matter, which are harmful to human lungs and hearts. Children, the elderly, and people with asthma are especially vulnerable to these pollutants. When fewer people drive private cars, cities experience measurable improvements in air quality, which can reduce hospital visits and premature deaths.

Reducing traffic also lowers noise levels, which many urban residents find exhausting and stressful. Constant engine noise, horns, and braking can interfere with sleep and concentration. Quieter streets allow people to hear birdsong, conversation, and the everyday sounds of community life. In this way, the shift toward walking and transit improves not only physical health but also the emotional quality of city living.

Public transportation, when well designed, can move far more people through a given amount of space than private cars can. A single bus or train can carry dozens or even hundreds of passengers, while the same number of people in cars would fill many lanes of road and require vast amounts of parking. This efficiency frees up land that can be used for parks, housing, and businesses, making cities more livable and economically productive.

Walking and transit also promote social connection. When people move through their neighborhoods on foot or on shared vehicles, they are more likely to encounter neighbors, shop at local businesses, and feel part of a community. Streets designed for pedestrians tend to be safer and more active, which can deter crime through what urban planners call natural surveillance. Car-dependent environments, by contrast, often isolate people inside their vehicles.

Economic arguments support this transition as well. Car ownership is expensive, with costs for purchase, insurance, fuel, maintenance, and parking adding up to a significant share of household budgets. Public transit offers a far cheaper alternative, and walkable neighborhoods can reduce household transportation expenses substantially. Local businesses also tend to benefit when foot traffic increases, as pedestrians stop more often than drivers passing through.

Equity is an important consideration in this discussion. Not everyone can drive, whether because of age, disability, or income, and car-centered planning has historically left these residents with limited options. A strong public transportation network gives people access to jobs, healthcare, education, and social life regardless of their ability to own or operate a vehicle. Expanding these options is therefore a matter of fairness as well as sustainability.

Successful examples from around the world show that this shift is achievable. Cities such as Copenhagen and Amsterdam have built extensive networks of bike lanes, sidewalks, and rail lines, and a large share of their residents walk, cycle, or take transit for everyday trips. Their experiences demonstrate that car dependence is not inevitable but rather the result of policy choices that can be changed.

Still, the transition faces real obstacles. Many existing cities were built around cars, and retrofitting them is expensive and politically difficult. Some residents worry that changes to road layouts or parking will disrupt their lives or businesses. Public transit systems require sustained funding for maintenance, staffing, and expansion, and they must be reliable enough to earn public trust. Overcoming these challenges requires patient planning and clear communication with the public.

Effective strategies can help address these concerns. Cities can build protected bike lanes and widen sidewalks to make walking and cycling safer and more comfortable. They can invest in frequent, reliable bus and rail service and integrate different transit options so that riders can switch easily between them. Pricing policies, such as congestion charges or reduced parking availability, can encourage people to reconsider driving for short trips.

Technology may also play a role. Real-time transit tracking, mobile payment systems, and trip-planning apps make public transportation easier to use, especially for newcomers to a city. Shared mobility services, such as bike and scooter sharing, can fill gaps between home, transit stops, and final destinations. Thoughtful integration of these tools can make multimodal travel more convenient than driving alone.

Individual choices matter as well, though they are most effective when supported by good infrastructure. A person who chooses to walk or ride the bus for a daily commute contributes to cleaner air and less congestion, and collective habits can gradually reshape social norms. When transit and walking are the easy and obvious choices, more people will make them without needing to be persuaded.

Environmental considerations provide additional motivation. Transportation is one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries, and reducing reliance on private cars is a key part of efforts to address climate change. Public transit powered by electricity or other low-emission sources can dramatically cut the carbon footprint of urban travel, and walking produces no emissions at all.

Looking ahead, the shift toward walking and public transportation represents a broader vision of what cities can be. Instead of places dominated by traffic and pollution, they can become spaces where people move easily, breathe cleaner air, and interact with one another. This vision requires commitment from governments, businesses, and residents alike.

Ultimately, the move away from private cars is not about eliminating driving entirely but about creating balanced transportation systems in which walking and transit are safe, convenient, and attractive. Such systems would improve public health, protect the environment, strengthen communities, and expand opportunity for all residents. As cities continue to grow, choosing these options now will shape the quality of urban life for generations to come.

Thornwald had kept the Sunken Gate for four hundred and twelve years, and in all that time he had never once been tired of it until the morning he realized he was tired of everything.

He stood where he had always stood, between the black stone pillars at the bottom of the ravine, his hands resting on the hilt of a sword so old its crossguard had worn smooth as river pebbles. Moss grew in the cracks of his armor. Birds nested in the plume that had long since rotted from his helm. None of it bothered him anymore. Very little did.

The Gate was a door into the old city beneath the mountain, and the city was full of things that should not wake. For four centuries Thornwald had turned them back. He had buried the cult of the Pale Choir under a rockslide, sealed the drowned hall where the tide-kings whispered, and broken the spine of a wyrm that had tried to crawl up through the cistern. Villages in the valley below had grown into towns, and the towns into a small kingdom, and none of them had ever learned his name. That was as it should be.

He had not been alive, not in the way the villagers were alive. The magic that bound him to the Gate had kept his heart beating through winters and wars, had knit his wounds closed and kept his lungs filling with air he had no need of. It had made him strong. It had made him patient. It had also made him unable to die, and somewhere around the second century he had begun to understand that this was not a gift.

The first adventurers arrived in the spring. There were four of them: a broad-shouldered woman with a bow across her back, a young man who talked too much, a quiet scholar with ink on her fingers, and a half-elf who kept glancing at the Gate as if it might bite. They had come for the treasure the old histories promised, and they stopped short when they saw him.

He told them to leave. They did not leave. The young man laughed and asked whether he was a ghost, and Thornwald said no, that he was only very old, and very tired.

Over the next several days they camped at the mouth of the ravine and argued among themselves within earshot of him, which he suspected was deliberate. The scholar came to speak with him each evening, asking careful questions about the seals and the bindings. She wrote down his answers. Sometimes she asked about the years, and he told her what he remembered, which was more than he wanted to remember.

On the fifth night she sat beside him on a flat stone and said, "There's a way to end it, isn't there? The binding. If someone else took up the Gate, you could be released."

"There is," he said.

"And you want that."

He looked at the stars through the gap in the ravine walls. "I want it more than I have wanted anything in a very long time."

She was quiet for a while. Then she said, "Why haven't you done it yourself?"

"Because the Gate needs a guardian, and the magic that binds me only transfers to one who accepts it freely. And because every guardian before me who was offered release refused it, and I was the one who took the oath after the last one died, and I did not understand then what I was agreeing to."

"And the others? Your predecessors?"

"They chose to stay. Each one believed that someone must. I believed it too."

The half-elf came to them then, and the scholar told him the whole of it. He listened with his hand on the hilt of his dagger, though the threat had long since passed.

"You're offering us the power to hold the Gate," he said. "Forever."

"Yes," said Thornwald. "The power to hold it, and the curse of never ending. I will teach you the words. You will feel the binding settle into your bones like cold water. In a few decades you will stop feeling the cold. In a century you will wonder what the sun is for."

The broad-shouldered woman, who had been silent until now, spoke for the first time. "And you want us to take that so you can stop."

"Yes."

"No," she said simply.

The young man protested. The scholar looked troubled. But the woman only shook her head. "We didn't come here to become you," she said. "We came for gold and a story to tell in taverns. That's a bad trade, and I'm not making it."

Thornwald felt something shift in his chest, something he had not felt in longer than he could measure. It was not quite disappointment. It was closer to grief, though he could not have said for what.

"I understand," he said.

They packed their things the next morning. The scholar lingered at the edge of the ravine and asked whether there was anything she could do. He told her no, but thanked her for asking. She hesitated, then offered him a small clay bottle of water from her pack, the kind travelers carry, and he took it because refusing would have hurt her.

"Will you be all right?" she asked.

He thought about the question honestly. "I will be what I have always been," he said. "That is not the same as all right, but it is what I have."

They walked up out of the ravine, and their voices faded, and the birds returned to their nesting, and Thornwald stood alone between the black stone pillars with the clay bottle in his hand.

He did not know how long he stood there. The sun crossed the gap in the walls and moved on. Somewhere beneath the mountain, something shifted in the old city and went still again, and he felt the familiar weight of the Gate settle more firmly into place.

He uncorked the bottle and drank. The water was cold and tasted of clay and of the scholar's hands. Then he set the bottle carefully on the stone where she had sat, and he turned back to the dark doorway, and he took up his post once more, because no one else had come to take it from him, and the Gate still had to be kept.
