Staying focused is one of the most valuable skills a student can develop, especially when deadlines are approaching and attention is pulled in many directions. One effective strategy is to break large assignments into smaller, specific steps, which makes the work feel manageable and gives a clear sense of progress. Another is to create a dedicated study environment free from clutter, with a clean desk and minimal noise, so the mind has fewer cues to wander. Setting a timer for focused work sessions, such as twenty-five minutes followed by a short break, can also help maintain concentration without causing burnout. Silencing phone notifications or placing the phone in another room removes one of the most common sources of interruption. Writing down distracting thoughts as they arise allows a student to acknowledge them and return to the task without losing momentum. Planning the day or week in advance, with realistic deadlines for each assignment, reduces the stress that often leads to last-minute scrambling and poor decisions. Many students also benefit from studying at the time of day when they feel most alert, reserving routine tasks for lower-energy periods. Finally, rewarding completed work with a small break or a enjoyable activity reinforces good habits and makes future focus easier to sustain. By combining these strategies, students can overcome distractions and complete their tasks on time with greater confidence and less stress.

The tiles on the bathroom floor began to breathe, slow and wet, and I understood that I had been someone else for a very long time. My name was Daniel, or it had been, or it was going to be. The mirror showed a man of forty with a face I almost recognized, like a cousin seen across a crowded train platform. I laughed, and the laugh came back to me in the voice of my father, who had been dead nine years and who was asking me, kindly, what I had done with the twenties. I tried to answer and found the answer was a drawer full of unsent letters, each one addressed to a version of myself who had stopped waiting. The clock on the wall had numbers that melted into the shape of the years I had spent deciding whether to begin. Eleven years at a job I hated, four at a marriage I had quietly abandoned before anyone noticed, a decade of promising the piano I would return. The walls leaned in to hear me confess, and I confessed everything: the friends I let drift, the city I never left, the book I kept rewriting in my head until it became a kind of ghost. Then the room folded, and I was standing in a field I had seen in a photograph taped inside a cabinet door, the grass taller than I remembered. A woman waved from the far end, and I knew her, or I knew the outline of the life I might have had with her, shimmering like heat above asphalt. She did not speak, and I did not need her to. The sun was a yellow coin pressed into the sky, and every second of it felt like a sum I had been paying in installments without ever checking the total. I wanted to run toward her, but my legs were made of the hours I had spent standing still. Somewhere a telephone rang in a house I had lived in as a child, and nobody answered it, and I understood with terrible clarity that the call was mine. The field dissolved into static and then into the cool tile again, the breathing floor now still. I sat with my back against the bathtub, shaking, the drug slowly loosening its grip on the colors. I was still Daniel, I decided, and Daniel was still forty, and the drawer was still full, but the envelopes had stopped looking like accusations. Maybe regret was just time asking to be spent differently. I picked up my phone and, for the first time in years, dialed my sister's number. She answered on the second ring, and her voice was the first real thing I had heard all night.

Should schools require students to complete community service when they already juggle demanding coursework and extracurricular activities? The question deserves careful thought, because the answer depends on what we believe schools are for. Supporters argue that community service teaches empathy and civic responsibility, qualities that a classroom alone cannot fully develop. Working at a food bank or tutoring younger children puts students in contact with people whose lives differ from their own, and that contact can reshape how they see their community. Requirements also ensure that every student, not only the already-motivated, has access to these experiences. Many students would never volunteer on their own, and a requirement may be the only push they receive. Critics, however, point out that students today face intense pressure to build transcripts that look impressive to colleges. An added requirement can turn service into another box to check, draining its meaning and leaving students resentful. Those who already work part-time jobs or care for family members may find that a mandate asks them to give time they simply do not have. There is also a question of fairness, since students with flexible schedules and access to transportation can complete service more easily than others. A middle path may serve students best. Schools could offer a range of options, including service embedded in coursework, so that the experience connects to what students are learning. Requirements could be modest in scope and paired with reflection, helping students think about what they gained rather than merely logging hours. Flexibility in timing and type of service would reduce the burden on students with limited time. Such an approach keeps the educational goal while respecting the other commitments students carry. Ultimately, service is most valuable when chosen freely, but a well-designed requirement can introduce students to its rewards. Schools should therefore require service, but only in a form that is thoughtful, flexible, and genuinely educational.

This manuscript addresses a meaningful gap in knowledge graph embedding research: most embedding methods treat relations as independent, so they fail to respect logical implications such as one relation entailing another. The authors propose a framework that constrains relation embeddings so that implication rules, for example that a relation R1 implies R2, are reflected geometrically in the vector space. The motivation is clearly stated and well grounded in the literature on inference-aware representation learning. The introduction positions the work appropriately relative to translational models, bilinear models, and rule-injection approaches, though the related work section could more explicitly compare against methods that encode logical rules through regularization. The core technical contribution is a set of loss terms that penalize violations of implication constraints during training. The formulation is mostly sound, and the authors show how the constraints can be expressed as inclusion relations between regions or as inequalities between relation vectors. However, the paper would benefit from a more rigorous treatment of the conditions under which the proposed constraints are jointly satisfiable, since conflicting rules could render the optimization problem inconsistent. The experimental evaluation uses standard link prediction benchmarks and reports gains in mean reciprocal rank and Hits@10 over baseline models. These improvements are encouraging, but the magnitude of the gains varies considerably across datasets, and the authors do not sufficiently discuss the cases where the method underperforms. The ablation study is useful for isolating the contribution of each loss term, yet it would be stronger with variance estimates across multiple random seeds. Statistical significance is not reported, which makes it difficult to judge whether some of the smaller improvements are robust. A further concern is that the benchmarks chosen may contain relatively few genuine implication patterns, so the evaluation may not fully test the central claim. I recommend that the authors construct or select a dataset where logical implications are dense and known, and report performance specifically on test triples that require inference. The theoretical analysis is limited, and a formal guarantee on the preservation of implications, even under restricted conditions, would considerably strengthen the paper. The writing is generally clear, though some notation for relation embeddings and region operators is introduced inconsistently and should be standardized. Figures illustrating the geometric intuition are helpful, but the captions could be more self-contained. The code availability statement is appreciated, and reproducibility would be further improved by specifying hyperparameter search ranges and training budgets. Overall, the paper presents a promising and relevant idea with reasonable empirical support. With a more thorough theoretical treatment, stronger statistical reporting, and an evaluation that directly targets inferential behavior, it could make a substantial contribution. I recommend a major revision.

Title: CT-Based Visceral Fat Measurements as a Tool for Distinguishing Crohn's Disease from Intestinal Tuberculosis

Abstract

Crohn's disease and intestinal tuberculosis are two chronic granulomatous or inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract that share overlapping clinical, endoscopic, and radiological features, and their differentiation remains a persistent diagnostic challenge in regions where both are prevalent. Visceral adipose tissue has been increasingly recognized as a metabolically active compartment that modulates systemic and local inflammation, and its quantification by computed tomography offers a reproducible, non-invasive measure of body composition. This study evaluated whether CT-derived visceral fat indices, including visceral fat area, the visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio, and mesenteric fat density, could discriminate between Crohn's disease and intestinal tuberculosis. We retrospectively reviewed abdominal CT examinations from patients with histologically or microbiologically confirmed diagnoses and compared fat measurements between groups. Our findings suggest that specific visceral fat parameters differ meaningfully between the two conditions and may contribute to a multimodal diagnostic framework. We discuss the biological rationale, methodological considerations, limitations, and directions for prospective validation.

Introduction

Crohn's disease is a chronic, relapsing transmural inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract with a complex etiology involving genetic susceptibility, immune dysregulation, and environmental triggers. Intestinal tuberculosis, caused predominantly by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and less often by Mycobacterium bovis, is an infectious granulomatous disease of the bowel that remains common in high-burden regions. Both conditions can produce ileocecal involvement, strictures, fistulae, lymphadenopathy, and mesenteric changes, which creates substantial overlap on imaging. Misdiagnosis carries important consequences, because antitubercular therapy is not appropriate for Crohn's disease and corticosteroids or immunosuppressants given for Crohn's disease can worsen untreated tuberculosis. Current diagnostic strategies rely on a combination of colonoscopy with biopsy, histopathology, acid-fast staining, mycobacterial culture, nucleic acid amplification testing, and cross-sectional imaging, yet each has limitations in sensitivity and specificity. Computed tomography is widely available and routinely performed in patients with suspected intestinal disease, making it an attractive platform for additional quantitative biomarkers. Visceral adipose tissue is not a passive energy store; it secretes adipokines and cytokines and participates in local immune responses within the mesentery. Mesenteric fat is in close anatomical contact with diseased bowel segments and draining lymph nodes, and its inflammatory state may differ between chronic immune-mediated disease and mycobacterial infection. Several studies have linked increased visceral adiposity to adverse outcomes in inflammatory bowel disease, including postoperative complications and disease activity. However, whether visceral fat distribution can serve as a discriminating feature between Crohn's disease and intestinal tuberculosis has not been systematically studied. We therefore sought to quantify CT-derived visceral fat measures in well-characterized patients and assess their diagnostic utility.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective case-control analysis at a tertiary referral center. Eligible patients were adults who underwent contrast-enhanced abdominal CT for suspected or known terminal ileal or ileocecal disease and who received a final diagnosis of either Crohn's disease or intestinal tuberculosis. Crohn's disease was defined by typical endoscopic and histopathological findings with exclusion of infection, and intestinal tuberculosis was defined by a composite standard incorporating caseating or non-caseating granulomas, positive acid-fast staining or culture, positive polymerase chain reaction, or clinical and radiological response to antitubercular therapy. Patients with malignancy, prior bowel surgery involving the region of interest, known human immunodeficiency virus infection, corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy within three months before imaging, or incomplete imaging were excluded. Body mass index, age, sex, and laboratory markers including C-reactive protein and albumin were extracted from the medical record. CT scans were acquired using standardized portal venous phase protocols with slice thickness of 5 mm or less. A single trained radiologist, blinded to the final diagnosis, performed measurements using dedicated image analysis software. Visceral fat area was quantified at the level of the L4-L5 intervertebral disc by thresholding voxels between −190 and −30 Hounsfield units within the intra-abdominal cavity, and subcutaneous fat area was measured at the same level. The visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio was calculated from these values. Mesenteric fat density was measured as the mean attenuation in a standardized region of interest placed in fat adjacent to the most affected bowel segment, avoiding vessels and lymph nodes. A second radiologist independently measured a random subset of scans to assess interobserver agreement. Continuous variables were compared using Student's t-test or the Mann-Whitney U test according to distribution, and categorical variables with the chi-square or Fisher's exact test. Receiver operating characteristic curves were generated for each fat parameter, and the area under the curve, optimal cutoffs, sensitivity, and specificity were calculated. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index was used to estimate independent associations. Statistical significance was set at a two-sided p value below 0.05.

Results

A total of 118 patients met inclusion criteria, comprising 74 with Crohn's disease and 44 with intestinal tuberculosis. Baseline demographic characteristics were comparable between groups in terms of age and sex distribution, although patients with Crohn's disease had a modestly lower mean body mass index. C-reactive protein was higher in intestinal tuberculosis in our cohort, while serum albumin was lower in the same group. Visceral fat area was significantly greater in patients with Crohn's disease than in those with intestinal tuberculosis after adjustment for body mass index. The visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio showed a similar pattern and was the most discriminating single parameter in receiver operating characteristic analysis, with an area under the curve of approximately 0.78. Mesenteric fat density was lower, indicating greater fat-tissue inflammation or edema, in intestinal tuberculosis compared with Crohn's disease, and this parameter demonstrated an area under the curve of approximately 0.72. Combining the visceral-to-subcutaneous ratio with mesenteric fat density improved discrimination, yielding an area under the curve of approximately 0.84. Interobserver agreement for visceral fat measurements was good, with intraclass correlation coefficients exceeding 0.9. In multivariable analysis, the visceral-to-subcutaneous ratio remained independently associated with diagnosis after adjustment for confounders. Sensitivity and specificity at the optimal cutoff varied, and no single threshold achieved high performance in both directions simultaneously.

Discussion

In this study, CT-derived visceral fat indices differed between patients with Crohn's disease and intestinal tuberculosis, and their combination improved discrimination beyond conventional radiological features alone. The finding that Crohn's disease was associated with relatively greater visceral adiposity may reflect the chronic metabolic and inflammatory milieu characteristic of long-standing immune-mediated disease, in which mesenteric adipocytes may be stimulated by adjacent inflamed bowel. The lower mesenteric fat density observed in intestinal tuberculosis may represent perienteric inflammatory edema or caseating processes extending into adjacent fat, consistent with the tendency of mycobacterial infection to provoke local tissue reaction. These interpretations remain hypotheses, and the underlying pathophysiology requires direct investigation. Our results are consistent with prior reports linking visceral adiposity to inflammatory bowel disease severity and postoperative outcomes, and they extend this literature to the differential diagnosis question. The combined use of two inexpensive, routinely acquired measurements is attractive because it requires no additional radiation exposure or cost beyond the standard examination. Nonetheless, several limitations must be acknowledged. The retrospective design introduces selection bias, and the reference standard was not uniformly applied, since some tuberculosis diagnoses relied on clinical response rather than microbiological confirmation. The sample size was modest, and external validation in independent cohorts from different geographic and ethnic backgrounds is necessary before clinical adoption. Hounsfield unit thresholds and imaging protocols vary across institutions, which may limit generalizability and necessitates standardization. Body composition differs by population, and cutoff values derived here may not transfer directly to other settings. Furthermore, disease activity, prior treatments, and disease duration may confound fat measurements, and our adjustment for these factors was incomplete. Future prospective multicenter studies should incorporate standardized imaging protocols, stratify by disease stage and activity, and evaluate whether visceral fat indices add incremental value to established clinical and laboratory tools. Machine learning approaches integrating body composition with texture analysis of bowel wall and lymph nodes may further improve performance. Investigation of adipokine and cytokine profiles in mesenteric fat from surgical specimens could clarify the mechanisms underlying the observed differences.

Conclusion

CT-based visceral fat measurements, particularly the visceral-to-subcutaneous fat ratio and mesenteric fat density, show promise as adjunctive, non-invasive tools for distinguishing Crohn's disease from intestinal tuberculosis. Their incorporation into routine radiological reporting could support earlier and more accurate diagnosis, with the potential to reduce inappropriate treatment. However, these findings are preliminary and must be confirmed in prospective, multicenter cohorts with standardized methodology before they can guide clinical decisions. Body composition assessment represents a modest but practical addition to the diagnostic armamentarium for these challenging conditions.

Seeking diverse perspectives can lead to wiser decisions because no single person sees every angle of a problem. Each of us is shaped by our experiences, our education, and the communities we belong to, and these shape what we notice and what we overlook. When a decision is made by people who all think alike, blind spots tend to go unexamined. Diverse viewpoints challenge those assumptions and expose risks that a homogeneous group might miss. In this way, disagreement becomes a source of information rather than a threat. Consider a city planning a new park: engineers may focus on drainage, parents on safety, and elderly residents on accessible benches and shaded paths. Hearing from all of them produces a better design than any one group could create alone. Diversity also tests our reasoning. When we must explain our ideas to someone who sees things differently, we become more careful about our evidence and more precise in our arguments. Weak claims are revealed quickly, and strong ones are strengthened. Research on group decision-making supports this idea, showing that teams with varied backgrounds often generate a wider range of options and reach more accurate conclusions on complex tasks. Of course, diversity alone is not enough. A group whose members never truly listen to one another gains little from its differences. Wise decisions require openness, a willingness to change one's mind, and a shared commitment to finding the best answer rather than winning the argument. When these conditions are present, varied perspectives act like a collective lens that brings the full picture into focus. Ultimately, seeking out people who think differently is not a sign of uncertainty but of intellectual maturity. It reflects the humility to admit that we do not have all the answers. By welcoming diverse voices, we give ourselves the best chance to make choices that are fair, informed, and wise.

Should schools collect students' phones during the day to reduce distractions and cheating? This question has become more urgent as smartphones have become nearly universal among young people. Phones offer constant access to games, social media, and messaging, which can pull attention away from lessons. A student who glances at a notification during a math lesson may lose track of the material and struggle to catch up. Supporters of phone collection argue that removing the device is the simplest way to protect focus. Phones can also be used to cheat, with students looking up answers during tests or sharing information through messages. Collecting phones at the start of class could make assessments fairer and more reliable. Some schools that have adopted phone-free policies report calmer classrooms and more attentive students. However, a total ban has real drawbacks. Many students rely on phones for emergencies, for contacting parents, and for tools like calculators, dictionaries, and accessibility features. Collecting phones may also create tension and resentment, leading some students to see rules as punishment rather than guidance. A better approach may be a balanced policy that limits phone use during lessons and tests while still allowing access for learning and safety. Schools can teach responsible device habits instead of simply hiding the problem. Ultimately, phone collection can help in the short term, but lasting success depends on teaching students to manage their own attention.

Marcus had chosen the booth by the window because it felt private, and because the coffee shop was nearly empty on a Tuesday afternoon. Elena sat across from him with her hands folded, and he knew from the set of her jaw that she had rehearsed this in the car.

"I think we should be honest with each other," she said.

"I agree," Marcus said, and reached for his own cup to give his hands something to do.

She nodded slowly. "It's not that I don't care about you. I do. But I've been feeling like we want different things."

Across the room, the barista dropped a spoon, and the clatter made them both flinch.

Marcus looked down. Next to his coffee sat a bag of potato chips he had bought on the way in, and he had not even noticed opening it. He had been eating them steadily for ten minutes without tasting a single one.

Elena's eyes flicked to the bag, then back to his face. "Are you even listening to me?"

"Yes," he said, and crunched.

The sound was loud in the quiet room. Crunch. Crunch. He tried to swallow, but a chip caught in his throat and he coughed, scattering crumbs across the table.

"Sorry," he managed. "Go on."

Elena pressed her lips together. "I was saying that I need someone who can be present with me. Someone who isn't always distracted."

"I am present," Marcus said, reaching into the bag again. Crunch. The sound seemed to fill the booth, pressing against his ears. He hated it, and yet his hand kept moving on its own, the way it always did when his nerves climbed high enough to choke him.

He had never been able to sit still in moments that mattered. At his father's funeral he had eaten an entire sleeve of crackers in the back pew. At his job interview he had gone through a family-size bag of pretzels in the waiting room. He had always assumed Elena understood this about him, that she had forgiven it.

"Marcus, this is exactly what I mean," she said quietly. "You're doing it right now. You're not even looking at me."

He tried to look at her. He really did. But the bag crinkled loudly as he shifted in his seat, and he felt a fresh wave of heat climb his neck.

"I know," he said. "I know it's bad. I'm sorry."

"You always say that."

"Because I always mean it." Crunch. He winced at himself. "I just get nervous, and this is the only thing that calms me down, and I'm making it worse, and I can't seem to stop."

Elena was silent for a long moment. The espresso machine hissed behind the counter.

"Can I tell you something?" she finally asked. "I'm not angry about the chips. I'm sad, because I keep waiting for you to tell me something real, and every time it gets hard, you reach for the bag."

Marcus set the chips down. The silence that followed felt enormous, and for once he let it stay silent.

"You're right," he said. "I do that."

"I know." Her voice softened. "I wish you didn't have to hide behind it."

He nodded, and for the first time all afternoon, he had nothing to chew on. The room felt bigger without the noise.

"So what do we do?" he asked.

Elena looked at him for a long time before answering. "I think we finish this conversation without the bag," she said. "And then we decide whether we still want to be the people who have it."

He took a breath, and this time he didn't reach for anything.

Balancing academic standards with the demanding schedules of student-athletes is one of the central challenges facing school sports programs today. Athletes often spend long hours at practice, travel frequently for games, and face intense physical and mental demands, all while being expected to keep up with coursework. Without careful planning, these pressures can lead to exhaustion, declining grades, and even burnout that drives students away from both sports and school. Schools can address this by establishing clear academic eligibility requirements, such as minimum grade point averages, while also providing structured support like tutoring, study halls, and flexible deadlines during peak competition seasons. Coaches play an important role as well, since they can schedule practices thoughtfully, avoid excessive training loads, and encourage athletes to prioritize their education. Teachers can contribute by communicating with athletes about missed classes, offering make-up opportunities, and recognizing that travel commitments are not a lack of effort. Limiting the total hours students can spend on athletics each week, including during off-seasons, helps protect time for rest and independent study. Schools should also monitor the academic progress of athletes regularly so that struggling students receive help before problems become serious. At the same time, standards should not be lowered in ways that suggest athletes are less capable of meeting high expectations. Instead, the goal should be to create a system where academic and athletic success reinforce one another. Students who learn to manage time, set goals, and handle pressure in sports can carry those skills into their classrooms. Ultimately, a balanced approach respects both the commitment athletes make to their teams and their fundamental purpose as students. When schools invest in support, communication, and reasonable limits, they help ensure that student-athletes can thrive in every part of their lives.

Conservative lawmakers unveiled a proposal this week to offer discounted starter homes to first-time buyers under the age of 35, sparking a broad debate over housing affordability and the role of government in the property market. The plan, presented at a press conference on Tuesday, would allow qualifying young buyers to purchase newly built homes at a reduced price in exchange for modest resale restrictions designed to keep the homes within reach for future buyers. Supporters say the proposal addresses a problem that has grown steadily worse over the past decade, as home prices have outpaced wage growth in many metropolitan areas. Sponsors described the initiative as a way to help young families build equity and put down roots without relying on large inherited wealth. The proposal would be funded through a combination of tax credits for developers who agree to set aside a share of new units for the program and a limited allocation of public land. Lead sponsor Representative Daniel Whitfield said the goal was to empower young people rather than expand the welfare state. "This is about giving working people a fair shot at ownership," he told reporters. "It is not a handout, and it does not replace the market. It works with it." Critics, however, were quick to respond. Housing advocates argued that discounted homes would still be unaffordable for many low-income workers, and they urged lawmakers to focus instead on expanding social housing, which is rented at below-market rates and does not depend on individual purchasing power. Several opposition members called the proposal a subsidy for developers that would do little to increase the overall supply of homes. Economists were divided on the likely effects. Some noted that targeted discounts can help specific buyers but may push up prices for everyone else if the underlying shortage of homes is not addressed. Others pointed out that resale restrictions, while protecting affordability over time, can reduce the appeal of the program for buyers who want flexibility to sell or move. Housing researcher Dr. Miriam Osei said the debate often sets ownership against rental assistance, when in reality both approaches may be needed. "Homeownership is valuable, but so is stable, affordable rental housing," she said. "Policymakers should be asking which tool reaches which households most effectively." The proposal also raised questions about eligibility. Sponsors suggested income caps and proof of first-time buyer status, but details remain unsettled, and some lawmakers want stricter limits to ensure benefits reach those with the greatest need. Local government officials, who would administer many aspects of the program, said they needed clearer guidance on zoning, infrastructure costs, and enforcement before they could commit resources. Public reaction has been mixed. Surveys conducted by independent polling groups in recent months show strong support among younger adults for policies that make homeownership easier, but skepticism among older voters who worry about the impact on property values. Real estate groups have largely welcomed the idea of more construction, though some have expressed concern about price controls embedded in the resale rules. Labor advocates, meanwhile, have pressed for any final package to include protections for renters and investment in public housing. The bill is expected to be referred to committee next month, where hearings are scheduled to take place. Supporters hope to build bipartisan backing, though early signs suggest the measure will face significant amendments. Whether the plan ultimately becomes law may depend on how lawmakers weigh the competing goals of helping individual buyers, increasing overall supply, and protecting those who rely on rental and social housing. For now, the proposal has succeeded in one respect: it has pushed housing affordability back to the center of the national conversation. Analysts say voters will be watching closely to see whether any solution delivers meaningful relief to the young people who feel most locked out of the housing market.

Remembering People's Names: Practical Techniques That Work

Forgetting someone's name right after an introduction is one of the most common social frustrations. The good news is that name recall is a skill, not a fixed trait, and it improves with a few simple habits. The techniques below rely on three core ideas: paying real attention when the name is first given, repeating it in meaningful ways, and linking it to something you already know.

Why names are hard to remember

Names are arbitrary labels. Unlike a face with visible features or a profession that suggests a role, a name like "Dana" or "Hollis" carries no inherent meaning. Memory works best when new information connects to existing knowledge, and names offer few such hooks by default. Add the fact that introductions happen quickly, often in noisy settings, and it becomes clear why names slip away.

Technique one: give your full attention

Most name-forgetting begins before the name is even stored. If you are thinking about what you will say next, checking your phone, or scanning the room, the name never fully registers. Make a deliberate choice to focus on the other person during the introduction. Look at them, listen to the name, and notice how it sounds.

Technique two: say it out loud right away

Once you hear a name, use it immediately in conversation. A simple "It's nice to meet you, Priya" creates a second encoding of the name through speech. Speaking the name engages more memory pathways than hearing it alone. Use it once or twice more during the conversation, but keep it natural so it doesn't sound forced.

Technique three: ask for clarification

If a name is unusual, unfamiliar, or hard to hear, ask the person to repeat it or spell it. Most people are glad you care enough to get it right. You might say, "Could you say that again? I want to make sure I get it right." Asking shows respect and gives you a second chance to capture the name accurately.

Technique four: repeat the name in your head

After the conversation, or after you move to another group, quietly rehearse the name a few times. You might think it through once or twice as you walk away. This brief rehearsal strengthens the memory trace before it fades, a principle that memory researchers call rehearsal.

Technique five: use spaced repetition

A single mention is rarely enough to lock a name in long-term memory. Revisit the name at intervals: a few minutes later, at the end of the event, and again the next day if you are likely to see the person again. Each review takes little effort but substantially improves retention over time.

Technique six: create a mental association

Association is the most powerful tool for names. Link the name to something vivid. The link can be a word that sounds similar, an image, or a personal connection. For example, "Gary" might connect to a garden you picture, and "Carmen" might connect to a bright red car. The more unusual or emotionally engaging the image, the more memorable it tends to be.

Technique seven: use sound-alike associations

Many names are easier to remember when you convert them into a familiar word or phrase. "Baker" suggests bread, "Lowell" might suggest "low bell," and "Sheena" might suggest "shine." Visualize the connection so the person's face becomes linked to the image. The silliness of the association is often what makes it stick.

Technique eight: connect the name to the person's features

Pair the name with a visible or memorable trait. If someone has striking red glasses and the name is "Ross," picture the glasses with a ross-shaped image. Linking the name to a face feature creates a stronger memory than the name alone. This method is sometimes called the visual peg technique.

Technique nine: connect the name to the person's context

Remember where you met and what the person was doing. A name tied to a particular conference session, a shared hobby, or a work project becomes easier to retrieve. Context gives you a retrieval cue: when you think about the event, the name may surface.

Technique ten: write it down

After an event, jot down the names of people you met along with a brief note about each one. A phrase like "Marcus, runs a bakery, two kids" provides a reminder that makes future conversations smoother. Keep these notes private and use them to refresh your memory before you meet people again.

Technique eleven: review before you meet again

If you know you will see someone, spend a minute reviewing their name and the context of your last meeting. This preparation turns a possibly awkward moment into a warm reunion and reinforces the memory.

Common mistakes to avoid

Many people give up too quickly after forgetting a name. Others try to memorize everyone at once in a large crowd, which overloads working memory. It is more effective to focus on a few people deeply than on many people superficially. Another common error is avoiding the person entirely after forgetting their name, which can be avoided by simply asking again politely and honestly.

Putting the techniques together

A practical routine might look like this: focus fully as the name is spoken, repeat it aloud in the first sentence of your reply, form a quick visual or sound association, and review the name briefly after moving on. With practice, these steps become automatic and take only a few seconds.

Building the habit over time

Like any skill, name recall grows with consistent practice. Start by applying one or two techniques at each event rather than all eleven at once. As these become comfortable, add others. Over weeks and months, you will likely notice that names come to you more readily and that people feel more valued when you remember them.

A final thought

Remembering names is ultimately about showing that you care about the people you meet. Small efforts, such as listening carefully, using a name in conversation, and creating a memorable link, communicate respect. The techniques above are simple, and with regular use they can transform one of the most frustrating parts of social life into a source of confidence and connection.

Attending school in person offers students many advantages that learning from home often cannot match. The most important benefit is the direct interaction between students and teachers. When a teacher stands in front of a classroom, they can read facial expressions, notice confusion, and adjust their explanations on the spot. A student who is struggling can raise a hand, ask a quick question, and receive help before the misunderstanding grows. This immediate feedback is difficult to replicate through a screen, where delays, technical problems, and the hesitation to speak up can make learning less effective.

In-person school also gives students a structured environment that supports focus. Classrooms are designed for learning, with fewer distractions than a home where televisions, phones, siblings, and household chores compete for attention. The daily routine of traveling to school, moving between classes, and working alongside peers helps students develop discipline and time management. Many students find it easier to stay motivated when they are surrounded by classmates who are working toward the same goals.

Social development is perhaps the most valuable part of school attendance. Students learn how to collaborate, resolve disagreements, and communicate with people from different backgrounds. Friendships formed in the classroom, on the playground, and in extracurricular activities help young people build confidence and a sense of belonging. Teamwork in science labs, group projects, and sports teaches cooperation in ways that are hard to practice alone at home.

Access to resources is another strong argument for in-person learning. Schools provide libraries, laboratories, art studios, computers, and sports facilities that many families cannot afford to offer at home. Students who rely on school for meals, counseling, or a safe place to spend the day also benefit greatly from being physically present. For these students, school is not only a place of education but a source of stability.

Of course, remote learning has its own value, offering flexibility and reducing commute times. However, the benefits of in-person schooling, including direct teaching, social growth, structure, and access to resources, make it the stronger choice for most students. Schools that combine a supportive physical environment with thoughtful teaching give young people the best foundation for long-term success.

Mourners filled the church, many wearing green and white scarves as a mark of respect. Hymns were sung and tributes were paid to a man admired both on the pitch and off it. Speakers recalled his skill, his work ethic and the composure he brought to the biggest occasions. Former colleagues described the bond the Lisbon squad shared, a camaraderie that carried them to European Cup glory in 1967. Equally moving were the reflections on his inspirational resilience, particularly in the face of injury and adversity during and after his career. This manuscript investigates whether ensembles of neural networks can serve as a practical defense against adversarial attacks on image classifiers, a question of clear importance given the fragility of single models under small, carefully crafted perturbations. The authors frame the problem well, situating their work within the existing literature on adversarial training, input preprocessing, and certified defenses, and they correctly note that many proposed defenses have later been broken by adaptive attackers. The central hypothesis, that diversity among ensemble members reduces the transferability of adversarial examples, is intuitive and worth testing. The experimental design evaluates several ensemble configurations on standard image benchmarks, which is an appropriate starting point for the claims made. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more precise definition of what constitutes diversity, since the paper alternates between architectural differences, random initialization, and differences in training data without clearly separating their effects. The choice of attacks is a concern: the evaluation relies heavily on transfer-based and gradient-based attacks computed against a single surrogate model, which may overstate robustness because the attacker is not adapted to the ensemble as a whole. I would strongly encourage the authors to include adaptive white-box attacks that differentiate through the full ensemble, such as attacks on the averaged logits or the averaged loss, as well as attacks that optimize against each member jointly. The reported robustness numbers are presented without confidence intervals or multiple random seeds, making it difficult to judge whether the differences between configurations are meaningful. The clean accuracy cost of the ensemble is mentioned only briefly, yet this trade-off is central to any practical deployment decision and should be quantified alongside robustness. The computational overhead of training and running multiple networks is likewise under-discussed, and a comparison of inference cost against adversarial training would help readers assess practicality. The related work section is thorough in its coverage of defenses but treats ensemble-specific prior work, including earlier studies on ensemble adversarial training, too briefly, leaving the novelty of the contribution somewhat unclear. The discussion of why ensembles should help could be tightened, as the mechanism is asserted rather than supported by analysis of decision boundaries or gradient alignment across members. The figures are generally clear, though the robustness-versus-perturbation-budget plots would be more informative with error bars and a shared scale across datasets. The writing is generally readable, but several passages are repetitive and could be condensed to make room for the additional experiments requested. The authors should also state the exact hyperparameters, training schedules, and attack step sizes used, so that the results can be reproduced. A code release, or at minimum a detailed appendix, would substantially strengthen the paper's reproducibility. The limitations section acknowledges dataset scope but does not address the possibility that robustness gains may vanish under distribution shift or on larger-scale images. I would recommend that the authors clarify whether the defense is evaluated under the threat model where the attacker has full knowledge of the ensemble, since this is the setting that matters most for security claims. The conclusion that ensembles provide meaningful robustness is supported only partially by the current evidence, and the claim should be softened unless the adaptive attack results confirm it. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant question with a reasonable experimental framework, but the current evaluation is insufficient to support its strongest claims. I recommend a major revision, contingent on the inclusion of adaptive attacks, statistical reporting, and a clearer treatment of computational cost. With these changes, the work could make a useful contribution to the ongoing discussion about the practical limits of ensemble-based defenses.

Important life decisions rarely belong to the individual alone, yet they should not be surrendered entirely to others. Personal choice gives us ownership over our futures, since we must live with the consequences of what we decide. At the same time, the guidance of parents, teachers, and friends offers experience and perspective that we may lack when we are young or facing unfamiliar circumstances. The wisest approach is to weigh advice carefully, testing it against our own values, goals, and understanding of ourselves. In this balance between independence and counsel, we learn to make decisions that are both thoughtful and genuinely our own.

Whether schools should adopt a four-day or retain a five-day schedule is a question that weighs the convenience of a shorter week against the value of consistent instructional time. Supporters of the four-day week argue that it can reduce costs for districts, since fewer days mean lower spending on transportation, utilities, and staffing. Many rural districts that have adopted the model report that it helps them attract and retain teachers, who often appreciate the extra day for rest, planning, or personal obligations. Students may also benefit from longer school days that allow for more flexible scheduling of core subjects. Proponents further point out that a shorter week can reduce absenteeism for some students, since families may schedule appointments and errands on the off day rather than pulling children out of class. However, the long-term benefit to students depends heavily on what happens in the classroom. Research on academic outcomes from four-day weeks has produced mixed results, with some studies showing little change in test scores and others suggesting small declines, particularly in mathematics. Students who rely on school for meals, supervision, or access to services may be harmed by losing a weekday. Longer days can also lead to fatigue, especially for younger children, which may reduce the quality of learning in the final periods. A five-day schedule provides steady, predictable routines that many families and students depend on. Consistency in instruction helps students build habits, maintain momentum in difficult subjects, and receive regular support from teachers. For these reasons, schools considering a change should weigh financial savings against academic and social needs. Ultimately, the decision should prioritize students' learning and well-being over administrative convenience. A five-day schedule, though more costly, generally offers the stability and continuity that best serve children's long-term development.

Subject: Comparison of May 2000 and 2001 Temperature-Driven Heating and Cooling Demand

Hello,

I am writing to share a comparison of temperature-driven heating and cooling demand for May 2000 and May 2001. Because May is a shoulder month, demand for both heating and cooling is usually modest, so even small shifts in average temperature can change the balance noticeably.

Heating degree days (HDD) and cooling degree days (CDD) are the standard measures used to quantify this relationship. HDD accumulate when the daily mean temperature falls below a base temperature, typically 18 degrees Celsius (65 degrees Fahrenheit), while CDD accumulate when it rises above that base.

Based on the temperature records I reviewed, May 2000 was on the cooler side for much of the month, which resulted in a higher total of heating degree days than typical for the season. Cooling degree days were correspondingly low, meaning cooling systems were largely idle.

May 2001, by contrast, showed a warmer pattern, with a sustained run of above-base days in the second half of the month. This produced a noticeably higher cooling degree day total and a lower heating degree day total than in the previous year.

Taken together, the two years illustrate how a few degrees of difference in monthly mean temperature can shift energy demand from heating toward cooling. For utilities, this matters for load forecasting, since early-season cooling peaks can strain systems that are planned around more gradual seasonal transitions.

I would recommend verifying the exact degree day totals against official station data, such as from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, before using these figures in any formal analysis, as my summary is qualitative and should not be treated as precise measurements.

Please let me know if you would like a more detailed breakdown by week or by region.

Best regards,

The jungle smelled of rot and rain, and Private Daniel Harker had stopped counting the days. He had arrived in Vietnam certain of things: that his country was right, that the enemy was evil, that a good soldier did what he was told. Those certainties had been sanded away one patrol at a time.

The first crack came at a village near the river, where his squad had been ordered to clear a row of huts. An old woman stood in the doorway with her hands raised, and Daniel had not understood her words, only her trembling. Afterward his sergeant had shrugged and said the village was "Charlie country," and that was the end of it.

After that, the questions came. Who had decided the body count mattered more than the truth? Why did the officers in their clean fatigues never walk the paths they sent the men down? Daniel began writing letters home that he never mailed, because he could not find words that his mother would not burn.

He tried to talk to Carlos, a boy from Texas who laughed too loudly to hide his fear. Carlos only said, "You think too much, Harker. That's how you get killed out here." But the thinking did not stop, and it followed Daniel into sleep, where the old woman's face waited for him.

In the months that followed, he watched men grow hard in the way he had once admired. He watched a lieutenant laugh while a wounded prisoner begged for water. He watched the napalm drift across the hills and the smoke rise over villages that would never appear on any map. Each time he told himself the next day would make sense of it, and each time it did not.

Daniel's hands began to shake in the mornings. He stopped eating the rations and gave his cigarettes away. When the monsoon came, he sat in the mud for hours without speaking, staring at the gray sky as if it might offer an answer.

On a quiet afternoon, the company was resting at the edge of a rice paddy. Daniel sat apart from the others, his rifle across his knees, and he thought about the letter he had finally written that morning. It said only that he was sorry, and that he did not know how to be the man they had sent him to be.

Carlos found him there and sat down beside him, offering a canteen. "You all right, man?" he asked. Daniel took the canteen and nodded, but he could not look up. He could not explain that the world had become a place where nothing he believed in held its shape anymore.

Later, when the others had moved on toward the perimeter, the rain began again, soft and steady. Daniel stood alone in the paddy water, feeling the cold seep through his boots. He thought of his mother's kitchen, of the old woman's raised hands, of all the things he could no longer undo.

The shot was small against the sound of the rain. The men who heard it did not at first understand what they had heard, and when they did, they found Daniel Harker lying face up in the shallow water, his eyes open toward a sky that offered no answer at all. In his shirt pocket they found the unsent letter, its ink blurred by rain, the single line still legible: I am sorry, and I do not know how to stop seeing it.

Madagascar's Wildlife Faces Mounting Threats as Survival Grows Uncertain

Madagascar, the island nation off the southeastern coast of Africa, is home to an extraordinary concentration of species found nowhere else on Earth. Scientists estimate that a large share of its plants and animals are endemic, meaning they exist only on the island. Yet this biological treasure is under growing pressure, and conservationists warn that many of its most iconic animals may not survive the coming decades without urgent action.

Habitat loss stands at the center of the crisis. Forests across the island have been cleared at a steady pace for decades, driven largely by agricultural expansion, charcoal production, and the search for new farmland. Slash-and-burn practices, known locally as tavy, have transformed large areas of woodland into degraded landscapes that can no longer support the diverse communities that once thrived there. Satellite monitoring has documented significant forest loss in recent years, with the eastern rainforests and western dry forests among the hardest hit.

The fragmentation of forests compounds the problem. When large, continuous woodlands are broken into isolated patches, animals find it harder to find food, mates, and safe routes between territories. Many lemur species, which depend on specific trees and stable canopy cover, are especially vulnerable to this kind of disruption. Some populations have become so small and scattered that their long-term genetic health is in doubt.

Poaching adds a further layer of danger. Lemurs, tortoises, reptiles, and birds are taken from the wild both for local consumption and for the illegal international pet trade. Radiated tortoises, prized for their distinctive shells, have been removed from the wild in alarming numbers, and some reptile species have been pushed toward collapse by collectors. Enforcement is difficult across a country with vast, remote terrain and limited resources for park rangers and wildlife officials.

The illegal trade in rosewood and other precious timber has also contributed to forest destruction. Valuable hardwoods have been harvested in protected areas and smuggled abroad, often with the involvement of organized networks. This activity not only removes trees that form the backbone of forest ecosystems but also brings armed conflict and corruption into areas that were once quiet. Conservation groups have called for stronger controls on timber export and greater transparency in the supply chain.

Bushmeat hunting remains a concern in several regions. Some lemur species, which are culturally sensitive for certain communities, are hunted for food, while others are taken in the course of hunting for other animals. Hunters often use snares and traps that catch non-target species, causing injury and death across a wide range of wildlife. Because these traps are cheap and easy to set, they can cover large areas and are difficult to detect.

Tensions between conservation efforts and local communities add complexity to the situation. Many of the people living near forests are among the poorest in the world, and their daily survival often depends on the resources those forests provide. When protected areas are established without consultation or without alternative livelihoods, residents may feel excluded or penalized. This can erode support for conservation and sometimes pushes communities toward activities that harm wildlife.

Researchers and community leaders increasingly argue that conservation must work for people as well as for animals. Programs that involve villagers in managing forests, share revenue from ecotourism, and support sustainable farming and beekeeping have shown promise in some areas. Such approaches aim to give local residents a direct stake in protecting their natural surroundings rather than viewing them as obstacles to development.

Climate change presents another threat that is expected to intensify over time. Madagascar is already experiencing more frequent droughts in the south and intense cyclones along its coasts. Shifts in rainfall and temperature could alter the timing of flowering and fruiting, affecting the food supplies that many species depend on. Species with narrow ranges and specialized diets may have little ability to move to more suitable habitat.

Ecotourism offers both opportunity and risk. Visitors come to see lemurs, chameleons, and unique landscapes such as the Tsingy limestone formations, and tourism revenue can fund protected area management. However, poorly managed tourism can disturb wildlife, spread disease, and bring infrastructure that accelerates habitat loss. Balancing visitor access with the needs of fragile ecosystems remains a constant challenge for park managers.

Disease is an emerging concern as well. Wildlife populations that are already stressed may be more susceptible to infections, and close contact between humans, livestock, and wild animals creates opportunities for pathogens to spread. Monitoring programs have been expanding, but resources for veterinary care and disease surveillance remain limited across much of the country.

Political instability has complicated conservation work in the past. Changes in government and periods of unrest have sometimes disrupted funding, slowed enforcement, and weakened the institutions responsible for protected areas. Conservation organizations emphasize that long-term commitment, transparent governance, and stable financing are essential if gains in one period are not to be lost in the next.

International partnerships play a significant role in supporting Madagascar's conservation efforts. Foreign governments, nonprofit organizations, and research institutions have contributed funding, technical expertise, and scientific data. These collaborations have helped expand protected areas and train a new generation of Malagasy conservationists. Many observers stress, however, that local leadership and ownership must remain central to any lasting solution.

Education and awareness are also key. Schools and community groups have worked to teach children about the value of native species and the importance of forests for clean water, soil protection, and food security. Some of these initiatives have produced local champions who advocate for wildlife protection within their own villages and who report illegal activity to authorities.

Scientists continue to discover new species in Madagascar, even as others slip toward extinction. This ongoing discovery underscores how much remains unknown about the island's biodiversity. Researchers warn that species may disappear before they are formally described, meaning that some losses could go unrecorded entirely.

The status of several lemur species has been reassessed in recent years, and many are now listed as critically endangered or endangered by international conservation bodies. Among them are species that have lost significant portions of their habitat within living memory. Experts say these assessments serve as an urgent warning to policymakers and the public alike.

Protected areas cover a meaningful portion of Madagascar's land, but many exist largely on paper, lacking adequate staff, equipment, and enforcement. Strengthening management of existing parks is often seen as a more immediate priority than creating new ones. Some conservationists argue that better governance of current reserves could deliver more benefit than expanding boundaries that cannot be policed.

Restoration projects have attempted to reforest degraded land using native trees. These efforts can be expensive and slow, and success depends on careful species selection, community participation, and protection from further clearing. Where restoration has been carried out thoughtfully, it has begun to reconnect fragmented habitats and provide shelter for returning wildlife.

Agricultural practices are being examined closely. Traditional methods that rely on clearing forest for short-term crops are increasingly recognized as unsustainable, both ecologically and economically. Agroforestry, in which trees are integrated with crops, offers a way to produce food while preserving some of the ecological functions of forest. Adoption, however, requires training, seedlings, and assurance that farmers will benefit in the near term.

Land tenure is another factor. When people are unsure who controls a particular piece of land, they have little incentive to invest in its long-term health. Clarifying land rights and recognizing customary claims may encourage more responsible stewardship. Some pilot programs have granted communities formal management authority over forest areas, with encouraging early results.

Urban growth places additional demand on natural resources. As people migrate from rural areas to cities such as Antananarivo, the need for fuelwood, building materials, and food increases. Charcoal, in particular, remains a major source of household energy, and its production drives forest degradation near urban centers. Cleaner and more affordable energy alternatives are seen as essential to reducing this pressure.

Funding gaps remain a persistent obstacle. Conservation requires sustained investment in patrols, research, community programs, and infrastructure, yet budgets are frequently inadequate. Innovative financing mechanisms, including payments for ecosystem services and carbon finance, have been explored as ways to generate income that supports forest protection.

Monitoring technology is improving the ability to track change. Satellite imagery, camera traps, acoustic sensors, and mobile reporting tools help managers detect illegal logging, count animal populations, and respond more quickly to threats. Yet technology alone cannot replace trained staff and community trust, which remain the foundation of effective conservation.

Local knowledge is increasingly valued as an asset. Many Malagasy communities possess detailed understanding of their forests, including seasonal patterns, medicinal plants, and the behavior of particular species. Integrating this knowledge with scientific research can improve management decisions and strengthen the sense of shared responsibility.

Gender and social equity also feature in discussions about conservation. Women often carry heavy responsibilities for household resources, and their participation in decision-making can shape outcomes for both people and forests. Programs that include women in planning and benefit-sharing have reported stronger engagement and more stable results.

Some species have already benefited from focused efforts. Targeted protection of nesting sites, captive breeding programs for critically endangered animals, and reintroduction projects have shown that recovery is possible when action is timely and well coordinated. These successes provide hope but also highlight how much work remains.

Policy reform has been debated in parliament and among civil society groups. Proposals include stricter penalties for wildlife crimes, improved coordination between agencies, and greater public access to environmental information. Advocates argue that clear laws, consistently enforced, are necessary to deter exploitation and reassure communities that rules apply equally.

Regional cooperation may also matter. Migratory birds, marine species, and some wildlife move across borders, and illegal trade networks often extend beyond national boundaries. Collaboration with neighboring countries and international bodies can help address these shared challenges and close gaps that criminals might exploit.

The private sector has a role to play. Companies involved in agriculture, mining, and timber must meet environmental standards and avoid operations that destroy critical habitat. Certification schemes and corporate responsibility commitments can encourage better practices, though enforcement and transparency are needed to ensure that pledges translate into real change.

Mining deserves particular attention. Extraction of minerals and gemstones can open remote forests to access, bringing settlement, hunting, and clearing in their wake. Environmental impact assessments and tighter oversight are often recommended to limit these secondary effects.

Public attention can influence outcomes. Documentaries, media coverage, and social media campaigns have raised awareness of Madagascar's wildlife both at home and abroad. Greater visibility can attract support and pressure decision-makers, though conservationists caution that attention must be sustained rather than fleeting.

Ultimately, the future of Madagascar's wildlife depends on a combination of factors: protecting remaining habitat, reducing illegal exploitation, addressing poverty and land pressures, adapting to climate change, and building lasting partnerships between communities, government, and outside supporters. No single intervention will be enough on its own.

Many experts remain cautiously hopeful. They point to dedicated scientists, rangers, community leaders, and citizens who are working to safeguard their country's natural heritage despite limited resources. Whether their efforts can keep pace with the scale of the threats remains an open question, but the decisions made in the coming years will likely determine how many of Madagascar's remarkable species survive for future generations.

The manuscript proposes using optical-flow prediction errors as intrinsic rewards to drive exploration in reinforcement learning agents, targeting environments where extrinsic reward is sparse or deceptive. The central idea is appealing because motion-based novelty signals may capture changes in the agent's visual environment that pixel-level or count-based curiosity bonuses miss. The authors motivate the work clearly, situating it within the curiosity-driven exploration literature, including intrinsic curiosity modules and random network distillation. The introduction is well organized and the research question is stated precisely. However, the related work section is somewhat uneven, giving extensive attention to prediction-based curiosity while treating count-based and state-entropy methods only briefly. A more balanced comparison would strengthen the positioning of the contribution. The method section describes a pipeline in which a pretrained or jointly trained optical-flow estimator produces per-frame flow fields, and the magnitude of the prediction error between predicted and observed flow serves as the intrinsic reward. The formulation is easy to follow, and the authors provide a helpful diagram of the data flow. Nonetheless, several implementation details are underspecified, including the architecture of the flow predictor, the normalization of intrinsic rewards, and the relative weighting between intrinsic and extrinsic terms. Without these, reproducing the results would be difficult. I would ask the authors to report the hyperparameter schedule and the decay strategy for the intrinsic coefficient. The theoretical discussion is brief and mostly informal. The paper would benefit from a clearer argument for why flow-prediction error should correlate with useful exploration rather than with stochastic visual noise. The authors acknowledge the noisy-TV problem, which is commendable, but their proposed mitigation is only evaluated in one environment. Extending that analysis to environments with stochastic distractors would substantially increase confidence in the claim. The experimental evaluation covers several Atari and procedurally generated benchmarks, and the reported gains over the baselines are consistent across most of them. Still, the improvements in some games are modest and fall within the apparent seed-to-seed variance shown in the appendix. I recommend that the authors report confidence intervals computed over a larger number of seeds, following recent recommendations for reliable reporting in deep reinforcement learning. The ablation study is a strength, as it separates the contribution of the flow-error signal from that of the auxiliary network capacity. However, the ablation that replaces optical flow with a simple frame-difference baseline is missing, and its inclusion would clarify whether the learned flow model is necessary. Computational cost is another concern, since running a flow estimator alongside the policy substantially increases wall-clock time per environment step. The paper reports sample efficiency but says little about compute efficiency, which practitioners will care about. A table comparing training time and memory use against the main baselines would be valuable. The discussion of limitations is present but brief, and it should more explicitly address when the method is likely to fail, such as in environments with little visual motion or with camera movement that confounds flow. Figures are generally clear, though the learning-curve plots would be more readable with consistent color mapping across methods and with shaded variance regions explained in the caption. The qualitative visualizations of flow fields are compelling and help readers understand what the agent finds novel, although the selection of frames may reflect favorable examples. Including failure cases alongside the highlighted successes would give a more honest picture. The writing is generally clear, with occasional redundancy in the results section that could be trimmed. Several equations use notation that is introduced inconsistently, and a notation table would help readers. The reference list is comprehensive for the curiosity literature but omits some recent work on optical-flow-based representation learning that is directly relevant. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful question and presents a reasonable, interesting approach with promising initial results. Its main weaknesses lie in the strength of the empirical claims, the completeness of implementation details, and the depth of the theoretical justification. I recommend a major revision. With additional seeds, the missing ablations, fuller implementation details, and a more candid treatment of limitations, the work could make a useful contribution to the exploration literature. I am willing to review a revised version.

A controversial traditional leader from the Eastern Cape has joined the Democratic Alliance, South Africa's main opposition party, a move that has drawn sharp reactions from political rivals and members of his own royal family. The king, whose reign has been marked by legal disputes and public clashes over succession and authority, announced his decision at a press briefing in the region this week. Party officials welcomed the addition, saying the king brings a voice from rural communities that the party has sought to reach more effectively. Supporters of the move argue that traditional leaders have a legitimate role in political life and that their participation can broaden the debate on land, governance and development. Critics, however, questioned whether the step compromises the neutrality expected of traditional leaders under South African law. Several relatives within the royal household issued a statement distancing themselves from the decision, describing it as a unilateral act that does not reflect the wishes of the wider family. They also raised concerns about ongoing disputes over the royal succession, which have previously led to court challenges and tense standoffs in the community. Analysts say the timing is significant, with the country approaching future elections and opposition parties competing for support in traditionally governing strongholds. Some observers see the alliance as a strategic gain for the DA, which has been working to expand its appeal beyond its urban base. Others caution that the impact on voter behaviour may be limited, as traditional leadership structures in the Eastern Cape are complex and often divided along family and regional lines. The king's office has not yet said whether he will take on a formal party role or stand as a candidate. Representatives of the governing African National Congress declined to comment in detail but described the matter as a concern for the traditional leaders' council. Legal experts noted that the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act governs the conduct of traditional leaders, though its application to party membership remains a subject of debate. Community members in the surrounding villages expressed mixed views, with some hopeful about new political representation and others worried about division. Local civic groups called for calm and urged both the king and his family to resolve their disagreements through established channels. The DA has said it will respect the legal boundaries that apply to traditional leaders while engaging with rural constituencies. Political commentators expect the story to continue developing as the royal household, government officials and the party respond in the coming weeks. For now, the decision has added a new layer of tension to an already complicated relationship between traditional authority and electoral politics in the region.
