Should teenagers be required to be home by 10 p.m. on school nights? Supporters of a curfew argue that it protects young people from the dangers of late-night life and helps them get the sleep they need. Opponents counter that such rules treat responsible teens like children and ignore individual differences. Weighing these views carefully shows that a school-night curfew can be a reasonable policy, but only when it is flexible and paired with trust.

The most persuasive argument for a curfew is safety. Late-night hours are linked to higher rates of car accidents, impaired driving, and risky behavior among teenagers, many of whom have less driving experience and judgment than adults. A set hour for coming home gives parents a clear expectation and reduces the chance that a teen ends up in a dangerous situation after dark. For families who struggle to keep track of their children's whereabouts, a curfew can provide a helpful structure.

Sleep is an equally important reason. Teenagers need roughly eight to ten hours of sleep each night, yet many fall well short because their biological clocks shift later during adolescence. A 10 p.m. curfew encourages a bedtime that allows students to rest before early school start times. Better sleep is linked to stronger concentration, improved mood, and fewer health problems, so a curfew can support academic performance as well as physical well-being.

Critics raise fair concerns, however. A rigid rule can feel unfair to a seventeen-year-old with a steady record, a part-time job, or a family obligation that ends late. Strict limits may also push teens toward secretive behavior rather than honest communication with their parents. Good decision-making develops through practice, and a curfew that never adjusts may leave young people unprepared for independence when they turn eighteen.

The strongest approach, then, is a curfew that is reasonable and responsive. Parents could set a 10 p.m. weeknight limit for younger teens while allowing older, trusted students to earn later hours through responsible behavior and open communication. Exceptions for school events, jobs, or emergencies would keep the rule practical. Such a system protects safety and sleep without sacrificing the trust that helps teenagers grow into capable adults.

Students should be allowed to use cell phones at school because these devices have become valuable tools for learning and safety. Phones give students quick access to dictionaries, research databases, translation apps, and educational videos that can deepen their understanding of a lesson. They also let students stay in touch with parents during emergencies, which can feel especially important in a world where school safety is a serious concern. Many teachers already use digital platforms for assignments, quizzes, and class communication, so phones can help students keep up with these tools. Trusting students with phones also teaches responsibility, since they must learn to manage their time and attention in a setting where self-control matters. Schools can set clear rules, such as keeping phones silent during class and banning their use during tests, to reduce distractions while still benefiting from technology. Ultimately, allowing phones with reasonable limits prepares students for a digital society better than banning them entirely.

South Korea's political landscape remains shaped by the removal of former President Park Geun-hye, whose impeachment and ouster in 2017 set off a chain of consequences that continue to influence the country's leadership, governance, economy, and diplomacy. The Constitutional Court upheld her impeachment in March 2017, making her the first democratically elected South Korean president to be removed from office. The decision followed months of mass protests in Seoul and other cities, with hundreds of thousands of citizens calling for her resignation over a scandal involving her close confidante, Choi Soon-sil. Choi was found to have exerted improper influence over government affairs and to have pressured large conglomerates to contribute funds to foundations she controlled. The revelations struck at public trust in institutions and gave new momentum to demands for political accountability. Park was later convicted of bribery, abuse of power, and related charges, and she received a lengthy prison sentence. In 2021 she was granted a presidential pardon, a decision that sparked fresh debate about justice, fairness, and the role of political considerations in the country's legal system. Her case also exposed deep divisions between conservative and progressive camps that have long defined South Korean politics. Her successor, Moon Jae-in, was elected in May 2017 on a platform promising reform, transparency, and a more equitable distribution of economic opportunity. His administration pursued anti-corruption measures and sought to curb the power of the chaebol, the family-controlled conglomerates that dominate the economy. Critics argued, however, that the government struggled to deliver on some of its promises, particularly regarding real estate prices and employment for young people. The political pendulum swung again in 2022, when Yoon Suk-yeol of the conservative People Power Party won a narrow victory over the progressive Democratic Party candidate. Yoon campaigned on a platform of prosecutorial reform and tougher stances toward North Korea, and his election was widely seen as a reaction to the policies of the previous administration. Yoon's tenure has also been marked by intense partisan conflict, particularly with an opposition-controlled National Assembly that has repeatedly clashed with the executive branch over budgets, legislation, and appointments. The Park scandal has also reshaped how corruption is perceived and prosecuted in South Korea. Civic groups, the media, and younger voters have grown more vocal in demanding transparency from both public officials and private business leaders. Several prominent chaebol executives have faced trials and convictions for bribery and embezzlement, and the country has seen continued debate over whether the justice system treats powerful figures more leniently than ordinary citizens. Reform advocates argue that structural changes, including stronger independent oversight bodies and clearer rules on political funding, remain necessary to prevent a repeat of the abuses that marked the Park era. On the economic front, the political turmoil of 2016 and 2017 coincided with slowing growth, rising household debt, and concerns about the sustainability of the export-driven model that has powered the economy for decades. Investors watched closely as uncertainty over the presidency created questions about policy continuity, particularly for large corporations with global operations. Subsequent governments have grappled with demographic challenges, including a rapidly aging population and a record-low birth rate, which weigh on long-term growth prospects. Efforts to diversify the economy into areas such as semiconductors, batteries, and digital services have gained urgency as competition from China and other regional rivals intensifies. Foreign relations have also been affected by domestic politics. Park's government had pursued a hardline stance toward North Korea, including the suspension of the Kaesong Industrial Complex in 2016, and it moved to deploy the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system, a decision that strained ties with China. Her removal prompted a shift in tone under Moon, who pursued engagement with Pyongyang and sought to ease tensions, although those efforts produced limited concrete results. Yoon's government has returned to a firmer posture, strengthening security cooperation with the United States and Japan and emphasizing deterrence against North Korean nuclear and missile threats. Relations with Japan, historically fraught over wartime history, have seen both cooperation and renewed friction as each administration has adopted different approaches. Looking ahead, analysts say the legacy of Park's removal will continue to shape South Korean politics for years to come. The episode demonstrated the strength of civic activism and the capacity of institutions to hold leaders accountable, but it also revealed the depth of polarization and the enduring challenges of building public trust. Whether future leaders can address corruption, revitalize the economy, and navigate a complex regional security environment will depend in part on their willingness to learn from a period that transformed the country's political culture.

Researchers in Scotland have launched a new tracking programme to study harbour seal populations, which have shown worrying declines in several coastal regions over the past two decades. The project, led by marine biologists working along the Moray Firth and the Northern Isles, is fitting seals with lightweight satellite tags that record their movements, diving patterns, and time spent hauled out on land. Scientists hope the data will reveal where the animals feed, which waters they rely on for breeding and moulting, and how they respond to changes in their environment. Harbour seals are a protected species in Scotland, and their numbers have been affected by factors including disease outbreaks, pollution, entanglement in fishing gear, and disturbance from boats and tourism. Early results suggest that some seals travel considerable distances, sometimes covering hundreds of kilometres between feeding grounds and resting sites. Conservation officials say this information is essential for designing protected areas that cover the places seals truly use, rather than relying on broader assumptions. Local fishing communities have been invited to take part in the project by reporting sightings and helping to recover tags that are shed or washed ashore. Researchers emphasise that the work is non-invasive, with tagging carried out by trained teams using methods approved under strict animal welfare guidelines. The programme is expected to run for three years, with findings used to inform management plans and future monitoring efforts across the region. Conservationists say that a clearer picture of seal movements could help reverse the decline and ensure these animals remain a fixture of Scotland's coastline.

Collaboration offers many advantages in school, at work, and in everyday life. When students work together, they can share ideas and approach problems from different angles, which often leads to stronger solutions than any one person could produce alone. Group projects also help students develop communication skills, since they must explain their thinking, listen to others, and negotiate roles. In the workplace, teams bring together people with varied expertise, allowing companies to complete complex tasks that would be impossible for a single employee. Collaboration also encourages accountability, because each member's contribution matters and the group succeeds or struggles together. Working with others can reduce individual stress, as tasks are divided and people can rely on one another for support and encouragement. Beyond formal settings, everyday cooperation, such as neighbors helping one another or families sharing household responsibilities, builds trust and strengthens community bonds. Collaboration additionally fosters empathy, since working closely with people from different backgrounds helps us understand their perspectives. It also promotes creativity, as brainstorming with others sparks new ideas that might never arise in isolation. Finally, the habit of collaborating prepares people for a world that increasingly values teamwork, adaptability, and the ability to build meaningful relationships. For these reasons, learning to work well with others is one of the most valuable skills a person can develop.

Stepping outside of familiar skills can feel uncomfortable at first, but it is one of the most reliable ways to build confidence, knowledge, and personal growth. Most people spend much of their time doing what they already know how to do well. This comfort is understandable, since mastery feels good and mistakes feel costly. Yet a life lived entirely within known territory tends to stop expanding, and the abilities we once prided ourselves on can begin to feel like the limits of who we are.

Confidence is one of the first things that grows when we try something new. A person who has never cooked a meal from scratch may feel nervous about entering a kitchen, but after successfully preparing a simple dish, that person has evidence of their own capability. Each small success becomes a reference point for the next challenge. Over time, these experiences teach us that we are not fixed in our abilities and that effort can produce real results.

Knowledge expands in a similar way. When we learn a skill outside our usual domain, we discover connections we would never have noticed otherwise. A writer who learns basic programming may begin to think about structure and logic in new ways, and a scientist who takes up painting may see color and form more carefully. These crossovers often make us better at our original pursuits, because they give us new tools and new perspectives on familiar problems.

Stepping beyond familiar skills also forces us to face the experience of being a beginner. This can be humbling, and that humility has value. Beginners ask questions, accept correction, and pay close attention, qualities that are sometimes harder to practice once we consider ourselves experts. Being willing to look foolish for a while is a skill in its own right, and it helps us stay curious throughout life.

Personal growth often comes from the discomfort itself. When we struggle with an unfamiliar task, we learn to manage frustration, to break problems into smaller steps, and to ask for help. These habits carry over into other areas, from school and work to friendships and family life. A person who has learned to keep going through a difficult new skill is better prepared to handle other setbacks with patience.

There are practical ways to begin. A student might join a club outside their academic interests, take an elective in an unfamiliar subject, or volunteer for a project that requires new abilities. Even small changes, such as reading a book from a different genre or learning a few phrases in a new language, can open doors. The goal is not to abandon what we are good at but to add to it, creating a broader and more flexible set of skills.

Of course, stepping outside our comfort zone does not mean taking reckless risks. It means choosing challenges that stretch us while still being achievable with effort and support. Good teachers, mentors, and friends can help us find that balance. Celebrating progress, however modest, keeps motivation alive and reminds us that growth is gradual.

In the end, the decision to try something new is a decision about the kind of person we want to become. Each unfamiliar skill we take on adds a layer of confidence, a bit of knowledge, and a new way of seeing the world. The process is rarely smooth, but the rewards accumulate over time. By stepping beyond what we already know, we give ourselves the chance to discover what else we are capable of becoming.

The manuscript investigates whether reinforcement learning can be used to decide the timing of adversarial attacks against agents that play Atari games. The central idea, learning when to attack rather than attacking at every step, is a sensible and practically motivated framing, since attack budgets are often limited in real deployments. The authors position their work within the broader literature on adversarial perturbations for deep reinforcement learning policies, and the related work section is generally well organized. However, the introduction would benefit from a clearer statement of the threat model, including what the attacker can observe, what perturbations are permitted, and how the budget is defined. The paper's contribution is described as a timing policy, yet the abstract sometimes reads as though the authors are proposing a new perturbation method, and this ambiguity should be resolved. The methodology section describes a learned attack scheduler trained with a policy gradient approach, which is appropriate for the sequential decision structure of the problem. Nevertheless, the reward formulation for the attacker is only partially specified, and it is unclear whether the reward penalizes unnecessary attacks or only rewards degradation of the victim's score. Clarifying this would make the approach reproducible. The choice of victim agents is a strength, as the authors evaluate against several pretrained Atari agents with differing architectures. Still, all victims appear to come from a single training pipeline, which limits how far the conclusions generalize. The experiments compare the learned timing policy against random attack timing and against always-on attacks. These baselines are reasonable, but the authors should also include a heuristic baseline, such as attacking when the victim's value estimate drops, to show whether learning adds value beyond simple rules. The results table reports mean episode return with standard deviations over only three seeds, which is too few to support the claimed improvements with confidence. The authors should report confidence intervals or run significance tests across a larger number of seeds. The ablation on the attack budget is informative and shows that the learned policy is most advantageous when budgets are tight, which is a useful practical finding. The figure illustrating attack timing across an episode is helpful, though the axis labels are small and the caption does not explain the color coding. The discussion of transferability, namely whether a timing policy learned against one victim works against another, is promising but underdeveloped and currently rests on a single cross-victim experiment. The paper also does not analyze the computational cost of training the attacker relative to the baselines, which matters for judging practicality. Regarding ethics, the authors briefly note the dual-use nature of the work but do not discuss defenses in any depth, and a short section on mitigations would strengthen the paper considerably. The writing is generally clear, although several sentences in the methods section are long and could be split for readability. Some notation is introduced inconsistently, with the state and observation symbols used interchangeably, which may confuse readers unfamiliar with partially observable settings. The limitations section is brief and should address the single-game focus, the small number of seeds, and the restricted victim pool. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant question with a reasonable approach and a useful practical framing. The main concerns are the underspecified threat model and reward, the thin statistical evidence, and the missing heuristic baseline. I recommend a major revision addressing these points before the work can be considered for acceptance.

The Face on Mars, a mesa in the Cydonia region photographed by NASA's Viking 1 orbiter in 1976, has fascinated the public for decades, with many people suggesting it was carved by an ancient alien civilization. However, a careful examination of the evidence shows that the Face is a natural landform shaped by ordinary geological processes. When the image was first released, its resolution was low, and the shadows created by the morning sun gave the rock formation an eye-like and mouth-like appearance. Human visual systems are strongly tuned to detect faces, a tendency known as pareidolia, which explains why we perceive facial features in clouds, rock outcrops, and electrical outlets. In 1998, the Mars Global Surveyor captured the same area again under different lighting conditions, and the higher-resolution image showed no face at all, only an irregular hill with eroded slopes. Scientists studying these images found that the apparent features disappeared when the angle of sunlight changed, confirming that shadows were responsible for the illusion. The surrounding terrain of Cydonia contains many similar mesas and buttes that were formed by wind erosion over millions of years. Mars has a thin atmosphere and frequent dust storms, which have been powerful enough to sculpt rock formations into irregular shapes. Geologists recognize that the Face belongs to a family of mesas that form when layered sedimentary rock is eroded, leaving behind resistant caprock on top of softer material below. There is no evidence of the regular geometric patterns, tool marks, or construction materials that would be expected from an artificial structure. Instead, the Face has the uneven surfaces and gradual slopes typical of natural erosion. The idea of an ancient Martian civilization also faces a practical problem, since no other artifacts, roads, or structures have ever been found in the region. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and a single image taken under misleading lighting does not meet that standard. The growth of the Face myth in popular culture, including books and films, has reinforced public belief despite the scientific explanation. Some enthusiasts continue to argue for an artificial origin, pointing to the symmetry of the features, yet symmetry alone is common in natural formations as well. The discovery of the Face is therefore best understood as a case study in how human perception can misread ambiguous images. Better imaging technology allowed scientists to resolve the mystery, demonstrating the value of careful observation and repeated measurement. Mars continues to reveal evidence of past water and geological activity, which is a far more compelling story than a hidden monument. The truth about the Face is that it reflects the planet's natural history, shaped by wind, dust, and time. Understanding this landform helps students appreciate both the power of science to correct false impressions and the wonder of Mars itself.

This manuscript proposes a neural decision tree architecture for regression that combines learned target discretization with probabilistic routing of inputs through the tree. The motivation is sound, since classical regression trees produce piecewise constant predictions that can be coarse, while many neural approaches sacrifice the interpretability that makes trees attractive. The authors frame the contribution clearly in the introduction and position it reasonably within the literature on differentiable decision trees and soft routing. The central idea, treating the continuous target as something to be partitioned into learned bins rather than fitted directly, is an interesting departure from standard split-based regression. The paper is generally readable, and the overall structure follows a conventional and appropriate progression from background to method to experiments. However, several aspects of the exposition need strengthening before the work can be considered ready for publication. The description of the discretization module is the weakest part of the methods section, as the mapping from continuous targets to discrete bins is not specified precisely enough for a reader to reimplement it. It is unclear whether the bin boundaries are fixed after initialization, learned end to end, or re-estimated during training, and this distinction materially affects both behavior and reproducibility. The probabilistic routing mechanism is described more thoroughly, including the sigmoid gating at each internal node, but the authors should clarify how routing probabilities are normalized across leaves. The loss function combines a reconstruction-style term with a regularization term whose weighting is set by hand, and the paper offers no sensitivity analysis showing how results depend on this choice. The experimental section evaluates the method on a collection of public regression benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the selection of datasets is narrow in size and domain. Several of the datasets are small, and with limited sample sizes the reported improvements may fall within the variance across random seeds. The authors report means without standard deviations or confidence intervals, and this should be corrected throughout the results tables. The baselines are a reasonable set, including gradient boosted trees, a standard regression tree, and a multilayer perceptron, but the comparison omits recent differentiable tree ensembles that address the same problem. Including such methods would give a clearer picture of where the proposed approach stands. Training time and inference cost are mentioned only briefly, yet they are important for a method whose appeal partly rests on efficiency and interpretability. The ablation study removes the discretization module and the probabilistic routing separately, which is a sensible design, but the paper does not isolate the effect of the number of bins, which seems a central hyperparameter. The interpretability claims are the most attractive part of the work, but they are supported only by a single illustrative tree visualization on one dataset. A more systematic analysis, such as examining whether learned bins correspond to meaningful target ranges or whether routing decisions are stable across runs, would substantiate these claims. The related work section is thorough in its coverage of neural trees but somewhat thin on classical probabilistic and soft regression tree models, which have a long history and are directly relevant. The theoretical discussion is limited, and a short analysis of the approximation or consistency properties of the model would meaningfully strengthen the contribution. The notation is mostly consistent, although the symbol used for the number of bins is overloaded with a related quantity in one of the equations, which may confuse readers. Several figures lack informative captions and would benefit from axis labels and clearer legends. The writing contains a number of overlong sentences in the discussion section that could be tightened for readability. Code availability is mentioned, and the authors are encouraged to release a complete implementation with configuration files so that the reported numbers can be reproduced. Overall the paper addresses a meaningful problem with a plausible and original mechanism. The core idea merits publication interest, but the claims about accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability currently rest on evidence that is too limited to fully support them. I recommend a major revision that addresses the methodological specification, the statistical reporting, the breadth of baselines, and the depth of the interpretability analysis.

The topic refers to a message attributed to Thomas Jefferson, but I should be careful: Jefferson wrote extensively about education, self-improvement, and industriousness, and he famously believed in the value of diligent study and a disciplined use of time. However, I'm not aware of one specific, documented quotation that matches "using time wisely and pursuing personal goals through hard work and commitment" word for word. The essay below draws on Jefferson's broader views and his well-known practice of organizing his days, without attributing a specific invented quote to him.

Thomas Jefferson believed that a person's character and usefulness depended largely on how they spent their time. Although he lived in an age very different from our own, his ideas about education and self-discipline remain relevant to students today. He was a man of remarkable energy who read widely, kept detailed records of his daily activities, and organized his schedule with care. His commitment to learning shaped everything from his architectural designs at Monticello to his work founding the University of Virginia. Jefferson understood that knowledge and accomplishment do not arrive by chance but are built through steady effort over many years. For a student, this message is a powerful reminder that time is a limited resource that should never be wasted. Every hour spent reading, practicing, or thinking carefully is an investment in the person one hopes to become. Jefferson himself rose early, worked through much of the day, and devoted his evenings to study and correspondence. Such habits were not glamorous, but they produced a lifetime of achievement. Pursuing personal goals requires more than good intentions, because intentions alone do not write essays, master languages, or build careers. Commitment means returning to difficult work even when motivation fades and progress feels slow. Hard work, in this sense, is less about talent and more about persistence and the willingness to keep going. Many students assume that success belongs only to the naturally gifted, yet history suggests that disciplined effort often matters more than raw ability. Jefferson's own story reflects this truth, as he was a self-taught student who continually pushed himself to learn new subjects. He studied law, mathematics, science, languages, and agriculture, showing that curiosity combined with dedication can open many doors. Using time wisely also means knowing where to direct one's energy and resisting distractions that offer only temporary pleasure. A student who plans each week, sets clear objectives, and reviews progress regularly is far more likely to reach their goals. Such planning does not eliminate challenges, but it gives shape and purpose to everyday effort. Commitment also involves accepting setbacks as part of the process rather than as signs of failure. Each mistake can teach a lesson that brings a person closer to mastery. In the end, Jefferson's example encourages young people to treat their time as precious and their goals as worthy of sustained effort. By working diligently and staying committed to what matters most, a student can build a future shaped by their own choices. The message is timeless: those who use their days with purpose and perseverance are the ones who turn their dreams into reality.

Car-free communities promise a different way of living, one built around walking, cycling, and public transit rather than private automobiles. Such places offer clear advantages, but they also raise serious practical questions that planners must address. The most significant benefit is improved public health. When residents walk or bike for everyday trips, they gain regular physical activity, which can reduce rates of obesity, heart disease, and depression. Air quality also improves, since removing vehicle traffic cuts emissions of pollutants linked to asthma and other respiratory illnesses. Streets without cars are quieter and safer, particularly for children, who can play outdoors without the constant threat of traffic. Car-free design often encourages stronger community life as well, because people who move slowly through their neighborhoods are more likely to meet their neighbors, shop at local businesses, and feel invested in shared spaces. Economically, residents may save considerable money by avoiding the costs of buying, insuring, fueling, and maintaining a car. Environmental benefits extend beyond air quality, as reduced driving lowers greenhouse gas emissions and land once devoted to parking can be converted into parks, housing, or gardens. However, these advantages come with real challenges. Access to jobs, hospitals, and specialized services may be limited if transit is inadequate, which can disadvantage people who cannot easily walk or bike long distances. Emergency services must still reach every home quickly, requiring careful planning of narrow or pedestrian-only routes. People with disabilities, the elderly, and families carrying heavy loads may find car-free living especially difficult without well-designed alternatives. Businesses that rely on deliveries or large-vehicle access can face higher costs or logistical problems. Property values and housing affordability may also shift, as desirable car-free neighborhoods can attract wealthier residents and drive up prices. Successful car-free communities therefore depend on thoughtful planning, reliable public transit, accessible design, and policies that ensure the benefits are shared fairly among all residents.

Every summer, Elias stood at the edge of the lake while his friends cannonballed into the cold water, laughing. He would only smile and shake his head. Water beaded and rolled off his skin like mercury, and it never seemed to want him. At parties, he reached past the water pitchers and reached instead for the cans of cola, cherry soda, and ginger ale. His grandmother once told him that his great-grandfather had been the same, a man who could walk through rain without a drop touching him. Elias had never tested the story, and he had no wish to. Still, one evening he found an old photograph tucked inside a book, showing a man on a riverbank, dry as dust while the river rushed past his boots. On the back, in faded ink, someone had written: Keep away from the water, and it will keep away from you.

A teenager on the autism spectrum has admitted to making a series of fake bomb threats that targeted schools, airports, and businesses across the United States, federal prosecutors said. The young man, whose name is being withheld because he is a minor, pleaded guilty to charges related to the hoaxes, which forced evacuations, delayed flights, and triggered emergency responses in several states. Investigators said the threats were sent through anonymous online accounts and phone calls, and that digital records eventually led them to the suspect. Authorities said each false alarm pulled police, bomb squads, and other first responders away from real emergencies while costing communities significant time and money. Defense attorneys argued that the teen's autism contributed to impulsive behavior and a limited understanding of how seriously the threats would be taken, and they asked the court for a sentence focused on treatment and supervision. Prosecutors countered that the scope and repetition of the threats demanded accountability, though they acknowledged the defendant's diagnosis as a factor in sentencing. Disability advocates expressed concern that the case could fuel unfair stereotypes about autistic people, stressing that the vast majority of autistic individuals never commit crimes of this kind. A sentencing hearing has been scheduled, and the court will determine the terms of supervision, any mandated mental health services, and restitution owed to the affected agencies and businesses. Officials urged anyone who receives threatening communications to report them immediately to local law enforcement.

Exploring Technology Careers and the Value of Early Work Experience in IT and Computer Science

Technology careers offer some of the most varied and rewarding paths available today. Whether you are a student, a career changer, or someone simply curious about what the field has to offer, this page will help you understand the range of roles, the skills they require, and why early work experience can make such a difference. The information here is meant as a starting point for your own research and decision-making.

The world of information technology and computer science is broad. It includes software development, data analysis, cybersecurity, network administration, cloud computing, systems engineering, user experience design, technical support, database management, and many other specialties. Each area has its own tools, vocabulary, and daily tasks, so no single description can capture the entire field.

Software developers design, build, test, and maintain applications and systems. Their work might involve creating a mobile app, writing the logic behind a web service, or improving the performance of a large database-driven platform. Developers typically need strong problem-solving skills, familiarity with one or more programming languages, and the habit of reading and writing clear documentation.

Data analysts and data scientists collect, clean, and interpret information to support decisions. They use statistical methods, spreadsheets, query languages, and visualization tools to turn raw numbers into useful insight. Many organizations rely on this work to understand customers, manage risk, and plan operations.

Cybersecurity professionals protect systems, networks, and data from unauthorized access and damage. They monitor for threats, respond to incidents, test defenses, and help organizations meet security standards. Demand for these skills has grown steadily as more of daily life moves online.

Network and systems administrators keep the infrastructure that organizations depend on running smoothly. They configure servers, manage user accounts, monitor performance, and troubleshoot outages. These roles often serve as an entry point into deeper technical specialties.

Cloud engineers design and manage computing resources hosted by providers over the internet. Their responsibilities include deploying applications, controlling costs, ensuring reliability, and automating routine tasks. Cloud skills are widely sought after across industries.

User experience and interface designers focus on how people interact with technology. They conduct research, create prototypes, and test designs to make products easier and more pleasant to use. This role blends technical knowledge with an understanding of human behavior.

Technical support and help desk specialists are often the first point of contact for people who have problems with their devices or software. They diagnose issues, guide users through solutions, and document recurring problems so they can be fixed at their source. These positions build patience, communication skills, and broad technical familiarity.

Database administrators and engineers store, organize, and protect the data that applications depend on. They design schemas, tune queries, manage backups, and ensure data integrity. Careful attention to detail is essential in this work.

Quality assurance testers examine software to find defects before it reaches users. They write test cases, run automated and manual tests, and report issues clearly. This role is a valuable way to learn how software is built and maintained.

Across all these roles, certain core skills appear again and again. Logical thinking and problem-solving are fundamental. Comfort with at least one programming or scripting language is valuable in many positions. Clear written and spoken communication matters because technical work must be explained to colleagues and clients who may not share the same background. Teamwork, adaptability, and a willingness to keep learning are also important, since tools and best practices change quickly.

Formal education provides a strong foundation. Degrees in computer science, information systems, software engineering, and related fields teach theory, mathematics, and principles of design. However, a degree is not the only route into the field. Bootcamps, online courses, professional certifications, and self-directed projects can also prepare people for technical work, and many employers now consider demonstrated skill alongside formal credentials.

This is where early work experience becomes especially valuable. Practical experience shows employers that you can apply knowledge to real problems, work within constraints such as deadlines and budgets, and collaborate with others. It also helps you discover which areas genuinely interest you, which is difficult to know from coursework alone.

Internships are one of the most common ways to gain early experience. A typical internship places a student or recent graduate within a team for a defined period, often a summer or semester. Interns may contribute to real projects, attend team meetings, learn workplace tools, and receive mentorship. Many companies use internships as a pipeline for full-time hiring, so they can be a significant step toward a first job.

Part-time and co-op positions provide similar benefits while allowing students to balance work with their studies. Co-op programs, which alternate periods of academic study with periods of paid employment, are offered by many universities and can extend over a full academic year or more. Students in these programs often graduate with both a degree and a significant body of professional experience.

Volunteer work and open-source contributions also count as meaningful experience. Helping a nonprofit build or maintain a website, contributing bug fixes to a public software project, or organizing a community technology event can demonstrate initiative and technical ability. Such work can be documented in a portfolio and discussed in interviews.

Personal projects deserve attention as well. Building a small application, analyzing a public dataset, setting up a home server, or automating a repetitive task all require applying knowledge in a concrete way. Sharing these projects publicly, with clear explanations of what you built and why, gives others a window into your abilities.

Early experience offers several specific advantages. It builds a professional network, since colleagues, mentors, and supervisors can later become references or sources of opportunity. It develops professional habits such as meeting deadlines, communicating progress, accepting feedback, and working in version-controlled environments. It also helps you clarify your career goals. Some people discover a passion they had not expected, while others learn that a particular path is not a good fit, which is valuable information in itself.

Early experience can also strengthen your confidence. Technical fields can feel intimidating, especially to newcomers who see experienced professionals working fluently with complex tools. Real-world practice gradually demystifies these tools and helps build a sense of competence. Mistakes made in a supportive environment are a normal and important part of learning.

For those just starting out, a few practical steps can help. Begin by identifying areas that genuinely interest you, and explore them through free or low-cost resources. Build a small portfolio of projects, and keep a record of what you learned from each one. Look for opportunities through your school's career services, professional organizations, local meetups, and online communities. When applying, tailor your resume to highlight relevant projects and skills, and be prepared to explain your reasoning in technical interviews. Ask questions freely, and seek out mentors who are willing to share their experience.

It is also worth remembering that career paths in technology are rarely linear. Many professionals move between roles, specialties, and even industries over the course of their careers. Early experience does not lock you into a single track. Instead, it gives you a foundation from which to make informed choices as your interests and circumstances evolve.

Employers in many sectors now hire for technical roles, including healthcare, finance, education, manufacturing, government, and entertainment, not only in traditional technology companies. This means that technology skills can open doors across a wide range of industries, and that domain knowledge in a particular field can be a strong complement to technical training.

Diversity and accessibility remain important goals within the technology community. Many organizations and educational programs work to broaden participation by offering scholarships, mentorship programs, and internships targeted at underrepresented groups. Prospective students and job seekers can take advantage of these opportunities and, where possible, help create them for others.

Finally, a note on continuous learning. Technology changes rapidly, and skills that are in high demand today may be less relevant in a few years. Successful professionals tend to develop the habit of learning new tools, reading technical materials, and reflecting on their own work. Early experience helps establish this habit, because it teaches you how to learn on the job, which is one of the most transferable skills you can develop.

In summary, technology careers are diverse, dynamic, and full of opportunity. Early work experience, whether through internships, co-ops, volunteering, or personal projects, helps you test your interests, build practical skills, establish professional relationships, and grow in confidence. Approach your exploration with curiosity and persistence, and take advantage of the many pathways available to you.

Detective Ray Dolan had worked the night shift for eleven years, and in all that time nothing had unsettled him the way the house on Calloway Street did. He had not planned to drive past it. His cruiser simply turned onto the block at two in the morning, the way a tired hand finds a familiar light switch in the dark.

The porch light was on. It had been off when the Hendersons moved out in the spring, and he knew because he had responded to the burglary alarm that followed. Now the bulb burned a steady yellow, and a rocking chair moved slowly back and forth, though there was no wind.

He stopped the car and sat with the engine running. The radio murmured dispatch codes he barely heard. He told himself to call it in, to note a possible welfare check, but his thumb hovered over the handset and did not press.

He stepped out. The air smelled of cut grass and something sweeter underneath, like lilacs left too long in a vase. The front door stood open an inch. He had a flashlight in one hand and his service weapon holstered at his hip, and he found that he was counting his steps the way he had been taught in the academy.

Inside, the house was empty. The carpet had been pulled up, the walls stripped, the rooms hollow. Yet on the kitchen counter sat a single coffee mug, still warm to the touch, with a faint ring of lipstick on the rim. Ray had not seen a woman in the house, and he had no idea whose mug it was.

He backed out slowly, as though the floorboards might give way. Halfway down the walk, his phone buzzed in his jacket pocket. He pulled it out and saw the screen read Owen, his son, who was sixteen and had not called him voluntarily in four months.

He answered. For a moment there was only breathing on the line, then a soft voice, too calm for a teenager.

"Dad, you need to go home," Owen said.

"Owen, it's two in the morning. Where are you? Is your mother with you?"

"Mom's asleep. I'm in my room. Dad, you were just on Calloway, weren't you?"

Ray felt the cold settle in his stomach. "How would you know that?"

"Because she told me you'd come. She said you always come back to the same places when you can't let go of something." There was a pause, and then a sound like a chair creaking, the same rhythm that had been drifting in the empty house. "She wants you to stop looking for her. She says the mug is hers, and she's still drinking from it."

The line went dead. Ray stared at the screen, then dialed Owen's number. It rang six times before a sleepy voice answered, his ex-wife Karen, groggy and irritated.

"Ray? Do you know what time it is?"

"Is Owen home?"

"Of course he's home. He's asleep in his bed, where he should be. Why?"

Ray looked back at the house. The porch light flickered once, then steadied. The rocking chair had stopped.

"No reason," he said. "Tell him I called. Tell him I'm sorry."

He drove home without turning on the radio. In the morning, he would ask Owen about the call, and he would hear his son laugh and say he had been asleep all night. But that night Ray sat in his kitchen with the light off, staring at the mug he had carried out of the Calloway house without ever remembering picking it up. Its rim bore a faint stain of red, and when he touched it, it was warm.

Investigators traced the drone to the operator, who was later interviewed about the incidents. In court, the man admitted to breaching aviation and drone regulations that prohibit flying in restricted airspace and over people and buildings without permission. Eurozone economic recovery gathers pace as business activity and consumer spending show steady improvement across member states. Inflation has moved closer to the European Central Bank's target, but officials caution that price pressures in some sectors remain stubborn. Against this backdrop, policymakers are beginning to discuss the gradual withdrawal of monetary stimulus that was introduced during the downturn. Market participants have adjusted their expectations, with bond yields rising as investors price in the possibility of higher interest rates. ECB officials have signaled that any tightening will be data-dependent and carried out cautiously to avoid derailing the recovery. Economists note that the timing of such moves will be closely watched, since premature action could weigh on investment and households already facing elevated borrowing costs. For now, the central bank appears poised to balance the strengthening economy against the need to keep inflation firmly anchored.

The National Asset Management Agency (Nama), the Irish state body set up to deal with bad loans from the financial crisis, has faced fresh allegations of improper payments and refinancing fees linked to its sale of a portfolio of Northern Ireland property loans to the US investment firm Cerberus Capital Management.

The sale, which involved a large book of loans secured against commercial and residential property in Northern Ireland, was one of several disposals Nama carried out to recover money for the Irish taxpayer after the collapse of the country's banking sector.

Documents and claims that have emerged in recent weeks suggest that certain fees charged in connection with the refinancing of borrowers' debts may not have been properly accounted for or disclosed.

Critics argue that the arrangements raise questions about whether the value realised for the public purse was maximised, and whether conflicts of interest were adequately managed during the process.

Nama has consistently maintained that its disposals were conducted under rigorous commercial processes, with independent advice and oversight, and that all transactions complied with its legal and governance obligations.

A spokesperson for the agency said it took allegations of this kind seriously and would examine any specific concerns raised with it through the appropriate channels.

Cerberus has also rejected any suggestion of wrongdoing, saying that its acquisition of the loans was carried out transparently and in line with the terms agreed at the time of sale.

The allegations centre on payments made to intermediaries and advisers involved in restructuring or refinancing the loans after they were transferred to the new owner.

Some borrowers in Northern Ireland have reportedly said they were charged fees they did not expect or understand when their loans were refinanced, a claim that has added to public unease about the sale.

Political representatives from across the Northern Ireland and Irish political spectrum have called for greater transparency, with several demanding that the relevant files be made available for scrutiny.

Calls have also been made for an independent review of the sale, with supporters arguing that only a fully independent examination can restore public confidence in how the portfolio was handled.

Nama is subject to oversight from the Oireachtas, Ireland's parliament, and its committees have previously examined the agency's disposals in detail.

Officials have said that any review would need to balance the desire for openness with legitimate commercial confidentiality, particularly where private companies and individual borrowers are involved.

Financial analysts note that large loan portfolio sales of this kind are complex, often involving multiple layers of fees, servicing arrangements and legal costs, all of which can be difficult for the public to assess.

They add that the distinction between standard transaction costs and improper payments can be hard to draw without detailed access to the underlying contracts and invoices.

Legal experts say that any finding of impropriety would depend on the specific terms of the sale agreement, the applicable regulations, and evidence showing how particular payments were authorised.

For now, the allegations remain unproven, and no formal finding of wrongdoing has been made by any regulatory or judicial body.

The matter has nonetheless prompted renewed attention to the wider question of how the state handled the aftermath of the banking crisis and whether lessons have been fully learned.

Campaigners representing indebted homeowners and small businesses have argued that the sale highlighted an imbalance between the interests of distressed borrowers and those of large international investors.

They have called for clearer protections for borrowers whose loans are sold, including stronger rights to information and fairer treatment in any subsequent refinancing.

Nama has previously defended its record, pointing out that it has repaid significant sums to the Irish state and that its work helped stabilise the public finances during a severe downturn.

Critics counter that the agency's achievements should not shield particular transactions from scrutiny, and that openness is essential to maintaining trust in public institutions.

Further information is expected as parliamentary committees and other bodies consider whether to take up the matter in more detail.

Until then, the central questions remain open: whether the fees were properly disclosed, whether the sale delivered the best outcome for taxpayers, and whether borrowers were treated fairly throughout the process.

The Electoral College has served as the mechanism for choosing American presidents for more than two centuries, yet its flaws have become increasingly difficult to defend. At its core, the system produces results that can contradict the clearly expressed will of the voters, as occurred in 2000 and 2016, when candidates won the presidency while losing the national popular vote. A nationwide popular vote would ensure that the candidate receiving the most votes from American citizens becomes president, aligning the outcome with basic democratic principles. Under the current arrangement, a small number of states decide most elections, leaving voters in safe states largely ignored by campaigns that focus their resources on a handful of battlegrounds. A national popular vote would require candidates to seek support from every region, giving voters in rural areas, urban centers, and every state a meaningful reason to be heard. The principle of one person, one vote is a cornerstone of American democracy, yet the Electoral College weights votes unequally, since a voter in a small state exercises more influence per person than a voter in a large state. Critics argue that the system protects smaller states, but a direct national count would still give every citizen an equal voice regardless of geography. Concerns about the loss of federalism are real, yet the states would still administer their own elections, and the national count would simply be the sum of those results. Supporters of the current system often point to its role in encouraging broad coalitions, but a popular vote would similarly reward candidates who build support across the nation rather than only in key states. The prospect of a recount or dispute in a close national race is a legitimate concern, yet procedures for nationwide tabulation and verification could be designed to address it. Moreover, the Electoral College's winner-take-all allocation in most states means that millions of votes cast for losing candidates within a state are effectively discarded. A popular vote would eliminate this distortion and ensure that every ballot counts toward the final tally. Some have proposed the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact as a path forward, though a constitutional amendment would provide the most durable and direct solution. Ultimately, the presidency is a national office, and the choice of its occupant should reflect the considered preferences of the nation as a whole. Replacing the Electoral College with a popular vote would strengthen public confidence in elections and affirm the principle that the people themselves should decide who leads them. Such a reform would modernize the nation's highest democratic institution and bring it closer to the ideal of equal representation that Americans have long claimed to hold.

Marcus Henley had always believed he was destined for greatness, and lately he had decided that greatness looked a lot like the Consortium of Quiet Hands.

He had found the advertisement pinned inside a dusty bookshop on Harrow Street, tucked between a flyer for tarot readings and a notice about lost cats. It was written on heavy cream paper with no return address, only a single line: Those who have the patience to be unseen may apply. Marcus had read it four times before slipping it into his coat pocket like a love letter.

The application arrived by mail two weeks later, sealed with black wax. It asked for a personal history, a list of accomplishments, and a demonstration of discretion. Marcus took it as a personal challenge.

He sat at his kitchen table with a fountain pen and a bottle of cheap red wine, and he began to write with the seriousness of a man composing his own legend.

He started with his childhood, describing how the neighborhood dogs always seemed to know he was nearby. He wrote about his mother's cat, which had gone missing the spring he turned eleven, and how he had felt a strange calm in the days that followed. He did not mention that he had buried it in the garden behind the shed, under the tomato plants, because he thought that detail was too obvious.

Next came his professional experience. He wrote that he had worked as a night janitor at the Alder Street clinic for three years, and that he took pride in knowing the building's routines better than anyone. He described the locked supply room where he sometimes sat in the dark, listening to the hum of the refrigerators and imagining what he would do if the right person wandered in alone.

He wrote about Denise Okafor, who had worked the front desk and had once told him to stop leaving smudges on the glass doors. He described how he had waited for her in the parking structure one February evening, and how the security camera on level three had been broken for weeks, which he considered a fortunate coincidence. He wrote that he had made her last moments quiet and that no one had heard anything, and he seemed quite pleased with himself about this.

The guild's application asked for a demonstration of discretion, so Marcus offered a few examples of what he considered his finest work. He wrote about the man from the laundromat who had argued with him about a dryer, and the woman who had rear-ended his car on the interstate and then screamed at him in the shoulder lane. He did not use their names, but he gave the dates and the streets, and he described their final expressions with a poet's care.

He wrote that he believed in the purity of anonymous action, and that he had never once been caught, though he admitted with a touch of regret that a detective named Ruiz had recently started asking questions at the clinic. He said he found Ruiz amusing, a bloodhound with no nose, and he signed off by saying he looked forward to proving himself worthy of the Consortium's quiet hands.

He reread the letter twice, tapping the pen against his chin, and felt a warm satisfaction spreading through his chest. He folded the pages neatly, sealed them in a plain envelope, and wrote the guild's address on the front in careful block letters.

On his way to the post office the next morning, he passed a police cruiser parked across the street from his apartment. He waved at the officer inside, who did not wave back, and Marcus decided the man was simply too shy to acknowledge a fellow professional.

At the counter, the postal clerk weighed the envelope, stamped it, and asked if he wanted tracking. Marcus said no, because real members of a secret society would never want their mail tracked, and he felt quite clever about this too.

He walked home whistling, already imagining the black wax seal, the whispered welcome, and the first assignment that would mark him as one of the chosen.

Three days later, a plain van pulled up outside the clinic on Alder Street. Detective Ruiz stepped out with a folder under one arm, and beside her walked a woman in a gray coat who had received an unusually detailed letter that morning. The letter had been postmarked from the city's east side, and it had been sent, unbeknownst to its author, to the Office of the District Attorney rather than to any secret guild.

Ruiz opened the folder on the hood of the van and laid out the photographs. The woman in the gray coat read the first page, then the second, and then looked up at the clinic's glass doors with an expression that was almost sympathy.

Marcus Henley was sitting at his kitchen table that morning, humming and polishing a pair of shoes, when two officers knocked on his door. He opened it with a smile, already prepared to greet the guild's emissaries, and he did not understand until the handcuffs closed around his wrists that the Consortium of Quiet Hands had never existed at all.

He kept talking as they led him down the stairwell. He told them about his mother's cat, about the parking structure, about the laundromat man, and he seemed to believe that each detail was another line on his application. The officers exchanged glances and said nothing, and Ruiz, watching from the curb, wrote every word in her notebook.

Later, in the interview room, Marcus asked when he would hear back from the guild. Ruiz slid a single cream-colored card across the table, the same heavy paper as the original advertisement. It read, in neat letters, Thank you for your confession. Your patience has been noted.

Marcus stared at it for a long time, and for the first time in his life, he had nothing to say.

Discouragement is a feeling every student encounters at some point, whether after a failed exam, a rejected application, or a goal that seems too distant to reach. Left unchecked, it can convince us to abandon our ambitions before we have truly tried. Overcoming it requires two qualities that work together: persistence, the willingness to keep working when progress is slow, and self-belief, the conviction that our efforts can actually lead to success. Persistence gives us the discipline to continue, while self-belief gives us the reason to continue. Consider a student who struggles with mathematics and receives a low grade on the first test. Instead of accepting that result as a permanent judgment, she can treat it as information about where she needs to improve. By practicing daily and seeking help, she gradually builds skills that once seemed out of reach. Each small improvement strengthens her belief that she can succeed, and that belief in turn motivates further effort. Self-belief is not the same as arrogance; it is the honest recognition that ability can be developed over time. Setbacks will continue to appear, but they need not define the outcome. Those who persist through discouragement often discover that the obstacles they feared were far less permanent than they imagined. In the end, the goals we achieve are shaped not only by talent but by the courage to keep going when giving up would be easier.

Whether summer learning assignments should be created by students or teachers is a question that touches on the purpose of summer break, the role of educators, and the nature of meaningful learning. Summer is often the only extended stretch of the year when students are free from the rigid schedules of school, and the way we design their learning during that time matters a great deal. Those who favor teacher-created assignments argue that educators possess expertise that students lack. Teachers understand the curriculum, know which skills students tend to lose over the break, and can identify the gaps that need attention before the next school year begins. Without this guidance, students might spend their time on topics they find enjoyable but that do little to prepare them for what comes next.

Teacher-designed assignments also offer consistency and fairness. When every student in a class receives the same expectations, it becomes easier to measure progress and to ensure that all learners are held to comparable standards. This matters especially for students who come from households where parents may not have the time or knowledge to guide learning at home. A well-structured packet from a teacher can provide a clear path that these students might otherwise lack. In this sense, teacher-created work can serve as a form of equalization, offering every student access to the same quality of planning.

Furthermore, teachers are accountable to schools and districts in ways that shape assignments to meet official learning goals. Summer work created by educators can be aligned with state standards, upcoming unit plans, and assessments that will follow in the fall. This alignment reduces the chance that students will arrive in September unprepared for the material they are expected to master. Teachers can also build in checkpoints and feedback loops, so that the work is not merely completed but meaningfully reviewed.

Yet there is a compelling case for student-created assignments, and it deserves serious consideration. Learning is most powerful when the learner has a stake in the process. When students design their own summer projects, they are more likely to feel ownership over the outcome and to remain motivated throughout the break. A student who chooses to investigate a question about marine biology, build a small business plan, or document a family history brings curiosity and energy that an assigned worksheet may not inspire. Self-directed learning can cultivate the very skills that schools aim to develop, including independence, planning, and the ability to set and pursue goals.

Student-created assignments also foster metacognition, the awareness of one's own learning. When young people must decide what they need to learn and how they will demonstrate it, they are forced to reflect on their strengths and weaknesses in a way that passive completion of teacher tasks rarely requires. This reflection can produce learners who are more capable of managing their own education over time, a skill that will serve them well beyond the classroom. Advocates of this approach often point out that adults rarely face predetermined assignments in their professional lives; they must identify problems and develop solutions on their own.

Still, student-created work carries real risks. Young learners may not have the judgment to identify what they most need to learn. A student who is struggling with fractions might instead choose a project on video game design, not realizing that the foundational gap will widen over the summer. Without oversight, students may set goals that are too ambitious or too vague, leading to frustration or unfinished work. For this reason, a model in which students design assignments under teacher supervision may offer the best of both approaches, combining student autonomy with educational expertise.

Such a collaborative model might work in several ways. Teachers could provide a menu of approved options that students choose from, each aligned with important skills and content. Alternatively, students could propose their own projects, which teachers would review and refine before the break begins. Some educators have suggested a hybrid structure in which every student completes a required core of teacher-designed review while also pursuing a personal learning project of their own choosing. This arrangement acknowledges that both structure and freedom have roles to play in learning.

Ultimately, the question is not simply who should hold the pen, but what outcome summer learning is meant to achieve. If the primary goal is to prevent learning loss and prepare students for the grade ahead, teacher-created assignments have clear advantages in precision and alignment. If the primary goal is to nurture curiosity, independence, and lifelong learning habits, student involvement becomes increasingly important. A thoughtful system would recognize that these goals are not mutually exclusive and would seek ways to honor both.

In conclusion, neither students nor teachers should bear sole responsibility for summer learning assignments. Teachers bring expertise, consistency, and curricular knowledge that protect students from wasted time and widening gaps. Students bring motivation, personal interest, and the developing capacity for self-direction that make learning meaningful. The most effective approach is likely a partnership, in which educators provide the framework and students help shape the path within it. By sharing this responsibility, schools can make summer learning something students look forward to rather than something they simply endure.

Staying active is one of the most valuable habits a person can build, and its benefits reach far beyond physical health. When we commit to regular exercise, we also strengthen our character and our capacity to grow. Physical activity teaches discipline, because showing up on days when we feel tired or unmotivated requires a quiet kind of determination. Each small victory, such as finishing a longer run or mastering a new skill in the gym, builds confidence that carries over into other areas of life. Athletes and active people also learn that progress is rarely linear, and this lesson prepares them to handle setbacks in school, work, and relationships. Resilience grows through repeated effort, as the body and mind adapt to challenges and learn to recover from difficulty. An active lifestyle also reduces stress and improves mood, giving people a clearer mind to face problems calmly. Those who feel strong and capable in their own bodies often find it easier to support others who are struggling. Team sports and group activities teach cooperation, empathy, and the importance of depending on one another. Many volunteers and community leaders first discovered their sense of responsibility through shared physical pursuits. Staying active, then, is not only about personal fitness but about becoming someone who can lift others up. In the end, the habit of movement shapes both who we become and how we contribute to the people around us.

Subject: A Few Parables for the Office Ladder

Hi everyone,

I wanted to share a handful of short, humorous parables I've been collecting about life in the workplace hierarchy. Some of them are a little silly, and some are a little too true.

The first is about the eager new hire who wanted to climb the ladder quickly. On her first day she asked the manager how to get promoted. The manager replied, "Stop asking how to get promoted and start doing the job you already have." She went back to her desk and wondered whether that was a riddle or a rebuke.

The second tale concerns the middle manager named Gerald, who discovered that his title had grown longer each year while his actual authority had shrunk. By the time he was "Senior Associate Director of Strategic Alignment," he could not approve a stapler purchase without three meetings and a spreadsheet.

Another parable tells of the two rival vice presidents who competed for the corner office. Each spent so much energy undermining the other that the building was sold, and both found themselves working from the same cramped coffee shop downtown, still arguing about the thermostat.

There is also the story of the manager who believed that the secret to survival was to agree with everyone. In meetings he nodded at every proposal, so when the company changed direction three times in one quarter, he was praised for his flexibility and quietly promoted to a position nobody could remember creating.

A cautionary fable describes the ambitious employee who wrote a brilliant memo and sent it to the entire company, including the cleaning staff and the board. He was recognized for his initiative, though his office was relocated to the basement near the copier, which everyone agreed was a tasteful lesson in visibility.

Consider the wise old employee who had outlasted six reorganizations. When asked her secret, she said she simply kept a plant on her desk, a spare sweater in her drawer, and a calm expression at all times. "Reorganizations come and go," she said, "but the plant needs watering, and that gives me something real to care about."

Then there is the tale of the team that held a meeting to discuss the agenda for the next meeting. After four hours they agreed to schedule a follow-up, and the minutes ran to forty pages, none of which anyone read, though everyone signed them with great dignity.

One parable warns against the manager who wanted to be loved by everyone. He rarely delivered bad news, so his team learned to read his silences as either approval or impending doom, and they spent more time decoding his moods than doing their work.

Finally, the story of the overworked executive who never took a vacation. One day she collapsed in the elevator, and as the doors opened, her colleagues looked at one another and asked, "Who will approve the travel expenses now?" It was the first time anyone had considered that she might have been human all along.

These parables are, of course, exaggerations, but like all good jokes they carry a grain of truth. I hope they gave you a smile this week.

Warm regards,
