Reducing our reliance on personal cars offers significant benefits for the environment, society, and the economy. As cities and towns grow, the number of vehicles on the road has increased dramatically, creating problems that affect everyone. Addressing these problems by encouraging alternatives to private car ownership is therefore a worthwhile goal for communities today.

The environmental advantages are perhaps the most widely recognized. Passenger vehicles are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, releasing carbon dioxide and other pollutants as they burn fossil fuels. Fewer cars on the road would mean lower emissions, contributing to efforts to slow climate change. Cars also release nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter, which degrade air quality and are linked to respiratory illness. Cleaner air would reduce asthma attacks, heart disease, and premature deaths, especially in neighborhoods located near busy highways. Vehicles also demand vast amounts of land for roads and parking, which fragments natural habitats and increases stormwater runoff that pollutes rivers and streams. Reducing car dependence would allow more land to remain green and support local ecosystems.

Social benefits follow closely behind the environmental ones. Communities designed around walking, cycling, and public transit tend to be more connected, because people encounter their neighbors more often on sidewalks and at bus stops. Such neighborhoods can foster a stronger sense of belonging and civic engagement. Reducing car use also improves road safety, since traffic accidents claim tens of thousands of lives each year in many countries, and fewer cars means fewer collisions. Children, older adults, and people with disabilities often struggle to get around in car-oriented environments, so better transit and safe pedestrian routes expand their independence. Access to jobs, schools, and healthcare becomes more equitable when people are not forced to spend large sums on a vehicle to participate fully in society.

Economic arguments are equally compelling. Owning a car is expensive, with costs for purchase, insurance, fuel, maintenance, parking, and depreciation often adding up to thousands of dollars per year for a single household. Many families could redirect this money toward savings, housing, education, or local businesses if they relied less on personal vehicles. Public transit and active transportation are generally far cheaper per trip for both individuals and governments, and investment in them can create jobs in construction, operation, and maintenance. Local economies can also benefit, since pedestrians and cyclists tend to patronize nearby shops and restaurants more often than drivers passing through quickly. Reduced spending on road expansion and parking infrastructure would free public funds for other priorities.

Reducing reliance on personal cars is not a call to abandon them entirely, since many people depend on vehicles for work, travel, and daily life. Rather, it is a call to build a balanced transportation system that gives people real choices. Improving public transit, creating safe bike lanes, and designing walkable neighborhoods can together make these alternatives practical for more people. Such changes would yield cleaner air, healthier and more connected communities, and stronger local economies. For these reasons, a shift away from car dependence deserves serious consideration by policymakers and citizens alike.

Nokia has challenged a small startup's use of the name "HERE," raising concerns about potential trademark confusion in the technology market. The dispute centers on the word "HERE," which Nokia has long associated with its mapping and location services business, known as HERE Technologies. The company, which was spun off and sold a majority stake in the mapping unit in recent years, argues that the startup's use of a similar name could mislead customers into believing the two businesses are connected. The startup, a small firm operating in the location or software space, has not yet publicly responded in detail to the complaint. Trademark experts note that disputes like this often hinge on whether the names are similar in appearance, sound, and meaning, and whether they operate in overlapping markets. Because "here" is a common English word, the startup may argue that it cannot be monopolized in general use, while Nokia may counter that its specific branding in mapping gives it strong protection. Legal observers say such disagreements are frequently settled through negotiation, such as a rebranding agreement, rather than litigation. Smaller companies facing challenges from large corporations often weigh the cost of legal defense against the expense of changing their name. The outcome could affect how other startups choose names that include common words. Industry analysts point out that brand recognition is valuable in mapping and navigation, where users rely on trusted names for accurate data. Nokia has emphasized that it wants to protect its customers from confusion rather than stifle competition. Critics of the complaint argue that large firms should not use trademark law to crowd out smaller innovators with modest resources. Supporters of Nokia's position say that protecting established brands is necessary to maintain clear market signals. The dispute is still in its early stages, and it remains unclear whether the matter will be resolved privately or move to a formal legal proceeding. Both parties have been contacted for further comment, and updates are expected as the situation develops. Observers will be watching closely to see how the case is handled and what precedent it may set for similar naming conflicts.

How Emerging Transportation Technologies and Urban Planning Are Reshaping City Mobility, Infrastructure, and Sustainability

Cities have always been shaped by how people and goods move through them. For much of the twentieth century, that shaping favored the private automobile, with wide roads, large parking areas, and low-density suburbs built around driving. Today, a convergence of new transportation technologies and changing urban planning philosophies is pushing cities in a different direction. This page explains the main forces at work, what they mean for daily life, and why they matter for long-term sustainability.

The first major shift is the move toward electrification. Electric vehicles, including cars, buses, delivery vans, and motorcycles, produce no tailpipe emissions, which improves local air quality even when the electricity that charges them comes from a mix of sources. Cities are responding by installing public charging stations, setting aside curbside charging spaces, and in some cases requiring new buildings to include charging infrastructure. Electric buses have become increasingly common in transit fleets, and many transit agencies have set targets for converting their entire fleets over the coming decades.

Electrification also changes the relationship between the vehicle and the grid. An electric vehicle parked for most of the day can, in principle, store energy and return it during periods of high demand, a concept often called vehicle-to-grid integration. This could help cities balance renewable energy sources such as solar and wind, which fluctuate with weather and time of day. Realizing this potential requires coordination between utilities, city governments, and vehicle manufacturers, and the technical and regulatory details are still being worked out in many places.

Shared mobility is another significant trend. Bike-sharing and scooter-sharing programs allow people to take short trips without owning a vehicle, and car-sharing services let households give up a second car while still having access to one when needed. Ride-hailing services have changed expectations about convenience, though their effect on congestion and emissions is debated. Some studies suggest that ride-hailing adds to traffic in dense areas, while others find it replaces some trips that would otherwise have been made by transit or walking. The net impact likely depends on local conditions and how services are regulated.

Automated vehicles represent a longer-term and more uncertain change. Vehicles capable of driving themselves under some or all conditions are being tested in many cities, and some limited driverless services already operate in certain areas. Proponents argue that automation could improve safety, since most serious crashes involve human error, and could make mobility more accessible for people who cannot drive. Critics point out that automated vehicles could increase total driving if they make travel easier and cheaper, which would work against congestion and sustainability goals. Public policy will largely determine which outcome becomes more likely.

Micromobility, meaning small, lightweight vehicles used for short trips, has grown rapidly. Electric bicycles and scooters can cover distances that many people would not walk, and they can connect transit stations with homes and workplaces, a function often called the first-mile and last-mile problem. Cities have had to develop rules about where these devices can be parked, how fast they may travel, and how riders should share space with pedestrians. Clear rules and dedicated infrastructure tend to produce better outcomes than unregulated growth.

Urban planning has responded to these technologies with new ideas about how cities should be laid out. One influential concept is the transit-oriented development model, which concentrates housing, jobs, shops, and services near high-capacity transit stations. By placing destinations within a short walk of rail or bus rapid transit, these developments reduce the need for driving and make transit more financially viable. Many cities now use zoning reforms to allow denser construction near transit corridors.

Another planning approach is the complete street. A complete street is designed to accommodate all users, including pedestrians, cyclists, transit riders, motorists, and people with disabilities. Typical features include wider sidewalks, protected bike lanes, median islands for crossing, shorter crossing distances, curb extensions, and transit priority lanes. Research has linked these designs to fewer crashes, more walking and cycling, and more economic activity along commercial streets.

The superblock is a more recent idea that has been tested in several European cities. A superblock groups several city blocks together and restricts through traffic within the group, leaving local streets for residents, pedestrians, and small vehicles. The space freed from traffic can be used for trees, seating, play areas, and small businesses. Supporters argue that superblocks reduce noise and pollution, improve safety, and create more usable public space, though some residents and businesses have raised concerns about how traffic is redirected to surrounding streets.

Parking policy has become an important lever for planners. For decades, many cities required new buildings to provide a minimum number of parking spaces, which raised construction costs and encouraged driving. A growing number of cities have eliminated or reduced these minimums, and some have introduced maximum limits or charged market rates for on-street parking. These changes aim to reduce car dependence and free land for housing and other uses. Evidence from cities that have made such changes suggests that parking supply does affect how much people drive, though the size of the effect varies.

Congestion pricing is a policy tool that charges drivers for entering or using certain roads during busy times. Several cities have adopted congestion charges, and results have generally included reduced traffic volumes and faster travel for those who continue to drive, along with revenue that can fund transit improvements. Public acceptance is often the main challenge, and designs that return revenue visibly to transportation services have tended to be more popular. Pricing can also be combined with road space reallocation to give more room to buses, bicycles, and pedestrians.

Bus rapid transit and light rail are being upgraded with features that make them faster and more reliable. Dedicated lanes, level boarding platforms, off-board fare payment, and traffic signal priority can cut travel times substantially. Because these systems carry many passengers in a small footprint, they can serve dense corridors more efficiently than private cars and at lower cost per passenger than many new subway lines. Cities with limited budgets have found these options especially attractive.

Digital technology is making transit more responsive. Real-time arrival information, mobile payment, and trip planning apps help riders make decisions with better information. Some agencies use data from fare cards and mobile devices to adjust service levels and routes. Mobility-as-a-service platforms attempt to combine transit, bike-sharing, ride-hailing, and other modes into a single payment and planning system. The success of these platforms depends on interoperability, fair pricing, and whether they actually reduce car use rather than simply adding options.

Freight and goods movement are also changing. Growth in online shopping has increased the number of delivery vehicles in cities, contributing to congestion, double parking, and emissions. Some cities are experimenting with consolidation centers at the edge of the urban core, where goods are transferred to smaller electric vehicles or cargo bikes for final delivery. Time-restricted loading zones and off-peak delivery schedules can also reduce conflicts with other road users. Planners increasingly treat freight as part of the mobility system rather than a separate concern.

Green infrastructure is becoming part of transportation design. Streets with planted medians, bioswales, and permeable pavement can absorb stormwater, reduce flooding, and cool surrounding areas during heat waves. Tree canopy along streets provides shade that makes walking more comfortable, which supports the goal of shifting trips away from cars. These features often cost less to maintain over time than conventional drainage systems, and they deliver co-benefits for public health and property values.

Infrastructure for emerging technologies must be planned carefully to avoid waste. Charging networks need to be placed where vehicles will actually park, and grid connections must be upgraded in step with demand. Sensors and communication networks for connected vehicles require standards so that equipment from different manufacturers can work together. Cities that plan these systems early, rather than retrofitting them after problems emerge, tend to achieve smoother transitions and lower long-term costs.

Equity is a central concern in all of these changes. New mobility services often begin in wealthier neighborhoods where demand is highest and profits are most likely, which can leave lower-income areas with fewer options. Digital payment requirements can exclude people without bank accounts or smartphones. Gentrification can follow transit improvements, displacing the residents those improvements were meant to serve. Planners and policymakers are increasingly using equity impact assessments, community engagement, and affordability requirements to address these risks.

Public health is closely tied to transportation choices. Cities that make walking, cycling, and transit safe and convenient tend to see more physical activity, which is associated with lower rates of heart disease, diabetes, and some cancers. Reducing vehicle emissions and traffic noise can lower rates of asthma and other respiratory conditions. Road traffic injuries remain a major cause of death worldwide, and street designs that slow vehicles and separate them from vulnerable users can save lives.

Data is playing a growing role in planning decisions. Traffic sensors, transit smart card records, mobile phone data, and crowdsourced reports allow planners to understand travel patterns in more detail than traditional surveys provided. These tools can help identify where improvements are most needed and evaluate whether interventions work as intended. At the same time, collecting and using personal location data raises privacy concerns, and cities need clear rules about what data is gathered, how long it is kept, and who can access it.

Governance and funding determine whether these ideas succeed. Many transportation projects span multiple jurisdictions, involve private companies, and depend on long-term commitments that outlast political cycles. Public-private partnerships, dedicated transportation funds, and regional coordination bodies can help, but they also require transparency and accountability. Community participation, including input from people who do not normally attend public meetings, can improve project design and build support.

Climate goals provide much of the urgency behind these changes. Transportation is one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries, and reducing it requires changes in vehicle technology, energy supply, and the amount of driving people do. Land use decisions have long-lasting effects, since a neighborhood built for cars will tend to keep generating car trips for decades. Planning that brings homes and destinations closer together can reduce the distance people need to travel, which lowers emissions regardless of the vehicle type.

Adaptation to climate change is also a transportation concern. Extreme heat can buckle roads and rail lines, heavy rain can overwhelm drainage, and rising sea levels threaten coastal infrastructure. Planners are considering these risks when designing new facilities, choosing materials, and deciding where to invest in protection or relocation. Transportation networks that can keep functioning during disruptions provide greater resilience for the whole city.

Cities differ widely in their circumstances, and no single model fits all of them. A dense city with strong transit may focus on expanding capacity and reducing parking, while a sprawling region may need to invest in frequent bus service and connections between suburban centers. Cities in rapidly growing countries face the challenge of building mobility systems before car ownership becomes entrenched, while older cities must retrofit streets and buildings that were designed for another era. Learning from other cities is valuable, but local conditions, politics, and culture shape what is possible.

Measuring success requires clear goals and good indicators. Common measures include the share of trips made by walking, cycling, and transit; average travel times; traffic fatalities and injuries; emissions and air quality; the share of residents living within a short walk of frequent transit; and the affordability of transportation for households. Tracking these indicators over time helps cities learn which policies work and adjust those that do not.

The future of city mobility is not predetermined. Technologies such as electric vehicles, automated systems, and shared services could either support a more sustainable and equitable urban future or reinforce existing patterns of car dependence and sprawl. The outcome will depend on choices made by planners, governments, businesses, and residents. Understanding the connections between technology, infrastructure, and land use is the first step toward making those choices well.

For readers who want to learn more, useful starting points include national and regional transportation agencies, university urban planning programs, and international organizations that publish research on sustainable urban mobility. Many cities also publish their own plans and progress reports, which offer concrete examples of how these ideas are being applied.

Naomi Long, the Northern Irish politician and leader of the Alliance Party, has built a political career marked by persistence, reinvention, and a notable ability to withstand sustained public attacks. Born in Belfast, Long entered politics during a period when Northern Ireland was still working through the lingering divisions of the Troubles, and her rise has been shaped by the region's complex politics of identity and power.

Long first came to prominence as a councillor on Belfast City Council, where she developed a reputation for pragmatic, locally focused work. Her early career demonstrated a willingness to engage across the community divide, a stance that set her apart in a political landscape still largely organized around unionist and nationalist blocs.

She was elected to the Westminster Parliament as the MP for Belfast East in 2010, a seat she held until 2017 when she stepped down from the Commons to focus on her role in the Northern Ireland Assembly and her party's wider strategy. That decision reflected her commitment to devolved government and to the institutions established under the Good Friday Agreement.

Her path has not been without setbacks. Long faced electoral challenges and periods when the wider political climate turned against the centrist and cross-community positions she championed. Like many politicians in Northern Ireland, she has had to navigate a polarized environment in which moderate voices can struggle to gain ground.

Long has also been the target of personal attacks, including criticism aimed at her character, her record, and her decisions. Political opponents and commentators have at times questioned her motives, and the scrutiny that comes with high office has been intense. Observers note that she has generally responded by returning to policy substance rather than engaging in the sharpest rhetorical exchanges.

Supporters point to this approach as evidence of composure under pressure. They argue that her focus on constituency concerns, public services, and the practical functioning of government has helped her maintain credibility even among those who disagree with her politics.

Long's leadership of the Alliance Party has been central to her public profile. Under her direction, the party has sought to broaden its appeal and to position itself as a voice for those who reject sectarian politics. The party's growth in recent election cycles has been widely noted as a sign of shifting attitudes among some voters.

Her tenure has also involved efforts to address divisive issues in Northern Ireland, including questions of identity, culture, and the future of power-sharing arrangements. Long has consistently argued that the region's institutions must function for everyone, a message that has resonated with some constituencies and drawn criticism from others.

Critics have argued that her centrist approach can leave the party caught between competing camps. Others contend that a middle-ground stance is precisely what Northern Ireland needs to move beyond entrenched divisions. This debate reflects broader arguments about whether consensus politics can deliver lasting change.

Long's resilience has been tested not only by political rivals but also by the wider pressures of public life, including the demands on her time and the strain of constant media attention. Those close to her describe a determination to keep the focus on the work rather than on the noise surrounding it.

As Northern Ireland continues to navigate its political future, Long's career offers a lens through which to view the challenges facing moderate politicians in the region. Her journey illustrates both the obstacles to cross-community politics and the enduring appeal of a pragmatic, inclusive approach to governance.

Looking ahead, the question for Long and her party is whether their steady, consensus-oriented message can translate into sustained electoral gains and meaningful influence over the direction of Northern Irish politics. Her record suggests a politician who values endurance, and whatever the outcome of future contests, her ability to weather difficult periods has already become a defining feature of her public career.

The manuscript addresses a timely problem: reducing the parameter count of recurrent neural networks through tensor-train decomposition of their weight matrices, with the decomposition ranks adapted during training via Riemannian optimization on the manifold of fixed-rank tensor-train tensors. The motivation is clearly stated, and the authors correctly situate their work relative to prior low-rank compression methods for recurrent architectures, though the related work section would benefit from a more explicit comparison with existing Riemannian and tensor-train training approaches. The core idea of treating the tensor-train cores as points on a quotient manifold and performing retraction-based updates is sound and well motivated, and the derivation of the Riemannian gradient in the appendix appears correct on inspection. However, the adaptive rank mechanism, which increases or decreases ranks according to a singular value threshold, is described only at a high level, and the authors should specify the threshold schedule, the frequency of rank updates, and how rank changes interact with the momentum state of the optimizer. The experiments cover language modeling and sequence classification benchmarks, which is a reasonable choice, but the reported compression ratios are given without the corresponding parameter counts or FLOP measurements, making it difficult to judge the practical efficiency gains. Baseline coverage is incomplete: the comparison omits strong recent pruning and quantization methods that would offer a more demanding reference point. The reported accuracy degradation is small, yet the results table lacks variance estimates across random seeds, so it is unclear whether the differences from the baselines are statistically meaningful. The ablation studying fixed versus adaptive ranks is a useful contribution and supports the central claim that adaptation improves the accuracy-compression tradeoff, though more configurations would strengthen this conclusion. The authors provide code, which is commendable and will aid reproducibility, but the hyperparameter search procedure for the baselines is not described, raising questions about fairness of the comparison. The discussion of computational overhead from the retraction and projection steps is brief and should quantify wall-clock training time relative to standard training. Several notational inconsistencies appear between the main text and the algorithm box, particularly in the indexing of the TT-cores, and these should be corrected before publication. The limitations section acknowledges the restriction to a single recurrent architecture but does not discuss sensitivity to initialization of the tensor-train ranks. Overall the paper presents a technically interesting and potentially useful method with a coherent theoretical basis. Its empirical claims are promising but currently under-supported, and I recommend a major revision addressing the baseline comparison, statistical reporting, efficiency measurements, and clarity of the adaptive rank procedure.

India has suspended defence contracts with Rolls-Royce amid an investigation into alleged bribery connected to an aircraft-engine deal, officials said. The move marks a significant escalation in scrutiny of one of the British manufacturer's long-standing relationships with the Indian military. Government sources said the suspension would remain in place while investigators examine the allegations, which centre on payments linked to the procurement of engines. Rolls-Royce has been a supplier to India's defence establishment for decades, providing engines for a range of aircraft and maritime platforms. Officials familiar with the matter said the probe was prompted by concerns raised over the conduct of certain intermediaries involved in past transactions. The company has previously faced allegations of improper payments in several markets, and it has said it takes such matters seriously and cooperates with investigations. Industry analysts noted that the suspension could affect ongoing maintenance and support work, as well as pending bids for future programmes. Defence procurement officials said alternative arrangements were being assessed to ensure that operational readiness is not compromised. Opposition figures called for a transparent inquiry and urged authorities to publish the findings once the investigation is complete. Legal experts said the case would likely turn on documentary evidence of payments and the role of agents in securing the original contracts. Rolls-Royce did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the latest development. Diplomatic observers said the matter could also weigh on trade and defence cooperation between India and the United Kingdom. Investigators are expected to review contract records, financial transfers and correspondence spanning several years. No charges have been announced at this stage, and officials cautioned that the allegations remain unproven. The government said it would share further details when the examination reaches a conclusion. The outcome of the probe will be closely watched by other foreign suppliers operating in India's defence sector.

A new attack in Jakarta has renewed concern about the direction of militancy in Indonesia, with investigators pointing to a generation of attackers who appear younger and less experienced than those behind earlier bombings in the country. Officials said the assailants showed limited training and planning compared with militants of the early 2000s, when networks linked to regional groups carried out coordinated and deadly strikes. Security analysts say the change reflects both the weakening of established extremist organizations and the effect of years of sustained police operations. Counterterrorism units have arrested large numbers of suspected militants over the past decade, many of them tied to older networks that once trained and financed attackers. Those arrests, analysts argue, have disrupted the pipelines that used to move recruits through camps, safe houses, and bomb-making workshops. As a result, a growing share of would-be attackers appear to act with minimal guidance, sometimes radicalized online and sometimes through small informal circles of friends. Police said that surveillance of known extremist figures, financial tracking, and monitoring of communication channels have made it harder for plotters to coordinate across cities. Several recent incidents were stopped before they could be carried out, which officials cited as evidence that intelligence gathering has improved. Still, the Jakarta attack showed that gaps remain, particularly when individuals with no prior criminal records slip past monitoring. Investigators are examining the backgrounds of the attackers, including their online activity, family histories, and any contact with known militant figures. Preliminary findings suggest that at least some of the suspects had limited formal education and little experience with weapons or explosives. That profile has prompted debate among experts about whether the threat is shrinking or simply becoming harder to detect. Some warn that loosely organized individuals can be just as dangerous as trained operatives, since they can strike with fewer warning signs. Others argue that the lack of sophistication means that the attacks are less likely to cause mass casualties. Community leaders and religious figures have also been drawn into the discussion, with many calling for expanded programs aimed at young people susceptible to extremist messaging. Some local governments have begun funding outreach initiatives that work with families, schools, and former militants to challenge violent ideas. Officials say these efforts are essential because enforcement alone cannot address the underlying grievances and online influences that draw recruits in. Human rights advocates have urged that any expanded surveillance be carefully limited by legal safeguards to prevent abuse. Within the government, there is recognition that balancing security with civil liberties will remain a difficult task. The Jakarta attack has also intensified scrutiny of how online platforms handle extremist content. Researchers note that digital spaces allow isolated individuals to find propaganda, instructions, and a sense of belonging without ever meeting an organized group. Pressure is mounting on technology companies to remove such material more quickly and to cooperate with authorities. Meanwhile, the victims and their families are receiving support from government agencies and charities. Authorities have pledged a thorough investigation and promised to share findings as they become available. For now, police say the city remains on heightened alert while they work to determine whether the attackers had any links to wider networks.

Subject: Wholesale Electricity Price Indices and Trading Volumes for November 5, 2001

Hello team,

I am writing to share a summary of wholesale electricity price indices and trading volumes for delivery on November 5, 2001. The purpose of this note is to give everyone a consistent reference point for the day's market activity.

Trading for this delivery date was conducted across the usual forward and day-ahead markets, with activity concentrated in the peak and off-peak blocks. Overall liquidity was moderate, reflecting the seasonal shift into lower-demand conditions in early November.

Price indices for the peak block settled noticeably above the off-peak block, which is consistent with the typical daily load pattern. Peak prices were driven primarily by evening demand, when heating loads began to rise and generation availability was tighter.

Off-peak prices remained comparatively stable through the overnight hours. Low demand and adequate baseload generation kept the off-peak index well below the peak level for most of the period.

Forward curve movements over the preceding week had already priced in a modest rise in demand for the delivery date, so the actual settlement was broadly in line with expectations.

Weather was a key factor throughout. Temperatures in the relevant regions were cooler than the seasonal average, which supported heating demand and added upward pressure to the peak index.

Should schools allow students to carry cell phones for safety and communication with parents? This question has become increasingly important as phones have grown from simple devices into constant companions for young people. Supporters argue that phones give students a reliable way to reach their parents in an emergency, whether that is a medical problem, a lost ride, or a situation at school that feels unsafe. In an era when school shootings and other crises have made families anxious, many parents feel more comfortable knowing their child can call or text them at any moment. Phones can also help students coordinate rides, check on younger siblings, and stay in touch with family members after school. Critics, however, point out that phones are a major source of distraction in classrooms, pulling attention away from lessons and toward games, social media, and messages. Teachers often report that phones make it harder to maintain focus and that they interfere with group work and discussion. Phones also create problems with cyberbullying, the sharing of embarrassing images, and cheating during tests. Some researchers suggest that constant access to phones can increase student anxiety, since children may feel pressure to respond to messages at all hours. A reasonable middle path may be to allow phones during non-instructional time, such as before school, during lunch, and after the final bell, while keeping them silenced and stored during class. Schools could also provide an emergency phone in the main office so that students who truly need to contact family can do so without a personal device. This approach respects both the safety concerns of parents and the educational goals of teachers. In the end, the goal should not be to choose between safety and learning but to design policies that protect both. Clear rules, consistent enforcement, and open communication among students, parents, and staff can help make that balance possible.

Officials from the small villages of Dull, Scotland, and Boring, Oregon, have announced they are considering a formal sister-community partnership in an effort to draw more visitors to both towns. The idea was first raised during an informal exchange of letters between local council members earlier this year. Residents of both communities have shown interest in the proposal, which could bring cultural exchanges, joint tourism campaigns, and shared promotional materials. Dull, a village in Perthshire, is best known for its ancient parish church and its association with the Scottish Highlands. Boring, a small community in the Portland metropolitan area, has long drawn curious travelers who stop to photograph its welcome signs. Supporters argue that the shared names offer a lighthearted hook that could attract media attention and encourage people to explore both places. Local business owners in each town have expressed cautious optimism about the potential boost to seasonal trade. Some suggested a joint souvenir line, while others proposed an annual exchange of visiting delegations. Tourism representatives from both regions said a partnership could also help highlight local history, food, and crafts that rarely receive wider recognition. Critics on both sides have questioned whether a novelty pairing can sustain long-term interest without substantial investment. Council members acknowledged those concerns and said any formal agreement would need a clear budget and measurable goals. A preliminary planning committee is expected to meet early next year to review possible terms. The committee will include representatives from local government, the chamber of commerce, and community groups. If approved, the partnership could be formalized through a signed charter. Organizers stressed that the goal is to build genuine friendship and cooperation rather than rely solely on the humor of the town names. Residents hope the effort will bring new visitors, fresh ideas, and renewed pride to both communities.

Remote education offers a valuable lifeline for students who struggle to attend school in person. Students dealing with serious illness often miss weeks or months of class, and online learning allows them to keep pace with their peers without being physically present in a classroom. A student recovering from surgery or managing a chronic condition can join lessons from a hospital bed or from home, reducing the fear of falling behind. Bullying is another reason some students feel unsafe at school, and remote learning can provide a sense of security by removing them from the environment where they are being harmed. Learning from home allows these students to focus on their studies rather than on avoiding a tormentor in the hallway or cafeteria. Remote education also gives students flexibility in how and when they learn, which can be essential for those whose health or emotional wellbeing fluctuates from day to day. Recorded lessons can be paused and revisited, and assignments can often be completed on a schedule that fits a student's energy levels. Online platforms also make it easier for students to communicate privately with teachers, which can encourage those who feel too anxious to speak up in a crowded classroom. Many students facing challenges at school find it easier to ask questions through a message than to raise their hand in front of others. Remote education can also keep students connected to their school community through virtual clubs, counseling sessions, and group projects. This connection helps prevent the isolation that often accompanies illness or bullying. Of course, remote learning is not a perfect solution, and it requires reliable internet access, a quiet place to study, and support from parents and staff. Schools must ensure that these students are not left behind by those gaps in access. When these conditions are met, however, remote education can transform a difficult situation into an opportunity to keep learning. In the end, it offers students a path to education that protects their health and dignity while preserving their future.

The rain had stopped by the time Mara reached the edge of the city, and the silence felt heavier than the storm had been. Vines wound up the sides of the office towers like green rope, and birches pushed through the cracks in the avenues. She climbed through a shattered lobby window and found a dry room on the fourth floor, where a faded sofa sat beneath a skylight choked with moss. She ate the last of her dried apricots and listened. Birds called somewhere far below, and water dripped steadily through the ceiling tiles. As the light faded, she built a small fire in an old metal waste bin and watched the shadows stretch across the walls. Something rustled in the corridor outside, then went still. She told herself it was a fox, or the wind moving loose paper. She checked the door latch twice and wedged a steel chair beneath the handle. Near midnight, she woke to a faint scraping sound, slow and deliberate, like fingernails drawn along concrete. She held her breath and reached for the knife at her belt. The scraping paused, then started again, moving closer to her door. She saw no light beneath it and heard no footsteps, only that patient, dragging rhythm. Her heart pounded so loudly she feared it would give her away. Then, just as suddenly, the sound stopped entirely. For a long time she waited, counting her breaths until the window turned gray with dawn. When she finally eased the door open, the corridor was empty, though the dust on the floor bore a trail of marks that led to the stairwell. She followed them down with her knife raised, but at the bottom the trail simply vanished into a tangle of roots. Outside, the morning sun touched the ruined towers, and Mara understood that the city was not as empty as it appeared. She shouldered her pack and walked toward the open country, never once looking back.

Abe had hoped the G7 would endorse a joint commitment to boost spending as a way to shore up a global economy that he argued was losing momentum. Several European leaders and officials were reluctant to adopt such a pledge, citing concerns about public debt levels and the risks of additional government borrowing. The discussions, held on the sidelines of the summit, reflected a growing divide among advanced economies over how best to respond to slowing growth. Abe has argued that raising the sales tax, currently scheduled to rise from 8 percent to 10 percent, could derail a fragile recovery in Japan. Officials close to the prime minister have said he is weighing whether to postpone the increase, a decision that would require careful justification to voters and markets. Critics of a delay warn that Japan's public debt, already among the largest in the developed world, could grow even faster without fiscal discipline. Supporters counter that consumer spending has weakened since the last tax hike and that the economy needs more time to gain traction. Market analysts said the outcome of the G7 talks underscored the limits of Abe's economic agenda on the international stage. Government officials insisted that Japan would continue to pursue its own measures regardless of the summit's outcome. They said a final decision on the consumption tax would be made after reviewing the latest economic data in the coming months. For now, the failed push leaves Abe with a difficult balancing act between fiscal responsibility and the political imperative of sustaining growth.

Choosing Nutritious Dog Food and Treats: A Practical Guide

Feeding your dog well starts with understanding what goes into their bowl. Good nutrition supports healthy skin, strong muscles, steady energy, and a long life. This guide explains how to evaluate ingredients, mineral balance, and nutrient content so you can make informed choices.

Start by reading the ingredient list, which manufacturers must present in descending order by weight as it was added to the food. Ingredients listed first make up the largest share of the product, so a named animal protein such as chicken, beef, or salmon near the top is a good sign. Be cautious when the first few items are mostly grains or fillers, since these tend to provide less biologically useful protein.

Look for specific ingredient names rather than vague terms. "Chicken meal" or "salmon" is more transparent than "meat by-products" or "animal digest," which do not tell you the source. Whole foods such as sweet potatoes, peas, carrots, and blueberries can add fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants, though they should complement rather than replace a quality protein source.

Pay attention to the guaranteed analysis on the label, which lists minimum protein and fat and maximum fiber and moisture. These numbers are a starting point but do not fully describe nutritional value, because two foods with identical protein percentages can differ greatly in digestibility and amino acid profile.

Moisture content can distort comparisons between products. Wet food often contains 75 to 82 percent water, while dry kibble typically contains around 10 percent. A canned food that looks higher in protein may actually be similar to a dry food once water is removed.

To compare fairly, convert both products to a dry-matter basis. First subtract the moisture percentage from 100 to find the dry-matter fraction. Then divide each nutrient percentage by that fraction and multiply by 100. For example, a canned food listing 10 percent protein and 78 percent moisture has a dry-matter protein of 10 divided by 22, or about 45 percent, while a dry kibble with 26 percent protein and 10 percent moisture has about 29 percent on a dry-matter basis.

Dry-matter comparisons are especially useful when deciding between food types or when evaluating a diet switch. They reveal the true nutrient density you are feeding, which matters for puppies, senior dogs, and dogs with specific health needs.

Mineral balance is equally important. Calcium and phosphorus must be present in the right ratio, generally between about 1:1 and 2:1 for adult dogs, because imbalances can contribute to skeletal problems over time. Puppies and large-breed dogs are particularly sensitive to excess calcium, which can disrupt normal bone development.

Excess supplementation can be as harmful as deficiency. Adding calcium to a complete diet, or feeding large amounts of bone-based products, can upset the balance. Unless your veterinarian recommends a supplement, a commercially balanced complete food is generally the safest approach.

Trace minerals such as zinc, copper, iron, manganese, and selenium also need to be balanced. Zinc and copper, for instance, interact with each other, and both can cause problems when given in excess. Reputable manufacturers formulate to established nutrient profiles, so choosing foods that state compliance with AAFCO nutrient profiles is a helpful signal.

Look for a statement on the label indicating that the food is complete and balanced for a specific life stage, such as growth, adult maintenance, or all life stages. This statement confirms the product was formulated to meet defined nutritional standards or was tested through feeding trials.

Life stage matters. Puppies need higher levels of protein, calcium, and calories to support rapid growth, while senior dogs may benefit from adjusted calories, joint support, and easily digestible protein. Choose a formula appropriate to your dog's age, size, and activity level.

Calorie needs vary widely. Active working dogs require substantially more energy than sedentary companions, and small breeds typically have a higher calorie requirement per pound of body weight. Use the calorie information on the package, often given in kilocalories per cup or per can, to plan portions carefully.

Treats deserve the same scrutiny as meals. Treats should generally make up no more than about 10 percent of daily calories, so the remaining 90 percent should come from a complete diet. Excessive treats are a common cause of unintended weight gain in dogs.

Check treat ingredient lists using the same principles as food. Simple treats with recognizable ingredients, such as single-ingredient dried meat, plain vegetables, or freeze-dried protein, are often a good choice. Avoid treats heavy in sugar, salt, artificial colors, or unnecessary additives.

Be mindful of foods that are toxic to dogs. Grapes and raisins, onions, garlic, chocolate, xylitol-sweetened products, and macadamia nuts should never be given as treats. If your dog has eaten any of these, contact your veterinarian promptly.

Consider your dog's individual health. Dogs with allergies, kidney disease, pancreatitis, or heart conditions may need prescription or therapeutic diets. Always consult your veterinarian before making major dietary changes for a dog with a medical condition.

When switching foods, transition gradually over seven to ten days. Mix a small proportion of the new food into the old, increasing the new portion each day. This helps prevent digestive upset and allows you to observe how your dog responds.

Monitor your dog's body condition regularly. You should be able to feel the ribs with light pressure, see a visible waist from above, and notice a tucked abdomen from the side. Adjust portions if your dog is gaining or losing weight unexpectedly.

Watch for signs that a food may not agree with your dog. Persistent itching, ear infections, chronic gas, loose stools, or dull coat can all indicate an intolerance or allergy. Keep notes on changes and share them with your veterinarian.

Store food properly to preserve nutrients and prevent spoilage. Keep dry food in its original bag inside an airtight container in a cool, dry place, and use it within the period recommended after opening. Refrigerate opened canned food in a sealed container and use it within a few days.

Price does not always reflect quality, and expensive labels do not guarantee better nutrition. Focus on the criteria discussed here, including named protein sources, complete and balanced statements, appropriate life-stage formulation, and sound mineral ratios, rather than marketing claims.

Be cautious with trendy claims such as grain-free, raw, or boutique diets. Grain-free diets have been linked in some studies to heart disease in dogs, and raw diets carry risks of bacterial contamination. Discuss any unusual diet with your veterinarian before committing to it.

Your veterinarian is your best partner in selecting a diet. They can evaluate your dog's health, body condition, and lifestyle, and recommend specific products or adjustments. Regular checkups allow early detection of problems that diet may influence.

In summary, choose foods with clearly named ingredients, compare products on a dry-matter basis, confirm mineral balance and a complete and balanced statement, match the formula to your dog's life stage, and keep treats to a small portion of daily calories. With these principles, you can make confident decisions that support your dog's health for years to come.

This paper investigates how gradients propagate through deep neural networks, with particular attention to the interplay between skip connections and initialization strategies. The authors frame the problem clearly, situating vanishing and exploding gradients within the broader literature on training very deep architectures. The theoretical analysis of signal propagation under different initialization schemes is a strength, as it provides concrete variance-based arguments rather than relying solely on empirical observation. The derivation of conditions under which residual connections preserve gradient magnitude across layers is well organized and easy to follow. However, several of the key assumptions, such as independence of activations and linearity near initialization, are stated but not sufficiently justified for the non-linear regimes where the networks are actually trained. The experiments cover a reasonable range of depths and architectures, but they are limited to image classification benchmarks, which leaves open whether the conclusions transfer to sequence modeling or other domains. The comparison against baseline initializations would be more convincing with multiple random seeds and reported variance, since several of the reported improvements are small relative to the apparent noise. The ablation study isolating the contribution of skip connections from that of initialization is a valuable addition, though the authors should clarify how learning rate schedules were tuned for each configuration. The discussion of computational overhead is brief, and a more explicit accounting of training time and memory costs would help practitioners judge the trade-offs. The related work section is thorough but would benefit from engaging more directly with normalization-based approaches, which often address the same gradient stability concerns. Figures are generally clear, although the gradient norm plots would be more informative on a log scale with per-layer breakdowns. The writing is precise, with only minor issues in notation consistency between the theory and experimental sections. Overall, the paper makes a useful contribution, and I recommend minor revisions addressing the assumptions, statistical reporting, and scope of the empirical evaluation.

This paper addresses an important problem: reducing the computational and memory cost of neural networks by training models with binary activations and weights. The authors propose a probabilistic training scheme that treats binary parameters as stochastic variables, which allows gradient-based optimization to proceed despite the non-differentiability of binarization. The motivation is clearly stated, and the connection to hardware efficiency, particularly for edge devices where bitwise operations are cheap, is well argued. The theoretical framing of the stochastic binarization is a strength, as it gives the method a principled basis rather than relying solely on heuristic straight-through estimators. However, the experimental section would benefit from a more thorough comparison against recent quantization baselines, since several competing methods report strong accuracy at similar bit widths. The paper would also be stronger with ablations isolating the contribution of the probabilistic component from other design choices, such as the choice of scaling factors or the learning rate schedule. Reported speedups are given in terms of theoretical operation counts, and actual wall-clock measurements on target hardware would make the efficiency claims more convincing. The discussion of variance in the gradient estimator is brief, and a more detailed analysis of how sampling noise affects convergence would be valuable. Overall, the work is a useful contribution, and I recommend minor revisions that add stronger baselines, ablations, and empirical timing results.

A wedge-tailed eagle has become the unlikely adversary of a New South Wales farmer after the bird struck and badly damaged his agricultural drone during a crop survey last week. The farmer, who asked not to be named, said he was flying the drone about 30 metres above a paddock when the eagle swooped in and clipped one of the rotors, sending the device spiralling into a fence line. He recovered the drone with a cracked frame and a broken propeller, and no one was hurt. Wedge-tailed eagles are Australia's largest raptors, with wingspans that can exceed two metres, and they are known to defend their territory aggressively, especially during nesting season. Wildlife experts say encounters like this are becoming more common as drones are used more widely for mapping, spraying and livestock monitoring in rural areas. Some birds appear to view drones as rivals or intruders, while others may be curious about the unfamiliar objects. Ornithologists note that the eagle was likely protecting a nearby nest, though they have not confirmed this. Drone operators are being urged to check for active nests before flying and to maintain greater altitude where raptors are known to be present. The farmer said he has since moved his survey flights to early mornings and is considering a visual deterrent for the rotors. Industry groups representing aerial operators say they are working with conservation bodies to develop guidelines that protect both wildlife and the growing drone sector. Meanwhile, the farmer says he is simply relieved the eagle was not seriously injured in the collision. Conservation officials have reminded the public that wedge-tailed eagles are protected under Australian law and should never be harassed or disturbed.
