Polytrichum piliferum is a species of moss in the family Polytrichaceae, commonly known as the bristly haircap moss. It is recognized by its tufted growth form, with dense clusters of upright stems that give the plant a bushy, cushion-like appearance.

The stems of this moss are typically unbranched or sparsely branched and can reach several centimeters in height. The leaves are narrow, lance-shaped, and tightly arranged around the stem, often appearing stiff when dry. A distinctive feature is the long, hair-like point at the tip of each leaf, which gives the species its name "piliferum," meaning hair-bearing.

Like other members of its genus, the leaves have a set of lamellae, or thin plates, on the upper surface along the midrib. These structures help distinguish Polytrichum from many other mosses and are an important aid in careful identification.

The sporophytes, or spore-producing structures, rise on long stalks above the leafy shoots. Each capsule is typically covered by a hairy calyptra, a protective cap derived from the female reproductive tissue, which is a characteristic seen across the haircap mosses.

Polytrichum piliferum is widely distributed across the temperate and boreal regions of the Northern Hemisphere. It is frequently found in the Arctic, mountain areas, and cooler lowland zones.

This species prefers open, sunny or lightly shaded habitats where soils are dry to moderately moist. It commonly colonizes heathlands, dry grasslands, sandy or acidic soils, and disturbed ground such as roadsides and forest clearings.

The moss plays an ecological role in pioneer communities by stabilizing loose soil and contributing to the gradual formation of organic layers. Its dense tufts also help retain moisture and provide shelter for small invertebrates.

When identifying this moss in the field, look first for the robust, tufted habit and the stiff, pointed leaves with hair-like tips. Examining the leaf cross-section or the upper surface under a hand lens will reveal the lamellae that confirm membership in the genus Polytrichum.

Several similar species can be confused with Polytrichum piliferum, including other haircap mosses such as Polytrichum juniperinum and Polytrichum commune. Differences in leaf shape, lamellae count, stem size, and capsule characteristics are the most reliable ways to separate them.

Microscopic examination is often necessary for certain determinations, particularly when specimens are immature or poorly developed. Careful attention to leaf anatomy and the presence or absence of sporophytes can greatly improve accuracy.

Collectors should note the habitat, substrate, and associated plant species when recording specimens. This information supports both accurate identification and broader ecological studies of bryophyte distribution.

Because mosses respond sensitively to environmental change, Polytrichum piliferum can serve as a useful indicator of habitat conditions. Shifts in its abundance may reflect changes in soil chemistry, moisture levels, or disturbance regimes.

Protecting open heathland and dry grassland habitats helps conserve populations of this species. Avoiding trampling and maintaining natural soil conditions are simple steps that support its long-term survival.

For further study, botanical field guides, bryophyte keys, and regional herbarium collections provide reliable reference material. Engaging with local naturalist groups can also offer valuable hands-on learning opportunities.

Whether observed for scientific research or personal interest, Polytrichum piliferum offers an accessible introduction to the diversity and ecology of mosses. Its distinctive form and widespread presence make it a rewarding subject for learners at every level.

This paper investigates whether random weight pruning can improve the robustness of neural networks to adversarial attacks, a question of practical interest given the cost of adversarial training. The authors frame random pruning as a lightweight alternative that removes connections without regard to learned importance, and they hypothesize that the resulting sparser networks are less sensitive to small input perturbations. The motivation is clearly stated and well situated within the existing literature on sparsity and robustness, though the related work section could more directly address prior findings that pruning can sometimes degrade robustness. The experimental setup evaluates several architectures on standard image benchmarks against common attacks such as FGSM and PGD, which is an appropriate choice for an initial study. However, the paper would benefit from stronger adaptive attacks, since robustness claims based only on fixed attacks can be misleading when the defense is not designed with the attacker in mind. The reported improvements in robust accuracy are modest and, in several configurations, appear to fall within the variance across random seeds, yet the paper does not report confidence intervals or the number of runs. The ablation comparing random pruning against magnitude-based and gradient-based pruning is a valuable addition and helps isolate whether randomness itself contributes to the effect. Nonetheless, the authors should clarify whether the observed gains persist at matched levels of clean accuracy, as a trade-off in clean performance could explain part of the apparent robustness. The theoretical discussion is brief and largely heuristic, and a more formal account of why random sparsity should attenuate adversarial gradients would strengthen the contribution. The writing is generally clear, though some figures lack axis labels and sufficient captions to be interpreted independently. The code and hyperparameters are described at a high level, and releasing the full implementation would greatly improve reproducibility. The discussion of limitations is minimal and should be expanded to address transferability of the findings to larger models and datasets. It would also help to test whether the method generalizes beyond image classification to other domains such as natural language or tabular data. The paper's central claim is plausible and potentially useful, but it currently rests on evidence that is not yet sufficient to establish it firmly. Overall, I recommend a major revision, with the primary requests being adaptive attack evaluation, statistical reporting across seeds, and a clearer analysis of the clean-accuracy trade-off. With these additions, the work could make a meaningful contribution to the study of efficient robustness methods.

I don't have the full text of this specific paper, so I can't review its actual claims, experiments, or figures. What follows is a review written against the title and the general methods it describes, framed as a reviewer's assessment of what such a paper would need to demonstrate. Treat it as a template to be checked against the real manuscript.

The paper addresses high-resolution autoregressive image generation, a problem where sequential pixel-by-pixel modeling becomes prohibitively expensive as image size grows. The authors propose two ideas: a multiscale pixel ordering, which generates coarse structure before fine detail, and progressive color-bit modeling, which predicts the most significant bits of each channel before the least significant ones. Both ideas are well motivated, since they reduce the effective sequence length and align the generation order with how humans perceive images. The overall framing of the problem is clear and the contribution is easy to identify. The novelty relative to prior work on multiscale and hierarchical autoregressive models should be stated more explicitly, because coarse-to-fine generation has appeared in several earlier lines of research. The authors should clarify which component is responsible for the gains, since two simultaneous changes make attribution difficult. An ablation isolating the multiscale ordering from the bit-level progression would substantially strengthen the empirical section. The method description would benefit from a precise formalization of the ordering, including how conditioning dependencies are defined across scales. Notation is mostly consistent, though a few symbols are reused for different quantities in the methods and experiments sections. The figures illustrating the generation order are helpful, but an additional visualization of intermediate samples at each scale and bit level would make the mechanism far easier to follow. The experimental setup should specify the datasets, resolutions, model sizes, and training budgets used for each comparison. Fair comparison with baselines requires matched parameter counts and compute, and the paper should state whether this was controlled. Reported metrics such as FID and likelihood measures should be accompanied by confidence intervals or results over multiple seeds. The inference cost of the proposed ordering should be reported directly, including wall-clock sampling time, since fewer sequential steps do not necessarily translate into faster sampling. A discussion of memory requirements at high resolution would also be valuable, given that memory is often the binding constraint. The results on the largest resolution are the most important evidence for the paper's central claim, so their presentation deserves particular care. The authors should report failure cases or regimes where the method underperforms, which would increase confidence in the conclusions. Qualitative samples are presented, but the selection procedure for those samples should be disclosed to rule out cherry-picking. The related work section covers the main autoregressive image models but could address diffusion-based high-resolution methods more thoroughly, since those are the principal competitors. A comparison against a strong diffusion baseline would be informative even if the autoregressive approach does not win on every metric. The limitations section is brief and should address dependence on the chosen ordering, potential artifacts at scale boundaries, and generalization beyond the training distribution. The code and trained models should be released or the level of detail should be sufficient for reproduction. Hyperparameter choices are listed, but the sensitivity of results to the number of scales and bit levels is not explored and should be. Overall, the paper presents a promising and sensibly motivated direction, and its acceptance depends on whether the ablations, compute-matched comparisons, and reproducibility details support the claims. With those additions, the work would be a useful contribution to efficient high-resolution generative modeling. I recommend a major revision before the manuscript can be considered for publication.

Choosing a career is one of the largest decisions a person will make, yet many teenagers are asked to commit to a future path before they have had any real chance to discover who they are. Allowing young people time to explore their interests before settling on a career path is therefore not a luxury but a practical necessity. Adolescence is a period of rapid growth, during which personal values, talents, and passions take shape in ways that cannot always be predicted. A student who declares an intention to become an engineer at fourteen may later find that her real fascination lies in storytelling, music, or community health. Without room to experiment, that discovery may come years later, often at considerable financial and emotional cost. Exploration allows teenagers to test their assumptions against real experiences rather than relying on guesses or the expectations of others. Trying a part-time job, joining a club, volunteering, or taking an unfamiliar class can reveal strengths and dislikes that no aptitude test could capture. Such experiences also teach valuable skills, including resilience, adaptability, and the ability to learn from failure. Critics sometimes argue that a late start will leave young people behind their peers, but this view overlooks how quickly people can build new skills when they are motivated by a genuine interest. Many successful professionals changed direction in their twenties or thirties, bringing with them broader perspectives that enriched their work. Early specialization can also narrow opportunities, since a rigid plan may close doors that a more flexible approach would keep open. Schools have an important role to play in supporting this exploration by offering a wide range of courses, mentorship programs, and career counseling that encourages curiosity rather than premature decisions. Parents and teachers can help most by asking open questions about what students enjoy and why, rather than pressing them toward a predetermined outcome. Exploration does not mean drifting aimlessly, and students still benefit from setting goals and reflecting on their progress. The aim is to create a balance between direction and discovery, so that young people move toward a future they have chosen with knowledge rather than fear. A choice made after genuine exploration is more likely to sustain motivation through the difficulties that every career involves. Ultimately, giving teenagers time to explore is an investment in their long-term well-being as well as in the broader society that will benefit from their diverse talents. Careers chosen with care tend to be more satisfying, and satisfied workers tend to be more productive and resilient. For these reasons, society should treat exploration not as a delay but as the foundation of a thoughtful and fulfilling working life.

Problem solving is more than finding the right answer quickly; it is a process that builds lasting understanding. When students learn to define a problem clearly, they first identify what is known, what is unknown, and what the goal actually is. Next, encourage them to explore several possible approaches rather than settling on the first idea that comes to mind. Teachers can prompt this exploration with questions such as "What else could we try?" or "How would this look if we approached it differently?" Comparing approaches helps students see that many paths can lead to a solution and that each has strengths and trade-offs. Mistakes and dead ends should be treated as valuable information that reveals misunderstandings and sharpens reasoning. Praising effort, strategy, and persistence, not just correct answers, signals that the process itself matters. Over time, students who practice this way develop confidence, flexibility, and the habit of reflecting on how they solved a problem. These skills prepare them not only for tests but for real-world challenges where the right answer is not obvious at the start.

Unusual Edible Plants and Fruit Trees for Compact Spaces and Indoor Growing

Growing food does not require a large garden. Many unusual edible plants and fruit trees can thrive in small balconies, windowsills, patios, and even indoor rooms with good light. Choosing the right species and giving them proper care makes it possible to harvest fresh, distinctive food year-round.

Dwarf citrus trees, such as Meyer lemon, calamondin, and Kumquat, are among the most popular choices for indoor growing. They stay compact, produce fragrant blossoms, and bear fruit when given bright light and consistent watering. Calamondin, a small citrus hybrid, is especially tolerant of container life.

Fig trees bred for containers, such as Little Miss Figgy and Petite Negra, can be kept small through regular pruning. They need full sun for several hours a day and a pot with good drainage.

Pineapple guava, also called feijoa, is a shrub with edible flowers and sweet, aromatic fruit. It grows well in large pots and tolerates cooler temperatures better than many tropical fruits.

Dwarf pomegranate varieties offer bright red fruit and ornamental flowers on a shrub that rarely exceeds three feet in a container. They prefer hot, dry conditions and a sunny location.

Goji berry, or wolfberry, is a hardy shrub that produces clusters of red berries. It can be grown in a large container and tolerates some neglect, though it benefits from support as it grows.

Strawberry plants grown in hanging baskets or vertical towers are a practical choice for small spaces. Alpine varieties produce small, intensely flavored fruit and can be grown indoors near a bright window.

Microgreens, including radish, sunflower shoots, and pea shoots, are harvested within about two weeks of sowing. They need only shallow trays, a growing medium, and steady light.

Sprouting seeds such as mung beans, lentils, and alfalfa require no soil at all. They can be grown in a jar with water and rinsed twice daily, producing crisp food in three to five days.

Ginger and turmeric rhizomes grow well in deep pots indoors. They prefer warm, humid conditions and indirect light, and they are harvested by digging up the underground stems once the foliage begins to die back.

Chili peppers, especially ornamental varieties like Thai and Hungarian types, can be grown in pots on a sunny windowsill. Their colorful fruits and compact shape make them both useful and decorative.

Dwarf banana varieties, such as Dwarf Cavendish, can fruit in large containers when kept warm and well-fed. They need significant light and humidity to produce fruit, so they are best suited to greenhouses or sunrooms.

Herbs such as basil, mint, and lemongrass are classic container plants. Mint should be grown in its own pot, since it spreads aggressively.

Container growing requires attention to drainage, light, and nutrients. Pots should have drainage holes, and plants should be fed with a balanced fertilizer during active growth.

Light is often the limiting factor indoors. A south-facing window provides the most natural light, and full-spectrum grow lights can supplement it when daylight is insufficient.

Pollination can be a challenge for indoor fruit trees. Gently brushing flowers with a small paintbrush or shaking the branches helps transfer pollen when there are no insects present.

Choosing self-fertile varieties simplifies fruiting, since a single plant can produce fruit without a partner. Many dwarf citrus and some fig varieties are self-fertile.

Regular pruning keeps compact trees within their intended size and encourages better fruit production. Removing crossing or crowded branches improves airflow and light penetration.

Watering should be consistent but not excessive. Allow the top layer of soil to dry slightly between waterings, and check that containers drain freely to prevent root rot.

Repotting every one to three years refreshes the soil and gives roots room to grow. Moving to a container only slightly larger than the current one is usually best.

Pests such as spider mites, scale, and aphids can appear on indoor plants. Regular inspection, wiping leaves, and using insecticidal soap are effective early responses.

Starting with a few plants and learning their needs is a sensible approach. Over time, experience with light, water, and temperature will help you grow a more varied and productive collection.

This manuscript investigates whether a sequence-based representation of molecules, SMILES strings, can be combined with a variational autoencoder to learn a continuous latent space that supports both accurate property prediction and goal-directed molecular design. The authors frame the work as a response to the difficulty of searching discrete chemical space, and the motivation is clearly articulated in the introduction. The premise is timely and relevant to the computational chemistry and machine learning communities. The literature review covers the main prior approaches to SMILES-based generative modeling, although it would benefit from a more explicit discussion of graph-based and fragment-based alternatives that address known shortcomings of string representations. The central methodological contribution is an encoder-decoder architecture trained jointly with a property predictor, which shapes the latent space so that nearby points tend to share chemically relevant properties. The description of the architecture is generally detailed, though several hyperparameters, including the latent dimensionality and the weighting between reconstruction and regression losses, are reported without justification or sensitivity analysis. A recurring concern is the validity of decoded SMILES, and the authors should report validity, uniqueness, and novelty rates alongside the more commonly emphasized metrics. The property prediction experiments use standard public benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the choice of baselines is somewhat narrow and omits several recent strong models. The reported improvements over baselines are modest in some tasks, and the manuscript does not provide confidence intervals or multiple random seeds, making it difficult to judge whether the gains exceed run-to-run variation. The latent-space optimization experiments are the most interesting part of the paper, as they demonstrate that gradient-based or Bayesian optimization in the continuous space can propose candidates with improved target properties. However, the evaluation relies heavily on a single surrogate objective, and the authors should test whether the optimized molecules remain synthetically accessible and drug-like under established scoring functions. The paper would also be strengthened by including a comparison against a simple genetic algorithm operating directly on SMILES, which serves as an important reference point in this field. The qualitative analysis of the latent space, including interpolation and visualization, is helpful for building intuition, but it is presented without quantitative measures of smoothness or continuity. The discussion of limitations is brief and should expand on the dependence of the approach on the training distribution and its tendency to generate molecules outside the domain of the training data. Reproducibility is partially supported by the stated availability of code, but the manuscript should specify the exact data splits, preprocessing steps, and random seeds used. The figures are clear and well labeled, although the caption for the latent-space projection does not state which dimensionality-reduction method was applied. The writing is generally fluent, though some sections repeat claims about novelty that are not fully substantiated by the experiments. The related work section would benefit from clearer positioning of this contribution relative to recent transformer-based and diffusion-based molecular generators. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful problem with a reasonable and interpretable approach, and its core ideas are sound. Its main weaknesses lie in the breadth of baselines, the lack of statistical rigor, and the limited evaluation of the designed molecules, all of which can be addressed in revision. I recommend a major revision, with the expectation that the authors strengthen the empirical evaluation before the work can be considered for publication.

Mucus can turn green or yellow during illness, and the color often reflects what is happening inside your airways. The main cause is white blood cells, especially neutrophils, which travel to the site of an infection to fight invading germs. These cells contain enzymes and pigments, including myeloperoxidase, which give them a greenish or yellowish tint as they accumulate in mucus. Because of this, a change in mucus color usually signals that your immune system is actively responding to an infection, most often a viral or bacterial one. However, color alone cannot reliably tell you whether an infection is bacterial or viral, since colds and flu frequently produce green or yellow mucus without any antibiotic need. Mucus that is lighter yellow usually indicates a mild immune response, while deeper green may reflect a more concentrated accumulation of immune cells. Dehydration or dry air can also darken mucus, so color is only one clue among several. If green or yellow mucus is accompanied by fever lasting more than ten days, shortness of breath, chest pain, or symptoms that worsen after initially improving, you should consult a doctor.

In the year 1981, in a Brooklyn apartment above a shuttered pizzeria, a plumber named Mario Mancini sat at his kitchen table staring at a single sheet of paper that refused to make sense.

He had been hired by the city to calculate the optimal layout of sewer pipes beneath Flatbush, and his numbers had come back with a result that could not possibly be true.

The total length of pipe required, he had found, was exactly negative four hundred meters.

Mario checked his arithmetic. He checked it again. He recalculated using the metric system, then the imperial system, then a method he had learned from a pamphlet at the library, and every time the answer came back the same: negative four hundred meters.

He called his brother Luigi, who worked at the same firm and who was a far more confident man than Mario.

Luigi arrived in a flurry of opinions and a fur coat despite the summer heat. He looked at the paper, laughed, then stopped laughing, then sat down very heavily on a chair.

"This is not possible," Luigi said. "Pipes do not have negative length. Length is a fundamental property of the physical world."

"Then explain it," Mario said.

Luigi could not explain it. Neither could the engineers at the firm, nor the professors at the university, nor the editors of the three journals to which Mario submitted his findings.

The journals rejected the paper on the grounds that it was nonsense. The reviewers, however, could not agree on what kind of nonsense it was. One called it an error of decimal placement. Another called it an insult to Euclid. A third wrote only, in shaking handwriting, "Please stop sending this."

Within a month the city had three separate committees investigating the matter, and none of them could reach a conclusion.

The committee on mathematics said the number was impossible but could not prove it wrong.

The committee on physics said the number was irrelevant because, in their view, nothing had ever really had a length, and the measurements were merely a social agreement.

The committee on the philosophy of science declared that reason itself had collapsed and that the city should consider the matter closed by vote.

It was voted closed. The sewers were dug anyway, by a crew that ignored the paperwork and simply followed the old maps.

Mario, meanwhile, could not stop thinking about the negative number. He began to see it everywhere. The bricks in his building seemed to be missing a few inches. The stairs leading down to the subway had one fewer step than they should. His own shadow sometimes lagged a little behind him on the pavement.

He went to see a priest, who told him that some mysteries were not meant to be solved. He went to see a psychiatrist, who told him that the mystery was in his head. He went to see a fortune teller, who told him that the number was a sign and that he should go to the sewers.

So Mario went to the sewers.

They were dark and damp and smelled of centuries. He walked for hours, guided by a flickering lamp and his own growing certainty that the tunnels were not behaving as tunnels should. Corridors bent back on themselves. Pipes ran uphill and then down again into the same spot. Once he passed a junction where three of the same pipe emerged from one wall, each labeled with the same serial number.

At the bottom of the deepest shaft he found a door made of riveted iron. It bore no handle, only a small plaque reading, in careful engraving, "Here the arithmetic ends."

Mario pushed. The door swung open onto a room lit by no visible source, where a gathering of mathematicians, physicists, and bureaucrats sat in silence around a long table. They all looked up at him with the same tired expression.

"You are the plumber," said a woman at the head of the table. "We have been waiting for someone to notice."

"Notice what?"

"That the pipes were never the point. The negative length is only the first crack. Reason is not a building you can repair with a wrench. It is a bridge, and the bridge has been slowly collapsing for years, and you are standing on the last plank."

Mario looked around the table. The faces were not cruel, only resigned. The room smelled faintly of ink and burnt sugar.

"Then what do we do?" Mario asked.

The woman smiled sadly and pushed a clipboard toward him. On it was a single blank form, labeled in neat letters: Application for Repair of Logic, Department of Impossible Works.

"You fill it out," she said. "And then you go back up and pretend you never came down here. That is what everyone does. It is also, I am afraid, why we are still here."

Mario picked up the pen. He wrote his name, then paused, then wrote a second name beneath it: Luigi.

Above him, faintly, he heard the sound of a pipe ringing as it fell a distance it could not possibly have fallen.

A Venezuelan musician's violin was damaged during recent street demonstrations, prompting an outpouring of public support from fellow artists and citizens. The musician, who had been performing at a protest in the capital, was playing near a gathering of demonstrators when the instrument was broken amid the crowd's movement. Witnesses said the violinist continued to play for several minutes before being forced to stop. Video of the moment circulated widely on social media, drawing sympathy from people across the political spectrum. Within days, local music schools and orchestras announced plans to donate instruments and offer repair assistance. Several well-known Venezuelan artists publicly condemned the damage and called for the protection of cultural expression during public gatherings. Supporters also launched an online fundraising campaign to help cover the cost of repairs and a replacement violin. Many described the musician's performance as a symbol of resilience and of music's role in public life. Letting students design their own summer learning projects offers benefits that a fixed curriculum rarely provides. When students choose what to study, they begin with genuine curiosity, which makes the work feel less like an obligation and more like an adventure. This sense of ownership often leads to deeper engagement, as students are willing to spend extra hours on a question they personally care about. Self-directed projects also teach planning skills, since students must define a goal, break it into manageable steps, and decide how to measure their progress. Along the way, they learn to manage their time without constant supervision, a skill that will serve them well in college and in careers. Failure becomes a more useful teacher in this setting, because a project that goes wrong invites students to reflect on what happened and try a different approach. Many students discover unexpected interests during these projects, sometimes leading to lifelong passions or future career paths they had never considered. Design choices also strengthen critical thinking, as students must evaluate sources, weigh competing ideas, and decide what evidence is good enough to support their conclusions. Collaboration can be part of the process as well, since students who share goals often learn to communicate, negotiate, and share responsibility. Personalized projects allow students with different strengths and learning styles to pursue paths that suit them, rather than being measured against a single standard. Summer, which is free from the pressures of grades and standardized tests, provides a particularly good setting for this kind of exploration. Students can take intellectual risks without fear that a single misstep will harm their academic record. Teachers and mentors still play an important role by offering guidance, asking probing questions, and helping students set realistic expectations. Over time, this kind of learning builds confidence, as students see that they can identify problems worth solving and carry them through to completion. Finally, self-designed projects remind students that learning does not stop when the school year ends. By giving young people the freedom to shape their own summer, schools can cultivate curious, motivated, and independent learners who are prepared for a lifetime of growth.

After-school involvement gives students something that classroom learning alone cannot: a space to grow at their own pace, discover their interests, and test their abilities in a supportive environment. Whether through sports, clubs, music, volunteering, or student government, these activities offer young people chances to step outside their usual routines and take on new challenges. Such experiences matter because they help shape who students become, not only what they know.

Personal growth is one of the most visible benefits of after-school participation. When students commit to a team or a project, they learn to set goals, manage their time, and keep going when things get difficult. A debate club member, for example, must research thoroughly, organize arguments, and respond calmly under pressure. Over time, these habits build confidence, and students begin to see themselves as capable of handling responsibility.

After-school activities also strengthen relationships. Students who spend regular time with teammates, bandmates, or fellow volunteers develop friendships based on shared purpose rather than convenience alone. These bonds often cross the boundaries of grade level, background, and social group, helping students learn to work with people who think differently from them. Strong relationships with peers and adult mentors can also provide emotional support during stressful periods.

Mentorship is another important part of this picture. Coaches, club advisors, and program leaders often serve as trusted adults who offer guidance beyond the subject matter of the activity. A coach may encourage a student to persevere after a loss, while an advisor may help a student think through a difficult decision about college or career. These relationships can make a lasting difference in how young people view their own potential.

Involvement also prepares students for future opportunities. Colleges and employers often look for evidence of initiative, leadership, and teamwork, and sustained participation in extracurricular activities provides that evidence. Beyond applications, the skills students practice after school, such as communication, collaboration, and problem-solving, transfer directly to academic and professional settings. Students who learn to lead a small team or plan an event gain experience that will serve them for years.

Not every student has equal access to these opportunities, however. Transportation, family obligations, and cost can keep some young people from participating, and schools and communities should work to remove these barriers. Offering free programs, providing transportation, and scheduling activities at times that fit students' lives can help ensure that the benefits reach everyone who wants them.

In the end, after-school involvement is not simply a way to fill the hours between school and home. It is an investment in students' character, their relationships, and their futures. When young people are given meaningful ways to contribute and connect, they leave these experiences more confident, more capable, and better prepared for the world ahead.

Late Pulmonary Metastasis of Eccrine Sweat Gland Carcinoma: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

Abstract

Eccrine sweat gland carcinoma is a rare malignant adnexal tumor of the skin, and late recurrence or distant metastasis is uncommon but clinically important. We describe a patient in whom pulmonary metastasis developed approximately one decade after surgical excision of a primary eccrine carcinoma. The case highlights the need for prolonged surveillance in patients with this diagnosis and reviews the relevant literature.

Introduction

Eccrine sweat gland carcinoma (ESGC) is a rare cutaneous malignancy arising from the secretory or ductal components of eccrine sweat glands. It accounts for a very small fraction of skin cancers, and its incidence is difficult to establish precisely because of its rarity and frequent misclassification in earlier series. The tumor most often presents as a slowly enlarging, sometimes ulcerated nodule on the head, neck, or extremities, and it may be mistaken for more common lesions such as basal cell carcinoma or pyogenic granuloma. Histologically, ESGC displays a range of architectural patterns, and the diagnosis relies on careful morphologic evaluation supported by immunohistochemistry. Historically, the prognosis was considered guarded, with local recurrence and regional nodal spread reported in a meaningful proportion of cases. Distant metastasis, particularly to the lungs, is documented but infrequent. The timing of metastasis is also variable, and the literature contains reports of recurrence occurring many years after initial treatment. This temporal pattern has important implications for follow-up strategies, which are not yet standardized. We report a case of pulmonary metastasis occurring roughly ten years after surgical removal of a primary ESGC, and we discuss its implications for long-term monitoring.

Case Presentation

A patient was initially treated surgically for a cutaneous eccrine sweat gland carcinoma approximately ten years before the presentation described here. The primary tumor was excised with margins that were reported as clear at the time of the original procedure. Follow-up during the early postoperative years was reported as unremarkable, and no clinical or radiologic evidence of recurrence was identified during that interval. The patient subsequently returned with respiratory symptoms that prompted diagnostic imaging. Chest computed tomography demonstrated one or more pulmonary nodules, some of which showed increasing size on serial assessment. Further evaluation was undertaken to determine the nature of these lesions and to exclude a second primary malignancy. Tissue sampling was pursued, and the pulmonary lesion was examined histologically. Morphologic features were considered in comparison with the original primary tumor, and immunohistochemical profiling was used to support the diagnosis of metastatic eccrine carcinoma. The concordance of the pulmonary tissue with the prior cutaneous specimen was judged to be consistent with metastatic disease rather than an independent primary lung neoplasm. The patient was then referred to a multidisciplinary team for management planning. Treatment decisions considered the extent of pulmonary involvement, the patient's overall condition, and the available therapeutic options for metastatic adnexal carcinoma. The clinical course following these decisions is summarized in the subsequent sections.

Pathological Findings

Histological examination of the primary cutaneous tumor had shown a neoplasm composed of nests and cords of atypical epithelial cells with infiltrative growth into the dermis. Areas of ductal differentiation and cytologic atypia were noted, and mitotic activity was present. In the pulmonary specimen, the tumor cells exhibited comparable architectural and cytologic features. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for markers of epithelial and glandular differentiation, supporting a sweat gland origin. The pattern of staining was reviewed alongside the primary tumor, which aided in establishing the metastatic relationship. Care was taken to exclude other entities that can present with similar morphology in the lung, including adenocarcinoma of other sites and metastatic carcinoma from unrelated primaries. The overall pathological assessment favored metastatic eccrine sweat gland carcinoma. We emphasize that accurate pathological correlation with the original lesion is essential, since definitive attribution of metastasis depends on comparing histology and immunoprofile across specimens. Limitations of the available archival material, including the age of the primary specimen, were acknowledged in the interpretation.

Discussion

The present case illustrates that eccrine sweat gland carcinoma can recur or metastasize long after apparently curative excision. Pulmonary dissemination is a recognized pattern of distant spread in this tumor, and our observation of a metastasis presenting approximately a decade after surgery underscores that the risk does not necessarily dissipate within the first few years. Prior reports have described recurrences and metastases occurring over extended intervals, though the total number of documented cases remains small, limiting the strength of conclusions that can be drawn. The mechanisms underlying such prolonged latency are not well understood, and possibilities include dormancy of disseminated tumor cells, microenvironmental factors that permit later outgrowth, and incomplete initial clearance that was undetectable at the time of surgery. Prognostic factors associated with adverse outcomes in ESGC have been proposed in the literature, including tumor size, depth of invasion, lymphovascular involvement, and high mitotic rate, but these have not been validated in large prospective cohorts. Treatment of metastatic disease is complicated by the rarity of the tumor, which means that evidence derives largely from case reports and small series. Options reported in the literature include surgical resection where feasible, systemic chemotherapy regimens borrowed from other carcinomas, and, in selected cases, radiotherapy for symptom control. Given the absence of tumor-specific trials, decisions must be individualized. Our case supports a clinical recommendation for extended surveillance of patients with eccrine carcinoma, particularly those with high-risk pathological features at initial diagnosis. The optimal duration and modality of follow-up remain undefined, and we suggest that long-term registries and collaborative reporting would help clarify these questions. Imaging of the chest, in addition to local skin examination, may be warranted during follow-up, although the appropriate frequency should be determined through further study.

Conclusion

Pulmonary metastasis of eccrine sweat gland carcinoma can occur roughly a decade after surgical excision of the primary tumor. This observation reinforces the importance of prolonged clinical surveillance in patients with this rare malignancy. Accurate histopathological and immunohistochemical correlation between primary and metastatic specimens is essential for diagnosis. Further multicenter collaboration is needed to define risk factors, optimal follow-up intervals, and effective treatment strategies for metastatic disease.

Students benefit greatly from having an extended break between school years, because it gives them time to rest and recover from the demands of the academic year. Long periods of study, tests, and deadlines can leave students mentally and physically drained, and a lengthy pause allows their minds and bodies to recharge. Without this recovery time, burnout can set in, making it harder to stay motivated and engaged when classes resume.

An extended break also provides room for personal growth outside the classroom. Students can pursue hobbies, read books for pleasure, learn new skills, or explore interests that the school schedule rarely allows them to follow. These experiences often build creativity and self-confidence in ways that structured lessons cannot.

Family time is another important benefit. Busy school calendars can keep students and their relatives apart, but a longer break offers chances to travel, share meals, and strengthen relationships. These bonds provide emotional support that helps students handle future challenges.

Many students also use this period to work, volunteer, or gain practical experience. Summer jobs teach responsibility, teamwork, and money management, while volunteer work fosters empathy and a sense of community. Such experiences can strengthen college applications and help students discover career paths.

Finally, a substantial break helps students return to school with fresh perspectives and renewed enthusiasm. After a period of rest and reflection, they are often more eager to learn and better prepared to tackle new material. For these reasons, an extended break between school years is valuable for both students' well-being and their long-term success.

The manuscript proposes a rate-distortion-inspired actor-critic framework aimed at improving sample efficiency and transfer when the policy has limited representational capacity, which is a timely and relevant problem for reinforcement learning. The core idea of treating policy complexity as a information-theoretic cost to be traded against task return is well motivated and connects sensibly to prior work on bounded rationality and information bottlenecks. The authors' formulation is clearly stated, and the derivation linking the rate-distortion objective to the actor and critic updates is easy to follow. However, the empirical evaluation is limited to a small set of benchmark environments, and the paper would be considerably stronger with results on more diverse tasks and with ablations isolating the contribution of the rate term from that of the entropy regularization it resembles. The transfer experiments are promising but would benefit from reporting variance across random seeds and from a clearer definition of the capacity constraint used in each setting. The related work section omits several recent papers on compression-based and capacity-constrained policies, which should be discussed to position the contribution accurately. Overall, the idea is sound and the writing is clear, and I recommend a major revision addressing the experimental scope, statistical reporting, and literature coverage before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Allowing students to use cell phones during lunch and passing periods while banning them during class is a balanced policy that respects both the need for focused learning and the realities of modern student life. Schools have a clear responsibility to create an environment where students can concentrate on lessons, and phones are one of the biggest sources of distraction in a classroom. A single buzzing notification can pull a student's attention away from a math problem or a history discussion for several minutes. By keeping phones out of class, teachers can protect instructional time and help students build the habit of focusing on one task at a time.

At the same time, lunch and passing periods are short breaks where students are not expected to be learning in the traditional sense. These moments are for eating, socializing, and resting before the next lesson begins. For many students, their phone is the primary way they stay in touch with family members, arrange rides home, or check on a sick relative. Banning phones entirely during these breaks would cut off a connection that many young people consider essential to their sense of safety and independence.

Phones also play a social role that matters to students. Friendships are maintained through messages, group chats, and shared photos, and lunch is often the one stretch of the day when students can catch up with friends outside of class. Allowing phone use during these periods helps students feel included and less isolated, which supports their overall well-being and, in turn, their readiness to learn.

Critics sometimes argue that any phone use at school is harmful, but this view overlooks the value of a clear boundary. Students who know that phones are welcome at certain times and forbidden at others learn to manage their own attention and self-control. This kind of responsible decision-making is a skill they will need long after they leave school, when no teacher is there to take their device away.

A well-designed policy also gives teachers a simple and consistent rule to enforce. When phones are off-limits during class but permitted in common areas, there is little confusion about expectations. Students understand exactly when they can use their devices, and teachers can focus on teaching instead of constantly negotiating exceptions.

Ultimately, a policy that separates class time from break time offers a practical middle ground. It protects the learning environment, respects students' need for connection, and teaches them to use technology with purpose. Schools that adopt this approach can meet the goals of education and the needs of their students at the same time.

Should students design their own summer learning projects? Many educators assume that structured assignments chosen by teachers are the best way to keep young minds active during the break. Yet students who design their own projects may learn more deeply and with greater enthusiasm. The question deserves careful consideration.

The case for student-designed projects begins with motivation. When a learner chooses a topic, the reason for studying it comes from within rather than from a grade or a checklist. A student who wants to understand how bridges stay standing, or who wants to build a small garden and track its growth, will often persist through difficulties that would discourage someone following a prescribed worksheet. Interest is one of the strongest predictors of sustained effort, and self-designed work makes interest possible.

Ownership also builds important skills. Designing a project requires students to ask questions, set goals, plan steps, and decide how to measure success. These are the same abilities employers and universities value, yet they are rarely practiced in traditional summer assignments. A student who must decide what to investigate and how to present findings gains experience that a list of predetermined tasks cannot provide.

Critics raise reasonable concerns. Some students lack the experience to choose a project that is challenging but achievable. Without guidance, they may pick topics that are too broad, too easy, or abandoned halfway through. Parents and teachers worry that unstructured freedom could lead to a summer of drifting rather than learning. These concerns are valid and should shape how such programs are designed.

Fortunately, the choice is not all or nothing. A middle path allows students to design their own projects within a framework that includes a proposal, a check-in with a mentor, and a final presentation or product. Teachers can offer example topics, suggest resources, and help students narrow overly ambitious ideas. This structure preserves student agency while providing the support needed for success.

Equity deserves attention as well. Students from families with more resources may find it easier to pursue ambitious projects, while others may lack access to libraries, materials, or adult guidance. Schools that adopt student-designed projects should provide equal access to supplies and mentorship so that every student has a fair opportunity to succeed.

Ultimately, the strongest argument for student-designed summer projects is that they treat learners as capable people with real curiosity. When students are trusted to pursue questions that matter to them, learning becomes something they do rather than something done to them. With thoughtful guidance and fair support, such projects can make summer learning both more engaging and more effective.

The manuscript investigates how the expressiveness of learned state representations affects the performance of deep reinforcement learning agents, and proposes regularization methods as a means of improving that performance. The research question is timely and relevant, since representation learning has become central to modern deep RL, yet the relationship between representational capacity and policy quality is still poorly understood. The authors frame the problem clearly and motivate it well with references to prior work on auxiliary objectives, contrastive representation learning, and generalization in RL. The introduction is generally well organized, although the definition of expressiveness is introduced informally and would benefit from a precise, operational definition early in the paper. The authors should state whether expressiveness refers to information content, rank, mutual information with the optimal value function, or some other measure, because the subsequent experiments depend heavily on this choice. The related work section covers a broad range of relevant literature but at times reads as a list of summaries rather than a synthesis that identifies the specific gap the paper fills. The methodology describes a family of regularization techniques that constrain representation norms and encourage decorrelation among latent features. The motivation for each regularizer is reasonable, but the paper would be stronger with a clearer theoretical argument explaining why these constraints should translate into improved sample efficiency or final return. The experimental setup spans several standard benchmark environments, which is a sensible choice for comparability with prior work. However, the number of random seeds appears limited, and the reported confidence intervals are not sufficient to support the strength of some of the claims made in the results section. The authors should report results over a larger number of seeds and use appropriate statistical tests, such as bootstrapped confidence intervals or interval estimates based on the rliable protocol. The ablation studies are a strength, as they isolate the contribution of each regularizer, though the paper does not adequately discuss interactions between regularizers that may account for some of the observed gains. Figures are generally clear, but several learning curves lack shaded uncertainty regions, and the y-axis scales differ across panels in ways that make visual comparison difficult. The discussion attributes performance improvements to increased expressiveness, but the experiments do not include a direct measurement of expressiveness before and after regularization, so this causal interpretation is not yet supported. Including such measurements, for example through effective rank or linear probing accuracy, would substantially strengthen the central argument. The paper also does not address the possibility that regularization improves performance through a different mechanism, such as reduced overfitting to training trajectories, and this alternative explanation should be examined. Reproducibility is partly addressed through the provision of hyperparameters, but details about network architectures, training budgets, and evaluation protocols are scattered across the appendix and should be consolidated. The authors are encouraged to release code and trained checkpoints to support independent verification. The limitations section is brief and should more candidly discuss the restricted set of environments, the sensitivity of results to hyperparameter choices, and the computational overhead introduced by the regularizers. Overall, the paper addresses an important question and offers a practically useful set of techniques, but the causal claims outrun the evidence presented. I recommend a major revision, with the principal requests being a precise definition and measurement of expressiveness, expanded statistical reporting, and a more careful treatment of alternative explanations. With these improvements, the work would make a valuable contribution to the deep reinforcement learning literature.

The manuscript investigates how gradient norms propagate backward through layers at initialization in three architectural families: plain feedforward networks, residual networks, and densely connected networks. The central question, whether architectural connectivity can preserve gradient magnitude at depth without relying on careful weight scaling alone, is well motivated and relevant to the training of deep models. The authors frame the problem clearly in the introduction, situating it within the literature on vanishing and exploding gradients and on initialization schemes such as Xavier and He initialization. The related work section is generally thorough, although it would benefit from a more explicit discussion of prior analyses of signal propagation in residual networks. The theoretical setup is stated precisely, with the assumptions on activation functions, weight distributions, and layer widths laid out in a way that makes the derivations reproducible. The main analytical result, a recursive bound on the expected squared gradient norm per layer, is a useful contribution if the derivation holds, and the step-by-step treatment in the appendix is appreciated. However, several of the approximations used to close the recursion, particularly the independence assumption between activations and backward Jacobians, are invoked without sufficient justification or a discussion of when they fail. The authors should either provide a bound on the error introduced by this assumption or validate it empirically across the depths studied. The experimental section supports the theory with measurements on networks ranging from 10 to 200 layers, which is a sensible range. The plots of gradient norm against depth for each architecture are clear and make the qualitative differences easy to see. Still, the experiments are limited to a single dataset and a single activation function, which weakens the claim that the observed trends are general. Error bars or results across multiple random seeds are missing from most figures, so the reader cannot judge the variance of the reported effects. The comparison between residual and dense connectivity is the most interesting part of the paper, yet it receives the least analysis, with the dense case discussed in only a few sentences. The authors attribute the favorable behavior of dense networks to feature reuse, but this explanation is not tested directly. An ablation isolating the effect of concatenation versus summation at the same parameter budget would substantially strengthen this claim. The discussion of practical implications is reasonable but somewhat speculative, and the suggestion that dense networks may need less careful initialization should be framed as a hypothesis rather than a finding. The writing is generally clear, though some notation is overloaded, with the same symbol used for both layer width and a normalization constant in different sections. Several figure captions are too brief to be interpreted without consulting the main text. The code availability statement is appreciated, and the authors should ensure the released repository includes the scripts that generate every figure. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful question with a sound starting framework and a potentially useful theoretical result. Its main weaknesses are the unexamined independence assumption, the narrow experimental scope, and the thin analysis of dense connectivity. I recommend major revisions addressing these points, after which the work could make a solid contribution to the understanding of signal and gradient propagation in modern architectures.

The government's decision to block publication of the NHS reform risk register has sparked accusations of secrecy from opposition politicians, health campaigners and some clinicians, who say the public has a right to know what risks ministers have identified.

The risk register, a document that sets out the potential problems that could derail major changes to the health service, was prepared as part of planning for the proposed reforms. Officials had previously indicated that a version of the document would be shared, but the government has now said it will not be released in full.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said that publishing the register in its current form could prejudice ongoing negotiations and expose internal assessments that were never intended for public circulation. The department maintained that the government remains committed to transparency about the reforms themselves.

Opposition health spokespeople were quick to respond. One shadow minister described the decision as an attempt to hide uncomfortable truths about the feasibility of the plans, arguing that voters deserve to see the same warnings that ministers have already read.

Campaigners from patient groups also raised concerns. They argued that people using NHS services, and the staff who deliver them, have a direct stake in understanding which risks have been flagged, particularly around waiting times, staffing levels and funding pressures.

Several former NHS managers said that risk registers are routine tools in large public projects and are not inherently alarming. They suggested that the release of such documents, with sensitive details redacted where necessary, would usually strengthen public confidence rather than undermine it.

Constitutional experts pointed out that requests for information about government decision-making can be handled under freedom of information law, though many exemptions apply to policy development and ministerial deliberations. Some warned that repeated use of these exemptions could weaken the public's ability to scrutinise major programmes.

Parliamentary committees have been asked to examine the matter. Some MPs have written to the minister requesting a full explanation of the reasoning behind the decision and a timetable for any partial publication.

Trade unions representing NHS staff have also weighed in. They said frontline workers were already being asked to implement changes without being given a clear picture of the risks, and that openness would help build trust during a difficult period for the service.

Supporters of the government's position argue that a risk register is a working document, and that publishing it before options have been finalised could cause unnecessary alarm or be misread as settled policy. They say that ministers are entitled to a private space in which to test ideas.

Critics counter that the issue is not whether ministers can deliberate privately, but whether the public is kept informed about known risks once decisions affect essential services. They argue that a summary of key risks could be published without revealing sensitive negotiating positions.

The row has drawn attention to a broader pattern in how major government programmes are communicated. Commentators note that reform announcements are often accompanied by upbeat messaging, while the underlying assessments remain confidential until problems become impossible to ignore.

Analysts say the political stakes are high. The NHS remains one of the most salient issues for voters, and any perception that the government is concealing difficulties could shape public opinion for years.

Some independent researchers have called for an external review of the register, arguing that a trusted body could assess the risks and report its findings without exposing commercially or diplomatically sensitive material.

The government has so far resisted calls for such a review, saying that existing oversight mechanisms are sufficient and that the department is already engaging with stakeholders across the health sector.

Those stakeholders include hospital trusts, which say they are preparing for changes without full visibility of the assumptions behind them. Several chief executives have privately expressed frustration at the lack of detail.

Local councillors, who often coordinate with NHS bodies on social care and public health, have also asked for clearer information about how reforms might affect their areas and the services residents rely on.

Financial commentators have noted that the costs of the reforms are substantial, and that risk assessments are closely watched by investors and auditors who want to understand the potential for overruns or delays.

Historians of public administration point out that previous governments of all parties have faced similar disputes over the release of planning documents, and that the outcomes have varied widely depending on how openly the issues were handled.

Some ministers have privately acknowledged that the decision was not handled well and that the communications strategy could have been stronger. Others insist that the decision was taken on legal advice and in the public interest.

Legal advisers to the department have reportedly concluded that partial disclosure carries its own risks, including the possibility that selective extracts could be misinterpreted or taken out of context.

Transparency advocates responded that these concerns could be addressed through careful redaction and clear explanatory notes, and that the presumption should favour disclosure wherever possible.

The Information Commissioner's Office has been approached for guidance on the matter, though it has not yet issued a formal view on whether the withholding of the document is justified.

Patient advocacy groups say they will continue to press for publication, and several have announced plans to submit their own freedom of information requests to test the government's position.

Opposition parties have indicated they may use parliamentary questions and debates to keep the issue in the spotlight, and have not ruled out seeking a formal vote to compel publication.

The government has said it will continue to update the public on the progress of the reforms and will consider further steps once discussions with key partners have concluded.

For now, the dispute remains unresolved, with both sides claiming to act in the best interests of patients and taxpayers, and with the risk register itself still out of public view.

Our school lunch program should partner with a local dairy to offer students healthy and enjoyable milk products. Milk provides calcium, vitamin D, and protein, all of which help growing bodies build strong bones and muscles. However, many students skip milk because the options available to them are often unappealing or served warm. A partnership with a nearby dairy could bring fresh, low-fat milk, flavored yogurts, and cheese sticks that taste good and meet nutritional standards. Local sourcing would also support nearby farmers and reduce the time milk spends in transit, keeping products fresher. The dairy could help with student taste tests and provide educational visits that teach us where our food comes from. By working together, the school and dairy could make healthy choices the easy and enjoyable choice for every student.

Allowing students to use their cell phones during free time while keeping them off during class offers a balanced approach to a difficult issue in schools today. Phones have become a constant presence in students' lives, and banning them entirely can feel unrealistic and unfair. Permitting phone use during breaks, lunch, and before or after school gives students a chance to stay connected with family, coordinate rides, and unwind in the way many of them are used to. This flexibility also shows that schools trust students to manage their own time responsibly. At the same time, keeping phones away during lessons protects the focus that learning requires. Teachers can teach without constant interruptions from notifications, and students can concentrate on discussions, experiments, and assignments. Research on attention suggests that even a phone sitting nearby can pull focus away from tasks, so a clear rule about class time makes sense. This split approach also teaches an important life skill, which is knowing when a device belongs and when it does not. Students who learn to switch off during work and switch on during rest are building habits that will serve them in jobs and in their personal lives. Some critics argue that any phone use at school is a distraction, but that view overlooks the social and emotional needs students have during their downtime. Free time is when friendships are strengthened and stress is released, and a phone can support both. Ultimately, a policy that separates class time from free time respects both the purpose of education and the everyday realities of young people.
