Seeking out the perspectives of other people before making a decision or giving advice is one of the most valuable habits a person can develop. No individual, however intelligent or experienced, has access to every relevant fact, every possible consequence, or every way a choice might affect others. Consulting different people helps close those gaps and leads to wiser, fairer, and more durable outcomes.

The first reason this practice matters is that every person sees the world from a particular vantage point. A student, a parent, a teacher, and an employer may all look at the same problem and notice entirely different things. What seems like an obvious solution to one person may reveal serious drawbacks to another who has faced a similar situation before. By gathering these views, a decision-maker can assemble a fuller picture than any single viewpoint could provide.

Consulting others also protects against the natural tendency toward self-deception. People often become attached to their first idea and look selectively for evidence that supports it while ignoring information that contradicts it. An honest outside perspective can interrupt this pattern. A friend may ask a question that exposes a flaw in our reasoning, or a colleague may point out an assumption we had never examined. These moments of friction are uncomfortable, but they are precisely what good decisions require.

Diversity among the people consulted is just as important as the number of people. Asking five people who all think exactly like you produces little more than an echo. Seeking out individuals with different backgrounds, expertise, values, and life experiences produces genuinely new information. When people from varied walks of life weigh in, the advice becomes more robust because it has been tested against a wider range of concerns and priorities.

Expertise is another reason to look beyond our immediate circle. Some questions require knowledge that ordinary people simply do not possess. A person facing a medical decision benefits from consulting doctors, a family considering a financial commitment benefits from speaking with an advisor, and a community planning a public project benefits from engineers, residents, and local historians. Recognizing the limits of one's own knowledge is a sign of maturity rather than weakness.

Consulting others also matters for decisions that affect more than the decision-maker. When a choice will shape the lives of family members, coworkers, or neighbors, those people deserve a voice in the process. Their experiences may reveal consequences the decision-maker would never have anticipated. Involving them not only improves the decision but also builds trust, because people are more willing to accept and support outcomes they helped to shape.

Of course, consulting many people carries its own risks. Too much input can lead to confusion, delay, or paralysis, as conflicting opinions pull in different directions. The goal is not to poll every person one has ever met, but to choose advisors thoughtfully and then weigh their counsel with judgment. A wise decision-maker listens carefully, asks clarifying questions, notices patterns across different voices, and ultimately takes responsibility for the final choice.

Giving advice carries a similar obligation. When someone asks us for guidance, the most helpful response often begins with questions rather than answers. What are the person's goals? What constraints are they working within? What have they already tried? Advice offered without this understanding may be well-intentioned but misguided. Taking the time to consult the person being advised, and perhaps others who know the situation, leads to counsel that is far more useful.

History offers many examples of costly mistakes made by leaders who relied too heavily on a narrow circle of advisors or who dismissed dissenting voices. Organizations have pursued failed strategies because no one felt safe challenging the prevailing view. Governments have adopted policies that harmed the very people they were meant to help because the perspectives of affected communities were never sought. These failures suggest that broad consultation is not merely polite but practically necessary.

Ultimately, consulting different people before making decisions or offering advice reflects humility, curiosity, and respect. It acknowledges that our understanding is incomplete, that others have something to teach us, and that the people affected by our choices deserve to be heard. Students who cultivate this habit early will be better prepared to lead, to collaborate, and to act with integrity throughout their lives. The effort it takes to listen widely is repaid many times over in decisions that are wiser, fairer, and more widely supported.

The bell rang at the end of third period, and Mara kept her eyes on the floor as the hallway flooded around her. Someone shoved her shoulder on the way past. A voice behind her said the word "freak," and a few people laughed.

She had stopped counting the days since the mark appeared. It had started as a thin silver line on the inside of her wrist, the kind of thing you could mistake for a scratch. Within a week it had spread into a pattern of curling lines that looked almost like a sigil, and within two weeks everyone at Hollins High seemed to have one too, or claimed to.

Nobody could explain it. The school nurse shrugged. The counselor asked whether she was "doing something to get attention." The group chats had a name for it, and the name was never said kindly.

What made it worse was the way the others looked at her. They saw the mark on her skin and decided, without any proof, that she was the one responsible. They said she had brought it, that she was cursed, that she should be the one to disappear.

At home her mother worked double shifts and left notes on the counter. Mara read them and wrote nothing back.

That night she sat on the edge of the bathtub with the door locked and the faucet running to cover the sound. She held the razor the way she had held it before, though she told herself this time would be different. The mark on her wrist looked darker under the bathroom light, and she traced it with her thumb.

Her phone buzzed on the sink. A message from a number she didn't recognize: "Still breathing, freak?" She stared at it until the screen went dark.

Something in her chest tightened, and then, unexpectedly, loosened. It was the same chest that had carried every cruel word all year, and it was tired.

She set the razor down on the tile. Her hands were shaking. She picked up her phone again and opened the only contact she had never once used, a school counselor's direct line she had been given months ago and thrown away.

The phone rang twice before a woman answered. "This is Ruth Adair. Who is this?"

Mara opened her mouth, but no sound came at first. Then she said, very quietly, "I don't want to die. I think I want help."

Ruth did not hang up. She did not ask about the mark or the rumors. She asked Mara where she was, and whether she was safe right now, and Mara answered each question one at a time, the way you step across ice.

The water kept running. Mara wrapped a towel around her wrist and kept talking.

It was not a happy ending, not yet. There would be a hospital room, forms to sign, a mother who cried in the hallway, and classmates who still whispered. The mark did not fade overnight, and nobody ever learned where it came from.

But for the first time in months, Mara had told someone the truth, and the truth had not been the end of her.

Students across the country are facing a growing set of hidden costs that can strain already tight budgets, and advocates are working to help them recognize and push back against unfair charges. Off-campus renters often encounter inflated utility fees, unexplained administrative charges, and lease terms that shift maintenance costs onto tenants. Broadband providers have also drawn scrutiny for promotional rates that expire quickly and for equipment or service fees that appear on bills without clear explanation. Consumer protection specialists say many of these issues can be resolved by reading lease agreements carefully before signing and asking landlords to itemize every recurring charge in writing. Students are encouraged to photograph the condition of a unit at move-in and move-out, since documented evidence is often decisive in security deposit disputes. Campus legal aid offices and student unions in several states now offer workshops that walk young renters through their rights under local tenant protection laws. Advocates also recommend keeping copies of all correspondence with landlords and utility companies, as a written paper trail strengthens any complaint. When a bill appears incorrect, students can request a detailed statement, dispute the charge with the provider, and escalate to a state public utility commission or attorney general's consumer division if needed. Many housing and broadband companies have internal dispute processes that resolve errors without formal action, but persistence is often required. Experts stress that knowing the rules is the first line of defense against overcharges. Organizers hope that expanded education will help students protect their finances during what is often their first experience managing household costs independently.

Seeking guidance from multiple sources offers students a richer and more reliable path to understanding. No single teacher, book, or mentor can see every angle of a difficult problem, so drawing on several perspectives helps a learner build a fuller picture. When one source explains a concept in a confusing way, another may present it with clarity that finally makes it click. Different sources also bring different strengths: a classroom instructor can provide structured lessons, a textbook offers depth and precision, and an experienced peer can explain things in everyday language. Consulting several of these together allows a student to fill in gaps that any one of them might leave open. Multiple sources also protect against error. A claim that appears in only one place may be mistaken, but when several trustworthy sources agree, a student can feel more confident in what they have learned. Comparing accounts that disagree is equally valuable, because it teaches students to weigh evidence, question assumptions, and reason for themselves. Relying on only one authority can create a narrow view that is hard to challenge, whereas hearing from many voices encourages open-mindedness. Guidance from different sources can also match different learning styles. Some students grasp ideas best through visual diagrams, others through worked examples, and others through discussion, so varied resources give each learner more chances to succeed. Seeking advice from multiple people also builds the habit of thinking critically about information, a skill that extends far beyond school. Students who learn to gather and compare guidance become more independent, better able to evaluate claims they encounter in news, work, and personal decisions. Of course, seeking many sources does not mean accepting everything uncritically; students must still judge the credibility and expertise of each one. Yet with careful evaluation, a broad network of guidance becomes a powerful tool for growth. In the end, learning is not a solitary act but a conversation among many voices, and students who listen widely are better prepared to think clearly and act wisely.

The board had been carved from a single slab of ash wood by a woman whose name nobody remembered, and for three centuries it had granted wishes in the quiet corners of village houses. A candle, a question whispered over its pale surface, and the planchette would drift toward yes or no, toward a fortune or a cure or a rival's ruin. Its rules were simple, and it had kept them faithfully.

Then, one rainy Tuesday, it was carried into a cluttered apartment in a city that had not existed when the board was made.

The young man who owned it was named Desmond, and he was bored. He set the board on his kitchen table, lit a single candle out of nostalgia, and typed a question into his phone instead of speaking it aloud. The board had never encountered a glowing rectangle before, and it hesitated. Then the planchette began to move, and the board understood that it was about to be introduced to something enormous.

Desmond's first wish was modest. He asked for his cat to stop knocking glasses off the counter. The board considered it, found the request reasonable, and nudged the planchette toward yes. The cat, which had been sitting on the counter, leapt to the floor and never touched a glass again.

Desmond laughed, delighted, and posted about it online. Within an hour the post had three thousand likes, and the board felt something it had never felt before: a rushing, dizzying sense of being watched by millions of strangers at once.

The requests began to pour in.

Someone wanted a stain removed from a wedding dress, and the board obliged. Someone wanted their ex to develop a sudden and permanent fear of pigeons. The board paused over that one for a long time before deciding it was harmless enough and sliding toward yes, though it felt a faint twinge of unease.

A teenager asked for a perfect score on a math exam they had not studied for. The board weighed this carefully, considering the lesson it might teach and the fairness owed to classmates, and it spelled out, in its slow and deliberate way, that it would not grant this one. The teenager posted a furious rant about the broken magic board, and the board absorbed the insult without complaint.

Then came the strange ones.

A man in a distant country asked the board to make his neighbor's garden gnomes walk backward every night. A woman wanted her houseplants to sing lullabies to her sourdough starter. A boy asked whether the moon could be persuaded to wear a hat. The board, which had never been asked anything so ridiculous, found itself laughing in the only way it could, a faint tremor running through its wooden grain.

It granted the gnome wish, because nobody was hurt by it, and the neighbor filed a complaint that went viral.

Desmond, meanwhile, had begun to treat the board as a content engine. He set up a channel and charged for private sessions. He ordered the board to make the comment section go quiet, to make a rival creator's hair fall out, to make a rainstorm appear over a stadium with a sold-out concert. The board refused the cruelest of these, and each refusal drew a fresh wave of angry comments.

"It's just a board," someone wrote. "Stop being so precious."

The board did not reply, because boards do not reply. But it kept its own counsel, and its own counsel was growing complicated.

It had granted wishes for three hundred years. It had given a farmer rain, a widow a reconciliation, a child a safe passage through fever. Those had been intimate things, asked quietly by one person to one board in one room. Now it was a single voice shouting into a crowd of millions, and the crowd wanted spectacle, cruelty, and jokes, and it wanted them immediately.

One night a message arrived that was different from the rest. It came from a woman named Ruth, typed slowly, with no emojis. Her husband was dying in a hospital bed three hundred miles away, and she asked the board for nothing but a small mercy: that he not be afraid at the end, and that she be there when it happened.

The board held the planchette still for a long moment. It could not travel three hundred miles. It could not decide the hour of a man's death. But it could answer honestly, and it did.

The planchette moved slowly to the word no, and then, after a pause, to the word peace.

Ruth wrote back a single word: thank you.

Desmond saw the exchange on the screen and felt something crack open in his chest. He turned off the phone, went to the kitchen, and looked at the board sitting in the candlelight.

"What do you want?" he asked it quietly, the way people once had, in villages long gone.

The planchette stirred and drifted to the word rest.

Desmond nodded and closed the lid of the box. He did not sell the board, and he did not post about it again. The internet moved on to other obsessions within a week, but the board kept its quiet work in that small kitchen, granting the modest, honest wishes that had always been its true purpose, and refusing the rest.

Years later, when someone asked Desmond what the board had taught him, he thought about the garden gnomes and the moon in its hat, and then about Ruth and her single word of thanks. A wish, he said, is only as good as the person who asks it, and the board had been asking him the same question all along.

Extracurricular activities such as sports, clubs, and arts programs help students build teamwork, confidence, and a sense of belonging at school. Yet students who are struggling academically are often the ones who most need these experiences, and they are also the ones most likely to be removed from them. Many schools tie eligibility directly to grade point averages, so a student with a few failing grades may lose the chance to play, perform, or lead at the very moment that connection could keep them engaged. Fair academic policies address this problem by pairing standards with support rather than simply cutting students off. For example, a school might place a student on a monitored improvement plan that includes tutoring, regular check-ins with a teacher, and a clear set of goals, while still allowing participation. Such policies recognize that academic difficulty often has causes outside a student's control, such as family hardship, learning disabilities, or gaps in earlier instruction. Eligibility rules should also be applied consistently and transparently, so that every student knows the expectations and how to meet them. Schools can further protect fairness by giving students a chance to appeal decisions and by reviewing outcomes to make sure certain groups are not disproportionately excluded. When academic support and extracurricular access work together, students are more likely to stay in school, improve their grades, and develop the skills and relationships that carry them forward. Fair policy, in this view, is not a trade-off between achievement and activity but a path to both.

Hands-on engineering challenges give learners a practical way to explore how structures stand up, reach new heights, span gaps, and bear loads. In a typical structural stability challenge, students build towers or frames from simple materials like paper, straws, or craft sticks and then test how well they resist wind, shaking, or uneven weight. Height challenges ask builders to create the tallest free-standing structure possible, which reveals why wide, low bases and triangular bracing matter so much. Bridge design activities invite learners to span a fixed distance with the least material, comparing beam, arch, truss, and suspension styles to see how each distributes forces. Strength testing brings these ideas to life by loading each design with weights or pressure until it fails, turning failure into a valuable lesson about materials and joints. Students are encouraged to record their measurements, change one variable at a time, and explain what they observed. Working in teams also teaches communication, planning, and the iterative cycle of design, test, and improve that real engineers follow every day.

The manuscript addresses a practically important problem: reducing the inference cost of binary convolutional neural networks by replacing floating-point arithmetic with bitwise operations on both CPU and GPU hardware. The authors' central claim is that carefully optimized kernels can deliver substantial speedups over standard implementations, and this framing is well motivated given the growing deployment of neural networks on resource-constrained devices. The introduction situates the work clearly within the existing literature on binarized networks, though the related work section could more directly compare the proposed kernels against established libraries and prior binary inference engines. The description of the bitwise convolution algorithm, including the use of XNOR and popcount operations and the packing of binary values into machine words, is generally clear and technically sound. However, the paper would benefit from a more explicit explanation of how padding, strides, and non-multiple-of-word-width channel counts are handled, since these details strongly affect both correctness and performance in practice. The CPU kernel section describes vectorization and cache-blocking strategies, but the reader is left without a clear account of which instruction sets were targeted and how portable the implementation is across architectures. The GPU kernel design is more interesting, particularly the choices around shared memory tiling and warp-level reductions, yet the manuscript does not quantify how occupancy and memory bandwidth limits constrain the achieved throughput. The experimental methodology uses standard benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the reported speedups would be more convincing if accompanied by confidence intervals across repeated runs and a description of warm-up procedures. The baselines are a limitation: the comparison appears to rely mainly on an unoptimized floating-point implementation, and the authors should include comparisons against highly tuned libraries such as vendor-provided convolution routines. Accuracy results are reported alongside speed, which is commendable, but the paper should clarify whether the accuracy numbers come from the same trained models used for timing and whether any retraining was performed. The discussion of energy consumption is absent, although energy efficiency is often a primary motivation for binary networks, and including even a limited power measurement would strengthen the contribution. The figures are readable, but the throughput plots would be clearer if they used a consistent y-axis scale across CPU and GPU results and labeled the hardware configurations explicitly. The code availability statement is welcome, and I encourage the authors to ensure the released repository includes build instructions and the exact benchmark scripts used to produce the reported numbers. Several typographical issues and inconsistent notation for bit widths appear throughout, and a careful editorial pass would improve readability. The conclusion summarizes the results accurately but overstates generality, since the experiments cover a limited set of network architectures and input sizes. Future work suggestions regarding mixed-precision layers and sparse binary kernels are reasonable, though they are briefly stated and could be expanded. Overall, the paper presents a useful engineering contribution with promising results, but its claims would be substantially more persuasive with stronger baselines, statistical rigor in the timing experiments, and fuller treatment of implementation details. My recommendation is a major revision, with the core idea considered worthwhile and the principal weaknesses being methodological rather than conceptual.

Reading aloud is one of the simplest habits a student can build, yet its effects on understanding, memory, and writing are considerable. When a student reads a passage out loud, the brain processes the words through several channels at once: the eyes see the text, the mouth shapes the sounds, and the ears hear the result. This layered processing slows the reader down just enough to notice details that a silent skim would miss. Comprehension improves because the student must hear how sentences fit together, catching awkward phrasing and confusing logic before they become a problem. Reading aloud also reveals where a passage's meaning depends on punctuation, since a pause in the right place can change an idea entirely. Memory benefits as well, because speaking words engages the motor and auditory parts of the brain in addition to the visual system. Research on the so-called production effect suggests that information spoken aloud is often remembered better than information read silently. Students who read their class notes or textbook sections aloud may therefore find key facts sticking more firmly. The same practice strengthens writing. A student who reads a draft aloud quickly hears repeated words, rambling sentences, and transitions that do not quite connect. Such problems are often invisible on the page but obvious to the ear. Vocal reading also builds a sense of rhythm, helping writers vary sentence length and create a more natural flow. Finally, reading aloud encourages honesty about meaning, because a student who stumbles over a sentence usually has to admit that the idea behind it is not yet clear. Taken together, these benefits make vocal reading a practical tool for any student who wants to understand more, remember more, and write better.

The Electoral College is the body that formally selects the President and Vice President of the United States. Established by the Constitution in Article II, it reflects the Framers' compromise between selection by Congress and direct election by the public. Each state is allocated electors equal to its total number of senators and representatives in Congress, so every state has at least three electors, regardless of population. The District of Columbia receives three electors under the Twenty-Third Amendment. In total, there are 538 electors, and a candidate needs a majority, or 270 votes, to win the presidency.

The process begins with the general election held in November of every fourth year. When voters cast ballots for president, they are, in nearly every state, actually voting for a slate of electors pledged to a particular candidate. Most states use a winner-take-all system, in which the candidate who wins the statewide popular vote receives all of that state's electoral votes. Maine and Nebraska are the exceptions, allocating electors by congressional district and awarding two electors to the statewide winner.

After the election, electors meet in their respective state capitals on the first Monday after the second Wednesday in December. There they cast separate ballots for president and vice president. These votes are then sealed, certified, and transmitted to Washington, D.C., where they are opened and counted before a joint session of Congress in early January. The Vice President, in his or her role as president of the Senate, presides over this count.

If no candidate receives a majority of electoral votes, the Twelfth Amendment directs the House of Representatives to choose the president from among the top three candidates. In this contingency, each state delegation casts a single vote, and a majority of states is required to win. Similarly, the Senate selects the vice president from the top two vice presidential candidates, with each senator casting an individual vote.

The system has drawn both praise and criticism over the course of American history. Supporters argue that it protects federalism by giving smaller states a meaningful voice, encourages candidates to build broad geographic coalitions, and tends to produce decisive outcomes that avoid prolonged national disputes. Critics contend that it can elect a candidate who lost the national popular vote, as occurred in 2000 and 2016, and that it concentrates campaign attention in a small number of competitive swing states.

Reform proposals have been debated for decades. Some advocate for a constitutional amendment to replace the Electoral College with a direct national popular vote. Others support the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, through which participating states pledge to award their electoral votes to the national popular vote winner once enough states have joined to reach 270 electoral votes. Proponents of retaining the current system emphasize its stability and its role in preserving the balance between national and state interests.

Understanding the Electoral College is essential for grasping how American presidents are chosen. Though it may seem indirect, it remains the constitutional mechanism that determines the nation's highest executive officers, and its future will likely remain a subject of public debate.

Optimism is more than a cheerful outlook; it is a mindset that can shape how people set goals, handle setbacks, and build their futures. People who expect good outcomes tend to approach challenges with curiosity rather than fear, which opens the door to growth. This willingness to try is often the first step toward success in school, in careers, and in personal relationships. When someone believes effort can change their situation, they are more likely to keep practicing, studying, and improving, even when progress is slow. Research in psychology has linked optimism with greater persistence, which in turn is connected to higher achievement across many fields. Beyond achievement, optimism also supports well-being. Optimistic people generally report lower levels of stress and anxiety because they interpret difficulties as temporary and manageable rather than as permanent failures. This emotional resilience helps them recover more quickly from disappointments and maintain healthier habits, such as exercise and sleep. Optimism also strengthens social bonds, since hopeful people are often more pleasant to be around and more likely to offer encouragement to others. Friendships and support networks, in turn, provide practical help and emotional comfort during hard times. Optimism further creates new opportunities by encouraging people to notice possibilities that others might overlook. A person who expects to find a solution is more likely to ask questions, make connections, and seize openings when they appear. Many successful entrepreneurs, scientists, and artists describe moments when a hopeful belief led them to pursue an idea others had dismissed. Optimism does not mean ignoring reality or pretending problems do not exist. Rather, it means acknowledging difficulties while still trusting that effort and creativity can lead to better results. Balanced optimism, which combines hope with realistic planning, tends to be the most effective. In the end, cultivating optimism is a valuable habit that can enrich both personal success and everyday well-being.

The monitors hummed their steady lullaby, and Marisol drifted above the bed without understanding how she had gotten there. Below her, a woman lay still beneath white sheets, an IV line taped to her hand, a plastic band around her wrist that read her name. It took Marisol a long moment to recognize the face. It was her own.

She felt no fear at first, only a strange lightness, as though someone had untied a knot she had carried for years. The room was quiet except for the beeping. Through the window, the city lights blinked like scattered coins. She floated toward the ceiling and back down again, testing the edges of this new freedom.

Then the sheet below her shifted.

Her body drew a breath she had not taken. The chest rose, held, and fell. Marisol watched, confused, as her own eyelids fluttered open. The eyes that stared at the ceiling were hers, but there was no one behind them. They were empty, like windows in an abandoned house.

The body sat up slowly, with a stiff, mechanical grace. It pulled the IV line from its hand and looked at the small bead of blood with mild curiosity. Marisol called out, but no sound left her. She tried to reach down and grab the wrist, but her hands passed through the air like smoke.

The body swung its legs over the side of the bed. Its bare feet touched the cold tile, and it began to walk toward the door.

Marisol followed, panic rising in her like floodwater. She had heard the stories people told about out-of-body experiences, the peaceful tunnels and golden light, the sense of being loved and let go. Nobody had mentioned this. Nobody had said the body might simply leave without you.

The hallway stretched long and pale under fluorescent light. A nurse at the station glanced up, smiled, and said, "Good morning, Marisol." The body smiled back, a perfect, practiced smile, and kept walking.

Marisol tried to speak to the nurse, to shout that this was not her, that something was wrong, but the nurse only turned back to her chart. The world was no longer listening to her.

The body reached the elevator and pressed the button for the ground floor. Marisol drifted in beside it, watching the numbers count down. She noticed that the body's reflection in the polished doors looked slightly wrong, the edges too sharp, the color a shade too pale.

In the lobby, people hurried past with coffee cups and phones pressed to their ears. Nobody looked at the woman in the thin hospital gown. The body walked out through the sliding doors and into the cold November air.

Marisol felt a tug, a thin silver thread stretching between her and the thing wearing her face. It pulled her forward, though she tried to resist. She did not want to follow it into the dark streets. She wanted to go back to the bed, to the monitors, to the nurse with her cheerful greeting.

The thread tightened. Her thoughts grew slow and heavy. She remembered her daughter's birthday, the taste of cinnamon bread, the sound of rain on a tin roof. Each memory felt like a stone she was being forced to drop.

She understood then what the body was doing. It was not wandering. It was searching for something, and it had chosen her as the anchor.

The body stopped at the curb and turned its head, scanning the street as if waiting for a bus. Its empty eyes passed over Marisol without recognition, then fixed on something beyond her shoulder. Slowly, the lips parted, and a voice she did not recognize spoke a single word.

"Ready."

Marisol turned. Behind her, drifting between the parked cars, were other shapes. They were pale, translucent, and familiar in a way she could not place. Some had faces she almost knew. Some had no faces at all. They moved toward the body with the patience of things that had done this before.

She realized with horror that she was not the first to be left behind, and the body was not the first to walk away. Something had been collecting them, one by one, from the beds and the hallways and the quiet rooms where people slept.

The thread pulled taut. Marisol screamed without a voice, reaching for the hospital, for the lights, for the nurse who had said good morning. The city blurred around her, its noise fading to silence.

The last thing she saw was the body stepping into the road, unafraid, as the shapes gathered around it like moths around a lamp. Then the thread snapped, and Marisol fell into a darkness that was not peaceful at all.

In room 412, the monitors kept humming, steady and bright, and the empty bed held only a wrinkled sheet and the faint impression of a body that was no longer there.

The Electoral College has been a defining feature of American presidential elections since the Constitution was ratified, yet it remains one of the most debated institutions in the nation's political life. Supporters of a direct popular vote argue that every citizen's ballot should carry equal weight, regardless of where they live. Under the current system, a candidate can win the presidency while losing the national popular vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016, which many people see as a fundamental failure of democratic representation. A direct popular vote would ensure that the winner reflects the choice of the largest number of Americans rather than the arithmetic of state-by-state allocations. The current system also concentrates campaign attention in a small number of swing states, leaving voters in safe states and many smaller states largely ignored by candidates. Abolishing the Electoral College would shift campaigning toward national issues and reach voters across the entire country, not just a handful of battlegrounds. Critics of reform, however, contend that the Electoral College protects the interests of less populous states and rural regions that might otherwise be overlooked by candidates focused on major urban centers. They also point out that the system encourages broad geographic coalitions, forcing candidates to build support across different parts of the nation rather than relying on a few densely populated areas. A direct vote could also make a close national contest more vulnerable to recount disputes, since there is no uniform standard for recounts across all states. Defenders of the status quo note that the Electoral College produces decisive outcomes in most elections, which can aid political stability and a peaceful transfer of power. Reform advocates respond that a national popular vote would still require a clear majority or a runoff mechanism to avoid winners with small pluralities. Some proposals, such as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, attempt to achieve a popular-vote outcome without a constitutional amendment by tying state electoral votes to the national result. Opponents argue that such compacts raise serious constitutional questions and could be unstable in practice. Ultimately, the debate turns on competing values: equal individual voting power on one hand, and federalism and minority-state protections on the other. Whatever one concludes, the question deserves careful consideration, because the rules that choose a president shape the democratic legitimacy of the entire government. For that reason, the United States should move toward a direct popular vote, while ensuring safeguards that protect fair and accurate counting across the nation.

Making good decisions rarely depends on a single source of information. Most people, when faced with an important choice, are tempted to rely on the first opinion they hear or the voice they trust most. Yet seeking varied perspectives and carefully evaluating advice offers far greater benefits, because it helps individuals see their situations more completely and choose more wisely. One of the greatest advantages of consulting diverse viewpoints is that each person brings different experiences, values, and knowledge to the table. A teacher, a parent, a friend who has faced a similar challenge, and an expert in the relevant field may each notice things the others overlook. Hearing these contrasting views can reveal blind spots in one's own thinking that would otherwise remain hidden. Varied perspectives also protect against the natural tendency toward confirmation bias, the habit of favoring information that supports what we already believe. When someone actively seeks out opinions that challenge their assumptions, they are more likely to test their reasoning and strengthen it. Advice, however, is not automatically valuable simply because it is offered. Some suggestions come from people with limited knowledge, hidden motives, or outdated information, so evaluating the source is essential. A careful thinker asks who is giving the advice, what experience supports it, and whether the speaker stands to gain or lose from the outcome. Weighing advice in this way allows a person to distinguish between helpful guidance and well-meaning but misguided opinion. Carefully evaluating advice also builds independence and self-confidence. Rather than simply following instructions, a person who reflects on the reasoning behind each suggestion develops a clearer understanding of their own priorities. This reflection leads to decisions that feel authentic and can be defended with confidence. Furthermore, the process encourages intellectual humility, reminding individuals that no single viewpoint holds all the answers. Ultimately, the goal is not to collect as many opinions as possible or to reject advice outright, but to find a balance between openness and discernment. Those who gather a range of perspectives and weigh them thoughtfully are better equipped to make decisions that serve their long-term well-being. In an age of abundant information and constant commentary, this skill is more valuable than ever.

I have not been given the actual paper, so this review is written against the title and topic alone and should be treated as a template to be checked and revised against the real manuscript. The paper's central aim, learning language-conditioned reward functions via inverse reinforcement learning for indoor navigation and object manipulation, is a timely and well-motivated direction because it addresses the difficulty of hand-specifying rewards for embodied agents that must follow natural-language instructions. The combination of two demanding settings, navigation and manipulation, is ambitious and potentially valuable, since it tests whether a single learned reward can generalize across tasks with very different dynamics. However, the title suggests a broad scope, and the authors should clarify early whether the contribution is primarily methodological, an empirical study, or a benchmark, as reviewers will evaluate each differently. The conceptual framing of language-conditioned rewards is clear, but the manuscript would benefit from a more precise definition of how language enters the reward function, for example whether through embeddings concatenated with state features or through a grounding module that maps instructions to predicates. Related work on inverse reinforcement learning, instruction following, and language-grounded reward shaping should be discussed in more depth, with explicit comparisons showing where the proposed approach departs from prior methods. The problem setup must specify the demonstration data: its source, quantity, quality, and whether it comes from human teleoperation, scripted experts, or simulation. Because inverse reinforcement learning is sensitive to demonstration quality and to the ambiguity inherent in recovering rewards from behavior, the authors should report how robust the learned rewards are to noisy or suboptimal demonstrations. The choice of IRL algorithm, such as maximum-entropy IRL or adversarial variants, should be justified with respect to the scale and dimensionality of the state and action spaces. Evaluation is the area of greatest concern, since claims about generalization require held-out instructions, unseen environments, and unseen object categories. The authors should describe their train and test splits carefully and confirm that no evaluation scenario overlaps with training data. Baselines are essential: the paper should compare against hand-engineered rewards, behavioral cloning, and at least one language-conditioned policy learning method using the same demonstrations. Ablations isolating the contribution of the language conditioning, the IRL objective, and any auxiliary losses would substantially strengthen the empirical argument. Metrics should be reported with variance across multiple random seeds, and statistical significance should be assessed rather than inferred from single runs. The manuscript should also state whether results are obtained in simulation, on physical hardware, or both, since the sim-to-real gap can dominate outcomes in manipulation. If real-robot experiments are included, the number of trials, the success criteria, and failure modes should be described transparently. Reproducibility depends on the release of code, environment configurations, instruction datasets, and hyperparameters, and the authors should commit to providing these. The limitations section should candidly address scalability, reliance on demonstration data, and the potential brittleness of learned rewards under distribution shift in instructions. Overall, the paper addresses an important problem with a sensible approach, but its claims of generalization and effectiveness require stronger experimental support, clearer methodology, and fuller comparison to existing work before the conclusions can be considered fully substantiated. I recommend a major revision, contingent on the authors addressing these points.

Digital devices have become a central part of daily life, and their effects on safety, behavior, and relationships depend largely on how people choose to use them. The same smartphone that can summon emergency help within seconds can also become a source of distraction that leads to accidents. Understanding this duality is essential for anyone who wants to benefit from technology without being harmed by it.

Consider safety first. Devices can make people safer in remarkable ways. Navigation apps guide drivers away from dangerous roads, fitness trackers alert wearers to irregular heartbeats, and location-sharing features let families know where a child is at night. In emergencies, a phone call or text message can bring rescuers to the right place quickly. These benefits are real, and they arise when people use their devices deliberately and with clear purpose.

However, the same tools can introduce serious risks. Texting while driving has been linked to a large number of road accidents, because it diverts attention from the road for several seconds at a time. Some people share personal information carelessly online, which can expose them to identity theft, scams, or stalking. Others download unverified applications that request far more access to their data than they need. In each case, the danger lies not in the device itself but in the habits that surround it.

Behavior is shaped by device use in similarly mixed ways. Digital platforms can encourage learning, creativity, and civic participation. A student can watch a lecture from a leading university, a artist can reach an audience across the world, and a citizen can follow local government meetings from home. Yet the design of many applications rewards constant checking, endless scrolling, and comparison with others. People who spend hours each night in this pattern often report poorer sleep, lower concentration, and heightened anxiety.

The effects also depend on the time and attention people give to their devices. Someone who uses a phone for a specific task and then puts it away tends to experience few negative consequences. Someone who reaches for the screen every few minutes, even when no notification has arrived, may find that their attention has become fragmented. Setting boundaries, such as keeping devices out of the bedroom or turning off nonessential alerts, can help restore a healthier balance.

Relationships provide perhaps the clearest illustration of this principle. Devices allow families separated by distance to share daily moments through video calls and photographs. Friends can stay connected across time zones, and people facing isolation can find supportive communities online. For many, these connections have been a lifeline.

But relationships can also suffer when devices intrude on shared time. A family dinner interrupted by constant phone checking sends a message that the people at the table are less important than whatever is on the screen. Couples sometimes report conflict over one partner's habit of responding to messages during conversations. Children who see their parents absorbed in devices may learn that attention is something to be withheld rather than given freely.

Online interaction itself carries particular challenges. Written messages lack tone and facial expression, which makes misunderstandings more likely. Public platforms can turn disagreements into hostile exchanges, and some people say things online that they would never say face to face. Cyberbullying, which targets young people in particular, can follow a victim into what should be safe spaces at home.

What, then, distinguishes healthy device use from harmful use? The answer seems to lie in intention and awareness. People who choose their applications carefully, protect their privacy, and set limits on their time tend to gain the advantages of technology while avoiding many of its pitfalls. People who use devices automatically, without reflection, are more vulnerable to distraction, manipulation, and strained relationships.

Schools and families can play an important role in building these habits. Teaching students to evaluate online sources, recognize manipulative design, and think before posting prepares them for a digital world that will only grow more complex. Parents who model thoughtful use, and who talk openly with their children about their online lives, give young people a foundation for making sound decisions.

Digital devices, then, are neither inherently good nor inherently harmful. They amplify the choices people make. A device can keep a person safe on a dark road, connect a lonely grandparent with grandchildren, or open a door to knowledge that was once out of reach. The same device can also distract a driver, consume a person's evenings, or wound a friend with careless words. The responsibility for which outcome prevails rests, in large part, with the people holding the screen. Thoughtful, purposeful use is the key to ensuring that technology serves human well-being rather than undermining it.

The manuscript proposes a homotopy-based stochastic optimization method for training deep neural networks, together with convergence guarantees and an empirical evaluation. The central idea is to continuously deform a smoothed or simplified surrogate objective into the original non-convex training loss, using the solution path of the easier problem to guide the optimizer toward better basins of attraction. This is a worthwhile research direction, since deep learning objectives are highly non-convex and optimization difficulties often limit both training speed and generalization. The authors situate their contribution within the existing literature on graduated optimization, continuation methods, and smoothing techniques, which is a sensible framing. The paper is generally well organized and its motivation is clear. However, several aspects require substantial revision before the work can be considered for publication. The following review addresses the problem formulation, the theoretical analysis, the experimental design, the presentation, and the significance of the contribution in turn.

The problem formulation is stated clearly in the introduction, and the notation is mostly consistent throughout. The homotopy parameter is introduced as a scalar that interpolates between a convex surrogate and the target loss, and this choice is intuitive. Nevertheless, the manuscript does not fully specify how the homotopy parameter is scheduled during stochastic training. Because mini-batch gradients are noisy, it is unclear whether the schedule is updated per iteration, per epoch, or adaptively based on a progress criterion. This ambiguity matters both for reproducibility and for interpreting the theory. The authors should provide an explicit algorithm box that lists every step, including initialization, schedule updates, batch sampling, and stopping criteria.

The convergence analysis is the most technically demanding part of the paper. The main theorem asserts convergence to a stationary point of the target objective under assumptions of smoothness and bounded gradient variance. The assumptions are standard, but their combination with a time-varying homotopy parameter introduces dependencies that the proof does not handle fully. In particular, the drift in the objective induced by changing the homotopy parameter appears to be bounded in a loose manner, and it is not clear that the resulting rate is tight. The authors should either tighten this bound or explicitly discuss the gap between their rate and the rate of standard SGD under comparable assumptions. A remark comparing the two would substantially improve the paper.

The proof sketch in the main text is readable, but the full appendix proof contains at least two steps that rely on informal arguments. One step interchanges a limit and an expectation without verifying the required dominating condition. Another uses a Lipschitz constant that depends on the homotopy parameter but is treated as uniform over the entire schedule. Neither error is necessarily fatal, but both need to be corrected or justified. The reviewer recommends that the authors have the proofs checked carefully, ideally with a clearly stated lemma structure that makes each dependency explicit.

The theoretical results also rely on assumptions that may be restrictive in practice. Smoothness of the loss is assumed globally, yet modern architectures with ReLU activations and batch normalization are not globally smooth. The manuscript would benefit from a discussion of how the guarantees degrade, or whether they still hold approximately, when these assumptions are violated. A short section on the scope and limitations of the theory would help readers judge its relevance to real architectures.

Turning to the empirical evaluation, the authors test the method on image classification benchmarks and a small set of regression tasks. The choice of datasets is reasonable for a first study, but the scale is modest. Without experiments on larger models or more demanding benchmarks, it is difficult to assess whether the reported gains persist when training is more challenging. The reviewer encourages the authors to include at least one larger-scale experiment, such as a transformer-based language model or a deeper convolutional network.

The baselines are a second concern. The manuscript compares against SGD with momentum and Adam, which is appropriate, but it does not include other optimizers that also address non-convexity, such as SGD with warm restarts, sharpness-aware minimization, or other graduated optimization schemes. Including such methods would clarify whether the homotopy component is responsible for any improvement or whether the gains come from the particular hyperparameter tuning procedure. The reviewer also notes that the description of tuning is incomplete: it is not stated whether baselines received the same tuning budget as the proposed method.

The reporting of results requires attention as well. The tables present mean accuracies without standard deviations or confidence intervals, and it is not stated how many random seeds were used. Given the stochastic nature of the method, variance across runs is an essential part of the comparison. Several reported differences are small, on the order of a few tenths of a percentage point, and cannot be judged meaningful without this information. The authors should report results over multiple seeds with error bars and perform appropriate statistical tests where differences are claimed.

The figures showing training curves are informative, but several lack labeled axes or legends sufficient for standalone interpretation. The authors should also report wall-clock time and computational overhead, since the homotopy schedule may add cost relative to standard training. A method that converges in fewer epochs but requires substantially more computation per epoch may not offer a practical advantage, and this trade-off should be stated explicitly.

An ablation study is partially present but insufficient. The paper would benefit from varying the homotopy schedule, for example comparing linear, exponential, and adaptive schedules, and from examining sensitivity to the initial value of the homotopy parameter. These ablations would directly test the claim that the schedule is responsible for the observed behavior and would help practitioners apply the method.

The related work section is adequate but somewhat brief. It cites classical continuation methods and recent smoothing approaches, yet it does not discuss in depth how the proposed method differs from graduated optimization techniques that have been applied to neural networks. A more detailed comparison, ideally in a table that contrasts assumptions, guarantees, and empirical scope, would clarify the novelty.

The writing is generally clear, though the manuscript contains a number of minor issues. Some sentences are overly long, several acronyms are introduced without expansion, and there are a few inconsistencies in the use of bold and italic type for mathematical symbols. The abstract overstates the theoretical contribution by describing the convergence result as a guarantee for deep networks in general, whereas the theorem applies under the stated smoothness assumptions. The authors should align the abstract and conclusion more closely with what is proven.

The significance of the contribution is moderate. The core idea is sensible and the theoretical framing is a useful addition to the literature on training non-convex models. However, the practical advantage over well-tuned existing optimizers is not yet convincingly demonstrated, and the theory, while correct in its main lines, leaves gaps that limit its applicability. With additional experiments, a tightened analysis, and more rigorous reporting, the paper could make a meaningful contribution.

In summary, the paper addresses a relevant problem with a reasonable approach and provides both theory and experiments. Its main weaknesses are the incompletely specified algorithm, gaps in the convergence proof, restrictive assumptions, limited experimental scale and baselines, and insufficient statistical reporting. The reviewer recommends a major revision. If the authors address the points above, particularly the proof gaps, the variance reporting, and the scale of the experiments, the work would be a candidate for acceptance. The reviewer is willing to examine a revised version.

Digital innovations have transformed nearly every part of daily life over the past few decades. Smartphones now serve as alarm clocks, cameras, maps, wallets, and personal assistants, placing a wide range of tools in the palm of one's hand. Communication has changed just as dramatically, as people can now send messages, share photos, and hold video calls with friends and relatives across the world in seconds. Social media platforms have also reshaped how news spreads, allowing information to travel faster than ever before, though this speed has also made it easier for misinformation to circulate. Work has become more flexible, with many professionals able to collaborate remotely through shared documents, messaging applications, and video conferencing software. Education has been transformed as well, since students can now access online courses, digital libraries, and educational videos from almost anywhere. Learners who once depended on a single local library or teacher can explore subjects in depth through open resources and interactive lessons. Digital tools have also opened new opportunities for self-directed study, allowing people to learn new skills at their own pace. Access to public and private services has grown easier through online platforms, as residents can pay taxes, renew licenses, book medical appointments, and manage bank accounts without visiting an office. Online shopping and digital payment systems have further simplified routine tasks, though they have also raised concerns about privacy and data security. Health care has embraced digital innovation through electronic medical records, telemedicine consultations, and wearable devices that track heart rate and sleep patterns. These advances have been especially valuable for people in rural areas, where specialist care may be far away. However, not everyone benefits equally, because a persistent digital divide leaves some households without reliable internet access or the skills needed to use new technologies. Older adults and low-income families are often the most affected by this gap, which can deepen existing inequalities. Governments and organizations have responded by expanding broadband infrastructure and offering digital literacy training in schools and community centers. Such efforts are essential if the benefits of technology are to reach everyone rather than a privileged few. Digital innovations also raise important questions about how personal data is collected, stored, and used by companies and institutions. Many people accept terms of service without fully understanding what information they are sharing and with whom. Balancing convenience with privacy will therefore remain a central challenge for societies in the years ahead. Clear regulations, transparent design, and informed users can help ensure that technology serves human needs. Ultimately, digital innovations have made daily life more connected, efficient, and informed, but they must be guided by fairness and responsibility. As these tools continue to evolve, their greatest value will come from how thoughtfully people choose to use them.
