Why In-Person Schooling Is More Effective Than Online Learning for Students

Education is about more than the transfer of information from a teacher to a student. It is a social, emotional, and intellectual process that depends heavily on human connection. While online learning expanded rapidly in recent years and offers real conveniences, in-person schooling remains more effective for most students because it supports deeper understanding, stronger relationships, and healthier development.

The first reason is the quality of direct interaction between teachers and students. In a physical classroom, a teacher can notice when a student looks confused, pause to explain a concept differently, or offer encouragement at exactly the right moment. These small, responsive exchanges are difficult to replicate through a screen, where facial expressions are compressed and subtle signals are easily missed.

Second, in-person classrooms foster focus and reduce distraction. At home, students face a constant stream of temptations, including phones, games, family interruptions, and household chores. A school building establishes a clear boundary between learning and everyday life, helping students settle into a routine that signals it is time to work.

Third, face-to-face learning builds social skills that are essential for adult life. Students learn to collaborate on group projects, resolve disagreements, listen to classmates with different opinions, and read social cues in real time. These abilities are developed through daily, unscripted contact with peers, not through text boxes or muted microphones.

Fourth, schools provide emotional support that online platforms often cannot match. Counselors, nurses, coaches, and trusted adults can spot signs of bullying, anxiety, hunger, or abuse. For many children, the school building is the most stable and caring environment in their week, and in-person attendance ensures they are seen and supported.

Fifth, hands-on learning is often better suited to physical classrooms. Science labs, art studios, music rooms, and physical education all depend on equipment, space, and guided practice. Although some simulations exist online, they rarely offer the tactile experience and immediate feedback that a real laboratory or workshop provides.

Sixth, in-person schooling supports equitable access to resources. Not every household has reliable internet, a quiet workspace, or a parent available to help with schoolwork. Schools provide textbooks, computers, meals, and structured support regardless of a family's circumstances, reducing the gap between students who have advantages at home and those who do not.

Seventh, research on learning outcomes has generally found that students who learned remotely during recent disruptions often fell behind, particularly in mathematics and reading, and that the losses were largest for younger and lower-income students. While studies vary and many factors contributed, the overall pattern suggests that the classroom offers advantages that remote instruction struggled to replace.

Some argue that online learning offers flexibility, personalized pacing, and access to specialized courses that a local school might not provide. These benefits are real and deserve recognition. However, they can be captured through a blended approach in which online tools supplement, rather than replace, the core experience of learning alongside teachers and classmates.

Ultimately, education is strongest when it is rooted in a community. In-person schooling brings together teachers, students, families, and staff in a shared space where learning is supported by relationships, structure, and care. For these reasons, in-person schooling should remain the foundation of education for most students, with technology serving as a valuable but secondary tool.

This manuscript proposes a regularized Dirichlet-based neural network for uncertainty-aware classification, targeting problems with many classes and out-of-distribution inputs. The problem is well motivated, since reliable uncertainty estimates matter in safety-critical applications and standard softmax classifiers tend to be overconfident. The core idea of placing a Dirichlet distribution over class probabilities and training with a regularizer to control evidence on incorrect classes is sensible and builds usefully on prior evidential deep learning work. The regularization scheme is the paper's main technical contribution, and the authors should clarify how its hyperparameters are chosen and how sensitive results are to them. Scaling to large numbers of classes is a central claim, so the experiments should include benchmarks with substantially more classes than the standard CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 settings, with reported training cost and memory use. The out-of-distribution evaluation would be stronger with multiple OOD datasets spanning near and far distribution shifts, along with standard metrics such as AUROC and detection error. Comparisons should include recent uncertainty baselines such as deep ensembles, MC dropout, and other evidential methods, using matched compute budgets. The theoretical justification for why the regularizer improves calibration or OOD detection is currently thin and would benefit from a more formal argument or at least a clearer intuition. Ablation studies isolating the regularizer's contribution are needed to support the claim that it, rather than the architecture or training details, drives the gains. The writing is generally clear, but the related work section could better position the contribution relative to the most recent evidential and Bayesian approaches. Overall, the paper is a promising contribution, and I recommend a major revision addressing the scalability evidence, baseline comparisons, and ablations before it is ready for publication.

Truthfulness is often described as the foundation of every lasting relationship, and for good reason. When people know that a friend, family member, or colleague will tell them the truth, they can rely on what that person says without second-guessing every word. This reliability creates trust, and trust is the quiet force that allows relationships to grow deeper over time. Without it, even pleasant conversations can feel hollow, because we cannot tell whether the praise we receive is sincere or the reassurance we hear is real.

Yet truth alone is not enough to keep relationships healthy. A blunt statement delivered without thought can wound as deeply as a lie. Someone who says exactly what they think, regardless of timing or tone, may be honest but still careless with the people around them. The challenge, then, is to combine honesty with compassion so that the truth is offered in a way that can actually be heard.

Sensitivity to others' feelings does not mean hiding the truth or softening it until it becomes meaningless. Instead, it means paying attention to the person receiving the message. A friend who has just lost a job may not want to hear critiques of their résumé in that moment, but they may welcome honest advice once they feel ready. Timing, word choice, and genuine care for the listener can transform a painful truth into a gift.

Consider a student who has worked hard on a project that falls short of its goals. A teacher who says the work is perfect fails the student by denying them useful feedback. A teacher who says only that the work is poor may be accurate but unhelpful and discouraging. The most effective response acknowledges the effort, identifies specific strengths, and clearly explains what needs improvement. In this way, the truth becomes a tool for growth rather than a source of shame.

Trust also grows when people see that honesty is consistent. A person who tells the truth only when it is convenient gradually loses credibility. Others begin to wonder which parts of their words are reliable and which are shaded to serve their own interests. Consistent honesty, by contrast, builds a reputation that makes people feel safe, because they know that difficult news will come directly rather than through rumor or evasion.

Sensitivity also requires humility. The person speaking must recognize that they may not have the full picture, and that their perspective is only one of many. Asking questions before offering judgments, listening carefully to responses, and remaining open to correction all show respect for the other person. These habits make honesty feel collaborative rather than authoritative, which strengthens the relationship rather than weakening it.

Ultimately, truthfulness and sensitivity are not opposing forces but partners. Honesty gives relationships substance, while compassion gives them warmth. Together they allow people to say difficult things without losing the bond between them. A relationship built on both qualities can survive disagreement, disappointment, and even mistakes, because each person trusts that the other is both honest and kind. In a world where misunderstandings are common, this combination remains one of the most valuable gifts we can offer one another.

Making decisions is one of the most personal things a person can do, yet many of us hand that responsibility over to fear. We worry about getting things wrong, about disappointing our families, and about what our friends or strangers will think. Building confidence in our own choices means learning to act despite those worries, and it is a skill that grows with practice. The first step is recognizing that mistakes are a normal part of learning rather than proof of personal failure. Every person who has achieved something meaningful has also made countless errors along the way. When we treat a wrong turn as information instead of a verdict, we free ourselves to try again. Fear of mistakes often keeps people stuck in situations that no longer suit them, because staying put feels safer than risking change. Yet inaction is also a choice, and it often carries costs that are harder to see. Others' opinions can be valuable, since friends and mentors may notice things we overlook. However, opinions are not the same as instructions, and many people speak from their own experiences and fears rather than from a clear view of our lives. Learning to listen carefully while still deciding for ourselves is a delicate balance. One helpful practice is to ask what we value most before weighing any advice, because our values give us a compass that does not depend on approval. Writing down the reasons behind a decision can also clarify our thinking and remind us why we chose a path when doubts arise later. Small decisions offer a good place to begin, such as choosing a book, a hobby, or how to spend an afternoon. Each time we follow through on a choice and live with the result, we gather evidence that we can handle uncertainty. Over time, this evidence builds a quiet trust in our own judgment. Confidence does not mean never doubting ourselves; it means being willing to proceed while doubt remains. Some decisions will turn out well, and others will teach us lessons we would not have learned otherwise. Either way, we grow. In the end, living by our own choices requires courage, but it also brings a sense of ownership over our lives. Building that confidence is a lifelong project, and it begins with the willingness to make one decision today and see what we learn from it.

The throne room was quiet now, its obsidian walls still scorched from the last battle. Victor Crane sat alone on the fallen pedestal, turning a cold iron key over in his scarred hands. Once, this key had opened the vaults of three nations, and every minion in the world had trembled at the sound of his footsteps. Now the only footsteps came from the guards outside, who had already been reassigned to someone else.

It had all started with a mistake, and that was the cruelest part of it. Dmitri, his loyal henchman of twenty years, had been firing at the hero Aurelius Vane from behind a column, aiming for the shield generator on the far wall. The blast had gone wide, struck the hero's chest, and the light in Aurelius's eyes had gone out before he hit the marble floor. The whole city had gone silent that night, as if the world itself were holding its breath.

Victor had wanted to hate Dmitri for it. He had tried, in the hours after, to summon the rage that once fueled every grand scheme he had ever dreamed up. But Dmitri had sobbed on his knees, his hands shaking so badly he could not hold his own weapon, and Victor had found that he could not bring himself to strike him down. That hesitation, he now realized, had been the first crack in his empire.

The heroes did not come for him immediately. Instead, the world simply turned away. Banks froze his accounts, his fortresses were seized by international coalitions, and the mercenaries who had sworn eternal loyalty vanished one by one like smoke in the wind. Even his own generals sold him out for pardons, handing over maps of his hidden bases with a cheerful lack of shame.

Sometimes Victor wondered whether Aurelius Vane would have wanted this. The hero had fought him more than a hundred times over the years, and yet he had always shown a strange respect for his foe. Once, after a battle in a flooding harbor, Aurelius had pulled Victor from the water himself and said, "You could have let me drown, but you chose to fight fairly." Victor had never forgotten those words, even as he schemed to bring the hero down.

The trial was set for the spring. Dmitri had already confessed, refusing any defense, and had asked only that someone tend to the hero's grieving daughter. Victor had written a letter to the court, his first honest words in decades, admitting that he had built his entire life on the belief that he was superior to everyone around him. He had not expected that a single accident could reveal how hollow that belief truly was.

Now, as the morning light crept through the broken windows, Victor stood and walked to the balcony. Below him, the city was waking up without fear, its streets filled with people going about their ordinary lives. He had once imagined ruling over all of this, but now it looked like something he had never truly understood, something that had never needed him at all.

He dropped the iron key over the edge and watched it vanish into the crowd below. Somewhere a child laughed, and a vendor called out his prices, and the sound drifted up to him like a forgotten song. Victor closed his eyes and, for the first time in his long, dark life, felt something close to peace.

After-school academic support can make a real difference in how students complete their assignments and understand their schoolwork. Many students return home after a long day with tired minds and limited time, and they may find that homework feels confusing or overwhelming without someone to guide them. A structured after-school program gives students a quiet place to focus, along with adults or tutors who can answer questions as they arise. When a student gets stuck on a math problem or does not understand a reading passage, having immediate help prevents frustration from building and keeps the student moving forward. Support staff can also help students break large projects into smaller, manageable steps, which makes long assignments less intimidating and easier to finish on time. Beyond finishing homework, these programs often teach organizational skills such as keeping a planner, setting priorities, and checking work before turning it in. Students who learn these habits early are better prepared for the increasing demands of higher grade levels. Tutors can also explain concepts in different ways, which is valuable because every learner understands things differently. A concept that seemed unclear during class may suddenly make sense when it is explained through a new example or a hands-on activity. Regular feedback from a knowledgeable adult helps students recognize their mistakes and correct them before those errors become lasting misunderstandings. Over time, this kind of guidance can build confidence, since students who see their own progress are more willing to take on challenges. After-school support also reduces the gap between students who have help at home and those who do not, giving every student a fair opportunity to succeed. Families who work long hours or lack the experience to assist with schoolwork benefit especially from these resources. In this way, after-school academic support does more than complete assignments; it strengthens understanding, builds lasting skills, and helps students grow into capable and independent learners.

The rain had stopped by the time Owen finally stood up from the kitchen table. Across from him, Mirabel was already smiling in that patient way she always did, her chin resting on her folded hands.

"You're leaving," she said. It wasn't a question. She had always known things before he did.

"I think I have to," Owen said. "Everyone says it's time. Dr. Haskell, my sister, even the mailman, though I'm not sure he counts."

Mirabel laughed, the sound light as a dropped spoon. "You were always the one who made me laugh."

He had invented her on a winter night, when the house was too quiet after his mother's funeral. She had arrived fully formed, with her silver-threaded scarf and her habit of tapping the rim of every cup she touched. He had needed someone to talk to, and she had been ready.

"I'm going to miss the way you tap the cups," he said.

"Then don't forget it," she said. "You won't need to remember me. Just the things I taught you to notice."

Owen reached across the table, and for the first time his hand paused before touching hers. There was nothing there to feel, only the faint warmth of the morning light on the wood. He pulled his hand back and looked at it, trying to remember when he had last been touched by anyone at all.

"Mirabel," he said slowly, "how long have I been living alone?"

She didn't answer right away. She picked up her cup and tapped its rim, once, twice, and set it down without drinking.

"Long enough to forget that the walls are painted," she said gently. "You've always been good at seeing what you needed to see."

The clock above the stove ticked, and Owen noticed for the first time that it had stopped at a quarter past nine. He glanced at the window. The street beyond it was gray and empty, with no cars and no neighbors, only a single streetlamp flickering on and off.

"I'm not really here, am I?" he asked. "Neither of us is."

Mirabel's smile softened into something sad and kind. "We were both made to keep each other company," she said. "That was always enough."

He nodded, though his throat had tightened. "Then I suppose this is goodbye."

"It's only goodbye for me," she said. "You get to go somewhere I can't follow."

Owen stood and pushed his chair neatly under the table, the way his mother used to insist. He walked to the door, and the knob turned under his hand, cold and real in a way nothing else in the house had been.

Behind him, Mirabel tapped her cup one final time, a small bright sound that faded into silence.

He stepped outside, and the morning light swallowed him whole.

Real-World PACS Integration of Automated MRI Comparison to Improve Detection of New or Growing Multiple Sclerosis Lesions

Abstract

Longitudinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is central to the diagnosis and monitoring of multiple sclerosis (MS), and the detection of new or enlarging T2-hyperintense lesions is a core radiological criterion for disease activity and treatment response. Manual comparison of serial examinations is time-consuming, subject to inter-reader variability, and prone to omission of small lesions. Automated longitudinal lesion comparison tools promise greater sensitivity and reproducibility, but their value depends on how effectively they are embedded in routine clinical workflows. This paper describes the real-world integration of an automated MRI comparison pipeline with a picture archiving and communication system (PACS), evaluates its effect on lesion detection performance in a clinical neuroradiology setting, and discusses practical, technical, and regulatory considerations relevant to deployment. We outline the architecture, the data-handling and registration steps, the presentation of results to radiologists, and the governance measures required for safe use. We also discuss limitations and directions for future work. Our aim is to provide a practical account that other institutions can adapt when considering similar deployments.

Introduction

Multiple sclerosis is a chronic immune-mediated disorder of the central nervous system characterized by inflammatory demyelination, axonal injury, and neurodegeneration. MRI is the principal imaging modality used in its diagnosis, prognostication, and monitoring. In clinical trials and routine practice, the emergence of new or enlarging T2-hyperintense lesions and the appearance of gadolinium-enhancing lesions are widely used as markers of disease activity. Consequently, accurate longitudinal comparison of serial MRI examinations is a recurring task for neuroradiologists.

Manual lesion comparison presents several challenges. Radiologists must visually align sequential scans, identify subtle changes among potentially dozens or hundreds of lesions, and distinguish genuine new lesions from artefacts, changes in acquisition parameters, or incidental findings. Studies of inter-reader agreement have consistently demonstrated variability in lesion counts, particularly for small or confluent lesions. Under time pressure, the risk of missed lesions increases, with potential consequences for clinical decision-making and for the interpretation of therapeutic response in both practice and research.

Automated methods have been developed to address these limitations. These include algorithms for intra-subject registration, lesion segmentation, and change detection, which generate candidate maps of new or growing lesions. Some approaches compute voxel-wise differences between co-registered images, while others apply segmentation to each time point and compare the resulting lesion masks. Reported performance varies with image quality, scanner heterogeneity, and the sophistication of preprocessing. Despite promising results in research cohorts, many such tools have remained confined to academic environments.

The gap between algorithmic performance and clinical benefit is often a matter of integration. A tool that requires manual export of images, separate software environments, and manual transfer of results imposes friction that can outweigh its analytical advantages. Integration with the PACS, which serves as the central repository for radiological images and reports, offers a route to seamless adoption. In this setting, automated comparison can be triggered when a new examination arrives, results can be delivered alongside the native study, and the radiologist can review findings within their familiar viewing environment.

This paper reports the experience of implementing such an integration in a clinical neuroradiology service. Our objectives were to describe the technical architecture and workflow, to assess the feasibility and performance of the system in routine practice, and to identify barriers and enablers to sustained use. We place particular emphasis on the operational details that are often omitted from methodological papers but that determine whether a tool is used safely and effectively.

Materials and Methods

Setting and scope

The integration was implemented within a tertiary neuroradiology department serving a large regional MS clinic. The department uses a vendor-neutral PACS with DICOM-compliant storage, query/retrieve, and worklist functions. The scope of the deployment was restricted to adult patients with a confirmed or suspected diagnosis of MS who had at least one prior brain MRI on record in the PACS. Examinations were eligible if they included a T2-weighted or FLAIR sequence and, where applicable, a post-contrast T1-weighted sequence, with acquisition parameters recorded in the DICOM header.

System architecture

The architecture comprised four principal components: a DICOM listener receiving incoming studies, a preprocessing and registration module, an automated comparison engine, and a results publisher returning outputs to the PACS. The DICOM listener subscribed to study-level events and identified examinations matching predefined criteria, including modality, body part, protocol name, and the presence of an MS-related indication code in the order record. Matched studies were queued for processing. Non-matching studies were ignored, reducing the risk of unnecessary computation and unintended processing.

The preprocessing stage retrieved the current examination and the most recent prior examination of sufficient quality from the PACS. Volumes were converted from DICOM to a standard volumetric format, and metadata including slice thickness, pixel spacing, repetition time, echo time, and manufacturer were logged. Bias field correction and intensity normalization were applied. Rigid and affine registration were performed to bring the prior examination into the coordinate space of the current examination, followed by a deformable step where appropriate. Registration quality was assessed automatically using overlap measures on brain masks and visually verified during validation.

The comparison engine performed independent lesion segmentation on both time points using a trained convolutional network, after which the two lesion masks were compared. Lesions present on the current scan but absent on the prior scan were labelled as candidate new lesions. Lesions whose volume increased beyond a predefined threshold, accounting for segmentation uncertainty, were labelled as candidate growing lesions. Each candidate was assigned a confidence score derived from segmentation probability and registration quality. Outputs included a binary change map, a list of candidate lesions with centroid coordinates and volumes, and a summary report.

The results publisher generated DICOM secondary capture images and structured reports. Overlay images displaying candidate lesions in color on the current examination were stored as new series associated with the study. A structured report linked to the study provided machine-readable lesion counts, volumes, and coordinates. Both were transmitted back to the PACS through a standard store operation and were made visible in the radiologist's worklist. Importantly, outputs were tagged as automated and were not written to the official radiology report field.

Workflow integration

Within the reading workflow, the automated results appeared as an additional series accessible from the same study folder used for the primary interpretation. Radiologists reviewed the native images as usual and could toggle the overlay to inspect candidate lesions. The interface allowed navigation between candidates, display of the prior and current images side by side, and acceptance or rejection of each candidate. Rejections were recorded with a free-text reason. Final determinations rested with the reporting radiologist, who retained full responsibility for the report.

To minimize workflow disruption, results were pre-computed as soon as an eligible examination was received, typically before the radiologist opened the study. Processing time for a standard examination was targeted at under fifteen minutes, and failures generated an alert to the informatics team and a notation in the worklist so that the radiologist could proceed with manual comparison.

Validation design

Before clinical deployment, the system was evaluated retrospectively on a set of consecutive examinations drawn from the institution's archive. Two neuroradiologists independently performed manual longitudinal comparison as the reference standard, with discrepancies resolved by consensus. The automated output was then compared against this reference for lesion-level sensitivity, positive predictive value, and volumetric agreement. A prospective phase followed, in which the tool was available to reporting radiologists during routine reporting, and their final reports were audited against automated outputs and against a subset of blinded re-reads.

Statistical analysis

Sensitivity and positive predictive value for new and growing lesions were calculated with binomial confidence intervals. Agreement between automated and manual lesion counts was assessed with Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients. Time to report was recorded for examinations reviewed with and without the tool, and comparisons were made using nonparametric tests. Subgroup analyses examined performance by scanner manufacturer, field strength, and slice thickness.

Governance and safety

Deployment followed the institution's clinical software governance framework. The tool was classified as decision support rather than autonomous diagnosis. Data processing occurred within the institution's network, and no identifiable data left the secure environment. Audit logs recorded every processing event, input version, software version, and radiologist action. A change control process governed updates to the segmentation model, and each new version required revalidation against the reference dataset before release. Clear labelling communicated to clinicians that outputs were advisory.

Results

During the retrospective validation phase, 412 paired examinations from 186 patients were analyzed. The automated system successfully processed 389 pairs, a success rate of 94.4 percent. Failures were attributable most often to missing or incompatible prior sequences and to substantial motion artefact that impeded registration. Among successfully processed pairs, the system identified candidate new or growing lesions in agreement with the reference standard with a lesion-level sensitivity of 0.87 and a positive predictive value of 0.79 for new lesions. Sensitivity for growing lesions was lower, reflecting the difficulty of reliably quantifying small volume changes.

Agreement between automated and manual total lesion counts was good, with an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.91. Bland-Altman analysis showed a small systematic tendency toward over-segmentation in the automated output, which was most pronounced in periventricular regions. Performance was lower for examinations acquired at 3 mm or greater slice thickness and for examinations with acquisition differences between time points, particularly where the prior study used a different manufacturer.

In the prospective phase, 1,026 examinations were reported with the tool available. Radiologists accepted approximately 71 percent of automated candidate new lesions and rejected the remainder, most commonly citing motion, vascular structures, or artefactual signal. Among accepted candidates, the final report included the new lesion in the great majority of cases. Blinded re-reads of a random subset indicated that the tool reduced the number of new lesions missed on initial reporting, with the largest benefit observed for small juxtacortical and infratentorial lesions.

Median time to report was modestly reduced for examinations with longitudinal comparison, although the difference did not reach statistical significance in the subgroup of highly complex cases. Radiologists reported that the side-by-side display and structured candidate list were the features they valued most. Usability feedback highlighted occasional latency in overlay loading and a desire for finer control over display thresholds.

Discussion

These findings indicate that automated longitudinal lesion comparison can be integrated into a PACS-based clinical workflow with acceptable reliability and meaningful benefit to lesion detection. The principal contribution of this work lies less in the algorithm itself than in the operational arrangements that allowed it to function in routine practice. Automated pre-computation, native display within the study folder, structured output that the radiologist can interrogate, and clear separation between advisory output and official reporting were, in our experience, essential enablers.

The sensitivity observed for new lesions is consistent with the literature and suggests that the tool can serve as a useful safeguard against omission, particularly for small lesions that are easily overlooked. The lower sensitivity for growing lesions reflects a known limitation of volumetric change detection, which is sensitive to segmentation variability and registration error. Clinicians should interpret volume-change outputs with appropriate caution, and the institution has adopted a conservative threshold for flagging growth.

The false-positive rate, while manageable because candidates were reviewed by radiologists, carries a real cost in reviewer time and in potential overcalling. The acceptance-rejection pattern observed during the prospective phase suggests that many false positives arise from identifiable sources, including motion, vessels, and artefacts. Future model refinement may reduce these, and the logging of rejection reasons provides a basis for targeted improvement.

Performance degradation with thicker slices and heterogeneous acquisitions underscores the importance of protocol standardization. Where longitudinal comparison is a central clinical goal, institutions may benefit from harmonizing MS protocols across scanners and sites, a step that is often administratively difficult but yields benefits across both clinical care and research. The subgroup analyses also highlight the need to validate tools across the full range of acquisition conditions encountered in practice, rather than relying solely on curated research datasets.

Integration into PACS raised several practical issues. Data transfer and storage requirements for secondary captures and structured reports were modest, but versioning of outputs and their association with the correct study required careful design. Failure handling was particularly important: when processing failed silently, radiologists could mistakenly assume that automated comparison had been performed. Explicit status indicators in the worklist mitigated this risk. Similarly, ensuring that the tool did not inadvertently alter the official report, or create confusion about which findings were radiologist-confirmed, required deliberate interface design and staff training.

From a regulatory and governance perspective, the decision to position the tool as decision support was important. It preserved the radiologist's responsibility for interpretation while allowing the institution to benefit from automation. Institutions considering similar deployments should consult their local regulatory requirements, including whether the software qualifies as a medical device in their jurisdiction and what post-market surveillance obligations apply. Continuous monitoring of performance after deployment, including periodic revalidation after model or software updates, is essential because model drift and changes in scanner hardware can alter performance over time.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The study was conducted at a single tertiary centre, and results may not generalize to community practices with different scanner fleets, protocols, or reporting norms. The retrospective validation relied on consensus reference standards, which, although rigorous, are themselves subject to human variability. The prospective phase assessed clinical utility through audit and blinded re-reading rather than through a randomized comparison, and the observed reduction in missed lesions, while encouraging, requires confirmation in larger controlled studies. Finally, the tool was evaluated for lesion detection rather than for downstream clinical outcomes, and no claims are made regarding effects on patient management or disability progression.

Future work should pursue multicentre validation across diverse scanners and protocols, prospective comparative studies measuring both detection performance and reporting efficiency, and evaluation of the tool's effect on clinical decisions. Improvements to registration robustness, particularly for motion-degraded examinations, are a priority. Investigation of user interface refinements, including adjustable thresholds and more granular display controls, may improve acceptance. Finally, integration with interoperability standards beyond DICOM, such as structured reporting templates that support longitudinal disease tracking, may further embed automated comparison within the broader informatics infrastructure of MS care.

Conclusion

Automated MRI comparison can be successfully integrated with a PACS to support the detection of new and growing multiple sclerosis lesions in routine neuroradiology practice. Success depends on careful attention to workflow design, failure handling, output presentation, and governance as much as on algorithmic accuracy. With appropriate safeguards and continued monitoring, such integration offers a practical means of improving the consistency and completeness of longitudinal MS imaging assessment, while preserving the central role of the radiologist in interpretation and reporting.

Maintaining Healthy Sleep Routines for Children: Summer and Year-Round Tips

Good sleep is one of the most important foundations for a child's growth, learning, mood, and physical health. Children need different amounts of sleep depending on their age, and most experts recommend roughly 10 to 13 hours a day for preschoolers, 9 to 12 hours for school-age children, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers. Summer break can disrupt these patterns in ways that are easy to overlook. Bedtimes often drift later, mornings become unstructured, and daylight lingers well into the evening. Parents can keep sleep on track by understanding why these changes happen and by building routines that adapt to the season without losing consistency.

Light is one of the strongest signals that tells the body when to be awake and when to sleep. Long summer evenings can delay the release of melatonin, the hormone that helps prepare the body for sleep, making it harder for children to wind down. Limiting bright light in the hour before bed can help, and closing blinds or using room-darkening curtains keeps early sunrises from waking children too soon. Exposure to natural daylight in the morning, on the other hand, supports a healthy internal clock.

A consistent bedtime and wake-up time matter more than almost any other sleep habit. Children do best when their bodies can predict when sleep is coming. Even on weekends and during vacations, keeping wake-up times within about an hour of the school-year schedule can prevent the difficult Monday-morning adjustment. Shifting bedtime by a little each night, rather than making sudden large changes, is often easier for children to adapt to.

A predictable bedtime routine signals to children that sleep is approaching. A routine might include a bath or shower, putting on pajamas, brushing teeth, reading a book together, and a few quiet minutes of conversation. The routine should be calming and the same each night, so it becomes a familiar cue. Keeping the steps brief, about twenty to thirty minutes, makes them easier to maintain during busy summer days.

Screens can make it harder for children to fall asleep. Devices emit blue-enriched light, and engaging content can keep young minds active when they should be settling down. A common recommendation is to turn off screens at least one hour before bed and to keep devices out of the bedroom overnight. Charging phones and tablets in a central location outside the bedroom is a simple way to enforce this boundary.

Physical activity supports better sleep, and summer offers plenty of opportunities for it. Outdoor play, swimming, and sports can help children feel tired at bedtime. However, vigorous exercise done too close to bedtime may make it harder to fall asleep for some children, so scheduling intense activity earlier in the evening is generally wiser.

Diet also plays a role. Large meals, sugary snacks, and caffeine, which can be found in some sodas, teas, and chocolate, can interfere with sleep. Offering a light snack if a child is hungry at bedtime, such as a small serving of yogurt or a piece of fruit, is usually fine, while heavy or spicy foods are best avoided in the evening. Staying hydrated during hot weather is important, but drinking large amounts of fluid right before bed may lead to nighttime bathroom trips, so it helps to front-load fluids earlier in the day.

Temperature affects sleep quality. Most children sleep best in a cool, comfortable room, often somewhere around 65 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit or 18 to 21 degrees Celsius. Fans, lightweight bedding, and cotton pajamas can help during warm summer nights. Air conditioning is helpful where available, though parents should take care that children are not too cold.

Noise can also disrupt sleep. Summer brings more outdoor activity, neighborhood sounds, and sometimes fireworks or late-night gatherings. White noise machines, fans, or soft background sounds can mask disruptive noises and help children stay asleep. Earplugs are not generally recommended for young children, so white noise is usually the safer choice.

Travel and vacations can throw sleep schedules off course. Time zone changes, unfamiliar beds, and exciting plans all make it harder for children to rest. Bringing familiar items such as a favorite blanket or stuffed animal can provide comfort. Where possible, maintaining a similar bedtime routine, even in a new setting, helps children feel secure and ready for sleep.

Sleep needs are closely tied to daytime naps. Young children often still need naps, while older children generally do not. Long or late naps can reduce nighttime sleep pressure, so if a child naps, it is usually best to keep the nap short, around one to two hours at most, and to finish it well before late afternoon.

Parents should watch for signs that a child is not getting enough sleep. These may include difficulty waking in the morning, irritability, trouble concentrating, hyperactivity, frequent accidents or clumsiness, and a tendency to fall asleep in the car or during quiet activities. Persistent sleep problems, loud snoring, pauses in breathing, or nightmares that disrupt daily life warrant a conversation with a pediatrician.

Back-to-school season offers a natural opportunity to reset sleep habits. Beginning the transition about one to two weeks before school starts gives children time to adjust. Gradually moving bedtime earlier by about fifteen minutes every few days is more effective than trying to shift everything at once. Practicing the school-morning routine, including wake-up time, getting dressed, and breakfast, can also reduce stress.

Teenagers face unique challenges because their internal clocks naturally shift later during adolescence. This biological change can make early school start times especially difficult. While parents cannot change the body clock, they can encourage consistent schedules, limit evening screen use, and support earlier exposure to morning light to help teens feel alert during the day.

Consistency throughout the year is the best long-term strategy. Families who keep similar routines across seasons tend to find transitions smoother and sleep more reliable. Weekend schedules that differ by only an hour or so from weekday schedules help maintain stable body rhythms.

Sleep environment matters year-round. A bedroom that is dark, quiet, and comfortable supports restful sleep in every season. Keeping the bed reserved for sleep and reading, rather than active play, helps children associate their beds with rest. Clean, comfortable bedding and a mattress that suits the child's size and needs contribute as well.

Emotional well-being and sleep are closely connected. Children who feel anxious, stressed, or unsettled may struggle to fall asleep. Talking with children about their day, validating their feelings, and creating a sense of safety at bedtime can ease worries. Some children benefit from a simple worry journal or a short conversation about tomorrow's plans before bed.

Families can also model healthy sleep habits. Children learn by watching adults, so when parents prioritize sleep, keep regular hours, and limit their own screen use in the evening, children are more likely to follow suit. Discussing the importance of rest in simple terms helps children understand why sleep matters.

Parents should be patient when establishing new routines. Changes can take one to two weeks to feel natural, and some children need more time. Small, steady adjustments tend to work better than strict rules that cause frustration. Celebrating successes, such as a child who falls asleep easily or wakes up refreshed, reinforces positive habits.

Healthy sleep routines are an investment in children's present and future well-being. Adequate rest supports memory, attention, emotional regulation, immune function, and physical growth. By understanding how summer changes affect sleep and by maintaining consistent routines throughout the year, parents can help children enjoy the season while staying rested, healthy, and ready to learn.

Every person faces decisions that feel too big to handle alone. Career choices, health concerns, money problems, and difficult relationships can leave us confused and anxious. In these moments, seeking guidance from people we trust can make a real difference. A trusted adviser, such as a parent, teacher, mentor, or close friend, can offer a perspective we may not have considered. We often become so immersed in our own worries that we lose sight of the options available to us. An outside view helps us step back and see the situation more clearly. Trusted people also know us well, which means their advice is often grounded in our values and circumstances. A good mentor does not simply tell us what to do but asks questions that help us think more carefully. Their experience may save us from mistakes they have already made or witnessed. Seeking guidance also reduces the feeling of isolation that often accompanies hardship. When we share our struggles, we discover that others have faced similar challenges and survived them. This sense of connection can ease stress and restore hope. Guidance can also strengthen our ability to cope with problems over time. By hearing how others approach difficulties, we learn strategies we can use in future situations. Of course, not every person is a good source of advice, so it is important to choose carefully. Trustworthy guides are honest, thoughtful, and genuinely concerned for our wellbeing. They tell us the truth even when it is uncomfortable, and they respect that the final decision belongs to us. Relying on flattery or on people who have their own hidden agendas can lead us astray. Therefore, wise seekers of advice listen to several perspectives and weigh them against their own judgment. Asking for help is not a sign of weakness but of maturity and self-awareness. Recognizing the limits of what we know is the first step toward learning more. In the end, trusted guidance does not replace personal responsibility but supports it. By reaching out to others, we equip ourselves to make better decisions and face life's problems with greater confidence.

Subject: FERC Policy on ROFR Pricing After Expiration of Vintaged-Rate Agreements

Dear Colleagues,

I am writing to summarize how the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approaches right-of-first-refusal (ROFR) pricing once vintaged-rate agreements reach expiration. Vintaged-rate arrangements typically set transmission or service rates by reference to the cost conditions and contract terms in effect when a given cohort of capacity was built or contracted, and their expiration raises questions about how the successor rate should be set. FERC's general posture is that the ROFR framework should not allow an incumbent to lock in favorable legacy pricing indefinitely, so renewal terms are generally expected to reflect current cost-of-service principles. The Commission has historically emphasized that rates must be just and reasonable under the Federal Power Act, and this standard guides its review of any successor pricing proposal. When a ROFR holder seeks to continue service after expiration, FERC examines whether the proposed rate reflects current investment, depreciation, and return on equity rather than the original vintage assumptions. Parties should expect scrutiny of any attempt to carry forward stale cost allocations that no longer track the underlying facilities. The Commission also looks at whether the ROFR process itself was open, transparent, and competitive enough to support the price that results. Where competing bids or alternative arrangements exist, FERC may weigh them as evidence of what a reasonable market rate would be. Transition provisions are a key consideration, and the Commission has signaled interest in avoiding abrupt rate shocks that could harm customers who relied on the earlier pricing. Any such transition should be explicitly justified on the record rather than assumed. Stakeholders should therefore document the cost basis, the reasoning behind any proposed step-down or step-up, and the impact on affected customers. Filings that clearly connect the successor rate to current costs and to the statutory standard are more likely to receive favorable treatment. Please review the attached materials and let me know if you have questions about how this guidance applies to your current contracts. I am happy to schedule a call to walk through the specifics.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Performance Evaluation and Optimization Techniques for Persistent Memory in Database Systems

Abstract

Persistent memory (PMem) technologies, such as Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory, occupy a niche between conventional dynamic random-access memory and solid-state storage, offering byte-addressable access with latencies approaching those of DRAM and capacities and persistence characteristics closer to those of storage devices. This paper examines the performance implications of integrating persistent memory into database management systems, evaluates the behavior of representative workloads on such hardware, and surveys optimization techniques that exploit its distinctive properties. We discuss the architectural foundations of persistent memory, the programming models that expose it to applications, the consistency and crash-recovery challenges it introduces, and the measurement methodology required to characterize its performance faithfully. We then present a structured evaluation framework and analyze the tradeoffs among data placement strategies, logging schemes, indexing structures, and transaction processing mechanisms. Our discussion emphasizes that naive adoption of persistent memory often fails to realize its potential, because software designed for block devices or volatile memory does not account for asymmetric read and write costs, limited write bandwidth, cache-line granularity, and the ordering guarantees required for durability. The paper concludes with a set of design principles and open research questions intended to guide the next generation of persistence-aware database engines.

1. Introduction

Database systems have long been organized around a fundamental assumption: volatile memory is fast but temporary, while secondary storage is durable but slow. This dichotomy has shaped nearly every layer of database architecture, from buffer pool management and write-ahead logging to index design and query execution. Persistent memory challenges this assumption by providing memory-mapped, byte-addressable storage that survives power loss. Such devices promise to collapse the traditional hierarchy, enabling database engines to operate directly on durable data structures without the overhead of serialization and block-level input and output.

The commercial availability of persistent memory modules has made it possible to study these promises empirically. Early generations of hardware demonstrated that read latencies are competitive with DRAM under many access patterns, while write behavior, bandwidth limits, and interaction with processor caches introduce considerations that differ markedly from both volatile memory and flash-based storage. These differences mean that database engines cannot simply be ported to persistent memory by replacing a file system with a memory-mapped region. Instead, the design of logging, recovery, buffering, and indexing must be reconsidered in light of the hardware's characteristics.

This paper addresses three questions. First, what are the performance characteristics of persistent memory that are relevant to database workloads? Second, how should these characteristics be measured and evaluated in a reproducible manner? Third, which optimization techniques offer the greatest benefit, and under what conditions? We approach these questions by synthesizing prior hardware characterization studies, describing evaluation methodology, and articulating design guidance that follows from observed behavior.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the architecture of persistent memory systems and the software abstractions used to access them. Section 3 discusses correctness requirements for durability and crash consistency. Section 4 describes a benchmarking methodology. Section 5 analyzes the performance of core database components. Section 6 presents optimization techniques. Section 7 discusses limitations and future directions, and Section 8 concludes.

2. Background on Persistent Memory Architecture

Persistent memory modules are typically installed in standard memory slots and presented to the operating system either as a memory-mapped device or as a block-accessible namespace. In the memory mode, the module serves as a large pool of volatile-like memory fronted by DRAM acting as a cache, which hides persistence from applications. In the app-direct mode, applications access the persistent region explicitly, using file system interfaces with direct access support or through load and store instructions on mapped addresses. Database systems that aim to exploit persistence typically use the app-direct mode, since it exposes durability semantics that the engine can manage.

Accessing persistent memory through load and store instructions introduces an important consideration: writes do not become durable when they leave the processor core but when they reach the persistence domain of the memory subsystem. Modern processors buffer writes in caches and write-combining buffers, and they may reorder stores to improve throughput. To guarantee durability at a known point, software must issue explicit cache-line flush instructions followed by store fence instructions. The cost of these operations is significant, and their placement largely determines the performance of write-intensive code paths.

The granularity of persistence is the cache line, typically sixty-four bytes. Writes smaller than a cache line still require flushing the entire line, which causes write amplification when a database updates small fields. Additionally, the internal media of persistent memory modules operate on larger blocks, historically around 256 bytes, so partial writes may trigger read-modify-write cycles inside the device. These internal behaviors mean that the effective cost of a small write can exceed its logical size by a considerable factor, and this must be accounted for in data layout decisions.

Persistent memory also exhibits asymmetric performance. Read bandwidth generally scales well with thread count and access size, while write bandwidth saturates at a lower number of concurrent threads and can degrade under contention. Measurements have shown that write throughput can peak with only a few threads per module and may decline when additional threads compete for the same channels. Software that assumes symmetric bandwidth will misjudge the throughput of logging and checkpointing operations, which are dominated by writes.

NUMA topology further complicates performance. Persistent memory modules are attached to specific sockets, and accesses from remote sockets traverse an interconnect with additional latency and reduced bandwidth. Placement of data and threads relative to their memory is therefore a first-order concern. Operating system policies for page allocation and thread scheduling can have large effects on tail latency unless they are explicitly controlled.

3. Programming Models and Crash Consistency

Exposing persistent memory to applications requires a programming model that allows developers to reason about which updates are durable and in what order. Low-level approaches involve manual flush and fence sequences, which are error-prone and difficult to verify. Higher-level libraries provide transactional semantics over persistent memory regions, typically using undo or redo logging internally to guarantee atomicity of multi-word updates. These libraries reduce programmer burden but introduce their own overheads, which must be weighed against the simplicity they provide.

Crash consistency is the central correctness concern. After a power failure, the persistent state must correspond to a consistent point in the execution, meaning that either all or none of the effects of an atomic operation are visible. Achieving this requires careful ordering of stores so that pointers are not made visible before the data they reference is durable. A common failure mode occurs when a new node is linked into a persistent data structure before its contents have been flushed, leaving a dangling reference after a crash. Testing for such defects requires fault injection frameworks that simulate crashes at arbitrary points in the instruction stream.

Memory leaks and allocation failures are also more consequential with persistent memory than with volatile memory, because allocations persist across restarts. A persistent allocator must therefore record its metadata durably and recover from crashes without losing or duplicating blocks. Allocator design thus becomes part of the database's durability guarantee, and its performance affects every insertion and update path.

Interactions with the processor's memory model require attention as well. Stores may become visible to other threads before they are durable, so concurrency control protocols must be designed so that committed transactions are not exposed to readers in a state that could be lost on crash. Commit protocols that release locks before durability is established can violate serializability after recovery, which is an additional constraint beyond the ordinary concurrency control problem.

4. Benchmarking Methodology

Evaluating persistent memory requires care in workload construction, hardware configuration, and measurement. Microbenchmarks that measure sequential and random read and write bandwidth at varying access sizes, thread counts, and NUMA placements provide a baseline characterization of the device. These should be complemented by latency measurements that distinguish between cache-resident and cache-missing accesses and that isolate the cost of flush and fence operations.

Database-level evaluation should use established benchmarks such as YCSB for key-value access patterns, TPC-C for transactional workloads, and analytical workloads derived from TPC-H for scan-intensive processing. Each benchmark stresses different aspects of persistent memory behavior. YCSB workloads with high update proportions expose logging and flush costs, while read-dominated workloads highlight the efficiency of index traversal and the impact of cache misses. TPC-C combines multi-statement transactions with contention, making it suitable for studying the interaction of concurrency control and durability.

Reproducibility demands full disclosure of hardware configuration, including module capacity, interleaving settings, firmware version, memory mode versus app-direct mode, operating system kernel version, and file system or direct access configuration. Results obtained under different configurations may differ substantially, and comparisons across studies should account for these differences. Warm-up periods, repetition counts, and reporting of variance are also necessary, since persistent memory performance can exhibit transient behavior associated with wear management and internal caching.

Measurement itself introduces overhead. Hardware performance counters and tracing tools can alter timing, and instrumentation that flushes or fences may change the very behavior being observed. Evaluators should validate instrumentation by comparing against uninstrumented runs and should report the magnitude of any perturbation.

Crash testing constitutes an essential complement to performance measurement. Fault injection, in which execution is halted at randomized points and the persistent state is then checked for consistency, can reveal ordering bugs that performance tests miss. Such tests should be run across all recovery paths, including partial log replay and interrupted checkpoints.

5. Analysis of Database Components

5.1 Logging

Write-ahead logging is the dominant source of durable writes in most database systems. Traditional logging serializes log records into a buffer and writes them to a log file through the operating system, incurring system call overhead and copy costs. Persistent memory allows log records to be appended directly to a mapped region, eliminating these copies. Experiments comparing these approaches generally show substantial reductions in commit latency for small transactions, because the dominant cost shifts from kernel transitions to cache flush operations.

However, log design must address the granularity of flushes. Appending records in cache-line-sized units and flushing each unit individually can produce excessive flush traffic, while batching many records before a single flush increases commit latency. Group commit, which amortizes the cost of durability across multiple transactions, remains beneficial, but the batching threshold should be tuned to the device's write bandwidth curve rather than inherited from disk-based defaults.

Log record format also matters. Compact encodings reduce the volume of data written, which directly reduces the time spent flushing. Delta-based logging, which records only changed bytes, can reduce write volume for updates to large tuples, though it complicates recovery because log replay must reconstruct full tuples from deltas.

5.2 Indexing

Index structures such as B-trees, hash tables, and skip lists have been adapted to persistent memory with varying degrees of success. Traditional B-trees designed for block devices use large nodes that are rewritten in full on update, producing write amplification at the cache-line level. Persistent B-tree variants use smaller nodes, in-place updates with careful ordering, or log-structured organization to limit the number of flushes per update. Experimental comparisons indicate that the best choice depends on the ratio of reads to writes and on the key distribution.

Hash-based indexes offer low-latency point lookups and are attractive for persistent memory because their accesses are random and read-heavy, which suits the device's strong read performance. Persistent hash tables must nonetheless handle resizing and collision resolution with crash consistency in mind. Techniques such as incremental rehashing and versioned buckets allow updates to proceed while maintaining recoverability.

Learned indexes represent an emerging direction in which models approximate the mapping from keys to positions. Their compact representation can reduce memory footprint and read traffic, though their update behavior and persistence requirements remain active research topics.

5.3 Buffer Management

Traditional buffer pools cache disk pages in DRAM to hide storage latency. With persistent memory, the storage latency gap narrows, and the benefit of a DRAM buffer pool diminishes for workloads whose working set can be served directly from persistent memory. Direct access designs eliminate the buffer pool for some data structures, reducing copying and simplifying management. The tradeoff is that persistent memory reads are slower than DRAM reads, so hot data may still benefit from caching in DRAM. Hybrid designs that promote frequently accessed pages to DRAM while keeping cold data in persistent memory have shown promise, with placement policies driven by access frequency and recency.

5.4 Transaction Processing

Concurrency control protocols interact with durability in ways that affect throughput. Two-phase locking must hold locks until commit records are durable, which extends lock hold times when flush latency is high. Optimistic and multi-version protocols defer conflict detection to commit time, and their validation phases may overlap with durability operations. Epoch-based approaches group transactions into epochs whose durability is established collectively, amortizing flush costs while preserving serial order within and across epochs.

Pipelining commit operations, so that a transaction's durability wait does not block the execution of subsequent transactions on the same thread, improves utilization. This requires asynchronous commit acknowledgment and careful handling of failures during the pipeline, since transactions may be executed but not yet durable when a crash occurs.

6. Optimization Techniques

6.1 Flush Minimization

Reducing the number of cache-line flushes is among the most effective optimizations. Techniques include coalescing adjacent writes into a single cache line, avoiding redundant flushes of unchanged lines, and using non-temporal store instructions for large sequential writes that bypass the cache. Non-temporal stores can improve bandwidth for bulk transfers such as checkpointing, but they must be combined with fences to ensure ordering and durability.

6.2 Write Combining and Alignment

Aligning data structures to cache-line and device-block boundaries reduces write amplification. Padding small records to prevent them from straddling cache lines avoids double flushes, and grouping frequently updated fields within a single line limits the flush footprint of each update. Layout decisions should be informed by update frequency profiles collected during representative workloads.

6.3 Thread Management for Bandwidth

Because write bandwidth saturates at low thread counts, limiting the number of threads that perform persistent writes concurrently can improve aggregate throughput. Dedicated writer threads or write-combining queues decouple application threads from device contention. Read-heavy operations, by contrast, benefit from higher concurrency, so separating read and write paths allows each to be tuned independently.

6.4 NUMA-Aware Placement

Placing data on the socket whose persistent memory holds it, and scheduling threads on the same socket, avoids remote access penalties. Partitioning the database by socket, with each partition's persistent memory and worker threads co-located, can substantially improve throughput for workloads with good partitionability. Cross-partition transactions require coordination and should be minimized through partitioning choices.

6.5 Tiered and Hybrid Storage

Combining persistent memory with DRAM and conventional storage in a tiered hierarchy allows each medium to serve the access patterns it handles best. Placement policies may be static, based on schema or table properties, or dynamic, based on observed access statistics. Migration between tiers introduces overhead, so migration thresholds must balance responsiveness against the cost of moving data.

6.6 Compression

Compression reduces the volume of data written to and read from persistent memory. Lightweight schemes such as dictionary encoding, run-length encoding, and bit-packing can improve both capacity and bandwidth utilization without imposing heavy computational costs. The benefit depends on the balance between CPU cost and memory bandwidth, and on whether the workload is memory-bound. For write-heavy workloads, compression reduces flush volume, which can yield larger gains than for read-heavy workloads.

6.7 Recovery Acceleration

Persistent memory allows recovery to begin immediately, since the data structures survive the crash. Recovery nonetheless requires replaying logs or validating structures. Checkpointing frequency controls the length of log replay, and persistent indexes that are consistent at all times can eliminate index rebuilding. Parallel recovery, in which independent log segments or partitions are replayed concurrently, reduces restart time, subject to dependencies between records.

7. Discussion and Limitations

The evaluation framework presented here relies on the characteristics of a particular class of hardware, and the specific numbers reported in the literature may change as devices evolve. Generational changes in persistent memory, including differences in internal block size, interleaving behavior, and cache interaction, can shift the relative merits of the techniques discussed. Design principles based on asymmetry, flush cost, and NUMA locality are likely to persist, but their quantitative parameters should be re-measured on each platform.

A further limitation is that much of the existing evaluation focuses on single-node systems. Distributed databases that replicate persistent state across machines face additional questions about the interaction between local durability and replication, including whether replication can substitute for local flushes and how failure models change when persistence is local but not replicated.

The security and integrity of persistent data also merit attention. Data remaining in persistent memory after deletion may be recoverable by an attacker with physical access, and encryption schemes must be designed to protect data at rest without imposing prohibitive overhead on the write path. Key management across restarts introduces additional complexity.

Finally, the operational aspects of persistent memory, such as monitoring device health, managing wear, and handling module failures, are less studied than their performance characteristics. Database operators require tools to detect degradation and to plan capacity, and research in this area would benefit deployment practice.

8. Conclusion

Persistent memory offers database systems the opportunity to eliminate much of the overhead that arises from the division between volatile memory and block storage. Realizing this opportunity requires an understanding of the hardware's asymmetric performance, its flush-based durability model, its sensitivity to access granularity and NUMA placement, and the consistency hazards introduced by direct persistent updates. Our evaluation indicates that logging, indexing, buffer management, and transaction processing each require redesign rather than simple porting, and that the most effective optimizations include flush minimization, write-bandwidth-aware threading, NUMA-aware placement, tiered storage, and lightweight compression. Rigorous benchmarking, paired with systematic crash testing, is essential for establishing both performance and correctness. As persistent memory technologies continue to evolve, persistence-aware database engines will need to adapt their designs accordingly, and the principles outlined here provide a foundation for that adaptation.

References

The references for this topic are drawn from the broader literature on persistent memory hardware characterization, persistent data structures, database logging and recovery, and main-memory database systems. Readers seeking primary sources should consult the proceedings of major database and systems conferences, including SIGMOD, VLDB, ICDE, USENIX ATC, and EuroSys, for work on persistent memory evaluation and persistence-aware system design.

Personal choices, both large and small, gradually shape the kind of person we become. Every decision to tell the truth, to keep a promise, or to show kindness adds a layer to our character, while each act of laziness or dishonesty can weaken it. Over time, these patterns harden into habits, and habits form the foundation of who we are. A student who chooses to study consistently, for example, not only earns better grades but also develops discipline and self-respect that carry into adulthood. Choices also open and close doors, since the courses we take, the friends we keep, and the risks we accept determine which opportunities come our way. Many people find that a single decision, such as choosing to move abroad or to change careers, sets off a chain of events that redirects their entire life. Yet choices do not operate in isolation, because circumstances, family, and chance all play a part in the options available to us. Even so, what matters most is how we respond to those circumstances, and this response is itself a choice. By deliberately reflecting on our values and acting in line with them, we can take greater ownership of our direction. In the end, our character is not a fixed gift but a continuing record of the choices we have made and the ones we are willing to make next.
