Venus is often called Earth's twin because the two planets are similar in size, mass, and composition. Yet the resemblance ends almost as soon as one looks closer. Venus has a surface temperature of roughly 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, and its atmosphere is dense enough that the pressure at the surface is about ninety times that of Earth's. Clouds of sulfuric acid drift overhead, and the planet rotates so slowly that a single Venusian day is longer than its year. Given these hazards, some people argue that resources should be spent on safer destinations such as Mars or the Moon. I believe that exploring Venus is worthwhile precisely because of its difficulties, and that the challenges themselves are reasons to go.

The most compelling reason to study Venus is scientific. Venus and Earth formed from similar material at similar distances from the Sun, so the paths their histories took offer a natural experiment. Earth developed stable oceans, a climate that has supported life, and a carbon cycle that keeps temperatures within a livable range. Venus, by contrast, appears to have undergone a runaway greenhouse effect that boiled away any water and trapped enormous quantities of carbon dioxide. Understanding why these two worlds diverged would sharpen our understanding of planetary habitability in general.

That understanding has practical consequences. Climate scientists use planetary comparisons to test their models of how greenhouse gases can reshape a world. Venus offers an extreme case that no laboratory or computer simulation can fully reproduce. Learning what drove its atmosphere to such a state could help us better understand the risks of changes on our own planet, even though Earth is nothing like Venus today.

Venus also raises open questions about geology and the interior of rocky planets. Its surface appears geologically young, with evidence of widespread volcanic resurfacing, and some researchers think the planet may still be volcanically active. Determining whether this is true, and how its crust and mantle behave without plate tectonics, would tell us much about how rocky planets evolve. Studying Venus would thus address questions that Earth alone cannot answer.

The difficulties of exploring Venus are real, but they are not insurmountable. Landers such as the Soviet Venera probes survived for up to a few hours on the surface in the 1970s and 1980s and returned the only close-up images of the planet's terrain we have. Engineers have since proposed materials, cooling systems, and designs that could extend the lifespan of a lander considerably. Long-duration missions may be difficult, but short and medium-length missions are feasible and would still return valuable data.

Another approach avoids the surface altogether. Orbiters and high-altitude balloons or aerial platforms could operate in the upper atmosphere, where temperatures and pressures are far more tolerable. The atmosphere of Venus contains layers that are relatively mild, and some proposals suggest that floating vehicles could make detailed measurements there for extended periods. These options allow scientists to gather information while sidestepping the most extreme conditions.

The cost of such missions must also be weighed against their value. Space exploration is expensive, and every mission competes with other priorities. However, the knowledge gained from Venus has applications beyond planetary science, including advances in materials engineering, electronics that survive high temperatures, and autonomous systems for harsh environments. Investments made for Venus can therefore produce benefits that extend well beyond the planet itself.

There is also a broader cultural argument. Humans have always been drawn to difficult frontiers, and the decision to explore a hostile world reflects curiosity and ambition. Venus is a reminder that our own planet is not the only possible outcome for a world of its size, and studying its extremes deepens our appreciation for the conditions that make Earth habitable.

Exploring Venus will not be simple or cheap, and some missions will fail. Yet the planet offers a rare opportunity to compare two worlds that began alike and ended very differently. The dangers it presents are a measure of how much there is to learn, and they are a reason to pursue exploration with careful planning and sustained commitment. Venus is worth the effort.

This manuscript proposes an unsupervised framework for decomposing scenes into foreground objects and sequential background segments using a probabilistic generative model. The problem is well motivated, since learning object-centric representations without annotations remains an important goal for representation learning and downstream reasoning. The authors position their approach clearly against prior slot-based and mixture-based methods, and the related work section covers the relevant literature in a generally fair way. The central idea of modeling background as a sequence of segments rather than a single monolithic component is an interesting contribution and addresses a real limitation of earlier methods that treat all non-object pixels as one layer. The generative formulation is described with reasonable mathematical clarity, and the inference procedure, which relies on variational approximation, is laid out in sufficient detail to be followed. However, several assumptions underlying the model are stated without adequate justification, particularly the conditional independence structure between segments and the choice of priors over segment ordering. The experiments are conducted on synthetic datasets, which are useful for controlled analysis but limit claims about generalization to natural images with clutter, occlusion, and lighting variation. The authors should include results on at least one real-world or more complex benchmark to support their broader claims. Quantitative comparisons rely mainly on adjusted Rand index and mean intersection over union, and while these are standard, additional metrics such as boundary accuracy or sensitivity to the number of segments would strengthen the evaluation. The ablation study is informative but does not isolate the effect of the sequential background component from other architectural choices, making it difficult to attribute performance gains to the core contribution. Computational cost and training stability are discussed only briefly, and reporting wall-clock time, memory requirements, and variance across random seeds would help readers judge practical applicability. The qualitative figures are helpful, yet some failure cases are shown without analysis, and a discussion of when and why the model fails would improve transparency. The paper would also benefit from clearer notation, as several symbols are reused with changing meanings across sections, which complicates verification of the derivations. Code and trained model release would greatly increase reproducibility, and the authors should commit to making these available. Overall, the paper presents a promising and reasonably original direction, but the empirical support and the justification of modeling assumptions need strengthening before the central claims can be considered well established. I recommend major revision.

Experts Weigh AI's Promise and Peril as Robots Enter Elder Care

Debate over the future of artificial intelligence intensified this week as researchers, policymakers, and industry leaders gathered to discuss how the technology may reshape daily life. Supporters argue that AI could boost productivity, accelerate scientific discovery, and help address labor shortages across health care and other essential fields. Critics counter that the same systems could deepen inequality, spread misinformation, and concentrate economic power in the hands of a few large companies. Among the most closely watched applications is the use of robots in elder care, where demand is rising as populations age in many countries. Proponents say companion robots and automated assistants can help seniors take medications on schedule, monitor vital signs, and reduce feelings of loneliness. Several nursing homes have piloted robotic pets that respond to touch and voice, and some families report that their relatives seem calmer and more engaged. Caregivers, however, raise concerns about whether machines can truly replace human attention, empathy, and judgment. Advocacy groups warn that cost-cutting could lead facilities to substitute technology for staff rather than supplement them. Privacy is another flashpoint, since many monitoring devices collect detailed data on residents' movements, sleep, and conversations. Researchers emphasize that older adults should have a meaningful say in whether and how such tools are used. Some studies suggest that people who receive regular social contact show better health outcomes, which has led some clinicians to argue that technology should encourage human connection rather than replace it. Ethicists also point to questions of consent, particularly for residents with cognitive decline who may not fully understand what they are agreeing to. Regulators in several regions are beginning to examine standards for medical and care-related AI, including requirements for testing, transparency, and accountability. Industry representatives generally support oversight but caution that rules should not stifle innovation that could benefit patients. Labor unions have pressed for protections ensuring that automation does not eliminate jobs or erode working conditions for care workers. Economists expect that AI will change the structure of many occupations, creating new roles even as it displaces others. Education and retraining programs, they argue, will be essential to help workers adapt. Beyond elder care, debate continues over AI's influence on education, creative industries, and public discourse. Some commentators foresee a future of abundance in which routine tasks are handled by machines and people pursue more meaningful work. Others warn of a more troubling path marked by surveillance, job insecurity, and widening social divides. Most experts agree that outcomes will depend less on the technology itself than on the choices societies make about how to design, govern, and deploy it. As the conversation continues, many say the central question is not whether AI will transform society, but who will shape that transformation and whose interests it will serve.

Intergenerational partnerships, in which young people and older adults work, learn, or create together, offer benefits that extend well beyond the activities themselves. Such relationships help students develop teamwork, communication skills, social confidence, and independence in ways that classroom instruction alone rarely achieves. When a teenager and a retired engineer build a model bridge together, for example, they must divide tasks, negotiate ideas, and combine their different strengths toward a shared goal. The younger partner brings fluency with new technology, while the older partner contributes patience and hard-won practical knowledge, and each learns to value the other's perspective. This kind of collaboration teaches teamwork in its most authentic form, because success depends on mutual respect rather than on competition or conformity. Communication is strengthened in a similar way, since working across a generational gap requires students to explain their thinking clearly and to listen carefully to views that may differ sharply from their own. Students learn to adjust their vocabulary, to ask thoughtful questions, and to recognize that good communication is a two-way exchange rather than a one-sided presentation. Over time, these experiences translate into greater fluency in everyday conversations with teachers, employers, and peers. Social confidence also grows through intergenerational contact, particularly for students who feel uncertain in group settings. Interacting regularly with an adult who shows genuine interest in their ideas can make a young person more willing to speak up, share opinions, and take social risks. The relationship offers a low-pressure environment in which mistakes are met with encouragement rather than judgment, which allows students to test their voices and gradually become more assured. Finally, intergenerational partnerships foster independence by placing students in roles where they must make decisions and take responsibility. Rather than being directed at every step, young participants often plan tasks, solve problems, and follow through on commitments. Older partners can offer guidance without taking over, encouraging students to trust their own judgment and learn from the outcomes. In this way, such partnerships prepare young people not only to work well with others but also to act capably on their own, making them more self-reliant members of their communities.

The Reaper's ledger had never been drawn by lottery before, but the Council of the Dead had grown tired of arguments over who would have to walk beside the man. So they filled a great bronze drum with the names of every soul who had ever been wronged by the tyrant, and the Reaper turned the crank. Ines Varga, a seamstress whose brothers had vanished into his prisons, heard her name called in the hush of the gray hall. She did not weep, and she did not protest. She simply rose and took her place in the line of nine. The dictator arrived with his medals still pinned to his chest, bellowing that he had been promised a throne. The nine said nothing as they approached him. Ines walked at the front, her hands folded, and when the gates of the underworld opened she stepped aside to let him pass first. He stumbled over the threshold and looked back with confusion, searching their faces for a flicker of fear or fawning. He found only a patient silence. The Reaper closed the gate behind them with a soft, final click. Ines turned toward the light that was her own and felt, for the first time in decades, that her brothers could finally rest.

The manuscript presents a benchmark suite intended to let researchers quickly assess reinforcement learning algorithms across a set of targeted behavioral environments. The motivation is well grounded, since many existing benchmarks are large and slow to run, which discourages rapid iteration and comparison. The authors clearly articulate the gap they aim to fill and position their work reasonably against established suites such as Atari and MuJoCo-based collections. The design choice to organize environments around specific behavioral competencies, such as exploration, credit assignment, and generalization, is a useful and interpretable contribution. However, the paper would benefit from a more precise definition of each targeted behavior, since the current descriptions leave ambiguity about what an environment must test to count as belonging to a given category. The experimental section reports results for several baseline algorithms, but it does not include variance across random seeds or confidence intervals, which limits confidence in the reported rankings. Computational cost is claimed to be low, yet the paper does not provide wall-clock timings or hardware specifications that would allow readers to verify this. The authors should also justify the chosen difficulty calibration and explain whether it remains stable across different algorithm families. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing the full code, configuration files, and exact versions of dependencies, and the current submission only partially addresses this. The discussion of limitations is brief and should expand on potential overfitting of algorithm design to the suite itself. Overall, the work is a practical and potentially valuable tool, but the claims of speed, discriminative power, and behavioral targeting require stronger empirical support. I recommend a major revision addressing these points before the paper can be considered for acceptance.

Students should be allowed to use their cell phones during lunch and free periods because these short breaks are meant for rest and personal time, not constant supervision. After hours of focused classwork, students need a chance to step back, relax, and recharge their minds. Phones offer a simple way to do this, whether by listening to music, chatting with friends, or catching up on news from home. Many students also rely on their phones to stay in touch with family members, especially those who commute, have part-time jobs, or have responsibilities outside of school. Allowing phone use during these periods gives them a way to manage those obligations without leaving campus or missing important messages. Restricting phones entirely can also create unnecessary tension, as students feel treated like children who cannot be trusted with a few free minutes. Trust, when extended thoughtfully, tends to encourage responsible behavior in return. Schools can still set clear expectations, such as keeping phones out of cafeteria lines and avoiding disruptive sounds, which preserves order without banning devices outright. Lunch and free periods are also a natural time for students to handle personal tasks like scheduling appointments, reading assigned material for other classes, or checking school portals. Many adults use their phones on their own breaks at work, and learning to manage that habit at school is valuable preparation for adult life. Some critics worry that phones will distract students from socializing face to face, but many students use their phones to coordinate meetups and stay connected with friends who share their interests. A balanced policy would give students flexibility while holding them accountable for their conduct. Ultimately, allowing phone use during lunch and free periods respects students as capable young people and acknowledges the real role these devices play in their daily lives. With clear rules and mutual trust, schools can make these breaks both restful and productive.

Outdoor basketball offers a simple and accessible way for students to stay active while enjoying the fresh air and open space of a public court or school yard. Playing the game regularly builds cardiovascular endurance, as sprinting, jumping, and quick changes of direction raise the heart rate and strengthen the lungs over time. It also develops coordination, balance, and agility, since dribbling, passing, and shooting all require precise control of the body. Because the sport involves running up and down the court for extended periods, it helps improve stamina and can contribute to healthier body weight and stronger bones and muscles. Beyond the physical benefits, outdoor basketball supports mental well-being by giving players a healthy outlet for stress and tension after a long day of classes. The rhythm of bouncing the ball and the focus required to track a moving game can create a calming, meditative state that clears the mind. Exercise in natural light, such as the sunshine and open air found outdoors, has been linked to improved mood and reduced feelings of anxiety. Basketball also builds confidence as players improve their skills, celebrate small victories, and learn to handle both wins and losses with resilience. Working as a team fosters communication, cooperation, and a sense of belonging, which are valuable for emotional health. Enjoyment is perhaps the most important reason many people keep playing, since the game is fun, social, and endlessly engaging. Pickup games allow players of different backgrounds and abilities to meet, share friendly competition, and form lasting connections. Unlike many structured activities, outdoor basketball requires little equipment and no membership, so it is open to nearly anyone with a ball and a court. Players can practice alone, shooting free throws or working on dribbling drills, or join a group for a lively game. The variety of play keeps the activity fresh, as every session offers new challenges and opportunities to learn. For students seeking a balance between work and rest, outdoor basketball provides a rewarding way to stay fit, relieve stress, and genuinely enjoy their free time. Encouraging more young people to step onto the court may therefore be one of the simplest and most effective investments in a healthier, happier school community.

The Cane Ridge Revival: Historical Impact, Excesses, and Lessons for Spiritual Awakening

The Cane Ridge Revival took place in August 1801 at Cane Ridge, near Paris, in Bourbon County, Kentucky, and it became one of the most famous events of the Second Great Awakening. Organized in part by Barton W. Stone, a Presbyterian minister, the gathering was intended as a sacramental occasion, a communion meeting that would draw families together for several days of worship. Estimates of attendance vary widely, but contemporary and later accounts suggest that between ten and twenty thousand people may have come, many traveling long distances on foot, horseback, or in wagons. The crowds were so large that preachers spoke from several stands at once, and worshippers gathered in clusters across the grounds to hear them. Historians generally regard the precise numbers as uncertain, since the figures come largely from observers who had strong opinions about the event.

The frontier setting shaped the character of the meeting. Kentucky in the early nineteenth century was a region of new settlements, scattered churches, and a shortage of ordained clergy, and many people had little regular access to preaching or the sacraments. The revival addressed these needs by bringing together people from different denominations, including Presbyterians, Methodists, and Baptists, who preached a message of personal conversion and the free offer of salvation. Methodists in particular, with their circuit-riding preachers and emphasis on emotional religious experience, were effective at reaching frontier communities. The meeting thus reflected both the religious hunger of the period and the practical difficulties of providing for it.

Accounts of the revival describe dramatic physical responses among participants. People reportedly fell down in a condition sometimes called the "falling exercise," while others jerked, barked, danced, or lay motionless for long periods. Some observers described spiritual ecstasy and joyful weeping, while others were disturbed by what they saw as disorder and emotional excess. These phenomena were not entirely new to revivalism, but the scale at Cane Ridge made them especially visible and controversial. Participants interpreted these experiences as evidence of the Holy Spirit at work, whereas critics viewed them as hysteria or manipulation.

The revival also produced significant theological and institutional consequences. Its emphasis on individual conversion, the universal offer of the gospel, and the authority of personal religious experience helped to shape the broader character of American evangelicalism. Many of the participants who went home from Cane Ridge carried this spirit into new congregations, camp meetings, and missionary efforts. Within a few years, camp meetings had spread across the Ohio Valley and into other parts of the South and West, becoming a central feature of frontier religious life.

The Cane Ridge gathering also contributed to tensions within the Presbyterian Church. Many Presbyterian leaders were uneasy with the emotional displays and with the willingness of ministers from different traditions to cooperate. Some clergy worried that the revival undermined doctrinal precision and the orderly structure of church government. These concerns helped lead to a series of disputes that eventually divided Presbyterians in Kentucky and beyond, and Stone himself later broke away from the Presbyterian Church. He and others formed independent congregations that sought to restore what they regarded as primitive Christianity, a movement that later contributed to the Restoration Movement, including the Christian Church and the Disciples of Christ.

Critics of the revival raised several concerns about its excesses. The emotional intensity could overwhelm people, and some participants later reported confusion, fear, or lasting distress. The large open-air gatherings made it difficult for ministers to exercise pastoral oversight, so enthusiasm sometimes outran careful teaching. There were also worries about the enthusiasm of some preachers, whose sensational methods could encourage people to value dramatic experiences over sustained discipleship. Such concerns were not limited to Cane Ridge, but the event became a reference point for debates about how religious emotion should be understood and channeled.

Historians have offered varied assessments of the revival's significance. Some emphasize its role in reshaping American religion, arguing that it helped create a more democratic and participatory form of Christianity that appealed to ordinary people. Others focus on the social dimensions of the event, noting that it brought together people across class and regional lines while still reflecting the hierarchies and exclusions of the period. Enslaved and free African Americans attended some revival meetings and were in several cases converted, and their participation contributed to the growth of Black churches, though the revival's racial dynamics were complicated and often unequal. Scholars continue to debate how much the revival was a religious turning point and how much it expressed broader frontier anxieties and aspirations.

For those seeking to promote spiritual awakening today, the Cane Ridge Revival offers several lessons. First, genuine renewal often grows out of community, prayer, and shared worship rather than from spectacle alone. Second, emotional sincerity is valuable, but it should be grounded in sound teaching and accountable leadership. Third, the care of people during and after intense religious experiences matters, since healthy faith requires follow-up, discipleship, and pastoral attention. Fourth, cooperation across differences can strengthen witness, though it also requires clear commitments about shared beliefs. Finally, the revival reminds communities that awakening can reshape not only individual lives but also the institutions and relationships that surround them.

A careful reading of Cane Ridge therefore avoids both uncritical celebration and blanket dismissal. The event reveals the power of faith to draw people together and to transform their sense of purpose, while also showing the risks of unchecked enthusiasm and institutional strain. Those who study it can learn how to value heartfelt devotion while maintaining reflection, humility, and care for others. In this sense, the revival remains a useful case study for anyone interested in how spiritual movements begin, grow, and sometimes fracture.

This manuscript examines how the geometry of ReLU networks relates to the effectiveness of ensemble-based defenses against adversarial attacks on image classifiers. The authors motivate the study well, noting that piecewise-linear decision regions create local structure that adversaries can exploit, and that ensembling is a common but incompletely understood response. The introduction is clear and situates the work reasonably within prior literature on adversarial robustness, though it could engage more directly with recent work on gradient masking and its pitfalls. The theoretical section characterizes linear regions and boundary distances for ensemble members, and the derivations appear mostly sound, although some steps relating region volume to robustness rely on assumptions that are stated only briefly. The authors should clarify whether their bounds hold for the specific architectures evaluated or only under idealized conditions. The experimental design covers several standard datasets and a range of attack strengths, which is a strength. However, the evaluation relies heavily on fixed-budget PGD and FGSM attacks, and the paper would be considerably more convincing with adaptive attacks designed specifically to defeat ensemble defenses. Reporting robust accuracy under such adaptive threat models is essential before claims of improved robustness can be accepted. The ablation studies are informative, particularly the comparison of ensemble diversity measures, but the diversity metric is introduced without a clear justification for why it should correlate with robustness. Figures showing decision boundary geometry are helpful, yet the captions are too brief and several plots lack axis labels or consistent color scales. Statistical reporting is inconsistent: some results include confidence intervals over multiple seeds while others report single runs, making it difficult to judge whether reported gains exceed run-to-run variance. The related work section is thorough in citing ensemble defenses but underrepresents theoretical analyses of ReLU expressivity, which would strengthen the framing. Code availability is mentioned, which is commendable, but the repository lacks documentation for reproducing the main tables. The discussion acknowledges limitations but does not address computational overhead, which is a practical concern since ensembles multiply inference cost. Overall, the paper offers a useful geometric perspective and a promising direction, but the robustness claims require stronger adaptive evaluation, more consistent statistical reporting, and tighter connection between theory and experiments. I recommend a major revision before the work can be considered for publication.

This paper proposes a dynamic knowledge graph framework for tracking entity locations and states as they evolve across narrative text. The authors address a real gap, since most knowledge graph construction methods treat facts as static triples and struggle with temporal change. The motivation is clearly stated, and the introduction situates the work well within prior research on event extraction, temporal knowledge graphs, and narrative understanding. The problem definition is precise, distinguishing between location changes and state changes such as possession, condition, or social relations. The related work section is thorough, though it could more directly compare against recent neural approaches to entity tracking in procedural text. The proposed architecture combines a span-based entity recognizer with a transition model that updates a graph node's attributes after each sentence. This design is intuitive and easy to follow, which is a strength. However, the paper does not sufficiently justify why the transition model is conditioned only on the current sentence rather than on a longer window of context. Several narrative phenomena, such as flashbacks and implicit movement, may require broader context. The formalization of the graph update rules is mostly clear, but some notation is overloaded, with the same symbol used for both node embeddings and attribute vectors in different sections. The experimental setup uses two annotated corpora, one of fiction and one of news-style narrative, which is a sensible choice for testing generality. Nevertheless, the annotation guidelines are described only briefly, and no inter-annotator agreement score is reported for the state labels, which raises concerns about label reliability. The baselines include static knowledge graph extraction and a rule-based tracker, but the absence of a strong neural sequence-labeling baseline weakens the comparison. The main results show consistent improvements in location accuracy, with gains of roughly six to nine points over the static baseline. The improvements for state tracking are smaller and less consistent across corpora, and the authors acknowledge this but attribute it mostly to annotation noise without providing evidence. The ablation study is a valuable addition, showing that removing the update gate causes the largest performance drop. However, the ablations would be more convincing with variance estimates across multiple random seeds. The error analysis is informative, identifying common failure cases such as coreference errors when multiple characters share pronouns and ambiguous movement verbs. These observations suggest concrete directions for future work that the authors could have developed further. The discussion of limitations is brief and should be expanded to cover dataset size, English-only evaluation, and the reliance on sentence-level segmentation. The paper would also benefit from a more detailed comparison of computational cost, since the update step runs for every sentence and may scale poorly for long novels. The figures are clear, although the architecture diagram omits the gating mechanism described in the text, which may confuse readers. The writing is generally fluent, though some paragraphs in the methods section are dense and would benefit from restructuring. Code and data release is mentioned, which is commendable, but the repository link was not functional at the time of review. Reproducibility would be improved by providing hyperparameter settings and training details in a table. The ethical considerations section is appropriate for a study on textual data, though it could address potential misuse for surveillance-like tracking of individuals in news text. Overall, the paper presents a sound and useful idea with reasonable execution. Its main contributions are the update formulation and the empirical demonstration of gains on location tracking. I recommend a minor revision, contingent on stronger baselines, reported annotation agreement, seed-level variance, and a more complete discussion of limitations.

Market participants should keep in mind that conditions in late 2001 were shaped by the broader energy market environment of that year, including shifting supply expectations and changing storage levels. Any analysis built on these conditions should account for those factors.

This paper proposes a method for estimating uncertainty in neural networks by replacing the non-differentiable max and argmax operations with probabilistic approximations that can be propagated through the network. The central idea is practical: the authors aim to obtain calibrated uncertainty estimates without the substantial computational cost of ensembles or Bayesian sampling. The motivation is clearly stated and well situated within the existing literature on uncertainty quantification, which makes the contribution easy to understand. The mathematical derivation of the probabilistic approximations is sound and carefully presented, though some steps would benefit from more explicit justification of the independence assumptions made. The experimental evaluation covers standard benchmarks and compares against common baselines such as Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles, which is appropriate, but the paper would be stronger with results on larger-scale datasets and with an analysis of how the approximation error scales with the number of classes. The reported runtime savings are promising, yet the authors should specify the hardware and implementation details more fully so that the efficiency claims can be reproduced. Overall, the paper is a solid contribution with a clear method and encouraging results, and I recommend minor revisions addressing the assumptions, scalability analysis, and reproducibility details.

Making major life choices is rarely a solo act, even when the decision feels deeply personal. Careers, relationships, education, and where to live all carry consequences that stretch far into the future, and few of us have enough experience to see every path clearly on our own. This is why seeking trusted guidance has long been valued across cultures and generations. A wise mentor, a thoughtful parent, or an experienced friend can offer perspective that our own emotions often obscure. When we are excited, anxious, or afraid, our judgment can narrow, and an outside voice can widen the view again. Trusted advisers also bring knowledge we may lack, such as how a particular industry works, what a degree really leads to, or what early warning signs to watch for in a relationship. Their experience gives us access to lessons they learned, sometimes painfully, so that we do not have to repeat every mistake ourselves. Guidance also helps us test our assumptions. A good adviser asks questions we have avoided, challenges the story we tell ourselves, and points out gaps in our reasoning. Such honesty can feel uncomfortable, yet it is exactly what makes the advice valuable. Equally important is the trust itself, which means choosing advisers whose intentions are sincere and whose judgment we have reason to respect. Not everyone who offers an opinion has our best interests at heart, so discernment matters. Seeking guidance does not mean surrendering responsibility for our choices. The final decision remains ours, and we must weigh advice against our own values, goals, and circumstances. The strongest approach combines several perspectives rather than relying on a single voice. In the end, seeking trusted guidance reflects humility and wisdom rather than weakness. It acknowledges that no one has complete knowledge of their own future, and that thoughtful people benefit from the insight of others. Those who seek such counsel often make choices they can stand behind, even when the outcomes are uncertain.

The manuscript proposes a control variate to reduce the variance of second-order Monte Carlo gradient estimators in stochastic computation graphs, extending first-order pathwise and score-function methods to Hessian-vector and higher-order gradient quantities. The problem is well motivated, since second-order information is increasingly needed for meta-learning, curvature-aware optimization, and sensitivity analysis, yet naive estimators suffer from prohibitive variance. The authors derive the control variate from a Taylor-style decomposition of the integrand and show that it remains unbiased when its expectation is known or analytically tractable, which is a clear and useful property. The theoretical section is generally rigorous, though the assumptions on differentiability and integrability of the graph's stochastic nodes should be stated more explicitly, particularly for discrete latent variables where reparameterization fails. The variance analysis would be stronger with a formal bound comparing the proposed estimator against the baseline score-function-of-score-function estimator, rather than relying primarily on empirical curves. The experiments cover a reasonable range of synthetic benchmarks and a small reinforcement learning task, but they would benefit from larger-scale problems and wall-clock cost comparisons, since the control variate adds computational overhead. Ablations isolating the contribution of each component of the proposed control variate are limited and should be expanded to support the claimed mechanism. The related work section omits some relevant literature on doubly-reparameterized and Rao-Blackwellized gradient estimators, and situating the contribution against these would sharpen the novelty claim. Several notational inconsistencies between the main text and the appendix make the derivations harder to follow and should be corrected. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful gap with a sound core idea, and I recommend a major revision that strengthens the theoretical bounds, broadens the empirical evaluation, and clarifies the assumptions and notation.

Persistence and purposeful effort are often described as the keys to success, yet their real value lies in how they shape a person's character and their influence on others. Success is rarely the product of a single brilliant moment. Instead, it tends to emerge from steady, deliberate work carried out over long stretches of time, often when no one is watching and little progress is visible.

Consider the difference between effort and purposeful effort. Effort alone can be scattered, repeated without direction, or spent on tasks that do not matter. Purposeful effort, by contrast, is aimed at a clear goal and adjusted when the goal or the method proves mistaken. A student who studies every night without a plan may improve slowly, but a student who identifies weak areas, seeks feedback, and revises their approach will usually advance faster. Purpose gives effort its direction.

Persistence is what keeps purposeful effort alive when enthusiasm fades. Every worthwhile goal eventually meets obstacles: a difficult concept, a failed attempt, a period of doubt. At these moments, the temptation to quit is strongest, and the people who continue are often not the most talented but the most willing to keep going. Persistence does not mean refusing to change course; it means refusing to abandon the purpose itself simply because the path has become hard.

History offers many examples of this quality. Scientists have repeated experiments dozens of times before a result held up. Writers have revised a single manuscript for years. Athletes have trained through injuries and setbacks to return to competition. Their achievements are usually remembered as moments of triumph, but those moments were built from countless ordinary days of effort that did not feel significant at the time.

Yet success, on its own, is an incomplete measure of a life. The more lasting question is what that success does for others. Persistence and purposeful effort affect the people around us, sometimes more than we realize. A person who keeps working through difficulty teaches others, by example, that difficulty can be survived. A teacher who refuses to give up on a struggling student may change that student's sense of what is possible.

Positive influence grows from this kind of modeling. People learn more from what they observe than from what they are told. When a parent keeps a commitment despite exhaustion, or a coworker patiently helps a colleague master a new skill, they demonstrate values that others carry forward. These small acts of steady care accumulate into a meaningful effect on families, workplaces, and communities.

Purposeful effort also strengthens the bonds of trust that make cooperation possible. People are more willing to rely on someone who reliably does what they say they will do. Over time, a reputation for diligence and follow-through becomes a source of influence, allowing that person to be trusted with responsibility and to guide others through shared work.

It is worth distinguishing persistence from stubbornness. Stubbornness refuses to learn from failure, while persistence adapts. A persistent person asks whether the current strategy is working, listens to criticism, and remains open to better methods. This balance matters, because effort aimed in the wrong direction can cause harm as well as waste time. Purpose must be guided by honest reflection.

Persistence also requires attention to one's own wellbeing. Rest, reflection, and support from others are not signs of weakness; they make sustained effort possible. Those who push relentlessly without pause often burn out, while those who pace their work and care for themselves can keep contributing for years. A balanced approach allows persistence to become a lasting practice rather than a brief burst of exertion.

For students, the implications are clear. Academic success depends less on natural ability than on regular practice, honest self-assessment, and the willingness to return to difficult material. Students who set specific goals, track their progress, and seek help when needed tend to build both skill and confidence. These habits extend beyond school, shaping how they will approach careers, relationships, and civic life.

Finally, persistence and purposeful effort connect the individual to something larger than themselves. When a person commits to meaningful work and sees it through, they contribute to a shared body of knowledge, craft, or care that others can build upon. Each generation inherits the results of earlier persistence, and each person has the opportunity to add to that inheritance.

In the end, persistence and purposeful effort are keys to success because they transform ambition into achievement. They are keys to positive influence because the way we work teaches others how to work, how to face difficulty, and how to care about what matters. Success measured only by personal gain is fragile, but success that uplifts others endures. The task for each of us is to choose meaningful goals, pursue them with patience and direction, and let our steady effort become a source of good for those who follow.

This manuscript investigates whether head-direction circuits inspired by biology can emerge in recurrent neural networks and whether such circuits support navigation-related representations and connectivity. The topic is timely and sits at a productive intersection of computational neuroscience and machine learning, building on the long line of work on ring attractor models of the fly and rodent head-direction system. The authors frame their contribution clearly, and the introduction situates the study well within prior literature on grid cells, place cells, and path integration. The central claim, that biologically plausible constraints on connectivity give rise to a stable angular representation, is interesting and worth testing. The model architecture is described in sufficient detail to be reproduced, which I appreciate. However, the connection between the trained network and the biological system remains largely qualitative, and the manuscript would benefit from more direct quantitative comparisons to empirical head-direction tuning curves and connectivity statistics. The analysis of the learned weight matrices is a highlight, as it shows a clear ring-like organization, but the authors should report how robust this structure is across random seeds and hyperparameter choices. The ablation experiments are informative, yet the paper does not adequately justify why certain biological constraints were included while others were omitted. I would also ask for a more careful treatment of the drift problem, since the reported angular error accumulates over long trajectories and the discussion of how visual or landmark cues correct it is brief. The figures are generally clear, though several panels lack error bars or statistical tests, which makes some of the differences between conditions hard to assess. The related work section could better acknowledge recent contributions on path integration in trained recurrent networks, as the novelty relative to these studies is not fully established. Methodologically, the training details, including optimizer settings and stopping criteria, are reported, which supports reproducibility. The code availability statement is welcome, and I encourage the authors to release trained model checkpoints as well. Some claims in the discussion, particularly about implications for neural circuit mechanisms in animals, go beyond what the modeling results can support and should be softened or explicitly framed as hypotheses. The writing is generally readable, but several passages are repetitive and could be condensed. Overall, the study is a solid and potentially valuable contribution, and I recommend a major revision addressing the quantitative comparisons, robustness analyses, and the scope of the biological claims.

In-person schooling offers benefits that remote learning struggles to replicate. Chief among them is the quality of direct human interaction between students and teachers. A teacher in a classroom can read a student's expression, notice confusion before it turns into failure, and adjust an explanation on the spot. Remote lessons often flatten these moments into a screen, where a hand raised may go unseen and a quiet struggle may go unnoticed for weeks.

Social development is another strong argument for physical classrooms. Children learn to cooperate, negotiate, resolve conflicts, and read social cues largely through everyday contact with peers. Recess, group projects, and lunch conversations build skills that cannot be fully practiced through a video call. These experiences also help students form friendships that support their well-being and sense of belonging at school.

In-person learning also supports healthier routines. Attending school in a building creates a clear separation between home life and academic work, which helps students focus and stay motivated. Without that structure, many learners, especially younger ones, struggle with procrastination, irregular sleep, and reduced physical activity. The daily commute and schedule of a school day teach punctuality and self-discipline in ways that are harder to build at a kitchen table.

Equity is a further consideration. Schools provide access to libraries, laboratories, computers, internet connections, free meals, and trained counselors that not every family can supply at home. Students from low-income households or crowded living conditions are often the most harmed when learning moves online, widening existing gaps in achievement. In-person schooling helps ensure that educational opportunity does not depend entirely on a family's resources.

Remote learning does have real advantages, including flexibility, reduced travel, and access for students who are ill, geographically isolated, or unable to attend. These benefits are genuine and deserve respect. However, they are best understood as supplements to in-person instruction rather than full replacements. A balanced approach can preserve the flexibility of online tools while keeping the classroom at the center of education.

In the end, the strengths of in-person schooling lie in its human connection, its social growth, its structure, and its fairness to all students. Those qualities are difficult to replace with a screen. For most students, a well-run physical classroom remains the most effective place to learn and grow.

Setbacks are an unavoidable part of life, and how we respond to them often shapes who we become. Overcoming difficulty builds resilience, deepens wisdom, and paves the way for lasting achievement. Each obstacle tests our character and reveals strengths we may not have known we possessed.

Resilience is the first gift that setbacks offer. When a plan fails, a person must decide whether to give up or to try again. Each time someone chooses to continue, they strengthen the capacity to bounce back. Over time, this capacity becomes a reliable inner resource that carries them through future hardships.

Wisdom grows from the lessons that failure teaches. A poor grade, a rejected application, or a lost friendship can reveal habits that need changing or assumptions that proved false. Those who reflect honestly on their mistakes gain insight that no textbook could provide. In this way, painful experiences become teachers.

Consider the experience of many famous inventors and scientists. Thomas Edison reportedly made thousands of unsuccessful attempts before developing a working light bulb. Rather than seeing each failure as a dead end, he treated each one as information about what did not work. His persistence transformed repeated setbacks into one of the most important inventions of his era.

Achievement often follows naturally from this combination of resilience and wisdom. People who have survived difficulties tend to approach new challenges with greater patience and clearer judgment. They understand that progress is rarely a straight line, so they plan for detours and remain focused on long-term goals. Their accomplishments are often more meaningful because they were earned through struggle.

Setbacks also build empathy. Someone who has experienced failure is better able to understand the struggles of others. This understanding can make a person a more supportive friend, colleague, or leader. Shared hardship often creates bonds that success alone cannot produce.

It is important to note that overcoming setbacks does not mean enduring them alone or ignoring real pain. Seeking help from family, mentors, or professionals is a sign of good judgment, not weakness. Resilience grows stronger when it is supported by a community that encourages recovery and growth.

Ultimately, the value of setbacks lies not in the difficulty itself but in what we do afterward. By facing obstacles with courage, reflecting on what they teach us, and continuing forward with renewed purpose, we transform adversity into strength. In this sense, setbacks are not the opposite of success but an essential part of the journey toward it.

Should schools require students to join an after-school activity? Many people believe that they should, and the reasons are persuasive. Such a requirement would support students' health, strengthen their social lives, and keep them safe during the hours when they are most likely to get into trouble. Sports, clubs, and arts programs encourage physical activity, which many young people do not get enough of in an age of screens and long hours of sitting. Structured activities also give students a reason to move, practice skills, and build healthy habits that can last a lifetime. Socially, after-school programs introduce students to peers they might never meet in class, helping them develop friendships, teamwork, and communication skills. Students who feel connected to a group are also less likely to feel isolated or lonely, which can protect their mental health. Safety is another important concern, since the afternoon hours between the end of school and the end of a working day are a period when unsupervised teenagers face higher risks of accidents, substance use, and poor choices. A required activity ensures that students have a supervised place to go. Critics argue that requiring participation infringes on personal freedom and ignores students who have jobs, family duties, or other responsibilities. These concerns deserve respect, and any policy should include flexibility for students with legitimate needs. Still, a well-designed requirement could offer a wide range of options, from robotics to chess to volunteering, so that every student can find something that fits their interests. Schools already require students to attend classes, learn subjects, and meet academic standards, and extending that responsibility to the hours after the final bell is a natural step. In the end, a thoughtful requirement would benefit students far more than it would burden them.

Daniel woke up on a Tuesday morning with a dry mouth, a stiff neck, and a notification count he could not explain. His phone sat on the nightstand, screen glowing with messages from classmates he barely knew. Someone had tagged him in a video. He tapped it, expecting a prank, and found himself staring at his own bedroom door, lit by the hallway lamp.

In the video, Daniel was standing in his boxer shorts, holding a toaster and humming a tune that sounded like a jingle for a cereal brand that did not exist. He was talking, but the words came out slurred and urgent. He was explaining, with great seriousness, why the moon owed him forty dollars.

Daniel did not remember any of it. He had taken his Ambien at eleven, as he did most nights during finals week, because the anxiety about organic chemistry kept him awake otherwise. The pills worked, mostly, but he had read the warnings on the bottle and the warnings had never felt like they applied to him.

The video had been posted by a roommate of a friend, a girl named Priya who lived two floors below him in the dorm. She had captioned it "when your neighbor is the moon's accountant." By lunchtime it had been shared four thousand times. By dinner it had a name: Moon Accountant Guy.

Daniel spent the afternoon reading the comments. Some were cruel. Many were delighted. A few were strangely earnest, asking whether the moon really did owe anyone money, and whether he had been right about it. One user had made a sound effect track set to the toaster hum, and it was spreading faster than the original clip.

He went to his student health center that afternoon, sitting in a waiting room full of people who looked as tired as he felt. The nurse practitioner listened carefully, then gave him a gentle lecture about combining sedatives with irregular sleep. She told him that complex sleep behaviors were a known side effect, and that he should never take the medication without a full seven or eight hours of sleep ahead of him.

Daniel nodded and promised to stop. He asked whether he should delete the video from the internet, and she laughed and told him that was not how the internet worked. She suggested he talk to someone about his anxiety, which he had been avoiding for months.

That night he set his alarm, locked his bedroom door, and placed his phone across the room so he could not reach it. He also put a chair against the door and took the pill bottle to his roommate, Marcus, asking him to hide it somewhere difficult to find. Marcus agreed, though he was clearly enjoying the situation more than he admitted.

Over the next week, the story of Moon Accountant Guy changed shape. A local radio station played the audio clip, and a comedian referenced it in a set that went viral in its own right. A bakery near campus began selling a pastry called the Accountant, which was mostly cinnamon and resentment. Daniel did not know whether to feel flattered or humiliated, and he suspected the answer was both.

The student newspaper ran an interview with him, arranged by Priya, who had started to feel guilty about posting the video in the first place. Daniel talked honestly about his insomnia, his fear of failing his exams, and the way the pills had quietly taken over his nights. He asked readers to take sleep medication seriously and to talk to a doctor before relying on it.

The article was not as popular as the video, but it reached the people who needed it most. Several students messaged him privately to say they had been taking the same medication in the same way, and that they were going to stop. One of them thanked him for being the reason they finally asked for help.

Daniel still got recognized on campus now and then. Someone would call out "Hey, moon guy," and he would wave, smile, and keep walking. He had come to accept that he would always be a little bit famous for the worst night of his sleep life.

Six weeks later he began seeing a counselor twice a week. The organic chemistry exam went better than expected, mostly because he had slept through the night for the first time since September. He never found out whether the moon really owed anyone money, but he decided it was probably not his problem to settle.

The village bell had not rung in forty years, and when it began to clang that gray autumn morning, Tomas the cooper's apprentice was the only one awake to hear it. He ran from the barrel shed with his apron still tied on, expecting a fire, and instead found the sky over the hills darkened by wings. The dragon came low over the mill, and its breath turned the water wheel to ash in a single gust. People screamed and scattered toward the church, and Tomas, who had never held a sword and was considered by most of the village to be a clumsy dreamer, stood frozen in the square. Then he noticed a glint among the rubble of the old chapel, where the ground had split open in the night. Half buried in the earth lay a shield of pale silver, its surface etched with runes that pulsed faintly like a heartbeat. Beside it was a sword whose blade was clear as river glass, and a helm shaped like a crown of woven thorns. He had no idea who had left them there, but the moment his fingers touched the shield, a warmth ran up his arm and settled in his chest. The helm settled over his head as though it had been fitted for him all along. The sword sang when he lifted it, a low note that rang through the bones of his hands. Above him the dragon wheeled, roaring, and its eye fell upon the single small figure standing in the chapel ruins. A voice, deep and ancient, seemed to rise from the silver itself, and it spoke as clearly as if it were whispering in his ear. It named him Champion of the Ember Gate and told him that the beast had come seeking the one who would answer its challenge. The villagers stared as the boy climbed the broken stones toward the open field beyond the church. Old Marta, who had buried three husbands and two sons, grabbed his sleeve and begged him to run. Tomas gently removed her fingers and said that he did not think running would save anyone now. He walked out into the open where the dragon could see him, and he raised the glass sword high. The beast descended in a thundering rush, its talons spread wide and its jaws glowing orange. Tomas did not know how to fight, but the shield moved before he told it to, catching the fire in a sheet of silver light. The sword cut through the air in a line of brilliance, and the dragon shrieked as it struck a wing. The duel lasted until the sun climbed above the hills, and by the end Tomas was bleeding from a dozen small wounds. When the final blow came, he drove the glass blade into the creature's chest, just beneath the place where its heart beat like a drum. The dragon crashed to the field, and for a long moment the village was silent. Then Marta began to cry, and the others cheered, and the bell rang once more across the valley. Tomas sat down in the grass and laughed until the tears came, and the silver shield lay quiet at his side, its runes gone dark and cool. Years later, the bards would sing of the cooper's apprentice who became the Champion of the Ember Gate. Tomas would always say that he was no hero, only a boy who happened to be standing in the right place when the legend chose to find him.

This paper proposes a method for learning joint node distributions in networks by exploiting conditional independence structure, with applications to both node classification and density estimation. The problem is well motivated, since modeling dependencies among nodes is central to many graph learning tasks, and the conditional independence framing offers a principled way to keep the model tractable. The authors position their approach clearly against existing graph neural network and probabilistic graphical model baselines, and the dual use for classification and density estimation is a notable strength. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more detailed analysis of the assumptions behind the conditional independence structure and how sensitive results are when those assumptions are violated on real-world graphs. Overall, the contribution is promising, but stronger empirical evidence on diverse datasets, along with clearer ablation studies and reproducibility details, would be needed to support the claims fully.

Nighttime restrictions, such as curfews that limit when teenagers may be outside or driving, are often introduced with the goal of keeping young people safe. Supporters argue that fewer teens on the streets late at night can reduce exposure to accidents, crime, and dangerous peer situations. Research on juvenile curfews has produced mixed results, however, and many studies find only modest effects on youth crime and victimization. Restrictions can also create safety concerns of their own, since teens who must be home early may be pushed toward unsupervised spaces or hurried driving to meet deadlines. Beyond safety, curfews affect independence, because learning to manage time, transportation, and personal decisions is an important part of growing up. Teenagers who are given reasonable freedom and responsibility often develop better judgment, while overly strict limits may leave them less prepared for adult life. Daily routines are shaped as well, as early curfews can cut into part-time jobs, extracurricular activities, study groups, and time with friends. Families must therefore balance protection with trust, and the most effective rules are often flexible, clearly explained, and tied to a teen's age and maturity. Ultimately, nighttime restrictions are not inherently good or bad, but their value depends on whether they support both the safety and the developing autonomy of young people.

Considering diverse perspectives before making important decisions is one of the most valuable habits a person can develop. Every individual sees the world through a particular lens shaped by experience, culture, and circumstance, which means no single viewpoint captures the full picture of a complex problem. When we deliberately seek out other viewpoints, we expose our assumptions to scrutiny and discover blind spots we would otherwise miss. A decision made in isolation may seem sound to the person who made it while overlooking consequences that someone with a different background would immediately recognize. Diverse perspectives also help us test the strength of our reasoning, since arguments that survive challenge from thoughtful people are generally more reliable than those that have never been questioned. Consider a community deciding whether to build a new highway: engineers, residents, environmentalists, and small business owners will each notice different costs and benefits. Listening to all of them does not guarantee agreement, but it makes the eventual choice more informed and more legitimate in the eyes of those it affects. Such openness also builds trust, because people who feel heard are more likely to accept outcomes they did not initially prefer. Of course, weighing many voices takes time and patience, and there is a risk of getting stuck in endless deliberation when action is needed. The goal, then, is not to seek unanimous approval but to gather enough varied insight to make a responsible judgment. Ultimately, the willingness to consider perspectives unlike our own reflects intellectual humility and a commitment to fairness. Those qualities lead to wiser decisions and stronger communities, which is why they deserve to be cultivated from an early age.
