Loganair, the Scottish regional airline, has announced that its chief executive is stepping down, prompting the company to begin the search for a successor. The airline said the departure was a matter of personal decision and thanked him for his leadership during his tenure. Under his guidance, Loganair has continued to operate its extensive network of routes linking the Scottish islands and mainland with airports across the United Kingdom and Europe. The board has indicated it will move quickly to identify a replacement who can maintain the airline's growth and service standards. Until a new chief executive is appointed, the existing senior leadership team will oversee day-to-day operations.

The manuscript proposes a method for musical style transfer operating on neural audio representations, and it frames evaluation as a cover-song generation task. This framing is a sensible and ambitious choice, since cover generation asks whether a system can preserve the melodic and harmonic identity of a source recording while altering its stylistic character. The authors are to be commended for tackling a problem that sits at the intersection of audio signal processing, music information retrieval, and generative modeling. The central question is well motivated, and the paper is generally readable. However, several issues need attention before the work can be considered a solid contribution.

The introduction establishes the context reasonably well, situating style transfer within the broader history of image and audio generation. It would benefit from a more careful discussion of how prior work on timbre transfer, genre conversion, and voice conversion differs from the proposed approach. At present, the related work section lists many methods but does not clearly articulate what gap the present method fills. A short paragraph explicitly stating the novelty would help readers evaluate the contribution.

The choice of neural audio representation is a key design decision, and the paper describes it at a high level without enough detail for reproduction. The authors should specify the architecture, the training objective, the dimensionality of the latent space, and how the representation is decoded back into waveform or spectrogram form. Without these details, it is difficult to judge whether the reported gains stem from the core idea or from incidental engineering choices.

The paper's treatment of content preservation is a strength. The authors separate melodic content from stylistic attributes and attempt to measure each independently. The use of chroma-based and pitch-contour metrics to assess whether the generated cover retains the original melody is appropriate. However, the reliance on a single pitch-tracking algorithm for ground truth introduces a potential source of systematic error, and the authors should either validate this choice or report results with an alternative tracker.

Style fidelity is harder to measure, and the manuscript acknowledges this difficulty. The authors use a classifier trained to distinguish genres as a proxy for stylistic match. This is a reasonable starting point, but it has known limitations. A classifier may reward superficial timbral cues while ignoring harmonic idiom, rhythmic feel, or arrangement conventions that listeners perceive as central to a style. The authors should discuss this limitation explicitly and, if possible, add a complementary measure.

The subjective evaluation is where the paper is most in need of strengthening. The listening test is described briefly, with only a sentence about the number of participants and no details on recruitment, expertise, or the exact question wording. Given that perceptual quality is the ultimate target of the work, a more thorough description is essential. Reporting inter-rater agreement, the distribution of ratings, and whether participants were blind to the condition would substantially increase confidence in the findings.

The statistical analysis of the listening test is minimal. The authors report mean scores with standard deviations but do not indicate whether differences between the proposed method and the baselines are statistically significant. Given the modest sample size implied by the description, a formal test such as a Wilcoxon signed-rank or a mixed-effects model would be appropriate, and effect sizes should be reported alongside p-values.

The baselines are a mixed set. Some are classical signal-processing methods that are reasonable comparisons, but the strongest recent neural baselines are absent or only briefly mentioned. Including at least one state-of-the-art generative model, even if adapted to the task, would make the comparison more convincing. The authors should also justify why certain stronger alternatives were excluded.

The ablation study is useful and shows that removing the content-disentanglement component degrades melodic preservation, which supports the central design claim. However, the ablation does not isolate the contribution of the representation itself from that of the training data. A version of the model trained on a different corpus would clarify whether the results generalize beyond the dataset used.

The dataset description needs more care. The paper states that the training corpus contains several thousand recordings but does not characterize its genre balance, recording quality, or the degree of overlap between training and evaluation songs. Potential leakage between training and test sets, particularly when covers of the same underlying composition appear in both, is a serious concern for cover-song tasks and must be addressed explicitly.

Licensing and provenance of the audio used for evaluation should also be stated. Many music datasets carry restrictions, and the paper should confirm that the authors had the right to use and publish results on the recordings, and whether any audio samples are released with the paper.

The results section presents the main quantitative findings in a clear table. The table would be more informative if it included confidence intervals and per-genre breakdowns, since aggregate numbers can hide substantial variation across musical styles. Some genres may be inherently harder to transfer, and this would be scientifically interesting to report.

The qualitative examples provided as audio links are valuable, and the authors deserve credit for including them. However, the paper should state clearly which examples were selected, and whether they are representative or chosen to highlight successes. Including a randomly sampled subset alongside curated examples would reassure readers about the typical quality of outputs.

The discussion section is somewhat brief and tends to restate results rather than interpret them. A more substantive discussion would examine failure cases, such as when the generated cover drifts from the original harmony or when the stylistic transformation introduces artifacts. Understanding why the method fails in specific conditions would be as informative as the reported successes.

Ethical considerations deserve more attention than the single paragraph devoted to them. Style transfer and cover generation raise questions about artist consent, attribution, and the potential for misuse in producing imitations of specific performers. The authors should discuss these issues and describe any safeguards or policy recommendations they consider appropriate.

The reproducibility statement promises code release upon publication, which is welcome, but the paper would be stronger if the code, model weights, and evaluation scripts were available to reviewers during review. Clear documentation of hyperparameters, random seeds, and compute requirements should accompany any release.

The writing is generally clear, though several sentences in the methods section are dense and would benefit from simplification. Some notation is introduced without definition, and a table of symbols would help. The figures are legible, but the spectrogram comparisons would be easier to interpret with labeled axes and matched color scales across panels.

The paper's conclusion summarizes the contributions accurately but overstates the generality of the results. Claims that the method establishes a new standard for musical style transfer are not fully supported by an evaluation on a single corpus with a limited set of baselines. The authors should moderate these claims or provide evidence across additional datasets.

Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful problem with a reasonable approach and includes a thoughtful evaluation framework. Its main weaknesses lie in the incomplete description of the method, the limited statistical rigor of the perceptual evaluation, the absence of strong recent baselines, and potential data leakage concerns. These issues are addressable within a revision cycle.

My recommendation is major revision. The core idea merits publication, but the authors need to provide the missing methodological detail, strengthen the statistical analysis, broaden the comparison, and temper the conclusions. With these changes, the work could make a useful contribution to the growing literature on neural music generation and evaluation.

Authenticity and honesty are often treated as moral ideals, but they are also practical tools for building the kind of life most people want. Friendships that last are rarely built on impressive performances or carefully managed images. They grow from the willingness to show who we really are, including our doubts, our mistakes, and our ordinary tastes. When a person lets others see the real self, they give those around them something real to respond to, and that is the foundation of trust.

Consider how most people feel when a friend pretends to enjoy something they actually dislike, or agrees with an opinion only to avoid conflict. Such moments may seem harmless, yet they create a quiet distance. The friend begins to wonder whether they are truly known, and the relationship becomes a little less solid. Honesty, by contrast, gives a friendship weight. A friend who tells us a hard truth gently and with care shows that they respect us enough to be sincere, and that respect is far more valuable than flattery.

Authenticity also matters for the relationship a person has with themselves. Every time someone pretends to be someone they are not, they carry a small burden of pretense. They must remember which version of themselves they showed to whom, and they must work to maintain it. Over time this effort can leave them feeling tired, unseen, and uncertain of their own worth. Living honestly removes that weight. A person who acts in line with their values does not need constant approval to feel secure.

Self-respect grows naturally from this kind of integrity. When someone keeps their promises, admits their errors, and speaks truthfully even when it is uncomfortable, they build a record of conduct they can be proud of. This inner evidence matters. It reassures a person that they are reliable and principled, and it makes it easier to stand firm when pressure arrives. Self-respect is not arrogance; it is the quiet confidence that comes from knowing one has acted with honesty.

Of course, authenticity does not mean saying every thought aloud without regard for others. Honesty should be paired with kindness and good judgment. There is a difference between being truthful and being cruel, and the best friends know how to speak plainly while still caring for the feelings of the person in front of them. Choosing words thoughtfully, timing difficult conversations well, and listening as much as speaking are all part of honest friendship.

Authenticity also invites others to be authentic in return. When one person drops the mask, it often makes it easier for another to do the same. Friendships can then move beyond small talk into deeper conversations about fears, hopes, and personal growth. These connections are rare and precious, and they tend to endure through changes in circumstance because they rest on mutual understanding rather than convenience.

In the end, the value of authenticity and honesty lies in what they make possible. They allow us to form friendships based on trust rather than performance, and they allow us to respect ourselves because our actions match our beliefs. Though it can feel risky to be truly seen, the rewards are lasting: relationships that feel like home and a sense of self that does not depend on the approval of others. Young people who learn this early are better prepared to build a life that is both meaningful and secure.

Joining at least one extracurricular activity is one of the most valuable choices a student can make during their school years. Classroom learning builds knowledge, but extracurricular activities build the skills and character that knowledge alone cannot provide. Students who participate in clubs, teams, or organizations gain experiences that shape them far beyond the walls of a classroom. One of the most important benefits is the development of teamwork. Whether on a soccer field, in a debate club, or in a school band, students learn to work toward a common goal with people who have different strengths and personalities. They learn to listen, compromise, and rely on others, which are abilities that employers consistently value. Extracurricular activities also teach time management. A student who balances homework, practice, and rehearsals must plan carefully and prioritize tasks. This discipline often proves more useful than any single lesson taught in school. Beyond practical skills, these activities help students discover their interests and passions. Many students do not know what they enjoy until they try something new. A student who joins the robotics club may find a lifelong interest in engineering, while another who joins the school newspaper may discover a talent for writing. Such discoveries can influence academic choices and even future careers. Extracurricular involvement also builds confidence. Performing in front of an audience, competing in a tournament, or leading a club meeting pushes students beyond their comfort zones. Each success, and even each failure, teaches resilience and self-belief. Students who feel confident in one area often carry that assurance into their classes and social lives. Furthermore, these activities create a sense of belonging. High school and college can feel overwhelming, and it is easy for students to feel isolated. Joining a group gives them a community of peers who share their interests and support their growth. Friendships formed through shared activities often last for years. Critics sometimes argue that extracurricular activities take time away from studying. While it is true that balance matters, a well-chosen activity rarely harms academic performance and often improves it. Students involved in activities tend to be more motivated and better organized. The key is to choose wisely rather than overcommit. Even a single activity, pursued with genuine effort, can make a meaningful difference. Colleges and scholarship committees also recognize the value of extracurricular involvement. They look for applicants who show initiative, commitment, and the ability to contribute to a community. A student who has stuck with an activity over several years demonstrates dedication that grades alone cannot display. Yet the most important reason to join is not to impress others but to grow as a person. Extracurricular activities give students the chance to explore, fail, improve, and succeed in a supportive environment. They turn school from a place where students simply attend classes into a place where they actively build themselves. For these reasons, every student should find at least one activity that sparks curiosity and commit to it. The rewards will extend far beyond graduation.

Travelers often find that Britain offers an exceptional mix of landmarks, cultural heritage, and chances to practice English, which together make a visit both memorable and rewarding. The country's famous sites, such as Stonehenge, the Tower of London, and the cathedrals of York and Canterbury, bring history to life in a way that textbooks cannot. Standing among ancient stones or walking through centuries-old castles allows visitors to feel connected to the people who built and lived in these places. Beyond these famous monuments, smaller towns and villages preserve traditions that reveal the everyday history of the nation. Museums across the country, many of them free to enter, display everything from Roman artifacts to modern art, giving travelers a broad view of the culture. Literature is another attraction, since visitors can follow in the footsteps of Shakespeare in Stratford-upon-Avon or explore the Brontë family's home in Haworth. Theater, music, and festivals add further richness, with London's West End and regional events offering performances that appeal to many tastes. Food and local customs, such as afternoon tea and pub culture, give travelers a chance to participate in daily life rather than simply observe it. For learners of English, Britain provides a natural setting in which to hear the language spoken in many accents and dialects, from the rhythms of Glasgow to the speech of Liverpool. Conversations with shopkeepers, guides, and fellow travelers create authentic opportunities to practice listening and speaking. Reading signs, menus, and newspapers builds vocabulary in real contexts that feel immediate and useful. Many visitors also enroll in language schools or join community events, which offer structured practice alongside cultural exploration. Because English is so widely spoken, travelers can ask questions and seek help with relative ease, which builds confidence over time. The combination of learning and sightseeing means that a single trip can serve multiple purposes at once. Students in particular benefit from immersion, as they encounter idioms, humor, and expressions that are rarely fully captured in classrooms. Such experiences often leave lasting improvements in fluency and comprehension. Ultimately, Britain's landmarks, heritage, and language environment work together to create a journey that enriches both the mind and the imagination. For many travelers, the lessons learned along the way prove as valuable as the sights themselves.

The manuscript addresses an important and practical problem: how to train deep reinforcement learning agents that behave safely by learning from human demonstrations enriched with graded feedback on the quality of individual actions. The motivation is clear, since pure reward-driven learning often produces policies that exploit reward loopholes or take unsafe actions during exploration, and demonstrations alone can be insufficient when the demonstrator's behavior is imperfect or narrow. The authors frame graded feedback as a richer signal than binary approval or rejection, which is a reasonable and under-explored direction. The introduction situates the work adequately within the imitation learning and reinforcement learning from human feedback literature, although the related work section could engage more directly with recent safe RL methods such as constrained policy optimization and shielding approaches. The core contribution is a training framework that combines behavioral cloning from demonstrations with a learned preference or quality model that scores individual actions on a graded scale. The formulation is described with enough detail to follow, but several equations use notation that is introduced inconsistently, and a consolidated table of symbols would improve readability considerably. The method's design choices, including how graded labels are mapped to loss weights, are justified mostly by intuition rather than by ablation, and the paper would be stronger with a sensitivity analysis on the grading scale granularity. The experimental section evaluates the approach on a set of continuous control and grid-world benchmarks, which is appropriate for the claims, though the choice of environments is narrow and does not include a domain with genuinely high-stakes safety constraints. Baselines include standard behavioral cloning, generative adversarial imitation learning, and a reward-shaping variant, which provides a fair comparison, but the absence of a comparison with a constrained RL baseline weakens the central safety claim. Reported safety metrics, such as the frequency of constraint violations during evaluation, show consistent improvements over the baselines, yet the paper does not report variance across seeds for all configurations, making it difficult to judge whether some gaps are statistically meaningful. The authors should clarify how constraint violations are defined in each environment and whether the same definition was applied to all methods. The qualitative examples of learned behavior are helpful for intuition, but they are selected by the authors and would be more convincing alongside a systematic failure-mode analysis. The discussion acknowledges some limitations, particularly the dependence on the quality and consistency of human graded labels, but it does not address how label noise or annotator disagreement would affect the learned safety model. Given that the method relies on human judgments of action quality, a study of annotator reliability, cost, and the effort required to collect graded feedback would substantially strengthen the practical relevance of the work. The paper also does not discuss the risk that the learned quality model itself may be miscalibrated in states far from the training distribution, which is precisely where safety guarantees matter most. The theoretical discussion is limited to a short proposition that restates known properties of weighted behavioral cloning, and it does not provide a bound on safety behavior, so claims about safety should be presented as empirical rather than guaranteed. The writing is generally clear, though some paragraphs in the methods section are dense and would benefit from a step-by-step summary of the training pipeline. Figures are legible and well chosen, but the learning curves lack confidence intervals and the axes are not labeled with units in two plots. The reproducibility statement is brief; the authors should release code, hyperparameters, and the exact protocol used to simulate or collect graded feedback. The literature review omits several recent works on preference-based reward learning and safe imitation, which would help readers position the contribution more precisely. The ethical considerations section is minimal and should discuss who provides the graded feedback, potential biases in annotator judgments, and the implications of deploying such agents in human-facing settings. Overall, the paper presents a promising and sensible idea with a reasonable initial empirical validation. However, the safety claims are currently supported mainly by limited experiments and lack statistical rigor, robustness analysis, and comparison with strong safe RL baselines. I recommend a major revision. With additional seeds and confidence intervals, a constrained RL comparison, an analysis of label noise and out-of-distribution behavior, and clearer reporting of the methodology, the work could make a valuable contribution to safe learning from human feedback.

The rain had not stopped for nine days, and Teodora Vance had decided that the rain was listening to her.

She stood at the edge of the drowned highway with a rusted tire iron in one hand and a child's plastic lunchbox in the other. Inside the lunchbox were three dried peaches, a button, and a folded letter she had written to nobody. The mud came up to her shins and sucked at her boots each time she shifted her weight.

Along the ridge, the riders appeared in a line against the grey sky. There were six of them, their motorcycles caked in clay, their faces wrapped in strips of cloth. One of them raised a hand, and the others stopped.

Teodora did not run. Running, she had learned, made men curious in the wrong way.

The rider in front came down the slope on foot, slow and deliberate. He carried a rifle slung across his back and a machete on his hip. Behind him the engines idled, coughing blue smoke into the wet air.

"You're alone," he said.

"No," Teodora said. "I have the Marshal with me. He's up the ridge, behind the water tower. He has a very good eye."

The rider glanced up at the skeleton of the water tower, then back at her. There was nobody there. There had never been anybody there. The Marshal had died in a flood that had taken the whole valley three springs ago, but Teodora had not yet found a way to tell the truth about him, and the lie had grown comfortable.

"The Marshal," the rider repeated. He sounded almost amused.

"He tells me when people are lying," Teodora said. "He is telling me now that you are lying."

The rider laughed, a short, wet sound. "What am I lying about?"

"About the radio. You said you had a radio that could reach the coast. You don't. Your man at the back has been holding a dead handset since the bridge."

Behind the line, a younger rider shifted and looked down at the thing in his hand. It was a radio, and it was dead, and everyone present knew it.

"Where did you learn that?" the leader asked.

"The water told me," Teodora said. "It runs downhill, and it carries everything with it. Mud, bodies, news. If you listen carefully you can hear what comes down from the north."

She was not sure she believed this. But she had noticed, over nine days of rain, that the water did carry things. A cracked boot. A shotgun shell. Once, the sound of a woman singing three valleys away, which had made her weep for an hour.

The leader took a step closer. Up close he looked tired, not cruel, his eyes red-rimmed above the cloth. "We're not here to hurt anyone," he said. "We're looking for fuel. For a place to dry out. Our people are sick."

"Your people are always sick," Teodora said. "The sickness is in the mud. It gets into the lungs and stays there."

He nodded slowly, as though she had said something wise. "You know that?"

"I know that the Marshal knows that."

The leader turned his head toward the water tower again, squinting. Teodora watched his shoulders loosen by a fraction, the way a man's shoulders do when he has decided to humor someone he pities.

"Tell your Marshal we'll take the north road," he said. "Tell him we won't come back this way."

"He already knows," Teodora said. "He said you would say that."

The leader smiled, and for a moment he looked like a man who had once had a family, a kitchen, a dog that barked at thunder. Then the smile went away, and he turned and climbed back up the slope.

The riders watched her for a long time before they rode off. When the last engine faded into the rain, Teodora sat down on the wet asphalt and opened the lunchbox. She took out one of the dried peaches and held it to her nose. It smelled of nothing at all.

"You did well," she said to the empty ridge.

Silence answered her, which was the best kind of answer she had received in a long time.

She stayed there until the light began to fail, then stood, shouldered her pack, and walked toward the water tower. At its base she paused and spoke to the air. "We can go now. They've gone north."

The rain fell on the broken steel and the flooded fields and the highway that led nowhere. Teodora kept walking, and she did not look back, because she had been told that looking back in a place like this was how you lost your way.

Graham Taylor, the former England manager and well-loved football figure, was remembered with warmth and gratitude at his funeral, where mourners gathered to celebrate a life devoted to the game. The service brought together family, friends, former players, and figures from across the football world to honour a man whose influence extended far beyond the pitch.

Taylor was best known for his long and distinguished career in management, which included spells at several English clubs and his time as manager of the national team. Those who knew him spoke of his passion, his dedication, and his genuine care for the people around him.

Family members took centre stage during the service, sharing memories that painted a picture of a devoted husband, father, and grandfather. Their tributes offered a glimpse of the man behind the managerial career, one who valued loyalty, hard work, and kindness.

Former players who had worked under Taylor also paid their respects, recalling his tactical insight and his ability to get the best out of those in his charge. Many described him as a demanding but fair coach who commanded deep respect in the dressing room.

Fellow managers and football administrators attended in large numbers, a testament to the esteem in which Taylor was held across the sport. Several spoke about the lasting impact of his work and the example he set for those who followed.

The atmosphere was one of reflection and affection rather than sorrow alone, as attendees shared stories and laughter alongside their tears. Many left the service feeling that they had been reminded of what made Taylor so special.

Supporters who had followed his teams over the years also marked the occasion, with some sending messages of thanks and others recalling moments of triumph and disappointment shared with him. His connection to fans was a recurring theme throughout the day.

The funeral closed with a celebration of his achievements, a fitting tribute to a career that left a clear mark on English football. Taylor's legacy, many agreed, would live on through the players he developed, the teams he built, and the families he loved.

Mountain rescue teams in Wales and Scotland carried out several operations over the weekend to bring stranded hikers to safety after conditions on the peaks deteriorated sharply. Teams reported high winds, heavy rain, and near-zero visibility as cloud descended across exposed ridgelines. In one incident in Snowdonia, a group of four walkers became disoriented after leaving a marked path and were located by volunteers using thermal imaging equipment late in the evening. In the Scottish Highlands, a separate team reached two climbers who had been sheltering in a gully for several hours after a fall left one of them with a suspected leg injury. Rescuers stabilized the injured climber and brought both to a waiting ambulance using a stretcher lowered over difficult terrain. Local officials said the operations involved more than fifty volunteers across the two regions and lasted into the early hours of Sunday. In a further incident, a pair of hikers became stuck on a rough forestry track after their vehicle could not handle the flooded surface, and they reportedly drove over a locked barrier and damaged the vehicle's undercarriage to reach a parking area closer to their intended route. Police later confirmed that the pair would face a review of their conduct, and that the cost of recovering the vehicle would be assessed. Mountain rescue spokespeople urged anyone planning walks in the coming days to check the forecast, carry suitable clothing and navigation equipment, and tell someone their route and expected return time. Teams also reminded the public that calling for help early is far safer and less costly than waiting until conditions worsen. No fatalities were reported in any of the incidents over the weekend, though officials described the situation as a sharp reminder of the risks posed by sudden changes in mountain weather.

The manuscript proposes combining randomized image patch shuffling with adversarial training to improve the robustness of convolutional neural networks by encouraging reliable local feature learning. The central idea is intuitive and worth exploring: shuffling patches disrupts global spatial structure, which may force the network to rely on local texture and shape cues, and pairing this with adversarial training could reduce sensitivity to small perturbations. The motivation is clearly stated in the introduction, and the related work section situates the method reasonably well among data augmentation and adversarial defense approaches. However, the paper does not sufficiently articulate why patch shuffling should specifically yield reliable local features, and the theoretical justification relies largely on intuition. The methodology section describes the shuffling procedure and training objective, but several hyperparameters, including patch size, shuffling probability, and the adversarial perturbation budget, are introduced without a clear rationale or sensitivity analysis. The experiments are conducted on standard benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the choice of baselines is limited and omits several recent robust training methods that would provide a stronger comparison. The reported robustness gains are promising, yet the paper does not report variance across random seeds, making it difficult to judge whether observed improvements are statistically meaningful. The evaluation against adaptive attacks is also insufficient, since the defense may appear stronger than it is if the attacks do not account for the shuffling step. Ablation studies isolating the contribution of patch shuffling from adversarial training are partially provided but would benefit from more thorough coverage. The discussion of computational overhead is brief, and readers would benefit from a clearer account of training time relative to baselines. The figures are generally clear, though some qualitative examples lack explanation of what features the model is actually attending to. The writing is mostly clear but contains repetitive passages in the results section that could be condensed. Code availability is mentioned, which is commendable, though the released repository would benefit from documentation for reproducing the main tables. Overall, the core idea is interesting and the empirical results are encouraging, but the paper needs stronger theoretical grounding, more rigorous statistical reporting, and more comprehensive adaptive evaluation before its claims can be fully accepted. I recommend a major revision.

Facial-expression recognition technology offers several potential benefits in education and mental health support. In classrooms, it could help teachers notice when students appear confused, bored, or disengaged, allowing them to adjust lessons in real time. For students who find it hard to speak up, such tools might provide a quiet signal that a teacher should check in. In mental health settings, the technology could assist clinicians by tracking changes in mood or affect between appointments, offering additional context for their assessments. It may also help therapists and counselors identify signs of distress that patients do not verbalize, which is especially valuable for people who struggle to describe their feelings. Early detection of worsening symptoms could lead to faster intervention, potentially reducing the severity of depression, anxiety, or other conditions. Automated tools could also extend support to schools or communities with few counselors, helping to close gaps in access to care. However, these benefits depend on accuracy, and expression alone does not reliably reveal what someone is feeling. Responsible use would therefore require careful validation, transparent consent, and human judgment rather than reliance on machine outputs. With these safeguards in place, facial-expression recognition could become a useful complement to the empathy and expertise of educators and clinicians.

This manuscript investigates infinite-width Bayesian neural networks and their connection to Gaussian processes, representation learning, and practical prediction, a topic of considerable current interest. The central claim, that wide networks under appropriate priors converge to Gaussian processes whose kernels can be computed in closed form, is well motivated and builds clearly on the neural network Gaussian process literature. The authors situate their contribution relative to prior work on kernel limits and lazy training regimes, though the related work section could be more thorough in discussing finite-width corrections. The theoretical derivations are generally sound, and the main theorem is stated with clear assumptions about activation functions and weight initialization. However, the proof sketch in the appendix omits several steps that are non-trivial, particularly the control of the approximation error uniformly over the input domain, and I would ask the authors to include these arguments in full. The notation is mostly consistent, but the distinction between the prior-induced kernel and the posterior predictive kernel is occasionally blurred, which may confuse readers less familiar with the area. The experimental section evaluates regression on several standard benchmarks and compares against finite-width networks trained with ensembles and against sparse Gaussian process baselines. The comparisons are informative, yet the hyperparameter tuning protocol for the baselines is not described, making it difficult to assess whether the reported gains reflect the method or differences in tuning effort. Confidence intervals or results over multiple random seeds are absent for most tables, and this weakens the strength of the claimed improvements in calibration. The representation learning analysis is the most novel portion of the paper, as it argues that finite-width feature learning can be partially recovered through a correction to the infinite-width kernel. This argument is interesting, but the evidence presented is largely qualitative, consisting of visualizations of learned features rather than quantitative measures of representation quality. I encourage the authors to adopt established metrics such as centered kernel alignment or linear probing accuracy to support this part of the claims. The discussion of computational cost is helpful, showing that the kernel computation scales favorably for moderate dataset sizes, but the authors should clarify the regime in which the method becomes impractical. Scaling beyond tens of thousands of training points would require approximations that the paper does not evaluate. The writing is generally clear, though several paragraphs in the introduction repeat points made in the related work section and could be condensed. Figures are legible, but axis labels in the calibration plots are too small to read comfortably in print. The limitations section acknowledges the restriction to fully connected architectures, which is appropriate, yet it would be stronger if it also discussed the dependence of results on the chosen activation function. Overall, the paper makes a useful contribution by clarifying the relationship between infinite-width limits and practical predictive models. I recommend a major revision addressing the completeness of the proofs, the reporting of variance across seeds, the description of baseline tuning, and quantitative evaluation of the representation learning claims. With these changes, the work would be a valuable addition to the literature.

Self-driving cars promise safer roads, fewer traffic jams, and greater mobility for people who cannot drive, but their widespread adoption also carries serious drawbacks and societal risks. One major concern is safety in unpredictable situations, since autonomous systems can struggle with unusual road conditions, construction zones, or erratic human behavior that falls outside their training data. Software errors and cybersecurity vulnerabilities add another layer of risk, as a hacked or malfunctioning vehicle could endanger passengers and pedestrians alike. The question of accountability is also unresolved, because when a self-driving car causes a crash, it is unclear whether the manufacturer, the software developer, the owner, or the passenger should bear responsibility. Economically, the shift could eliminate millions of jobs held by professional drivers, including truckers, taxi drivers, and delivery workers, many of whom have few easy paths to comparable employment. Privacy is another worry, since these vehicles collect detailed data on where people go, when they travel, and who they travel with, creating opportunities for surveillance and misuse. There are also equity concerns, as expensive autonomous technology may first be available only to wealthier communities, widening existing gaps in access to transportation. Public trust could be damaged by high-profile accidents, slowing adoption even when the technology is objectively safer than human drivers. Urban planning may be affected as well, since cheap, always-available autonomous rides could increase total vehicle miles traveled and congestion rather than reduce them. Finally, the transition period, in which autonomous and human-driven vehicles share roads, may itself be hazardous because each behaves in ways the other does not expect. For these reasons, society should pursue self-driving technology carefully, with strong regulation, transparent testing, and policies that protect workers and ensure fair access.

The guards came for Tomas Veyra at four in the morning, as he had known they would for eleven months. He did not struggle. He had written his last letter to his daughter the night before, and he had already made peace with the cold stone of the corridor and the long walk toward the courtyard.

But the procession did not turn left toward the courtyard. It turned right, through a door he had never seen opened, into a narrow room that smelled of disinfectant and old paper.

A man in a gray coat sat behind a steel desk. He did not stand. He slid a folder across the table and said, in a voice without malice, "Sit down, Mr. Veyra. We have very little time."

Tomas sat. He did not touch the folder.

"You are not going to be executed tonight," the man said. "Your name will be on the official record as having died in custody. The death certificate is already signed. A body will be cremated this morning, and it is not yours."

Tomas stared at him. "Why would you do this?"

"Because a government that kills its critics in the dark is afraid of them, and a government that lets them vanish quietly is merely embarrassed." The man tapped the folder. "Someone in the ministry decided you were more useful alive and gone than dead and martyred. I am only the one who carries out the decision."

Tomas opened the folder. Inside was a passport in the name of Daniel Hale, a citizen of a neighboring republic. There was a birth certificate, a work permit, a bank card, and a photograph of a man with a thinner face and a short gray beard. The photograph was unmistakably him, only altered by someone skilled.

"You will be taken to the border before dawn," the man said. "A driver will take you across at Kessler Pass. From there you are on your own. You will not be able to contact anyone from your former life. Not your daughter, not your old colleagues, not anyone who knew your face."

The word daughter caught in Tomas's throat. "Anya," he said. "She thinks I am dead already. She has been told so."

"Yes. That is the cost of this, and I will not pretend otherwise." The man looked at the desk for a moment. "She will grow up believing her father was a traitor who was executed. That is the story the state has chosen for her. It is a cruel story, and I am sorry."

Tomas closed his eyes. He thought of her small hand in his at the market, years ago, when she had insisted on carrying the bread herself.

"Why tell me?" he asked. "Why not simply let me go without knowing?"

"Because you would have found out eventually, and you would have spent your new life looking over your shoulder for a knock on the door. I would rather you know that the door is no longer there."

A clock ticked somewhere in the building. Tomas opened his eyes.

"What do I do now?"

"You get in the car. You do not look back. You do not write to anyone. And you learn to answer to a name that is not yours." The man almost smiled. "You may find that Daniel Hale is a more forgiving person than Tomas Veyra was. Some people do."

Tomas picked up the passport and turned it over in his hands. The cover was blue and unfamiliar. He had never been anyone but himself.

"Who arranged this?" he asked. "Who would risk so much for one prisoner?"

The man stood and buttoned his coat. "People who remember what you wrote. Some of them are in the ministry, some are not. A few of them are your readers, though you will never know which ones." He moved toward the door. "Good luck, Mr. Hale."

The car was waiting in the alley behind the prison, its engine running low. The driver did not speak. Tomas sat in the back seat with the folder on his knees and watched the city lights thin out behind them.

The road climbed into the hills. Snow had begun to fall, soft and steady, covering the fields in white. Tomas pressed his forehead against the cold window and tried to imagine a face he had never worn.

At Kessler Pass the guards at the checkpoint barely glanced at the passport. A bored officer stamped it, handed it back, and waved them through. The barrier lifted. Tomas felt the car roll forward and cross an invisible line that had defined the whole of his adult life.

He did not look back. He had been told not to, and he found, to his surprise, that he did not want to.

On the far side of the border the sky was beginning to lighten in the east. The driver stopped beside a small bus station and got out without a word, leaving the engine running a moment longer before he drove away.

Tomas stood alone on the platform with the folder under his arm. A woman with a basket of eggs passed him and nodded politely, and he nodded back, testing the unfamiliar motion.

"Good morning," she said.

"Good morning," he replied, and hearing his own voice speak the foreign name in his head, he found that it sounded, very faintly, like a beginning.

He bought a ticket to the coast, where no one knew him, and sat on a hard wooden bench while the sun rose over the hills. He thought about Anya, and he wrote her name on the inside cover of the folder in pencil, so small it could barely be read.

He would not be able to send her a letter. Not now, perhaps not ever. But he would remember her, and he would live carefully, quietly, and well, for as long as he was allowed.

The bus arrived with a groan of brakes and a cloud of diesel. Tomas Hale climbed aboard, found a seat by the window, and watched the snow melt on the glass as the road carried him toward the sea.

Modern innovations have transformed the way people live, making everyday tasks faster, easier, and more convenient. In communication, smartphones and video calls allow families and colleagues to stay connected across great distances, often at little or no cost. At work, cloud software and automation help people collaborate in real time and free them from many repetitive chores, so they can focus on more creative and meaningful tasks. Shopping has also changed dramatically, as online stores and digital payment systems let consumers compare prices, read reviews, and receive goods at their doorstep. In scientific research, powerful computers and advanced instruments allow scientists to analyze enormous datasets and make discoveries that once would have taken decades. Taken together, these advances show how technology can improve both our personal lives and the progress of human knowledge.

Concerns are mounting over the reliability of rail services and the level of investment in the line linking Inverness with Sutherland and Caithness, the Far North Line. Passengers and local business groups say repeated cancellations, delays and ageing rolling stock have eroded confidence in one of the most remote rail routes in the United Kingdom. Community representatives argue that the railway is a vital lifeline for students, patients travelling to hospital appointments, and workers in the region's energy and tourism sectors. Many residents say they have little alternative to the train, given long distances and limited bus connections across the Highlands. Rail industry observers note that the single-track nature of much of the route, combined with severe weather exposure along the coast and across exposed moorland, makes consistent performance difficult to maintain. Maintenance backlogs on track, signalling and bridges have also been cited by campaigners as contributing factors to disruption. Local councillors have called on Transport Scotland and Network Rail to publish a clear timetable of planned upgrades and to explain how funding will be allocated over the coming years. Some have pressed for longer-term commitments rather than short-term repairs that they say fail to address underlying weaknesses. Operators have acknowledged the frustration and say that engineering work and weather-related incidents are being managed as efficiently as possible. They point to recent investment in new trains and infrastructure as evidence of progress, though critics argue the benefits have not yet been felt on the ground. Business leaders in Caithness warn that unreliable services discourage visitors, deter investment and make it harder for employers to attract staff to the area. Tourism operators, who rely on the scenic route to draw visitors, have also raised concerns about the impact of cancellations on bookings. Campaign groups have launched petitions and are seeking meetings with ministers to press for a review of service standards. They want independent monitoring of punctuality and reliability figures, which they say would give passengers a more accurate picture of day-to-day performance. Transport Scotland has said it remains committed to improving the line and will consider stakeholder feedback as it develops future plans. Whether those plans deliver the reliability that communities are demanding will be closely watched in the months ahead.

The last of the trench lines had gone quiet three nights earlier, and Corporal Idris Vance had stopped counting the days since. He walked east through the broken orchard with his rifle slung and his boots full of mud, because walking was the only thing left that still made sense to him.

The war had started over a river that no one remembered anymore. It had grown into a machine that ate boys and spat out orders, and Vance had fed it for longer than he could honestly account for. Somewhere behind him, the generals were still drawing lines on maps that the artillery kept erasing. He had heard the rumor that both sides were preparing a final push, and he understood with a flat certainty that he would not be there for it.

He left the rifle in a ditch just past the second ruined farmhouse. The metal was cold and heavy, and setting it down felt like the first honest thing he had done in months. He kept his canteen, his ration tin, and the photograph of his sister tucked inside his shirt, its corners soft from handling.

The orchard gave way to a field of tall grass that hissed when the wind moved through it. At the edge of the field stood a stone wall, older than the war by centuries, its top courses collapsed in places. He sat down against it and let his eyes close for a while.

When he opened them, the light had changed. It was not dusk exactly, nor dawn, but a thin amber glow that seemed to come from everywhere at once. The grass was still there, but it was greener, and the air smelled of woodsmoke and bread.

He stood slowly, his knees protesting. The wall ran on ahead of him, and along it, half-buried in moss, he saw a small iron gate he did not remember passing. It stood open a crack, and through the gap he glimpsed a kitchen window with a yellow curtain and a kettle on the stove.

He pushed the gate and it swung without a sound. Beyond it was not a house but something like a house seen through water, its edges shimmering and uncertain. A table sat in the middle of a courtyard, laid with two cups and a loaf of dark bread. The bread was still warm, he could tell from the steam.

Vance hesitated at the threshold. The war had taught him to distrust anything too kind, and this place was kind in a way that felt almost cruel. Yet his body ached for rest, and his heart ached for something he could not name.

He stepped inside. The courtyard was quiet except for the faint crackle of a fire he could not see. On the table lay a folded letter addressed in handwriting he recognized with a jolt: his mother's careful, looping script, the one she had used when he was small and away at school.

He sat and unfolded it. The paper was thin and smelled faintly of lavender. She wrote about the apple tree in the back garden, how it had finally borne fruit after years of nothing. She wrote about the neighbor's dog, who had taken to sleeping on their porch. She wrote that the river at the bottom of the hill had been running high that spring, and that she hoped he would come home before the summer floods.

He read it twice. Then a third time. His eyes stung, and he pressed the back of his hand against them until the sting passed.

The kettle began to whistle somewhere beyond the wall. He could hear it clearly, the same thin sound that had woken him every morning in his childhood. He wanted to go toward it, and at the same time he understood that he could not.

A figure moved at the edge of the courtyard. It was not his mother, though it wore her shawl. It was a girl of perhaps nine, barefoot on the cold stones, holding a jar of something that glowed faintly gold. She looked at him with an expression he recognized from the faces of the villagers he had passed on the road months ago, the ones who had watched the soldiers go by without wanting to know their names.

"You're in between," she said. Her voice was matter-of-fact. "Most people who come through here are."

"Between what?" Vance asked.

She shrugged. "The places. The war is one place. This is another. There's a bit of home stuck here, like a splinter in a thumb. It doesn't belong to either side, so it just sits and waits."

He looked at the letter again. "Can I stay?"

The girl considered this with the seriousness of a child. "You can stay as long as you like. But the splinter only lasts so long. Eventually it either works its way out or it gets buried."

He thought of the field beyond the gate, the grass hissing in the wind, the rifle lying cold in the ditch. He thought of the river at the bottom of the hill, running high in a spring he had not seen in three years.

"Which way is out?" he asked.

She pointed past the table, toward a second gate he had not noticed, its iron bars rusted through in places. Beyond it lay the orchard again, and beyond that, faintly, the road running west.

"That way goes home," she said. "The other way goes back to the trenches. Both are real. You just have to pick one."

Vance folded the letter carefully and tucked it inside his shirt beside the photograph of his sister. Then he stood, lifted the untouched cup from the table, drank the last of the cold tea in it, and set it down again.

"Thank you," he said.

The girl nodded and turned back toward the kitchen, the jar of gold light swaying in her hand. Vance walked to the second gate, pushed it open, and stepped through into the orchard.

The air was cold and the sky was gray. Somewhere far behind him the guns had started up again, a dull rolling thunder that promised nothing good. He did not turn around. He walked west along the broken road, one foot in front of the other, while the wind carried the faint sound of a kettle whistling on a stove he would never see again.

Sarah Payne's brothers have spoken about the lasting trauma they continue to carry after their sister was abducted and murdered by Roy Whiting in 2000. Sarah, aged eight, disappeared in July of that year while playing near her grandparents' home in West Sussex, England. Her disappearance sparked a nationwide search that drew widespread public attention and grief. Her body was later found in a field in Kent, and Whiting was subsequently convicted of her murder.

Her brothers, who were children at the time, described how the events of that summer shaped the rest of their lives. They recalled the fear and confusion that gripped their family as the search unfolded day after day. One of them said that the sense of safety they had once taken for granted disappeared overnight. Both have spoken of nightmares, anxiety, and difficulty trusting others in the years that followed.

The brothers also described the strain the case placed on their family. Their parents, Sara and Michael Payne, campaigned publicly for changes to child protection laws, and the family became a focus of intense media scrutiny. The brothers said that being in the public eye as children added another layer of difficulty to an already devastating loss. Growing up with such a high-profile tragedy meant that they were often reminded of what had happened.

Mental health professionals who have worked with families affected by child murder say that siblings in such cases often face long-term effects, including depression, guilt, and survivor's grief. The brothers said that they have sought support over the years, though they admitted that the pain has never fully faded. They emphasized that Sarah's memory remains central to their lives and that they want her to be remembered for who she was, not only for how she died.

The case led to the introduction of the Sarah's Law scheme in England and Wales, which allows parents to request information about individuals with convictions for child sex offences. The brothers have said they hope that their experiences will encourage others affected by similar crimes to seek help. Their account serves as a reminder of the enduring impact that such crimes have on the families left behind.

Improving academic performance on important exams begins with a clear plan that breaks large goals into manageable weekly tasks. Students who review their past mistakes, rather than simply rereading notes, tend to make faster progress because they can target the specific concepts that keep costing them points. Consistent practice under timed conditions also builds both accuracy and confidence, so that the real exam feels familiar rather than threatening. Setbacks are inevitable, whether it is a disappointing practice score or a day when nothing seems to stick, and how a student responds to them matters more than the setback itself. Instead of treating a poor result as proof of inability, a resilient student asks what went wrong, adjusts the study approach, and tries again with a fresh strategy. Support from teachers, classmates, and family can make this process far less lonely and help keep motivation steady over the long months of preparation. Ultimately, perseverance turns academic challenges into opportunities for growth, teaching students that ability is built through effort and reflection.

This paper addresses a practical limitation of BERT-based summarization by proposing an extended architecture that handles documents beyond the standard 512-token input limit, which is a relevant and well-motivated problem for real-world long-document tasks. The core idea of adapting positional handling and segment-level encoding to process longer inputs is sensible, and the authors clearly situate their contribution against prior work on hierarchical and sparse-attention approaches. However, the experimental section would be substantially strengthened by reporting results on a broader range of long-document benchmarks, along with ablations isolating the contribution of each architectural change. The computational cost of the proposed extension, including memory and training time relative to baselines, is mentioned only briefly and should be quantified more thoroughly. Overall, the work is a useful incremental contribution, and I recommend minor-to-major revisions focused on stronger empirical validation and a more detailed analysis of efficiency trade-offs.
