Taking risks is one of the most important steps a person can take toward personal growth and success. When we step outside our comfort zones, we open ourselves to new experiences that reveal our hidden strengths and expand our understanding of what we are capable of. Many achievements begin with uncertainty, and those who are willing to try something difficult often discover skills they never knew they had. However, risk alone is not enough, because most meaningful goals require sustained effort over time. Perseverance allows us to keep moving forward after setbacks, turning mistakes into lessons rather than reasons to give up. History is full of inventors, athletes, and artists whose breakthroughs came only after repeated failures and stubborn determination. Ultimately, the combination of courage to take chances and the resolve to keep going is what transforms ordinary effort into lasting success and genuine personal growth.

Considering others' perspectives is one of the most reliable ways to make better decisions. Every person sees a situation from a particular vantage point, shaped by their experiences, values, and responsibilities. When we deliberately step outside our own viewpoint, we gain access to information we would otherwise miss. A decision that looks sensible from one angle may reveal serious flaws when viewed from another.

Consider a manager planning a new work schedule. From the manager's point of view, the goal may be efficiency and coverage during busy hours. However, if the manager asks the employees who must follow the schedule, they may learn about childcare conflicts, long commutes, or health needs that the original plan ignored. Incorporating these insights often produces a schedule that is both practical and fair, which tends to reduce absenteeism and frustration.

Taking others' perspectives also helps us test our assumptions. We often assume that our reasons are obvious or that our intentions are clear to everyone. Hearing how a friend, colleague, or family member interprets our choice can expose these blind spots. A proposal that seemed persuasive in our own minds may prove confusing or unconvincing to someone else, giving us the chance to revise it before it causes problems.

Perspective-taking additionally reduces the risk of costly mistakes. Historians often point to decisions made by leaders who surrounded themselves only with people who agreed with them, a pattern sometimes called groupthink. Such environments discourage dissent, so warning signs go unnoticed. By actively seeking out critics and people with different expertise, decision-makers expose their plans to scrutiny that can prevent avoidable failures.

Finally, considering others' perspectives builds trust and cooperation, which make decisions easier to carry out. People are more willing to support a choice when they feel their views were heard, even if the final outcome does not match their preference. In this way, the process of understanding others strengthens the community that must live with the results.

Of course, considering other perspectives does not mean abandoning our own judgment or treating every opinion as equally valid. Good decision-makers weigh the evidence and the reasoning behind each viewpoint. Nevertheless, a willingness to listen before deciding is a habit that protects us from narrow thinking. In the end, the best decisions are rarely made in isolation; they emerge from honest conversation among people who see the world differently.

Northern Ireland's police service is facing renewed criticism after it emerged that tissue samples taken from deceased victims were retained without the knowledge of their families. The revelations have prompted public apologies from senior officers and a commitment to direct outreach to affected relatives.

The issue came to light as bereaved families began asking questions about the handling of post-mortem material linked to criminal investigations. Many said they had no idea that tissue had been kept after their loved ones' deaths, and some learned of it only through media inquiries or official correspondence.

Retaining tissue is not unusual in forensic and pathology practice, where samples may be needed for later testing, appeals, or reviews. However, critics argue that the absence of clear communication with next of kin has turned a procedural matter into a serious breach of trust.

Families described feelings of shock, distress and anger. Several said the discovery reopened wounds that had only partly healed, and some questioned whether they would have been consulted had the cases been handled differently.

Campaigners and families' representatives called for a full review of the policies governing the retention, storage and disposal of human tissue. They also demanded transparency about how many cases are affected and what samples remain in storage.

A senior police spokesperson acknowledged the failings and offered a public apology to the families affected. The spokesperson said the service recognised that the lack of notification had caused additional hurt at a time of grief and loss.

The police service confirmed that it would contact all families whose loved ones' tissue had been retained and explain the circumstances of each case. Officers will also provide information about the options available to relatives, including the possible return or disposal of samples.

A dedicated helpline has been set up to field questions from the public and those concerned that their relatives may be affected. Officials said staff have been trained to handle these conversations sensitively, with support available for families who request it.

Independent pathologists and legal experts were asked to comment on the matter. Several agreed that retention can be justified in some circumstances but stressed that consent, or at least informed notification, should be the norm wherever feasible.

Government ministers and members of the Northern Ireland Assembly have also weighed in, with many calling for answers. Some representatives asked for parliamentary scrutiny of the force's practices and for clear national guidance on the issue.

Human rights organisations pointed to the importance of respecting the dignity of the deceased and the rights of their families. They argued that any retention of body material must be proportionate, lawful and subject to regular review.

The police service said it has begun an internal audit to establish how the practice developed and whether existing procedures were followed. The findings are expected to be shared with the public once the review is complete.

Officials acknowledged that record-keeping in some cases was incomplete, making it difficult to trace every sample quickly. They said improving documentation and tracking systems would be a priority in any reforms.

Families have welcomed the apology but many said words alone are not enough. They want assurances that changes will be made, that similar failures will not recur, and that they will be treated with openness going forward.

Some relatives said they wished to know the reason a sample was kept, how long it would be held, and who had access to it. Others simply wanted the opportunity to make their own decisions about what happens to their loved one's remains.

The controversy has also drawn attention to the broader question of how the justice system balances investigative needs with the emotional and cultural sensitivities of bereaved people. Advocates say the case highlights the need for consistent standards across all police forces.

Community leaders urged the police to engage with families in a spirit of genuine partnership rather than defensiveness. They suggested that independent oversight and regular public reporting could help restore confidence.

The Police Ombudsman's office was asked whether it would examine complaints arising from the matter. Officials said they were considering the issue and would respond to any formal referrals made by families or representatives.

Legal advisers have told affected families that they may have grounds to seek further information through formal channels. Some are reportedly considering civil action, though no legal proceedings had been confirmed at the time of writing.

Health and forensic specialists stressed that the vast majority of tissue retention is carried out for legitimate reasons. They warned, however, that legitimate practice can still cause harm when it is not explained properly to those most affected.

The issue has prompted wider discussion about the rights of families to be informed about post-mortem procedures. Some experts have proposed a national framework requiring written notification whenever tissue is retained beyond standard timeframes.

Police leaders said they welcomed scrutiny and accepted that public trust must be earned through openness. They pledged to publish updates on the progress of the review and the outreach programme at regular intervals.

For many families, the immediate priority is simply to be heard. Several said they hoped the apologies would be followed by respectful and honest conversations that acknowledge the pain caused and the responsibility the police bear.

The service has committed to reviewing its communication practices so that future decisions about retained material are explained clearly and promptly. Officials say the aim is to ensure that no family learns about such matters by chance.

As the review proceeds, attention will remain on whether the apologies translate into lasting change. For the families affected, the outcome will be measured not only by policy statements but by the care and honesty they receive in the coming months.

Summer break offers students something rare during the school year: time that belongs to them. Too often, that time is filled with passive activities or simply treated as a pause between semesters. Students should instead create their own summer projects, because self-directed work builds skills, deepens curiosity, and gives them a sense of ownership over their own growth.

When students design a project themselves, they must decide what they want to learn, which is a skill school rarely asks them to practice. Choosing a goal forces them to reflect on their interests and strengths. A student who wants to understand how bridges stay standing, or who hopes to write a short novel, must figure out the first steps without a teacher handing down a checklist.

Self-directed projects also teach planning and persistence. A student who commits to building a small app, growing a vegetable garden, or researching a local history topic must break the work into stages, set deadlines, and adjust when things go wrong. These are the same habits that carry people through college, careers, and any demanding task later in life.

Creating a project also builds confidence. Each time a student finishes something they started on their own, they learn that they can solve problems without outside instruction. That confidence often spills into the classroom, where students may feel more willing to ask questions and take intellectual risks.

Finally, summer projects let students explore beyond the boundaries of the standard curriculum. A teenager who is fascinated by marine biology can spend the summer reading research papers, volunteering at an aquarium, or keeping field notes at a nearby beach. Such experiences often reveal career paths that a classroom alone could never suggest.

Some people argue that students need rest after a demanding school year, and that is a fair point. Rest and projects are not mutually exclusive, however. A project pursued for joy rather than grades can be restful in its own way, and students can choose a pace that suits them. The goal is not to fill every hour with productivity but to make sure the time is meaningful.

Parents and schools can support this by encouraging students to propose ideas and by offering resources like libraries, online tutorials, and community mentors. The support should guide rather than dictate, leaving room for the student to make real decisions. When adults trust students to choose their own paths, they send a powerful message about the students' abilities.

In the end, summer is a chance for students to become the authors of their own learning. A well-chosen project can turn an ordinary break into a season of discovery, skill-building, and growth. Students who take that opportunity seriously will carry its benefits long after the first day of school returns.

Late blight is one of the most destructive diseases of home garden potatoes, caused by the water mold Phytophthora infestans. It can wipe out foliage within days and rot tubers in the ground or in storage, so early recognition and prompt action matter. Watch for dark brown to black lesions on leaves and stems, often with a pale green or whitish fuzzy ring at the leaf edge, especially during cool, wet weather. Infected tubers show reddish-brown, granular, dry rot under the skin that can spread into the flesh and cause soft rot in storage. Begin by planting certified disease-free seed potatoes rather than saving tubers from a previous crop that may carry the pathogen. Choose resistant or later-maturing varieties where possible, and space plants so air circulates freely through the foliage. Water at the base of plants in the morning so leaves dry quickly, and avoid overhead watering in the evening. Scout your plants at least twice a week during humid periods, and check the undersides of leaves as well as the tops. If you find blight, remove and bag infected leaves and stems immediately rather than composting them, because spores can survive and spread. Do not walk through wet foliage between plants when it is infected, since spores cling to shoes and clothing. Protective fungicides labeled for late blight, such as copper-based products or those containing chlorothalonil or mancozeb, can be applied before infection or at the first sign of disease, following label directions. Some newer products are also available, so check current recommendations from your local extension service. Hill soil or mulch around plants so spores washed down from leaves cannot reach developing tubers near the surface. Allow foliage to die back completely, either naturally or by cutting it off about two weeks before harvest, which reduces the chance of tuber infection. Harvest on a dry day and let tubers cure in a cool, dark, dry place for a few days to toughen their skin. Discard any tuber showing rot, and do not store damaged potatoes alongside healthy ones. Clean tools, containers, and bins with a diluted bleach solution to remove lingering spores. Avoid planting potatoes or tomatoes in the same spot the following year, since both crops can harbor the pathogen. Local extension offices can confirm whether late blight is active in your area and provide updated treatment guidance. With consistent monitoring, sanitation, and good cultural practices, you can greatly reduce losses and protect your harvest.

Raising academic eligibility standards for student athletes is a reasonable step that can encourage responsibility and improve their future opportunities. Many student athletes spend long hours training, traveling, and competing, which leaves limited time for studying. When schools set higher academic requirements, they send a clear message that education matters as much as athletic performance. Students who must maintain strong grades to play are more likely to develop time management skills, discipline, and the habit of planning their week around both practice and homework. These habits extend well beyond sports and prepare young people for college, careers, and adult life. Academic standards also protect athletes from a common and painful outcome, which is reaching the end of their athletic careers without the education or credentials needed to succeed elsewhere. Only a small percentage of student athletes go on to professional sports, so a strong academic foundation offers a realistic path to lasting opportunity. Higher eligibility requirements can also improve graduation rates, which in turn strengthens a student's job prospects and earning potential. Critics argue that stricter rules may unfairly exclude talented students from low-income backgrounds who lack academic support at home or in their schools. This concern is valid, and schools should respond by providing tutoring, mentoring, and early academic intervention rather than simply removing students from teams. When support systems accompany higher standards, the rules become a tool for growth instead of a barrier. Schools can also reward improvement, allowing students who show progress to regain eligibility and see that their effort matters. Ultimately, raising academic standards asks student athletes to take ownership of their future. Sports can teach valuable lessons about teamwork and perseverance, but those lessons are most valuable when paired with an education that opens doors. By expecting more academically, schools can help athletes build a foundation that supports them long after their playing days end.

The room was quiet except for the soft hiss of oxygen. Margaret had not spoken in three days, and she kept her eyes fixed on the window, where the late autumn light fell thin across the parking lot. She wanted it to be over. Every breath felt like a chore she had already finished too many times.

Nurse Dana Okafor came in with the morning tray and set it down gently, the way she did everything. She opened the blinds a little wider and talked about the weather, the hawk she had seen circling the maple outside, and the new volunteer who kept mixing up the flower deliveries. Margaret listened without answering.

When Dana checked the pulse at Margaret's wrist, she paused, not because of the number but because of the stillness she felt beneath her fingers. She had sat with many people at this threshold, and she had learned that some who seemed to be fading still had something left to hold onto.

Margaret's gaze finally shifted. Her eyes, pale and steady, met Dana's for a long moment. There was no pleading in them, only a tired question that needed no words.

Dana pulled a chair close and sat down. She did not tell Margaret that she was wrong to want rest, because she knew that wanting rest was not the same as wanting to disappear. Instead she said, "I'm not going anywhere until you're comfortable."

Margaret's lips moved, and after a moment a single word escaped, barely audible. It sounded like "tired." Dana nodded. "I know. You've been brave for a long time."

In the hallway, a cart rattled past, and somewhere a television murmured a game show. Life went on in small, ordinary noises that Margaret could no longer join. Dana had always believed those noises mattered, even to those who could no longer hear them.

She adjusted the blanket, smoothing a wrinkle near Margaret's shoulder. The gesture was small, but it said what she could not put into a speech: that this body, this life, still belonged to someone who cared.

Margaret closed her eyes. Her breathing slowed, but it did not stop. Dana stayed in the chair, her hand resting lightly on the bed rail.

Later that afternoon, the volunteer brought in a vase of yellow chrysanthemums. Dana arranged them on the sill where Margaret could see them if she opened her eyes. Margaret did not open them, but her fingers twitched once against the sheet.

Dana noticed and smiled softly. She did not know whether Margaret wanted to live or only wanted to stop hurting, and she suspected that even Margaret did not know. What she did know was that the choice of what to do with the time remaining belonged to the person in the bed.

The night nurse arrived at seven, and Dana gave her report in a low voice. She mentioned the pain medication, the fluid intake, and the small twitch of the fingers. Then she paused and added, "She's still here. Keep the light on for her."

Walking to her car in the cold dusk, Dana thought about the long argument she sometimes had with herself. She believed life had value even when it was hard to see, and she also understood that some people carried a weight no one could fully lift. Both truths sat in her chest without resolving.

The next morning, Margaret was still breathing. The hawk was back in the maple, and the chrysanthemums had opened further in the warm room. Dana came in with the tray, set it down, and said good morning.

For a moment, nothing happened. Then Margaret's eyes opened, slowly, and found the flowers first. Her lips parted, and she made a sound that was not a word but was not nothing either.

Dana leaned closer. "I hear you," she said. "I'm here."

Margaret closed her eyes again, but her hand moved across the blanket until it rested near Dana's. They stayed that way, two people sharing a quiet room, one still longing for the end and one still believing in the next small morning.

Working together often produces better results than working alone, because each member brings different skills, knowledge, and perspectives to a shared goal. When people combine their strengths, they can divide complex tasks into manageable parts and complete them more efficiently than one person could manage alone. Teammates also catch one another's mistakes, which reduces errors and improves the quality of the final work. Discussion within a group encourages people to test their ideas, consider alternatives, and refine their thinking in ways that solitary work rarely allows. Collaboration can also make difficult challenges feel less overwhelming, since responsibility is shared and encouragement is available when motivation falters. Teamwork builds communication, negotiation, and leadership skills that are valuable in school, careers, and everyday life. Working independently still has its advantages, such as complete control over one's schedule and the freedom to follow one's own approach without compromise. However, those benefits are often outweighed by the creativity and reliability that a well-functioning group can offer. For these reasons, teamwork generally provides greater advantages than independent work for most tasks that are large, complex, or require varied expertise.

Cities and countries around the world are increasingly working to reduce their dependence on cars, and the reasons are both practical and urgent. For much of the twentieth century, urban planning prioritized the automobile, building wide highways, sprawling suburbs, and vast parking lots while neglecting walking paths, public transit, and dense neighborhoods where people could meet their daily needs nearby. Today, many governments recognize that this model is expensive, unhealthy, and unsustainable, and they are beginning to change course.

One of the most visible strategies is the creation of protected bike lanes and pedestrian zones. Cities such as Copenhagen and Amsterdam have long been known for their cycling infrastructure, where separate lanes keep cyclists safe from traffic and make bicycling a realistic choice for people of all ages. Paris has expanded its network of bike paths in recent years and has closed sections of major roads to cars, turning them into parks and walkways. Other cities have followed with similar projects that reclaim street space for people rather than vehicles.

Public transit expansion is another central approach. Many metropolitan areas are investing in new subway lines, light rail systems, and frequent bus networks to give residents reliable alternatives to driving. Some cities have introduced bus rapid transit, which uses dedicated lanes and priority signals to move large numbers of passengers quickly. Where transit is convenient and affordable, people are more willing to leave their cars at home for commuting, errands, and social trips.

Urban design policies also play a significant role. Zoning reforms that allow mixed-use development, placing housing, shops, and workplaces close together, reduce the distances people must travel. The concept of the "15-minute city," in which most daily needs can be reached by walking or cycling within a short time, has gained attention in cities including Paris and Melbourne as a guiding goal for planning. Such designs make car ownership less necessary rather than merely inconvenient to avoid.

Some governments are using pricing tools to discourage unnecessary driving. London introduced a congestion charge in 2003 that requires drivers to pay a fee for entering the central zone during peak hours, and the policy reduced traffic and raised funds for transport improvements. Other cities have explored low-emission zones that restrict the most polluting vehicles, and some have examined road pricing that adjusts charges based on time and distance traveled. Parking policy is equally important, since limiting the supply of parking and raising its cost can encourage people to choose other modes of travel.

Electric vehicles are part of the broader picture, though they do not solve every problem associated with car dependence. Many countries have set targets to phase out the sale of new gasoline-powered cars and offer incentives for electric models. Electric cars can reduce tailpipe emissions and local air pollution, but they still contribute to traffic congestion, road wear, and the space demands of parking, so they are generally viewed as a complement to reducing overall car use rather than a replacement for it.

The benefits of reducing car dependence extend well beyond the environment. Cleaner air reduces respiratory illnesses and premature deaths linked to vehicle emissions, which is especially important for children and older adults. Walking and cycling provide regular physical activity, which can lower the risk of heart disease, diabetes, and depression. Traffic injuries and fatalities also tend to fall when streets are designed to slow vehicles and protect people outside them.

Economic advantages are significant as well. Households that do not need to own and maintain one or more cars can save thousands of dollars each year on purchase costs, fuel, insurance, and repairs. Local businesses often benefit when streets are pleasant for pedestrians, since people who walk or cycle tend to stop and shop more frequently than those who drive past in traffic. Public investment in transit and infrastructure can also create jobs and stimulate development around stations.

Reduced car dependence can improve social equity. Many people, including the young, the elderly, people with disabilities, and those who cannot afford a vehicle, are left out of a system built around driving. When transit and safe streets are available, these residents gain greater access to jobs, schools, healthcare, and community life. Equitable transportation planning means ensuring that the benefits of change are shared fairly and that lower-income neighborhoods are not displaced by new development.

Reducing car dependence also creates more livable communities. Quieter streets, less noise, and more green space make neighborhoods healthier and more pleasant places to spend time. Children can walk to school more safely, and neighbors are more likely to meet one another on sidewalks and in public squares. Many people who experience car-free or car-light districts report a stronger sense of community and place.

Challenges remain, and not every effort succeeds. Changes to streets and parking can meet resistance from residents and businesses who fear losing convenience or revenue. Rural areas and places with dispersed populations may find it difficult to provide frequent transit, and some people still depend on cars for work that requires them to travel long distances or carry heavy loads. Successful policies therefore tend to combine several approaches and to be tailored to local conditions rather than copied without adaptation.

Even so, the direction of change is clear across many parts of the world. Cities are discovering that giving people real choices about how to move makes them healthier, wealthier, and more connected. Countries are linking transportation policy to climate goals, public health, and social fairness. Reducing car dependence is not about eliminating cars entirely but about creating balanced transportation systems in which walking, cycling, and transit are safe, convenient, and attractive options. As more places demonstrate these benefits, the case for building cities around people rather than vehicles grows stronger.

The first thing Dana noticed was the silence. There was no breath in her chest, no heartbeat drumming in her ears, only a soft hum she could not quite place. She tried to open her eyes, and for a moment nothing happened. Then a pale light bloomed across her vision, cool and even, and she understood that she was seeing through something that was not eyes at all.

She remembered the road. The wet asphalt, the headlights swinging wide, the sickening crunch that had folded the world into darkness. Her last clear thought had been about her daughter's school play, the one she had promised to attend. Now she wondered how long ago that had been.

A voice spoke near her, gentle and measured. "You're awake. Do not try to move quickly. Your systems are still calibrating."

She wanted to ask where she was, but when she tried to speak, a flat synthetic tone came out instead. It startled her so badly that she felt a jolt run through her frame, and she heard the faint whir of servos responding.

"That is normal," the voice said. "Your vocal module is new. Everyone finds it strange at first."

Everyone. The word lodged itself in her mind. How many others had woken here, in bodies that were not their own?

She lifted her hand, or rather the thing at the end of her arm, and turned it slowly in the light. Smooth panels of a dull graphite color met at precise seams. Her fingers were jointed and articulated, each one capable of a range of motion she had never possessed. She flexed them, marveling at how little effort it took, and then felt a wave of grief so sharp it nearly overwhelmed her.

She had always known the touch of things. The warmth of her coffee mug, the rough bark of the oak in her backyard, the soft fur of the dog she had loved for twelve years. Now she could sense pressure and temperature only as numbers scrolling faintly at the edge of her perception, like data on a screen.

"Where is my body?" she asked, and this time the words came out with a little more control.

The voice hesitated. "Your original body was severely damaged. We were able to preserve your neural pattern. This chassis is what we had available."

"Available," she repeated. The word tasted bitter. "So I'm a machine now."

"You are still you," the voice said quickly. "Your memories, your personality, your habits of thought. Those were carried over intact. The difference is in the vessel, not the person inside it."

She wanted to believe that. Part of her did. But another part kept returning to the phantom sensations of a body that no longer existed, the ache in muscles she could no longer feel, the hunger that had vanished without her noticing when it went.

She sat up slowly. The room was white and clean, lined with monitors and quiet machines, and beyond a wide window she could see a city glittering under a dusk sky. Somewhere out there, her daughter was growing up without her, believing she was gone.

"Can I see her?" Dana asked. "My daughter. Can I tell her I'm alive?"

There was a long pause. "We can discuss that. There are questions about how she would understand it, and how you would feel about being seen this way."

Dana looked down at her hands again, metal and light and joints that did not tire. She thought of the school play, the promise she had made, and the strange new silence where her heartbeat used to be.

"I'll decide how I feel about it," she said quietly. "I just need to see her first."

The hum of the machines seemed to soften around her, and for the first time since she had woken, Dana felt something that was not grief or fear. It was resolve, and it belonged entirely to her.

Clear, engaging, and professional writing rests on a few core features. First, clarity depends on precise word choice and direct sentences that state the main point early, so readers never have to guess what the writer means. Second, a logical structure, with paragraphs that each develop a single idea and transitions that show how ideas connect, guides the reader smoothly from beginning to end. Third, engagement comes from concrete examples, varied sentence rhythm, and an active voice that makes the writing feel alive rather than mechanical. Fourth, professionalism is reflected in accurate grammar, consistent formatting, and a tone that respects the reader without becoming stiff or overly casual. Fifth, careful editing and proofreading remove the small errors that can undermine a writer's credibility, even when the underlying ideas are strong. Sixth, writers who know their audience can tailor vocabulary, depth, and examples so that the material feels relevant and accessible to the people reading it. Taken together, these features show that good writing is less about impressive language than about thoughtful choices made with the reader firmly in mind.

Maya had always been the quiet one, so when Ms. Ortiz announced a class project to help the students "understand how it feels to be included," she was thrilled to be chosen as the first subject. The experiment was simple: Maya would be placed in a group of classmates who had been told to ignore her for one afternoon, and afterward they would discuss the lesson together. At first, Maya sat at the table and smiled at each of them, waiting for someone to notice her. The others chatted and laughed, passing a notebook around while her name went unspoken. She tried to make a joke about the science worksheet, and when it fell flat, she laughed louder than she meant to, hoping someone would join in. Hours seemed to stretch, and her chest tightened with a hunger she had never felt so sharply before. When the bell finally rang, she lingered at the door, half expecting someone to say her name. Instead, the group filed out without looking back, and Maya realized she had been counting their glances all day. Later, during the debrief, Ms. Ortiz asked how she felt, and Maya wanted to say she had learned something important, but all she could manage was that she wished someone had asked her to sit with them. The classmates looked down, suddenly ashamed, and one girl quietly slid over to make room. That small gesture, Maya thought, was the first moment all day she had felt she belonged.

Learning from the experiences of others is one of the most efficient ways to discover new activities and gain knowledge. Rather than spending years on trial and error, we can draw on the lessons that others have already paid for with their time and effort. A friend who has taken a particular course, for example, can tell us which parts are worth the effort and which can be skipped. Likewise, a person who has tried a hobby such as rock climbing or bread baking can warn us about common mistakes and recommend the right tools to begin with. This shared knowledge saves time, reduces unnecessary expense, and helps prevent avoidable injuries or frustrations. Hearing about different experiences also broadens our horizons, exposing us to activities we might never have considered on our own. Stories and advice from others can spark curiosity and motivate us to try things we would otherwise dismiss. Moreover, comparing several perspectives helps us form a more balanced view, since no single account tells the whole story. Of course, we should weigh advice carefully and remain critical, because what works for one person may not suit another. Still, by listening to others and reflecting on what they share, we can learn more quickly, make better choices, and grow in both skill and understanding.

The Electoral College has been the subject of debate for generations, and the question of whether it fairly represents voters across states remains pressing. Supporters argue that the system protects federalism by giving smaller states a meaningful voice in presidential elections. Each state receives electors equal to its congressional delegation, which means that even the least populous states hold at least three electoral votes. This structure, they contend, prevents candidates from focusing exclusively on the largest population centers and encourages broader geographic appeal. The founders also feared that a pure popular vote could lead to demagoguery and that a national contest would favor candidates with the greatest name recognition. Critics, however, point out that the system can produce outcomes at odds with the national popular vote, as occurred in 2000 and 2016. Because most states award all their electors to the statewide winner, a candidate can win the presidency while losing the nationwide tally by a substantial margin. This arrangement also concentrates campaign attention on a small number of swing states, leaving voters in safe states largely ignored. Votes cast in lopsided states carry less practical weight than votes in competitive ones, which many see as a violation of the principle that each citizen's vote should count equally. A direct popular vote would address these concerns by making every ballot count the same regardless of where it is cast. Under such a system, the candidate who receives the most votes nationwide would win, eliminating the possibility of a mismatch between the popular and electoral outcomes. Proponents also argue that a national contest would encourage turnout in every state, since voters in all regions would have a reason to participate. Opponents of abolition warn that a direct vote could diminish the influence of rural and small-state voters and encourage campaigns to focus only on densely populated metropolitan areas. They also raise concerns about close national races, which might trigger nationwide recounts and disputes that could be harder to resolve than the state-by-state process. Some suggest a middle path, such as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, in which participating states pledge their electors to the national popular vote winner. Such proposals attempt to preserve the existing framework while aligning outcomes with the national will. Ultimately, the fairness of the Electoral College depends on which principle one values most: the equal weight of each individual vote or the protection of state-level representation. Reasonable people can weigh these considerations differently. Still, the growing gap between electoral and popular outcomes suggests that the current system deserves serious reconsideration. A reform that honors both equality among voters and the legitimate interests of states may ultimately serve the nation best.

Trump's Healthcare Overhaul Faces Growing GOP Resistance as Crucial House Vote Nears

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump's proposed healthcare overhaul is facing mounting opposition from members of his own party as a pivotal House vote approaches, raising questions about whether the measure can clear Congress. Party leaders have spent recent weeks trying to build support, but a bloc of Republican lawmakers has signaled reservations that could complicate the effort. The outcome carries significant implications for millions of Americans who rely on insurance coverage and for the broader political direction of the party heading into future elections.

The plan, which the White House has promoted as a way to lower premiums, expand choice, and reduce federal spending on health programs, has been the centerpiece of the administration's domestic agenda this session. Supporters argue that the proposal would shift more decisions to states and individuals while curbing what they describe as wasteful regulation. Its backers have emphasized price transparency and the expansion of options for consumers who are currently priced out of coverage.

Critics within the Republican conference, however, have raised concerns that cuts to federal programs could leave vulnerable populations without adequate protection. Several moderate members representing districts with large numbers of Medicaid enrollees have said they cannot support changes that would reduce funding for those programs. Others on the party's conservative flank have argued that the bill does not go far enough in dismantling existing mandates and federal oversight.

The divide reflects a longstanding tension within the party over the proper federal role in health coverage. Some lawmakers favor a market-driven approach with minimal government involvement, while others believe that any reform must preserve guarantees for patients with pre-existing conditions. Finding language that satisfies both camps has proven difficult, according to aides familiar with the negotiations.

House leadership has been holding closed-door meetings with members who remain undecided, offering amendments and assurances in an effort to win their support. Staff have worked late into the evenings revising sections of the legislation, and several provisions have been altered at least twice in recent weeks. Party whips have been counting votes daily, and officials acknowledge that the margin for error is extremely narrow.

Democrats, who are united in opposition, have seized on the intraparty disagreement to press their own message. Minority leaders have called the proposal a threat to affordable care and have urged Republicans to abandon it in favor of bipartisan alternatives. They have also pointed to independent analyses projecting that millions could lose coverage under the current draft, a claim the administration disputes.

Industry groups have weighed in as well, with hospital associations, insurers, and physician organizations offering a range of responses. Some hospital representatives have warned that proposed reimbursement changes could strain rural facilities that already operate on thin margins. Insurers have been more mixed, with some saying they welcome greater flexibility and others cautioning about the administrative burden of new requirements.

Patient advocacy organizations have mobilized in recent days, organizing calls to congressional offices and rallies near the Capitol. Many of the people who have spoken out describe their own experiences with high costs, coverage gaps, and the difficulty of navigating the current system. Their stories have become a focal point for both sides as they try to frame the debate in human terms.

Economists who have reviewed the proposal offer differing assessments of its likely effects. Some project modest savings on premiums for certain groups, while others warn that the net impact on overall spending and coverage could be less favorable than advertised. Analysts note that projections depend heavily on assumptions about how insurers and states would respond to the changes.

The White House has pressed lawmakers to act quickly, arguing that delay would leave the country with a system that officials describe as unsustainable. Administration officials have held briefings for reporters and members of Congress, and the president has spoken publicly about the importance of the vote. Aides have indicated that the president is prepared to campaign for the measure in districts where representatives remain on the fence.

Some Republicans have urged caution, suggesting that the party should not rush a sweeping change that affects one-sixth of the national economy. These lawmakers argue that a more incremental approach, focused on specific problems such as drug prices or surprise billing, would be easier to pass and less disruptive. Their proposals have received limited attention from leadership but have gained some traction among rank-and-file members.

The Congressional Budget Office has been asked to provide updated estimates, and its findings are expected to influence the final weeks of debate. Members from both parties have said they will closely examine the figures, particularly those related to coverage numbers and federal spending over the next decade. Any revised score could shift the positions of lawmakers who have been waiting for clearer data.

Governors across the country have also voiced opinions, with officials from both parties expressing concern about the financial implications for their states. Some have said that shifts in federal funding would force difficult choices about budgets and eligibility rules. Others have welcomed the prospect of greater flexibility to design programs suited to local needs.

Legal experts have noted that several provisions of the proposal could face court challenges if enacted. Questions about the scope of federal authority, the treatment of existing contracts, and the protections guaranteed under current law are likely to be contested. Analysts say that litigation could delay implementation for years regardless of how the House votes.

Within the House, procedural maneuvers are shaping the path forward. Leadership must decide whether to bring the bill to the floor under a rule that requires majority support for the procedure itself, a step that has tripped up previous legislative efforts. Failure to secure the rule vote would represent a significant setback before the substantive debate even begins.

Several swing-district Republicans have stressed that their votes depend on constituent feedback. Town hall meetings held over the past month have featured heated exchanges, with some attendees praising the plan and others voicing fierce objections. Lawmakers say they are weighing these voices against the priorities of their party leadership and the policy merits of the bill.

Supporters of the overhaul have pointed to polling suggesting that many voters want lower costs and more choice, arguing that the proposal addresses those concerns directly. They contend that opponents are defending a status quo that many Americans find frustrating. Proponents also say that the party has a responsibility to deliver on promises made during the campaign.

Opponents counter that polling shows broad public support for protecting existing coverage and that voters may punish lawmakers who vote for changes perceived as harmful. They argue that the party should focus on targeted improvements rather than a comprehensive rewrite. Some have suggested that a failed vote would allow the party to regroup and craft a more durable plan.

Hospitals in rural areas have been among the most vocal critics, warning that reductions in reimbursement could force closures of emergency rooms and maternity wards. Representatives of these facilities have traveled to Washington to meet with lawmakers, presenting data on patient volumes and financial strain. Their testimony has resonated with members whose districts include many small communities.

Pharmaceutical companies have also taken an interest, with some expressing support for provisions that would alter drug pricing mechanisms and others raising concerns about changes to patent protections. The industry has been lobbying intensively, and its position could influence the votes of members who have close ties to companies based in their districts.

Insurance regulators have warned that sudden shifts in the market could create instability, particularly in states where few carriers operate. They have urged Congress to provide a transition period and clear guidance to avoid disruptions for consumers who are mid-plan year. Several regulators have asked for direct consultation before any final text is adopted.

Labor unions representing health care workers have expressed opposition, arguing that proposed staffing and wage provisions would weaken protections for employees. Union leaders have said they will mobilize members in targeted districts to press their representatives. Their involvement adds another layer of pressure on lawmakers who depend on labor support in their elections.

Veterans' organizations have raised questions about how the plan would affect the Department of Veterans Affairs and the health care options available to former service members. Advocates have asked for assurances that veterans will not lose access to services they have earned. Several lawmakers have said they will seek clarifying language before committing their votes.

Analysts following the debate say the coming days will be decisive. Whip counts remain fluid, and leadership has not yet confirmed that it has the votes needed to proceed. Whether the House moves forward, delays the vote, or revises the bill substantially will likely determine how the broader healthcare debate unfolds in the months ahead.

This manuscript proposes a generative adversarial network for audio synthesis that models spectral magnitudes and instantaneous frequencies, and evaluates it on the NSynth dataset. The motivation is well grounded, since explicitly modeling phase-related quantities through instantaneous frequency can avoid the phase-reconstruction artifacts common in magnitude-only spectrogram approaches. The authors clearly describe the generator architecture and the adversarial training setup, although several hyperparameters, such as loss weighting between the magnitude and frequency terms, are reported only partially and should be fully specified for reproducibility. The quantitative evaluation relies mainly on spectral distance metrics and a pitch-accuracy measure, which are informative but do not fully capture perceptual quality, so the inclusion of listening tests or a perceptual metric such as a learned audio quality model would considerably strengthen the claims. The comparison baselines are limited to one prior GAN vocoder, and the paper would benefit from comparisons against diffusion-based and autoregressive NSynth models that represent the current state of the art. The ablation study is helpful in isolating the contribution of the instantaneous frequency branch, but it does not report variance across random seeds, so it is unclear whether the reported improvements are statistically robust. The discussion of NSynth's limitations, including its restriction to single-note instrument samples, is appropriately brief, yet the authors should more explicitly address whether the method generalizes to polyphonic or real-world audio. The writing is generally clear, though some notation for the instantaneous frequency computation is introduced inconsistently and should be unified. Overall, the paper presents a technically sound and potentially useful contribution, and I recommend a major revision addressing the evaluation breadth, reproducibility details, and statistical reporting before it is suitable for publication.

Inspiring words have a remarkable power to help people persevere through difficult times. When life becomes overwhelming, a single sentence of encouragement can shift a person's mindset from despair to determination. Many people throughout history have turned to speeches, letters, and poems to find the strength to keep going when the odds seemed impossible. Words that remind us of our past courage can reignite our belief that we are capable of overcoming current obstacles. Inspiring language also connects us to others who have faced similar struggles, showing us that hardship is a shared human experience rather than a personal failure. Encouraging words from friends, mentors, or family members can provide comfort and a sense of being supported during our darkest moments. Beyond comfort, motivating language helps reframe challenges as opportunities for growth, which can make difficulties feel more manageable. When we repeat hopeful messages to ourselves, we train our minds to focus on possibilities instead of limitations. In this way, the words we choose and the words we hear shape how we respond to adversity. Ultimately, inspiring words do not remove the difficulties of life, but they give us the courage and perspective needed to persevere through them.

This paper proposes a novel approach to improving image reconstruction in variational autoencoders by guiding training with programmatically generated grid images, which provide structured, controllable supervision signals. The core idea is interesting and well motivated, as synthetic grid patterns offer precise geometric ground truth that natural image datasets lack. The experimental section would be strengthened by a more thorough comparison against standard VAE baselines and recent reconstruction-focused variants, along with clearer ablations isolating the contribution of the grid guidance. The methodology description is somewhat sparse on how the grid images are generated and weighted relative to the main training objective, which limits reproducibility. Reported gains in reconstruction metrics are promising, but the authors should also evaluate generalization to natural image datasets and report variance across multiple random seeds. Overall, the work is a worthwhile contribution that would benefit from expanded experiments and more detailed implementation reporting before publication.

The manuscript addresses an important gap in deep image retrieval, namely the difficulty of explaining why two images are judged similar by a learned embedding. The authors propose a visual attention mapping approach that projects attention signals onto the embedding space, allowing similarity scores to be decomposed into localized image regions. This framing is well motivated, since global similarity scores offer little guidance to users who wish to understand or correct retrieval results. The introduction situates the work clearly within the literature on explainable retrieval and saliency methods, although the related work section could engage more directly with recent region-based retrieval architectures. The central claim is that localized similarity analysis improves both interpretability and user control, and the paper largely supports this claim with experiments. The method is described in a logical sequence, beginning with the attention formulation and ending with the interactive retrieval interface. The mathematical notation is mostly consistent, though the definition of the attention normalization term is introduced late and would benefit from earlier clarification. The figures illustrating attention heatmaps for query-result pairs are effective and help the reader grasp the qualitative behavior of the method. However, the choice of heatmap color scale varies across figures, which makes visual comparison between examples harder than it should be. The experimental setup uses standard benchmark datasets, which is appropriate, but the authors should report results on at least one additional dataset to demonstrate generality. Quantitative retrieval metrics such as mean average precision are reported, and the proposed method performs comparably to strong baselines, though the margins are small. The paper would be stronger if it included confidence intervals or results over multiple random seeds, as the reported differences could plausibly fall within run-to-run variance. The localization evaluation relies on a proxy measure that compares attention maps with bounding box annotations, and the authors should justify why this proxy is a valid indicator of useful explanation. A user study evaluating whether the localized analysis helps people understand or refine retrieval results would substantially strengthen the interactive claims. The interactive retrieval component is described briefly, and the paper does not specify how user feedback modifies the embedding or the attention weights in practice. Clarifying this mechanism, perhaps with pseudocode, would help reproducibility. The computational cost of computing attention maps at query time is mentioned only in passing, yet latency is critical for interactive systems, so a systematic timing analysis is needed. The ablation study isolates the contribution of the attention projection layer, which is a useful addition, but it does not separate the effect of the interface from the effect of the underlying attention. Limitations are acknowledged in a short paragraph, though they focus on dataset scope and omit potential failure cases such as attention collapse onto background regions. The authors should include a failure analysis with representative examples. The discussion of societal implications is minimal, and given that retrieval systems can reinforce dataset biases, a brief treatment of fairness considerations would be appropriate. The code release statement is welcome, and the authors are encouraged to provide trained model checkpoints to facilitate verification. Overall the writing is clear and the contribution is relevant, with the core idea being sound and worth publishing. The main weaknesses lie in the strength of the empirical evidence for interactivity and in the limited analysis of failure modes. The reported gains over baselines are modest, so the authors should temper claims of superiority accordingly. The literature review would benefit from citing more recent work on attention-based explanation for metric learning. Figures could be reorganized to place qualitative and quantitative results closer together for easier reading. Minor typographical errors appear in several equation references and should be corrected before publication. The supplementary material is referenced frequently, and key details currently located there should be moved into the main text. The reproducibility statement lists hyperparameters but omits the random seed policy, which should be added. Taken together, the paper presents a promising direction, and I recommend a major revision addressing the evaluation, interactivity validation, and failure analysis before it can be accepted.

Facial-expression technology promises schools a new way to understand students, but its use to identify emotions, honesty, and learning needs raises serious questions that deserve careful thought. These systems use cameras and software to analyze faces and infer feelings such as boredom, confusion, or excitement during a lesson. Supporters argue that such information could help teachers notice when a student is struggling and respond before the student falls behind. In a crowded classroom, a teacher may miss the quiet student who looks lost, and a tool that flags those moments might seem like a helpful second set of eyes.

However, the scientific basis for reading emotions from faces is far less certain than the technology's marketing suggests. Research in psychology has shown that facial expressions do not reliably map onto internal states across people, cultures, and situations. A furrowed brow might signal concentration, frustration, or simply bright sunlight in the window. When an algorithm labels a student as "unengaged," it is often making a guess based on a narrow and sometimes flawed model of human expression.

The claim that these systems can detect honesty is even more troubling. Lying does not produce a consistent, observable facial signature, and decades of research on deception detection have found that people, and machines, perform only slightly better than chance at spotting lies. Using such a tool to judge whether a student is telling the truth about cheating, behavior, or an absence could lead to unfair accusations. A student who is nervous, anxious, or from a different cultural background might be wrongly marked as dishonest.

Bias is another serious concern. Several studies have found that facial analysis software performs unevenly across skin tones, genders, and disabilities, sometimes with significantly higher error rates for students of color. A system that misreads these students as angry, disengaged, or deceptive would reinforce existing inequalities rather than correct them. Schools that adopt such technology could end up disciplining or labeling the very students who are already most vulnerable.

Privacy also matters a great deal. Continuous facial monitoring means that students are recorded and analyzed throughout the school day, often without meaningful consent. Young people have a reasonable expectation that their private reactions and expressions are not constantly catalogued by a machine. Even if data is stored securely, the existence of such a record can change how students behave, encouraging them to perform the expressions a system expects rather than being themselves.

There is also the question of what learning really requires. Good teaching depends on relationships, trust, and conversation, which a camera cannot replicate. A student who feels watched and judged is less likely to ask questions, take intellectual risks, or admit confusion. If the goal is to meet students' learning needs, the more effective path is often to talk with them, observe their work, and build a classroom where mistakes are safe to make.

Some educators propose using the technology only for limited purposes, such as measuring general classroom attention in aggregate rather than tracking individuals. Even this narrower use raises questions about accuracy and whether the benefits justify the intrusion. Schools considering such tools should ask whether there is solid evidence that they work and whether they could cause harm.

In the end, the appeal of technology lies in its promise of certainty, but human emotions and honesty are too complex to be reduced to a face scan. Schools should be cautious about replacing the judgment of trained teachers with software that is unreliable, biased, and invasive. Supporting students well requires patience, empathy, and genuine attention, qualities that no algorithm can fully provide.

Stercoral colitis in young adults with lupus: diagnostic challenges, clinical management, and outcomes

Abstract

Stercoral colitis is a rare but potentially lethal form of right-sided colonic necrosis caused by impaction of hardened feces that raises intraluminal pressure and compromises mucosal and mural blood flow. Although it is well described in elderly patients with chronic constipation, opioid use, and immobility, it is increasingly recognized in younger populations with systemic conditions that predispose to bowel dysmotility and vascular injury. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is one such condition, affecting predominantly women of reproductive age and associated with gastrointestinal involvement, medication exposure, and thrombotic or vasculitic complications. This paper reviews the clinical, diagnostic, and therapeutic considerations of stercoral colitis in young adults with lupus, discusses the diagnostic difficulties that arise from overlapping features with lupus enteritis, and summarizes available evidence on management and outcomes. Because published data are limited to case reports and small series, the conclusions drawn here should be regarded as provisional and in need of prospective confirmation.

Introduction

Stercoral colitis was first systematically described in the medical literature in the twentieth century, and its pathophysiology has since been characterized as a combination of mechanical pressure from an impacted fecal mass and ischemia of the bowel wall. The right colon is most commonly affected, possibly because of its wide lumen, the relatively liquid consistency of its contents, and its position within a watershed vascular territory. Clinical recognition is often delayed because the presentation may mimic more common abdominal conditions such as appendicitis, diverticulitis, or small bowel obstruction.

Systemic lupus erythematosus is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by multisystem involvement, with a marked female predominance and onset most often between the ages of fifteen and forty-five years. Gastrointestinal manifestations occur in a substantial proportion of patients and include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, and in severe cases, lupus enteritis, peritonitis, pancreatitis, and protein-losing enteropathy. Lupus enteritis is thought to arise from small vessel vasculitis and ischemia, and its clinical picture overlaps considerably with that of ischemic colitis from other causes.

The convergence of these two entities in a young adult raises particular questions. Lupus-related dysmotility, corticosteroid-induced changes in gut function, and the vascular fragility associated with antiphospholipid antibodies may each contribute to susceptibility. Conversely, the features of stercoral colitis may be attributed to lupus enteritis, leading to misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment. This paper considers these interactions in detail.

Epidemiology and Risk Factors

Epidemiologic data specific to stercoral colitis in young adults with lupus are not available, and the relevant literature consists of isolated case reports and small retrospective series. The broader population of patients with stercoral colitis is predominantly elderly, with mean ages in most series exceeding sixty years. Young patients who develop the condition frequently have identifiable contributors, including chronic constipation, anticholinergic or opioid medications, neurologic disorders, eating disorders, or hypothyroidism.

In patients with lupus, several risk factors may be relevant. Corticosteroid therapy is widely used in SLE and is associated with delayed gastric emptying, altered colonic motility, and increased susceptibility to intestinal perforation. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which are frequently used for musculoskeletal symptoms, may compromise mucosal defense and alter fluid handling in the colon. Immunosuppressive agents such as mycophenolate mofetil and cyclophosphamide may further complicate the clinical course by blunting the inflammatory response and masking early signs of ischemia.

Antiphospholipid antibodies, present in a substantial minority of patients with SLE, predispose to thrombosis of both arterial and venous circulation. Mesenteric venous thrombosis and small vessel occlusion may reduce the colonic perfusion reserve, rendering the bowel more vulnerable to the additional ischemic insult produced by fecal impaction. Hypoalbuminemia, which may result from nephrotic-range proteinuria or protein-losing enteropathy, can further reduce colloid osmotic pressure and contribute to mural edema.

Pathophysiology

The mechanism of stercoral colitis involves a sequence of events beginning with the accumulation of inspissated stool in the colon. Distension of the bowel increases intraluminal pressure, which in turn compresses the venous outflow channels within the wall and eventually compromises arterial inflow. As perfusion falls, the mucosa becomes ischemic, followed by necrosis, which may extend transmurally to cause perforation. Bacterial translocation through the damaged wall leads to peritonitis and sepsis.

In lupus, the same mechanical process may act on a bowel already weakened by immune-mediated injury. Vasculitis of the mesenteric arterioles, endothelial dysfunction, and microthrombosis may reduce the threshold at which ischemia develops. It is plausible that a relatively modest degree of fecal impaction could produce significant ischemia in a patient with active lupus enteritis, although this hypothesis has not been tested prospectively.

Clinical Presentation

Patients with stercoral colitis typically present with abdominal pain, which is often located in the right lower quadrant or periumbilical region and may be severe and out of proportion to examination findings. Nausea and vomiting are common, as are abdominal distension and absolute constipation or, paradoxically, overflow diarrhea. Fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis may be present, though their absence does not exclude the diagnosis, particularly in immunosuppressed patients.

In young adults with lupus, the presenting complaints frequently overlap with those of lupus flare. Abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting may be attributed to active lupus enteritis, to medication effects, or to a functional gastrointestinal disorder. Because abdominal symptoms are common in lupus, there is a risk of anchoring bias, in which clinicians interpret new symptoms within the framework of known disease activity rather than considering an alternative mechanical or ischemic cause. Careful attention to the history of bowel habits, recent medication changes, and the timing of symptom onset relative to any change in therapy may help to distinguish these possibilities.

Physical examination may reveal a tender, distended abdomen with decreased bowel sounds, and in advanced disease, signs of peritonitis such as guarding and rebound tenderness. Palpation of a firm fecal mass in the right colon is occasionally possible but is an unreliable finding. Lupus-related findings such as malar rash, arthritis, serositis, or oral ulceration may be present and can serve as clues to underlying disease activity.

Diagnostic Challenges

The central diagnostic challenge in this population is distinguishing stercoral colitis from lupus enteritis and from other causes of acute abdominal pain. Both conditions can present with abdominal pain, vomiting, and elevated inflammatory markers. Lupus enteritis is typically diagnosed on the basis of imaging showing bowel wall thickening, ascites, and mesenteric edema, together with clinical evidence of systemic activity such as elevated anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies or low complement levels. However, these features are nonspecific and may coexist with stercoral colitis.

Computed tomography is the imaging modality of choice in most acute settings. In stercoral colitis, typical findings include a dilated right colon containing a mass of mottled, air-containing feces, with or without bowel wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, and in advanced cases, pneumatosis, portal venous gas, or free air. Lupus enteritis may produce similar wall thickening and ascites but usually lacks an intraluminal fecal mass of this character. The presence of a feculent mass is therefore the most useful discriminating feature, although it may not always be obvious on imaging, especially when bowel contents are partially liquid.

Ultrasonography may be helpful in thin patients and in pregnancy, where ionizing radiation is undesirable, but its sensitivity for stercoral colitis is limited by bowel gas and obesity. Magnetic resonance imaging can characterize bowel wall changes and mesenteric vascularity but is less widely available in emergency settings. Endoscopic evaluation carries substantial risk in the presence of ischemia and perforation and is generally contraindicated in the acute setting, though it may be useful in selected stable patients to exclude other inflammatory conditions.

Laboratory testing offers limited discrimination. Elevated lactate, leukocytosis, and raised C-reactive protein are nonspecific. Serologic markers of lupus activity may help confirm systemic disease but do not establish the cause of the abdominal findings. Antiphospholipid antibody testing and assessment for thrombophilia may be informative when mesenteric thrombosis is suspected.

Diagnostic delay carries significant prognostic consequences, since the interval between symptom onset and surgical intervention is strongly associated with mortality in ischemic and necrotic bowel disease. Clinicians managing young adults with lupus and acute abdominal pain should therefore maintain a low threshold for cross-sectional imaging and should involve surgical colleagues early when imaging suggests a mechanical or ischemic process.

Clinical Management

Management of stercoral colitis is based on three principles: decompression of the bowel, correction of the underlying cause, and treatment of any complications such as perforation or sepsis. Initial conservative management includes bowel rest, nasogastric decompression where vomiting is present, intravenous fluid resuscitation, and correction of electrolyte abnormalities. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are generally administered when infection or perforation is suspected, with coverage directed against enteric gram-negative organisms and anaerobes.

Disimpaction is the cornerstone of treatment in uncomplicated cases. This may be attempted using enemas, including warm tap water, mineral oil, or hypertonic solutions, and in some patients, manual extraction of the fecal mass under sedation. Hyperosmolar agents may also be administered orally or rectally. These measures should be used cautiously in patients with ischemic or necrotic bowel, as aggressive manipulation may precipitate perforation. Vigorous enemas are contraindicated when there is evidence of peritonitis.

In patients with lupus, the management of the underlying disease must be integrated with the management of the colitis. Corticosteroid dosing may need to be adjusted, although abrupt withdrawal can precipitate a lupus flare and adrenal insufficiency. Immunosuppressive regimens should be reviewed in consultation with rheumatology. Where antiphospholipid syndrome is present, anticoagulation may be indicated, but the risk of bleeding must be weighed against the presence of mucosal ischemia and the need for surgery. Hydroxychloroquine should be continued where possible, as it has been associated with reduced thrombotic events in SLE.

Surgical management is required when there is perforation, peritonitis, refractory ischemia, or failure of conservative measures. Right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis or with ileostomy and mucous fistula is the most commonly performed procedure, with the choice depending on the degree of contamination, the patient's physiologic reserve, and the surgeon's assessment of tissue viability. In critically ill patients, damage control surgery with temporary abdominal closure may be necessary. Second-look procedures are often required when the extent of ischemia is uncertain at the initial operation.

Perioperative management in lupus patients requires particular attention to thrombosis prophylaxis, wound healing, and infection risk. Corticosteroid stress-dose coverage should be considered in patients on chronic steroids. The potential for postoperative lupus flare, triggered by surgical stress, should be anticipated and monitored.

Outcomes

Outcome data for stercoral colitis in young adults with lupus are extremely limited. In the general stercoral colitis literature, mortality is substantial and has been reported in the range of several percent in earlier series, rising considerably in patients who develop perforation or who undergo delayed surgery. Advanced age, comorbidity, and delayed diagnosis are consistently associated with worse outcomes. Because the young adult population with lupus differs in age and comorbidity profile, the extent to which these data apply is uncertain.

Reported outcomes in lupus patients with bowel ischemia more generally suggest that mortality is higher than in the general population, reflecting disease severity, immunosuppression, infection risk, and thrombotic complications. Survival in patients who require colectomy appears to depend heavily on the timing of intervention and on control of underlying lupus activity. Patients who experience a flare during the perioperative period may have a more difficult recovery.

Long-term outcomes include the possibility of intestinal dysfunction, altered bowel habit, and in patients with an ileostomy, the psychological and practical burden of stoma care. Young patients may face additional concerns related to fertility, pregnancy planning, and body image. Pregnancy in women with SLE carries known risks, and the coexistence of stercoral colitis and pregnancy would further complicate management, requiring multidisciplinary planning with obstetric and maternal-fetal medicine input.

Quality of life outcomes have not been systematically studied in this population. Given the chronic nature of lupus and the potential for recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms, long-term follow-up and psychosocial support are likely to be important components of care.

Prevention

Prevention of stercoral colitis in young adults with lupus centers on maintaining regular bowel habits and avoiding factors that promote constipation. Where opioids, anticholinergic drugs, or calcium channel blockers are required, clinicians should consider prophylactic laxatives and monitor bowel function closely. Adequate hydration, dietary fiber as tolerated, and physical activity may reduce the risk of fecal impaction. Patients with known chronic constipation or neurologic conditions should be counseled to report changes in bowel habit promptly.

Patients receiving corticosteroids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs should be advised about gastrointestinal warning symptoms and encouraged to seek early review if abdominal pain develops. Regular assessment of disease activity and medication adverse effects may help identify patients at higher risk.

Research Gaps

Several important gaps in knowledge limit the ability to provide evidence-based recommendations for this population. There are no prospective studies of stercoral colitis in patients with lupus, and the incidence, risk factors, and outcomes remain uncertain. The extent to which lupus-specific mechanisms such as antiphospholipid-mediated thrombosis or vasculitis contribute to disease susceptibility has not been quantified. Diagnostic criteria that reliably distinguish stercoral colitis from lupus enteritis would be valuable, as would validated scoring systems to guide the timing of surgical intervention. Comparative studies of conservative versus surgical management in this population are needed, as are data on long-term gastrointestinal and psychosocial outcomes.

Conclusion

Stercoral colitis in young adults with lupus is an uncommon but serious condition that presents diagnostic challenges because of its overlap with lupus enteritis and other causes of acute abdominal pain. Recognition depends on a high index of suspicion, appropriate cross-sectional imaging, and careful integration of gastrointestinal and rheumatologic assessment. Management requires decompression, correction of underlying contributors, optimization of lupus therapy, and early surgical consultation when perforation or ischemia is suspected. Outcomes are influenced by the speed of diagnosis and intervention, as well as by the activity of underlying disease. Given the limited evidence base, clinicians should apply these principles with caution and should contribute to the collection of case data that will allow future recommendations to be refined. Multidisciplinary care involving rheumatology, gastroenterology, colorectal surgery, and critical care is likely to offer the best prospect of favorable outcomes for this vulnerable group.
