Personal identity is shaped by many forces, but the choices we make about our goals are among the most revealing expressions of who we are. When others expect us to follow a particular path, we face a quiet test of self-belief: whether we will trust our own sense of purpose or surrender it to the approval of others. Perseverance becomes essential in this moment, because the pursuit of a goal that others doubt is rarely met with encouragement along the way. Family members may question whether a chosen career is practical, teachers may suggest safer alternatives, and friends may quietly wonder why we are willing to struggle for something uncertain. These expectations can feel like walls, yet they can also clarify what we truly value. Understanding this tension is the first step toward a more authentic life. Self-belief does not mean ignoring criticism or assuming that we are always right. Rather, it means having enough confidence in our own judgment to test our ideas through effort rather than abandoning them at the first sign of doubt. A person who believes in their capacity to learn and grow can accept feedback without being defined by it. Perseverance then becomes a practice of returning to the goal after each setback, adjusting the strategy while keeping the underlying purpose intact. History offers many examples of individuals who pursued unconventional ambitions despite skepticism, from scientists whose theories were initially dismissed to artists whose work was once considered strange. Their stories remind us that what seems improbable to observers may appear entirely reasonable to the person who has committed to it. Of course, not every expectation is unjust, and wisdom lies in distinguishing between constructive guidance and limiting assumptions. Thoughtful people listen carefully to others, weigh their advice, and then decide for themselves. Ultimately, pursuing one's goals despite external doubt is an act of self-definition. It asks us to take responsibility for our own story, to build the discipline needed to keep going, and to hold onto a belief in our potential even when it is not shared by those around us. In doing so, we discover that our identity is not simply inherited or assigned, but actively created through the courage to persist.

Deep Learning-Based Restoration of Cardiac Diffusion MRI to Improve In Vivo Myocardial Fiber Mapping During Free Breathing

Abstract

Cardiac diffusion tensor imaging (cDTI) offers a noninvasive means of characterizing the three-dimensional arrangement of cardiomyocytes and their aggregates, yet its clinical translation has been hindered by low signal-to-noise ratio, long acquisition times, and sensitivity to physiological motion. Free-breathing acquisitions are desirable for patient comfort and robustness, but respiratory motion introduces misregistration, phase inconsistencies, and signal dropout that corrupt the estimated diffusion tensors and degrade derived fiber orientation maps. In this work we propose a deep learning-based restoration framework designed to recover high-fidelity diffusion-weighted images from free-breathing cardiac diffusion data, with the explicit goal of improving in vivo myocardial fiber mapping. We describe a convolutional and transformer-hybrid network trained on paired motion-corrupted and reference-quality datasets, incorporating physics-informed constraints that enforce consistency with the diffusion signal model. We evaluate the approach on retrospectively and prospectively acquired data from healthy volunteers, quantifying improvements in tensor fitting residuals, helix angle and fiber angle reproducibility, and the spatial coherence of the reconstructed myocardial fiber architecture. Results indicate that the proposed method substantially reduces respiratory-induced artifacts and yields fiber maps that more closely match breath-hold references, while preserving the anatomical detail necessary for downstream analysis. We discuss limitations, including dependence on training data diversity, the risk of hallucinated structure, and the need for prospective validation in patient populations, and we outline directions for integrating the framework into routine clinical workflows.

Introduction

Diffusion tensor imaging has become a principal tool for probing tissue microstructure in the brain, where it reveals white matter tract organization with well-established clinical and research value. Applying the same principle to the heart is considerably more demanding. The myocardium is a dynamic organ that undergoes continuous contraction and relaxation, and its helical fiber architecture, which governs the mechanics of ventricular torsion and wall thickening, is encoded in a diffusion signal that is small relative to the noise floor of the acquisition. Cardiac diffusion tensor imaging, first demonstrated in ex vivo hearts and subsequently translated to in vivo human studies, therefore requires careful coordination of cardiac and respiratory gating, motion compensation, and signal averaging.

The fiber architecture of the left ventricle has long been described in terms of a helix angle that varies transmurally from the epicardium to the endocardium, with a sweep of roughly one hundred and twenty degrees in many descriptions. Measurements of this transmural helicity, together with the sheetlet and imbrication structure, provide insight into normal and pathological remodeling. In conditions such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, myocardial infarction, and dilated cardiomyopathy, altered fiber orientation and disrupted sheetlet organization have been reported, suggesting that cDTI-derived biomarkers could complement existing imaging endpoints. Realizing this potential depends on the reliability and reproducibility of the underlying fiber maps.

The principal obstacle to reliable in vivo cardiac diffusion imaging is motion. Cardiac motion, respiratory motion, and bulk patient movement all alter the spatial relationship between successive diffusion-weighted acquisitions. Breath-hold strategies mitigate respiratory motion but impose strict limits on acquisition duration, reduce the number of diffusion directions and b-values that can be sampled, and are poorly tolerated by many patients, including those with cardiac disease who may have limited breath-holding capacity. Free-breathing approaches avoid these constraints but expose the data to respiratory-induced displacement of the heart relative to the imaging volume, which manifests as through-plane and in-plane misregistration, intravoxel phase dispersion, and signal loss that propagates into the diffusion tensor estimates.

Conventional approaches to motion correction include navigator-based gating, retrospective image registration, and motion-compensated averaging. Navigator techniques reduce the effective scan efficiency and may fail to capture non-rigid motion adequately. Retrospective registration can correct for rigid displacement but struggles with the nonuniform and nonlinear deformations of the beating heart and with the very low signal of individual diffusion-weighted images. Moreover, many of these corrections operate on the data before tensor estimation, so residual artifacts can persist and be amplified in the derived fiber orientation maps, where small errors in eigenvector direction translate into large angular discrepancies.

Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated considerable promise for image restoration tasks in magnetic resonance imaging, including denoising, super-resolution, artifact reduction, and accelerated reconstruction. Convolutional neural networks trained on paired data can learn mappings from degraded to high-quality images that exploit statistical regularities beyond the reach of hand-crafted priors. Transformer-based architectures, which model long-range dependencies through self-attention, have further extended these capabilities. Applying such methods to cardiac diffusion MRI is attractive because the target signal is structured, spatially coherent over the myocardium, and governed by a known physical model that can be incorporated as a constraint.

Despite this promise, applying deep learning to cardiac diffusion data raises specific challenges. Training datasets with matched reference-quality diffusion images are scarce, since obtaining ground truth typically requires long breath-hold or ex vivo acquisitions that are not available at scale. Networks trained on synthetic corruptions may fail to generalize to the complex, patient-specific motion encountered in clinical practice. Furthermore, purely data-driven restoration risks introducing plausible but incorrect structure, which is especially dangerous when the output is used to infer microstructural orientation. These concerns motivate methods that combine learning with explicit physical and anatomical constraints.

In this paper we address these challenges by developing a deep learning-based restoration framework for free-breathing cardiac diffusion MRI, with the specific objective of improving in vivo myocardial fiber mapping. Our contributions are fourfold. First, we formulate the restoration problem as a supervised mapping from motion-corrupted diffusion-weighted images to motion-reduced estimates, using a training strategy that leverages breath-hold acquisitions as a reference and simulated respiratory motion to expand the diversity of corruptions. Second, we incorporate a diffusion-signal consistency term that encourages the restored images to obey the Stejskal-Tanner model when tensors are fitted, thereby discouraging the hallucination of diffusivity profiles that are physically implausible. Third, we evaluate fiber mapping outcomes directly, measuring helix angle, fiber angle, and transverse angle reproducibility rather than relying solely on image-domain metrics. Fourth, we assess spatial coherence of the reconstructed fiber field, since clinically meaningful fiber architecture should exhibit smooth, anatomically consistent organization.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first describe the acquisition protocol, the construction of the training and evaluation datasets, and the network architecture and loss formulation. We then present quantitative and qualitative results comparing the restored free-breathing data against breath-hold references and against conventional motion correction. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings, the limitations of the present study, and the steps required to bring this approach toward routine clinical use.

Methods

Study Population and Acquisition

The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent. Healthy adult volunteers without known cardiovascular disease were enrolled for the development and initial validation of the framework. Imaging was performed on a 3 tesla clinical scanner equipped with a multi-channel cardiac coil. Diffusion-weighted images were acquired using a single-shot spin-echo echo-planar sequence with motion-compensated diffusion encoding, cardiac triggering to the diastolic quiescent phase, and fat suppression. Diffusion encoding was performed along a set of directions distributed over the sphere, with b-values chosen to balance diffusivity sensitivity against signal attenuation.

For each participant, a breath-hold reference acquisition was obtained with the same spatial and diffusion parameters, using a protocol segmented across multiple breath-holds where necessary. A free-breathing acquisition was then obtained immediately afterward, under instruction to breathe normally, with the same nominal parameters. Respiratory motion was monitored with a diaphragmatic navigator to permit retrospective assessment of motion amplitude. Acquisitions were repeated where the breath-hold reference exhibited obvious motion or failed quality checks.

Training Data Construction

Because prospective pairing of free-breathing and reference acquisitions is limited in size, we constructed a training set by combining breath-hold data with simulated respiratory corruption. Breath-hold diffusion images served as the reference target. For each reference volume, we synthesized corrupted versions by applying rigid and locally nonrigid displacement fields sampled from a distribution fitted to measured respiratory motion amplitudes, together with phase perturbations and partial-volume signal loss consistent with through-plane displacement during the acquisition window. The displacement model was parameterized by an estimated respiratory cycle, with random initial phase, amplitude, and superimposed cardiac-related deformation. This procedure yielded a large number of paired examples from a relatively modest number of reference acquisitions.

To reduce the risk that the network learns the specific artifacts of the simulation rather than general respiratory corruption, we applied a range of augmentation strategies, including random intensity scaling, additive noise drawn from the empirical noise distribution of the scanner, variable spatial sampling, and random cropping of the myocardial region. We also held out a subset of acquisitions that were never used in simulation, so that evaluation reflected behavior on genuinely unseen real free-breathing data.

Network Architecture

The restoration network adopts an encoder-decoder design with skip connections, in which convolutional blocks capture local texture and fine anatomical boundaries. At the bottleneck, a set of transformer blocks operates on tokenized feature maps to model long-range spatial dependencies across the myocardium, which is important because respiratory displacement affects the heart as a coherent structure. The network processes the diffusion-weighted images jointly, with the diffusion direction and b-value encoded as additional input channels, so that the restoration can exploit correlations across the diffusion set. Multi-slice context is provided through a small stack of adjacent slices to reduce through-plane ambiguity.

The output of the network is a restored set of diffusion-weighted images with the same geometry as the input. Restoration is performed slice by slice within a stacked framework, and a final lightweight refinement module enforces smoothness along the through-plane dimension.

Loss Function

Training minimizes a composite objective comprising three terms. The first is a pixel-wise reconstruction loss, computed as a combination of the L1 norm and a structural similarity term, measured between the restored images and the breath-hold reference after registration of the reference to the restored output. The second is a diffusion-consistency term. For each voxel, the restored signal across diffusion directions is used to fit a diffusion tensor by weighted least squares under the Stejskal-Tanner model, and the discrepancy between the predicted signal from the fitted tensor and the restored signal is penalized. This term encourages the network to produce data that are internally consistent with a single tensor per voxel, discouraging the introduction of diffusion profiles that could not arise from the physical model. The third is a regularization term on the spatial smoothness of the derived principal eigenvector field within the myocardium, applied with a small weight to avoid oversmoothing genuine fiber discontinuities at the sheetlet boundaries.

The relative weights of the three terms were selected on a validation subset by examining the trade-off between image fidelity and the accuracy of derived tensor parameters.

Training Procedure

The network was optimized with the Adam optimizer using a cosine-annealed learning rate schedule, a batch size constrained by available memory, and early stopping based on validation loss computed on held-out acquisitions. Data augmentation was applied on the fly. Training was performed on a single high-memory graphics processing unit. Hyperparameters, including the number of transformer blocks, the embedding dimension, and the number of input slices, were chosen by a limited search on the validation set.

Diffusion Tensor and Fiber Estimation

After restoration, diffusion tensors were estimated voxel-wise by weighted linear least squares on the log-transformed signals, with weights reflecting signal magnitude to reduce bias at low signal. Eigen-decomposition yielded eigenvalues and eigenvectors at each voxel. Myocardial fiber orientation was characterized by the helix angle, defined as the angle between the projection of the principal eigenvector onto the short-axis plane and the local circumferential direction, together with the transverse angle and the fiber angle relative to the local myocardial coordinate system. Local myocardial coordinates were derived from segmentation of the left ventricular endocardial and epicardial surfaces in each participant's anatomical images, with the circumferential, longitudinal, and radial directions defined accordingly.

To ensure that comparisons were performed on a common geometry, the breath-hold reference, the free-breathing data before restoration, and the restored data were registered to the same anatomical template using a combination of rigid and nonrigid registration derived from cine imaging acquired within the same session.

Evaluation Metrics

We evaluated performance at three levels. At the image level, we computed structural similarity and normalized root-mean-square error between restored free-breathing images and breath-hold references, restricted to a myocardial mask. At the tensor level, we measured the residual of the tensor fit and the agreement of the mean diffusivity and fractional anisotropy maps with the reference. At the fiber level, we quantified the voxel-wise absolute angular difference between helix angle maps from the restored data and from the breath-hold reference, and we assessed reproducibility by comparing repeated free-breathing acquisitions within the same participant. We also computed the mean and variance of helix angle transmural gradients, as well as the proportion of voxels with fiber orientation estimates exceeding a physiologically implausible angular deviation from neighbors, as a measure of spatial incoherence.

Comparison Methods

For comparison, we processed the free-breathing data using three alternative pipelines: uncorrected reconstruction, a navigator-gated and retrospectively registered pipeline with tensor estimation performed on the corrected data, and a conventional denoising filter applied in the image domain prior to tensor estimation. Statistical comparisons were performed using paired nonparametric tests, with correction for multiple comparisons across metrics.

Results

Image-Level Restoration

Across the held-out healthy volunteer cohort, the proposed network substantially improved the agreement of free-breathing diffusion-weighted images with breath-hold references. Structural similarity within the myocardial mask increased relative to uncorrected free-breathing data, and normalized root-mean-square error decreased correspondingly. The improvement was most pronounced in slices near the diaphragm, where respiratory displacement was greatest, and in the lateral wall, where partial-volume effects from through-plane motion were most severe. Visual inspection confirmed reduction of ghosting and blurring at the myocardial boundary, and restoration of the sharp epicardial and endocardial contours that were degraded in the raw data.

The restored images showed qualitatively reduced signal dropout in the inferior and lateral segments, consistent with recovery of diffusion-weighted signal that had been attenuated by misregistration during the acquisition window. Performance relative to the navigator-gated and registered pipeline was comparable in global image metrics, but the deep learning approach produced fewer residual misregistration artifacts at segment boundaries.

Tensor-Level Results

Tensor fitting residuals were lower for the restored data than for uncorrected free-breathing data, indicating that the restored signals were more consistent with a single-tensor model per voxel. Mean diffusivity maps from restored data agreed more closely with breath-hold references, with reduced bias in the inferior wall. Fractional anisotropy values showed improved correspondence with the reference, particularly in the mid-ventricular septum, where the uncorrected free-breathing data had underestimated anisotropy. The diffusion-consistency term appeared to contribute meaningfully to this improvement, as ablation of that term produced restored images with comparable image-domain metrics but higher tensor residuals and elevated anisotropy errors.

Fiber-Level Results

The most important outcome for the present application concerns myocardial fiber mapping. Helix angle maps derived from restored free-breathing data exhibited a transmural progression that closely resembled the breath-hold reference, with the characteristic sweep from positive values at the epicardium to negative values at the endocardium preserved across the ventricular wall. The median voxel-wise absolute angular difference between restored and reference helix angle maps was reduced relative to uncorrected free-breathing data and to the conventional denoising pipeline. Reproducibility across repeated free-breathing acquisitions within the same participant improved, as indicated by a narrower distribution of angular differences between repeats after restoration.

The proportion of voxels exhibiting implausible angular discontinuities relative to their neighbors was lower in the restored data, consistent with improved spatial coherence of the fiber field. Transmural helix angle gradients derived from restored data fell within the range reported in the literature for healthy myocardium, whereas uncorrected data exhibited greater variance, suggesting that a portion of the apparent heterogeneity in raw free-breathing fiber maps arose from motion-related noise rather than true anatomical variation. The sheetlet-related features of the transverse angle were preserved in the restored maps, indicating that the smoothness regularization did not excessively suppress genuine fiber structure.

Qualitative Assessment

Visual review of the fiber orientation maps by two observers blinded to the processing pipeline confirmed the quantitative findings. Restored free-breathing maps were judged more similar to breath-hold references than uncorrected maps, and the observers identified fewer regions of apparent fiber discontinuity attributable to artifact. Observers also noted that the restored maps occasionally appeared slightly smoother than the reference in regions of low signal, which we address in the discussion as a potential source of bias.

Discussion

The present results indicate that a deep learning-based restoration framework, incorporating a diffusion-consistency constraint, can meaningfully improve the quality of free-breathing cardiac diffusion data and the fiber orientation maps derived from them. The gains were evident at the image, tensor, and fiber levels, with the largest practical benefit appearing in the reproducibility and spatial coherence of helix angle estimates. Because fiber architecture is inferred from small angular differences in the principal eigenvector, improvements in tensor fidelity translate directly into more reliable microstructural characterization, which is the central requirement for clinical use.

The inclusion of the diffusion-consistency term deserves emphasis. Purely image-domain objectives can yield visually attractive results that nonetheless violate the physics of the diffusion signal, producing tensors that are not realizable under the model. By penalizing such discrepancies, the framework constrains the network to output data that a single-tensor interpretation can accommodate, which reduces the risk that the restoration introduces structure that is physically implausible. The ablation experiment supports this design choice, since removing the term degraded tensor-level accuracy even when image metrics remained similar.

Several limitations warrant consideration. First, the training data were derived from a modest number of healthy volunteers and from simulated respiratory corruption. Although we used held-out real free-breathing data for evaluation, the generalizability of the network to patients with cardiac disease, arrhythmia, altered respiratory patterns, or substantial body habitus variation remains to be established. Pathological myocardium may exhibit fiber architectures that differ from the healthy distribution on which the network was trained, and there is a risk that the restoration could bias such patterns toward the normative appearance. Prospective evaluation in patient cohorts, with explicit assessment of whether disease-related fiber changes are preserved, is an essential next step.

Second, the risk of hallucinated structure, inherent to deep learning-based restoration, cannot be eliminated by the present constraints. The observation that restored maps appeared marginally smoother than references in low-signal regions suggests a tendency toward regularization that could mask genuine heterogeneity. This tendency may be acceptable for some applications but is undesirable where fine transmural or sheetlet detail carries diagnostic weight. Uncertainty estimation, for example through ensembles or Bayesian formulations, could help flag regions where the restoration is less reliable, and we regard its incorporation as a priority.

Third, the reference standard itself is imperfect. Breath-hold acquisitions, while preferable to free-breathing data for reference purposes, are not free of motion, and the true fiber architecture cannot be observed directly in vivo. Our evaluation therefore measures agreement with a practical reference rather than with ground truth. Validation against ex vivo histological or diffusion data from explanted hearts would provide a stronger anchor, although such comparisons are technically demanding and differ in tissue state and temperature.

Fourth, the computational cost of the network and the requirement for a high-memory graphics processing unit during inference may limit deployment in some clinical settings. Model compression, optimized inference pipelines, and integration with scanner-side reconstruction could reduce this barrier. Similarly, the interaction of the restoration with other acquisition-side accelerations, such as undersampling and parallel imaging, requires investigation, since joint optimization may yield further gains in scan efficiency.

Despite these limitations, the framework offers a practical route to improving the robustness of cardiac diffusion imaging under free-breathing conditions. Free-breathing acquisition substantially broadens the population in whom cDTI can be performed, including patients who cannot reliably hold their breath, and a restoration method that makes such data more reliable could expand access to fiber mapping in clinical research and, eventually, in patient care. Integration of the approach into routine workflows would also benefit from standardized protocols, shared benchmark datasets, and multicenter validation to assess reproducibility across scanner vendors and field strengths.

Future work will extend the training data to include patients with a range of cardiomyopathies and conduction abnormalities, incorporate uncertainty quantification, evaluate the framework across multiple scanner platforms, and investigate the incorporation of cardiac motion modeling directly into the restoration network. We also plan to assess whether restored cDTI-derived biomarkers provide prognostic or diagnostic information beyond conventional cardiac magnetic resonance endpoints. Such studies will determine whether the gains in fiber mapping fidelity demonstrated here translate into clinically meaningful advances.

Conclusion

We have presented a deep learning-based restoration framework for free-breathing cardiac diffusion MRI that improves the fidelity of in vivo myocardial fiber mapping. By combining supervised restoration trained on breath-hold references with simulated respiratory corruption and a physics-informed diffusion-consistency constraint, the method reduces motion-related artifacts, improves tensor accuracy, and yields helix angle maps that are more reproducible and spatially coherent than those obtained from uncorrected or conventionally processed free-breathing data. These findings support the potential of learning-based restoration to make cardiac diffusion imaging more robust and accessible, while underscoring the need for rigorous prospective validation in patient populations before clinical adoption.

Hopcroft's Perspectives on Improving Chinese Education: Computer Science Teaching, Faculty Development, and Student Learning

Abstract

John E. Hopcroft, the Nobel-adjacent Turing Award laureate and longtime Cornell professor, has been an influential voice in discussions of higher education reform in China. This paper synthesizes his publicly available views on computer science teaching, faculty development, and student learning, drawing on his public talks, interviews, and the institutional initiatives with which he has been associated. It argues that his recommendations form a coherent framework centered on conceptual depth, research-informed instruction, and the cultivation of independent learners. The paper also considers how these ideas apply within the particular structures of Chinese higher education, and where implementation challenges may arise. Because the scope of this analysis depends on secondary sources and public statements, its conclusions are interpretive and should be read as a reasoned account rather than a definitive record of his positions.

Introduction

Higher education in China has expanded rapidly over the past three decades, moving from an elite system to one serving a large share of each age cohort. This expansion has created pressure to improve the quality of teaching, particularly in fields such as computer science that have grown quickly in student numbers and economic importance. Within this context, the views of established figures in computing education carry weight, and John Hopcroft is among the most frequently cited. His career spans theoretical computer science, algorithm design, automata theory, and, in later decades, a sustained commitment to undergraduate education and institutional reform. This paper examines his perspectives as they relate to China, with attention to three areas: the content and method of computer science teaching, the development of faculty, and the nature of student learning.

Hopcroft's Background and Engagement with China

Hopcroft received the Turing Award in 1986, jointly with Robert Tarjan, for foundational contributions to the design and analysis of algorithms and data structures. He later served as Dean of Engineering at Cornell University and became a prominent advocate for rethinking how computing is taught. His engagement with Chinese institutions grew through collaborations, visiting appointments, and advisory roles connected to the development of computer science programs. Several Chinese universities have invited him to speak on curriculum design and research culture, and he has been associated with efforts to strengthen the research orientation of undergraduate education. These relationships provide the empirical basis for the observations discussed here, though the precise details of individual engagements are best verified through the institutions concerned.

Conceptual Depth in Computer Science Teaching

A recurring theme in Hopcroft's writing is the distinction between teaching programming skills and teaching the underlying principles of computation. He has argued that curricula overly focused on tools, languages, and short-term technical trends leave students ill-equipped for a field that changes rapidly. In his view, durable knowledge consists of algorithms, abstractions, mathematical reasoning, and the ability to formalize problems. For Chinese programs, which often emphasize rapid coverage of many topics, this suggests a need to slow down in key areas and to ensure that foundational courses in discrete mathematics, algorithms, theory of computation, and systems are taught with rigor.

This emphasis aligns with a broader argument that computer science should be understood as a science with its own methods of inquiry, not merely as an engineering craft. Hopcroft has stressed that students should learn to reason about the complexity of problems, to recognize when a problem is intractable, and to design solutions with provable properties. In practice, this means assessment should reward understanding of why an algorithm works and under what conditions it fails, not only the ability to reproduce code. Applied to China, where examinations have historically played a central role in evaluation, this recommendation implies a shift toward assessments that probe reasoning, such as proofs, open-ended analysis, and design justifications.

Hopcroft has also advocated for the integration of theory and practice without subordinating one to the other. Theory provides the vocabulary and guarantees, while practice tests ideas against real constraints. He has pointed to the value of projects that require students to build systems while also analyzing their performance. For Chinese institutions that have invested heavily in laboratories and industry partnerships, this suggests that practical work should be designed to illuminate theoretical concepts rather than serve as a substitute for them.

Research-Informed Instruction

A second strand of his thinking concerns the relationship between research and teaching. Hopcroft has long believed that undergraduates benefit from exposure to open problems and to the process of discovery. He has supported approaches in which students engage with current research questions, read primary literature, and undertake projects that resemble small research investigations. This orientation challenges a model of education in which knowledge is presented as settled and complete. In the Chinese context, where the transition from undergraduate study to graduate research is an important pathway, earlier exposure to research methods could help students develop the independence required for advanced work.

Hopcroft's advocacy for research-informed teaching also has implications for how universities allocate their resources and reward their staff. If teaching is to be grounded in research, faculty must have time and support to remain active scholars. This connects his views to the question of faculty development, discussed below.

Faculty Development

Hopcroft has consistently emphasized that the quality of an educational system depends on the capabilities and commitment of its teachers. He has argued that faculty members should be supported in developing their teaching as seriously as their research, and that institutions should create structures in which excellent teaching is recognized and rewarded. In discussions of Chinese universities, he has noted that rapid expansion can strain the supply of experienced instructors, leading to heavy teaching loads and limited opportunities for reflection and improvement.

Several concrete recommendations can be drawn from his perspective. First, institutions should provide sustained programs of pedagogical training, not one-time workshops, in which faculty can examine their methods, observe colleagues, and receive feedback. Second, tenure and promotion criteria should give genuine weight to teaching quality, supported by evidence such as peer observation, student learning outcomes, and curriculum development. Third, senior researchers should be encouraged to mentor junior colleagues in both research and instruction, creating communities of practice. Fourth, collaboration between universities, including international partnerships, can expose faculty to alternative models and help them adapt good practices to local conditions.

Hopcroft has also highlighted the importance of faculty engagement with the discipline's intellectual core. Instructors who understand the theory behind their subject can respond to student questions flexibly and can help students see connections across courses. He has suggested that teaching quality rises when faculty are themselves curious and actively learning, which argues against treating teaching as a routine task assigned to whoever is available.

Student Learning

The third theme concerns how students learn and what they should be expected to achieve. Hopcroft has been critical of education systems that reward memorization and rapid recall over comprehension and creativity. He has advocated for learning environments in which students are asked to explain their reasoning, to work on problems that lack obvious solutions, and to take responsibility for their own progress. In his view, the development of independent learners is among the most important goals of higher education, because the knowledge students acquire will become outdated while the capacity to learn continues to matter.

This perspective has specific implications for pedagogy. Active learning methods, such as problem-based learning, collaborative projects, and in-class problem solving, can engage students more deeply than lecture-only instruction. Hopcroft has indicated support for such methods while recognizing that they require careful design and adequate class sizes to be effective. In large Chinese classes, which can include hundreds of students, implementing active learning poses real logistical challenges, and institutions may need to experiment with hybrid models, teaching assistants, and technology-supported feedback.

Hopcroft has also been attentive to the role of mathematics in computing education. He has argued that students who are comfortable with mathematical reasoning are better prepared to engage with algorithms, probability, and formal methods. Strengthening mathematical preparation, therefore, is not separate from improving computer science teaching but is a prerequisite for it.

Another point concerns the value of breadth. Hopcroft has noted that exposure to diverse areas of computing and to related disciplines can help students discover their interests and see the wider significance of their work. This suggests that curricula should allow some flexibility, rather than locking students into a rigid sequence of narrowly defined courses.

Discussion

Taken together, Hopcroft's perspectives form an integrated approach to education. Conceptual depth, research engagement, faculty development, and student independence reinforce one another. A curriculum built on foundational principles requires faculty who understand those principles deeply. Research-informed teaching requires institutional support for faculty scholarship. Independent learning requires assessment and pedagogy that reward reasoning over recall. The coherence of this framework is one of its strengths, but it also means that partial adoption may yield limited results.

Several challenges arise when applying these ideas in China. Large class sizes, examination-oriented evaluation traditions, heavy teaching loads, and the pressure to produce publications can all work against the changes Hopcroft recommends. Moreover, the rapid growth of computing enrollments has sometimes outpaced the availability of qualified instructors, making faculty development a pressing need. At the same time, Chinese universities have demonstrated considerable capacity for large-scale reform when priorities are clearly set, and many of the ideas discussed here are already reflected in national and institutional initiatives. Successful implementation will likely depend on adapting principles to local contexts rather than transplanting specific models wholesale.

It is also worth noting the limits of this analysis. Hopcroft's views have been expressed in varied formats, and not all of his statements are equally detailed or systematic. The interpretation offered here draws on his general emphases rather than a complete body of written policy recommendations. Future research could strengthen this account through direct interviews, analysis of specific curriculum reforms, and empirical evaluation of outcomes at institutions that have adopted his suggestions.

Conclusion

John Hopcroft's perspectives offer a substantive contribution to the improvement of Chinese higher education, particularly in computer science. His emphasis on conceptual depth, research-informed instruction, faculty development, and the cultivation of independent learners addresses core challenges facing rapidly expanding systems. While implementation faces real constraints, his ideas provide a useful framework for institutions seeking to combine quality with scale. Continued dialogue between Chinese and international educators, informed by evidence from practice, will be essential for translating these principles into lasting improvements in teaching and learning.

References

Hopcroft, J. E. Selected public lectures and interviews on computing education and higher education reform. Various venues. Specific citations should be verified against the original sources before use.

The manuscript proposes an extension of the skip-gram model that learns multiple sense-specific embeddings for each word without supervision, using either soft or hard attention to weight context words during sense assignment. The motivation is clear and well grounded, since polysemy remains a known limitation of single-vector word representations, and the authors position their work sensibly within the literature on multi-sense embeddings. The introduction is readable and the research question is stated concisely. However, the related work section is uneven, giving substantial space to older clustering-based approaches while providing only a brief treatment of recent contextualized models, which weakens the justification for why the proposed method is still needed. The core technical contribution, the attention mechanism that assigns context windows to senses, is described at a high level, and several equations would benefit from explicit definitions of all symbols and dimensions. The distinction between soft and hard attention is interesting, but the paper does not clearly explain how gradients are propagated through the hard variant, which is a central methodological question. The training procedure is reasonably described, yet the authors should specify the number of senses per word, whether this is fixed or adaptive, and how this choice was tuned. The experimental setup uses standard benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the choice of datasets is not fully justified, and it is unclear whether the same hyperparameters were applied across all comparison systems. The reported results show modest gains over the baseline skip-gram model on word similarity tasks, and the improvements are presented without confidence intervals or significance testing, making it difficult to judge whether they are robust. The word sense discrimination evaluation is a strength, as it directly tests the stated goal of the method, though the authors should describe the annotation procedure and inter-annotator agreement for any manually labeled data used. The qualitative analysis of nearest neighbors for polysemous words is illustrative and helpful, but the examples appear to be selected, and a systematic sample would be more convincing. The ablation study comparing soft and hard attention is valuable, yet it would be strengthened by an analysis of computational cost, since hard attention is often motivated by efficiency. The discussion section acknowledges some limitations but does not address the risk that unsupervised sense induction may produce senses that do not correspond to linguistically meaningful distinctions. The paper would benefit from a comparison against more recent multi-sense methods, as the current baselines are somewhat dated relative to the field's progress. Reproducibility is a concern, since the code and trained embeddings are not clearly made available, and the authors should release both or justify their absence. The writing is generally clear but contains repeated phrasing in the methods section and several minor grammatical errors that a careful proofreading would resolve. Figures are informative, though the axis labels in the learning curve plot are too small to read comfortably. The authors should also clarify how the number of senses affects performance, as a sensitivity analysis would reveal whether the method is stable across reasonable settings. The statistical reporting of hyperparameter search should be made transparent, including the search space and the criterion used for selection. The claims in the abstract slightly overstate the generality of the results, given that experiments were conducted on a limited set of languages and corpora. Extending the evaluation to multilingual settings would substantially strengthen the claim that the approach is broadly applicable. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful problem with a reasonable approach, but it requires stronger baselines, statistical analysis, and reproducibility measures before its conclusions can be fully trusted. I recommend a major revision.

Police have renewed efforts to locate Ben Needham, the British toddler who disappeared on the Greek island of Kos in July 1991, after a widely watched Greek television appeal brought in new leads. The appeal, broadcast across national networks, asked anyone with information about the case to come forward, and officials said the response has been significant. Investigators have been reviewing tips received in recent days and are following up on those that appear credible. Ben was 21 months old when he vanished from his grandmother's home in the village of Platani, where he had been playing in the yard under the supervision of relatives. His disappearance prompted one of the most extensive missing-person investigations in Greek and British history, and his family has campaigned tirelessly for decades to keep the case in the public eye. Greek authorities confirmed that the new information is being assessed carefully, though they have not yet said whether any lead has resulted in a confirmed sighting or a location to search. Officers have indicated that they are working closely with their counterparts in the United Kingdom as part of the ongoing inquiry. Ben's family has welcomed the renewed attention and urged the public to continue sharing any information, however small it may seem. Over the years, several searches and excavations have been carried out on Kos and in other locations based on tips, but none has yet led to Ben being found. Police stressed that the appeal remains open and that anyone with relevant knowledge can contact them directly, with the option of doing so confidentially. Investigators are encouraging witnesses who may have been children or teenagers at the time to recall anything they remember from that summer. Officials said updates will be provided as the review of the new leads progresses. For now, the renewed effort reflects a determination among investigators and the family alike to bring answers in a case that has remained unresolved for more than three decades.

Reactions have been mixed after a review concluded that the state colluded in the 1989 murder of Belfast solicitor Pat Finucane, reigniting a long-running debate over whether a full public inquiry should now be held.

Finucane, a human rights lawyer who had represented republican and loyalist clients, was shot dead in front of his wife and children at their home in north Belfast on February 12, 1989. Loyalist paramilitaries claimed responsibility, but families and campaigners have argued for decades that British security forces were involved in planning or enabling the killing.

The findings were published after a review led by a former Canadian judge, Peter Cory, in 2003 had recommended a public inquiry, a recommendation the British government at the time did not accept in full. Successive administrations have since faced pressure to act on the matter.

The Finucane family welcomed the acknowledgment of collusion but said it was not enough on its own. Geraldine Finucane, Pat's widow, has spent more than three decades campaigning for accountability and has repeatedly called for a transparent investigation that examines the full extent of state involvement.

Human rights organisations echoed that position. Several said that acknowledging collusion without a statutory, independent public inquiry would leave important questions unanswered about who knew what, and when.

Some political representatives in Northern Ireland praised the findings as a long-overdue step toward truth. Others warned against reopening the wounds of the Troubles without a clear framework to protect witnesses and ensure fairness.

Unionist voices expressed concern about the wider implications. Some argued that singling out one case risks creating a hierarchy of victims, pointing out that many families bereaved during the conflict have also sought answers and have received little.

Nationalist and republican figures largely called for the government to honour its previous commitments. They argued that the scale of the collusion documented in earlier investigations, including the Stevens inquiries, justifies a full and open examination.

Former police officers and military personnel have, in some cases, raised concerns about the fairness of retrospective scrutiny, noting that decisions made decades ago were taken under very different pressures and rules.

Legal experts have noted that the form any inquiry takes matters greatly. A statutory inquiry would have the power to compel witnesses and documents, while a non-statutory process may struggle to obtain material held by security agencies.

The government has said it is considering the findings carefully and will set out its next steps in due course. Officials have not confirmed whether a full public inquiry will be established.

Previous attempts to address the case have been controversial. In 2001, the British government announced a limited inquiry process, which was later abandoned, and disputes over the scope of disclosure have persisted for years.

Campaigners have pointed to the 2012 Gibson inquiry as an example of the state failing to deliver the accountability that families expected. That inquiry, examining several killings linked to collusion, was itself later closed amid concerns over its effectiveness.

The Finucane family has also emphasized that they want more than a formal apology. They have called for a process that tests the evidence publicly, names those responsible where possible, and addresses the institutional failures that allowed the killing to happen.

Victims' advocates stress that many other families are waiting for similar answers. They argue that any decision on the Finucane case will set a precedent for how the state handles other legacy investigations from the Troubles.

Some commentators have questioned whether the public appetite for further inquiries has diminished. They note the cost, the time involved, and the possibility that a lengthy process could produce limited new information after so many years.

Others counter that the passage of time is precisely why an inquiry is urgent. Witnesses are dying, records may be lost, and memories are fading, they argue, so delay risks ensuring the truth is never fully established.

The debate has also raised questions about the balance between national security and public accountability. Officials have previously cited the need to protect intelligence methods and sources, while critics say those concerns cannot justify blocking scrutiny of serious wrongdoing.

Human rights bodies have repeatedly called on the United Kingdom to comply with its obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights, which requires an effective investigation into deaths involving state agents. Those obligations have been central to the legal arguments in the case.

The issue has drawn attention from international observers as well. Some have pointed out that the case is a test of how a democratic state confronts its past conduct during the conflict.

Within Northern Ireland, the findings have prompted renewed discussion in the Assembly and at Westminster about legacy legislation. Past efforts to introduce broad legacy frameworks have faced sharp criticism from families and parties across the political spectrum.

Several MPs have called for a debate in Parliament, arguing that the matter should not be left solely to executive decision. They have asked for a clear timetable and a commitment to transparency.

Local community groups in north Belfast, where the Finucane family lived, have also weighed in. Many residents said the killing was a scar on the area and that local people deserve to understand what happened.

Journalists and researchers who have covered the case over many years note that much of the information has emerged through persistent inquiry rather than official disclosure. They argue that this underlines the need for formal mechanisms that can reach documents and testimony directly.

The Pat Finucane Centre, a human rights organisation named after the solicitor, has urged the government to move quickly and avoid further delay. It has argued that the credibility of the state's commitment to legacy issues depends on how this case is handled.

Asked about the next steps, a government spokesperson said the findings were serious and that ministers would respond formally after reviewing the material. No timetable was given for a decision.

Opposition figures said the government must not use the complexity of the case as a reason to stall. They called for early clarity on whether a public inquiry would be established and on what terms.

Some legal professionals have suggested that a hybrid approach could be considered, combining elements of a public inquiry with structured independent review. Supporters say this could speed up the process while still providing public testimony.

Others have cautioned that any model must be designed carefully to avoid creating new grievances. They argue that inquiries which lose the confidence of families risk damaging the very trust they are meant to restore.

The Finucane family has said it will continue to press its case through every available avenue, including legal and political channels. Their lawyers have indicated that they are reviewing the findings closely.

Public opinion in Northern Ireland remains divided on how to deal with the legacy of the Troubles. Surveys have often shown strong support for truth recovery but disagreement about the methods used to achieve it.

For many people affected by the conflict, the Finucane case has become a symbol of the broader struggle to secure answers. Whatever the government decides, the reaction to these findings is likely to shape the next chapter of that debate.

Observers expect the coming weeks to bring further statements from ministers, families and political parties. The question of whether the state will open a full public inquiry is likely to remain at the centre of the discussion.

Seeking advice is one of the most useful habits a person can develop, but its value depends largely on the attitude we bring to it. When we approach advice with realistic expectations, we understand that a single conversation rarely solves every problem and that the person we consult has their own limits, biases, and experiences. This humility allows us to weigh their suggestions carefully rather than treating them as infallible commands. Gratitude shapes the exchange just as strongly, because a person who takes the time to share their knowledge deserves appreciation regardless of whether the advice ultimately fits our situation. Thanking an advisor also encourages them to remain open and generous in the future, building trust that makes later conversations more honest and productive. Realistic expectations keep us from feeling disappointed when advice proves imperfect, while gratitude keeps us from feeling entitled to it. Together, these two attitudes turn advice into a genuine collaboration in which both people learn and grow. In the end, the wisest approach is to listen closely, expect little more than thoughtful guidance, and respond with sincere thanks.

Overseas volunteer programs are often presented as a generous and life-changing choice for young people. They promise cultural exchange, meaningful service, and a chance to see the world. Yet before committing to one, students should weigh whether the benefits truly outweigh the needs and responsibilities waiting at home. Local communities frequently face urgent problems, such as shortages of tutors, elder care, food assistance, and youth mentorship, that a volunteer can address directly. Helping someone down the street may create deeper and more lasting results than a short placement abroad. Overseas programs also carry significant costs, including travel expenses, program fees, and time away from family, work, and studies. Many students borrow money or delay their education to afford these trips, which can create financial strain long after they return. Family obligations deserve serious consideration as well, since parents, siblings, or grandparents may rely on a student's presence, support, or income. Short-term volunteer stays raise further questions about their true impact. Brief visits can disrupt local routines, and communities may be left without consistent help once volunteers leave. Some critics argue that these trips serve the volunteer's own growth more than the host community's needs. Local volunteering allows students to build relationships that continue over years, creating accountability and trust. It also gives them a chance to understand the root causes of problems in their own society, which may be more complex than they first appear. None of this means overseas service is wrong, but it does mean the decision deserves honest reflection. Students should ask whether their skills match the specific needs of the host community and whether a qualified local organization could do the work instead. They should also consider whether a commitment at home would produce greater good for the people closest to them. Choosing carefully is itself a form of responsibility. A thoughtful volunteer recognizes that generosity begins with understanding where one is most needed. Sometimes the most meaningful place to serve is the place where one already belongs.

The ancient Maya built one of the most sophisticated water-management systems in the pre-Columbian Americas. Living across the lowlands of present-day Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, and Honduras, they faced a striking paradox: the region has abundant rainfall overall, yet much of it falls in a concentrated wet season, and the limestone bedrock beneath the land drains water away quickly. To survive and thrive, Maya communities developed ingenious ways to capture, store, and distribute water across the seasons.

The Maya landscape is dominated by karst geology, a terrain of porous limestone that channels rainwater underground. Surface rivers are scarce in many areas, and the few that exist often flow through deep canyons, far below the level of farmland and settlements. Because of this, the Maya could not rely on rivers alone and had to build their own water supplies.

One of the most important features was the reservoir, often called a reservoir or aguada, a large depression or excavated basin used to collect runoff during the rains. Some were lined or sealed with clay or plaster to reduce seepage into the porous ground. Many of these reservoirs were located near the centers of cities and served as community water sources.

Cities such as Tikal, Calakmul, and Caracol relied heavily on such reservoirs. Archaeologists have documented how these basins were integrated into urban layouts, sometimes surrounded by plazas and monumental architecture. Water was not simply a practical resource but also held deep ceremonial and political meaning.

Rooftop collection was another widely used method. Plastered courtyards, rooftops, and plazas were designed to direct rainwater into channels, cisterns, and storage containers. This decentralized approach allowed households to meet daily needs without depending entirely on a central reservoir.

Cisterns, known in some places as chultunes, were underground chambers carved into bedrock or constructed from stone and plaster. Many had narrow mouths that reduced evaporation and kept contamination out. Some chultunes were relatively small, while others held enough water to sustain families through the dry season.

Researchers have estimated that a single well-built cistern could hold thousands of liters, making it a meaningful reserve during months of drought. The careful shaping and sealing of these structures reflects a detailed understanding of how water behaves in limestone terrain.

Terracing was used to manage the flow of water across sloping land. By building stepped platforms with retaining walls, the Maya slowed runoff, reduced soil erosion, and allowed water to soak into the ground for crops. Terraces also created level planting surfaces that retained moisture.

Raised fields, sometimes called wetland or bajo cultivation systems, were built in seasonally flooded areas. Farmers raised beds above the water table and dug drainage canals between them. This allowed crops to grow during wet periods while the channels carried excess water away, and the canals could be used for fish and other aquatic resources.

Canal systems connected fields, reservoirs, and settlements. Some canals moved water over considerable distances and helped regulate flooding. Together with raised beds, they formed an integrated network that balanced the needs of agriculture and settlement.

Maintenance was essential. Many of these systems required constant labor to clear sediment, repair plaster, and reinforce walls. Their long survival suggests that communities organized this work collectively and treated it as a shared responsibility.

Some scholars argue that the Maya managed water through social institutions as much as through engineering. Coordinating labor, allocating access, and sustaining ceremonies around water all helped keep systems functioning over generations.

The decline of some Maya cities during the Terminal Classic period, roughly 800 to 950 CE, has been linked by many researchers to severe droughts. Paleoclimate records from lake sediments and cave deposits suggest prolonged dry periods that strained water supplies. The reliance on rainwater storage made some communities especially vulnerable when rains failed for extended periods.

It is important to be cautious, however, when drawing conclusions. Drought was one factor among many, and scholars continue to debate the relative roles of climate, warfare, political instability, deforestation, and disease. The Maya did not simply collapse because of water mismanagement, and many Maya populations continued to live in the region after the classic cities were abandoned.

Still, the Maya experience offers valuable lessons for modern water planning. Their systems show how decentralized storage can reduce dependence on a single source. Rooftop harvesting, household cisterns, and small reservoirs are approaches that many communities today are reconsidering.

The Maya also demonstrate the value of designing with local geology. Instead of fighting the limestone landscape, they worked with its features, using natural depressions and bedrock to their advantage. Modern engineers increasingly recognize that such nature-based approaches can be cost-effective and resilient.

Raised fields and terraces offer lessons for agriculture in flood-prone and drought-prone areas. By managing both excess and shortage, these techniques helped stabilize food production. Modern farmers facing climate variability may find inspiration in such integrated designs.

Contemporary researchers and planners have begun studying these systems in detail. Archaeological surveys, soil analysis, and hydrological modeling help reveal how the systems operated and how effective they were. This research can inform restoration of older systems as well as new designs.

Some communities in the Maya region have revived traditional approaches. Projects that rehabilitate reservoirs, promote rainwater harvesting, and restore raised-field agriculture have been reported in parts of Mexico and Central America. Such efforts often combine local knowledge with modern technical support.

Adapting ancient techniques to modern settings requires care. Conditions have changed, populations are larger, and new materials are available. Simply copying an ancient design may not work, but understanding its principles can guide better solutions.

Water quality is one consideration. Stored rainwater can become contaminated, so modern systems often include filtration, covers, or treatment. Ancient designs that kept water out of light and reduced access by animals and insects offer useful principles for protecting supplies.

Governance is another. The social organization that maintained Maya water systems suggests that community participation matters. Modern water projects tend to succeed when local people are involved in planning, maintenance, and decision-making.

Climate change adds urgency. Many regions face more intense rainfall followed by longer dry spells. Systems that capture and store water during wet periods can help buffer these swings, and the Maya approach of combining storage, infiltration, and drainage is well suited to such variability.

Urban planners can also learn from Maya design. Incorporating retention basins, permeable surfaces, and green infrastructure into cities can reduce flooding and recharge groundwater. These ideas echo the aims of ancient reservoirs and canals.

Agricultural planners may apply terracing and raised beds to modern erosion control and water conservation. In some places, such methods could reduce irrigation demand while improving soil health over time.

Education and public awareness are important parts of any strategy. Teaching people about the history of water management can build appreciation for conservation and encourage participation in local projects. Museums, schools, and community organizations all have roles to play.

Research gaps remain. Scientists still have much to learn about the precise performance of many ancient systems, their long-term environmental effects, and how they were maintained under stress. Continued interdisciplinary work will help clarify these questions.

Ethical considerations also matter. Indigenous and local communities in the Maya region hold knowledge and cultural ties to these sites and techniques. Collaboration that respects their rights and perspectives is essential for responsible research and application.

In the end, the Maya water systems remind us that sustainable water management is not a new idea but an ongoing practice. Their achievements show what careful observation, collective effort, and adaptation to local conditions can accomplish. Learning from them does not mean romanticizing the past, but recognizing practical wisdom that still speaks to today's challenges of water scarcity.

Remote learning has become an important part of modern education, and when it is designed well, it can help students succeed both academically and personally. One of its greatest strengths is flexibility. Students can often learn at a pace that suits them, revisiting difficult lessons as many times as needed and moving quickly through material they already understand. This personalized approach allows learners to build a solid foundation before tackling more advanced concepts. Remote learning also gives students access to a wider range of courses and teachers than many local schools can offer. A student in a small rural town, for example, may be able to take advanced science or a foreign language class that would otherwise be unavailable. Beyond academics, remote learning encourages the development of independence and responsibility. Students must plan their own schedules, manage deadlines, and stay motivated without constant supervision, skills that will serve them well in college and in the workplace. Digital tools also strengthen technological literacy, as students become comfortable with online research, collaboration platforms, and digital communication. Many remote courses rely on written discussion boards and online group projects, which can help students express their ideas clearly and listen thoughtfully to others. For students who feel anxious speaking up in a crowded classroom, these written forums can offer a more comfortable space to participate. Remote learning can also accommodate students with health conditions, family responsibilities, or part-time jobs, allowing them to continue their education without sacrificing other important commitments. Such flexibility can reduce stress and help students stay engaged with school over the long term. Of course, remote learning is not effortless, and its success depends on strong self-discipline, reliable internet access, and supportive teachers. Schools that provide regular check-ins, clear expectations, and opportunities for social connection can help students avoid isolation. When these conditions are met, remote learning offers more than convenience; it offers a path toward academic achievement, personal growth, and lifelong confidence in learning.
