The paper addresses an important and timely problem: understanding which internal units of a generative adversarial network are causally responsible for specific visual content, and using that understanding to improve output quality. The authors' use of semantic segmentation as a lens for mapping feature units to human-interpretable concepts is a sensible and practical choice that grounds the analysis in measurable quantities. The causal framing, which involves ablating or intervening on feature units and observing the resulting changes in segmented regions, is a stronger approach than purely correlational visualization and deserves credit. However, the manuscript would benefit from a clearer definition of what constitutes a causal effect in this setting, since intervening on a unit can produce changes that are difficult to attribute cleanly to a single concept. The experimental section would be strengthened by evaluations across multiple GAN architectures and datasets, as results on a single model risk overstating generality. The authors should also report variance across random seeds and provide confidence intervals for their key measurements, which is currently missing. Comparisons against established interpretability baselines, such as GAN Dissection and network dissection methods, are necessary to demonstrate that the proposed causal procedure offers a real advance. The improvement method is promising, but the paper does not sufficiently explain how selected units are modified or why those modifications generalize beyond the tested cases. Quantitative improvement claims should be accompanied by standard image quality metrics such as FID and by a human evaluation to confirm perceptual gains. The discussion of limitations is brief and should expand on failure cases, computational cost, and sensitivity to the quality of the segmentation model. Figures are generally informative, but several lack sufficient captions to be interpreted without reading the main text. The related work section overlooks some recent literature on causal inference in deep networks, which would help position the contribution more precisely. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code, trained model checkpoints, and the exact hyperparameters used for ablation. Overall, the paper presents a useful direction with solid motivation, but it requires more rigorous validation and clearer methodological detail before its conclusions can be fully trusted. I recommend a major revision.

Remote schooling options have become an important part of modern education, offering students flexibility, access, and new ways to learn. While some people worry that online learning cannot match the classroom experience, remote options bring real advantages that benefit a wide range of learners. Their value lies in the way they expand opportunities, respect individual needs, and prepare students for a changing world.

One of the most significant advantages of remote schooling is flexibility. Students can often set their own schedules, allowing them to balance academics with jobs, family responsibilities, athletic training, or artistic pursuits. A student who works part-time to support a household, for example, may find that online courses make it possible to keep up with coursework without sacrificing income. This flexibility can make the difference between finishing a degree and dropping out.

Remote learning also removes geographic barriers. A student living in a rural town far from a university or specialized high school can still access advanced courses, rare languages, or career-focused programs. Families who move frequently, such as military households, can keep their children enrolled in a consistent curriculum regardless of where they are stationed. In this way, remote options help ensure that a student's education is not limited by the accident of where they happen to live.

Another benefit is the opportunity for personalized pacing. In a traditional classroom, the teacher must move through material at a speed that suits the average student, which can leave some learners bored and others struggling to keep up. Remote courses often allow students to spend extra time on difficult concepts, replay recorded lectures, or move quickly through material they already understand. This individualized approach can build confidence and deepen understanding.

Remote schooling can also serve students who face health challenges. Those with chronic illnesses, compromised immune systems, or conditions that make commuting difficult may find that learning from home allows them to stay engaged with school rather than falling behind. Similarly, students who experience anxiety in crowded or noisy environments may feel more comfortable and focused in a familiar setting. For these learners, remote options can protect both their health and their educational progress.

Beyond accommodating special circumstances, remote learning builds valuable skills that matter in the modern workforce. Students who complete online coursework must manage their time, communicate through digital tools, and take responsibility for their own progress. These habits of self-direction and independence are increasingly expected in many careers, where employees often collaborate remotely and manage their own deadlines. Learning these skills early gives students a practical advantage.

Remote options also encourage digital literacy. Students become comfortable with video conferencing, online research databases, collaborative documents, and learning management systems. These tools are now common across industries, and familiarity with them can ease the transition into college and employment. Far from being a poor substitute for education, online learning can teach students how to use technology thoughtfully and productively.

Cost can be another consideration. Remote courses may reduce expenses related to transportation, housing, and campus fees, making education more affordable for some families. Students who would otherwise need to relocate for a particular program may be able to stay at home and save money. Although not every online option is inexpensive, many provide a lower-cost pathway to valuable credentials.

Remote schooling further expands access to a diverse range of voices and perspectives. Online classrooms can connect students from different cities, states, and even countries, exposing them to viewpoints they might never encounter in their own communities. Discussion forums and virtual group projects can create meaningful exchanges that broaden understanding and cultivate empathy. This global connection enriches the learning experience for everyone involved.

Teachers and institutions also benefit from remote options. Schools can reach larger audiences, offer specialized courses that would be impractical to run in a single building, and experiment with new teaching methods. Recorded lessons can be reviewed again and again, and digital resources can be updated quickly as knowledge advances. These innovations can improve the quality of instruction for students in both online and in-person settings.

It is important to acknowledge that remote learning is not perfect and does not suit every student. Some learners thrive on the structure and social energy of a physical classroom, and others need hands-on laboratory or athletic experiences that are difficult to replicate online. Success in remote education also depends on reliable internet access, a quiet place to study, and strong self-motivation. Schools should therefore support remote students with clear expectations, regular check-ins, and access to technology.

Even with these challenges, the advantages of remote schooling are substantial. It offers flexibility, breaks down geographic and personal barriers, supports individualized pacing, and helps students who face health or circumstantial difficulties. It develops independence and digital skills while often reducing costs and broadening access to diverse perspectives. When thoughtfully designed and properly supported, remote options give students more choices and more ways to succeed.

Ultimately, the goal of education is to help every learner reach their potential, and remote schooling is one of the most promising tools for doing so. Rather than replacing traditional classrooms, it can work alongside them, giving students the freedom to choose the path that best fits their lives. By embracing these options, schools can meet students where they are and open doors that might otherwise remain closed. The advantages are clear, and they deserve to be recognized and expanded.

The manuscript proposes a voxel-based variational autoencoder for reconstructing and generating three-dimensional crystal structures together with their atomic compositions. The central idea is to represent a crystal as a discretized three-dimensional grid in which each voxel encodes local atomic occupancy and chemical identity, allowing standard convolutional architectures to be applied to a domain where atoms otherwise appear as irregular point sets. The authors frame this as a generative tool for materials discovery, and the topic is timely given growing interest in inverse design and machine-learning-driven exploration of crystal chemistry. The motivation is clearly stated in the introduction, and the review of prior work on graph-based and point-cloud generative models for materials is reasonably thorough, though it would benefit from a more direct comparison with recent diffusion-based crystal generators.

The method section describes the voxelization procedure, the encoder and decoder architectures, and the loss function, which combines a reconstruction term with a Kullback-Leibler regularizer on the latent distribution. The description of the voxel encoding is mostly easy to follow, but the manuscript does not fully specify how the grid resolution was chosen relative to the typical interatomic distances of the training materials. This matters because coarse voxels can blur neighboring atoms while fine voxels greatly increase memory and training cost. A short ablation or sensitivity analysis on resolution would substantially strengthen the methodological claims.

A related concern is the handling of periodic boundary conditions. Crystals are periodic, yet the description suggests that the voxel grid is treated as a finite cell, and it is unclear whether atoms near cell faces are wrapped or padded. Failure to respect periodicity can introduce artifacts that a reconstruction metric may not detect, so the authors should clarify this point and ideally show that generated structures remain physically sensible when tiled.

The treatment of atomic composition is a strength of the work, since it attempts to encode species within the same representation as geometry rather than treating them as a separate prediction task. However, the manuscript should explain how the one-hot or embedded chemical channels are handled during decoding, in particular how the model resolves cases where several species compete for the same voxel. The current text leaves this step underspecified, which makes the reproducibility of the reported compositional results uncertain.

The experimental setup uses a dataset drawn from a public materials database, with a train-validation-test split described in the appendix. The choice of database is appropriate, and the preprocessing steps for removing duplicate and unstable entries are reasonable. Nevertheless, the main text should report the dataset size, the distribution of unit cell sizes, and the range of chemical elements represented, since these factors strongly influence the difficulty of the reconstruction task and the generalizability of the conclusions.

The evaluation relies primarily on voxel-wise reconstruction accuracy and on a composition match score. These are sensible first-order metrics, but they do not directly measure physical validity. The authors should consider reporting metrics such as the fraction of generated structures that are charge-neutral or that pass a basic interatomic distance check, as well as energy estimates from a surrogate or density functional theory on a subset of samples. Without such measures, it is difficult to judge whether the generated crystals are chemically plausible or merely visually similar to the training data.

The novelty and novelty-related claims deserve careful framing. Voxel representations of molecules and materials have been explored before, and the manuscript should more explicitly delineate what is new, whether that is the particular encoding of composition, the variational formulation, or the generative sampling strategy. A clearer statement of contribution would help readers situate the work relative to existing literature.

The results figures show representative reconstructions alongside ground-truth structures, which is helpful. However, the figures would be more informative if they included error maps highlighting where the reconstruction fails, as well as examples of failure cases rather than only successful ones. Balanced reporting of failures is important for judging the reliability of the method.

The latent space analysis is intriguing, with interpolation experiments suggesting smooth transitions between structures. The authors interpret these as evidence of a meaningful latent organization, but the claim should be tempered unless the interpolated intermediates are checked for physical validity. Interpolations between two stable crystals may pass through configurations with unphysical bond lengths, so a quantitative check is needed before drawing strong conclusions.

The paper compares the proposed model against a baseline variational autoencoder operating on flattened descriptors. The improvement reported over this baseline is noticeable, yet the baseline appears relatively weak, and the comparison would be more convincing against a stronger contemporary generative model such as a graph-based VAE or a crystal diffusion model. Including such a comparison would clarify whether the advantage is due to the voxel representation itself or simply to the architectural choices.

Statistical reporting is limited. The results are presented as single-run numbers in most tables, and the manuscript does not report variance across random seeds or confidence intervals. Given the stochastic nature of variational training, multiple runs with reported standard deviations are needed to establish that the observed differences are robust.

The hyperparameter selection process is described only briefly. The authors state that the latent dimensionality and the weight on the KL term were tuned on the validation set, but they do not report the search space or the sensitivity of results to these choices. Providing this information, possibly in a supplementary table, would aid reproducibility.

Computational cost is mentioned but not quantified in detail. Training time, GPU memory requirements, and inference speed per generated structure would help practitioners evaluate whether the approach is feasible at scale, particularly since voxel grids grow cubically with resolution and can become expensive for large unit cells.

The discussion section makes several broader claims about the potential of the approach for accelerating materials discovery. While the aspiration is reasonable, these claims go beyond what the experiments establish, since no new materials are experimentally synthesized or validated computationally in the study. The authors should either soften these statements or add a validation step that supports them.

The limitations section acknowledges that the method is restricted to structures that fit within a fixed-size cell and that very large or disordered systems are not addressed. This candor is appreciated. I would encourage the authors to expand on additional limitations, including the restriction to a limited set of elements in the current training data and the potential for the model to memorize training structures rather than generalize.

The writing is generally clear, with a logical flow from motivation to method to results. Some sentences in the methods section are long and contain nested clauses that could be simplified. A thorough proofreading pass would also catch a number of minor inconsistencies in notation, particularly in the use of symbols for the latent variable and the reconstruction loss across sections.

The figures are of acceptable quality, though several axis labels are small and the color scales in the error maps are not always accompanied by sufficient explanation. Captions should be more self-contained so that readers can interpret each panel without consulting the main text.

The references are appropriate in number and cover the major strands of related work, though a few relevant recent contributions on generative models for crystals appear to be missing. The authors should check the citation list for completeness and for consistent formatting.

The code and data availability statement indicates that the implementation will be released upon publication. This is commendable, and I would strongly encourage the authors to release trained model weights and the exact preprocessing scripts alongside the code so that the results can be independently reproduced.

The ethical considerations are minimal, which is appropriate for a materials modeling study. However, the authors should briefly acknowledge the dual-use potential of generative models for materials, namely that the same tools could in principle be used to propose hazardous compounds, and state what safeguards, if any, they consider appropriate.

Overall, the manuscript addresses an interesting and relevant problem with a reasonable and original-seeming representational choice. The core idea is promising, and the paper would be a useful contribution to the field. However, several issues must be addressed before the conclusions can be considered fully supported: the handling of periodicity and composition decoding needs clarification, the evaluation should include physically grounded metrics and stronger baselines, statistical reporting must be improved, and the claims in the discussion should be moderated to match the evidence.

My recommendation is major revision. The work has clear potential, and with the additional analyses and clarifications outlined above, it could become a solid and reproducible contribution. I would be glad to review a revised version addressing these points.

This paper attempts to reproduce R2D2, a differentiable closed-form meta-learning method for few-shot classification, and to provide an open-source TensorFlow implementation of it. The authors address a worthwhile problem, since reproducibility has been a persistent concern in the meta-learning literature, and an independent implementation can meaningfully increase confidence in the original claims. The manuscript is clearly organized, and the description of the closed-form ridge regression solver and the Woodbury-based formulation is accessible to readers familiar with few-shot learning. The implementation details, including the choice of backbone, data augmentation, and training schedule, are reported with reasonable thoroughness, which makes the reproduction effort credible. However, the reported accuracies on standard benchmarks fall somewhat short of the original paper's numbers, and the discussion of this gap is brief and does not clearly identify its likely causes. The authors should provide variance across multiple random seeds and confidence intervals so readers can judge whether the differences are statistically meaningful. A more systematic ablation of the sensitivity to the regularization hyperparameter and the number of training episodes would strengthen the claims about robustness. The comparison to the original PyTorch or other reference code, if available, would help isolate whether discrepancies stem from framework differences or from algorithmic choices. The open-source release is a clear strength, and the authors should ensure the repository includes pinned dependency versions, pretrained checkpoints, and scripts that reproduce every table in the paper. Some figures would benefit from clearer axis labels and more informative captions. Overall, the work is a useful and well-executed reproduction effort, and with additional statistical rigor and a more careful analysis of discrepancies, it would make a solid contribution to the reproducibility literature.

The palace of Vhalen Ar rose from the desert like a crown of glass, and its floors were laid with a mosaic that shimmered whenever the sun touched it. Tovan the artisan had set the first tiles of that floor twenty years earlier, when he was young and his hands were steady.

Now his hands were bound, and he was brought before the Vizier in chains.

"The Hall of Dawn is cracked," the Vizier said. "The mosaic has lost its light, and only you know how it was made."

Tovan looked down at the dull stones beneath his feet. He had known they would come for him one day, when the magic in the floor began to fade.

"I cannot repair what I did not understand," he said quietly. "The light came from the sorcerer who guided my hand, not from my tools."

The Vizier's eyes narrowed. "Then you will be guided again. The sorcerer is dead, but his binding remains in the old stones. You will kneel and work, and the binding will do the rest."

They chained him to the floor of the Hall of Dawn, one ankle to a ring of iron set into the marble. The guards stood at the doors with spears, and the Vizier watched from a high seat with his fingers tapping on the arm of his chair.

Tovan began to work. He lifted a broken tile, pressed a new one into the mortar, and felt the cold pull of something ancient reaching up through his fingers. The mosaic warmed beneath him. Colors bloomed across the floor, gold and blue spreading like water across sand.

"Faster," the Vizier called.

Tovan worked faster. The light grew brighter, and the pull grew stronger. He realized, with a sinking heart, that the binding did not merely guide his hands. It was drawing something from him, the way a well draws water from the earth.

He tried to stop. The guards stepped forward, and the Vizier raised one finger. "Keep working."

Tovan returned to the stones. His breath grew thin. His vision blurred at the edges. The mosaic glowed so fiercely now that the walls seemed to pulse with it.

Then he felt the cold reach his left leg. It crept up from his ankle, through the bone and muscle, and settled in his knee like frost on a window. He cried out and tried to pull away, but the iron ring held him fast.

"The binding asks for a price," said a voice in his memory, the sorcerer's voice, gentle and sad. "Every great thing costs something."

The leg went numb, then gray, then something worse. Tovan screamed as the light drank deeper, and the color flooded the last empty space in the floor.

When it was over, he lay gasping on the marble. The Hall of Dawn blazed with light, brighter than it had been in a hundred years. The Vizier rose from his chair, smiling.

Tovan looked down at his leg. It was still there, but it was no longer flesh. It had become a thing of pale stone, veined with gold, the same as the tiles he had set. He could not feel it at all.

"Good," the Vizier said. "The palace is whole again. You may rest now."

The guards unlocked the chains, and two of them lifted him by the arms. He tried to stand and found he could not, for his stone leg would not bend.

"What will become of me?" he asked.

The Vizier turned away toward the glowing floor. "You will stay here," he said. "You are part of the mosaic now, and the palace needs its artisans close."

They carried Tovan to a small chamber off the hall and left him there with a jug of water and a single narrow window. Through it he could see the desert, pale and endless, under a sky he could no longer reach.

He thought of his workshop by the river, of the clay pots he used to glaze, of the sound his tools made against the stone. He thought of his daughter, who had been eight years old the last time he saw her.

That night the palace hummed around him, and the floor beneath his bed sang softly with stolen light.

Tovan lay awake and listened, his stone leg cold against the blanket, and he understood at last what the sorcerer had meant. The binding had not been a guide. It had been a hunger, and it had been waiting for him all along.

In the morning the Vizier came to inspect the Hall of Dawn, and he found the mosaic perfect, flawless, and burning. He did not look at the artisan in the small chamber, for he had already forgotten Tovan's name.

Outside, the sun climbed over the desert and struck the palace glass, and every tile in the floor flared gold in reply.

This manuscript investigates whether abstract syntax tree (AST) path representations, combined with sequence decoding, improve code summarization and natural-language code captioning. The topic is timely and well motivated, since generating concise natural-language descriptions of source code remains a practical challenge for documentation and program comprehension. The authors frame the problem clearly and situate their work within prior encoder-decoder approaches, which makes the contribution easy to follow. The core idea of encoding syntactic paths between AST leaves is sensible, as it offers a structured inductive bias that token-only models may lack. However, the introduction could more precisely state what gap remains unaddressed, since several recent transformer-based systems already exploit structural information in related ways. The related work section is broadly adequate but would benefit from a more systematic comparison of path-based encoders against graph neural networks and pretrained code models. The methodology describes how AST paths are extracted and sampled, yet the description of path length limits, width constraints, and handling of out-of-vocabulary terminals is incomplete. Readers would need these details to reproduce the results. The choice of sequence decoder, whether recurrent or attention-based, is justified in only a sentence, and an ablation comparing decoder variants would strengthen the argument. The datasets are described as standard benchmarks, but the paper should report split sizes, deduplication procedures, and the languages covered, since data leakage is a known concern in this area. The evaluation relies primarily on BLEU and ROUGE, which correlate imperfectly with human judgments of summary quality. Including human evaluation or a learned metric would make the findings more convincing. The results tables show consistent gains over the baselines, but the reported differences are small and no variance across random seeds is given. Statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are needed before claiming superiority. The qualitative examples are helpful for illustrating model behavior, yet they appear to be cherry-picked, and a sample of failure cases would give a more honest picture. The discussion attributes improvements to the syntactic structure of paths, but no experiment isolates this factor directly, so the causal claim is overstated. An ablation that removes path information while keeping model capacity constant would address this concern. The limitations section is brief and should acknowledge the restriction to a small set of programming languages and the sensitivity to parser quality. Ethical considerations are not discussed, though the work could affect documentation practices and should note potential misuse or over-reliance on generated comments. The writing is generally clear, though some sentences in the methods are dense and could be simplified. Figures are legible, but the architecture diagram omits the dimensions of intermediate representations, which would help readers. The reference list is current and includes the major relevant works. Overall, the paper offers a reasonable empirical study with a plausible central idea, but the claims currently outpace the evidence. I recommend a major revision that adds ablations isolating the path representation, reports variance and significance, expands the evaluation beyond n-gram metrics, and provides complete implementation details. With these changes, the work could make a useful contribution to the code summarization literature.

Dutch River-Basin Planning: Making Room for Rivers

The Netherlands lies largely at or below sea level, and much of its territory is shaped by three major rivers: the Rhine, the Meuse, and the Scheldt. Because these rivers carry water from many countries upstream, the Dutch have long depended on careful planning to keep their land safe from flooding. Over the past several decades, that planning has shifted from simply raising and strengthening dikes toward a broader strategy that gives rivers more space. This approach is often called "Ruimte voor de Rivier," meaning Room for the River.

The core idea is that a river needs room to carry high water safely. When floodplains are narrowed by embankments and land development, water rises higher and faster during peak flows. By deliberately lowering the land in certain areas and moving dikes further from the riverbank, planners allow the river to spread out during floods. This reduces the water level at critical points downstream and lowers the risk of dike failure.

Several specific measures make this strategy work. Dike relocation pushes embankments back to create wider floodplains, giving water more room to flow. Excavation of floodplains lowers ground levels so that the river can reach higher ground during high discharge. Side channels, sometimes called nevengeulen, are dug alongside the main river to carry extra water during floods while remaining dry or lightly flooded at normal levels. Weirs and sluices allow managers to control flows and water levels within the system.

Flood safety is only one goal of this planning. The Dutch government and regional water authorities, known as waterschappen, also aim to improve landscape quality. Restored floodplains can create attractive open landscapes, recreational areas, and cultural heritage features that connect residents to their river environment. Many projects include walking and cycling routes, nature viewpoints, and preserved historic villages and farmsteads.

Ecological improvement is a third major objective. Before the modern era, Dutch rivers were dynamic systems with shifting channels, seasonal flooding, and diverse habitats such as wetlands, gravel banks, and riparian forests. Canalization and dike building removed much of this variety. Expanded floodplains allow natural processes to return, supporting plants, birds, fish, and insects that depend on periodically flooded land. Projects along the Rhine and Meuse have reported increased biodiversity in restored areas.

Planning in the Netherlands is organized across multiple levels of government. National authorities, including Rijkswaterstaat, manage the main rivers and set policy frameworks. Provinces and regional water boards handle many local decisions, while municipalities coordinate land use. The Delta Programme, a national initiative begun after severe flooding in 1953 and updated regularly, sets long-term goals for water safety and freshwater supply. This multi-level structure allows projects to balance national safety standards with local interests.

Stakeholder participation is an important part of the process. Farmers, landowners, nature organizations, residents, and businesses all have interests in how river land is used. Planners typically hold consultations, negotiate compensation for affected landowners, and seek designs that serve several purposes at once. This integrated approach, sometimes called multifunctional or dual-use design, aims to avoid conflicts and build broad public support.

Financing these projects requires substantial investment and coordination. Costs are shared among national, regional, and sometimes European sources, and projects are often bundled with other infrastructure work to improve efficiency. Long-term maintenance of floodplains, channels, and structures is also necessary to keep them functioning as intended.

Dutch experience has attracted international interest. Countries facing similar pressures from rising river flows and climate change have studied Room for the River as a model. The Dutch approach demonstrates that water management can be combined with spatial planning, nature conservation, and public amenity. Its lessons are that flood protection works best when rivers are treated as systems and when planners look for solutions that benefit many goals together.

Sources of uncertainty remain. Climate change may bring more intense rainfall and higher peak discharges, and planners must design for conditions that are not fully known. Ongoing monitoring, adaptive management, and periodic review of standards help the Netherlands respond as new information emerges.

Advanced automotive technology is transforming how we travel, and it offers significant benefits for road safety, energy independence, and the environment. One of the most important advances is the development of driver-assistance systems such as automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping assist, and adaptive cruise control. These tools help prevent crashes caused by human error, which is a factor in the vast majority of traffic accidents. Electronic stability control and advanced airbag systems have also reduced injuries and deaths in collisions. Beyond safety, electric and hybrid vehicles are reducing the world's dependence on oil. Because electric motors can run on electricity generated from a variety of sources, drivers are less tied to fluctuating petroleum markets and the geopolitical tensions that often accompany them. Fuel efficiency improvements in conventional engines, such as turbocharging and direct fuel injection, further reduce the amount of gasoline each vehicle consumes. These changes also benefit the environment by lowering tailpipe emissions of carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and particulate matter. Cleaner air improves public health, particularly in dense urban areas where traffic pollution is concentrated. Battery technology continues to improve, which may make electric vehicles more affordable and practical for millions of households. Connected vehicle systems can also optimize routes and traffic flow, reducing congestion and the wasted fuel that idling in traffic creates. Critics note that battery production and electricity generation still carry environmental costs, and these must be addressed through responsible mining and cleaner power grids. Even so, the overall trajectory is promising. Governments, manufacturers, and drivers all have roles to play in encouraging these technologies. If these innovations are adopted widely and thoughtfully, they can make roads safer, reduce our reliance on oil, and help protect the planet for future generations.

Respectful behavior and emotional self-control are two qualities that quietly shape the course of a person's life. Though they may seem like simple habits, they have a powerful effect on the relationships we build and the success we achieve. Respect tells others that their thoughts, feelings, and time matter, and this message encourages trust and cooperation. When people feel valued, they are more willing to listen, share ideas, and support one another. Emotional self-control works alongside respect by helping us respond thoughtfully instead of reacting impulsively. A person who can pause before speaking in anger is far less likely to say something hurtful that cannot be taken back. Over time, this restraint helps prevent small disagreements from growing into lasting conflicts. Consider a workplace where colleagues treat each other with courtesy and manage their frustrations calmly. Such an environment tends to be more productive because people can focus on solving problems rather than defending themselves. Teachers, employers, and leaders often notice these qualities and trust individuals who display them consistently. Strong relationships built on respect also open doors to mentorship, collaboration, and new opportunities. Friends and family members who feel safe with us are more likely to stand by us during difficult times. Emotional self-control is also essential for personal growth, since it allows us to learn from criticism instead of becoming defensive. When mistakes happen, people who respond with composure can take responsibility, make amends, and move forward. This capacity for recovery is often what separates those who progress steadily from those who remain stuck. Self-control does not mean suppressing emotions entirely, but rather recognizing them and choosing constructive ways to express them. Respect, in turn, requires us to listen carefully, consider other perspectives, and acknowledge differences without belittling anyone. Together, these habits create a foundation of credibility that people rely on in every area of life. Those who practice them often find that others are more willing to cooperate and to offer second chances. Such goodwill can be more valuable than talent alone, because it multiplies the effects of every skill a person possesses. Ultimately, respectful behavior and emotional self-control are not limitations but strengths. They allow us to build relationships that endure and to pursue goals with greater clarity and resilience. Young people who cultivate these qualities early are investing in a future where both their connections and their accomplishments can flourish.

Persistence, practice, and learning from mistakes are three qualities that together help people reach their goals. Although each one matters on its own, their greatest power comes from working together over a long period of time. Many people imagine that success comes from talent alone, but a closer look at most accomplished people reveals years of steady effort behind their achievements.

Persistence is the willingness to keep going when progress is slow or when obstacles appear. Goals rarely come within reach on the first try, and people who give up at the first sign of difficulty seldom see the results they want. A person who keeps working through setbacks gives themselves many more chances to succeed than someone who stops early.

Practice turns intention into skill. Repetition builds the habits, knowledge, and confidence needed to perform well when it counts. A musician who practices scales every day, or a student who works through problems each week, gradually develops abilities that once seemed out of reach. Consistent practice also makes difficult tasks feel more familiar, which reduces fear and frees the mind to focus on improvement.

Learning from mistakes is what makes practice truly effective. Errors reveal exactly where understanding is weak or where a method is failing, which gives a person precise information about what to change. Those who treat mistakes as lessons rather than failures can adjust their approach and avoid repeating the same problems. In this way, every error becomes a step toward a better result.

These three qualities reinforce one another in a cycle. Persistence keeps a person practicing even when results are discouraging, and practice creates opportunities to make mistakes. Mistakes, in turn, provide the feedback that makes practice more useful, which encourages the person to keep going. Over time, this cycle produces steady growth that can lead to remarkable outcomes.

Consider the example of a student preparing for a difficult exam. At first, she may score poorly on practice tests and feel tempted to quit. If she persists, reviews her wrong answers carefully, and practices regularly, she will gradually identify her weak areas and strengthen them. By the time the exam arrives, her earlier mistakes will have become the foundation of her success.

Similar patterns appear in fields far beyond the classroom. Athletes refine their technique through countless repetitions and by studying their errors on video. Writers revise their drafts many times, learning from each round of feedback. Entrepreneurs test ideas, notice what fails, and adjust their strategies. In every case, the path to success runs through ongoing effort and honest reflection.

Of course, persistence without reflection can become stubbornness, repeating the same mistakes indefinitely. Likewise, practice without attention to errors may simply reinforce bad habits. The most effective learners combine determination with a willingness to change direction when the evidence suggests it. They ask themselves what is working, what is not, and what they can do differently.

Developing these qualities takes time, and it often requires patience with oneself. A person should expect setbacks and view them as a normal part of growth rather than a sign of inadequacy. Small, regular efforts tend to be more sustainable than occasional bursts of intense work. Over months and years, these small efforts add up to significant change.

Ultimately, persistence, practice, and learning from mistakes offer a practical framework for achieving almost any goal. They do not guarantee success in every case, since circumstances and luck also play a role. Yet they give people the best chance of turning their aspirations into reality. By committing to keep going, practicing with purpose, and learning from every error, anyone can move steadily toward the goals they hope to achieve.

The UK government's proposal to merge income tax and National Insurance contributions has sparked debate among economists, employers, and workers, with critics warning of significant administrative and fairness challenges. Under the plan, the two separate charges on earnings would be combined into a single system, a change that supporters say would simplify the tax code and reduce confusion for millions of taxpayers.

Currently, income tax and National Insurance are levied separately, with different thresholds, rates, and rules. National Insurance is paid on earnings and is linked to entitlements such as the State Pension and certain benefits, while income tax applies to a broader range of income sources. Merging them would require careful redesign to address these differences.

Supporters argue that a unified system would make it easier for people to understand what they pay and why. They also say it could close gaps that allow some high earners and certain income types to face lower overall charges than workers with similar incomes.

However, the plan raises a number of concerns. One of the most prominent is the question of how entitlement to state benefits and pensions would be protected if National Insurance were absorbed into income tax. Campaigners fear that the link between contributions and entitlements could be weakened or lost.

Employers have also raised worries about administrative costs. Payroll software, accounting systems, and HR processes would all need to be updated, and small businesses in particular may struggle with the transition. Some payroll professionals have warned that poorly managed change could lead to errors and delays in wages.

Employer contributions present another complication. National Insurance is paid by both employees and employers, and the employer share is a significant cost for businesses. Any merger would need to determine how employer obligations would be structured, and whether firms would face higher or lower bills overall.

The treatment of self-employed workers is also under scrutiny. Self-employed people pay National Insurance through a different mechanism, and integrating them into a combined system could affect millions of freelancers, contractors, and sole traders.

Economists point to the potential for winners and losers. Depending on how rates and thresholds are set, some households could pay more while others pay less. Analysts say the distributional impact will depend heavily on design choices that have yet to be fully explained.

Transition arrangements are another area of concern. Any reform of this scale would likely take years to implement, and during that period taxpayers and businesses would need clear guidance. Critics argue that the government must publish detailed plans and costings before any legislation is passed.

Trade unions have called for safeguards to ensure that workers are not left worse off, particularly those on lower incomes. They have also urged ministers to consult widely with employers, accountants, and pension experts before making decisions.

The Treasury has said that any changes would be designed to be fair and to protect public services. Officials have indicated that consultation will take place, though no final decisions have yet been announced.

Tax experts also note that a merged system would need to address the different treatment of savings, dividends, and pension income. Without careful alignment, the reform could create new distortions in how people choose to earn and save.

Political reaction has been mixed. Some opposition figures have welcomed the goal of simplification but questioned whether the government has the capacity to deliver such a complex reform. Others have raised concerns about the timing, given wider pressures on household budgets.

Campaign groups focused on pensioners and disabled people have asked for assurances that existing benefits will not be cut or made harder to claim. They say that clarity on these issues is essential before public trust can be built.

Looking ahead, the success of any merger will depend on the detail of the proposals and the quality of implementation. Policy analysts recommend phased introduction, extensive testing of IT systems, and a public information campaign to help people adjust.

For now, the proposal remains at an early stage. Stakeholders across the economy are watching closely, aware that changes to how the country raises its largest sources of revenue carry far-reaching consequences. Whether the reform delivers simplicity without sacrificing fairness will be the central test as details emerge in the months ahead.

The manuscript proposes residual energy-based language models trained with noise-contrastive estimation, aiming to improve perplexity and text generation quality over standard autoregressive baselines. The central idea is sound and well motivated, since energy-based residual formulations offer a principled way to reweight a pretrained base distribution without retraining it from scratch. The authors position their contribution clearly within the literature on energy-based modeling and noise-contrastive estimation, and the introduction gives a fair account of why sequence-level scoring might complement local next-token prediction. The paper is generally readable and the problem statement is precise, which I appreciated as a reviewer. However, several aspects of the method require more careful justification before the claims can be fully accepted. The choice of noise distribution is central to noise-contrastive estimation, and the manuscript treats it somewhat briefly, so I would like to see a more systematic analysis of how the noise model affects convergence and the quality of the learned energy. The derivation of the training objective is mostly correct, but the step relating the partition function estimate to the final loss is compressed and could be expanded for readers less familiar with the technique. The experimental section reports perplexity improvements on standard benchmarks, which is encouraging, yet the magnitude of the gains is modest and the variance across random seeds is not reported. Without error bars or multiple runs, it is difficult to judge whether the improvements are statistically meaningful. The baselines are a reasonable selection, but the authors should also compare against a stronger base model of comparable size to rule out the possibility that the gains stem from additional parameters or training compute. The generation experiments rely heavily on automatic metrics, and the paper would be considerably stronger with human evaluation on fluency, coherence, and factuality. The qualitative examples included in the appendix are informative, but they appear to be hand-picked, and I recommend including randomly sampled outputs to give a more honest picture. Some of the claims about text quality in the abstract go beyond what the experiments demonstrate, and I would encourage the authors to temper this language. The ablation study is a welcome addition, though it examines only one hyperparameter in isolation. Interactions between the noise distribution, the number of negative samples, and the temperature parameter could meaningfully change the conclusions, and a more complete grid would help. The discussion of computational cost is underdeveloped. Energy-based models typically require additional sampling or normalization steps at inference time, and the paper should quantify the resulting latency and memory overhead relative to the baselines. Practitioners will need this information to assess whether the approach is worth adopting. The related work section covers the main threads of research competently but omits some recent efforts on hybrid autoregressive and energy-based decoding, which are directly relevant to the proposed method. Adding these comparisons would clarify what is genuinely new. The notation is mostly consistent, although the symbol used for the base distribution changes between the methods and experiments sections, which caused some confusion during reading. A unified notation table would resolve this. Figures are clear, but the axis labels in the perplexity plots are small and the legend obscures part of the data for one configuration. The reproducibility statement mentions that code will be released, which is commendable, but the paper should also specify the exact training data splits, tokenization, and preprocessing steps so that results can be replicated independently. Hyperparameters are listed for the main model but not for several baselines, and this asymmetry should be corrected. The limitations section is brief and mostly lists future work rather than acknowledging weaknesses of the current approach. A more candid discussion of failure modes, such as degenerate outputs under certain sampling settings or sensitivity to the quality of the base model, would strengthen the paper's credibility. The ethical considerations are addressed in a single sentence, and given that improved generation quality can amplify misuse risks, a fuller treatment would be appropriate. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful question with a reasonable technical approach and shows promising initial results. I recommend a major revision. The core contribution is worth publishing once the statistical reporting, baseline fairness, human evaluation, computational cost analysis, and claims are brought in line with the evidence. With these revisions, the work would make a useful contribution to the study of energy-based language modeling.

The workshop had been silent for eleven weeks. Elias Varn kept the lights off most days now, preferring the gray light that leaked through the single high window. His blueprints were still pinned to the walls, curling at the corners, the lattice of his turbine design faded from months of sun.

Before the accident, he had been the kind of man who woke before dawn with equations already unspooling in his head. He had shown the city council a model of a wind-and-tide hybrid grid that could power three districts without a single coal plant. They had called him visionary in the newspapers. His daughter had called him Papa Ingenieur, and she had drawn him with wings.

The fire at the coastal plant had taken his right hand and most of the hearing in his left ear. The doctors had been kind and precise about what he would never do again. Fine assembly was impossible. Soldering was impossible. The surgeons spoke of adaptation, of assistive devices, of a life redirected rather than ended.

Elias had nodded through every conversation, feeling like a stranger to his own body. The man who had built things was gone, and the man who remained could not even hold a pencil steady enough to sketch a bolt.

His wife tried to fill the silence with gentle questions. Did he want to teach? Would he consider consulting from a desk? He answered yes to everything and meant nothing by it. Each offer only reminded him of the distance between the work he had loved and the work that was left to him.

Some nights he sat in the dark and imagined the grid he had dreamed of, humming along the coast, lights coming on in kitchens he would never see. It was a beautiful ache, and it hollowed him out.

He began to think about the old ferry pier at the end of the harbor road. He walked there one evening in late October, the wind cold and sharp, the water black beneath the planks. He stood at the edge for a long time, his one good hand gripping the railing until his knuckles ached.

He thought about his daughter's drawing. He thought about the wings she had given him, and how he had never once believed he could fly.

A gull landed on the railing a few feet away and regarded him with bright, unbothered eyes. Elias almost laughed. The bird had no blueprint, no plan, no grand design, and yet it was perfectly at home in the wind.

His phone buzzed in his coat pocket. It was a message from his daughter's school, a reminder about a science fair she had entered. The project was called "Turbines in the Tide." Her teacher had added a note: she asked whether her father might come to see it, because she wanted him to know she had built it from his old notes.

Elias read the message three times. His throat tightened, and the cold seemed to recede from his face.

He stepped back from the railing. His legs shook, and he sat down heavily on the damp bench beside the pier, pressing his good hand against his mouth. For a long while he simply breathed, the sound of the waves filling the space where his thoughts had been.

He did not feel healed. The pain remained, sharp and immediate, and he knew it would not vanish because of a text message. But something had shifted, a small thread pulled taut in the place where despair had been pulling him under.

He called his wife from the bench. She answered on the first ring, her voice tight with the fear she had been carrying for weeks. He told her where he was, and that he was coming home, and that he needed help. He said it plainly, without ornament, the way he would once have stated the load on a beam.

She began to cry, and he let her. Then he stood, slowly, and began the long walk back along the harbor road.

That night he sat at the kitchen table with his daughter's project notes spread before him. He could not hold a pencil, but he could read, and he could speak. He could tell her what he remembered about tidal flow and how to model the blade pitch, and he could let her hear the excitement in his voice when she got it right.

He was not the engineer he had been. Perhaps he never would be again. But the grid was not the only thing worth building, and the wind, he realized, had always been about more than the turbines it turned.

This manuscript compares invertible generative flows operating on molecular graphs with sequence-based approaches for molecule generation, a timely and relevant question for computational chemistry and drug discovery. The authors motivate the study clearly, noting that graph-based flows offer exact likelihood computation and invertibility, while sequence-based models such as SMILES generators benefit from mature architectures and simpler training pipelines. The experimental design evaluates both families on standard benchmarks, which is a strength, since it allows direct comparison across validity, uniqueness, and novelty metrics. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more detailed description of how the flow's invertibility constraints are enforced for discrete graph structures, as this is a non-trivial technical point that is only briefly addressed. The reported validity rates are encouraging, but the authors should clarify whether post-hoc chemical correction steps were applied, since these can inflate the apparent performance of either approach. The comparison would also be strengthened by including a fair baseline with matched parameter counts and training compute, as differences in model size could otherwise confound the conclusions. The discussion of drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility is somewhat superficial, and I encourage the authors to report these properties with standard scoring functions and distributional comparisons to the training data. Statistical reporting is limited to single runs in most tables, and multiple random seeds with confidence intervals would make the reported differences more trustworthy. The related work section omits several recent graph-based and autoregressive generative models that address similar trade-offs, and situating the contribution relative to these would sharpen its novelty claim. The figures are clear overall, although the latent-space visualizations would benefit from annotation explaining what structure the reader should observe. The code and trained checkpoints are described as available upon request, and public release would substantially improve reproducibility and allow independent verification of the results. Overall, the paper addresses a useful question with a sound general approach, and I recommend a major revision focused on controlled comparisons, statistical rigor, and clearer technical exposition before the work can be considered for publication.

Commander Elena Ruiz stared through the viewport at the star field that had, a moment ago, been a smear of light. The drive had engaged without warning during the test burn, folding space around the ship like a sheet pulled taut, and now the nearest stars sat where no star should be.

For a long time she said nothing. Her crew floated behind her, equally silent, as the ship's instruments scrambled to confirm what their eyes already told them. They were four light-years from home, a distance they had crossed in less than a minute of ship time.

The first message home took nearly five years to arrive, and when the reply came back, it was a single line from the mission director: Are you alive? Elena laughed until she cried, then sent back a full report.

Over the following decades, the discovery unfolded slowly. The drive, which the engineers named the Ruiz Lattice, turned out to depend on a geometry of spacetime that no one had fully mapped. Every test raised new questions, and every answer opened three more doors.

Elena spent her later years in the lab rather than the cockpit. She watched young physicists argue over equations she had only half understood, and she found herself grinning like a child at the chalkboards covered in new notation.

A generation after the first jump, the Lattice could carry cargo to the outer planets in days. Then it could carry crews. Then came the survey probes, dozens of them, each sending back images of worlds that had once been points of light in a telescope.

There were setbacks, of course. A coolant failure destroyed an early research vessel and its crew, and the program paused for two years while the engineers rebuilt their safety protocols from the ground up. Elena attended the memorial and spoke only briefly, saying that the stars would still be there when they were ready.

Her grandson, Mateo, was the first in the family to study the Lattice formally. He was clever and impatient, and he had the family habit of asking the wrong question at the right time. He showed her a model one evening that suggested the drive might work in reverse, and she felt the old awe return.

She was ninety-one when the first crewed vessel reached the Kepler cluster. The live feed showed a blue-green world turning beneath the ship, and the mission commander, a woman who had been born the year Elena first jumped, gasped audibly on the open channel.

Elena watched the broadcast from a chair in her garden, a blanket over her knees. She did not feel the same disbelief she had felt in the cockpit so long ago. Instead she felt something warmer and more restless, the sense that the universe had finally begun to open its doors.

Mateo sat beside her with a tablet full of new calculations. He was already talking about the next theoretical leap, a drive that might not need the Lattice at all, and his excitement was contagious. Elena nodded, though she knew he could not see her smile in the fading light.

The stars were beginning to appear over the rooftops. Elena had seen them from the ship, from the lab, and from this garden, and each time they seemed to be calling her to come closer. She had spent her life answering that call, and she found she was not finished yet.

This manuscript proposes a hybrid architecture that combines neural networks with regression trees, reframing continuous value prediction as a classification problem, and evaluates it on age and height estimation. The motivation is sound, since discretizing a continuous target can make learning more stable and can yield predictive distributions rather than single point estimates. The authors are clear about this framing in the introduction, which helps the reader understand the intended contribution. However, the related work section is thin and largely omits the literature on ordinal regression, distributional regression, and classification-based regression approaches such as label distribution learning, which are directly relevant and should be discussed. The architecture itself is described at a high level, and several implementation details needed for reproduction are missing, including how bin boundaries are chosen, how many leaves the tree contains, and how gradients are propagated through the discrete splitting decisions. The authors should clarify whether the tree is fixed, learned jointly with the network, or constructed in a separate stage. The mathematical formulation would benefit from a more careful derivation, particularly the loss function that combines the classification objective with any regression-based decoding of the output. The choice of cross-entropy over bins versus an expected-value decoding step should be justified, since the two can behave quite differently near bin boundaries. The experimental setup relies on standard age and height datasets, which is appropriate, but the paper does not state clearly whether the train, validation, and test splits respect subject identity, a point that matters a great deal for face-based age estimation where the same person may appear many times. The reported metrics are mean absolute error and root mean squared error, which are reasonable, yet the authors should also report results stratified by age range or height range, since errors at the extremes of the target distribution are often much larger and can be masked by averages. Baselines are limited to a plain regression network and one classification-based variant; stronger and more recent baselines, including ordinal regression methods and modern gradient-boosted tree implementations, should be included to support the claim of improvement. Statistical significance is not assessed, and with the small margins reported in the results table, confidence intervals or repeated runs with different random seeds are needed before the improvements can be considered reliable. The ablation study is a welcome addition, but it removes components one at a time without examining interactions, and it would be more informative to vary the number of bins and the tree depth to show sensitivity. The qualitative examples are helpful for intuition, though they are selected without explanation and may not represent typical behavior. The discussion of limitations is brief and should address dataset bias, since age and height datasets often skew toward particular demographic groups, and the authors should discuss how this could affect fairness and generalization. Ethical considerations deserve more attention given that age estimation from images has real privacy and misuse implications, and the paper should state its intended use cases and any safeguards. The writing is generally clear, though several sentences in the methods section are long and could be simplified for readers less familiar with tree-based models. Figures are legible, but the axis labels in the error distribution plots should include units and the captions should be more self-contained. The code availability statement is vague, and releasing the implementation along with trained weights and split indices would substantially improve the paper's value to the community. Overall, the core idea is interesting and potentially useful, but the paper requires stronger baselines, statistical validation, more complete methodological detail, and a fuller treatment of fairness and ethics before its claims can be fully supported. I recommend a major revision.

Sunlight may be doing more to the body than producing vitamin D, according to a growing body of research into how ultraviolet exposure could influence weight gain and diabetes risk. Scientists have observed that animals kept under controlled UV conditions sometimes show shifts in metabolism, including changes in how they store fat and process blood sugar. Some of these effects appear to run through the skin, where UV light triggers the release of signaling molecules that may travel through the bloodstream. One area of interest is nitric oxide, a compound that UV light can release from skin stores, which affects blood vessel function and may play a role in glucose regulation. Early studies in mice have linked UV exposure to altered insulin sensitivity, though the results vary depending on the wavelength, dose, and duration of exposure. Researchers caution that most of this work has been done in animals, and it is not yet clear how closely these findings apply to people. Human studies have produced mixed results, with some observational data suggesting that people who spend more time outdoors have lower rates of obesity and type 2 diabetes, while others find no clear link once factors like physical activity and diet are accounted for. Confounding variables are a particular challenge, since people who spend more time in the sun may also be more active, have different incomes, or live in regions with different food environments. Dermatologists also stress that UV exposure carries well-established risks, including skin cancer and premature skin aging, so any metabolic benefit would need to be weighed against those dangers. Experts say there is currently no evidence that sunbathing or tanning beds should be used to manage weight or blood sugar. Some scientists are exploring whether the effects could be harnessed through safer means, such as targeted compounds that mimic the beneficial signaling without UV damage. Others are investigating whether seasonal patterns in metabolism, which vary with the amount of sunlight across the year, might partly explain why diabetes diagnoses and weight trends fluctuate in some populations. Large, long-term human trials are needed to determine whether these associations reflect cause and effect. Until such research is complete, public health guidance on sun exposure is unlikely to change. The possible connection remains an intriguing but unresolved question, and researchers emphasize that it should not be interpreted as a reason to seek out more UV exposure.
