The kitchen light was the only one on when Mira came downstairs. Her father sat at the table with his coat still on, staring at the phone face-down in front of him as if it might ring if he waited long enough.

Her brother Eli had been gone for four days. The police had come twice, then stopped coming. Now there were only the posters on the telephone poles and the casseroles nobody wanted to eat.

Mira poured herself a glass of water and stood by the sink. She had learned that silence was safer than speech in this house lately.

Her father slammed his palm on the table. "Why didn't you stop him?"

She flinched, though she had heard the question a dozen times already. "I didn't know he was going to leave."

"You were in the same room."

"I was reading," she said quietly. "He said he was going to Marcus's."

He stood so fast the chair scraped across the tile. For a moment she thought he might hit the cabinet, or the wall, or something that would make the noise stop. Instead he pressed both hands over his face and made a sound that was not quite a word.

Mira set down her glass. She crossed the kitchen slowly, the way she would approach a dog that had been hurt, and stood beside him without touching him.

"I'm scared too," she said.

He lowered his hands. His eyes were red and furious, but underneath the fury she saw something smaller and more frightened, and it looked a lot like her own.

"I know you are," he said roughly. "I'm sorry. I'm not angry at you."

"I know." She hesitated. "Can I sit with you?"

He nodded and dropped back into the chair. Mira pulled out the one beside him and sat close enough that their elbows touched.

They didn't talk for a long time. The refrigerator hummed. Somewhere outside a car passed, and both of them turned toward the window before realizing it wasn't Eli's.

Eventually her father said, "He used to fall asleep on my shoulder in the car."

"I remember," Mira said. "He always complained his neck hurt after."

A small laugh broke out of him, cracked and wet. "He never once complained to me."

"He complained to me," she said. "All the time."

They sat with that for a while. The anger hadn't gone anywhere, she could tell, but it had loosened its grip, the way a fist does when it finally gets tired.

Later, when the clock said past midnight, her father reached over and squeezed her hand. It was the first time he had held it since the disappearance.

"Tomorrow we call the detective again," he said. "Together."

"Okay," Mira said.

She didn't know if Eli would come home. She didn't know if the anger would ever fully leave the house. But for the first time in four days, the kitchen felt like a place where two people could sit in the same grief without breaking each other.

She left the light on when they finally went upstairs, just in case.

The manuscript addresses an important and timely problem: adapting models to new data distributions without labeled target data, in settings where data cannot be centralized due to privacy, bandwidth, or regulatory constraints. The authors clearly motivate the decentralized setting and position their work relative to federated learning and classical unsupervised domain adaptation, which helps readers see the contribution. The proposed method combines local feature alignment with a consensus mechanism across nodes, and the description of the algorithm is generally clear enough to follow. However, the theoretical analysis relies on assumptions, such as bounded heterogeneity between source and target distributions and a specific communication topology, that are stated but not sufficiently discussed in terms of how restrictive they are in practice. The experiments cover several standard image benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the paper would benefit from evaluation on a more realistic, non-image workload and from reporting variance across random seeds. The baselines include centralized and federated adaptation methods, yet the comparison omits some recent decentralized approaches that would provide a stronger reference point. The communication cost analysis is useful, though the authors should report wall-clock time and energy overhead alongside the number of communication rounds. Ablation studies convincingly show the contribution of the consensus term, but the sensitivity to hyperparameters such as the mixing weight and learning rate is only partially explored. Overall, the paper is a solid contribution with a sound core idea, and I recommend a major revision addressing the assumptions, the experimental breadth, and the reporting of statistical variability.

Success is rarely a straight line. Most people who achieve something meaningful have faced moments when their plans fell apart, their efforts seemed wasted, or their confidence was shaken. Yet these setbacks often turn out to be valuable teachers, and they become more useful when paired with the right kinds of support. Education, family, and work each play a distinct role in helping people move through difficulty and eventually reach their goals.

Setbacks can take many forms. A student might fail an important exam, a worker might lose a job during an economic downturn, or a family might face illness or financial strain. In each case, the immediate reaction is often discouragement. However, the experience can also reveal weaknesses in study habits, career planning, or personal resilience that might otherwise remain hidden. A failed test, for example, can show a student exactly which concepts need more attention. A lost job can push someone to learn new skills or consider a field they had never explored.

Education is one of the most important sources of support in overcoming setbacks. Good teachers do more than deliver information; they notice when a student is struggling and offer encouragement, alternative explanations, or extra help. Schools and colleges often provide tutoring centers, counseling services, and academic advising that help students recover from poor performance. Education also gives people the tools to understand their own difficulties. A student who learns to analyze problems, research solutions, and manage time is better equipped to handle future challenges. In this way, education supports success not only by providing knowledge but by building the capacity to keep learning after a fall.

Family is perhaps the most personal form of support. Parents, siblings, grandparents, and other relatives can provide emotional stability when everything else feels uncertain. A family member who listens without judgment can help a person process disappointment and regain perspective. Families also offer practical help, such as a place to stay during a job search, money for school expenses during a hard year, or simply a reminder of past accomplishments. Equally important, families often instill values like perseverance and honesty that shape how a person responds to failure. Children who grow up seeing their parents recover from hardship often learn that setbacks are temporary and survivable.

Work provides another layer of support, and it can be especially powerful because it links recovery to purpose and income. Good employers offer training programs, mentorship, and feedback that help employees grow after a mistake or a demotion. Coworkers can share knowledge, introduce new opportunities, and offer a sense of belonging. Even a difficult job can teach discipline, teamwork, and the ability to take criticism constructively. Many people find that their first job, though modest, gives them the experience and confidence to pursue better positions later. Work also restores a sense of control, which can be deeply reassuring after a period of uncertainty.

These three sources of support often work together. A student who struggles in school may find encouragement from a parent, which motivates them to seek tutoring, and that effort may eventually lead to an internship that opens a career path. Similarly, an adult who loses a job may draw on family support while retraining through a community college, and the new skills may lead to stable employment. The strength of this network lies in its overlap, since no single source must carry the full burden of recovery. When education, family, and work reinforce one another, a person is more likely to bounce back and continue forward.

It is worth acknowledging that not everyone has equal access to these forms of support. Some students attend underfunded schools, some families lack resources, and some workers face discrimination or unstable employment. These inequalities make it harder for certain people to recover from setbacks, and they remind us that communities and institutions have a responsibility to widen access to help. Public investment in education, family assistance programs, and fair workplace policies can give more people the chance to turn difficulties into growth.

In conclusion, setbacks are a natural part of the path to success, and they need not be final. Education offers knowledge and guidance, family provides emotional and practical strength, and work supplies structure, skills, and renewed purpose. Together, these sources of support help people learn from their failures and rebuild with greater understanding. Success, then, is not the absence of setbacks but the ability to recover from them with the help of those around us.

Romance as Love, Imagination, and a Literary Tradition

The word "romance" carries many meanings, and understanding them helps us appreciate one of the oldest and most enduring forms of storytelling. At its heart, romance refers to narratives centered on love, adventure, and the extraordinary, often set in worlds that stretch beyond everyday experience. The term itself traces back to the Old French word "romanz," used for vernacular texts written in the French language rather than Latin. Over time, the word came to describe a particular kind of story rather than a language.

Medieval romances emerged in the twelfth century, when poets in France began composing long verse narratives about knights, ladies, quests, and courtly devotion. Chrétien de Troyes, who wrote in the second half of the twelfth century, is often regarded as a foundational figure in this tradition. His works, such as Erec et Enide and Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, explored the tensions between love, duty, honor, and personal identity. These early tales established patterns that would shape European literature for centuries.

The Arthurian legends became the most celebrated source of romance material. Stories of King Arthur, Camelot, the Knights of the Round Table, and the quest for the Holy Grail offered rich territory for writers. Sir Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, completed in the late fifteenth century and printed by William Caxton in 1485, gathered many of these tales into a single influential English work. Malory's version shaped how later generations imagined the legend.

Romance was never limited to Arthurian material. Medieval writers also drew on classical antiquity, producing works about Troy, Alexander the Great, and Aeneas. Others told tales of Tristan and Iseult, whose doomed passion became one of the most retold love stories in Western culture. Still others explored fairy lands, magical objects, and encounters with the supernatural. This variety reveals how romance served as a flexible framework for imagining human emotion.

A central feature of romance is its treatment of love as a force that transforms the lover. In many medieval texts, love is not simply a pleasant feeling but an ennobling discipline that demands courage, loyalty, and self-sacrifice. The courtly love tradition, which developed alongside these narratives, idealized the lady as an object of devotion and the lover as one who proves himself through service and deeds. Scholars continue to debate how literally these conventions reflected real social practices.

The imaginative dimension of romance is equally important. Romance invites readers to leave the ordinary world and enter spaces shaped by wonder. Enchanted forests, mysterious castles, shape-shifting figures, and perilous journeys create an atmosphere in which the boundaries between the real and the marvelous are deliberately blurred. This imaginative freedom allowed authors to explore questions about identity, desire, and moral conduct without the constraints of realism.

Romance also served as a vehicle for moral and social reflection. Through their heroes and heroines, these stories asked what it means to be virtuous, how one should balance personal desire against public obligation, and what forms of courage and kindness matter most. Many romances end with characters achieving a harmony between love and responsibility, though others depict the costs of failing to find that balance.

The tradition did not end with the Middle Ages. In the early modern period, Renaissance writers revived and reshaped romance for new audiences. Ludovico Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, published in 1516, combined chivalric adventure with wit and complicated plots of love and madness. Edmund Spenser's The Faerie Queene, published in 1590 and 1596, used romance structures to celebrate virtue and the Tudor world. These works demonstrate how romance could carry deep cultural and political meaning.

The novel's rise in the eighteenth century marked a significant transformation. Writers such as Samuel Richardson, Henry Fielding, and later Jane Austen drew on romance conventions while grounding them in more realistic settings and psychological detail. The question of marriage, courtship, and personal choice became central to the novel, and many of these works retained the romance interest in the power of love to test and reveal character.

Romantic literature of the nineteenth century broadened the meaning of the term further. The Romantic movement in poetry and fiction emphasized emotion, nature, individual imagination, and the sublime. Writers such as Walter Scott, whose historical novels blended adventure, chivalry, and national history, helped popularize romance as a mode that combined the past with feeling. The Romantic emphasis on intense inner experience continued to influence later literature.

In the modern era, romance has taken many forms, from gothic novels and historical fiction to contemporary genre fiction. The romance novel, often focused on the development of a love relationship with a hopeful resolution, has become one of the most widely read categories of popular fiction. This modern genre retains the older tradition's interest in desire, obstacles, and the transformative power of love.

Literary critics have long debated the value and definition of romance. Some have dismissed it as escapist or sentimental, while others have recognized its complexity and cultural importance. Northrop Frye, the Canadian literary theorist, argued that romance represents a fundamental narrative pattern in literature, involving quests, trials, and the restoration of a lost ideal. This perspective encourages readers to see romance as a deep structure rather than a minor category.

Understanding romance also means recognizing its relationship to myth and folklore. Many romantic narratives draw on older stories of heroes, transformations, and otherworldly journeys. The fairy tale, with its enchanted princesses and brave young heroes, shares structural features with medieval romance. These connections show how romance grows out of a shared human impulse to tell stories about longing and transformation.

The language of romance has also influenced everyday speech. Phrases such as "a romantic gesture" or "a romantic getaway" reflect the broader cultural association of romance with love, beauty, and idealism. This popular sense of the word, though different from its literary origins, reveals how deeply the tradition has shaped our expectations about relationships and the imagination.

Studying romance offers several benefits for readers. It introduces the history of storytelling, reveals the evolution of literary forms, and invites reflection on how societies have understood love. It also encourages readers to consider the role of imagination in shaping human experience. By reading romances from different periods, students can compare how each era defined courage, devotion, and happiness.

When approaching a romance text, readers may find it helpful to consider several questions. What is the setting, and how does it shape the events? What does the hero or heroine value, and how is that value tested? How does love change the characters, and what obstacles stand in the way? What moral lessons, if any, does the story offer? These questions help readers move beyond plot summary toward deeper interpretation.

Many classic romances remain accessible today. Readers interested in medieval examples might begin with Chrétien de Troyes in translation or with Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur. Those drawn to Renaissance romance could explore Spenser or Ariosto. Scott's novels offer an entry point into the Romantic period, while Austen provides a bridge between romance conventions and the realist novel. Each work rewards careful attention to its historical context.

The enduring appeal of romance lies in its combination of emotional intensity and imaginative range. It speaks to universal experiences of longing, loyalty, and transformation while allowing writers to explore possibilities beyond ordinary life. Across centuries and cultures, romance has offered a space where love and imagination meet, inviting each generation to find meaning in its stories.

In conclusion, romance is best understood as a rich and evolving tradition rather than a single genre with fixed rules. From medieval verse tales of knights and ladies to modern popular fiction, it has consistently explored the power of love and the possibilities of the imagination. Its history reminds us that stories about desire and devotion have always been central to human culture, and that they continue to shape how we think about ourselves and one another.

Reducing car dependence in suburban communities has become an important goal for planners, residents, and local governments seeking a more sustainable and equitable future. Many suburbs were built after the Second World War around the assumption that every household would own at least one car, and as a result, homes, shops, schools, and offices are often separated by long distances with few safe routes for walking or cycling. Changing this pattern offers significant benefits, but it also raises real challenges that communities must confront thoughtfully.

One of the most important benefits is improved public health. When residents can walk or bike to nearby destinations, they tend to get more daily physical activity, which can lower the risk of obesity, heart disease, and diabetes. Reduced driving also means fewer traffic accidents, which are a leading cause of injury and death among young people. Cleaner air is another advantage, since vehicle emissions contribute to smog, respiratory illness, and climate change. Quieter streets and fewer cars can make neighborhoods more pleasant places to live, especially for children and older adults.

Economic benefits are also substantial. Car ownership is expensive, with costs for purchase, insurance, fuel, maintenance, and parking often adding up to thousands of dollars per year for a household. Families that rely less on cars can redirect that money toward housing, education, or savings. Local businesses may also benefit, because pedestrians and cyclists are more likely to stop at neighborhood shops than drivers passing through quickly. Walkable commercial areas can increase property values and generate steady tax revenue for municipalities.

Social benefits deserve attention as well. Communities designed for walking and transit tend to encourage casual interaction among neighbors, which can build trust and a stronger sense of belonging. Young people who cannot yet drive gain greater independence when they can reach friends, jobs, and activities on their own. Older residents who no longer drive can remain connected to family, healthcare, and social life rather than becoming isolated.

Despite these advantages, the challenges are considerable. Suburban infrastructure is deeply tied to car travel, and retrofitting it is expensive. Building sidewalks, bike lanes, crosswalks, and transit stops requires large investments, and many towns have limited budgets. Zoning rules often prohibit the mixed-use development that makes walking practical, so changing these regulations can be politically difficult and slow.

Transit service presents its own difficulties. Buses and trains work best when population density is high enough to support frequent routes, but many suburbs are spread out and have low density. Without frequent and reliable service, residents may find transit impractical for work, shopping, or appointments, and they will continue to drive. Transit agencies also face ongoing operating costs and pressure to keep fares affordable.

Cultural attitudes and personal preferences matter too. Many people value the privacy, space, and convenience that come with a private yard and a car in the driveway. Some residents worry that new development will bring traffic, noise, or changes to neighborhood character. Balancing these concerns with the goal of reducing car use requires careful public engagement and clear communication about the benefits and tradeoffs.

Equity is another important consideration. Lower-income households are often the ones most affected by car dependence, since they may have limited access to reliable vehicles or spend a larger share of their income on transportation. Yet policies that improve walkability can sometimes raise housing costs and displace existing residents if they are not carefully designed. Communities must therefore pair investment in alternatives with protections for affordable housing.

Successful strategies often combine several approaches at once. Mixed-use zoning can bring homes, shops, and offices closer together. Safe sidewalks and bike networks can make short trips easy and enjoyable. Improved transit, including on-demand shuttles and better bus connections, can serve areas where fixed routes are not practical. Carpooling programs, car-sharing services, and employer incentives can also reduce the number of vehicles on the road.

Technology may help or complicate these efforts. Ride-hailing apps and electric vehicles offer new options, but they do not necessarily reduce the total number of trips or the space devoted to roads and parking. Planners must consider whether new technologies genuinely move communities toward less car dependence or simply change the form of car use.

Ultimately, reducing car dependence in suburbs is a long-term project rather than a quick fix. It requires patience, sustained funding, and cooperation among governments, developers, and residents. The benefits for health, finances, community life, and the environment are significant, but they will only be realized if communities address the practical, political, and equity challenges along the way. With thoughtful planning, many suburbs can become places where people have real choices about how they move.

Optimism is more than a cheerful outlook; it is a habit of mind that shapes how people handle difficulty, how they treat others, and how they feel about their own lives. Researchers who study well-being have found that optimistic people tend to report greater life satisfaction and lower levels of stress. This connection matters because it suggests that the way we interpret events can be as important as the events themselves.

One reason optimism supports personal well-being is that it changes how setbacks are understood. A person who expects things to improve is more likely to see a failed test or a canceled plan as a temporary problem rather than a permanent verdict. This perspective encourages persistence, because it makes effort seem worthwhile. Over time, this steady willingness to try again builds confidence and a sense of control over one's future.

Optimism also influences physical health. Some studies have linked a hopeful outlook with better sleep, stronger immune responses, and a greater tendency to take care of oneself through exercise and regular medical checkups. While optimism alone cannot cure illness, it can encourage the daily choices that keep people healthy. The mind and body are closely connected, and a positive expectation about the future often leads to actions that protect long-term health.

The benefits of optimism extend beyond the individual into their relationships with others. Optimistic people tend to assume the best about the intentions of those around them. When a friend forgets to reply to a message, an optimistic person is more likely to think the friend is busy rather than uninterested. This generous interpretation reduces unnecessary conflict and allows relationships to remain warm even during small misunderstandings.

Hopeful people also tend to be better company. Their expectation of good outcomes makes them pleasant to be around, and their enthusiasm can be contagious. Friends and coworkers often feel encouraged after spending time with someone who approaches challenges with calm confidence. This emotional energy can strengthen bonds, because people naturally want to spend time with those who make them feel capable and supported.

Optimism plays an important role in cooperation as well. When people believe that a shared project can succeed, they are more willing to contribute their time and ideas. A team led by someone who expresses confidence in the group's abilities often performs better than one that expects failure. In this way, optimism becomes a shared resource that benefits everyone involved.

It is important to note that optimism does not mean ignoring problems or pretending that every situation will turn out well. Realistic optimism acknowledges difficulty while still holding a belief that effort can make a difference. This balanced approach is more useful than blind positivity, because it allows people to prepare for challenges while remaining motivated. Healthy relationships also depend on honesty, and optimism that respects the truth can strengthen trust.

Anyone can cultivate optimism with practice. Keeping a simple journal of things that went well each day can train the mind to notice positive experiences. Reframing negative thoughts by asking what might be learned from a difficult event also builds a more hopeful outlook. Spending time with supportive people reinforces the idea that good relationships are possible and worth pursuing.

In conclusion, optimism supports personal well-being by helping people cope with stress, maintain healthy habits, and find meaning in their experiences. It also strengthens relationships by encouraging generous interpretations, creating warmth in social interactions, and inspiring cooperation. Because optimism can be learned and practiced, it offers a valuable path toward a more fulfilling life shared with others.

The manuscript proposes biologically inspired neural networks for video prediction and evaluates them against two sets of benchmarks: human-like visual familiarity effects and neural responses recorded from the macaque visual system. The central claim is that architectural features drawn from the primate visual pathway improve predictive accuracy while also reproducing signatures of familiarity, such as reduced responses to repeated or predictable stimuli. The motivation is clearly stated and well situated within the literature on predictive coding and neural alignment of deep networks. The study is ambitious in scope, combining a machine learning task with two distinct neurophysiological comparisons, which is a strength because it tests the model against independent sources of biological evidence. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more precise description of how the biological inspiration is implemented, since the architectural mapping from cortical areas to network modules is described only at a high level. The video prediction results are reported on a single dataset, and the authors should include additional datasets or ablations to show that the gains are not specific to the benchmark chosen. The familiarity analysis would be stronger with statistical tests that account for multiple comparisons and with a clear baseline model that lacks the biologically motivated components. The macaque comparison relies on representational similarity analysis, and the authors should justify the choice of similarity metric and report how sensitive the results are to it. It is also unclear whether the neural recordings were collected for this study or drawn from an existing public dataset, and the provenance and preprocessing steps should be documented in full. The discussion occasionally overstates the implications for biological mechanism, given that a network matching neural data at the population level does not establish that the same computations occur in the brain. Code and trained model weights should be released to allow replication. Overall, the work makes a useful contribution at the intersection of machine learning and systems neuroscience, and I recommend major revisions addressing the points above before publication.

The traveler woke in a waiting room lit by a flickering blue glow, and a dial tone hummed somewhere beneath the floor. A sign on the wall read "Please Wait While We Connect You," and beneath it, a progress bar crawled toward a hundred percent without ever reaching it. He tried to stand, but his legs had been replaced by a loading spinner that turned endlessly, and every step he took produced only the sound of modem handshakes screeching through his skull. A pop-up window appeared before him, demanding that he accept a license agreement he could not read, its text scrolling forever in a font that bled into static. He clicked "Accept" and was immediately asked to restart his soul. Through a cracked doorway he glimpsed a corridor of beige computer towers, each humming with the fan noise of a dying machine, their screens displaying green text he could not understand. A voice from one of them whispered that his files were corrupted and that he had been moved to the recycle bin. He searched for an exit, but every door he opened led to a blue screen announcing a fatal error, and the error code was always his own name. Somewhere a floppy disk ejected with a mechanical clunk, and a faint chorus of old dial-up sounds rose to a crescendo. He wandered past rows of forgotten chat rooms where users typed greetings to no one, their usernames fading one by one into grey. A banner ad promised him free access to a world he had lost long ago, and when he clicked it the screen filled with the logo of a browser that no longer existed. The cursor followed him everywhere, blinking patiently, waiting for a command he could never remember. He tried to type a password, but the field asked for the name of his first pet, his childhood street, and his mother's maiden name, and each answer dissolved as he reached for it. Overhead, a system tray clock ticked backward through decades, and with each tick a little more of the room went pixelated and dim. At last he sat down before the oldest machine in the corridor, its screen reading "Press any key to continue." He pressed every key he could find, and the machine simply replied, "Timed out. Please try again later," and the waiting room began its long reboot, again and again, forever.

Learning at home has become a common experience for students, and its success depends largely on two factors: motivation and support. Without the structure of a classroom, students must rely on their own drive to start assignments, manage their time, and stay focused on their goals. Those who feel genuinely curious about a subject tend to thrive, because their interest carries them through lessons that might otherwise feel tedious or distracting. Motivation, however, is not always constant, and many students struggle when their enthusiasm fades. This is where support becomes essential. Parents, teachers, and friends can help by setting clear expectations, checking in on progress, and offering encouragement when work feels overwhelming. A parent who creates a quiet study space and a daily routine gives a student the foundation needed to concentrate. Teachers who respond promptly to questions and provide thoughtful feedback keep students connected to the material and to the learning community. Peer support also matters, since study groups and conversations with classmates can make the work feel less isolating. Technology plays a role as well, offering tools for organization, communication, and access to resources that a student might not find otherwise. Yet technology can also become a source of distraction, which again returns the question to self-discipline and guidance. Students who lack either motivation or support may fall behind, feel anxious, or disengage entirely. For these learners, schools and families must work together to identify problems early and provide help. When both motivation and support are present, however, learning at home can be rich, flexible, and deeply rewarding. It allows students to explore subjects at their own pace and develop independence that will serve them well beyond their school years. Ultimately, the home is neither a guaranteed success nor a guaranteed failure; it is a setting whose outcomes depend on the student's own commitment and the care of those around them.

Students should be allowed to use their phones during lunch and free time at school because these breaks are meant for rest and social connection, not instruction. Phones give students a way to decompress, listen to music, or catch up with family and friends after a demanding morning of classes. Many students also use lunch periods to finish homework or review notes, and a phone can make that work more efficient. Banning phones entirely during these times treats students as though they cannot be trusted to manage their own downtime, which can damage the sense of responsibility schools hope to build. Restricting phones can also push students toward unsupervised corners of the campus where they are harder for staff to see, which may create more problems than it solves. Schools that allow limited phone use with clear expectations, such as no videos of other students and no disruptive noise, show that rules can be reasonable and enforceable. Furthermore, phones are a practical safety tool, letting students reach parents quickly in an emergency or after a school incident. Ultimately, trusting students with phones during free time, paired with clear and fair guidelines, teaches them self-control in a setting where the stakes are low.

Gerald Pruitt had never succeeded at anything in his forty-one years, and he was determined that today would be no different. He had decided to become a villain. The plan was simple: he would sneak into the city's central water reservoir and dump a bottle of food coloring into it, just to watch the town panic.

The bottle was the first problem. It was not food coloring but a jar of his late aunt's raspberry jam, which he had grabbed in the dark kitchen. He told himself the effect would be dramatic enough anyway.

The reservoir gate was the second problem. Gerald had read about it online and assumed it was unlocked, since nobody in his small town ever locked anything. It was locked. He spent twenty minutes climbing the fence, got his jacket caught on the barbed wire, and fell into a drainage ditch.

Muddy and bleeding slightly from one palm, he crawled through a storm culvert that he was fairly sure led to the reservoir. It did not. It led to the basement of the municipal building, where the town's emergency generator was housed.

Gerald stood up in the dim light and saw a small red light blinking on a control panel. Beside it, a laminated sheet warned that the generator's cooling system had failed and that the backup valve must be opened manually within the hour or the unit would overheat.

He had no idea what the valve was, but he had a jar of jam, a flashlight, and nothing better to do. He pried open a panel with a screwdriver he found in his pocket, which he had been carrying for no reason he could remember, and found a large wheel labeled in faded letters.

The wheel was stiff. Gerald put his full weight on it, then his knee, and finally his whole body. It gave way with a screech, and a rush of cold water began pouring through a pipe somewhere above him.

Upstairs, a night-shift technician named Dolores Ruiz heard the alarm she had been ignoring for an hour. She ran down the stairs, saw a soaked and filthy man sitting on the floor in a puddle, and screamed.

Gerald raised his hands and tried to explain, but all he managed was, "I was going to poison the water."

Dolores looked at the open valve, the cooling fluid spreading across the concrete, and the dial that had been climbing toward the red zone. Then she looked back at Gerald.

"You stopped a meltdown," she said.

"I did what?"

She called it in. By sunrise, a crew had arrived and confirmed that the generator would have overheated within forty minutes, cutting power to the hospital's ventilators and the water pumps for three neighborhoods.

The local paper ran a photo of Gerald wrapped in a emergency blanket, holding a jar of jam. The headline read: LOCAL MAN SAVES TOWN, SAYS HE WAS "JUST PASSING THROUGH."

Gerald read it twice at the kitchen table. He had never been a hero, and he was not sure he wanted to be one now. But when the mayor showed up at his door with a handshake and a plaque, he found he could not bring himself to correct the record.

He still had the jam, though. He decided he would keep that part to himself.

Marlowe woke, as he always did now, with the taste of burnt coffee on his tongue and a stranger's name pressing at the back of his teeth. Tessa. Not his name. Never his name.

He lay still in the gray light of a rented room in a city he did not recognize and tried to hold on to the warning. It had been written on the inside of his wrist in ballpoint, the way he had written it every night for what might have been fifty nights, or five hundred. The ink had faded to a bruise-colored smudge. He could still make out the words if he squinted: Don't drink the second cup.

He had written it, he was almost sure, to himself. Some earlier version of him had been frightened enough to leave a note on his own skin.

The dreams always started the same way. He would be in someone's body, feeling their weight and their hunger, and then the switch would come, like a hand pulling a sheet off a table. He would wake in a different life, a different bed, and the only thread connecting them was the caffeine. Every life began with a cup of coffee, and every cup was the thing that let the cycle turn over.

He reached for the pot on the nightstand out of habit, then stopped. His hand shook. He could feel the craving sitting under his ribs like a second heartbeat, patient and insistent. He had been an addict in every life he could remember, and he suspected he had been one in lives he had forgotten.

Marlowe got up and went to the sink. He filled a glass with tap water and drank it slowly, letting it cool his throat. Then he found a pen in the drawer and began writing on the back of his other hand, because the wrist was getting crowded.

Coffee is the door. Stay awake without it.

He looked at the words for a long time. They seemed both urgent and absurd, the kind of advice that would sound ridiculous to anyone who had not lived through this. He tried to imagine explaining it to Tessa, or to the man whose face he had glimpsed in the mirror two lives ago, and he could not find a way to begin.

The first morning he had tried to stop, in whichever life that was, he had lasted four hours before the headache drove him to a café. The barista had smiled and said, "The usual?" and he had said yes before he could think. The cup had been hot and sweet and the switch had come that night, as certainly as sunset.

So this time he would try differently. He had written himself a list on the inside of his arm, a sequence of small steps: water, a walk, cold air on the face, a book read aloud. Each one was a rung on a ladder he hoped would hold his weight long enough to reach the top.

He went out into the street. The city was waking up around him, shopkeepers lifting shutters, a bus sighing at the corner. The smell of coffee drifted from a doorway, rich and bitter, and his whole body leaned toward it like a plant toward light.

Marlowe kept walking. He counted his steps, then the streetlamps, then the cracks in the pavement. He thought about the people he had been and the people he had touched, all of them tangled together in a chain he could not see the end of.

By noon his head was pounding and his hands would not stay still. He sat on a bench in a small park and pressed his palms against his eyes until he saw sparks. Someone walked past with a paper cup, and the scent hit him so sharply that he gasped.

He did not get up. He stayed on the bench, breathing, while the sun moved across the sky and the craving rose and fell like a tide. Somewhere in the middle of the afternoon he realized he had not thought about Tessa for almost an hour.

That was new. He held onto it.

When evening came he was shaking and exhausted, but he was still himself, still Marlowe, still awake. He walked back to the rented room and sat on the edge of the bed in the dim light, looking at the words on his skin.

The dreams would come tonight, he was almost certain. They always did. But maybe, if he could stay awake long enough, the switch would not catch him. Maybe the warnings were not meant to be obeyed in the moment but to be carried forward, a message passed hand to hand across a long relay of selves.

He thought of the first person in the chain, the one who had written the first warning, and wondered what that person had been running from. He wondered whether they had ever succeeded, or whether they had simply handed the problem down to him like a stone too heavy to set aside.

He picked up the pen again and wrote one more line on his forearm, pressing hard so the ink would last.

If you're reading this, you made it through one more day. Keep going.

Then he turned off the light, lay back, and forced his eyes to stay open against the dark.

Summer learning projects offer middle and high school students a chance to explore ideas beyond the constraints of the regular school year, yet a central question remains unsettled: should teachers or students be the ones to design these projects? Each group brings distinct strengths, and the strongest answer may lie in a thoughtful partnership rather than a clear winner.

Teachers are trained to understand how learning develops over time. They know which skills students need next, how to sequence material so that it builds logically, and how to assess whether a project has achieved its goals. A teacher-designed project can ensure that summer work reinforces core competencies in reading, mathematics, and writing, which is especially valuable for students who experienced learning loss during disrupted school years. Teachers also understand the practical realities of a classroom, such as what a reasonable workload looks like and how to make expectations clear.

Students, however, have something teachers cannot fully replicate: direct knowledge of their own interests, curiosity, and frustrations. A project that a student helps shape is more likely to hold their attention through the long, unstructured weeks of summer. When students choose a topic, such as building a small weather station, documenting the history of their neighborhood, or researching a question about marine life, they tend to invest more effort and develop a stronger sense of ownership. Student-led design also builds skills in planning, self-direction, and decision-making that will serve them well beyond school.

The risk of student-only design is that motivation alone does not guarantee rigor. A young person may choose a project that feels exciting but teaches little that is new, or may underestimate the time and effort a meaningful investigation requires. Without guidance, some students will drift, and the summer may pass with little academic growth. Teacher-only design carries the opposite risk: projects can become rigid assignments that students complete for a grade rather than for genuine interest, which undermines the very curiosity that summer learning is meant to encourage.

A balanced model addresses both concerns. Teachers could establish learning goals and provide a range of approved options, while students select among them or propose their own projects for approval. This structure preserves academic standards while giving students meaningful choice. It also creates a natural checkpoint where a teacher can help a student narrow an overly ambitious idea or strengthen a vague one. Such collaboration treats students as capable partners without abandoning the professional judgment that teachers bring.

Schools that adopt this approach should also consider how students with different needs will be supported. Some students arrive at summer with strong self-direction, while others need more structure to begin and sustain a project. A collaborative model can flex to meet these differences, offering more guidance to students who need it and more independence to those ready for it. Clear rubrics and regular check-ins help ensure that all students, regardless of their starting point, have a fair opportunity to succeed.

In the end, the question of who should design summer projects is less about choosing a single authority and more about recognizing complementary strengths. Teachers provide expertise, structure, and a sense of where learning should go, while students provide motivation, relevance, and personal investment. When these perspectives meet, summer learning can become something students value rather than endure. The most effective projects are likely to be those that teachers and students build together, with each contributing what they know best.

Considering diverse perspectives is one of the most reliable ways to make decisions that are both fairer and more effective. When people with different experiences, backgrounds, and ways of thinking examine a problem together, they are more likely to notice details that a single viewpoint would miss. This advantage matters in every setting where decisions affect other people, including schools, workplaces, governments, and communities.

The first reason diverse perspectives improve decisions is that they reduce blind spots. Every person carries assumptions shaped by their upbringing, education, and daily environment, and these assumptions often operate without us realizing it. A city planner who has always commuted by car may not think about the needs of people who rely on buses or who cannot drive. When someone from a different situation joins the conversation, those hidden assumptions become visible and can be tested.

A second reason is that diversity improves the quality of thinking itself. When a group contains only people who agree, discussions tend to move quickly toward a single answer, and few people question it. Disagreement forces each participant to explain their reasoning more carefully, to defend claims with evidence, and to consider objections. Research on group problem solving has repeatedly suggested that groups with varied backgrounds can produce more accurate and creative solutions, although the benefits depend on the group being willing to listen to one another.

Fairness also depends on who is included in the discussion. Decisions made without input from affected groups often impose burdens on those groups without anyone intending harm. A school that adopts a new schedule without consulting parents who work night shifts, or a hospital that designs a waiting area without asking elderly patients, may create problems that were easily foreseeable. Including those voices allows decision makers to anticipate consequences and to share costs and benefits more evenly.

Diverse perspectives also build legitimacy. People are more likely to accept a decision, even one they dislike, when they believe their concerns were heard and considered. A policy developed by a narrow group can seem arbitrary or self-serving to those left out, which can lead to resistance, low compliance, or repeated conflict. When a broader range of people has contributed, the outcome is more likely to be trusted and sustained over time.

Of course, diversity does not automatically produce good decisions. A group that is diverse in appearance but unwilling to share honest views gains little from its differences. Some participants may be ignored, interrupted, or pressured to conform, which means the benefits are lost. Effective use of diverse perspectives requires a deliberate process, including clear ground rules, opportunities for everyone to speak, and a habit of asking why others see things differently.

Leaders play an important role in making this process work. They can set the tone by welcoming criticism, by asking questions before stating their own opinions, and by explaining how input shaped the final decision. When leaders treat disagreement as useful information rather than as a threat, participants feel safer offering honest views. This kind of culture takes time to build, but it strengthens an organization's ability to learn and adapt.

Consider a community deciding where to build a new park. If only residents from one neighborhood take part in the planning, the park may suit their preferences but neglect families who lack transportation, older residents who need benches and shade, or young people who want space for sports. A planning process that actively seeks input from all these groups is more likely to produce a park that serves the whole community. The result is not only fairer but also more useful, because it is more likely to be used and valued.

Some people worry that considering many perspectives will slow decisions or lead to compromises that satisfy no one. These concerns are worth taking seriously, since endless discussion can paralyze a group. Yet the goal is not to hear every opinion indefinitely but to gather enough varied input to make an informed choice. A well-structured process can balance thoroughness with efficiency, setting deadlines and clear criteria while still giving meaningful weight to different views.

In the end, diverse perspectives make decisions fairer because they bring in the voices of people who might otherwise be overlooked, and they make decisions more effective because they expose errors, reveal new options, and test ideas against a wider range of experience. These benefits are not guaranteed, and they require honest participation, open minds, and deliberate methods. Still, the evidence and everyday experience both suggest that taking many viewpoints seriously is among the most dependable ways to reach good collective choices.

This paper addresses the problem of modeling how entities change state across the steps of a process description, a task central to procedural text understanding. The authors frame the problem clearly and motivate it well, noting that many downstream applications such as question answering over procedures and process extraction depend on tracking entity states accurately. The related work section is thorough and situates the contribution relative to prior approaches based on sequence labeling and neural state-tracking models. The proposed architecture is described with sufficient detail to be reproduced, and the choice to represent states as structured predicates rather than free-form labels is a sensible design decision. The experimental setup uses a recognized benchmark, which allows meaningful comparison with prior systems. However, the reported gains over the strongest baseline are modest, and the paper would benefit from significance testing across multiple random seeds to establish that the improvements are robust. The error analysis is informative but limited to aggregate categories; a more detailed breakdown of failure cases, particularly for implicit state changes that are never stated explicitly in the text, would strengthen the claims. The ablation studies convincingly show that the auxiliary entity-linking objective contributes to performance, though the paper should clarify how sensitive results are to the weighting of this loss term. The writing is generally clear, although some notation in the methods section is introduced inconsistently and should be standardized. Overall, the paper makes a useful incremental contribution, and I recommend a minor revision that addresses the statistical reporting and the depth of the error analysis.

Architectural Typologies of Historic Homes in Kocaeli as a Means of Preserving Local Identity and Cultural Heritage

Abstract

This paper examines the architectural typologies of historic residential buildings in Kocaeli, a province in northwestern Turkey bordering the Sea of Marmara and the Gulf of İzmit. Residential architecture is among the most immediate expressions of local identity, and the homes of Kocaeli record centuries of economic, social, and environmental adaptation. The study proposes that a systematic classification of these typologies can support heritage preservation by linking material form to cultural meaning. The argument is developed through a review of regional history, a description of principal building types, an analysis of construction materials and spatial organization, and a discussion of threats to preservation together with recommendations for policy and practice. The paper concludes that typological documentation is a practical foundation for sustaining the distinctive character of Kocaeli's built environment.

Introduction

Historic houses are more than shelters. They embody the knowledge of builders, the needs of households, and the resources available in a particular place and period. In Turkey, regional residential traditions have long been recognized as carriers of cultural memory, yet many of them have been studied unevenly. Kocaeli occupies a distinctive position within this landscape. Its coastal plains, river valleys, and forested hillsides, together with its role as a corridor between Istanbul and Anatolia, produced a building culture shaped by both local practice and external influence. Despite this richness, the residential heritage of the province has received less sustained attention than that of larger historic centers.

The purpose of this paper is to describe the principal architectural typologies of historic homes in Kocaeli and to consider how their documentation can contribute to the preservation of local identity. A typology, in the sense used here, is a classification of building types based on shared formal, structural, and functional characteristics. Such classification allows researchers and conservators to recognize patterns, compare examples, and identify those features that are most significant for conservation. The approach also helps to counter the tendency to treat individual buildings in isolation, which can obscure the wider cultural system to which they belong.

The paper proceeds as follows. The next section outlines the historical and geographical context of Kocaeli. This is followed by a methodological note, a description of the principal typologies, an analysis of materials and construction techniques, a discussion of spatial organization and social life within the house, a consideration of threats to preservation, and a set of recommendations. The paper then offers concluding remarks on the relationship between typology and identity.

Historical and Geographical Context

Kocaeli has been inhabited for millennia, and its settlement history reflects its strategic location on routes linking the Bosphorus with the interior of Anatolia. The region passed through Byzantine, Seljuk, and Ottoman administrations, and each period left traces in its urban fabric and domestic architecture. During the Ottoman era, towns such as İzmit developed as commercial and administrative centers, while smaller villages and coastal settlements sustained agrarian and maritime livelihoods.

The physical geography of the province is varied. The northern coast along the Black Sea-facing shore and the southern shore of the Gulf of İzmit present different climatic and topographic conditions from the interior hills. The Gulf of İzmit has historically supported fishing and shipbuilding, and the Sakarya and other rivers provided fertile alluvial land. Rainfall is comparatively high by Turkish standards, and humidity is pronounced in lowland zones. These conditions influenced roof pitches, the use of timber, the orientation of openings, and the choice of protective finishes.

Industrialization in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries transformed the province. Textile, chemical, and automotive industries expanded rapidly, drawing migrants from across the country and reshaping settlement patterns. This transformation brought new building forms and materials, and it placed considerable pressure on older neighborhoods. The tension between economic development and heritage conservation is therefore central to any consideration of Kocaeli's historic homes.

Methodological Note

The typological analysis presented here is based on a synthesis of published regional studies, architectural surveys, and documented examples of residential buildings across several districts of the province. Classification proceeds from observable characteristics, including plan form, number of storeys, roof type, construction system, facade composition, and the relationship between the house and its plot. Where possible, dating has been inferred from stylistic features, inscriptions, and documentary sources, although the paper acknowledges that many buildings have been altered and that precise chronologies are often uncertain.

The paper treats typology as a tool rather than a fixed taxonomy. Categories are indicative and overlap in practice, and hybrid forms are common. The analysis aims to capture dominant patterns while remaining open to local variation. Limitations include the uneven availability of documentation and the difficulty of accessing private properties. These limitations are noted where they affect the strength of the conclusions.

Principal Architectural Typologies

Several broad types can be identified among the historic homes of Kocaeli. The first is the timber-framed house with infill, often described in Turkish architectural literature as a himiş or hımış-type construction, in which a load-bearing timber skeleton is filled with masonry, mud brick, or lighter infill. This system offered resistance to seismic activity, a significant consideration in a region of the North Anatolian Fault, and it allowed flexible arrangements of openings and partitions.

The second type is the masonry house of stone or brick, typically found in more prosperous urban settings and in buildings associated with commercial or civic functions. These houses frequently display more substantial walls, stone plinths, and carefully crafted entrances. In some cases they reflect the influence of urban building standards introduced during periods of Ottoman administrative consolidation.

The third type is the vernacular rural house, usually single or two storeys, with a simple plan organized around a central hall or a sequence of rooms opening onto an open or semi-enclosed courtyard. These houses are often closely tied to agricultural use, incorporating storage, animal shelter, and work areas. Their roofs commonly use locally available tiles and timber, and their facades reflect the practical needs of the household rather than formal display.

A fourth category comprises coastal and waterfront dwellings, which respond to proximity to the sea and to maritime occupations. These buildings may incorporate timber balconies, lighter construction, and orientation strategies that take advantage of breezes and views. Some examples show the influence of boatbuilding techniques in joinery and in the treatment of structural elements.

A fifth group consists of transitional and early modern houses, which combine traditional spatial patterns with newer materials and facade treatments. These buildings are significant because they document the period of change and often represent the most endangered part of the heritage, since they are sometimes regarded as less valuable than older examples despite their historical importance.

Materials and Construction Techniques

The materials used in Kocaeli's historic homes reflect local availability and climatic demands. Timber, particularly oak, pine, and chestnut, provided structural members, floors, roof frames, and decorative elements. Local stone was used for foundations and plinths, while mud brick and fired brick formed infill and load-bearing walls. Roof coverings were commonly clay tiles, which were well suited to the region's rainfall. Lime-based mortars and plasters were used throughout, and these materials were generally compatible with the breathing qualities of traditional walls.

Construction techniques demonstrate considerable craft knowledge. Timber connections were often secured with pegs and interlocking joints rather than metal fasteners, allowing flexibility under lateral loads. The arrangement of infill and bracing contributed to the seismic performance of the building. Plasters and finishes were applied in layers, and surface treatments such as lime washes protected walls from moisture while contributing to the characteristic appearance of each settlement.

The conservation of these materials requires specialist understanding. Repairs using incompatible cement mortars or impermeable coatings can trap moisture and accelerate decay. Likewise, replacement of traditional timber with untreated or mismatched material can alter the structural behavior of the building. The documentation of typologies therefore includes not only form but also the material and technical systems that sustain it.

Spatial Organization and Social Life

The internal organization of historic homes in Kocaeli reflected family structure, social customs, and the division of labor. Many houses included a central space or hall that served as a circulation and gathering area, with rooms arranged around it. Separation between public and private zones, and in some households between male and female spaces, shaped the arrangement of entrances, staircases, and reception rooms. Kitchens and service areas were often placed to the rear or on lower floors, while upper floors provided sleeping quarters and more formal rooms.

Courtyards, gardens, and orchards extended the domestic realm into the plot. These open spaces accommodated household production, storage, and sociability, and they contributed to the microclimate of the dwelling. The relationship between house and garden is an important element of identity, since it expresses patterns of land use and everyday life that are increasingly rare in urbanized settings.

Decorative features, such as carved window frames, painted ceilings, and ornamental eaves, also conveyed meaning. These features varied by region, class, and period, and they offer valuable evidence for understanding local tastes and the exchange of craft knowledge. Their documentation contributes to the broader cultural narrative of the province.

Threats to Preservation

Historic homes in Kocaeli face several interrelated threats. Rapid urbanization and land speculation have led to demolition and replacement of older buildings, particularly in areas adjacent to transport corridors and industrial zones. Economic pressures encourage owners to modify or extend properties in ways that disregard their historical character. Changes in household structure, including the division of large houses into smaller units, can damage plans and finishes.

Environmental factors compound these pressures. High humidity, seismic activity, and the degradation of timber by moisture and insects threaten structural integrity. Inappropriate repairs, the use of modern cement-based materials, and the removal of original roof coverings can accelerate deterioration. Neglect is also a significant problem, particularly where owners lack the resources or knowledge to maintain traditional buildings.

Legal and administrative frameworks present additional challenges. Protection may depend on the registration of individual buildings or on the designation of conservation areas, and gaps in inventory and enforcement can leave vulnerable properties unprotected. Public awareness of the value of vernacular architecture is uneven, and the loss of a single building may go unnoticed outside its immediate community.

Discussion: Typology, Identity, and Heritage

The relationship between architectural typology and local identity lies in the recurrence of forms across time and space. When a community recognizes a particular house type as its own, that recognition reflects shared memory, practices, and aesthetic values. Typological documentation makes these shared characteristics visible and allows them to be articulated in planning, education, and conservation. It also helps distinguish between features that are essential to the character of a place and those that are incidental or later additions.

A typological approach further supports the protection of groups of buildings rather than isolated monuments. The streetscape, the rhythm of plots, and the relationship between houses and public spaces are all part of identity, and these qualities are often lost when individual buildings are considered without reference to their context. Conservation strategies informed by typology can therefore address both architectural fabric and urban character.

There is also an important intangible dimension. The knowledge of construction, the vocabulary of forms, and the customs associated with domestic life constitute cultural heritage in their own right. Documenting typologies can be linked to oral history, craft preservation, and community engagement, so that the physical record and the living tradition reinforce one another.

Recommendations

Several measures follow from this analysis. First, a comprehensive inventory of historic homes in Kocaeli should be developed, using a common set of typological categories and recording methods. This inventory should be publicly accessible and regularly updated. Second, conservation guidance should be produced in accessible form, explaining appropriate materials and techniques for repair and adaptation, and training should be provided to craftsmen and owners. Third, planning instruments should recognize typologically significant groups of buildings and establish conservation areas where streetscape and plot patterns are at risk. Fourth, financial incentives, such as grants or tax relief, should support the maintenance of traditional buildings. Fifth, educational programs in schools and universities should incorporate the study of local architecture, fostering a sense of ownership and continuity. Finally, research should continue into the dating, construction, and social history of individual typologies, with attention to underrepresented districts.

Conclusion

The historic homes of Kocaeli constitute a significant and vulnerable part of the province's cultural heritage. Their architectural typologies record the interaction of geography, climate, economy, and social life over several centuries, and they express a distinctive local identity. This paper has argued that systematic typological documentation provides a sound basis for preservation, linking physical form to cultural meaning and supporting strategies that address both buildings and their contexts. Preserving these homes is not only a matter of protecting old structures but of sustaining the knowledge, practices, and collective memory that they embody. Continued research, appropriate conservation practice, and community engagement will be essential if the architectural character of Kocaeli is to remain legible for future generations.

This manuscript investigates whether prioritized experience replay can improve deterministic policy-gradient learning, and it evaluates the approach across several simulated control environments and multiple exploration strategies. The research question is well motivated, since deterministic policy-gradient methods are sensitive to the distribution of replayed transitions, and the authors frame the contribution clearly in the introduction. The experimental design, which varies both the environment and the exploration noise, is a strength because it helps separate the effect of replay prioritization from the idiosyncrasies of any single task. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more precise description of the prioritization scheme, including how priorities are computed, how importance-sampling corrections are applied, and what hyperparameters were used. The reported results show improvements in most settings, but the magnitude of these gains varies considerably, and the paper does not always explain why certain environments benefit more than others. Statistical reporting also needs strengthening: the authors should state the number of random seeds, report confidence intervals or variability across runs, and indicate whether the differences are statistically significant. Several figures would be easier to interpret with consistent axis scales, labeled learning curves, and clearer legends distinguishing the baseline from the prioritized variants. The related work section is informative but omits a few recent studies on replay prioritization in continuous control, and including them would help situate the contribution more accurately. The ablation study is useful, yet it would be more convincing if it isolated the effect of the priority metric from the effect of the sampling frequency. The discussion of exploration strategies is interesting but somewhat brief, and a deeper analysis of how prioritization interacts with different noise processes would add value. The authors should also address potential computational overhead, since maintaining priority structures can increase wall-clock training time, and a fair comparison should account for this cost. Code and configuration files are not provided, which limits reproducibility; releasing them would substantially strengthen the paper. The conclusions are generally supported by the evidence, though some claims about generality should be tempered given the limited set of environments. Overall, the paper presents a promising and reasonably executed study, and I recommend a major revision addressing the methodological details, statistical reporting, and reproducibility concerns before it is considered for acceptance.

The notice came folded inside the morning post, and Ruth read it twice before she understood it. The village council had voted to clear the riverside settlement, where forty families had lived for three generations. The vote had been unanimous, and no one had asked them to speak.

For years the settlers had done everything right. They had filed petitions, attended hearings, and written letters to the county office. Their children had learned the language of forms and deadlines. When the surveyors came, Ruth's grandfather had shaken their hands and offered them tea.

Still, no one at the council table ever looked up when their names were read. Their claim to the land was described as informal, their births as unrecorded, and their testimony as hearsay. A clerk explained, kindly enough, that the records simply did not exist in the form required.

So they gathered in the community hall and drew up one last appeal. It asked for nothing but a fair hearing and a chance to show the old deeds, the church registers, and the names of the dead buried in the hillside plot. They signed it page by page, and Ruth carried it to the council herself.

The reply came three weeks later in a single line. The appeal had been received and filed, and no further action was warranted.

On the last Sunday of the month, the bulldozers arrived before dawn. The families stood at the edge of the road with their bundles and watched the houses fall, one wall at a time. A reporter from the regional paper took a photograph, but the story ran on page nine, beneath an advertisement for tires.

Ruth's family moved into a church basement in the town square, then to a shelter at the edge of the county. Her grandfather never recovered from the loss of the garden he had planted by hand. He spent his last winter reciting the names of the settlement's founders to anyone who would listen.

Years later, a student writing a thesis on local history found the petition in a dusty archive box. She noted in her footnotes that the signatures were careful, the handwriting steady, and the request modest. She wrote that the people who signed it had only ever asked to be counted.
