Online schooling has grown from a niche alternative into a mainstream option for students of all ages and for adults returning to learning. Its benefits lie in flexibility, accessibility, personalization, and the development of skills that matter in the modern workplace. Understanding these advantages helps explain why so many learners now choose to study online.

The most obvious benefit is flexibility. Traditional schools operate on fixed schedules, with set start times, rigid class periods, and a physical location that every student must reach. Online schooling allows learners to structure their days around their own needs. A student who is most alert in the evening can study then, and a parent can balance childcare with coursework. This adaptability makes education possible for people who might otherwise be shut out of it.

Accessibility is closely related to flexibility. Students who live in rural areas, far from well-funded schools or specialized programs, can enroll in courses that would otherwise be unavailable to them. Students with chronic illnesses, physical disabilities, or anxiety that makes crowded classrooms difficult can learn from home in an environment that suits them. Online platforms can also provide captioning, screen readers, and other tools that support diverse learning needs.

For adults, online education offers a path back into learning after years away from the classroom. Working professionals can earn degrees or certificates without leaving their jobs. People changing careers can acquire new skills at a pace that fits their finances and obligations. Retirees and lifelong learners can pursue subjects purely for personal enrichment. The absence of a commute and the option to study part-time reduce many of the barriers that discourage older students.

Online courses also tend to be personalized in ways that traditional classrooms struggle to match. Many programs allow students to revisit recorded lectures, pause to take notes, and replay difficult explanations as often as needed. Adaptive software can identify weak areas and offer targeted practice. Students can move quickly through material they already understand and devote more time to concepts that challenge them.

Cost is another significant advantage. Online programs often charge lower tuition than their on-campus equivalents, and they frequently eliminate expenses for housing, transportation, and campus fees. Students can keep their existing homes and jobs, which reduces the financial strain of higher education. For many families, these savings make the difference between pursuing a degree and abandoning the idea altogether.

Online learning also builds independence and self-discipline. Because students must manage their own schedules and meet deadlines without constant supervision, they develop time-management and organizational skills that serve them throughout life. They learn to seek out information, communicate clearly in writing, and take responsibility for their progress. These habits are valuable in nearly every career.

Digital literacy is an added benefit. Students who learn online regularly use video conferencing, collaborative documents, learning management systems, and online research tools. This familiarity prepares them for remote and hybrid workplaces, which have become common across many industries. Employers increasingly value candidates who can work effectively in digital environments.

Collaboration, though sometimes thought to be weaker online, can be strong in well-designed courses. Discussion boards, group projects conducted through shared documents, and video meetings allow students from different cities, countries, and backgrounds to exchange ideas. Such interactions expose learners to perspectives they might never encounter in a local classroom. Many online students also report building meaningful relationships with classmates and instructors.

Online schooling does not suit everyone, and it carries real challenges. Some learners need the structure and social contact of a physical classroom, and isolation can affect motivation. Reliable internet access and a quiet study space are not guaranteed for every student. Still, these challenges can be addressed through good course design, regular check-ins, and community support, and they should not overshadow the genuine benefits the format offers.

In conclusion, online schooling provides flexibility, accessibility, personalization, affordability, and the development of independence and digital skills. It opens doors for students who face geographic, physical, or financial barriers and gives adults the chance to learn, retrain, and grow at their own pace. As educational institutions continue to refine their online offerings, these benefits are likely to reach even more learners in the years ahead.

Critics have offered a warm but measured response to the latest stage adaptation of the Harry Potter saga, praising its dazzling visual effects and strong ensemble performances while voicing concerns about its running time and dense plotting.

The production, which opened to audiences this autumn, has quickly become one of the most talked-about theatrical events of the year. Reviewers across the country gathered in the stalls on opening night, many arriving with high expectations shaped by decades of devoted fandom.

Many reviewers singled out the staging for special praise. Illusions that conjure flying broomsticks, shifting castle corridors, and spectral figures drifting across the stage were described as genuinely breathtaking. Several critics noted that the production team had clearly invested heavily in the mechanics of the show.

The set design drew equal admiration. Towering structures rise and fall with precise timing, transforming the stage from a bustling classroom to a shadowy forest within seconds. Lighting designers were credited with creating moods that move easily between whimsy and menace.

Performances also earned consistent praise. The actor playing the young wizard at the center of the story was widely described as sincere and emotionally grounded, avoiding caricature while still capturing the character's famous determination. Supporting cast members, particularly those portraying the headmaster and the story's antagonist, were singled out for memorable turns.

Critics also observed that the cast handled the demands of the material with notable discipline. Scenes requiring quick changes in tone rarely felt forced, and the actors managed the transitions between humor and darkness with apparent ease.

Yet the praise was not unqualified. Nearly every reviewer raised the question of length. With a running time that stretches well past the standard theatrical evening, some felt the production tested the patience of audiences, particularly younger viewers attending with families.

The plot itself drew mixed reactions. Those familiar with the source material found the story's many threads satisfying to see realized, but others felt the sheer volume of characters, subplots, and backstory could leave newcomers struggling to follow events. A few critics suggested that the adaptation assumes a level of prior knowledge that not every ticket holder will possess.

Pacing emerged as a recurring concern. Several reviewers argued that the middle act lingers too long over exposition, while the final act arrives in a rush that leaves some emotional beats underdeveloped. Others, however, defended the structure as a faithful reflection of the novels' own sprawling ambition.

Despite these reservations, the overall verdict from the critical community leans positive. Many described the production as a visual feast that justifies its ticket price, even if it does not always achieve the economy of a tightly written drama.

Theatre enthusiasts have responded with enthusiasm, and box office figures reported in the production's first weeks suggest strong demand. Advance bookings for the coming months reportedly outpace those of several other major productions currently running in the city.

The creative team has acknowledged the feedback in interviews. The director said the company was aware of the length concerns and was reviewing the running order, though no changes have yet been announced. The composer, meanwhile, spoke about the challenge of scoring a story that spans many years and a wide emotional range.

Industry observers note that adapting a beloved and sprawling work presents unusual difficulties. Every production must balance the expectations of devoted readers with the needs of audiences encountering the story for the first time, and the balance is rarely easy to strike.

Some commentators have compared the production to earlier stage and screen adaptations, arguing that its ambition sets it apart. Its reliance on live spectacle, they say, gives it a distinct identity, even if it cannot match the intimacy of the books.

Ticket holders leaving the theatre on opening weeks offered a range of views. Many said they were delighted by the magic on display, while others admitted they had felt the evening's length by the final scene. Almost all agreed that the central performances were memorable.

Educators and families have also weighed in. Some parents said the production was suitable for older children but cautioned that its darker passages might unsettle younger viewers. Others praised the way it treats themes of courage, friendship, and loyalty with seriousness.

Looking ahead, the production's future will likely depend on whether its creators can address the criticisms without sacrificing the qualities reviewers most admired. Trimming the running time could broaden its appeal, while clearer storytelling might help newcomers feel more welcome.

For now, the show stands as a significant achievement in large-scale theatre. Its spectacle and performances have earned genuine admiration, and its shortcomings, though real, have not dimmed the excitement surrounding it.

Whether the production will endure beyond its initial run remains to be seen. Its success will ultimately be measured not only by reviews but by the audiences who continue to fill the seats long after the opening night buzz has faded.

Critics seem to agree on one point: the magic, at least, is real.

The manuscript proposes input-conditioned adaptive convolutions for generative adversarial networks, with the stated aims of improving image generation quality and increasing the flexibility of local features. The central idea is sound and well motivated, since static convolution kernels share identical weights across all inputs, which can limit how well a generator adapts its local texture and structure to varying latent codes. The authors situate their work reasonably within the literature on dynamic filters, conditional normalization, and style-based generators, although the related work section would benefit from a more explicit comparison with prior dynamic convolution methods and their computational trade-offs. The method description is clear at a high level, but several implementation details, such as how the kernel-generating network is parameterized, how kernels are normalized to maintain training stability, and where in the generator the adaptive layers are inserted, are described too briefly to permit faithful reproduction. The experimental section evaluates on standard benchmarks and reports Fréchet Inception Distance and Inception Score, which is appropriate, but the authors should also report precision and recall or a similar diversity-sensitive metric, since FID and IS alone can mask mode collapse. The ablation study is a strength, as it isolates the contribution of the adaptive kernels from the added parameter count, yet a control with a static convolution of matched capacity would make the argument considerably stronger. The reported improvements are modest on some datasets, and the paper would be more persuasive with multiple random seeds and confidence intervals, since GAN training is known to exhibit substantial run-to-run variance. The qualitative results are visually plausible, but the selection of showcased samples should be described, and additional uncurated samples or a user study would help substantiate claims about local feature flexibility. The authors' claim that the method improves local feature flexibility would be better supported by an analysis of the learned kernels or the feature maps themselves, rather than inferred solely from final image metrics. The computational cost, including training time, memory use, and inference latency relative to the baseline, is not adequately discussed, which matters for practical adoption. The limitations section is brief and should acknowledge the sensitivity of the approach to training hyperparameters and its potential applicability to other generator architectures. The writing is generally clear, though some sentences in the introduction are repetitive and the notation for kernel generation shifts between sections and should be unified. Figures are informative, but the architecture diagram would benefit from labeled tensor dimensions so readers can trace the adaptive layers through the network. The mathematical formulation of the adaptive convolution should include the full loss terms and any regularization used, so that the training objective is unambiguous. The paper does not clearly state whether code and pretrained models will be released, and I strongly encourage the authors to make their implementation publicly available. Comparisons against recent strong baselines, such as StyleGAN variants or diffusion-based generators where relevant, would contextualize the gains more fairly. The authors should also discuss potential misuse of higher-fidelity generative models and briefly outline mitigations. Overall, the contribution is a plausible and useful incremental advance, and I recommend a major revision addressing the reproducibility details, statistical rigor, and baseline comparisons before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Electric rays are cartilaginous fish belonging to the order Torpediniformes, found in oceans around the world. Their most remarkable feature is a pair of kidney-shaped electric organs located on either side of the head, which are made of modified muscle tissue called electrocytes. These electrocytes are stacked in columns and arranged in a way that allows them to add their voltage together, much like batteries connected in series. Depending on the species, an electric ray can discharge anywhere from about 8 to over 220 volts, although the current is typically low and the shock is rarely dangerous to humans. Rays use these discharges to stun or immobilize prey such as fish and crustaceans before eating them. The shocks also serve as a defense mechanism, deterring predators and warning off threats that might otherwise attack. Electric rays can deliver repeated pulses in quick succession, which makes their hunting especially effective against fast-moving prey. Scientists believe the electric organs evolved from muscle tissue, and the rays' nervous systems are adapted to control the discharges precisely. Some electric rays also use their electric fields to help locate prey, since their sensory organs can detect the faint bioelectric signals that living animals produce. Because they spend much of their time buried in sand or mud on the seafloor, these rays rely on electricity as a powerful tool for survival. Learning about electric rays helps us better understand the diversity of adaptations that have evolved in marine life.

The manuscript addresses an important and timely problem: how to leverage large pools of unlabeled speech to improve automatic speech recognition when labeled data is scarce, and whether the resulting representations generalize across acoustic and linguistic domains. The authors frame the work clearly, situating self-supervised speech representation learning within the broader trajectory of contrastive and masked-prediction objectives and motivating the study with the practical cost of transcription. The central claim, that pretraining on unlabeled audio yields substantial word error rate reductions in low-resource semi-supervised settings, is plausible and consistent with prior findings, though the magnitude of the gains should be verified against the strongest supervised baselines. The experimental design compares several pretraining objectives and fine-tuning regimes, which is a strength, but the paper would benefit from a more explicit statement of the labeled-data fractions used, since conclusions about semi-supervision depend heavily on this choice. The cross-domain robustness evaluation is a valuable component, yet the selection of target domains appears somewhat narrow, and the authors should justify why these particular corpora represent meaningful distribution shifts, such as changes in accent, recording conditions, or spontaneous versus read speech. The reported results would be more convincing with multiple random seeds or confidence intervals, as differences between some configurations are small enough that run-to-run variance could account for them. The ablation on the amount of unlabeled pretraining data is informative, but the authors do not clearly separate the effect of data quantity from data diversity, which limits the generality of the recommendations they offer. The description of hyperparameters and training schedules is mostly adequate, although a few key settings, including learning rate warmup and the masking strategy details, are underspecified and would hinder reproduction. The authors should release code and pretrained checkpoints, or at minimum precise configuration files, to allow independent verification of the main results. The related work section is thorough in covering self-supervised speech models but could more directly compare against recent semi-supervised pseudo-labeling approaches, which are strong competitors in the same setting. The discussion of cross-domain failure cases is a welcome addition, as it honestly identifies conditions under which the learned representations degrade, and this analysis could be expanded with error breakdowns by speaker group or noise condition. The writing is generally clear, though some sections repeat results already presented in tables, and tightening these would improve readability. Figures showing learning curves across labeled-data fractions would strengthen the central argument and make the trade-offs easier to interpret at a glance. The computational cost of pretraining is discussed only briefly, and a more explicit accounting of compute budgets relative to baselines would help readers judge the practical value of the approach. Ethical considerations around the collection and use of unlabeled speech data, including consent and representation of underrepresented speakers, receive little attention and should be addressed. Overall, the paper presents a useful empirical study with promising results, and I recommend a major revision that addresses the statistical reporting, baseline comparisons, data specification, and reproducibility concerns before the work can be considered for acceptance.

First impressions are quick and convenient, but they are rarely complete. We form them within seconds, relying on appearance, behavior in a single setting, or a few words overheard from across a room. Such judgments help us navigate crowded situations, yet they also invite error, because they reduce a whole person to a fragment. Getting to know someone is the process that challenges these fragments and gradually replaces them with a fuller picture.

Consider a classmate who seems aloof at first, quiet and reserved while others chatter during lunch. Many people would label such a person as unfriendly or uninterested. Spending time together, however, often reveals a different story. The quiet student may be shy in groups but warm and funny one-on-one, or may be carrying worries that make social settings exhausting. Discovering this does not excuse the first impression as wrong so much as show that it was incomplete.

Familiarity also exposes the contradictions that every person contains. A teacher who appears strict in class might turn out to be deeply patient during office hours, or a loud and confident friend might admit to constant self-doubt. These contradictions are not signs of hypocrisy but evidence of a complex inner life that no single observation can capture. Learning to hold such contrasts together is a mark of maturity in how we judge others.

Shared experiences accelerate this process. Working together on a difficult project, traveling, or facing an unexpected problem shows how someone behaves under pressure, which is often more revealing than their everyday demeanor. A person who seemed careless may prove remarkably dependable when it matters, while someone who appeared dependable may buckle under stress. These moments disclose character in ways that casual conversation rarely can.

Getting to know someone also requires patience and a willingness to be wrong. It means asking questions, listening closely, and allowing a person to unfold at their own pace. Those who rush to conclusions miss the subtler qualities that emerge only over time. Curiosity, rather than certainty, becomes the key to understanding.

Ultimately, the gap between first impressions and true personality reminds us to approach others with humility. Every person we meet carries stories, values, and struggles that are invisible at a glance. By taking the time to know someone, we not only correct our assumptions but also open ourselves to connections that might otherwise never have formed.

Demand for homeless accommodation in Hull has risen sharply in recent months, according to local charities and council workers, as cuts to support services leave more people struggling to find and keep a safe place to live. Outreach teams report that referrals for emergency beds have climbed steadily since the spring, with some hostels operating at or near full capacity for most of the week. Support workers say the pressure is compounded by reduced funding for drug and alcohol services, mental health outreach and housing advice, which many residents rely on to avoid losing their tenancies. Local voluntary organisations warn that when these services are scaled back, people often reach crisis point more quickly, making them harder and more expensive to help. One charity manager said her team was turning away several people each week because there were simply no available places, a situation she described as unprecedented in her years of work in the city. Council officials acknowledge the growing strain but say they are working with partners to make the best use of limited resources and to prevent homelessness where possible. Housing advisers point to a shortage of affordable private rented accommodation as a further factor, with landlords leaving the market and rents remaining high relative to local incomes. Residents who have experienced homelessness in Hull described the difficulty of moving between temporary placements, sofas and night shelters while waiting for a more permanent solution. Campaigners are calling on the government and local authorities to restore funding for support services, arguing that early intervention is both more humane and more cost-effective than emergency responses. Some have also urged the expansion of supported housing schemes that combine a stable home with help to address the underlying causes of homelessness. The council has said it will review current provision in the coming months, with a report expected to be presented to councillors early next year. Charities say they will continue to monitor demand closely and hope the review leads to a sustained increase in support. For now, those working on the front line say the need is greater than they have seen in many years, and the human cost of that gap is becoming increasingly visible across the city.

Whether students should attend school in person or learn remotely from home is a question that has grown more urgent since the widespread shift to online education. Each option offers distinct advantages and drawbacks, and the right answer depends on the needs of individual students as well as the communities they live in. On balance, in-person schooling remains the stronger default, though remote learning has real value in specific circumstances.

The most compelling argument for in-person school is the quality of direct human interaction. Teachers can read a confused expression, notice when a student is struggling, and adjust a lesson on the spot. A good teacher in a classroom can pose a follow-up question, redirect a distracted pupil, or encourage a shy student to speak. These small moments are difficult to replicate through a screen.

In-person learning also supports social development. Children learn cooperation, conflict resolution, empathy, and communication largely by interacting with peers. Recess, group projects, lunch conversations, and extracurricular activities teach skills that no worksheet can fully capture. For younger students especially, the classroom is where they learn how to function in a community outside their families.

Structure and routine matter as well. Attending school at set hours creates habits of punctuality, focus, and self-discipline that carry into adult life. Many students at home face distractions such as household chores, video games, or unsupervised time, which can make it harder to stay on task. The physical separation between home and school helps many young people mentally shift into learning mode.

Access to resources is another important factor. Schools provide libraries, laboratories, art studios, sports facilities, counselors, nurses, and meals for many children who depend on them. When students learn remotely, these benefits can disappear, and the gap between well-resourced and under-resourced families can widen. A student without reliable internet, a quiet place to study, or a responsible adult at home may fall far behind.

Remote learning, however, has genuine strengths that should not be dismissed. It offers flexibility for students with chronic illnesses, those with severe anxiety, or those who must care for family members. Students who live far from school, or who travel frequently for athletic or artistic training, may benefit from being able to learn on their own schedule. For some, remote study allows deeper focus, since they can work at their own pace without the pressure of a crowded room.

Remote learning also builds independence and digital literacy. Students who manage their own assignments and deadlines develop skills that will serve them in college and in many modern workplaces. Online tools can give learners access to courses, experts, and materials their local schools may not offer.

Yet the experience of recent years revealed significant problems with remote learning as a long-term replacement for classrooms. Many students fell behind in core subjects, and the losses were largest among younger children and those from low-income households. Reports of rising loneliness, anxiety, and disengagement among students who spent extended periods at home raised serious concerns about mental health. Learning that depends on self-motivation tends to fail the students who most need guidance.

These findings suggest that the choice need not be all or nothing. A hybrid approach can combine the relationships and supervision of the classroom with the flexibility of home study. Schools might offer remote options for students with specific medical or family needs while keeping in-person instruction as the foundation. Such arrangements require careful planning, including reliable technology and clear expectations, but they acknowledge that students differ.

Ultimately, in-person schooling should remain the primary model for most students, because it best supports academic achievement, social growth, and emotional well-being. Remote learning should be available as a thoughtful option for those who genuinely need it, not as a substitute that leaves students isolated and behind. By investing in strong classrooms and flexible support, schools can give every student the best chance to learn and grow.

Religious activists played central roles in twentieth-century American struggles for social and political justice, drawing on faith traditions to challenge injustice. Martin Luther King Jr., a Baptist minister, led the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, grounding civil rights demands in Christian teachings on love and human dignity. Black churches served as organizing hubs, providing meeting spaces, leadership, and networks that sustained movements such as the 1960s sit-ins and the Freedom Rides. Dorothy Day, a Catholic social activist, co-founded the Catholic Worker Movement in 1933, combining direct aid to the poor with advocacy for labor rights and nonviolent resistance to war. Abraham Joshua Heschel, a Jewish theologian, marched alongside King in Selma in 1965 and described his participation as "praying with my feet." Quaker and other pacifist groups, including the American Friends Service Committee, worked for peace, prisoner rights, and aid to refugees, earning a Nobel Peace Prize in 1947. Religious coalitions also shaped labor and immigrant rights, as clergy supported strikes, sanctuary efforts, and advocacy for fair treatment of workers. These activists often faced opposition, arrest, and violence, yet their work helped reshape American law and public conscience. Their legacy shows how moral and spiritual convictions can inspire sustained collective action for justice.

A Widow's Journey Through Grief After Hillsborough

Sheffield, England. Nearly four decades after the Hillsborough disaster, one widow is sharing her memories of the husband she lost and the family life they built together before that fateful day in April 1989. Her account offers a deeply personal window into the human cost of a tragedy that shocked the nation and reshaped the fight for justice in British football.

The disaster occurred on April 15, 1989, at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, during the FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest. Ninety-seven Liverpool supporters died as a result of crushing injuries in the crowd, and many more were injured. For the families left behind, the loss was sudden, senseless, and, in the years that followed, compounded by a long struggle for the truth.

The woman, who asked that her identity be kept private, described her husband as a devoted father and a man who lived for the people around him. They had married young and built a modest but happy home, filled with the everyday rituals that define a family: Sunday lunches, school runs, and evenings spent talking over cups of tea.

He was a man of routine, she recalled, and football was woven into the fabric of their lives. He had followed Liverpool since boyhood, and going to matches was something he shared with his friends and, when they were old enough, his children. That Saturday in April was meant to be an ordinary outing, one of many.

She remembers the morning clearly. He was in good spirits, joking as he got ready and promising to be home in time for dinner. She waved him off without a second thought, a moment she has replayed countless times since.

The hours that followed were agonizing. As news of the disaster spread, she waited with a mounting sense of dread, unable to reach anyone who could tell her what had happened. Like many families, she spent a long and terrible night not knowing whether he was alive.

Confirmation came in the early hours, and with it a grief she describes as impossible to put into words. The house that had been full of his voice and laughter fell suddenly silent. Her children asked questions she struggled to answer, and she found herself trying to hold the family together while she herself was falling apart.

In the immediate aftermath, daily life became a series of tasks she could barely manage. Funeral arrangements, the phone calls, the visitors, and the paperwork all arrived at once. She leaned heavily on relatives, friends, and neighbors, many of whom had their own losses to bear.

She speaks of the strange burden of carrying on for her children. Even as she grieved, she felt a responsibility to keep routines going, to make sure birthdays were marked and holidays were not entirely lost to sadness. Those efforts, she admits, were often exhausting.

The loss of her husband also meant the loss of a partner in the countless small decisions of family life. She described the quiet moments as especially painful, the times when she turned to tell him something and remembered he was gone.

Over time, she says, her grief changed shape without ever fully leaving. There were years when it felt raw and overwhelming and others when she could think of him with a gentleness that brought comfort. Anniversaries, she explained, remain difficult, bringing back the memories of that day with particular force.

The wider context of Hillsborough added another layer to her suffering. In the days and weeks after the disaster, many fans were wrongly blamed for the tragedy, with false allegations circulated in parts of the press. For the families, the injustice of being blamed for their loved ones' deaths compounded their pain.

She recalls the anger she felt at those accusations. Her husband, she insists, was not a troublemaker but an ordinary man who went to watch his team with a sense of pride and belonging. The suggestion that he or others like him had caused their own deaths was, to her, an unbearable insult.

The families campaigned tirelessly for decades to uncover the truth. They pressed for official inquiries, challenged inaccurate findings, and demanded accountability from those responsible. Their persistence eventually led to new investigations and, in time, a clearer public understanding of what happened that day.

Many of those campaigns were led by women who, like her, had lost husbands, sons, and fathers. Together they formed a powerful community, drawing strength from shared experience and a common determination that their loved ones would not be forgotten.

She describes the support of this community as essential to her own healing. Meeting others who understood the particular pain of losing someone in such circumstances helped her feel less alone. Shared memorials, marches, and gatherings gave her a place to honor her husband alongside others.

Official acknowledgment of the truth came in stages. Inquiries over the years examined the causes of the disaster, and a later independent panel reviewed previously undisclosed documents. Its findings, published in 2012, concluded that the disaster was caused by failures of policing and stadium safety, and that the initial narrative blaming fans had been false.

She welcomed those findings but says they could never restore what was lost. Justice, she said, mattered deeply, yet no official conclusion could bring her husband back or return the years she and her children had been denied with him.

The inquests into the deaths were a long and emotional process. Families sat through testimony, listened to detailed accounts of what their loved ones endured, and waited years for legal resolution. She remembers the courtroom as a place of both sorrow and hope.

Eventually, in 2016, a new inquest jury returned verdicts of unlawful killing for the 96 victims whose deaths were examined, with the 97th victim later dying in hospital. For many families, the verdicts were a vindication that the truth had finally been formally recognized.

She described the moment the verdicts were read as one of mixed emotions. Relief and pride sat alongside a sadness that the process had taken so long and had cost so much. Her husband's name, she said, was finally spoken with the dignity it deserved.

Raising her children without their father has shaped each of them in different ways. She says they have grown into thoughtful, resilient adults who carry their father's warmth and sense of humor. Many of their conversations return to him, and she treasures these shared memories.

She keeps photographs and small keepsakes around the house, including the scarf he wore to matches and a few letters he wrote before they were married. These objects, she says, help her feel close to him and give her grandchildren a sense of the grandfather they never met.

Her grandchildren, she notes with a smile, have heard stories about their grandfather's love of football and his habit of humming old songs while he cooked. Passing those stories down has become a way of keeping him present in the family.

She reflects on the ways the disaster changed her understanding of life. She learned how fragile it can be and how quickly ordinary days can end. She also learned about the strength people find in one another when tragedy strikes.

Asked what she would most like people to remember about her husband, she paused before answering. He was kind, she said, funny, and deeply loyal to the people he loved. He was not a statistic or a headline but a man with dreams, habits, and a family who adored him.

She hopes that by sharing her story, others will understand that behind every name associated with Hillsborough was a real person with a life full of meaning. Each of the 97 men, women, and children who died, she said, had people who missed them every day.

The anniversary of the disaster is always a time of reflection for her. She attends memorial services, visits the places connected to that day, and spends time with family and friends who understand what it means. These moments, she says, are both painful and necessary.

She also takes comfort in the progress that has been made in stadium safety and in the understanding of crowd management. While nothing can undo the loss, she believes lessons learned from Hillsborough have helped protect countless fans in the years since.

Looking back, she describes her life as one shaped by love, loss, and perseverance. The grief has never fully left, but it has been joined by memories of joy, pride in her family, and gratitude for the community that stood beside her.

As the interview drew to a close, she spoke again about her husband. She said that if she could tell him one thing, it would be that the family he left behind has kept going, that his children and grandchildren carry his spirit, and that he has never been forgotten.

Her story stands as a reminder of the lasting impact of the Hillsborough disaster, not only on the city of Sheffield and the city of Liverpool, but on the countless families whose lives were changed forever that spring afternoon in 1989.

Across the world, cities are rethinking how people move, and these changes are reshaping the rhythm and character of urban life. For much of the twentieth century, many planners assumed that the automobile would define the modern city, and entire neighborhoods were built around highways, parking lots, and wide arterial roads. That approach brought convenience to some residents but also produced noise, pollution, traffic deaths, and streets that felt hostile to anyone on foot or on a bicycle. Today, a growing number of communities are questioning that legacy and experimenting with alternatives.

Car-free communities are among the most visible of these experiments. In places such as Venice, the historic center has long banned private motor traffic, so residents rely on boats, bicycles, and their own feet. Smaller projects in Europe and North America have followed, closing main streets to cars and turning them into plazas where children play and cafes spill onto the pavement. Proponents argue that such spaces make neighborhoods quieter, safer, and more socially connected.

Transportation choices more broadly are also changing the way people live. Cities including Copenhagen, Amsterdam, and Utrecht have invested heavily in bicycle infrastructure, with protected lanes, dedicated signals, and secure parking. In these cities, cycling is not a niche hobby but an everyday habit for commuters of all ages. The result is less congestion and fewer emissions, along with a public health benefit from regular physical activity.

Public transit has been transformed as well. Subway systems, light rail, and bus rapid transit lines have expanded in many metropolitan areas, offering residents alternatives to driving. When transit is frequent, reliable, and affordable, it can reduce the number of cars needed and free up land once devoted to parking. Some cities have converted former parking spaces into parks, bike lanes, or outdoor seating.

These shifts carry economic consequences. Local businesses often find that pedestrians and cyclists spend money in shops and restaurants more frequently than drivers who pass through quickly. Reduced car ownership can also lower household expenses, since car payments, insurance, fuel, and maintenance represent a significant share of many family budgets. At the same time, transitions can be uneven, and low-income residents may be displaced when improvements raise nearby property values.

Equity remains a central concern in this debate. Car-free initiatives must ensure that people with disabilities, the elderly, and workers with irregular schedules are not left behind. Accessible sidewalks, reliable paratransit, and affordable transit passes are essential if these changes are to benefit everyone. Otherwise, the gains may be concentrated among wealthier residents who can afford to live in newly desirable areas.

Looking ahead, the future of urban mobility will likely combine several approaches rather than relying on a single solution. Walking, cycling, transit, shared vehicles, and carefully managed private cars may each play a role in different places. The most successful cities will be those that design streets for people first and treat transportation as a means to build communities rather than simply to move vehicles. In this sense, the choices cities make about how people travel are also choices about what kind of life they want their residents to lead.

This manuscript proposes a reinforcement learning framework in which multiple cooperative goal-setting agents jointly generate training curricula intended to remain balanced across task difficulty and skill coverage. The problem is well motivated, since hand-designed curricula scale poorly and automated curriculum learning is an active area with real practical value. The authors position their contribution clearly relative to prior work on teacher-student curriculum models and self-play, and the related work section is generally thorough. The core idea of decomposing curriculum design across cooperating agents, each responsible for a different axis of balance, is interesting and plausibly novel in its specific formulation. However, the paper's central claim that the resulting curricula are "balanced" is never defined operationally, and the reader is left to infer the intended meaning from context. A formal metric for balance, or at least a clear qualitative definition with justification, would substantially strengthen the work. The reward design for the goal-setting agents is described only briefly, and it is unclear how cooperation is enforced when individual agents' incentives may diverge from the shared objective. The experimental section evaluates on two benchmark environments, which is a reasonable start, but both are relatively small and the results may not transfer to larger or more heterogeneous task distributions. The baselines are limited to a single fixed curriculum and one prior automated method, and stronger comparisons against recent curriculum learning approaches would make the claimed improvements more convincing. Reported gains are given without confidence intervals or details on the number of random seeds, so it is difficult to judge whether the differences exceed run-to-run variance. The ablation study is informative in isolating the contribution of the cooperative component, though the removal of inter-agent communication is treated as a binary condition when a graded analysis would be more revealing. The hyperparameter choices are listed in an appendix, which is helpful for reproducibility, but the paper does not report the compute budget or training time, which limits practical assessment. Code availability is mentioned as forthcoming, and releasing the implementation upon publication would greatly aid verification. The discussion of failure cases is brief, and a more candid analysis of when the curricula collapse or overfit to particular task orderings would benefit readers. The writing is generally clear, though several figures lack informative captions and the notation for the joint policy is introduced inconsistently across sections. The theoretical motivation for the cooperative objective is sketched but not developed, and a short formal analysis of convergence or of the stability of the joint curriculum would add rigor. Overall, the paper offers a promising and reasonably original direction, but its claims of balance and cooperative benefit need sharper definitions, broader experiments, and more statistically grounded evidence before the conclusions can be considered fully supported. I recommend a major revision.

Presidential elections should be decided by the national popular vote because every citizen's ballot should carry equal weight regardless of where they live. Under the Electoral College, a candidate can win the presidency while losing the national popular vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016, which undermines public confidence in the outcome. Today, campaigns concentrate their time, money, and attention on a small number of swing states, leaving voters in safe states largely ignored. A national popular vote would encourage candidates to campaign everywhere and to address the concerns of all Americans, not just those in battleground regions. Critics argue that the Electoral College protects smaller states, but a direct vote would still give every state a voice through its share of the total electorate. Moving to a national popular vote would also simplify the process, eliminating the risk that a handful of electors could disregard the will of the voters. For these reasons, the nation should adopt a national popular vote to determine who wins the presidency.

In the high-profile Nina Wang inheritance saga, Peter Chan Wing-kwong, a Hong Kong businessman and former associate of the late Nina Wang, has been convicted of forging a will in an attempt to claim her vast fortune. Wang, Hong Kong's richest woman and chairwoman of the Chinachem property group, died in 2007 after a long illness, leaving behind an estate valued at billions of dollars. Chan had long asserted that he was the rightful heir, presenting a document he said was a will drafted by Wang that named him as her beneficiary. Prosecutors argued that the document was a fabrication, and the court heard extensive evidence challenging its authenticity, including forensic analysis of the signatures and the circumstances in which the will was produced. The trial drew intense public attention in Hong Kong, given the enormous sums involved and the long-running legal battles that had followed Wang's death. Chan's supporters maintained his innocence throughout the proceedings, insisting that the will was genuine and that he had been unfairly targeted. Ultimately, the court found the evidence sufficient to convict him of forgery and related offences, rejecting his claim to the estate. The verdict was widely reported as a major moment in a dispute that had divided Wang's relatives, business associates, and the broader public for years. Chan's conviction also raised questions about how estates of such magnitude are administered and how disputed wills are investigated. Legal observers noted that the case highlighted the vulnerabilities that can arise when large fortunes pass without an undisputed succession plan. Sentencing and any further appeals were expected to follow, and the matter was closely watched by the financial and legal communities in Hong Kong. The outcome brought a significant, though not necessarily final, chapter to one of the most closely followed inheritance disputes in the city's history.

Should the president be chosen by direct national popular vote rather than through the Electoral College? The question strikes at the heart of American democracy, because it asks whether every citizen's vote should carry equal weight in selecting the nation's highest office. A direct popular vote would embody the principle that each person's ballot should count the same, regardless of where they live. Under the current system, a voter in a populous state often has a vote that carries less weight than a voter in a small state, because electoral votes are allocated by state and each state receives at least three. Supporters of reform argue that a national popular vote would end this inequality and ensure that the winner reflects the choice of the majority of Americans. The Electoral College also produces the troubling possibility that a candidate can win the presidency while losing the national popular vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016. Such outcomes can erode public confidence in the legitimacy of elections. Critics of the current system further note that presidential campaigns concentrate their time and money in a handful of swing states, leaving voters in safe states largely ignored. A national vote would encourage candidates to speak to every region and to every voter. Defenders of the Electoral College, however, contend that it protects the interests of smaller states and rural areas that might otherwise be overlooked by candidates focused only on dense population centers. They point out that the framers designed the system as a compromise between election by Congress and election by popular vote, and that it reinforces the federal character of the nation. Supporters also argue that the requirement to win a broad coalition of states encourages candidates to build national support rather than rely on a single region. A direct popular vote could, in their view, lead to a fragmented political landscape in which a candidate wins with only a small plurality. Some proposals attempt to address this concern by requiring a runoff election when no candidate receives a clear majority. Others, such as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, seek to achieve direct election indirectly by having participating states pledge their electoral votes to the national popular winner. Such approaches raise their own constitutional and practical questions. Ultimately, the debate turns on competing values: equal individual representation on one side, and federalism and regional balance on the other. Each side offers serious arguments, and reasonable citizens can disagree. Still, the principle that the nation's leader should be chosen by the clear will of its people is compelling. A democracy should strive to make every vote count equally, and a direct popular vote, with safeguards against fragmentation, would move the nation closer to that ideal.

Long before written history, the fertile lands between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers and the Levant hosted some of the earliest complex societies on Earth. Excavations at sites such as Jericho, Tell Abu Hureyra, and Göbekli Tepe reveal that settled communities and early farming took root in the Fertile Crescent during the Neolithic period, roughly 10,000 years ago. At Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, archaeologists have uncovered thousands of clay tablets bearing proto-cuneiform script, which record administrative and economic activity and mark the emergence of writing around 3300 BCE. Temple complexes such as the ziggurats and monumental architecture at Eridu and Ur show how religious institutions organized labor, trade, and food storage in early city-states. In the Levant, sites like Ebla in northern Syria yielded a large archive of cuneiform tablets, illuminating the diplomacy, commerce, and political rivalries of the third millennium BCE. Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, produced an alphabetic script and extensive literary texts that reveal the religious and cultural life of a major Late Bronze Age trading port. Excavations at Megiddo, Hazor, and Lachish document fortified cities, shifting political power, and destruction layers that help date the rise and fall of regional kingdoms. Trade networks linking these cities to Egypt, Anatolia, and the Indus region are evident in imported goods such as lapis lazuli, obsidian, and cedar timber. Together, these discoveries show that Mesopotamian and Syrian-Palestinian societies developed through interconnected cycles of agricultural innovation, urbanization, writing, and political competition. Ongoing research continues to refine these timelines, and scholars regularly revise interpretations as new excavations and scientific dating methods emerge.

Subject: Invitation to the Conference on ADHD Diagnosis, Ritalin Prescribing, and the Disease Promotion Controversy

Dear Colleague,

I am writing to invite you to an upcoming conference that will examine some of the most debated questions in contemporary psychiatry and pharmacology. The event will bring together clinicians, researchers, legal scholars, patient advocates, and policymakers to discuss attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the prescribing of methylphenidate, commonly sold as Ritalin, and the legal controversy surrounding allegations that the condition has been promoted beyond what the evidence supports.

ADHD is one of the most frequently diagnosed neurodevelopmental conditions in children and adults. Diagnostic rates have risen substantially over the past two decades, and this rise has prompted sustained public and professional debate. Some observers see the increase as evidence of better recognition and treatment of a real and impairing disorder. Others question whether diagnostic thresholds have widened, whether symptoms are overidentified in certain populations, and whether commercial interests have influenced how the condition is described and treated.

Methylphenidate remains one of the most widely prescribed stimulant medications for ADHD. Its benefits in reducing core symptoms are supported by a substantial body of clinical research, yet questions persist about long-term outcomes, appropriate dosing, prescribing patterns across regions and age groups, and the potential for misuse and diversion. The conference will address these clinical and public health dimensions with attention to both the strength of the evidence and its limitations.

The legal dimension of the discussion has drawn considerable attention. Lawsuits and regulatory inquiries have raised allegations that certain parties promoted ADHD diagnosis or stimulant treatment in ways that misrepresented risks, benefits, or the underlying science. Some of these matters have resulted in settlements, while others remain contested. Panelists will examine the outcomes of these proceedings, the standards of evidence courts have applied, and what they mean for manufacturers, prescribers, and regulators.

Several sessions will focus on diagnostic practice. These will consider how clinicians assess ADHD, the role of rating scales and clinical interviews, the importance of ruling out alternative explanations such as sleep disorders, anxiety, trauma, and learning differences, and the challenges of diagnosing adults and individuals from underrepresented communities. We will also look at how diagnostic criteria have evolved across editions of the diagnostic manuals and how those changes have affected prevalence estimates.

A separate panel will address prescribing practice. Presenters will review data on prescribing trends, the role of primary care versus specialist care, the use of stimulants alongside behavioral interventions, and the monitoring requirements for patients on long-term treatment. Attention will also be given to shortages, regulatory controls on controlled substances, and the implications for patients who depend on consistent access.

We have also planned a session dedicated to patient and family perspectives. Individuals living with ADHD and their caregivers will describe their experiences with diagnosis, treatment decisions, side effects, and the stigma that can accompany both the condition and its medication. Their insights are central to understanding what is at stake in these debates.

Researchers presenting at the conference will share recent findings on the neurobiology of ADHD, genetic and environmental risk factors, and the outcomes of both pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments. Where studies disagree, presenters have been asked to explain the methodological differences that may account for the divergence.

The conference is designed to be balanced rather than advocacy-driven. Speakers have been selected to represent a range of viewpoints, including those who view current practice as appropriate, those who consider it excessive, and those who believe it is inadequate for people who need help. We believe that a careful, evidence-based exchange serves patients better than polarized argument.

The program will include moderated panel discussions, invited presentations, and a poster session for early-career researchers. Continuing education credits are expected to be available for eligible clinicians, pending accreditation approval, and we will confirm details in the coming weeks.

Registration is now open, and early registration is encouraged, as space in some sessions will be limited. Students and patient advocates may apply for reduced-fee places, and information about these options is available on the conference website.

We will also host a virtual participation option for those who cannot attend in person. Recordings of selected sessions will be made available afterward to registered attendees, subject to speaker consent and applicable privacy considerations.

The organizing committee welcomes suggestions for topics or speakers. If you have research, clinical experience, or lived experience that you believe would contribute to the program, please reply to this message with a brief description and we will consider it for inclusion.

Thank you for your interest in this important area. We hope you will join us for what promises to be a rigorous and wide-ranging discussion.

With kind regards,

The Conference Organizing Committee

Please visit the conference website for the full program, speaker biographies, venue details, and registration information. If you have questions about any aspect of the event, please contact the committee directly by replying to this email.

The manuscript proposes a graph neural network representation with claimed theoretical expressivity gains over standard message-passing architectures, and evaluates it on minimum vertex cover optimization. The motivation is clear and relevant, since minimum vertex cover is an NP-hard combinatorial problem that serves as a useful testbed for whether learned models can capture structural properties beyond the reach of 1-WL-bounded networks. The theoretical contribution is the most important part of the paper, and the authors should state their expressivity result as a formal theorem with precise assumptions, including the class of graphs, the input features, and the model's depth and width. The proof sketch in the main text is too brief to verify, so I recommend moving a complete argument to the appendix and clarifying which separations are proven and which are only demonstrated empirically. The experimental setup would benefit from a stronger set of baselines, including classical approximation algorithms such as the maximal matching 2-approximation and greedy heuristics, as well as established neural combinatorial optimization methods. Reporting only approximation ratios on synthetic random graphs is insufficient, and the authors should include structured graph families and real-world instances to test generalization. The paper should also report results across multiple random seeds with variance or confidence intervals, since differences between methods are otherwise hard to interpret. Ablations isolating the contribution of the proposed representation from increases in parameter count or training compute would strengthen the causal claim. The related work section omits several recent lines of research on expressive GNNs and learned vertex cover solvers, and should be expanded to position the contribution accurately. Overall, the core idea is promising and potentially significant, but the current manuscript does not yet fully support its theoretical and empirical claims, and I recommend a major revision.

Schools should not require students to participate in extracurricular activities, because students are best positioned to decide how they spend their own time. Extracurriculars such as sports, clubs, music, and volunteer work offer real benefits, but those benefits depend on genuine interest and commitment. When a student is forced into an activity they do not care about, the experience often breeds resentment rather than growth. A student who is compelled to join the chess club may spend every meeting watching the clock instead of learning strategy or making friends. Freedom of choice also allows students to pursue passions that a school might not offer, such as robotics, animation, or a part-time job that teaches responsibility. Requirements can also burden students who already have demanding schedules, including those who care for siblings, work to support their families, or manage health challenges. For these students, a mandatory activity could mean less sleep, lower grades, or a harder time keeping up with academics. Critics argue that required participation builds teamwork and discipline, and that some students would never try anything without a push. This is a fair point, but encouragement and access can achieve the same goal without coercion. Schools can advertise a wide range of options, offer introductory sessions, and make activities affordable and easy to reach. Mentors and teachers can personally invite students who seem isolated, which is often more effective than a rule. Voluntary participation also tends to produce more committed members, since students who choose an activity usually show up, contribute, and take pride in their work. Requiring participation may also weaken the sense that these activities belong to the students themselves. Clubs and teams thrive when they are built around shared enthusiasm rather than attendance records. There is also a question of fairness, since a mandatory system may favor students whose families can afford equipment, travel, and fees. Choice does not eliminate these barriers, but it allows schools to focus their resources where they are most needed. Ultimately, the goal of education is to prepare young people to make responsible decisions about their own lives. Letting students choose their activities gives them practice at that skill, while still supporting them with guidance and opportunity. Schools that trust students in this way are more likely to raise adults who take initiative and commit to what they value.

Wanda Group's Chinese-themed entertainment complex is putting new pressure on Walt Disney Company's ambitions in China's booming theme park market. The development, which combines attractions, hotels, and retail space, is designed to draw domestic visitors who increasingly prefer experiences rooted in Chinese culture, history, and folklore. Industry analysts say the project reflects a broader shift in consumer tastes, as younger Chinese travelers show growing interest in homegrown brands and storytelling. Wanda has positioned the complex as a showcase for Chinese heritage, incorporating local legends and traditional architecture into its design. Disney, which operates Shanghai Disneyland and has long been seen as a leader in the Chinese market, has faced questions about how to keep its appeal strong amid this competition. Analysts note that Shanghai Disneyland has performed well since opening, but rivals are rapidly expanding their offerings in tier-two and tier-three cities. Wanda's approach also benefits from lower land and development costs in some regions, allowing it to compete on price as well as theme. Industry observers caution that the outcome will depend on execution, visitor satisfaction, and the ability to sustain attendance after the initial opening rush. Disney has not publicly announced a direct response to the project, though the company continues to invest in its China operations. As China's leisure economy grows, the contest between international giants and domestic developers is expected to intensify in the coming years.

Mexicans reacted with a mix of dismay and anxiety this week after Donald Trump's election victory, as many in the country braced for what his return to power could mean for trade, migration, and the peso. In Mexico City, shoppers and commuters spoke openly about their worries, with several saying they feared a return to the tariff threats and harsh rhetoric that marked Trump's first term. Economists warned that uncertainty alone could weigh on investment decisions in the months ahead. The Mexican peso came under pressure in the hours after the results became clear, reflecting investor nervousness about the direction of bilateral relations. Analysts noted that Mexico is the largest trading partner of the United States, and that roughly four-fifths of its exports are sent north. Business leaders in the manufacturing sector, particularly in automotive and electronics production, expressed concern that proposed tariffs could disrupt supply chains that have been built over decades. Many factory owners in border states such as Nuevo Leon, Chihuahua, and Coahuila said they were already reviewing contingency plans. Farmers, too, voiced unease, pointing to the importance of agricultural exports such as avocados, tomatoes, and cattle to the American market. Migration emerged as another central concern. Trump campaigned on a promise of large-scale deportations and tighter border controls, and advocacy groups on both sides of the border said they were preparing for increased enforcement. Families with relatives in the United States expressed fear about possible separations, while some community leaders called for emergency planning and legal assistance. Mexican government officials said they would seek to maintain constructive dialogue with the incoming administration. President Claudia Sheinbaum, who took office recently, struck a measured tone, emphasizing sovereignty while reaffirming a willingness to cooperate on shared priorities such as security and trade. Her administration has said it will defend Mexican interests and pursue negotiations grounded in mutual respect. Not all reactions were negative. Some business owners said they hoped a pragmatic relationship could emerge, arguing that the economic integration built under the USMCA trade agreement gives both countries strong incentives to avoid a trade war. Others pointed out that Trump's first administration ultimately renegotiated NAFTA rather than abandoning it, and they expressed cautious optimism that similar compromises might be reached. Still, the prevailing mood in many parts of the country was one of wariness. In cafes and markets, residents spoke of feeling overlooked in a political debate in which Mexico often serves as a symbol rather than a partner. Some younger voters said they worried about job prospects and the cost of living if economic tensions escalated. Religious leaders and civil society groups called for compassion toward migrants and urged policymakers on both sides to avoid rhetoric that stigmatizes Mexicans. Analysts cautioned that the coming months will be critical. Key decisions on tariffs, immigration enforcement, and the future of the USMCA review process could reshape the relationship for years. For now, Mexicans appear to be watching closely, hoping for stability while preparing for a period of uncertainty.

The Quaker Tapestry is a large embroidered work that tells the story of the Religious Society of Friends, commonly known as Quakers, from its origins in seventeenth-century England to the present day. The idea began in 1981, when Anne Wynn-Wilson, a Quaker from Hertfordshire, England, proposed that Friends create a visual record of their history and beliefs. Her suggestion grew into a collaborative project involving thousands of people across many countries, including Britain, the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. Each panel was designed and stitched by different groups of volunteers, who worked in meeting houses, schools, and community centers. The finished work consists of 77 individual panels, each measuring about one meter square, that together form a continuous narrative. Panels depict scenes such as George Fox preaching, the persecution Quakers faced in early Britain, the founding of Pennsylvania by William Penn, and Quaker involvement in abolition, relief work, and peace efforts. The stitching techniques were varied, drawing on the skills and traditions of the many contributors, and the designs were drawn from historical research and community discussion. The project took several years to complete, with the final panels finished in the late 1980s. The tapestry was first exhibited in full in 1990 and has since been displayed at venues in Britain, the United States, and elsewhere. Its public exhibitions have served both as educational displays and as occasions for dialogue about Quaker values such as simplicity, equality, and nonviolence. The work is now housed in the Friends Historical Library and has been shown to visitors who may have little prior knowledge of Quakerism. Today the Quaker Tapestry is regarded as a notable example of community textile art and as a lasting record of a faith tradition shaped by collective participation.

The manuscript addresses an important practical problem: reducing the memory and bandwidth footprint of large neural networks through product quantization guided by activation statistics. The central premise, that weight reconstruction error should be weighted by the magnitude and distribution of the activations that multiply those weights, is well motivated and aligns with a growing body of post-training compression work. The authors are right to frame compression as an optimization over the function the layer computes rather than over raw weight-space distance alone. The paper is clearly written in most sections, and the problem statement is easy to follow.

The second contribution, concerning structural redundancy, is the most interesting part of the work. The authors observe that rows of a weight matrix often share correlated patterns, and they argue that exploiting this redundancy before quantization can reduce codebook size without a proportional loss in accuracy. This observation is plausible and worth investigating, but the manuscript would benefit from a more precise definition of what constitutes structural redundancy in the experiments. At present the reader must infer the metric from figures, and a formal definition with a sensitivity analysis would make the claim much stronger.

The treatment of row permutations deserves particular attention. Reordering rows so that similar vectors fall into the same subspace before quantization is a known technique, but the authors extend it by making the permutation activation-aware. This is a reasonable extension, yet the paper does not clearly separate the gain attributable to the permutation from the gain attributable to the activation weighting. An ablation that applies each component independently, and then jointly, would isolate their effects and make the conclusions more convincing.

The experimental section covers several architectures, including a convolutional network and a transformer, which is a welcome breadth. However, the models are relatively small compared with the systems that motivate the work, and the authors should acknowledge whether the observed trends hold at larger scales. Reporting results on a single benchmark per architecture also limits the generality of the conclusions. Additional tasks, or at least a discussion of why the chosen benchmarks are representative, would help.

The baselines are a mixed strength. The authors compare against standard product quantization and a scalar quantization method, which are appropriate, but they omit several recent activation-aware post-training quantization approaches that address similar goals. Including at least one of these would position the contribution more accurately within the literature. The authors should also state whether baseline hyperparameters were tuned with the same budget as the proposed method, since unequal tuning can distort the comparison.

Reported accuracy figures are given with a single run in most tables. For compression results, where calibration data selection can introduce variance, multiple seeds or calibration subsets should be used, and standard deviations should be reported. Without this, it is difficult to judge whether the differences of a few tenths of a percentage point are meaningful. The authors partly address this in the appendix, but the main-text claims rely on the single-run numbers.

The calibration procedure itself needs more detail. The paper states that activation statistics are collected from a small held-out set, but it does not specify the size of that set, how it was sampled, or how sensitive the results are to its composition. Because the method's advantage depends on these statistics being representative, this is a material omission. A short study varying the calibration set size would be valuable.

The compression ratios reported are expressed in bits per weight, which is a useful convention. However, the paper should also report the overhead of storing codebooks, permutation indices, and any auxiliary scaling factors, since these can meaningfully reduce the effective compression at small layer sizes. Presenting the total storage cost, including metadata, would give a more honest picture of the memory savings.

Latency and throughput are discussed only briefly. Compression is often motivated by inference speed, yet quantized weights require dequantization or specialized kernels, and the permutation step may add runtime cost. The authors should report measured inference latency on at least one hardware platform, along with the cost of the permutation and codebook lookup, so that readers can assess the practical trade-offs.

The theoretical analysis is limited. The paper offers an intuitive justification for activation weighting but does not provide a bound on the output error introduced by quantization under the proposed objective. A simple analysis for a single linear layer, showing how the expected output error relates to the activation covariance, would substantially strengthen the methodological contribution.

The related work section is adequate but somewhat brief. It would benefit from a clearer comparison of how product quantization differs from vector quantization and low-rank factorization in terms of both accuracy and hardware compatibility. A concise table summarizing these methods along a few shared axes would help readers place the contribution.

The writing is generally clear, though several passages repeat the same claim in slightly different words, which lengthens the introduction without adding information. Tightening these sections would improve readability. The notation is mostly consistent, but the symbol used for the activation covariance changes between the method and experiments sections, and this should be unified.

Figures are informative in most cases. The plot of error against bits per weight is effective, but the legend is small and the curves for the two strongest methods are difficult to distinguish in grayscale. Larger markers or distinct line styles would resolve this. The permutation illustration would also benefit from an accompanying caption that explains what the color encoding represents.

The authors provide code, which is commendable and greatly aids reproducibility. The repository should include the exact calibration data sampling procedure and the random seeds used for each reported result, so that the tables can be reproduced without guesswork. A brief README describing the pipeline end to end would further lower the barrier to reuse.

The ethical and broader impact discussion is minimal and appropriately so for a compression methodology, but a sentence noting that compressed models may inherit or amplify biases present in the original weights, and that accuracy should be checked across subgroups, would be a responsible addition.

The paper's claims are generally supported by the evidence presented, though several are stated more strongly in the abstract and conclusion than the experiments warrant. In particular, the phrase describing the method as broadly applicable should be qualified, since the results cover only a narrow set of architectures and tasks. Moderating these claims would improve the alignment between the text and the data.

In summary, the paper tackles a relevant problem with a sensible combination of activation-aware weighting and structural preprocessing. The core idea is promising and the empirical results are encouraging. The main weaknesses are the lack of ablations separating the two components, limited baselines, single-run reporting, incomplete accounting of storage overhead, and insufficient latency analysis. Addressing these issues would make the contribution considerably more convincing.

My recommendation is major revision. The work has merit and could make a useful addition to the compression literature, but the claims need stronger experimental support and more careful qualification before the paper is ready for publication.
