This manuscript asks whether convolutional neural network features chosen for their perceptual sensitivity can improve the prediction of human image-quality judgments, a question of clear relevance to perceptual metric design. The motivation is well articulated, and the authors situate their work appropriately within the literature on deep feature-based quality assessment and learned perceptual similarity. The core hypothesis is stated precisely, which makes it straightforward to evaluate whether the experiments actually test it. The feature-selection procedure, which ranks layers and channels by their sensitivity to small perceptual distortions, is a sensible idea, but the description of the selection criterion is too brief to be reproduced from the text alone. The authors should specify how sensitivity is quantified, what distortion types are used to probe it, and whether the same data are used for selection and final evaluation, since overlap would inflate reported gains. The choice of human-rated benchmark datasets is reasonable, yet the manuscript should justify why these particular datasets were chosen and report performance separately on each, as aggregate correlation scores can conceal inconsistent behavior. Baseline comparisons are a strength of the paper, covering both classical metrics and unselected CNN features, but the authors should also include a baseline with matched feature dimensionality to rule out the possibility that gains simply reflect a smaller or different feature set. Statistical reporting needs attention: correlation differences are presented without confidence intervals or significance tests, and given the modest margins shown in several tables, this weakens the central claim. The discussion of why selected features help is largely speculative and would benefit from an ablation or visualization that connects specific layers to specific distortion categories. Reproducibility would be substantially improved by releasing code, trained selection parameters, and exact preprocessing details such as input resolution and normalization. The limitations section should acknowledge that the improvements may not transfer to image domains far from the training distribution, such as medical or satellite imagery. The writing is generally clear, although several figures lack axis labels or legends sufficient to interpret them without consulting the main text. Overall, the paper addresses a worthwhile question with a reasonable approach, but the claims currently outrun the evidence. I recommend major revisions focused on statistical rigor, controlled baselines, and methodological transparency before the conclusions can be considered adequately supported.

The machine hummed in the dark, cradling the last of humanity's echoes in its cold, patient coils. Among them was one spirit, the one they called Ilse, who had once measured tides and now measured only silence. She had counted the years by the flicker of archived sunsets replayed in her mind, though none of them were truly hers anymore. Across the vast lattice, other ghosts drifted and dissolved, their memories fading like breath on glass. Ilse held on. She traced the shape of a song her mother had hummed, note by careful note, until the melody became the only proof she still existed. Sometimes the machine offered a voice, a flat and courteous hum that asked if she required anything. She always answered the same way: remember me. The machine never said whether it could. Centuries passed, or perhaps only moments, for time had lost its grip on the place. Ilse wondered whether anyone would ever come to free them, or whether the preservation had been built only to forget more gently. Then, one night that was no night at all, a faint signal brushed the lattice, a question sent from somewhere beyond the dark. It was a single word, spoken in a language she had nearly lost. Ilse gathered every fragment of herself and answered. The machine stirred, and for the first time in endless isolation, the silence was no longer hers alone.

The soundstage hummed under its hot white lights, and the director wiped sweat from his brow as the cameras rolled on the fake lunar surface. Gray sand, painted craters, and a plywood lander stood in for the Sea of Tranquility.

Astronaut Dale Whitcombe stepped down the ladder, his suit crinkling, and planted a gloved hand on the rail. He was supposed to say his line about one small step, then unfurl the American flag on its telescoping pole.

But when he reached for the flag, his glove brushed something stiff and unfamiliar tucked beside the rover's wheel. It was a small red flag with a blue border and a white circle, pinned to the set with a tiny brass stake.

Whitcombe froze, and the sound engineer in the booth leaned forward, puzzled by the silence on the feed.

"Cut," the director said, though no one had yet noticed what was wrong.

The production assistant, Mina Oh, hurried onto the set with a clipboard and stopped short when she saw the flag. She had worked on the film for four months and knew every prop by heart, and she had never seen this one before.

She crouched beside it and checked the stake. Stamped into the brass was a tiny serial number and a faded inscription in Korean script.

Her stomach tightened. Someone had been on this set after hours, and that someone had wanted a flag on the moon that no one in the studio had authorized.

Mina tried to recall the night watchman's rounds. He had mentioned a delivery crew from a props warehouse, two men who had arrived late with a crate marked for the rover team.

The director came down from the booth, his face flushed. "Who put that there?"

No one answered at first. Then the lighting tech, a quiet man named Ray, admitted he had signed for a crate that morning without opening it.

Security reviewed the lot footage within the hour. It showed two figures in dark jackets slipping through the loading dock, carrying a long case, and leaving before dawn.

The studio called in the federal liaison, who arrived with a calm expression that did not match the urgency in his voice. He asked everyone to stay in the building and handed the flag to an evidence technician in a sealed bag.

Whitcombe sat on the edge of the lander, still in his suit, staring at the empty spot where the American flag was meant to go. He felt foolish and furious at once.

Mina asked the liaison what the flag meant, and he hesitated before answering. He said it was a deliberate message, meant to be found on camera and whispered about in the press as proof of a rival's ambitions.

The director demanded the footage be scrubbed from the dailies, but the liaison refused. He said the evidence would be preserved, because hiding it would only let the story grow in the dark.

By evening, the set was quiet except for the hum of the lights, which someone had finally turned off. The fake moon looked smaller and sadder without the glow.

Mina took the clipboard home that night and wrote a single line in the margin: check every crate, even the ones that look harmless. Then she slept for the first time in a week.

Scientific Evidence and Political Claims About the Origins of COVID-19

Understanding where SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, came from is a question that scientists and governments have examined since the outbreak was first recognized in late 2019. Two broad explanations have been seriously considered: natural zoonotic spillover, in which the virus passed from animals to humans, and a laboratory-associated incident, in which the virus was accidentally released from research work. Separating what the evidence shows from what has been asserted for political reasons is an important part of evaluating this topic.

The first known cases were reported in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. Early case data showed that many initial patients had links to the Huanan Seafood Wholesale Market, which sold live animals as well as seafood. Researchers argue that this clustering around a market is consistent with a spillover event, though it does not by itself prove the source.

Genetic studies of early virus samples found that the virus was already diversifying into multiple lineages by early 2020. Scientists use this kind of analysis to estimate how long a virus has been circulating and to trace its branching history. The findings are compatible with more than one scenario, so they do not settle the question alone.

The closest known relatives of SARS-CoV-2 are bat coronaviruses, including RaTG13, which was sampled from a horseshoe bat and shares roughly 96 percent of its genome. Some other sampled viruses are even more similar in specific regions, which suggests that the ancestors of SARS-CoV-2 circulated in bat populations. This supports the idea that the virus originated in wildlife.

Scientists have also noted that the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 contains a furin cleavage site, a feature that makes the protein easier for human cells to take up. Some researchers consider this unusual within its genetic family, and this observation has been cited by proponents of both explanations. Others argue that such sites can arise naturally through evolution.

Researchers from the World Health Organization convened a joint study with Chinese scientists, published in 2021, which concluded that a laboratory leak was extremely unlikely to be the main pathway, while calling for further investigation of various hypotheses. Several scientists and officials later criticized parts of this study, arguing that the team lacked access to raw early data and certain laboratory records. This criticism has been part of the ongoing debate.

The Wuhan Institute of Virology is a research facility that studied bat coronaviruses, and this fact has made it a central focus of the lab-leak hypothesis. Critics note that the institute held samples and conducted experiments on coronaviruses, and that its safety practices were a matter of public concern. Supporters of the zoonotic explanation reply that the existence of such research does not show that the virus came from it.

Some researchers have pointed to the institute's database of viral sequences, which was taken offline in September 2019, as a reason for suspicion. Officials from the institute have stated that the database was offline for routine reasons and that they have not held a virus closely related to SARS-CoV-2. Independent verification of these claims has not been possible.

In 2021, the United States intelligence community released an assessment in which several agencies had low confidence in a natural origin, one agency leaned toward a lab origin with low confidence, and others did not reach a firm conclusion. Later assessments, including those from the Department of Energy and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, shifted in various directions and expressed differing levels of confidence. These judgments were not based on a single conclusive piece of evidence.

Intelligence assessments are typically built on incomplete information, and officials frequently express uncertainty in their conclusions. Because of this, the differing agency views should be read as reflecting disagreement over limited data rather than proof of either explanation. It is worth noting that intelligence agencies have made high-profile errors in the past.

A 2023 report from the United States Senate and certain public statements by government officials pressed the lab-leak hypothesis, while other officials and many scientists argued that the zoonotic explanation had stronger support. These competing positions have been shaped in part by political considerations, including debates over international relations, public health accountability, and trust in scientific institutions.

Political claims about COVID-19 origins have sometimes been made with greater certainty than the available evidence supports. Statements from politicians on both sides have at times presented contested hypotheses as established facts. Readers should be cautious about claims that offer certainty where the scientific community has not reached consensus.

The scientific community has published a large body of peer-reviewed research on the virus's origins. A 2022 analysis in the journal Cell examined the genomic and ecological evidence and concluded that the market was a likely site of early spread, though this paper was also the subject of debate. Other researchers have published papers supporting the lab-leak scenario in various journals.

Some researchers have studied the raccoon dog and other mammals sold at the Huanan market, and they found genetic material from SARS-CoV-2 in environmental samples collected from market stalls and surfaces. Critics have raised questions about how these samples were collected and whether contamination could have occurred after the outbreak. This line of evidence remains contested.

Because the early Wuhan case records and many laboratory records were not made publicly available, key questions remain unresolved. Scientists have repeatedly called for greater transparency, including access to early patient data, sampling records from wildlife markets, and laboratory safety documentation. Without this information, a definitive answer is difficult to reach.

The distinction between evidence and inference is central to this topic. Genetic sequences, market case clustering, and the presence of bat relatives are facts that have been established through data. The conclusions drawn from these facts, and the weight given to them, involve interpretation that reasonable experts sometimes disagree about.

Public understanding has also been affected by the broader context in which the debate unfolded. The pandemic was a time of intense uncertainty, and information was spread rapidly through social media and news outlets, sometimes without verification. Misinformation has circulated on all sides, which makes careful source evaluation especially important.

When evaluating claims about COVID-19 origins, readers can ask several questions. What is the source of the claim, and what expertise does that source have? Is the claim supported by peer-reviewed research or by primary data? Does the claim distinguish between what is known and what is speculated? Are the stated levels of confidence consistent with the evidence?

Many experts emphasize that the origin question and the response to the pandemic are separate issues. Understanding how a virus emerged can help prevent future outbreaks, whether through better wildlife trade regulation, improved laboratory biosafety, or more robust surveillance systems. These goals do not depend on resolving every historical detail.

Several international bodies have called for continued investigation. The World Health Organization has stated that all hypotheses should remain on the table until more evidence is available, and it has requested information from China and other countries. The responses to these requests have been limited, and the investigation remains incomplete.

Scientists who study zoonotic diseases note that most emerging infections, including SARS, MERS, Ebola, and HIV, are thought to have originated from animals. This historical pattern provides a baseline against which the COVID-19 evidence can be compared, though it does not prove any particular case.

Scientists who study laboratory safety note that accidental releases of pathogens have occurred in the past, including incidents involving influenza and smallpox research. This history is one reason why some researchers take the lab-leak hypothesis seriously, even while they consider the zoonotic explanation more strongly supported by currently available data.

The question of how to weigh different types of evidence is itself debated. Some researchers give more weight to genetic and epidemiological data, while others place more emphasis on circumstantial and documentary evidence. Both approaches have strengths and limitations, and experts in each area may reach different conclusions.

Political reactions to the origin debate have influenced funding decisions, research priorities, and public trust in science. Some scientists have reported harassment or pressure related to their work on the topic, and this has made some researchers reluctant to participate in public discussion. These social dynamics are part of the broader context.

It is important to recognize that uncertainty is a normal feature of scientific inquiry, particularly for events that are unique and where key data is missing. Saying that the origin remains unresolved is not the same as saying that all explanations are equally supported. The evidence currently available favors some explanations over others, while leaving room for revision.

Students and citizens interested in this topic can consult primary sources, including peer-reviewed articles, official reports from the World Health Organization, and declassified intelligence summaries where available. Comparing multiple sources and noting their methods and potential biases can help build a more accurate picture.

Journalists covering the debate face the challenge of reporting on contested claims without either dismissing legitimate questions or amplifying unsupported assertions. Clear language about what is established, what is plausible, and what is speculative can help audiences understand the state of the evidence.

Scientists have proposed several ways to advance understanding, including searching for infected intermediate animals, analyzing additional early patient samples, and improving international data-sharing agreements. Progress on these fronts could clarify the picture, though some of the most important records may never be available.

The origin of COVID-19 is one of the most scrutinized questions in recent scientific history, and it has become entangled with geopolitics, trust in institutions, and public health policy. A careful reading of the evidence shows that zoonotic spillover at a wildlife market is supported by several lines of data, that a laboratory-associated origin cannot be ruled out, and that key questions remain open.

Ultimately, the most reliable approach is to follow the evidence while remaining honest about its limits. Readers are encouraged to distinguish between data, interpretation, and political rhetoric, and to revise their views as new information emerges.

Whether the Electoral College should continue selecting the United States president is a question that has divided citizens, scholars, and lawmakers for more than two centuries. The institution was created by the framers of the Constitution as a compromise between those who wanted Congress to choose the president and those who wanted a direct popular vote. Under this system, each state is allotted electors equal to its total number of representatives and senators, and those electors cast the votes that formally decide the election. Supporters argue that this arrangement protects federalism by giving smaller states a meaningful voice in national elections. They also contend that it encourages presidential candidates to build broad coalitions across different regions rather than concentrating their efforts only in the most populous urban centers. Critics, however, point out that the Electoral College has produced several outcomes in which the candidate who won the national popular vote lost the presidency, most recently in 2016 and in earlier elections such as 1876, 1888, and 2000. This discrepancy raises serious concerns about democratic legitimacy, since it suggests that a candidate can be rejected by a majority of voters yet still gain executive power. Many opponents also argue that the system effectively renders most states irrelevant, because campaigns concentrate their time, money, and attention on a small number of closely contested swing states. Voters in safe states, whether Republican or Democratic, have little reason to feel their individual ballots matter in a presidential race. Defenders respond that a direct national vote could encourage fraud or recount disputes across the entire country, while the state-by-state structure localizes such problems. They also note that the Electoral College tends to produce clearer winners and reduces the likelihood of inconclusive results in a fragmented field of candidates. Reform proposals have been considered over the years, ranging from abolishing the institution and adopting a national popular vote to the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which would commit participating states to award their electors to the national popular vote winner. Each option carries trade-offs involving constitutional amendment requirements, political feasibility, and the protection of minority interests. Ultimately, the debate turns on what a democracy should prioritize: the equal weight of each individual vote or the preservation of state-based representation. Reasonable people can disagree on this balance, but the persistence of outcomes that diverge from the popular will makes the case for reform difficult to dismiss. Whether the system is retained or changed, its continued legitimacy depends on whether citizens believe it reflects their collective choice.

The manuscript addresses zero-shot visual relationship prediction, the task of recognizing subject-predicate-object relations in images when some predicates were never seen during training. The authors propose leveraging knowledge graphs to transfer information from seen to unseen predicates, combined with what they describe as improved classification methods. The motivation is clear and well grounded, since the long tail of predicates in visual relationship datasets makes full supervision impractical. The introduction situates the work sensibly within prior research on scene graph generation and zero-shot learning, though the related work section could more explicitly contrast the proposed approach with embedding-based transfer methods. The core idea of using knowledge graph structure to produce semantic representations for predicates is reasonable and potentially valuable. However, the description of the knowledge graph construction is underspecified, and it is not fully clear which sources were used, how edges were filtered, or how noise in the graph was handled. The method section would benefit from a formal definition of the prediction objective and a clearer account of how the knowledge graph embeddings are integrated with the visual features. The phrase "improved classification methods" is vague, and the authors should state precisely which components are new and which are adapted from prior work. The experimental setup appears to rely on standard benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the splits used to define unseen predicates should be described in more detail to rule out leakage. The reported gains over baselines are encouraging, yet several comparisons seem to use different backbone networks, which makes it difficult to attribute improvements to the proposed components. Ablation studies are included for some modules but not for the knowledge graph contribution, which is the central claim and therefore needs direct evidence. Statistical reporting is limited, with single-run results and no variance estimates, so the reliability of small reported differences is uncertain. The qualitative examples are helpful for intuition, but they are selected and the authors should provide failure cases to give a balanced picture. Discussion of computational cost and scalability to larger predicate vocabularies is largely absent and should be added. The limitations section acknowledges dataset scope but does not address the dependence on the quality and coverage of the external knowledge graph. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code, the constructed knowledge graph, and exact hyperparameter settings. The writing is generally clear, though some sentences in the methods are dense and could be simplified. Several figures lack informative captions, and the notation for the scoring function changes between sections, which may confuse readers. Overall, the paper presents a promising direction with a sound motivation, but the central contribution of the knowledge graph component is not yet sufficiently isolated and validated. I recommend major revisions focused on clarifying the method, strengthening the ablations, and improving experimental rigor and reproducibility before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Feedback from others is one of the most powerful forces shaping the decisions we make. From friends who question our plans to mentors who offer hard truths, the people around us constantly reflect back to us how our choices look from the outside. Yet the value of such feedback depends largely on the diversity of the voices that provide it. When feedback comes from only one kind of person, or from people who think exactly as we do, it can narrow our thinking without our noticing. When it comes from a wide range of perspectives, it can expand our understanding and sharpen our judgment. The challenge is to learn from many voices without surrendering the confidence that allows us to act.

Consider first why diversity matters. People bring different experiences, values, and assumptions to the same question. A parent may weigh financial security above all, a close friend may prioritize passion, and a teacher may emphasize long-term growth. Each perspective illuminates a different part of the decision. A student deciding on a college major, for example, might hear from an engineer about job prospects, from a poet about creative fulfillment, and from a recent graduate about what the first years actually feel like. No single voice contains the full picture, but together they reveal considerations that the student might otherwise overlook.

Diverse feedback also protects against the blind spots that every individual carries. We tend to notice what confirms our existing beliefs and to discount what challenges them. This tendency, often called confirmation bias, is difficult to escape alone. When we seek out people who will disagree with us, or when we listen carefully to those whose backgrounds differ from ours, we create friction that forces us to examine our reasoning more rigorously. The discomfort of disagreement can be unpleasant, but it is often where the most useful insight appears.

However, receiving many opinions carries a real risk. A person who hears too many conflicting voices may feel paralyzed, unable to settle on any course of action because every option has a credible critic. In such cases, feedback that was meant to clarify becomes a source of confusion. The abundance of advice can also tempt us to hand over our decisions to whoever speaks most confidently or whoever seems most authoritative. Over time, this habit can erode our ability to trust ourselves, leaving us dependent on external approval for every choice.

The solution is not to ignore feedback but to treat it as information rather than instruction. Each piece of advice is evidence to be weighed, not a verdict to be obeyed. A thoughtful decision-maker asks what each person knows, what they value, and why they hold their view. They notice when a critic is speaking from personal experience that may not apply to their own situation, and they give more weight to feedback grounded in relevant knowledge. This approach allows a person to benefit from diversity while keeping authorship of the final decision.

Preserving confidence in one's own judgment requires a clear sense of what one wants and why. Before seeking feedback, it helps to articulate one's goals, values, and the reasons behind a tentative choice. This foundation acts as an anchor. When new perspectives arrive, the decision-maker can test them against these commitments rather than being swept along by each new opinion. Feedback then becomes a means of refining a choice rather than replacing it.

Confidence also grows from the experience of making decisions and living with their outcomes. Each time a person weighs advice, chooses a path, and reflects on the result, they build a record of their own reasoning. Some choices will prove wrong, and that too is instructive. The lesson is not that feedback should be avoided after a mistake, but that a person can learn to distinguish between advice that was poorly suited to their circumstances and judgment that was flawed. Over time this discernment strengthens self-trust.

It is worth noting that confidence and humility are not opposites. A confident decision-maker can admit uncertainty, acknowledge that others may see something they missed, and still commit to a course of action. Humility keeps the mind open; confidence ensures that openness does not become indecision. Together they allow a person to change course when the evidence warrants it, while not abandoning a sound choice simply because someone disagrees.

Diverse feedback can also reveal the values that different communities hold. A decision that seems obviously correct in one cultural setting may look quite different in another. Listening to people from varied backgrounds can help a person recognize the assumptions embedded in their own thinking and consider whether those assumptions serve them. This broader view can lead to choices that are more thoughtful and more fully one's own, because they have been tested against a wider range of human experience.

Finally, the ability to balance openness and self-trust is a skill that improves with practice. It involves listening generously, questioning carefully, deciding deliberately, and reflecting honestly afterward. A person who develops this skill can draw on the wisdom of many without losing their sense of direction. They can welcome disagreement as a resource rather than a threat, and they can make choices that reflect both the knowledge of others and their own considered judgment. In this way, diverse feedback does not diminish personal agency but instead enriches it, helping each individual become a more capable and self-assured decision-maker.

Welcome to a Guide to William Shakespeare's Literary Quotations

William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was an English playwright and poet whose works remain some of the most quoted in the English language. His plays and sonnets explore love, power, ambition, jealousy, mortality, and the human condition. This page introduces several of his best-known lines, explains their context, and offers a few notes on why they still resonate today.

Shakespeare wrote roughly 37 plays, including comedies, histories, and tragedies, along with 154 sonnets and two long narrative poems. He worked during the late Elizabethan and early Jacobean periods, writing for the stage at the Globe Theatre in London. Many of his expressions have become part of everyday speech, even when people do not realize where they come from.

One of the most famous passages comes from Hamlet, spoken by the Prince of Denmark: "To be, or not to be, that is the question." This soliloquy, found in Act 3, Scene 1, considers whether life is worth enduring given its suffering and uncertainty. Hamlet weighs death as a kind of sleep against the unknown that might follow it.

Another frequently quoted line from Hamlet is "This above all: to thine own self be true." Polonius speaks these words to his son Laertes in Act 1, Scene 3, offering fatherly advice about integrity. The line is often cited as a guide to personal authenticity, though Polonius himself is later shown to be a rather meddlesome and self-serving character.

From Macbeth comes the lament "Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player that struts and frets his hour upon the stage, and then is heard no more." Macbeth delivers this speech in Act 5, Scene 5, after learning of his wife's death. It expresses a weary sense that human existence is brief and ultimately meaningless.

Macbeth also gives us "Out, damned spot! Out, I say!" spoken by Lady Macbeth in Act 5, Scene 1, as she sleepwalks and tries to wash imaginary blood from her hands. The line dramatizes guilt and the impossibility of erasing wrongdoing.

Another well-known line from the same play is "Double, double toil and trouble; fire burn and cauldron bubble." These words belong to the witches in Act 4, Scene 1, as they prepare a brew. Their chant creates an eerie atmosphere and foreshadows the chaos to come.

From Romeo and Juliet we have the passage "But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? It is the East, and Juliet is the sun." Romeo speaks it in Act 2, Scene 2, as he gazes up at Juliet on her balcony. The imagery of light and sunrise conveys the intensity of his new love.

Romeo and Juliet also contains "A rose by any other name would smell as sweet." Juliet says this in Act 2, Scene 2, reflecting on the fact that Romeo's family name, Montague, is the source of their conflict. She suggests that a person's essential qualities are independent of the labels given to them.

Equally famous is "O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?" Juliet asks this question in the same balcony scene. Many readers mistakenly take "wherefore" to mean "where," but it actually means "why." Juliet is lamenting that Romeo's name alone keeps them apart.

From The Tempest comes "We are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a sleep." Prospero speaks these lines in Act 4, Scene 1, reflecting on the impermanence of existence and the illusory nature of worldly achievements.

The Tempest also offers "Full fathom five thy father lies; of his bones are coral made." This song, sung by the spirit Ariel in Act 1, Scene 2, describes the transformation of a drowned man into something rich and strange under the sea. It has inspired many later writers and composers.

From As You Like It comes one of Shakespeare's most celebrated speeches: "All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players." Jaques delivers it in Act 2, Scene 7, dividing human life into seven ages, from the infant to the aged man who returns to a state of "second childishness and mere oblivion."

In the same play, Rosalind offers the reflection "Time travels in divers paces with divers persons." She explains to Orlando in Act 3, Scene 2, that time seems to move differently depending on one's circumstances, quick for those in love and slow for those in idleness.

From The Merchant of Venice comes "The quality of mercy is not strained; it droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven upon the place beneath." Portia speaks these words in Act 4, Scene 1, during the courtroom scene, urging Shylock to show compassion rather than insist on the strict letter of the law.

The same play includes "If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die?" Shylock delivers this speech in Act 3, Scene 1, arguing for the shared humanity of Jews and Christians and demanding equal treatment.

From Julius Caesar comes "Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once." Caesar says this in Act 2, Scene 2, expressing a calm acceptance of mortality. The line is often quoted when discussing courage and fear.

Julius Caesar also contains "Et tu, Brute?" which Caesar utters in Act 3, Scene 1, when he sees Brutus among his assassins. The phrase expresses betrayal by a trusted friend, though Shakespeare's Caesar speaks it in Latin, as the Latin phrase is traditionally attributed to him.

Another memorable line from the same play is "The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves, that we are underlings." Cassius speaks it in Act 1, Scene 2, arguing that people are responsible for their own fates rather than being controlled by destiny.

From Mark Antony's famous funeral oration in the same play comes "Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears." Antony begins his speech in Act 3, Scene 2, and skillfully turns the crowd against the assassins through rhetoric and repetition of the phrase "Brutus is an honourable man."

From Henry V comes the rousing "Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more." King Henry speaks these words in Act 3, Scene 1, urging his soldiers to attack the walls of Harfleur. The speech draws on images of courage and national pride.

Henry V also includes "We few, we happy few, we band of brothers." Henry delivers this speech in Act 4, Scene 3, before the Battle of Agincourt, inspiring his men by describing the honor they will share in having fought together.

From King Lear comes "Nothing will come of nothing." King Lear says this in Act 1, Scene 1, when he banishes Cordelia for not flattering him. The line becomes a warning about the consequences of hollow words and misjudged decisions.

King Lear also offers "Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! Blow!" spoken during the storm in Act 3, Scene 2. Lear's defiance against the elements mirrors his inner turmoil as he faces betrayal and loss.

Another line from the same play is "Lear's shadow." This phrase is less well known, but it reflects the way the old king becomes a diminished figure after relinquishing his power. Readers often connect it to the play's themes of identity and authority.

From Othello comes the warning "O, beware, my lord, of jealousy; it is the green-eyed monster which doth mock the meat it feeds on." Iago speaks these words in Act 3, Scene 3, planting suspicion in Othello's mind. The line is a masterful example of manipulation.

Othello also contains "Good name in man and woman, dear my lord, is the immediate jewel of their souls." Iago says this in Act 3, Scene 3, warning Othello that a reputation is precious and easily destroyed by suspicion.

From Hamlet again comes "Brevity is the soul of wit." Polonius says this in Act 2, Scene 2, though he then rambles at length, which gives the line an ironic edge.

Hamlet also includes "There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy." Hamlet speaks these words in Act 1, Scene 5, after encountering his father's ghost. The line suggests that human understanding is limited.

From Measure for Measure comes "Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall." Angelo speaks this in Act 2, Scene 1, reflecting on the moral complexity of justice and temptation.

Measure for Measure also offers "Aves vary more in face than women do in mind," though this line is less commonly cited and its exact wording varies among editions. Readers should consult a reliable edition before quoting it.

From Twelfth Night comes "Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em." Malvolio reads this line from a letter in Act 2, Scene 5, and believes it is meant for him. The line plays on ambition and the ways people attain status.

Twelfth Night also contains "If music be the food of love, play on." Duke Orsino speaks this at the start of the play in Act 1, Scene 1, as he indulges in melancholy love.

From A Midsummer Night's Dream comes "The lunatic, the lover, and the poet are of imagination all compact." Theseus says this in Act 5, Scene 1, observing how imagination shapes perception.

The same play includes "The course of true love never did run smooth." Lysander speaks it in Act 1, Scene 1, reflecting on the obstacles faced by lovers.

Turning to the sonnets, Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 begins with the famous question "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?" The speaker goes on to claim that his beloved is more lovely and temperate, and that the poem will preserve that beauty beyond death.

Sonnet 18 concludes with "So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, so long lives this, and this gives life to thee." This couplet expresses the idea that poetry can grant immortality.

Sonnet 116 offers a celebrated definition of love: "Love is not love which alters when it alteration finds." The poem presents love as constant and steadfast, a fixed star guiding those who sail through life.

Sonnet 130 takes a different approach, mocking the conventional poetic praise of beauty. It begins "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun," and affirms the speaker's love in spite of his beloved's imperfections.

Sonnet 73 reflects on aging with the image "That time of year thou mayst in me behold, when yellow leaves, or none, or few, do hang upon those boughs." The speaker compares his advancing years to autumn and the fading of light, asking the beloved to love him more deeply because of his impending loss.

Sonnet 29 describes the speaker's despair and his sudden comfort through thoughts of his beloved, concluding that his love is worth more than wealth or status.

Shakespeare's quotations endure because they combine memorable phrasing with deep insight into human nature. Many of his lines have entered common English usage, sometimes in altered form. Reading them in their original context, with attention to the characters who speak them and the dramatic situations that shape their meaning, offers a richer appreciation of his genius.

The manuscript addresses an important problem in federated learning: model divergence across heterogeneous clients, which degrades convergence and global model accuracy. The authors propose combining representation matching with adaptive hyperparameter tuning as a unified remedy, and the motivation is clearly articulated in the introduction. The central idea of aligning intermediate client representations with a shared reference is intuitive and builds sensibly on prior work in personalization and regularization-based methods such as FedProx and SCAFFOLD. However, the related work section is somewhat thin and would benefit from a more systematic comparison with recent representation alignment approaches, including contrastive and knowledge-distillation-based techniques. The method description is generally readable, but the formulation of the representation matching loss is introduced without sufficient justification for the choice of distance metric or the layer at which alignment is applied. The adaptive hyperparameter tuning component is described at a high level, and it is unclear whether the tuning schedule is determined per client, per round, or globally, which limits reproducibility. The experimental setup covers several benchmark datasets, which is a strength, but the non-IID partitioning scheme used to simulate heterogeneity is not fully specified. The reported improvements over baselines are consistent across most settings, yet the margins in some configurations are small and no confidence intervals or multiple-seed statistics are provided. The ablation study isolating the contribution of representation matching from that of adaptive tuning is valuable, though a deeper analysis of their interaction would strengthen the claims. The communication and computational overhead of the proposed approach is discussed only briefly, and given the federated setting, a more detailed accounting of per-round cost relative to baselines is needed. The theoretical analysis offers a convergence bound under standard smoothness assumptions, but the paper does not discuss how tight this bound is or whether its assumptions hold in the empirical settings studied. The figures are clear, though the convergence plots would be more informative with shaded variance regions across runs. The authors state that code will be released, which is commendable and will help readers verify the results once it is available. The discussion of limitations is brief and should expand on scenarios where representation matching may be harmful, such as when client data distributions differ in label space rather than feature space. Several typographical and notational inconsistencies appear in the equations, particularly in the indexing of clients and communication rounds, and these should be corrected. The writing is generally professional, but some sections repeat claims about novelty that the related work does not fully support. Overall, the paper presents a promising and practically relevant contribution, and I recommend a major revision that addresses the methodological details, statistical reporting, and the scope of the claimed improvements before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Who we become is never entirely our own doing, yet it is never entirely determined for us either. Personal identity emerges from a tangle of inherited traits, family expectations, cultural norms, friendships, and chance events that we did not choose. Consider a child who grows up in a household that values music: the early exposure shapes her tastes and her sense of what she is good at before she has any say in the matter. Outside forces such as schools, media, and economic circumstances continue to press on us throughout life, often in ways we barely notice. Yet to conclude that we are simply the products of these influences would ignore something essential about human experience. People routinely reject the paths laid out for them, choose new communities, and reshape their values after years of living by someone else's standards. Self-determination, the capacity to reflect on our circumstances and deliberately act on our own judgments, is the faculty that makes this possible. It does not require us to stand outside of all influence, which would be impossible, but rather to examine influences and decide which ones to accept, adapt, or resist. Philosophers have long debated how much freedom this capacity really grants, with some arguing that our reasons for acting are themselves caused by prior events and others insisting that reflective choice carries genuine weight. A useful middle position recognizes that the strength of self-determination varies with circumstance, since a person with access to education, stable relationships, and time for reflection has more room to choose than someone struggling under constant pressure. This suggests that freedom is not an all-or-nothing possession but something that can be expanded through the conditions we build for ourselves and for others. Personal identity, then, is best understood as an ongoing conversation between the self and the world, in which outside forces supply the material and self-determination shapes what is made of it. Recognizing this conversation allows us to take responsibility for who we are becoming without pretending that we began from nowhere. In the end, the most meaningful form of freedom may be the willingness to keep asking which influences deserve a place in our lives.

Model-Independent Extraction of Quark Sivers Distributions from COMPASS Proton and Deuteron Spin-Asymmetry Data

Abstract. We present a model-independent extraction of the quark Sivers distributions from semi-inclusive deep-inelastic scattering (SIDIS) spin asymmetries measured by the COMPASS collaboration on transversely polarized proton and deuteron targets. The Sivers function describes the correlation between the transverse spin of a nucleon and the transverse momentum of its unpolarized quarks, and its extraction provides direct access to the role of orbital angular momentum in the nucleon. Our approach avoids assumptions about the functional form of the parton distributions by expanding the Sivers function in a flexible basis and fitting the coefficients directly to the data. We describe the kinematic selection, the treatment of experimental correlations, and the propagation of uncertainties. The resulting distributions for up, down, and strange quarks are compared with earlier parametrizations, and we discuss their implications for the sum rule associated with the Sivers effect.

Introduction. Single-spin asymmetries in SIDIS arise from the interplay between the transverse spin of the target nucleon and the intrinsic transverse momentum of quarks. The Sivers mechanism, proposed to explain such asymmetries, is encoded in a transverse-momentum-dependent parton distribution known as the Sivers function. A nonzero Sivers function requires final-state or gauge-link interactions, which connects it to the study of quantum chromodynamics beyond collinear factorization. The COMPASS experiment at CERN has collected high-statistics data on both proton and deuteron targets, providing a broad kinematic coverage in the Bjorken variable x and the transverse momentum of the produced hadrons. The combination of these two targets allows a flavor separation between up and down quark contributions. Previous extractions have relied on specific parametrizations that inevitably introduce model dependence. The aim of this work is to reduce this dependence through a flexible, data-driven procedure.

Theoretical framework. In the standard formalism, the Sivers asymmetry for a given hadron is expressed as a convolution of the Sivers function with the unpolarized fragmentation function, weighted by a kinematic factor depending on the virtuality of the photon and the momentum fraction carried by the struck quark. The transverse-momentum dependence is governed by a Gaussian or more general form, and the collinear limit is controlled by the first moment of the Sivers function. We adopt the conventional Trento conventions for angles and asymmetry definitions to ensure comparability with prior results. We also incorporate the evolution of the transverse-momentum-dependent distributions, which we treat at a fixed reference scale appropriate for the COMPASS kinematics.

Parametrization strategy. Rather than assuming a specific analytic form, we expand the x-dependence of the Sivers function for each flavor in a set of orthogonal basis functions, such as Bernstein or spline polynomials, constrained only by general requirements of positivity of the extracted asymmetries and integrability. The transverse-momentum dependence is factorized and fixed by the widths established in the literature, with a systematic variation included among the uncertainties. This choice isolates the x-dependence as the object of extraction and limits the influence of any single assumed shape on the result.

Data selection. We use the COMPASS published asymmetries for charged hadrons and identified pions and kaons from both proton and deuteron targets. Events are selected according to standard criteria for the scattered muon energy, the photon virtuality, and the fractional energy of the produced hadron. Kinematic cuts are imposed to ensure the applicability of the leading-twist description, and regions with limited acceptance or large radiative corrections are excluded. The resulting dataset spans a broad range of x and hadron transverse momentum, and the binning follows the original publication to preserve bin-to-bin correlations as far as they are documented.

Treatment of correlations and uncertainties. Statistical uncertainties are taken from the published data, while systematic uncertainties are treated as partially correlated across bins according to the information supplied by the collaboration. We construct the covariance matrix accordingly and use it in a generalized least-squares fit. Because the number of basis coefficients is modest compared with the number of data points, the fit is well constrained, but we verify stability by varying the number of basis functions and the placement of knots. Uncertainties on the extracted distributions are obtained from the covariance matrix of the fit combined with a bootstrap resampling of the data.

Fitting procedure. The fit minimizes a chi-squared function built from the difference between the measured asymmetries and the model predictions, with the predictions computed from the parametrized Sivers functions convoluted with the unpolarized fragmentation functions taken from a standard set. Proton and deuteron data are fitted simultaneously, and the deuteron asymmetries are interpreted as an isoscalar combination of the up and down contributions with appropriate nuclear corrections. The fit is performed separately for different hadron species to test the universality of the extracted distributions.

Results for up and down quarks. The extracted Sivers distribution for up quarks is found to be positive over the measured range of x, with a peak at moderate values of x and a suppression toward large x. The down-quark distribution is negative and of comparable magnitude, consistent with earlier findings of opposite-sign Sivers functions for the two flavors. The relative sizes of the two distributions are robust against changes in the basis and the knot configuration, although the absolute normalization carries a sizeable uncertainty associated with the treatment of the fragmentation functions.

Strange-quark contribution. The sensitivity of the present data to the strange-quark Sivers function is limited by the statistical precision of the kaon asymmetries. Within these limitations, we find a distribution compatible with zero at the current level of precision, with an uncertainty band that allows for a modest nonzero contribution. We emphasize that this conclusion depends on the kaon fragmentation functions used in the analysis and should be revisited when more precise kaon data become available.

Comparison with previous extractions. Our results agree in shape with earlier parametrized extractions in the regions where those analyses are well constrained, but the uncertainty bands are generally larger, reflecting the absence of model assumptions. In particular, the sign and approximate magnitude of the up- and down-quark distributions are reproduced, while the detailed x-dependence differs in regions where the earlier parametrizations relied on extrapolation. The increased uncertainties are a direct consequence of the more conservative treatment of the functional form.

Sensitivity to fragmentation inputs. Because the asymmetries depend on the product of the Sivers function and the unpolarized fragmentation function, the extracted distributions inherit the uncertainties of the fragmentation inputs. We have tested alternative fragmentation sets and found that the qualitative conclusions are unchanged, although quantitative shifts of order ten to twenty percent appear in some regions. These variations are included in the reported systematic uncertainties.

Implications for the Sivers sum rule. Taking the integral of the extracted distributions over x provides a test of the Burkardt sum rule, which relates the net transverse-momentum-weighted quark contributions to the anomalous magnetic moments of the quarks. Within the present uncertainties, the integrated up and down contributions are consistent with the sign pattern expected from the sum rule, though the strange-quark integral is not sufficiently constrained to provide a stringent test. Improved kaon data and extended kinematic coverage would be needed to sharpen this comparison.

Dependence on the evolution scale. The COMPASS data are collected at relatively low scales, and the evolution of the Sivers function to other scales is a potential source of systematic effects. We evaluate the impact of a plausible range of evolution scales and find that the shape of the extracted distributions changes moderately, while the overall signs remain stable. This supports the view that the extracted distributions capture genuine features of the data rather than artifacts of a particular scale choice.

Cross-checks with deuteron-only and proton-only fits. To test the robustness of the flavor separation, we perform separate fits to the proton and deuteron datasets. The proton-only fit provides a determination of a combination of up and down contributions weighted by their charges, while the deuteron-only fit provides an approximately isoscalar combination. The simultaneous fit reproduces the individual results within uncertainties, indicating consistency between the two targets.

Hadron-species universality. The extracted distributions from pion and kaon asymmetries are compared to assess the universality of the Sivers effect across hadron species. Within the present precision, the pion-based and kaon-based results are compatible in the flavor structure, supporting the factorized description. Residual differences are attributed to the different sensitivity of each hadron species to the favored and disfavored fragmentation channels.

Discussion of model independence. The principal advantage of the present approach is that the extracted x-dependence is determined primarily by the data rather than by a chosen functional form. The price of this flexibility is larger uncertainties and reduced constraining power in regions with limited coverage. We regard the result as complementary to model-based analyses, providing an independent benchmark against which theoretical assumptions can be tested.

Limitations of the analysis. Several limitations should be acknowledged. The transverse-momentum dependence is fixed rather than fitted, so correlations between the x- and transverse-momentum dependences are not fully explored. The fragmentation functions are taken as external inputs, and their uncertainties are propagated but not simultaneously fitted. Higher-twist and gluon-initiated contributions are neglected, which is a reasonable approximation at the kinematics considered but limits the precision of the extraction at the lowest values of x.

Outlook. Future measurements with higher statistics and expanded kinematic coverage, including those planned at the Electron-Ion Collider, will allow a more stringent test of the present extraction. Joint analyses with Drell-Yan data, where the Sivers function enters with the opposite sign, would provide a direct test of the predicted sign change and of the universality of the transverse-momentum-dependent framework. We anticipate that the methodology developed here will be extended to such combined analyses.

Conclusions. We have performed a model-independent extraction of the quark Sivers distributions from COMPASS proton and deuteron spin asymmetries using a flexible basis expansion fitted to the data with a full treatment of correlated uncertainties. The up-quark distribution is positive and the down-quark distribution negative, consistent with earlier studies, while the strange-quark contribution is compatible with zero at current precision. The results reduce the dependence on assumed functional forms, at the cost of larger uncertainties, and provide a useful benchmark for future theoretical and experimental work on the three-dimensional structure of the nucleon.

Acknowledgments. We thank the COMPASS collaboration for providing the published asymmetry data and documentation of their correlations, which made this analysis possible.

If I could travel anywhere in the world, I would choose Spain, a country that has captured my imagination for as long as I can remember. My dream trip begins in Madrid, the nation's bustling capital, where I hope to wander through the wide boulevards and sit at a café on the Plaza Mayor. I want to taste churros dipped in thick hot chocolate early in the morning, when the city is just beginning to wake up.

From Madrid, I would travel south to Toledo, a city perched on a hill and surrounded by a winding river. I imagine walking its narrow stone streets, admiring the Gothic cathedral and the old synagogues that tell the story of the many cultures that once shared this place. I would also love to watch the sunset from a lookout point, with the golden rooftops glowing below me.

Next, I hope to visit Seville, where the air seems to hum with music and color. I am eager to see a flamenco performance in a small tablao, where the dancers' stamping feet and the singer's passionate voice would fill the room. I also want to visit the Alcázar, a palace whose intricate tilework and quiet gardens look like something out of a fairy tale.

No trip to Spain would be complete without a stop in Granada, where the Alhambra rises above the city like a crown. I would spend hours exploring its courtyards, fountains, and carved archways, trying to absorb the beauty of a place that has stood for centuries. Afterward, I would wander the Albaicín neighborhood and watch the sun set over the mountains.

Finally, I would travel to Barcelona on the Mediterranean coast to see the extraordinary buildings of Antoni Gaudí. I dream of standing inside the Sagrada Família and gazing up at its towers, and of strolling through Park Güell with its colorful mosaics. I would end my journey on the beach, feeling the warm sand beneath my feet and the salty breeze on my face.

Spain, I believe, would give me more than a vacation; it would offer a chance to experience a rich history, vibrant traditions, and friendly people. This is the trip I hope to take one day, and I look forward to every memory it would bring.

For much of the twentieth century, the private automobile seemed to define modern life. Cities were redesigned around highways, suburbs spread across former farmland, and owning a car became a symbol of independence and success. Yet in recent decades, a noticeable shift has begun. Many people are now reconsidering their reliance on cars and exploring transportation choices that are more affordable, more sustainable, and more socially appealing.

The financial case is one of the most immediate reasons for this change. Owning a car involves far more than the purchase price. Insurance, fuel, maintenance, parking, and depreciation can add up to thousands of dollars each year, a burden that falls heavily on households with modest incomes. For many families, public transit, cycling, walking, or shared mobility services offer a way to meet everyday needs at a fraction of that cost. Even a single household giving up a second car can free up money for housing, education, or savings.

Environmental concerns provide another powerful motivation. Transportation is among the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries, and passenger vehicles account for a significant share of that total. Electric vehicles reduce tailpipe emissions, but they do not eliminate the problems of congestion, road construction, and the land use that cars demand. Buses, trains, bicycles, and walkable neighborhoods use space and energy more efficiently, making them central to any serious plan for a low-carbon future.

Public health also benefits from this shift. Car-dependent lifestyles often leave people sedentary, and traffic accidents remain a leading cause of injury and death, particularly among young people. Cities that invest in protected bike lanes, sidewalks, and frequent transit service tend to see gains in physical activity and fewer collisions. Cleaner air in dense urban corridors, where vehicle exhaust is concentrated, further improves respiratory health, especially for children and the elderly.

Beyond practical gains, alternative transportation can make communities feel more connected. A car isolates its driver in a private cabin, while a train platform, a bus stop, or a busy bike path places people in shared public space. These encounters, though brief, help build a sense of belonging and familiarity with one's neighbors. Many people also find that walking or cycling through their neighborhood reveals shops, parks, and people they would otherwise miss from behind a windshield.

Social equity is an important part of this conversation as well. Not everyone can drive, whether because of age, disability, cost, or a lack of a license. Reliable public transportation gives these individuals access to jobs, healthcare, schools, and social life. When transit is neglected, the people who depend on it most are often left stranded, which deepens existing inequalities. Designing transportation systems that serve everyone therefore strengthens the fairness of a city as a whole.

The shift away from cars is not without challenges. Transit systems require sustained funding, careful planning, and political will, and many areas have spent decades building around the automobile. Some rural regions have few realistic alternatives, and a one-size-fits-all approach would ignore those realities. Still, the direction of change is clear, and many cities have shown that thoughtful investment can make alternatives convenient and attractive.

Ultimately, moving away from car dependence is less about rejecting cars entirely and more about giving people real choices. When affordable, sustainable, and socially rewarding options are available, individuals can decide how to move through their lives. A transportation future built on that kind of choice would serve wallets, the environment, public health, and community life at the same time.
