Consulting multiple people before making a decision is one of the most practical habits a person can develop. Every individual sees the world through a particular lens shaped by their experiences, knowledge, and values. When we rely on only our own perspective, we risk overlooking important details that others would notice right away. Seeking several opinions helps us see the full shape of a problem rather than just one side of it.

One of the clearest benefits is the chance to uncover blind spots. People are often unaware of their own biases, assumptions, and gaps in knowledge. A trusted friend may point out a flaw in our reasoning, while a mentor with years of experience may warn us about consequences we had never considered. Hearing these observations allows us to correct course before a mistake becomes costly.

Multiple advisors also bring a range of expertise. A decision about choosing a college, for example, might benefit from the input of a teacher who knows our academic strengths, a parent who understands our finances, and a current student who can describe daily life on campus. Each person contributes a different kind of knowledge, and together they paint a far more complete picture than any single source could provide.

Consulting others can also reduce the emotional pressure that clouds judgment. When we are anxious or excited about a choice, our feelings may distort how we evaluate the options. An outside voice offers a calmer, more detached viewpoint that can ground us in reality. Talking through a problem often clarifies our own thinking, even before anyone else responds.

Diverse opinions help test the strength of our ideas. If a plan survives scrutiny from several people with different backgrounds, we can feel more confident that it is sound. If it falls apart under questioning, we learn that it needed more work. In either case, the process strengthens the final decision.

There is, of course, a risk of seeking too much advice. Hearing conflicting opinions can produce confusion or paralysis, leaving a person unable to act. The goal is not to gather endless input but to select a thoughtful group of advisors whose insights are relevant and whose judgment we respect. Limiting the conversation to a few well-chosen voices keeps the process productive.

Ultimately, the responsibility for a decision still belongs to the person making it. Other people can inform and challenge our thinking, but they cannot live our lives for us. Consulting others simply ensures that we make that choice with better information, clearer reasoning, and a wider understanding of what is at stake.

Facial expression technology uses cameras and software to read the emotional signals that students display during a lesson, such as confusion, boredom, frustration, or interest. Proponents argue that this information could help teachers personalize instruction and improve engagement in ways that were difficult to achieve in crowded classrooms. Traditional teaching relies heavily on the teacher's ability to notice which students are lost or disengaged, but a single instructor managing twenty-five or more students can easily miss the quiet learner in the back row. Automated systems could, in theory, track these patterns continuously and alert the teacher when a large share of the class appears puzzled by a particular concept. This would allow the teacher to pause, revisit the material, or offer a different example before misunderstanding becomes entrenched. Personalization could go further by adjusting the pace of an online lesson, suggesting easier practice problems to a student who appears frustrated, or offering more challenging material to one who seems bored. Such adaptive approaches might help students feel that their learning is being responded to rather than simply delivered. Engagement is closely linked to motivation, and students who feel understood are often more willing to participate. Supporters also point out that technology could give shy students a private channel for signaling confusion that they might otherwise never voice aloud. However, the reliability of these systems is a serious concern. Research on emotion recognition has shown that facial expressions do not map neatly onto internal feelings, and a furrowed brow may signal concentration rather than confusion. Misreading students could lead teachers to make poor decisions based on inaccurate data. There are also questions of accuracy across different cultures, ages, and individuals with conditions that affect facial movement, since systems trained on narrow datasets may perform unevenly. Privacy presents another major issue, because continuous monitoring of children's faces creates a detailed record of their emotional lives. Students may feel watched and anxious, which could undermine the very engagement the technology is meant to build. Data collected in schools could also be stored, shared, or misused by companies or third parties in ways families never agreed to. Consent is complicated when young students cannot fully evaluate these risks and parents may feel pressured to accept them. Schools considering such tools should therefore demand transparent evidence of accuracy and clear limits on how data is collected and retained. Any system should be treated as one input among many, rather than a replacement for a teacher's professional judgment and knowledge of each child. Teachers should also receive training to interpret the information critically and to recognize when the software is likely wrong. Ultimately, facial expression technology offers a tempting promise of more responsive teaching, but that promise must be weighed against scientific uncertainty and the rights of young people. Engagement is best built through relationships, meaningful tasks, and trust, and technology should support those foundations rather than substitute for them. If carefully limited and rigorously evaluated, these tools might play a modest role in helping teachers notice students who need help. Without those safeguards, however, they risk turning classrooms into places of surveillance where children learn to perform emotions rather than explore ideas.

Choosing a graduation timeline is one of the most personal decisions a student can make, and it deserves careful thought. A traditional four-year path is not the right fit for everyone, and treating it as the default can leave some students feeling rushed or stuck. A timeline that matches your goals allows you to pursue the courses, internships, and research that will truly prepare you for your future. It also gives you room to grow as a person, whether that means working for a year to understand what you want to study or taking an extra semester to pursue a double major or study abroad. Financial circumstances matter too, since a flexible schedule can make it possible to work part-time or reduce debt without sacrificing your education. Students who accelerate may save money and enter the workforce sooner, but they should also ask whether they are building enough depth and experience along the way. Ultimately, the value of a graduation timeline lies in its alignment with who you are becoming, not in how quickly you finish. By choosing deliberately, students can turn their years of study into a foundation for lasting personal and professional growth.

Marcus had made a rule years ago: love was a story people told to make the hard parts bearable. He repeated it at dinner, at the hardware store, and at his sister's wedding, where he stood at the back with his arms folded. His son Eli, nine years old, once asked him whether he loved his mother. Marcus said that love was a word, nothing more, and sent Eli to bed without dessert for the question.

The house was quiet after the divorce. Marcus kept the same mugs in the cupboard, though only one of them ever got used. He told himself this was practical, since the others were nicer than the chipped ones he had bought alone.

On Tuesdays he drove Eli to soccer practice and sat in the folding chair at the edge of the field. Eli dribbled badly and laughed at his own mistakes, and Marcus felt something tighten in his chest that he refused to name.

Late at night he sometimes opened the old box in the closet. Inside were birthday cards written in a loopy hand, a ticket stub from a concert they had gone to in their first year, and a photograph of himself asleep on a couch with a small child curled against his ribs. He always closed the box before he could look too long.

One evening Eli came home with a crayon drawing from school. It showed three stick figures holding hands under a yellow sun, and the teacher had written in careful letters: Eli's family. Marcus stood at the counter holding it and said nothing for a long time.

"Do you think that's wrong?" Eli asked from the doorway. "It's just what Mrs. Adler told us to draw."

"It isn't wrong," Marcus said, and his voice came out rougher than he intended. "It's a fine drawing."

Eli shrugged and went to wash his hands. Marcus stared at the sun in the corner of the paper, its edges pressed hard into the page as if the child had gone over them many times.

That night he did not open the box. Instead he took the chipped mug down from its hook and filled it with coffee, then sat at the kitchen table and watched the steam curl upward. He told himself he was tired.

On Sunday he took Eli to the lake. They skipped stones until Eli's arm grew sore, and when the light started to fade, the boy leaned against his father's side without asking. Marcus did not move away.

"Dad," Eli said quietly, "do you still think love is just a word?"

The lake went gold and then gray. Marcus thought of the couch, the sleeping child, the loopy handwriting in the box, the sun drawn in crayon.

"No," he said. "I think I was wrong about that."

Eli nodded as if this were the most ordinary thing in the world, and they sat there together until the first stars came out over the water.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus kept his old rule to himself, though it no longer felt like a rule so much as a wall he had grown tired of standing behind. He bought a new set of mugs and put them on the shelf beside the chipped one, which he refused to throw away.

This paper proposes applying information bottleneck regularization to the discriminator in adversarial learning to curb overfitting and stabilize training. The core idea is well motivated, since a discriminator that memorizes training samples can give vanishing or misleading gradients to the generator, and constraining the mutual information between inputs and learned representations offers a principled way to address this. The authors clearly situate their work within prior GAN stabilization literature, and the method is simple enough to be adopted with minimal architectural changes. However, the experimental section would benefit from a more thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of the bottleneck term from other regularizers, such as spectral normalization or gradient penalties, that are often used alongside it. The reported improvements in Fréchet Inception Distance are promising, but the paper should include variance across multiple random seeds and report results on additional datasets to support its generality claims. The theoretical analysis linking the bottleneck to generalization bounds is sketched rather than fully developed, and a more rigorous derivation would strengthen the paper's contribution. Hyperparameter sensitivity, particularly for the bottleneck weight, is only briefly discussed, and a sensitivity analysis would help practitioners apply the method reliably. Overall, this is a promising and readable contribution, and I recommend a major revision addressing the experimental rigor and theoretical depth before acceptance.

Cirrhosis in Children: Causes, Symptoms, and Effects

Cirrhosis is a condition in which healthy liver tissue is gradually replaced by scar tissue, which disrupts the liver's ability to filter blood, process nutrients, and make essential proteins. While it is most often associated with adults, cirrhosis can also occur in children, and it is important for parents and caregivers to recognize its signs early.

In children, cirrhosis is relatively uncommon, but it can develop from a range of underlying conditions. Some children are born with liver problems, while others develop liver damage later in childhood. Because the liver has a remarkable capacity to repair itself, damage may go unnoticed for a long time before cirrhosis becomes evident.

One of the most significant causes of cirrhosis in children is biliary atresia, a condition in which the bile ducts are blocked or absent. Bile cannot drain from the liver, which leads to inflammation and scarring. Biliary atresia is typically diagnosed in infancy and is a leading reason for liver transplantation in young children.

Other inherited metabolic and genetic disorders can also cause cirrhosis. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes a protein to build up in liver cells and damage them over time. Wilson disease leads to copper accumulation in the liver and brain. Galactosemia, tyrosinemia, and glycogen storage diseases can likewise injure the liver.

Chronic viral hepatitis, particularly hepatitis B and hepatitis C, is another possible cause. Long-term infection causes persistent inflammation that can lead to scarring. Autoimmune hepatitis, in which the immune system attacks liver cells, is a further cause and can occur at any age in childhood.

Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease has become more common in children, largely in association with obesity and insulin resistance. Over years, fat accumulation and inflammation may progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis. Certain medications, toxins, and prolonged use of some supplements may also injure the liver.

Some children develop cirrhosis after a severe injury to the liver or as a complication of other chronic illnesses, including cystic fibrosis, which can affect the bile ducts. In many cases, however, the cause remains unclear even after thorough testing.

Symptoms of cirrhosis in children can be subtle at first. Common early signs include fatigue, poor appetite, and difficulty gaining weight or growing at the expected rate. Children may also appear pale or develop yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes, a condition called jaundice.

As the disease progresses, more noticeable symptoms may appear. The abdomen may swell because of fluid accumulation, a condition known as ascites. Veins on the abdominal wall may become more visible, and the spleen may enlarge. Children may bruise or bleed easily because the liver produces fewer of the proteins needed for clotting.

Itching is another frequent symptom, caused by bile salts building up in the skin. Some children have dark urine or pale, greasy stools. Changes in mental function, such as confusion, sleepiness, or difficulty concentrating, can signal a serious complication called hepatic encephalopathy.

Because cirrhosis affects nutrition, children may experience delayed growth and development. Vitamin deficiencies are common, particularly of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, because fat digestion depends on bile. Bone health may also suffer, increasing the risk of fractures.

Diagnosis usually involves a combination of blood tests, imaging such as ultrasound, and sometimes a liver biopsy. Doctors check liver enzymes, bilirubin levels, and clotting measures to assess how well the liver is functioning. Specialized tests may be used to identify the underlying cause.

The effects of cirrhosis can be serious. Portal hypertension, or high blood pressure in the veins that supply the liver, can cause enlarged veins in the esophagus that may bleed. Infections, including bacterial peritonitis, become more likely because of fluid buildup in the abdomen.

Hepatic encephalopathy can range from mild confusion to coma and is caused by toxins that the damaged liver can no longer clear from the blood. Growth failure and developmental delays may have lasting effects on a child's health and learning, which is why early nutritional support is important.

Liver cancer, known as hepatocellular carcinoma, is a rare but serious risk in people with long-standing cirrhosis, and regular monitoring is recommended for those affected.

Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the disease. Doctors may prescribe medications to control itching, reduce fluid buildup, or manage infections. Nutritional support, including specialized formulas and vitamin supplements, is often essential. Surgery to treat blocked bile ducts may be considered in certain infants with biliary atresia.

When the liver fails or complications become severe, liver transplantation may be the only option. Transplantation has greatly improved survival for children with end-stage liver disease, and many go on to lead active lives afterward.

Preventing some causes of childhood cirrhosis is possible. Vaccination protects against hepatitis A and B, healthy eating and regular physical activity help prevent fatty liver disease, and caution with medications and household chemicals reduces the risk of liver injury.

Parents who notice persistent fatigue, yellowing of the skin, abdominal swelling, poor growth, or easy bruising in their child should seek medical advice promptly. Early diagnosis and specialist care offer the best chance of managing the disease and protecting the child's long-term health.

This manuscript investigates how colour is represented within deep neural networks trained for visual recognition, and how those internal representations compare with the structure of human colour vision. The question is timely and well motivated, since convolutional and transformer-based models now routinely match or exceed human accuracy on object classification, yet it remains unclear whether they encode colour in ways that resemble the human visual system. The authors frame their contribution around two linked aims: characterising the geometry of colour representations across network layers, and testing whether that geometry predicts recognition performance and alignment with psychophysical data. The introduction situates the work clearly within the literature on representational similarity analysis and colour opponency, and the background on the cone-based trichromatic architecture of human vision is accurate and useful for readers from machine learning backgrounds. The methods section describes the networks studied, the stimulus sets, and the procedure for extracting activations, which is adequate for replication in principle. However, the stimulus construction is under-specified, and it is not stated whether colour stimuli were presented in a calibrated colour space such as CIELAB or in raw RGB, a distinction that substantially affects the interpretation of any claimed correspondence with human perception. The authors use representational dissimilarity matrices to compare networks with human similarity judgements, but they do not report the noise ceiling for the human data, so readers cannot tell how close the best-performing model comes to the reliability limit of the behavioural measurements. The statistical analysis would also benefit from correction for multiple comparisons across layers and networks, since many of the reported differences are modest and some reach significance only at uncorrected thresholds. The finding that intermediate layers show opponent-like axes is the most interesting result, and the figures illustrating this are generally clear, though the colour maps used in several panels are not perceptually uniform and may mislead readers about the magnitude of effects. The ablation experiments, in which colour information is removed by converting images to greyscale or by shuffling hue channels, are a valuable addition and convincingly show a drop in accuracy on colour-diagnostic categories. Nevertheless, the authors should discuss more carefully whether these ablations test colour representation specifically or instead disrupt low-level texture and contrast statistics that co-vary with hue. The comparison to human performance on the same ablated stimuli is limited to a small sample of participants, and the authors should either expand this sample or temper their conclusions about human-model correspondence accordingly. The discussion draws a fairly strong conclusion that networks learn a colour space resembling that of human observers, and this claim goes beyond what the evidence supports, since similarity in linear decoding does not establish similarity in mechanism. The authors would strengthen their argument by testing whether the observed structure persists across multiple random seeds and training regimes, as a single trained model may reflect idiosyncratic choices. Relatedly, the paper would benefit from a more explicit comparison with prior work that reported opponent-like channels in early convolutional layers, so the novelty of the present contribution is clearer. The reporting of hyperparameters and the code availability statement are appreciated, and the commitment to releasing activations and analysis scripts will aid reproducibility considerably. Overall, the paper addresses an important question with a sound general approach and several genuinely informative results. Its principal weaknesses are the under-specified stimulus calibration, the absence of a noise ceiling, the limited human sample, and conclusions that outrun the evidence. I recommend major revision, and I believe that with these issues addressed the work would make a useful contribution to the study of shared representations between biological and artificial vision.

The manuscript addresses an important and well-motivated problem: procedural text, such as cooking recipes, science lab protocols, and assembly instructions, describes a sequence of actions that continually alter the entities involved, and answering questions about such text requires tracking what exists, what properties those entities have, and how those properties change over time. The authors frame this clearly and situate their work within the broader literature on process comprehension and entity-state modeling, which gives readers a useful orientation. The introduction is generally well organized, although the motivation could be sharpened by offering a concrete example early on, showing a passage, the questions it should answer, and where existing systems fail. Such an example would make the stakes immediately apparent to readers outside the immediate subfield.

The related work section covers relevant prior efforts on event extraction, neural state tracking, and reading comprehension over science texts. However, the coverage of recent transformer-based approaches feels thinner than the rest of the review, and several comparisons are asserted rather than demonstrated. The authors should either expand this section or explicitly state the scope of their literature search so that readers can judge its completeness.

The proposed model architecture is described with reasonable clarity. The core idea of maintaining an explicit, updatable representation of entity attributes across steps, combined with a question-answering module that queries this representation, is sound and intuitive. The authors deserve credit for separating the state-tracking component from the answer-prediction component, since this modularity makes the contribution easier to assess. Still, several equations and the description of the update gating mechanism are underspecified, and I could not fully reconstruct the training procedure from the text alone.

The experimental setup relies on established benchmarks for procedural comprehension, which is appropriate. The inclusion of multiple baselines, spanning rule-based systems, recurrent models, and pretrained language models, provides a fair picture of the landscape. However, the authors should report results over multiple random seeds, along with variance estimates, since differences between the top systems appear small enough that single-run numbers may not be reliable.

The ablation study is one of the paper's stronger elements. Removing the attribute-tracking component and the state-change detector separately shows that each contributes to performance, and the analysis of which question types benefit most is informative. I would encourage the authors to go further by reporting performance broken down by the number of intervening steps between an action and a question, since this would directly test the central claim that explicit tracking helps over long procedures.

The error analysis is useful but brief. The examples of failure cases are helpful for understanding the model's limitations, particularly cases involving implicit state changes, where an entity transforms without being named, and coreference across long spans. A more systematic categorization of errors, with counts, would strengthen the section considerably.

Regarding reproducibility, the authors state that code will be released, which is commendable. The hyperparameter table is helpful, but the paper should also specify preprocessing steps, tokenization choices, and the exact dataset splits used, since small differences in these can meaningfully affect results on this kind of task.

The discussion section acknowledges several limitations, including reliance on English-language recipes and the assumption that state changes are explicitly described in text. I appreciate this candor. I would add that the approach may not generalize to procedures where important state changes are implied by domain knowledge rather than stated, and the authors could discuss how their model might incorporate such knowledge.

The writing is generally clear, though some sentences are unnecessarily long and several technical terms, such as "state slot" and "attribute gate," are introduced without sufficient definition at first use. A careful copyedit would improve readability. The figures are mostly informative, but the architecture diagram omits the dimensionality of the intermediate representations, which would help readers follow the data flow.

Ethically, the work poses minimal concerns, as it concerns text comprehension in benign domains. The authors might briefly note potential downstream uses, such as assistive systems for people following instructions, to contextualize the contribution.

In terms of significance, the paper makes a credible incremental advance in an active area. Its central idea is reasonable and its empirical gains are plausible, but the evidence supporting the claim that explicit tracking is the primary driver of improvement would be more convincing with the additional analyses suggested above.

I recommend a revision before acceptance. The core contribution is sound and worth publishing, but the authors should strengthen the statistical reporting, clarify the model and training details, expand the error analysis, and tighten the related work and presentation. With these changes, the paper would make a solid contribution to the literature on procedural question answering.

This manuscript addresses the training of neural networks whose weights are restricted to low-bit, discrete values, using a variational Bayesian framework to handle the non-differentiability that makes such models difficult to optimize with standard gradient methods. The motivation is well grounded, since low-precision and discrete-weight networks promise substantial reductions in memory, computation, and energy for deployment on edge hardware. The authors frame the problem clearly and situate their approach within the broader literature on binarized and quantized networks, although the related work section could more carefully distinguish their method from straight-through estimator approaches and from prior probabilistic quantization schemes. The core idea of placing a discrete distribution over each weight and optimizing a variational objective is sound and potentially useful, and the derivation of the evidence lower bound for the discrete case is generally correct and easy to follow. However, several steps in the gradient estimation procedure rely on approximations whose bias is not quantified, and the paper would benefit from a formal or empirical analysis of how this bias affects convergence. The experimental section evaluates the method on standard image classification benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the choice of baselines is limited, and the comparison omits several recent quantization-aware training methods that would provide a stronger reference point. The reported accuracy gaps between the proposed method and full-precision baselines are presented favorably, yet the paper does not always state how many random seeds were used or report variance, making it difficult to judge whether the improvements are statistically meaningful. Ablation studies examining the choice of prior, the number of samples drawn during training, and the temperature schedule are helpful, though some of these results appear only in the appendix and deserve more prominence. The computational cost of the variational training procedure relative to standard training is discussed briefly, but a clearer account of wall-clock time and memory overhead would help practitioners assess the trade-offs. The figures are generally clear, although the training curves would be more informative with confidence bands and a consistent axis scale across experiments. The writing is largely precise, but certain notational choices, particularly the reuse of symbols for both the variational parameters and the weight values, cause confusion in the middle sections and should be revised. The authors provide code, which is commendable and will aid reproducibility, but the documentation accompanying it should specify the exact hyperparameters used for each reported result. The discussion of limitations is brief and focuses mainly on dataset scope, whereas the more substantive limitations concerning the scalability of the method to larger architectures and the sensitivity to initialization are only hinted at. Extending the experiments to a language modeling or detection task would test whether the approach generalizes beyond the vision setting used here. The theoretical contribution is modest but clearly stated, and the paper does not overclaim its novelty, which I appreciate. Overall, the work is a reasonable contribution with a sound core idea, but it requires stronger baselines, more rigorous statistical reporting, and a fuller treatment of approximation error before its claims can be fully supported. I recommend a major revision, and I would be glad to review a revised version.

This paper addresses the problem of adversarial attacks on image classification models by proposing randomized input defenses, a family of techniques that apply stochastic transformations to inputs before they reach the classifier. The motivation is clear and timely, since small, imperceptible perturbations can cause deep networks to misclassify images with high confidence, and defenses that avoid costly retraining are attractive in practice. The authors position their approach against deterministic preprocessing defenses, arguing that randomness makes it harder for an attacker to craft perturbations that survive the transformation. The related work section gives a reasonable overview of gradient masking, input transformation defenses, and adversarial training, although it could more directly compare against recent randomized methods such as random resizing and padding. The core method is described with enough detail to be understood, but the paper would benefit from a more formal statement of the threat model, particularly whether the attacker is assumed to be oblivious to the defense, has full white-box knowledge, or can adapt to the randomness. The experiments on standard benchmarks show meaningful reductions in attack success rates across several attack methods, which supports the central claim. However, the evaluation relies heavily on attacks that do not account for the randomization, and this raises concerns that the reported robustness may be overstated. The authors should include adaptive attacks, such as expectation over transformation, to demonstrate that the gains persist under a stronger adversary. The ablation study is useful for isolating the contribution of each randomization component, though the chosen hyperparameter ranges appear narrow and their sensitivity is not fully explored. Clean accuracy trade-offs are reported, and the drop in accuracy on unperturbed inputs is modest, which is a positive result that deserves more discussion. The computational overhead of the defense, including inference latency and the number of samples needed for stable predictions, is mentioned only briefly and should be quantified more fully. Figures are generally clear, but the qualitative examples would be more convincing with a broader selection of images and failure cases. The statistical reporting is limited, as the paper does not clearly state the number of runs or provide confidence intervals for the main results. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code and the exact random transformation parameters used in each experiment. The discussion section acknowledges some limitations but understates the risk that randomness can be circumvented by stronger attacks. The conclusion appropriately notes that randomized defenses are not a complete solution to adversarial robustness. Overall, the paper makes a useful contribution and is well organized, but its claims of robustness need stronger support through adaptive evaluation before they can be accepted. I recommend a major revision.

Sinn Féin has won the Foyle constituency from the SDLP, as Mark Durkan lost his parliamentary seat to Elisha McCallion.

The result marks a significant shift in one of Northern Ireland's most closely watched constituencies, where the SDLP had held a strong position for decades. Durkan, a former party leader who had represented Foyle since 2005, conceded defeat after the count in Derry/Londonderry.

McCallion, a Sinn Féin candidate from the city, was declared the winner after a count that ran late into the night. Her supporters gathered at local party offices to celebrate the outcome, which many described as a long-awaited breakthrough.

Durkan had long been considered one of the most recognisable figures in Northern Irish politics, having served as deputy first minister and as leader of the SDLP. His defeat was seen by many observers as a reflection of changing voter priorities in the city.

Sinn Féin has steadily grown its support across Northern Ireland over the past decade, and the Foyle result is widely regarded as a sign of that momentum. The party has also argued that its message on housing, health services and the cost of living resonated strongly with voters.

The SDLP, which has historically drawn much of its support from the nationalist community in Derry and across the north-west, faced a difficult campaign. Party officials acknowledged that the result was a painful one for the organisation.

Local commentators noted that the contest was closely fought, with turnout higher than expected in several wards. Election officials said the count was conducted in line with standard procedures, with results announced as each stage was completed.

Durkan thanked his supporters and staff in a short statement, saying he was proud of the work he had carried out for the people of Foyle over many years. He also congratulated McCallion on her victory.

McCallion, speaking after her election, pledged to represent all residents of the constituency regardless of how they had voted. She said she would prioritise issues affecting families, young people and local businesses.

Political analysts said the result would prompt the SDLP to reassess its strategy in the north-west and beyond. Some suggested the party would need to rebuild its connections with voters who felt overlooked in recent years.

Sinn Féin's gain in Foyle also has implications for the wider balance of power at Westminster and in the Northern Ireland Assembly, though the immediate impact will depend on how seats are allocated across the region.

Business leaders in Derry welcomed the emphasis on economic development in the campaign, calling for early engagement with the new representative on infrastructure, investment and employment.

Community groups in the city said they hoped the new MP would focus on tackling deprivation in some of the constituency's most disadvantaged areas. Several charities have requested meetings in the coming weeks.

Voters interviewed outside polling stations described a range of motivations, with many citing the cost of living and public services as their top concerns. Others said they had been considering a change for some time.

The outcome also reflected broader shifts in Irish nationalist politics, where Sinn Féin has increasingly competed for votes that once went almost exclusively to the SDLP. This trend has been visible in several recent elections across the island.

Durkan's career has spanned several decades, including a period as a key negotiator during the peace process that led to the Good Friday Agreement. Many observers expect his contribution to be recognised in the years ahead.

McCallion's election will be closely examined by party colleagues and rivals alike, as she takes on the responsibilities of representing one of the most politically significant seats in the north-west.

Political commentators said the coming months would test both parties, with the SDLP needing to define its future direction and Sinn Féin needing to demonstrate it can deliver for its newly won constituency.

Local residents are expected to watch closely as the new representative settles into the role, with many hoping for clear progress on the issues that dominated the campaign in Derry and the surrounding area.

Solar Impulse's Record-Breaking Flight Marks Major Step in Round-the-World Journey

Solar Impulse, the Swiss-led solar-powered aircraft project, has achieved a record-breaking flight that marks a major milestone in its ambitious effort to circle the globe using only the sun for energy. The achievement has drawn attention from aviation experts, engineers, and environmental advocates around the world. Mission organizers said the flight demonstrates that clean energy can power long-distance travel, even if it remains a technical challenge. The aircraft, with a wingspan comparable to that of a large commercial airliner, is powered by more than 17,000 solar cells embedded across its wings. Its body is built from carbon fiber, keeping its weight remarkably low for an aircraft of its size. Engineers designed the plane to store surplus solar energy in lithium-ion batteries, allowing it to fly through the night. The record flight covered a distance that surpassed previous solar-powered flight benchmarks, according to project representatives. Pilots on the mission described the experience as demanding, citing long hours at the controls and the need for intense concentration. The aircraft flies at relatively slow speeds, which conserves energy but requires careful management of weather and wind conditions. Weather remains one of the greatest risks for solar flight, since clouds and storms can reduce the energy the panels collect. Mission planners spent years studying seasonal patterns and atmospheric conditions to choose the safest routes. The project was founded by Swiss pilot Bertrand Piccard and engineer Andre Borschberg, who both took turns flying the aircraft during earlier stages. Their original goal was to show that renewable energy could support aviation and inspire investment in cleaner technologies. Supporters say the flight has already influenced conversations about sustainable transportation. Industry analysts note that while the aircraft cannot carry passengers or heavy cargo, its engineering lessons may apply to drones, aerial surveying, and other lightweight applications. Researchers involved in the project have shared data on battery performance, lightweight materials, and solar energy management. Several universities and technology companies have expressed interest in collaborating on follow-up research. The record flight also served as a public demonstration, drawing crowds and media coverage at stops along the route. Local officials in host cities welcomed the aircraft as a symbol of innovation and environmental responsibility. Schoolchildren in several countries followed the journey through live updates and educational materials provided by the team. Critics have questioned whether solar aviation can ever be scaled to commercial levels, citing the limits of current battery and solar panel technology. Project leaders acknowledge these concerns but argue that pioneering flights are essential for driving progress. They point out that many aviation breakthroughs once seemed impractical before becoming standard. Energy experts say improvements in battery density and solar cell efficiency could eventually expand what solar aircraft can achieve. The mission team has reported that each stage of the journey has revealed new insights that will guide future designs. Safety remained a central concern throughout the flight, with ground crews monitoring the aircraft and weather at every moment. Pilots followed strict protocols for landing, rest, and emergency procedures. The team also coordinated with aviation authorities to ensure compliance with international flight regulations. Following the record flight, organizers said they plan to continue the journey with additional legs in the coming months. Each remaining segment will test the aircraft against different climates, altitudes, and flight durations. The team hopes the completed circumnavigation will stand as proof that solar energy can power meaningful achievements beyond the ground. For now, the record-breaking flight stands as a significant step forward, offering encouragement to those who believe clean technology can reshape the future of travel.

The manuscript addresses an important and practical problem: semi-supervised classification when the unlabeled pool contains samples from classes that do not appear in the labeled set. Such out-of-distribution contamination is common in real deployments, and standard self-training can degrade badly under it because confidently wrong pseudo-labels propagate through training. The authors propose a confidence-aware self-training framework that estimates the reliability of pseudo-labels and filters or reweights unlabeled samples accordingly, and this framing is well motivated. The introduction clearly positions the work relative to open-set semi-supervised learning and safe semi-supervised learning, which is helpful for readers outside the immediate subfield. The problem statement is precise, and the assumptions about the labeled and unlabeled distributions are stated explicitly, which I appreciated. The core contribution, a confidence estimation module that separates in-distribution from irrelevant samples during iterative pseudo-labeling, is described with enough detail to be understood conceptually. However, the method section would benefit from a more explicit algorithm box that specifies each step of the training loop, including how thresholds are initialized and updated. The notation is mostly consistent, although the symbol used for the confidence score is overloaded in two places and should be disambiguated. The loss function combines a supervised term, a pseudo-label term, and a regularization term, but the weighting coefficients are not justified beyond a brief statement that they were tuned on validation data. A sensitivity analysis over these coefficients would substantially strengthen the paper. The authors should also clarify whether the validation set used for tuning contains irrelevant-class samples, since this choice materially affects the reported gains. The experimental setup covers several image classification benchmarks, which is appropriate, and the choice of baselines includes standard self-training, FixMatch-style consistency methods, and recent open-set approaches. The inclusion of multiple contamination ratios is a strength, as it shows how performance degrades as the proportion of irrelevant data grows. Nonetheless, the results table reports means without standard deviations, and with only a few random seeds the reader cannot judge whether the reported improvements are statistically meaningful. I encourage the authors to report variance across at least five runs and to include significance tests for the main comparisons. The ablation study isolates the contribution of the confidence estimator and the reweighting scheme, which supports the central claim, though an ablation removing the threshold update rule would also be informative. The analysis of failure cases is brief, and a qualitative discussion of which irrelevant classes are most often misclassified as in-distribution would add useful insight. The computational overhead of the confidence module is mentioned only in passing, and a clear comparison of training time against the baselines would help practitioners assess the method's cost. The related work section is thorough but somewhat list-like, and a more critical comparison that highlights the specific limitations of prior methods would sharpen the paper's novelty claim. Several recent papers on calibration for pseudo-labeling are cited but not discussed in relation to this work, and the authors should address whether calibrated confidence scores could replace the proposed estimator. The theoretical motivation relies on an informal argument about error propagation, and a formal bound or at least a clearer proposition would make the contribution more rigorous. The authors should also state the conditions under which the method is expected to fail, such as when irrelevant classes are visually similar to target classes. The discussion of limitations is present but short, and it would be strengthened by noting the dependence on the quality of the initial labeled set. Reproducibility is partially addressed through a statement that code will be released upon acceptance, which is acceptable, but hyperparameter ranges and the full training schedule should appear in an appendix. The figures are clear, although the axis labels in the contamination-ratio plot are too small to read comfortably in print. The writing is generally fluent, with a few awkward sentences in the abstract that could be tightened. Overall, the paper presents a useful and timely idea with reasonable empirical support, but the statistical reporting, theoretical grounding, and clarity of the method description need improvement before the claims can be fully accepted. I recommend a major revision, and I believe the work could become a solid contribution once these issues are addressed.

The manuscript addresses the problem of learning sentence representations from multiple contextual text sources while handling out-of-vocabulary words through positional methods, a topic of clear practical relevance. The motivation is well articulated in the introduction, which argues convincingly that sentence embeddings trained on a single corpus inherit that corpus's biases and vocabulary gaps. The authors situate their work within the literature on distributed sentence encoders and contextual embeddings, though the related work section could more explicitly contrast their approach with subword-based solutions such as byte-pair encoding. The central idea of combining several contextual sources into a single representation is sensible, and the decision to treat each source as a separate view before fusing them is a reasonable design choice. The positional method for out-of-vocabulary words, which encodes a token's position relative to known context words, is the most novel contribution and deserves more careful justification. The paper would benefit from a formal definition of this positional encoding, since the current description relies heavily on intuition and an informal example. It is unclear how the positional signal interacts with the fusion mechanism, and a diagram or equation showing the full pipeline would greatly aid comprehension. The experimental setup uses three benchmark datasets, which is a reasonable number, but the authors should justify why these were chosen over larger or more diverse alternatives. The baselines include averaged word embeddings and a single-source sentence encoder, yet stronger recent baselines are absent, which limits the strength of the comparative claims. Hyperparameter settings are reported for the proposed model but not for several baselines, raising concerns about fairness of the comparison. The results table shows consistent gains on most tasks, but the improvements on two of the datasets are small and no significance testing is reported. I would strongly encourage the authors to include confidence intervals or paired statistical tests to support their claims. The ablation study is a welcome addition, as it isolates the contribution of the positional component from that of multi-source fusion. However, the ablation only removes components one at a time, and the authors should consider whether interactions between components change the conclusions. The analysis of out-of-vocabulary performance is particularly informative, showing that the positional method helps most on rare named entities and technical terms. Nonetheless, the evaluation of out-of-vocabulary words uses a relatively small subset, and the authors should report how many such tokens appear in each test set. The error analysis section offers useful qualitative examples but does not quantify the failure modes systematically. A breakdown of errors by sentence length, syntactic complexity, or domain would make the analysis more actionable for future researchers. The discussion of computational cost is missing entirely, which is a notable omission given that multiple contextual sources increase training and inference time. Readers would need to know how the method scales with the number of sources and the size of the vocabulary. The reproducibility statement mentions that code will be released, which is commendable, but the paper does not specify the exact corpora used for each contextual source. Providing precise dataset versions, preprocessing steps, and random seeds would substantially improve reproducibility. The writing is generally clear, although several sentences in the methods section are overly long and contain nested clauses that obscure the meaning. Figures are legible, but the axis labels in the learning curves are too small to read comfortably in print. The notation is mostly consistent, though the symbol for the fused representation changes between the methods and experiments sections, which may confuse readers. Minor typographical errors appear in the references, including inconsistent capitalization of proper nouns in several entries. The limitations section acknowledges dependence on the quality of the contextual sources, which is an honest and important caveat. It would be valuable to also discuss potential biases introduced by the sources and how the positional method might propagate them. The ethical considerations are briefly addressed, but a more thorough discussion of how the model could be misused, for example in surveillance of text, would strengthen the paper. Overall, the work presents a promising direction with a potentially useful technique for handling rare vocabulary in sentence representations. The main weaknesses lie in the insufficient formal grounding of the positional method, the limited baselines, and the absence of statistical testing. I recommend a major revision addressing these points, after which the contribution could be a valuable addition to the venue. I would be glad to review a revised version once the authors have addressed these concerns.

Penicillin V Potassium in Veterinary Medicine: Uses, Pharmacology, Dosing, and Storage

Penicillin V potassium is an oral, acid-stable penicillin antibiotic used in veterinary medicine to treat infections caused by susceptible gram-positive bacteria. It is the potassium salt of phenoxymethylpenicillin and belongs to the beta-lactam class of antibiotics. Its main advantage over penicillin G is that it survives stomach acid well enough to be given by mouth. Veterinarians most often prescribe it for infections involving streptococci, staphylococci that do not produce penicillinase, and certain anaerobic bacteria. It is commonly used for dental and oral infections, skin and soft tissue infections, and some respiratory infections. Because its spectrum is narrow, a culture and sensitivity test is valuable when the causative organism is uncertain.

Pharmacologically, penicillin V works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis. It binds penicillin-binding proteins, which disrupts the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, leading to weakened cell walls and bacterial death. Because mammalian cells lack cell walls, the drug is relatively selective for bacteria. Absorption from the gastrointestinal tract is reasonable but variable, and food can reduce the amount absorbed, so administration timing relative to meals matters. The drug is distributed widely in body fluids but penetrates the central nervous system poorly unless inflammation is present. It is excreted mainly unchanged by the kidneys, so renal function influences how long it remains active in the body.

Dosing varies considerably by species, body weight, the infection being treated, and the clinical judgment of the veterinarian. Commonly cited dosages for dogs and cats fall roughly within the range of 10 to 50 mg per kilogram of body weight per dose, given two to four times daily. Dosing intervals and durations should always be confirmed with a veterinarian, and treatment is typically continued for at least several days beyond apparent clinical improvement. Animals with reduced kidney function may require adjusted dosing intervals. Owners should never change the dose or stop treatment early without consulting the prescribing veterinarian.

Penicillin V is generally well tolerated, but adverse effects can occur. Gastrointestinal upset, including vomiting, diarrhea, and reduced appetite, is the most common complaint. Hypersensitivity reactions such as rash, itching, facial swelling, or more serious allergic responses are possible, and any suspicion of an allergic reaction warrants immediate veterinary attention. Long-term or repeated use can disrupt the normal intestinal flora and may promote antimicrobial resistance. Penicillin V should not be given to animals with a known penicillin allergy, and caution is advised in animals with significant kidney disease.

Penicillin V potassium tablets and oral solutions should be stored according to the manufacturer's labeling, generally at controlled room temperature and protected from moisture and excessive heat. Reconstituted oral suspensions often have limited shelf lives and may require refrigeration, so the label should be checked carefully. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets that are not the intended recipients. Unused or expired medication should be disposed of through an appropriate pharmacy or veterinary take-back program rather than flushed or thrown in household trash. Accurate dosing equipment, such as an oral syringe, helps ensure correct measurement of liquid formulations.

Creativity enriches learning because it encourages students to ask questions, explore alternative answers, and connect ideas that seem unrelated at first. When a student draws a diagram to understand a math problem or writes a story to remember a historical event, they engage with the material in a way that makes it their own. Creativity also drives discovery, since many of history's breakthroughs began with someone willing to imagine what had not yet been seen or tested. Scientists, inventors, and artists alike rely on creative thinking to step beyond established methods and try new approaches. Beyond the classroom, creativity shapes everyday life by helping people solve problems at home, at work, and in their communities. Simple choices, such as rearranging a small kitchen for efficiency or finding a new way to resolve a disagreement, reflect creative thought applied to ordinary challenges. For these reasons, nurturing creativity in young people is not a luxury but a necessity for building curious, adaptable, and thoughtful citizens.

Replacing the Electoral College with a nationwide popular vote for president and vice president would make the American electoral system more democratic, because every vote would count equally regardless of where a citizen lives. Under the current system, a candidate can win the presidency while losing the national popular vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016. Such outcomes strike many citizens as fundamentally unfair, since they suggest that the will of the majority can be overridden by a mechanism that few Americans fully understand. A direct popular vote would ensure that the candidate with the most support nationwide becomes president.

The Electoral College also distorts campaign behavior in ways that harm the broader public. Because most states award all their electoral votes to the statewide winner, candidates concentrate their time, money, and attention on a small number of swing states. Voters in safe states, whether Republican or Democratic, are often ignored during campaigns, while voters in competitive states receive far more attention than their numbers would justify. A national popular vote would require candidates to seek support in every region, including rural areas, cities, and states that are currently considered uncontested.

Critics of abolishing the Electoral College often argue that it protects smaller states by giving each state a minimum of three electoral votes. However, a national popular vote would still give every voter a voice, and candidates would have to build broad coalitions that include citizens in less populous states. The current system already allows a small number of states to decide elections, which means that residents of small states are not as influential as they might appear. A nationwide vote would spread influence more evenly across the population.

Supporters of the Electoral College sometimes claim that it encourages broad geographic support, requiring candidates to win across different regions. Yet the system can reward a candidate who wins narrow victories in several states while ignoring large numbers of voters nationwide. A popular vote would reward candidates for winning the genuine support of the most citizens, which is a more direct measure of national consensus. It would also remove the risk of so-called faithless electors, who occasionally cast votes contrary to their pledges.

Concerns about recounts and close elections are also relevant. A national popular vote could create the possibility of a close nationwide result that requires a recount across many states, which would be logistically complex. Still, the country already manages large and complicated electoral processes, and clear federal standards for counting and recounts could address these challenges. Most democracies around the world elect their leaders by direct popular vote or through systems that do not depend on a separate intermediary body.

Ultimately, replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote would align presidential elections with the basic democratic principle that each citizen's vote should carry equal weight. It would reduce the influence of swing states, encourage candidates to engage with all Americans, and ensure that the winner reflects the choice of the most voters. For these reasons, a direct national vote is a reform worth serious consideration.

Oversized national flags across India are repeatedly tearing in strong winds, prompting growing concern over costly maintenance and what critics describe as poor planning. Several large tricolour installations, including some towering over public squares and government complexes, have suffered visible damage in recent months during gusty weather. Residents and local officials have reported flags shredded at the edges or split along their length within days of being hoisted. Maintenance crews are often called in to replace or repair the fabric, and each replacement carries a significant expense for the agencies responsible. Public finance observers note that the recurring cost of frequent replacements could add up quickly across multiple sites. Some experts argue that the flags were chosen for their sheer size without adequate consideration of wind loads, fabric durability, or the local climate. Others point out that high-quality materials designed to withstand strong gusts can be considerably more expensive upfront. Engineers have suggested that proper mounting systems, reinforced hoisting poles, and wind-rated fabrics could reduce the damage substantially. Critics say such technical planning should have been part of the initial project approval rather than an afterthought. Officials responding to the concerns have generally acknowledged the problem and said that reviews of procurement and installation standards are under way. Some agencies have reportedly begun inspecting flagpoles and considering shorter replacement cycles for the most exposed locations. Advocates for stricter oversight have called for clear guidelines on specifications, budgets, and maintenance schedules for large flag installations. They argue that transparency about spending would help the public judge whether the investment is justified. For now, the torn flags remain a visible reminder of the gap between ambitious displays of national pride and the practical realities of keeping them intact.

Venus is often called Earth's twin because the two planets are similar in size, mass, and bulk composition, yet their surface conditions could hardly be more different. This contrast makes Venus a valuable subject for scientific study, since it offers a natural laboratory for understanding how planetary climates can run away into extreme greenhouse states. Its surface temperature exceeds 460 degrees Celsius, and its crushing atmosphere, composed mostly of carbon dioxide, exerts a pressure about ninety times that of Earth's at sea level. Studying these conditions helps scientists refine models of climate change and better understand the long-term evolution of rocky planets. Venus may also hold clues about whether it once had oceans and possibly habitable conditions, questions that bear directly on the search for life elsewhere. However, the same hostile environment that makes Venus scientifically compelling also presents severe engineering challenges. Spacecraft must survive intense heat, corrosive sulfuric acid clouds, and enormous pressure, and most previous landers have survived only minutes or, at best, a few hours on the surface. Recent advances in high-temperature electronics, heat-resistant materials, and autonomous operation offer hope that future missions could endure far longer. Improved power systems and better thermal insulation would allow landers to conduct extended experiments rather than brief snapshots. Aerial platforms, such as balloons or aircraft drifting through the more temperate upper atmosphere, could also provide continuous observations of winds, chemistry, and cloud behavior. Each of these technologies must be tested and refined before they can be trusted with a mission costing hundreds of millions of dollars. Ultimately, the scientific rewards of exploring Venus justify the difficulty, because a better understanding of our sister planet could reveal fundamental truths about the forces that shape all planets, including our own.

Good decisions rarely come from a single point of view. When people with different experiences, training, and assumptions examine the same problem, they notice things that any one person would miss. This is the core reason why gathering diverse perspectives can lead to wiser decisions, and it is a lesson that applies to families, schools, businesses, and governments alike.

Consider first how individual judgment works. Every person sees the world through a particular lens shaped by upbringing, profession, culture, and personal history. That lens is useful because it highlights certain details, but it also hides others. An engineer may focus on efficiency and overlook how a design affects daily users. A community organizer may understand residents' needs yet underestimate the budget constraints facing the city. Neither view is wrong, but each is incomplete.

Diversity of perspective helps by exposing these blind spots. When a group includes people who see the problem differently, questions get asked that might otherwise go unspoken. Someone raises the uncomfortable possibility that a plan will fail, or points out an assumption everyone had taken for granted. These challenges can feel frustrating in the moment, yet they often prevent costly mistakes.

Research in psychology and organizational behavior supports this intuition, although the picture is nuanced. Studies have found that diverse groups often perform better on complex problems because members process information more carefully. When everyone in a room thinks alike, people tend to agree quickly and stop searching for alternatives. When views differ, the group has to explain its reasoning, which forces a more thorough examination of the evidence.

History offers many examples. Scientific progress often depends on researchers from different fields combining their methods. Medicine has improved as clinical trials have included more varied populations, revealing how treatments affect different bodies in different ways. Public policy has sometimes failed precisely because planners never consulted the people most affected by their decisions.

Diversity alone, however, does not guarantee wisdom. A group with many viewpoints can still reach poor conclusions if its members do not listen to one another or if the process is dominated by a few loud voices. What matters is how the perspectives are gathered and weighed. Inclusive discussion requires that each person feel safe to speak, that ideas are judged on their merits, and that the group is willing to change its mind when good arguments emerge.

Leaders play an important role in making this happen. A wise leader actively seeks out people who disagree, asks open-ended questions, and resists the temptation to treat their own view as the default. Such a leader also makes clear how the final decision will be reached, so that participants understand their input was genuinely considered rather than collected for show.

There is also a question of fairness. Decisions made with broad participation tend to be more widely accepted, even by those who lose the argument. People are more willing to support a policy when they believe their voice was heard. This legitimacy matters because a wise decision that no one will carry out is of little practical value.

Gathering diverse perspectives does take time and effort. Meetings run longer, disagreements can be uncomfortable, and consensus is harder to reach. These costs are real, and not every decision warrants an elaborate process. A minor choice may not need a full range of viewpoints, while a decision with far-reaching consequences almost always does.

For students, this lesson applies directly to their own learning. Group projects are often frustrating because classmates approach problems differently, yet those differences frequently produce stronger work than any one student could create alone. Learning to listen to viewpoints that challenge our own is a skill that will serve us throughout life.

In the end, wisdom is less about being right from the start and more about being willing to test our ideas against the views of others. A diverse group offers a built-in check on error, a source of new information, and a richer understanding of what is at stake. By seeking out perspectives unlike our own, we give ourselves the best chance of making decisions we can stand behind.

Should students be required to maintain a B average in order to take part in sports and extracurricular activities? Supporters of such rules argue that school is the primary purpose of a student's time, and that athletics and clubs should not come at the expense of learning. A minimum grade standard sends a clear message that academic responsibility comes first, and it gives students a concrete reason to stay on top of their classwork. Many coaches and advisors also note that students who struggle in class often benefit from the structure and accountability that teams provide, so a grade requirement can act as a motivator to seek help rather than simply a punishment. On the other hand, critics point out that the students most likely to fall below a B average are often the ones who would benefit most from the sense of belonging that activities offer. Removing them from a team or club may push them further away from school, which can increase the risk of dropping out. Grades also reflect many factors beyond effort, including family responsibilities, learning disabilities, and unequal access to tutoring or quiet study space. A single eligibility cutoff may therefore punish students for circumstances they cannot easily control. Some schools have tried to find a middle ground by keeping students eligible while requiring mandatory study halls or academic probation plans. These approaches allow students to keep participating while receiving targeted academic support. Such programs ask more of schools in terms of staffing and money, but they address the underlying cause of poor performance rather than just its symptom. Ultimately, the question is whether eligibility rules are meant to reward achievement or to correct struggling students. A B average requirement works well for students who are already close to that standard, but it may be less effective for those who need the most help. Schools should weigh both goals carefully before deciding how strict their rules should be. A thoughtful policy would protect academic progress while keeping the door open for students who are working to improve.

Extending school days to create a four-day week may seem like a practical solution to budget pressures and teacher shortages, but it can harm students' learning and weaken family time. The four-day model typically lengthens each school day by roughly an hour so that the total instructional hours remain the same. Although this sounds reasonable on paper, the longer days place considerable strain on young learners whose concentration naturally fades after several hours of structured study. Younger children, in particular, may struggle to remain attentive during extended lessons, and their academic gains can suffer as a result. Teachers also face greater fatigue, which can reduce the quality of instruction in the final periods of the day. Students who already have difficulty focusing may fall further behind when the day stretches longer and offers fewer natural breaks. Research on instructional time suggests that learning depends more on the quality and pacing of lessons than on simply adding minutes, and a poorly managed longer day may produce diminishing returns. Furthermore, the loss of a full weekday removes a regular opportunity for remediation, tutoring, and enrichment that many students depend on. Families are affected as well, because the longer school day shortens the hours between dismissal and bedtime. Working parents may find that after-school schedules become more difficult to arrange, especially when they must cover the lost weekday with childcare. Children who return home later may have less time for homework, meals, physical activity, and rest, all of which support healthy development. Many households also rely on time together during evenings to strengthen relationships and communicate about school and life. When school runs later into the afternoon, this shared time becomes compressed, and parents may feel less involved in their children's education. Transportation can also become a challenge, since bus schedules and carpool arrangements are often built around the traditional day. Community members who depend on school-based services, such as meals and counseling, may find access reduced when the school week is shortened. For these reasons, districts considering a four-day week should carefully weigh the academic and family costs before adopting a schedule that extends each day. Alternatives such as improved staffing, targeted budget reform, or flexible scheduling within a five-day week may better protect students' learning and preserve the family routines that support it.
