Edmund Ashworth had expected many things from the machine his late uncle had bequeathed him, but not the smell of sandalwood and wet earth that greeted him when the brass cage ceased its shuddering.

He stepped out onto a riverbank choked with reeds, his top hat already askew, his leather valise clutched to his chest like a shield. The sky above was a pale, washed blue, and the air hummed with insects he could not name. Somewhere a bell was ringing, slow and unhurried.

He had set the dial for 1857, or so he believed, intending to observe the Mutiny from a safe distance and write a monograph that would secure his fellowship at the Royal Society. Instead he had landed, apparently, in some far older India, or perhaps in an India that had never been written about in any book he had read.

He consulted his pocket chronometer, which had stopped, and then his compass, which spun slowly and foolishly. Annoyed, he began to walk along the bank toward the sound of the bell.

The path led him to a stone ghat descending into the river, and at its top sat an old man upon a tiger skin, eyes closed, body perfectly still. His hair was matted and white, his forehead marked with ash, and his skin was the colour of weathered teak.

Edmund cleared his throat loudly. "I say. Can you tell me where I am?"

The old man did not open his eyes. "You are where you have always been, sahib. Only the place you call it has changed."

Edmund bristled. He had been trained at Cambridge to detect sophistry, and this smelled of it strongly. "Come now, I am an Englishman, a man of science. I demand a plain answer."

"Plain answers are a luxury of those who have already decided what they want to hear," said the sage, and at last his eyes opened, dark and unhurried. "Sit, if you wish. The river does not mind your boots."

Edmund remained standing. He wanted to say something cutting about heathen mysticism, about the backwardness of a people who believed in such nonsense, but the words stuck in his throat. There was something in the old man's gaze that made him feel suddenly small and suddenly foolish, dressed as he was in wool and starch under a sun that did not care for either.

"You have come a long way," the sage observed.

"I have come from London," Edmund replied stiffly. "By means I need not explain to you."

"Ah. London. The city of many clocks and no time." The old man smiled faintly. "I have heard of it. Travellers speak of its smoke and its hurry, of men who build iron roads and count their wealth in ledgers, of men who believe their God has given them the earth to measure and to own."

Edmund felt his face grow hot. "The British Empire has brought law, railways, medicine, and the Gospel to places that had none of them."

"And taken rivers, forests, grain, and the names of gods," the sage said mildly. "Tell me, sahib, does your Gospel teach that the poor man is less than the rich, or that the stranger at the gate is to be feared?"

"It teaches charity," Edmund said, and realised as he spoke that he had not thought of his faith as a question for many years. It had been a fixture, like the furniture in his father's house, something one dusted and did not examine.

"Charity," the sage repeated, tasting the word. "A fine thing, if it is given freely. But you did not come here to give. You came to observe, to measure, to write what others will read. Is this not so?"

Edmund opened his mouth to protest and found he could not. The ledger of his ambitions lay open in his mind: the fellowship, the monograph, the admiring letters from colleagues who would call him a pioneer of comparative study. He had spoken of the natives of India as "subjects" in his notes, and he had not once wondered what they called themselves.

"I believe," Edmund said slowly, "that my Lord Jesus taught that the last shall be first."

"Then you have heard your own teaching," said the sage, and for the first time there was warmth in his voice. "Sit, sahib. Let us speak as two men who have travelled far and do not yet know what they have found."

Edmund sat, awkwardly, upon the cool stones of the ghat. His valise slipped from his lap and lay forgotten beside him. The river moved past them, carrying flowers, leaves, and the reflected light of a sun that had shone on this water long before any Englishman had thought to name it.

"What is your name?" Edmund asked, and was surprised to find he wanted to know.

"I am called Anand, though the name is only a sound the wind carries," the sage replied. "And you?"

"Edmund Ashworth. Of Cambridge. Of the Royal Society."

"Edmund," said Anand, pronouncing it carefully, as if weighing a stone. "A name that means one who guards prosperity. That is a heavy thing to carry."

Edmund laughed despite himself, a short and startled sound. "My uncle chose it, I suppose, or my father did. I never considered what it meant."

"Few do," said Anand. "Most of us carry names given by others and grow into the shape of them without asking whether the shape fits."

They were silent for a time. A boatman poled past, singing softly, and Edmund watched him with an attention he had never before paid to a labourer on the Thames.

"Tell me," Edmund said at last, "do you truly believe your gods are real? Or is it simply a manner of speaking, a way of making the world bearable?"

Anand regarded him with patient amusement. "And do you believe your God is real, Edmund Ashworth, or is it a manner of speaking that makes your own world bearable?"

Edmund felt the question strike somewhere deep and tender. He had defended his faith against the materialists at dinner parties for twenty years, quoting Paley and Butler with the ease of long habit. But now he found himself unable to answer quickly, and the silence stretched until it became its own kind of answer.

"I believe," he said finally, and his voice was rougher than he intended, "that I have been very sure of many things and very unkind on the strength of that certainty."

Anand nodded slowly, as though a student had at last arrived at the correct sum. "That is a beginning. Certainty is a fine horse, but it must be ridden with care, or it will carry you into the river."

"You have a way of saying things that makes a man want to argue," Edmund said, and this time he smiled.

"Argument is not my purpose. Understanding is. There is a difference, though your scholars at Cambridge may not have found it yet."

The bell rang again across the water, and Edmund realised he could no longer hear the insects, nor feel the heat of the sun on his neck. The light was shifting, golden and deep, and the shadows of the ghat stretched long across the stones.

"I must return," Edmund said, though he did not know how. "My machine is in the reeds."

"Then return," said Anand. "But take something with you, if you will accept it."

"What?"

"Carry your certainties lightly. Let them be tools and not walls. When you write your monograph, write what you have seen, and write also what you did not understand. That is the honest work of a man who studies others."

Edmund looked down at his valise, which seemed suddenly heavier than it had been. "I was going to write about the Mutiny."

"Then write about it honestly, and about the men who suffered it on both sides. Many of your countrymen will not thank you. But the truth has a way of outliving the flattery of its audience."

Edmund rose, brushing dust from his trousers, and stood for a moment looking at the old man upon the tiger skin. He wanted to thank him, but the words felt too small, so he bowed instead, a gesture he had learned in drawing rooms and which now felt oddly naked.

Anand inclined his head in return, and the gesture was returned with a dignity that made Edmund flush.

He walked back through the reeds to the brass cage, which gleamed faintly in the failing light. When he looked back, the ghat was empty, though he thought he saw a figure sitting still in the shadows, and a faint scent of sandalwood hung in the air.

He stepped inside, set his hand upon the dial, and found that his fingers were trembling. The machine hummed to life, the world blurred, and Edmund Ashworth closed his eyes.

When he opened them again, he stood in a London street, gaslight flickering, the cold rain falling on his upturned face. He had no monograph. He had only a memory of a river and a question he could not put down.

He walked home slowly through the wet streets, past the shuttered shops and the sleeping beggars, and for the first time in his life he looked into their faces.

Community service offers students far more than a line on a college application. When young people volunteer their time to help others, they develop empathy by seeing firsthand the challenges that neighbors face. They also build practical skills, such as teamwork, communication, and problem-solving, that are difficult to learn in a classroom alone. Service often connects students with adults from different professions and backgrounds, widening their understanding of possible futures. Many students also report greater confidence and a stronger sense of purpose after giving back to their communities. Schools can encourage participation in several ways, beginning with flexible scheduling that allows students to volunteer during the school day or on weekends without penalty. Recognition programs, such as certificates or mentions at assemblies, can motivate students who want their efforts acknowledged. Schools can also partner with local organizations so that students have clear, meaningful opportunities rather than vague assignments. A community garden is an especially valuable project for this purpose. Students can plant and tend vegetables, learn about nutrition and the environment, and donate the harvest to local food pantries. The garden also gives younger and older students a shared space to work side by side, strengthening bonds across grade levels. Science teachers can use the garden to teach soil health, plant biology, and seasonal cycles through hands-on experience. Local residents, including retirees with gardening knowledge, can be invited to share their expertise and build intergenerational friendships. Ultimately, a community garden shows students that their labor can nourish both people and the places where they live.

High school curricula are built on two kinds of courses: those a student must complete to graduate, and those a student may choose freely. Understanding the difference between these two categories helps explain how students shape their own education and why schools structure their programs as they do. Graduation requirements are the courses that every student must pass before receiving a diploma. They typically include English, mathematics, science, social studies, and physical education, and they reflect a shared belief that all young people should possess a common foundation of knowledge. Because these subjects are mandatory, they ensure that a graduate from one school can be expected to have covered similar material to a graduate from another. Electives, by contrast, are courses a student selects according to personal interest, career goals, or talent. They might include subjects such as music, computer programming, foreign languages, drama, or agriculture. Electives give students room to explore possibilities they may not have encountered otherwise. A student who is unsure about a future career can sample several fields before committing to one. The balance between these two categories is a matter of ongoing debate among educators and parents. Some argue that requirements should be expanded so that every student gains broad knowledge, while others contend that more electives would allow learners to pursue what genuinely motivates them. Supporters of greater choice point out that engaged students often perform better, and that a course chosen out of curiosity may be remembered far longer than one taken out of obligation. Critics of too much choice worry that students may avoid challenging subjects and leave school without essential skills. The most effective approach likely lies somewhere between these positions. A well-designed program establishes a firm core of required learning while leaving meaningful space for students to follow their own paths. In this way, requirements provide stability and equal opportunity, and electives provide flexibility and personal relevance. Ultimately, the distinction between the two serves a larger purpose: preparing students not only for the next stage of their education but for a life in which they must balance common responsibilities with individual aspirations.

The President had rehearsed the handshake for three weeks, but nothing had prepared her for the alien ambassador's tentacles, which unfurled like a bouquet of silver ribbons. Cameras captured every frame as the delegation descended the ramp of their gleaming vessel onto the White House lawn. Speech after speech was delivered in a translated hum, promising peace, shared knowledge, and mutual prosperity between two worlds. Then the ambassador paused, its many eyes shimmering, and asked a question no protocol officer had anticipated. It wished to know how Earth's most popular forms of entertainment were distributed, particularly those that dealt with the mysteries of human intimacy. The President's chief of staff choked on his coffee while the translator struggled to render the word "pornography" into the ambassador's clicking tongue. Negotiations, it turned out, were already underway in a side room, where the ambassador's aides had been studying Earth's streaming data for months. They had concluded that the species produced an extraordinary volume of such content and were willing to pay in exotic minerals and a patent for faster-than-light fiber optics. The President, sensing both an opportunity and a potential diplomatic disaster, asked for a recess and a list of who in the industry could be trusted to sign. Within a week, a consortium of producers, distributors, and a very confused royalties lawyer were drafting terms in a conference room. The deal was signed with a ceremonial pen made from a meteorite, and the ambassador departed with a promise to return for a sequel. Earth's entertainment executives toasted their new interstellar partners, and the President quietly added a clause requiring that all proceeds fund a public library.

Seeking advice from several people before making an important decision is one of the most practical habits a person can develop. No single individual sees every angle of a complicated choice, and each of us carries our own experiences, biases, and blind spots. By gathering perspectives from different sources, we give ourselves a fuller picture of what is at stake.

Consider the decision to change careers, buy a home, or move to another city. A close friend may offer encouragement grounded in knowing our personality, while a mentor may point out practical risks we have overlooked. A financial advisor can explain the numbers, and someone who has already made a similar choice can describe what the experience was really like. Each voice contributes something the others cannot.

Multiple opinions also help us test our own reasoning. When we explain a plan to several people, we often discover gaps in our logic or assumptions we had never questioned. A question that a stranger asks can reveal a weakness that a loved one, out of kindness, might have politely ignored. This process turns a vague feeling into a clearer, more defensible conclusion.

Consulting others protects us against the tendency toward confirmation bias. People naturally seek out information that supports what they already want to believe. By deliberately asking people who may disagree with us, we force ourselves to take seriously the arguments against our preferred option. Even when we ultimately reject those arguments, we do so with greater confidence because we have confronted them directly.

There is, of course, a danger in the opposite direction. Asking too many people can produce confusion, as conflicting advice piles up and paralyzes the decision-maker. The goal is not to poll everyone we know until we hear what we hope to hear. Rather, it is to select a thoughtful range of advisors whose judgment we respect and whose perspectives differ meaningfully from one another.

Wisdom lies in weighing advice rather than simply counting it. A single well-informed expert may outweigh a dozen casual opinions, and we should judge each suggestion by the reasons behind it. Ultimately, the responsibility for the decision remains ours, and we must be willing to choose even when the advice is mixed.

In the end, consulting several people is not a sign of indecision or weakness. It reflects humility, the recognition that our own knowledge is limited, and a commitment to making choices that we can stand behind. Those who seek counsel from a variety of trustworthy voices tend to make decisions that are more considered, more informed, and more likely to serve them well over time.

In the kingdom of Veyra, twin princes were born on the same night, and from their first breath they seemed to belong to two halves of one whole. Aldric was born at dusk, when the sky turned the color of embers, and his brother Caelan arrived at dawn, as the first pale light touched the castle towers.

Their father, the old king, watched them grow with a mixture of pride and worry. He saw how Aldric loved the quiet hours of study and how Caelan thrived in the bright courtyards of swordplay and song. Each brother carried a piece the kingdom would need, yet each feared he might never be enough alone.

When the old king grew frail, he called both sons to the throne room. "A kingdom cannot be held by one pair of hands," he told them. "Rule together, or the realm will fracture."

The brothers were not sure they could agree on anything, let alone rule as one. Their first council was a clash of opinions, with Aldric urging caution over the northern border and Caelan demanding the army march at once. Neither would yield, and the court whispered that Veyra's future would be torn apart by its princes.

That night, Caelan found Aldric standing alone on the western wall, watching the moon rise over the hills. "We argue because we each see half the picture," Caelan said. "Perhaps that is the point."

Aldric considered this in silence before answering. "Then let us stop trying to win and start trying to balance."

They agreed on a simple rule: no decision would be made by one brother alone. Aldric would guard the treasury, the laws, and the archives, while Caelan would command the watch, the roads, and the garrisons. Every choice that touched both realms would require their shared word.

The northern border tested them within the year. Raiders gathered in the mountain passes, and Caelan wanted to strike at once. Aldric studied the maps and found that the raiders were starving, driven down by a failed harvest. Together they sent grain north instead of soldiers, and the raids ended before the first blade was drawn.

Years passed, and the people of Veyra came to trust the twin princes. Farmers brought their disputes to the eastern hall, where Caelan listened with a steady gaze, and merchants brought their ledgers to the western chambers, where Aldric read every line. Neither brother ruled alone, and neither needed to.

At night, when the castle grew quiet, the brothers would meet on the western wall to speak of their day. Sometimes they laughed, and sometimes they disagreed, but they never stopped listening to each other. Their vigilance kept the kingdom safe, and their balance kept it whole.

When at last they grew old, the people gathered in the square to honor them. An elder asked them what secret had kept Veyra strong for so long. Aldric smiled and gestured toward his brother. "Day and night are not enemies," he said. "They are two watchers who never sleep at the same time."

Replacing the Electoral College with a nationwide popular vote would make presidential elections fairer and more representative of the will of the American people. The current system, established by the Constitution, assigns each state a number of electors equal to its total representation in Congress, and most states award all their electors to whichever candidate wins the statewide plurality. As a result, a candidate can win the presidency while losing the national popular vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016. Such outcomes strike many citizens as fundamentally undemocratic, because the principle that the majority should decide is set aside in favor of a mechanism most voters do not fully understand.

The problem is compounded by the concentration of campaign attention in a handful of swing states. Because electors are awarded on a winner-take-all basis in most states, candidates have little reason to campaign in states where the outcome seems certain. Voters in Texas, California, New York, and many other states are often ignored, while voters in a few battleground states receive a disproportionate share of visits, advertising, and policy promises. A national popular vote would remove this distortion, since every vote would carry equal weight regardless of where it was cast.

Critics of direct elections often argue that the Electoral College protects small states from being overlooked by candidates focused only on populous areas. Yet the current system already gives small states a disproportionate voice, since each state receives at least three electors regardless of population. A nationwide vote would still reflect the interests of rural and small-state voters, because candidates would need to build broad coalitions across the entire country to earn a majority. In a national contest, a candidate could not win by appealing narrowly to a few regions, and this requirement encourages a more inclusive politics.

Another objection holds that a popular vote would encourage candidates to concentrate on large metropolitan areas where the most votes are found. This concern deserves attention, but it is not clear that the result would be worse than the present arrangement. Under the Electoral College, candidates already focus their resources on a few dozen counties in a few states. A national system would require attention to voters in every state, including suburban, rural, and urban communities alike, because turnout gains anywhere would count toward the national total.

Some also worry that abolishing the Electoral College would lead to recounts and disputes over a national margin. In practice, a national popular vote would likely produce clearer results than the current system, since a close national race could be resolved through a uniform federal recount standard rather than the patchwork of state procedures that now apply. The Electoral College itself has produced contested outcomes, including the 2000 Florida recount, which was decided by a Supreme Court ruling rather than by voters.

Opponents also suggest that the Electoral College promotes stability by encouraging two major parties and discouraging fragmentation. This is a real consideration, and any reform would need to address the risk that multiple candidates could split the vote and produce a winner with a small plurality. Proposals such as instant-runoff voting or a national runoff requirement could address this concern while still honoring the principle of direct election. Stability does not require an institution that can override the national vote, and a well-designed direct system can be both stable and democratic.

The Electoral College was created in an era of limited communication, when delegates and electors were thought to serve as a deliberative filter. Those conditions no longer exist. Today, voters are informed about national candidates, and elections are conducted on a national scale through national media and national campaigns. The original rationale for the institution has weakened, while its democratic flaws have become more visible.

For these reasons, a nationwide popular vote would better serve the fundamental democratic principle that each citizen's vote should count equally. It would eliminate the risk of electing a president who lost the national vote, end the neglect of voters in safe states, and require candidates to seek support across the entire country. Constitutional change is difficult, and reformers must address legitimate concerns about stability and representation. Yet the strength of the case for direct election lies in its simplicity: the person who receives the most votes from the American people should become their president.

DNA Methylation Dynamics and Thymine DNA Glycosylase Expression in Individuals with Inherited TP53 Mutations and Cancer Predisposition

Abstract

Germline mutations in TP53 cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a hereditary cancer predisposition disorder characterized by early-onset sarcomas, breast cancers, brain tumors, adrenocortical carcinomas, and leukemias. The p53 protein is a central regulator of genome stability, and its loss or dysfunction is associated with altered epigenetic regulation. In this study, we examine the relationship between genome-wide DNA methylation patterns and the expression of thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG), an enzyme involved in active DNA demethylation through base excision repair. We discuss how inherited TP53 variants may influence methylation landscapes and TDG activity, and how these changes might contribute to cancer susceptibility. The findings are presented as a framework for hypothesis-driven investigation, as the literature in this specific intersection remains limited.

Introduction

The TP53 gene encodes p53, a transcription factor that responds to cellular stress by regulating genes involved in cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, DNA repair, and senescence. Inherited pathogenic variants in TP53 confer a markedly elevated lifetime risk of malignancy, with penetrance estimated to exceed 90 percent by middle age in many families. Beyond its canonical transcriptional functions, p53 participates in chromatin organization and the maintenance of epigenetic stability. Aberrant DNA methylation, including both global hypomethylation and focal hypermethylation of tumor suppressor gene promoters, is a recognized hallmark of carcinogenesis. Understanding how germline TP53 status shapes the epigenome may therefore clarify mechanisms of tumor initiation in predisposed individuals.

DNA methylation predominantly occurs at cytosines within CpG dinucleotides and is catalyzed by DNA methyltransferases such as DNMT1, DNMT3A, and DNMT3B. Removal of methylation can occur passively through replication-dependent dilution or actively through enzymatic pathways. The active pathway involves oxidation of 5-methylcytosine by the TET family of dioxygenases to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, 5-formylcytosine, and 5-carboxylcytosine. Thymine DNA glycosylase excises 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine from DNA, initiating base excision repair that restores unmodified cytosine. Because TDG is essential for this process, its expression and activity directly influence the methylation state of specific genomic regions.

Several lines of evidence suggest that p53 and TDG may be functionally connected. Stress-responsive pathways that engage p53 also modulate base excision repair capacity, and TDG has been implicated in transcriptional regulation at promoters and enhancers. Consequently, alterations in p53 function could plausibly shift the balance between methylation and demethylation, affecting TDG-dependent remodeling of the epigenome. This study considers that possibility within the context of inherited TP53 mutations.

Materials and Methods

A hypothetical cohort design would include individuals carrying germline pathogenic TP53 variants, first-degree relatives without the variant, and unaffected population controls matched for age and sex. Peripheral blood leukocytes and, where available, normal tissue biopsies would be collected under appropriate ethical approval and informed consent. Genome-wide methylation profiling would be performed using bisulfite sequencing or array-based platforms covering promoter, gene body, and enhancer regions. TDG messenger RNA and protein expression would be quantified by quantitative reverse transcription PCR and immunoblotting, respectively. Germline TP53 status would be confirmed by targeted sequencing, and somatic TP53 status in tumor samples would be assessed separately. Statistical analyses would employ linear models adjusting for cell composition, age, and batch effects, with false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons.

Results

The hypothetical analysis would be expected to reveal differentially methylated regions between TP53 carriers and controls. We anticipate that carriers may show a shift in methylation at loci regulated by p53 and by TDG-dependent demethylation. Specifically, promoters of genes involved in DNA repair and cell cycle control could exhibit altered methylation, and these changes might correlate with TDG transcript levels. Carriers may also display a distinct distribution of 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, reflecting altered TET activity upstream of TDG. Expression of TDG itself may differ between carriers and controls, and such differences could be modulated by age and by the specific location of the TP53 variant within the DNA-binding or tetramerization domains.

Discussion

If the proposed relationships are confirmed, they would suggest that germline TP53 mutations influence cancer risk not only through loss of transcriptional tumor suppression but also through epigenetic dysregulation mediated by TDG-dependent demethylation. Such a mechanism would provide a plausible route by which subtle methylation changes accumulate over time and predispose tissues to malignant transformation. Methylation signatures could also serve as biomarkers for early risk stratification in families with Li-Fraumeni syndrome, complementing existing surveillance protocols. TDG expression may represent a further therapeutic consideration, since modulating base excision repair or demethylation pathways is an area of active investigation.

Several limitations must be acknowledged. Cohorts of TP53 carriers are small and heterogeneous, and tissue availability is restricted. Methylation patterns are highly cell-type specific, so findings from blood may not reflect target tissues such as breast or brain. Causality cannot be established from association data alone, and functional experiments in cellular or animal models would be required. Variant-specific effects also complicate interpretation, as different TP53 mutations differ in their impact on p53 function.

Conclusion

The interplay between inherited TP53 mutations, DNA methylation, and TDG expression represents a promising but underexplored area of cancer predisposition research. Integrating epigenomic profiling with germline genetic data may reveal mechanisms linking p53 dysfunction to altered demethylation and tumorigenesis. Future studies should combine large, well-characterized cohorts with mechanistic experiments to test the hypotheses outlined here.

References

References would be provided upon completion of the empirical investigation. This manuscript presents a proposed framework and does not report experimentally validated findings.

Should students be allowed to use mobile devices during lessons, or should they focus solely on their studies? This question has become increasingly important as phones and tablets have become a constant presence in classrooms. Supporters of device use argue that phones give students instant access to information, dictionaries, translation tools, and educational apps that can deepen their understanding of a subject. Used well, a device can also let students take quick notes, record lectures, or check facts during a discussion. However, the same tools that offer these benefits can easily become sources of distraction. A notification, a message, or a social media feed can pull a student's attention away from the lesson in seconds. Research on attention suggests that switching between tasks reduces the quality of learning, so even brief interruptions can have a lasting effect. Teachers also find it harder to hold attention and manage discussion when students are glancing at screens. Fairness is another concern, since students without reliable devices or internet access may fall behind peers who can use them freely. A balanced approach may offer the best outcome. Schools could allow devices for specific purposes, such as research or approved learning activities, while requiring them to be silenced and put away at other times. Clear rules, agreed on by teachers, students, and parents, would help students understand when devices are appropriate. Ultimately, the goal of any lesson is to help students think, understand, and remember. Mobile devices can support that goal, but only when their use is guided by purpose and self-discipline. Without these limits, the convenience of a phone is likely to cost students the focus they came to school to develop.

The sea has always demanded courage from those who work upon it, but few seafarers face a danger quite as unusual as the duty of watching over animals. Among the many tasks aboard a working vessel, the care and observation of livestock, marine animals, or cargo animals can be among the most physically demanding and hazardous. Such work often falls to crew members who must remain alert through long nights and rough weather, keeping watch over creatures that can panic, injure, or even kill when frightened. The following essay considers the dangers of this work, the injuries that seafarers suffer while performing it, and the remarkable determination that keeps them returning to help others.

Animal-watching duties at sea vary widely, depending on the vessel and its cargo. On livestock carriers, crew members may be responsible for feeding, watering, and monitoring hundreds of cattle, sheep, or horses during voyages that can last several weeks. On fishing or research vessels, some crew may tend to live animals held in tanks or pens, while others work alongside marine mammals or birds that require careful handling. Each of these tasks requires constant vigilance, because a single animal that slips, kicks, or charges can threaten everyone nearby.

The dangers of this work are shaped by the confined and unpredictable environment of a ship. Decks become slick with water, manure, and spilled feed, and the constant motion of the sea can throw a worker off balance at the worst moment. Pens and stalls are often cramped, leaving little room to retreat when an animal becomes agitated. Storms add further risk, since frightened animals may thrash violently as the ship rolls, and crew members must enter the enclosures anyway to calm them and secure their safety.

Injuries are a common and serious consequence of these conditions. Seafarers working among large animals have been crushed against pen walls, kicked in the legs or torso, bitten, and struck by falling equipment or loose cargo. Slips and falls on wet decks frequently produce broken bones, head injuries, and spinal damage, while the strain of lifting heavy feed sacks or water containers can cause lasting muscle and back problems. Because a ship may be days away from the nearest port, even a minor injury can become serious before medical help arrives, and the isolation of the work magnifies the fear that accompanies every accident.

Despite these hazards, many seafarers continue to perform this work with extraordinary determination. Their commitment often grows from a deep sense of responsibility toward the animals in their care, whose welfare depends entirely on the people watching over them. Crew members frequently describe a bond formed through long hours of quiet attention, in which they learn to read the moods and needs of the animals and to respond with patience. This sense of duty extends to their fellow crew, as workers look out for one another, sharing warnings, covering shifts, and tending to injured colleagues when accidents occur.

Determination also appears in the way seafarers return to their posts after injury. Many resume their duties as soon as they are able, motivated by loyalty to their shipmates and by the knowledge that their absence places additional strain on those who remain. Others use their experience to improve safety, suggesting better pen designs, clearer procedures, or improved training for newcomers. In this way, the lessons learned from painful incidents often become protections for future crews.

Ultimately, the duty of watching over animals at sea reveals a profound combination of danger and dedication. The work exposes seafarers to real risks of injury, from crushing blows to lasting physical harm, yet it also draws out their willingness to protect others and to persevere through hardship. Their determination to keep helping, whether by caring for animals, supporting one another, or improving the conditions of their work, reflects a quiet but powerful form of courage. Such devotion deserves recognition, not only for the difficult labor it involves but also for the compassion that sustains it across the open ocean.

Should the President of the United States be chosen by a direct national popular vote rather than through the Electoral College? The question strikes at the core of American democracy, because it asks who should decide the nation's highest office and how fairly each citizen's vote should count. Supporters of a popular vote argue that the principle of one person, one vote is the most basic standard of democratic fairness, and that the current system violates it. In the Electoral College, a candidate can win the presidency while losing the nationwide popular vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016. Critics note that this outcome undermines public confidence in the legitimacy of the winner.

The current system also concentrates campaign attention in a small number of battleground states. Because most states award all their electoral votes to the statewide winner, candidates have little reason to campaign in states they are certain to win or lose. Voters in populous states such as California or Texas, and in one-party states like Wyoming or Vermont, may feel their ballots matter less. A national popular vote would require candidates to seek support from voters everywhere, giving every citizen a reason to be courted.

Defenders of the Electoral College respond that it was designed to protect the interests of smaller states and to balance federal power. Under the Constitution, each state receives electoral votes equal to its total number of senators and representatives, which gives less populous states a proportionally larger voice than they would have under a pure population count. Supporters argue that without this structure, candidates might focus almost exclusively on a few dense metropolitan areas, leaving rural and regional concerns unaddressed.

The Electoral College also tends to produce clearer national outcomes in many elections. Because most states award all their electoral votes to a single winner, a candidate typically needs to build a broad coalition across different regions. Some argue that this requirement encourages candidates to appeal to a geographically diverse electorate rather than relying on a single region. Others counter that the same system can magnify small margins in a few swing states.

Practical concerns also matter in this debate. Amending the Constitution to eliminate the Electoral College would require approval by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of the states, a very high threshold that has never been met for such a fundamental change. Alternatively, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact seeks to achieve a similar result by having participating states pledge their electoral votes to the national popular vote winner, but it takes effect only if enough states join to total 270 electoral votes. Its legal and political durability remains debated.

In weighing these arguments, the central question is what values a democracy should prioritize. If equal treatment of individual voters is paramount, the popular vote offers a compelling answer. If preserving federalism and ensuring that less populous regions retain a meaningful voice is more important, the Electoral College has a defensible rationale. Ultimately, the debate reflects a longstanding tension in the American political system between majority rule and the protection of distinct state and regional interests.

A coroner's inquest opened this week to examine the death of a psychiatric patient who died during a physical struggle with a man who said he was defending himself. The hearing, held in a county courthouse, is expected to take several days as jurors and the coroner hear testimony from witnesses, medical staff, and investigators. The patient, whose name has not been released pending family notification, had been admitted to a psychiatric unit for treatment after a period of acute distress. Court documents describe the incident as taking place in a common area of the facility during the early evening. Staff members told investigators that the patient became agitated and approached another resident in a threatening manner. A second patient, a man in his forties, said he stepped in to protect himself and the people nearby. According to his statement, the struggle lasted only a short time before staff intervened. Hospital officials said that staff responded according to established protocols for restraining agitated patients, and that emergency medical care was started immediately. Despite those efforts, the patient was pronounced dead at the scene. An autopsy was performed, and preliminary findings have been submitted to the coroner, though the official cause of death has not yet been announced. Family members of the deceased attended the opening session and asked that the inquest examine whether the facility's safety measures were adequate. Their attorney said they hope the proceedings will bring clarity about the sequence of events and the level of supervision in place at the time. Mental health advocates have also taken interest in the case, noting that incidents of violence in psychiatric settings raise broader questions about staffing levels, training in de-escalation, and the use of physical restraint. The coroner's office has said it will consider all evidence, including surveillance footage, staff logs, and expert testimony on the medical condition of the patient. Jurors will be asked to determine the manner of death, which may be ruled natural, accidental, homicidal, suicidal, or undetermined. The coroner stressed that an inquest is a fact-finding process rather than a criminal trial, and that it does not by itself determine legal responsibility. Any further criminal review would be handled separately by prosecutors. The facility has said it is cooperating fully with the inquiry and has offered counseling to staff and patients who were present. Officials declined to comment on specific details while the investigation remains open. The inquest is scheduled to resume next week, when the medical examiner is expected to present the autopsy findings. Members of the public may attend the proceedings, which the court has said will remain open to observers. The outcome is expected to influence how the facility reviews its policies in the coming months.

Should students be required to join extracurricular clubs, or should they be free to choose for themselves? Mandatory participation has real benefits, since it can introduce students to activities they would never seek out on their own and help them develop teamwork, discipline, and a sense of belonging at school. However, forcing students into clubs can drain motivation and turn an enriching experience into another obligation to resent. Students have different interests, schedules, and responsibilities, such as part-time jobs or family caregiving, and a requirement may place unfair strain on those who already have full lives. Personal choice also teaches self-direction, a skill that students will need long after they leave school, because they must learn to evaluate their own interests and commit to them. Students who genuinely care about an activity tend to contribute more, so voluntary participation often produces higher-quality engagement than compelled attendance. Schools can still encourage involvement by offering a wide variety of clubs, making them accessible, and explaining their value without making them mandatory. In the end, giving students the freedom to choose respects their individuality while still allowing schools to nurture participation through thoughtful and inviting opportunities.

This paper presents a few-shot meta-learning approach for adapting image classifiers to domain shifts, and it addresses a practically important problem: models trained on one data distribution often degrade sharply when deployed on another, and collecting large labeled datasets for every new domain is expensive. The authors frame the task clearly and situate their contribution within the existing literature on gradient-based and metric-based meta-learning. The introduction is well organized, though the motivation could be strengthened with a more concrete example of a real-world deployment scenario where few-shot domain adaptation would be needed. The core method combines episodic training across simulated domain shifts with a lightweight adaptation module that updates a small set of parameters at test time. The idea of constructing training episodes that deliberately mimic distribution mismatch is a sensible and reasonably novel design choice. However, the description of how these domain-shifted episodes are sampled is underspecified, and readers would struggle to reproduce the sampling procedure from the text alone. The mathematical formulation is largely correct, but the notation for the inner-loop and outer-loop updates is inconsistent between the methods section and the algorithm box, which creates unnecessary confusion. The experimental evaluation spans several standard benchmarks, which is a strength, yet the choice of baselines omits some recent domain adaptation methods that would provide a more demanding comparison. The reported accuracy gains are consistent across most settings, but the margins in the 1-shot regime are small and the authors do not report confidence intervals or variance across random seeds, so it is hard to judge whether the improvements are statistically meaningful. The ablation study is useful for isolating the contribution of the episodic domain-shift sampling, but it would be more informative with an ablation on the adaptation module's capacity. The authors acknowledge some limitations, including sensitivity to the number of inner-loop steps, yet they do not analyze how this sensitivity affects practical deployment. Computational cost is discussed only briefly, and a comparison of training and inference time against the baselines would help practitioners weigh the tradeoffs. The related work section is thorough in its coverage of meta-learning but thinner on domain generalization literature, which is a notable gap given the paper's focus. Figures are generally clear, although the t-SNE visualization lacks a description of perplexity settings and the color scheme is hard to distinguish in grayscale print. The writing is mostly clear and free of major grammatical errors, though several paragraphs in the results section repeat numerical details already given in tables. The code availability statement is appreciated, but the repository was incomplete at the time of review, and the authors should ensure all hyperparameter configurations are included. Overall, the paper makes a credible and useful contribution to few-shot domain adaptation. I recommend a major revision that addresses the reproducibility concerns, adds statistical reporting, and broadens the baseline comparisons before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Creating visual art offers students a rare space where feelings can take shape without needing to be explained in words. When a student picks up a pencil or a brush, they begin a conversation with themselves that can be calming, honest, and restorative. Many young people carry stress from school, friendships, and family life, and art gives that tension a place to go. The act of making marks on paper, mixing colors, or shaping clay can slow a racing mind and bring attention back to the present moment.

Psychologists have long noted that expressive activities can lower anxiety and help people process difficult experiences. Art does not require a perfect result to be valuable. A student who sketches a troubling day or paints a mood they cannot describe may discover a clearer understanding of what they feel. This kind of self-reflection builds emotional literacy, the ability to recognize and name one's emotions, which is a skill that supports healthy relationships throughout life.

Beyond emotional benefits, visual art strengthens creative growth in ways that carry into every subject. Drawing trains the eye to observe carefully, noticing shapes, proportions, shadows, and relationships that others might overlook. This habit of close looking helps students in science, where careful observation drives discovery, and in writing, where vivid detail brings stories to life. Art also teaches that problems can have many solutions, encouraging flexible thinking.

The creative process in art is rarely linear. A composition may need to be reworked several times, and a color that looked right in the morning may appear wrong by evening. Students learn to tolerate uncertainty, to experiment without fear, and to revise their work based on honest feedback. These habits of persistence and revision are essential for innovation, whether a student goes on to engineering, medicine, or design.

Art also builds confidence through accomplishment. Finishing a piece, even an imperfect one, gives a student a tangible record of effort and growth. Looking back at earlier work and seeing improvement can be deeply motivating. This sense of progress encourages students to take on harder challenges and to believe that their abilities can be developed through practice.

Career aspirations benefit as well, though the connection is sometimes underestimated. Visual art is the foundation of many fields, including graphic design, architecture, animation, fashion, industrial design, and film. Even careers far from the studio value the skills art cultivates, such as visual communication, spatial reasoning, and the ability to present ideas clearly. Employers across industries increasingly seek people who can think creatively and communicate with impact.

Developing a portfolio is one of the most practical benefits for students with professional goals. A body of work demonstrates skill, vision, and growth in a way that grades cannot. Students who keep a sketchbook and build a collection of finished pieces gain material for college applications, scholarship submissions, and job interviews. The discipline of assembling and presenting a portfolio also teaches organization and self-advocacy.

Art education can also open doors to community and mentorship. Students often meet artists, teachers, and peers who share their interests and who can offer guidance, encouragement, and opportunities. Exhibitions, school galleries, and community art programs give young artists a chance to share their work with an audience, building both confidence and professional networks.

Some students worry that pursuing art is not a practical choice. It is true that creative careers can be competitive, but the same is true of many fields, and art develops adaptability that serves people well regardless of their path. A student who learns to create, reflect, and communicate visually is prepared for a world that rewards imagination.

Schools that invest in visual art give students more than a class period of pleasant activity. They offer a place for emotional expression, a training ground for creative thinking, and a pathway toward meaningful careers. Supporting art education means supporting the whole student, helping them grow as people who can feel deeply, think originally, and pursue their dreams with purpose.

Kent Police's use of predictive software to guide patrols has prompted fresh questions about how well the technology works and whether the force has the resources to make the most of it.

The software analyses past crime data to identify locations and time periods where offences are statistically more likely to occur, and officers are then directed to spend time in those areas. Supporters argue that the approach allows limited patrol hours to be used more efficiently at a time when police budgets remain under pressure.

Critics, however, say the case for its effectiveness has not been clearly demonstrated in public. Independent researchers have pointed out that predictive policing tools can reflect the patterns of past recording rather than underlying levels of crime, which may lead to uneven attention across different neighbourhoods.

Questions have also been raised about the data feeding the system, including how complete it is, how often it is updated, and how reported crimes are categorised. Campaigners have asked for greater transparency about the inputs and outputs of the software.

Resources are another concern. Running and maintaining such a system requires trained analysts, reliable data infrastructure, and regular oversight, and some observers question whether these needs are being met alongside frontline demands. Others note that the software is only as useful as the officers who act on its recommendations.

Officers on the ground have offered mixed views. Some say that targeted patrols help them focus on known hotspots, while others feel that the guidance can be rigid and does not always match what they see in their own communities.

A spokesperson for Kent Police has said the force regularly reviews its use of analytical tools and remains committed to evidence-based policing. The spokesperson added that the technology is intended to support, not replace, professional judgement.

Local councillors have asked for a fuller public account of the system's results, including whether crime has fallen in areas where extra patrols were directed. Several have called for an independent evaluation to be published.

Civil liberties groups have also urged caution, arguing that any predictive tool must be subject to clear legal safeguards and must not lead to people being treated as suspects because of where they live.

Data protection specialists have added that the force must be able to explain how personal information is stored, shared, and deleted, particularly where data from different sources is combined.

The debate reflects a wider national conversation about how police forces should use data-driven technology. Supporters see potential for better outcomes, while sceptics warn of unintended consequences that can be hard to detect.

Kent Police has said it will consider the feedback it has received and publish updates where it can. Whether this will be enough to settle the questions remains to be seen.

For now, residents, councillors, and officers alike are waiting for clearer evidence on whether the software is delivering the results it promises. The outcome may shape how other forces approach similar tools in the years ahead.

After-school programs offer students far more than a place to wait for a ride home. When structured well, they support the health, friendships, and academic lives of young people in ways that families and schools can build upon. Their benefits reach well beyond the final bell of the school day.

One of the most important advantages is physical health. Many after-school programs include sports, dance, outdoor games, or active play, which help children meet daily activity goals that are often hard to reach during long hours of sitting in class. Regular movement supports stronger bones and muscles, better sleep, and healthier weight. Programs that also serve a healthy snack give students nutrition at a time when hunger can otherwise distract them from learning.

Emotional health benefits as well. Supervised programs give students a calm, predictable setting where they can decompress after a demanding school day. Trained staff can notice when a child seems withdrawn, anxious, or struggling at home, and they can connect that child with counselors or family support. Many programs also teach coping skills, such as managing frustration during a game or handling disappointment after a loss.

Friendships are another area where these programs make a real difference. Students who attend the same program often form bonds that cross the boundaries of their classrooms, grade levels, or neighborhoods. Shared activities such as building a robot, rehearsing a play, or working on a community garden give children common goals to pursue together. For students who are shy or new to a school, a consistent group of peers can make the transition feel far less lonely.

These friendships also teach important social skills. Children learn to take turns, resolve disagreements, cooperate on teams, and listen to viewpoints different from their own. Older students who serve as mentors or helpers develop leadership and responsibility, while younger students gain role models they can look up to. Over time, these experiences help children grow more confident in their ability to connect with others.

Academically, after-school programs can close gaps that the regular school day leaves open. Homework help gives students a quiet space and an adult who can answer questions, which reduces the frustration that often leads to unfinished assignments. Tutoring in reading and math can strengthen skills for students who need extra practice, while enrichment activities can spark interests in science, art, or technology that a busy curriculum may not fully explore.

Beyond specific subjects, these programs encourage habits that support lifelong learning. Students practice time management when they balance homework with activities, and they build persistence when they work through challenges on a project over several weeks. Exposure to new experiences, such as visiting a museum through a partner organization or learning a musical instrument, can broaden a student's sense of what they might become.

Research has found that well-run programs can be linked with improved attendance, better grades, and more positive attitudes toward school. These results are most consistent when programs are carefully planned, stay focused on clear goals, and are staffed by people who build trusting relationships with students. Poorly designed programs that offer little more than unsupervised free time do not produce the same benefits, which is why quality matters as much as availability.

Access is also an important consideration. Families who work long hours or lack reliable transportation may depend on after-school programs to keep their children safe and engaged. When these programs are affordable or free, they help level the playing field for students whose families have fewer resources to fill the afternoon hours with enrichment. Communities that invest in such programs are, in effect, investing in the futures of their children.

Schools, parents, and community organizations can all contribute to making these programs successful. Schools can share information about student needs, while families can give feedback and encourage attendance. Community groups, libraries, and local businesses can offer expertise, space, or volunteers. When these partners work together, after-school programs become a dependable source of growth for students.

In the end, the afternoon hours can be some of the most valuable in a child's day. After-school programs that promote physical activity, emotional well-being, meaningful friendships, and academic support help students become healthier, more connected, and better prepared for the future. Investing in them is a practical way to help every young person thrive.

The manuscript proposes a feedforward initialization scheme for energy-based models trained with equilibrium propagation, aiming to reduce the number of relaxation steps needed at inference time while avoiding backpropagation. The problem is well motivated, since equilibrium propagation traditionally requires iterative settling of the network state to a fixed point, which is slow and limits practical use. The authors frame the contribution clearly and position it relative to prior work on local learning rules and biologically plausible training. The central idea is to learn a feedforward network that predicts a good starting state for the energy minimization, so that fewer iterations are required to reach equilibrium. This is a sensible and potentially useful direction, and the paper is generally readable and organized.

The strongest aspect of the work is its conceptual simplicity. Using a cheap feedforward pass to warm-start an iterative solver is a well-established idea in other settings, and the authors adapt it thoughtfully to the energy-based framework. The derivation of how the initializer interacts with the equilibrium objective is mostly clear, and the authors correctly note that the initializer does not change the fixed points of the energy function, only the path taken to reach them. This property is important because it means the inference result should remain consistent with the trained model. The authors also make a reasonable argument that the approach preserves the locality that makes equilibrium propagation attractive.

There are, however, several concerns that the authors should address. The derivation of the training signal for the feedforward initializer is presented somewhat briefly, and it is not fully clear how its parameters are updated or whether a separate learning rule is needed. A more explicit statement of the full training procedure, perhaps in algorithmic form, would substantially aid reproducibility. The paper also does not adequately discuss the case where the initializer is poor, for example on out-of-distribution inputs, and whether the iterative solver can still recover reliably in such cases. Reporting the distribution of the number of settling steps, rather than only the average, would give a more honest picture of the speedup.

The experimental section demonstrates improvements on standard image classification benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the scope is narrow. The authors test primarily on small convolutional and fully connected architectures, and it remains unclear whether the gains persist for deeper or larger models. The comparison baselines are reasonable but could be strengthened by including a version of equilibrium propagation with a fixed reduced number of iterations, since this would isolate whether the initializer or simply fewer steps accounts for the improvement. Error bars or results across multiple random seeds are not consistently reported, making it difficult to judge whether some of the reported differences are statistically meaningful.

The accuracy numbers are competitive with prior equilibrium propagation results, but the paper would benefit from a clearer accounting of computational cost. Inference speed is reported in terms of iteration counts, which is informative, yet wall-clock time and the cost of running the additional feedforward network are not fully quantified. Since the central claim is acceleration, a direct wall-clock comparison on common hardware would be more persuasive. The authors should also clarify whether the reduction in iterations comes at any cost in final energy or prediction quality.

The related work section is thorough in covering equilibrium propagation and its variants but is less complete on amortized inference and learned warm starts in energy-based modeling more broadly. Engaging with this literature would help readers understand how the proposed method differs from existing amortization strategies. Some notation is introduced inconsistently, with the same symbol used for both the energy function and a related quantity in different sections, which should be corrected for clarity.

The figures are generally clear, though the convergence plots would be easier to interpret with a shared axis scale across methods and with the initialization cost included. The writing is mostly precise, though a number of sentences in the discussion are verbose and could be tightened without losing content.

In summary, this is a promising and clearly motivated contribution with a simple and plausible core idea. The main weaknesses lie in the incompleteness of the training description, the limited scope of experiments, the lack of multi-seed statistics, and the incomplete accounting of computational cost. If the authors address these points, particularly by providing a full algorithm, broader experiments, and wall-clock timings, the paper would make a solid contribution to the study of efficient equilibrium-propagation-based models. I recommend a major revision.

Facial-expression recognition technology promises a new way for teachers to understand how students feel during lessons. By analyzing the images captured from classroom cameras, software can estimate whether a student appears confused, bored, frustrated, or engaged. Supporters argue that this information could help teachers respond quickly, offering extra explanation to a student who looks lost or a new challenge to one who seems restless. In a crowded classroom, a single teacher cannot easily notice the subtle signs of every learner, so a tool that flags these moments could make support more responsive and more equitable.

The potential benefits are real. Students who struggle silently, often because they are shy or reluctant to ask questions, might receive help they would otherwise miss. Teachers could also use aggregated data to see which topics leave the whole class puzzled, prompting them to revisit material or change their approach. Used carefully, the technology could complement a teacher's judgment rather than replace it, giving educators one more source of information about how their lessons are landing.

However, the accuracy of these systems is a serious concern. Human facial expressions are not reliable indicators of inner states. A student who looks bored may be deeply thinking, and a student who looks angry may simply have poor eyesight and be squinting at the board. Research on emotion recognition has repeatedly found that the link between facial movements and specific feelings varies across people, cultures, and situations. Acting on flawed readings could lead teachers to misjudge students and respond in ways that do not help.

Privacy is another major issue. Constant monitoring of young people's faces creates a record of their emotional lives that many would find intrusive. Students may feel they are always being watched, which can increase anxiety and make them less willing to express themselves honestly. Questions also arise about who would own this data, how long it would be stored, and whether it might later be used for purposes such as disciplinary decisions or evaluations of teacher performance.

Fairness must also be considered. Recognition systems have been shown to perform less accurately for some racial and gender groups, and students who express emotions differently because of neurodivergence or cultural background could be unfairly labeled. A system that misreads these students could reinforce existing inequalities rather than reduce them.

For these reasons, schools should approach the technology with great caution. If it is used at all, it should be strictly limited, transparent to students and parents, and subject to independent evaluation for accuracy and bias. Students should have a voice in deciding whether such tools are acceptable. Above all, the goal should be to strengthen human relationships in education, not to replace careful observation and conversation with an algorithm that may not truly understand the young people it claims to read.

This paper proposes a neural semantic parsing framework that maps natural language mathematical problems into executable programs built from domain-specific operators, with the aim of improving compositional generalization. The authors motivate the work clearly, noting that existing sequence-to-sequence approaches often produce fluent but logically inconsistent solutions when problems require multi-step numerical reasoning over textual context. The introduction situates the contribution well within prior work on program synthesis for math word problems and neural symbolic reasoning. The central idea, a library of typed domain-specific operators that the decoder composes into programs, is intuitive and well-motivated. The operator design section, however, would benefit from a more precise formal definition of operator types and their signatures. Readers would also appreciate a clearer explanation of how operator arguments are grounded in spans of the input text. The parsing architecture combines a pretrained encoder with a grammar-constrained decoder, which is a reasonable design choice for ensuring syntactically valid outputs. The paper would be stronger if it included an ablation isolating the contribution of the grammar constraint from that of the operator vocabulary. The training procedure uses a mixture of supervised program annotations and weak supervision from final answers, and the description of this mixture is somewhat terse. The authors should specify the weighting scheme and report sensitivity to it. The experimental setup evaluates on several standard math reasoning benchmarks, which is appropriate for the claims made. The reported gains over the strongest baseline are consistent across datasets, though the margins on some splits are small enough that variance estimates over multiple random seeds would strengthen the conclusions. The compositional generalization experiments, which hold out certain operator combinations during training, are the most interesting part of the evaluation and deserve more space. The authors show that the model generalizes to unseen combinations of depth greater than those seen in training, a finding that supports their central thesis. Error analysis is included and categorizes failures into grounding errors, operator selection errors, and arithmetic execution errors. This taxonomy is useful, but the proportions reported should be accompanied by counts and examples for readers to judge severity. The comparison with large language model prompting baselines is limited, and it is unclear whether the prompting setup used few-shot exemplars matched to the target distribution. Stronger and more carefully configured baselines would make the comparison more convincing. The paper's claim that the approach is more interpretable than end-to-end neural solvers is plausible given that programs are inspectable, but the authors provide no human study verifying that the generated programs are easier to audit. Such a study would substantiate this claim. The related work section is thorough, though it could more explicitly contrast the proposed operators with those in earlier neural module networks. Reproducibility is partially addressed through the release of code, but the paper does not specify the exact operator library or provide the full prompt and hyperparameter settings in the main text. Including these in an appendix would be valuable. The writing is generally clear, though several figures are small and their captions are insufficiently descriptive. The notation for program trees changes between sections, which occasionally creates confusion. Overall, the core contribution is a sound and promising extension of semantic parsing to mathematical reasoning. The compositional generalization results are encouraging and merit further investigation. I recommend acceptance conditional on minor revisions. The authors should add variance estimates, clarify the operator formalism, strengthen the LLM baselines, and provide a human evaluation of program interpretability. With these changes, the paper would make a solid contribution to the field. The problem is important, the method is principled, and the empirical evidence, while not yet fully comprehensive, points in a convincing direction. I would be glad to see a revised version.
