Education and effort in school can have a lasting influence on students' future careers and earnings. Students who build strong skills in reading, math, and critical thinking gain access to a wider range of jobs and training programs. Consistent effort, such as completing assignments, seeking help when needed, and pursuing challenging courses, also teaches discipline and perseverance that employers value. Over time, these habits can lead to higher education, certifications, and promotions that translate into greater earning potential. While school success does not guarantee a particular outcome, it provides a foundation that opens doors and helps students make informed choices about their futures.

Gathering diverse perspectives before making a decision is one of the most valuable habits a person or group can develop. When people with different backgrounds, experiences, and expertise contribute their views, they expose blind spots that a single viewpoint would likely miss. Each individual tends to approach problems through a familiar lens, and that lens can limit the range of options considered. Hearing from others challenges assumptions and encourages people to examine why they believe what they believe. Diverse input also leads to more thorough analysis, since different people notice different risks, consequences, and opportunities. Decisions shaped by many viewpoints are often more fair, because they take into account the needs of a wider group of people who will be affected by the outcome. Such decisions also tend to earn greater trust and buy-in, since those who contributed feel heard and are more likely to support the result. Furthermore, the process of weighing competing ideas sharpens critical thinking and reduces the danger of groupthink, where a desire for agreement overrides careful judgment. Ultimately, seeking out diverse perspectives does not mean giving up one's own judgment, but rather strengthening it with a richer set of information. In an increasingly complex world, the ability to listen to and learn from others is essential to making wise and lasting choices.

The afterlife, it turned out, had a queue. Marisol arrived at the Gates of Eternal Repose on a Tuesday, still wearing her hospital bracelet, and was handed a numbered ticket: 48,212,907.

A pleasant voice over the speakers assured her that her call was important and that her wait would be brief.

She sat in a long hall of pale marble, its ceiling lost in soft golden light. Angels drifted past with clipboards, smiling in the way people smile when they cannot help you.

Beside her, a retired fisherman named Tomas sighed and said he had been waiting since Easter. He had already been transferred twice, once to Purgatory Services and once to a department that no longer existed.

The paradise beyond the hall was visible through a frosted window: rivers of light, gardens without weeds, music that sounded like someone reconciling with a lost friend. Every so often a door would open, a lucky soul would step through, and the crowd would murmur with envy.

Marisol had expected judgment. She had prepared herself for fire, for reckoning, for the weight of her small cruelties. She had not prepared for hold music.

The hold music was a single phrase of a harp melody, looping forever, and it was slightly out of tune.

After nine hours, a cherub at the front desk told her that her file was incomplete. Her birth certificate was missing, and so was a notarized statement of her good intentions.

"We have a form for that," the cherub said, sliding a document across the counter. It was four hundred pages long and written in a language that shifted when she looked away.

She filled out the first page. It asked for her mother's maiden name, and she realized she could no longer remember it, which made her cry in a way she had not cried while dying.

Tomas, two seats over, was furious on her behalf. He wrote letters to the Supervisor of Souls, a being no one had ever seen, and received replies that thanked him for his feedback.

A woman in a grey shawl joined the line and quietly mentioned that she had once been a case worker in the mortal world. She said the afterlife was simply a larger version of the same systems, staffed by the same weary people, and that the cruelest part was the hope they kept selling.

Years passed, or perhaps only days. Marisol lost track. The marble grew dusty, the golden light dimmed to a tired amber, and the harp melody began to sound like a warning.

Eventually her number came up on a glowing board. She rushed to the counter with trembling hands.

The cherub looked at her file, frowned, and said her application had been closed as abandoned. She would need to start again from the beginning, and the queue had been reorganized.

Marisol laughed, then wept, then laughed again. Tomas patted her shoulder and told her that, in his experience, the trick was to make friends with the hold music.

So they did. They sat together in the endless hall, humming the broken harp tune, trading stories of the lives they had left behind, and waiting for a door that might never open.

Mara had spent most of her life hiding the thin white line that ran across her left forearm, a souvenir from a bicycle accident when she was nine. She wore long sleeves in summer and turned her arm away whenever a camera appeared. Her reflection had become a place she visited only briefly, always looking for what was wrong.

When she met Daniel, she expected him to notice the scar eventually, and she braced herself for the questions that usually followed. Instead, he never asked about it in the first weeks they spent together. He simply held her hand the way anyone would, his thumb moving over the inside of her wrist without any hesitation.

One evening, while they were cooking together, she reached for a pan and her sleeve slipped up. Daniel glanced at the scar, then went back to chopping onions as if it were nothing unusual. She waited for him to say something, but he only asked whether she wanted more garlic.

Later that night, lying on the couch with a blanket over both of them, she finally asked him why he had never mentioned it. He thought for a moment before answering. He said the scar was part of how her arm had been shaped by her own life, and that it made her hands look like they had done real things.

Mara did not know what to say. She had spent so many years believing that her body was something to be corrected or concealed that his words felt almost foreign. She felt tears gather, not out of sadness exactly, but from a strange relief.

The following weekend, Daniel took her to the lake, and she wore a sleeveless blue dress without thinking about it until she was already standing in the sun. She felt the warmth on her skin and noticed the scar in the bright light. For once, she did not immediately look away.

Over the following months, Daniel kept showing her the same quiet acceptance. He traced the small scar above her eyebrow from a childhood fall and told her it looked like a tiny comma, a pause in a sentence that still made sense. He never treated her marks as flaws to fix, only as parts of her history.

Mara began to notice how much lighter she felt when she stopped pulling her sleeves down. She started to see her body less as a list of problems and more as a record of everything she had survived. The mirror became less of an enemy and more of a familiar friend.

She still had days when the old critical voice returned, whispering that she should cover up and be less visible. On those days, she would think of Daniel's thumb moving across her wrist, unbothered and gentle. Slowly, she learned to speak to herself with the same patience he offered her.

Years later, when a young cousin asked her about the faint line on her arm, Mara smiled and told the story of the bicycle and the hill and the stubborn determination to ride it again. Her cousin listened with wide eyes and then asked if it hurt. Mara laughed and said it had, but that she had healed, and that the mark was a reminder of how far she had come.

Her cousin nodded seriously and said it looked like a secret map. Mara agreed that it might be, and she realized she was no longer afraid of anyone asking. What she had once wanted to hide had become a part of her story she could share freely.

Daniel had given her something more valuable than comfort. He had shown her that being loved did not depend on being flawless, and that acceptance from someone who truly sees you could help you see yourself. Her self-worth had not come from becoming someone new, but from finally recognizing the person who had been there all along.

Setbacks are a normal part of life, and they can be some of the most valuable experiences a person ever has. Although failure is often painful, it can teach lessons that success rarely provides. When people face setbacks, they are forced to examine what went wrong, and that examination can lead to growth.

Consider the process of learning to ride a bicycle. Almost every child falls off at least once, and those falls are not wasted effort. Each fall teaches the rider something about balance, speed, and steering. The scraped knees are a small price for the knowledge gained. In the same way, many of the skills people develop in adulthood are shaped by early mistakes.

One reason setbacks are so useful is that they reveal weaknesses clearly. A student who receives a poor grade on a test learns exactly which topics need more attention. A runner who loses a race can see where their pacing fell apart. Success can hide flaws, because a person who wins may never notice what could have been better. Failure makes those flaws visible and gives the person a reason to address them.

Setbacks also build resilience. Resilience is the ability to recover from difficulty and keep moving forward. People who have experienced disappointment and survived it often discover that they are stronger than they expected. Each time someone bounces back, their confidence in their own ability to cope grows. Over time, this confidence makes future challenges feel more manageable.

It is important, however, to approach setbacks with the right attitude. Someone who sees every failure as proof of their own inadequacy may give up entirely. A more helpful approach is to view a setback as information rather than a verdict. The question should not be "Am I bad at this?" but rather "What can I learn from what just happened?" This shift in perspective turns a discouraging moment into an opportunity.

Many famous people have credited their achievements to lessons learned through failure. Inventors have described hundreds of unsuccessful experiments before finding a working design. Writers have collected stacks of rejection letters before a single book was published. Athletes have lost important competitions and then trained harder to win later. These examples suggest that persistence through difficulty is often a key part of eventual success.

Setbacks can also encourage creativity. When the first plan fails, people are pushed to find another path. Some of the best solutions to problems come from the need to try something different. A closed door can lead a person to discover a window they would never have noticed otherwise. In this way, setbacks can redirect a person toward goals they might not have considered before.

Relationships can benefit from setbacks as well. When people struggle, they often reach out to friends, family, or mentors for support. These moments can deepen connections and remind people that they do not have to face difficulties alone. Sharing a setback can also make others feel more comfortable being honest about their own struggles.

Of course, not every setback leads to a positive outcome automatically. Learning from failure requires effort, reflection, and sometimes outside guidance. A person must be willing to honestly assess their mistakes without excessive blame or denial. They must also be willing to adjust their methods and try again. Setbacks offer the raw material for growth, but growth still depends on the choices a person makes afterward.

Schools can play an important role in helping students understand this. When teachers treat mistakes as part of the learning process rather than as failures to be punished, students are more likely to take risks and attempt difficult problems. A classroom where students feel safe to be wrong is one where real learning can happen. Encouraging students to reflect on their errors can help them develop habits that will serve them throughout their lives.

Parents and caregivers can also support children through setbacks. Rather than rushing to fix every problem, they can ask questions that help the child think through what happened and what to try next. Praise for effort and strategy, rather than only for results, can teach children that their abilities can improve with practice. Children who learn this lesson early are often more willing to tackle challenges later.

In the workplace, setbacks are equally common. A project may fail, a deadline may be missed, or a proposal may be rejected. Organizations that treat these moments as opportunities to study what went wrong often become more innovative and effective over time. Employees who feel supported after a mistake are more likely to speak up about problems early, which can prevent larger failures in the future.

Personal goals follow a similar pattern. Someone who wants to get in shape may gain weight back after a period of progress, or someone learning a language may struggle to hold a conversation. These experiences can be discouraging, but they also reveal what habits need to change. A person who adjusts their routine, sets more realistic expectations, and keeps going is far more likely to reach their goal than someone who quits after the first disappointment.

It is also worth remembering that setbacks can change the direction of a life for the better. A person who fails to get into their first choice of college may discover a program they love at another school. A business that fails may lead its founder to a more successful venture. A job loss may open the door to a career that better fits a person's talents. In hindsight, many people see that the setback was a turning point rather than an ending.

Finally, setbacks teach humility and perspective. They remind people that they do not have complete control over outcomes and that effort, luck, and circumstance all play a role. This understanding can make people more compassionate toward others who are struggling. It can also help them celebrate success more meaningfully, knowing how hard it was to reach.

In conclusion, setbacks are not simply obstacles to be avoided. They are chances to learn, to strengthen character, and to find better ways forward. Those who meet failure with curiosity and determination often end up closer to their goals than they would have been otherwise. The next time a setback arrives, it may be worth asking not only what it has taken away, but also what it has to teach.

Should high schools require arts education, or should students be free to choose their own courses? Supporters of required arts classes argue that the arts develop skills that matter in every field, including creativity, discipline, and the ability to think from multiple perspectives. A student who has never performed on stage, sketched from observation, or analyzed a painting may never discover a talent or interest that could shape the rest of their life. Requirements also ensure that students from low-income families, who may have no access to art programs outside school, receive exposure they would otherwise miss. On the other hand, students are not all the same, and forcing everyone into the same courses can feel like a waste of time for those with clear goals in science, engineering, or trades. Time spent on a required art class is time not spent on advanced mathematics, a second language, or a career-focused elective. Choice also builds responsibility, since students who select their own courses must think about their strengths and future plans. A middle path may serve students best: require a basic exposure to the arts in early years, then allow students to choose advanced arts courses based on their interests. This approach introduces everyone to creative work while still respecting individual goals. Ultimately, the question is not whether the arts matter, but how schools can make them accessible without ignoring what each student needs to succeed.

School partnerships with local businesses can give students valuable chances to explore careers through job shadowing, internships, and guest speakers who share real workplace experience. These programs help students connect classroom learning to practical skills and can clarify their interests before they commit to a college major or training path. However, partnerships also carry costs, such as the time teachers must spend coordinating with employers and the risk that businesses may promote their own interests or offer opportunities unevenly across different student groups. Schools must therefore weigh these benefits against the administrative demands and design partnerships carefully to ensure they are equitable and educational.

The manuscript addresses an important and underexplored question: whether neural architectures can learn recursive divide-and-conquer strategies for combinatorial problems rather than merely memorizing input-output mappings. The authors position their contribution well within the literature on algorithmic reasoning and neural execution, and the motivation for seeking inductive biases that mirror recursive decomposition is convincing. The paper's central claim is that a recursive controller with shared parameters across subproblems can generalize to larger instances than those seen during training, and this is the claim the evaluation must ultimately support. The related work section is thorough in covering pointer networks, neural GPUs, and graph neural approaches to combinatorial optimization, though it would benefit from a clearer comparison against classical hybrid methods that already exploit divide-and-conquer structure. The formal description of the architecture is generally clear, with the recursion depth, merge operator, and base-case handling specified in sufficient detail to be reproduced. However, the paper does not state how the merge operator is constrained to remain valid across subproblem boundaries, and I would ask the authors to clarify this, since invalid merges could silently produce infeasible solutions. The training procedure relies on supervised targets generated by an exact solver, which raises the question of whether the model learns the recursion or simply imitates the solver's outputs on a narrow distribution. The experiments on sorting-like and partitioning tasks show encouraging in-distribution accuracy, but the length-generalization results are reported only for two problem sizes beyond training, which is too few to support a strong conclusion about scaling. I would strongly encourage evaluation at several held-out sizes with confidence intervals across multiple random seeds, as the current single-run figures make variance impossible to judge. The ablation study is valuable, particularly the comparison with a non-recursive baseline of matched parameter count, but the authors should also ablate the parameter-sharing choice, since that is the component most directly tied to the paper's thesis. The discussion of failure cases is brief and would be more useful with concrete examples showing where the recursion breaks down on problems with irregular subproblem sizes. Reproducibility is partially addressed through the released code, yet the hyperparameter search procedure and compute budget are not reported, which limits fair comparison with future work. The writing is generally clear, though several figures have unlabeled axes and the notation for subproblem indices changes between sections, which should be unified. The theoretical section offers a loose argument about expressivity but does not establish any bound on the depth needed to solve instances of a given size, and a stronger statement here would substantially raise the paper's impact. The authors also do not discuss the computational cost of their approach relative to the classical algorithms it imitates, which matters for any practical claim of advantage. Some claims in the introduction, such as that the method "discovers" novel divide-and-conquer strategies, go beyond what the evidence shows, since the learned decompositions are not analyzed or compared with known algorithms. I recommend that the authors either provide an analysis of the learned recursion or temper this language. Overall, the paper contains a promising idea and a competent initial implementation, but the empirical evidence for generalization is currently too limited to support the central claim. I would rate the submission as a weak accept conditional on a more extensive length-generalization study, clearer treatment of merge validity, and a more cautious framing of the discovery claims. With these revisions, the work could make a meaningful contribution to the study of neural algorithmic reasoning.

Setbacks are often viewed as failures, yet they can serve as powerful guides for personal growth and achievement. When a plan falls apart, it forces a person to pause, reflect on what went wrong, and consider what could be done differently. This process builds self-awareness, revealing strengths to rely on and weaknesses to address. Many successful people have described early defeats as turning points that taught them patience, humility, and persistence. Overcoming a difficult experience also builds resilience, giving a person greater confidence to face future challenges. Rather than discouraging progress, setbacks can redirect energy toward more meaningful goals and better strategies. In this way, the obstacles we encounter become lessons that shape character as much as any success. Ultimately, the path to achievement is rarely a straight line, and those who learn from their setbacks are the ones who grow the most.

The wind off the ridge had teeth that day, and Tom Harrow felt every one of them through his thinning coat. He had been walking the survey line for six hours, boots crusted with snow, his theodolite strapped across his back like a sleeping animal. Nobody had paid him in four months, and the debts from the last winter still sat in his chest like stones.

He almost missed the figure lying in the drift below the saddle of the hill. It was a man, or what remained of one, curled against a boulder with his hands tucked into his armpits. Tom slid down the slope on his heels and knelt beside him. The stranger's lips were gray, and when Tom touched his cheek, the skin was waxy and stiff.

Frostbite, Tom thought, and something worse than frostbite if the man had been out long. He should have built a fire right there. He should have cut the man's wet clothes away and wrapped him in his own spare blanket, then half-carried him to the cabin two miles south. Those were the things a decent man would do, and Tom knew it.

But beneath the saddle, just visible where the snow had blown thin, was a band of dark quartz running through the rock. Tom had seen that kind of vein before, in the old reports from the district office. The men who staked it first would own the hill for a generation. A claim like that could pay off every debt he owned and then some.

The stranger coughed weakly and whispered something that might have been water or might have been a name. Tom stood up and looked at the vein, then at the man, then at the vein again. The wind pushed against his back as though urging him along.

He told himself the man would be found eventually, that someone else would come along the trail, that the cold was not his doing. He told himself a surveyor's first duty was to his survey. None of it sounded convincing, even to him.

He pulled a stake from his pack and began driving it into the frozen ground beside the vein. Each blow of the mallet rang out across the empty hillside. The stranger's breathing grew shallower with every swing, but Tom kept his eyes fixed on the rock.

By the time he had marked the corners of the claim, the light was failing. He wrote the coordinates in his field book with fingers he could barely feel. Then he finally looked down at the figure in the snow, which had gone very still.

Tom knelt again and pressed two fingers to the man's neck. Nothing moved beneath them. He sat back on his heels and stared at the sky, where the first stars were pricking through the clouds.

He could still go for help. The cabin was two miles away, and a man could make it in under an hour if he ran. But the claim papers needed filing in town by the end of the week, and a body on the hill would mean questions, inquiries, a delay that might cost him the vein.

He stood and gathered his gear, moving stiffly, ignoring the hollow feeling spreading under his ribs. He did not look back at the boulder as he started down the trail toward town. The snow fell softly behind him, filling in his footprints one by one.

In town the next morning, the clerk at the district office stamped his papers without looking up. Tom signed where he was told and collected his copy of the claim. He felt lighter than he had in months, and he hated himself for it.

Three days later, a search party found the stranger's body near the saddle, half-buried under fresh snow. A deputy came to the boarding house asking questions about the surveyor who had been working that line. Tom answered politely, saying he had seen no one on the hill that week.

The deputy wrote it down and thanked him for his time. Tom watched him ride away and told himself the lie would hold. It held for a while, though the cold seemed to follow him into every room afterward.

That spring, workers came up the ridge with picks and drills and began opening the vein. The ore assayed richer than anyone had hoped, and the company's agents shook Tom's hand on the porch of the office. They offered him a percentage of the sale, and he accepted it without argument.

The money paid his debts and bought him a proper coat. It also bought him a house with a stove that never seemed to warm the kitchen corners. At night he sometimes dreamed of the drift beneath the saddle, of gray lips moving around a word he never learned.

Years passed, and the mine grew into a small town with a school and a church. Tom grew older, his hands spotted and stiff with the same cold that had taken the stranger. He never returned to the saddle, but the wind still came off that ridge every winter, and he always heard it.

Once, a young surveyor came to his door asking about the old claim records. The boy had an honest face and bright eyes, and he thanked Tom warmly for the directions. Tom watched him walk away down the road and thought about how easily a man could choose the wrong thing.

He had built a fortune on that single afternoon, and it had not kept him warm. In the quiet of his study, Tom sometimes took out his old field book and turned to the page with the coordinates. Beside them, in his own shaky hand, he had written a single word that he never let anyone read: forgive.

Contact-Line Pinning and the Stability of Surface Nanobubbles Under Pressure Reduction and Heating: Theoretical and Simulation Perspectives

Abstract

Surface nanobubbles are gaseous domains, typically tens to hundreds of nanometers in width and only a few nanometers to tens of nanometers in height, that persist at solid-liquid interfaces far longer than classical dissolution theory would predict. Their stability has been a long-standing puzzle, and a substantial body of theoretical and molecular simulation work now suggests that the three-phase contact line plays a central role. This paper reviews how contact-line pinning governs nanobubble response to two experimentally and industrially relevant perturbations: reduction of the ambient liquid pressure and elevation of temperature. We outline the theoretical frameworks, including modified Young-Laplace analyses, line-tension corrections, and gas-diffusion models with pinned boundaries, and we synthesize predictions from molecular dynamics and continuum simulations. The central conclusion is that pinning shifts the balance between Laplace pressure and gas supersaturation, allowing stable states that would be unstable for free-surface bubbles, and that pressure reduction and heating act on this balance through distinct mechanisms. We discuss the implications for the interpretation of experiments and for applications in flotation, microfluidics, and heterogeneous nucleation.

1. Introduction

Surface nanobubbles were first reported through atomic force microscopy and optical methods on hydrophobic substrates immersed in water. Their apparent lifetimes, often exceeding hours to days, conflict with the Epstein-Plesset prediction that a gas bubble in undersaturated liquid should dissolve on timescales of microseconds to milliseconds at this size scale. Several explanations have been proposed, including gas supersaturation maintained near the interface, surface contamination, and the stabilizing effect of pinned contact lines. Among these, contact-line pinning has attracted particular attention because it provides a geometric constraint that modifies the internal pressure and the rate of gas exchange with the surrounding liquid.

The contact line, where the gas, liquid, and solid meet, is a region of high curvature and strong chemical or topographic heterogeneity. When the line is pinned, its position does not follow the changes in volume that a free-moving bubble would undergo, and the contact angle evolves in a manner that alters the Laplace pressure. Understanding this coupling is essential for predicting how nanobubbles respond to changes in external conditions. This paper focuses on two such conditions: pressure reduction, relevant to degassing and cavitation-like processes, and heating, relevant to thermal processing and to the thermodynamics of gas solubility.

2. Classical Background

For a spherical cap bubble of radius R and contact angle theta, the Laplace pressure difference across the gas-liquid interface is given by the relation of the capillary pressure to surface tension gamma and curvature. For a free bubble in equilibrium with liquid at ambient pressure P_l, the internal gas pressure satisfies P_g = P_l + 2 gamma / R. Gas diffusion out of the bubble is driven by the difference between the dissolved gas concentration at the interface, which is raised by the Laplace pressure via Henry's law, and the bulk concentration. For a bubble in undersaturated liquid, the net flux is outward and the bubble shrinks, with the classical Epstein-Plesset lifetime scaling with the square of the radius divided by the diffusivity and the degree of undersaturation.

For a surface nanobubble, the relevant geometry is a truncated sphere with a pinned contact line of base radius r. Basic geometry relates the radius of curvature to the base radius and contact angle, and the Laplace pressure then depends on both. The Epstein-Plesset result must therefore be modified to account for the reduced exposed surface area and the diffusion field, which is strongly constrained near the solid. Several authors have shown that the diffusive flux from a pinned cap scales differently with size than from a free sphere, and that the flux can be suppressed sufficiently to allow long lifetimes when the bulk liquid is only moderately undersaturated.

3. Role of Contact-Line Pinning

The contact line may be pinned by surface roughness, chemical heterogeneity, or the formation of a contaminant layer. Pinning means that the base radius remains fixed while the contact angle may vary within a range bounded by advancing and receding angles. This hysteresis gives the system a set of metastable configurations. When the bubble volume is reduced by gas loss, the contact angle decreases, which increases curvature and therefore Laplace pressure, which in turn increases the interfacial gas concentration and tends to drive further loss. However, the fixed base radius limits the reduction in interfacial area and thus limits the diffusive flux, creating a balance that can sustain the bubble.

Line tension, the excess free energy per unit length of the contact line, introduces an additional correction that becomes important at nanometer scales. Theoretical treatments including line tension show that the effective contact angle depends on the base radius, and that the stability condition for a pinned bubble can shift significantly when line tension is non-negligible. Estimates of line tension are uncertain, typically in the range of about one piconewton, and the sign and magnitude strongly influence whether the pinned state is energetically favorable relative to a dissolved state.

4. Response to Pressure Reduction

Reducing the external liquid pressure increases the pressure difference between the gas inside the bubble and the surrounding liquid. Within a constant-gas-content model, the bubble expands to maintain mechanical equilibrium. For a pinned contact line, expansion is constrained, so the contact angle must increase and the curvature must decrease. This reduces the Laplace pressure and lowers the interfacial gas concentration, which decreases the outward diffusive driving force. Under certain conditions, pressure reduction can therefore stabilize a nanobubble by suppressing dissolution, although it also lowers the ambient gas solubility, which acts in the opposite direction.

The net effect depends on the relative magnitude of these competing influences. Theoretical analyses suggest that for sufficiently large pinned bubbles, the reduction in Laplace pressure dominates and the bubble becomes more stable as pressure falls. For very small bubbles, the increase in effective gas concentration from reduced ambient pressure can dominate, leading to a critical radius below which bubbles dissolve regardless of pinning. Molecular dynamics simulations of argon or nitrogen nanobubbles on graphitic or hydrophobic surfaces have reproduced qualitatively this non-monotonic behavior, with a critical size set by the balance of these terms.

Simulations also indicate that pressure reduction can induce transitions in the contact-line structure. As the contact angle increases past a threshold, the contact line may depin and advance across a chemical or topographic step, producing an abrupt change in base radius. Such events are sensitive to the local energy landscape and are only partially captured by continuum models, which tend to assume a single pinning threshold.

5. Response to Heating

Heating affects nanobubble stability through several coupled channels. First, the gas solubility in water generally decreases with increasing temperature, which raises the effective supersaturation for a given dissolved concentration and tends to promote gas release from the bubble. Second, surface tension decreases approximately linearly with temperature, reducing the Laplace pressure for a given geometry and therefore reducing the interfacial gas concentration. Third, the gas diffusivity increases with temperature, accelerating diffusive transport and thus accelerating dissolution if the bubble is undersaturated in its surroundings. Fourth, thermal expansion of the gas increases the internal pressure for a fixed amount of gas, which can push the contact line outward or increase the contact angle depending on pinning strength.

Theoretical models that combine these effects predict that heating generally destabilizes pinned nanobubbles, with the dominant mechanism depending on the dissolved gas concentration in the bulk. When the bulk liquid is near saturation at the initial temperature, the reduction in solubility upon heating can drive substantial gas release. Simulations incorporating temperature-dependent solubility, surface tension, and diffusivity have shown that bubbles on hydrophobic surfaces exhibit a temperature window of metastability that narrows as the gas content in the bulk is reduced.

A distinct prediction is that local heating from the substrate, rather than uniform heating of the liquid, can create thermal gradients that drive Marangoni flows and alter the local gas concentration near the contact line. Such effects can either stabilize or destabilize the bubble depending on the flow direction and on whether the line remains pinned. These gradient-driven effects are sensitive to geometry and are an active area of simulation work.

6. Simulation Methods and Findings

Molecular dynamics simulations have been the primary tool for resolving the molecular structure of the contact line and the gas-liquid interface at nanoscales. Simulations of Lennard-Jones or water-based systems have reproduced nanobubble formation and persistence, often under conditions of mild supersaturation induced by solvent exchange or by imposed gas concentration. Pinning in simulations is typically imposed through substrate heterogeneity, such as atomic-scale defects or patterned hydrophilic regions, and the response to pressure changes is monitored by varying the simulated system pressure or by coupling to a barostat.

Continuum simulations, based on solving the Navier-Stokes equations with interface tracking and diffusion of dissolved gas, complement molecular approaches by reaching larger length and time scales. These models require boundary conditions at the contact line, and the choice of condition, such as a pinned base radius or a Gibbs-type contact angle law, strongly affects predicted lifetimes. Comparisons between these approaches indicate that continuum models capture the qualitative stabilization by pinning but may underestimate the sensitivity of lifetime to line tension and to nanoscale gas-density fluctuations.

Across published simulations, several consistent findings emerge. Pinned bubbles show extended lifetimes compared with unpinned bubbles at identical gas content. Pressure reduction stabilizes larger pinned bubbles while destabilizing very small ones. Heating reduces the window of stability and, in most configurations, accelerates dissolution, though the magnitude of the effect depends on the initial dissolved gas concentration and on the strength of pinning.

7. Discussion

The theoretical picture that emerges is that contact-line pinning provides a kinetic and geometric barrier to nanobubble dissolution, and that the response to pressure and temperature is governed by how these external variables shift the balance between Laplace pressure, gas solubility, and diffusive flux. Pressure reduction tends to stabilize larger pinned bubbles by lowering interfacial curvature, while heating tends to destabilize them through combined reductions in solubility and surface tension and increases in diffusivity. The competition between these effects produces critical sizes and temperature windows that can, in principle, be tested experimentally.

Several caveats apply. The magnitude of line tension and the true strength of pinning are not well determined experimentally, and their values can change the sign of predicted responses. Molecular simulations are constrained by short timescales and small system sizes, so the extrapolation to experimentally observed lifetimes of hours or days requires careful justification. Continuum models depend on assumed boundary conditions that may not capture the stochastic depinning events observed in simulations. The interpretation of experimental observations is further complicated by the difficulty of distinguishing true gas nanobubbles from contamination layers or from reduced-density interfacial regions.

8. Implications and Future Directions

Understanding how pinning affects nanobubble response to pressure and temperature has practical relevance. In flotation and in mineral processing, nanobubbles on particle surfaces influence attachment and selectivity, and their response to temperature changes in process streams may alter performance. In microfluidic devices, unintended nanobubble formation or dissolution can affect flow and sensing. In heterogeneous nucleation studies, the stability of pre-existing gas domains on substrates bears directly on nucleation barriers and on the interpretation of cavitation thresholds.

Future work should combine multiscale modeling with carefully controlled experiments in which pressure and temperature are varied independently while contact-line pinning is characterized, for example through chemically patterned substrates of known geometry. Measurements of line tension, diffusivity under confinement, and gas concentration near the interface would constrain the parameters that currently dominate uncertainty. Improved simulation methods capable of resolving stochastic depinning and long-time diffusion would also help bridge the gap between molecular and continuum descriptions.

9. Conclusions

Contact-line pinning is a central factor in the stability of surface nanobubbles, providing geometric and kinetic constraints that counteract the rapid dissolution predicted by classical theory. Reduction of ambient pressure can stabilize sufficiently large pinned bubbles by reducing Laplace pressure, while also imposing a critical-size threshold below which dissolution dominates. Heating generally destabilizes pinned nanobubbles through decreased solubility, decreased surface tension, and increased diffusivity, with the net response depending on initial gas content and pinning strength. Theory and simulations agree qualitatively on these trends, though quantitative predictions remain sensitive to line tension, substrate heterogeneity, and boundary conditions at the contact line. Resolving these uncertainties will require tighter coupling between simulation and experiment.

References

The references for this paper would be drawn from the established literature on surface nanobubbles, contact-line physics, and gas-liquid interfacial thermodynamics, including foundational work on Epstein-Plesset dissolution, line-tension theory, and molecular dynamics studies of nanobubble stability. Specific citations should be verified against the primary literature before submission.

Why In-Person Schooling Is More Beneficial Than Online Classes

Education is about more than the transfer of information from a teacher to a student. It is also about growing as a person, learning to work with others, and developing the habits that will carry students through adulthood. For these reasons, in-person schooling offers benefits that online classes cannot fully replicate. Physical classrooms create conditions in which students learn more effectively, more socially, and more healthily.

The most obvious advantage of in-person learning is the direct relationship between teachers and students. A teacher in a classroom can see when a student looks confused, notice a furrowed brow or a hesitant pause, and adjust the lesson on the spot. Online, that same teacher may only see a grid of small, frozen faces, or no faces at all. Important signals get lost, and struggling students can slip through unnoticed.

In-person classes also reduce the distractions that come with learning from home. At home, a student may be tempted by a phone, a television, a bed, or a sibling who needs attention. A classroom sets clear expectations about when it is time to focus. The physical separation between "school" and "home" helps the brain understand that it is time to work, which supports concentration and discipline.

Social development is another major reason to favor in-person school. Students learn to read body language, resolve disagreements, share materials, and cooperate on group projects. These skills are learned through daily, unscripted interaction, such as chatting before class, working through a difficult partner assignment, or cheering for a classmate at lunch. Online platforms can imitate some of this, but they rarely capture the spontaneity of real human contact.

Friendship and a sense of belonging also depend heavily on shared physical spaces. Many students describe their closest friendships as beginning in the hallways, on the sports field, or in the cafeteria. A school community gives young people a place where they feel known and valued. Students who feel connected to their school are more motivated to attend, participate, and persevere when work becomes difficult.

Extracurricular activities are central to a well-rounded education, and they are much harder to deliver online. Band practice, theater rehearsals, science labs, sports teams, debate clubs, and art studios all require physical equipment, shared space, and hands-on participation. Students who join these activities gain confidence, leadership experience, and a sense of purpose that complements their academic work.

Laboratory and hands-on learning provide another clear advantage. Students learn chemistry by mixing substances, biology by dissecting specimens, and physics by testing forces. Woodworking, engineering, cooking, and music all rely on tactile experience. While simulations and videos have value, they cannot fully substitute for the experience of handling real materials and troubleshooting real problems.

In-person schooling also supports the mental health of many students. Schools provide access to counselors, nurses, and trusted adults who can notice warning signs of depression, anxiety, abuse, or neglect. Students who are isolated at home may have no one outside their family who checks on their well-being. A school building can serve as a safety net that online learning often lacks.

Routine and structure are valuable for young people, and school provides both. Regular start times, scheduled meals, and a predictable daily rhythm help students develop self-regulation and time management. Online learning can blur these boundaries, leading some students to sleep irregularly, skip meals, or fall behind without anyone noticing.

Equity is an important consideration as well. Not every family has reliable internet access, a quiet place to study, or a parent available to supervise schoolwork. In-person schools level the playing field by providing computers, meals, libraries, and supervised study spaces. When learning moves entirely online, students with fewer resources are often the ones who suffer most.

Critics of in-person schooling sometimes point out that online classes offer flexibility, reduce commuting time, and allow students to learn at their own pace. These are real benefits, and online tools can be valuable as supplements to classroom instruction. However, flexibility alone does not guarantee learning, and many students need the external structure that a classroom provides.

Health concerns, including contagious illnesses, can make remote learning seem safer in certain circumstances. Yet the experience of recent years showed that prolonged remote schooling carried serious costs in learning loss, social isolation, and mental strain. Schools can and should adopt sensible health measures, such as ventilation, hygiene practices, and flexible sick-day policies, without abandoning the benefits of in-person instruction.

Ultimately, in-person schooling provides something that screens cannot: a shared physical community where students learn from skilled teachers, practice social skills, build lasting friendships, and grow into capable adults. Online learning has a place as a tool, but it should not replace the classroom as the foundation of education. Students deserve schools where they can be seen, challenged, and supported face to face.

Should students choose the design of their summer learning projects with teacher guidance? This question matters because summer projects can either deepen a student's interest in learning or become another assignment completed out of obligation. Allowing students a voice in how their projects are designed can make them more meaningful, while teacher guidance helps ensure that those projects are realistic, rigorous, and aligned with educational goals.

The strongest argument for student choice is that motivation grows when people care about what they are doing. A student who selects a topic, a format, or a method is more likely to invest effort and persist through difficulties. When a student decides to build a model of a local watershed or to write a series of short stories inspired by a family history, the project belongs to them in a way that a prescribed assignment rarely does. Ownership often leads to deeper learning because the student must think carefully about what they want to know and how they will find out.

Choice also builds skills that extend well beyond the classroom. Designing a project requires students to define a question, plan steps, estimate time, gather resources, and adjust when something does not work. These are the same abilities needed in college, in careers, and in everyday life. Students who practice making these decisions while still in school may become more confident and self-directed learners. Without any opportunity to shape their own work, they may never develop these habits.

However, unlimited freedom can lead to problems. Some students, especially younger ones or those who have little experience with independent work, may choose projects that are too broad, too easy, or too vague to produce real learning. A student who wants to "learn about space" over the summer may end up with a collection of loosely connected facts rather than a focused investigation. This is where teacher guidance becomes valuable. A teacher can help a student narrow an idea, identify appropriate resources, and set measurable goals that make the project achievable.

Teacher guidance also protects against projects that are unsafe, unrealistic, or unequal in their demands. Not every family has access to the same materials, transportation, or free time in the summer. A teacher who understands the community can suggest projects that students can complete without spending money they do not have or relying on resources their school does not provide. Teachers can also make sure that the project meets curriculum standards, so that the time students spend over the break supports what they will need when school resumes.

Guidance does not have to mean control. The most effective approach may be a shared process in which the teacher sets the boundaries and the student fills them in. For example, a teacher might require that each project address a particular skill, such as scientific reasoning or persuasive writing, while allowing students to choose the subject. The teacher might then meet with each student to review a draft proposal, offering feedback on feasibility and suggesting improvements without dictating the final result. This balance respects the student's voice while still providing the structure that helps them succeed.

Some critics argue that teachers should design all summer work because they have professional training and a clearer view of what students need. Expertise is certainly important, and a teacher's perspective can reveal gaps in a student's knowledge that the student may not recognize. Yet a project designed entirely by an adult may feel like homework in disguise, and students may complete it simply to satisfy the requirement. A collaborative model keeps the advantages of expert judgment while still letting students pursue questions that matter to them.

Another concern is fairness. If some students receive more guidance than others, those with supportive families or access to outside help may have an advantage. Schools can address this by scheduling regular check-ins, providing written templates for project proposals, and offering examples of strong projects. These supports help make the process accessible to every student, regardless of their background, and they reduce the chance that choice will widen existing gaps.

Assessment is another consideration. When students design their own projects, grading becomes more complicated because the work may vary widely in topic and format. Teachers can address this by creating clear criteria that focus on the quality of thinking and the process rather than on a single correct outcome. Rubrics that assess how well a student defined a question, used evidence, and reflected on their results can apply across many kinds of projects. This approach allows fair evaluation without requiring every student to do the same thing.

Reflection is an important part of any summer project. Asking students to write about what they planned, what changed, and what they learned helps them connect the experience to their broader education. A teacher who reviews these reflections can see how each student is growing and can offer guidance for the next school year. Reflection turns a project from a finished product into a learning experience that the student can understand and build upon.

Time and workload also deserve attention. Summer is meant to be a break, and projects should not feel like a second school year. When students help design their work, they can choose a scope that fits their schedule and their interests. Teachers can help by establishing reasonable time expectations and encouraging students to plan for rest as well as study. This shared planning can reduce stress and make the project feel like an opportunity rather than a burden.

Parents and families can play a role as well. When a student explains their project idea at home, family members may offer ideas, resources, or encouragement. Teachers can invite this involvement by sharing project goals with families and suggesting ways they might support their child without taking over the work. Strong partnerships among students, teachers, and families make it more likely that the project will be completed thoughtfully and with pride.

Ultimately, the question is not whether students should have a voice in their learning, but how much voice is appropriate at each stage of their development. Younger students may need more structure, while older students may be ready for greater independence. A flexible approach that adjusts to each learner respects both their autonomy and their need for guidance.

In conclusion, students should choose the design of their summer learning projects, but they should do so with the support of teachers. Student choice fosters motivation, ownership, and important skills, while teacher guidance keeps projects focused, realistic, and fair. When these two forces work together, summer projects can become some of the most meaningful learning a student experiences all year.

North Korea's claim in January 2016 that it had successfully tested a hydrogen bomb was met with widespread skepticism from international observers and nuclear experts. Pyongyang announced that the underground blast was its first thermonuclear test, a significant step beyond the atomic devices it had detonated in earlier years. However, seismologists measured the seismic signal at roughly magnitude 5.1, a yield far smaller than what a true hydrogen bomb would typically produce. Analysts noted that the modest size of the tremor was more consistent with a boosted fission weapon, which uses a small amount of fusion fuel to enhance a conventional nuclear reaction. Researchers at institutions including the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization and several universities examined the data and reached similar doubts. Some experts argued that the test was valuable to North Korea as a demonstration of progress even if it did not reach full thermonuclear capability. Others questioned whether the government's claims were intended mainly for domestic audiences and as a political message to rivals. Independent verification proved difficult because North Korea restricts access to its test sites and does not allow outside inspectors. Radioactive sampling from the region provided limited information, leaving many conclusions dependent on estimates rather than direct evidence. Officials in South Korea, Japan, and the United States expressed their own uncertainty while condemning the test as a violation of United Nations Security Council resolutions. The episode highlighted the challenges of verifying nuclear activity in a closed state. Debate over the true nature of the device continued among analysts for years afterward. The uncertainty surrounding the 2016 test remains a notable example of how difficult it can be to assess nuclear claims without transparency.

The manuscript addresses an important and practical problem: learning transferable visual representations when labeled data is scarce, a setting common in medical imaging, remote sensing, and specialized industrial inspection. The authors propose a self-supervised pretraining framework intended to produce features that remain effective under limited labeled supervision, and they evaluate it against established contrastive and masked-image baselines. The motivation is clearly stated, and the introduction situates the work reasonably well within the existing literature on label-efficient learning. The central contribution, a modified augmentation and sampling strategy combined with an auxiliary consistency objective, is described with enough detail to follow the logic. However, the description of the training procedure leaves several hyperparameters unspecified, including the learning rate schedule, the temperature parameter, and the batch size used during pretraining, which limits reproducibility. The experimental section evaluates on three benchmark datasets and reports linear probing and low-shot fine-tuning results at 1, 5, and 10 percent label fractions, which is an appropriate design for the claims being made. The reported gains over the strongest baseline are consistent across label fractions, which supports the authors' central claim. Nonetheless, the magnitude of improvement in the 10 percent setting is small, and the paper does not report variance across random seeds, so it is difficult to judge whether the differences are statistically meaningful. The ablation study is useful, but it removes components one at a time without examining interactions, and the authors should discuss whether the auxiliary objective contributes independently of the augmentation changes. The comparison with recent masked autoencoder methods is incomplete, since those baselines were run with default settings that may not be tuned for the low-data regime. The related work section would benefit from a more critical discussion of prior label-efficient methods such as semi-supervised pseudo-labeling, which compete directly with the proposed approach in practice. The qualitative analysis of learned features, including the attention visualizations, is suggestive but anecdotal, and quantitative measures of feature quality would strengthen the argument. The computational cost of the method is mentioned only briefly, and a clearer account of training time and memory requirements relative to baselines would help practitioners assess trade-offs. The authors state that code will be released, which is commendable, though the current manuscript does not include a link or repository. The limitations section acknowledges dataset scope but does not discuss potential failure modes, such as sensitivity to domain shift between pretraining and downstream data. Figures are generally clear, although the axis labels on the low-shot accuracy plot are too small to read comfortably at print size. Some notation is introduced inconsistently, with the same symbol used for both the projection head output and the encoder representation in different sections. The writing is generally clear, though several paragraphs in the methods section are dense and would benefit from a summary diagram of the full pipeline. The abstract overstates the generality of the results by implying applicability to all image recognition tasks, whereas the experiments cover only classification on natural-image benchmarks. The statistical reporting should be revised to include confidence intervals or standard deviations across at least three runs. The authors should also clarify how the label fractions were sampled, since class balance in the subsets can substantially affect low-shot results. Overall, the paper is a sound and useful contribution with a clear idea and reasonable experiments, but it requires additional rigor in reporting, a fuller set of tuned baselines, and more cautious claims before it is ready for publication. I recommend a major revision.

This paper addresses semi-supervised few-shot image classification, a setting where a model must learn new categories from very few labeled examples while also exploiting a pool of unlabeled images. The authors propose using soft labels to propagate information from labeled to unlabeled samples, combined with task-adaptive network components that adjust feature representations to each episode. The problem is well motivated, since labeled data is scarce in many real applications and unlabeled data is comparatively cheap. The introduction clearly situates the work within prior meta-learning and transductive approaches, which helps the reader understand the gap being filled. The core idea of replacing hard pseudo-labels with soft assignments is sensible, as it reduces the damage caused by early misclassifications on unlabeled data. The task-adaptive component is a reasonable extension, though the paper would benefit from a more precise explanation of how the adaptation parameters are computed and whether they add significant overhead. The method section is generally readable, but some notation is overloaded across episodes, support sets, and unlabeled pools, and a summary table of symbols would improve clarity. The experimental setup covers standard few-shot benchmarks, which allows direct comparison with established baselines. The reported gains over strong baselines are encouraging, but the margins in some settings are small and the paper does not report variance across multiple random seeds, making it hard to judge significance. The ablation studies are useful in isolating the contribution of soft labels versus task adaptation, yet they would be more convincing with a broader range of unlabeled-to-labeled ratios. The authors should also clarify how the amount of unlabeled data affects performance, since this is central to the semi-supervised claim. Results on out-of-distribution unlabeled samples are mentioned only briefly and deserve a more thorough analysis, as real unlabeled pools are rarely clean. Computational cost comparisons are limited, and training and inference time relative to competing methods would help practitioners weigh the trade-offs. The related work section is thorough but could more explicitly discuss why prior transductive methods fail under label noise. Figures are generally clear, though the qualitative examples do not show failure cases, which would give a more balanced picture. The writing is mostly fluent, with a few passages that repeat claims about novelty without new supporting evidence. Code availability is a welcome commitment, and releasing exact hyperparameters and episode sampling procedures would greatly aid reproducibility. The conclusion accurately summarizes the contributions but somewhat overstates generality beyond the benchmarks tested. Overall, the paper presents a useful and plausible idea with solid but incomplete empirical support. I recommend a minor revision that adds variance reporting, broader ablations on unlabeled data, a clearer method description, and a more candid discussion of limitations.

Helping young students explore career options before committing to a specific path is one of the most valuable things schools and families can do. At an age when many students are still discovering their interests, strengths, and values, early exposure to a wide range of careers can open doors they might never have considered. A student who has only ever imagined becoming a doctor or a teacher may not realize that careers in engineering, environmental science, graphic design, or public health also exist and could suit them well. Exploration gives students a broader picture of what is possible. Career fairs, guest speakers, job shadowing, and school-sponsored visits to workplaces all allow young people to see real professionals at work and ask honest questions about their daily routines. These experiences often matter more than any aptitude test, because they show students what a job feels like rather than just what it is called. Exploration also helps students connect what they learn in class to the world beyond school. A math lesson on statistics becomes more meaningful when a student hears how a data analyst uses it to solve problems. Similarly, a writing assignment gains purpose when a student understands how journalists, lawyers, and marketing specialists rely on clear communication. Early exploration can also reduce pressure. When students feel they must choose a single path too soon, they may make hasty decisions or feel anxious about falling behind. Being encouraged to try different options, and to understand that interests can change, lets them approach the future with curiosity rather than fear. Of course, exploration should not become an endless list of possibilities that leaves students feeling confused. Good guidance balances breadth with reflection, helping students note which experiences energized them and which left them indifferent. Teachers and counselors can support this by encouraging journals, class discussions, or simple self-assessments. In the end, the goal is not to force an early decision but to build a foundation of self-knowledge. Students who explore thoughtfully are better prepared to commit to a path later, and more likely to choose one that genuinely fits who they are and who they hope to become.

Community service has long been a fixture of school life, but a central question remains: should students participate voluntarily, or should it be required? Those who favor voluntary service argue that genuine motivation is what gives service its meaning. When students choose to help, they are more likely to invest their full effort, reflect honestly on their experiences, and develop a lasting commitment to civic life. Forced participation, by contrast, can turn a meaningful activity into a checkbox, leaving students resentful and learning little beyond how to complete a requirement. Supporters of mandatory service, however, point out that many students would never seek out such opportunities on their own, and that a requirement ensures every student gains exposure to the needs of their community. Many young people discover a passion for service only after being introduced to it, so an obligation can serve as a valuable first step rather than a barrier. A middle path may offer the strongest answer: schools could require a minimum commitment while giving students real choice over where and how they serve. This approach respects individual interests while still ensuring broad participation. Ultimately, the goal of community service is to cultivate responsible, caring citizens, and the best method is one that balances freedom with a shared expectation of contribution.

Cashaw: Meaning and Historical Uses

Cashaw is a regional English name for a group of winter squashes and pumpkins, most commonly associated with the American South. The word is believed to derive from the Narragansett term askutasquash, a term for green or unripe squash that was eaten raw, and it passed into English through early colonial contact with Algonquian-speaking peoples of New England. Over time, the word was adapted into various spellings, including cushaw, cashaw, and cushau, and it gradually came to refer to a specific family of squash in Southern usage. Cushaws are typically distinguished by their long, curved necks attached to a bulbous base, a shape that sets them apart from round pumpkins. Their flesh is often firm, sweet, and light in color, and the fruit is valued for its keeping quality, since cured cushaws can be stored through much of the winter. Botanically, cushaws belong to the species Cucurbita mixta, although many varieties are grown under the same common name. Early settlers and Indigenous farmers cultivated these squashes alongside corn and beans in the traditional Three Sisters system. Because the vines are vigorous and productive, cushaws became a dependable food source in Southern kitchens and farm gardens. In the kitchen, cushaws were commonly baked, boiled, stewed, or mashed, and they were used in pies, breads, and preserves. Southern cooks prized them for pies because the dense flesh produced a rich, smooth filling. Some families also made cushaw butter and pickled the fruit as a way of preserving it for later use. Beyond the vegetable itself, cushaw is also the name of a tree. The cushaw tree, known scientifically as Acacia greggii in some regional contexts and more widely as a name for certain small trees in the Southwest, has been referred to by this term in folk and local usage, though common naming for this tree is inconsistent. Because of this variation, readers should consult regional botanical references when identifying a specific tree. The tree name seems to have arisen independently of the squash, and the overlap in naming has caused occasional confusion in older records. In historical documents, cushaw appears in plantation records, farm journals, and cookbooks from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Writers often listed it among staple crops, which shows how central it was to rural diets. The squash was also mentioned in regional literature as a symbol of homestead abundance and of traditional Southern foodways. Today, cushaws are grown by heritage seed enthusiasts and small farms that wish to preserve older crop varieties. Many gardeners value them for their ornamental appearance, their long storage life, and their connection to regional culinary history. Interest in heritage vegetables has helped keep the name cushaw in active use. Understanding the word's origins, its variant spellings, and its dual use as a squash and tree name offers insight into how language, agriculture, and cultural exchange have shaped American food traditions.

After-school activities offer students far more than a way to fill the hours between the final bell and dinner. They serve as a setting where young people build friendships, discover talents, and begin to picture the kind of work they might one day do. When students take part in clubs, sports, arts programs, or volunteer groups, they step into communities that extend beyond their classrooms and neighborhoods.

One of the most valuable gifts of after-school involvement is the chance to form friendships around shared interests. In a robotics club or a school choir, students meet peers who care about the same things they do, which makes it easier to connect and build trust. These relationships often feel more relaxed than those formed during the school day, because students are there by choice rather than obligation. Over time, these bonds can grow into lasting friendships that offer support through the challenges of adolescence.

After-school activities also teach students how to work with people who differ from them. A soccer team, a theater production, or a community service project requires members to coordinate schedules, share responsibilities, and resolve disagreements. Students learn to listen to different viewpoints, to compromise when necessary, and to celebrate the successes of others. These social skills are easy to underestimate, yet they shape how young people communicate and cooperate for the rest of their lives.

Beyond social growth, after-school programs give students a low-pressure environment to explore possible career paths. A student who joins the debate team might discover a passion for law or public speaking, while one who volunteers at an animal shelter could become curious about veterinary medicine. Because these activities are voluntary, students can experiment freely, trying something new without the fear of a poor grade. Each experience becomes a piece of information about what they enjoy and what they do well.

Many after-school activities also provide hands-on experience that connects directly to future work. Students in a school newspaper learn writing, editing, and deadline management, while those in a coding club practice problem solving and logical thinking. Such experiences give students concrete skills and examples they can later describe in college applications or job interviews. They also help students see that the abilities they develop in one setting can transfer to many different careers.

Mentorship is another important benefit that often emerges from after-school involvement. Coaches, club advisors, and program leaders frequently take an interest in their students' goals and offer guidance about education and work. A teacher who sponsors the science club might suggest a summer research program, or a community volunteer might introduce a student to a professional in a field of interest. These adult relationships can open doors that students would otherwise never have known existed.

Of course, not every activity will lead to a lifelong career, and that is perfectly acceptable. The purpose of after-school involvement is not to lock students into a single path at a young age. Instead, these experiences help students build confidence, curiosity, and a sense of identity. Whether a student ultimately becomes an engineer, a nurse, an artist, or a teacher, the habits of commitment and collaboration gained through extracurricular life will remain useful.

For these reasons, schools and communities should continue to invest in after-school programs and make them accessible to all students. Transportation, cost, and scheduling can prevent some young people from participating, and removing these barriers would allow more students to benefit. When every student has the opportunity to join a club, team, or volunteer group, the entire community gains young people who are socially capable, future-minded, and ready to contribute.

A constructive outlook can be one of the most valuable habits a student develops, because it shapes how they treat others and how others respond to them. Students who approach classmates with kindness, curiosity, and encouragement tend to attract friends who enjoy their company and trust them. When a student focuses on solutions rather than complaints, teachers and mentors are more likely to offer extra help, recommendations, and second chances. This positive attitude also makes it easier to handle setbacks, since a student who believes mistakes are opportunities to learn will keep trying instead of giving up. Over time, these friendships and relationships create a support network that makes challenging schoolwork feel more manageable. In the end, a constructive outlook does more than improve a student's mood; it builds the connections and resilience that lead to lasting academic success.
