A positive outlook is more than a cheerful personality trait. It is a way of interpreting events, expecting good things, and believing that effort can lead to meaningful results. Although it may seem like a small mental habit, a positive outlook can shape how people treat one another, how they handle stress, and how they approach the ordinary routines of daily life. Understanding its influence can help students see why optimism is worth cultivating.

One of the clearest effects of a positive outlook appears in relationships. People who expect the best from others tend to communicate with warmth and patience. When a friend forgets a plan, an optimistic person is more likely to assume an honest mistake rather than deliberate neglect. This generous interpretation reduces conflict and keeps small misunderstandings from growing into resentment. Over time, such habits build trust, because others learn that they can make mistakes without being judged harshly.

Positivity also affects the way people give and receive support. Optimistic individuals are often more willing to ask for help, since they believe help is available and that others want to assist. They are also more likely to offer encouragement, which strengthens bonds within families, classrooms, and workplaces. A supportive atmosphere makes people feel safe enough to share their struggles, and this openness deepens friendships in ways that superficial cheerfulness never could.

Emotional well-being is closely tied to outlook as well. Research in psychology has linked optimism with lower levels of anxiety and depression, although the exact relationship is complex and influenced by many factors. A person who expects things to turn out reasonably well is less likely to spiral into hopelessness after a setback. Instead of seeing a single poor grade as proof of failure, an optimistic student might view it as a sign that a different study method is needed.

Optimism does not mean ignoring problems. A realistic positive outlook acknowledges difficulty while maintaining confidence in the ability to cope. This balance is important because denial can be just as harmful as pessimism. People who face challenges honestly, yet still believe in their capacity to improve, tend to recover more quickly. They are able to name what is wrong, make a plan, and keep moving forward without being overwhelmed.

Stress management is another area where outlook makes a difference. When faced with a demanding schedule, optimistic people often focus on what they can control and set manageable goals. They may break a large project into smaller steps and celebrate each completed part. This approach reduces the sense of being buried under obligations. In contrast, a pessimistic outlook may lead to procrastination, since the task seems impossible from the start.

Physical health may also benefit from a hopeful mindset. Some studies have suggested that optimistic people report better overall health and may be more consistent with healthy habits such as exercise and regular sleep. While optimism alone cannot replace medical care or good nutrition, it can encourage people to take care of themselves because they believe their efforts will matter. Motivation and belief in positive outcomes often go hand in hand.

In everyday life, a positive outlook changes the texture of ordinary experiences. A rainy morning becomes an opportunity to slow down rather than a source of irritation. A crowded bus can be an occasion to people-watch or listen to music instead of fuming. These small shifts accumulate, making daily life feel more pleasant and less exhausting. Over weeks and months, they can influence overall satisfaction with life.

Work and school performance can also be shaped by optimism. Students who believe their abilities can grow tend to persist longer when material is difficult. They are more likely to ask questions, seek feedback, and try new strategies. Employees with a hopeful view of their careers may be more open to learning and more resilient when projects fail. In both settings, persistence often matters as much as raw talent.

It is important to recognize that a positive outlook is not fixed at birth. Many people can develop it through practice. Keeping a gratitude journal, reframing negative thoughts into more balanced ones, and spending time with encouraging people are all useful habits. Mindfulness exercises can help individuals notice their automatic reactions and choose more constructive responses. Like any skill, optimism strengthens with consistent effort.

Some critics argue that encouraging positivity can place unfair pressure on people who are suffering. Someone facing grief, illness, or injustice may not feel ready to look on the bright side, and being told to "just be positive" can feel dismissive. This concern is valid. A healthy approach to optimism respects emotional reality and allows room for sadness, anger, and grief. Positivity should be a source of strength, not a demand to suppress genuine feelings.

Communities also benefit when many members hold a hopeful outlook. Neighbors who believe in the possibility of improvement are more likely to work together on local projects, such as cleaning a park or organizing a food drive. Schools with optimistic teachers and students may foster stronger cooperation and a sense of shared purpose. Collective optimism can create momentum that supports larger social change.

Finally, a positive outlook shapes the stories people tell about their lives. Those who view their past experiences as sources of learning often describe themselves as capable and growing. This narrative can influence future choices, encouraging people to pursue goals they might otherwise avoid. Over time, the stories we tell ourselves become part of who we are.

In conclusion, a positive outlook influences relationships, emotional well-being, and everyday life in meaningful ways. It encourages generosity and trust with others, supports healthier responses to stress, and makes ordinary experiences more rewarding. Because optimism can be developed and must be balanced with honesty about difficulty, it is a valuable quality for students to cultivate. Approached thoughtfully, a hopeful outlook can help people live with greater connection, resilience, and purpose.

Eli had always believed freedom was something you took, not something you were given. At sixteen, he hated the curfew, the locked car keys, and the way his father, Thomas, watched him over the rim of his coffee cup as if he were a problem to be solved. The argument that night started over a party Eli had already decided to attend. Voices rose, doors slammed, and Eli shoved past his father toward the driveway. Thomas grabbed his arm, and Eli wrenched free with a force he didn't measure. His father stumbled backward down the porch steps and struck the edge of the concrete with a sound Eli would hear for the rest of his life. For a long moment Eli simply stood there, waiting for his father to get up and shout at him again. Thomas did not move. The ambulance lights painted the neighborhood red and blue, and a police officer asked Eli questions he answered in a voice that didn't sound like his own. At the funeral, relatives whispered about the boy who had ruined everything. Eli had won the right to come and go as he pleased, and now there was no one left to tell him no. He drove past the party house the following weekend and felt nothing but the empty passenger seat beside him. Freedom, he discovered, had no weight at all, and that was the worst thing he had ever learned.

Title: Discriminatory Policing Experiences and Abdominal Obesity: Examining Gendered Racial Health Disparities

Abstract

Abdominal obesity is a robust predictor of cardiometabolic disease, and its distribution varies substantially across racial and gender groups in the United States. A growing body of research suggests that exposure to discriminatory policing, including stops, searches, verbal harassment, and use of force, may contribute to these disparities through psychosocial and physiological pathways. This paper reviews the conceptual and empirical literature linking discriminatory policing experiences to central adiposity, considers how gender shapes both the form and consequences of police contact, and discusses the implications for public health research and intervention. We argue that policing should be treated as a structural determinant of health and that gendered analyses are essential for understanding racial disparities in abdominal obesity. We note throughout that the evidence base is still developing, that most studies are observational, and that causal claims must be made cautiously.

Introduction

Abdominal obesity, typically operationalized by waist circumference or waist-to-hip ratio, is more strongly associated with insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and cardiovascular events than is body mass index alone. Because visceral adipose tissue is metabolically active and sensitive to stress hormones, the accumulation of fat in the abdominal region is of particular interest to researchers studying the health effects of chronic psychosocial adversity.

Racial and ethnic disparities in obesity are well documented. Non-Hispanic Black women in the United States have among the highest rates of abdominal obesity, while patterns among men vary by group and by measure. Mexican American and Native American populations also show elevated rates in many surveys. These patterns cannot be explained by individual behaviors such as diet and physical activity alone, which has led researchers to examine structural and social exposures, including residential segregation, neighborhood disadvantage, occupational stress, and experiences of racial discrimination.

Policing represents a distinct and understudied form of institutional contact. Unlike many forms of discrimination, police encounters can be sudden, coercive, and in some cases physically dangerous. They occur in public spaces, are often witnessed by others, and can carry the threat of arrest, injury, or death. For communities subject to heavy policing, these encounters may be frequent and cumulative. Research on policing and health has grown since the mid-2010s, with particular attention to the mental health consequences of stops and use of force, but the link to metabolic outcomes such as abdominal obesity has received comparatively less attention.

This paper synthesizes evidence on this relationship. We first review the theoretical pathways connecting stress and discrimination to abdominal fat accumulation. We then examine empirical studies of police contact and health, paying attention to measurement challenges. Next we consider gender, which shapes both the patterns of policing and the physiological and social responses to it. We conclude by discussing limitations and directions for future research and policy.

Theoretical Pathways

The most widely cited framework linking stress to abdominal obesity is the allostatic load model, which describes how repeated activation of physiological stress systems produces cumulative wear on the body. Chronic or repeated activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis can elevate circulating cortisol, and sustained cortisol exposure has been associated with preferential deposition of visceral fat, increased appetite for energy-dense foods, and impaired glucose regulation. Acute stressors can also trigger sympathetic nervous system responses that alter metabolic function.

Discrimination-based stress models extend this logic. Experiences of unfair treatment are thought to generate chronic threat appraisals, hypervigilance, and anticipatory stress, which may persist even when no specific encounter is occurring. Police contact may be especially potent because it combines unpredictability, authority, and the possibility of severe harm. Individuals may modify their behavior to avoid encounters, for example by limiting outdoor activity, avoiding certain neighborhoods, or altering travel routes, and such avoidance could reduce physical activity and social engagement, further contributing to weight gain.

Behavioral pathways are also plausible. Stress and fatigue can influence sleep quality and food choices, and some individuals may use food or other coping strategies to manage distress. Financial consequences of policing, such as fines, court fees, legal costs, and lost employment following arrest, may constrain access to healthy food and health care. Neighborhood-level effects are relevant as well: heavily policed areas often overlap with areas of limited access to supermarkets, parks, and safe spaces for exercise.

Finally, there may be pathways operating through social relationships and community trust. Police contact can erode trust in institutions, including health systems, which may reduce engagement with preventive care and delay diagnosis of metabolic conditions. Collective stress within communities may also shape social norms and access to resources.

Empirical Evidence on Policing and Health

Empirical research on policing and health has used several designs. Cross-sectional surveys have asked respondents about stops, searches, harassment, and use of force, and have linked these experiences to self-reported health outcomes. Longitudinal cohort studies have tracked individuals over time, allowing investigators to examine temporal ordering. Ecological studies have related area-level measures of policing intensity, such as stop rates or arrest rates, to population health indicators. Quasi-experimental designs are rare but increasingly used, exploiting variation in policing practices or policy changes.

Findings from this literature have generally linked police contact to poorer mental health, including depressive symptoms, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress symptoms. Associations with physical health outcomes are less consistent but have been reported for hypertension, sleep disturbance, and self-rated health. Fewer studies have directly measured abdominal obesity as an outcome. Those that have typically rely on self-reported waist circumference or measured anthropometry within health surveys, and the number of such studies is limited.

Several measurement challenges complicate interpretation. Police contact is often underreported, particularly for stops that do not result in arrest, and recall of stressful encounters may be biased by current distress. Respondents who have been stopped may differ systematically from those who have not in ways that confound associations with health. Researchers must also distinguish between discriminatory policing, meaning contact that is disproportionate or unjustified relative to behavior, and policing contact in general, since the health consequences of the two may differ.

Gendered Dimensions

Gender shapes both the patterns and the consequences of policing. Men, particularly young men, are stopped, searched, arrested, and subjected to force far more often than women, and the most extreme forms of police violence are disproportionately directed at men. Women, however, experience policing differently. They may face gender-specific forms of misconduct, including sexual harassment and assault during stops or detention, and they often bear the indirect costs of policing when partners, sons, or other family members are arrested or incarcerated. Women are frequently responsible for caregiving and household management in these circumstances, which can magnify stress and economic strain.

These gendered patterns interact with racial patterns. Black women may experience both racial and gender-based discrimination in policing contexts, and their experiences may be less visible in public discourse focused on men. Research on gendered racism suggests that intersecting forms of discrimination produce distinct health effects that cannot be captured by examining race or gender alone. For abdominal obesity, the gendered distribution of body fat and the sex-specific effects of stress hormones may mean that the same policing exposure produces different metabolic consequences for men and women.

Sex differences in fat distribution are relevant. Women typically accumulate more subcutaneous fat, while men more often accumulate visceral fat, although these patterns shift after menopause and vary across populations. Estrogen appears to influence fat distribution and may modify stress responses, meaning that hormonal status is a potential effect modifier. Few studies have examined these interactions, and more research is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.

Gendered stress exposures also differ in form. Men may experience stops and force as direct threats to physical safety and masculinity, which some researchers have linked to the suppression of emotional distress and reliance on maladaptive coping. Women may experience policing as a source of fear for family members and as a threat to their own sexual safety. Both pathways may contribute to chronic stress, but they may do so through different biological and behavioral routes.

Implications for Research and Policy

Future research should prioritize longitudinal designs with repeated measurement of both policing exposure and anthropometric outcomes, including waist circumference measured by trained staff rather than self-report. Studies should be powered to test sex-stratified and race-stratified associations and their intersections. Researchers should also measure potential mediators, including cortisol, sleep, physical activity, food insecurity, and financial strain, to clarify mechanisms. Natural experiments, such as changes in stop-and-frisk policies or consent decrees, offer opportunities for stronger causal inference.

Policy implications follow from this evidence, though they should be framed with appropriate caution. If discriminatory policing contributes to cardiometabolic disease, then reducing unnecessary and disproportionate contact could be considered a public health strategy. Reforms that limit stops to those supported by evidence, improve accountability for misconduct, provide alternatives to police response for mental health and social crises, and reduce the financial burden of legal system involvement may all have health benefits. Health systems can also play a role by screening for experiences of police contact and related stress, integrating trauma-informed care, and addressing the financial and neighborhood conditions that compound risk.

Clinicians should be aware that patients from heavily policed communities may carry cumulative stress that affects metabolic health, and that mistrust of institutions may affect engagement with care. Care approaches that emphasize respect, continuity, and shared decision-making may improve outcomes.

Limitations

This review has several limitations. The evidence linking policing to abdominal obesity is sparse, and most available studies are cross-sectional, limiting causal inference. Measurement of policing experiences is inconsistent across studies, and self-report may be subject to recall and reporting bias. Reverse causation is possible in some designs, for example if individuals with higher body weight are more likely to be stopped due to perceived physical characteristics, although this direction is less commonly hypothesized. Residual confounding by socioeconomic position, neighborhood conditions, and health behaviors is likely. The studies reviewed are concentrated in the United States, limiting generalizability to other settings. Finally, the interpretation of racial and gender categories requires care, since these categories are socially constructed and often combine heterogeneous populations.

Conclusion

The relationship between discriminatory policing and abdominal obesity is plausible, supported by theoretical models of stress and discrimination, and consistent with broader evidence linking policing to mental and physical health. However, direct empirical evidence remains limited, and the mechanisms and magnitude of effects are not yet well established. Gender is central to understanding these patterns, as men and women experience policing differently and may respond to it through distinct biological and behavioral pathways. Addressing gendered racial health disparities in abdominal obesity will require integrating policing into the study of structural determinants of health, using longitudinal and mechanistic designs, and considering policy changes that reduce unnecessary and discriminatory police contact. Continued research in this area is warranted, and conclusions should be presented with the caution that the current evidence demands.

Deep Learning Prediction of Station-Level Car-Sharing Demand for Vehicle Distribution and Operational Planning

Abstract

Car-sharing systems have become an important component of urban mobility, yet their operational efficiency depends heavily on the spatial and temporal distribution of vehicles across stations. Imbalances between demand and supply lead to empty stations in some locations and congestion of idle vehicles in others, reducing service quality and profitability. This paper investigates whether deep learning models can accurately predict station-level car-sharing demand and whether such predictions can support improved vehicle redistribution and operational planning. We propose a spatiotemporal forecasting framework that combines convolutional and recurrent components with contextual features describing land use, weather, calendar effects, and nearby points of interest. The framework is evaluated on historical trip records from a free-floating and station-based car-sharing dataset spanning several months. We compare the proposed model against seasonal naive baselines, autoregressive integrated moving average models, gradient boosted trees, and standard long short-term memory networks. Results indicate that the proposed architecture reduces mean absolute error and improves the detection of demand peaks relative to all baselines. We further translate forecasts into a vehicle redistribution plan using a mixed-integer optimization model and simulate the operational consequences. Simulated outcomes show a reduction in unmet demand and in relocation distance compared with a rule-based rebalancing policy. We discuss implications for operators, limitations of the dataset and the modeling assumptions, and directions for future work.

Introduction

Car-sharing services allow users to access vehicles on a short-term basis without ownership, and they have expanded rapidly in cities across Europe, North America, and Asia. Two principal operational models exist. In station-based systems, vehicles are picked up and returned at fixed locations. In free-floating systems, vehicles may be parked within a defined service area. Both models share a fundamental operational challenge: the demand for vehicles is spatially and temporally uneven, and user trips tend to produce directional imbalances that accumulate over the course of a day. A station that receives more arrivals than departures will fill up, forcing users to seek alternatives, while a station that loses vehicles faster than it regains them will be depleted.

Traditional responses to this imbalance include manual relocation by operator staff, incentive schemes that encourage users to return vehicles to underserved locations, and static reallocation policies based on historical averages. These approaches are labor-intensive, reactive, or insensitive to short-term variation. Accurate forecasts of station-level demand allow an operator to anticipate shortages and surpluses before they occur, transforming rebalancing from a reactive to a proactive activity. Forecasting therefore sits at the center of operational planning for car-sharing.

Demand forecasting for shared mobility has been studied in the context of bike-sharing, ride-hailing, and taxi services, where a substantial literature has developed around both statistical and machine learning methods. Early work relied on time series techniques such as autoregressive models and exponential smoothing, which capture temporal autocorrelation but struggle with the spatial dependencies that characterize transportation networks. Subsequent work introduced regression trees, support vector machines, and ensemble methods, which accommodate heterogeneous input features but generally treat each location independently. Neither family explicitly models the interaction between neighboring locations, which is essential when vehicles flow between stations.

Deep learning offers a natural framework for capturing both spatial and temporal structure. Convolutional neural networks can extract spatial patterns from grid-based representations of demand, while recurrent architectures, including long short-term memory networks and gated recurrent units, model sequential dependencies over time. Hybrid architectures that combine these components have achieved strong results in urban flow prediction. However, most published work has focused on aggregated demand for taxis or bicycles, and comparatively little attention has been paid to car-sharing at the level of individual stations, where data are sparser, more volatile, and more directly tied to operational decisions.

This paper addresses that gap. Our contributions are threefold. First, we develop a spatiotemporal deep learning model tailored to station-level car-sharing demand that incorporates contextual features and an explicit representation of inter-station relationships. Second, we benchmark the model against a range of established baselines using a consistent evaluation protocol. Third, we connect forecast accuracy to operational outcomes by embedding predictions in a vehicle redistribution optimization and measuring its effect on unmet demand and relocation cost in simulation. Our aim is not only to improve predictive metrics but to demonstrate that these improvements translate into more effective planning decisions.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on demand forecasting in shared mobility and on deep learning for spatiotemporal prediction. Section 3 describes the data, preprocessing procedures, and feature construction. Section 4 presents the proposed model and the baselines. Section 5 reports predictive performance. Section 6 describes the redistribution optimization and the simulation experiments. Section 7 discusses implications, limitations, and future directions, and Section 8 concludes.

Related Work

Research on car-sharing has examined user behavior, the spatial placement of stations, fleet sizing, and the economics of operation. A substantial body of work addresses the vehicle relocation problem, in which an operator moves vehicles among stations to meet anticipated demand. Early formulations treated relocation as a static problem solved from a snapshot of vehicle counts, while later studies incorporated stochastic demand and dynamic decision-making. The quality of any relocation policy depends critically on the accuracy of the demand information available to it, which motivates the study of forecasting as a precursor to optimization.

Statistical time series methods have long been used for transportation demand prediction. Seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average models capture trends and periodic patterns in aggregated counts and remain competitive benchmarks when data are regular and abundant. Exponential smoothing methods provide a simple alternative with low computational requirements. These approaches are interpretable and robust but typically model each series in isolation, which limits their ability to represent the flow of vehicles between neighboring stations.

Machine learning methods extended the feature space available to forecasters. Gradient boosted decision trees can incorporate weather variables, holidays, and categorical descriptors of location, and they often perform well on tabular data with nonlinear interactions. Random forests and support vector regression have similarly been applied to bike-sharing and taxi demand. Such models are attractive in practice because they require less tuning than neural architectures and produce feature importance measures that support interpretation. Nevertheless, their treatment of spatial dependence is indirect, typically relying on the inclusion of neighborhood aggregates as additional features.

Deep learning has transformed spatiotemporal forecasting in urban computing. Convolutional architectures were applied to grid-based representations of crowd flow and taxi demand, treating the city as an image in which each pixel holds a count of events. Recurrent networks were then used to model the temporal evolution of these maps, and hybrid models combined convolutional encoders with recurrent sequence models. Graph-based approaches, including graph convolutional networks and attention mechanisms, have further improved the representation of irregular spatial structure, since stations do not necessarily lie on a regular grid and the relevant neighborhood is defined by the network rather than by geometry.

Applications of these methods to car-sharing have been more limited. Some studies have used recurrent networks to forecast total system demand, while others have examined station-level prediction for bike-sharing with convolutional and graph-based models. Work specifically targeting station-level car-sharing demand, and linking the resulting forecasts to vehicle distribution decisions, remains relatively sparse. Moreover, many studies evaluate models only on predictive error without assessing whether lower error produces better operational outcomes, an omission that this paper seeks to address.

Data

The empirical analysis uses trip records from a station-based car-sharing operator in a mid-sized metropolitan area. Each record contains the identifier of the originating and destination station, the start and end timestamps, the trip duration, and the vehicle identifier. The dataset covers approximately eighteen months of operation and includes a network of several hundred stations distributed across residential, commercial, and mixed-use zones. Vehicle availability snapshots are recorded at fifteen-minute intervals, allowing reconstruction of the number of vehicles present at each station through time.

Demand at a station is defined as the number of rental requests originating there in a given interval, which we treat as the target variable for forecasting. Because operators are primarily concerned with unmet demand, we also record the number of requests that could not be fulfilled due to the absence of available vehicles. Where available, these censored observations are flagged, and we describe below how they are handled in training.

Preprocessing involved several steps. Records with implausible durations, missing timestamps, or inconsistent station identifiers were removed. Trips with durations under two minutes were treated as likely erroneous and excluded. Timestamps were converted to local time, and daylight saving transitions were handled explicitly. Station-interval counts were then constructed on a fifteen-minute grid, yielding a three-dimensional tensor indexed by station, time interval, and channel, where the channels represent departures, arrivals, and vehicle availability.

Contextual features were drawn from several external sources. Weather observations included temperature, precipitation, wind speed, and visibility, aggregated to the same temporal resolution as the demand data. Calendar features included hour of day, day of week, a holiday indicator, and a school-term indicator. Land use and point-of-interest counts were computed for a buffer around each station, distinguishing commercial, residential, transport, and leisure categories. Public transit proximity was measured as the distance to the nearest rail or bus stop. These static descriptors were held constant over time, while dynamic features varied with the interval.

The data were partitioned chronologically to avoid leakage. The first twelve months served as the training set, the subsequent three months as the validation set used for hyperparameter selection and early stopping, and the final three months as the held-out test set. This ordering reflects the deployment scenario, in which models are trained on past data and applied to future periods. All normalization parameters were estimated on the training set and applied to the other partitions.

Exploratory analysis revealed several properties relevant to modeling. Demand exhibits strong daily and weekly periodicity, with pronounced peaks during weekday commuting hours and on weekend afternoons. Station-level series are sparse at certain locations, with many intervals containing zero requests, which complicates training with standard squared-error losses. Demand is also strongly correlated among geographically proximate stations, supporting the premise that spatial structure carries predictive information. Finally, weather effects are nonlinear: moderate precipitation reduces leisure trips but may increase short trips in commercial areas, and extreme temperatures suppress overall demand.

Methods

Problem Formulation

Let the station network be represented by a set of N stations, and let y_{i,t} denote the number of rental requests at station i during interval t. The forecasting task is to predict the vector of demands across all stations over the next H intervals, given observations over the preceding L intervals together with contextual features. Formally, we seek a function f that maps the historical tensor and the contextual features to predicted demand for each station and each future interval. The horizon H is set to four intervals, corresponding to one hour, which matches the time scale of operational rebalancing decisions.

Proposed Architecture

The proposed model, which we term the spatiotemporal demand network, consists of three components. A spatial encoder processes the demand and contextual features at each time step using a graph convolution in which the adjacency matrix is constructed from a combination of geographic distance and observed flow. The adjacency weights are defined by a Gaussian kernel on station distance, multiplied by an empirical co-movement coefficient estimated from the training period, and sparsified by retaining only the strongest connections for each station. This construction allows the model to propagate information between stations that are both nearby and behaviorally linked.

The temporal component is a stacked gated recurrent network that consumes the sequence of spatial embeddings and produces a latent state summarizing recent history. Gating mechanisms were chosen for their stability and parameter efficiency relative to standard recurrent units. To capture the strong periodicity of the data, we augment the input sequence with representations of the same interval on the previous day and the previous week, providing the model with explicit access to seasonal context.

The output component is a fully connected decoder that maps the latent state, combined with the calendar and weather features for the forecast horizon, to predicted demand for each station and interval. Because demand is non-negative and frequently zero, the decoder produces the parameters of a negative binomial distribution rather than a point estimate alone. The mean and dispersion parameters are learned jointly, and the training objective is the negative log-likelihood of the observed counts. This probabilistic formulation accommodates overdispersion and yields predictive intervals that can inform robust operational decisions.

Censored observations, in which demand exceeded available supply, were handled by treating the observed count as a lower bound. For these intervals the likelihood contribution is replaced by the survival function of the distribution evaluated at the observed count, which discourages the model from learning that stations with frequent stockouts have low underlying demand. This adjustment is important because naive training on fulfilled trips would systematically understate demand at constrained locations.

Training used the Adam optimizer with a learning rate schedule that decreased when validation loss plateaued. Dropout was applied to recurrent connections and to the decoder. Batches were constructed by sampling contiguous windows across the training period, and early stopping terminated training when validation likelihood failed to improve for a fixed number of epochs. Hyperparameters, including the number of graph convolution layers, the hidden dimension of the recurrent network, the sparsity threshold of the adjacency matrix, and the dropout rate, were selected by grid search on the validation set.

Baseline Models

We compare the proposed model against four baselines. The seasonal naive forecast predicts the demand at each station and interval to equal the value observed one week earlier at the same time of day, providing a minimal but strong reference for periodic data. A seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average model was fitted separately to each station series, with orders selected by information criteria on the training period. A gradient boosted regression tree model was trained on a tabular representation in which the lagged demand values, contextual features, and aggregated neighborhood demand served as predictors. Finally, a standard long short-term memory network was trained on each station series independently, without any spatial component, to isolate the contribution of the graph structure.

For fair comparison, all models were trained on the same partition and evaluated on the same test intervals. Where a model produced point forecasts, these were evaluated directly; where a model produced distributional forecasts, the mean was used for point metrics and the full distribution for probabilistic metrics.

Evaluation Metrics

Predictive performance was assessed using mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and mean absolute percentage error computed over non-zero actual values to avoid division by zero. Because operational decisions depend heavily on peak demand, we additionally report error restricted to the top decile of intervals by observed demand. For probabilistic forecasts we report the negative log-likelihood and the empirical coverage of ninety percent prediction intervals. Coverage close to the nominal level indicates well-calibrated uncertainty.

Results

Predictive Performance

Table 1 summarizes forecasting accuracy on the held-out test set. The proposed spatiotemporal demand network achieved the lowest mean absolute error among all models, improving on the best baseline by a meaningful margin. The gradient boosted model performed second best, benefiting from its ability to incorporate contextual features and neighborhood aggregates. The standard recurrent network without spatial structure outperformed the seasonal autoregressive model but fell short of the spatiotemporal approach, suggesting that inter-station information provides predictive value beyond temporal patterns alone. The seasonal naive forecast, despite its simplicity, performed respectably, underscoring the strength of weekly periodicity in the data.

Performance differences were most pronounced during peak periods. On the top decile of intervals, the proposed model reduced error relative to the strongest baseline by a larger proportion than it did across all intervals. This is consequential because peak intervals are where stockouts concentrate and where accurate anticipation yields the greatest operational benefit. The probabilistic model also produced well-calibrated predictive intervals, with empirical coverage of ninety percent intervals close to the nominal level, whereas the gradient boosted model's implicit uncertainty estimates, obtained through quantile adjustments, showed noticeable under-coverage during high-demand periods.

Analysis by station type revealed heterogeneity. Stations in commercial districts exhibited the highest forecast errors, reflecting volatile weekday patterns and sensitivity to events. Residential stations were predicted more accurately, owing to their regular commuting and weekend rhythms. Stations with low overall volume were difficult for all models, as sparse counts yield high relative variance. The proposed model narrowed this gap somewhat, which we attribute to its use of neighborhood information to borrow strength from nearby, better-observed stations.

Ablation experiments confirmed the contribution of each component. Removing the graph convolution and training the recurrent network on individual station series increased error, consistent with the baseline comparison. Removing the previous-day and previous-week seasonal inputs degraded performance most strongly at longer horizons. Removing contextual weather and point-of-interest features produced a smaller but consistent deterioration, with the largest effects observed during precipitation events and holidays. Replacing the negative binomial output with a Gaussian output reduced calibration and slightly worsened peak-period accuracy, supporting the choice of a count-appropriate distribution.

Sensitivity to the forecast horizon was also examined. Accuracy declined as the horizon lengthened, as expected, but the proposed model degraded more gracefully than the baselines. At a horizon of four intervals the advantage over the strongest baseline remained clear, and the model continued to outperform alternatives at the longer horizons considered in supplementary experiments. This robustness matters for operations, because rebalancing trucks may require lead time and forecasts must remain useful beyond the immediate interval.

Vehicle Distribution and Operational Planning

Forecasts were transformed into a vehicle redistribution plan through a mixed-integer optimization model. At the start of each planning cycle, the model observes the current vehicle counts at all stations and the predicted demand over the planning horizon. It determines which vehicles to relocate from surplus stations to deficit stations, subject to constraints on the number of available staff and vehicles, the capacity of each station, travel times between stations, and a time window within which relocations must be completed. The objective minimizes a weighted combination of expected unmet demand and total relocation distance, with penalties reflecting the relative cost of lost trips and operational travel.

To reflect forecast uncertainty, the optimization can be run in a scenario-based mode in which demand realizations are drawn from the predictive distribution. In this study we report results for the deterministic version using the mean forecast and for a robust variant that hedges against the upper quantile of demand at each station. The robust variant prioritizes stations with high predicted variance, which is useful when the cost of a stockout is high.

We compared the redistribution policy driven by the proposed forecasts against three alternatives: a rule-based policy that moves vehicles from stations whose current count exceeds a fixed threshold to those below a lower threshold; a policy driven by the seasonal naive forecast; and a policy driven by the gradient boosted forecast. Each policy was evaluated in a discrete-event simulation that replays the test-period demand. The simulator models user requests as arrivals to the station network, assigns vehicles according to availability, and executes relocations on the schedule produced by each policy. Relocation durations depend on travel times estimated from the road network, and staff capacity is enforced.

Simulation outcomes are reported in terms of unmet demand, defined as the fraction of requests that could not be served, and total relocation distance. The proposed forecast-driven policy reduced unmet demand relative to the rule-based policy and relative to the seasonal naive and gradient boosted alternatives. It also achieved lower relocation distance than the rule-based policy, indicating that anticipatory rebalancing requires fewer and more targeted moves. The robust variant further reduced unmet demand during peak periods at a modest increase in relocation distance, illustrating the trade-off between service reliability and operating cost.

These results support the central premise that predictive accuracy translates into operational value, although the magnitude of improvement depends on the cost structure and the staffing available to the operator. Sensitivity analysis showed that gains were largest when relocation capacity was constrained, since in that regime the timing and location of moves matter most. When capacity was abundant, the rule-based policy approached the performance of the forecast-driven policy, indicating that forecasting is most valuable when resources are scarce.

Discussion

The findings indicate that deep learning models incorporating spatial structure can improve station-level demand prediction for car-sharing, particularly at peak periods where accurate forecasts matter most. The superiority of the spatiotemporal architecture over the standalone recurrent network suggests that inter-station dependencies carry information that is not recoverable from each station's history alone. The advantage over gradient boosting indicates that explicit modeling of temporal and spatial structure provides benefits beyond what tabular methods can extract from engineered neighborhood features, although the gradient boosted model remained a strong and practical alternative.

The probabilistic formulation contributes to operational usefulness in ways that point metrics do not capture. Operators can use predictive intervals to set safety margins for vehicle staging, to prioritize stations where the upper tail of demand is large, and to communicate uncertainty to planners. The calibration results suggest that the negative binomial specification adequately represents the overdispersed count process observed at most stations, though performance at very low-volume stations warrants further investigation.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. The dataset derives from a single operator in one metropolitan area, and the generalizability of the learned relationships to other cities, fleet compositions, and pricing structures is uncertain. Transferability could be assessed by applying the trained model to a different network or by fine-tuning on limited local data, an avenue we consider promising. The contextual features, while informative, were drawn from external sources of varying granularity, and errors in those sources may propagate into forecasts.

The simulation omits several real-world complexities. It assumes that users respond to availability in a fixed manner and does not model demand substitution across transport modes or the behavioral response to changes in service levels. It treats relocation as perfectly executed, ignoring delays, breakdowns, and staff variability. These simplifications were necessary to isolate the effect of forecast quality, but field validation would be required before operational deployment. A pilot study in which forecast-driven rebalancing is compared against current practice over a controlled period would provide stronger evidence.

The choice of graph construction also influences results. The adjacency structure combines geographic distance with empirical co-movement, and the sparsity threshold was selected on validation data. Alternative constructions, such as those based on learned attention or on infrastructure connectivity, may yield different performance, and the optimal construction could depend on the city. Future work could learn the graph jointly with the forecasting model, reducing reliance on heuristic choices.

Operational deployment raises additional considerations. Forecast systems must be retrained regularly to adapt to changes in user behavior, fleet expansion, and new station openings, and the computational cost of retraining must fit within the operating cycle. Monitoring procedures should detect distribution shift, such as that caused by changes in pricing or by external events like major public gatherings or construction. Finally, the integration of forecasts with human decision-making remains important; planners need interpretable outputs and the ability to override automated recommendations when local knowledge indicates otherwise.

Several directions for future research follow from this work. Multi-task models that jointly forecast demand, vehicle availability, and relocation requirements could provide a more integrated basis for planning. Reinforcement learning approaches could allow policies to be learned directly from operational outcomes rather than through a two-stage forecast-then-optimize pipeline, although such methods require careful safety evaluation. Extending the analysis to free-floating systems, where vehicles are not confined to stations, would require modeling demand on a continuous spatial domain and is an important next step. Incorporating user-level data, where privacy regulations permit, could improve the representation of individual travel behavior.

Conclusion

This paper has presented a spatiotemporal deep learning framework for predicting station-level car-sharing demand and has shown how these predictions can inform vehicle distribution and operational planning. The proposed model combines graph-based spatial encoding, gated recurrent temporal modeling, and a count-appropriate probabilistic output, and it outperforms established baselines on held-out data, with the largest gains during peak periods. Embedding forecasts in a redistribution optimization and simulating the resulting operations demonstrated reductions in unmet demand and relocation distance relative to a rule-based policy, with benefits concentrated where vehicle resources are constrained. While the evidence supports the value of forecast-driven planning, its generalization to other systems and its performance under real operating conditions require further validation. We believe that accurate, uncertainty-aware demand forecasting is a practical foundation for more responsive and efficient car-sharing operations, and we hope this work encourages wider adoption of such methods in shared mobility planning.

Should students be required to join an after-school activity? This question divides parents, educators, and students alike, and the answer depends on what we believe schools are for. Requiring participation has real benefits, but it also carries costs that deserve serious attention.

The strongest argument for a requirement is that many students would never choose to join an activity on their own, even though it would benefit them. A shy student who never speaks up in class might discover confidence on the debate team. A student who spends every afternoon alone at home might find friends in the chess club. Without a requirement, these students may simply never take the first step.

Structured activities also offer clear advantages for development. Research on youth programs has linked consistent participation in sports, music, and clubs to better school attendance, stronger grades, and improved social skills. A requirement could spread these benefits more fairly, reaching students whose families lack the time, money, or knowledge to enroll them in outside programs.

A requirement can also build a sense of community. When everyone is involved in something, the school becomes more than a place students attend for a few hours each day. Shared activities create traditions, rivalries, and friendships that cross the usual lines between cliques and grade levels.

However, forcing participation raises serious concerns about personal freedom. Students are not all alike, and an activity that excites one teenager may bore or stress another. A required activity that a student dislikes can create resentment toward school in general, which is the opposite of what educators intend.

There is also the problem of unequal burdens. Students who work part-time jobs to support their families, care for younger siblings, or commute long distances may find a mandatory activity nearly impossible to fit into their lives. A requirement could penalize the very students who already have the least flexibility.

Schools must also consider whether they have enough resources to offer meaningful choices. A requirement only makes sense if there are enough quality options to suit diverse interests, from robotics and theater to volunteering and gardening. Without that variety, students would simply be assigned to whatever happens to have room.

A middle path may serve students better than a strict mandate. Schools could require students to participate in some activity for a set period but allow them to choose among many options. They could also offer incentives, such as academic credit or recognition, to encourage participation without compelling it.

Ultimately, the goal should be to help students grow, not merely to fill their schedules. A well-designed requirement, one that offers real choice and accommodates different circumstances, might achieve that goal. A rigid requirement that ignores individual needs is more likely to produce compliance than genuine engagement.

For these reasons, schools should encourage after-school participation strongly while stopping short of making it mandatory for everyone. Students deserve both guidance and the freedom to find their own path. The best schools will be those that make activities so appealing and accessible that students want to join, rather than those that simply insist they must.

This manuscript proposes an attention-enhanced variant of BioBERT for classifying radiology reports and evaluates it against baseline models and human readers. The topic is timely and clinically relevant, since automated report labeling can support large-scale data curation, quality monitoring, and clinical decision support. The authors correctly identify that radiology reports are dense, domain-specific, and often contain negation, uncertainty, and hedged language, which makes them a meaningful testbed for biomedical language models. The motivation for adding an attention mechanism on top of BioBERT is reasonable, although the manuscript would benefit from a clearer explanation of what the attention layer adds beyond the self-attention already present in the transformer. The related work section covers prior rule-based and neural approaches to report labeling adequately, but it could more explicitly position the contribution against recent clinical language models and fine-tuning strategies. The dataset description is a strength, as it specifies the source institution, report volume, and label schema, but the authors should report inter-annotator agreement for the reference labels and describe how disagreements were resolved. The train, validation, and test splits are described, yet it is not clear whether splits were made at the patient level, which is important to avoid leakage across reports belonging to the same individual. The baselines include a TF-IDF logistic regression model, a CNN, and vanilla BioBERT, which is a sensible set, but the authors should also consider a stronger rule-based system such as NegEx-style pipelines to contextualize gains. Reported metrics include accuracy, macro F1, and AUROC, and the choice of macro-averaged measures is appropriate for imbalanced label distributions. However, confidence intervals or results from repeated runs with different random seeds are absent, so the reported improvements of roughly one to two points may not be statistically distinguishable from variance. The authors should apply a formal significance test, such as a paired bootstrap or McNemar's test, to support their claims of superiority. The comparison with human readers is a particularly valuable component, yet the protocol for recruiting readers, their level of training, the time allotted per report, and the reading conditions are insufficiently described. Without these details it is difficult to judge whether the comparison is fair or whether the model is outperforming a weak human reference. The per-class analysis reveals that performance drops considerably on rare findings, and this limitation deserves more discussion, since clinically important conditions are often the least frequent. The error analysis is brief, and a more systematic categorization of false positives and false negatives, for example by negation, hedging, or template variation, would make the findings more actionable. Attention visualizations are included as qualitative evidence of interpretability, but the authors should be cautious in claiming that attention weights explain model decisions, and they should either validate these visualizations against clinician judgments or temper their language. The ablation study isolating the contribution of the attention module is welcome, though it would be strengthened by reporting parameter counts and training costs for each variant. The discussion acknowledges single-institution data as a limitation, and I encourage the authors to evaluate on at least one external dataset, since generalization across hospitals with different report templates is a central concern for clinical deployment. Reproducibility would improve with the release of code, model checkpoints, hyperparameters, and a detailed description of preprocessing steps, including how report sections were segmented. Overall, the work is a useful incremental contribution with a sound design in several respects, but the claims of improvement and human-level performance require stronger statistical support, fuller methodological detail, and external validation before the conclusions can be considered reliable. I recommend a major revision.
