Collaborative science experiments offer students benefits that go well beyond the knowledge of the subject itself. When learners work together to design, carry out, and interpret an experiment, they practice the scientific method as a shared activity rather than a solitary exercise. Each member of a group can contribute a different strength, whether it is careful measurement, creative hypothesis building, or clear record keeping. This division of labor helps students recognize that science is rarely the work of one isolated genius and is instead a cooperative human effort. Working in teams also encourages students to articulate their reasoning aloud, which strengthens their understanding of concepts they might otherwise memorize without truly grasping. When a classmate questions a result or proposes a different explanation, the student must defend or revise their thinking, and this back-and-forth sharpens critical thinking. Collaboration also exposes students to errors in a low-stakes setting, so that a failed trial becomes a shared lesson rather than a personal failure. Such experiences can reduce anxiety about science, especially for students who feel intimidated by the subject when working alone. Communication skills develop naturally as group members must explain procedures, negotiate roles, and reconcile disagreements about data. Social bonds also form through these shared tasks, helping students build friendships and a sense of belonging in the classroom. Teachers often observe that quieter students gain confidence when they have a defined role within a small group. Collaborative work additionally mirrors the conditions of professional research laboratories, preparing students for future academic and workplace settings. Learning to share equipment, divide tasks fairly, and respect differing viewpoints are valuable habits that extend far beyond the science classroom. Of course, collaboration must be structured carefully, since groups can fall into patterns where one student does most of the work while others remain passive. Clear roles, individual accountability, and reflective discussion help ensure that every member participates meaningfully. When these conditions are in place, the collaborative science experiment becomes a powerful setting for both intellectual and social growth. In this way, the shared laboratory bench teaches students not only how the natural world works but also how people can work together to understand it.

Self-driving cars promise to transform transportation, but their arrival brings real safety concerns that deserve careful attention. Foremost among these is the problem of software reliability. Autonomous vehicles depend on complex code and machine learning systems, and any flaw in perception, planning, or control could lead to a crash. Unlike human drivers, who can draw on intuition and common sense, these systems may fail in unexpected ways when they encounter situations outside their training data.

Sensor limitations present another serious risk. Self-driving cars rely on cameras, radar, lidar, and ultrasonic sensors to understand their surroundings. Heavy rain, fog, snow, glare from the sun, or a dirty sensor can degrade their view of the road. Even a partially obscured stop sign or a pedestrian wearing unusual clothing could confuse the system at a critical moment.

The question of responsibility after an accident is also unresolved. When a human driver causes a collision, the blame is usually clear. When an automated system causes harm, liability may fall on the manufacturer, the software developer, the owner, or some combination of them. This ambiguity can slow justice for victims and discourage companies from prioritizing safety.

Cybersecurity threats add yet another layer of danger. A vehicle that is connected to the internet and controlled by software could be targeted by hackers. Malicious actors might disable brakes, manipulate steering, or gain access to personal data. Because a single vulnerability could affect thousands of identical vehicles, the consequences of such an attack could be widespread.

Human factors also complicate the picture. Many current systems require drivers to remain alert and ready to take control, yet people tend to lose focus when a machine handles most of the work. Studies of partially automated driving have shown that drivers may take longer to respond to emergencies than they would if they were fully engaged. This gap between human attention and machine capability can create dangerous situations.

Ethical dilemmas arise as well. Engineers must decide how a vehicle should behave in unavoidable accident scenarios, such as choosing between striking one person or swerving into another. Programming these decisions raises difficult moral questions, and there is no universal consensus on the right answers.

Finally, the transition period itself poses risks. Roads will likely contain a mix of human-driven and autonomous vehicles for many years, each behaving in different ways. Unpredictable interactions between these groups could increase accident rates until the technology and traffic rules mature.

Despite these concerns, self-driving cars may eventually save lives by removing human error, which causes most traffic deaths today. However, that potential can only be realized if safety remains the top priority. Rigorous testing, transparent reporting, clear legal frameworks, and strong cybersecurity standards are essential. Society must weigh the promise of autonomous vehicles against their risks and insist that they meet high standards before they share our roads.

The manuscript proposes a reinforcement learning method that ranks candidate actions and recasts policy optimization as a supervised learning problem, and the central idea is appealing: by converting a sequential decision problem into a ranking-based classification objective, the authors hope to inherit the stability and tooling of supervised learning. The motivation is clearly stated, and the introduction does a reasonable job situating the work relative to policy gradient methods, value-based approaches, and recent offline reinforcement learning techniques that also reuse supervised objectives. The core contribution, as I read it, is a loss function that penalizes the policy when a higher-ranked action under estimated returns receives lower probability mass than a lower-ranked one. This is a sensible construction, and the connection to listwise ranking losses from information retrieval is a welcome bridge that the authors could make more explicit. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more careful derivation of why the ranking objective is a valid surrogate for expected return. At present the argument moves from ranking consistency to policy improvement somewhat informally, and I would like to see a theorem or at least a precise statement of the conditions under which the induced policy is guaranteed to improve or converge. The assumptions behind this step, such as the quality of the return estimates used to form the ranking, deserve explicit treatment. The experimental section evaluates the method on a standard set of continuous control benchmarks and a discrete-action suite, which is an appropriate choice for an initial study. The reported gains over the baselines are encouraging, but the comparisons raise several concerns. The baselines appear to be run with default hyperparameters, and it is not clear whether the same tuning budget was applied to each method. Given how sensitive policy optimization is to learning rates and entropy coefficients, this could materially affect the conclusions. I would ask the authors to report results across multiple random seeds with confidence intervals, and to include learning curves rather than only final-performance tables. The ablation study is useful but incomplete. It isolates the ranking loss from the choice of return estimator, yet it does not separately test the effect of the list length used for ranking, which seems likely to matter a great deal in practice. Additional ablations on how the ranking candidates are sampled would also strengthen the paper, since sampling strategy plausibly drives much of the observed behavior. The related work section covers the main policy gradient and offline RL literature competently but omits a few relevant threads, including preference-based policy optimization and recent work that frames reinforcement learning as sequence modeling. Discussing these would clarify where the contribution sits. The writing is generally clear, though some notation is overloaded, and the authors should define the ranking operator and the candidate set formally before using them in the loss. Reproducibility is partially addressed: the authors state that code will be released, which I commend, but the paper should also list all hyperparameters, compute budgets, and the exact return-estimation procedure in an appendix. Limitations are mentioned only briefly and should be expanded to discuss computational overhead from ranking many candidate actions, behavior in stochastic or partially observable environments, and the potential for the method to inherit biases from the return estimator. In summary, the paper presents a promising and reasonably original idea with encouraging empirical results, but the theoretical justification is underdeveloped and the experimental evidence needs stronger controls and statistical reporting. I recommend a major revision. With a formal treatment of the surrogate objective, a fairer and more thorough empirical comparison, and an expanded discussion of limitations, the work could make a useful contribution to the growing literature on reframing reinforcement learning as supervised learning.

Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 is a federal civil rights law that prohibits discrimination against students with disabilities in schools that receive federal funding. Under this law, students who have a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, such as learning, reading, concentrating, or walking, may be eligible for accommodations even if they do not need special education services. West Hartford Public Schools, located in Connecticut, follow these federal requirements and maintain their own procedures for identifying eligible students. Families who suspect their child may need support can contact their child's school principal, school counselor, or the district's Section 504 coordinator to request an evaluation. The district reviews referrals and gathers information from teachers, parents, medical providers, and, where appropriate, existing academic data to determine whether a student qualifies. Evaluation teams typically include school staff familiar with the student and a knowledgeable decision-maker, and parents are invited to participate in these meetings. If a student is found eligible, the team develops a written 504 plan that describes the disability, the accommodations and supports to be provided, and the staff responsible for implementing them. Common accommodations include extended time on tests, preferential seating, modified assignments, access to assistive technology, breaks during the day, and adjustments to classroom or building access. Unlike an Individualized Education Program under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, a 504 plan does not typically include specialized instruction, though the two frameworks can overlap in practice. Parents have procedural protections under Section 504, including the right to review their child's records, to receive written notice of decisions, and to request an impartial hearing if they disagree with an eligibility or placement decision. The district is responsible for periodically reviewing each student's plan to confirm that it remains appropriate as the child grows and as needs change. Students who transfer into West Hartford from another district are generally expected to receive comparable services while the district completes its own review. Schools also provide information about the grievance process and the name of the coordinator responsible for handling concerns related to Section 504. Families are encouraged to review the district's current policy documents and student handbook, since specific procedures, timelines, and forms may be updated from year to year. For the most current details, parents and community members should contact the West Hartford Public Schools central office or the district's website directly.

The European Space Agency has awarded a contract to Astrium UK for the development of a next-generation microwave sounder for weather satellites. The agreement marks a significant step in Europe's effort to strengthen its capacity for observing the atmosphere from space. Microwave sounders measure radiation emitted by the atmosphere at different frequencies, allowing scientists to build profiles of temperature and humidity at multiple altitudes. These measurements feed directly into numerical weather prediction models that forecasters rely on every day. The new instrument is intended to improve the accuracy and vertical resolution of such data compared with earlier generations of sensors. ESA officials said the project forms part of a broader programme to ensure continuity of satellite observations for operational meteorology across Europe. Astrium UK, the British arm of the aerospace group, will lead the design and development work under the terms of the contract. The company has a long history of building instruments and spacecraft for European and international missions. Engineers at the firm will be responsible for the sounder's electronics, antenna systems, and calibration hardware. Industry analysts noted that the award reflects the strength of the UK space sector within the European supply chain. The contract also supports jobs and research capability at Astrium's facilities in Britain. Project managers said the development timeline will span several years, with testing and qualification planned before any launch. The sounder is designed to operate on polar-orbiting satellites, which pass over the planet's poles and provide global coverage. Such orbits allow the instrument to observe the entire atmosphere repeatedly over the course of each day. Meteorologists have long emphasized that data from these satellites is among the most valuable inputs to forecasts beyond a few days ahead. Improved sounding capability is expected to benefit severe weather warnings, climate monitoring, and aviation planning. Researchers also see potential gains in understanding atmospheric processes that influence long-term climate patterns. ESA has stressed that the data will be made widely available to national weather services and the scientific community. Officials said that open access policies are central to maximizing the societal value of publicly funded satellite missions. The agency also highlighted the importance of maintaining a reliable pipeline of instrument technology for future missions. Development of microwave sounders demands precision engineering, including careful control of thermal conditions and stable calibration over the instrument's operational life. Engineers must also manage the challenges of interference and the need to measure extremely faint signals. The contract includes provisions for rigorous testing to verify performance before the instrument is integrated with its host spacecraft. ESA representatives expressed confidence that the partnership would deliver a robust and capable instrument. Astrium UK executives welcomed the award and said their team was ready to begin work on the design phase. The announcement was received positively by the meteorological community, which has been seeking dependable sources of atmospheric data. Further details on the satellite mission and launch schedule are expected to be released in the coming months as the programme progresses.

Remote education has become an important tool for keeping students on track when illness or emergencies prevent them from attending school. Illness can keep a child at home for weeks, and natural disasters, family crises, and public health emergencies can close schools entirely. Without a way to keep learning, students can fall behind in their coursework, lose momentum, and struggle to return to their classmates. Remote education offers a practical solution to this problem by allowing learning to continue wherever the student happens to be.

The most useful forms of remote education combine live instruction with recorded lessons. Live video classes allow students to ask questions, participate in discussions, and feel connected to their teachers and peers. Recorded lessons give students flexibility, letting them watch material at their own pace and review difficult concepts as many times as they need. When a student is too sick to concentrate for long periods, short recorded segments can be far more manageable than a full school day of live instruction.

Digital tools also make it easier for teachers to share assignments, collect completed work, and give timely feedback. Learning platforms can organize readings, quizzes, and projects in one place, so students always know what is expected of them. This structure helps students feel that they are still part of their class rather than isolated from it. Clear routines matter a great deal, especially for younger students who need consistency to stay engaged.

Remote learning is not only about academics. Students who are ill or dealing with an emergency often feel anxious, lonely, or overwhelmed, and regular contact with teachers and classmates can provide reassurance. A brief daily check-in, a message from a friend, or a video call with a counselor can remind a student that they have not been forgotten. These connections support both mental health and motivation, which are essential for learning.

Of course, remote education has real limitations. Not every household has reliable internet access or a quiet place to study, and some students may not have a suitable device. Schools that want to use remote learning effectively must address these gaps by lending equipment, providing printed materials, and offering flexible deadlines. Equity should guide every decision, so that a student's access to education does not depend on their family's income or location.

Teachers also need support to make remote education successful. Preparing lessons for both in-person and online delivery takes extra time, and educators need training in the tools they are expected to use. When schools invest in professional development and reasonable workloads, teachers can design remote lessons that are engaging rather than simply a recording of a classroom session. Well-prepared teachers are the foundation of any effective remote program.

In the end, remote education is a valuable safety net for students facing illness or emergencies. It protects academic progress, supports emotional well-being, and keeps students connected to their school community. With thoughtful planning, adequate resources, and a commitment to equity, schools can ensure that a missed week or month does not become a permanent setback. Keeping students learning, even when they cannot be in the classroom, is a goal worth pursuing.

Remote learning and in-person schooling each offer distinct advantages and challenges, and the right choice often depends on a student's circumstances, temperament, and goals. One of the clearest benefits of studying remotely is flexibility. Students can often set their own schedules, which allows those with jobs, caregiving duties, or chronic health conditions to keep up with their education. Remote learning also removes the cost and time of commuting, giving students hours back each week that can be spent studying, sleeping, or pursuing other interests.

Another advantage is access. Students who live in rural areas, who are far from a suitable campus, or who cannot afford to relocate can reach courses and programs that would otherwise be out of reach. Online formats also frequently allow students to replay recorded lectures, pause to take notes at their own pace, and revisit difficult material as many times as needed.

However, remote study has real drawbacks. The most common is a loss of structure. Without a classroom, a fixed start time, and classmates present, many students struggle with procrastination and motivation. Self-discipline becomes essential, and students who lack it can fall behind quickly. Isolation is another concern. Much of learning happens through informal conversation, questions asked after class, and the sense of belonging that comes from sharing a physical space with peers and teachers.

In-person schooling addresses many of these weaknesses. Face-to-face instruction makes it easier for teachers to notice when a student is confused, and it allows for immediate feedback, discussion, and debate. Students can form study groups, join clubs, play sports, and build friendships, all of which support social development and emotional well-being. For younger students especially, the daily routine of attending school provides stability and supervision that remote arrangements may not easily replicate.

Yet in-person schooling carries its own costs. Commuting can consume significant time and money, and rigid schedules may be difficult for students with work or family obligations. Physical campuses can also be crowded or noisy, which some students find distracting, and students with certain disabilities may face barriers that remote options could reduce.

Technology plays a large role in how well remote learning works. A reliable internet connection, a suitable computer, and a quiet place to study are not equally available to all students. Those who lack these resources may find remote study frustrating or unworkable, which raises questions about fairness. Schools that adopt remote options must therefore consider how to support students who do not have equal access.

Ultimately, neither format is universally better. Remote learning suits self-motivated students who need flexibility and who have dependable technology at home. In-person schooling tends to serve students who benefit from structure, social interaction, and direct access to teachers. Many institutions have found that a blended approach, combining online and classroom elements, can capture the strengths of both. Students weighing their options should consider their learning habits, responsibilities, and personal preferences before deciding which path will serve them best.

UK mortgage lending has risen this year as more households move forward with home purchases, according to recent market data. Lenders have reported steady demand from first-time buyers and movers, helped in part by a gradual easing of borrowing costs. However, analysts warn that affordability pressures, including high property prices and elevated living costs, could restrain further growth in the coming months. Some economists expect lending to stabilise rather than accelerate sharply, depending on the path of interest rates and wage growth. Industry observers say the outlook will remain closely tied to household incomes and the broader health of the housing market.

Dandelions: Folklore, History, Ecology, and a Sustainable Rubber Source

Few plants are as familiar as the dandelion. Its bright yellow flowers appear in lawns, roadsides, and meadows across the temperate world, and its name comes from the French "dent de lion," meaning "lion's tooth," a reference to the jagged edges of its leaves. Though often dismissed as a weed, the dandelion has a long and surprisingly rich story. It has shaped folk traditions, fed and healed people for centuries, supports countless insects, and is now being studied as a source of natural rubber. This page explores each of these themes.

The dandelion has accumulated a great deal of folklore. In many European traditions, blowing the seed head and counting the puffs was a way of telling the time or predicting the hour. Children have long made wishes as they blow the fluffy seeds into the wind, believing the wish will be carried away. In some regions, the first dandelion seen in spring was considered a sign that the season had turned. Folk healers in various cultures associated the plant with protection and vitality, and it appeared in charms and home remedies. Its tenacious roots and its ability to return after being cut gave it a reputation for resilience that people admired and sometimes feared.

The plant's name appears in many languages with links to its appearance or to the local sense of its character. In English, its common names include "blowball," "cankerwort," and "priest's crown," each reflecting a different observation or belief. Such names show how closely people once watched the plants around them and how deeply those observations entered everyday speech.

Dandelions have a long record of use as food. Young leaves, harvested before the plant flowers and becomes bitter, have been eaten in salads for centuries and are rich in vitamins A, C, and K as well as minerals such as potassium and iron. The flowers have been made into wine, syrup, and fritters, and the roasted root has been ground as a coffee substitute, a practice that became especially common during periods of scarcity. Herbalists have used the root and leaves as a mild diuretic and a digestive bitter, and modern research has examined the plant for anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, though more evidence is needed before firm medical claims can be made.

Historically, dandelion preparations appear in European herbals from the medieval period onward, and the plant was cultivated in some gardens for its medicinal and culinary value. Its use spread with European settlers to North America and elsewhere, where it became naturalized. The plant's wide distribution today is partly the result of this long association with human activity.

From an ecological standpoint, the dandelion is far more valuable than its reputation suggests. Its bright flowers are among the first sources of nectar and pollen in early spring, when few other plants are blooming. Bees, hoverflies, beetles, and other pollinators depend on these resources as they emerge from winter dormancy. Because dandelions bloom over a long season, they provide food across a span of months in many regions.

The plant also plays a role in soil health. Its deep taproot can reach far below the surface, drawing up nutrients and loosening compacted soil. When the leaves die back and decompose, they return these nutrients to the topsoil. Dandelions are also a food source for various birds and small mammals, and their seeds are eaten by finches and other seed-eating species.

Dandelions reproduce by apomixis, a process in which seeds form without fertilization, so each seed is a genetic copy of the parent plant. This allows a single successful plant to colonize new ground quickly, which helps explain its success across diverse habitats. Their wind-dispersed seeds can travel considerable distances, further aiding their spread.

Despite their value, dandelions can be a nuisance in cultivated lawns and agricultural fields, where they compete with crops and turf grasses. Management approaches range from hand removal to targeted mowing, and many people now choose to tolerate them because of their early-season benefit to pollinators.

Natural rubber, the elastic material obtained from the latex of plants, has long been dominated by the Pará rubber tree, Hevea brasiliensis. Concerns about disease, labor conditions, deforestation, and supply concentration have prompted researchers to look for alternative sources. Among these, the Russian dandelion, Taraxacum kok-saghyz, has attracted particular attention.

Taraxacum kok-saghyz produces latex in its roots, and the rubber it contains is chemically similar to that of the Pará tree. The plant was studied intensively in the twentieth century, especially during the Second World War, when access to Southeast Asian rubber was disrupted. Research programs in the United States and elsewhere explored its cultivation, though it was eventually overshadowed by synthetic rubber, which became cheaper and more practical.

Interest has returned in recent years as concerns about sustainability and supply security have grown. Breeding programs have worked to increase the rubber content and root biomass of cultivated dandelion varieties, and some researchers have focused on mechanizing harvest and processing. Work continues on improving yields, reducing the cost of extraction, and making the resulting rubber suitable for demanding products such as tires.

The potential advantages are notable. Dandelions are temperate plants that can be grown in regions far from the tropical zones where Hevea is cultivated, which could diversify supply chains. They are herbaceous and can be harvested annually, potentially requiring less land-clearing than tree plantations. Because they can be grown in rotation with other crops, they might also fit into existing agricultural systems.

Challenges remain. Current yields of rubber per hectare are generally lower than those of mature rubber trees, and the cost of processing the roots into usable rubber is still a barrier. Researchers are also examining the agronomic demands of the crop, including its needs for water, fertilizer, and pest control. Whether dandelion rubber can compete economically at large scale is not yet settled, and the answer will depend on continued research and investment.

Even so, the dandelion offers a striking example of how a common plant can serve many purposes. It has inspired stories and wishes, nourished people, supported ecosystems, and may one day help supply a material essential to modern life. Looking at the humble dandelion with fresh attention can reveal how much value grows in the places we often overlook.

How to Connect a Home Wi-Fi Router to a Modem and Laptop

A home network starts with two devices: the modem, which links your home to your internet service provider, and the router, which shares that connection wirelessly with your devices. Before you begin, gather the modem, the router, the power adapters for both, and an Ethernet cable, which usually comes in the router's box. Place the modem and router near each other, ideally close to a power outlet and a central spot in your home for good wireless coverage. Start by turning off the modem and unplugging it from power, then wait about thirty seconds so it can reset. Connect one end of the coaxial cable from your internet provider to the modem's cable input, and tighten the connector by hand so it is secure. Plug the modem's power adapter back in and wait several minutes until its status lights show that it is online, which usually means a steady power light and a steady internet or link light. Next, take the Ethernet cable and plug one end into the modem's Ethernet port, which is often labeled LAN or Ethernet and not the one used for phone lines. Plug the other end into the router's port labeled WAN, Internet, or sometimes a differently colored port set apart from the numbered LAN ports. Connect the router's power adapter and switch the router on, then wait a few minutes for its lights to stabilize. Once the router is powered and its internet light is on, your network is physically connected and ready for configuration. Find the Wi-Fi network name, or SSID, and the password printed on the label of the router, since you will need them to join from your laptop. On your laptop, open the Wi-Fi menu from the taskbar or menu bar and select the network name that matches your router's label. Enter the password when prompted, and make sure you type it exactly, since passwords are case-sensitive. Once connected, your laptop should show the Wi-Fi symbol with full or near-full signal bars and indicate that the network has internet access. If the laptop reports that the network has no internet access, restart the modem and router by unplugging each, waiting thirty seconds, and plugging them back in, starting with the modem. You can also open a web browser and visit a common website to confirm that pages load normally. For better security, many routers allow you to change the Wi-Fi password and network name through a settings page, which is usually reached by typing an address such as 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1 into a browser. The exact address and login details are printed on the router's label, and you should change the default administrator password the first time you log in. Remember to write down any new network name and password you choose so you can reconnect your devices later. If you have trouble, consult your router's manual or your internet provider's support website, since setup steps can vary between models. With the modem and router properly connected and your laptop joined to the network, your home internet is ready for everyday use.

Dear friend,

I have been thinking about you and the difficult decision you are facing. I know how heavy it can feel to carry a choice that could shape the months and years ahead, and how easy it is to lie awake turning every option over in your mind. I want you to know that you are not alone in this, and that I am praying for you.

Scripture reminds us that we are invited to bring our anxieties to God, and that He cares for the details of our lives. Proverbs 3:5-6 encourages us to trust in the Lord with all our heart and not lean on our own understanding, and I find real comfort in those words when I am uncertain.

I am asking God to grant you clarity, the kind that comes not from forcing an answer but from quiet, honest prayer. I am praying that He would settle your heart and guard your thoughts from fear.

I am also praying for wisdom. James 1:5 tells us that if any of us lacks wisdom, we should ask God, who gives generously without finding fault. I believe He will meet you in that request.

Please remember that trusting God does not mean you will always know the outcome in advance. It means believing that He is present in the process, whatever path you choose.

I hope you will give yourself grace in this season. Some decisions feel impossible because they matter so much, and it is natural to want certainty before you move. Often, peace comes as we take the next faithful step rather than waiting for every question to be answered.

If it helps, consider writing down what you know, what you fear, and what you hope for. Seeing these things on paper can sometimes bring surprising clarity and help you hear what your heart is trying to say.

I also encourage you to seek counsel from people you trust, people who know you well and who pray with you. You do not have to carry this alone, and wise friends can help you see blind spots without taking the decision out of your hands.

As you pray, you might simply say, "Lord, I do not know what to do, but my eyes are on You." That honest prayer is powerful, and God hears it.

I am also praying that you would feel His peace settle over you, even before the decision is made. The peace of God, as Philippians 4:7 describes it, guards our hearts and minds, and it is available to us in the middle of uncertainty.

Please take care of yourself while you wait. Rest when you can, eat well, step outside for fresh air, and allow yourself moments of joy. Clear thinking often comes more easily when we are cared for.

I want you to hold onto the truth that God's love for you does not depend on which choice you make. He walks with you on every road, and He can redeem even the paths we wish we had not taken.

Whatever you decide, I will be here to listen, to pray, and to celebrate with you or sit with you through the hard parts. You have my support and my prayers.

Lean into God's faithfulness, which has carried you through before and will carry you again. Trust that He is working even now, in ways you may not yet see.

Thank you for allowing me to walk alongside you in this. I am grateful for you and for the courage you show in facing this moment.

May the Lord bless you, guide your steps, and give you the peace that surpasses understanding. You are held, you are loved, and you are never alone.

With love and prayers,

[Your Name]

This paper addresses a timely and important problem in algorithmic fairness: how to maintain fair predictions when the sensitive attributes used to define groups are noisy, incomplete, or subject to change over time. The authors motivate their work clearly, noting that many fairness interventions implicitly assume that protected attributes are accurately recorded and stable, an assumption that rarely holds in practice. The framing of the problem is a strength, as it connects fairness research to real deployment concerns in areas such as lending, hiring, and healthcare. The paper situates its contribution against prior work on fairness constraints, reweighting, and adversarial debiasing, and the related work section is generally well organized. However, the literature review would benefit from a more explicit discussion of work on noisy or missing sensitive attributes, since several recent papers tackle closely related questions and their omission weakens the claimed novelty. The central proposal is a metric-based approach that aims to learn predictors robust to perturbations in the sensitive attribute, and the intuition behind this is sound. The use of a fairness metric as the optimization target, rather than a surrogate constraint, is a sensible design choice that gives the method a clearer interpretation. The formal definitions are mostly precise, although the notation for the perturbation model shifts between sections, which can make the theoretical development harder to follow. The assumptions underlying the robustness guarantees are stated, but the authors should discuss more carefully when these assumptions are likely to hold and what happens when they are violated. The theoretical analysis is a notable component of the paper, and the main theorem provides a bound that is intuitive and useful. Nevertheless, the proof sketch in the appendix skips several steps that a reader would need to verify the result independently, and I recommend expanding it. It would also help to state explicitly whether the bound is tight or merely sufficient. The experimental section evaluates the method on several standard tabular benchmarks, which is appropriate for the scope of the claims. The choice of datasets is reasonable, though the inclusion of at least one larger or more recent dataset would strengthen confidence in generality. The baselines include both classical fairness methods and a few robust learning approaches, which allows a meaningful comparison. However, some baselines appear to be run with default hyperparameters, and the authors should confirm that all methods received comparable tuning effort. Results are reported as averages over several random seeds, but the reported variances are sometimes large relative to the differences between methods, and the paper occasionally describes small gaps as clear improvements. More careful statistical reporting, such as confidence intervals or significance tests, would make the empirical conclusions more credible. The ablation study is informative and isolates the contribution of the robustness component, which I found helpful for understanding where the gains come from. The sensitivity analysis over the perturbation rate is a welcome addition and shows that performance degrades gracefully, though the range explored could be wider. The figures are generally clear, but several axis labels are too small to read at print size and the legend is ambiguous in one plot. The paper's code and data processing details are described in reasonable depth, but a public repository with reproduction instructions would substantially improve reproducibility. The discussion section acknowledges limitations, including the restriction to binary sensitive attributes, and this candor is commendable. I would encourage the authors to go further and discuss the potential for the method to be misused, for example to mask underlying disparities by optimizing a metric that does not capture the harms of concern to affected communities. The conclusion summarizes the contributions accurately without overstating them. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful gap and offers a principled approach with reasonable theoretical and empirical support. Its main weaknesses lie in the incomplete treatment of related work, the need for more rigorous statistical reporting, and some gaps in the theoretical exposition. I recommend a major revision. With these issues addressed, the paper could make a useful contribution to the fairness literature.

Jaw Joint Disorders as a Cause of Facial Pain and Their Treatment

The temporomandibular joint, commonly called the TMJ, connects the lower jaw to the skull just in front of each ear. It allows the jaw to open, close, slide, and rotate during chewing, speaking, and yawning. When this joint or the muscles that move it become irritated or damaged, the result can be a group of conditions known as temporomandibular disorders, or TMDs. These disorders are one of the more common causes of persistent pain in the face, jaw, and head.

Pain from jaw joint disorders is often felt in the cheek, temple, ear, or jaw itself, and it may be dull and aching or sharp with movement. Many people also notice pain that worsens while chewing, yawning, or talking for long periods. Some describe a clicking, popping, or grinding sound when they open their mouth, and others experience a feeling that the jaw gets stuck or locks in place for a short time.

Because the nerves that serve the jaw also serve the teeth, ears, and surrounding face, pain from the joint can be mistaken for a toothache, earache, sinus problem, or headache. This overlap is one reason these disorders are often misdiagnosed or diagnosed only after a long search. A careful history and examination are important for telling them apart.

There are several main categories of TMD. Muscle disorders involve pain and tenderness in the chewing muscles and are the most frequent type. Joint disorders involve problems with the disc that cushions the joint, the bones, or the joint capsule. These can include disc displacement, where the disc slips out of its normal position, and arthritis, which causes inflammation and wear of the joint surfaces.

Several factors are thought to contribute to these conditions. Teeth grinding and clenching, especially during sleep, place heavy repeated loads on the joint and muscles. Injury to the jaw or face, such as a blow or whiplash, can damage the joint structures. Arthritis, including osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, can affect the joint directly. Stress and anxiety are commonly linked to muscle tension and clenching, and poor posture of the head and neck may also play a role.

It is worth noting that the exact cause in any individual case is often unclear, and several factors frequently act together. Research on TMDs continues, and some of the older beliefs about causes, such as the idea that bite alignment alone determines the problem, are no longer considered well supported.

Diagnosis usually begins with a detailed discussion of symptoms, including when the pain started, what makes it better or worse, and whether the jaw has locked or clicked. The clinician then examines the jaw movement, listens to the joint, and presses on the muscles to check for tenderness. Imaging such as X-rays, computed tomography, or magnetic resonance imaging may be used when there is concern about bone changes or disc position, but it is not needed in every case.

Many people with jaw joint pain improve with conservative, non-surgical treatment. Education about the condition is often the first step, along with advice to avoid habits that stress the joint. Patients are commonly encouraged to eat softer foods, avoid wide yawning, chewing gum, and biting nails, and to rest the jaw when it is sore.

Self-care measures can help considerably. Applying warm or cold packs to the painful area may ease discomfort. Gentle jaw exercises, prescribed by a clinician or physical therapist, aim to restore range of motion and reduce muscle tension. Relaxation techniques, stress management, and good posture also form part of many treatment plans.

Medication can be useful for short-term relief. Over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen or naproxen can reduce pain and swelling. Muscle relaxants may be prescribed for patients with significant muscle tightness, usually for a limited period. Some people benefit from low doses of certain antidepressants or other medications that can help with chronic pain and sleep disturbance.

A custom-made occlusal splint, sometimes called a night guard, is a common treatment for people who grind or clench their teeth. The splint is worn over the teeth, usually at night, to protect the teeth and reduce the load on the joint and muscles. Splints can relieve symptoms, although they manage the problem rather than cure the underlying cause, and their long-term use is typically reviewed by a dentist.

Physical therapy is an important option for many patients. A physical therapist may use manual techniques such as gentle mobilization of the joint and soft tissue massage, along with exercises to improve jaw control and posture. Therapy is often tailored to the individual and may continue for several weeks or months.

Some patients are offered injections into the joint or surrounding muscles. Options include corticosteroids to reduce inflammation, local anesthetics to ease pain, and botulinum toxin to relax overactive chewing muscles. Hyaluronic acid injections are sometimes used to lubricate the joint, although evidence for their benefit varies. These treatments are generally considered when conservative measures have not provided enough relief.

Cognitive behavioral therapy and other psychological approaches can help people who have chronic pain. These methods teach ways to manage pain, reduce catastrophic thinking, and lessen the muscle tension that stress produces. They are often used alongside physical treatments rather than on their own.

Surgery is generally reserved for severe cases that have not responded to other treatments. Procedures range from minimally invasive arthroscopy, in which a small camera and instruments are used to clean and repair the joint, to open joint surgery and joint replacement. Because surgery carries risks and the results can vary, it is usually considered only after careful evaluation.

Lifestyle habits can influence how the condition behaves over time. Regular exercise, good sleep, and managing stress can reduce the frequency of flare-ups. Avoiding caffeine or alcohol in excess may help some people who clench at night, though the evidence for this is modest.

Dietary adjustments can ease symptoms during painful periods. Soft foods such as yogurt, soups, mashed potatoes, eggs, and cooked vegetables place less demand on the jaw. Cutting food into small pieces and chewing on both sides of the mouth can also reduce strain.

Posture deserves attention because the head and neck influence the jaw. Forward head posture, common among people who spend long hours at computers or on phones, can increase tension in the muscles of the neck and jaw. Keeping screens at eye level and taking regular breaks to move and stretch may help.

Sleep quality is closely linked to jaw pain. Many people grind their teeth during sleep without realizing it, and waking with a sore jaw, headache, or worn teeth can be a sign of this. A dentist or doctor may recommend a sleep evaluation if snoring or breathing interruptions are also present, since sleep-disordered breathing is connected to bruxism.

Children and adolescents can also develop jaw joint problems, although the causes and treatments may differ from those in adults. Growth changes, injury, and habits such as thumb sucking can play a part. Pediatric cases are usually managed with a gentle, conservative approach under professional supervision.

Pregnancy and hormonal changes have been associated with changes in jaw pain in some women, although the connection is not fully understood. Women are more commonly affected by TMDs than men, and the reasons for this are still being studied.

Long-term outlook varies. Many people experience pain that improves within a few weeks or months, particularly when the condition is caught early and managed with simple measures. For others, symptoms come and go over years. Chronic pain can be frustrating, but most people can achieve meaningful improvement with an approach that combines education, self-care, and appropriate professional treatment.

Anyone with jaw pain that lasts more than a few days, that is accompanied by swelling, fever, or difficulty opening the mouth, or that follows an injury should seek medical or dental advice. A dentist, doctor, or physical therapist can help identify the cause and recommend a suitable plan. Early assessment makes it easier to manage the condition and prevent it from becoming a long-term problem.

The manuscript addresses the automated discovery and interpretation of task hierarchies within linearly-solvable Markov decision processes (LMDPs), a framework in which the Bellman equation becomes linear in the desirability function, enabling efficient analytical and computational methods. The authors' central motivation, that hierarchical structure can be recovered from the solution itself rather than hand-specified, is well chosen and addresses a genuine gap in the literature on hierarchical control. The paper's conceptual framing is clear, and the connection drawn between subtask decomposition and the factorization of the desirability function is a promising direction. The related work section is thorough and places the contribution appropriately among prior efforts in options frameworks and hierarchical reinforcement learning. However, the formal definition of a task hierarchy in the linearly-solvable setting is introduced somewhat abruptly, and the authors should state more explicitly which structural properties the hierarchy must satisfy for the discovery procedure to be guaranteed to terminate and produce a unique decomposition. The algorithm for hierarchy discovery is described at a high level, and pseudocode with complexity analysis would substantially improve reproducibility. The interpretation component, which is claimed as a key contribution, is supported mainly by qualitative examples, and the authors should provide a more systematic criterion for judging whether a recovered hierarchy is meaningful to a human analyst. The experiments are limited to two gridworld domains of modest size, and I would encourage evaluation on larger or more stochastic environments to test scalability and robustness. Baseline comparisons are present but narrow; including at least one established hierarchical method would clarify where the proposed approach offers genuine advantages. The reported results appear consistent with the claims, although the paper would benefit from variance estimates across random seeds and a discussion of sensitivity to the hyperparameters governing the decomposition. Several figures are difficult to read at print resolution, and the axis labels and legends should be enlarged. The mathematical notation is mostly consistent, but the distinction between the state cost and the terminal cost is occasionally blurred, which could confuse readers new to the LMDP formalism. The discussion section acknowledges limitations but does not address the possibility that discovered hierarchies may reflect artifacts of the chosen state representation. I recommend a major revision: the core idea is sound and of interest, but the theoretical guarantees, algorithmic detail, and empirical scope need to be strengthened before the claims can be fully evaluated.

Online learning has transformed higher education by opening doors for students who might otherwise be unable to pursue a degree. Many learners today balance full-time jobs, caregiving responsibilities, and household duties alongside their studies. For these students, the flexibility of online courses can make the difference between giving up on education and achieving their goals. This essay examines the key benefits of online learning for students with work and family commitments.

The most significant advantage is scheduling flexibility. Traditional classes meet at fixed times and places, which can conflict with shift work, commuting, or the needs of young children. Online courses often allow students to watch lectures, complete readings, and submit assignments at hours that fit their own lives. A nurse who works night shifts, for example, can study in the early morning, while a parent can complete coursework after the children are asleep.

Geographic freedom is another important benefit. Students who live far from a college campus no longer need to relocate or spend hours commuting each week. This saves money on transportation and housing, and it preserves time that can be devoted to family and employment. Students in rural areas or those caring for relatives who cannot be left alone can access programs that would otherwise be out of reach.

Online learning also reduces many of the hidden costs of education. Commuting, parking, and campus fees add up quickly, and these expenses can strain the budgets of working families. Many online programs also provide digital textbooks or open educational resources, which can lower the cost of materials. Although tuition varies widely, the overall financial burden can be easier to manage when students do not have to leave their jobs.

Self-paced options offer further relief for students facing unpredictable demands. A sudden work deadline, a child's illness, or a family emergency can disrupt a student's plans. Some online courses allow learners to pause, catch up, or adjust their pace within reasonable limits, which can help them avoid falling behind or withdrawing entirely. This adaptability encourages persistence during difficult periods.

Online learning also builds skills that are valuable in the modern workplace. Students must manage their own time, communicate through digital platforms, and stay motivated without constant supervision. These abilities are highly regarded by employers and often translate directly into professional success. Many students also find that the technology they use in their courses strengthens their digital literacy.

Finally, online programs can make education feel more personal and manageable for adult learners. Students can apply what they learn to their own jobs and family situations in real time, which often deepens understanding. Discussion forums and virtual groups also connect learners who share similar challenges, creating a sense of community across distances.

Despite these benefits, online learning is not without difficulties. Students must still find dedicated study time, and the lack of in-person interaction can be isolating for some. Strong self-discipline and reliable internet access are essential. However, with thoughtful planning and institutional support, these challenges can be managed.

In conclusion, online learning offers students with work and family commitments flexibility, affordability, and access that traditional education often cannot match. By allowing learners to fit education into their existing responsibilities, online programs help more people earn degrees and advance their careers. As higher education continues to evolve, online learning will remain a vital pathway for students whose lives demand both achievement and balance.

Subject: Why Major Banks Are Lagging Despite Favorable Rates, and Where Better Long-Term Value May Lie

Dear Team,

I wanted to share some thoughts on a question that has been coming up frequently: why major banks have underperformed even though interest rates have been relatively favorable for their core business. Higher rates typically widen the spread between what banks earn on loans and what they pay on deposits, so on the surface the environment should have been a tailwind. The reality has been more complicated, and understanding why matters for any decision about bank stocks.

The first factor is deposit costs. As rates rose, banks had to compete harder to keep depositors, and many customers moved money into higher-yielding accounts or money market funds. That shift compressed the margin benefit that rising rates were expected to deliver. Banks that relied heavily on low-cost checking balances saw those advantages erode.

The second factor is the value of existing assets. Many banks had locked in long-term securities and loans at lower yields during the prior low-rate period. As rates climbed, the market value of those holdings declined, and some institutions faced unrealized losses on their bond portfolios. Those losses weighed on capital ratios and investor sentiment, even when they did not immediately hit earnings.

The third factor is credit and loan growth. Higher borrowing costs slowed demand for loans in several categories, including commercial real estate and mortgages. Banks also set aside larger provisions for potential credit losses as economic uncertainty persisted. Slower loan growth combined with higher provisions limits how much of the rate advantage actually reaches the bottom line.

The fourth factor is regulatory and capital pressure. Regulators have pushed for stronger capital buffers and liquidity, particularly following the regional bank stress of recent years. Compliance costs and capital requirements can constrain buybacks and dividend growth, which are often central to a bank stock's total return.

The fifth factor is market structure. Investors have been rotating toward growth sectors, and financials as a group have sometimes been treated as a cyclical proxy for the broader economy. When growth expectations are uncertain, bank valuations tend to compress, regardless of near-term earnings.

Turning to which banks may offer better long-term prospects, it helps to focus on characteristics rather than names. Institutions with a durable base of low-cost deposits, diversified revenue streams that include fee income from payments, wealth management, and capital markets, and conservative underwriting tend to be more resilient across rate cycles. Strong capital positions that allow for consistent dividends and buybacks are also valuable.

Large universal banks with diversified operations have historically weathered difficult periods better than smaller, more concentrated lenders, though their valuations often reflect that stability. Some regional banks with strong deposit franchises and disciplined credit management may offer more upside if their balance sheets are sound, but they carry higher idiosyncratic risk. Investors should look closely at each bank's net interest margin trends, deposit betas, credit quality, and capital ratios.

Before acting on any of this, I would recommend a few steps. Review recent quarterly filings and earnings calls to understand management's outlook on deposits and net interest income. Compare valuations such as price to tangible book value and forward earnings against peers and historical averages. Consider how each bank fits within your broader portfolio and risk tolerance.

It is also worth acknowledging the limits of this analysis. Bank performance depends heavily on the path of interest rates, the health of the broader economy, and regulatory developments, all of which are difficult to predict with confidence. My view reflects general patterns rather than a specific recommendation, and individual circumstances should guide any investment decision. Consulting a qualified financial advisor is a sensible step before making changes.

I am happy to discuss any of these points in more detail or walk through specific institutions if that would be useful.

Best regards,

[Your Name]

Stricter academic eligibility requirements for student athletes have sparked considerable debate among educators, coaches, and families. Supporters argue that athletic scholarships and competition are secondary to the core purpose of college, and that tougher standards ensure players are genuinely earning their degrees. However, critics worry that rigid cutoffs may unfairly penalize students who face learning difficulties, disadvantaged schooling, or the heavy time demands of training and travel. Such rules can also push athletes toward easier courses or less rigorous majors simply to protect their eligibility, which undermines the educational goals they were meant to advance. Some students may be dropped from teams just as they are beginning to improve academically, removing the structure and support that helped them succeed in the first place. Financial stakes add further pressure, since losing eligibility can mean losing a scholarship and the opportunity to afford college at all. Reformers therefore suggest a more balanced approach, pairing clear academic benchmarks with tutoring, mentoring, and flexible recovery paths. Ultimately, the central question is how to protect academic integrity while still giving every student athlete a fair chance to succeed in both the classroom and competition.

It began on a Tuesday, when Eliot heard the melody through the wall of his apartment. It was faint at first, a thread of notes rising and falling like someone humming in a distant room. He assumed it was the neighbor's radio.

The next night it was louder, and he realized it had no source he could place. The tune wound through the walls, under the floorboards, and into the hum of the refrigerator.

He tried to name it. It sounded like a lullaby he had known as a child, but when he reached for the words, his memory slid away like wet glass.

By Friday he had stopped sleeping. He lay awake listening, counting the phrases, waiting for the melody to resolve into a final chord. It never did. Each phrase ended in a question that the next phrase refused to answer.

He began to write the notes down on the back of envelopes, then on the walls in pencil, then on his own forearms. The handwriting grew smaller and more frantic as the days passed. He noticed that his pencil moved in time with the music, whether he wanted it to or not.

His reflection started to hum along. He would catch it in the bathroom mirror, lips parted, eyes half closed, as though listening to something he could not hear. He tried to stop, but his mouth kept shaping the notes.

Mara, his sister, called on Sunday. He could hear her voice from across the line, bright and worried, but the melody rose beneath her words until he could no longer tell which sounds were hers. He hung up in the middle of a sentence.

He went outside to escape it, but the streets were full of the same tune. A bus driver hummed it. A child on a swing sang it without knowing the words. The pigeons seemed to bob their heads in its rhythm.

He understood, then, that the melody was not coming from anywhere. It was waiting for him to finish it.

He returned home and sat at the piano he had never learned to play. His fingers found the first phrase, then the second. The notes came easily, as though they had always lived in his hands.

At the end of each phrase he paused, and the silence rang with the question the melody had been asking all week. He felt a terrible calm settle over him. The answer was simple, and he knew it would be the last thing he ever played.

He pressed the final key.

The room went quiet, and then the quiet began to sing.

Mara found him three days later, sitting upright at the piano, his hands resting on the keys. The room was spotless. The walls were bare, every pencil mark scrubbed away. On the music stand lay a single sheet of paper covered in neat, unhurried notes that ended in a chord no one had ever heard.

Her neighbor later swore she could still hear the melody drifting through the building, faint and patient, humming beneath the floorboards.

This manuscript investigates how the noise inherent in stochastic gradient descent interacts with the local curvature of the loss landscape, as measured by the Hessian, and argues that this interaction biases training toward flatter minima. The central question is important and well motivated, since the relationship between flat minima and generalization remains a major topic in deep learning theory. The authors' decomposition of the gradient noise covariance into components aligned with the top Hessian eigenvectors is a clear and useful framing that connects the analysis to prior work on implicit regularization. The theoretical derivation of the stationary distribution under a continuous-time approximation is carefully stated, and the assumptions behind it are mostly made explicit. However, the central claim depends on the approximation that minibatch noise is well described by isotropic or Hessian-proportional Gaussian noise, and the manuscript does not sufficiently test how well this holds for the non-convex, non-Gaussian gradient distributions encountered in practice. The empirical section would be considerably stronger with experiments on more architectures and datasets, particularly larger-scale models where the Hessian must be estimated approximately. The paper also needs clearer ablations separating the effect of learning rate from the effect of batch size, since both change the noise scale and the step size simultaneously. Several figures report sharpness metrics without specifying how they were computed, which makes the reported comparisons difficult to reproduce or interpret. The discussion of how these results relate to prior sharpness-aware and flatness-based generalization measures is brief and would benefit from a more direct comparison. The authors should also address the known sensitivity of sharpness measures to parameter reparameterization, since a flatness claim is only meaningful if the chosen metric is invariant to such changes or the authors justify its use. The writing is generally clear, though some derivations in the appendix contain notational inconsistencies that should be corrected. Overall, the paper makes a valuable contribution, but the conclusions are currently stronger than the evidence supports, and I recommend a major revision addressing the approximation validity, experimental scope, and metric definitions.

The manuscript addresses an important and timely problem: how decentralized learners can adapt sequentially to a stream of domains while respecting privacy constraints, with collaborator selection guided by Wasserstein distance. The topic sits at the intersection of federated and decentralized learning, domain adaptation, and differential privacy, and the authors are right that these threads are rarely studied together. The central idea, using an optimal-transport distance to decide which peers to collaborate with, is intuitive and well motivated, since peers whose data distributions are close to one's own should in principle yield more useful updates. The introduction does a reasonable job of framing the problem and situating it relative to prior work on federated domain adaptation and gossip-based decentralized optimization.

The related work section is broad but at times reads as a list of citations rather than a critical synthesis. The authors would strengthen their positioning by explicitly stating what gap their method fills that existing decentralized domain adaptation approaches do not. In particular, a clearer comparison with methods that already use distribution-distance measures for peer or client selection would help readers judge the novelty of the Wasserstein-based selection rule.

The problem formulation is clearly stated, with domains arriving sequentially and each node maintaining a local model that is periodically mixed with selected neighbors. The notation is mostly consistent, although a few symbols are overloaded, and a summary table of notation would improve readability considerably. The assumptions underlying the analysis, such as bounded gradients, smoothness of the loss, and bounded Wasserstein distances between domains, are stated, but the paper should discuss how restrictive these are in practice and whether they hold for the neural architectures used in the experiments.

The proposed algorithm combines three components: a sequential adaptation schedule, a privacy mechanism based on noise injection into shared updates, and a neighbor selection step that ranks peers by estimated Wasserstein distance. Each component is individually reasonable, but the interaction between them is the most interesting and least examined aspect. Noise added for privacy can distort the distance estimates used for selection, and the paper does not sufficiently analyze this feedback effect. A clearer treatment of how estimation error in the Wasserstein distance propagates into the selection decisions would be valuable.

The privacy analysis relies on a standard differential privacy composition argument across communication rounds and domains. The derivation appears largely correct under the stated assumptions, but the privacy budget accounting is presented somewhat informally, and it is unclear whether the reported epsilon values account for the additional information leaked through the selection step itself. Since selecting neighbors based on data-dependent distances can reveal information about local distributions, the authors should either include this leakage in their accounting or argue explicitly why it is negligible.

The theoretical convergence result provides a bound on the expected suboptimality after the final domain, expressed in terms of the number of communication rounds, the noise level, and a term capturing domain shift. The bound is informative, but the dependence on the domain-shift term is loose, and the authors do not discuss whether the bound becomes vacuous under realistic levels of heterogeneity. A remark on tightness, or a comparison against the bounds for non-adaptive decentralized SGD, would help readers interpret the result.

The experimental section evaluates the method on several image classification benchmarks partitioned into domains, with a range of network topologies and privacy budgets. The breadth of settings is commendable, and the inclusion of multiple topologies is a welcome feature. However, the baselines are limited to a small number of decentralized methods, and several recent federated domain adaptation approaches are absent. Including stronger and more recent baselines would make the claimed improvements more convincing.

The ablation studies isolate the contribution of the Wasserstein-based selection by comparing it against random selection and against selection based on a simpler statistic such as mean feature distance. These ablations are useful and largely support the claim that the Wasserstein criterion helps, although the margins are modest in several settings and the reported variance is not always large enough to rule out noise. Additional random seeds or confidence intervals would be needed to make the differences statistically convincing.

The reported results show consistent gains over the baselines in most configurations, particularly in settings with high domain heterogeneity, which is where the method is designed to help. In low-heterogeneity regimes the advantage largely disappears, which is an honest result the authors acknowledge, and it suggests the method's benefit is conditional rather than universal. The paper would benefit from stating this conditionality more prominently in the abstract and conclusion.

The computational cost of estimating pairwise Wasserstein distances is not adequately addressed. Exact optimal-transport computation scales poorly with sample size and dimension, and the paper mentions an approximation but does not quantify the resulting error or its effect on neighbor selection. A runtime comparison and an analysis of the approximation quality would clarify whether the approach is practical at scale.

Communication overhead is discussed in terms of the number of messages exchanged per round, but the cost of transmitting the auxiliary statistics needed for Wasserstein estimation is not counted. Since these statistics may be as large as the model updates themselves in some configurations, the communication analysis should be revised to include them in the total cost. This is a notable omission given that communication efficiency is a central motivation for decentralized learning.

The paper's treatment of privacy in the experiments is somewhat narrow. Privacy is evaluated mainly through the formal epsilon values, with no empirical attack-based evaluation such as membership inference. Including such an evaluation, even briefly, would show whether the formal guarantees translate into meaningful protection against realistic adversaries.

The writing is generally clear, although some sections are dense and would benefit from careful editing. The figures are informative, but several plots use similar colors and markers that make the curves hard to distinguish, and the captions could state more clearly what each panel shows. Minor typographical issues and inconsistent capitalization of method names appear throughout and should be corrected before publication.

Reproducibility is partially supported. The authors state that code will be released and provide most hyperparameters, but details such as the learning-rate schedule for each domain, the exact Wasserstein approximation settings, and the random seeds are missing from the main text. Providing a complete configuration table in the appendix would substantially improve reproducibility.

The limitations section is brief and mostly restates assumptions rather than discussing failure modes. A more candid discussion would address the sensitivity of neighbor selection to noisy distance estimates, the reliance on the availability of a sufficiently rich pool of peers, and the open question of how the method behaves when domains do not follow a clean sequential order. Such a discussion would make the contribution easier to assess and to build upon.

The ethical implications are not discussed. Since the method is intended for privacy-sensitive settings, a short statement on the intended applications, potential misuse, and the limits of the privacy guarantees would be appropriate. This is a minor point but would round out the manuscript.

Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful problem with a reasonable and somewhat novel combination of ideas, and the empirical results are encouraging. The main weaknesses lie in the insufficiently analyzed interaction between privacy noise and distance-based selection, the narrow set of baselines, the omitted cost of communicating Wasserstein statistics, and the limited empirical privacy evaluation. I recommend a major revision. If the authors address the analysis of the noise-selection interaction, expand the comparisons, and clarify the computational and communication costs, the work could make a solid contribution to the decentralized and privacy-preserving learning literature.
