Thomas Jefferson is remembered as a statesman, but his daily habits reveal a man deeply committed to productive living and preparation. He rose early, often before dawn, and filled his days with reading, writing, farming, and experimentation. At Monticello he kept detailed records of his garden, noting the planting and harvesting of dozens of crops, which shows a steady discipline and a belief in careful observation. He also designed inventions and tools, such as a improved plow and a dumbwaiter, reflecting his conviction that useful knowledge should be applied to everyday needs. Jefferson believed that an active mind and body were essential to a free and virtuous citizen, and he often wrote about the value of agriculture as a source of independence and moral strength. His extensive correspondence and his founding of the University of Virginia further demonstrate his commitment to learning as a lifelong pursuit. Rather than resting on past accomplishments, he continued to read, plan, and build well into his later years. For students today, Jefferson's example suggests that preparation and purposeful activity are not merely habits of efficiency but foundations of a meaningful and responsible life.

Olympic Committee Official Arrested in Brazil Over Alleged Ticket Scheme

Pat Hickey, the former president of the Olympic Council of Ireland and a longtime figure in the International Olympic Committee's governance structure, was arrested in Rio de Janeiro in August 2016 in connection with an alleged scheme to resell Olympic tickets at inflated prices. Brazilian police acted on a warrant issued as part of an investigation into the sale of tickets for the Rio Games, which opened that same month.

Authorities alleged that hospitality packages and tickets allocated to national Olympic committees and sporting federations were being diverted to ticket resellers rather than distributed to fans or the sporting community as intended. Investigators said the arrangement could have generated substantial profits for those involved, at the expense of ordinary spectators who had been priced out of the market.

Hickey, who was in his late seventies at the time, had served as a senior figure in the Olympic movement for decades and was widely known for his role in European and Irish sport. His arrest drew immediate attention because it placed a sitting member of the IOC's extended circle under scrutiny during the Games themselves.

Police reportedly seized documents, electronic devices, and other materials during searches linked to the inquiry. Officials said the evidence gathered would be used to determine the extent of any wrongdoing and whether additional individuals or companies had participated in the alleged resale operation.

Hickey was initially held in custody, and his lawyers contended that he had done nothing wrong and that the accusations were unfounded. Supporters argued that the allegations required proper legal scrutiny before any conclusions could be drawn about his conduct.

The arrest came as the Rio Games faced a range of criticism, including concerns about budget overruns, unfinished infrastructure, and public spending. Critics said the ticketing controversy reflected broader problems with transparency and accountability in the planning and delivery of the event.

The International Olympic Committee responded to the case by stating that it took the allegations seriously and was cooperating with Brazilian authorities. The organization said that it expected all members to adhere to its ethical standards and that it would review the matter in line with its own rules.

Following his arrest, Hickey was released on bail after a relatively short period in detention, though he remained subject to conditions while the investigation continued. Legal proceedings in Brazil moved slowly, and the case was closely followed by sports journalists and governance watchdogs.

Hickey was also linked to a wider set of inquiries concerning the Olympic Council of Ireland and allegations that funds and ticketing arrangements had been mishandled. Investigators examined whether financial irregularities extended beyond the Rio ticket resale and whether officials had used their positions for personal benefit.

Separately, the Olympic Council of Ireland faced questions about its governance and internal oversight. Members and observers called for clearer procedures for handling tickets, hospitality, and financial arrangements, arguing that such safeguards were essential to protect the integrity of national Olympic bodies.

The case also prompted discussion within the wider sports community about how tickets allocated to national committees are distributed and monitored. Some commentators suggested that greater transparency, auditing, and public reporting could help prevent similar problems at future major events.

Hickey maintained his innocence throughout the early stages of the process. His representatives said he would contest any charges in court and argued that the case had been publicized in a way that unfairly damaged his reputation before the facts were established.

As the investigation progressed, Brazilian prosecutors continued to assemble evidence, interview witnesses, and review financial records connected to the ticket sales. Officials indicated that the inquiry was complex, involving multiple parties and a significant volume of documentation.

Observers noted that major sporting events often attract ticketing irregularities, given high demand and limited supply. They said the Hickey case highlighted the need for robust rules on secondary sales and for clear consequences when officials are found to have breached those rules.

The Rio ticketing scandal also drew attention to the role of intermediaries and hospitality companies that handle large volumes of tickets on behalf of sporting bodies. Questions were raised about how such firms are selected, supervised, and held accountable for their dealings.

Sports governance experts said the affair could influence reforms within the Olympic movement, particularly regarding conflicts of interest and the oversight of officials who hold multiple positions. Some argued that stronger ethics enforcement was needed to restore public confidence.

For fans, the controversy served as a reminder of the frustration many experienced when trying to secure tickets to the Games. Many had reported difficulties navigating the official sales process, and the allegations suggested that some seats had been unfairly diverted away from the public.

Hickey's case remained under investigation in the months after his arrest, and the final outcome depended on the results of the Brazilian legal process. Until charges were formally tested and resolved, officials stressed that the allegations should be treated as unproven.

The episode underscored the scrutiny that accompanies the staging of the Olympic Games, where large sums of money, international attention, and high-profile officials intersect. How the case is ultimately resolved is likely to be watched closely by sports bodies, regulators, and the public alike.

Drew Barrymore's career has been one of Hollywood's most remarkable transformations, moving from precocious child star to respected actor, savvy producer, and accomplished director. Born on February 22, 1975, into the famous Barrymore acting family, she was introduced to audiences at just 11 months old in the 1976 film Altered States, though her breakout came later. Her early career was marked by fame that arrived almost before she could understand it. At age seven, she starred in Steven Spielberg's E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, playing Gertie, the young sister who befriends the alien. The film became one of the highest-grossing movies of its era and turned Barrymore into a household name. Yet the intense spotlight also brought struggles, and by her early teens she had battled substance abuse and spent time in rehabilitation, experiences she has spoken about openly in later years. Barrymore's turning point came in the years following that period, as she worked to rebuild her life and reclaim control of her career. She returned to the screen with a series of roles that showed her range, beginning with films that let her demonstrate maturity and emotional depth. Her performance in Boys on the Side in 1995 earned critical attention and signaled that she was more than a former child star. She followed it with a string of popular films, including the romantic comedy The Wedding Singer in 1998 opposite Adam Sandler, which became a box office success. In 1999 she appeared in Ever After, a retelling of the Cinderella story that reached a wide audience and showcased her charm. Her career continued to gain momentum with Charlie's Angels in 2000, an action comedy that made her a major commercial presence. Barrymore also demonstrated a willingness to take risks, appearing in a variety of genres and working with notable directors throughout the early 2000s. Alongside her acting, she began building a production company, Flower Films, which she co-founded with Nancy Juvonen. The company became a vehicle for developing projects and putting her creative instincts to work behind the camera. Through Flower Films, Barrymore helped produce films and television programs, giving her greater influence over the stories being told. Her producing work reflected a commitment to character-driven material and projects that resonated with her personal sensibilities. In the 2010s and beyond, Barrymore expanded her footprint into television, hosting her own daytime talk show, The Drew Barrymore Show, which premiered in 2020. The program became known for its warm tone, celebrity interviews, and segments on everyday topics, earning her multiple daytime Emmy recognitions. Her success as a host added another dimension to her public image and business ventures. Barrymore's most significant step behind the camera came when she made her feature directorial debut with Whip It in 2009. The film, a coming-of-age story about a teenager who joins a roller derby team, was well received by critics for its energy and sincerity. It marked a clear statement that Barrymore intended to shape her work from the director's chair as well as in front of the lens. She has continued to pursue both acting and directing, balancing the demands of each while maintaining a busy schedule across film and television. Industry observers often point to her resilience and adaptability as central to her longevity. Few performers have managed to move so successfully from childhood fame to lasting adult careers. Barrymore's path shows how a former child star can reinvent herself through acting, producing, and directing. Her career stands as a case study in durability, creative growth, and the ability to take ownership of one's professional identity over decades in the entertainment business.

Making community service a graduation requirement for high school students would give young people meaningful experiences that extend far beyond the classroom. Schools today prepare students with academic knowledge, yet many graduate without understanding the needs of the neighborhoods they live in or the ways they can contribute to them. Requiring service would help close that gap by connecting learning to real problems, such as food insecurity, environmental cleanup, and support for the elderly. Students who volunteer often develop empathy, communication skills, and a sense of responsibility that are difficult to teach through lectures alone. Critics argue that a required activity cannot be truly voluntary, and they worry that forced service may breed resentment rather than generosity. That concern is worth taking seriously, but it does not outweigh the benefits when the program is designed thoughtfully. Schools can offer a wide range of options so that students can choose work that matches their interests, whether that means tutoring younger children, helping at an animal shelter, or assisting with a local festival. Structured reflection, such as short written responses or group discussions, can help students understand what they learned and why their work matters. Service requirements also promote equity, since students from wealthier families are more likely to have access to volunteer opportunities through private networks. A school-based requirement ensures that every student, regardless of background, gains exposure to civic life. Many states already encourage or mandate service in some form, and early evidence from these programs suggests that students who serve are more likely to vote, stay engaged in their communities, and report higher confidence in their own abilities. Communities benefit as well, because schools can become partners in addressing local needs that agencies alone cannot meet. To make the requirement fair, schools should set a reasonable number of hours, provide transportation when needed, and recognize service that happens outside school as well as within it. Accountability matters too, so that the requirement is taken seriously and not treated as a box to check. Ultimately, community service teaches students that they are part of something larger than themselves. A graduation requirement would not create that understanding on its own, but it would give every student a chance to discover it. For that reason, schools should adopt service requirements and design them with care, flexibility, and a genuine commitment to the people they serve.

Staying active is one of the most reliable ways to move toward meaningful goals and to find real satisfaction in the work we do. When people remain engaged, they keep making progress, even if the steps are small. Momentum builds over time, and each completed task reinforces the belief that effort leads to results. Inactivity, by contrast, tends to create a cycle of hesitation, where delayed action makes the next step feel even harder. Staying in motion breaks that cycle and keeps ambitions from fading into wishful thinking. Activity also sharpens focus, since working on a concrete task forces a person to clarify what matters most. Goals that stay abstract are easy to postpone, but goals broken into daily actions become manageable and visible. Beyond progress, active engagement brings a sense of satisfaction that passive waiting rarely provides. Many people find that the greatest pleasure in work comes not from the final reward but from the process of solving problems and improving skills. Each challenge met with effort teaches patience, resilience, and confidence. Over time, these qualities shape a person's character as much as their accomplishments. Activity also fosters connection, because working alongside others creates opportunities for collaboration and shared purpose. Such relationships often make work more rewarding and help people sustain their efforts during difficult periods. Of course, activity without reflection can lead to exhaustion or aimless busyness, so the key is purposeful action. Setting clear priorities and pausing to evaluate progress ensures that energy is well spent. In this way, staying active becomes not a burden but a source of direction and fulfillment. Ultimately, those who remain engaged in their work are more likely to achieve their goals and to discover lasting satisfaction in the journey itself.

Schools across the country are debating whether students should be allowed to use mobile devices during the school day, and I believe that a carefully limited policy allowing responsible use during breaks and emergencies would serve students better than a complete ban. Phones have become a central part of how young people communicate, stay informed, and feel safe. A total prohibition ignores these realities and asks students to give up a tool that many of them rely on every day. Breaks are a natural time for students to relax, check in with family, or catch up with friends, and a short period of phone access can help them reset before returning to class. Many students also need to coordinate rides, manage after-school commitments, or respond to family needs that arise during the day. Emergencies are an even stronger reason to permit access. In a crisis, such as a medical problem, a lockdown, or a severe weather event, a phone can be the fastest way to contact parents, emergency services, or a trusted adult. Schools already have emergency plans, but those plans work best when students can communicate their location and condition quickly. Responsible use, however, must be clearly defined. Phones should remain silent during class time, and devices should be stored out of sight during lessons unless a teacher grants permission for a learning activity. Schools could set clear rules that prohibit recording other students, accessing inappropriate content, or using devices to cheat on tests. Violations should lead to proportionate consequences that teach responsibility rather than simply punishing students. Teachers and administrators would also need guidance and training to enforce these rules consistently and fairly. Some critics worry that phones will distract students and disrupt learning, and these concerns deserve serious attention. Yet limiting use to breaks and emergencies addresses much of this worry, since the majority of instructional time would remain phone-free. Students who learn to manage their devices during brief windows may also build self-discipline that will serve them well in college and the workplace. A thoughtful, balanced policy treats students as young people capable of responsibility while still protecting the learning environment. Ultimately, allowing responsible mobile device use during breaks and emergencies strikes a sensible balance between focus and safety. It respects students' needs to communicate and feel secure while preserving the classroom as a place of learning. With clear rules, fair enforcement, and trust built over time, schools can create an environment where technology supports education rather than undermining it.

Gratitude, kindness, and helping others are simple values, yet together they have the power to build a more respectful and compassionate world. Each day offers countless small chances to practice them, and these moments shape how people treat one another. Gratitude begins with noticing the good things we often take for granted, such as a friend's patience, a teacher's effort, or a stranger's smile. When people take time to express thanks, they strengthen their connections and remind others that their actions matter. Kindness is the natural companion of gratitude, because a person who feels appreciated is more likely to offer kindness in return. A small gesture, like holding a door or listening without interrupting, can change the mood of an entire afternoon. Helping others goes a step further by turning good feelings into real action. Volunteers who tutor children, neighbors who check on the elderly, and students who share their notes all show that compassion becomes meaningful when it is put into practice. Respect grows in the same soil, because treating someone with dignity means recognizing that their experiences and feelings are valid, even when they differ from our own. Communities that practice these values tend to be more inclusive, since people feel safe enough to speak honestly and to ask for help. Schools benefit especially, as classrooms where students support one another often see less conflict and more cooperation. Families, too, become stronger when members show gratitude at home and kindness in daily routines. These habits also spread outward, inspiring others to follow similar patterns. One person's generosity can encourage a friend, and that friend may then encourage someone else. Over time, such ripples can transform a neighborhood, a school, or even a nation. Compassion does not require wealth, power, or fame, only attention and willingness. Every individual therefore holds a part of the responsibility for creating a kinder world. By choosing gratitude, practicing kindness, and helping others, young people can begin that work today. In the end, a more respectful and compassionate world is not a distant dream but a future we build together, one thoughtful choice at a time.

The paper addresses regret guarantees for contextual bandits using overparameterized neural networks analyzed through the neural tangent kernel framework, a timely and technically ambitious topic. The authors tackle a genuine gap by extending NTK-based analysis, which has mostly been developed for supervised learning, to the exploration-exploitation setting of contextual bandits. The problem is well motivated, since practitioners routinely use neural networks as reward models in bandit applications while theory has lagged behind. The reduction from the bandit setting to a sequence of regression problems with neural network function approximation is clearly stated and makes the contribution easy to follow. The main regret bound is presented with its assumptions, including requirements on network width, the minimum eigenvalue of the NTK Gram matrix, and the scale of the reward noise, and these assumptions are stated explicitly, which I appreciate. However, the paper would benefit from a more thorough discussion of how restrictive the width requirement is, since the bound may only be non-vacuous at widths that are impractically large for the experiments considered. The theoretical analysis relies on the network remaining close to its initialization throughout training, a lazy-training regime whose relevance to realistic feature learning should be discussed more candidly. The empirical section is useful but limited, with synthetic experiments that validate the sublinear regret trend and only a small number of baselines, such as linear UCB and neural bandits without the theoretical exploration bonus. I would like to see experiments on standard contextual bandit benchmarks and an ablation over network width and training steps to test whether the theory's predicted dependencies hold in practice. The proof sketch is readable, though some steps in the concentration argument for the confidence sets are compressed to the point that a reader would need to consult the appendix to verify them. Notation is mostly consistent, but the symbol used for the effective dimension is overloaded with a related quantity in a later section, which can cause confusion. The related work section covers linear and kernelized bandits well but could engage more with recent neural bandit papers that offer alternative analyses. Overall, the contribution is a solid and meaningful step toward theoretically grounded neural contextual bandits, and I recommend acceptance conditional on a clearer discussion of the width and lazy-training assumptions and expanded empirical validation.

The manuscript proposes a deep-learning image compression framework that combines learned analysis and synthesis transforms with hyperprior-based entropy modeling. The topic is timely and well within the scope of current work on neural image codecs, and the authors are right that accurate probability estimation for quantized latents is the central lever for rate-distortion performance. The introduction motivates the problem clearly, situating the work against both classical transform codecs and earlier end-to-end learned approaches. The writing is generally clear, though some passages in the methods section would benefit from tighter notation and a more consistent use of terms such as latent, bottleneck, and hyperlatent. The overall ambition is appropriate, and the paper has the potential to be a useful contribution to the compression literature.

The core idea is a two-level latent hierarchy in which a hyperprior network conditions the entropy model for the main latents on side information extracted from those latents. This is a natural extension of the scale-hyperprior line of work, and the authors frame it honestly as an incremental but principled refinement. The architecture description is sufficient for a reader familiar with variational image compression to reconstruct the model, which is a strength. However, the paper would be more convincing if it stated explicitly which components are new and which are carried over from prior work, since at present a reader must work this out by comparing against the cited baselines. A short paragraph or a table listing the differences from the closest prior architecture would resolve this.

The training objective is the standard rate-distortion Lagrangian, with the rate term computed from the learned entropy model and the distortion term measured as mean squared error. The use of additive uniform noise as a differentiable surrogate for quantization is described correctly, and the authors are transparent about the mismatch between training and test-time quantization. That said, the discussion of how this mismatch affects the final bitrate is thin. Since the rate estimates during training are only approximations of the actual code length, the authors should report the gap between estimated and realized bits on the test set, for example through actual arithmetic coding of the bitstreams. Without this, the claimed rate savings rest partly on an estimate that the reader cannot verify directly.

The experimental section evaluates the codec on standard benchmark datasets and reports rate-distortion curves against JPEG, JPEG2000, BPG, and at least one prior learned codec. The curves are presented clearly and the choice of baselines is reasonable, though the omission of a more recent learned codec with context-adaptive entropy models weakens the claim of state-of-the-art performance. The authors should either include such a comparison or temper the language in the abstract and conclusions. The use of both PSNR and MS-SSIM is welcome, as the two metrics can disagree substantially at low bitrates, and the paper handles this disagreement reasonably in the discussion. The reported Bjøntegaard delta figures are useful summaries, but their computation should be described more precisely, including the interpolation method and the rate range used.

The ablation study is one of the more valuable parts of the paper, isolating the contribution of the hyperprior, the choice of activation functions, and the number of latent channels. The results suggest that the hyperprior accounts for most of the gain over the baseline, which is a sensible and useful finding. However, the ablations are run on a single random seed, and the differences between some configurations are small enough that run-to-run variance could plausibly account for them. The authors should report means and standard deviations over several seeds, or at minimum acknowledge this limitation explicitly. Reporting training time and parameter counts for each ablated variant would also help readers judge the efficiency trade-offs.

The computational cost of the proposed model is discussed only briefly. Neural codecs are often criticized for their decoding latency and memory footprint, and this is especially relevant when the entropy model is autoregressive or requires sequential decoding. The paper states that its hyperprior design avoids sequential dependencies in the main latent decoding, which is an advantage, but it does not quantify encoding and decoding time on a stated hardware configuration. Adding these measurements, even on a single GPU and a single CPU, would make the practical claims much more concrete and allow fair comparison with other learned codecs.

The discussion of limitations is present but short. The authors acknowledge that performance was evaluated primarily on natural images at moderate resolutions and that generalization to medical, satellite, or synthetic imagery was not tested. This is an honest statement, but the paper would benefit from a more substantive discussion of failure modes, such as behavior on high-frequency textures, text, or images with heavy compression artifacts in the training data. A qualitative figure showing reconstructions in these difficult cases would help readers understand where the model's advantages end.

The related work section is generally accurate and covers the main threads of learned compression, including scale-hyperprior models, autoregressive context models, and more recent transformer-based approaches. Some citations appear to be given without enough discussion of how the present work differs from them, and a few statements about the relative performance of prior methods would benefit from being qualified to the specific datasets and metrics under which they were measured. A more explicit positioning paragraph would help the reader see where this contribution fits.

Reproducibility is a concern that the authors partly address. The paper specifies the optimizer, learning rate schedule, batch size, and number of training iterations, which is commendable. However, it does not state whether code and trained model weights will be released, and several architectural hyperparameters, such as the kernel sizes and channel widths of the hyperprior network, are given only in a figure rather than in a table. Releasing the code and a configuration file would substantially improve the paper's value to the community and is strongly encouraged.

The figures are generally well designed, with legible axes and sensible color choices, though a few rate-distortion plots would be easier to read with a log-scale bitrate axis and clearer legends. The qualitative comparison figure is informative but would benefit from zoomed-in crops highlighting regions where differences between codecs are most visible, such as edges and fine textures. Captions could also be more self-contained, since at present several require the reader to consult the main text to understand the experimental setting.

The statistical reporting is adequate in most places but inconsistent in others. Some tables report results to three decimal places with no uncertainty estimate, while others report only the best configuration without the spread across runs. A uniform convention, with error bars or confidence intervals where multiple runs are available, would make comparisons more reliable. The authors should also clarify whether the test images were held out from any hyperparameter tuning, since using the test set for model selection would inflate the reported gains.

Overall, the paper presents a sound and useful refinement of hyperprior-based learned image compression, with a clear motivation, a reasonable experimental design, and a valuable ablation study. Its main weaknesses are the limited verification of rate estimates against real bitstreams, the single-seed ablations, the absence of a comparison with the most recent context-adaptive codecs, and the lack of runtime measurements. These issues are addressable and do not undermine the core contribution. I recommend a major revision, with the expectation that the authors will add the missing comparisons, report variance across seeds, measure encoding and decoding cost, and release their code. With these changes, the paper would make a solid contribution to the learned compression literature.

Subject: Modeling the Rate and Market Effects of Shifting Utility Debt Costs to Noncore Customers

Dear Team,

I am writing to propose a modeling effort to examine how shifting utility debt costs to noncore customers could affect electricity rates and the health of competitive markets. Noncore customers, such as large commercial and industrial users who can choose among electricity suppliers, are often the customers most sensitive to changes in their rate structures. Before any cost-allocation decision is made, we need a clear picture of its likely consequences.

The model should begin by establishing a baseline of current utility debt, the associated financing costs, and how those costs are currently recovered across core and noncore customer classes. From there, we can simulate alternative allocation scenarios that move some share of debt service onto noncore customers. Each scenario should track changes in average and marginal rates for each customer class over a multi-year horizon.

A key output is the price differential between utility service and competitive supply offers available to noncore customers. If the added charges make the utility rate significantly higher than market alternatives, customers may switch suppliers or relocate, which could erode the revenue base that supports the debt in the first place. The model should estimate these switching and attrition effects under a range of elasticity assumptions.

We should also examine how the allocation affects competition itself. Higher non-bypassable charges can reduce the economic advantage of competitive suppliers and discourage new market entrants, potentially concentrating supply among fewer providers. Conversely, a well-designed allocation may preserve incentives for efficient supply and avoid distorting price signals. The model should include indicators of market concentration and supplier participation.

Distributional impacts deserve careful attention as well. Residential and core customers may see rate relief under some scenarios, while noncore customers bear a larger share, and small commercial customers may fall somewhere in between. We should quantify these effects and identify where they may create cross-subsidy concerns.

Sensitivity analysis will be essential, since results depend heavily on assumptions about customer response, interest rates, load growth, and the timing of debt retirement. I recommend testing the most influential assumptions and reporting ranges rather than single-point estimates.

Finally, the findings should be presented in a form that regulators, stakeholders, and utility leadership can readily interpret. I suggest a short summary of trade-offs alongside the detailed technical results.

I would welcome your input on the data sources, scenario definitions, and timeline. Please let me know a good time to meet this week to discuss next steps.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

A central focus of the investigation is the gap between boys and girls, with evidence suggesting that girls often drop out of sport and active play earlier and at higher rates than boys. Campaigners welcomed the inquiry as an overdue step toward tackling inactivity, which they say carries long-term risks for both physical and mental health.

Success in life is rarely the product of talent alone. Three qualities, authenticity, optimism, and ambition, often work together to shape how far a person can go and how satisfying the journey becomes. Each one supports the others, and each can fail without the rest.

Authenticity matters because it keeps a person grounded in who they really are. When someone pursues goals that reflect their own values rather than the expectations of others, they tend to persist longer through difficulty. A student who chooses a field out of genuine curiosity is more likely to keep studying when the material gets hard than one who is simply chasing a parent's approval. Authenticity also builds trust, since people are drawn to those who are honest about their strengths and weaknesses.

Optimism provides the emotional fuel that makes effort feel worthwhile. Setbacks are inevitable, whether a failed exam, a rejected application, or a project that collapses halfway through. A hopeful outlook does not ignore these problems; instead, it encourages people to ask what can be learned and what to try next. Research on resilience suggests that people who expect their efforts to eventually pay off are more likely to keep trying, which in turn increases the chances that they will succeed.

Ambition gives direction to both authenticity and optimism. Without a clear aim, a person may feel authentic and hopeful yet drift without accomplishing much. Ambition turns good intentions into concrete plans, such as setting a goal, breaking it into steps, and measuring progress along the way. However, ambition must be tempered, because an unhealthy obsession with achievement can lead to burnout, dishonesty, or the sacrifice of relationships that matter.

The most successful people usually balance these qualities rather than maximizing any single one. Someone who is ambitious without authenticity may climb the ladder only to find it leans against the wrong wall. Someone who is optimistic without ambition may wait for good things to happen without acting on them. Someone who is authentic without optimism may give up at the first obstacle.

In the end, success is best understood not as a single destination but as a way of living that combines self-knowledge, hope, and purposeful effort. Students who cultivate all three are better prepared not only for their careers but also for the personal fulfillment that gives those careers meaning.

Venus is often called Earth's twin because the two planets are similar in size, mass, and bulk composition. Both are rocky worlds with iron cores, silicate mantles, and thin crusts, and both formed from the same region of the early solar system. Despite these resemblances, Venus has evolved into a place that is almost completely hostile to life. Its surface temperature averages about 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, and this heat comes from a runaway greenhouse effect driven by a carbon dioxide atmosphere roughly ninety times denser than Earth's. The atmospheric pressure at the surface is about ninety times that of Earth at sea level, comparable to the pressure found roughly 900 meters beneath the ocean. Clouds of sulfuric acid droplets cover the planet, reflecting sunlight and trapping heat while producing a corrosive environment that would quickly destroy most materials. Winds at the cloud tops circle the planet in only four Earth days, far faster than the planet's slow rotation, which takes about 243 Earth days. Scientists have debated whether the upper atmosphere, where temperatures and pressures are closer to Earth's, could harbor microbial life, and the 2020 report of phosphine gas sparked interest, though that finding remains disputed. Any life there would still face intense ultraviolet radiation, high acidity, and the lack of liquid water in usable form. Studying Venus therefore helps researchers understand how a planet with Earth-like beginnings can diverge so dramatically, offering a warning about the fragility of climate balance. Future missions, such as NASA's VERITAS and DAVINCI and ESA's EnVision, aim to answer lingering questions about its geology and history. Ultimately, Venus shows that similarity in origin does not guarantee a similar fate.

The tunnel smelled of wet clay and something sharper, like burnt metal. Diglett had lost count of the days since the men with the loud machine had pulled it from the soil of Route 11 and dropped it into a glass box lined with cold stone. Its three heads ached from pressing against the walls, and its claws had grown ragged from scraping at the seams.

Every morning a figure in a white coat would peer through the glass and tap notes onto a board. Diglett learned to hide its faces when the door opened, to lie flat and still so they would think it sleeping. It listened carefully. The men spoke of weights and temperatures and something they called a growth curve, and once they said the word "dual," which meant nothing to Diglett.

Hunger sharpened its thinking. Diglett began to dig in the only direction it could: down. The floor of the box was thin concrete laid over packed earth, and beneath it the soil was soft and familiar. Night after night, it scraped a little more, pushing the loosened dirt into the corner where the cleaning crew never looked.

Something was changing inside it as well. The digging came easier each night. Its body felt longer, its muscles denser, and its three heads moved in a strange rhythm as though they were learning to share a single purpose. Diglett did not understand it yet, but it did not fear the change. It only knew it had to get home.

On the thirty-first night, the concrete finally gave way with a soft crack. Diglett slipped through into the earth and felt the world close around it like an embrace. Cool, damp soil pressed against its skin, and the smell of roots and worms rushed into its senses. It burrowed upward and then sideways, guided by a pull it had carried since birth, the pull of the colony beneath the hill.

The tunnels grew wider as it neared home. Diglett passed the old root that marked the eastern boundary, then the stone where the Sandshrew family liked to sun themselves. Its three heads swayed as it went, and it noticed that it moved faster now, the earth parting before it with almost no effort.

At last the great central chamber opened before it. Dozens of Diglett and a few Dugtrio were gathered there, their dirt-streaked faces turning toward the sudden noise. For a moment no one spoke. Then an elder Dugtrio stepped forward, eyes narrowing as it studied the newcomer.

"You are Diglett," the elder said slowly. "You went up into the light and did not come back."

"I was taken," Diglett said, its voice coming out in three overlapping tones that startled even itself. "Glass walls, metal machines, men who counted me. But I dug my way out."

A murmur rippled through the chamber. Several young Diglett backed away, unsettled by the strange new voice.

The elder tilted its head. "You speak with more than one mouth."

"I do," Diglett answered, and it let its three heads rise together, each one turning to meet a different face in the crowd. "I have become something new. The men called it a dual evolution. I think I simply grew into what I was always meant to be, shaped by every tunnel I dug in the dark."

Slowly, the elder bowed its head. Others followed, one by one, until the whole chamber rang with the soft sound of earth shifting under many feet.

Diglett took a deep breath of familiar air and felt the last of the glass box fall away from its heart. It was home, and it was no longer small. It was Dugtrio now, and the tunnels stretched endlessly ahead, waiting for it to dig.

Persistent Childhood Nightmares and Night Terrors: Could They Be Linked to Later Psychotic Experiences?

Nightmares and night terrors are common among children, and most children outgrow them without lasting effects. However, when these sleep disturbances persist or are especially frequent, researchers have begun asking whether they may signal something more important about a child's developing mind. One area of interest is whether persistent childhood sleep disturbances are associated with psychotic experiences during adolescence.

Nightmares are vivid, distressing dreams that usually occur during REM sleep, and children typically wake up and can recall the dream in detail. Night terrors, by contrast, usually happen during non-REM sleep, often in the first few hours of the night, and the child may scream, thrash, or appear frightened while remaining largely unresponsive and typically not remembering the episode in the morning.

Psychotic experiences are unusual perceptions or beliefs, such as hearing voices, feeling watched, or holding unusual suspicions. They are not the same as a psychotic disorder, and many young people who report such experiences never develop a diagnosable condition. Still, they are an important focus for research because they can be distressing and may signal increased risk for later mental health difficulties.

Several longitudinal studies have found that children who experience frequent or persistent nightmares show a higher likelihood of reporting psychotic-like experiences later in adolescence. The association appears in multiple populations, though the strength of the link varies between studies.

Researchers have proposed several explanations for this connection. One possibility is that shared biological factors, such as differences in sleep regulation or brain development, influence both sleep disturbance and the later emergence of psychotic symptoms. Another is that disrupted sleep may affect emotional processing, making it harder for the brain to distinguish between internal experiences and external reality.

Stress and trauma offer another explanation. Children exposed to adversity often have more frequent nightmares, and adversity is also a known risk factor for psychotic experiences. In this case, the nightmares might reflect underlying distress rather than directly causing later symptoms.

It is important to note that a link does not mean that childhood nightmares cause psychosis. Most children who have nightmares do not develop psychotic experiences, and many factors contribute to adolescent mental health. The association is best understood as a risk marker that may help identify children who could benefit from closer attention.

For parents and caregivers, the practical message is that occasional nightmares are normal, but ongoing, severe, or worsening sleep disturbances deserve professional attention. A pediatrician or mental health professional can assess the child, rule out medical causes such as sleep apnea, and discuss whether further evaluation is appropriate.

Good sleep habits can support children in general. Consistent bedtimes, calm pre-sleep routines, limiting screen time before bed, and creating a comforting sleep environment may all help reduce disruptions.

Children who have persistent nightmares may also benefit from emotional support. Talking openly about fears, validating feelings, and helping the child feel safe can make a difference. If a child reports hearing voices, feeling persecuted, or experiencing other unusual perceptions, families should seek professional advice promptly, as early support can be helpful.

Treatments exist for persistent nightmares. Imagery rehearsal therapy, a structured approach in which the person rewrites the nightmare's ending and rehearses it while awake, has been shown to reduce nightmare frequency in both adults and children. Cognitive behavioral approaches may also help when nightmares are linked to anxiety or trauma.

Research in this area is still developing. Many studies rely on self-reported symptoms, which can be imprecise, and more long-term research is needed to clarify the direction and mechanisms of the association. Scientists are working to determine whether treating childhood nightmares might reduce later risk, but this has not yet been firmly established.

Understanding these connections can help clinicians, educators, and families recognize when a child may need extra support. Awareness of the possible link encourages earlier conversations and assessment, which can improve outcomes for young people who are struggling.

If you are concerned about a child, speaking with a healthcare provider is the best next step. They can offer guidance tailored to the child's situation, provide reassurance where appropriate, and connect the family with further resources if needed.

Tensions over the draft Wales Bill deepened this week as politicians, legal experts and campaigners clashed over whether the proposed legislation hands Cardiff enough real power or leaves Westminster with excessive control. Supporters of the bill argue that it provides a clearer and more stable settlement for the Senedd, setting out in statute what the devolved institutions can and cannot do. They say this would end the years of confusion that followed the earlier reliance on a conferred-powers model. Critics, however, contend that several provisions retain significant reserved powers, allowing the UK Government to intervene in areas that are nominally devolved. Plaid Cymru has described the draft as a missed opportunity, warning that it falls short of the expectations raised by the Senedd's own calls for reform. Labour figures in Wales have largely welcomed the bill as a step forward, while acknowledging that further refinements may be needed during its passage through Parliament. Constitutional lawyers have pointed to the scope of the proposed reservations and the mechanisms for overriding decisions made by the Senedd. Some argue these powers could be used sparingly, while others warn that their mere existence risks chilling policy experimentation in Wales. Business groups have called for greater clarity on how the new arrangements will affect cross-border trade and regulatory consistency across the United Kingdom. Campaigners for a stronger devolution settlement say the bill should include clearer limits on Westminster's ability to legislate in devolved areas without consent. The Welsh Government has said it will examine the text closely and submit detailed responses during the consultation period. Officials in London maintain that the draft strikes a sensible balance between national coherence and local autonomy. They point to new commitments to consult the Senedd and to a formal process for resolving disputes between the two governments. Opposition parties have pressed ministers for a fuller justification of the reserved powers, arguing that the burden of proof should rest with Westminster. Several cross-party committee members have said they will table amendments aimed at narrowing the scope of central control. Public opinion on the issue remains divided, with polling suggesting many voters are unsure how the changes would affect everyday public services. The debate is expected to intensify as the bill moves to its next stage, with both sides preparing for a contest over the wording of its key clauses. Whatever the outcome, the question of how much authority Wales should hold within the Union is likely to remain central to Welsh politics for years to come.

Year-round schooling has gained attention as an alternative to the traditional calendar that gives students a long summer break. Supporters argue that shorter, more frequent breaks could improve learning, while critics point to the value of extended rest and family time. Weighing these views carefully shows that year-round schooling offers real benefits, though its success depends on how it is implemented.

The most frequently cited advantage of year-round schooling is the reduction of summer learning loss. Research in education has long documented that many students lose some of the academic skills they gained during the previous year over the summer months. This loss tends to fall hardest on students from low-income families, who may have fewer opportunities for reading, enrichment, and structured activities during the break. By spacing instruction more evenly across the year, schools can reduce this gap before it widens.

Shorter breaks also make it easier for students to retain information. Traditional schedules often require teachers to spend the first several weeks of each fall re-teaching material that students have forgotten. Year-round calendars, with breaks of three to six weeks spread throughout the year, allow lessons to build on one another without long interruptions. Students are therefore more likely to arrive at each new unit with the knowledge they need.

Proponents also point to the benefits for student well-being. Frequent breaks can help prevent burnout, giving young people regular opportunities to rest and recharge. Teachers, too, may experience less exhaustion when their work is divided into shorter blocks with recovery periods in between. Some schools that have adopted this model report improved attendance and fewer behavioral problems, though these results vary.

However, the traditional summer break has its own value that should not be dismissed. For many families, summer is the only extended period when parents and children can travel, spend time together, or take part in activities that school schedules do not allow. Summer also offers unstructured time, which many child development experts consider important for creativity, independence, and emotional growth. Students who spend long stretches in a rigid academic environment may miss these experiences.

Another concern involves practical arrangements. Year-round schedules can complicate childcare, especially for working parents whose employers do not align with the school calendar. Families with multiple children on different tracks may find coordinating schedules difficult. Extracurricular programs, sports leagues, and summer jobs that teenagers rely on are also structured around the traditional calendar, and a change in the school year can disrupt these commitments.

Cost is a further consideration. Keeping school buildings open for most of the year requires additional spending on utilities, maintenance, and staffing, though some districts offset this by using facilities more efficiently. Whether the financial trade-off is worthwhile depends heavily on local circumstances and available resources.

The research on academic outcomes is mixed. Some studies find modest gains in test scores and retention for students in year-round programs, particularly those at risk of falling behind. Other studies find little difference between the two calendars once factors such as socioeconomic status and school quality are accounted for. This inconsistency suggests that the calendar alone is not the decisive factor in student success.

Implementation appears to matter greatly. Year-round schools that provide enrichment programs, tutoring, and engaging activities during intersession breaks tend to report better results than those that simply shorten the summer and add days to the calendar. Teacher training, community involvement, and clear communication with families all influence whether the change succeeds.

It is also worth considering how the school calendar fits with students' broader lives. Learning does not stop when the school doors close, and what students do during their free time shapes their development as much as what happens in the classroom. A well-designed break, whether in summer or spread throughout the year, can support this broader growth.

Ultimately, year-round schooling offers meaningful advantages in reducing learning loss, improving retention, and supporting student and teacher well-being. These benefits are most likely to be realized when schools use the calendar thoughtfully, with strong enrichment and support during shorter breaks. At the same time, the traditional summer break provides rest, family time, and unstructured experiences that remain valuable. Rather than declaring one calendar superior, communities should consider their own students' needs, families' circumstances, and available resources when deciding which schedule will serve them best.

The manuscript investigates whether the perceptual sensitivity of neural-network features can serve as a predictor of agreement with human image-quality judgments and of their usefulness for image generation, a question of clear relevance to both perceptual metrics and generative modeling. The authors frame the problem well and situate their work within the existing literature on learned perceptual similarity measures, though the related work section would benefit from a more explicit comparison with recent feature-based quality metrics. The methodology for quantifying perceptual sensitivity is described in reasonable detail, but the paper should specify how sensitivity is operationalized, since the choice of layer, normalization, and distance function substantially affects the results. The human-judgment experiments are a strength, yet the authors should report inter-rater reliability, the number and background of participants, and the exact question wording so that agreement figures can be properly interpreted. The statistical analysis reports correlation coefficients, but it does not clearly account for confounds such as image content, distortion type, or dataset-specific biases, and I would ask for controlled comparisons or a held-out evaluation set. The claim that higher perceptual sensitivity improves usefulness for image generation is supported by only a limited set of generative models, and the authors should either broaden this evaluation or temper the conclusion accordingly. The ablation studies are informative, but several key baselines are absent, and including simple pixel-based and established metrics would clarify whether the proposed approach offers a genuine advance. The discussion of limitations is brief and should address failure cases, computational cost, and the risk that learned features inherit biases from their training data. The figures are generally clear, although some plots lack confidence intervals, which makes it difficult to judge whether reported differences are meaningful. Overall, the paper addresses an important question with promising results, and I recommend a major revision that strengthens the statistical reporting, expands the baselines and generative evaluation, and clarifies the experimental protocol before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Cities across the world are rethinking how people move, and one of the most promising changes is reducing our reliance on private cars. Doing so can improve the health of residents, clean the air they breathe, and make neighborhoods more pleasant places to live. The benefits extend well beyond transportation, touching public health, the environment, the economy, and the everyday experience of city life.

Air pollution is one of the most pressing urban health problems today. Vehicle exhaust releases fine particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, and other pollutants that irritate the lungs and worsen conditions such as asthma and heart disease. Because these emissions occur at street level, people who live and work near busy roads are exposed to the highest concentrations. Fewer cars on the road would directly reduce these harmful levels.

Traffic also contributes to climate change through carbon dioxide emissions. Transportation is responsible for a significant share of greenhouse gases in many countries, and passenger cars are a major part of that total. Shifting trips to walking, cycling, and public transit cuts these emissions and helps cities meet their climate targets.

Physical health offers another strong argument. People who walk or cycle as part of their daily routine tend to get more exercise, which lowers the risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. Cities that invest in safe sidewalks and bike lanes give residents easy ways to build activity into their lives without needing a gym membership or a dedicated workout schedule.

Road safety improves as well. Motor vehicle collisions cause thousands of deaths and serious injuries in cities each year, and pedestrians and cyclists are among the most vulnerable. When streets are designed for slower speeds and fewer cars, the number of crashes tends to fall. Protected bike lanes and traffic-calmed neighborhoods protect everyone, including drivers.

Noise is a quieter but real burden on urban life. Constant traffic noise disrupts sleep, raises stress levels, and can affect children's learning. Reducing car dependence lowers ambient noise, allowing residents to enjoy calmer homes and more peaceful public spaces.

Space is another consideration. Parking lots and wide roads consume enormous amounts of land that could be used for housing, parks, or community gathering places. When cities need fewer parking spaces, they can convert these areas into green space that cools neighborhoods, absorbs rainwater, and supports wildlife.

Public transit is central to making car reduction work. Buses, trams, and subways can move large numbers of people efficiently, but they need frequent service, reliable schedules, and convenient routes to attract riders. Cities that invest in these systems give residents a practical alternative to driving for daily commutes and errands.

Affordability matters too. Owning and operating a car is expensive, with costs for purchase, insurance, fuel, maintenance, and parking adding up quickly. Households that rely less on cars can save considerable money, which can be spent on food, housing, or education. This benefit is especially important for low-income families.

Equity should guide these changes. Not everyone can easily give up a car, particularly people with disabilities, shift workers, or residents of areas poorly served by transit. Effective policy must ensure that alternatives are accessible to all, rather than simply making driving more difficult for those with few options.

Some critics argue that restricting cars will harm businesses or inconvenience drivers. Evidence from cities that have pedestrianized shopping streets suggests otherwise in many cases, as walkable areas often attract more foot traffic and spending. Still, planners should consult local businesses and communities to address legitimate concerns.

Mixed-use development can make car reduction easier. When homes, shops, schools, and workplaces are located near one another, people can reach most of their needs on foot or by bicycle. Compact, connected neighborhoods reduce the distances that require driving and make public transit more viable.

Technology can complement these efforts. Electric vehicles produce no tailpipe emissions, which improves local air quality compared with gasoline cars. Shared mobility services, such as bike-sharing and car-sharing, can also help people access transportation without owning a vehicle. However, technology alone cannot solve congestion or land-use problems, so it should supplement rather than replace broader strategies.

Several cities offer useful examples. Copenhagen has built an extensive network of cycling infrastructure, and a large share of its residents commute by bicycle. Paris has expanded bike lanes and restricted cars in parts of its center. These efforts show that determined planning can change travel habits over time.

Implementing these changes requires a range of policies. Cities can expand transit service, build protected bike networks, set congestion pricing, limit parking, and create low-emission zones. Each measure works best when combined with the others, since no single policy changes behavior on its own.

Public support is essential for success. Residents are more likely to accept new policies when they understand the benefits and have a voice in planning decisions. Community consultations, pilot projects, and transparent data about outcomes can build trust and help adjust plans as needed.

Timing and gradual change also matter. Abrupt restrictions can provoke backlash, while phased improvements allow people to adapt. Cities can start with modest steps, such as adding bike lanes on one street or extending bus hours, and expand successful projects over time.

Reducing reliance on cars is not about eliminating them entirely. Many people will always need vehicles for certain trips, and some areas will remain car-dependent. The goal is to offer real choices so that driving is one option among many rather than the only practical one.

The health benefits alone make a compelling case. Cleaner air reduces respiratory illness, active travel reduces chronic disease, and safer streets prevent injuries. These gains translate into lower healthcare costs and more productive, happier residents.

Environmental gains extend across the region. Lower emissions help protect ecosystems, and reduced runoff from paved surfaces can improve water quality. Cities that prioritize trees, green corridors, and permeable surfaces can also manage heat during summer months more effectively.

Social life benefits as well. When streets are safer and more pleasant, people spend more time outdoors, meet neighbors, and use public spaces. Walkable neighborhoods foster a sense of community that car-oriented suburbs often lack.

Economic arguments support change too. Studies in several cities have found that improved cycling and walking infrastructure can increase local retail activity and property values. Investment in transit can attract employers who want accessible locations for their workers.

Resilience is another advantage. Cities with diverse transportation options can better withstand disruptions such as fuel price spikes, extreme weather, or road closures. A network that includes walking, cycling, and transit keeps people moving when any single mode is unavailable.

Governments must also consider the needs of freight and emergency services. Delivery vehicles, ambulances, and fire trucks require efficient routes, and planners should design policies that keep these services running smoothly while still prioritizing people over private cars.

Measuring progress helps keep efforts on track. Cities can monitor air quality, traffic volumes, transit ridership, crash rates, and public health indicators to evaluate whether their policies are working. Clear targets and regular reporting make it easier to adjust strategies and maintain public confidence.

In conclusion, reducing reliance on cars offers a practical path toward healthier, cleaner, and more livable cities. Through thoughtful planning, equitable policies, and sustained public engagement, urban areas can improve air quality and well-being for everyone. The challenge is significant, but the rewards for present and future generations make it well worth pursuing.

The library's reading room was packed that Saturday morning, with children perched on cushions and parents lingering at the back. Margaret Hollis, a retired schoolteacher with silver hair and reading glasses on a beaded chain, held the worn copy of "The Princess and the Pea" with the calm authority of someone who had done this for thirty years.

She had barely reached the second page when a small boy in a dinosaur shirt shouted that the princess was going to get squished. Several children giggled. Margaret smiled and asked him to wait for the ending.

Then the radiator clanked loudly, startling a toddler into tears. Her mother scooped him up and hurried toward the door, and the wooden chair beneath her squeaked across the floor.

Margaret raised her voice slightly and continued. The princess, she read, had been awakened by a pea hidden beneath twenty mattresses.

A teenager near the window began loudly ordering food on his phone, asking for extra fries in a voice that carried across the room. Someone shushed him, which made him laugh even louder.

Margaret lost her place on the page. She pressed her finger to the line and tried again, her voice tightening.

The dinosaur boy stood up on his cushion and announced that he could hear a dragon in the walls. His older sister told him to sit down, and the two began arguing so fiercely that a stack of picture books toppled from the display shelf.

A man in a gray jacket at the back stood up and complained loudly that this was supposed to be a quiet reading, not a circus. His wife tugged at his sleeve, but he ignored her and kept talking.

Margaret closed the book with a snap. Her hands trembled slightly on the cover. For a moment, nobody spoke.

"I have read this story aloud four hundred times," she said, her voice sharp enough to cut through the room. "Four hundred times, and I have never once had to shout over a radiator, a telephone, and a grown man who thinks he is the king of this castle."

The man in the gray jacket flushed red and sat down heavily. The teenager pocketed his phone. Even the dinosaur boy went quiet, staring at her with wide eyes.

Margaret took a long breath and opened the book again. Her voice softened as she found her place. "Now," she said gently, "where were we?"

A little girl in the front row raised her hand. "Is the princess still sleeping?" she asked.

Margaret smiled, and for the first time that morning, the room leaned in together. "Not for long," she said, and began to read.

This paper proposes a latent covariance regularization term for variational autoencoders aimed at encouraging disentangled visual representations while preserving reconstruction fidelity. The problem is well motivated, since disentanglement in VAEs is known to trade off against reconstruction quality, and a method that addresses both objectives simultaneously would be a useful contribution. The authors frame the approach clearly, situating it relative to beta-VAE, FactorVAE, and total-correlation-based methods, and this positioning is helpful for readers unfamiliar with the subfield. The core idea of penalizing off-diagonal entries of the latent covariance matrix is intuitive and easy to implement, which is a practical strength. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more precise derivation explaining why decorrelation of latent dimensions should correspond to disentanglement, since correlation is only a second-order proxy for statistical independence. The theoretical section would be strengthened by discussing the conditions under which this proxy fails, such as when true factors are nonlinearly dependent. The experimental setup uses dSprites and 3D Shapes, which are standard benchmarks, and this choice allows reasonable comparison with prior work. Nevertheless, the authors should justify why they did not evaluate on more complex natural image datasets, where disentanglement is harder and the stakes for reconstruction quality are higher. The reported disentanglement metrics, including the DCI and MIG scores, are appropriate, but the paper would be more convincing with confidence intervals across multiple random seeds. Currently, the results appear to come from single runs, which makes it difficult to judge whether the reported gains exceed run-to-run variance. The reconstruction comparisons rely mainly on mean squared error, and adding a perceptual or structural similarity measure would give a fuller picture of visual quality. The ablation study isolating the regularization coefficient is valuable, yet the sensitivity analysis is limited to a narrow range of values. A broader sweep would show whether the method is robust or requires careful tuning per dataset. The authors acknowledge the tradeoff between the regularization strength and reconstruction loss, and the accompanying plots illustrate it well. It would be useful, however, to report how the chosen coefficient was selected, and whether a validation split was used to avoid tuning on the test metrics. The related work section is thorough in citing prior disentanglement methods but gives less attention to recent alternatives based on causal or structural assumptions, which are relevant competitors. The writing is generally clear, though some notation is overloaded, with the same symbol used for both the covariance matrix and a loss weight, which can confuse readers. Figures are informative, but several axis labels and legends are too small to read at print size. The limitations section is brief and should more explicitly address the reliance on synthetic benchmarks and the lack of a formal identifiability guarantee. Overall, the contribution is modest but practical, and the idea of combining covariance regularization with a reconstruction-preserving objective is worth exploring. With stronger statistical reporting, a broader evaluation, and a clearer theoretical justification, the paper could make a more substantial case. I recommend a major revision before the work can be considered for acceptance.
