The paper examines importance resampling as a method for off-policy evaluation, asking when the approach is applicable and where its limitations lie. The authors position the technique as a practical alternative to standard importance sampling, which can suffer from high variance when the behavior and target policies diverge. The motivation is clear and well grounded in the reinforcement learning literature, and the problem is of genuine practical importance for settings where live experimentation is costly or risky. The theoretical analysis of applicability conditions is a strength, as it gives practitioners concrete guidance on when resampling can be trusted. The discussion of limitations is candid, particularly regarding bias introduced by the resampling step and sensitivity to the effective sample size. The extension to policy optimization is the most ambitious contribution, but the manuscript would benefit from a more thorough empirical comparison against established baselines such as doubly robust estimators. Some of the experimental settings appear small in scale, and it is unclear whether the reported gains persist in higher-dimensional or more stochastic environments. The notation is occasionally inconsistent between the derivation sections and the algorithm descriptions, which makes reproducing the results harder than necessary. Clearer documentation of hyperparameter choices and the code release would substantially improve reproducibility. Overall, the paper is a solid contribution with a useful framing of trade-offs, and I recommend a minor revision that addresses the empirical scope and presentation issues.

Egypt has agreed to purchase two French warships that were originally intended for Russia, a deal that highlights shifting defense partnerships in the Mediterranean region. The vessels, Mistral-class amphibious assault ships, were built by French shipyards under a contract signed with Russia in 2011 but were never delivered after France suspended the arrangement following Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014. Egyptian officials confirmed the purchase as part of a broader effort to modernize their naval fleet and strengthen their capacity for power projection and humanitarian missions. Defense analysts note that the Mistral class is well suited to troop transport, helicopter operations, and disaster response, capabilities that Egypt has sought to expand in recent years. The transaction is also seen as a significant commercial win for France, which has been working to find buyers for vessels that had been sitting idle for years. Paris has framed the sale as a responsible outcome that keeps advanced military technology out of the hands of a government it considers a security concern. Russia, which had already paid a portion of the original contract price, has been a point of discussion in negotiations over how those funds are handled. Officials from both countries have declined to disclose the full financial terms of the agreement. Egypt has long been one of the largest importers of French military equipment, including Rafale fighter jets and naval frigates, and this purchase reinforces that relationship. Regional observers say the deal also reflects Cairo's efforts to diversify its arms suppliers beyond traditional sources. Naval experts expect the ships to be refitted to Egyptian specifications before entering service, a process that could take several months. The acquisition is expected to bolster Egypt's presence in the eastern Mediterranean and Red Sea at a time of heightened maritime tensions in the region.

A man armed with an axe threatened shop staff during a failed cash robbery in Gravesend on Saturday evening, police said. Officers were called to the shop on a busy high street shortly before 8 p.m. after reports that a masked man had entered the premises demanding money from the till. Witnesses said the suspect brandished the axe and shouted at employees, who retreated to the back of the store. Staff managed to raise the alarm, and the man fled empty-handed when he was unable to access the cash register. No one was physically injured, though two employees were treated at the scene for shock. Police have cordoned off the area while forensic officers examine the store and collect CCTV footage from nearby businesses. A spokesperson said detectives are appealing for any witnesses or anyone with dashcam footage from the surrounding roads. The suspect is described as a man of slim build, around six feet tall, wearing dark clothing and a face covering. Local residents expressed alarm at the incident, with several saying they had not expected such violence in the area. Anyone with information is asked to contact police directly or submit details anonymously through a crime reporting line.

Virtual learning has become an important option for students who face challenges that make traditional school attendance difficult. Many students balance their education with jobs, family duties, medical needs, or long commutes, and a rigid daily schedule can leave them struggling to keep up. Online learning offers a different structure, one that can adapt to the lives students actually lead.

One of the greatest advantages of virtual learning is flexibility in attendance. Students who must miss a class because of an illness or a family appointment can often access recorded lectures, digital notes, and assignments without falling far behind. Instead of losing an entire day of instruction, they can review material at a time that suits their recovery. This reduces the anxiety that many students feel when they know they cannot be physically present.

Scheduling is another area where virtual learning can make a real difference. Traditional schools operate on fixed bell schedules that leave little room for other commitments. Online courses, by contrast, frequently allow students to complete lessons during early mornings, evenings, or weekends. A student who works a shift at a restaurant in the afternoon might prefer to study late at night, and virtual platforms make that possible without forcing a choice between income and education.

Responsibilities outside school, especially caregiving, are often overlooked in discussions about education. Some students look after younger siblings, support a parent with a chronic illness, or manage household tasks while a family member works long hours. For these students, attending a school building five days a week may simply be impossible. Virtual learning allows them to fulfill family obligations while still making progress toward a diploma.

Virtual learning also supports students who are working to support themselves or their families. Many teenagers hold part-time jobs to contribute to household expenses, and some older students are returning to education after years in the workforce. Online programs let these learners set their own pace, sometimes completing coursework in shorter bursts between work responsibilities. This can prevent the frustration of having to drop out entirely.

Health considerations are an important part of this picture as well. Students with conditions such as asthma, autoimmune disorders, or anxiety may find that attending a crowded classroom affects their wellbeing. Virtual learning can provide a safer and calmer environment in which they can focus on their studies. It also allows students to schedule medical treatments without sacrificing their academic progress.

Despite these benefits, virtual learning is not a perfect solution, and it requires careful planning. Students need reliable internet access, a quiet place to study, and a good deal of self-discipline. Without support, some learners may feel isolated or fall behind when they do not have clear deadlines. For this reason, the most effective virtual programs combine flexibility with regular check-ins from teachers and counselors.

Schools can strengthen these programs by offering structured support alongside flexible scheduling. Regular video meetings, clear weekly goals, and accessible tutoring can help students stay connected to their teachers and classmates. Schools can also provide devices and internet access to families who cannot afford them, ensuring that technology does not become another barrier.

In the end, virtual learning should be seen as one tool among many for helping students succeed. It is not a replacement for in-person education, but it offers meaningful support for students whose attendance, schedules, or outside responsibilities would otherwise keep them from learning. When designed thoughtfully, it can help students stay engaged, earn their credentials, and build a future that fits the reality of their lives.

Independent work plays a vital role in shaping how students learn and succeed in their academic lives. When students are given the opportunity to research, plan, and complete tasks on their own, they develop skills that extend far beyond any single assignment. This form of learning encourages responsibility, builds confidence, and prepares young people for the demands of higher education and the workplace.

One of the most significant benefits of independent work is the development of self-discipline. When no teacher is standing over a student's shoulder, the student must decide when to begin a task, how to manage their time, and when to take a break. Over time, these decisions become habits that help students stay organized and focused. Those who learn to manage their own schedules are better equipped to meet deadlines in university courses and in professional settings.

Independent work also strengthens critical thinking. Working alone requires a student to evaluate sources, weigh different ideas, and reach conclusions without immediate guidance. Each time a student struggles through a difficult problem and eventually solves it, their ability to reason through complexity grows. This process turns passive knowledge into active understanding, which is far more durable than memorized facts.

Furthermore, independent work fosters a sense of ownership over learning. When students choose topics, set goals, or determine how to approach a question, they become invested in the outcome. This personal investment often leads to greater motivation and curiosity. A student who has chosen a research question is more likely to pursue it with enthusiasm than one who has simply been handed a worksheet.

Independent work also builds self-confidence. Successfully completing a task without constant assistance gives students proof of their own abilities. This confidence encourages them to take on harder challenges and to view mistakes as opportunities to learn rather than as signs of failure. Students who trust their own judgment are more willing to ask thoughtful questions and to participate actively in class discussions.

Finally, the skills gained through independent work support lifelong learning. The world changes quickly, and no education can teach every skill a person will need. Students who learn how to find information, evaluate it, and apply it independently will continue to grow long after they leave school. In this sense, independent work is not merely a tool for passing exams but a foundation for a lifetime of personal and professional growth.

Plans for a new school campus in Dalbeattie have been put on hold after funding complications emerged, local officials confirmed this week. The project, which was intended to replace ageing buildings and provide modern classrooms for pupils in the town and surrounding area, had been expected to move forward by the end of the year. Council representatives said the delay stems from a shortfall between the estimated cost of construction and the funds currently committed to the scheme. Officials are now reviewing the budget to identify where additional money might come from. Options under consideration include applying for further government grants, revisiting the scope of the design, and exploring partnerships with private investors. Parents and staff at the existing schools have expressed frustration at the setback, with many saying the current buildings are in need of significant repair. Some parents raised concerns about overcrowding and the condition of facilities that they say are no longer suitable for the number of pupils enrolled. Education leaders stressed that the delay will not affect the quality of teaching in the meantime, but acknowledged that the wait for improved facilities will be longer than originally planned. A spokesperson for the council said that the priority is to secure a funding package that is realistic and sustainable over the long term. No revised timetable has been announced, but officials said they expect to update the public once the financial review is complete. Community groups have called for greater transparency about how the original budget was set and why the shortfall was not identified earlier. The council has agreed to hold a public meeting in the coming weeks to answer questions and outline the next steps. Local residents will be watching closely as the outcome will shape education provision in Dalbeattie for many years to come.

Westminster was thrown into a heated debate on Monday as political leaders gathered to discuss the government's legislative programme outlined in the Queen's Speech, against a backdrop of election fallout and renewed scrutiny of the state's handling of the Grenfell Tower disaster. Opposition MPs seized on the speech to question whether the government had the mandate and the focus needed to deliver its promises after a result that many analysts described as a significant setback for the ruling party. Ministers defended the programme, arguing that it addressed housing, public services and economic stability, and insisted that the government remained committed to the priorities voters had identified. Critics countered that several flagship measures lacked detail and that the speech did too little to address the concerns raised by a fragmented and volatile electorate. The debate quickly turned to Grenfell Tower, where a fresh round of questioning focused on the pace of remediation work and the replacement of dangerous cladding on residential buildings across the country. Survivors and bereaved families, several of whom were present in the public gallery, have repeatedly called for faster progress and greater accountability for those responsible for the fire. Opposition spokespeople argued that the government had been too slow to act on the recommendations of the public inquiry and had failed to deliver the justice and rehousing that residents were promised. Government representatives responded that substantial funding had been committed and that significant progress had been made, though they acknowledged that more needed to be done. The exchanges grew sharp at times, with several members accusing their opponents of exploiting a tragedy for political gain. Speaker's intervention was required on more than one occasion to restore order to the chamber. Commentators noted that the combination of a contested election result and an unresolved national grievance placed considerable pressure on the government to demonstrate decisive leadership. Whether the legislative agenda can win the confidence of a skeptical public and a determined opposition remains an open question. Further debate on the individual bills is expected in the coming weeks, with the Grenfell inquiry's outstanding recommendations likely to remain a focal point of parliamentary scrutiny.

This paper proposes a method for learning reusable value representations that transfer across reward functions and policies in reinforcement learning. The problem is well motivated, since agents that must be retrained from scratch for every new reward or policy are expensive to deploy in practice. The authors frame the contribution clearly, separating the goal of transferring knowledge across reward functions from the goal of transferring across policies, which helps the reader follow the argument. The related work section covers successor features, universal value function approximators, and multi-task representation learning, although it could more directly compare the proposed approach against recent methods that address the same transfer setting. The core technical idea of decomposing value functions into reward-independent features and reward-dependent weights is sound and builds sensibly on prior successor feature formulations. The derivation of the learning objective is mostly clear, though a few steps in the approximation of the expectation over policies would benefit from more explicit justification. The experimental setup includes a range of continuous control and discrete navigation tasks, which is a reasonable spread for testing generality. However, the choice of baselines is somewhat narrow, and the paper would be stronger with comparisons against more modern transfer and meta-learning methods. The reported gains over baselines are consistent across tasks, but the magnitude of improvement varies considerably, and the authors do not always explain the cases where transfer underperforms. Ablation studies isolating the contribution of the representation learning component from the reward decomposition are helpful and support the central claims. The paper would benefit from reporting variance across more random seeds, since several of the differences shown are modest and the confidence intervals overlap in places. Hyperparameter sensitivity is discussed only briefly, and a more thorough analysis would help readers judge how robust the method is to tuning. Computational cost and training time are not compared against baselines, which is an important omission for a method intended to save effort in deployment. The theoretical analysis offers useful intuition but does not provide guarantees on transfer performance under explicit assumptions about reward or policy similarity. Some notation is introduced inconsistently between sections, which made parts of the methodology harder to verify on first reading. The figures are generally informative, though several learning curves lack axis labels or clear legends for the shaded regions. Code availability is mentioned, which is commendable and would greatly aid reproducibility if released in full. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant and practical problem with a reasonable and mostly well-supported approach. I recommend a major revision that strengthens the baselines, adds statistical rigor, clarifies notation, and includes computational cost analysis before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Should students with average grades be allowed to participate in school sports? Many schools answer this question with academic eligibility rules that require a minimum grade point average, and these rules deserve careful thought. On one hand, the purpose of school is education, and athletics are meant to support that mission rather than replace it. A student who is failing several classes may be better served by spending extra time on schoolwork than on the practice field. On the other hand, average students are not failing, and they often gain a great deal from sports. Athletics teach discipline, teamwork, time management, and resilience, skills that transfer directly to the classroom and beyond. For many students, the team is also a source of belonging, and removing that connection could push them toward disengagement. Average students who participate in sports may also find that the structure of practices and games helps them organize their week and stay focused. Critics argue that eligibility standards should be higher to encourage stronger academic effort, but this assumes that a single grade threshold accurately measures student potential and effort. Grades reflect many factors, including learning differences, family circumstances, and access to resources, so a rigid rule can punish students who are working hard but struggling. A more balanced approach would allow average students to play while providing academic support such as tutoring, study halls, and monitoring by coaches and teachers. Such a system keeps students engaged in both academics and athletics rather than forcing a choice between them. Schools could also set a clear warning threshold, so that a student whose grades slip receives help before losing eligibility entirely. This gives students a chance to recover and reinforces the idea that sports and studies are connected. Ultimately, sports should reward commitment and growth, not just high marks. Average students deserve the same opportunities to learn from athletics as their higher-achieving peers. Allowing them to participate, supported by thoughtful academic guidance, serves the broader goal of education. Schools should therefore focus on helping every student succeed rather than excluding those who fall in the middle.

Rose O'Neal Greenhow: Spy, Socialite, and Her Final Voyage

Rose O'Neal Greenhow was a Washington, D.C. socialite who became one of the most effective Confederate spies of the American Civil War. Born around 1813 in Montgomery County, Maryland, she was raised in a well-connected family and grew up with a keen interest in politics. Her Washington home on Lafayette Square made her a central figure in the city's social life, drawing senators, diplomats, and military officers into her circle. Widowed in 1840 after her husband Robert Greenhow died, she used her social position to build a wide network of contacts.

When the war began in 1861, Greenhow offered her services to the Confederacy. She maintained a correspondence with Confederate officials and passed along information gathered through her Washington acquaintances. Her most notable early contribution was relaying details of Union army plans before the First Battle of Bull Run in July 1861. Her messages reportedly reached Confederate General P. G. T. Beauregard, who used the information to prepare his forces. Historians generally credit her intelligence with helping the Confederacy achieve its victory at that battle.

Greenhow operated through a series of couriers, codes, and cipher messages. She also reportedly used a young woman, Bettie Duvall, and others to carry information across the lines. Her activities drew the attention of federal authorities, who had begun monitoring suspected Southern sympathizers in the capital. Detectives from the Union's secret service, led by Allan Pinkerton, kept her under surveillance.

In August 1861, federal agents placed Greenhow under house arrest at her Washington residence. Searches of her home reportedly turned up cipher materials and correspondence. She was held under guard for several months, and her case became a notable episode in wartime relations between the Union government and civilians in border regions. During her confinement she continued to pass messages through intermediaries, which only deepened federal suspicion.

In May 1862, Greenhow was transferred to the Old Capitol Prison in Washington, which held many political prisoners and suspected spies. Conditions there were harsh, though she was not subjected to the worst treatment given to some detainees. Her confinement lasted until the summer of 1862, when federal authorities decided to send her south. She was released and deported to the Confederacy, along with her young daughter, Rose Greenhow, who had been imprisoned with her.

After returning to the South, Greenhow was welcomed as a heroine. She traveled to Europe on a mission for the Confederate government, seeking support for the Southern cause among British and French leaders. She published a memoir, My Imprisonment and the First Year of Abolition Rule at Washington, which portrayed her treatment in a sympathetic light and was popular in the Confederacy and abroad. Her writings were intended to rally support for the Confederate cause in Europe.

In 1864, Greenhow was sent back to the Confederacy with dispatches for Confederate leaders. She was aboard the blockade runner Condor, which was attempting to slip past Union warships off the coast of North Carolina. The ship was operating at night in an effort to evade the Union blockade that had long constrained Southern trade.

On the night of October 1, 1864, the Condor ran aground near the mouth of the Cape Fear River, close to Fort Fisher, when it attempted to enter the port of Wilmington. The vessel was spotted by Union forces and came under fire, and the ship was damaged in the attempt to escape. Accounts differ on the exact sequence of events, but the ship grounded on a sandbar in the shallow waters near the coast.

As the ship sank or was abandoned, Greenhow attempted to reach shore in a small boat. The boat capsized in the surf, and she drowned. Her body was recovered and buried with honors at Oakdale Cemetery in Wilmington, North Carolina. Confederate officials and the public mourned her, and she was honored as a martyr to the Southern cause.

The dispatches she was carrying were reportedly lost in the sea, along with much of the cargo. The loss of the messages deprived the Confederacy of whatever information she had intended to deliver, though historians do not agree on the strategic consequences. Her death also removed one of the war's most famous female operatives from active service.

Greenhow's life illustrates the important but often overlooked role women played in Civil War intelligence. Many women, both Union and Confederate, gathered information, carried messages, and used their social access to gain military secrets. Their work frequently took place in drawing rooms, boarding houses, and social gatherings rather than on battlefields.

Historians have debated the accuracy of Greenhow's claims and the extent of her influence on Bull Run. Some sources suggest she exaggerated her role, while others argue her intelligence was genuinely valuable. Her own memoir and wartime reports should be read with this in mind, since they were written partly to promote the Confederate cause.

Her case also highlights the difficulties the Union faced in dealing with civilian dissent in Washington. Federal authorities had to balance security concerns with the legal and political challenges of detaining a woman of high social standing. The episode prompted discussion about the treatment of civilian prisoners during the conflict.

Greenhow's daughter, Rose, was also a notable figure in her mother's story. The young girl was imprisoned alongside her mother and was later sent south with her. Accounts of their confinement and release helped shape public sympathy for Greenhow in the Confederacy.

Today, Greenhow is remembered as a complex figure: a skilled intelligence gatherer, a persuasive writer, and a controversial wartime personality. Her story is studied by historians of espionage, gender, and the Civil War. Visitors to Wilmington can still find her grave at Oakdale Cemetery.

Her life also raises questions about the ethics and legality of espionage during wartime. Both sides regarded spies as dangerous, and the penalties for espionage could be severe. Greenhow's willingness to take risks for her cause made her an example of the personal courage and conviction that defined many wartime figures.

The circumstances of her death remain a subject of interest for maritime and local historians. The shipwreck near Fort Fisher took place in a dangerous stretch of coast known for shifting sandbars and heavy surf. Local records, newspaper accounts, and salvage reports from the period provide much of what is known about the wreck.

Modern researchers continue to examine archival records, including Union surveillance files, Confederate correspondence, and postwar memoirs. These sources do not always agree, so historians must weigh evidence carefully. Her story therefore serves as a useful case study in how to assess wartime testimony.

Greenhow's reputation has varied over time. In the decades after the war, Southern writers often celebrated her as a heroine, while Northern accounts portrayed her more critically as a dangerous agent. Later historians have tried to separate myth from documented fact.

Understanding her role requires attention to the broader context of Washington society in the 1850s and 1860s. The capital was a city of divided loyalties, where many residents had family ties to the South. Social networks of this kind made it easier for information to move between opposing sides.

Her story also reflects the wider problem of security in a divided nation. Union officials worried about leaks from government offices, and Confederate leaders relied on sympathizers in the North. This mutual distrust shaped many decisions made during the war.

When studying Greenhow, students should consider the sources behind each claim. Memoirs, official reports, and newspaper articles all have different purposes and biases. Comparing them helps build a more reliable account of events.

The Civil War's intelligence efforts were often informal and improvised. Neither side had the sophisticated organizations that later became common. Greenhow's network, though small by later standards, shows how personal relationships could become military assets.

Her case is also useful for understanding the role of women in public life during the nineteenth century. Women were generally excluded from formal politics and the military, yet they found ways to influence events through private networks and social influence. Greenhow exemplifies this paradox.

The Confederacy's use of Greenhow as a publicity figure after her release shows how both sides valued propaganda. Her memoir and European mission were designed to build support for the South abroad. Such efforts were an important part of the war's diplomatic dimension.

Greenhow's death in 1864 came at a time when Confederate fortunes were declining. Union forces were tightening their control of the coast, and the blockade was becoming more effective. Her final voyage reflects the desperation of blockade running during the war's later stages.

The shipwreck off North Carolina also illustrates the dangers faced by blockade runners generally. Many ships were lost to storms, grounding, or capture, and crews faced severe risks. Greenhow's death was one of the most widely reported losses of the period.

Fort Fisher, near the scene of the wreck, was a major Confederate defense that guarded the approach to Wilmington. Its capture by Union forces in January 1865 was a significant blow to the Confederacy. The area's history is closely tied to the blockade and to Greenhow's final days.

Greenhow's grave in Wilmington has become a point of interest for visitors interested in Civil War history. The cemetery contains the graves of many Confederate soldiers and civilians. Her burial there reflects the regard in which she was held in the city.

In summary, Rose O'Neal Greenhow's career combined intelligence work, social influence, imprisonment, and a dramatic death at sea. Her story offers insight into the Civil War's espionage, the role of women in wartime, and the difficulties of separating fact from legend. Studying her life encourages careful reading of historical sources and a fuller understanding of the conflict.

Energy-Selective Electron Transport and Localization in an Interacting Quasiperiodic Chain under Electric Fields

Abstract

We investigate energy-selective electron transport and localization in a one-dimensional interacting quasiperiodic chain subjected to a static electric field. The model combines nearest-neighbor hopping, a quasiperiodic on-site potential of Aubry-André type, a uniform linear potential representing the applied field, and a short-range density-density interaction between electrons. Using a combination of exact diagonalization for small systems, density-matrix renormalization group calculations for larger chains, and time-dependent propagation of wave packets, we characterize how transport depends on the energy of injected electrons. We find that the quasiperiodic potential generates a mobility edge separating extended from localized single-particle states, and that the applied field shifts and partially smears this boundary through Wannier-Stark localization. Interactions modify the picture in a nontrivial way: they can delocalize certain states that are localized in the noninteracting limit, while in other energy windows they enhance localization through many-body dephasing. We quantify these effects using the inverse participation ratio, the level-spacing statistics, the entanglement entropy, and the frequency-resolved conductance computed via the Landauer-Büttiker formalism adapted to finite chains. Energy-selective transport emerges because electrons injected at energies below the mobility edge propagate ballistically or diffusively, whereas those above it undergo localized, Bloch-oscillation-like motion with suppressed net current. The interplay between field strength and interaction strength yields a rich phase diagram containing extended, localized, and intermediate regimes, the last exhibiting multifractal wavefunctions and subdiffusive transport. We discuss the relevance of these results to ultracold-atom quantum simulators, where quasiperiodic lattices and tunable interactions are routinely realized, and to solid-state realizations in engineered heterostructures. Our findings suggest a route to energy-filtering devices based on quasiperiodic order and provide benchmarks for numerical studies of many-body localization in driven systems.

Introduction

The transport of electrons through disordered media has been a central problem in condensed matter physics since Anderson's seminal demonstration that sufficiently strong disorder can localize single-particle wavefunctions. In three dimensions, this localization transition occurs at a finite disorder strength, separating metallic from insulating phases, while in one and two dimensions all states are localized for any nonzero random disorder in the noninteracting limit. Quasiperiodic potentials provide an intermediate class of disorder that is deterministic yet aperiodic, and the Aubry-André model is the canonical example in which a localization transition occurs at a finite critical strength even in one dimension.

The Aubry-André model describes spinless fermions hopping on a one-dimensional lattice in the presence of an incommensurate cosine potential whose wavelength is irrational relative to the lattice spacing. Its localization transition is self-dual and occurs at a potential strength equal to twice the hopping amplitude. Beyond this critical point, all eigenstates become exponentially localized, while below it all states are extended. Generalizations including mobility edges, obtained by modifying the quasiperiodic potential, have revealed that energy-dependent localization can occur, separating energy windows of extended and localized states within a single spectrum. Such mobility edges are of particular interest because they allow the transport character to depend sensitively on the energy of the carriers.

An external electric field introduces a linear potential gradient into the chain. In a perfectly periodic lattice, this gradient converts the continuous band into a ladder of Wannier-Stark states and produces Bloch oscillations, with the carrier executing a bounded spatial motion rather than drifting steadily. When disorder is present, the Stark ladder is perturbed, and the combined influence of field and disorder can produce localization even in systems that would otherwise be extended. The field thus provides a tunable knob that can shift the energy window in which states are localized, making it a natural control parameter for energy-selective transport.

Electron-electron interactions add a further layer of complexity. In the noninteracting setting, localization is robust, but the presence of interactions raises the question of whether localization survives in the thermodynamic limit. Many-body localization, a phenomenon in which interacting systems fail to thermalize in the presence of strong disorder, has been established numerically and, in some settings, experimentally. Interactions can also lead to delocalization by providing dephasing channels or by enabling resonant energy exchange among localized excitations. The competition between these effects is particularly delicate in quasiperiodic systems, where the absence of true randomness can alter the nature of the many-body dynamics.

Despite substantial progress on each of these ingredients separately, a unified understanding of how electric fields and interactions jointly control energy-selective transport in quasiperiodic chains remains incomplete. In particular, it is not fully established how the field-induced shift of the mobility edge depends on interaction strength, nor how the intermediate phase between extended and localized regimes manifests in transport observables. Addressing these questions is important both for fundamental understanding and for potential applications in energy-filtering and quantum-simulation settings.

In this work we study a minimal model that captures these ingredients. We consider interacting spinless fermions on a one-dimensional lattice with nearest-neighbor hopping, a quasiperiodic potential with a tunable mobility edge, a uniform electric field, and nearest-neighbor interactions. We combine several numerical approaches to access both the single-particle and many-body regimes, and we compute transport observables that directly probe the energy dependence of conduction. Our aim is to map the phase diagram as a function of field and interaction strengths and to identify signatures that could be tested in cold-atom experiments.

Model and Methods

We consider a chain of L lattice sites with open boundary conditions. The Hamiltonian is H = H_hop + H_qp + H_F + H_int, where H_hop = -t sum_j (c_j^dagger c_{j+1} + h.c.) describes nearest-neighbor hopping with amplitude t, which we set to unity as the energy scale. The quasiperiodic potential is H_qp = sum_j V cos(2 pi beta j + phi) n_j, where beta is an irrational number, which we take to be the golden ratio conjugate, phi is a phase offset, V is the amplitude, and n_j = c_j^dagger c_j is the local density operator. A mobility edge can be introduced by generalizing the potential to a form that depends on the energy-dependent parameter alpha, but for the present work we focus on the standard Aubry-André form with the mobility edge determined self-consistently from the single-particle spectrum.

The electric field enters through H_F = F sum_j j n_j, where F is the field strength in units of t per lattice spacing. The interaction term is H_int = U sum_j n_j n_{j+1}, which describes nearest-neighbor repulsion of strength U. We work at fixed particle filling, typically one-third or one-half, depending on the system size and the question addressed.

For small chains, up to approximately sixteen sites, we perform exact diagonalization of the full many-body Hamiltonian. This yields complete spectra and eigenstates from which we compute the inverse participation ratio, the level-spacing ratio, and the entanglement entropy of half the chain. For larger systems, we employ the density-matrix renormalization group with bond dimensions up to several hundred, which allows us to access chains of up to around one hundred sites for the ground state and low-lying excited states.

To probe dynamics and transport, we prepare wave packets localized in energy windows by applying spectral projectors constructed from the single-particle eigenstates, and we evolve them under the full Hamiltonian using time-evolving block decimation. We track the center-of-mass position, the spreading width, and the local current. From the long-time behavior of the spreading, we extract the dynamical exponent characterizing ballistic, diffusive, subdiffusive, or localized dynamics.

Energy-resolved transport is quantified through a two-terminal Landauer-Büttiker approach adapted to finite chains. We attach semi-infinite leads at both ends, modeled as clean tight-binding chains, and compute the transmission function T(E) using the Green's function method. Interactions are treated within a mean-field or time-dependent Hartree-Fock approximation for the conductance calculation, with the full many-body treatment reserved for the spectral and dynamical analysis. We extract the linear-response conductance as a function of Fermi energy and identify energy windows of high and low transmission.

Results: Single-Particle Localization and the Mobility Edge

In the noninteracting limit with zero field, the spectrum of the Aubry-André chain exhibits a sharp localization transition at V = 2t. For V < 2t, the eigenstates are extended and display ballistic transport with a transmission close to unity throughout the band. For V > 2t, all eigenstates are exponentially localized, with the localization length scaling as the inverse of the logarithm of the ratio V/2t.

When the quasiperiodic potential is tuned to produce an energy-dependent localization threshold, we observe a mobility edge E_c that separates an extended band segment from a localized one. States with energies below E_c have inverse participation ratios scaling as 1/L, consistent with extended wavefunctions, while states above E_c have finite inverse participation ratios independent of system size. The level-spacing ratio distribution follows the Poisson statistics characteristic of localized phases on the localized side and the Wigner-Dyson statistics on the extended side.

Turning on the electric field F shifts the spectrum relative to the lattice and introduces Wannier-Stark localization. For weak fields, the extended states near the mobility edge are only modestly perturbed, but the Stark potential breaks the translational symmetry of the Bloch states and causes the mobility edge itself to move in energy. We find that the shift is approximately linear in F for small F and saturates at larger F, where the field dominates the spectrum and the localization character becomes largely determined by the Stark ladder. In the intermediate regime, we observe that the mobility edge broadens into a finite-width crossover region containing multifractal wavefunctions, whose inverse participation ratios scale as a fractional power of L.

Energy-resolved transmission reflects this structure directly. Electrons injected at energies below the field-shifted mobility edge exhibit near-unit transmission across a finite-length chain, while those above it show exponentially suppressed transmission with the length. The transition is sharp in the thermodynamic limit but smooth in finite systems, and we extract the effective mobility edge from the energy at which the average transmission falls to one half.

Results: Interaction Effects

Introducing nearest-neighbor interactions modifies the picture substantially. At weak interaction strength U, the single-particle mobility edge persists, and the energy-selective character of transport is preserved, though the edge is shifted slightly. The interaction introduces a dephasing mechanism that can broaden transmission resonances but does not generally delocalize the localized states at this level.

At intermediate interaction strength, we observe a regime in which interactions delocalize states that are localized in the noninteracting limit. This arises because two-particle processes can connect localized configurations to a continuum of many-body states, providing a pathway for transport that is absent for single particles. The effect is most pronounced for energies close to the mobility edge, where localized and extended single-particle states are nearly degenerate and interaction-mediated mixing is most efficient. The delocalization manifests as an increase in the entanglement entropy and a shift of the level-spacing ratio toward Wigner-Dyson values.

At strong interaction strength, the behavior is dominated by many-body localization for states above the mobility edge, consistent with the expectation that strong disorder and interaction together suppress thermalization. The entanglement entropy grows only logarithmically in time after a quench, and the local observables retain memory of their initial conditions. Below the mobility edge, the strong interaction can instead induce a crossover to a thermal-like regime with diffusive transport, though the finite-size effects in our calculations make a definitive distinction difficult.

The interplay between field and interaction is particularly rich. The field tends to localize carriers through Wannier-Stark physics, while interactions can either assist or oppose this localization depending on energy and density. We find that for a range of parameters, the field-induced localization is partially reversed by interactions, leading to a non-monotonic dependence of the conductance on F. This reentrant behavior provides a distinctive signature of the joint influence of the field and interactions.

Results: Dynamics and Transport

Wave-packet dynamics confirm the energy selectivity inferred from the static spectrum. Packets prepared below the mobility edge spread ballistically in the noninteracting limit, with a width growing linearly in time, and retain a substantial fraction of their weight in the extended band. Packets prepared above the edge remain localized, with the width saturating after a short transient. The Bloch-oscillation-like motion expected in the presence of the field appears as a bounded oscillation of the center of mass, with a period set by the field strength.

In the interacting case, packets near the mobility edge exhibit subdiffusive spreading with a dynamical exponent between the localized and diffusive values, consistent with a multifractal, intermediate phase. The exponent varies continuously with the interaction strength and the field, providing a quantitative measure of the phase boundary. Current-voltage characteristics computed within the Landauer framework show an energy-dependent threshold consistent with the dynamical picture, and the position of this threshold tracks the field-shifted mobility edge.

Discussion

Our results establish that the combination of a quasiperiodic potential, an electric field, and interactions produces a controllable form of energy-selective transport. The mobility edge provides the basic energy filter, the field allows its position to be tuned, and interactions provide an additional knob that can either sharpen or blur the filter depending on the energy and interaction strength. The intermediate multifractal regime is particularly interesting because it offers a possible route to tunable, partially transmitting energy windows whose width can be adjusted electrically.

Several caveats should be noted. Our exact diagonalization and DMRG calculations are limited to finite systems, and the distinction between genuine localization and slow delocalization at long times is subtle, particularly in the interacting regime. The mean-field treatment of interactions in the conductance calculation neglects correlations that may be important near the mobility edge. Finite-size scaling and longer time-evolution studies would help clarify these issues.

Experimentally, the model can be realized with ultracold atoms in optical lattices. Quasiperiodic potentials are generated by superimposing two incommensurate optical standing waves, electric fields correspond to gravitational or magnetic gradients, and tunable interactions are provided by Feshbach resonances. Single-site-resolved imaging and quench protocols allow direct measurement of wave-packet dynamics and entanglement, providing a route to test the predictions made here. Solid-state realizations in engineered heterostructures or photonic analogs may also be possible, though with less control over the interaction parameter.

Conclusion

We have studied energy-selective electron transport and localization in an interacting quasiperiodic chain under an electric field. The system exhibits a field-tunable mobility edge separating extended and localized states, a multifractal intermediate regime near the edge, and an interaction-dependent competition between localization and delocalization. These features combine to give energy-selective transport whose character can be controlled by the field and interaction strengths. Future work should address larger system sizes, more controlled treatments of many-body transport, and direct experimental realization in quantum simulators.

The authors thank colleagues for useful discussions on quasiperiodic localization and many-body dynamics.

The value of realistic goals is often overlooked in a culture that celebrates constant ambition and the pursuit of exceeding every expectation. From an early age, students are encouraged to aim high, dream big, and never settle for less than extraordinary. While ambition can be a powerful motivator, it can also become a source of unnecessary pressure and disappointment. Realistic goals offer a more sustainable path to growth because they are grounded in an honest understanding of one's abilities, time, and circumstances. When a goal is attainable, each step forward builds confidence and reinforces the belief that effort leads to results. By contrast, goals that are constantly out of reach can lead to frustration, burnout, and a sense of failure even when real progress has been made. Setting realistic targets also encourages better planning, since a person must consider the resources and steps needed to succeed. Students who aim for achievable milestones often develop discipline and resilience because they learn to measure their progress honestly. Exceeding expectations is admirable, but it is rarely the result of simply demanding more from oneself at every moment. Many people who go beyond what others expect have first mastered the fundamentals through steady, attainable steps. Constant ambition without a foundation of realism can lead people to take on too much, neglect their health, and damage relationships with family and friends. Realistic goals, on the other hand, leave room for rest, reflection, and the unexpected challenges that life inevitably brings. They allow a person to adjust course without feeling that everything has been lost. In school, a student who sets a realistic goal of improving one grade at a time may ultimately achieve more than one who attempts an impossible leap and gives up. Over the long term, the habit of setting honest, achievable goals builds a healthier relationship with success and failure alike. Ambition still has its place, but it works best when it is guided by realism. The most meaningful accomplishments often come from steady progress rather than from chasing perfection. In the end, realistic goals are not a sign of low aspirations but of wisdom about how growth truly happens.

Welcome to Story Explorers: A Literature-Based ELA Program

Our literature-based English Language Arts program helps students read closely, think critically, and write with confidence. At its heart is a simple idea: the best way to learn how stories work is to read great stories carefully. Each unit centers on a high-quality piece of fiction, chosen for its rich characters, memorable settings, and clear examples of literary craft.

Students begin every unit by previewing the text. They consider the title, the cover, and any opening passages, and they make predictions about what the story will explore. These predictions become a baseline that students revisit as they read.

As they read, students practice identifying the core story elements. They learn to recognize characters and to distinguish between major and minor roles. They trace how the setting shapes the mood and the choices characters make. They follow the plot from the initial situation through the rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution.

A central focus is point of view. Students learn to identify whether a story is told in first person, close third person, or from an omniscient perspective. They discover how the narrator's position affects what readers know and how they feel about the characters.

Conflict is another key concept. Students classify conflicts as internal or external, such as a character struggling with a decision or facing an opposing force like nature, society, or another person. They explain how conflicts drive the plot and reveal character.

Theme receives special attention. Rather than asking for a single correct answer, the program teaches students to build a theme statement from evidence. They identify recurring ideas, examine how the author develops them, and test their interpretations against the full text.

Vocabulary instruction is woven into each reading. Students encounter unfamiliar words in context and learn strategies for determining meaning, including using surrounding sentences, identifying word parts, and consulting reference sources. Academic vocabulary, such as "foreshadowing," "symbolism," and "characterization," is taught explicitly so students can discuss literature with precision.

Discussion plays a vital role. Students participate in structured conversations in small groups and whole-class settings. They learn to build on classmates' ideas, respectfully challenge interpretations, and support their claims with specific passages.

Close reading routines help students slow down and examine individual sentences and paragraphs. Teachers model how to annotate a text by marking patterns in word choice, repeated images, and shifts in tone. Students then practice these routines independently.

Writing is taught as a natural extension of reading. After analyzing a story, students write short responses that answer focused questions about a single element, such as how a character changes or why an author chose a particular setting. These responses build toward longer analytical essays.

The writing process is explicitly modeled. Students brainstorm, draft, revise, and edit, with teachers demonstrating each stage using sample student work. Peer feedback sessions give students practice offering constructive suggestions.

Evidence is at the center of every claim. Students learn to introduce quotations smoothly, explain how a quoted passage supports their argument, and avoid simply summarizing the text. They practice embedding short quotes and blocking longer ones according to standard conventions.

Organization receives careful instruction. Students learn to structure paragraphs with a clear topic sentence, supporting evidence, and analysis. They practice using transitions that signal relationships between ideas, such as comparison, contrast, cause, and effect.

Narrative writing is also part of the curriculum. Students draw on what they observe in published stories to craft their own scenes, paying attention to point of view, dialogue, pacing, and sensory detail. Imitating published models helps them internalize the techniques they admire.

Reading comprehension is assessed in several ways. Teachers use exit tickets, short quizzes, and conversation checklists to monitor understanding during the unit. Periodic performance tasks ask students to apply what they have learned to a new passage.

Differentiation ensures that every learner is supported. Teachers provide leveled guiding questions, sentence starters for writing, and graphic organizers for plot and character analysis. Advanced readers receive extension prompts that invite deeper comparison across texts.

Read-alouds give students access to complex texts they might not yet read independently. Teachers model fluent expression, pause to think aloud about meaning, and invite students to predict what will happen next. This practice builds listening comprehension and shared vocabulary.

Independent reading is encouraged throughout the year. Students select books from a classroom library organized by genre and reading level. They keep reading logs, record questions, and share recommendations with peers.

Text sets connect each unit to related works. After reading a central novel or story, students may explore a poem, a nonfiction article, or a short film that addresses a similar theme. Comparing texts sharpens analytical thinking and broadens background knowledge.

Authentic purposes for reading and writing motivate students. Projects may include creating a podcast episode about a character, designing a book trailer, or writing a letter to the author. These tasks show students that literary analysis has real audiences and real value.

Family engagement strengthens learning at home. Teachers send monthly letters describing the current text, suggest discussion questions for dinner-table conversations, and share ideas for encouraging reading outside of school.

Professional development supports the teachers who deliver the program. Educators participate in workshops on text selection, questioning techniques, and writing instruction. They also meet in collaborative teams to plan lessons, analyze student work, and refine their practice.

Text selection follows clear criteria. Stories are chosen for literary merit, age-appropriate content, cultural diversity, and their ability to spark meaningful discussion. The program includes works from many eras and many voices so that students encounter a wide range of perspectives.

Progress monitoring guides instruction. Teachers review data from reading assessments and writing samples to identify skills that need reinforcement. Small-group lessons target specific needs, and students track their own growth through goal-setting conferences.

Students build independence over time. In the early weeks of a unit, teachers provide substantial scaffolding. Gradually, they release responsibility, asking students to choose their own evidence, design their own discussion questions, and draft their own analytical paragraphs.

The program's ultimate goal is to create lifelong readers and writers. By learning to analyze story elements closely, students gain tools they can apply to any text they encounter, whether in school, at work, or for pleasure. They become thoughtful interpreters of literature and clear communicators of their ideas.

We invite you to explore Story Explorers and discover how great literature can transform the way students read, think, and write.

Lincolnshire Police has confirmed that one of its service dogs has been euthanised following two reported biting incidents, which are currently under investigation. The dog, a trained police working dog, was withdrawn from duty while the complaints were assessed by the force. A spokesperson said the decision was made after careful consideration of the dog's behaviour and the welfare of both the animal and the public. Venus, often called Earth's twin because of its similar size and mass, offers scientists a compelling opportunity to study how a planet can evolve in dramatically different ways. Exploring it could reveal valuable insights into the runaway greenhouse effect, which has raised its surface temperature to roughly 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Understanding these processes may also help researchers better grasp the long-term future of Earth's own climate. Beyond climate science, Venus's thick atmosphere, rich in carbon dioxide and laced with sulfuric acid clouds, provides a natural laboratory for studying atmospheric chemistry under extreme conditions. Missions could also investigate whether the planet once had liquid water and possibly a more hospitable environment in its distant past. Some scientists have even proposed that microbial life could persist in the cooler, pressurized layers of the upper atmosphere, though this remains highly uncertain and debated. Technological progress is another potential benefit, since engineers must develop heat-resistant materials, long-lasting electronics, and innovative landing systems to survive the planet's surface conditions. However, the challenges are formidable, as the surface pressure is about ninety times that of Earth's, enough to crush most spacecraft within hours. The corrosive sulfuric acid clouds further complicate missions by threatening instruments and communication systems that must operate in a hostile chemical environment. Power generation is also difficult, because the thick clouds block sunlight, limiting the effectiveness of solar panels for long-duration missions. Engineers must therefore balance scientific ambition against practical limits, choosing between short-lived surface landers and orbiters or high-altitude balloons that drift through more temperate layers. Cost remains a significant concern, since such missions demand substantial funding that must be weighed against other priorities in planetary science and Earth-focused research. Despite these obstacles, international cooperation and steady technological advancement could make Venus exploration increasingly feasible in the coming decades. Ultimately, the planet serves as both a cautionary tale and a scientific treasure, offering lessons that reach far beyond its own scorching surface.

Facial emotion recognition in classrooms promises to help teachers spot student distress early and respond with timely support. Cameras and software could flag signs such as sadness, anxiety, or frustration, allowing counselors to reach out before a struggling student falls behind or withdraws. For students who hide their feelings, this technology might offer a quiet way to be noticed. However, facial expressions do not reliably reveal inner states, since people express emotions differently across cultures, personalities, and situations. A student who looks bored may simply be concentrating, while a student who appears calm may be deeply troubled. Misreading these signals could lead to unnecessary intervention, embarrassment, or unfair labeling. Constant monitoring may also make students feel watched and judged, which can increase stress rather than reduce it. Privacy is another serious concern, because biometric data about young people is sensitive and could be stored, shared, or misused. A more balanced approach would treat any automated signals as a prompt for human attention rather than a diagnosis, with consent, clear limits, and trained adults making the final decisions. Ultimately, the most reliable support comes from trusting relationships between students and teachers, which no algorithm can fully replace. Schools should therefore use such tools cautiously, if at all, and prioritize open communication and care.

Every four years, Americans are reminded that their presidential vote does not always count equally, and the Electoral College is the reason. The system was designed in 1787 as a compromise between those who wanted Congress to choose the president and those who wanted a direct vote by the people. Today, that compromise has outlived its purpose and now distorts the democratic process. A direct popular vote would ensure that every citizen's ballot carries the same weight, regardless of where they live. Under the current system, a voter in Wyoming or Vermont has far more influence per person than a voter in California or Texas, because electoral votes are allocated by population but with a minimum of three per state. The result is that a small number of states hold disproportionate power. Most states are ignored entirely during campaigns, as candidates concentrate their time and money on a handful of swing states. Voters in safe states, whether Republican or Democratic, have little reason to expect candidates to address their concerns. A national popular vote would encourage campaigns to speak to the whole country rather than a narrow slice of it. The winner-take-all method used by nearly every state also magnifies small margins into large electoral victories. A candidate can win a state by a fraction of a percentage point and receive all of its electoral votes, while the millions of voters who supported the other side are effectively erased from the outcome. This means the final tally can differ sharply from the will of the majority. Critics of direct voting often argue that it would undermine federalism by ignoring the interests of smaller states. However, the presidency is a national office, and the president represents all citizens, not individual states. Federalism is well protected in Congress, where the Senate gives each state equal representation regardless of size. Eliminating the Electoral College would not threaten that structure. Another common concern is that a direct vote would lead to recounts across the country and create legal confusion. In reality, the country already conducts nationwide vote tallies, and modern vote-counting technology is far more reliable than it was in the eighteenth century. A single national count would be simpler and more transparent than the current patchwork of state-by-state procedures. Some defenders of the Electoral College claim it promotes stability by requiring broad geographic support. Yet a candidate who wins a majority of the national vote demonstrates broad support by definition, since millions of voters from every region would have chosen them. A popular vote does not require geographic balance to be meaningful; it requires only that every citizen's preference is counted. Direct elections are also the norm in nearly every other democracy that elects a head of government by popular vote. Americans have accepted the principle of one person, one vote in every other election, from congressional races to state governorships. Applying the same principle to the presidency would make the nation's highest office consistent with its democratic values. Public opinion has increasingly supported this change, with polls in recent decades showing majorities of Americans favoring a national popular vote. Constitutional amendment is difficult, but the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact offers another path, in which participating states commit their electoral votes to the national popular winner. Whatever method is chosen, the goal is the same: to make the presidency answer to the people as a whole. The Electoral College once reflected the realities of a young nation with slow communication and limited transportation. Those conditions no longer exist, and the system's flaws have become harder to justify. Replacing it with a direct popular vote would honor the principle that every citizen deserves an equal voice. It is time for the United States to elect its president the way it elects almost everything else: by counting every vote equally.

Schools should allow students to use cell phones during designated times because phones have become valuable tools for learning and daily life. Many students already carry devices that can access research databases, translation tools, and educational apps that support their studies. Allowing phone use at set times, such as during lunch, between classes, or in a supervised study hall, gives students structured access without disrupting instruction. Phones also provide a practical safety benefit, since students can contact family members quickly during emergencies or schedule changes. Banning phones entirely can create an unhealthy dynamic in which students feel distrusted and are more likely to hide their devices and use them secretly. Designated times teach responsibility by asking students to manage their own attention and follow clear rules, skills they will need in college and in the workplace. Teachers can also incorporate phones into lessons, using polling tools, digital notes, or quick research tasks that make classroom activities more engaging. Parents often rely on phones to stay in touch with their children, and reasonable access during the school day reduces anxiety for families and students alike. Scheduled phone time can also serve as a break that helps students recharge before returning to focused work. Schools can set clear expectations, such as keeping phones silent and out of sight during class, to minimize distractions while still providing access. Students who learn to use technology appropriately during set periods are better prepared to handle constant connectivity in adult life. A thoughtful policy that balances access with boundaries respects students as capable young people while protecting the learning environment. For these reasons, schools should adopt policies that allow cell phone use during designated times rather than imposing blanket bans.

Volunteering to transport livestock after World War II played a meaningful role in the recovery of war-torn regions in Europe and Asia. As farms were destroyed and food supplies ran short, animals such as cattle, pigs, horses, and poultry became essential for restoring agriculture and providing protein to hungry families. Volunteers, many of them young people, helped move these animals across borders and devastated landscapes, often under difficult conditions with limited resources. Their work supported relief organizations and local communities that depended on livestock for plowing fields, producing milk and eggs, and rebuilding household economies. The humanitarian impact extended beyond the animals themselves, as reliable food sources reduced malnutrition and gave displaced families a foundation for returning to normal life. Many volunteers also reported a deep sense of purpose, knowing that their labor directly contributed to the survival and dignity of people who had lost nearly everything. Working alongside people from different nations fostered friendships and mutual understanding during a period when the world was seeking reconciliation. For many participants, the experience taught patience, responsibility, and empathy toward both animals and people in need. The personal rewards often lasted long after the program ended, shaping later careers in agriculture, veterinary care, and public service. Some volunteers described the satisfaction of seeing a healthy animal delivered to a farm that would soon feed a village. Others valued the chance to contribute to peace in a practical, hands-on way rather than through politics or speeches. Looking back, the transport of livestock stands as a quiet but important chapter in postwar recovery, showing how ordinary acts of service can help rebuild both communities and lives.

The manuscript proposes an end-to-end framework for learning active contours to perform two-class image segmentation, using polygon area supervision together with neural rendering. The central idea is to predict a parametric contour for each image and then rasterize it differentiably so that the segmentation loss can be computed against area-level targets rather than dense pixel masks. This is a practically motivated direction, since polygon-level or area annotations are often cheaper to obtain than full pixel-wise labels, and the authors make a reasonable case for this in the introduction. The paper is generally clearly written and well organized, and the problem framing is easy to follow. The related work section covers classical snake and level-set methods as well as recent deep learning approaches to contour prediction, although it could more explicitly position the contribution relative to weakly supervised segmentation methods that also rely on coarse or box-level supervision. The authors should consider a more precise statement of what is novel, because the combination of differentiable rendering and contour parameterization has appeared in several recent works, and the distinction is not yet sharply drawn. The methodology section describes the contour parameterization, the neural renderer, and the area-based loss in reasonable detail. The use of a differentiable polygon rasterizer is a sensible choice, but the manuscript would benefit from a more careful discussion of gradient behavior near contour vertices, where small displacements may produce discontinuous changes in the rendered mask. The area supervision term is intuitive, yet the paper does not fully address the ambiguity that arises when a single area value is consistent with many spatially different masks. The authors partially acknowledge this in a limitations paragraph, but a formal analysis or an ablation isolating its effect would strengthen the claims considerably. The loss function combines the area term with a regularization term that penalizes contour length and curvature, and the weighting of these terms is set by a grid search whose range is not reported. Providing sensitivity curves for these hyperparameters would help readers judge how robust the method is. The network architecture is described adequately for reproducibility at a high level, although some implementation details, such as the number of contour control points, the initialization strategy, and the number of rendering iterations, are either absent or scattered across the appendix. The experimental setup uses two medical imaging datasets and one natural image benchmark, which is a reasonable choice for demonstrating generality across domains. However, the paper reports results on only a small number of splits, and the variance across runs is not clearly shown, which makes it difficult to assess whether the reported improvements are statistically meaningful. The baselines include a standard U-Net trained with full pixel masks, a weakly supervised U-Net trained with the same area labels, and a classical active contour method. The comparison with the fully supervised U-Net is informative, as it sets an upper reference, and the authors report that their method closes most of the gap. The comparison with the weakly supervised baseline is the more important one for the paper's claims, and the reported margin there is modest on two of the three datasets. The authors should discuss whether this margin is consistent across training set sizes, since data efficiency is a central motivation of the approach. A learning-curve experiment varying the number of labeled images would substantially strengthen the paper's argument. The qualitative results are helpful and show that the predicted contours follow object boundaries reasonably well in typical cases. The failure cases figure is appreciated, as it reveals that the method struggles with thin structures and with objects that have multiple disconnected components, which is a limitation that deserves more prominent discussion in the main text. The paper also does not state clearly whether the method can handle topology changes, and since the contour representation is a single closed curve, this restriction is significant for many real segmentation tasks. Code availability is mentioned, which is commendable, but the repository link was not functional at the time of review, and the authors should verify that the code and trained weights will be accessible. The writing contains several minor issues, including inconsistent notation for the rendering operator, a few figure captions that do not fully describe the panels, and some repeated sentences in the introduction. The conclusion summarizes the results appropriately but somewhat overstates the generality of the findings given the limited number of datasets. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant problem with a reasonable technical approach, and the empirical evidence is promising but not yet fully convincing. I recommend a major revision that clarifies novelty, adds a data-efficiency study and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, reports variance across runs, and expands the discussion of limitations related to topology and thin structures. With these changes, the work could make a useful contribution to weakly supervised segmentation research.
