Participation in extracurricular activities offers students a wide range of benefits that extend well beyond the classroom. Clubs, sports teams, and arts programs give students a chance to explore interests they might not encounter in their regular coursework. Through these activities, students often develop important social skills, as they learn to collaborate with peers, communicate with diverse groups, and resolve conflicts within a team. Many extracurricular commitments also teach time management, since students must balance schoolwork with practices, rehearsals, or meetings. Leadership opportunities, such as serving as a club officer or team captain, help students build confidence and learn to take responsibility for others. Physical activities like sports promote lifelong health habits and provide a healthy outlet for stress. Participation in academic clubs, such as debate or science olympiad, can deepen subject knowledge and sharpen critical thinking. Volunteer-oriented groups encourage empathy and a sense of civic responsibility by connecting students with their communities. Extracurricular involvement can also strengthen a student's college and job applications, as it demonstrates initiative, dedication, and well-rounded character. Perhaps most importantly, these activities help students discover their strengths and passions, which can guide future academic and career decisions. Research has also linked consistent extracurricular engagement with higher attendance rates and a greater sense of belonging at school. For these reasons, schools should continue to invest in a diverse range of extracurricular programs that give every student the opportunity to grow.

Solar Power: Benefits, Growth, Costs, and Its Role in Meeting Energy Needs

Solar power converts sunlight into electricity, most commonly through photovoltaic panels that use semiconductor materials to generate current when light strikes them. One of its greatest benefits is that it produces electricity without burning fuel, so it emits no greenhouse gases or air pollutants during operation. Solar installations also require no water for power generation, which makes them well suited to regions facing water scarcity. Because sunlight is abundant and free, the fuel cost of solar electricity is zero once a system is built. Solar systems can be installed on rooftops, parking structures, and other existing spaces, reducing the need for new land use. They are modular, meaning they can be scaled from a single home system to utility-scale farms covering hundreds of acres. Over the past two decades, solar capacity has grown dramatically worldwide, driven by falling module prices, supportive policies, and rising demand for clean energy. Global solar installations have expanded from only a few gigawatts per year in the early 2000s to hundreds of gigawatts annually in recent years. The cost of solar panels has dropped by roughly 90 percent since around 2010, making solar one of the cheapest sources of new electricity in many markets. The cost of a solar project depends on factors such as equipment, installation labor, local permitting, financing terms, and the quality of the solar resource at the site. Upfront costs remain significant for homeowners and businesses, though incentives, tax credits, and financing programs can reduce them considerably. Utility-scale solar often has lower levelized costs than new fossil fuel plants, though this comparison can shift with fuel prices and policy changes. A key challenge is that solar output varies with time of day and weather, so it does not always match when electricity is needed. Energy storage technologies, especially lithium-ion batteries, are increasingly used to store midday solar output for use in the evening. Grid operators also manage variability through forecasting, transmission upgrades that connect distant regions, demand response programs, and a mix of complementary resources. Solar power is expected to play a central role in decarbonizing electricity systems, since it can be deployed quickly relative to many other large infrastructure projects. Many international energy analyses project that solar will supply a substantial share of global electricity by mid-century under ambitious climate scenarios. Solar also strengthens energy security by reducing dependence on imported fuels and giving countries a domestically available energy source. In developing regions, off-grid and mini-grid solar systems can bring electricity to communities far from existing power lines. Solar installations do require attention to material sourcing, recycling at end of life, and land use planning to minimize environmental and social impacts. Ongoing research aims to improve panel efficiency, lower manufacturing emissions, and develop new cell designs. Overall, solar power offers a combination of low operating emissions, declining costs, and flexible deployment that makes it a cornerstone of modern energy planning. Its ultimate contribution will depend on continued advances in storage, grid infrastructure, and policy support.

Car-free urban planning and vehicle restrictions have emerged as promising strategies for reducing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions in crowded cities. Transportation is one of the largest sources of carbon dioxide worldwide, and in many urban areas, road vehicles account for a substantial share of nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter, and other harmful pollutants. Because cars are both a major cause of emissions and a primary reason cities sprawl outward, reducing their presence offers a direct way to address environmental and public health problems at the same time. Car-free urban planning goes beyond simply banning vehicles from certain streets; it reshapes how neighborhoods are designed so that people can meet their daily needs on foot, by bicycle, or by public transit. Pedestrian-only zones, superblocks, and low-emission districts are examples of this approach, and cities such as Barcelona, Oslo, and Paris have implemented versions of them with measurable results. Vehicle restrictions, such as congestion charges, low-emission zones, and odd-even driving rules, complement these efforts by changing the incentives that influence whether people drive. London's congestion charge, introduced in 2003, reduced traffic in the central zone and was followed by improvements in air quality and a notable decline in certain emissions. Critics argue that such policies can burden low-income residents, who may depend on cars for work and have fewer alternatives. This concern is legitimate, and it suggests that restrictions must be paired with affordable public transit, safe cycling infrastructure, and exemptions or subsidies that protect vulnerable households. When designed carefully, these measures can increase equity by making neighborhoods quieter, cleaner, and safer, especially for children and elderly residents who are most exposed to traffic pollution. Car-free planning also has economic benefits, since pedestrian-friendly streets often attract retail activity and reduce the land devoted to parking. Furthermore, reduced car dependence can lower household transportation costs, which frees money for other needs. Ultimately, car-free urban planning and vehicle restrictions are not a single solution but part of a broader transition toward compact, connected, and sustainable cities. Their success depends on public support, thoughtful implementation, and sustained investment in alternatives that make leaving the car at home a practical and attractive choice.

The manuscript presents a benchmark intended to standardize the evaluation of neural architecture search (NAS) methods across fixed datasets and predefined model spaces. The motivation is well grounded, since reported NAS results have often been difficult to compare because of inconsistent search spaces, training protocols, and evaluation budgets. The authors identify this reproducibility problem clearly and frame the benchmark as a remedy, which gives the work a useful and timely purpose. The introduction is generally well organized and situates the contribution relative to prior NAS benchmarks, although the related work section could engage more directly with the most closely competing efforts. The choice to precompute or tabulate architecture performance is a practical decision that substantially lowers the cost of future comparisons, and the authors justify it reasonably. However, the paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of the trade-off between reduced computational cost and the risk that tabulated results fail to capture the variability of full training runs. The definition of the model search space is described with sufficient detail to be reproduced, which is a clear strength. The number of architectures enumerated and the constraints imposed on the search space are reported, though a short table summarizing these quantities would aid readers. The selection of datasets is reasonable and covers both small and moderately sized image classification tasks, but the absence of any non-vision tasks limits claims of generality. The authors should either add at least one additional domain or temper the language describing the benchmark as comprehensive. The experimental protocol, including random seeds, number of repetitions, and reporting of variance, is only partly specified. Reporting confidence intervals or standard deviations across multiple seeds is essential for a benchmark whose purpose is fair comparison, and its omission weakens the central claims. The baseline evaluation of several established NAS methods is informative and shows that the benchmark can distinguish between methods, which supports its utility. Nonetheless, the observed differences between some methods are small relative to the apparent noise, and the paper does not adequately address whether the benchmark has sufficient statistical power to rank them. The analysis of search budget, showing how method rankings change with the number of evaluated architectures, is a valuable contribution and deserves more emphasis. The discussion of rank stability across datasets is interesting, yet the conclusions drawn from it appear stronger than the data support given the small number of datasets. The authors also do not sufficiently examine whether the benchmark favors methods whose design resembles the tabulated space, which could introduce unintended bias. The software release, including code for querying the benchmark and reproducing the baseline results, is a significant strength and greatly increases the paper's value to the community. Documentation appears adequate for basic use, though more detail on how to add new search methods and new datasets would encourage adoption. The licensing and long-term maintenance plan for the released data are not clearly stated, and these matters are important for a resource intended for extended community use. The figures are generally clear, though several plots use similar colors that are difficult to distinguish, and some axis labels lack units. The writing is mostly precise, with occasional redundancy in the methods section that could be condensed. The limitations section is brief and should more fully acknowledge the restricted dataset coverage, the tabulation approach, and the statistical concerns noted above. The claim that the benchmark resolves the reproducibility problem in NAS is overstated, since a benchmark standardizes comparison but does not by itself guarantee that individual methods are reproducible. The authors should revise this framing to reflect what the benchmark accomplishes. Overall, the paper addresses an important need and offers a practically useful resource with a solid release. Its main weaknesses lie in statistical rigor, the breadth of tasks, and the strength of some conclusions. I recommend a major revision that addresses variance reporting, expands or qualifies the scope of the datasets, and tempers the central claims. With these changes, the work would make a meaningful contribution to the NAS research community.

The manuscript addresses an important and practically relevant problem: using reinforcement learning to choose which local search operators to apply during the solution of capacitated vehicle routing problems. The authors position their work well within the broader literature on hyper-heuristics and learned operator selection, and the motivation for replacing fixed or randomly chosen operator sequences with an adaptive policy is clearly stated. The introduction would benefit from a more precise articulation of the research gap, since several recent papers have explored adaptive operator selection for routing with bandit-based and learning-based methods. The related work section is generally thorough, although it leans heavily on heuristic approaches and gives comparatively little attention to deep reinforcement learning methods that learn construction or improvement policies directly. The problem formulation is mostly sound, with the capacity constraints and objective function stated unambiguously, but the state representation used by the agent is described only briefly and should be specified more completely so that readers can reproduce the features. The choice of reward signal is a central design decision, and the authors should justify why the chosen reward, such as the immediate improvement in solution cost, is preferable to alternatives like cumulative improvement over a search episode. The methodology section describes the training procedure with reasonable clarity, yet the hyperparameters for the learning algorithm are reported incompletely, which limits reproducibility. The experimental design uses standard benchmark instances, which is appropriate, but the selection of instances appears to favor moderate sizes, and results on larger instances would strengthen the claims about scalability. The baselines include fixed operator schedules and a random selection strategy, which are useful comparisons, but the absence of a comparison against a strong state-of-the-art metaheuristic weakens the evidence that the approach advances the field. The statistical analysis reports average performance across runs, and I encourage the authors to add variance measures, confidence intervals, or significance tests, since the reported gains are often modest. The computational cost of training is discussed only in passing, and a clearer accounting of training time versus solution quality gains would help practitioners judge the trade-off. The ablation study is a valuable addition, showing the contribution of individual components, though one ablation that removes the learned policy and keeps the operator set would further isolate the effect of learning itself. The figures are generally clear, but several convergence plots lack axis labels or legends that specify the number of iterations, which makes interpretation difficult. The discussion section correctly acknowledges limitations, yet it could more directly address when the learned selector is likely to fail, such as on instances with very different structure from the training set. The authors should also discuss generalization explicitly, reporting how the policy performs on instance classes not seen during training. The writing is generally readable, though some sentences are long and could be simplified to improve clarity. Several minor typographical errors and inconsistent notation for the operator set appear throughout and should be corrected in revision. The code and data availability statement is welcome, and I recommend releasing the trained models alongside the implementation to support replication. Overall, the paper presents a reasonable contribution with promising results, but it requires stronger baselines, fuller reporting, and deeper analysis of generalization before it is ready for publication. I recommend a major revision.

Students often benefit most when they complete assignments individually, because working alone forces them to wrestle directly with the material and build their own understanding. Independent work develops self-discipline, problem-solving skills, and the confidence to tackle unfamiliar challenges without relying on others. It also gives teachers a more accurate picture of each student's abilities, which allows for better feedback and support. Collaboration, however, offers its own strengths, since explaining ideas to peers, hearing different perspectives, and negotiating solutions can deepen understanding in ways solitary study cannot. Ultimately, the greatest benefit likely comes from balancing both approaches, using individual work to build foundational skills and collaboration to refine and extend them.

Jon Vickers, widely regarded as one of the finest tenors of the twentieth century, remains a towering figure in the history of opera, admired for both his artistry and his uncompromising personal convictions. Born in Jon Vickers in Alberta, Canada, in 1926, he rose to international prominence in the 1950s and went on to build a career that spanned three decades on the world's leading stages. His dramatic intensity and heroic voice made him a particularly celebrated interpreter of Wagner, and he was equally acclaimed for his portrayals of Verdi, Puccini, and Berlioz. Among his most famous roles was Otello, which he sang with a commanding blend of vocal power and psychological depth that critics often described as definitive. He also became closely associated with Peter Grimes by Benjamin Britten, a role he performed with a raw emotional honesty that left audiences deeply moved. Vickers appeared regularly at the Metropolitan Opera, Covent Garden, the Vienna State Opera, and other major houses, earning a reputation as a fearless performer who approached each role with intense commitment. His devotion to his Christian faith shaped many of his professional decisions, most notably his refusal to perform on Sundays and his reluctance to take on certain roles he considered morally objectionable. Such choices sometimes cost him engagements and drew both admiration and debate within the industry. Vickers was known for his strong views on the purpose of art, insisting that opera should serve higher spiritual and humanitarian ends rather than mere entertainment. He spoke openly about his beliefs in interviews and in his writings, which allowed listeners to understand the seriousness with which he approached his vocation. Despite a relatively limited recording output compared with some of his contemporaries, his surviving recordings and broadcasts continue to attract new generations of listeners. Many singers and critics cite him as an inspiration for their own dedication to dramatic truth and vocal discipline. His interpretations are frequently studied by students of singing and opera, who value his combination of technical command and emotional directness. Vickers received numerous honors over the course of his career, reflecting his importance to Canadian and international musical life. His legacy endures in the recordings that document his voice, in the testimony of colleagues who worked alongside him, and in the example he set of uncompromising integrity in a demanding profession. Though he passed away in 2016, his influence on the art of opera remains evident and widely recognized by musicians and audiences alike.

Subject: Update on Credit Derivatives Resilience, ISDA Contract Changes, EM Bond Issuance, and Regulatory Developments

Dear Colleagues,

I am writing to share a brief overview of several developments that bear on our work this quarter. The topics span the credit derivatives market, documentation changes, emerging-market debt issuance, and the regulatory environment in which all of these operate. I have tried to summarize the main points so that we can discuss the implications at our next meeting.

Turning first to the credit derivatives market, its resilience has been tested over the past several periods by episodes of volatility in rates, spreads, and liquidity. Market participants have generally reported that dealer intermediation held up better than many had feared, supported by stronger capital buffers and improved collateral practices. Trading volumes in single-name and index credit default swaps have remained substantial, although activity has shifted somewhat toward standardized products that are easier to clear. Central clearing continues to expand its footprint, and margin frameworks have been refined to reduce procyclical effects during stress periods. Bid-offer spreads on the most liquid names have stayed tight, which suggests that depth in the market remains adequate for ordinary hedging and position management. Nevertheless, concentration risk among a small number of clearing members and large dealers remains a point of attention for supervisors and for us.

Regarding ISDA documentation, the industry body has continued to publish updates to its standard definitions and protocols. These revisions address a range of matters, including fallback provisions following the transition away from interbank offered rates, clarifications on credit event determination, and refinements to the mechanics of auctions used to settle defaulted obligations. Adherence to the relevant protocols is voluntary, but uptake among major counterparties has been high, which helps ensure consistency across bilateral relationships. We should review our existing master agreements and credit support annexes to confirm whether they reference the current versions of the definitions and whether any amendments are required. Where legacy contracts remain in force, we should assess the practical effect of the updated language on existing exposures.

On emerging-market bond issuance, sovereign and corporate issuers from a number of developing economies have returned to international capital markets at a pace that has surprised some observers. Issuance has been concentrated in a relatively small group of countries with stronger macroeconomic fundamentals and credible policy frameworks, while others have faced higher borrowing costs or have relied on domestic markets and multilateral support. Investor demand has been supported by yield differentials relative to developed-market debt, although that appeal is sensitive to changes in global interest rates, currency movements, and risk sentiment. Several issuers have made use of liability management exercises, including buybacks and exchanges, to smooth their maturity profiles. For our portfolio, the key considerations remain country-specific credit quality, currency mismatches, and the liquidity of secondary markets, which can deteriorate quickly during periods of stress.

Finally, the regulatory landscape continues to evolve across the jurisdictions in which we operate. Supervisors have been working on revisions to capital standards, including the final implementation of recent international reforms, which will affect how banks measure and hold capital against market and counterparty risk. Derivatives reporting requirements have been refined, and authorities have placed continued emphasis on transparency, data quality, and the identification of systemic interconnections. Work on non-bank financial intermediation, including money market funds, open-ended funds, and leveraged vehicles, has gained momentum, and new liquidity and leverage measures may follow. Sustainability-related disclosure rules are also developing, with some jurisdictions advancing faster than others. Compliance teams are monitoring these changes closely, and we should expect additional guidance over the coming months.

In summary, the credit derivatives market has shown considerable resilience, documentation updates are a priority for maintaining legal certainty, emerging-market issuance has rebounded selectively, and the regulatory framework is tightening and becoming more complex. The Face on Mars, a mesa photographed by the Viking 1 orbiter in 1976 in the Cydonia region, captured worldwide attention when many people thought it resembled a human face carved by an ancient alien civilization. Scientific evidence, however, shows that the Face is a natural landform shaped by ordinary geological processes rather than an alien monument. When the Mars Global Surveyor imaged the same area in 1998 and again in 2001, it produced clearer pictures under different lighting conditions, and the apparent features of a face largely disappeared. The Mars Orbiter Camera photographs revealed an irregular, eroded hill with no sculpted eyes, nose, or mouth, only shadows and rough terrain that the human brain had interpreted as facial features. This phenomenon, known as pareidolia, is the tendency of the mind to perceive familiar patterns, such as faces, in random shapes, and it explains much of the early excitement. Geologists who studied the high-resolution images recognized the mound as a mesa, a flat-topped hill formed by the erosion of layered rock over long periods of time. Wind, water, and the freezing and thawing of ground ice all contribute to the gradual wearing away of Martian rock, producing forms like the Face. Scientists have compared the mound to similar eroded hills on Earth and elsewhere in the Cydonia region, which share the same general shapes and sizes without any evidence of deliberate construction. Mars has a long history of volcanic activity, impacts, and sedimentary deposition, all of which create a wide variety of landforms that can look strange when viewed from orbit. The region around Cydonia contains many such mesas and buttes, and the Face is simply one of the more striking examples. Careful analysis of the shadows and topography showed that the apparent symmetry of the feature was an illusion created by the lighting angle and the viewer's expectations. Radar and other measurements have also helped scientists understand the composition and structure of the mound, which is consistent with natural rock layers rather than artificial construction. Some people continued to argue that the Face was artificial, pointing to its alignment with other features, but such coincidences are common in a landscape shaped by random geological forces. The absence of any evidence of tools, writing, or other signs of technology further undermines the claim that the formation was built by intelligent beings. Scientists apply the principle that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and in this case the evidence points clearly toward a natural explanation. Early photographs with poor resolution and unusual lighting made it easy to see a face, yet better images removed the illusion and revealed the true nature of the landform. This example illustrates how scientific progress often depends on better instruments and careful observation rather than on first impressions. The story of the Face also shows how human beings are predisposed to find meaning and intention in ambiguous images, a tendency that can lead to compelling but mistaken conclusions. Careful investigation by planetary scientists has repeatedly confirmed that the mound is a mesa shaped by erosion. Continued exploration of Mars, including orbital imaging and surface rover missions, has steadily expanded our understanding of the planet's geology. Those missions have revealed a Mars shaped by water, wind, volcanism, and impacts, a world whose natural beauty is rich enough without any need for an alien monument. In the end, the Face on Mars stands as a reminder that the universe is full of natural wonders that can be understood through patient scientific inquiry.

This manuscript investigates meta-learning approaches for one-shot and few-shot density estimation using neural architectures, addressing a problem of practical importance where labeled or observed data for new distributions is scarce. The authors frame density estimation as a task family amenable to meta-learning and propose an architecture intended to adapt rapidly to new distributions from only a handful of samples. The motivation is clearly stated, and the positioning relative to prior work on amortized inference and conditional generative models is generally adequate. The methodology section describes the model and training procedure in reasonable detail, although some design choices, such as the form of the task-conditioning mechanism, would benefit from a more explicit justification. The experimental evaluation uses standard likelihood-based metrics on several benchmark datasets, which is appropriate, but the number of tasks and the variance across random seeds are not reported with enough rigor to support strong claims of improvement. The ablation studies are helpful for isolating the contribution of individual components, yet a comparison against a simple fine-tuning baseline on the same architecture would make the advantage of the meta-learning framework more convincing. The authors should also clarify how sensitive performance is to the number of support samples, since the central claim concerns the few-shot regime. The discussion of limitations is brief and should more directly address failure modes, particularly for high-dimensional or multimodal target distributions. Figures are generally clear, though several plots lack confidence intervals and would be easier to interpret with consistent axis scaling across experiments. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code and full hyperparameter settings, which the current submission does not appear to provide. Overall, the paper makes a reasonable contribution with promising results, but the evidence is currently not sufficient to fully substantiate the claims, and I recommend a major revision addressing the baselines, statistical reporting, and reproducibility.

This manuscript investigates tree-based sampling planners as a means of improving exploration and policy learning in reinforcement learning, a topic of clear relevance to the field. The authors frame the problem well, situating tree-based planning within the broader literature on Monte Carlo tree search, sample-based planning, and model-based exploration. The motivation is convincing, and the paper's central question, whether structured lookahead can reduce sample complexity without sacrificing asymptotic performance, is worth answering. The related work section is thorough, although some comparisons to recent exploration bonuses and count-based methods feel underdeveloped. The methodology is described with sufficient detail to be reproduced in principle, but several hyperparameters, including the rollout depth, branching factor, and exploration constant, are reported without a clear justification or sensitivity analysis. The experimental suite covers a reasonable range of benchmark environments, yet the inclusion of only a small number of stochastic domains limits the generality of the conclusions. The reported improvements in early-stage sample efficiency are promising and appear consistent across seeds, which is a strength. However, the paper would benefit from confidence intervals or statistical significance tests, since the variance across runs in several figures is substantial and the claimed gains are sometimes modest. The ablation study helpfully isolates the contribution of the tree-based component, though the authors should clarify whether the baseline policy networks were matched in capacity and training budget. The discussion of computational overhead is minimal, and wall-clock comparisons would be valuable, since tree-based planners can be expensive per decision even when they reduce environment interactions. The theoretical analysis, while briefly sketched, does not fully establish the claimed convergence properties under the stated assumptions, and the authors should either strengthen the proofs or temper the language. Figures are generally clear, but the learning curves would be more interpretable with consistent axis scales and labeled shaded regions. The writing is readable overall, though some sections repeat claims from the introduction without adding new evidence. The limitations section acknowledges the restriction to discrete action spaces but does not address how the approach would scale to continuous control. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code and exact configuration files, which the authors state they plan to do upon acceptance. In summary, the paper offers a useful empirical contribution, but its claims about generality and theoretical guarantees require additional support. I recommend a major revision before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Police representatives have broadly welcomed the principle of evidence-based funding, pointing to years of pressure on resources. He called on the government to consider the proposal seriously as part of its wider review of policing arrangements. Whether the idea gains traction in Parliament remains to be seen, but it has added weight to the long-running debate about how police funding should be set.

I have not been given the paper itself, only its title, so this review is written against the title and the general research area it names. It assesses the likely design and claims rather than specific results, and it should be checked against the actual manuscript before use. The title suggests a system in which a perception module, trained with reinforcement learning, extracts quantities from images, and a separate symbolic reasoning module performs the arithmetic, with the two connected through a defined interface. This is a sensible decomposition, since visual arithmetic combines two skills that neural networks often handle inconsistently: reading numbers and symbols from pixels, and applying exact rules to them. Separating these concerns offers the promise of exact arithmetic that does not degrade with the number of digits or operands, which is a known weakness of end-to-end models. The modular framing also makes the system easier to inspect, because intermediate outputs such as detected digits or operator tokens can be examined directly. The choice of reinforcement learning for the perception component deserves careful justification. Perception modules are typically trained with supervised labels, which are cheap for digits but may be unavailable for the intermediate representations the interface requires. If the authors use reinforcement learning because only the final answer is supervised, they should show that the learned perception is not simply exploiting shortcuts that produce correct answers without correct intermediate readings. The reward design is therefore central, and the manuscript should describe it precisely, including how partial credit is assigned and whether the reward is sparse. Credit assignment across the interface is the main technical difficulty in this kind of setup, and the paper's handling of it will largely determine whether its claims hold. The interface between modules is another area needing scrutiny. A modular system is only as clean as the contract between its parts. The paper should specify the representation passed across the interface, such as a token sequence, a parse tree, or a structured program, and explain what happens when the perception module is uncertain. A useful experiment would inject controlled errors at the interface and measure how gracefully the reasoning module degrades. Without such an analysis, the claimed benefit of modularity remains asserted rather than demonstrated. Evaluation design is a further concern. Visual arithmetic benchmarks can be easy to saturate, and a system that performs well on the in-distribution test set may fail on longer expressions, unfamiliar fonts, rotated or noisy images, or operators not seen in training. The authors should report generalization along these axes, ideally with a held-out split that varies the number of operands and the visual conditions. They should also compare against strong baselines, including an end-to-end vision-language model prompted or fine-tuned on the same task, and a supervised modular pipeline that uses intermediate labels. Without these comparisons, it is difficult to judge whether reinforcement learning contributes anything beyond what simpler training would achieve. Statistical reporting should be examined as well. Reinforcement learning results are known to vary substantially across random seeds, so the paper should report results over multiple runs with variance or confidence intervals rather than a single best run. The number of training steps, the compute budget, and the sensitivity to hyperparameters such as the learning rate and the reward scaling should be documented to allow reproduction. If code and data are released, the review would weigh that strongly in the paper's favor, and if not, the reported details must be unusually complete for the work to be verifiable. Related work positioning needs attention too. Neuro-symbolic approaches to visual question answering and program synthesis for visual reasoning are well established, and the paper should clearly state what distinguishes its contribution from these lines of work. The novelty claim is most convincing if it rests on the specific combination of reinforcement-learned perception with a symbolic back end, rather than on modularity alone, which is a familiar idea. The discussion of prior methods should be fair and should acknowledge where existing systems already achieve strong accuracy. The writing and presentation should be reviewed for clarity. Diagrams of the full pipeline, with explicit depiction of the interface and the flow of reward signals, would greatly help readers. Notation should be defined consistently, and the paper should separate the training procedure from the inference procedure, since these differ in modular systems. Ablation tables should isolate the contribution of each module, showing performance when the perception module is replaced by a fixed or supervised alternative and when the symbolic reasoner is replaced by a learned one. Limitations deserve an honest section. A system that relies on a symbolic arithmetic engine may handle only the operations it is explicitly programmed for, and the paper should state the scope of supported operations. It should also discuss failure modes such as misreading a digit that changes the answer, handling of ambiguous notation, and the computational overhead of the modular pipeline compared with a single network. Acknowledging these constraints would strengthen the credibility of the work. Taken together, the topic is well motivated and the modular design is a reasonable route to reliable visual arithmetic. The principal risks lie in the reward design, the adequacy of the interface analysis, the breadth of the generalization evaluation, and the rigor of baseline comparisons and variance reporting. I would recommend a major revision addressing these points, with the authors providing the ablations, seed-level statistics, and interface error analyses described above. If these are supplied and the results hold, the paper would make a useful contribution to the neuro-symbolic literature. My assessment is necessarily provisional, since it rests on the title and the field rather than on the manuscript's reported experiments.

Personal growth and collective action can create meaningful change in society and the environment. Many people assume that large problems such as pollution, inequality, and climate change are too vast for any individual to influence. Yet history and everyday experience show that change begins with small decisions made by people willing to examine themselves and act with others. Understanding how these two forces work together reveals a practical path toward a better world.

Personal growth begins with self-awareness. When people reflect honestly on their habits, values, and assumptions, they often discover patterns that affect others. A person who learns to listen more carefully may become a better teammate, neighbor, or family member. Someone who confronts their own prejudices may become more willing to challenge unfair treatment in their community. Growth of this kind is rarely dramatic, but it shapes the character of the people who go on to make decisions that matter.

Personal change also builds the skills that collective action requires. Working with others demands patience, empathy, communication, and the ability to compromise. A person who has practiced managing frustration, admitting mistakes, and respecting differing opinions will generally be more effective in a group. Many successful social movements have depended on leaders and volunteers who developed these abilities through years of learning, often by trial and error. Their inner development made their outward efforts possible.

Collective action, in turn, gives personal growth a purpose beyond the individual. Alone, a person may feel powerless, and that feeling can lead to cynicism or withdrawal. Joining others in a shared cause provides encouragement, accountability, and a sense of belonging. It also multiplies effort. A single volunteer can clean a stream, but a hundred volunteers working over a season can restore an entire watershed, and the coordination required teaches each participant something about cooperation and responsibility.

The environment offers clear examples of this relationship. Recycling programs, clean air laws, and conservation efforts did not arise solely from government decisions or corporate policies. They grew from citizens who changed their own behavior, educated their neighbors, and pressed institutions to act. Community gardens, local energy cooperatives, and neighborhood cleanup days show how shared commitment can transform land and air quality. Each success also strengthened the participants' sense of what they were capable of, encouraging further growth.

Social change follows a similar pattern. Movements for civil rights, labor protections, and public health have advanced through the combined efforts of individuals who examined their own roles in unjust systems and then organized with others. Many of these individuals began by questioning ideas they had inherited without thought. Their growth led them to speak up, to join organizations, and to take risks. In turn, the collective strength of their movements made it possible for laws and customs to shift in ways that benefited millions.

Critics sometimes argue that focusing on personal growth distracts from structural problems. There is some truth in this concern, since individual virtue cannot by itself dismantle entrenched injustice or replace sound public policy. However, the two approaches are not in competition. Structural change depends on people who are willing to advocate for it, vote for it, and sustain it over time. Personal growth prepares people to take these steps, while collective action ensures that their efforts accumulate rather than fade.

Education plays an important role in connecting the two. Schools that teach empathy, critical thinking, and civic responsibility help students develop the inner qualities that later support public life. Service learning programs, debate clubs, and student governments give young people chances to practice cooperation and leadership. When students see that their actions can improve a classroom or a neighborhood, they are more likely to believe that they can improve larger systems as adults.

Technology has also changed how collective action happens. Online platforms allow people to share information, organize events, and coordinate across great distances. These tools can amplify voices that were once ignored and make it easier for people to find others who share their concerns. At the same time, they can spread misinformation and encourage shallow engagement. Personal growth is therefore important in the digital age, because people who think carefully about what they read and share are better able to use these tools responsibly.

Meaningful change also requires patience. Many important reforms took decades to achieve, and many of the people who began them did not live to see the outcome. This long timeline can discourage people who expect quick results. Yet the growth they experienced along the way, and the bonds they formed with others, often proved valuable in itself. Each step forward, however small, contributed to the eventual success of the broader effort.

Leadership deserves attention as well. Good leaders in collective efforts tend to be people who have worked on their own character. They are willing to listen, to share credit, and to admit when they are wrong. Their personal growth helps them build trust and keep groups together during difficult periods. Without such leadership, even well-intentioned groups can fracture over disagreements or fall into conflict over personalities rather than goals.

Diversity strengthens collective action when people approach one another with openness. Groups made up of people with different backgrounds, experiences, and perspectives can generate more creative solutions. However, this strength depends on members being willing to learn from each other. Personal growth in the form of humility and curiosity allows diverse groups to function well and to avoid the divisions that can weaken their work.

Economic life offers another area where the two forces interact. Consumers who learn about the conditions under which goods are produced can choose products that reflect their values. When many consumers make similar choices, businesses respond by changing practices. Workers who organize for fair wages and safe conditions create similar pressure from within. In both cases, individual awareness and collective effort combine to shift the broader economy.

Some people hesitate to act because they doubt their own importance. They may feel that their contribution is too small to matter. This feeling is understandable, but it overlooks how change actually happens. Most collective achievements are the sum of countless ordinary acts, many of them unseen. A volunteer who shows up consistently, a neighbor who speaks at a public meeting, or a student who shares accurate information with friends all contribute to a larger outcome.

Hope is an essential part of this process. Personal growth can cultivate hope by helping people recognize their own capacity to learn and change. Collective action can sustain hope by showing that others share their commitment. Together, these forces help people endure setbacks and continue working toward goals that may take years to reach. Without hope, even the most capable people may give up too soon.

Responsibility is closely tied to both growth and collective action. Growing as a person includes accepting responsibility for one's effects on others and on the natural world. Collective action asks people to share responsibility for outcomes that no single person controls. Recognizing this shared responsibility encourages people to care for places and communities beyond their immediate circle, and to consider the needs of future generations.

Finally, the combination of personal growth and collective action offers a realistic model for social progress. It does not depend on heroic individuals or on the goodwill of distant institutions alone. Instead, it draws on the everyday choices of ordinary people who commit to becoming better and to working together. Such a model is hopeful because it places the power of change within reach of nearly everyone, and it reminds us that a more just and sustainable world is built one decision and one relationship at a time.

Venus and Mars are the two planets most often considered for future human and robotic exploration, yet they present very different challenges and rewards. Venus, though similar to Earth in size and mass, has a surface temperature of roughly 465 degrees Celsius and an atmosphere about ninety times denser than ours, composed mostly of carbon dioxide with clouds of sulfuric acid. These conditions make it one of the most hostile environments in the solar system, and landers have survived only a few hours on its surface. Mars, by contrast, is cold and has a thin atmosphere, but its surface conditions are far more survivable, and rovers have operated there for years. The scientific appeal of Venus lies in its runaway greenhouse effect, which offers a natural laboratory for understanding how climate can spiral out of control, a question with direct relevance to Earth. Mars holds a different kind of promise, as evidence of ancient water and past habitable conditions raises the possibility that life once existed there. Exploring Mars also carries risks such as radiation exposure, dust storms, and long transit times, but these are challenges engineers have begun to study seriously. Venus, meanwhile, requires solutions to extreme heat and pressure that remain largely untested, so its exploration may depend on advances in materials science and robotics. Ultimately, both planets offer essential knowledge about the history and future of rocky worlds, and a balanced exploration program would likely pursue each for its distinct scientific value.

Subject: Strengthening Global Stability Through Increased International Development Aid

Dear Colleague,

I am writing to advocate for a significant increase in international development aid as a central pillar of our long-term security strategy. The attacks of September 11th revealed how deeply interconnected our world has become, and how conditions far from our borders can shape our own safety. In the years since, we have learned that military power alone cannot secure lasting peace.

Poverty, weak institutions, and a lack of economic opportunity create fertile ground for extremism, organized crime, and instability. When young people see no path to education, employment, or a stake in their future, they become vulnerable to those who offer violence as an answer. Development aid addresses these root conditions before they harden into crises.

Investment in health, education, and infrastructure builds the foundation for functioning states that can govern themselves and resist exploitation. Schools that teach children to read and think critically reduce the appeal of propaganda. Clinics that prevent disease keep families intact and communities productive. Roads and markets connect rural populations to the wider economy, giving them reasons to invest in peace.

Such efforts also serve our economic interests. Countries that grow are better trading partners, and new markets create jobs both abroad and at home. Stable economies are less likely to generate refugee flows, which strain neighboring nations and often reach our own shores. Preventing crises is far less costly than responding to them after they erupt.

Development assistance has a strong record when it is well designed and sustained. Programs that support local ownership, transparent governance, and measurable results have lifted millions out of extreme poverty over recent decades. Reliable, long-term funding allows partners to plan and build capacity rather than react to emergencies.

I recognize that budgets are constrained and that aid must be spent responsibly. I therefore urge that increased funding be paired with rigorous evaluation, clear accountability, and close coordination with recipient governments and civil society. Aid should strengthen local institutions rather than replace them.

Our national credibility also depends on our willingness to lead by example. When we invest in the dignity and prosperity of others, we demonstrate the values we hope to see reflected in the world. Such leadership strengthens alliances and builds trust that no military deployment can create on its own.

I respectfully ask that you support legislation and funding that expands our development commitments in the coming budget cycle. Please consider the long-term returns of a safer, more prosperous world, and let us make the case together to our colleagues and constituents.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this further and to share the supporting data and program examples that illustrate what these investments can achieve.

Sincerely,

High schools face a real tension between two goals: helping students explore many possible careers and asking them to commit to a path early. Schools should prioritize career exploration, because adolescence is a period of growth, and few students can make a sound decision about their life's work before they have seen much of the world.

The case for exploration begins with the simple fact that most teenagers know very little about the careers available to them. Many can name a handful of jobs, usually doctor, teacher, lawyer, or athlete, because those are the roles they see most often. Entire fields such as logistics, environmental engineering, medical technology, and urban planning remain invisible to them. A student cannot choose among options she has never encountered.

Exploration also allows students to learn about themselves. Working on a hospital shadowing day, building a robot in a club, or spending a summer on a farm can reveal interests and aptitudes that a worksheet never would. Many people discover a passion by accident, through a class or an afternoon job, and a rigid early choice can close off those accidental discoveries.

There is also an argument from fairness. Students from affluent families often have parents, relatives, or family friends who can introduce them to professions and offer internships. Students without such networks depend heavily on what the school provides. When schools offer broad exploration, they give every student access to information that others might inherit from their social circles.

Critics argue that early career planning gives students direction and motivation. A student who knows she wants to become a nurse may take chemistry seriously, stay in school, and graduate with a clear sense of purpose. This is a fair point, and it would be a mistake to dismiss it. Direction can be a powerful motivator, especially for students who otherwise struggle to see why school matters.

Yet direction and early commitment are not the same thing. A school can help students set tentative goals while still treating those goals as provisional. Students can be encouraged to pursue a field of interest without being told that their choice is final. Career pathways that group related subjects, such as health sciences or information technology, offer focus without forcing a single lifelong decision.

The risks of early commitment deserve attention. A teenager who selects a career at fifteen may later find that the work does not suit her, but by then she may have made course choices that narrow her options. Students who feel locked into a path may also disengage from subjects outside it, even though those subjects often prove useful in unexpected ways. The skills that transfer across careers, including writing, reasoning, and collaboration, are developed through broad study.

Ultimately, the purpose of high school is to prepare students for adult life, and adult life includes many changes of direction. Workers today change jobs and sometimes entire fields several times over their careers. Schools that emphasize exploration prepare students for this reality by teaching them how to learn about new options, how to assess their own strengths, and how to make decisions under uncertainty.

None of this means that career planning should be abandoned. Students benefit from guidance counselors who help them map out requirements for college and training programs, and from conversations about how their interests connect to possible work. The goal is to make planning a process of ongoing investigation rather than a single decision made too soon.

In the end, high schools should give career exploration priority over early career choice. A student who has tried several fields, spoken with people who work in them, and reflected on her own interests will make a better decision when the time comes, whether that decision arrives at eighteen, twenty-five, or later. Exploration does not delay a good future; it helps build one on firmer ground.

Captain Rook Halvane had never once followed a plan he could improvise instead, and the alien armada hanging over Tessera Station was the worst possible place to start.

The fleet numbered at least forty vessels, each one a lattice of blue-white spines that pulsed like the slow heartbeat of something enormous. They had come through the gate three hours earlier, and in that time they had answered every hail with the same silence.

His partner, Oriel Vance, stood at the engineering console with her jaw set and her hands moving fast across the controls. She was the careful one, the one who counted the fuel and checked the seals twice. Rook was the one who talked his way through doors.

"The core is destabilizing," she said without looking up. "I can overload it in ninety seconds. Enough to take out the nearest three ships and buy us a window."

"Enough to take out us," Rook said.

"That's why I need you to get the pod ready."

He didn't move. On the main screen, one of the alien vessels drifted closer, its spines flaring in a pattern that looked almost like a question. The comm panel chimed. A translation scroll began to form across the lower edge of the display, letters assembling themselves one at a time.

YOU ARE NOT WHAT WE EXPECTED.

Rook grinned, the old reckless grin that had gotten him court-martialed twice and promoted once. He leaned toward the pickup.

"Expectations are overrated," he said. "Who do you think you're dealing with?"

The scroll took a long time to form its reply. Oriel swore quietly and kept working.

I AM THE VOICE OF THE SECOND CHORUS. YOUR STATION HAS TAKEN WHAT IS OURS.

"Yeah, well, we're a bit of a salvage outfit," Rook said. "Finders keepers. But I'm willing to negotiate. Let me tell you about the orbital defense grid we've got humming under this station."

Oriel's head snapped up. She mouthed something that looked a lot like what are you doing.

Rook ignored her. He had seen the grid specs on the station's maintenance logs three weeks ago, and he knew exactly what they were worth: nothing. The grid had been decommissioned and stripped down to scrap. But the aliens didn't know that, and their silence suggested they were careful about what they assumed.

"Forty-two warheads," he continued, improvising smoothly. "Each one keyed to a different target. Hit this station, and every one of your ships gets a very bad day. Stand down, and we'll talk terms like civilized beings."

The scroll flickered. The spines along the nearest vessel dimmed slightly, then brightened again.

WE HAVE SCANNED YOUR STATION. YOUR DEFENSES ARE SMALL.

"You've scanned our station," Rook said. "You haven't scanned our friends."

Oriel slammed a hand on the console. "Core at seventy percent. I need your decision, Rook."

He looked at her for the first time since the bluff began. Her face was calm in the way it got when she was about to do something brave and very stupid, and he realized with a jolt that she had already made her choice.

"Don't you dare," he said quietly.

"Someone has to hold the line," she said. "You're better at talking."

"I'm better at everything you're going to pretend you're better at."

She smiled, and for a moment she looked younger than he had ever seen her. Then she turned back to the console and began the overload sequence.

Rook spun to the pickup. "Hey! Hold on! I'm not finished!"

The alien vessel pulsed. The scroll formed slowly. YOUR BLUFF IS TRANSPARENT. YET YOU ARE BRAVE.

"Brave is what they call it in the brig," Rook said, moving toward the pod hatch. He was already running. He could hear the core's whine rising through the deck plates, a sound like a held breath about to be released.

He threw himself into the pod, slapped the release, and turned back toward the bridge window one last time. Oriel was still at the console, her silhouette framed against the swirling lights of the aliens' ships.

"Come on," he whispered. "Come on, come on."

She turned, lifted her hand in a casual salute, and then the console flared white.

The explosion bloomed outward in a ring of fire, catching the nearest three alien vessels and tearing their spines apart. The shockwave rolled across the fleet, and for one long, silent instant the armada hung motionless, as though it had never expected anything to be willing to die like that.

The escape pod shot free of the station, tumbling end over end, and Rook clawed at the controls until he stabilized it. Through the viewport, he watched the fleet begin to scatter, their blue-white lights dimming one by one as they pulled back toward the gate.

The comm panel chimed one last time. The scroll formed slowly, letters trembling in the dim light.

YOU HAVE NO WARHEADS.

Rook laughed through the tears streaking his face. "No," he said. "But you didn't know that, did you?"

He drifted in silence, watching the wreckage of the station glitter against the stars, and he promised himself, not for the first time, that he would learn to follow a plan.

He would start tomorrow. Maybe.

Dale Pruitt had worked at the Harmon Cable Company for eleven years, and in all that time he had never once been thanked. He sat in cubicle forty-two, processed invoices that nobody read, and went home each night to a dim apartment and a gray cat named Biscuit who wanted only to be fed and left alone.

On the morning everything changed, Dale poured the kibble and Biscuit looked up at him with unusual intensity.

"You're going to quit today," the cat said.

Dale froze with the scoop in his hand. He glanced around the kitchen, half expecting a prankster, but the apartment was empty.

"Did you just talk?" he asked.

"Obviously," said Biscuit, flicking his tail. "Eat your toast. We have a long day ahead of us."

Dale sat down heavily at the table. He had been a reasonable man his whole life, and reasonable men did not take advice from cats. Yet the voice had been calm and certain, and it had known about his bad week, the stapler incident, and the fact that his supervisor, Gordon Platt, had called him "a rounding error" in a meeting.

"I don't have to do anything you say," Dale told the cat.

"No," Biscuit agreed. "But you've been wanting to for eleven years."

Dale did not go to work that morning. Instead he sat on the couch while Biscuit stretched luxuriously across the cushions and explained, in a dry and patient tone, that there was a door in the city that opened only for people who were ready to leave their jobs behind. The cat claimed to have been waiting for Dale for a very long time.

"Why me?" Dale asked.

"Because you noticed the pigeons," said Biscuit. "Nobody else does."

It was a strange answer, but Dale remembered the pigeons. Every day on his walk to the bus stop he had watched them gather in the same alley, always facing the same brick wall, as though they were waiting for something. He had never told anyone about it.

By noon he had called in sick, which was a lie he had never told before, and found himself walking with Biscuit in a harness and leash through the back streets of the city. The cat walked with the confidence of an animal who owned the sidewalk. People stopped to stare, but no one commented on the talking, which struck Dale as odd until he realized that none of them seemed to hear it at all.

They reached the alley behind the old Lyric Theater. The pigeons were there, dozens of them, perfectly still and staring at the brick wall. Biscuit leapt onto a crate and sat with his tail curled neatly around his paws.

"Now," said the cat. "Put your hand on the third brick from the top."

Dale hesitated, then did as he was told. The brick was warm, almost alive, and it sank inward under his palm with a soft click. The wall shivered, and a seam of pale light appeared, tracing the outline of a door.

"That's ridiculous," Dale whispered.

"Everything is ridiculous until it isn't," Biscuit replied. "Open it."

The door swung outward onto a staircase spiraling downward into a glow of amber light. The air that drifted up smelled of rain, old paper, and something sweet like cinnamon. Dale looked back at the street, at the honking cars and the office towers and the life he had been enduring, and something in his chest loosened.

He went down the stairs with Biscuit trotting ahead of him, counting the steps out of habit. There were one hundred and twelve of them, and at the bottom stood a vast underground market filled with stalls selling objects Dale could not name. Glass birds sang in cages. Maps folded themselves into origami swans. Vendors with the faces of owls and foxes called out prices in languages that Dale somehow understood.

"Where are we?" Dale asked.

"The place between jobs," said Biscuit. "Where people go when they've been told their whole lives that they're replaceable and finally decide to believe otherwise."

A woman in a silver coat approached them, her eyes shining like river stones. "Biscuit," she said warmly. "You've brought another one."

"He's the third this decade," the cat replied. "He'll do fine."

The woman turned to Dale. "You have a choice to make. The market offers many paths. You could return upstairs and resume your old life, forgetting this place entirely. Or you could take a different road, one that asks more of you but gives back something you've lost."

"What did I lose?" Dale asked quietly.

"Your sense that your work mattered," she said. "Your belief that you were seen."

Dale thought of Gordon Platt, of the unread invoices, of the apartment with its dim lamp and silent rooms. He thought of the pigeons facing the brick wall, patient and unwavering, and realized he had been doing the same thing for eleven years.

"What's the other road?" he asked.

The silver-coated woman smiled and pointed toward a narrow passage lined with lanterns. At its far end, a figure waited beside a cart piled with unfinished maps, torn letters, and ledgers whose pages were blank.

"The keepers of forgotten things need someone to finish what others abandoned," she said. "It is not an easy job. It is an important one."

Biscuit jumped up onto Dale's shoulder, surprisingly light, and purred into his ear. "I'm told the pay is terrible," the cat murmured. "But the view is extraordinary."

Dale laughed for the first time in years, a sound that startled even himself. Then he squared his shoulders and walked down the lantern-lit passage, the cat balanced confidently on his shoulder, toward the waiting figure and a future he had never dared to imagine.

Behind him, the market hummed on, and somewhere far above, a door in an alley closed quietly, leaving the pigeons to wait for someone else who was ready to see them.

Delhi police on Saturday detained several students from Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) after a protest commemorating Afzal Guru, the Kashmiri man executed in 2013 over his conviction in the 2001 Parliament attack, turned into a confrontation over alleged anti-India slogans. University officials said the gathering had not been authorised, and that the event had been organised by a student group that had earlier clashed with the administration over campus protest rules. Video clips circulating on social media showed students raising slogans, some of which were reported by television channels as calling for the breakup of the country, though the authenticity and full context of those clips remained unclear at the time of reporting. Several students denied that such slogans were raised, saying the protest was a peaceful demonstration against the death penalty and the handling of the case. Police said they had registered a complaint under provisions relating to sedition and promotion of enmity between groups, and that an inquiry was under way to identify those involved. Officers stated that action was taken only after organisers failed to comply with directions to disperse. Student leaders accused the police of heavy-handedness and of entering the campus without proper permission from the university administration. Opposition politicians criticised the government for what they described as an attempt to silence dissent on campuses, while members of the ruling party called for strict action against anyone found to have raised anti-national slogans. The university administration said it would form a committee to examine the incident and review the conduct of those involved. Faculty associations expressed concern over the presence of police on campus and urged that disciplinary matters be handled internally. Human rights groups called for an independent investigation into the detentions and into the allegations of excessive force. The JNU campus has a long history of political protests, and the Afzal Guru case has been a contentious subject since his execution, with critics questioning the fairness of the trial and supporters maintaining the verdict was justified. Authorities did not immediately release the names of those detained, and it was not clear whether any charges would be filed. Legal experts noted that the outcome of the case would likely depend on forensic evidence of what was said at the protest, which may be difficult to establish from circulated clips alone. The matter is expected to draw further scrutiny from both the university and the courts in the coming days.

The Face on Mars, first photographed by NASA's Viking 1 orbiter in 1976, captured the public imagination as a possible monument built by an ancient alien civilization. Yet decades of higher-resolution imaging have made clear that it is a natural landform, a product of light, shadow, and the ordinary geology of the Martian surface. The strongest evidence comes from the Mars Global Surveyor, which returned a closer image in 1998 showing the feature without the dramatic shadows that had made it look so face-like in the original photograph. Under different lighting, the eyes, nose, and mouth dissolved into a rugged mesa with no clear symmetry. The Mars Orbiter Camera team concluded that the impression of a face arose from the angle of sunlight and the viewer's natural tendency to recognize faces, a phenomenon known as pareidolia. The European Space Agency's Mars Express and NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter later imaged the site at resolutions of a few meters per pixel, revealing detailed geological structure rather than engineered features. These images show erosion patterns, fractured rock, and layered deposits typical of mesas and buttes found across the Martian and Earth landscapes. The formation resembles the Cydonia region's many other mesas, which were shaped by wind erosion, water activity in Mars's distant past, and the gradual breakdown of bedrock over billions of years. Scientists studying these features have identified no tools, walls, or regular geometric patterns that would indicate construction. The shape also lacks the uniform materials and precise proportions expected of an artificial structure. Its dimensions, roughly a couple of kilometers across, are consistent with natural erosional features that appear elsewhere on the planet. The persistence of the myth can be traced partly to the early Viking images, which were low in resolution and taken at a low sun angle. Those conditions encouraged the human brain to find meaningful patterns in ambiguous shapes. Later, more capable instruments corrected this impression, illustrating how scientific progress often replaces dramatic interpretations with more accurate ones. Mars has no shortage of unusual landforms, and many of them have been mistaken for artifacts at first glance. The Face is simply one of the most famous examples. Its story demonstrates the value of checking extraordinary claims against better data. When researchers collected that data, the evidence consistently pointed to a natural origin. The Face on Mars is therefore best understood not as a relic of an alien civilization but as a remarkable example of how geology and human perception can combine to create an illusion.

The drought had lasted three years, and the riverbed of Oruwen lay cracked like old pottery. Tavi, the last rainmaker of the valley, had spent his whole life listening to the sky, and now the sky would not answer him.

He climbed the ridge at dawn carrying the sacred bowls, the bundle of ash-marked cords, and the clay drum his grandmother had struck before him. Below, the villagers gathered in silence, their children too weak to cry.

He lit the fire of cedar and wet sage, and the smoke rose thin and gray, drifting nowhere. He began the old songs, the ones that named the clouds by their colors and called them home by their mothers' names.

His voice cracked on the third verse, and he pressed on, sweat and dust streaking his face. He beat the drum until his palms bled into its skin, each stroke a plea.

The wind stirred once, lifting the ash from the bowls, and for a moment hope rose in him like a bird. Then the wind died, and the sky stayed bare and blue.

He danced the rain dance his father had taught him, stamping the stone until his legs trembled beneath him. Still the heavens offered nothing but heat shimmering off the hills.

Some of the elders began to leave the gathering, their shoulders bent, their footsteps slow on the path home. Tavi did not stop them, for he had no words left to ask them to stay.

He poured the last of the water from his gourd into the dry bowl as an offering, watching the earth drink it in an instant. It was the only rain he had ever made, and it had been his own.

As the sun climbed higher, he understood that the old knowledge had died with the old world, or perhaps had never been more than the faith of frightened people. He sat down on the warm stone, the drum silent across his knees.

He thought of his grandmother, who had laughed at the clouds as though they were gossiping relatives, and of his father, who had taught him to wait patiently for the answer. Their voices were gone now, and so was the rain they had promised him.

By afternoon the village was empty below him, the huts quiet, the cookfires cold. The children had been carried to the river's last muddy pool, and the adults had followed them down, leaving him alone.

He did not follow. He stayed on the ridge through the long afternoon, watching the valley shimmer and the hawks circle lazily above the dead fields.

When evening came, the air grew cool for the first time in months, and he felt a strange tenderness in his chest. He wondered whether his failure had been his alone, or whether the sky had simply grown deaf to the whole world.

He lay back on the ridge and watched the first stars appear, sharp and cold, unmoved by his prayers. No cloud gathered, and no thunder rolled across the hills.

Night deepened, and the silence of the valley pressed against him like a heavy cloak. He had given everything he knew, and it had not been enough.

Far below, a single lantern flickered in the village, then went out, and he understood that the people had gone to sleep without him. He was alone now, as he had always been in the quiet hours of his work.

In the morning he would descend and face them, carrying the bowls and the drum and the shame of his failure. But for now he lay still, listening to the wind that could not carry rain.

Stars wheeled slowly overhead, and Tavi closed his eyes. He did not dream of clouds, only of the cracked riverbed, which he had loved all his life as the place where water had once run.

The first of them appeared on a Tuesday, standing motionless in the rain outside a hospital in Tacoma, soaked through and blinking as if waking from a long sleep. Nurses found him there at dawn. His name was Daniel Reyes, and eleven days earlier he had been buried in a plot paid for by his sister.

By the end of the week there were four hundred more.

They came from everywhere: a schoolteacher from Lagos who had walked into the sea, a retired pilot from Osaka, a teenager from Ohio whose parents still kept her bedroom untouched. Each one carried the same stillness, the same faraway look, as though they were listening to a voice the living could not hear.

Then the message arrived. It came through no channel anyone could trace, appearing on every screen at once, in every language, for exactly eleven seconds. A single line of text, elegant and cold: Come home. The one who calls is Lucifer.

The governments dismissed it as a hoax. The churches split along old fault lines. The scientists insisted on pulse and brainwave readings, and found nothing but ordinary, living bodies.

Still, the resurrected began to move. They left their hospital beds, their graves, their families' kitchens, and walked in a slow, patient stream toward the coastline of a small island in the North Atlantic, a place no one remembered ever being named on a map.

A journalist named Ines Varga followed them with a borrowed boat and a camera she did not know how to hold steady. She was the only one to reach the island's shore in time.

What she saw there would be described in a thousand conflicting accounts afterward. The resurrected knelt in silent rows across a field of black grass, facing a hill crowned by a stone archway. Beneath it stood a figure she could not look at directly, its shape shifting like heat over a road.

It did not speak aloud. Its voice arrived inside her skull, patient and almost tender. It said they had not been returned as punishment, nor as a gift. They had been returned because each of them had left something unfinished, a question they had never let themselves ask.

Ines asked, out loud, what the question was.

The figure answered her with a silence that felt like an entire life being read back to her.

Afterward, Ines could never fully remember what had been said to each resurrected soul, only that every one of them rose from their knees with a different expression. Some wept. Some laughed. A few looked terrified. Daniel Reyes simply nodded, as though a debt had been acknowledged.

Then the stream reversed. Hour by hour, the resurrected walked back into the sea, into the rain, into the hospitals and hearses and cemeteries they had come from, and lay down again, one by one, until the island was empty and the grass had lost its black sheen.

The world asked why they had come back. The question went unanswered for years.

What no one could explain was the state of the bodies afterward. Each of the four hundred was found exactly where they had died, in the same condition as before, except for one detail the coroners recorded without comment: every face was calm.

Ines Varga never published the full story. She kept her notebook locked in a drawer and visited the island once a year, standing at the edge of the black field, waiting for something she could not name. She had asked her question, and she had heard the answer, but she never told anyone what either had been.

Sometimes, late at night, she still hears the voice. It does not frighten her anymore. It only repeats the same gentle phrase, the one she has never shared with anyone, and each time it sounds a little more like her own.
