East Timor and Australia remain at odds over how to divide the revenue from the Greater Sunrise gas field, a large offshore deposit in the Timor Sea that holds billions of dollars' worth of natural gas and condensate. The dispute centers on where the maritime boundary should lie, with East Timor arguing for a median line that would place the field largely within its waters, while Australia has long favored a boundary that keeps more of the resource on its side. Negotiations have stretched over many years, and the two countries have sparred over the legal and historical basis for their competing claims. East Timor, one of the youngest nations in Southeast Asia, has pressed the issue as a matter of economic sovereignty, saying revenue from the field is vital to funding its development. Australian officials have countered that existing agreements and the treaty framework must be respected, and they have emphasized the importance of a fair and lasting settlement. Both governments have said they hope to reach a durable arrangement that allows the Sunrise project to proceed, though progress has been slow and the timeline for a final deal remains uncertain. Industry observers note that delays have held back development of the field, which has sat largely untapped for years despite its commercial potential. As talks continue, the outcome will shape not only the financial future of East Timor but also the broader relationship between the two neighbors in the Timor Sea.

Success rarely comes from effort alone, nor from rest alone, but from the careful balance between the two. Many students believe that the best way to achieve their goals is to work without stopping, spending long hours at their desks until exhaustion sets in. However, this approach often backfires, because a tired mind struggles to absorb information, solve problems, and remember what it has learned. Rest is not the opposite of productivity; it is an essential part of it. During sleep, the brain consolidates memories, and during breaks, it recovers the focus needed for demanding work. Purposeful effort, meanwhile, ensures that time spent working is used well. Effort directed toward clear goals produces far more progress than hours spent drifting between tasks without direction. Wise time management connects these two ideas by helping individuals decide what matters most and when to act on it. By planning their schedules, students can set aside focused blocks for challenging assignments while reserving time for exercise, friends, and relaxation. Prioritizing tasks by urgency and importance prevents the last-minute panic that leads to poor work and sleepless nights. Breaking large projects into smaller steps also makes them feel manageable and reduces the procrastination that often steals valuable hours. Good time management, however, does not mean filling every minute with activity. Leaving unstructured space in a schedule allows room for unexpected problems and for the reflection that often sparks new ideas. Many successful people, from athletes to scientists, have emphasized the value of recovery and routine. Their accomplishments reflect not just dedication but also the discipline to step away when necessary. Students can learn from this example by treating rest as a planned part of their routine rather than a reward earned only after exhaustion. Over time, a balanced approach builds healthier habits, greater resilience, and a more sustainable path toward long-term achievement. In the end, success depends less on how much time one spends working and more on how thoughtfully that time is used. Those who learn to balance purposeful effort with genuine rest are better equipped to reach their goals without sacrificing their well-being. Such balance is, therefore, not a limitation on ambition but a foundation for achieving it.

Local councils across England are set to receive a £168 million funding boost to tackle the growing problem of potholes, the government has announced. The money is intended to help authorities carry out repairs on damaged roads that have deteriorated over recent harsh winters and years of constrained budgets.

The allocation will be distributed among local highway authorities, with each council receiving a share based on the size and condition of its road network. Ministers said the investment would help motorists and cyclists by reducing the number of hazards on local streets and main routes.

Officials described the funding as a welcome step towards addressing a backlog of maintenance work that has built up over more than a decade. Many councils have struggled to keep pace with the rate at which roads are degrading, particularly after periods of heavy rainfall and freezing temperatures.

Road safety campaigners have long warned that poorly maintained surfaces pose risks to drivers, motorcyclists and cyclists, and that potholes can cause serious accidents and expensive vehicle damage. Insurance claims linked to road defects have also risen in recent years, placing additional pressure on local authorities.

However, the sector has responded to the announcement with caution. Representatives of local government have argued that £168 million falls well short of what is needed to bring the country's roads up to a satisfactory standard. Some industry bodies have estimated the total repair backlog to run into the billions of pounds.

Council leaders have pointed out that road maintenance competes with other pressing demands on limited budgets, including social care, education and housing. They have called for more sustained, long-term funding rather than one-off grants, arguing that short-term allocations make it difficult to plan large resurfacing schemes.

Engineers note that cheaper temporary fixes, such as filling potholes with cold asphalt, can provide quick relief but often fail within months. More durable solutions, such as full resurfacing or structural repairs, cost considerably more and take longer to deliver, which is why many experts favour preventative maintenance programmes.

Transport analysts have also highlighted regional disparities. Councils in areas with older infrastructure or harsher weather conditions may face greater repair costs, and some rural authorities manage extensive road networks with comparatively small tax bases.

The government has said it expects councils to use the money transparently and to report on how it is spent. Ministers emphasised that the funding forms part of wider efforts to improve transport infrastructure across the country.

Drivers in many areas have already reported increasing numbers of potholes on local roads, with some describing journeys that require constant vigilance and frequent detours. Local residents have welcomed the news but said they hope to see visible improvements soon.

Whether the £168 million will make a lasting difference remains to be seen. Critics argue that without a commitment to multi-year funding and a clear national strategy, the country may continue to face a cycle of temporary repairs and recurring damage.

For now, councils are expected to begin planning their repair programmes in the coming months, prioritising the most dangerous and heavily used routes. The announcement has renewed debate about how the nation should invest in the roads on which millions of people depend every day.

Tobias Wren had never believed in anything he couldn't film, so when his friends dared him to mock the old ritual at Hollow Creek, he grabbed his phone and grinned. The ritual was simple, according to the faded pamphlet in the general store: at midnight, stand in the circle of stones, speak your own name three times, and wait for the answer. Tobias thought it was the most ridiculous thing he had ever heard.

His friends, Dana and Marcus, stayed by the car while he walked the muddy path into the trees. The night air smelled of wet leaves and something sweeter underneath, like flowers left too long in a vase. The stones were older than he expected, moss-covered and leaning like tired old men around a fire pit with no fire.

He set his phone on a rock to record and stepped into the circle. "Okay, spirits of Hollow Creek," he said loudly, mocking the pamphlet's solemn tone. "I'm Tobias Wren, and I'm not scared of you." He laughed, then said it again in a silly voice, and once more for good measure.

The silence that followed was too complete. Even the crickets had stopped.

Then something answered, not from the trees but from inside the circle, in a voice that sounded like his own, only colder. "Tobias Wren," it said. "Thank you for calling me."

He laughed again, but it came out thin. He reached for his phone, but the rock beside him was empty. The recording light was gone. He turned around and saw the path behind him had vanished under a crawl of pale roots.

Dana and Marcus were honking the horn somewhere far off, the sound muffled as if through water. Tobias shouted for them, and his voice came back to him from every direction at once, layered and overlapping, a chorus of men who all sounded like him.

"You should not have mocked the circle," said the voice again. "Mockery is a kind of invitation."

He told himself it was a trick, some local prank set up by bored teenagers with a speaker and a fog machine. He searched the ground for wires and found only stone and moss. The air grew heavier, pressing against his chest like a hand.

The first thing he noticed was that the stones were no longer leaning. They had straightened, and each one bore a shallow carving at its base, a face with its mouth open. He had walked past those carvings without seeing them, and now he saw that every face had his nose, his crooked eyebrow, his nervous half-smile.

"We keep names," the voice said gently. "We keep everything that is spoken here. Yours was spoken three times."

Tobias fell to his knees, scraping his palms on the cold ground. He tried to say that he was sorry, that it had been a joke, that he would leave and never come back. The words came out, but they came out in the voice from inside the circle, and he realized with horror that his own name no longer belonged only to him.

Back at the car, Dana and Marcus waited until dawn. They heard the horn of a passing logging truck and went looking for help. When the sheriff's deputies walked the path at sunrise, they found the circle of stones standing tall in the mist.

In the center lay Tobias's phone, its screen still glowing with a recording that ran for three seconds and then went black. The deputies watched it once, and then they did not watch it again. The last frame showed the stones behind him, with one face carved fresh at the base of the nearest stone.

It bore a mouth stretched wide in a silent scream, and beneath it, cut neatly into the rock, were three words: TOBIAS WREN, KEPT.

The town of Hollow Creek still tells the story, and the pamphlet is still in the general store. Nobody there mocks the circle anymore, and nobody speaks their own name at midnight near the trees. Some of the older residents say that if you walk past the stones in the early morning, you can hear a young man's voice answer when you call out your name.

The Face on Mars, first photographed by NASA's Viking 1 orbiter in 1976, quickly captured the public imagination as a possible sign of an ancient civilization. Its appearance, a rough humanlike visage in the Cydonia region, seemed to suggest deliberate construction. However, decades of higher-resolution imaging and careful analysis have shown that the Face is a natural geological formation, shaped by erosion and light conditions rather than by any intelligent builders. The earliest images were low in resolution, and the human mind is strongly inclined to perceive faces in ambiguous shapes, a tendency known as pareidolia. When the Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft imaged the feature in 1998 and 2001 with far greater detail, the supposed eyes, nose, and mouth resolved into irregular hills, ridges, and shadows. The Mars Orbiter Camera photographs showed that the so-called face was simply one mesa among many similar landforms in the region. Geologists have noted that the Cydonia area contains numerous mesas and buttes formed through the long process of wind and water erosion acting on layered sediment and volcanic rock. These landforms share structural features with other eroded hills across the Martian surface, which indicates a common natural origin. Shadows play a critical role in how the Face appears, and the apparent features change dramatically depending on the angle of sunlight at the time an image is taken. In images captured under different lighting conditions, the facial outline becomes far less distinct or disappears altogether. This sensitivity to illumination is a hallmark of natural relief rather than of purposeful sculpture, which would typically show consistent and symmetrical detail. The 2001 high-resolution images revealed that the Face's symmetry is only approximate, with asymmetrical features that a deliberate designer would be unlikely to leave. Additionally, no evidence of tools, debris patterns, or construction materials has been found around the formation. The surrounding terrain shows no signs of organized engineering, such as roads, foundations, or regular geometric layouts. Scientists studying Mars have also established that the planet has a long history of geological activity, including volcanism, impact cratering, and flowing water in its distant past. These processes are fully capable of producing irregular hills that can be interpreted as faces by an observer. Taken together, the physical evidence points consistently toward a natural explanation. The Face on Mars is therefore best understood as a remarkable example of how geology and human perception can intersect to produce compelling but misleading images. Recognizing this distinction is an important lesson in scientific reasoning, showing why careful measurement should always be weighed against first impressions.

An optimistic outlook can be one of the most valuable tools a student carries into school, and its effects reach far beyond a single good grade. Optimism is the tendency to expect that effort will lead to positive results, and that setbacks are temporary rather than permanent. Research in psychology has linked this expectation to stronger academic performance, greater persistence, and better emotional health. Understanding why this is so helps explain why cultivating a hopeful mindset is worth the effort.

Achievement begins with persistence, and optimism fuels persistence. A student who believes that hard work will eventually pay off is more likely to keep studying after a disappointing test. By contrast, a student who assumes that failure reflects a fixed lack of ability may give up early. Optimistic students tend to treat mistakes as information, asking what went wrong and what to try next. This habit of learning from errors compounds over time, producing steady gains that talent alone rarely achieves.

Optimism also shapes how students approach challenges. Difficult assignments can feel overwhelming, but a hopeful student is more likely to break them into manageable steps and begin. Starting is often the hardest part of productivity, and optimism lowers the barrier by making progress feel possible. Confidence in eventual success encourages students to set clear goals and track their advancement. Over weeks and months, these small, consistent actions add up to substantial accomplishment.

The benefits of optimism extend into productivity more broadly. Optimistic people often manage their time with greater intention, because they believe their choices matter. They are more likely to plan ahead, seek help when needed, and recover quickly after distractions. Their energy is spent on solving problems rather than worrying about them. This focus allows them to accomplish more with the same amount of time and effort.

Emotional well-being is perhaps the most important, and least discussed, benefit of an optimistic outlook. Students face stress from exams, social pressures, and uncertainty about the future, and optimism can act as a buffer against these pressures. Hopeful students tend to report lower levels of anxiety and depression, partly because they interpret difficulties as temporary and manageable. This emotional resilience helps them bounce back from disappointment without lasting damage to their self-esteem. A calmer mind is also better able to concentrate and remember what it learns.

Optimism and well-being reinforce each other in a positive cycle. When students feel emotionally steady, they are more willing to take on challenges, which produces success, which in turn strengthens their hopeful expectations. Teachers, parents, and peers can encourage this cycle by recognizing effort as well as results and by framing mistakes as opportunities to grow. Schools that emphasize growth over rigid ranking help students build the confidence that optimism requires.

It is important to note that optimism does not mean ignoring real problems or pretending that everything will turn out well without effort. Unrealistic positivity can lead to complacency, and students still need honest feedback to improve. The most useful form of optimism is grounded in reality: it accepts difficulties while maintaining belief in one's capacity to respond to them. This balanced hopefulness supports both good judgment and good spirits.

In the end, an optimistic outlook offers students a practical advantage. It sustains effort through setbacks, makes challenges feel manageable, and protects emotional health under pressure. Students who cultivate this mindset are not guaranteed success, but they give themselves the best chance to learn, grow, and thrive. Optimism, in this sense, is less a gift that some people are born with and more a habit that anyone can practice.

School-based after-school programs offer students a valuable opportunity to grow academically, socially, and personally beyond the regular school day. When students have access to structured support and enrichment, they can strengthen their skills, explore new interests, and build confidence in ways that classroom time alone may not allow. One of the most important benefits is academic help. Many students struggle with particular subjects, and after-school tutoring gives them time to ask questions, review difficult material, and catch up without feeling rushed. Teachers and tutors can also identify learning gaps early and address them before they grow into larger problems. Enrichment activities add another dimension to these programs. Clubs in science, art, music, coding, and debate allow students to pursue passions that may not fit into a crowded daily schedule. These experiences can spark curiosity and encourage students to think about future careers or hobbies they might never have considered. After-school programs also provide a safe and supervised environment for students during hours when they might otherwise be unsupervised. This structure gives working families peace of mind and reduces the risk of students getting involved in unsafe or unproductive activities. Beyond supervision, the programs foster meaningful relationships between students and adults. Mentors who take an interest in a student's progress can become role models and trusted advisors. Students who feel known and supported at school are often more engaged, more motivated, and more likely to attend regularly. Social development is another important outcome. Group projects, team activities, and shared goals teach students how to cooperate, communicate, and resolve conflicts. These skills carry over into the classroom and into adult life. Confidence grows as well, since students who experience success in a new activity often begin to believe they can achieve more. Equity is also a key consideration. Students from low-income households may lack access to private tutoring, music lessons, or extracurricular camps that their wealthier peers can afford. School-based programs help level the playing field by offering these opportunities at little or no cost. In this way, they can narrow achievement gaps and expand opportunity for students who need it most. Finally, these programs benefit the broader school community. Engaged students tend to have better attitudes toward learning, which can improve the classroom environment for everyone. Families often feel more connected to the school when their children are thriving in these programs. In conclusion, school-based after-school programs provide academic support, enrichment, safety, mentorship, and equal access to opportunity. Investing in them is an investment in the futures of students and the communities they will one day lead.

Should schools operate year-round, or should they keep the traditional academic calendar? This question has divided parents, educators, and policymakers for decades. Traditional calendars, with a long summer break and shorter breaks throughout the year, have deep roots in American history, largely shaped by agricultural needs when children were required on farms during the harvest. Today, that rationale has faded, yet the calendar remains. Year-round schooling offers an alternative that spreads instructional time more evenly across the year. Supporters argue that this approach can address some of the most persistent problems in modern education. Among the strongest arguments for year-round schooling is the problem of summer learning loss. Researchers have long observed that many students, particularly those from lower-income households, lose ground in reading and mathematics over the long summer break. Shorter, more frequent breaks may reduce this decline because students spend less time away from structured learning. Teachers also report spending the first several weeks of each new school year reviewing material that students forgot over the summer. Year-round calendars could return that time to new instruction. Advocates also point to the benefits of more frequent breaks for student and teacher well-being. Shorter breaks spaced throughout the year may give students regular opportunities to rest and recover, which could reduce burnout and stress. Teachers, who often face heavy workloads, might also benefit from periodic time off that allows them to recharge without the long gap that can disrupt continuity in classrooms. Some families find that a schedule with predictable intervals of rest is easier to plan around than a single long summer. Financial considerations form another part of the debate. Year-round schools can make more efficient use of buildings and facilities, since they can stagger breaks so that only a portion of the student body is away at any time. In some districts, this has allowed schools to accommodate more students without constructing new buildings. Supporters argue that this efficiency can be especially valuable in crowded urban districts where space is limited. However, opponents raise serious concerns, and these deserve careful attention. The traditional summer break is a valuable time for many families. It allows children to travel, participate in camps, volunteer, work summer jobs, and spend unstructured time with relatives. Critics argue that a year-round calendar can make these experiences harder to arrange, especially for families who rely on summer programs or who want to coordinate vacations. Changing the calendar can also create logistical burdens for working parents, who may struggle to find childcare during the shorter, more frequent breaks. Opponents also note that the evidence on academic outcomes is mixed. Some studies have found modest gains in achievement for students in year-round schools, while others have found little difference compared to traditional schedules. Much of the research is complicated by the fact that year-round schools often differ in other ways, such as funding, class size, or student demographics. Because of these complications, it is difficult to say with confidence that the calendar alone produces better results. A further concern is the cost and disruption of transition. Switching from a traditional to a year-round schedule requires adjustments to transportation, food service, staffing contracts, and extracurricular activities. Teachers may need to renegotiate agreements, and families must reorganize their routines. These costs can be substantial, and they may outweigh the benefits if the change is not carefully planned and widely supported by the community. Ultimately, the choice between year-round and traditional calendars may depend less on a single right answer than on local circumstances. A district with overcrowded buildings, significant summer learning loss, and community support for the change may find year-round schooling to be a sensible choice. A district where families depend heavily on summer programs and where the academic benefits are uncertain may be better served by keeping the traditional calendar. Whatever the decision, it should rest on evidence, honest discussion with families and educators, and a clear understanding of what the community hopes schooling will achieve. The calendar is a tool, and its value lies in how well it serves students.

Illicit foreign wealth is inflating London's luxury property market, and campaigners are now calling for estate agents to be required to report suspicious transactions. Anti-corruption groups say that high-value homes in areas such as Mayfair, Knightsbridge and Kensington have long attracted buyers whose money may have originated from corruption, embezzlement or other crimes. Many of these purchases are made through shell companies or trusts, which can hide the true identity of the owner. Critics argue that this practice distorts prices, pushing up values for ordinary homeowners and first-time buyers who cannot compete with cash-rich overseas purchasers. Under current rules, estate agents are regulated as part of anti-money laundering frameworks, but many are not obliged to file formal suspicious activity reports unless they are directly involved in a transaction. Campaigners say this gap allows warning signs to go unreported. Proposals under discussion would require agents to flag unusual payment methods, opaque ownership structures and buyers with links to sanctioned or high-risk jurisdictions. Supporters argue that stronger reporting duties would help law enforcement trace the proceeds of crime and deter money from being parked in UK property. Industry representatives have raised concerns about the added compliance burden, particularly for smaller firms, and warned against creating a system that places excessive responsibility on frontline staff. Government officials have said they are reviewing the evidence and considering further measures to improve transparency in the property sector. Transparency advocates maintain that the existing register of overseas entities has been a useful step but has not gone far enough to tackle the problem. Whether the government will act on the calls remains uncertain, but pressure for change is growing as the scale of the issue becomes clearer.

Corwin Vance had been apprenticed to the Guildhouse of Ash for six years, and in all that time he had never once cast a spell that worked on the first try. His classmates called him the Sparrow, not kindly. His fingers trembled when he drew sigils, and his ink always smudged.

Across the courtyard stood Idris Thorne, the prodigy. At fourteen, Idris could ignite a lantern from across a room without speaking a word. The masters spoke of him in the same tone they reserved for weather and the stars. Everyone agreed the Ash Trial would belong to him.

The Ash Trial was an ancient contest held once a generation. Each candidate was given a sealed iron box and one hour to unlock it using only magic. The box contained a single flame, and whoever could draw it out without burning themselves would be named Warden of the Guildhouse.

Idris stepped up first. He wove a torrent of light around the box, his hands blazing with power, and the iron groaned and glowed red. The masters nodded. Then the lock flared, sparks scattered across the flagstones, and the box remained shut. Idris swore, his face pale with frustration, and sat down hard on the bench.

Corwin's turn came with the bell. He stared at the box for a long time. Everyone else had treated it as a wall to break through. Corwin noticed instead the faint silver thread running along its seam, thinner than a hair, the kind of pattern he had always traced out of boredom in the margins of his notebooks.

He had spent years tracing those threads because his own spells kept failing and he needed to understand why. Every failed working left a faint residue, a kind of map of where the magic had gone wrong. Corwin had learned to read these maps the way other students read textbooks. He knew that magic in the Guildhouse did not move in a straight line. It followed grain, like wood.

He pressed one finger lightly to the silver thread and whispered the smallest possible word, the one his first teacher had used to test whether a sigil was alive. The thread brightened, and a chain of faint lights ran away from his fingertip, looping through the iron like a river finding its bed.

Corwin realized the box was not locked by force at all. It was locked by a sequence, a chain of seven inverted signs layered beneath the surface, each one holding the next in place. Brute strength only tightened the chain. The key was to unravel it from the end, not the beginning.

He began to draw. His hands did tremble, and the first sigil smudged as always, but he did not stop to correct it. He let the smudge become part of the pattern, bending the flaw toward the silver grain. The second sign took him a quarter hour, and the third came easier, as though the box were guiding his hand.

The crowd began to murmur when the fourth sign lit without sparks. Idris leaned forward from his bench, frowning in confusion. The masters exchanged glances. Corwin felt the warmth of the flame inside the box rising to meet his work, the way a sleeper turns toward a voice.

By the sixth sign he could hear the box humming, a soft note like a struck bell held too long. He had only minutes left, and his palms were slick with sweat. The seventh sign was the hardest, a knot of overlapping lines that most mages would have needed a week to parse. Corwin closed his eyes, traced the grain one more time, and let his understanding carry the last stroke.

The box clicked open.

Inside lay the flame, small and steady, waiting. Corwin reached in and lifted it out with two fingers, and it did not burn him. The courtyard fell silent, then erupted into shouts.

Idris stood slowly, looking at the open box and then at Corwin with an expression that was half envy and half something like respect. "How?" he asked quietly.

Corwin shrugged, suddenly embarrassed by the attention. "I stopped trying to force it," he said. "I just listened to where it wanted to go."

The masters conferred briefly, then the eldest among them stepped forward and placed a silver ring on Corwin's finger. "The Warden is not the strongest mage," she said. "The Warden is the one who sees what the rest of us miss."

That night, Corwin sat alone in the library with his notebooks open, adding a new page of silver threads and smudged sigils. Somewhere below, Idris was still practicing his lightning spells, and Corwin could hear the crackle through the stone. For the first time in six years, he did not feel like a sparrow. He felt like a man who had found the shape of the world's hidden rules, and who knew now how to bend them.

This manuscript presents an automated approach to classifying radiology reports that combines an enhanced biomedical language model with an attention mechanism, addressing a practical need for scalable clinical text processing. The problem is well motivated, as manual labeling of radiology reports is time-consuming and limits the development of clinical decision support tools. The authors situate their work reasonably within the existing literature on biomedical language models, though the related work section could more directly compare against recent domain-specific transformers to clarify the specific gain offered by their enhancements. The architecture description is clear in its overall design, but several details, including the exact form of the enhancement to the base model and the attention formulation, would benefit from equations and pseudocode to allow reproduction. The experimental evaluation reports improvements in standard metrics such as precision, recall, and F1, which is encouraging, yet the paper would be stronger with confidence intervals or repeated runs across random seeds to establish that the gains are statistically meaningful. The dataset description should specify the source institution, report types, label schema, and annotation procedure, along with inter-annotator agreement, since these factors strongly affect generalizability. Ablation studies isolating the contribution of the enhanced language model versus the attention mechanism are needed to support the central claims about each component. The authors should also discuss error patterns qualitatively, particularly for rare or ambiguous findings, as these are where clinical utility is most often tested. Finally, the manuscript would benefit from a clearer discussion of limitations, including potential bias across patient populations and the need for external validation on data from other institutions before clinical deployment.

Should Schools Require Students to Join Extracurricular Activities?

Extracurricular activities are often described as an essential part of a well-rounded education. Sports teams, debate clubs, music ensembles, and science competitions teach skills that classrooms alone cannot always provide. Because of this, many schools have considered requiring students to take part in at least one activity. However, such a requirement raises serious questions about fairness, especially for students who already carry heavy responsibilities outside of school. Before any policy is adopted, it is worth examining whether a mandate would truly serve students or simply add another burden to their lives.

For many young people, family responsibilities are not a minor concern but a daily necessity. A student may be expected to care for younger siblings while a parent works a second job, or to help run a family business after classes end. Some students translate for relatives who speak little English, while others manage household chores that would otherwise go undone. A school requirement that ignores these realities could force such students to choose between their obligations at home and their obligations at school. Such a choice is not a fair one for a teenager to make.

Parental concerns also deserve serious attention. Many parents have legitimate reasons to be cautious about after-school programs, whether because of safety in certain neighborhoods, cultural expectations, religious commitments, or simply a desire to know where their child is at all hours. A compulsory activity might override these concerns without giving families a voice in the decision. Schools that wish to involve parents as partners should be wary of policies that treat family judgment as an obstacle rather than a valuable input. Respecting parental authority is part of respecting the community the school serves.

Transportation presents another practical barrier. Many students live far from school, and rural districts in particular may have limited bus service after the final bell. A student who must wait an hour for a ride, or who has no ride at all, faces real risks when activities run late into the evening. Traveling home in the dark can be unsafe, and some families simply cannot afford to drive their children back and forth. A requirement that does not account for these logistics may end up excluding the very students who most need the support that activities provide.

Supporters of mandatory participation make a reasonable argument. They point out that students who are pushed to try something new sometimes discover a passion they would never have found otherwise. Activities can build friendships, confidence, leadership skills, and a sense of belonging, which can be especially valuable for students who feel isolated. Some researchers have linked sustained involvement in extracurriculars to higher attendance and graduation rates. These benefits are real, and any honest discussion of the issue must acknowledge them.

Still, benefits that are available to all students are different from requirements imposed on all students. A middle path may serve everyone better than a strict mandate. Schools could offer a wide range of activities at different times, provide transportation stipends or late buses, and allow students to fulfill participation through family-approved options, such as community service, part-time work, or structured study. Such flexibility recognizes that engagement can take many forms and that students do not all start from the same place.

In the end, the goal of education is to help young people grow into capable and caring adults, and extracurricular activities are one important path toward that goal. Yet a requirement that disregards family duties, parental judgment, and the practical realities of travel home is unlikely to achieve it. Schools should instead focus on making activities welcoming, accessible, and worth choosing. When students want to participate, the benefits follow naturally. When they are forced, the experience may leave them resentful rather than enriched.

This manuscript examines how prosocial preferences and learned communication jointly shape cooperation in multi-agent negotiation games, a timely question given the growing use of learning agents in bargaining and resource-allocation settings. The authors frame the problem clearly, situating their work within the literature on social preferences in economics and emergent communication in multi-agent reinforcement learning. The motivation is convincing, and the introduction makes a reasonable case that the two factors have usually been studied in isolation. The research question is well defined, though the abstract could state the primary hypothesis more explicitly. The authors model negotiation as a repeated game with partial information, which is an appropriate choice for capturing the strategic tension between individual payoffs and joint welfare. The payoff structure is described in enough detail to reproduce the setup, which I appreciate. The prosocial preference parameter is introduced as a weighting between an agent's own reward and its partner's reward, a simple and interpretable formulation. However, the manuscript does not justify why this linear weighting is sufficient, and alternatives such as inequity aversion or reciprocity-based models are not discussed. The communication channel is implemented as a learned discrete message vocabulary, and the authors provide a reasonable account of how messages are trained through the policy gradient. The experimental design compares agents with and without prosocial preferences crossed with communication and no-communication conditions, which allows the interaction effect to be isolated. This factorial structure is a strength of the paper. The number of random seeds, however, is small for the claims being made, and the variance across runs is reported only in a single figure. Results show that prosocial preferences increase joint payoff in most configurations, and communication further improves cooperation when preferences are present. The effect sizes are meaningful, but the paper would benefit from confidence intervals and a formal statistical test for the interaction term. The authors also report that communication alone, without prosocial preferences, sometimes reduces payoff, an interesting finding that deserves deeper analysis. The manuscript offers a plausible explanation involving message-induced coordination on exploitative strategies, but this claim is supported only by anecdotal examples from the appendix. A quantitative analysis of message content and its correlation with outcomes would make this argument considerably stronger. The discussion section is thoughtful and acknowledges several limitations, including the restricted game family and the simplicity of the environment. I would encourage the authors to test their conclusions on at least one richer negotiation environment with asymmetric information. The related work section is thorough but occasionally lists papers without explaining how they differ from the present approach. Several figures are difficult to read at print size, particularly the message-frequency heatmaps, and axis labels should be enlarged. The writing is generally clear, though some sentences in the methods section are unnecessarily long and could be split for readability. The supplementary material includes hyperparameters, which supports reproducibility, but no code is provided at the time of review. Releasing the environment and training code would substantially increase the paper's value to the community. Overall, the study addresses an important question with a sound basic design and presents interesting preliminary findings. The central claims are plausible but require stronger statistical support and deeper analysis of the communication mechanism. I recommend a major revision before the manuscript is considered for publication.

The manuscript investigates parameter-efficient sparse convolution designs for deep neural networks and examines how sparsity patterns relate to model accuracy. The topic is timely, since sparse convolutions offer a practical route to reducing memory footprint and computation in convolutional architectures without abandoning the inductive biases that make them effective. The authors frame the problem clearly, situating their work within the broader literature on pruning, structured sparsity, and lottery-ticket-style sparse training. The motivation is persuasive, and the introduction does a reasonable job of explaining why the relationship between parameter count and accuracy deserves a more systematic treatment. However, the related work section is uneven, relying heavily on a small set of recent citations while underrepresenting earlier work on low-rank factorization and depthwise separable designs that address the same efficiency goals. A more thorough comparison of these alternatives would strengthen the positioning of the contribution. The paper proposes a taxonomy of sparse convolution designs, categorizing them by the granularity of sparsity, such as element-wise, channel-wise, and filter-wise patterns. This taxonomy is useful and easy to follow, and it provides a shared vocabulary that the community could adopt. That said, the boundaries between categories are sometimes blurred in practice, and several hybrid designs in the experiments do not fit cleanly into any one class. The authors should acknowledge this ambiguity explicitly. The experimental setup covers three benchmark datasets and four backbone architectures, which is a reasonable breadth for the scope claimed. Nevertheless, all datasets are image classification tasks at relatively small resolution, so the generality of the conclusions to detection, segmentation, or higher-resolution inputs remains untested. The authors should either temper their claims or include at least one experiment beyond classification. The training protocol is described in adequate detail, including learning rate schedules, batch sizes, and augmentation policies. However, the paper does not report the number of random seeds used for each configuration, and the reported accuracies appear to be single-run values. Given that differences between sparse designs are often a fraction of a percentage point, variance estimates are essential for judging whether the observed trends are meaningful. The central empirical claim is that accuracy degrades smoothly as parameter count decreases, with a sharp drop appearing only below a particular sparsity threshold. The figures supporting this claim are compelling and the trend is visually clear. Still, the threshold itself is identified somewhat informally, and the paper would benefit from a more principled method, such as fitting a piecewise model with a breakpoint and reporting confidence intervals on its location. The analysis of why certain sparsity patterns outperform others is the strongest part of the paper. The authors connect channel-wise sparsity to the preservation of feature diversity across layers, and they provide ablation evidence that supports this interpretation. The discussion of hardware implications is also valuable, since many sparse designs that look favorable on paper fail to deliver speedups on real accelerators. However, the latency measurements are reported on only one GPU model, and the authors should clarify whether their conclusions would hold on other hardware. The paper's treatment of the relationship between accuracy and parameter efficiency rests on the assumption that parameter count is the appropriate cost metric. In many deployment settings, floating-point operations or measured inference latency are more relevant, and these metrics do not always track parameter count. The authors partly address this in a supplementary table, but the main text should discuss the discrepancy more directly, since it affects how practitioners should interpret the results. Several figures would benefit from clearer labeling. In particular, the axis scales in the accuracy-versus-sparsity plots differ between panels, which makes visual comparison across architectures difficult. Consistent scaling or a shared legend would improve readability considerably. The captions also tend to restate the results rather than explain what the reader should look for, and a few captions omit the number of runs underlying each point. The writing is generally clear, though some sentences in the methods section are unnecessarily long and contain nested clauses that obscure the procedure. Tightening these passages would help reproducibility, which is already a strength given the code release mentioned in the abstract. The authors should confirm that the released code includes the exact sparsity masks and random seeds used in the reported experiments. The conclusion summarizes the findings accurately but overstates their generality in one place, claiming that the observed patterns hold across all convolutional architectures. The evidence covers only four backbones, all of which are residual or plain convolutional designs, and the claim should be restricted accordingly. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant question with a sensible experimental design and offers some genuinely useful insights about sparsity structure. Its main weaknesses are the limited task diversity, the absence of variance estimates, and several overstated generalizations. I recommend a major revision. With additional statistical rigor, a broader evaluation, and more careful framing of the conclusions, the work could make a solid contribution to the efficient deep learning literature.

Allowing students to use their phones during lunch and free periods while keeping them off during class time is a balanced policy that recognizes both the educational purpose of the classroom and the real social needs of young people. Schools exist first and foremost to teach, and the instructional period demands focused attention that a buzzing phone can easily disrupt. Research on attention suggests that even the presence of a phone on a desk can divide concentration, which is one reason many districts have moved toward clear no-phone rules during lessons. At the same time, students are not machines that should be expected to switch off their social lives for seven hours a day. Lunch and free periods offer a natural window where students can rest, talk with friends, and decompress after hours of demanding work. Phones are often the primary way teenagers stay in touch with family members, check on siblings, or coordinate after-school plans, and a total ban can leave them feeling cut off during the only unstructured time they have. Permitting phone use in these periods also treats students with a measure of trust and responsibility. Learning to manage one's own device use is itself an important skill, and a policy that asks students to switch off in class while allowing them to choose how to use free time gives them practice with self-regulation. Critics argue that even unstructured time can become a source of cyberbullying, unhealthy comparison, or endless scrolling, and these concerns deserve attention. Schools can address them by setting clear expectations about respectful behavior, encouraging students to use breaks for conversation or physical activity, and keeping open channels for reporting online harassment. Teachers can also model healthy habits by making sure free periods are not simply filled with screens. A policy of this kind works best when it is consistent, clearly communicated, and enforced fairly. When students understand that the rule exists to protect learning time while still honoring their need for connection, they are more likely to accept it. In the end, the balance between focus and freedom is not a compromise that weakens either goal but a practical arrangement that serves both. A school that protects instructional time while respecting students' breaks prepares young people not only to learn but to live thoughtfully in a world full of devices.

Reducing automobile use offers a wide range of benefits that extend across health, safety, finances, and the environment. Many people rely on cars for nearly every trip, yet the costs of this habit are often hidden in daily routines. By driving less and relying more on walking, cycling, public transit, and shared mobility, individuals and communities can improve their well-being in several important ways.

The health benefits are among the most immediate. Walking and cycling are forms of physical activity that help people maintain healthy weight, strengthen their hearts, and reduce the risk of chronic conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure. Commuting on foot or by bicycle can build exercise into everyday life without requiring a separate gym visit. In addition, less driving means less exposure to vehicle exhaust, which contains fine particles and nitrogen oxides linked to asthma and respiratory illness.

Safety also improves when fewer cars are on the road. Traffic collisions cause a significant number of injuries and deaths each year, and pedestrians and cyclists are especially vulnerable. Reducing the total number of vehicle trips lowers the chance of crashes, and communities that invest in safer streets for walking and cycling often see fewer serious accidents. Public transit, when well managed, is generally one of the safest ways to travel.

Financial advantages are equally compelling. Owning and operating a car involves costs for purchase or lease, insurance, fuel, maintenance, parking, and depreciation, which can add up to thousands of dollars annually. Households that drive less can redirect this money toward savings, housing, education, or other priorities. Walking, cycling, and transit are typically far cheaper, and they reduce the financial strain that high transportation costs place on lower-income families.

Environmental gains are perhaps the most widely recognized. Automobiles are a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, and driving less directly reduces the carbon dioxide that contributes to climate change. Fewer cars also mean less air pollution, cleaner water since less oil and debris wash off roads, and less land devoted to roads and parking lots. Communities with reduced car dependence tend to preserve more green space and support wildlife habitats.

Ultimately, reducing automobile use is not about eliminating cars entirely but about making more thoughtful choices about how we travel. Each trip taken on foot, by bicycle, or by transit contributes to a healthier body, a safer community, a stronger household budget, and a cleaner planet. These overlapping benefits show that changing transportation habits can produce advantages that reach far beyond the road itself.

Broccoli rabe, also known as rapini, is a leafy green vegetable that belongs to the turnip family, Brassicaceae, and is more closely related to turnips than to broccoli despite its name. It is believed to have originated in the Mediterranean region, where wild relatives of brassicas have grown for thousands of years, and it has been cultivated for centuries in Italy, where it remains a staple of regional cooking. The plant produces slender stems, leafy greens, and small clusters of buds that resemble tiny broccoli florets, which give it its common name. Its flavor is distinctly bitter and peppery, more pronounced than that of spinach or kale, and this bitterness is one of its most prized characteristics in traditional cuisine. In Italian cooking, broccoli rabe is often sautéed with garlic, olive oil, and red pepper flakes, and it is a classic pairing with sausage, as in the well-known dish orecchiette with sausage and rapini from Puglia. It also appears in pasta dishes, risottos, frittatas, and as a side vegetable alongside grilled meats and fish. Many cooks blanch the greens briefly in salted boiling water before finishing them in a pan, which tempers the bitterness and helps them keep a bright green color. To prepare it, trim the tough lower ends of the stems, rinse the greens thoroughly to remove grit, and cut them into manageable lengths. Cooking time is short; a few minutes of sautéing or blanching is usually enough to make the leaves tender while preserving some crunch in the stems. Broccoli rabe is low in calories yet provides a wide range of nutrients, including vitamins A, C, E, and K, along with folate and several B vitamins. It is also a good source of dietary fiber, calcium, iron, and potassium, which support digestion, bone health, and normal bodily functions. The vegetable contains glucosinolates, sulfur-containing compounds characteristic of cruciferous vegetables, which are studied for their potential role in supporting the body's natural detoxification processes. Its antioxidant content, including carotenoids and flavonoids, may help protect cells from oxidative stress. Because of its bitterness, some people find it an acquired taste, but pairing it with rich, salty, or acidic ingredients such as cheese, cured meats, lemon, or vinegar can balance its flavor. Broccoli rabe is widely available in the fresh produce sections of grocery stores during the cooler months, and it is best used within a few days of purchase. When selecting it, look for crisp, deeply colored leaves and firm stems without yellowing or wilting. Overall, broccoli rabe offers a flavorful, nutrient-dense addition to a wide variety of meals.

Bessie had always believed she was meant for something more than the milking stall. Each morning she watched the crows wheel above the pasture and dreamed of lights, of applause, of a stage where a cow could stand tall and be seen.

The farmer's daughter, Lila, often hummed while brushing Bessie's flank, and Bessie would lean into the rhythm as though it were music meant only for her.

One autumn afternoon, a sleek man in a pale suit climbed out of a silver car at the farm gate. He wore sunglasses though the sky was gray, and he carried a leather case that clicked when he set it down.

His name, he said, was Mr. Vance, and he represented a talent agency in the city. He had heard about a cow with an unusual gift, a cow who seemed to respond to melody.

Bessie's heart leapt. She stepped forward, eyes bright, and let out a low, trembling hum that rose and fell in the cool air.

Mr. Vance clapped slowly, his smile widening in a way that did not reach his eyes. Lila watched from the barn door, her brow creased with uncertainty.

He spoke to the farmer in hushed tones, pressing papers across the fence rail. Words like exclusive, contract, and generous drifted over the pasture.

The farmer signed without reading closely, eager for the money that promised to clear his debts. Lila tried to protest, but her father waved her silent.

That evening, Mr. Vance returned with a flatbed trailer and two men in gloves. Bessie was led up the ramp while she still believed she was going toward the spotlight.

The trailer rolled through the night, its engine droning, and Bessie hummed softly to herself to keep her courage up.

At the city warehouse, the lights were harsh and cold. There was no stage, only pens lined with concrete and a row of men with clipboards who spoke about weight and price.

Mr. Vance had not lied about one thing. Bessie was being displayed. But she was not being celebrated. She was being sold by the pound to the highest bidder.

She tried to hum again, but the sound caught in her throat. The men laughed at her, calling her a novelty, a gimmick, a joke that would fetch a fair price at market.

Days passed in the pen. Bessie stopped eating much. She stopped lifting her head when the buyers came through, stopped turning her ears toward voices.

She remembered Lila's humming and tried to recall the melody, but it slipped away like water through her hooves.

A buyer from a meatpacking firm came on the fourth morning, flipping through a ledger and making notes. Mr. Vance stood beside him, nodding and smiling as though he had done a favor for everyone involved.

Bessie no longer expected applause. She expected nothing at all. Her great dream had become a bright, empty room, and she had walked into it willingly.

The buyer tapped her flank, pronounced her healthy, and wrote a number on the page. Mr. Vance shook his hand and wished him a profitable season.

Bessie closed her eyes. Somewhere far away, she imagined the crows still wheeling over the green pasture, free and unbothered by ambition.

She did not hum again. The stage she had longed for had never existed, and the silence that settled over her was deeper than any she had known on the farm.

Choosing who we become is one of the most important decisions we can make, and it is one that many people never consciously consider. Much of our personality is shaped by family, friends, culture, and circumstance, yet we are not simply passive products of these forces. As we grow older, we gain the ability to reflect on the traits we have inherited and decide which ones to keep, which to refine, and which to let go. Being true to oneself means living in a way that matches our honest values rather than constantly bending to meet the expectations of others. When a person pretends to be someone else, they often feel tired, anxious, and disconnected from their own life. In contrast, someone who acts with authenticity tends to make decisions with greater confidence and clarity. Authenticity does not mean refusing to change, since a person who learns from experience and grows wiser is still being true to themselves. It also does not mean rejecting kindness or cooperation, because a genuine personality can be warm, generous, and considerate of others. Choosing our own personality requires courage, especially when friends or peers pressure us to conform. Yet the people who stand firm in their values often earn deeper respect and form more meaningful relationships. In the end, a life lived honestly is a life that belongs to the person living it.

Ray Dunning had not held a rifle in nine years, but when the delivery robot rolled past his porch that Tuesday morning, his hands went looking for one anyway. The machine was small and white, with a single amber light blinking on its back. It paused at the gate, as it always did, and waited for the latch to lift. Ray saw only a silhouette moving through the fog toward his wife's house, a shape that stopped too often and turned its head with too little warning. He remembered the dust of a village in another country, the stillness before a door opened, the way a shadow could become a man with a weapon in the time it took to blink. His heart hammered against his ribs as he gripped the porch rail, counting the seconds the way his sergeant had taught him. The robot beeped softly, a cheerful sound that meant nothing to him now. Ray lowered his voice and told it to stop, though it could not hear him over the wind. Then his daughter's car turned the corner, headlights sweeping across the yard, and the sound of her voice calling his name pulled him back to the porch, to the cold rail, to the present. The robot had already deposited its package and rolled quietly away. Ray stood there a long while, shaking, and finally understood that the threat had only ever been inside him.

Exploring How Elaboration Can Deepen Communication, Learning, and Personal Growth

Elaboration is the practice of adding detail, context, reasons, and examples to an idea so that it becomes richer and easier to understand. It is one of the most useful habits a person can develop, because it turns surface-level information into knowledge that holds together and can be used. When we elaborate, we move beyond simply stating a fact and begin to explain how it works, why it matters, and how it connects to what we already know.

In communication, elaboration helps listeners follow our thinking. A short statement such as "The project failed" leaves many questions open, while adding the causes, the lessons learned, and the next steps gives others a clear picture. Good elaboration anticipates what the listener might wonder and answers it before the question is asked. This makes conversations more efficient, reduces misunderstandings, and builds trust, since people can see the reasoning behind a claim.

Elaboration also strengthens learning. Psychologists who study memory have long observed that information connected to existing knowledge is easier to recall than isolated facts. When a student explains a concept in their own words, relates it to a familiar example, or asks how it might apply in a new situation, they build more pathways in memory. Each of these connections gives the mind another way to retrieve the idea later.

There are several practical techniques for elaboration. One is to ask "why" and "how" repeatedly about any statement you encounter. Another is to explain an idea to an imaginary listener who knows nothing about the subject. A third is to create analogies that link unfamiliar material to everyday experience. Writing a short summary and then expanding it with examples can also reveal gaps in understanding that were not obvious before.

Elaboration is not the same as adding noise. Padding a sentence with filler words or repeating the same point in different phrasing does not deepen meaning. True elaboration adds information, reasoning, or perspective that moves the idea forward. A useful test is to ask whether each added detail helps the reader or listener understand the point more fully.

The benefits extend beyond academic and professional settings into personal growth. Reflecting on experiences in detail, rather than merely recording that they happened, helps people notice patterns in their behavior and emotions. Someone who elaborates on a difficult conversation by considering what they felt, what the other person may have felt, and what they might do differently gains insight that a brief summary would miss. Over time, this kind of reflection builds self-awareness and resilience.

Elaboration also supports empathy. When we take the time to explain our perspective fully, we give others the material they need to understand us, and when we ask others to elaborate on theirs, we open the door to understanding views that differ from our own. Many disagreements persist simply because each side has only heard the shorthand version of the other's position.

Finally, elaboration is a habit that improves with practice. Beginners may find it tiring to expand every idea, but with repetition it becomes a natural way of thinking. Choosing one topic each day and examining it from several angles is a simple way to start. Over time, the habit of elaboration makes communication clearer, learning more lasting, and personal reflection more meaningful.
