This manuscript proposes a biologically inspired predictive-coding network for video prediction and evaluates whether its internal representations correspond to activity recorded from primate visual cortex. The question is timely and important, as it sits at the intersection of machine learning and computational neuroscience, and the authors are right to pursue a model that is both functional and neurally grounded. The paper is generally well motivated, and the core idea of using prediction error as the driving signal for hierarchical representation learning is a reasonable one given the predictive-coding literature. However, I have several concerns regarding the strength of the central claims, the rigor of the comparisons, and the clarity of presentation, which I detail below. In my assessment, the work is promising but requires substantial revision before its conclusions can be considered adequately supported.

The introduction does a reasonable job of situating the work within prior predictive-coding theories of cortical function, including the work of Rao and Ballard and subsequent extensions. The authors clearly articulate the gap they aim to fill: existing video prediction models are typically optimized for pixel-level accuracy without regard to biological plausibility, while neuroscience models of visual cortex often lack the capacity to process natural video. This framing is useful. That said, the related work section would benefit from a more systematic treatment of recent deep predictive models of neural responses, particularly those that have used self-supervised video objectives to explain temporal dynamics in cortex. Without this, it is difficult for the reader to judge how much of the proposed advance is novel.

The architecture description is detailed in parts but leaves important gaps. The paper specifies the hierarchical layout and the local learning rules, but the precise formulation of the error units, the update dynamics, and the number of inference iterations per frame are not fully stated in the main text. Reproducibility depends on these details, and I recommend that the authors move the complete equations and a pseudocode description into the main paper or a clearly referenced appendix. The authors should also justify the choice of recurrent connectivity and explain how temporal context is integrated across frames.

The training procedure and datasets are described adequately at a high level, but several questions remain. The authors should specify the exact video datasets used, their resolution and frame rate, the train-test splits, and whether any frames from the same clip appear in both training and evaluation sets. Information about compute budget, number of random seeds, and hyperparameter search procedures is also needed to assess the robustness of the reported results.

The baseline comparisons are the area of greatest concern. The paper compares the proposed network against a small set of models, but several strong and relevant baselines are absent, including recent convolutional and transformer-based video predictors and standard feedforward models whose intermediate layers have been used in neural-prediction studies. Without these comparisons, it is not possible to determine whether the predictive-coding mechanism itself contributes to the observed performance or whether the gains derive from architectural capacity or training differences. An ablation study removing the predictive-coding component while holding other factors constant would greatly strengthen the argument.

The primary prediction-accuracy results are reported as mean squared error and structural similarity on held-out video. These metrics are standard, and the proposed model shows improvements on several of them. However, the reported differences are often small, and the manuscript does not include confidence intervals or statistical tests. The authors should report variability across seeds and apply appropriate significance testing before claiming superiority.

The neural comparison constitutes the paper's central scientific claim, and here the evidence is less convincing than the framing suggests. The authors use representational similarity analysis and linear regression from model units to recorded neural responses to quantify correspondence. Linear predictivity scores are sensitive to the number of model features and to regularization choices, and the manuscript does not adequately control for these confounds. I recommend reporting noise-ceiling estimates for the neural data, so that readers can see how close any model comes to the reliability limit of the recordings, and comparing against null models with matched dimensionality.

The manuscript also reports that the predictive-coding model's representations correspond more closely to later visual areas than to early ones, and interprets this as evidence for hierarchical predictive processing. This interpretation is plausible but not uniquely supported. Many feedforward architectures show a similar gradient of correspondence along the cortical hierarchy, so the authors should explicitly test whether the predictive-coding model outperforms a matched feedforward control on the same layer-to-area mapping.

The discussion of biological plausibility is somewhat overstated. The model uses several mechanisms, such as non-local weight sharing and global normalization, that do not have clear counterparts in cortical circuitry. The authors acknowledge some of these limitations, but the abstract and conclusions describe the model as biologically inspired in terms that could mislead readers about the degree of correspondence. I recommend a more measured description and a dedicated paragraph enumerating the biological assumptions the model makes and those it violates.

The figures are generally clear, though several could be improved. The layer-wise correspondence plots lack error bars, and the color scales in the prediction-error visualizations are not consistent across panels, which complicates visual comparison. The caption for the architecture diagram omits the dimensionality of intermediate representations, which would help readers follow the model.

The writing is generally readable, but the manuscript contains several passages that are repetitive, and some technical terms are used before they are defined. A careful editorial pass would improve clarity. The authors should also ensure that all acronyms are defined at first use and that notation is consistent between the text and equations.

The limitations section is brief and should be expanded. In particular, the authors should discuss the restricted set of neural recordings, the possibility that the observed correspondence reflects shared low-level statistics of natural video rather than shared computational principles, and the extent to which results from a single species and recording modality can generalize.

The code and data availability statement is welcome, but the repository was not accessible at the time of review, and the authors should confirm that the released materials include trained weights, evaluation scripts, and the preprocessing pipeline needed to reproduce the main figures.

The ethics and data-use statement appears adequate, assuming the neural recordings were collected under the appropriate institutional approvals, and the authors should state these approvals explicitly in the methods section.

The conclusions are broadly consistent with the evidence presented, but they go beyond it in places. Statements that the model "explains" primate visual-cortex responses should be replaced with more precise language about predictive correspondence, given the limits of the analyses.

Overall, the paper addresses a worthwhile question and offers a potentially useful model. Its main weaknesses lie in insufficient baselines, limited statistical reporting, and an overstated neural interpretation. I recommend major revision. If the authors add the missing controls, report variability and noise ceilings, and temper their claims about biological correspondence, the contribution could be substantial and suitable for publication.

Digital tools have changed the way people manage their daily lives, making tasks that once took hours much faster and easier. Navigation apps help commuters find the best routes, while calendar and reminder applications keep busy schedules organized and reduce missed appointments. Online banking and payment services let people pay bills and track spending from home, saving time and making personal finances more transparent. Video calls and messaging platforms keep families and friends connected across long distances, which is especially valuable for those who live far from loved ones. However, these benefits depend on responsible use, such as protecting personal data, setting healthy limits on screen time, and verifying information before sharing it, so that technology truly serves everyday life.

Parents at Redhill Academy have voiced strong objections to the cost of the school's new mandatory branded trousers and skirts, which were introduced at the start of the autumn term. The uniform, featuring the school's crest and a specific shade of navy, must be purchased from a single supplier, with some parents reporting that a full set of items can cost well over a hundred pounds. Many families say the price is difficult to afford, particularly those with more than one child attending the academy. One parent, who asked not to be named, said she had been forced to choose between buying new uniform and covering other household bills this month. Others argued that the requirement to buy from one approved supplier removes the option of shopping around for cheaper alternatives. The school's governing body has defended the decision, saying the branded items help create a unified identity and that the supplier was chosen after a competitive tender process. A spokesperson said the academy had also set aside funds to help families who cannot afford the full cost, though parents have questioned how easy that support is to access. Several parents said they had not been given enough notice of the change before the new term began. Some have called for the school to allow unbranded trousers and skirts in a plain navy shade that meets the general dress code. Local councillors have said they will raise the matter at the next education committee meeting. The academy has agreed to review its uniform policy in the coming weeks, but no firm decision has yet been announced. Parents' groups say they will continue to press for a more affordable solution. The dispute has highlighted a wider debate about the rising cost of school uniforms and whether schools should mandate branded clothing that can only be bought from specific suppliers.

The manuscript proposes a difference-of-convex (DC) optimization framework for pruning dense neural network layers, and it addresses a relevant problem: reducing model size while retaining accuracy. The authors formulate pruning as a DC program, which allows the non-convex sparsity-inducing penalty to be handled through a sequence of convex subproblems with monotone decrease of the objective. The core algorithmic idea is sound and builds sensibly on prior work in DC algorithms for sparse regression. The complexity analysis is a strength, as the authors give per-iteration cost bounds in terms of layer width and number of samples and discuss how these scale to realistic layer sizes. However, the convergence guarantee is stated only to a critical point, and the manuscript should be clearer about how often the iterates reach a stationary point in the non-convex setting that practitioners actually encounter. The generalization analysis relies on a Rademacher complexity bound that depends on the norm of the pruned weights, and the link between the pruning procedure and the effective hypothesis class is not made fully rigorous. The authors should state explicitly whether the bound holds uniformly over all sparsity levels or only at the sparsity selected by the algorithm, since selection on training data can invalidate the bound. The experiments cover two image classification benchmarks and one tabular dataset, which is a reasonable starting point but limits claims of general applicability. Comparisons are made against magnitude pruning and a single structured pruning baseline, and stronger recent baselines, such as iterative lottery-ticket style methods or second-order pruning, would make the empirical case more convincing. Wall-clock time results are reported only for the pruning step and not for end-to-end retraining, so the practical efficiency claim in the title needs qualification. The ablation on the DC penalty parameter is informative, though the sensitivity to its initialization is not discussed and could affect reproducibility. Hyperparameter choices and random seeds are described, but code availability is not mentioned, and releasing an implementation would substantially aid verification. The related work section is thorough in its treatment of sparse regression but thinner on the neural network pruning literature from the past few years. Figures are clear, though the axis scales in the accuracy-versus-sparsity plots make small differences between methods hard to judge. The writing is generally precise, and the theorem statements are well organized, with proofs deferred to the appendix in an acceptable manner. Overall, the paper offers a technically interesting contribution with a mostly sound analysis, but the claims of efficiency and generalization should be tempered and supported by broader experiments and clearer theoretical caveats. I recommend a major revision before the work can be considered for publication.

Paraguay's Senate Prepares to Impeach President Fernando Lugo After Deadly Land Eviction Clashes

Paraguay's Senate moved this week to begin impeachment proceedings against President Fernando Lugo, following a violent confrontation over a land eviction that left several people dead. The clashes broke out in the northern region of Curuguaty, where police were carrying out a court-ordered eviction of families occupying a large estate. Officials said the operation turned violent when shots were fired, and both police officers and local farmers were among the casualties. The deaths quickly became a political flashpoint, with opposition lawmakers accusing the government of mishandling the operation and failing to protect public order. Supporters of the farmers, meanwhile, said the families had been left with no alternative and called the eviction an injustice rooted in Paraguay's long-running dispute over land ownership. Land distribution has been one of the most contentious issues in Paraguay for decades, with a small number of large landowners controlling a substantial share of the country's farmland. Lugo, a former Catholic bishop who took office in 2008 promising social reform, had made land redistribution a central pledge of his presidency. Critics argued that his government had not delivered on that promise and that the eviction exposed the tensions between his supporters and his political opponents. Opposition leaders in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies called for an immediate investigation into the events and demanded accountability from senior officials. Several legislators said that the violence had damaged public confidence in the government's ability to maintain order. Lugo's administration defended the legal basis for the eviction, stating that the occupation of the property had been declared illegal by the courts. Government spokespeople also expressed regret over the loss of life and pledged a full inquiry into how the confrontation had unfolded. The president's allies warned that impeachment would be an overreach and could destabilize Paraguay's democratic institutions at a fragile moment. Human rights groups called on all parties to ensure that the investigation was thorough, impartial, and transparent. They urged authorities to examine the conduct of both security forces and the occupiers. Observers noted that the Senate's move, if it advanced, would require a formal vote and would test the balance of power between the executive and legislative branches. Political analysts said the outcome would depend heavily on the strength of the evidence and on the shifting alliances within Congress. The Senate is expected to hold further sessions in the coming days to decide how to proceed. Lawmakers have not yet set a firm timetable for a vote. Farmers' organizations in the affected region said they would continue to press for a fair resolution to the land dispute. Many residents of Curuguaty expressed grief and anger, saying the deaths had left families devastated. Local churches held vigils for the victims, drawing crowds from across the community. The incident has drawn national and international attention to the unresolved question of land rights in Paraguay. Whatever the Senate decides, the episode is likely to shape the political debate in the country for some time.

A military helicopter crashed in Yemen this week, killing all crew members on board, according to officials familiar with the incident. The aircraft went down in a region already torn apart by the country's ongoing civil war between the internationally recognized government and Houthi forces. Military officials said the cause of the crash is under investigation, and they have not ruled out mechanical failure or hostile action. The crash comes as Yemen's humanitarian crisis deepens, with millions of people facing food insecurity, a collapsing health system, and widespread displacement. Aid agencies have repeatedly warned that the conflict has left much of the population dependent on humanitarian assistance, and that access to remote areas is often restricted by fighting. Military aviation is a critical lifeline in the conflict, used for troop movements, medical evacuations, and resupply missions to isolated garrisons. Losing an aircraft and its crew is a significant blow to forces already stretched thin by years of fighting. Local residents in the affected area described hearing a loud explosion before seeing smoke rise above nearby hills. Families of the crew members have been notified, and the names of the dead are expected to be released after the next of kin are informed. Analysts say the incident underscores the fragility of Yemen's security situation and the difficulty of achieving a lasting peace settlement. Efforts by UN envoys to restart political negotiations have repeatedly stalled, leaving the country's civilians to bear the brunt of the continued violence.

Newly released correspondence has shed light on objections raised in 2015 by Arlene Foster, then a senior figure in the Democratic Unionist Party and later First Minister of Northern Ireland, to Scotland's plans to recognise civil partnerships formed in Northern Ireland as same-sex marriages. The letters, made public recently, show the concerns Foster communicated about how the proposal would affect the legal status of couples who had entered civil partnerships under Northern Ireland law. At the time, same-sex marriage was not available in Northern Ireland, while civil partnerships were, creating a gap that Scottish lawmakers sought to address. Foster's objections centred on the principle that the recognition of such partnerships should not be altered in a way that the Northern Ireland Assembly had not decided. Supporters of the Scottish proposal argued that it would give legal clarity and fairness to couples who had moved between the two countries. Critics of Foster's position, including some equality campaigners, said her stance reflected broader resistance within unionist politics to same-sex marriage. The correspondence also reveals the diplomatic and constitutional sensitivities involved when legislation in one part of the United Kingdom touches on matters devolved to another. Officials in both administrations had been coordinating on the question, and the letters offer a window into the positions taken during those discussions. Northern Ireland would not legalise same-sex marriage until 2019, when Westminster intervened to bring it into effect after the devolved institutions had been suspended. Foster, who became DUP leader and First Minister, has since addressed her record on LGBT issues, although the released letters have drawn renewed attention to her earlier views. A spokesperson for the DUP was not immediately available to comment on the documents. The release has prompted calls from some MLAs for further transparency about how the matter was handled at the time. Campaign groups said the letters underline the importance of equal treatment for couples regardless of where in the UK they live. The full extent of the documentation and any further responses from the parties involved are expected to be reported as more material becomes available.

The manuscript proposes dilated convolutional networks as parallelizable alternatives to recurrent models for reading comprehension and other sequence-processing tasks, a motivation that is timely given the computational bottlenecks of sequential recurrence. The authors clearly articulate the core idea, which is that exponentially increasing dilation rates can give convolutional layers a large receptive field over the input without the training-time serialization that limits recurrent architectures. The experimental setup is a strength, as the comparison spans multiple benchmarks and reports both accuracy and wall-clock training speed, which is the right pair of metrics for a claim about efficiency. However, the baselines deserve scrutiny, since the recurrent models appear to be trained with hyperparameters that were not tuned to the same budget as the proposed architecture, which could overstate the gap in accuracy. The ablation on dilation schedules is informative, but the authors should also report variance across random seeds, as single-run differences on reading comprehension benchmarks are often within the range of run-to-run noise. The discussion of why dilated convolutions succeed on some tasks and underperform on others is thin, and a more careful analysis of failure cases, particularly for questions requiring long-range coreference, would strengthen the paper considerably. The related work section covers the main convolutional and recurrent sequence models adequately but omits some relevant recent work on attention-based alternatives, which weakens the positioning of the contribution. The reproducibility statement is welcome, though the authors should release the exact preprocessing pipeline, since tokenization choices can shift results on these benchmarks. Overall, the paper is a useful empirical contribution whose central efficiency claim is likely sound, but the accuracy comparisons need stronger controls and statistical reporting before the conclusions can be considered firmly established. I recommend a major revision.

The manuscript addresses a timely problem: generating diverse yet plausible future trajectories for safety-critical prediction, such as autonomous driving and pedestrian motion forecasting, where rare but dangerous outcomes must be represented. The authors propose using Determinantal Point Processes to enforce diversity among sampled trajectories while retaining plausibility through a learned generative model, which is a sensible combination of ideas. The motivation is clearly articulated, and the introduction does a good job situating the work relative to multimodal forecasting and diversity-promoting sampling methods. The mathematical formulation of the DPP kernel, including how quality and similarity terms are combined, is presented with reasonable clarity, though the derivation of the marginal and conditional sampling procedures would benefit from more explicit steps. The experimental evaluation covers multiple benchmarks, which strengthens the claims, but the choice of baselines is somewhat narrow, and several strong recent diversity-aware generators are absent from the comparisons. The metrics emphasize coverage and minimum-over-samples error, yet the paper provides limited analysis of plausibility beyond likelihood-based measures, which may not reflect physical or behavioral realism. The authors should clarify how safety-critical events are identified and whether the reported improvements hold specifically on the rare, high-risk subset rather than on average. Ablation studies on the diversity weight and kernel bandwidth are helpful, but the sensitivity results suggest the method may require careful tuning that is not fully discussed. Computational cost is mentioned only briefly, and a more detailed comparison of sampling latency, which matters for real-time deployment, would be valuable. The qualitative visualizations are informative, though the selection of examples appears curated, and additional failure cases would give a more balanced picture. The related work section is thorough in its treatment of trajectory forecasting but could engage more deeply with the literature on safety evaluation and adversarial scenario generation. Reproducibility is partially supported by the stated hyperparameters, but the absence of released code or precise training details limits independent verification. The writing is generally clear, though some notation is overloaded and several figures lack complete captions. Statistical significance testing across random seeds is not reported, making it difficult to judge whether the gains over baselines are robust. The authors should also discuss potential misuse risks, since generating plausible hazardous trajectories could be repurposed for adversarial testing of deployed systems. Overall, the contribution is incremental but useful, and the paper would be considerably strengthened by broader baselines, significance analysis, and a clearer treatment of rare-event evaluation. I recommend a major revision before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Segregated Libraries and Librarians in Tampa and Clearwater, Florida

Before the mid-twentieth century, public libraries in Florida were segregated by race, and African American residents were largely denied access to the main library facilities in cities like Tampa and Clearwater. Black Floridians therefore built their own reading spaces, often through churches, fraternal organizations, schools, and community clubs. These informal collections laid the groundwork for later formal branch libraries. In Tampa, the African American community in the Central Avenue and Ybor City neighborhoods relied heavily on such self-organized resources during the Jim Crow era. Black librarians and volunteers played a central role in maintaining these collections, often with limited funding and few books. Their work was an act of both education and resistance, affirming the value of literacy in a society that sought to restrict it. In Clearwater, African American residents similarly depended on segregated facilities and community initiatives to meet their reading needs. Local schools for Black students frequently had small library rooms that served as the primary access point to books for children and families. Librarians in these settings were frequently teachers or community members who took on library duties in addition to other responsibilities. Many worked without professional training in library science, since institutions that trained Black librarians were limited in number and southern access to them was restricted. The American Library Association's own segregation practices meant that Black librarians were often excluded from its meetings and professional networks. Segregated branches were typically housed in older, smaller, or repurposed buildings and were given fewer resources than white branches. Book collections at these branches were often outdated, with donated or discarded materials making up a large share of holdings. Despite these inequities, the branches became vital centers for civic life, hosting study groups, storytime, and community meetings. The librarians who staffed them became respected figures who guided readers, supported students, and preserved local history. Documentation of their contributions is incomplete, and historians have had to rely on oral histories, newspaper accounts, and church and school records to reconstruct this past. Such records reveal the persistence of community leaders who advocated for better facilities and equal access. Legal challenges to segregation in the 1950s and 1960s gradually opened formerly white-only library spaces to Black patrons. Integration did not immediately bring equal treatment, and many Black branches were closed or consolidated in the process. Some critics argue that integration reduced the cultural centrality of African American libraries and dispersed the community institutions that had been built around them. Others note that integration fulfilled a fundamental democratic promise of equal access to public knowledge. Today, local archives, historical societies, and university collections in the Tampa Bay area work to recover the stories of these libraries and the librarians who ran them. Public exhibits, oral history projects, and digitized photographs help bring this history to new audiences. Studying this history encourages readers to consider how libraries reflect and shape the social structures around them. It also highlights the importance of community leadership in building institutions that serve everyone. Visitors interested in this topic can explore local archives, consult published histories of Florida's African American communities, and speak with longtime residents whose families remember these libraries firsthand. Learning from these sources ensures that the contributions of segregated libraries and their librarians are recognized as a meaningful part of Florida's educational heritage.

Marla had always believed that loyalty meant doing whatever it took, even if it wasn't pretty. She sat at the corner booth of the Silver Spoon Diner, stirring cold coffee and glaring at the door, waiting for Tessa's boyfriend, Evan, to walk in.

Tessa was her oldest friend, the one who had once driven three hours through a snowstorm to bring her soup when she had the flu. Lately, though, Tessa seemed happier than she had in years, and that made Marla nervous. Evan was too charming, too attentive, and Marla had decided he was hiding something.

She had a plan. If Evan could be tempted, he would show his true colors, and Tessa would be spared the heartbreak of finding out later. It was a noble plan, she told herself, even if the method was a little ugly.

The bell above the door jingled, and Evan slid into the booth across from her without being asked. He smiled, polite and unbothered, and asked how she was doing.

Marla didn't answer right away. She had rehearsed a dozen lines in the car, all dramatic and clever, but now they felt thin and silly. She leaned forward, lowered her voice, and said something bold and clumsy about how she'd always noticed him.

Evan's smile faded into a look of confusion, then something closer to pity. He didn't flirt back. Instead, he set down his fork and said quietly that Tessa had told him Marla might do something like this, and that he had agreed to meet her anyway because he wanted to understand why she disliked him so much.

Marla's face burned. She had not expected him to be honest, and she had certainly not expected him to be kind about it.

He told her that he had been planning to propose to Tessa next month, and that he had been nervous about asking her friends for their blessing. He admitted that he had been hoping Marla would come around, not because he needed her approval, but because he knew how much Tessa valued her.

The words landed harder than any insult could have. Marla stared at her cold coffee, feeling foolish and small. She realized that her protective instinct had curdled into cruelty, and that she had been so busy guarding Tessa from a threat that didn't exist that she had almost lost her friend anyway.

She apologized, awkwardly at first, then more sincerely. Evan accepted it with a nod and offered to pay for her coffee, which only made her feel worse.

When she got home that night, she called Tessa and confessed everything, from the plan to the humiliating conversation. Tessa was quiet for a long time, then laughed softly and said she had always known Marla loved her, even when she was being impossible.

Marla hung up feeling lighter than she had in months, and resolved to be a better friend, one who trusted the people Tessa chose.

The manuscript addresses an important problem: how to estimate uncertainty in Q-values and use it to guide exploration in reinforcement learning. The authors propose using successor features as a basis for this estimation, which is a promising direction because successor features decouple environment dynamics from reward structure and could allow uncertainty to transfer across tasks. The motivation is clearly stated, and the introduction situates the work reasonably well within the literature on count-based exploration, bootstrapped ensembles, and Bayesian value estimation. The method section describes the successor feature formulation and the uncertainty estimator in enough detail to follow the derivation, though a few steps in the connection between feature-space covariance and Q-value variance would benefit from more explicit justification. The experimental setup covers a reasonable range of benchmark environments, including sparse-reward tasks where exploration matters most, which is appropriate for the claims being made. However, the baselines are somewhat limited, and the authors should include stronger contemporary exploration methods, such as random network distillation or ensemble-based approaches, to make the comparison convincing. The reported results show improvements in sample efficiency on several tasks, but the variance across seeds is not always shown, and some of the differences may not be statistically significant without further analysis. The ablation study is helpful in isolating the contribution of the uncertainty term, yet it would be stronger if it also examined sensitivity to the hyperparameters that govern the feature dimension and regularization. The discussion of computational overhead is brief, and readers would benefit from a clearer account of wall-clock cost relative to the baselines. The theoretical section offers a useful bound under linear function approximation, but it is unclear how well this analysis extends to the deep, nonlinear settings used in the experiments, and the authors should state this limitation directly. The related work section is thorough in places but omits some recent papers on uncertainty in successor representations that would sharpen the novelty claim. Figures are generally clear, though several plots would be easier to interpret with confidence intervals and consistent color schemes across methods. The writing is largely readable, with a few passages that are repetitive and could be condensed to improve flow. Code availability is mentioned, which is commendable and will aid reproducibility once the repository is fully documented. Overall, the paper presents a potentially valuable idea with a sound core contribution, but it needs stronger baselines, more rigorous statistical reporting, and clearer discussion of the gap between theory and practice before the conclusions can be considered fully supported. My recommendation is major revision.

The manuscript under review proposes Bayesian neural networks that place Gaussian-process function priors over network outputs, with the stated aim of improving uncertainty estimation and learning performance. The topic is timely, since practitioners increasingly need calibrated predictive uncertainty from deep models, and the authors correctly identify that standard weight-space priors on neural networks give poorly interpretable function-space behavior. The motivation is clearly articulated in the introduction, and the authors do a reasonable job situating their contribution relative to prior work on variational inference for Bayesian neural networks, deep kernel learning, and neural network Gaussian processes. The central idea of constraining the function-space distribution through a GP prior is well-motivated and has a meaningful conceptual appeal. However, the novelty relative to existing function-space inference methods needs to be stated more precisely, because several recent approaches also target function-space priors and the manuscript does not always make clear what is new. The related work section would benefit from a more systematic comparison, ideally in a table that lists the key properties of each competing method. The mathematical framework is generally sound in its outline. The authors define the joint model over inputs, latent network outputs, and observations, and derive a variational lower bound that is tractable under the stated assumptions. That said, several derivation steps are compressed to the point of being hard to verify, and the appendix does not fully resolve these gaps. In particular, the treatment of the inducing-point approximation and the choice of variational family for the GP component should be expanded so that a reader can reproduce the bound without reconstructing the omitted algebra. The authors should also state explicitly which terms in the objective are approximated and how the approximation error is expected to scale with the number of inducing points. Assumptions about kernel hyperparameters are a further concern. The manuscript appears to optimize kernel parameters jointly with network weights, but it is not entirely clear whether this is done by maximum likelihood or through a fully Bayesian treatment. This distinction matters for the uncertainty claims, since point-estimated hyperparameters can understate predictive variance. A sensitivity analysis showing how results change under different kernel choices, such as RBF, Matérn, and periodic kernels, would substantially strengthen the paper. The experimental section covers regression benchmarks, classification on standard image datasets, and an out-of-distribution detection task. The selection of baselines is reasonable, including deep ensembles, MC dropout, and mean-field variational inference, but the omission of stronger recent function-space baselines weakens the comparative claims. The authors should include at least one method that performs inference directly in function space, so that the advantage of the proposed prior can be separated from the advantage of the inference scheme. Reported improvements in negative log-likelihood are encouraging, yet the magnitude of several gains is small relative to the reported standard deviations, and the paper does not always report how many random seeds were used. Statistical significance testing, or at minimum a clear statement of variability across runs, should be added. Calibration is evaluated through expected calibration error on classification tasks, which is useful, but the authors should also report reliability diagrams and a proper scoring rule for regression calibration to give a fuller picture. The out-of-distribution experiments are the most compelling part of the evaluation, since they directly test the claimed uncertainty benefits, and the reported AUROC improvements are promising. However, the choice of out-of-distribution datasets is limited to a small number of pairs, and it is unclear whether the performance gap persists when the in-distribution and out-of-distribution data are more similar. Adding near-distribution benchmarks would clarify the scope of the method's advantage. Computational cost is discussed only briefly. Because GP priors and inducing-point methods add overhead, the authors should report wall-clock training time, memory usage, and inference latency alongside accuracy, and they should discuss how these costs scale with network size and dataset size. Without this information, practitioners cannot judge whether the uncertainty gains justify the additional expense. Reproducibility is partially addressed through a statement that code will be released, but at the time of review the repository link is not provided, and key hyperparameter settings such as learning rates, number of inducing points, and optimizer schedules are reported only for some experiments. A complete table of hyperparameters for every experiment should be included. The writing is generally clear, though some sections repeat material from the introduction and could be condensed. Several figures have small fonts and unlabeled axes, and the captions do not always state what is being plotted or how many runs are averaged. Minor typographical inconsistencies in notation, such as the alternating use of boldface for vectors and matrices, should be corrected. Overall, the paper addresses an important problem with a reasonable and interesting approach. Its main strengths are the clear motivation, the conceptually appealing use of function-space priors, and the promising out-of-distribution results. Its main weaknesses are insufficiently detailed derivations, limited baseline comparisons, unclear treatment of hyperparameters, incomplete statistical reporting, and absent computational cost analysis. I recommend a major revision. If the authors address the concerns about derivations, baselines, uncertainty statistics, and computational cost, the contribution could be a valuable addition to the literature on uncertainty estimation in deep learning.

Leadership troubles have deepened the crisis facing the UK's child sexual abuse inquiry, unsettling survivors who have waited years for answers and prompting fresh calls for parliamentary scrutiny.

The inquiry, established to examine institutional failures to protect children from sexual abuse across England and Wales, has been marred by upheaval at the top for much of its existence. Its progress has been repeatedly interrupted by changes in leadership, and critics say the instability has slowed hearings and weakened public confidence.

Survivors' groups said the latest developments have left many feeling abandoned. Several described a sense of exhaustion, noting that some had already given evidence only to see the process restart under new direction.

Campaigners argue that the inquiry's credibility depends on stability and clear accountability. They say that each change in leadership has forced the inquiry to revisit procedural questions, delaying work that should have been moving toward findings and recommendations.

The inquiry was set up in 2015 following revelations about institutions including schools, churches, care homes and local authorities that failed to act on allegations of abuse. Its remit was intended to be broad, covering decades of failures and the responses of public bodies.

Over the years, the inquiry has faced criticism over its pace, its costs and its handling of the participation of survivors. Some have questioned whether it has met the expectations set when it was first announced.

The recent leadership problems have revived those concerns. Commentators point out that the inquiry's authority rests on the trust of people who have experienced abuse, and that uncertainty at the top can quickly erode that trust.

Several survivors said they were not informed clearly about the reasons for the changes. Many expressed frustration that they learned of developments through media reports rather than direct communication from the inquiry.

Support organisations said that clear and timely communication is essential for people who are already vulnerable. They urged the inquiry to provide regular updates and to explain how decisions affecting hearings and timetables are being made.

Parliamentary figures have responded by calling for closer oversight. Some MPs have argued that Parliament should examine the inquiry's governance, budget and management to ensure it is delivering for survivors.

Advocates for greater scrutiny say that an inquiry of this scale and importance should not operate without meaningful accountability. They propose regular reporting to parliamentary committees and clearer mechanisms for raising concerns.

Others caution against political interference. They argue that an inquiry must remain independent in order to uncover the truth, and that any oversight should protect its autonomy while ensuring transparency.

The debate reflects a broader tension between independence and accountability that has accompanied the inquiry since its creation. Balancing those two principles has proved difficult, and the current crisis has brought that difficulty into sharp focus.

Legal and governance experts note that inquiries of this kind often face challenges in maintaining momentum over long periods. They say that strong leadership, adequate resourcing and clear terms of reference are essential to avoiding prolonged delays.

Survivors have repeatedly stressed that their participation is not merely procedural. For many, giving evidence is an act of considerable personal cost, and they want assurance that their testimony will lead to meaningful change.

Child protection organisations have echoed that concern, emphasising that the lessons of the inquiry must be applied to current safeguarding practice. They warn that delays risk leaving the same systemic weaknesses in place.

Local authorities and institutions named in the inquiry's work have also been watching the developments closely. Some have said they remain committed to cooperating fully, while others have called for the process to conclude efficiently so that lessons can be learned.

The government has said it values the inquiry's work and remains committed to seeing it through. Officials have stressed that the welfare of survivors is central to the process.

Nevertheless, pressure is growing for a more transparent account of what has gone wrong at the top of the inquiry. Calls have intensified for a clear timetable, published milestones and a commitment to regular public reporting.

Some observers suggest that a review of the inquiry's governance structure could help restore confidence. They argue that clearer lines of responsibility and defined decision-making processes could reduce the risk of future disruption.

Others believe the focus should remain on the substance of the inquiry rather than on internal management. They say that the real measure of success will be the quality of its findings and the implementation of its recommendations.

Whatever the outcome of the current debate, the impact on survivors is already clear. Many feel that their experiences have been pushed to the margins by administrative concerns, and they want those concerns addressed without further delay.

Survivors' representatives say they will continue to press for answers. They insist that the inquiry must be judged not by its internal difficulties but by whether it finally delivers the accountability and justice that victims have long been denied.

As Parliament considers how to respond, the question facing decision-makers is how to restore trust in a process that is central to confronting one of the most serious failures in the country's history.

Should Schools Prohibit Cell Phones Throughout the School Day?

Cell phones have become a constant presence in the lives of young people, and many schools have struggled to decide how much room these devices should have in the classroom. Some administrators argue that a full-day ban is the only way to protect learning, while others believe students should be trusted to use phones responsibly. After weighing both sides, I believe schools should prohibit cell phones throughout the school day, because the benefits to focus, social health, and equity outweigh the inconvenience of restricting a device that most students already carry.

The most important reason for a full-day ban is the protection of attention. Research on learning consistently shows that students perform better when they can concentrate on a single task for an extended period. A phone sitting on a desk, even when turned face down, creates a temptation that pulls at a student's mind. Notifications, messages, and the simple habit of checking the screen interrupt thinking and make it harder to absorb complex material. A school day is built around sustained effort, and a device designed to capture attention works against that purpose.

Critics of a ban often argue that a limited policy, such as allowing phones during lunch or between classes, would be enough. However, partial rules are difficult to enforce and tend to blur over time. A student who is permitted to check a phone during a break may find it hard to resist glancing at it during a lesson. A consistent rule that applies from the first bell to the last is clearer for students, teachers, and families, and it removes the constant negotiation that comes with exceptions.

Another reason to support a full-day ban is the effect of phones on social life inside the school. Much of the time students spend on their devices during the day is not spent on schoolwork or even on useful communication. Instead, phones often become a way to withdraw from the people around them. Students who would otherwise talk, play, and build friendships with classmates may retreat into their screens. Without phones, students are more likely to engage with one another face to face, which supports the social and emotional development that schools are meant to encourage.

A ban also helps address the problem of online conflict spilling into the school. Photos, rumors, and messages shared during the school day can quickly escalate into bullying or humiliation. When phones are away, there are fewer opportunities for these incidents to start or grow. Teachers and counselors often report that a phone-free environment leads to calmer hallways and fewer disputes that begin on a screen and end in a confrontation at school.

Some people worry that a ban would make it harder for students to reach their families in an emergency. This concern deserves a serious answer. Schools can and should maintain clear systems for emergency contact, such as access to the main office and phones available to students who need them. A well-designed policy can keep students safe without requiring every student to carry a personal device at all times. The existence of a safety concern does not require unlimited access to phones throughout the day.

Equity is another consideration. Students come from many different backgrounds, and not all of them have the same kind of device or the same quality of data plan. When phones are used for classwork or are expected to be present, students without them can be left behind. A uniform rule that applies to everyone removes that gap from the classroom and ensures that every student is on equal footing during instruction.

Opponents also argue that teaching responsible phone use is a valuable skill and that banning phones avoids the chance to teach self-control. This is a fair point, but schools already teach many skills through structure and boundaries. We do not expect students to learn to manage other distractions by being exposed to them without limits. A school's primary responsibility is to create conditions for learning, and a clear rule helps students develop habits of focus that will serve them later in life.

In the end, the case for a full-day ban rests on a simple idea: schools exist to educate, and anything that consistently interferes with that purpose deserves a firm limit. Cell phones offer many benefits outside the classroom, but during the school day their costs to attention, social connection, fairness, and safety are too high. A complete prohibition, paired with clear emergency procedures, gives students the best chance to learn, grow, and connect with the people around them.

Genetic research has become an important tool for understanding lobster biology, managing wild fisheries, and improving aquaculture practices. Scientists use DNA analysis to study how lobster populations are structured across the ocean, revealing which groups are genetically distinct and which are connected through larval dispersal. This information helps fishery managers define stock boundaries more accurately, so that conservation decisions match the actual biological units being harvested. Microsatellite and single nucleotide polymorphism markers are among the methods used to measure genetic diversity and track gene flow between populations. Genetic data also allow researchers to estimate effective population size, an indicator of how vulnerable a population may be to overfishing or environmental stress. In the American lobster, Homarus americanus, studies have examined whether heavily fished areas show shifts in genetic composition over time. Parentage analysis is another application, enabling scientists to identify which adults contribute offspring to a given area, which informs decisions about protecting spawning stock. Researchers also apply genetic tools to lobster health, including detecting pathogens and identifying genetic markers linked to disease resistance. Shell disease and certain viral infections have been investigated with molecular techniques that can identify the causative agents quickly and accurately. In aquaculture, selective breeding programs use genetic information to improve traits such as growth rate, survival, and feed conversion efficiency. Breeders can select broodstock based on genomic estimated breeding values rather than relying solely on observed performance. Genetic traceability is increasingly valuable as well, since DNA-based methods can confirm the origin of seafood products and help combat mislabeling and illegal harvest. Such tools support certification schemes and consumer confidence in sustainable sourcing. Genetic monitoring of hatchery-reared animals is important to prevent unintended genetic changes in wild populations when hatchery stock is released. Managers can use genetic data to assess whether released individuals interbreed with wild lobsters and whether this alters local adaptation. Environmental DNA, or eDNA, is an emerging approach in which water samples are analyzed for lobster genetic material, offering a non-invasive way to detect presence and estimate abundance. This method may complement traditional trap surveys and reduce costs for monitoring programs. Genomic resources for lobsters have expanded considerably, with reference genomes and transcriptome data supporting research into adaptation to temperature and ocean acidification. Understanding these adaptive genetic responses is essential as warming waters shift lobster distributions. Scientists must also consider ethical and governance questions, such as data ownership, benefit sharing with fishing communities, and the appropriate use of genetic information in management. Collaboration among geneticists, fishers, and policymakers helps ensure that research findings translate into practical benefits. Ongoing advances in sequencing technology are lowering costs and increasing the resolution of genetic studies. As these tools become more accessible, their integration into routine fisheries and aquaculture management is likely to grow. Continued investment in genetic research will strengthen the scientific basis for sustaining lobster resources for future generations.

This manuscript presents a method for fast mitochondria detection in connectomics datasets, and the authors address a practical bottleneck in large-scale electron microscopy reconstruction. The motivation is well articulated, as the sheer volume of data in modern connectomics makes computational efficiency a central concern. The validation of accuracy against manually annotated ground truth is appropriately performed and reported with standard metrics. However, the central claim of the paper is that the method is fast, and the evidence supporting this claim is currently insufficient. The manuscript reports runtime only for the proposed method, with no systematic comparison against competing approaches such as established deep learning segmentation pipelines or classical image processing baselines. Without such comparisons, readers cannot judge whether the reported speed is a genuine advance or merely reflects a favorable hardware configuration or dataset choice. The authors should benchmark all methods on identical hardware, using the same input volumes, batch sizes, and precision settings. Reporting wall-clock time alongside throughput in voxels per second and memory consumption would give a more complete picture. It would also help to state whether timings include preprocessing and postprocessing steps, since these can dominate total runtime in practice. The scaling behavior of each method with increasing volume size should be shown, as speed advantages at one scale may not persist at another. The authors should also clarify whether GPU and CPU implementations are compared fairly, and whether any baseline was tuned less carefully than the proposed method. A discussion of the speed-accuracy tradeoff is needed, since a faster method that sacrifices detection of small or atypical mitochondria may be unsuitable for downstream analyses. Error bars or variance across repeated runs should be provided to establish the reliability of the timing results. Finally, the authors should release code and configuration files sufficient to reproduce the benchmarks. I recommend major revision, contingent on the inclusion of a comprehensive and transparent speed comparison.

Why Freshwater Conservation Matters for Oceans, Communities, and Economies

Freshwater and the ocean are more connected than most people realize. Rivers carry water, sediment, and nutrients from inland watersheds to the sea, and the flow and quality of that water shape the health of coastal ecosystems. In Texas, this connection is especially visible along the Gulf of Mexico, where major rivers such as the Rio Grande, the Brazos, the Colorado, and the Trinity deliver freshwater to bays and estuaries. Estuaries like Galveston Bay, Matagorda Bay, and the Laguna Madre depend on a balanced mix of fresh and salt water to support fish, shrimp, oysters, and crabs. When too little freshwater reaches these bays, salinity rises, nursery habitats decline, and commercially important species suffer. Conserving freshwater inland therefore protects the ocean as well. Healthy river flows also keep sediment and nutrients at levels that support marsh plants and seagrass beds, which buffer shorelines against storms. Coastal wetlands absorb wave energy and reduce erosion, lowering the risk of damage to towns and infrastructure. Communities along the Texas coast benefit from this natural protection, which is far less expensive than many engineered alternatives. Freshwater conservation also supports the region's economy. Commercial and recreational fishing, tourism, and seafood processing all rely on productive bays and clean coastal waters. Oyster reefs and shrimp nurseries generate millions of dollars in annual economic activity, and these industries employ thousands of Texans. Losing these resources would reduce income for families and tax revenue for local governments. Water supply is another central concern. Texas has experienced prolonged droughts, and population growth continues to increase demand from cities, farms, and industry. Efficient irrigation, leak reduction in municipal systems, water reuse, and conservation programs help stretch existing supplies. Water planning that accounts for environmental flow needs ensures that rivers keep enough water to sustain ecosystems while still meeting human needs. Reducing pollution is equally important. Runoff from farms, streets, and industrial sites can carry fertilizers, sediment, and contaminants into waterways, creating dead zones and harming marine life. Practices such as riparian buffers, stormwater management, and careful nutrient use protect both freshwater and marine environments. The same actions that improve drinking water quality also reduce the burden on coastal ecosystems. Beyond Texas, the principles are the same. Many of the world's large river systems, including the Mississippi, the Nile, and the Ganges, deliver water and nutrients to coastal seas that support fisheries and livelihoods. Watershed-scale planning, which brings together upstream and downstream communities, offers a practical way to manage these shared resources. Individuals can contribute as well by fixing leaks, using water efficiently at home, supporting local watershed groups, and choosing sustainable products. Public agencies, researchers, and residents working together can build systems that keep rivers flowing, bays productive, and communities secure. Protecting freshwater is, in the end, an investment in the health of the ocean and the prosperity of the people who depend on it.

This manuscript investigates whether recurrent sentence encoders capture compositional structure by approximating their representations with tensor-product models and evaluating the resulting approximations on targeted tasks. The research question is well motivated, since understanding how neural encoders combine word meanings into sentence meanings remains a central open problem in representation analysis. The authors' decision to frame compositionality through tensor-product approximations is a sensible choice, because it provides an interpretable reference model against which the encoder's behavior can be measured. The introduction situates the work clearly within prior literature on probing and compositionality, although the related work section would benefit from engaging more directly with recent analyses of recurrent architectures. The methodology section describes how the tensor-product approximation is fitted, but the description of the role-filler assignments is somewhat terse and could be expanded to allow replication. The evaluation tasks are a strength, as they target specific compositional phenomena such as negation scope and argument ordering rather than relying solely on aggregate downstream accuracy. However, the paper does not report how sensitive the results are to the choice of approximation dimensionality, which is a significant gap given that this hyperparameter strongly affects the expressiveness of the reference model. The reported approximation error is encouraging, yet the authors should clarify whether low error reflects genuine structural alignment or merely the flexibility of the tensor-product family. Statistical reporting is inconsistent across experiments, with some results accompanied by confidence intervals and others by single point estimates. The ablation comparing unidirectional and bidirectional encoders is informative and supports the central claims about directionality. I would encourage the authors to include a control condition using randomly initialized encoders to establish a baseline for how much structure emerges from architecture alone. The discussion sometimes overstates the implications of the findings, particularly the claim that the encoder "implements" a compositional function, which the evidence supports only in a weaker sense. Figures are generally clear, though the axis labels in the dimensionality analysis are too small to read comfortably. The limitations section is brief and should address the restriction to English sentences and the relatively small set of constructions tested. The writing is generally clear, with a few passages in the methods that would benefit from tighter prose and consistent notation. Overall, the paper makes a useful contribution to interpretability research on sentence encoders. With more thorough sensitivity analysis, stronger baselines, and more measured claims, it would be a substantially stronger submission. I recommend a major revision.

Remote learning has become a familiar part of education, and when it is well designed, it can support students in three important areas: their academic performance, their mental well-being, and their connections with family. Each of these benefits deserves careful attention, because education is about more than test scores alone.

To begin with academic performance, remote learning allows students to work at a pace that suits their individual needs. A student who grasps a math concept quickly can move ahead, while a student who needs more time can revisit a recorded lesson as many times as necessary. Many online platforms also offer practice quizzes, instant feedback, and digital resources such as videos, interactive simulations, and reading libraries. These tools can make abstract ideas easier to understand and help students retain what they learn. Remote learning also builds independence, since students must plan their schedules, manage deadlines, and take responsibility for their own progress. These skills are valuable beyond the classroom and prepare students for college, careers, and lifelong learning.

Mental well-being is another area where remote learning can make a positive difference. Some students feel anxious in crowded hallways, noisy cafeterias, or classrooms where they fear being judged by peers. Learning from home can reduce these pressures and give students a calmer, more comfortable environment in which to focus. Students with health conditions, social anxiety, or disabilities may find that remote options allow them to participate more fully and with less stress. Flexible schedules can also leave room for rest, exercise, hobbies, and sleep, all of which support emotional health. Of course, remote learning can bring its own challenges, such as isolation or screen fatigue, so students benefit when schools provide regular check-ins, counseling access, and opportunities for healthy breaks.

Finally, remote learning can strengthen family connections. When students study at home, parents and caregivers often have a clearer view of what their children are learning and where they might need support. Family members can offer encouragement during difficult assignments, celebrate achievements, and share daily routines such as meals. Younger students in particular may benefit from having a trusted adult nearby during the school day. Families who work together to create a study space and a schedule often develop better communication and teamwork. These shared experiences can build trust and closeness that last well beyond the school year.

In conclusion, remote learning, when thoughtfully supported, can enhance students' academic progress, protect their mental health, and deepen their relationships with the people closest to them. Schools, families, and students all play a part in making this model successful. With the right balance of structure, flexibility, and human support, remote learning can be a meaningful and positive path to education.

Many Americans have long questioned whether the Electoral College still serves the democratic ideal of one person, one vote. Under the current system, a candidate can win the presidency while losing the national popular vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016. This outcome undermines public confidence in the legitimacy of the election itself. A direct popular vote would ensure that the candidate with the most support nationwide becomes president, aligning the result with the will of the majority. Critics of the Electoral College also point out that it concentrates attention on a small number of swing states, leaving voters in safe states largely ignored during campaigns. A national popular vote would require candidates to seek support from every region and every community, not just a handful of battlegrounds. The winner-take-all allocation within most states further distorts representation, since a candidate who wins a narrow plurality can claim all of a state's electors. Supporters of reform argue that this system effectively disenfranchises the millions of voters whose preferences are outvoted within their states. Defenders of the status quo cite federalism and the protection of smaller states, but a direct election could still give every voter equal weight regardless of geography. Reform proposals such as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact seek to achieve this goal without a constitutional amendment, though their legal durability remains debated. Any change should be designed to encourage turnout, since a national count would give voters in every state a reason to participate. Modern communication and data systems make accurate nationwide vote counting more feasible than it was when the Electoral College was created in 1787. Ultimately, a more representative system would strengthen democratic accountability and public trust in the outcome of presidential elections. Replacing the Electoral College with a direct popular vote is therefore a reform worth serious consideration.

Optimism is more than a cheerful outlook; it is a practical tool that helps people face difficulties and pursue their goals. When people believe that their efforts can lead to good outcomes, they are more willing to try, to persist, and to learn from setbacks. This belief shapes how they respond to the problems that inevitably arise in life. Instead of giving up at the first obstacle, optimistic individuals tend to see challenges as temporary and solvable. This mindset encourages them to look for new strategies rather than accepting defeat. Over time, this persistence can make a significant difference in what a person accomplishes. Research in psychology has supported this connection, finding that optimistic people often report better health, stronger relationships, and greater resilience under stress. Their hopeful expectations can also motivate them to take action that increases their chances of success. A student who believes she can improve her grades, for example, is more likely to study consistently, seek help from teachers, and stay committed to her goals. Optimism also helps people recover from failure. Rather than dwelling on mistakes, they focus on what they can change next time. This ability to bounce back allows them to keep moving forward when others might stop. Optimism does not mean ignoring real problems or pretending that everything will turn out perfectly. Instead, it means approaching difficulties with the confidence that effort and creativity can make a positive difference. Hopeful people are also often better at inspiring and supporting others, which can open doors to collaboration and new opportunities. In this way, optimism creates a cycle in which positive expectations lead to effort, effort leads to progress, and progress reinforces hope. Ultimately, optimism empowers people to overcome challenges and build meaningful success. It reminds us that the future is not fixed and that our attitudes can shape the paths we choose to take.

The manuscript investigates how anisotropic noise in stochastic gradient descent affects a model's ability to escape local optima, an important and timely question given the growing theoretical interest in the implicit regularization of SGD. The authors' central contribution, a linear stability analysis showing that noise aligned with high-curvature directions accelerates escape from sharp minima, is clearly motivated and connects well to existing work on flat-minima generalization. The theoretical derivations are generally sound and the assumptions are stated explicitly, although the reliance on a quadratic local approximation limits how directly the results transfer to deep, non-convex networks. The empirical section would be considerably stronger with experiments on more architectures and datasets, along with error bars across random seeds, since the reported improvements are sometimes within the range of run-to-run variability. The authors should also clarify how the noise covariance was estimated in practice, as this choice materially affects the conclusions and is currently under-specified. The discussion of related work omits several recent analyses of SGD noise structure that would help position the contribution more precisely. Overall, the paper offers a valuable and mostly rigorous perspective, and I recommend a minor revision addressing the empirical breadth, the estimation details, and the literature review.

Good decisions rarely come from a single point of view. When we face a difficult choice, our first instinct is often to trust the conclusion that feels most natural to us, but that feeling is shaped by our experiences, our fears, and our blind spots. Gathering multiple perspectives before deciding helps us see the situation more completely and test our assumptions against the judgment of others. The practice is valuable not because other people are always right, but because they notice things we cannot.

Consider a student choosing between two colleges. A parent may emphasize cost and stability, a teacher may focus on academic fit, and a friend who attended one of the schools may describe daily life on campus. Each person brings a different lens, and together they reveal considerations that no single voice would have raised. The student who listens to all three is far better equipped to weigh tradeoffs honestly than one who relies only on a glossy brochure or a single opinion.

Multiple perspectives also protect us from the trap of confirmation bias. People tend to seek out information that supports what they already believe, and they often dismiss evidence that challenges their preferences. When we deliberately ask people who disagree with us for their reasoning, we are forced to confront the strongest version of the other side. This process can strengthen our original view if it survives scrutiny, or it can persuade us to change course before a costly mistake.

Historical examples show the cost of deciding in isolation. Leaders who surrounded themselves only with agreeable advisors have repeatedly led their organizations into avoidable failures, because no one was positioned to voice doubts. By contrast, institutions that cultivate dissent and encourage open debate tend to catch errors early. The lesson extends beyond government and business to families, classrooms, and friendships, where a willingness to hear criticism often prevents small problems from becoming serious ones.

Gathering perspectives does require time and humility, and it has real limits. Seeking too many opinions can lead to paralysis, as contradictory advice piles up and no clear direction emerges. The goal is not to poll every person one has ever met but to identify a thoughtful range of viewpoints, including people with relevant expertise, people affected by the decision, and people willing to be honest. Knowing when enough input has been gathered is itself a skill that improves with practice.

Ultimately, the value of multiple perspectives lies in the quality of the final choice and the confidence that comes with it. A decision made after genuine consideration of several viewpoints is more likely to account for hidden risks and unintended consequences. Even when the outcome disappoints, the person who chose thoughtfully can take pride in the process. Wisdom, in the end, is less about never being wrong and more about being willing to learn from others before it is too late.
