Primary care is often the first place people turn when they feel persistently sad, hopeless, or unable to function, yet many primary care practices are not well equipped to manage depression as thoroughly as they manage other chronic illnesses. Clinics that routinely monitor blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol usually have established protocols, scheduled follow-ups, and tracking systems for those conditions. Depression, by contrast, is frequently assessed only briefly during a visit and may not receive the same structured, ongoing attention. One reason is limited time: a typical primary care appointment is short, and clinicians must address many competing concerns, leaving little room for in-depth mental health discussion. Another reason is the shortage of behavioral health staff, such as psychologists, social workers, and counselors, who can provide therapy or care coordination within the practice. Many clinics also lack embedded collaborative care models that pair a primary care clinician with a trained care manager and a psychiatric consultant. Without these supports, patients may wait weeks or months for a referral to a specialist, and some never complete the journey. Screening tools such as the PHQ-9 are widely recommended, but a positive result is only useful if the practice has a clear plan for what happens next. Treatment monitoring is another gap, since measuring symptom changes over time requires repeated assessments that many practices do not systematically perform. Medication management can also be challenging, as antidepressants often require several adjustments before they work well, and clinicians may feel less confident prescribing them than managing a stable diabetes regimen. Reimbursement structures add to the problem, because visits focused on mental health may be compensated less favorably than procedure-based or disease-management services. Stigma, both among patients and among some staff, can further discourage open conversations about mood. Training gaps matter as well, since many primary care clinicians receive limited instruction in psychotherapy and depression management during their education. Addressing these challenges requires investment in integrated behavioral health teams, dedicated time for mental health care, and payment models that reward ongoing depression treatment. Patients can help by asking their clinicians directly about screening, follow-up plans, and referral options. Ultimately, closing this resource gap would allow primary care to deliver depression care that is as consistent and well organized as the care provided for other chronic illnesses.

The studio hallway smelled of fresh paint and burnt coffee. Ellen had rehearsed her line for three days, but now that Walt Disney himself was standing across from her, every word had fled her mind. He looked up from his sketches, peering over his spectacles with a patient, expectant smile. "You're the one with the picture for the new feature, aren't you?" he asked. Ellen nodded too quickly and nearly dropped her portfolio. She cleared her throat twice before the words finally tumbled out. "It's called Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs," she said, then immediately winced. Walt's eyebrows lifted slightly, and he tapped his pencil against his chin. "Is that so? Seven dwarfs, you say?" Ellen felt her cheeks burn as she realized she had given the title with the wrong emphasis, as if she were apologizing for it. "Well, it's a working title," she stammered. "Or it could be. I mean, it's the one we've been using." Walt chuckled, a warm and rumbling sound that filled the small room. "Ellen, isn't it? Relax. A title is just a door. Let's see if it opens onto something worth walking through." He gestured to a stool, and she sat down gratefully, clutching her portfolio like a shield. For the next hour they talked about the drawings, the dwarfs' personalities, and the queen's dark mirror. By the time she left, the awkwardness had melted away, and she was fairly sure the title had survived its first test.

Cars have become so central to modern life that many people never question how much they depend on them. Yet the convenience of driving everywhere comes with serious costs to the air we breathe, the safety of our communities, and the money we spend each year. Reducing our reliance on cars would bring clear benefits in all three areas, and these benefits are worth taking seriously.

The most visible advantage is cleaner air. Vehicles are a major source of air pollution, releasing carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and fine particulate matter from their exhaust and tires. These pollutants are linked to asthma, heart disease, and other respiratory illnesses, and they affect children and older adults most severely. When fewer cars are on the road, neighborhoods near busy highways often see measurable improvements in air quality. Cleaner air means fewer emergency room visits and fewer sick days, which benefits both families and the wider economy.

Cleaner air also helps the climate. Transportation is one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions in many countries, and passenger cars contribute a significant share. Walking, cycling, and riding public transit produce far fewer emissions per person than driving alone. Even modest shifts in travel habits, multiplied across millions of people, can meaningfully reduce the carbon footprint of a city or region.

Safer travel is another important benefit. Motor vehicle crashes cause tens of thousands of deaths each year in many countries, and they injure many more people. Fewer cars on the road means fewer opportunities for collisions. Cities that invest in protected bike lanes, reduced speed limits, and well-designed pedestrian crossings tend to see lower rates of serious injury. Safer streets also give children the freedom to walk or bike to school independently, which supports their physical health and sense of independence.

Lower costs may be the benefit that touches people most directly. Owning and operating a car is expensive, with costs for purchase or lease, insurance, fuel, maintenance, parking, and depreciation adding up to thousands of dollars per year. Households that rely less on cars can redirect that money toward savings, housing, education, or other needs. Public transit passes, bicycles, and walking cost far less than a private vehicle, and they can make a real difference for families on tight budgets.

Reducing car dependence also strengthens communities. When people walk and bike more, they encounter their neighbors, patronize local shops, and feel a stronger connection to their surroundings. Streets designed for people rather than just cars tend to be quieter and more pleasant. Local businesses often benefit from foot traffic that drive-through or car-only commercial areas cannot generate.

Some people argue that cars are essential and that alternatives are impractical, especially in rural areas or for people with disabilities or demanding schedules. These concerns deserve respect, and no one should be forced to give up a car when it is truly necessary. The goal is not to eliminate cars entirely but to build choices so that people who can walk, bike, or take transit have good options to do so. Improved bus service, safe bike infrastructure, and compact neighborhoods with nearby shops all expand those choices.

Governments, employers, and individuals each have a role to play. Cities can invest in transit and cycling networks, zone for mixed-use development, and price parking more realistically. Employers can offer transit subsidies, flexible work arrangements, and secure bike storage. Individuals can try walking or cycling for short trips, carpool when possible, and consider whether every errand truly requires a car.

In the end, reducing our reliance on cars offers a rare combination of benefits: healthier air, safer streets, lower household expenses, and stronger communities. These gains reinforce one another, and the steps needed to achieve them are within reach. Choosing alternatives to driving is not a sacrifice but an investment in a cleaner, safer, and more affordable future for everyone.

Remote learning has opened new doors for students who have long been left out of traditional classrooms. For many learners, the physical school building presents barriers that have nothing to do with their intelligence or motivation. A student who lives in a rural village may face a long bus ride each day, while a student with a chronic illness may miss weeks of lessons because of hospital stays. Remote learning can reduce these obstacles by bringing education directly into the home or wherever a student can connect to the internet.

One of the greatest strengths of remote learning is its flexibility. Recorded lectures allow students to pause, rewind, and revisit difficult material at their own pace. A learner who needs extra time to understand a math concept can watch an explanation several times without feeling rushed or embarrassed. This kind of control can build confidence, especially for students who have previously felt left behind in a fast-moving classroom.

Remote learning also supports students who must balance school with other responsibilities. Many young people care for younger siblings, hold part-time jobs to support their families, or manage health conditions that require regular appointments. Online courses often allow these students to structure their study time around their real lives rather than forcing them to choose between education and survival. In this way, remote learning can help keep students enrolled who might otherwise drop out.

The digital environment can also make learning more comfortable for students who struggle socially. Some learners feel anxious speaking in front of large groups, and a crowded classroom can make participation feel overwhelming. In an online discussion forum or chat, a shy student may feel more able to share ideas thoughtfully. Written responses give students time to compose their thoughts, which can lead to deeper and more considered contributions.

Accessibility tools are another advantage that remote learning often provides. Digital texts can be adjusted in size, color, and font, and many platforms support screen readers, captions, and translation features. Students with visual or hearing impairments, or those learning in a second language, can often customize their materials to suit their needs. These features can make the curriculum more inclusive than a single printed textbook ever could.

Remote learning does not solve every problem, however, and its benefits depend on access to reliable technology. Students without a computer, stable internet, or a quiet place to work can fall further behind in an online setting. Schools and communities must therefore invest in devices, connectivity, and safe study spaces if remote learning is to serve everyone fairly. Without these supports, the promise of accessibility can quickly become a new form of inequality.

Teachers also play an essential role in making remote learning supportive. A good online teacher checks in regularly, responds to messages promptly, and notices when a student has stopped logging in. Personal feedback, encouraging comments, and small virtual meetings can help students feel seen and valued even when they are far from their classmates. Human connection remains central to learning, and remote education works best when it prioritizes relationships as well as content.

Finally, remote learning encourages the development of independence and self-direction. Students must learn to plan their time, manage their assignments, and seek help when they need it. These skills are valuable beyond the classroom and prepare young people for college, careers, and lifelong learning. When remote learning is thoughtfully designed, it does more than deliver lessons; it helps students become capable, confident, and resilient learners.

Indian courts and the government have intensified pressure on internet companies to remove offensive online content, a move that has reignited a debate over censorship, free expression, and the practical limits of content moderation. Officials argue that social media platforms have become channels for hate speech, misinformation, harassment, and material that can incite violence, and they say companies must act more quickly once such content is flagged. Several High Courts and the Supreme Court have in recent months heard petitions asking for stricter accountability from platforms, with judges questioning whether current takedown mechanisms are fast and effective enough. Under the country's information technology rules, intermediaries are generally required to remove unlawful content within specified timeframes after receiving a valid order from a competent authority. Government representatives have pointed to a rising volume of complaints about deepfakes, communal posts, and abusive material as evidence that the existing framework needs tightening. Technology companies, for their part, have said that the sheer scale of user-generated content makes it extremely difficult to review every post before or immediately after it appears. Industry representatives warn that overly broad or rapid removal demands could lead to the suppression of legitimate speech, including political commentary, satire, and news reporting. They also argue that vague legal standards leave platforms uncertain about what must be taken down, which can push them toward cautious over-removal. Digital rights advocates have echoed these concerns, saying that opaque orders and limited avenues for appeal risk chilling free expression among ordinary users. Some civil society groups have called for greater transparency, including public reporting of takedown requests and clearer reasons given to affected users. Companies have responded that they already operate large trust and safety teams and rely on a mix of automated tools and human reviewers to enforce their policies. Engineers at several firms say artificial intelligence can help identify certain categories of harmful material, but context-dependent cases such as sarcasm, regional languages, and political speech remain difficult to judge accurately. India's linguistic diversity, with dozens of major languages and countless dialects, compounds these challenges, as moderation systems often perform less reliably outside English and Hindi. Officials have acknowledged these difficulties but maintain that platforms must invest more in local-language capacity and grievance redressal. Government sources have indicated that further amendments to the rules may be considered, particularly around timelines for response and obligations to identify the originators of certain messages. Legal experts note that any such changes will face scrutiny under constitutional protections for free speech, which the Supreme Court has previously upheld while also permitting reasonable restrictions. The outcome of the ongoing court cases could significantly shape how liability and responsibility are divided between the state, platforms, and users. For now, the dispute reflects a broader global tension over who should decide what speech is acceptable online and through what processes. Industry groups have requested consultations before any new rules take effect, arguing that hasty regulation could have unintended consequences for users and small businesses alike. The government has said it remains open to dialogue while insisting that the safety and dignity of citizens cannot be compromised. Observers expect the debate to continue as courts weigh the competing claims and as platforms refine their policies to meet both legal demands and public expectations.

Extending the school day can offer real benefits for students and families, particularly when it provides time for academic support, enrichment activities, and physical exercise. Students who struggle with core subjects may gain valuable extra time with teachers to review difficult material and catch up before falling further behind. Longer days also allow schools to offer arts, music, sports, and clubs that many students would otherwise not have access to, helping them discover interests and build skills beyond the classroom. For working families, an extended schedule can reduce the strain of finding childcare after school, giving parents greater confidence and flexibility in their jobs. However, longer days are not without drawbacks, as younger children and tired adolescents may suffer from fatigue, reduced attention, and less time for rest, family meals, and unstructured play. Critics also argue that adding hours does not guarantee better learning if the extra time is filled with repetitive instruction rather than meaningful activities. Ultimately, extending the school day is beneficial only when it is carefully designed around student well-being, quality teaching, and community input. When schools focus on enrichment and support rather than simply adding more of the same, longer days can become a genuine advantage for students and their families.

The manuscript addresses a practically relevant problem: reducing gradient variance in policy-gradient reinforcement learning when the environment is subject to external disturbances that the agent cannot observe or control. The central proposal, an input-conditioned baseline that adapts to the state and disturbance-relevant features, is well motivated, since standard state-value baselines may fail to absorb variance that arises from exogenous noise. The authors correctly frame the estimator as unbiased with respect to the policy gradient, which is an important property that must be preserved for the method to be sound, and the derivation in the methods section appears to establish this under the stated assumptions. However, the assumptions themselves deserve more scrutiny, particularly the independence conditions between the disturbance process and the action, which are asserted rather than tested. The experimental section evaluates the method on three control benchmarks with synthetic disturbances, which is a reasonable starting point, but the disturbance models are limited to additive Gaussian noise and a single piecewise-constant signal, leaving open whether the gains generalize to structured or adversarial disturbances. The reported variance reductions are substantial in the figures, yet the paper does not report confidence intervals or the number of random seeds used, making it difficult to judge statistical reliability. The comparison set is also thin: the baselines include a standard learned value function and a constant baseline, but omit recent variance-reduction techniques such as control variates from action-dependent baselines, which would clarify where the proposed approach offers a genuine advantage. The ablation study isolating the contribution of the input conditioning is a strength and convincingly shows that the disturbance-aware features drive most of the improvement. The writing is generally clear, though the notation for the conditioning variables shifts between sections and should be unified. The related work section covers the policy-gradient literature adequately but gives insufficient attention to prior work on disturbance-robust reinforcement learning, which is a closely neighboring field. The computational overhead of the additional conditioning network is mentioned only briefly, and wall-clock comparisons would strengthen the practical claims. The limitations section acknowledges the restricted disturbance models but does not discuss the potential for the learned baseline to overfit to the training disturbance distribution. Reproducibility would benefit from released code and full hyperparameter tables, which are currently only partially provided. Overall, the core idea is promising and technically grounded, but the empirical evidence needs broader disturbance models, more baselines, statistical reporting, and a clearer treatment of distribution shift before the contribution can be considered fully established. I recommend a major revision, with the authors addressing these points and the underlying derivation being checked once more for the stated independence assumptions.

This manuscript investigates adversarial robustness in neural networks through the lens of input-space geometry, decision boundary structure, and Jacobian-based regularization. The topic is timely and relevant, since adversarial vulnerability remains one of the central unresolved concerns in deploying deep learning systems. The authors frame their contribution as a geometric account of why small input perturbations can flip predictions, and they propose that controlling the local behavior of the network's Jacobian can yield more stable decision surfaces. The motivation is clearly articulated in the introduction, and the authors do a reasonable job situating their work relative to prior adversarial training and certified defense literature. However, the paper would benefit from a sharper statement of what is new relative to existing Jacobian regularization methods, which have appeared in several prior studies. The related work section covers a wide range of threads but at times reads as a list of citations rather than a synthesis that identifies a specific gap the present work fills. The conceptual framework linking input-space geometry to decision boundary curvature is intuitive and largely well explained. The authors describe how local linearization of the network around an input can be used to approximate the distance to the nearest boundary, which is a useful and well-motivated idea. That said, the derivation connecting this linear approximation to robustness guarantees relies on assumptions that are not fully stated, and a reader would need to reconstruct several steps independently. I recommend the authors make these assumptions explicit and discuss under what conditions the approximation breaks down, particularly in highly nonlinear regions of the input space. The methodology section describes a regularization term that penalizes the Frobenius norm of the input-output Jacobian during training. The formulation is clear, and the authors provide implementation details sufficient to reproduce the core setup. Nevertheless, several hyperparameter choices, including the regularization coefficient schedule and the sampling strategy for evaluation points, are justified only briefly. Given that Jacobian penalties are known to be sensitive to these choices, a more systematic ablation would strengthen the paper considerably. I would also encourage the authors to report computational overhead, since computing or approximating Jacobians adds nontrivial cost to each training step. The experimental evaluation spans several image classification benchmarks and compares against standard adversarial training baselines under projected gradient descent attacks. The results show consistent improvements in robust accuracy at moderate perturbation budgets, which is encouraging. However, the strongest reported gains appear primarily under the attack used during training, and the paper provides limited evidence that the robustness transfers to adaptive attacks designed with knowledge of the defense. Evaluation against adaptive attacks, including those that target the regularized quantity directly, is essential before the robustness claims can be considered reliable. The authors should also clarify whether gradient masking could account for some of the observed improvements, as this is a well-documented failure mode for defenses that alter gradient behavior. The geometric analysis, which visualizes decision boundaries and measures margin distributions, is one of the more distinctive contributions of the paper. The visualizations are informative and help convey the intuition behind the method. Still, the figures are presented on low-dimensional slices of the input space, and it is unclear how well these slices represent the high-dimensional geometry that actually governs adversarial behavior. I suggest the authors either quantify this representativeness or temper their conclusions about the global structure of decision boundaries drawn from these slices. The margin distribution analysis would also be more convincing with confidence intervals across multiple random seeds. The discussion section offers thoughtful reflections on the trade-off between clean accuracy and robustness, and the authors acknowledge the well-known tension between the two. The reported drop in clean accuracy is modest, which is a positive finding worth highlighting. However, the discussion would benefit from a more candid treatment of limitations, including the scale of models and datasets tested, which are relatively small compared with contemporary architectures. It remains an open question whether the proposed regularization remains tractable and effective for large-scale models, and the authors should address this directly rather than leaving it implicit. The writing is generally clear and well organized, though some sections contain repetitive phrasing and a few notation inconsistencies that should be corrected. The mathematical notation for the Jacobian and the perturbation set changes between the methods and theory sections, which can confuse readers. Consolidating notation in a preliminaries section would improve readability. Several figure captions are also too brief to be interpreted without consulting the main text, and expanding them would help. Reproducibility is partially addressed through the description of the training procedure, but the authors do not state whether code and trained model checkpoints will be released. Public availability of code would substantially increase the value and credibility of the contribution, and I strongly encourage the authors to commit to releasing it. The appendix provides some additional experiments, though a few referenced results are not clearly located. Overall, the paper presents a coherent and potentially valuable perspective on adversarial robustness that connects geometric intuition with a practical regularization technique. The core idea is worth pursuing, and the initial empirical results are promising. However, the claims currently outpace the evidence in several respects, particularly regarding robustness against adaptive attacks, generalization to larger models, and the representativeness of the geometric analysis. I recommend a major revision. With clearer statements of novelty, a more rigorous adaptive attack evaluation, expanded ablations, and more careful treatment of limitations, the paper could make a meaningful contribution to the adversarial robustness literature. I look forward to seeing a revised version addressing these points.

This manuscript proposes a conditional generative adversarial network architecture for text-to-speech synthesis, combining multiscale discrimination with speech-specific evaluation metrics. The problem is well motivated, since adversarial training has the potential to close the perceptual quality gap that persists between neural TTS systems and natural human speech. The authors position their contribution clearly within the existing literature on GAN-based vocoders and acoustic models, and the related work section is generally thorough. The multiscale discriminator design is a sensible extension of prior work, operating on raw waveforms and downsampled versions to capture both fine-grained artifacts and longer-range prosodic structure. The conditioning mechanism, which feeds phonetic and duration information into the generator, is described with enough detail to be reproducible in principle, though a formal diagram of the full pipeline would substantially aid comprehension. The choice of speech-specific evaluation metrics is a strength, as the paper argues persuasively that generic image-derived measures such as FID do not transfer well to audio. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more rigorous justification of which metrics are used and why, including validation of their correlation with human judgments on the authors' own data. The main quantitative results report improvements in mean opinion score and objective measures over several baselines, which is encouraging. Nevertheless, the reported confidence intervals are wide relative to some of the claimed gains, and the authors should clarify whether the differences are statistically significant. The ablation study is informative for the multiscale component but is less complete for the conditioning design, and additional ablations would strengthen the central claims. The listening test protocol is described briefly, and details on rater recruitment, number of utterances per rater, and screening procedures should be expanded to allow assessment of validity. The paper would also benefit from a discussion of computational cost and training stability, since adversarial training is known to be sensitive to hyperparameters. Some figures contain small fonts and low-resolution spectrograms that make it difficult to judge the qualitative differences claimed in the text. The discussion of limitations is brief and should address generalization to unseen speakers, languages, and expressive speech styles. Overall, the work is a useful and promising contribution, and I recommend a major revision addressing the statistical reporting, evaluation protocol, and ablation coverage before the paper can be considered for acceptance.

Emergency services were called to the scene shortly after, and both drivers were taken to hospital, but the other motorist, a woman in her thirties, died from her injuries. Her unborn child also did not survive. Police said the investigation into the cause of the crash is ongoing and that they are reviewing traffic camera footage and witness statements. At a brief court appearance this week, the pregnant driver entered a plea of not guilty to the careless driving charge. Her legal representative told the court that the case would be contested and that the defense intended to examine the evidence in detail. Friends of the victim gathered near the crash site over the weekend to leave flowers and tributes. Family members described her as devoted, warm, and deeply loved by her community.
