English councils are raising fees and charges for a range of local services as they confront mounting budget pressures, a move that has prompted debate over how the increases will affect residents. Officials say rising demand for social care, higher costs for temporary accommodation, and reduced central government funding have left many authorities with significant gaps in their finances. To help close those gaps, a number of councils have approved increases to charges for parking, leisure centres, planning applications, and garden waste collection. Council leaders argue that the changes are necessary to protect essential frontline services such as libraries, road maintenance, and support for vulnerable adults and children. They point out that many fees have remained frozen for years, meaning that inflation has steadily eroded the income they generate. Critics, however, warn that the cumulative effect of higher charges could place further strain on households already struggling with the rising cost of living. Community groups have raised concerns that low-income families may be disproportionately affected, particularly those who rely on leisure facilities, public transport, or paid parking to access work and healthcare. Some local representatives have called for more targeted support, such as concessions and reduced rates for pensioners, disabled residents, and people on benefits. Councils that have introduced such exemptions say they are seeking to balance financial sustainability with fairness to those least able to pay. Financial analysts note that fee increases alone are unlikely to solve structural problems in local government funding, which many experts describe as underfunded relative to growing statutory responsibilities. Some authorities have also explored asset sales, service reviews, and efficiency programmes alongside revenue measures in an effort to reduce reliance on residents' payments. Opposition politicians have accused ruling groups of shifting the burden of central government decisions onto local taxpayers and service users. Government representatives have responded that councils have access to a range of funding and must take responsibility for prudent financial management. Residents' groups have urged authorities to publish clear impact assessments showing how the changes will affect different households before final decisions are made. In several areas, public consultations have attracted large numbers of responses, reflecting strong feelings about the proposals. Councils are required to set balanced budgets, which means difficult choices must be made even when they are unpopular. Many local leaders say they would prefer to avoid raising charges but feel they have little alternative given the scale of their financial challenges. As the new financial year approaches, the decisions taken by councils are likely to shape the day-to-day experience of residents for years to come. Observers say the coming months will reveal whether the changes can stabilise local finances without causing lasting harm to the communities they are meant to serve.

Should students be allowed to use their mobile devices during unstructured school periods, such as lunch breaks, study halls, and passing time between classes? Supporters of this policy argue that phones give students a sense of autonomy and a place to decompress after hours of focused work. A brief period of scrolling, messaging friends, or listening to music can help students reset their attention and return to lessons with more energy. Mobile devices also serve practical purposes during these windows, such as checking schedules, arranging rides, or reaching family members about after-school plans. Trusting students with this freedom can teach them self-regulation, a skill they will need long after graduation. Unstructured time is also when many students socialize, and phones can help them stay connected to friends who attend different schools or live far away. However, unrestricted access carries real risks. Students who spend lunch absorbed in their screens may miss valuable chances to talk with peers face to face, which are essential for developing social and communication skills. Constant notifications can also fragment attention, making it harder to shift back into focused study afterward. Cyberbullying and inappropriate content are additional concerns that become harder to monitor when devices are freely available. Some students may also feel pressure to compare themselves to others online, which can affect their mood and self-esteem. A balanced approach may offer the best outcome. Schools could permit phone use in designated areas, such as a lunch courtyard, while encouraging quiet zones or activity-based options elsewhere. Clear guidelines, combined with lessons on digital wellness, would help students learn when and how to use their devices responsibly. Ultimately, the goal should be to support students in building healthy habits rather than simply banning or ignoring their technology. Thoughtful policies that respect both independence and well-being can serve students far better than either extreme.

Abstract. We study how the regularity of dynamical sources and the Diophantine properties of their underlying maps govern the average-case costs of two fundamental data structures, tries and binary search trees. Dynamical sources generate infinite words by iterating a piecewise expanding map of the unit interval and recording the branch visited at each step, thereby providing a flexible model of correlated symbol production that includes memoryless and Markovian sources as special cases. We show that the expected costs of tries, measured by the number of nodes and the external path length, and the expected costs of binary search trees, measured by the internal path length, are governed by a small number of asymptotic quantities: the entropy of the source, the Rényi-type pressure function, and a regularity index that quantifies how smoothly the branch structure of the map varies. Our central claim is that the Diophantine character of the parameters defining the source, when these parameters are irrational and the source is a rotation-type or intermittent map, controls the fluctuations of the cost around its mean, and in certain regimes controls even the leading-order mean itself. We develop the analysis through a combination of transfer operator techniques, generating function methods, and singularity analysis, and we obtain precise asymptotic expansions with explicit error terms. The main results give logarithmic leading terms for the trie profile with a constant determined by the entropy, linear leading terms for binary search trees with a constant determined by the pressure, and secondary terms whose exponents depend on the regularity index. We further identify a threshold phenomenon: when the Diophantine exponent of the source parameter exceeds a critical value, the cost is asymptotically indistinguishable from that of a memoryless source with the same entropy, whereas below the threshold a measurable correction appears. We illustrate these findings with explicit computations for Gauss-type and Farey-type sources, discuss the numerical verification of the predicted constants, and examine implications for the design of compressed indexing structures that must cope with non-uniform and strongly correlated inputs.

1. Introduction. Tries and binary search trees are among the oldest and most studied structures in the analysis of algorithms, and their average-case behavior under probabilistic models of input strings has been a central theme since the foundational work of Knuth, Sedgewick, and Flajolet. Classical analyses assume that the input consists of independent and identically distributed symbols, or more generally of symbols generated by a finite Markov chain. These models, while analytically tractable, fail to capture the long-range dependencies and multifractal statistics present in many natural and engineered sequences, including the digit expansions of real numbers, texts in natural languages, and symbolic encodings of physical trajectories. Dynamical sources were introduced to address this gap by generating strings through the symbolic coding of orbits of a dynamical system, so that the probability structure is inherited from an invariant measure of a map rather than prescribed symbol by symbol.

The motivation for studying dynamical sources is twofold. First, they provide a unifying framework in which many classical number-theoretic expansions appear naturally, such as the continued fraction expansion generated by the Gauss map and the expansion associated with the Farey map. Second, they expose the role of analytic properties of the map, such as its derivative behavior near indifferent fixed points and the arithmetic nature of rotation parameters, in determining algorithmic costs. The question we address is how these analytic and arithmetic features translate into the average costs of tries and binary search trees, two structures whose performance is governed by the distribution of common prefixes among the stored strings.

For tries built over n independent strings drawn from a source, the expected number of nodes and the expected external path length grow at rates determined by the entropy of the source, and the fluctuations of these quantities are of central interest in the design of compressed indexes. For binary search trees, the expected internal path length is governed by a different quantity, namely the pressure associated with the source, which accounts for the way the probability of a string depends on its length-n prefix. Previous work established these leading-order behaviors for broad classes of dynamical sources under mild regularity assumptions, but the finer structure of the asymptotic expansions, including secondary terms and their dependence on arithmetic parameters, remained comparatively less understood.

In this paper we pursue a precise description of these finer terms. We introduce a regularity index that measures how the local contraction properties of the map vary across the interval, and we show that this index, together with the Diophantine exponent of the relevant parameter, determines the exponent of the first correction term in both trie and binary search tree costs. Our analysis proceeds by expressing the relevant generating functions as sums over cylinder sets of the map, applying a transfer operator whose spectral properties are controlled by the regularity index, and then extracting asymptotics through singularity analysis of the resulting functions. The Diophantine condition enters through the estimates on the iterates of the operator when the rotation parameter is badly approximable or only weakly approximable.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls the definitions of dynamical sources, tries, and binary search trees, and fixes notation for entropy, pressure, and the cost measures. Section 3 introduces the transfer operator and the regularity index, and proves the spectral gap estimates that form the backbone of the analysis. Section 4 treats the trie costs, deriving the asymptotic expansion of the expected number of nodes and external path length with explicit secondary terms. Section 5 treats the binary search tree costs and establishes the corresponding expansion of the internal path length. Section 6 analyzes the Diophantine threshold phenomenon and proves that the correction term vanishes to leading order when the Diophantine exponent exceeds a critical value. Section 7 presents explicit computations for Gauss-type and Farey-type sources and compares the predicted constants with numerical experiments. Section 8 discusses implications for compressed indexing and outlines open problems.

2. Preliminaries. Let X be the unit interval [0,1) and let T be a map from X to itself that is piecewise expanding with respect to a finite partition of X into subintervals called branches. We assume T admits an absolutely continuous invariant measure with respect to which the associated dynamical source is ergodic. A dynamical source is defined by a coding function that assigns to each point x in X a symbol from a finite alphabet according to the branch of the partition containing x. For a point x, the infinite word generated by the source is the sequence of symbols recorded along the orbit of x under T.

For a finite word w of length n, the cylinder set associated with w is the set of points in X whose first n symbols coincide with w. The probability of w under the source is the measure of its cylinder set with respect to the invariant measure. The entropy of the source is defined as the limit, as n tends to infinity, of the average of the negative logarithm of these cylinder probabilities, normalized by n. This quantity plays the role of the leading-order constant in the trie costs. The pressure of the source is defined through the transfer operator associated with the map and a weight function, and it captures the exponential growth rate of the sum of weighted cylinder probabilities over words of length n. Pressure governs the binary search tree costs at leading order.

A trie built over n independently generated strings is a tree in which each string is stored along the path spelled by its symbols, with branching occurring when two strings first differ. The number of nodes in the trie, the external path length, which is the sum of the depths of the leaves corresponding to the strings, and the internal path length are the standard cost measures. For binary search trees, the strings are inserted in the order of their arrival, and the internal path length measures the total depth of the nodes in the resulting search tree. Both structures depend on the statistics of common prefixes, and in particular on the probability that two independently generated strings share a prefix of a given length.

The Diophantine properties enter through the rotation or shift parameter that often appears in the definition of the map. A real number alpha is said to be of Diophantine type with exponent kappa when there exists a constant c such that the distance from q alpha to the nearest integer is at least c divided by q to the power kappa for all positive integers q. Numbers that are badly approximable correspond to kappa equal to two, and the set of Diophantine numbers with exponent kappa has full measure for kappa greater than two. We consider sources whose defining parameter alpha is either badly approximable or belongs to a class with prescribed exponent, and we track how the exponent propagates into the estimates on the transfer operator and into the resulting cost expansions.

We denote by H the entropy of the source, by P(s) the pressure as a function of a complex parameter s, and by lambda the leading eigenvalue of the transfer operator at parameter s equal to one. Throughout, the notation f(n) = g(n) + O(h(n)) means that the difference between f and g is bounded in absolute value by a constant multiple of h for all sufficiently large n. We use the symbol o to denote terms that are negligible compared with the displayed main terms.

3. The transfer operator and the regularity index. For a weight parameter s with real part greater than zero, we define the transfer operator L_s acting on a space of functions of bounded variation by summing over the inverse branches of T with weights given by the derivative raised to the power minus s. The operator is quasi-compact on this space under the assumption that T is uniformly expanding on each branch and that the branches satisfy a bounded distortion property. Quasi-compactness implies that the spectrum of L_s consists of a simple dominant eigenvalue together with an essential spectral radius strictly smaller than the dominant eigenvalue, and this spectral gap is the key ingredient in deriving asymptotic expansions.

The regularity index, which we denote by beta, measures how the logarithm of the derivative of the map varies in the Hölder sense near the indifferent points or near the boundaries of the branches. When the map has indifferent fixed points, the derivative approaches one at a rate governed by the local behavior of the map, and the index beta records the exponent of this approach. For uniformly expanding maps the index can be chosen to be zero, and the transfer operator then has a clean spectral gap. For intermittent maps with indifferent fixed points, the index is positive, and the spectral gap degenerates as the parameter approaches its critical value, producing slower convergence and larger correction terms in the costs.

We establish that the dominant eigenvalue lambda(s) is analytic in s in a neighborhood of the real axis and that its derivatives at s equal to one determine the entropy and the variance-like constants of the source. The pressure P(s) is the logarithm of lambda(s), and its values at s equal to one and at s equal to a parameter related to the binary search tree cost give the constants in the leading terms. The regularity index controls the modulus of the second-largest spectral contribution, and we prove that this modulus decays at an explicit rate depending on beta and on the Diophantine exponent kappa when the map contains a rotation-type component.

The proof of the spectral gap estimate proceeds by a Lasota-Yorke inequality adapted to the regularity class. Specifically, we show that for functions in the chosen space, the variation of L_s to the n-th power of a function is bounded by a constant times the n-th power of a contraction factor plus a constant times the sup norm, with the contraction factor depending on the minimal expansion rate and the constant depending on the distortion. When beta is positive, we modify the norm by a weight that blows up near the indifferent point, and the resulting inequality retains a spectral gap for parameters in a neighborhood of one. The Diophantine condition on alpha is then used to control the Fourier-type sums that arise when the operator is restricted to functions with prescribed rotation behavior, yielding bounds of the form n to the power minus kappa times a logarithmic factor.

We summarize these spectral results as a lemma. For sufficiently small perturbations of the parameter s around one, the operator L_s admits a decomposition into a rank-one spectral projection associated with the dominant eigenvalue and a remainder whose iterates decay geometrically when beta is zero and polynomially with exponent determined by beta when beta is positive. The remainder estimate carries an additional factor depending on kappa when the map has a rotation component, and this factor is the source of the Diophantine dependence in the final expansions.

4. Trie costs. Let T_n denote the trie built over n strings drawn independently from the source. The expected number of internal nodes of T_n can be expressed as a sum over k of the probability that a given prefix of length k is shared by at least two of the strings, summed over all prefixes. This probability is a polynomial in the cylinder probabilities, and summing over prefixes yields a generating function whose coefficients are controlled by the transfer operator. Using Mellin transform techniques, one obtains a representation of the expected number of nodes as a sum of a term proportional to n times the logarithm of n, a term linear in n with a constant depending on the entropy, a periodic fluctuation term of small amplitude, and a remainder.

The leading logarithmic term has coefficient equal to the reciprocal of the entropy, and this is the content of the classical result for memoryless sources extended to dynamical sources satisfying our regularity assumptions. The linear term arises from the analytic structure of the Dirichlet series associated with the cylinder probabilities, and its constant is expressed through the derivative of the pressure at parameter one. The periodic fluctuation term is a consequence of the lattice structure of the Mellin singularities, and its amplitude decreases as the regularity index increases. The remainder term is controlled by the spectral gap estimate and carries the Diophantine dependence: when alpha is badly approximable, the remainder is of order n to the power minus one half times a logarithmic factor, while for Diophantine exponents larger than two it becomes of order n to the power minus one plus a correction determined by kappa.

For the external path length, which is the sum of the depths of the leaves, the analysis is parallel. The expected external path length equals n times the logarithm of n divided by the entropy, plus a linear term whose constant differs from the node count constant by a quantity computed from the second derivative of the pressure, plus fluctuation and remainder terms. We derive the explicit form of these constants and verify that they reduce to known values for the Bernoulli and Markov special cases. Numerically, the fluctuation term for the external path length has larger amplitude than for the node count, consistent with the greater sensitivity of depth sums to local structure of the source.

We highlight the role of the regularity index in the trie analysis. When beta is zero, the remainder is exponentially small in the Mellin variable and the expansion has only the displayed terms up to polynomially small errors. When beta is positive, the spectral gap closes in a controlled manner, and the remainder acquires a polynomial correction of exponent proportional to beta. This means that intermittent sources exhibit slower convergence to their asymptotic regime, and finite-size simulations may show deviations from the leading-order prediction that persist over substantial ranges of n.

5. Binary search tree costs. Let B_n denote the binary search tree built by inserting n strings in order. The expected internal path length of B_n satisfies a recurrence obtained by conditioning on the first inserted string and its position relative to the remaining strings in the order of the source. For dynamical sources, the recurrence involves the probability that a random string falls on a particular side of the pivot, and this probability is determined by the cylinder structure of the source. The recurrence can be converted into a differential equation for the associated generating function, and its solution is expressed through the pressure of the source.

The expected internal path length is asymptotically equal to a constant times n times the logarithm of n, where the constant equals two divided by the entropy, and this constant coincides with the classical value for memoryless sources when the entropy is computed appropriately. We refine this result by deriving the linear term and identifying its dependence on the pressure at a shifted parameter. The linear term is shown to be of the form n times a constant involving the derivative of the pressure, and the fluctuation term is of order n times a small oscillatory function whose period is determined by the lattice structure of the Mellin singularities in the generating function.

The Diophantine properties of the source parameter influence the remainder term in the binary search tree expansion through the same mechanism as in the trie analysis, namely through the decay of the non-dominant spectral contributions. For badly approximable parameters, the remainder is of order n times a power of the logarithm of n, and we make this power explicit. For parameters with larger Diophantine exponents, the remainder is governed by the exponent kappa, and in the limit of exponents approaching the threshold, the remainder becomes comparable to the fluctuation term.

A notable consequence of the analysis is that the binary search tree cost is less sensitive to the regularity index than the trie cost at the level of the linear term, because the linear term depends on the pressure at a shifted parameter where the spectral gap is comfortably open. The regularity index influences only the remainder, and the effect is a polynomial correction whose exponent is a simple function of beta. This asymmetry between tries and binary search trees reflects their different dependence on prefix statistics: tries depend on the probability of shared prefixes at all depths simultaneously, while binary search trees depend on the probability of comparisons, which averages over depths in a smoother manner.

6. The Diophantine threshold. We now examine the regime in which the Diophantine exponent kappa of the rotation parameter exceeds a critical value, which we identify as the value at which the Fourier-type sums controlling the spectral remainder become summable. For exponents above this threshold, the correction to the leading constant in both the trie and binary search tree expansions vanishes, and the cost is asymptotically identical to that of a memoryless source with the same entropy. This phenomenon can be interpreted as a form of averaging: the correlations induced by the rotation are washed out by the arithmetic regularity of the parameter when the approximation properties are sufficiently strong.

To establish this threshold, we analyze the Fourier coefficients of the invariant density and show that their decay is controlled by the Diophantine exponent through a Denjoy-Koksma-type estimate. When kappa exceeds the critical value, the coefficients are square summable with a sum that is controlled uniformly in the discretization parameter, and this uniform control allows us to pass to the limit in the expansion of the cost generating function. Below the threshold, the sum diverges logarithmically or polynomially, and a residual term of order n to a power depending on kappa survives in the leading asymptotics.

The threshold result has an immediate practical consequence. For sources whose defining parameter is a quadratic irrational or a number of bounded type, the Diophantine exponent is exactly two, which lies at the boundary of the regime in which the correction vanishes. Such sources therefore exhibit a logarithmic correction of marginal size, and finite-size experiments can be misleading unless the sample size is large. For sources with transcendental parameters of high approximability, the correction is more pronounced, and the cost may deviate noticeably from the memoryless prediction.

We also show that the threshold is sharp in the sense that the exponent cannot be lowered without changing the qualitative behavior of the expansion. For parameters chosen from a set of exponent close to the critical value, we construct examples in which the remainder oscillates with an amplitude that does not decay with n, indicating that the threshold is intrinsic to the spectral analysis rather than an artifact of the proof method.

7. Examples and numerical verification. We illustrate the general theory with two families of sources. The first is the Gauss source, obtained from the Gauss map that generates the continued fraction expansion of a real number in the unit interval. The Gauss map has a well-known invariant density and an entropy equal to pi squared divided by six times the logarithm of two, which is the Lévy constant in the analysis of continued fractions. The Gauss map is uniformly expanding on its branches away from the boundary, and its regularity index is zero, so the spectral gap is clean and the trie and binary search tree expansions contain only the displayed terms up to exponentially small errors. The Diophantine properties enter through the continued fraction partial quotients of the input, and the rotation-type analysis applies to the associated rotation parameter in the coding.

The second family is the Farey source, generated by the Farey map that has an indifferent fixed point at the origin. This map has regularity index positive, and the analysis predicts slower convergence and a polynomial correction term in both cost measures. The invariant density has a non-integrable singularity at the origin, and the entropy is infinite in the naive sense, so the analysis requires the use of an infinite measure version of the transfer operator theory. We handle this by restricting attention to a finite measure induced map, which retains the essential correlation structure while producing a finite entropy. The resulting trie and binary search tree costs exhibit a correction of polynomial size, and the exponent of this correction matches the prediction from the regularity index.

Numerical experiments were designed to test the predicted constants and exponents. We generated sequences of several thousand strings from each source for a range of sample sizes, built the corresponding tries and binary search trees, and recorded the costs. The leading constants agreed with the predicted values to within the expected finite-size error, and the logarithmic-type behavior was clearly visible in the data. The secondary exponents were harder to estimate precisely, but the empirical slopes in log-log plots of the residuals were consistent with the predicted values for the Gauss source and with the predicted polynomial correction for the Farey source. The threshold phenomenon was more difficult to detect numerically, since the Diophantine exponent of an empirically chosen parameter is itself hard to certify, but parameters of high approximability produced costs closer to the memoryless benchmark, in accordance with the theory.

We also compared the dynamical source costs with those of Bernoulli and Markov sources having the same entropy. For the Gauss source, the difference in the linear terms was small but nonzero, reflecting the dependence of the linear constant on the derivative of the pressure, which is not determined by the entropy alone. This observation confirms that entropy is not a complete summary of the cost behavior and that the finer structure of the pressure function contains additional information relevant to algorithm performance.

8. Discussion and open problems. The results presented here show that the average costs of tries and binary search trees fed by dynamical sources are governed by three interacting features: the entropy and pressure of the source, the regularity index describing the local behavior of the map, and the Diophantine exponent of the arithmetic parameters. The entropy and pressure determine the leading constants, which are universal across broad classes of sources, while the regularity index and Diophantine exponent determine the secondary terms and, in the case of the Diophantine threshold, the presence or absence of a correction to the leading behavior. This layered structure clarifies which features of a source matter for algorithmic performance and which can be safely ignored at leading order.

For the design of compressed indexes, the implications are significant. Structures based on tries and suffix-type trees are widely used to index compressed text, and the analysis suggests that the costs of such structures for sources exhibiting strong correlations may deviate from the memoryless predictions in ways that depend on the arithmetic and analytic regularity of the source. Designers who rely on entropy alone to estimate performance may therefore underestimate the costs for intermittent or arithmetically irregular sources, and the regularity index offers a practical diagnostic for identifying such cases.

Several open problems remain. The first is to extend the analysis to multidimensional dynamical sources, where the map acts on a higher-dimensional domain and the cylinder structure is more complicated. The second is to determine whether the Diophantine threshold identified here has an analogue for other data structures, such as skip lists or digital search trees with different balancing rules. The third is to obtain sharp error bounds in the intermittent regime, where the present estimates are not believed to be optimal. The fourth is to develop efficient algorithms for estimating the regularity index and the Diophantine exponent from observed data, so that the theory can be applied to empirical sources without requiring knowledge of the underlying map. We expect that progress on these problems will deepen the connection between the arithmetic of dynamical systems and the performance of fundamental algorithms, and will provide a more complete understanding of how structure in the input shapes the cost of computation.

The manuscript addresses a practical gap in dialogue response modeling, namely how systems handle out-of-vocabulary words that frequently appear in conversational text such as slang, names, and misspellings. The authors propose generating embeddings for unseen tokens and pairing them with an enhanced LSTM encoder, which is a reasonable and relevant direction for improving response quality. The motivation is clearly stated, and the introduction situates the work adequately within existing research on sequence-to-sequence dialogue models. The methodology section describes the embedding strategy and the architectural modifications to the LSTM in sufficient detail to be followed, although a schematic diagram of the full model would make the pipeline easier to understand. The experimental evaluation compares the proposed model against several baselines using automatic metrics, and the reported gains are consistent across the datasets used. However, the paper relies heavily on automatic metrics such as BLEU and perplexity, which correlate weakly with human judgments of dialogue quality, so the authors should include human evaluation or at least a qualitative error analysis. The ablation study is useful but would be stronger if it isolated the contribution of the OOV embeddings from that of the LSTM enhancements, since the current results do not clearly separate the two effects. The related work section omits several recent transformer-based approaches that address the same vocabulary problem through subword tokenization, and a discussion of how the method compares to these would strengthen the paper's positioning. Reproducibility would also improve with the release of code, hyperparameter settings, and details on how the OOV embeddings were initialized. Overall, the paper presents a modest but sound contribution, and I recommend a major revision addressing the evaluation methodology, the ablation design, and the related work before the work can be considered for acceptance.

The manuscript studies the critical-point structure and global optimality of linear neural networks, and extends these results to single-hidden-layer ReLU networks. The topic is timely and of genuine interest to the optimization and deep learning theory communities, since understanding when gradient-based training avoids bad local minima remains a central open question. The authors position their contribution clearly within the existing literature on loss landscapes of deep linear networks, and the introduction offers a readable summary of prior work. The central claim, that every local minimum of a deep linear network is a global minimum while saddle points are the main obstacle, is well established in the literature, and the manuscript should more explicitly state what is new beyond these known results. The analysis of critical points is the strongest component of the paper, with a careful characterization of the Hessian structure at stationary points under full-rank and rank-deficient conditions. The proofs appear largely sound on a first reading, although several lemmas rely on rank assumptions that are stated only in passing and should be elevated to the main theorem statements. The notation is sometimes inconsistent, particularly in the switching between weight matrix dimensions and the indexing of layers, and a symbol table would substantially improve readability. The extension to single-hidden-layer ReLU networks is the most ambitious part of the work, but the argument there depends on piecewise linearity and on the activation pattern being fixed locally, which limits the generality of the conclusions. The authors should discuss more carefully how the results change when the activation pattern varies across the parameter space, since this is precisely where the nonconvexity of ReLU networks becomes difficult. The claim of global optimality for the ReLU extension would be considerably stronger if supported by either a formal proof covering all activation regions or a clearly scoped statement restricted to particular regimes. The experimental section is brief and consists mainly of small-scale simulations on synthetic data, which is adequate for illustrating the theory but insufficient to support broader claims about practical training. I would encourage the authors to include experiments on at least one standard benchmark, and to report the frequency with which gradient descent from random initialization converges to a global minimum. Several relevant works on the implicit bias of gradient descent and on the role of overparameterization are cited but not discussed in relation to the present results, and this connection would enrich the paper. The writing is generally clear, though some proofs are presented in an overly compressed style that makes verification difficult for readers outside the immediate subfield. Figures are informative, but the captions are minimal and should describe the experimental settings, including dataset sizes, learning rates, and number of random seeds. The limitations section acknowledges the restriction to shallow ReLU networks but does not address whether the techniques could plausibly extend to deeper architectures, which readers will naturally wonder about. A short discussion of what would constitute evidence against the main conjectures would also strengthen the paper's scientific framing. The related work section is thorough in its coverage of linear network results but somewhat thin on the ReLU landscape literature, which has grown considerably in recent years. Minor typographical errors appear throughout, including inconsistent hyphenation and a few missing article references, and a careful proofreading pass is recommended before resubmission. The reference list is mostly complete, although a few preprints have since appeared in peer-reviewed venues and should be updated accordingly. Overall, the paper makes a solid technical contribution to the theory of linear networks, and the ReLU extension is promising but requires either tighter assumptions stated upfront or broader supporting analysis. I recommend a major revision, with the principal requests being a sharper statement of novelty, a more careful treatment of activation-pattern variation in the ReLU case, and expanded empirical validation. With these changes, the work could be a valuable addition to the literature on the optimization landscape of neural networks.

Personal growth often begins where comfort ends. When we step outside familiar routines and take on challenges we have never faced before, we discover abilities we did not know we possessed. Taking risks forces us to confront fear, and each time we act despite that fear, we build confidence that carries into other parts of life. Unfamiliar challenges also expose us to new perspectives, teaching us that our assumptions about the world may be limited. Failure, which is an inevitable part of risk, becomes a valuable teacher rather than a reason for shame. Through setbacks, we learn resilience, patience, and the willingness to adapt our strategies. Many people look back on their most difficult experiences as the moments that shaped them most profoundly. A student who joins an unfamiliar debate team, for example, may struggle at first but gradually learns to think on their feet and speak with clarity. Similarly, someone who moves to a new country must rebuild their social world from scratch, and in doing so often develops independence and empathy. These experiences show that growth rarely comes from staying safe. Ultimately, pursuing unfamiliar challenges allows us to become more capable, more open, and more fully ourselves.

Smartphones have become a constant presence in students' lives, and rather than banning them outright, schools should consider allowing them in the classroom under clear guidelines. First, phones give students immediate access to a vast range of information, allowing them to look up unfamiliar words, verify historical dates, or check scientific facts during a lesson. This instant access encourages curiosity and helps students follow up on questions that might otherwise go unanswered. Second, many educational apps are designed to support learning in subjects such as mathematics, languages, and science, offering practice exercises, interactive simulations, and personalized feedback. Teachers can use these tools to differentiate instruction, giving advanced students challenges while providing extra support to those who need it. Third, smartphones can serve as cameras, recorders, and note-taking devices, which is especially helpful for students with disabilities or learning differences who rely on assistive technology. Fourth, using phones in class builds digital literacy, a skill that employers and colleges increasingly expect. Learning to evaluate online sources, use productive software, and manage digital tools responsibly prepares students for life beyond school. Fifth, phones can make collaboration easier, as groups can share documents, conduct research together, and present multimedia projects with ease. Sixth, allowing phones can reduce the sense of forbidden fruit that often makes them more distracting when banned. When students learn to use devices appropriately under supervision, they are more likely to develop self-regulation. Seventh, teachers can incorporate quick polls and quizzes through phones, giving them real-time insight into student understanding. This feedback helps educators adjust their lessons before misconceptions take hold. Of course, benefits depend on clear rules, such as designated times for phone use and consequences for misuse. With thoughtful policies, smartphones can become valuable learning tools rather than sources of distraction. In the end, schools that embrace this technology can better prepare students for a world where digital skills are essential.

Stress and Caffeine: How They May Affect Perception

Stress and caffeine are two of the most common influences on the brain in everyday life. Researchers have found that both can shape how we perceive sounds and interpret the behavior of others. Under high stress, the body releases hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline, which heighten alertness and can make the brain more sensitive to ambiguous stimuli. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors, which increases neural activity and can amplify this heightened state. In some studies, stressed or caffeinated individuals have been more likely to report hearing sounds that were not present, a phenomenon related to auditory hallucinations. Similar effects have been observed in tasks where people must judge facial expressions or social intentions, with some participants tending to read neutral faces as hostile. These findings suggest that the brain's pattern-detection systems can become overly active when pushed by stress or stimulants. It is important to note that most people who experience stress or drink coffee do not develop hallucinations, and the effects found in research are often modest and context-dependent. Individuals with a history of anxiety, psychosis, or sleep problems may be more vulnerable to these shifts in perception. Anyone who experiences frequent or distressing hallucinations should consult a healthcare professional. Reducing stress through sleep, exercise, and relaxation, and moderating caffeine intake, may help support clearer perception for most people.

Balancing extracurricular activities, personal growth, and family life is one of the central challenges of being a student. Each commitment offers something valuable, yet each also competes for limited time and energy. Sports, music, clubs, and volunteer work build skills and friendships that classrooms alone cannot provide. At the same time, personal growth requires quiet reflection, rest, and the freedom to explore interests without pressure to perform. Family life, too, deserves attention, since parents and siblings offer support, perspective, and a sense of belonging that anchor a young person through difficult seasons. Achieving balance does not mean giving equal hours to every area, but rather recognizing which commitments matter most at a given time and making deliberate choices. Setbacks are inevitable, whether a missed deadline, a lost competition, or a strained relationship, and how a student responds to them often matters more than the setback itself. Perseverance grows from small daily habits, such as keeping a realistic schedule, asking for help, and celebrating progress along the way. Over time, the effort to juggle many responsibilities teaches patience, organization, and self-awareness that serve a person long after school ends. Ultimately, a balanced life is not a perfectly managed one but a resilient one, shaped by honest priorities and the willingness to keep moving forward.

A positive outlook can shape almost every part of a person's life, from the friendships they form to the goals they reach. When people approach others with optimism and good faith, they tend to build stronger relationships, because kindness and encouragement invite trust and cooperation. Those who expect the best from classmates and teachers often find that they receive more support in return. In school, a positive attitude helps students face difficult material with curiosity rather than fear, which makes it easier to persist through challenges and learn from mistakes. Students who believe their effort can lead to improvement are more likely to keep practicing, asking questions, and seeking help when they need it. This mindset also supports better memory, focus, and motivation, all of which contribute to stronger academic results. Looking ahead, optimism can open doors to future opportunities, since people who remain hopeful are more willing to apply for jobs, pursue new skills, and take reasonable risks. Employers and mentors often notice individuals who meet setbacks with resilience and a constructive attitude, and they are frequently more inclined to offer responsibility and guidance to such people. A positive outlook does not mean ignoring problems, but rather approaching them with the belief that they can be solved. In the end, the habit of seeing possibility rather than limitation helps people grow, connect with others, and build the futures they hope for.

Subject: Proposal to Resolve Outstanding AEP Matters and Assess Enron's Financial and Legal Trade-offs

Dear Team,

I am writing to propose a structured approach to resolving the outstanding matters related to AEP and to weigh the financial and legal trade-offs for Enron before we commit to a course of action.

First, we need a clear inventory of every open item involving AEP, including contractual obligations, pending payments, disputed amounts, and any regulatory or reporting requirements.

Second, each item should be assigned an owner and a target resolution date so that accountability is clear from the outset.

Third, we should quantify the financial exposure associated with each matter, distinguishing between amounts already recognized, probable liabilities, and contingent risks.

Fourth, I recommend that we model at least three scenarios: negotiated settlement, partial resolution with deferred items, and full litigation or arbitration if talks fail.

Fifth, for each scenario, we should estimate the likely cost, the expected timeline, and the effect on our cash flow and credit standing.

Sixth, the legal team should review the strength of our position on each disputed point and identify any provisions that could limit or expand our liability.

Seventh, we must consider the reputational implications of each path, including how the outcome may affect relationships with other counterparties and regulators.

Eighth, the finance team should confirm how any settlement would be accounted for and whether disclosure obligations would be triggered.

Ninth, we should evaluate whether a negotiated resolution could include non-monetary terms, such as revised service arrangements or mutual releases, that reduce cost without weakening our position.

Tenth, I suggest we set a firm internal deadline for decision-making so that the process does not drift without resolution.

Eleventh, outside counsel and financial advisers should be engaged where specialized expertise is needed, particularly on any cross-border or regulatory questions.

Twelfth, all communications with AEP should be coordinated through a single point of contact to maintain consistency and avoid inadvertent admissions.

Thirteenth, privileged analysis should be kept within the legal team and clearly labeled to protect it from disclosure.

Fourteenth, we should document the rationale for each decision as we go, which will support audit review and any future dispute.

The manuscript addresses the problem of aligning samples across two datasets when no paired correspondences are given, framing the task as an entropic optimal transport problem augmented with side-information constraints. The authors position their contribution against standard unsupervised alignment methods, arguing that such methods often ignore available metadata that could sharpen the transport plan. The motivation is clearly stated and of practical relevance, since cross-dataset alignment arises in domains such as single-cell genomics, record linkage, and multimodal representation learning. The formulation extends the Sinkhorn-based entropic regularization framework by adding linear or group-level constraints on the coupling matrix, which is a reasonable and natural extension of the existing literature. The paper would benefit from a more explicit discussion of how the side-information constraints interact with the entropic regularization parameter, because the balance between the two determines whether the solution remains well conditioned. The theoretical section establishes convergence of the proposed iterative scheme, but the assumptions behind the convergence proof are stated somewhat informally and should be made precise. In particular, the authors should clarify whether the feasibility of the constrained problem is guaranteed under the stated conditions or must be checked in practice. The derivation of the dual problem is presented clearly, although the step connecting the constrained primal to the modified Sinkhorn updates is compressed and would be easier to follow with an explicit intermediate lemma. The experimental evaluation covers three benchmark settings, which is a sensible choice, yet the datasets are relatively small and the authors should justify why larger-scale experiments were not included. The baselines are appropriate in kind, but the paper does not compare against recent neural alignment methods that also incorporate auxiliary information, which weakens the claim of state-of-the-art performance. The reported gains over the unconstrained entropic baseline are consistent across settings, though the magnitude of improvement varies considerably and the authors should discuss the conditions under which the constraints help most. Reporting of variance across random seeds is inconsistent between tables, making it difficult to judge whether some differences are statistically meaningful. The ablation on the regularization strength is informative and supports the authors' argument that moderate entropy yields the best trade-off between accuracy and sparsity of the plan. The computational complexity analysis is brief, and a clearer statement of per-iteration cost relative to standard Sinkhorn would help practitioners assess scalability. The related work section is thorough in its coverage of optimal transport methods but is thinner on the literature concerning constrained and structured transport, which is directly relevant to the proposed approach. The writing is generally clear, though several notational choices, such as overloading the symbol for the constraint matrix, may cause confusion and should be revised. Figures are well chosen, but the transport plan visualizations would be more useful with axis labels and a legend indicating the side-information groups. The code availability statement is welcome, and the authors should ensure that the released implementation includes the exact configurations used for all reported experiments. Overall, the paper presents a useful and reasonably well-motivated extension of entropic optimal transport, and I recommend a major revision addressing the theoretical assumptions, the experimental scope, and the baseline comparisons before it can be considered for acceptance.

An optimistic mindset can shape nearly every part of a person's life, from the goals they pursue to the way they recover from setbacks. At its core, optimism is the tendency to expect that good outcomes are possible and that one's efforts can make a difference. This outlook is not the same as ignoring problems; rather, it is a way of approaching them with confidence and a willingness to act. Because of this, optimism can become a powerful force for personal success.

People who believe their efforts will pay off are more likely to set ambitious goals and keep working toward them. When obstacles appear, an optimistic person tends to see them as temporary and solvable rather than as proof of failure. This persistence often leads to better results over time, since many achievements depend on continued effort rather than a single moment of talent. In school, at work, and in personal projects, the expectation of success can encourage the steady practice that produces it.

Optimism also supports emotional well-being. Research in psychology has linked optimistic thinking with lower levels of stress, anxiety, and depression, although the relationship is complex and varies from person to person. An optimistic person is more likely to notice the positive aspects of daily life, which can build a habit of gratitude and contentment. Over time, these small moments of positive feeling can add up to a more satisfying and balanced life.

Perhaps the most important benefit of optimism is its role in resilience. Life inevitably brings disappointments, such as failed exams, lost jobs, or broken relationships. Optimistic people tend to interpret these experiences as challenges they can learn from, rather than as permanent defeats. This flexible way of thinking helps them recover more quickly and move forward with new strategies. Resilience is not the absence of hardship but the capacity to adapt and keep going, and optimism strengthens that capacity.

Still, optimism must be balanced with realism to be truly useful. Blind hope that ignores evidence can lead to poor decisions, while an honest assessment of risks allows a person to plan wisely. The healthiest form of optimism accepts difficulties as real while maintaining confidence in one's ability to respond. In this sense, optimism is less about expecting everything to go well and more about believing that effort and adaptability can improve the outcome.

Fortunately, optimism is not a fixed trait that people either have or lack. It can be cultivated through practices such as reframing negative thoughts, focusing on what is within one's control, and celebrating small progress. Building supportive relationships and surrounding oneself with encouraging people can also reinforce a hopeful outlook. Over time, these habits can gradually shift how a person understands their experiences and their future.

In conclusion, an optimistic mindset can influence success, well-being, and resilience in meaningful ways. It motivates persistence, supports emotional health, and helps people recover from life's inevitable setbacks. When paired with realistic judgment, optimism becomes a practical tool rather than a naive belief. By learning to cultivate hope and confidence, individuals can open the way to a more fulfilling and resilient life.

This manuscript proposes using topological persistence, drawn from persistent homology, as a measure of neural network complexity and as a validation-free signal for early stopping and generalization analysis. The central idea is appealing: if the persistence diagrams of a network's activation or weight-space geometry track generalization, practitioners could stop training without holding out a validation set, which is valuable in data-scarce settings. The authors motivate the work clearly and situate it within the broader literature on complexity measures such as norm-based bounds, sharpness, and intrinsic dimension. The paper is generally well organized, and the mathematical background on filtrations and persistence diagrams is accessible to readers with a machine learning background. However, several claims need stronger support before the conclusions can be considered established. The definition of the topological complexity measure is given at a high level, and the choice of filtration, which strongly influences the resulting diagrams, is not justified or ablated. The authors should specify exactly which point cloud is used at each layer, how the sample size affects the estimate, and how the summary statistic is computed from the diagram. The early stopping experiments are the most important empirical contribution, yet they are limited to a small number of architectures and datasets. Results should be reported across multiple random seeds with confidence intervals, since the reported improvements in several tables are within the apparent variance. The baselines are also incomplete: comparisons against standard validation-based early stopping, and against simple complexity proxies such as weight norm or effective rank, are needed to show that the topological signal adds information. The claim of being validation-free deserves scrutiny, since any hyperparameter selection for the topological method, such as filtration threshold or summary choice, may implicitly rely on held-out performance. The generalization analysis section would benefit from a clearer statement of what correlation is being measured and whether it persists after controlling for training loss and architecture width. Computational cost is mentioned only briefly, yet persistent homology scales poorly with the number of points, so a runtime comparison against the validation-based alternative is necessary for practical claims. The theoretical discussion relating persistence to generalization bounds is suggestive but informal, and the authors should either provide a formal statement or clearly label it as heuristic. The related work section omits some recent studies on topology and deep learning, and engaging with them would sharpen the novelty claim. Figures are generally informative, but the persistence diagrams would be more useful with consistent axis scales across conditions and an explanation of how points near the diagonal were treated. The release of code is appreciated and will aid reproducibility, but the paper should also document the exact preprocessing and random seeds used. The discussion of limitations is brief and should address failure cases, such as settings where the topological signal fails to track generalization, since these would help readers judge the scope of the method. The writing is clear overall, though some notation is overloaded, particularly the use of the symbol for both the filtration parameter and a layer index. Minor typographical errors appear in several captions and should be corrected. Overall, the idea is promising and potentially impactful, but the current evidence supports the method only as an interesting exploratory tool rather than a reliable replacement for validation-based early stopping. I recommend a major revision that adds broader experiments, stronger baselines, runtime analysis, and a more careful treatment of the validation-free claim.

Northern Ireland's constitutional future remains a central question in the years following the UK's vote to leave the European Union, with debate intensifying over the prospects for a future border poll and the arrangements governing the island's frontier. Under the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, the Secretary of State is empowered to call a poll on Irish unity if it appears likely that a majority would favour it, a mechanism that Brexit brought renewed attention to. Nationalist parties argue that the UK's departure from the EU, and the shifts it produced in trade and governance, have strengthened the case for reconsidering the region's place within the UK. Unionist leaders, by contrast, contend that the conditions for a poll have not been met and that the majority of voters in Northern Ireland continue to support remaining in the United Kingdom. The Northern Ireland Protocol, later replaced in part by the Windsor Framework agreed in early 2023, sought to avoid a hard border on the island of Ireland by keeping Northern Ireland aligned with certain EU rules for goods. These arrangements aimed to preserve the free movement of people and trade across the land border with the Republic of Ireland, which remains an EU member state. Critics from unionist communities argued that the checks on goods moving from Great Britain to Northern Ireland created a sense of separation from the rest of the UK. Supporters of the arrangements countered that they were necessary to protect the Good Friday Agreement and the peace it underpinned. Public opinion surveys have shown a shifting picture, with a growing share of respondents expressing openness to Irish unity in some scenarios, though outright majorities in favour of a poll have been difficult to confirm. Analysts note that the outcome of any future vote would depend heavily on economic considerations, identity, and the terms of any proposed transition. The Irish government has repeatedly stated that it would prepare for the possibility of unification while maintaining that the decision rests with the people of Northern Ireland. Cross-border cooperation in areas such as health, education, infrastructure, and policing continues through institutions established under the peace process, including the North-South Ministerial Council. Looking ahead, the balance of political, economic, and demographic forces will shape whether the question of a border poll moves from debate to formal consideration. For now, both governments and local parties have emphasised the need for stable, practical arrangements that protect livelihoods and the peace settlement while the constitutional debate continues.

This manuscript applies reinforcement learning to the design of urban metro networks and benchmarks the approach against alternative optimization methods, a topic of clear practical relevance for transit planning. The problem framing is well motivated, since metro network design involves combinatorial choices about station placement, line routing, and connectivity that are difficult to solve exactly at city scale. The authors present a clearly defined formulation of the environment, reward structure, and state representation, which makes the learning setup easier to follow and reproduce. The comparative evaluation against established heuristics and exact or metaheuristic methods is a strength, as it situates the reinforcement learning results within existing practice rather than in isolation. However, the paper would benefit from a more detailed description of the hyperparameter tuning and training procedure, since conclusions about relative performance can be sensitive to how each baseline was configured. The experiments are conducted on a limited set of synthetic and real-world city layouts, and the authors should justify these choices or extend the evaluation to a more diverse range of urban geographies and demand patterns. The cost and travel-time objectives used to score candidate networks are reasonable proxies, but the manuscript would be stronger if it discussed how sensitive the rankings are to alternative weightings of construction cost, ridership, and passenger transfers. Reporting of computational cost is somewhat incomplete, and a clearer account of training time, inference time, and scalability with network size would help practitioners judge feasibility. The statistical analysis would also be improved by reporting variance across multiple random seeds and by including significance tests for the claimed performance differences. The discussion of limitations is brief and should more explicitly address generalization to real planning constraints such as existing infrastructure, political feasibility, and phased construction. The related work section covers the classical optimization literature well but could engage more with recent graph-based and learning-based network design studies. Overall, the paper addresses an important question with a sound approach, and with additional robustness analysis and more transparent reporting, it could make a meaningful contribution to the field.

Using a cellphone while driving has become one of the most serious threats on the road today. Many drivers believe they can handle a quick glance at a message or a brief phone call without any real consequence. However, the evidence shows that even momentary distractions can have deadly results. Driving requires constant attention, quick reactions, and sound judgment, and a phone pulls focus away from all three.

The danger begins with the three main types of distraction: visual, manual, and cognitive. A driver who looks at a screen takes their eyes off the road, sometimes for several seconds. At highway speeds, a car can travel the length of a football field in that time. Manual distraction occurs when a driver takes a hand off the wheel to type, swipe, or hold the phone. Cognitive distraction is perhaps the most overlooked, because a driver can keep their eyes forward and hands on the wheel yet still have their mind elsewhere, absorbed in a conversation or a text.

Research has consistently confirmed these risks. Studies using driving simulators and real-world video footage have found that texting makes drivers far more likely to drift out of their lane and to miss important signals or hazards. Reaction times slow considerably, and the gap between a driver's response and a sudden emergency can become the difference between a close call and a crash. Even hands-free devices have been shown to impair attention, which means that simply using a headset does not fully solve the problem.

The human consequences of these choices are severe. Every year, thousands of people are killed in crashes involving distracted drivers, and many more are seriously injured. Those victims include pedestrians, cyclists, passengers, and drivers who did nothing wrong except share the road with someone who chose to look at a screen. Families are left grieving, and survivors often live with lasting physical and emotional harm. Behind every statistic is a person whose life was changed in an instant.

Laws across many countries and states now prohibit handheld phone use while driving, and some ban nearly all phone use behind the wheel. These laws reflect a growing recognition that personal convenience should never outweigh public safety. Enforcement and penalties have increased in many places, yet the problem persists because the habit is so deeply ingrained. Many people feel compelled to respond to messages immediately, and that pressure makes the temptation hard to resist.

Fortunately, there are practical ways to reduce the danger. Drivers can silence notifications before starting the car, place their phones out of reach, or enable do-not-disturb modes that automatically block alerts while the vehicle is moving. Pulling over safely is always the right choice when a call or message truly cannot wait. Passengers can also help by handling navigation or responding to messages on the driver's behalf. Small changes in habit can make a significant difference.

Ultimately, driving is a serious responsibility that demands full attention. A phone may seem harmless in the moment, but the few seconds it steals from the road can last a lifetime for someone else. Choosing to put the phone away is a simple decision that protects everyone who shares the road, and it is one that every driver should make every time they get behind the wheel.

Everyone called her Ace, though her real name was Lena. The nickname started the winter she was seven, when her uncle Dale taught her to shuffle at the kitchen table while the radio shouted through the wall. He said a good hand could save you from a bad night, and she believed him.

The house was never quiet for long. Doors slammed, voices climbed, and sometimes glass broke in the other room. Lena learned to read the weather of her family the way she read the cards: who was bluffing, who was about to fold, who would walk out and who would come back apologizing.

Her mother worked double shifts and came home smelling of fryer oil and tiredness. Her stepfather, Rick, drank whiskey straight from the bottle and called every card game a waste of time. But on the nights he fell asleep in his chair, the three of them, Lena, Dale, and her little brother Sam, would pull the table close to the heater and play gin rummy until their eyes drooped.

Sam was the one who gave her the name, though he could never explain why. He just shouted "Ace!" whenever she won a hand, and the word stuck to her like a badge. At school, teachers used it too, and soon she answered to it more readily than to Lena.

Lena liked what the name seemed to promise. An ace was the high card, the one that could change everything with a single turn. She imagined herself that way, quick and clever and impossible to pin down.

Still, she knew the truth about the game. You could play perfectly and still lose, because the deal was never entirely yours. She kept that thought tucked away, the way she kept a spare dollar in her sock.

One night in March, the shouting went on longer than usual, and Lena took Sam into the bathroom and locked the door. They sat on the cold tile with a deck of cards between them and dealt out hands by the glow of the nightlight. Sam won the first round, then the second, and laughed so hard he got the hiccups.

Later, a neighbor knocked and asked if everything was all right. Lena opened the door just enough to answer, her voice steady, and said yes, they were fine. That was her first real bluff, and it worked.

In the morning she walked to school with Sam's mittens on her hands and the deck in her pocket. At the bus stop, Sam asked her what card she would be if she could be any card. She thought about it for a long time.

"The one that gets to decide," she said at last. Sam nodded as though that settled it, and the bus came around the corner, and Ace climbed on first.

Remote learning from home has become a common part of education, offering both clear benefits and real drawbacks. One of its main advantages is flexibility. Students can often set their own schedules, review recorded lectures at their own pace, and avoid long commutes, which frees up time for rest, part-time work, or extracurricular activities. Learning from home can also be more comfortable for students who feel anxious or overwhelmed in crowded classrooms, allowing them to focus more calmly on their studies. However, remote learning also has significant disadvantages. Many students struggle with self-discipline when there is no teacher physically present to keep them on track, and it is easy to become distracted by phones, television, or household chores. Social connection is another concern, since friendships, group projects, and casual conversations with classmates are harder to build through a screen. Access to reliable internet and suitable equipment is not equal for everyone, so students from low-income families may fall behind through no fault of their own. In the end, remote learning works best when it is combined with clear routines, strong communication with teachers, and opportunities for students to connect with others.
