Venus presents some of the harshest conditions of any planet in the Solar System, with surface temperatures near 465 degrees Celsius and a crushing atmospheric pressure about 90 times that of Earth. These extremes destroy most electronics within hours, which is why past Soviet landers such as Venera 13 survived only about two hours on the surface. Rugged mechanical technology, including simple, heat-tolerant components and systems that do not depend on delicate silicon circuits, offers a promising way to overcome these limits. Such designs could enable long-duration missions that study the planet's dense clouds, volcanic terrain, and climate history, which may reveal important lessons about how a planet's atmosphere can spiral out of control. Although engineers still face serious challenges in materials, power, and communication, exploring Venus with resilient machines could transform our understanding of planetary habitability both within and beyond our Solar System.

This manuscript proposes an unsupervised method for learning graph-level representations by maximizing mutual information between whole-graph embeddings and local subgraph embeddings. The core idea, contrasting global and local views of the same graph, is well motivated and draws sensibly on the success of contrastive and mutual-information objectives in image and text representation learning. The authors position the work clearly against prior graph kernel and supervised GNN baselines, and the framing of why local-global agreement should capture structural information is a strength. However, the theoretical justification connecting the mutual information estimator to the downstream utility of the embeddings is somewhat under-developed, and the paper would benefit from a clearer argument about what invariances the objective encourages. The choice of subgraph sampling strategy is central to the method, yet the manuscript gives only a brief description and does not analyze how sensitive results are to sampling size or neighborhood radius. The experiments cover several standard graph classification benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the reported gains over the strongest baselines are often within the range of reported variance, and the statistical testing is not described. Ablations removing either the local or global component are included and are informative, though an ablation on the negative sampling scheme would strengthen the evidence that the gains come from the proposed objective. The comparison with recent contrastive graph methods appears limited, and the authors should either include more of these or justify their omission. Computational cost is discussed only qualitatively, and wall-clock training time and memory measurements would help readers assess practicality on larger graphs. The related work section is thorough in its coverage of kernel methods but could be more precise in distinguishing the proposed objective from existing local-global infomax variants. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code and by specifying all hyperparameter search ranges and random seeds. The writing is generally clear, though some notation is overloaded between node, subgraph, and graph embeddings and should be standardized. Overall, the paper presents a reasonable and promising contribution, but the empirical claims need stronger statistical support and the theoretical motivation needs tightening before the conclusions can be fully endorsed. My recommendation is a major revision.

This paper addresses the problem of learning controllable temporally extended actions, or options, from deep successor representations in stochastic environments. The authors aim to bridge two lines of work: successor representations, which encode expected future state occupancies and support fast transfer across reward functions, and hierarchical reinforcement learning, which relies on temporally extended actions to improve exploration and credit assignment. The motivation is clear and well grounded, since many real-world control problems are both stochastic and hierarchically structured. The introduction situates the work reasonably within the existing literature on options discovery, including eigenoption and bottleneck-based approaches, though the coverage of recent stochastic-environment option methods could be more thorough. The central contribution is a framework that derives option policies directly from the learned successor representation, rather than from a separately optimized intrinsic reward. This is a conceptually appealing design choice because it ties option construction to the same representation used for value estimation. The authors formalize the notion of controllability, defining an option as controllable when its termination and trajectory can be reliably steered by the agent. The formal definitions are mostly precise, although a few symbols are introduced before they are fully explained, which slightly impedes readability. The theoretical analysis establishes that, under certain assumptions on the transition kernel, the learned options converge to policies that maximize occupancy of a target set of states. The proof sketch is plausible, but the assumptions, particularly those concerning ergodicity and bounded stochasticity, are strong and deserve more discussion regarding when they hold in practice. The algorithm combines a deep neural network approximator for the successor representation with a learned termination function and an intra-option policy. The architecture description is adequate, yet several hyperparameters and training schedules are reported only briefly, which may hinder reproducibility. Experiments are conducted on a set of grid-world and continuous-control benchmarks with varying levels of transition noise. The choice to vary stochasticity explicitly is a strength, as it directly tests the claimed advantage in stochastic settings. The baselines include standard option-critic and flat deep Q-learning agents, which are appropriate comparisons, but the absence of a successor-representation baseline without temporal abstraction weakens the attribution of gains. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves higher sample efficiency and more stable learning curves across most noise levels. The improvements are most pronounced at moderate stochasticity, while at very high noise the advantage narrows, a finding the authors discuss candidly. Reported metrics are averaged over five random seeds, and confidence intervals are shown in most figures, although the small number of seeds limits the strength of statistical conclusions. Ablation studies isolate the contributions of the learned termination function and the successor-based option policy, and they support the claim that both components matter. An additional ablation on the discount factor would have helped clarify sensitivity, since the successor representation is known to be sensitive to this parameter. The qualitative analysis, including visualizations of learned options in grid worlds, is informative and helps readers understand the behavior of the discovered skills. The visualizations would benefit from a clearer legend and explicit annotation of stochastic transitions to aid interpretation. The related work section is concise and fair, although it could better acknowledge concurrent efforts that combine successor features with option discovery. Writing quality is generally good, with a logical flow from motivation to method to evaluation. Some sentences in the methods section are overly long and contain nested clauses that could be simplified. Notation is mostly consistent, though the distinction between the successor representation and the successor features is occasionally blurred. The discussion section appropriately notes limitations, including reliance on a fixed set of option initiation sets and the computational overhead of training the successor network. Future directions, such as extending the approach to partially observable settings and to learned state abstractions, are reasonable and well motivated. The authors provide code availability, which is commendable and substantially improves the potential impact of the work. Overall, the paper makes a meaningful and reasonably novel contribution at the intersection of representation learning and hierarchical control. The theoretical claims are promising but need tighter justification of their assumptions. The empirical evidence supports the main claims within the tested domains, though broader benchmarks and more seeds would strengthen confidence. I recommend a minor revision, with the primary requests being clarification of the theoretical assumptions, an expanded set of baselines, and additional ablations on key hyperparameters.

The manuscript investigates whether prioritized experience replay, a technique usually associated with value-based reinforcement learning, can serve as a regularizer for policy-gradient training in program synthesis. The motivation is sound, since program synthesis rewards are sparse and policy-gradient estimates are notoriously high-variance, so any stabilizing mechanism is worth examining. The authors frame the problem clearly and situate their work within prior literature on reinforcement learning for code generation, though the related work section could more explicitly distinguish their approach from off-policy corrections already used in actor-critic methods. The central claim is that replaying high-priority trajectories improves sample efficiency and reduces gradient variance, and this is a reasonable hypothesis to test. However, the paper does not clearly justify why prioritization by temporal-difference error, which is defined for value estimates, transfers meaningfully to a policy-gradient setting where no such error is directly computed. The authors should state explicitly which priority signal they use and how it is derived. The experimental setup covers a benchmark of synthesis tasks with a fixed set of baselines, which is appropriate in scope. Nevertheless, the baselines appear somewhat weak, and the authors should include a comparison against a standard entropy-regularized policy gradient and against uniform replay to isolate the contribution of prioritization itself. The reported improvements are modest, and the paper would benefit from confidence intervals or results over a larger number of random seeds, since single-run differences in this domain can be misleading. The ablation studies are a strength, particularly the analysis of the priority exponent, which shows how sensitive the method is to this hyperparameter. Still, the authors should report how the chosen exponent was selected, because if it was tuned on the same tasks used for evaluation, the reported gains may be optimistic. The writing is generally clear, though several sections repeat the same claims about variance reduction without providing supporting measurements. A plot of gradient variance over training for each method would substantially strengthen this claim. The discussion of limitations is brief and should be expanded to address the computational overhead of maintaining a priority buffer and the potential for replay to amplify rare but misleading trajectories. The authors also do not discuss how replay interacts with the on-policy assumptions of standard policy-gradient estimators, which is a substantive theoretical concern. Reproducibility is partially addressed through the provided hyperparameter table, but the code and the exact benchmark splits are not mentioned, and their release would greatly help the community. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant question with a plausible method and useful ablations. Its main weaknesses are the unclear definition of the priority signal, the limited statistical rigor, and the thin treatment of theory. I recommend a major revision, with the expectation that the authors can resolve these issues within the scope of the existing study.

Should students be permitted to use mobile devices during class for learning and safety reasons? This question has become increasingly urgent as smartphones have become nearly universal among young people. While some educators argue that phones are distracting and should be banned outright, a more balanced approach recognizes that mobile devices can support learning and protect student well-being when used thoughtfully and within clear limits.

The most compelling argument for allowing mobile devices is their educational value. Phones give students immediate access to a vast library of information, from encyclopedias and translation tools to scientific simulations and historical archives. A student who wonders about a word, a date, or a chemical reaction can find an answer in seconds, turning a passing curiosity into genuine inquiry. Many teachers already use devices for polls, quizzes, research projects, and collaborative documents, showing that these tools can make lessons more interactive and engaging.

Mobile devices also play an important role in personal safety. Students may need to contact a parent after a schedule change, report a medical concern, or reach emergency services during a crisis. In an era when school emergencies are a real concern, having a phone can provide a direct line to help. For students with medical conditions, such as diabetes or severe allergies, a device may also provide quick access to health information or emergency contacts.

Critics, however, raise legitimate concerns. Phones can pull attention away from lessons, and notifications from social media and messaging apps can fragment concentration. Research on the cognitive effects of constant device access suggests that the mere presence of a phone may reduce focus, even when it is turned off. Cyberbullying and the sharing of inappropriate content are also serious issues that schools must address.

These concerns do not necessarily justify a total ban, but they do argue for structure. Schools can establish clear policies that specify when devices may be used, such as during designated research activities or as part of teacher-directed lessons. Phones could be stored in lockers or pouches during instructional time and accessible during breaks or in emergencies. Such an approach preserves the benefits of technology while minimizing its distractions.

Ultimately, the goal of education is to prepare students to think independently and use tools responsibly. Banning phones entirely may deny students the chance to learn self-regulation, digital literacy, and responsible technology use, skills they will need throughout their lives. A thoughtful policy that allows purposeful device use, guided by teachers and supported by clear rules, offers the best path forward. Students deserve an environment that embraces both the promise and the pitfalls of the digital age.

The manuscript addresses an important and challenging problem: learning policies for MOBA games where agents must choose among discrete actions (such as which ability to cast) and also set continuous parameters (such as aim direction or cast distance) for each choice. The authors frame this as a hybrid action space and propose a architecture that pairs a discrete action head with a continuous parameter head, trained jointly, which is a sensible and well-motivated design. The related work section gives a fair overview of prior approaches to parameterized action spaces, though it would benefit from a more direct comparison with recent hybrid-action methods in other domains. The experimental setup uses a standard MOBA benchmark environment, and the choice of baselines is reasonable, but the paper should report results across multiple random seeds with confidence intervals, since the reported differences between methods are often small. The ablation study is a strength, as it isolates the contribution of the joint training objective from the architectural choices, although the authors should clarify how the continuous parameter head is conditioned on the sampled discrete action. The discussion of computational cost is limited, and given that MOBA training is expensive, readers would benefit from wall-clock comparisons and sample-efficiency curves. The theoretical justification for the gradient estimator used in the hybrid update is sketched rather than fully derived, and an appendix with the full derivation would strengthen the claims. Several figures have unlabeled axes or unclear legends, which makes the learning curves difficult to interpret without rereading the text. The authors should also state more explicitly what the code and environment configurations will be released, since reproducibility is a central concern for this kind of work. The writing is generally clear, though some notation for the hybrid policy distribution is introduced inconsistently between the methods and experiments sections. Overall, the paper makes a useful contribution with a sound core idea, and I recommend a major revision addressing statistical reporting, computational cost, derivation completeness, and presentation before acceptance.

This manuscript presents an empirical comparison of continual learning strategies for generative models trained sequentially across multiple image datasets. The topic is timely, since catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle when generative models must adapt to new data distributions without access to earlier training sets. The authors position their work well within the existing literature, though the related work section could more clearly distinguish their evaluation setting from prior studies focused on discriminative classifiers. The choice to benchmark replay-based, regularization-based, and architecture-based methods side by side is a strength, as it allows direct comparison under a shared protocol. However, the paper does not sufficiently justify why the chosen dataset sequences were selected, and the ordering of tasks appears to be fixed without analysis of how sensitive results are to task order. The evaluation relies heavily on Fréchet Inception Distance, and while this is a reasonable choice, the authors should supplement it with precision and recall metrics or human assessments to capture sample quality and diversity separately. The reported improvements of the replay-based approach over the baselines are meaningful, but the paper would benefit from confidence intervals or results across multiple random seeds to establish statistical reliability. Several figures showing generated samples are informative, yet their selection process is not described, raising concerns about cherry-picking. The hyperparameter tuning procedure is described only briefly, and it is unclear whether the same budget of tuning was applied to all compared methods. This matters because differences in tuning effort can produce misleading conclusions about relative performance. The memory footprint and computational cost of each strategy are discussed, which is valuable for practitioners, but these costs are not integrated into the main comparison. The authors should present a clear accuracy-versus-cost analysis to help readers select methods for resource-constrained settings. The discussion of forgetting dynamics is insightful, particularly the observation that early tasks degrade more rapidly under regularization methods. Nevertheless, the mechanistic explanations offered are speculative and would be stronger if supported by targeted ablation experiments. The limitations section is brief and should address the restricted resolution of the datasets, the use of a single model family, and the absence of very long task sequences. Reproducibility is partially supported through the release of code, but the paper should also specify the exact dataset splits and preprocessing steps used. The writing is generally clear, although several passages in the methods section are dense and would benefit from a summary table of all configurations. Overall, the paper provides a useful empirical baseline for the community and addresses an important gap in the literature. Its conclusions are reasonable given the evidence presented, but they are currently limited in generality by the narrow experimental scope. I recommend a major revision, with the primary requests being multi-seed evaluation, a fair and documented tuning protocol, and broader metric coverage. With these improvements, the contribution would be substantially more convincing and valuable to researchers and practitioners alike.

Ohio sits at a crossroads in its energy future, and the choices voters make in the coming elections could heavily influence how quickly the state moves away from coal and toward solar power. For decades, Ohio's economy has been closely tied to coal, with power plants, mines, and rail networks supporting thousands of jobs in the southeastern and eastern parts of the state. Now, as utilities retire aging coal units and developers propose new solar farms across the countryside, residents, business leaders, and local officials are watching closely to see what comes next. Federal policy is one of the biggest variables in this transition. Tax credits, grants, and regulatory standards set in Washington can make solar projects far more or less attractive to investors and utilities. Candidates who favor clean energy incentives often point to the economic opportunities of manufacturing solar panels, batteries, and related components, while those who prioritize fossil fuels frequently argue that coal and natural gas provide reliable and affordable baseload power. State-level decisions matter just as much. The Ohio legislature has the power to set rules for siting renewable energy projects, and in recent years lawmakers have debated measures that would give local governments more control over where solar farms can be built. Supporters of these measures say communities deserve a voice in land use decisions, while critics warn that restrictive rules could slow investment and drive developers to neighboring states. Ohio's energy debate also reflects longstanding tensions between urban and rural areas. Many farmers see solar leases as a way to earn steady income from land that might otherwise produce low margins, and some landowners have embraced the extra revenue. Others worry about the loss of farmland, changes to rural character, and the long-term fate of decommissioned panels. Coal communities face their own anxieties. Workers in mining and power generation often describe a sense of uncertainty about pensions, retraining programs, and whether new jobs will match the wages they once earned. Some regions have seen local tax revenue from coal plants shrink as facilities close, leaving school districts and county budgets under pressure. Advocates for a fast transition argue that the costs of inaction are growing. Air quality concerns linked to coal combustion, along with the health impacts of mining and ash disposal, have prompted calls for cleaner alternatives. Solar power has become one of the cheapest sources of new electricity in many parts of the country, and proponents say Ohio risks falling behind if it fails to attract the manufacturing and installation work that accompanies this growth. Skeptics counter that renewable energy alone cannot yet guarantee grid reliability during extended periods of low sunlight or peak winter demand. They argue that storage technology, transmission upgrades, and natural gas backup remain necessary, and that rushing the transition could raise electricity bills for households already struggling with costs. Utilities occupy a central place in this debate. Investor-owned companies must balance regulatory requirements, shareholder expectations, and customer rates while planning the retirement of large generating assets. Their long-term resource plans, which are subject to review by state regulators, will shape how much solar capacity gets built and how quickly older plants are closed. Environmental groups have pushed for ambitious clean energy targets, and some have challenged utility proposals they consider insufficient. Industry groups, meanwhile, have warned that overly aggressive timelines could strain the system. Elections affect each of these players. A change in the governor's office or in control of the legislature can alter the priorities of state agencies, including the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio. Local races for county commissioners and township trustees also matter, since these officials often make decisions about zoning, tax abatements, and permits for large energy projects. Voters in these races may not always connect their ballots to energy policy, but the consequences can be substantial. Looking ahead, analysts expect Ohio's energy mix to continue shifting over the next decade, though the pace and shape of that change remain uncertain. Much will depend on federal incentives, state legislation, market prices for natural gas and solar equipment, and the willingness of communities to host new projects. For many Ohioans, the question is less about whether the transition will happen and more about who will benefit, who will bear the costs, and how fairly the gains will be shared. As the next round of elections approaches, those questions are likely to remain at the center of the state's political conversation.

Reducing how much we rely on cars is one of the most practical steps a community can take toward becoming healthier, safer, and less stressful. Cars have become so central to daily life that many people drive even short distances that could easily be walked or biked. This habit carries costs that often go unnoticed. By choosing alternatives such as walking, cycling, public transit, and carpooling, residents can improve their own well-being while strengthening the places where they live.

Physical health is one of the clearest benefits. People who walk or bike to work and errands build exercise into their routines without needing to set aside extra time for a gym. Regular activity lowers the risk of heart disease, diabetes, and obesity, and it can improve sleep and mood. Because active travel is woven into everyday life, it is easier to sustain than occasional workouts.

Air quality also improves when fewer cars are on the road. Vehicle exhaust releases pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate matter, which are linked to asthma, lung disease, and other respiratory problems. Children, older adults, and people with existing health conditions are especially vulnerable. Cleaner air means fewer emergency visits and healthier neighborhoods for everyone.

Safety improves as well. Road crashes cause thousands of deaths and serious injuries each year, and fewer cars on the road means fewer opportunities for collisions. Communities that invest in protected bike lanes, sidewalks, and traffic-calmed streets tend to see fewer pedestrian and cyclist injuries. Slower traffic and better design protect not only people on foot or bicycle but drivers too.

Stress levels can also decline when people move away from heavy car dependence. Driving in congested traffic is known to raise blood pressure and frustration, and long commutes are consistently linked to lower life satisfaction. Choosing a walk, a bike ride, or a train trip can offer a calmer start and end to the day. Some people find that reading or simply looking around during transit gives their minds a welcome break.

Alternative transportation also builds stronger communities. When people walk and bike through their neighborhoods, they are more likely to greet neighbors, notice local businesses, and feel a sense of belonging. Streets full of pedestrians tend to feel more lively and watched over, which can deter crime. Shared spaces like public transit stations and shaded sidewalks become places where people connect.

Economic benefits follow naturally. Car ownership is expensive, with costs for fuel, insurance, maintenance, and parking adding up quickly. Households that rely less on cars can redirect that money toward housing, food, or savings. Local businesses also benefit, since people who walk or bike tend to shop at nearby stores more often than drivers who pass them by.

Environmental gains reinforce all of these advantages. Transportation is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, and reducing car trips helps slow climate change. Quieter streets with fewer vehicles also reduce noise pollution, which has been linked to stress and poor sleep. Green spaces and trees that replace parking lots and wide roads can cool neighborhoods and absorb rainwater.

Reducing car use does not require abandoning cars altogether, and it is not realistic for everyone in every situation. Many people live far from transit or must carry heavy loads, and their needs deserve respect. Still, communities can make alternatives more accessible through better public transit, safe crossings, bike networks, and zoning that places homes, schools, and shops closer together. Each small shift makes the next one easier.

Choosing alternative transportation is ultimately a choice to invest in health, safety, calm, and connection. A community that walks, rides, and shares its streets is one where people are more likely to be well and to look out for one another. The benefits reach far beyond the individual trip, shaping the kind of place we all call home.

Autonomous vehicles promise significant safety benefits for people who struggle to drive safely, including learners and impaired drivers. Most serious crashes today stem from human error, such as distraction, fatigue, poor judgment, or slow reaction times. Self-driving systems do not get tired, text on their phones, or drive under the influence of alcohol, which could eliminate many of these risks. For novice drivers, autonomous features could reduce the chance of inexperience leading to dangerous mistakes on unfamiliar roads. Learners who are still developing hazard perception might also benefit from vehicles that automatically maintain safe following distances and respond to sudden obstacles. People with medical conditions that affect driving, such as epilepsy, severe vision impairment, or sudden sedation effects, could gain safer independence through automated driving. Impaired drivers, whether affected by alcohol, drugs, or medication, could be transported safely without relying on their own judgment. However, these benefits come with real challenges that must be addressed. Current systems are not equally capable in all conditions, and they can struggle with heavy rain, snow, construction zones, or unpredictable pedestrian behavior. A learner or impaired person who relies heavily on automation may fail to develop or maintain the skills needed to handle emergencies when the system disengages. Handoff situations, where control must suddenly return to a human, are especially dangerous for someone who is drowsy, intoxicated, or inexperienced. There are also concerns about overconfidence, since drivers may trust automation more than they should. Liability is another unresolved issue, as it is unclear who is responsible when an automated vehicle causes a crash involving a learner or impaired occupant. Privacy and data collection raise further questions about how driving behavior and health information are stored and shared. Equity matters as well, because expensive autonomous technology may remain out of reach for the low-income communities that could benefit most. Ultimately, autonomous vehicles could greatly improve safety for learners and impaired drivers, but only if regulation, training, and system design account for their limitations and the realities of human behavior.

Making good decisions rarely depends on how intelligent we are alone; it depends heavily on the information and viewpoints we bring to the table. Gathering diverse perspectives before deciding is one of the most reliable ways to improve the quality of our choices. Every person sees the world through a particular lens shaped by experience, culture, profession, and temperament. When we rely only on our own vantage point, we risk overlooking facts, consequences, and alternatives that are obvious to someone else. A single viewpoint can feel complete simply because it is familiar, which makes it easy to mistake confidence for accuracy. Diverse perspectives challenge that comfort by introducing questions we would not have asked ourselves. Consider a town planning council deciding where to build a new park. Engineers may focus on drainage and cost, parents on safety and access, and older residents on benches and quiet corners. Each group notices things the others miss, and the final plan is stronger for including all of them. The same principle applies in smaller settings, such as a student choosing a college or a family deciding how to care for an aging parent. Hearing from people with different backgrounds also helps us identify our own assumptions. When someone disagrees with us respectfully, we are forced to explain our reasoning, and that process often reveals gaps we had not noticed. Sometimes we discover that our original position was sound, which gives us renewed confidence. Other times we find that our reasoning was incomplete or based on a belief we had never examined. Either outcome leaves us better prepared. There is also a moral dimension to seeking varied input. Decisions affect people, and those people deserve to have their concerns heard before outcomes are locked in. Inclusion builds trust, and decisions made with broad participation are more likely to be accepted and supported, even by those who did not get their preferred result. Of course, gathering perspectives is not the same as treating every opinion as equally valid. The goal is to collect relevant information and reasoned viewpoints, weigh them carefully, and then decide. Listening widely does not mean waiting forever, and it does not require agreeing with everyone. It requires openness, curiosity, and the discipline to test our first instincts against other minds. In an age when people often gather information only from sources that confirm what they already believe, the habit of seeking out different perspectives is more valuable than ever. It protects us from narrow thinking, sharpens our judgment, and helps us act with greater wisdom and fairness. Good decisions are rarely the product of a single mind working alone, and recognizing that is itself a sign of maturity.

The manuscript proposes quaternion-based equivariant neural networks for recognizing 3D point clouds and representing object pose, a timely and well-motivated direction given the growing use of point-cloud data in robotics, autonomous driving, and augmented reality. The central idea of exploiting quaternion algebra to encode rotations compactly and to build layers that are equivariant to SO(3) is conceptually appealing, and the authors articulate the connection between quaternion multiplication and rotation group structure clearly in the introduction. The related work section covers rotation-equivariant point-cloud architectures reasonably well, though it would benefit from a more explicit comparison with vector-neuron and tensor-field approaches, which address similar invariance goals through different mathematical machinery. The methodology is described with sufficient detail to be followed, and the derivation of the quaternion-valued convolution and the equivariance property is largely sound, although a few steps in the appendix skip intermediate algebra that a reader would need to verify the claims independently. The experimental evaluation on standard benchmarks for classification and pose estimation is a strength, as it allows direct comparison with established baselines under common protocols. However, the reported gains over the strongest baselines are modest in several settings, and the authors do not provide variance across random seeds or confidence intervals, so it is difficult to judge whether the improvements are statistically meaningful. The ablation study isolating the contribution of the quaternion parameterization from the equivariant layer design is valuable, but it would be strengthened by including a parameter-matched real-valued control. The paper reports inference speed and memory usage, which is helpful, yet the training cost of the quaternion layers, which may be substantially higher, is not discussed. The pose representation component is interesting, but the evaluation of pose error relies on a single metric, and reporting both rotation and translation errors separately, along with a failure-case analysis, would give a fuller picture. The qualitative visualizations are informative, though the color scales are not labeled, which hampers interpretation. The discussion of robustness to noise and partial occlusion is brief and would benefit from quantitative results, since real sensor data rarely matches clean benchmark conditions. The code availability statement is appreciated, but the authors should confirm that the released implementation reproduces the reported numbers, including hyperparameters and data preprocessing steps. Some notation is inconsistent between the main text and the figures, particularly in the use of conjugation and the ordering of quaternion components, and a unified notation table would reduce confusion. The limitations section acknowledges computational overhead but should also address generalization to point clouds with varying density and to object categories absent from the training set. Overall, the paper makes a worthwhile technical contribution with a sound core idea, but the empirical claims need stronger statistical support and more thorough robustness analysis before they can be considered fully substantiated. I recommend a major revision, with the expectation that the authors can address these concerns within a reasonable timeframe.

Understanding Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia Through Genetically Engineered Mice

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia, often abbreviated as CLL, is the most common form of leukemia in adults in Western countries. It is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow in which the body produces too many abnormal B lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell that normally helps fight infection. These cells tend to accumulate slowly over time, and many people with CLL have few symptoms for years. Because the disease develops over long periods and differs greatly from person to person, scientists need reliable tools to study how it begins and progresses.

One of the most valuable tools is the genetically engineered mouse model. Mice share many biological features with humans, and their genomes can be modified in precise ways to mimic the genetic changes found in human disease. Researchers can introduce or delete specific genes so that the mice develop leukemia-like conditions that resemble CLL in people.

To build these models, scientists often start by studying the genetic changes found in human CLL patients. Common alterations include deletions of certain chromosome regions, mutations in genes that control cell survival, and changes in signaling pathways that tell cells when to grow or die. Once these changes are identified, they can be recreated in mice to test whether they are responsible for disease development.

Some engineered mice carry a gene that drives excessive B cell growth, while others are designed to lose a gene that normally keeps cell growth in check. When these changes occur, the mice gradually develop an accumulation of abnormal B cells in the blood, spleen, and lymph nodes. Researchers then track the progression of the disease over weeks or months, much as doctors monitor patients.

These models allow scientists to observe the disease from start to finish under controlled conditions. They can examine how leukemia cells interact with their surrounding environment, including supportive cells in the bone marrow and lymph nodes. Such interactions are important because CLL cells often rely on signals from their surroundings to survive.

A major advantage of the mouse model is that it allows researchers to test potential treatments before they are tried in people. Scientists can give mice different drugs and measure whether the number of leukemia cells decreases, whether survival improves, and whether side effects appear. This process helps identify the most promising therapies and eliminates those that are unlikely to work.

Through this kind of research, scientists have identified several potential treatment targets. A treatment target is a molecule, such as a protein, that plays a key role in the disease and can be blocked or altered by a drug. Targets studied in CLL research include proteins involved in B cell receptor signaling and proteins that regulate programmed cell death.

Some therapies developed partly through this type of research have already become part of clinical care for CLL patients. These include drugs that inhibit signaling enzymes within leukemia cells and drugs that restore the natural ability of cells to undergo apoptosis, or controlled cell death. Such advances show how laboratory models can contribute directly to improved patient outcomes.

Mouse models are not perfect, however. Mice do not develop CLL in exactly the same way as humans, and a treatment that works well in mice may fail in people. For this reason, researchers use mouse studies as one step in a longer process that also includes laboratory experiments with human cells and carefully designed clinical trials.

Despite these limitations, genetically engineered mice remain a central tool in leukemia research. They allow scientists to ask precise questions about cause and effect that would be difficult or unethical to test directly in patients. Each new model adds to our understanding of how CLL develops.

Ongoing work continues to refine these models so they more closely reflect the diversity of human disease. Researchers are developing mice that carry multiple genetic changes found in patients, which may better represent the complexity of CLL. These efforts aim to improve the accuracy of preclinical testing.

The ultimate goal of this research is to find treatments that are more effective, better tolerated, and suitable for different types of patients. By combining genetic engineering with careful observation and testing, scientists hope to turn a slowly progressing disease into one that can be managed for many years with a good quality of life. Continued study of these mouse models will play an important part in reaching that goal.

This manuscript proposes a memory-augmented neural network architecture for streaming active learning, together with a class-margin sampling strategy for deciding which incoming examples to query for labels. The problem is well motivated, since labeling budgets are limited in streaming settings where data arrives continuously and cannot be stored or revisited indefinitely. The authors position their contribution clearly within the existing literature on active learning and online learning, and the related work section covers the main lines of prior research reasonably well. The central idea of pairing an external memory module with margin-based query selection is interesting and plausibly useful, because the memory can retain informative exemplars while the sampling rule prioritizes examples near decision boundaries. However, the paper would benefit from a more precise definition of the class-margin criterion, since the manuscript describes it at a high level and the reader cannot easily reproduce the exact selection score from the text alone. The architecture description is detailed in places but leaves open how the memory is updated, including the replacement policy, the memory capacity, and how stale entries are handled as the data distribution drifts. The experimental section evaluates the method on several benchmark streams, which is a strength, but the choice of datasets is narrow and the paper does not discuss whether results generalize to real-world streams with severe class imbalance or concept drift. The baselines are relevant, yet the authors should include at least one recent streaming active learning method that uses a comparable memory mechanism to make the comparison more convincing. Reported gains over the strongest baseline are modest on some datasets, and the manuscript does not provide confidence intervals or results across multiple random seeds, which makes it difficult to judge whether the differences are statistically meaningful. The ablation study is a helpful addition, but it isolates the memory component and the sampling strategy only partially, and a full factorial ablation would clarify which element drives the improvements. The computational cost of maintaining the memory and computing margins at each step is not quantified, which matters greatly for streaming applications where per-example latency is a practical constraint. The authors should report wall-clock time, memory footprint, and throughput alongside accuracy and label efficiency. The theoretical analysis, if any, is limited, and a brief discussion of regret or query-budget guarantees would strengthen the paper considerably. Figures are generally clear, although the learning curves would be easier to interpret with shaded variance bands and a consistent x-axis definition across datasets. Several sentences in the methodology section are repetitive and could be condensed to improve readability. The notation is mostly consistent, but the symbol used for the margin threshold appears with two slightly different definitions, which should be resolved. The limitations section is brief and should address failure modes, such as when the margin signal is unreliable in early training or when the memory becomes dominated by a single class. Code availability is mentioned, which is commendable, but the repository should include configuration files and scripts sufficient to reproduce the main tables. Overall, the paper presents a sound and promising idea with competent experiments, but it requires clearer specification of the method, broader empirical validation, statistical reporting, and a fuller treatment of computational cost. With these revisions, the contribution would be substantially more convincing. My recommendation is major revision.

GAMT deficiency: A Rare Inherited Creatine Disorder

GAMT deficiency is a rare, inherited metabolic disorder that affects how the body makes and uses creatine, a compound essential for energy storage in the brain and muscles. The condition is caused by variants in the GAMT gene, which provides instructions for the enzyme guanidinoacetate methyltransferase. This enzyme performs the second and final step in creatine synthesis, converting guanidinoacetate into creatine. When the enzyme is missing or works poorly, guanidinoacetate builds up in the blood, urine, and brain while creatine levels fall. The disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, meaning a child must receive a faulty copy of the gene from each parent to be affected. Parents who each carry one copy typically have no symptoms themselves. Because creatine is especially important for the brain, the most significant effects of GAMT deficiency involve the nervous system. Children often show developmental delay, with slower progress in learning to sit, walk, and talk than expected. Speech difficulties are common, and many affected individuals have limited or absent expressive language. Seizures, also called epileptic episodes, occur in many patients and can range from mild to severe and difficult to control. Behavioral problems, including hyperactivity, aggression, self-injury, and autism-like features, have also been reported. Movement difficulties may include low muscle tone, involuntary muscle movements, and problems with coordination. Intellectual disability is frequently present and ranges from mild to profound. Symptoms usually appear in infancy or early childhood, although the exact age of onset and severity vary widely between individuals. Doctors diagnose GAMT deficiency by measuring guanidinoacetate and creatine levels in blood and urine, and sometimes by analyzing brain tissue through magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Genetic testing of the GAMT gene confirms the diagnosis and can identify specific variants. Early diagnosis is important because treatment can reduce the buildup of harmful compounds and improve outcomes. The main treatment is oral creatine supplementation, which helps restore creatine levels in the body and brain. Doctors also commonly prescribe ornithine, which helps lower the amount of guanidinoacetate in the body. Dietary measures to limit arginine, a precursor of guanidinoacetate, are sometimes recommended, though these must be guided by a specialist. Treatment is most effective when started early, particularly before significant brain damage occurs. Seizures are managed with standard antiepileptic medications, and therapies such as speech, occupational, and physical therapy support daily functioning. Some patients experience partial improvement in symptoms with treatment, while others continue to have significant challenges. Because the disorder is rare, many cases go unrecognized for years, and families may need to see several specialists before receiving a diagnosis. Ongoing monitoring by a team that may include neurologists, metabolic specialists, and genetic counselors helps guide long-term care. Genetic counseling is also valuable for families who want to understand their risk of having another affected child. Research into GAMT deficiency continues, with a focus on improving treatments and understanding why outcomes differ between patients. Families are encouraged to connect with patient support organizations and rare disease networks for information and community. Awareness of GAMT deficiency among healthcare providers remains important so that affected children can be identified and treated promptly.

Flexible curfews for teenagers make sense because young people lead busy lives that do not always fit within a fixed schedule. Many teens hold part-time jobs to help their families, save for college, or simply gain early experience in the working world. A rigid curfew can force a teenager to leave a shift early or refuse a valuable opportunity, even when the work is responsible and closely supervised. A flexible approach would allow these students to finish their responsibilities without losing income or the chance to grow.

Family emergencies are another reason curfews should adapt to real circumstances. A teenager may need to care for a younger sibling while a parent works a late shift, drive a relative to the hospital, or help a family member through a crisis. In such moments, strict rules can make a difficult situation harder to manage. Parents and teens who communicate openly can agree on exceptions that protect safety while respecting the family's needs.

School responsibilities also deserve room in a teenager's schedule. Student council meetings, debate tournaments, theater rehearsals, and athletic events often run late and cannot always be planned around a set hour. Students who participate in these activities learn leadership, teamwork, and time management, skills that matter far beyond the classroom. A curfew that ignores these commitments may discourage the very involvement that helps young people succeed.

Critics argue that flexible curfews could lead to unsafe situations or weaken parental authority. These concerns are real and deserve attention. However, flexibility does not mean the absence of rules. Families can set clear expectations, require check-in calls, and define which activities qualify for extended hours. Structure and trust can coexist when both sides understand the purpose behind the rules.

In the end, a curfew should protect teenagers rather than punish them for living full and responsible lives. When it bends to accommodate work, family needs, and education, it teaches accountability instead of simply enforcing obedience. Flexible curfews, supported by open communication and sensible limits, prepare young people to balance competing duties, which is one of the most valuable skills they will need as adults.

The manuscript investigates how early-stage neural network training, the structure of learned weights, and the quality of training data jointly shape both the learning dynamics of a model and its susceptibility to compression. The central question is well motivated, since practitioners routinely prune, quantize, or distill networks without a clear account of which training decisions make compression more or less damaging. The authors frame the problem clearly in the introduction and position their work relative to the pruning and lottery ticket literature with reasonable care. However, the paper's contribution is difficult to isolate from the existing body of work, and the authors should state more precisely what finding is new. The experimental design covers three factors, which is ambitious, but the manuscript does not adequately explain how these factors were varied independently. Confounding between early training length, initialization scale, and dataset noise appears likely in several of the reported comparisons. The authors should provide a factorial or ablation table that makes each factor's effect visible in isolation. The choice of architectures is limited to two convolutional networks and one small transformer, which constrains how far the conclusions can be generalized. The discussion of results sometimes overstates claims, particularly where the paper states that early weight structure "determines" compressibility when the evidence only shows a correlation. Statistical reporting is inconsistent: some figures show error bars across seeds, while the main results table reports single runs. Readers cannot judge whether the reported differences exceed run-to-run variance. The authors should report means and standard deviations over at least five seeds for all headline comparisons. The data quality component is handled through label noise injection, which is a reasonable proxy but not the only relevant notion of quality. Duplication, class imbalance, and distribution shift are omitted, and the paper should acknowledge this scope restriction explicitly. The compression methods evaluated are magnitude pruning and uniform post-training quantization, which are standard but not representative of structured pruning or quantization-aware training. Including at least one method from each category would strengthen the claims about compression in general. The paper's figures are generally clear, though Figure 4 uses a color scale that is hard to interpret for readers with color vision deficiencies. The axis labels in several plots are abbreviated without definition in the captions. The methods section describes the optimizer and learning rate schedule but omits the weight decay value and warmup length, which are necessary for reproduction. The authors state that code is available, which is commendable, but the repository link was not functional at the time of review. Related work is cited thoroughly for pruning but thinly for the training dynamics literature, such as work on critical learning periods and early-phase gradient statistics. Adding these references would situate the early-training claims more firmly. The theoretical section offers a simplified linear model to motivate the empirical findings, but the assumptions of this model are not checked against the experiments. The authors should either validate the model's predictions or present it explicitly as heuristic intuition. Some of the notation is inconsistent, with the same symbol used for both the compression ratio and a regularization coefficient in different sections. The abstract summarizes the results accurately but emphasizes the transformer experiment, which is the weakest part of the evaluation given its small scale. The conclusion section repeats the abstract with little added interpretation and could instead discuss limitations and practical guidance for practitioners. Overall, the paper addresses a useful question with a reasonable experimental framework, but its claims currently exceed its evidence. I recommend major revision. With clearer factor isolation, multi-seed statistics, broader compression baselines, and more cautious causal language, the work could make a meaningful contribution. The authors have the foundation for a valuable study, and the revisions required are substantial but achievable. I would be glad to review a revised version.

Improving Single-Image 3D Shape Recovery by Combining Learned Depth, Surface Orientation, and Symmetry Cues

Abstract

Recovering the three-dimensional shape of an object or scene from a single photograph is an ill-posed problem, because many different surfaces can produce the same image. Recent learning-based methods have made substantial progress by predicting depth maps directly from pixels, yet depth alone often yields reconstructions that are locally plausible but globally inconsistent, with warped silhouettes, flattened curvature, and asymmetric artifacts on objects that should be symmetric. This paper proposes a unified framework that jointly exploits three complementary cues: learned monocular depth, predicted surface orientation (surface normals), and symmetry priors. We argue that depth provides global metric structure, surface normals encode fine local geometry and shading-consistent orientation, and symmetry supplies a strong global regularizer that constrains unobserved regions. We describe an architecture in which each cue is predicted by a dedicated branch, a consistency module that reconciles depth gradients with normal fields, and a symmetry-aware fusion stage that propagates information across mirrored regions. We formulate the recovery as a constrained optimization whose objective penalizes disagreement between depth and normals, enforces approximate reflection symmetry where it is detected, and preserves agreement with the input image. We evaluate the approach on standard benchmarks for single-view depth and shape estimation and on a set of man-made and natural object categories where symmetry is prominent. Results indicate improvements in depth error, normal accuracy, and chamfer distance relative to depth-only baselines, with the largest gains on symmetric objects and on occluded regions. We also analyze failure cases, including objects with weak or broken symmetry, and discuss the sensitivity of the method to the accuracy of the symmetry detector.

Introduction

Human observers routinely infer the shape of objects from single images, drawing on shading, texture, perspective, and prior knowledge about how objects are typically built. Reproducing this ability in computer vision has been a long-standing goal, with applications in robotics, augmented reality, graphics, and autonomous driving. The core difficulty is that the projection from three dimensions to two discards depth, so a single image is compatible with an infinite family of underlying scenes. Classical shape-from-shading and shape-from-texture methods attempted to resolve this ambiguity using hand-crafted assumptions about illumination, reflectance, and surface regularity, but these assumptions rarely hold in unconstrained photographs.

The advent of deep learning changed the landscape. Convolutional networks trained on large collections of images paired with depth sensor measurements can predict dense depth maps with reasonable accuracy, learning statistical regularities of real scenes that no explicit model encodes. These networks have been extended to predict surface normals, semantic labels, and full voxel or mesh representations. However, purely data-driven predictors tend to exhibit characteristic weaknesses. Depth maps often appear smooth but geometrically inconsistent, in the sense that the gradients of the predicted depth do not agree with the orientation the same network predicts for the surface. Predicted shapes may have silhouettes that drift from the object boundary, and the parts of an object that are self-occluded are frequently hallucinated poorly.

We observe that these weaknesses are partly due to treating each geometric quantity in isolation. Depth and surface orientation are not independent: the normal at a point is determined by the local derivatives of the depth field, so a method that predicts both should enforce this relation. Moreover, many objects of practical interest, including vehicles, furniture, tools, animals, and faces, possess approximate bilateral symmetry. Symmetry is a powerful prior because it allows information observed on one side of an object to inform the reconstruction of the other side, which is especially valuable for occluded surfaces.

This paper makes three contributions. First, we introduce a multi-branch network that predicts depth, surface normals, and a symmetry-plane hypothesis from a single image, with shared encoder features to promote coherence. Second, we propose a consistency-enforcing optimization layer that adjusts the depth field so that its gradients agree with the predicted normals while remaining faithful to the observed image evidence. Third, we develop a symmetry-aware fusion procedure that mirrors observed geometry across the detected symmetry plane and blends it with the network prediction according to confidence estimates. We show that these components work together and that each contributes to the overall gain.

Related Work

Monocular depth estimation has evolved from early patch-based regression and Markov random field formulations to deep encoder-decoder architectures trained with scale-invariant and gradient-based losses. Many approaches report errors on indoor and outdoor datasets using absolute relative error, squared relative error, and threshold accuracy metrics. Some works have emphasized the importance of multi-scale features and attention mechanisms for preserving fine detail, while others have focused on generalization across domains through large-scale mixed training.

Surface normal estimation has been studied both as a standalone task and as an auxiliary signal. Normals are attractive because they are less sensitive to global scale ambiguity than absolute depth and because they correlate strongly with shading. Several methods have shown that jointly predicting depth and normals improves both, and that enforcing their consistency through a differentiable loss reduces artifacts in planar and curved regions. Our work builds on this line of research but adds an explicit reconciliation step at inference time.

Shape recovery from single images has also been approached through learned voxel grids, point clouds, implicit signed distance functions, and parametric template deformation. Template-based methods exploit category-level priors and can produce complete shapes, but they are restricted to the categories they were trained on. Implicit representations offer higher fidelity but require substantial supervision. Symmetry has been used as a prior in classical reconstruction, for instance in detecting reflection planes in man-made objects and in exploiting repetitive structure in architectural scenes. Recent learning-based works have incorporated symmetry as a loss term or as an augmentation, but few have combined it with explicit depth-normal consistency in a single framework.

Method

Our system takes a single RGB image as input and produces a dense depth map, a dense normal map, a symmetry-plane estimate with an associated confidence map, and a final refined depth map. The encoder is a shared backbone that produces multi-scale feature maps. Three decoder heads predict depth, normals, and a symmetry representation. The symmetry head outputs a candidate reflection plane parameterized by a unit normal and an offset, together with a per-pixel mask indicating regions that are expected to be mirror-symmetric with respect to that plane.

The depth head is trained with a scale-invariant logarithmic loss combined with a multi-scale gradient matching term. The normal head is trained with an angular error loss against ground-truth normals derived from depth sensors where available. Because normals and depth are predicted from shared features, the network is encouraged to produce mutually compatible outputs, but compatibility is not guaranteed at inference, so we add an explicit refinement stage.

The refinement stage treats the final depth as the unknown and minimizes an energy with three terms. The first term is a data term that keeps the refined depth close to the network depth prediction, weighted by the depth confidence. The second term penalizes the difference between the gradients of the refined depth and the gradients implied by the predicted normals, which are obtained by converting the normal vectors into local slope estimates. The third term is a symmetry term that, for pixels inside the detected symmetric region, encourages the depth at a point to match the depth at its mirror image under the estimated reflection. Mirror correspondences are computed by reflecting pixel coordinates and resampling the depth map, with occlusion handling that discounts correspondences where the mirrored point lies outside the image or where the symmetry mask is low.

The energy is minimized with a sparse linear least-squares solver after linearizing the normal consistency term, which is valid because we operate in the depth domain with fixed normals. Because the mirror correspondence depends on the depth itself, we alternate between updating correspondences and solving the linear system for a small number of iterations. In practice convergence occurs within a few alternations.

The symmetry-aware fusion stage handles regions where the symmetry hypothesis is strong. For such regions, we construct a fused depth estimate by averaging the refined depth at each point with the refined depth at its mirror point, using weights derived from the confidence maps. This allows an observed side of an object to fill in an occluded or poorly predicted side. Where symmetry confidence is low, the fusion reduces to the identity and the refined depth is retained.

Training follows a two-stage protocol. The encoder and decoder heads are first trained jointly on depth, normal, and symmetry supervision, where symmetry supervision is derived from annotated reflection planes for objects in the training set. The refinement stage has no learnable parameters in our default configuration, although we also explore a variant in which the energy weights are predicted per image by a small network.

Experimental Setup

We evaluate on three groups of data. The first is a standard indoor depth benchmark containing RGB-D recordings of diverse scenes, used to measure depth accuracy and normal accuracy. The second is an outdoor driving dataset with sparse LiDAR ground truth, used to test robustness to scale and to large depth ranges. The third is a shape dataset of single objects rendered from multiple viewpoints, with complete ground-truth meshes, used to measure chamfer distance and volumetric intersection-over-union. For the shape dataset we create symmetry annotations by marking reflection planes for each category, and we report results separately for categories where symmetry is expected (vehicles, chairs, cabinets, and animals) and categories where it is weak or absent (irregular natural shapes and deformable objects).

Metrics include absolute relative depth error, root mean squared error, threshold accuracy at several ratios, mean and median angular error for normals, chamfer distance for shapes, and volumetric intersection-over-union. For symmetry detection we report the angular and offset error of the predicted plane relative to annotations, as well as the precision and recall of the symmetry mask.

We compare against several baselines. The depth-only baseline uses the same encoder with only the depth head and no refinement. The depth-and-normal baseline adds the normal head and joint training but no refinement or symmetry. A recent state-of-the-art monocular depth network serves as an external reference. Ablations remove each component of the refinement and fusion stages in turn.

Results

On the indoor benchmark, the full method reduces absolute relative depth error compared with the depth-only baseline and also reduces mean normal angular error relative to the depth-and-normal baseline. The most notable improvement appears in threshold accuracy at the strictest ratio, which indicates that the refinement stage sharpens depth in regions where the network was previously blurry. Joint training alone yields a modest improvement, and the explicit consistency term contributes the majority of the gain in normal accuracy, confirming that enforcing agreement between depth gradients and normals is beneficial even when both are predicted well.

On the outdoor dataset, improvements are smaller in absolute terms because the metric scale is dominated by distant regions with sparse supervision. Nevertheless, the consistency term reduces spurious depth ripples on road surfaces and building facades, which are planar and therefore well suited to normal-based regularization. The symmetry term has little effect here, as expected, since most outdoor scenes contain few mirror-symmetric objects of interest, although it still helps for parked vehicles.

On the shape dataset, the largest gains occur for symmetric categories. For vehicles and chairs, chamfer distance decreases substantially relative to the depth-only baseline, and volumetric intersection-over-union increases, particularly in the occluded back surfaces that the baseline frequently misestimates. The fusion stage is responsible for much of this improvement, and visualizations show that the back of a chair is reconstructed with plausible legs and backrest where the baseline produces a thin or missing structure. For animals, which are only approximately symmetric and whose symmetry plane is less reliable, the gain is smaller but still positive. For deformable and irregular categories, the symmetry term can slightly degrade results when the detected plane is wrong, and the confidence weighting does not always suppress such errors.

Symmetry detection accuracy is central to the method. When the predicted plane is within a few degrees of the annotated plane, the fusion yields consistent improvements. When the plane error exceeds roughly ten degrees, fusion can introduce mirrored artifacts, and in these cases we observe a small net decrease in accuracy. This motivates the confidence estimation, which we found to be well calibrated on held-out data but not perfect.

Ablation and Analysis

Removing the consistency term while keeping symmetry fusion reduces normal accuracy and leaves visible discontinuities at object edges. Removing the symmetry term while keeping consistency preserves most depth accuracy on non-symmetric scenes but loses the occlusion gains on objects. Using a fixed rather than confidence-weighted fusion weight increases errors on objects with partial symmetry, indicating that the confidence estimate carries useful information. Alternating the correspondence update for more than three iterations produces negligible changes, supporting our choice of a small number of iterations.

We also examined sensitivity to the weight on each energy term. Moderate weights on the consistency term produce the best trade-off; very large weights make the depth overly dependent on the predicted normals and transfer normal errors into depth, while very small weights recover the depth-only behavior. The symmetry weight shows a similar pattern, with performance peaking when the term is active only in regions with high symmetry confidence.

Limitations

The method inherits the limitations of its components. Symmetry is an assumption, and objects that are asymmetric in ways that matter for the task will be penalized by the symmetry term unless the confidence correctly identifies them. The refinement stage relies on predicted normals, so errors in normal estimation propagate into depth. The approach operates on a single view and cannot resolve scale ambiguity beyond what the depth network learns. Finally, the optimization adds computational cost, although it remains modest compared with the network forward pass.

Conclusion

We have presented a framework that improves single-image shape recovery by combining learned depth, surface orientation, and symmetry cues within a single pipeline. Enforcing consistency between depth gradients and predicted normals sharpens local geometry, while symmetry-aware fusion propagates observed structure into occluded regions. Experiments on indoor, outdoor, and object-level benchmarks show consistent gains, with the largest improvements on symmetric objects. Future work includes learning the refinement weights end to end, extending symmetry reasoning to partial and rotational symmetries, and integrating the framework with generative priors for regions that remain ambiguous even after symmetry is applied.

References

The reference list for a complete manuscript would cite the depth estimation, normal estimation, and shape reconstruction works discussed in the related work section, together with the benchmark datasets used in the experiments. Specific citations should be added and verified against the original publications before submission.

This paper proposes a non-autoregressive generative adversarial network framework aimed at fast speech synthesis, and it pairs this with an objective evaluation method that uses automatic speech recognition to assess the intelligibility of generated speech. The motivation is well grounded, since autoregressive text-to-speech models are slow at inference, and the non-autoregressive design offers a clear path to real-time generation. The adversarial training setup is described with reasonable detail, though the authors would strengthen the work by providing a more thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of the discriminator and the non-autoregressive decoder. The ASR-based evaluation is a sensible idea, as it offers a scalable complement to subjective listening tests, but the manuscript should clarify how sensitive the metric is to the choice of recognizer and whether it correlates with human judgments of naturalness and intelligibility. The experimental comparisons against baseline systems are informative, yet the reported speedups would be more convincing with measurements across multiple hardware configurations and with confidence intervals over repeated runs. Overall, the paper makes a useful contribution to fast speech synthesis and evaluation, and I recommend minor revisions addressing the ablation analysis, the validation of the ASR-based metric against human ratings, and the reporting of computational benchmarks.
