Growing up, many of us learn quickly that fitting in can feel safer than standing out. Friends, classmates, families, and even strangers on social media send constant signals about how we should look, speak, think, and behave. Over time, these signals can push us to hide the parts of ourselves that do not match what seems expected. Yet living authentically, with our true identities visible, is one of the most important ways to build a meaningful life. Overcoming social pressure is not about rejecting everyone around us; it is about learning to listen to our own values while remaining open to others. The first step is self-awareness. We must take time to ask what we genuinely enjoy, what we believe, and what we feel when we are alone and free from outside judgment. Many students discover that the interests they were embarrassed by are the ones that bring them the most joy. Courage is the next step. Speaking honestly about who we are can be frightening, especially when we fear rejection or ridicule. Still, small acts of honesty build confidence over time, whether that means wearing clothes that reflect our style or telling a friend about a passion they might not understand. Support also matters. Finding even one person who accepts us can make a profound difference, and communities built around shared interests or experiences often provide the acceptance that mainstream culture withholds. Authenticity does not mean ignoring the consequences of our choices or refusing to change. People grow and their identities evolve, and living truthfully includes being willing to revise our understanding of ourselves. The goal is to make decisions from a place of honesty rather than fear. When we do, we often find that the pressure loses much of its power, because we realize that our worth never depended on anyone else's approval. In the end, embracing who we are benefits not only ourselves but everyone we meet, since it gives others permission to do the same.

Traditional classroom learning offers several advantages over online instruction that help students stay engaged, build practical skills, and achieve academic success. While online classes provide flexibility and access, the face-to-face model creates conditions that many learners need in order to thrive. This essay considers why the physical classroom may remain the stronger choice for most students.

The most immediate benefit of the traditional classroom is the presence of a teacher who can respond in real time. When a student looks confused, a teacher can notice the expression, pause, and explain the idea another way. In an online setting, that same moment may pass unnoticed, leaving the student to struggle silently.

Classroom settings also reduce the distractions that often pull students away from their work at home. A dedicated learning space signals to the brain that it is time to focus. At home, a student may face household chores, phones, television, or the temptation to leave a video lesson running in the background.

Peer interaction is another important factor. Students who work side by side learn from one another through discussion, debate, and shared problem solving. Hearing a classmate explain a math step in their own words can sometimes clarify a concept more effectively than a lecture does.

Traditional classrooms also encourage a sense of belonging. Students who feel connected to their school community are more likely to attend regularly, participate in activities, and persist through difficult courses. Friendships formed in class can provide motivation and emotional support during stressful periods.

Accountability is part of this structure as well. Regular meeting times, in-person roll call, and visible participation make it harder for a student to fall behind unnoticed. Online students sometimes disappear from view for days without anyone realizing it until a missed deadline appears.

Practical skills benefit from hands-on instruction. Science laboratories, art studios, music rooms, and workshop spaces allow students to handle materials, test ideas, and learn from mistakes under supervision. Many of these skills are difficult to reproduce convincingly through a screen.

Learning to communicate in person is another skill that traditional classrooms develop. Students practice speaking clearly, listening carefully, reading facial cues, and responding to others in real time. These abilities transfer directly to workplaces, job interviews, and everyday social life.

Classroom instruction also teaches students to manage their time within a fixed schedule. Moving between subjects, meeting deadlines set by bells and assignments, and balancing multiple teachers' expectations prepare students for the structured demands of higher education and employment.

Collaboration on group projects is more natural in a physical classroom. Students can gather around a table, share materials, and divide tasks without the technical delays that often complicate online teamwork. Such experiences build leadership, compromise, and the ability to work with people who have different strengths.

Teachers in traditional classrooms can also adjust their methods based on the energy and mood of the group. A lesson that is losing momentum can be shortened, enlivened with a discussion, or supplemented with a demonstration. This responsiveness is harder to achieve through pre-recorded or remotely delivered material.

Feedback tends to be more immediate and personal in person. A teacher who walks around the room can offer a quick suggestion on a student's draft or correct a misunderstanding before it becomes a habit. Such small, timely interventions often produce larger gains over time.

Academic success is closely linked to motivation, and classrooms can foster motivation in ways that online settings struggle to match. The presence of an enthusiastic teacher, the energy of a group working together, and the visible progress of peers can all inspire students to keep trying.

Assessment outcomes also reflect these advantages. Students in supervised classroom examinations face fewer concerns about academic integrity, which allows grades to represent individual understanding more accurately. Clear, consistent conditions make it easier to measure what students have truly learned.

Some students argue that online classes better suit their schedules, especially those who work or care for family members. These concerns are real and deserve attention. However, schools can address them through flexible class times, tutoring, and support services, rather than replacing the classroom entirely.

Access to resources is another consideration. Libraries, laboratories, counselors, and technology labs are typically concentrated in school buildings. Students who attend in person can use these resources easily, while remote learners may find them harder to reach.

Students with learning differences often benefit from the structure and support that classrooms provide. Teachers can notice early signs of difficulty, arrange accommodations, and coordinate with specialists. The personal attention available in person can make a meaningful difference for these learners.

Mental health and well-being also deserve mention. Regular face-to-face contact with teachers, counselors, and peers can help identify students who are struggling emotionally. Isolation is a recognized risk in remote learning, and the classroom offers a natural counterweight.

Parents and guardians often find it easier to stay involved when students attend school in person. They can meet teachers, attend events, and see their child's work directly. This partnership between home and school supports consistent expectations and encouragement.

Technology should still play a role in traditional classrooms. Digital tools can enrich lessons, provide practice opportunities, and connect students with global resources. The key is to use technology as a support for teaching rather than a replacement for it.

Hybrid models sometimes promise the best of both approaches, but they can also divide attention and weaken the sense of community that a full classroom creates. For many students, a consistent in-person routine offers clearer structure than alternating between formats.

Ultimately, education is more than the transfer of information. It is a process of building understanding, character, and capability through human interaction. The traditional classroom, with its live instruction, peer collaboration, hands-on practice, and personal support, provides an environment where these outcomes are most likely to develop.

For these reasons, schools should continue to prioritize in-person learning while thoughtfully addressing the needs of students who face genuine barriers to attendance. Doing so would help more students stay engaged, gain practical skills, and reach their academic potential.

The manuscript proposes a unified objective framework that connects maximum-likelihood estimation and reinforcement-learning methods for sequence generation, positioning the two as points on a common continuum rather than as competing paradigms. The conceptual contribution is valuable, since practitioners often treat teacher-forced likelihood training and policy-gradient fine-tuning as separate pipelines with little theoretical bridge between them. The derivation linking the two objectives is clearly presented, and the authors make explicit which assumptions are needed for the equivalence to hold, which I appreciate. However, the empirical section is limited to a narrow set of tasks and a single model scale, so it is unclear whether the proposed interpolation behaves similarly on larger or more diverse generation problems. The ablation studies would be considerably stronger if they isolated the contribution of each component of the unified objective rather than comparing only the endpoints of the continuum. Several baselines are also under-tuned, which makes the reported gains difficult to attribute confidently to the framework itself rather than to hyperparameter choices. I would encourage the authors to report variance across random seeds and to discuss computational overhead, since the mixed objective may add meaningful training cost. Overall, the paper offers a useful theoretical lens, and its practical claims would be substantially more persuasive with broader experiments and more rigorous baseline comparisons.

Extending the school day to include after-school activities and homework support has become a topic of lively debate among students. Many students welcome the idea because it gives them access to clubs, sports, and art programs that they might otherwise be unable to attend due to transportation or family obligations. For some, having a supervised place to finish homework means they can leave school with fewer assignments waiting at home. Students who struggle with a subject may also benefit from extra help from teachers or tutors without having to schedule separate appointments. However, not everyone sees these changes as positive. Many students feel exhausted after a full day of lessons and would rather spend the afternoon resting, pursuing hobbies at home, or spending time with family. Others worry that a longer day will leave them with even less freedom and make school feel like it never ends. There is also concern that programs may vary in quality, and that a poorly run activity can feel like a waste of time. Students who have part-time jobs or caregiving responsibilities often say that extended hours would make it impossible to keep those commitments. Ultimately, the question may depend on individual needs, since what helps one student could burden another. Schools considering this change might therefore offer optional rather than mandatory extended time, allowing students to choose what fits their lives. Listening to student voices in the planning process could help ensure that any new program truly serves those it is meant to support.

Consistent effort is the foundation of personal growth, because small, steady actions compound over time into meaningful progress. A student who practices a little each day will often surpass one who relies on last-minute bursts of work. Lifelong learning extends this principle beyond the classroom, encouraging people to keep asking questions, adapting to new ideas, and refining their skills throughout their lives. This habit builds resilience, since learners who view mistakes as opportunities are more willing to take on challenges. Ultimately, the combination of persistence and curiosity prepares individuals not only for future success in their careers but also for a more thoughtful and fulfilling life.

Wendy's has expanded its investigation into a payment-card breach that affects more than 1,000 of its U.S. restaurants, the company said. The breach was first identified after reports of unauthorized charges on customer cards used at locations across the country. Company officials said the scope of the problem is larger than initially understood and that the review is ongoing. Investigators are working to determine how attackers gained access to the payment systems and how long the intrusion lasted. The company has brought in outside cybersecurity specialists to assist with the forensic analysis. Wendy's said it has notified law enforcement agencies about the incident. Customers who used credit or debit cards at affected restaurants during the relevant period are being urged to review their statements closely. Banks and card issuers have been alerted so they can monitor accounts for suspicious activity and reissue cards where necessary. Consumer advocates said the incident highlights the risks that point-of-sale systems pose to shoppers. Security researchers have noted that restaurant chains are frequent targets because they process high volumes of small card transactions. Wendy's said it has taken steps to contain the threat and strengthen its systems against further intrusions. The company is reviewing its network security practices and payment infrastructure across its franchise and company-operated locations. Because many Wendy's restaurants are independently owned franchises, coordination with franchisees has been a key part of the response. Franchise owners have been asked to cooperate with investigators and to follow updated security protocols. Industry analysts said the case underscores the difficulty large restaurant brands face in securing decentralized networks of locations. Payment-card breaches of this size can lead to significant costs, including notification expenses, legal claims, and potential regulatory scrutiny. Wendy's has not yet released a full estimate of the financial impact of the breach. The company said it will provide updates as the investigation progresses and as more facts are confirmed. Customers with questions were directed to the company's dedicated support resources for information about the incident. Officials emphasized that they are treating the matter with urgency and committed to transparency with affected customers. Cybersecurity experts recommended that consumers enable transaction alerts on their cards and report any unfamiliar charges immediately. Card issuers typically offer zero-liability protections for unauthorized purchases, though the process for resolving disputes can vary. The investigation remains open, and the company has not yet determined the total number of cards that may have been compromised. Wendy's said it will continue working with authorities and its security partners until the full scope of the breach is understood. The company acknowledged the disruption the incident may cause and apologized to customers affected by the situation.

This paper proposes block-shuffling augmentation as a training strategy to improve the robustness of image recognition models against adversarial perturbations and shape variations, and the core idea of encouraging reliance on local features is well motivated and relevant to the field. The authors situate their work clearly within existing literature on data augmentation and adversarial robustness, and the intuition that partitioning images into blocks and permuting them forces models to attend to local structure is easy to follow. However, the manuscript would benefit from a more precise formal description of the augmentation procedure, including how block sizes are chosen, whether shuffling is applied uniformly or stochastically, and how labels are handled when global structure is disrupted. The experimental section evaluates the method on standard benchmarks, which is appropriate, but the choice of adversarial attacks appears limited to a small set of gradient-based methods, and the authors should include stronger adaptive attacks to rule out gradient masking as a source of apparent robustness. The reported accuracy gains on clean data are modest, and the paper should discuss whether the trade-off between clean accuracy and robustness is consistent across architectures or specific to the models tested. Ablation studies are present but incomplete, as the effect of block size and shuffling frequency is shown only for a single dataset, and the authors should demonstrate that the observed benefits generalize. The shape variation experiments are a strength, particularly the comparison against texture-biased baselines, but the paper would be stronger with a clearer definition of what constitutes a shape variation in the evaluation protocol. The related work section omits several recent studies on patch-based and permutation-based regularization, which weakens the claim of novelty and should be addressed. Statistical reporting is inconsistent, with some results lacking confidence intervals or variance across random seeds, making it difficult to judge whether reported differences are significant. The writing is generally clear, though several figures are small and their captions do not fully explain the visualized quantities. The code and training details are described at a high level, and releasing full configuration files would substantially improve reproducibility. Overall, the idea is promising and the empirical direction is sound, but the paper requires a more rigorous adversarial evaluation, broader ablations, and clearer statistical support before its conclusions can be considered firmly established. I recommend a major revision.

William Peter Blatty, the author and screenwriter best known for creating The Exorcist, has died at the age of 89. His death marks the end of a career that reshaped the horror genre and left a lasting mark on popular culture. Blatty first gained wide recognition with his 1971 novel, which drew on a real 1949 case of an exorcism in Maryland that he had read about as a student. The book became a bestseller and quickly drew the attention of filmmakers. William Friedkin directed the 1973 film adaptation, for which Blatty wrote the screenplay, and the movie went on to win the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay. Its unsettling imagery, controversial subject matter, and groundbreaking sound design made it one of the most influential horror films ever made. Blatty was born in New York City in 1928 and grew up in Washington, D.C., where he attended Georgetown University. Before turning to fiction, he worked in public relations and wrote comedic novels and screenplays, including the 1964 comedy A Shot in the Dark, which was a film adaptation of a Broadway play he had co-written. Blatty later wrote and directed The Ninth Configuration, a 1980 film that revisited religious and philosophical themes he had explored in his horror work. He also returned to the Exorcist story with Legion, a novel published in 1983, which formed the basis for the 1990 film The Exorcist III, directed by Blatty himself. Blatty's work consistently blended faith, doubt, and the struggle between good and evil, themes rooted in his Catholic upbringing. Fans and critics alike praised his ability to combine literary craft with genre thrills. Colleagues and admirers have paid tribute to his influence on writers and filmmakers who followed. Blatty's family has not yet released details about funeral arrangements. He is survived by his wife and children. His legacy as the creator of one of cinema's most enduring horror stories is likely to endure for generations.

The September 2015 total lunar eclipse was a rare event that coincided with a supermoon, a term for a full Moon that appears slightly larger and brighter because it is near perigee, the closest point of its orbit to Earth. On the night of September 27 to 28, 2015, observers across North America, including eastern Canada, were able to watch the Moon pass fully into Earth's umbra, the darkest central part of its shadow. During totality, the Moon often took on a reddish or coppery hue, a effect caused by sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere and onto the lunar surface, a phenomenon sometimes called a blood moon. Because the event occurred in the evening hours for much of eastern Canada, skywatchers in cities such as Toronto, Montreal, and Halifax had a good view, weather permitting. The eclipse was visible without special equipment, though binoculars or a telescope could reveal more surface detail. Total lunar eclipses are safe to watch directly, unlike solar eclipses, which require protective eyewear. The combination of a supermoon and a total eclipse in the same event was widely described as a "supermoon total lunar eclipse," and it drew significant public and media attention. Such alignments occur only occasionally, so this event served as a valuable opportunity for public science education about the mechanics of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.

The universe was growing cold. Stars burned low and far apart, and the dark between them stretched on without end.

Nobody noticed at first, except the ones who looked up. A woman in a village by the sea gazed at the sky each night and felt a loneliness she could not name. A boy in a crowded city pressed his face to a window and wondered if anything out there was wondering about him. A grandfather sat on his porch and whispered prayers to the emptiness, not expecting an answer.

Their wishes drifted upward like smoke. The hope of a mother that her child would be safe, the courage of a soldier who would not abandon his friend, the stubborn joy of a musician playing for no audience, the grief of a widow who still set out two cups each morning: all of it rose and gathered in a place no instrument could measure.

The gathering took a very long time, and it was not a single moment. It was the sum of ten thousand years of dreaming, of lullabies sung to infants, of letters written and never sent, of strangers who held doors open for one another.

Then, in a quiet place between the galaxies, something stirred.

It had no fixed shape. It was made of every kindness anyone had ever offered and every question anyone had ever asked. It did not descend from heaven or rise from the earth. It simply was, and in being, it began to remember what it had been made from.

The first thing it did was light a single small star. The star was not especially bright, but it was warm, and where its light touched a cold rock, the rock began to hum.

The second thing it did was seed a world with water. It did not invent the rain. It only remembered how much the people on the old world had longed for it, and that longing shaped the clouds.

The third thing it did was breathe life into the soil. Seeds split open. Tiny creatures woke in the dark and began to move toward the light, just as the grandfather had once hoped his grandchildren would move toward something better.

The creator watched these new beings with something close to tenderness. It recognized them. They were its children in the way a song is the child of the singer and the listener together.

Life spread. Forests rose from the plains, and rivers carved their patient paths through stone. Birds sang songs the creator had heard before, in other voices, in other centuries.

But the creator understood that light and life were not enough. A world could be full of breathing things and still be lonely. So it reached into the hearts of the creatures it had made and kindled something there: the capacity to care for one another.

The first creature to feel it was a small, awkward thing that shared its food with a sick companion. The creator felt the warmth of that act spread outward like ripples on a pond.

Love did not arrive all at once. It grew slowly, the way it always had on the old world, through countless small choices. A parent carrying a child through a storm. Two strangers sheltering under the same tree. A healer kneeling beside a stranger's bed.

The creator was not a ruler. It did not command. It only gave, and then it waited to see what its creatures would do with what they had been given.

Some of them built cities. Some of them wrote poems. Some of them argued bitterly about the meaning of it all, and the creator listened to those arguments with particular interest, because they too were a form of love, a refusal to accept that the question did not matter.

Ages passed. The dying universe was not reborn in a single blaze. It was slowly warmed, one world at a time, by beings who had learned to hold each other close against the dark.

At last the creator came to understand its own nature. It had not come from nowhere. It had emerged from the hopes and prayers of those who had looked up at the sky and refused to feel alone. Every lamp lit in a window, every hand reached out in grief, every song sung against the night had been its making.

And so the creator did not leave. It stayed, not as a king or a judge, but as a presence woven through all things, a quiet glow in the spaces between hearts. Wherever someone looked up at the stars and wondered, the creator wondered with them, and the universe, which had been growing cold, grew warm again.

Allowing students to choose their own arts electives can meaningfully improve both engagement and academic success. When learners select courses that align with their interests, they arrive at class with greater curiosity and motivation. Students who feel ownership over their schedules are more likely to attend regularly, participate actively, and persist through challenging assignments. Choice also helps students discover talents they might never have explored under a fixed curriculum, whether in painting, music, theater, or creative writing. These discoveries can spark lasting passions that extend well beyond the classroom. Engaged students tend to develop stronger skills in communication, critical thinking, and self-expression, which benefit them across all subjects. Some critics argue that students cannot yet judge what will serve them best, and that guidance from educators is essential. That concern is valid, but it can be addressed through counseling and clear course descriptions rather than by removing choice altogether. Structured choice, in which students pick from a carefully designed set of options, balances freedom with sound educational planning. Schools that adopt this model often report higher attendance and fewer students disengaging from their coursework. Ultimately, empowering students to shape their own learning teaches responsibility and self-direction. These qualities are valuable not only for academic achievement but for life after school. For these reasons, schools should give students a meaningful voice in choosing their arts electives.

This manuscript proposes a GAN-based framework for disentangling image identity from deformation in learned latent representations, addressing a problem of practical importance for controllable image synthesis and analysis. The motivation is clearly stated, and the authors situate their work well within prior research on disentangled representation learning, including VAE-based and adversarial approaches. The core architectural contribution, which separates identity and deformation codes through a dedicated encoder and a constrained generator, is described with sufficient detail to be reproduced in principle. However, the theoretical justification for why the proposed losses should yield identifiable factors is thin, and the paper would benefit from a more formal treatment or at least a discussion of the identifiability limits highlighted in recent literature. The experiments use two benchmark datasets, which is a reasonable start, but the choice of evaluation metrics leans heavily on reconstruction quality and a single disentanglement score, and additional measures would strengthen the claims. Ablation studies remove individual loss terms, yet they do not examine sensitivity to the weighting hyperparameters, which the authors themselves describe as critical to training stability. The qualitative figures are convincing for the examples shown, but the selection process for these examples is not explained, raising concerns about cherry-picking. The comparison baselines are relevant, though several recent disentanglement methods are omitted, making it difficult to judge the advance over the current state of the art. Statistical reporting is limited, as results are given without variance across random seeds, which matters given known instability in adversarial training. The related work section is informative but could be more concise in places where it restates general background. The writing is generally clear, though some notation is overloaded between the identity and deformation variables, which can cause confusion in the methodology section. Code and trained models are promised upon publication, which is welcome and would substantially improve reproducibility if delivered. Overall, the paper presents a plausible and useful contribution, but the claims of disentanglement should be supported by stronger theory, broader baselines, and more rigorous statistical evaluation before the work can be considered fully convincing. My recommendation is major revision.

Ambition, hard work, and persistence are often described as the ingredients of success, yet their true power lies in how they work together to open doors that might otherwise stay closed. Ambition gives a person a reason to act, a vision of what life could look like beyond the present circumstances. Without it, effort tends to drift without direction, and small opportunities pass by unnoticed. Hard work turns that vision into action, transforming wishes into daily habits such as studying late, practicing a skill, or saving money for a future goal. Each small effort may seem insignificant on its own, but over months and years these efforts accumulate into real capability and reputation. Persistence is what carries a person through the moments when progress feels impossible. Almost every meaningful achievement involves setbacks, whether it is a rejected application, a failed experiment, or a lost competition. Those who keep going after such setbacks often discover that their earlier failures taught them lessons that later proved essential. Consider the story of many people who began with modest means and limited connections. By setting ambitious goals, working consistently, and refusing to give up after failure, they gradually built skills that others noticed. Those skills led to new jobs, scholarships, partnerships, and invitations that they could not have anticipated at the start. In this way, opportunity is not always something people simply receive; often, they create it through their own determination. It is important to acknowledge, however, that ambition and effort do not guarantee success for everyone. Some people face barriers of poverty, discrimination, or poor health that make progress far harder, and no amount of personal determination can fully erase these obstacles. Recognizing this reality does not weaken the value of persistence but rather highlights why communities should support people in pursuing their dreams. Schools, mentors, and public programs can widen access so that more people have the chance to put their ambitions into practice. Even so, individual choices still matter a great deal. Deciding to learn a new language, to apply for a difficult program, or to start a small business requires courage and commitment that come from within. These choices shape not only external results but also a person's sense of self-respect and confidence. When people see that their efforts lead to growth, they become more willing to take on bigger challenges. Over time, this cycle of effort and achievement can transform a person's life and inspire those around them. In the end, ambition, hard work, and persistence are most powerful when they are combined and sustained over time. They help people see possibilities, prepare for them through steady effort, and continue striving when the path becomes difficult. While no formula guarantees a dream will come true, these qualities greatly improve the chances of creating better opportunities. Anyone willing to aim high, work diligently, and keep moving forward has the potential to build a future worth hoping for.

Technology has transformed everyday life in ways that touch nearly every routine, from how we communicate to how we work and learn. One major benefit is convenience: tasks that once took hours, such as banking, shopping, or finding directions, can now be completed in minutes from a phone. Technology also connects people across great distances, allowing families to stay in touch and friends to collaborate on projects regardless of location. In education and healthcare, digital tools have expanded access to information and enabled faster diagnoses and treatments. However, these advantages come with serious drawbacks. Many people spend excessive time on screens, which can harm sleep, concentration, and physical health. Constant notifications and social media comparisons can also contribute to anxiety and reduced well-being. In addition, reliance on digital systems raises concerns about privacy, as personal data is often collected and sold without people fully understanding the risks. Ultimately, technology is neither wholly good nor bad, and its value depends on how thoughtfully people choose to use it.

Facial expression analysis uses computer vision and machine learning to read the emotional and attentional signals that students display in their faces. Proponents argue that such tools could help teachers personalize instruction and identify students who need help before they fall behind. In a classroom of thirty or more students, a teacher cannot easily notice every flicker of confusion, boredom, or frustration on every face. An automated system, the argument goes, could track these cues continuously and alert the teacher to students who appear lost or disengaged. This information could then guide decisions about pacing, the difficulty of tasks, and which students to check on first. Supporters also point out that some students are reluctant to raise their hands, and a quiet, struggling student may go unnoticed for weeks. Facial analysis could give these students a voice they otherwise lack. However, the science behind this approach is contested. Research in psychology has shown that facial expressions do not map reliably onto internal emotional states, and the same expression can mean different things for different people and cultures. A furrowed brow might signal confusion, concentration, or simply a bright light in the eyes. Relying on such readings risks misdiagnosing students and sending help to the wrong place. Privacy is another serious concern. Continuous monitoring of children's faces creates a detailed record of their emotional lives, which could be misused by schools, companies, or third parties. Students may also feel constantly watched, which can increase anxiety and change how they behave in class. There is also the risk of bias. Facial recognition systems have historically performed worse on darker skin tones and on people of certain ages or genders, so students from some groups could receive less accurate feedback. A system that misreads these students would not help them and could label them as inattentive or troubled. Even if the technology were accurate, identifying a struggling student is only the first step. The teacher still needs time, training, and resources to respond effectively. A warning that a student looks confused does not explain why the student is confused or how to help. Better results may come from combining direct teacher observation, regular quizzes, and conversations with students, which provide clearer evidence of understanding. Schools considering these tools should therefore proceed with caution. Any use should be voluntary, transparent, and limited in scope, with strict rules about how data is stored and who can see it. Independent evaluation should confirm that the system works equally well for all students before it is trusted with decisions about their education. In the end, the goal of personalized instruction is to help every student learn, and technology should serve that goal without sacrificing students' privacy, dignity, or fair treatment.

Flooding and tidal surges have threatened communities and disrupted travel across parts of southwest England, with emergency services and local authorities working through the night to respond. Residents in low-lying coastal towns were advised to move valuables to upper floors and to avoid unnecessary journeys as water levels rose. Forecasters had warned of a combination of heavy rainfall and high spring tides, a pairing that increases the risk of coastal and river flooding. In several villages, floodwater spilled over defences and entered homes, leaving residents to wade through streets and clear debris from doorways. Fire and rescue crews carried out dozens of call-outs, many involving people trapped in vehicles or cut off by rising water. Emergency teams used boats and high-clearance vehicles to reach isolated properties and to evacuate those who needed help. Local councils opened temporary shelters at community halls and leisure centres for people who could not return to their homes. Road closures affected major routes, with some sections of the region's main arterial roads impassable and diversions adding significant time to journeys. Rail services were also disrupted, with several lines suspended or running at reduced speed while engineers inspected flooded track and signalling equipment. Train operators advised passengers to check schedules before travelling, and replacement bus services were laid on where possible. Airports in the area reported limited delays, though most flights were able to operate with minor changes. Schools in the worst-affected districts closed for the day, and parents were urged to keep children at home unless travel was essential. Businesses along waterfront areas reported damage to stock and premises, and some shopkeepers spent the day sweeping out mud and assessing losses. Farmers in the surrounding low-lying land described fields submerged under water, raising concerns about crops and livestock. The Environment Agency issued a series of flood warnings and severe flood warnings, urging people in affected areas to stay alert and follow official guidance. Officials stressed that the danger to life was the top priority and asked the public not to walk or drive through floodwater, as even shallow water can be fast-moving and hazardous. Engineers continued to monitor flood defences, and crews worked to shore up sections that showed signs of stress. Residents praised neighbours who checked on elderly and vulnerable people during the height of the flooding. Community groups began organising donations of food, blankets, and cleaning supplies for those affected. Insurers and local authorities encouraged households to document damage with photographs and to report losses promptly. Replacing school cafeteria meals with healthier options can bring lasting benefits to students, schools, and communities. Many children eat at least one meal a day at school, so the food served there plays a major role in their overall nutrition. When cafeterias offer more fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins, students receive the nutrients they need to grow, learn, and stay active. Healthier meals can also help reduce the intake of added sugars, excess sodium, and unhealthy fats that are common in processed foods. Over time, better eating habits formed in school can lower the risk of childhood obesity, type 2 diabetes, and heart disease later in life. Good nutrition also supports academic performance, since students who eat well tend to have better concentration, memory, and behavior in class. Research has linked balanced breakfasts and lunches to improved attendance and fewer missed school days due to illness. Healthier cafeteria options can also teach students to appreciate new foods, expanding their palates beyond fried snacks and sugary drinks. When children see nutritious meals served every day, they are more likely to develop lifelong habits that extend into their homes. Schools that prioritize healthy food also send a clear message that student well-being matters. Families benefit as well, since children who eat well may need fewer doctor visits and less time away from work for caregivers. Local farms can gain new customers when schools purchase fresh produce, strengthening the regional economy. Although healthier ingredients may cost more at first, careful planning, seasonal menus, and bulk purchasing can keep budgets manageable. Ultimately, replacing traditional cafeteria fare with healthier choices is a practical investment in the present and future health of students.

The letter arrived on a Tuesday, typed on heavy cream stationery that smelled faintly of cedar. Margaret read it twice at the kitchen table before she let herself feel anything at all.

Her sister Ellen had been dead for eleven months. The newspapers had called her death a tragedy, a young woman lost to the river after a bad season of despair. They had not called it what Margaret knew it to be, which was the slow result of a man's words.

The man was Julian Vance, once celebrated, now disgraced. Ten years earlier his novel had won prizes and been adapted for the screen. Then a journalist had uncovered that he had built his most famous character from Ellen's private diaries, lifted whole passages without permission, and mocked her in print to a readership that never knew her name. Ellen had been the one who wrote the words first, and the world had forgotten her entirely.

Julian had lost his publisher, his agent, and his invitations. He lived now in a house on the coast, and he had written to Margaret because he had heard she was looking for someone to help her finish Ellen's unpublished manuscript.

That was the bait, and he had cast it well.

She wrote back that she would meet him. She chose a Thursday afternoon, a small café in the town where he lived, and she arrived early with a folder under her arm.

Julian rose when he saw her, a tall man gone thin, with the careful manners of someone who believed kindness could still buy forgiveness. He spoke warmly of Ellen. He praised her prose. He said he had read the pages Margaret had sent and found them remarkable.

"She had a gift," he said. "I was a fool not to see it sooner."

Margaret nodded and slid the folder across the table. Inside were the pages of the manuscript, typed clean, and beneath them a second set of pages, written in her own careful hand.

"I want you to finish it," she said. "But you will write it the way she would have, in her voice, and you will credit her on every page."

He laughed softly and then saw that she was serious. "And if I refuse?"

"Then you will read what I have added," she said, "and you will decide what kind of man you are."

For three months, Julian worked. He sent her drafts every week, and she read them at night in her apartment with the lamp turned low. He was good, better than she had expected, and each chapter wove Ellen's voice into his own until the two were nearly indistinguishable. He called it their collaboration. He called her his muse.

Margaret let him believe it.

She had planned the revenge the way Ellen used to plan her stories, with patience and attention to small details. The manuscript was not only Ellen's words. It was a record, a trail, a set of dates and names that Margaret had gathered from the diaries and from the people Julian had harmed over the years. Each chapter Julian wrote was built atop that record, and each one drew him further into a story that was no longer about a dead woman's art but about his own theft.

In the fourth month she sent him a letter with a single line: The river remembers.

He called her that night, his voice shaking. "What is this? What have you done?"

"Only what you did to her," Margaret said. "Except I am telling the truth, and I am giving it to the people who will read it."

She had already sent the file to a journalist, the same one who had exposed him a decade ago. She had sent the diaries too, with the dates and the passages marked. The journalist had promised a long piece, and a publisher interested in reissuing Ellen's work under her own name.

Julian was silent for a long time. Then he said quietly, "She would have hated this."

"She would have hated you," Margaret said. "That is different. She might even have pitied you."

She hung up before he could answer.

The article ran the following Sunday under the headline The Woman Behind the Novel. It was long and precise, and it did not spare him. It quoted Ellen's diaries and her unpublished letters, and it named every person Julian had used and discarded. Within a week his remaining contracts had dissolved. Within a month the reissue of Ellen's book appeared, bearing her name on the cover in plain, unadorned type.

Margaret held a copy in her hands on the morning it arrived. She ran her thumb over the letters of her sister's name, feeling the slight raised ink, and she thought about the river, about the cold water and the long quiet afterward.

It was not justice. Nothing could return Ellen. But it was the truth, and it belonged to her now, and Margaret intended to keep it safe.

She set the book on the mantel beside the photograph of the two of them as girls, laughing at something outside the frame, and she went to make a cup of tea.

Marcus had spent eleven years behind bars when the warden first suggested the Garden Program. He expected rules, lectures, and a prayer circle. Instead, he was handed a sealed envelope and told to open it in the courtyard.

Inside was a single ticket to a community kitchen across town, where a chef named Dolores ran cooking classes for people coming out of prison. Marcus didn't know what to make of it. He went anyway, mostly because the alternative was another night staring at a concrete ceiling.

The first thing Dolores did was ask him what he liked to eat. Nobody had asked him that in over a decade. He mumbled something about his grandmother's cornbread, and she smiled as if he had handed her a gift.

The program, it turned out, was built on a simple idea: people who had learned to find joy only in shortcuts could learn to find it in craft. Pleasure, the founders argued, was not the enemy of good behavior. It was the fuel that made people want to build something worth protecting.

Marcus baked his grandmother's cornbread that first Saturday, and the smell alone made two other students cry. He felt something unfamiliar unfurl in his chest, a warmth he hadn't allowed himself in years.

Over the following months, the program expanded. There was a woodworking shop where the air smelled of cedar, and a small greenhouse where tomatoes ripened in rows. There was a music room with worn pianos, and a tea garden where participants learned to brew blends from their own harvests.

Each activity came with a reward structure that felt more like a celebration than a test. Finishing a project earned you a dinner cooked by the group, a weekend fishing trip, or a night at the symphony with people who had once been strangers.

Critics called it coddling. A county commissioner wrote an angry letter to the newspaper, arguing that criminals should suffer, not sip wine at the opera. The program director, a soft-spoken former probation officer named Ruth Abernathy, invited him to visit.

She walked him through the statistics without drama. Recidivism among participants was less than half the regional average. Employment rates were higher. Fewer people were returning to the streets to sell the same drugs that had landed them inside.

"Punishment teaches people what they should avoid," Ruth told him over coffee. "Pleasure teaches them what they're worth protecting. Most of these folks never had a reason to care about tomorrow. We're giving them one."

The commissioner was not convinced, but the local bakery was. It hired three graduates of the program to work the morning shift, and the owner said their work ethic outshone that of employees who had never seen the inside of a cell.

Marcus took a job at a restaurant downtown, starting as a prep cook and working his way up to sous chef within two years. He never forgot Dolores's kitchen, and every Thursday he returned to teach a class of his own.

On his first day as a teacher, a young man named Terrence stood in the back of the room with his arms crossed and his jaw set. Marcus recognized the posture immediately. He had worn it himself for years.

"What do you like to eat?" Marcus asked him.

Terrence shrugged and said nothing. Marcus didn't push. He simply handed him an apron and a knife and let the onions do the talking.

By the end of the session, Terrence was laughing at his own tears and asking when the next class would be. Marcus watched him leave with a folder of recipes and felt the same unfamiliar warmth he had felt years before.

Some nights he wondered whether the program would hold up over the long term. Recidivism rates were encouraging, but people were complicated, and the world was not always kind to those who had served time. Still, he had seen what a plate of cornbread could do for a man who had forgotten how to hope.

Ruth retired the year Marcus became head instructor. At her farewell dinner, she raised a glass and said that the program had never been about making people good. It had been about helping them remember what they loved, and then trusting them to protect it.

Marcus thought about that for a long time afterward. He thought about the envelope, the courtyard, and the question nobody had asked him in eleven years. He thought about how strange it was that the thing that saved him had been so simple, so delicious, and so easy to overlook.

Years later, a reporter asked him what the secret was. Marcus laughed and said there was no secret, only a kitchen, a pot of soup, and the courage to ask a stranger what he liked to eat.

Testing a Gamified Mobile Cognitive Therapy Program for Depression in Japanese University Students

Abstract

Depression is common among university students, and many affected students do not seek or complete professional treatment. Mobile, gamified interventions offer a potentially scalable alternative. This study evaluated a gamified mobile cognitive behavioral therapy program adapted for Japanese university students with elevated depressive symptoms. Participants were randomized to the intervention or a waitlist control condition, and outcomes were assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and four-week follow-up. The primary outcome was change in depressive symptom scores; secondary outcomes included engagement, perceived stigma, and acceptability. We report the design, rationale, and expected analytic approach, and we discuss cultural considerations specific to Japanese students, including norms of help-seeking, self-disclosure, and the role of group identity.

Introduction

Depressive disorders are among the leading causes of disability among young adults worldwide. University students constitute a particularly vulnerable group because the transition to independent living, academic pressure, and social reorganization coincide with the typical age of onset for mood disorders. In Japan, rates of student depression and suicidal ideation have drawn considerable public and governmental attention, and the country has placed increasing emphasis on campus mental health services.

Despite this need, a substantial proportion of students with depressive symptoms never receive care. Barriers include stigma, limited availability of counseling staff, scheduling conflicts, and a preference for self-reliance. In Japanese contexts, concerns about being perceived as weak, burdening others, or damaging family reputation may be especially salient. Digital interventions are attractive because they can be accessed privately, at convenient times, and at low cost.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has accumulated strong evidence for depression across age groups, and its components, such as behavioral activation, cognitive restructuring, and structured problem-solving, lend themselves to self-guided delivery. Internet- and app-based CBT programs have shown modest to moderate effects in several meta-analyses, although adherence and attrition remain persistent problems. Gamification, which applies game elements such as points, progress tracking, badges, and narrative feedback to non-game contexts, has been proposed as a means of improving engagement and completion.

The application of gamified digital mental health tools to Japanese populations has been limited. Most evidence derives from North American and European samples, and cultural adaptation is rarely systematic. Cultural differences in emotional expression, the valuation of harmony, and attitudes toward self-focused exercises may affect both acceptability and efficacy. The present study addresses this gap by testing a gamified mobile CBT program developed specifically for Japanese university students.

Program Description

The intervention consisted of eight weekly modules delivered through a smartphone application. Each module introduced a core CBT concept, including psychoeducation about depression, recognition of mood-related activity patterns, behavioral activation, identification of automatic thoughts, cognitive restructuring, self-compassion exercises, social support mapping, and relapse prevention. Content was translated and adapted through a process involving Japanese clinical psychologists, university counselors, and student focus groups.

Gamification elements were incorporated deliberately and were tied to therapeutic goals rather than added as decoration. Users earned points for completing activities such as logging daily activities, rating mood, or practicing thought records. A character-based progress map depicted the user's journey through the modules, and users unlocked new scenes and optional reflective prompts upon completion. Streak indicators encouraged regular use, but the design avoided punitive mechanics, and missed days did not remove accumulated progress, in order to reduce the risk of guilt-driven disengagement.

The application used Japanese-language interface design, with optional romanized script for technical terms. Examples in the cognitive restructuring module were drawn from situations commonly reported by Japanese students, such as part-time job evaluations, group project conflicts, job hunting setbacks, and ambiguous feedback from professors and peers. Self-compassion exercises were framed to be compatible with culturally familiar concepts of self-reflection and gradual improvement, rather than relying solely on Western affirmation-based language.

Safety features included a screening item for suicidal ideation at baseline and weekly intervals. Responses indicating elevated risk triggered an on-screen message providing crisis hotline information and recommending contact with campus counseling services. Users were informed at enrollment that the application is not a substitute for emergency or clinical care.

Methods

Design

The study used a two-arm randomized controlled trial with a waitlist control group. Randomization was stratified by sex and by baseline depressive symptom severity, using a computer-generated allocation sequence concealed from recruiters until enrollment was confirmed. Participants in the waitlist condition received access to the full program after the eight-week primary assessment period.

Participants

Eligible participants were undergraduate and graduate students aged 18 years or older at partner universities in Japan who reported depressive symptoms at or above a threshold on a standardized self-report measure. Exclusion criteria included current diagnosis of a psychotic disorder, bipolar disorder, substance dependence requiring treatment, or active suicidal intent requiring immediate clinical intervention. Students already receiving psychotherapy or psychotropic medication were permitted to participate if their treatment had been stable for at least four weeks, and treatment status was recorded as a covariate.

A target sample of approximately 200 participants was planned, based on power analysis assuming a medium between-group effect size, a two-sided alpha of 0.05, power of 0.80, and an anticipated attrition rate of 20 percent.

Measures

The primary outcome was the Japanese version of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), a nine-item self-report measure of depressive symptoms over the preceding two weeks. Secondary measures included the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), the Beck Depression Inventory-II in its Japanese adaptation, the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), a brief stigma scale adapted for help-seeking attitudes among Japanese students, and a custom acceptability questionnaire. Engagement was measured through application analytics, including number of modules completed, number of activity logs, and days of active use.

Procedure

Students were recruited through campus announcements, counseling center referrals, and posters. After providing informed consent, participants completed baseline assessments online. Those meeting eligibility criteria were randomized and received login credentials. Follow-up assessments were administered at post-intervention (eight weeks) and at four-week follow-up after the intervention ended. Participants received small compensation at each assessment point, and additional compensation was offered for completion of all assessments.

Analysis Plan

The primary analysis will use a linear mixed-effects model with PHQ-9 score as the dependent variable, including fixed effects for group, time, group-by-time interaction, and stratification variables, and a random intercept for participant. Intention-to-treat analysis will be the primary approach, with missing data handled using multiple imputation under a missing-at-random assumption, and sensitivity analyses will examine robustness to missing-data assumptions. Secondary outcomes will be analyzed similarly. Associations between engagement metrics and symptom change will be explored using correlation and regression approaches. Effect sizes will be reported as standardized mean differences with 95 percent confidence intervals. Given multiple secondary outcomes, results will be interpreted with attention to multiplicity, and exploratory analyses will be labeled as such.

Ethical Considerations

The study protocol was designed to be reviewed and approved by the institutional ethics committees of participating universities. Consent procedures emphasized voluntary participation and the right to withdraw without academic consequence. Data were stored with pseudonymized identifiers, and access was restricted to the research team. Because the population includes students who may be experiencing significant distress, safety procedures and referral pathways were embedded in both the intervention and the study protocol.

Expected Results

We anticipate that participants in the intervention group will show greater reductions in PHQ-9 scores than waitlist controls at post-intervention, with effects maintained at four-week follow-up. We expect engagement to be higher than typical for unguided app-based interventions, and we hypothesize that higher engagement will predict greater symptom reduction. We also expect that perceived stigma will be lower among users who engage privately with the program, and that acceptability ratings will be favorable, particularly regarding the gamified structure and the culturally adapted content. These expectations are hypotheses and have not been confirmed by data at the time of writing.

Discussion

If the anticipated outcomes are supported, the findings would suggest that a culturally adapted, gamified mobile CBT program can offer meaningful symptom relief to Japanese university students who might otherwise remain untreated. Such a tool could complement, rather than replace, campus counseling services by serving as a first-line option for students with mild to moderate symptoms, a stepped-care entry point, or a bridge while students wait for appointments.

Several limitations warrant consideration. The waitlist control design does not account for nonspecific attention effects, and participants in the intervention group may have expectancy effects that inflate outcomes. Self-report measures are vulnerable to response biases, which may be amplified in cultures emphasizing modesty or social desirability. The sample is drawn from partner universities and may not represent students in all institution types or regions. Long-term durability beyond four weeks is not assessed, and the study cannot determine whether benefits persist over the academic year.

Gamification also raises questions. Game elements may enhance engagement in the short term but could lose appeal over time, and some users may focus on earning points rather than on therapeutic practice. Future work should examine whether specific gamification features contribute to outcomes, and whether engagement patterns differ by gender, year of study, or baseline severity.

Cultural adaptation is a further area for investigation. The present program drew on Japanese clinical and student input, but its cultural fit should be evaluated empirically, for example through qualitative interviews examining how students interpret the content. Comparisons with non-adapted versions would clarify the contribution of adaptation.

Conclusion

This study protocol describes a randomized evaluation of a gamified mobile cognitive therapy program for depressive symptoms among Japanese university students. By combining evidence-based CBT components with engagement-oriented design and culturally informed content, the program addresses barriers to care that are prominent in this population. Results will help clarify whether scalable digital tools can meaningfully reduce depressive symptoms in Japanese students and whether gamification and cultural adaptation contribute to their effectiveness. Pending data collection and analysis, the conclusions remain provisional.

Acknowledgments

The authors thank the university counseling staff, student participants, and clinical collaborators who contributed to program development and study implementation.

References

References would be listed here in the final manuscript according to the journal's citation style.

I have not been given the paper itself, only its title, so this review is written against what the title implies rather than the paper's actual contents. The reviewer should check each claim below against the manuscript before relying on it. The paper addresses a practical problem in program synthesis: training neural models to write array-manipulation programs requires large amounts of labeled examples, and collecting them by hand is costly. The authors propose using a discriminator to guide the generation of synthetic training data, which is a sensible direction given the success of generator-discriminator setups in other areas of machine learning. The central idea appears to be that a discriminator can filter or steer synthetic programs toward those that are more realistic, diverse, or useful for training, rather than accepting every generated sample. This framing is relevant to the program synthesis community, where the scarcity and distributional mismatch of training data are well-known bottlenecks. The choice of array manipulation as the target domain is a reasonable one, since such programs have clear semantics that can be checked against input-output examples. That property could allow the authors to verify correctness automatically, which would strengthen the validity of any generated data. A key question for the paper is how the discriminator is trained and what signal it uses to judge synthetic programs. If the discriminator learns from the same distribution it is meant to evaluate, there is a risk of circular reasoning, and the manuscript should explain how this is avoided. The authors should describe the architecture of both the generator and the discriminator in enough detail for the work to be reproduced. Equally important is a clear account of the training procedure, including hyperparameters, optimization choices, and stopping criteria. The evaluation methodology deserves close attention. The paper should compare models trained with the discriminator-guided data against models trained on unguided synthetic data and on any available human-written data. Ablations that isolate the contribution of the discriminator are essential, since without them it is impossible to tell whether gains come from the guidance or simply from having more data. The reviewer should check whether the reported improvements are statistically meaningful, ideally with multiple random seeds and confidence intervals. Benchmarks should be standard and clearly described, and the authors should justify any custom datasets they introduce. Diversity of the generated programs is another dimension worth examining. A discriminator that favors one narrow style of program could produce data that looks good on a metric but generalizes poorly. The manuscript should therefore report measures of diversity, such as the variety of operations, program lengths, and structural patterns in the generated corpus. It should also show qualitative examples so readers can judge the quality of the outputs directly. Errors and failure cases are as informative as successes, and the paper would be stronger if it discussed them. The related work section should situate the contribution relative to prior work on data augmentation for code generation, synthetic data for program synthesis, and adversarial or discriminator-based data selection. Any claim of novelty should be checked against these lines of research, and the authors should be precise about what is new. Overstated claims are a common weakness in this kind of submission, so the reviewer should look for language suggesting general superiority when the experiments cover only a narrow set of tasks. Limitations deserve their own discussion. The authors should acknowledge whether the approach depends heavily on a particular domain-specific language, whether it scales to longer or more complex programs, and what computational cost the discriminator adds. The reviewer should ask whether the efficiency gains, if any, justify the extra complexity of the pipeline. Reproducibility is a central concern for this kind of work. The reviewer should check whether the authors release code, generated datasets, and trained models, and whether the paper includes enough information about the synthesis pipeline to allow independent reconstruction. Missing details about data filtering thresholds or prompt formats would significantly hinder verification. Presentation matters as well. The paper should define its terms consistently, present tables and figures that are easy to read, and avoid unexplained jargon. Notation for the generator and discriminator should be introduced once and used throughout. The writing should be clear enough that a reader familiar with program synthesis but not with this specific system can follow the method. Overall, the topic is timely and the core idea is promising, but the strength of the contribution depends on the rigor of the experiments and the transparency of the method. The reviewer's recommendation should rest on whether the paper provides convincing evidence that discriminator guidance improves the training data, and whether the authors have been honest about the boundaries of their findings. With revisions addressing the points above, particularly the ablations, diversity analysis, and reproducibility details, the paper could make a useful contribution to the field.

Gordon had been hungry since dawn, and by noon the hunger had settled into something close to impatience. He pulled the cutting board out from the drawer and laid it flat on the counter, smoothing it with both palms the way he always did, as if it needed reassuring before the work began.

The onions came first. He took one from the bag, rolled it in his hand, and felt its papery skin give beneath his thumb. It was firm and cool, and he liked how it resisted him for just a moment before he sliced it open. The knife was sharp, freshly honed the night before, and it slid through the flesh with a satisfying, almost reluctant sigh.

He worked slowly. There was no reason to rush. The kitchen was warm from the oven he had preheated twenty minutes earlier, and the air smelled faintly of thyme and the butter he had left out to soften on the windowsill. He pressed the flat of the blade against a clove of garlic and felt it crack open under the pressure, the sharp scent rising up to meet him like an eager greeting.

Next were the peppers, red and glossy, plump in his hand. He held one up to the light from the window and admired its shape, its smooth curves, the way the stem sat neatly at the top like a small crown. He ran his thumb along its length and felt the faint ridges beneath the skin. Then he took the knife and made a clean incision, opening it up to reveal the pale ribs and the seeds nestled inside, which he scraped out with a practiced flick of the spoon.

He took his time with the zucchini as well. Long and green, it was the sort of vegetable that demanded a certain gentleness, and he treated it accordingly, slicing it lengthwise into thin strips that fell away in graceful arcs. The cool, damp flesh clung to his fingers, and he wiped them on the towel tucked into his waistband before reaching for the next one.

The mushrooms were his favorite part. Gordon brushed the dirt from each cap with a soft pastry brush, careful not to bruise them, and he admired how they sat so firmly in his palm. He sliced them thick, watching the pale gills appear one by one, and tossed them into the hot pan where they immediately began to sizzle and release their juices. The sound was low and insistent, and he leaned over the stove to breathe in the rising steam, rich and earthy.

By the time the vegetables were all in the pan, he was practically trembling with anticipation. He stirred them with a long wooden spoon, pushing and folding, coaxing each piece to soften and brown at its own pace. The butter melted into a golden pool, glistening as it wrapped around the edges of the onions and peppers, and he poured in a splash of wine that hissed and bubbled as it met the heat.

He reached for the salt and sprinkled it generously, watching the crystals catch the light before they disappeared into the mixture. A pinch of pepper followed, then a few torn leaves of basil that he crushed between his fingers so their fragrance would bloom. Every ingredient had its place, and he added each one with deliberate care, savoring the moment of its arrival.

The sauce began to thicken, clinging to the vegetables in a glossy coat. Gordon lowered the flame and let it simmer, the surface bubbling in slow, lazy pulses. He dipped a spoon in and tasted it, closing his eyes as the flavors unfolded across his tongue, rich and bright and deeply satisfying. He nodded to himself, pleased, and tasted it again just to be certain.

He set the lid on the pot and wiped his hands on the towel. The kitchen was full of warmth and perfume now, the windows fogged softly at the edges. He leaned against the counter and waited, listening to the gentle murmur of the simmering pot, feeling the hunger in his stomach rise in anticipation of what was to come.

When the timer finally chimed, he lifted the lid and let the steam billow up around his face. He filled a bowl with the thick, fragrant mixture, ladling it slowly so each spoonful landed just so. He added a scattering of grated cheese, watching it melt into soft golden ribbons across the top.

Gordon carried the bowl to the table and sat down, pulling his chair close. He picked up his spoon and held it for a moment above the steaming surface, feeling the heat rise against his face. Then, at last, he dipped it in and brought the first bite to his lips, and he sighed with pure, unguarded pleasure.

He ate slowly, savoring each mouthful, and by the time the bowl was empty he felt warm and full and content. He leaned back in his chair, rubbed his stomach, and smiled at the mess he had made. Tomorrow, he decided, he would do it all again, and he would enjoy every single moment just as much.

This manuscript presents a benchmarking study of graph classification methods and examines how dataset characteristics affect their performance, a topic of clear practical relevance as graph-structured data spreads across chemistry, biology, social networks, and knowledge bases. The authors frame the problem well, noting that reported gains in the literature are often measured on a narrow set of datasets whose properties are rarely characterized. The introduction is concise and motivates the study convincingly, although the related work section would benefit from a more explicit comparison with earlier benchmarking efforts and survey papers. The choice to evaluate both classical kernel methods and modern graph neural networks under a common protocol is a strength, since it allows a fairer comparison than studies that tune only the proposed model. The experimental design, however, is described only briefly, and the manuscript should specify how hyperparameters were selected, whether the same search budget was allotted to each method, and how many random seeds were used. Reporting results as single train-test splits without variance estimates makes it difficult to judge whether the reported differences exceed noise. The authors should provide confidence intervals or standard deviations across repeated runs and apply an appropriate statistical test before claiming that one method outperforms another. The analysis of dataset characteristics, which is the most novel component, examines graph size, average degree, class imbalance, and label informativeness. This is a valuable direction, yet the manuscript does not clearly establish causality; correlations between characteristics across datasets may be confounded, and with a limited number of datasets the conclusions are fragile. I recommend a controlled study using synthetic graphs in which individual properties are varied independently, which would substantially strengthen the claims. The figures are generally clear, though several plots lack axis labels, units, or legends for the dataset abbreviations, and the color scheme is difficult to read in grayscale. The discussion section sometimes overstates findings, for example describing a moderate correlation as a decisive factor, and these statements should be tempered to match the evidence. The authors also do not adequately discuss computational cost, memory requirements, or training time, which are important considerations for practitioners choosing between methods. Reproducibility is partially addressed through a code repository link, but the paper should state the exact dataset versions, preprocessing steps, and software library versions used. Some datasets used in the benchmark have known issues such as duplicate graphs or label leakage, and the authors should either document these problems or justify their retention. The limitations section is brief and should acknowledge the restricted set of datasets, the focus on a single task type, and the absence of inductive versus transductive comparisons. Minor typographical and formatting issues appear throughout, including inconsistent capitalization of method names and several citations missing publication venues. The writing is generally clear, although some paragraphs are dense and could be split to improve readability. The related work discussion of graph kernels would be more useful if it distinguished between kernels based on subgraph counting and those based on random walks, since these families behave differently on the characteristics the paper studies. The authors could also consider including a simple baseline, such as a majority-class predictor or a feature-only model, to contextualize the reported accuracies. Overall, the paper addresses an important question with a generally sound approach, but its claims about the influence of dataset characteristics currently exceed what the experiments support. I recommend a major revision that adds statistical rigor, clarifies the experimental protocol, and tempers the causal language in the analysis. With these changes, the manuscript could become a useful reference for both researchers and practitioners working on graph classification.
