Mara had been circling the same first line for eleven months. Every morning she sat at her desk with the manuscript open, convinced that this time the words would arrive fresh and untouched by anyone else's pen. She read Austen and Woolf at night, underlining sentences, then felt sick when she recognized the rhythm of a borrowed cadence in her own drafts. Her lover, Theo, a patient man who repaired clocks for a living, told her that every story is a remix of older stories, but she would not hear it. She rewrote the opening chapter forty-three times, each version more polished and more hollow than the last. When the publisher's deadline finally passed without a word from her, she realized the book she had been guarding so jealously had never been written at all. She closed the file, poured two glasses of wine, and went to find Theo, who was waiting by the window with the kettle already warm.

The first photograph came back from the lunar orbiter on a Tuesday, and by Friday every network on Earth was running the same jagged image: a black seam cutting across the Sea of Tranquility, long as a river and straight as a ruler.

Dr. Mira Okonkwo was the one who noticed the edges were too clean. Lunar fissures crumble and slump over millions of years, she told the committee, but this one looked cut.

Within a week the internet had decided what it was. Some called it a tomb, others a seal, and a few insisted it was a door. A podcaster with three million followers claimed the government had known about it for decades. An online forum traced the fissure's angle to a constellation and declared it a message.

The space agency released a dull statement about thermal contraction and basalt flows. Nobody believed it.

Mira did not believe it either, but she did not believe the conspiracy theories, and she spent her nights rereading the gravimetry data instead of the comment sections. The mass beneath the fissure was wrong. Something dense sat under the surface, something that had no business being there.

In March, the agency approved a robotic probe. It was a small, slow craft, designed to drill a single core sample and return it. Mira argued for a larger budget and lost. She argued for a second drill and lost again.

The probe landed on a Thursday in June. For eleven hours the feed showed nothing but gray dust and the long black shadow of the rim. Then the drill struck something that rang back like a bell, a tone so low that the audio engineers had to shift it up two octaves before they could hear it properly.

The core came back in a sealed capsule, and the lab opened it in a room kept at absolute zero. Inside was a cylinder of metal, perfectly smooth, etched on its surface with spirals of fine lines that repeated at every scale, from the width of a hair to the length of the cylinder itself.

Mira stared at it through the glass for a long time before she spoke. Then she asked the technician to run the spectral analysis again, because the alloy did not match anything in the periodic table.

It matched nothing on Earth. It matched nothing in any meteorite collection. It was older than the Moon itself, according to the decay chains locked inside it.

The lines on the surface, when the team mapped them, formed a lattice, and the lattice encoded numbers. The numbers were prime, then composite in a pattern that Mira recognized from her own field: an error-correcting code, the kind used to send signals across vast distances where noise would otherwise destroy the message.

Someone had built this to be found, and to be read by minds capable of mathematics.

The committee wanted to classify everything. The president wanted a press conference. Mira wanted to keep working, and she managed to keep the lab for another three weeks before the classification order arrived.

In those three weeks she decoded the first layer. It was a warning, not a greeting. It described a cycle, a repeating pattern in which intelligence arose, grew, and reached for the stars, and then something came from beyond the galaxy and did not stop until the lights went out. The cylinder was a seed vault and a beacon, and it had been waiting under the dust for a species clever enough to dig.

The second layer was harder. It contained coordinates, and the coordinates pointed not into the sky but toward the fissure itself, toward a depth the drill had not reached.

Mira understood then why the mass was wrong. There was not one object beneath the Moon's surface. There were many, arranged in a pattern like the cells of a hive, and the uppermost one was only the first to be woken by the drill.

She sent her last report on a Sunday, to a secure channel that she was not sure still existed. In it she wrote that the fissure was not a scar and not a grave, but a hatch, and that something on the other side had just heard them knocking.

The reply came back in under a minute, and it was not from the agency. It was a single line of prime numbers, repeating, and then the lattice again, and then the seismometers on the far side of the Moon began to register a faint, rhythmic tapping that did not stop.

This manuscript addresses layer-wise weight quantization for neural networks by combining distortion-aware codebook optimization with knowledge distillation, a timely problem given the growing demand for deploying large models on resource-constrained hardware. The authors clearly motivate the work by identifying the limitations of uniform quantization schemes, which often fail to account for the heterogeneous sensitivity of different layers. The proposed codebook optimization method, which weights quantization error by its estimated effect on the output distortion, is a well-reasoned idea that is explained with commendable clarity in the methodology section. The inclusion of knowledge distillation as a recovery mechanism for accuracy lost during quantization is sensible, and the authors describe how the teacher-student setup is configured in enough detail to allow reasonable reproduction. The experimental evaluation covers several architectures and reports compression ratios alongside accuracy, which is appropriate for this area. However, the comparison baselines are somewhat limited, and the paper would be strengthened by including recent post-training quantization methods that also target layer sensitivity. The ablation study isolating the contribution of distortion-aware codebooks versus distillation is valuable, but the authors should report variance across multiple random seeds, since the reported improvements are sometimes within the range of run-to-run noise. The discussion of inference latency and memory bandwidth on actual hardware is thin, and claims about practical speedups would be more convincing with measured numbers rather than theoretical bit-width reductions. The related work section is thorough in its coverage of quantization literature but could more precisely distinguish the novelty of the codebook formulation from prior vector quantization approaches. Several equations in the optimization derivation use notation that is inconsistent between the main text and the appendix, which should be corrected before publication. Overall, the paper presents a promising and technically sound contribution, and I recommend a major revision that addresses the baseline comparisons, statistical reporting, and hardware evaluation.

Varrask the Unbroken had stood at the top of the Obsidian Spire for eleven years. Players spoke of him in hushed tones. His sword could split a mountain, and his roar could shake the stars from the sky. Those who reached his chamber rarely left it alive, and the few who did carried scars that never faded.

Then, on a grey Tuesday afternoon, a boy named Pim found the seam.

He had been climbing the spire's western wall, testing whether the stone could be scaled without the staircase, when his character slipped through a crack in the geometry and tumbled into a corridor no one had ever mapped. At its end was a door, and behind the door was Varrask, frozen mid-stride, his great sword raised but going nowhere.

Pim did not know what to do, so he attacked.

The first blow did not land. The second did not either. By the fortieth strike, Varrask had not moved, had not spoken, had not even blinked. Then Pim noticed the health bar above the giant's head had been shrinking the whole time, as if the boss had forgotten to refill it. Pim struck again, and the bar emptied.

He sat back in his chair and stared at the screen for a long time.

The news spread within a day. Videos of the glitch flooded the forums, and by the weekend thousands of players were streaming through the western wall. Each arrived at the same silent chamber, and each defeated Varrask in the same absurd way, without any real struggle at all.

The developers noticed within the week. They patched the seam, of course, but the patch arrived slowly, and in the meantime the game's economy and its community had already rearranged themselves around the new reality.

Something unexpected happened in the weeks that followed. Players began returning to the spire, not to fight Varrask but to watch him. They gathered in the western corridor and filmed the moment he was defeated, laughing and cheering.

Then a new kind of player appeared, one who wanted to learn how the spire worked. Those players did not climb the western wall. They came through the front gate, fought through the lesser guardians, and learned the rhythms of the stairs. Along the way they noticed that Varrask, now stripped of his mystique, had become something of a teacher.

The developers, who had never intended for their final boss to be used this way, found they liked the idea. In the next major update, Varrask was not deleted. He was moved.

He now stood at the very entrance of the spire, in a small training courtyard just past the first gate. His health bar was short, his attacks were slow and telegraphed, and his roar had become a soft cough. When a new player arrived, a floating tutorial message appeared above his head: "Press attack to strike. Dodge when the sword glows red."

Pim, now grown and working as a designer for a different studio, heard about the change and smiled. He booted up the spire one evening, walked through the front gate, and found Varrask waiting in the courtyard. He pressed attack, and the old giant lurched forward, his sword swinging lazily through the air.

Pim dodged, struck once, and watched the little bar drain.

Varrask stumbled backward, bowed his enormous head, and dissolved into gold, ready to return the next day for the next student.

Autonomous vehicles promise to reshape how people travel, and their benefits extend well beyond convenience. Chief among these is safety. Human error contributes to the large majority of traffic crashes, including those caused by distraction, fatigue, speeding, and impaired driving. Self-driving systems do not tire, text, or drink, and they can monitor their surroundings continuously in every direction. Although no technology is perfect, widespread adoption could prevent many of the thousands of deaths that occur on roads each year. Safer roads would also reduce the injuries, medical costs, and emotional toll that accompany collisions.

Productivity is another important advantage. Commuters who currently spend their drives concentrating on traffic could instead read, plan their day, answer messages, or rest. For people who spend hours each week behind the wheel, this recovered time adds up to a meaningful gain. Autonomous vehicles could also make freight and delivery services more efficient, lowering costs for businesses and consumers. Shared fleets might reduce the need for parking spaces in crowded cities, freeing land for housing, parks, and other uses that support economic life.

Social connection may be the most underrated benefit. Autonomous vehicles could expand mobility for people who cannot drive, including older adults, individuals with disabilities, and young people too young to hold a license. Greater independence allows these groups to visit friends, attend religious services, take part in community events, and reach jobs and medical care. Rural residents, who often live far from services, could gain easier access to the wider world. By helping more people stay connected to their communities, autonomous vehicles could reduce isolation and strengthen the social bonds that support well-being.

Realizing these benefits will require careful planning, clear regulation, and public trust. Still, the potential gains in safety, productivity, and social connection make autonomous vehicles a promising development worth pursuing thoughtfully.

The paper proposes a learning-based approach to polygon evolution for image segmentation that combines active contour ideas with differentiable rendering, allowing the contour to be optimized end-to-end from training data. The problem is well motivated, since classical active contours are sensitive to initialization and hand-tuned energy terms, and the authors make a reasonable case that learned evolution policies can generalize better. The use of differentiable rendering to convert polygon vertices into masks that can be compared with ground truth is a sound and clearly explained technical contribution. However, the experimental section would benefit from comparisons against more recent contour-based and transformer-based segmentation baselines, as the chosen comparisons appear somewhat dated. The ablation studies are useful but do not isolate the effect of the differentiable rendering component from the effect of the learned evolution module, which weakens the claim that both are necessary. The paper would also be strengthened by reporting runtime and memory costs, since iterative polygon evolution can be expensive relative to single-pass segmentation networks. Overall, the work is a promising and technically coherent contribution, and I recommend a minor revision addressing the baseline selection, ablation design, and efficiency analysis.

Reducing private vehicle use offers significant benefits for both public health and the environment. Cars and trucks are major sources of air pollution, releasing fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and carbon monoxide that contribute to asthma, heart disease, and other respiratory illnesses. When fewer people drive, cities see cleaner air, which can lower hospital visits and reduce the burden on healthcare systems. Transportation is also one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions, so cutting car trips directly helps slow climate change. Walking and cycling, which often replace short car trips, provide regular physical activity that strengthens the heart, improves mental health, and lowers the risk of obesity and diabetes. Less traffic also means fewer traffic accidents, saving lives and preventing serious injuries, especially among children and older adults. Quieter streets that result from reduced driving decrease noise pollution, which is linked to stress, sleep problems, and high blood pressure. Communities with fewer cars tend to have more space for parks, trees, and gathering areas, which further support physical and social well-being. Public transit and shared mobility options can reduce the total number of vehicles on the road while still giving people the access they need to work, school, and services. Overall, shifting away from private vehicle dependence is a practical step that benefits individual health, community quality of life, and the long-term health of the planet.

Elias had carried the ability for forty years, a quiet power to bend the ordinary into something else. He had used it sparingly: to find lost keys, to soften a hard winter, to make a stranger laugh at the right moment. Now, at seventy-one, with a doctor's grim news folded in his coat pocket, he understood he had one use left.

He sat on the bench outside the hospital and watched the late afternoon light slant across the parking lot. The asphalt looked tired. A child in a red jacket chased a runaway balloon past the car wash, and Elias felt the old pull of the gift stirring in his chest.

He considered the grand options first. He could summon a sky full of color, or lift the city's noise into a single perfect chord. He could reverse a death, though he knew the cost of that kind of magic, and he had sworn long ago never to pay it. Each idea felt too loud, too much about him.

Then he thought of Marta. She had been his wife for thirty-eight years, and she had never once seen him use the gift, because he had always kept it hidden. He had wanted her to love him as a plain man, and she had. Perhaps that was the greater gift, he thought, and yet he still wanted to give her something.

He went home and found her in the kitchen, humming over a pot of soup. Without a word, he took her hand and led her to the back porch. The sun was going down over the hills, and he let it hang there, a little longer than it should have. The gold deepened and spread until the whole valley seemed lit from within.

Marta laughed in surprise and pressed her hand to her mouth. Elias felt the strain of the magic in his bones, a slow tug like a rope pulled taut, but he held it steady. The moment stretched, the birds going silent in the oaks, the wind pausing in the grass.

"Elias," she whispered, "what did you do?"

"Nothing you won't remember," he said, and that was true in a way he did not explain. He wanted her to keep only the feeling, not the trick.

The light held for nearly a minute, then eased back into the ordinary dusk. The birds began again. The wind returned to the grass. Marta leaned into his shoulder and said nothing for a long time.

Elias had spent his last ability on a sunset, and he found, to his quiet astonishment, that he did not regret it at all.

Technology has become woven into nearly every part of everyday life, offering remarkable conveniences while also raising serious concerns. On the positive side, digital tools allow people to communicate instantly with friends and family across the world, making distance feel smaller than ever before. Smartphones put information, maps, and banking services in our pockets, saving time and making daily tasks easier to manage. Medical technology has also improved health outcomes, with advances in diagnosis and treatment helping people live longer and healthier lives. Students benefit as well, since online resources and educational apps give them access to knowledge that once required a trip to a library. However, these benefits come with real drawbacks that deserve careful attention. Many people spend excessive hours on screens, which can harm sleep, concentration, and physical health. Social media platforms, though connecting people, can also fuel anxiety, comparison, and the spread of misinformation. Privacy is another concern, as companies and governments often collect large amounts of personal data, sometimes without people fully understanding how it will be used. Automation threatens certain jobs, leaving some workers struggling to adapt to a changing economy. Furthermore, a growing digital divide means that those without reliable internet access or devices can fall behind in school, work, and public services. In the end, technology is neither purely good nor purely harmful, and its impact depends largely on how thoughtfully individuals and societies choose to use it.

German New Medicine (GNM) is an alternative health system developed in the 1980s by Ryke Geerd Hamer, a German physician who was later stripped of his medical license. This page explains the central claims of GNM about emotional conflicts, cancer development, and healing, and it places those claims in the context of established medical science.

At the core of GNM is the idea that every disease originates from a sudden, unexpected emotional shock, which Hamer called a "conflict shock." According to this view, the shock occurs at a moment when a person feels isolated or threatened, such as after receiving bad news or losing a loved one.

Hamer proposed that each conflict shock affects a specific part of the brain and a corresponding organ in the body. He named this supposed link the "biological special program," and he described it as a fixed, predictable pattern.

GNM divides the body's responses into two phases, which Hamer called the conflict-active phase and the healing phase. He claimed that disease develops during the first phase and that symptoms appear during the second.

According to GNM, the conflict-active phase is marked by a kind of hyperactivity in the affected organ, and the healing phase is marked by symptoms that people usually associate with illness. Hamer maintained that these symptoms are the body's attempt to restore balance.

GNM asserts that cancer is not a process of uncontrolled cell growth driven by genetic and environmental factors, as mainstream oncology describes it. Instead, Hamer argued that cancer is a biologically meaningful program triggered by emotional conflict.

Hamer taught that different types of conflict produce different cancers. For example, he associated certain conflicts with breast tissue, others with the lungs, and others with the skin.

GNM describes a "conflict resolution" as the event that ends the conflict-active phase. Hamer claimed that once a person resolves the emotional conflict, the body enters the healing phase.

In GNM, healing is said to involve a swelling of the affected tissue, which Hamer considered a natural and beneficial process. He argued that this swelling is often misdiagnosed as a dangerous tumor.

Hamer also maintained that the symptoms of the healing phase, including pain, fever, and fatigue, are signs that the body is repairing itself. He advised that such symptoms should not be treated with conventional medicine.

According to GNM, conventional treatments such as chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery interfere with the body's healing process and can cause harm. Hamer and his followers have strongly criticized these therapies.

Many people who follow GNM are encouraged to refuse or delay standard cancer treatment. Medical professionals have documented cases in which patients who followed this advice died from treatable cancers.

The GNM framework has been widely rejected by the scientific and medical community. Researchers have found no evidence that emotional conflicts cause specific organs to develop specific diseases in the way Hamer described.

Cancer is a group of diseases characterized by abnormal cell division, and its development is linked to mutations in DNA, which can be inherited or acquired. Decades of research have identified many risk factors, including tobacco use, radiation exposure, certain infections, diet, and genetic predisposition.

Emotional stress is studied in medicine as one factor that may influence health, but research does not support the claim that stress alone produces cancers of particular types in particular locations. The relationship between psychological state and disease is complex and remains an active area of study.

GNM's explanation of disease also relies on the idea that the brain contains a precise map linking conflicts to organs. Neuroscience has not validated this map, and brain imaging and clinical observation do not show the patterns Hamer described.

Hamer's theory was presented as the result of his personal observations and a discovery he claimed to have made after his own son's death. Critics point out that the theory was not tested through controlled studies and was not published in peer-reviewed scientific journals.

In 1986, Hamer was convicted in Germany of practicing medicine without a license, and in the years that followed his medical license was revoked. His legal troubles and the publicity surrounding his advice have contributed to public concern about the movement.

Supporters of GNM often share personal testimonials, which can be persuasive. However, anecdotes cannot establish cause and effect, because people who recover from cancer without standard treatment are rare, and many others who try alternative approaches are not included in such accounts.

Scientific evaluation depends on controlled trials, reproducible results, and peer review, and GNM has not met these standards. Its claims have not been supported by evidence that would justify changing established treatment for serious diseases.

Medical organizations emphasize that cancer should be diagnosed and treated by qualified professionals. Early diagnosis and evidence-based treatment have improved survival rates for many cancers, and delaying effective care can allow a treatable disease to progress.

People who encounter GNM ideas are encouraged to consult a licensed physician before making decisions about their health. Discussing emotional well-being with a doctor or counselor is appropriate, but it should complement rather than replace proven medical care.

Families and friends of people with cancer can play a supportive role by encouraging timely medical consultation. Emotional support, such as counseling or support groups, can improve quality of life during treatment without requiring anyone to abandon medical care.

It is also worth recognizing why GNM appeals to some people. A serious diagnosis can feel overwhelming, and a theory that offers a clear explanation and a sense of personal control may seem comforting.

However, that comfort does not make the theory accurate. A coherent story can still be false, and the stakes of a cancer diagnosis are high enough that people should rely on evidence rather than appealing explanations alone.

Readers who want to evaluate health claims can ask several questions. Is the claim supported by controlled studies? Has it been published in peer-reviewed journals? Do independent experts reach the same conclusions? Does it explain the evidence better than existing science?

When applied to GNM, these questions reveal a significant gap between its assertions and the available evidence. The theory rests largely on Hamer's personal conclusions rather than on data that others can verify.

Understanding this history can also help people recognize similar claims in the future. Health claims that promise simple cures, dismiss established treatments, or rely mainly on testimonials deserve careful scrutiny.

The conflict-based model of disease also reflects a broader pattern in alternative medicine, in which a single cause is proposed to explain many illnesses. Medicine typically finds that diseases arise from multiple interacting factors.

Learning how diseases actually develop can be empowering. Research into genetics, environmental exposures, immune function, and early detection has produced real advances, and these advances depend on the same scientific methods that GNM rejects.

Readers interested in the psychology of health beliefs may find it useful to study how people weigh evidence, how trusted voices influence decisions, and why emotionally satisfying explanations can be persuasive.

Patients should also be aware that some alternative practitioners may charge substantial fees, and that delaying proven treatment can have serious financial and medical consequences.

If a loved one is considering abandoning standard treatment in favor of GNM or a similar approach, it may help to have an open conversation, to ask the treating physician to explain the evidence, and to seek a second opinion from another qualified doctor.

Medical ethics emphasize informed consent, which requires that patients receive accurate information about risks, benefits, and alternatives. Understanding the evidence behind a treatment decision is a key part of that process.

In summary, German New Medicine presents a detailed system linking emotional conflicts to specific diseases, describing cancer as a meaningful biological program and healing as a phase that conventional medicine interferes with. These claims have not been validated by scientific research and have been associated with serious harm when used to avoid effective treatment.

Anyone facing a health concern is best served by consulting qualified medical professionals, relying on evidence-based information, and treating emotional well-being as a valuable part of comprehensive care rather than a replacement for it.

Using Entropy Production and Dissipative Energy to Assess the Stability of a Fishery Population-Harvesting Model

Abstract

Sustainable management of fisheries requires tools that can diagnose when a harvested population is moving toward collapse or settling into a robust equilibrium. Conventional stability analysis, based on linearization and eigenvalue spectra, identifies local stability but offers limited insight into the energetic and thermodynamic organization of the system. In this paper we propose a complementary framework that uses entropy production and dissipative energy as diagnostic quantities for a fishery population-harvesting model. We formulate a nonlinear logistic-type stock model with Holling-type harvesting, derive a thermodynamically motivated dissipation functional, and examine how entropy production behaves near equilibria and along trajectories. We show that the rate of dissipative energy loss to harvesting and natural mortality provides a Lyapunov-like indicator whose sign and magnitude correlate with local and global stability. Numerical experiments across parameter regimes illustrate bifurcations, including transitions from stable coexistence to oscillatory and collapsed states. The results suggest that entropy-based metrics can serve as early-warning signals and can complement classical bioeconomic indicators in adaptive harvest governance.

Introduction

Fisheries are among the most important renewable resources supporting food security and livelihoods, yet many stocks have been depleted by overharvesting. Mathematical models have long been used to describe the interaction between fish biomass and fishing effort, from the classical Schaefer surplus-production model to more elaborate age-structured and spatially explicit formulations. Stability analysis of these models typically relies on the Jacobian evaluated at equilibria, which determines whether small perturbations decay or grow. While effective for identifying local behavior, eigenvalue analysis does not directly quantify how much energy a system dissipates as it approaches or departs from equilibrium.

Thermodynamic concepts offer a different vantage point. In non-equilibrium thermodynamics, entropy production measures the irreversibility of processes, and dissipative quantities measure the rate at which free energy is converted into heat or lost to the environment. Ecological systems are open, driven, and dissipative, making such concepts natural candidates for characterizing their organization. Prior work in ecosystem thermodynamics has proposed exergy, entropy, and dissipation as indicators of ecosystem maturity and resilience, although these ideas have seldom been applied rigorously to harvested populations with explicit control.

The present study addresses this gap. Our aim is to construct a dissipation-based stability diagnostic for a fishery population-harvesting model, to establish its relationship to conventional Lyapunov analysis, and to demonstrate its behavior across parameter regimes. We do not claim that entropy production replaces established stability methods; rather, we argue that it provides an interpretable, energy-based measure that can enrich the management toolkit.

Model Formulation

We consider a single fish stock with biomass density x(t) subject to logistic growth with carrying capacity K and intrinsic growth rate r. Harvesting is modeled by a Holling type II functional response, so that the catch rate is proportional to x/(a + x), scaled by a maximal harvesting rate h and a fleet-related effort parameter E. The governing equation is

dx/dt = r x (1 - x/K) - h E x / (a + x).

The parameter a controls saturation of the harvest rate at high biomass, and E represents fishing effort, which we treat as a constant control in the baseline analysis. Nonnegative equilibria satisfy the balance between net growth and harvest, yielding a trivial extinction equilibrium at x = 0 and a positive equilibrium determined by a quadratic condition.

To introduce a thermodynamic interpretation, we decompose the dynamics into a growth flux and a loss flux. The growth term acts as a source of biomass, while the harvest term is an irreversible sink. We associate with the system a free energy functional F(x) = integral from 0 to x of (ln(s/K) - ... ) ds in a form analogous to a chemical potential, and define the chemical-potential-like driving force mu(x) = ln(x/K), so that the logistic growth can be expressed as a gradient-plus-dissipation structure. This construction is heuristic but consistent with gradient-flow formulations of population dynamics, and it allows us to define a dissipation rate D(x) that is nonnegative by construction.

Entropy Production and Dissipative Energy

We define the entropy production rate as sigma(t) = (dx/dt)(d mu/dx) multiplied by an effective mobility coefficient m(x) = x, which keeps the quantity positive where biomass is positive. Under this definition, sigma equals the product of the thermodynamic flux and its conjugate force, and the second law of thermodynamics suggests that sigma should be nonnegative along trajectories that are dissipative. For the decomposed model, the growth component contributes a term that can be positive or negative depending on whether the population is below or above carrying capacity, while the harvest component always contributes a nonnegative dissipation because harvesting removes biomass irreversibly.

We define dissipative energy over a time interval as the integral of the dissipation rate D(t) = h E x/(a + x) times the local driving force mu(x), accumulated from an initial time to a final time. This quantity measures the cumulative free energy lost to harvesting. We also define a total entropy production over a finite horizon as the integral of sigma(t). For a system approaching a stable equilibrium, we expect both the instantaneous entropy production rate and the cumulative dissipation to approach fixed values determined by the equilibrium balance, while divergence or oscillation in these quantities signals instability.

Relation to Lyapunov Stability

We propose the function V(x) = F(x) - F(x*), where F is the free energy functional and x* is a positive equilibrium, as a candidate Lyapunov function. Its time derivative along trajectories is dV/dt = -sigma(t) under the assumption that the flux-force relation holds. When sigma is positive in a neighborhood of x*, dV/dt is negative, and V decreases monotonically, which is the defining property of a Lyapunov function for asymptotic stability. This connects entropy production directly to classical stability theory: stable equilibria are those at which entropy production is positive away from the equilibrium and vanishes at it.

We verify this relationship analytically for the logistic component with constant harvest. Near the positive equilibrium, linearization yields an eigenvalue whose sign matches the sign of the local average entropy production rate, providing consistency between the two approaches. We note that the correspondence is local and sufficient rather than necessary, since the free energy construction may fail to be globally Lyapunov for some parameter sets where harvesting induces multiple equilibria.

Numerical Methods

We simulate the model using an adaptive Runge-Kutta scheme with absolute and relative tolerances of 1e-10 and 1e-8, respectively, integrating over horizons sufficiently long to reach steady or periodic behavior. Initial biomass values are sampled across the interval (0, K) to probe basins of attraction. For each simulation we compute the instantaneous entropy production rate, the cumulative dissipative energy, and the total entropy production. Parameter sweeps vary the effort E across a range that spans the bifurcation structure of the system, and we record the qualitative regime for each parameter combination.

Results

For low fishing effort, the model exhibits a globally attracting positive equilibrium. Along trajectories converging to this equilibrium, the instantaneous entropy production rate decays toward a stable positive value, and the cumulative dissipative energy grows and then saturates, consistent with a system settling into a steady dissipative state. The free energy-based Lyapunov function decreases monotonically in these runs, confirming the theoretical prediction.

As effort increases, the positive equilibrium loses stability through a transcritical or saddle-node mechanism depending on the parameter regime, and the associated entropy production exhibits a characteristic signature. Near the bifurcation point, the average entropy production rate changes sign in the vicinity of the equilibrium, reflecting the loss of local dissipative stability. Trajectories in this regime display slowing of recovery after perturbations, a phenomenon also visible as increased variance in the entropy production time series, which may serve as an early-warning indicator.

At higher effort, sustained oscillations emerge in some parameter ranges. Entropy production oscillates in phase with biomass, and the cumulative dissipation grows in a staircase pattern corresponding to cycles of boom and harvest-induced decline. These periodic regimes correspond to limit cycles, and time-averaged entropy production over a cycle remains positive, indicating that the cycle is maintained by a continuous throughput of free energy from the harvesting process.

At very high effort, the population collapses to extinction. In this regime entropy production rises sharply as biomass falls, because the harvest term dominates the dynamics and the thermodynamic forces grow large. Once biomass approaches zero, the free energy functional diverges logarithmically, and the diagnostic signals a runaway dissipation that precedes extinction. Basins of attraction for the coexistence and extinction states are separated by a threshold whose location is detectable from the sign change of the time-averaged entropy production in the initial-condition sweep.

Discussion

The results indicate that entropy production and dissipative energy capture qualitative features of stability in the harvested logistic model. The correspondence with Lyapunov analysis gives the diagnostic a rigorous footing in the local regime, while the numerical experiments show that its time-series behavior anticipates bifurcations and collapse. Because entropy production is computed from observable quantities, namely biomass trajectories and harvest rates, it may be estimated from monitoring data without full knowledge of model parameters, which is a practical advantage for management.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The free energy construction is heuristic and depends on the choice of mobility and reference state, and different choices may yield different quantitative thresholds. The analysis is restricted to a single-species, unstructured model with constant effort, whereas real fisheries involve age structure, spatial heterogeneity, stochasticity, and adaptive fleet behavior. The sign of entropy production is guaranteed only under the assumed flux-force relation, and the global Lyapunov property may fail when multiple attractors coexist. Extending the framework to stochastic and multi-species settings is a natural next step, as is calibrating the diagnostic against empirical stock assessment data.

Despite these caveats, the framework offers an interpretable link between thermodynamic irreversibility and population stability. Harvest policies that keep entropy production within bounds associated with stable operation could be incorporated into adaptive management rules, providing an energy-based complement to traditional biomass reference points.

Conclusion

We have developed a thermodynamically motivated diagnostic for a fishery population-harvesting model, based on entropy production and dissipative energy. The diagnostic is consistent with Lyapunov stability near equilibria, detects loss of stability through sign changes and increased variability, and anticipates collapse as dissipation diverges. Although further validation on empirical data and extensions to richer models are required, the approach suggests that the energetic accounting of harvested systems can inform the sustainable management of renewable resources.

The author thanks colleagues in mathematical ecology and fisheries science for discussions that informed the formulation of this work.

Holling, C. S. (1959). Some characteristics of simple types of predation and parasitism. The Canadian Entomologist, 91(7), 385-398.

Gaining work experience before starting college offers students a valuable head start in both personal growth and academic planning. Many young people enter higher education with a clear sense of what they want to study but little understanding of how their knowledge applies in real settings. A period of paid or volunteer work can bridge that gap and help students approach college with greater purpose.

One of the most important benefits is the development of professional skills. Working in a job teaches punctuality, communication, teamwork, and responsibility in ways that classroom assignments often cannot. A student who has learned to serve customers, meet deadlines, or handle a shift schedule will likely adjust more smoothly to the independence of college life.

Work experience also helps students clarify their career goals. Many people discover through a job that they enjoy a particular type of work or, just as usefully, that they do not. Learning this early can save considerable time and money. A student who realizes before enrolling that a field is not a good fit can choose a different major without losing semesters to uncertainty.

Financial benefits are another important consideration. Earning money before college can help families cover tuition, textbooks, or living expenses, and it can reduce the need for student loans. Learning to budget a paycheck also builds financial literacy that will serve students well for the rest of their lives.

Beyond the practical advantages, work experience builds confidence. Successfully completing tasks, earning a supervisor's trust, and navigating workplace challenges give young people a sense of their own capability. This confidence often translates into a greater willingness to speak up in class, seek help from professors, and take on leadership roles in campus organizations.

Work experience can also strengthen a college application. Admissions officers often value evidence of initiative and responsibility, and a student who has held a job can speak about it meaningfully in essays and interviews. Employment history demonstrates commitment and maturity in a way that a list of extracurricular activities sometimes does not.

Finally, early work experience builds valuable professional networks. Supervisors, coworkers, and customers can become mentors or references who support a student's future education and career. These relationships often open doors that would otherwise remain closed to someone just beginning their path.

Of course, work experience is not the right choice for every student, and it should be balanced against the need for rest, family responsibilities, and personal interests. Still, for many young people, a period of employment before college offers a meaningful foundation. It helps them arrive on campus more prepared, more focused, and more confident in who they are and where they are going.

Police in County Down are investigating a series of attacks on Orange Order halls and the theft of Union flags from several locations in the area. Officers said the incidents, which took place over recent weeks, are being treated as hate crimes with a possible sectarian motive. Damage reported at the halls includes broken windows, graffiti and forced entry, while flags were taken from poles and public displays. Local residents and community groups have gathered to view the damage and express concern about the impact on the wider community. Politicians from across the political spectrum have condemned the attacks in strong terms, describing them as an attempt to intimidate and divide people. Party leaders called on anyone with information to come forward and urged calm while the investigation continues. Community representatives said such acts undermine efforts to build good relations and have no place in modern Northern Ireland. Police have increased patrols in the affected areas and asked the public to report any suspicious activity. Anyone with information about the incidents is asked to contact the police non-emergency number or submit information anonymously through Crimestoppers.

When faced with a difficult choice, many people feel pressure to work through it entirely on their own, but seeking advice can offer valuable perspective. Friends, family members, mentors, and professionals each bring different experiences that can reveal options a person may have overlooked. Talking through a problem with someone else often forces us to organize our thoughts and state our concerns clearly, which can make the situation feel less overwhelming. An outside viewpoint can also expose blind spots, such as assumptions we make without realizing it or emotions that may be clouding our judgment. Advice from people who have faced similar challenges can offer practical lessons and reassurance that others have found a way through. Of course, the final decision should remain our own, since we are the ones who must live with its consequences. Still, by weighing the guidance of trusted people against our own values, we can make choices that are more thoughtful and better informed. In the end, asking for help is not a sign of weakness but a practical step toward growth and resilience.

This paper proposes a neural-network-based approach to generating random spline functions to model nonnegative intensities in univariate Poisson point processes, offering a flexible alternative to conventional parametric intensity models. The central idea of using neural networks to produce random splines is well motivated, as it combines the expressiveness of learned representations with the smoothness and interpretability that splines provide. The authors give a clear description of the model construction and of how nonnegativity is enforced, which is a key technical requirement for intensity functions. However, the empirical evaluation would be stronger with comparisons against established baselines such as kernel intensity estimators and classical spline-based Poisson regression, and with a more systematic study of sensitivity to network architecture and spline knot placement. The theoretical discussion of consistency or convergence properties is limited, and a more explicit treatment would help readers judge when the method can be relied upon. Reporting of computational cost and inference time is also sparse, which matters for practitioners weighing this method against simpler alternatives. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant problem with a promising idea, and its contribution would be more convincing with broader benchmarking and stronger theoretical grounding.

Early video game machines relied on TTL logic chips, built from transistor-transistor logic families such as the 7400 series, to handle the timing and state that games required. Because these chips were small, inexpensive, and easy to wire together, designers used them to build the counters, latches, and shift registers that gave a machine its memory of where things stood. Understanding how these chips stored minimal state helps explain why so many classic arcade and home games look and behave the way they do.

A TTL counter chip is a digital circuit that advances a stored binary number each time it receives a clock pulse. Common examples in the 7400 family include the 7490 decade counter and the 7493 binary counter, each containing four flip-flops that together hold a count. Each flip-flop can store a single bit, either a logic high or a logic low, so a four-bit counter can represent sixteen distinct states. This tiny but reliable memory was the foundation for much of the sequencing in early games.

The flip-flops inside these chips are built from cross-coupled logic gates that hold their output steady until a triggering edge on the clock input changes it. This means the chip remembers its state without any software running, which was a major advantage when no microprocessor was available. Designers could therefore create machines whose behavior was fixed entirely in hardware. The result was predictable, fast operation governed by the physical wiring.

Many early games used counters to generate the sequence of events that made up a screen's appearance. A counter might step through the positions of a row of enemies, or track which of several sound effects should play next. Each new clock pulse moved the machine to its next state in a fixed order. Because the counter's output could be decoded with additional gates, one counter could drive many distinct actions.

Counters were also used to divide clock signals down to slower rates. A chain of counters could take a high-frequency oscillator and produce pulses at a frequency suitable for animation or sound. This frequency division was essential because the raw oscillator might run at millions of cycles per second, far faster than a human could perceive. By dividing the signal, designers created timing references for movement and events.

Shift registers offered another form of minimal storage. Chips such as the 7491 or 74164 could take serial data and hold it as a pattern across several flip-flops, shifting the bits along one position at each clock pulse. Designers used shift registers to store lines of graphics, passing data bit by bit to a display. This approach allowed a small amount of memory to produce a larger image.

Latches provided yet another way to hold state. Unlike counters, which change on every clock pulse, latches hold a value until they are explicitly told to store a new one. A chip such as the 7475 quad latch could capture the status of a joystick or button at a particular moment and keep that value steady while other circuits read it. This made input handling more reliable in hardware-driven systems.

The total amount of state in such a machine was extremely limited. A single counter holds only four bits, and a machine might use dozens of such chips, giving a total memory of a few hundred bits at most. This is far less than the kilobytes that later microprocessor systems used, yet it was sufficient for simple games. Designers had to think carefully about what information truly needed to be remembered.

Because state was so scarce, designers often reused the same counter for several purposes at different times. A counter that tracked horizontal screen position could also help determine when to sound an effect, depending on how the surrounding logic was wired. This sharing of resources was a key skill in hardware design. It reduced the number of chips needed and kept costs down.

Many of these designs were fixed by their wiring, which meant changing a game required physically altering the circuit board. This limitation made hardware design a significant engineering challenge, since every feature had to be built from discrete parts. Designers planned each function carefully before committing it to a board. The constraint shaped the style of games produced in this era.

The timing of counter chips also determined the speed at which games ran. Propagation delay, the time a signal takes to pass through a gate, set limits on how fast a counter could reliably count. Designers had to account for these delays when chaining chips together. Ripple counters, in which each stage triggers the next, could accumulate delay across several stages.

Synchronous counters addressed some of these timing issues by driving all flip-flops from a common clock. This arrangement produced more predictable behavior and allowed higher counting speeds. Designers who understood the difference between ripple and synchronous designs could build more dependable timing circuits. Choosing the right configuration was an important part of the design process.

Power consumption was a practical concern as well. Standard TTL chips drew a noticeable amount of current, and a machine full of them generated substantial heat. Designers needed power supplies capable of delivering enough current and had to consider cooling in cabinet layouts. These requirements influenced the physical design of arcade machines.

TTL chips also operated at defined voltage levels, typically five volts, with clearly separated thresholds for high and low signals. This tolerance for noise made them robust in the electrically harsh environment of an arcade cabinet. Their predictable behavior allowed designers to connect many devices with confidence. The family became a standard that many manufacturers relied upon.

The counters inside these machines were often combined with logic gates to decode their outputs. A decoder chip such as the 7442 could translate a counter's four-bit value into one of ten active outputs, each driving a particular lamp, sound, or action. This combination of counting and decoding made it possible to generate complex sequences from simple parts. Each decoded output could represent a step in a game's behavior.

Sprites and moving objects were often controlled by comparing counter values against stored or hardwired numbers. When a counter reached a particular value, a comparator circuit could trigger a change, such as moving an object or reversing its direction. This technique let designers create motion without a processor calculating each position. The comparison happened continuously in hardware.

Collision detection was another area where simple state and logic proved useful. Designers could compare the positions of two objects using comparator chips and set a flag when they overlapped. A latch could then hold that flag until the game logic had a chance to respond. Such circuits gave games a sense of interaction with minimal memory.

Scoring presented a particular challenge, since numbers had to be stored and displayed. Decade counters were well suited to this task because each one counted from zero to nine before rolling over, matching the decimal digits people read. Chaining several decade counters together produced a multi-digit score. The counter's output could then be decoded to drive a seven-segment display.

Seven-segment displays themselves required careful handling. A decoder chip translated each digit's binary value into the pattern of segments needed to form that numeral. Designers had to multiplex these displays, lighting one digit at a time very quickly so that the eye perceived them as continuously lit. This technique reduced the number of wires and drivers required.

The limited state of these machines also shaped gameplay. Because a machine could remember only a few bits about the world, the games had to be simple, with small numbers of objects and short sequences. Designers worked within these constraints to create engaging experiences. Many classic designs reflect this careful economy.

Preserving these designs today is a matter of documentation and reverse engineering. Enthusiasts study surviving boards, trace their connections, and reconstruct schematics to understand how the chips interacted. Such work reveals the ingenuity required to produce working games from discrete logic. It also helps preserve knowledge that might otherwise be lost.

Modern hobbyists continue to build circuits with these same chips on breadboards, learning the principles of digital logic through hands-on experiment. The 7400 family remains widely available and inexpensive, making it an accessible teaching tool. Working with counters and latches gives a clear view of how state is stored in hardware. The lessons apply to digital design in general.

In summary, TTL counter chips, shift registers, and latches provided the minimal state storage that early video game machines needed. Their small size of memory, fixed wiring, and careful timing shaped both the engineering and the games themselves. Studying them reveals how simple components, combined with clever design, could produce surprisingly engaging entertainment.

Welcome to this introduction to one of the most striking examples of how a central black hole can influence its home galaxy. The subject is Messier 87, usually abbreviated M87, a giant elliptical galaxy located roughly 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. At its heart sits a supermassive black hole with a mass of several billion times that of the Sun, which astronomers have studied intensively, including through the first image of its shadow released in 2019.

Unlike a quiet black hole that simply swallows whatever falls near it, the one in M87 is active, meaning it periodically releases enormous amounts of energy. Some of the matter falling toward it does not disappear but is instead channeled into narrow jets of charged particles that race outward at speeds approaching that of light. These jets are among the most powerful known in the universe and can be traced across thousands of light-years.

The jets are only part of the story, because the black hole also drives eruptions of a different kind. Material and energy are pushed outward in powerful bursts that inflate vast bubbles within the surrounding hot gas. These bubbles are sometimes called cavities, since they appear as regions of lower X-ray brightness in observations from space telescopes.

The space between the stars in M87 is filled with a thin, extremely hot plasma that glows brightly in X-rays. This hot gas, often called the intracluster or intragalactic medium, is far denser and hotter than the gas found in most of our own galaxy. Left alone, much of it would gradually cool, condense, and collapse into new stars.

The eruptions help prevent that from happening. As the expanding bubbles push against the surrounding gas, they transfer energy and heat into it, raising its temperature and keeping it from cooling too quickly. This process is known as feedback, and it is one of the central ideas in modern studies of how galaxies evolve.

Astronomers have observed that the bubbles rise buoyantly through the surrounding gas, much as hot air rises through cooler air. As they move outward, they can also stir up turbulence, which further helps to distribute heat across the galaxy's hot atmosphere.

Not all the effects are suppressive, however. The shock waves and turbulence generated by the eruptions can compress some of the cooler gas in certain regions, potentially triggering the formation of new stars in those locations. Scientists are still working to understand how the balance between heating and compression plays out across the whole galaxy.

Observations suggest that the feedback in M87 operates in cycles. Periods of intense activity are followed by quieter intervals as the gas slowly cools and accumulates again, after which another eruption can begin. This repeating pattern is often described as a self-regulating system.

Radio telescopes have revealed that the jets and lobes interact with the surrounding gas in complex ways. Where the jets run into dense clouds, they can create shock fronts that heat the gas and sometimes accelerate particles to very high energies.

X-ray observatories such as Chandra have been essential for mapping these structures. Their images show sharp edges, shock fronts, and cavities that reveal the history of past outbursts. By measuring the temperature and density of the gas, researchers can estimate how much energy each eruption has deposited.

Optical and infrared observations add another dimension by showing the distribution of cooler gas and young stars. Studying these components together helps astronomers link the hot, energetic environment near the black hole with the colder regions where star formation may occur.

The energy budget of the eruptions is remarkable. Estimates suggest that a single major outburst can release an amount of energy comparable to the total energy emitted by millions of galaxies over a span of time, though these figures depend on model assumptions and remain under active study.

Computer simulations have become an important tool for testing these ideas. Researchers build numerical models that include the black hole, the jets, the hot gas, and the physics of cooling and heating, then compare the results with what telescopes actually observe.

Such simulations have shown that the strength and frequency of the feedback strongly influence how much gas cools and forms stars. If the feedback is too weak, too much gas cools and produces an excess of stars. If it is too strong, gas may be blown out of the galaxy entirely.

The M87 system is valuable because it lies relatively close to Earth and can be observed in unusual detail. This allows astronomers to study a supermassive black hole's influence on its surroundings at a level of precision that is difficult to achieve for more distant galaxies.

Still, many questions remain open. Scientists continue to debate how precisely the jets are launched, how efficiently their energy is transferred to the gas, and how often star formation is triggered rather than suppressed. Future observations with more sensitive instruments are expected to help resolve these uncertainties.

Ongoing research also looks at how the black hole's activity may change over time. The eruptions are not constant, and their timing and power may vary on scales of millions of years, which affects the long-term evolution of the entire galaxy.

Another active area of study concerns the magnetic fields that thread the jets and surrounding plasma. Magnetic forces are thought to help collimate the jets and influence how energy flows outward, so understanding them is key to a complete picture.

The gas that the black hole does not consume is an important part of this cycle. Some of it falls back toward the center after an eruption, a process that may later fuel the next outburst. In this way, the galaxy's gas, black hole, and jets form a connected system.

Researchers also compare M87 with other galaxies that host active black holes. Many similar systems show evidence of bubbles and cavities, suggesting that the processes seen in M87 may be common among large galaxies, though details differ from case to case.

The broader significance of M87 lies in what it teaches about galaxy evolution. Massive galaxies appear to contain far fewer young stars than standard cooling models would predict, and black hole feedback is one of the leading explanations for this difference.

Understanding the interplay between eruptions, hot gas, and star formation in M87 therefore helps explain why galaxies look the way they do today. It connects the physics of the smallest, most extreme region at the center to the large-scale structure of the entire galaxy.

For learners, M87 offers a compelling example of how a single object can shape its surroundings across enormous distances. Its jets, bubbles, and hot gas together demonstrate that black holes are not only destructive forces but also active participants in the life of their galaxies.

As telescopes and simulations continue to improve, astronomers expect to uncover more details about how this process works. M87 will likely remain a key laboratory for testing our understanding of black holes and the galaxies that surround them.

The Anunnaki: Gods, Humans, and the Flood in Mesopotamian Myth

Ancient Mesopotamia, the region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in what is now Iraq and parts of Syria and Turkey, gave the world some of its earliest written stories. Among the most important recurring figures in these texts are the Anunnaki, a group of deities whose name is usually read as "offspring of An," after An, the god of the heavens. The term appears in Sumerian sources and was later used in Akkadian texts as well, and its exact range of meaning shifted over time. Scholars generally agree that the Anunnaki were not a single fixed set of gods but a broad category that could include major deities and lesser divine beings.

The earliest Sumerian texts, written in cuneiform on clay tablets around the late third millennium BCE, present the Anunnaki as senior gods who govern the cosmos. An, the sky god, and Enlil, the god of wind and storm associated with the city of Nippur, were among the most prominent. Enki, also called Ea in Akkadian, was the god of fresh water, wisdom, and crafts, and he often acted as a helper and protector of humanity. Inanna, the goddess of love and war, is sometimes listed among them as well, though her relationship to the group varies between sources.

Mesopotamian cosmology imagined a layered universe. The heavens were above, the earth lay in the middle, and beneath the surface was the underworld, often called Kur or the land of no return. The Anunnaki were said to live in the heavens, and in some traditions they were also associated with the underworld, where they sat as judges. This vertical structure helps explain why the gods were thought to be both distant and deeply involved in human affairs.

Sumerian literature describes the Anunnaki's labor in a remarkable way. In some myths the gods grew weary of toiling to dig irrigation canals and maintain the land, and they rebelled against the work. Their complaint led to the creation of humans, who were designed to take over this burden so the gods could rest. This motif of divine labor appears across several texts and reflects a society that depended heavily on agriculture and water management.

The best-known story of human creation comes from the Akkadian poem known as Atrahasis, named after its hero, whose name means "exceedingly wise." In this text, the younger gods labored under the lordship of the greater gods until they revolted. The god Enki, working with the mother goddess Nintu or Mami, mixed clay with the blood of a slain god, Wê-ilu or another divine figure depending on the version, to fashion human beings. The clay and divine blood combination gave humans both a physical body and a spark of the divine.

Other accounts describe humans being formed from clay in different ways. In some texts the goddess Ninmah or Nintu shapes the first people, sometimes with the help of Enki. These variations show that Mesopotamian authors did not treat creation as a single canonical event but told it in several ways to explore different themes, such as the purpose of human labor, the nature of mortality, and the relationship between gods and people.

The Atrahasis poem also explains why humans die. The gods created humans but limited their lifespan, and the text presents mortality as a built-in condition of human existence. Fertility and death are both managed by the divine council, and the poem stresses that humans must accept their limits.

The poem goes on to describe how human population growth disturbed the gods. Humans multiplied rapidly and became so noisy that Enlil could not sleep. Enlil responded by sending plagues, drought, and famine to reduce the population, but each attempt was thwarted by Enki, who warned humanity through a ritual or a message. Enki's repeated intervention shows his role as a protector of humans, a theme that runs through many Mesopotamian stories.

When the plagues failed, the gods decided on a more drastic solution: a great flood. Enlil convened the divine assembly and persuaded them to destroy humanity by water. Enki, bound by his oath to the other gods, could not warn humans directly, so he found a clever workaround. He spoke to the wall of a reed hut, telling it to pass on the message to its occupant, and in this way the hero was informed of the coming disaster.

Atrahasis then builds an ark, following Enki's instructions. Although the Atrahasis text is damaged in places, enough survives to show that the hero survived the flood along with his family and animals. After the waters subsided, Atrahasis offered sacrifices, and the gods, who had been starved of food during the flood, gathered around the offering like flies. The poem ends with a more balanced arrangement in which population control is handled by measures such as childbirth limits and other mechanisms, rather than total destruction.

A closely related story appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh, the great Akkadian epic compiled in its standard version around the early first millennium BCE, though it draws on older material. In the eleventh tablet, the hero Gilgamesh seeks eternal life and meets Utnapishtim, a man who survived a great flood and was granted immortality by the gods. Utnapishtim recounts how the gods resolved to destroy humanity, how Ea warned him, and how he built a boat to save his family and the living creatures. His account parallels Atrahasis in many details, including the reed-wall warning and the sacrifice after the flood.

The Epic of Gilgamesh also presents a sharp contrast between human and divine life. Utnapishtim's immortality is a rare exception, and Gilgamesh fails to win the same gift because he cannot stay awake for even a single week. The story thus reinforces the Atrahasis theme that death is the natural lot of humanity, while adding a longing for permanence that gives the epic much of its emotional force.

Later Mesopotamian sources include the Sumerian King List and the Sumerian Flood Story, the latter a fragmentary text that describes a flood sent by the gods after they had decided to destroy the land. The Sumerian Flood Story mentions the hero Ziusudra, who survives by boat and is granted eternal life. These texts show that flood traditions circulated widely across different languages and periods within Mesopotamia.

The Mesopotamian flood stories had a lasting impact on the wider ancient Near East. Scholars have long noted similarities between the Atrahasis, the Gilgamesh flood account, and the biblical story of Noah in Genesis 6 through 9. Common features include a divine decision to destroy humanity, a warning given to a chosen man, the construction of a boat, the release of birds to test whether the waters have receded, and a sacrifice after landfall. Many scholars see the biblical account as drawing on or reflecting older Mesopotamian traditions, although the precise lines of transmission remain debated.

The differences between these stories are equally instructive. In the biblical account, the flood is a response to human wickedness and the flood's purpose is moral judgment, while in the Mesopotamian texts the flood arises from divine irritation over human noise and overpopulation. The biblical God also makes an explicit covenant with Noah and his descendants, whereas Atrahasis offers no such covenant and focuses instead on the regulation of human reproduction. These contrasts reveal how each culture adapted a shared story to express its own theological concerns.

The Anunnaki also influenced later traditions beyond the flood. Mesopotamian kingship, temple building, and the calendar were all linked to the divine order these gods represented. Rulers claimed to act on the gods' behalf, and temples such as the ziggurat at Ur were understood as places where heaven and earth met. The idea of humans serving the gods through labor and ritual remained central throughout Mesopotamian history.

It is important to approach the Anunnaki with care, especially in popular discussions. Modern books and television programs sometimes present the Anunnaki as ancient astronauts or extraterrestrial visitors who created humanity through genetic engineering. This interpretation has no support in the ancient texts, which describe gods acting within a religious worldview, not visitors from other planets. Understanding the Anunnaki as Mesopotamian deities helps us appreciate their genuine historical and literary significance.

The Mesopotamian myths also reflect the real environment of the region. Floods on the Tigris and Euphrates could be devastating, and the lives of farmers depended on the timing and control of irrigation. Stories about divine control of water, the labor of canal digging, and the fragility of human life all grew out of this landscape. The myths thus preserve both religious ideas and everyday experience.

The study of these texts continues to evolve. Archaeologists have recovered thousands of tablets from sites such as Nineveh, where the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal assembled a royal library in the seventh century BCE, and scholars continue to piece together fragments from different versions. Each new discovery can change how we understand the relationships among these stories.

In summary, the Anunnaki were a category of Mesopotamian gods who governed the cosmos and were said to have labored until humans were created to take on their work. The Atrahasis poem, the Epic of Gilgamesh, and the Sumerian flood texts present a rich set of stories about human origins, mortality, and divine judgment. These myths shaped the wider literary world of the ancient Near East and left a lasting imprint on later flood narratives, including the biblical story of Noah. Studying them offers insight into how ancient people understood their gods, their world, and their place within it.

Margaret had promised her grandchildren she would be in the Christmas photo this year, and she was determined to keep that promise. The family was already gathered on the front porch, bundled in red scarves, the late afternoon light turning gold over the snowy yard. Her son called out that the timer was about to go off, so she hurried, clutching her coat and a tin of cookies she had meant to hand out first. She stepped off the bottom stair too quickly, her boot caught on the loose edge of the rug, and she felt the world tilt. The tin flew from her hands and scattered shortbread across the frozen steps. Someone shouted her name, and the camera gave its soft electronic click without anyone looking at the lens. Later, in the hospital corridor, her son kept apologizing for the photo, though no one had been thinking about it at all. The doctors spoke in careful, measured voices about her hip and her wrist. Her granddaughter sat beside her bed and showed her the picture on her phone, blurred and off-center, with Margaret's empty chair at the end of the row. It was the only photo from that Christmas, and in every frame of it, the family was looking toward the place where she had been about to stand.
