The colony ship Halcyon had been dead for three years when the first hunger riots began. Two hundred and eleven colonists remained on the frozen moon of Teskar, and the greenhouses had failed one after another, each collapse a little more final than the last. Mara Venn had been the colony's agronomist, and she was the one who had to tell them the truth.

The truth came from the cold lake beneath the ice shelf. Her team had drilled through forty meters of ice in the spring, expecting microbial mats or perhaps nothing at all. Instead they found a dense, pale biomass that moved with purpose. It shaped itself into filaments, then into lattices, and within a week it had begun to answer their signals with patterns of pulsing light.

ElanOduya, the colony's physician, was the first to suggest the obvious. Its cellular structure was rich in proteins and lipids, and the chemistry was compatible with human digestion. He said it carefully, as if the words might bruise someone.

Nobody spoke for a long time after that.

The colony council met in the old cargo bay, its walls stacked with sealed crates of seed stock that would never sprout. Thessaly Baum, who had lost a daughter to the cold the previous winter, wanted to act immediately. Her voice shook when she said that the children were already eating half-rations and that the adults were not much better off.

Caspian Reyes disagreed. He had spent four years studying the thing in the lake, and he had grown to believe it was communicating. He had recorded its light patterns, and he had begun to see structure in them, something that resembled grammar. He did not want to call it a person, but he could not bring himself to call it food either.

Mara listened to them argue for six hours. She kept waiting for someone to propose a third option, and no one did.

That night she went down to the lake alone. The ice had been cut into a viewing platform, and the water below glowed faintly, the way deep ocean life glows on Earth. She lay on the cold metal and watched the light ripple. Slowly, a cluster of pale filaments drifted toward the surface beneath her, and the light arranged itself into a pattern she recognized from Caspian's recordings. It was a greeting, or possibly a question.

She did not know what it meant. She only knew that it was looking at her, and that it was very much alive.

The next morning she told the council that she would not authorize harvesting. The room erupted. Thessaly accused her of condemning the children to death. Elan argued that the biomass was a resource like any other, and that moral objections were a luxury the dying could not afford. Caspian said nothing, but his hands were shaking.

Mara said she understood. She said she was not certain she was right. She said that if they chose to eat it, she would not stop them by force, but she would not help them do it, and she would ask every colonist to make that decision with open eyes rather than hiding from it behind words like resource or yield.

Thessaly walked out. Elan stayed, and after a long silence he asked Mara what she thought they should do about the children.

She had no answer that did not involve breaking something inside herself.

Over the following days the colony divided. Some families drew up plans to harvest carefully, taking only a small portion from the lake's edge and claiming it was enough to survive. Others refused to touch the water at all, preferring to starve slowly with their consciences intact. A small group began building a second, deeper drill, hoping to find a different source before the first ran out.

Caspian spent every night at the lake. He sent his recordings to the council, and his notes grew more desperate. He believed the biomass was learning from them, that the light patterns were becoming more complex each day. He thought it might be trying to communicate something important, perhaps a warning, perhaps a proposal, though he could not tell which.

Mara began to dream about the lake. In the dreams she was standing at its edge while the light rose toward her, and she could not tell whether it was reaching out in welcome or pulling her down.

Two weeks later, a child named Ilse Brandt fell through the ice at the edge of the shelf while playing near the drill site. The adults pulled her out within minutes, but she had swallowed a mouthful of the cold water, and she coughed up pale filaments onto the ice. The filaments twitched, then went still, then twitched again.

Ilse was not hurt, but the colony saw what had happened, and the argument reached its breaking point. Some people were now certain the biomass was a kind of mind, sensitive and aware. Others insisted that something aware could still be fed upon, and that the moral question was secondary to survival.

Mara found herself thinking about the first colonists who had come to Teskar, and the promises the company had made about a new world that would sustain them. She thought about how little any of them had known about what they were choosing to take from this place.

In the end the council did not vote. Instead, a crowd gathered at the lake on a freezing morning, and they asked Caspian to speak to the water one last time. He stood at the platform and sent out his strongest pattern, the one he had spent four years refining. The light below paused, then rose slowly toward the surface.

It formed a shape none of them had seen before. Caspian said later that it looked like a hand, open and empty, held up in the dark.

Nobody harvested that day. Nobody harvested the next day either, though the hunger did not ease, and some of the children grew too weak to stand. Mara sat with them and read to them from the Halcyon's old library, stories about other worlds and other choices, and she tried not to think about what they would do when there was nothing left to give.

Elan worked through the numbers every night and found no path that kept everyone alive without the lake. He told Mara this in a voice that had nothing left in it but exhaustion. She asked him whether he thought they were already doing the wrong thing by waiting. He said he did not know, and she believed him.

The colony had come to Teskar to build a future. Now it had to decide whether a future was worth building on what it would cost to live. Some of them began to think that starving with clean hands might be a kind of answer, and others believed that survival was the first duty of any people.

Mara did not believe either side had the whole truth. She believed the lake was waiting for them to decide what kind of people they were willing to be, and that the choice could not be made for them by a council or by the cold.

On the last night of the second month, Caspian walked to the lake alone and stood at the edge of the platform. He spoke to the water in the soft voice he used with frightened animals, and he told it that he was sorry. He did not know if the words meant anything to it, but he felt that they needed to be said.

The light below stirred, slowly, and rose toward him.

He stood very still, and did not look away.

Margaret had outlived the fever, the famine, and two husbands, but the cancer was patient in a way the others had not been. In her last spring, a neighbor brought her a pair of rescued greyhounds, thin and trembling, who curled against her blankets as if they had always belonged there. She painted them in watercolor each afternoon, their long legs and gentle eyes filling the pages of a sketchbook that grew heavier every week. At night, the pain dulled enough for her to wander again into the country she had dreamed since childhood, a place of silver rivers, towers of living glass, and skies where two dogs ran beside her without tiring. Her nurse said she smiled in her sleep, and when the dogs lay beside her on the last morning, she was painting one final wind-swept hillside. The sketchbook was found open on her bed, the brush still resting in the paint water, and the dogs would not leave the room for days.

How Unconventional Practices Can Solve Problems and Inspire Beneficial Change

Communities and organizations often rely on familiar routines because they have worked before. Yet routines can also hide problems, and when old methods stop producing results, unconventional practices offer a way forward. An unconventional practice is simply an approach that departs from standard procedure, whether in how decisions are made, how people meet, how work is organized, or how resources are shared. This page explains what these practices are, why they can be effective, and how to introduce them responsibly.

Consider first what makes a practice conventional. Conventions usually arise because they solved a real problem at some point, and they gain authority through repetition. Over time, however, the original problem may change while the convention stays the same. A meeting format designed for a team of ten may frustrate a team of sixty. A rule written for a small town may fail a city that has grown around it. Recognizing this gap between a practice and its purpose is the first step toward useful change.

Unconventional practices tend to succeed for several reasons. They bring new perspectives into problems that have been looked at the same way for years. They lower the cost of experimenting, since a small trial can reveal whether an idea is worth pursuing. They also invite participation from people who were previously left out of decisions, which often produces better information about what is actually happening on the ground.

Participatory budgeting is one example that has spread across many cities. Instead of a small group of officials deciding how public money should be spent, residents propose projects, vote on them, and sometimes help monitor the results. The practice changes who holds knowledge and authority, and it often reveals needs that officials had not noticed. Similar models now appear in schools, housing cooperatives, and workplaces.

Another example is the use of citizen assemblies, where a randomly selected group of people meets over several weekends to study an issue and recommend a course of action. Random selection can produce a group that reflects the wider population more closely than elected bodies or self-selected public meetings. Participants receive background materials and hear from experts with differing views, which helps them reason through difficult trade-offs.

Organizations have also adopted unconventional approaches to work itself. Some have experimented with results-only work environments, where employees are judged by outcomes rather than hours spent at a desk. Others use rotating leadership roles so that more people gain experience guiding a team. These changes can reduce burnout and build skills across the group, though they also require clear expectations and trust to work well.

Problem-solving methods can be unconventional as well. Design sprints compress weeks of planning into a few days of focused work, with teams prototyping and testing ideas with real users before committing resources. Pre-mortems ask a group to imagine that a project has already failed and then to explain why, which surfaces risks that optimistic planning often overlooks. Red teams assign people to argue against a proposal, strengthening it by exposing weak assumptions.

Communities have found creative ways to address long-standing challenges. Some neighborhoods have turned vacant lots into community gardens, which provide food, gathering places, and a sense of shared ownership. Others have set up tool libraries, where residents borrow equipment instead of buying items they will use only occasionally. Such arrangements reduce costs and strengthen social ties at the same time.

Unconventional practices also carry risks, and it would be misleading to present them as automatically beneficial. A new approach can fail, confuse people, or create new inequities if it is poorly designed. Some practices are adopted for their novelty rather than their results, and this can waste time and goodwill. Careful thinking about purpose, evidence, and fairness helps prevent these outcomes.

Evaluation is therefore essential. Before adopting a practice, it helps to state clearly what problem it is meant to solve and how success will be measured. Pilot programs allow a group to test an idea on a small scale and learn from the results. Gathering feedback from the people most affected, including those who may be skeptical, provides information that data alone cannot capture.

Leadership plays an important role in whether unconventional practices take root. Leaders who explain the reasons for a change, admit uncertainty, and invite criticism tend to build more trust than those who announce new rules without discussion. Showing willingness to adjust course when something is not working signals that experimentation is serious rather than performative.

Inclusion matters as well. Practices that rely on participation can unintentionally favor people who already have time, confidence, and social connections. Organizers may need to offer childcare, translation, flexible meeting times, or stipends to make participation possible for a wider range of people. Asking who is missing from a conversation is often as valuable as asking what the group thinks.

Cultural context shapes what will work. A practice that succeeds in one organization may meet resistance in another because of differences in history, hierarchy, or communication norms. Rather than copying a model exactly, groups can adapt its core principles to their own circumstances. Learning from other communities remains valuable, provided it is done with attention to local conditions.

Change can also be disruptive, and people may feel a sense of loss when familiar routines disappear. Acknowledging this feeling respectfully helps maintain morale. Explaining what will be kept, what will be different, and what support will be available reduces anxiety and makes it easier for people to engage with new ideas.

Timing influences outcomes too. Introducing a major change during a crisis may be difficult, while a period of relative stability can provide room to experiment. Some groups begin with low-stakes changes that build confidence before tackling more significant reforms. Sequencing changes thoughtfully allows people to develop skills and trust gradually.

Documentation helps preserve what is learned. Recording what was tried, what happened, and why decisions were made creates a resource for future members who may not know the history. It also helps the group avoid repeating mistakes and allows others to build on successful experiments.

Small wins deserve attention because they show that change is possible. Celebrating modest improvements, such as a shorter meeting or a faster approval process, can build momentum for larger efforts. Recognizing the people who contributed to these improvements reinforces a culture in which new ideas are welcomed.

Measurement should include both quantitative and qualitative indicators. Numbers can show whether costs fell or participation rose, but stories and direct observation can reveal whether people feel respected, heard, or more connected. Combining these sources gives a fuller picture of impact.

It is also worth considering when not to be unconventional. Some situations call for established procedures, especially where safety, legal compliance, or consistency are critical. Unconventional practices are most useful when the existing approach is clearly failing or when a problem is complex enough that new thinking is needed. Judgment about when to depart from convention is itself a skill.

Groups that succeed with unconventional practices tend to share certain habits. They stay curious, ask questions openly, and treat failures as information. They balance ambition with humility, recognizing that no single approach solves every problem. They also remain connected to their purpose, returning again and again to the question of whether a practice is helping people do what matters most.

In summary, unconventional practices can open new paths for communities and organizations facing problems that familiar methods no longer solve. They work best when they are chosen deliberately, tested carefully, shaped by local context, and designed to include the people they affect. Change of this kind is rarely instant, but a willingness to question assumptions and learn from experience can steadily improve how collective life is organized.

Lengthening the school day is often proposed as a simple way to boost academic performance and close achievement gaps, yet the idea deserves far more scrutiny than it usually receives. Before extending classroom hours, policymakers should consider the very real costs to students' health, their personal lives, and the practical realities of getting them to and from school. When these factors are weighed honestly, the case against a longer day becomes compelling.

The most immediate concern is fatigue. Adolescents already struggle to get adequate sleep, largely because their biological clocks shift later during puberty, making early mornings difficult. Many schools start before eight in the morning, and the national recommendation for teenagers is at least eight to ten hours of sleep each night. Adding hours to the end of the day compounds this problem, since students who are exhausted by mid-afternoon are poorly positioned to absorb new material. Learning requires attention and memory, and both decline when a student has been awake and working for too long.

Fatigue also affects the quality of instruction itself. A teacher facing a room of drowsy students may find that lessons take longer, that discipline problems increase, and that the energy needed for engaging teaching is harder to sustain. The added hours may therefore produce diminishing returns, with each additional period yielding less learning than the one before. Quantity of time does not automatically translate into quality of education.

Physical health is another consideration. Longer days can mean less time for exercise, less time for preparing nutritious meals, and reduced opportunities for the rest that growing bodies need. Students who spend most of their waking hours in a building may become more sedentary, which carries known risks for weight gain and long-term cardiovascular health. Schools that promote wellbeing should not be lengthening days in ways that undermine it.

Free time deserves equal attention. Young people need unstructured hours to pursue interests, rest, socialize, and simply be bored, which is often where creativity and self-direction take root. Part-time jobs, family responsibilities, and extracurricular activities such as sports, music, and volunteering already fill many students' afternoons. A longer school day would squeeze these activities, and for some students it would force difficult choices about which commitments to abandon.

Family life would also be affected. Many parents rely on predictable schedules to arrange childcare, work hours, and household routines. A later dismissal can disrupt these arrangements, particularly for working families who may lack the flexibility to adjust. Students who help care for younger siblings or contribute to household income would find their domestic responsibilities harder to manage. The burden of a longer day would fall unevenly, often on the families least able to absorb it.

Transportation presents perhaps the most practical obstacle. School bus systems are designed around existing schedules, and extending the day would require either new routes, additional buses, or a significant shift in timing that many districts cannot afford. Students who rely on buses could face long waits, and those who walk or cycle home would be traveling in darker conditions during the colder months. Safety concerns grow when students are commuting later into the evening.

Costs extend beyond transportation. Extending the day means paying staff for additional hours, which may include teachers, aides, custodians, and bus drivers. It may also require heating, cooling, lighting, and supervising buildings for longer periods. Districts facing tight budgets would need to divert funds from other priorities, such as smaller class sizes, counseling services, or arts programs, to cover these expenses.

Teachers themselves would bear significant strain. Educators already contend with lesson planning, grading, meetings, and professional development outside classroom hours. A longer day can intensify burnout and contribute to the staff shortages that many districts already face. A school that cannot retain experienced teachers is unlikely to improve outcomes, regardless of how many hours it operates.

Some proponents argue that longer days could benefit students who lack enrichment opportunities at home. This is a legitimate concern, and it deserves a response that does not rely on simply adding more hours to the existing structure. Targeted programs, after-school tutoring, and community partnerships can provide enrichment without imposing the same demands on every student. These alternatives allow families to choose what suits them rather than mandating a single schedule.

Equity, in fact, cuts in multiple directions. A uniform policy of longer days may appear fair, but it ignores the diverse needs of students with different home situations, health conditions, and talents. Some students thrive with extended structure; others need space and rest. A one-size-fits-all approach risks serving the average student while neglecting those at the margins.

Research on the relationship between instructional time and achievement is mixed. Some studies show modest gains from additional learning time, particularly in specific subjects and for struggling students. Other studies find little effect, especially when the added time is not used effectively. The evidence suggests that how time is spent matters more than how much time there is, which points toward improving teaching quality rather than simply extending the calendar.

Policymakers should therefore examine alternatives before committing to longer days. Later start times for adolescents, when supported by evidence, may address fatigue more directly. Reforms to curriculum, assessment, and instructional methods may yield better results without additional hours. Investments in tutoring and mentoring can target the students who most need extra support.

Public input is essential in any such decision. Parents, students, teachers, and community members each bring valuable perspectives about what their schools need. Decisions made without meaningful consultation risk producing policies that look sound on paper but fail in practice. Listening to those affected can help districts avoid costly mistakes.

Ultimately, the goal of education is to help young people learn, grow, and flourish. A longer school day may serve that goal in some contexts, but the arguments against it are substantial. Fatigue undermines learning, reduced free time limits development, and transportation and cost concerns create practical barriers that cannot be ignored. Before lengthening the school day, communities should be confident that the change will genuinely improve students' lives, not merely add hours to them.

Remote learning has become a significant part of modern education, offering students benefits that extend well beyond the convenience of studying from home. One of its most important advantages is flexibility. Students can often arrange their study schedules around work, family responsibilities, or personal commitments, which allows them to balance many demands on their time. This flexibility is especially valuable for adult learners and those who must care for relatives.

Remote learning also gives students access to a wider range of courses and instructors. A student in a small rural town, for example, may not have access to a specialized course in marine biology or advanced computer science at a local school, but an online program can bring that opportunity directly to them. Geography no longer limits educational choices in the same way it once did.

Another benefit is the development of independent study skills. Because online courses often require students to manage their own time, set goals, and seek out information, they build habits of self-discipline and responsibility. These skills are valuable in higher education and in the workplace, where self-direction is often expected.

Remote learning can also reduce costs. Students who learn online may save money on commuting, housing, and campus fees. For families facing financial pressure, these savings can make higher education more achievable.

Many students also find that remote learning suits their personal learning styles. Recorded lectures can be paused, rewatched, and reviewed as needed, allowing students to absorb difficult material at their own pace. Written discussion forums give quieter students time to think carefully before they respond, which can encourage participation that might not happen in a crowded classroom.

Finally, remote learning has helped make education more resilient. When illness, weather, or other disruptions prevent students from attending school in person, online tools help them keep learning. In this way, remote learning provides a dependable path to education that adapts to the circumstances of real life.

The manuscript proposes a flow-based approach to imitation learning that conditions on future dynamics in order to align the state-action distributions of the expert and the learning agent, with the stated aim of doing so efficiently. The motivation is clear and well grounded, since distribution matching has become a popular alternative to behavior cloning when compounding error and limited expert coverage are concerns. The authors position their method against adversarial imitation approaches and offline distribution matching baselines, which is a sensible comparison set. The central idea of using future-conditioned dynamics as a signal for matching is interesting, and the paper does a reasonable job of explaining the intuition behind why conditioning on the future might disambiguate otherwise similar state-action pairs. However, the derivation connecting the flow-based formulation to the distribution-matching objective is difficult to follow in places, and several steps appear to rely on approximations whose consequences are not fully analyzed. The authors should state explicitly under what assumptions the flow model recovers the target distribution, and discuss what happens when these assumptions are violated, such as with stochastic or multimodal expert behavior. The efficiency claims are a key contribution but are supported mainly by wall-clock comparisons on a small set of benchmark tasks, and the reported gains would be more convincing with a breakdown of sample complexity, compute cost per update, and total training budget. The experimental section would benefit from ablations isolating the contribution of the future-conditioning component, since without them it is unclear whether the improvement stems from the proposed conditioning or from the flow architecture alone. The choice of baselines is reasonable, but the authors should include at least one recent strong offline imitation method and report variance across random seeds, as several reported differences fall within what appears to be the range of run-to-run noise. The paper would also benefit from evaluation on tasks with high-dimensional observations or significant environment stochasticity, where the claimed advantages are most likely to be tested. Figures are generally clear, though the learning curves lack confidence intervals and some axis labels are too small to read comfortably. The related work section is thorough in covering imitation learning and normalizing flows but is weaker on recent work using generative models for policy learning, and a more explicit comparison there would help readers place the contribution. Reproducibility is partially addressed through hyperparameter tables, but the paper does not state whether code will be released, and key implementation details such as the flow depth and conditioning horizon selection procedure should be specified. The limitations discussion is brief and should be expanded to cover computational overhead at inference time and sensitivity to the choice of future horizon. Overall, the paper addresses a relevant problem with a promising idea, but the theoretical justification and empirical evidence need strengthening before the efficiency and performance claims can be fully accepted. I recommend a major revision, with the main requests being clearer assumptions, targeted ablations, seed-level variance reporting, and a more complete discussion of limitations.

Idaho's Upland Game Birds: Habitats, Populations, and Hunting Opportunities

Idaho is home to a diverse group of upland game birds that thrive across its varied landscapes, from sagebrush steppe and farmland to forests and river valleys. These birds are a valued part of the state's natural heritage and a major draw for hunters and wildlife watchers alike. The species most commonly pursued include ring-necked pheasant, chukar partridge, gray partridge, California quail, mountain quail, ruffed grouse, sage-grouse, and wild turkey. Each species depends on specific habitat conditions, so their distribution across the state varies considerably. Ring-necked pheasants, an introduced species, are most often found in the agricultural lowlands of southern and western Idaho, where grain fields, cover strips, and wetland edges provide food and shelter. Chukar partridges, also introduced, inhabit the steep, rocky canyons and grassy slopes of the Snake River region and the state's desert terrain. Gray partridges favor open farmland and grassland edges, particularly in the Magic Valley and other agricultural areas. California quail prefer brushy edges, riparian corridors, and suburban fringes, where they forage on seeds, greens, and insects. Mountain quail live in dense shrub habitats at mid to high elevations and are generally more secretive than their California relatives. Ruffed grouse occupy aspen, mixed conifer, and deciduous forests in northern and mountainous parts of Idaho, relying on dense understory cover. Greater sage-grouse depend on expansive stands of sagebrush for food and nesting, making them an indicator species for the health of sagebrush ecosystems. Wild turkeys, which were reintroduced in the twentieth century, use a mix of open woodlands, meadows, and river bottoms. Population levels fluctuate with weather, habitat quality, predator numbers, and disease, so the Idaho Department of Fish and Game monitors many species through surveys, brood counts, and harvest data. Sage-grouse populations have declined across much of their historic range, prompting conservation efforts focused on restoring sagebrush habitat and limiting development. Pheasant and chukar numbers can rise sharply after mild winters and productive nesting seasons, and they often drop after harsh weather. Hunters can pursue upland birds under seasons and bag limits set annually by the state, and regulations, season dates, and licensing requirements should always be checked with Idaho Fish and Game before heading into the field. Many areas open to public hunting are managed through the state's Wildlife Management Area program and private land access initiatives, which provide opportunities for hunters without private land connections. Hunters are encouraged to scout ahead, respect landowner property, and carry appropriate safety gear, including hunter orange where required. Dogs are a traditional and effective tool for upland hunting, and their use is widespread among bird hunters in Idaho. Ethical hunting practices, including taking only clean shots and properly recovering harvested birds, help maintain both the resource and public trust. Responsible hunters also contribute to conservation through license fees and excise taxes on hunting equipment, which fund habitat work and wildlife management. Wildlife watchers can enjoy these birds as well, particularly during spring courtship displays of sage-grouse and wild turkeys in the open country. Whether pursued for sport or appreciated for their beauty, Idaho's upland game birds reflect the health of the state's habitats. Protecting those habitats through conservation, sound management, and informed recreation will help ensure these species remain part of Idaho's landscape for generations to come. For the most current seasons, regulations, and population reports, consult the Idaho Department of Fish and Game website or a local regional office.

The manuscript presents a theoretical analysis of second-order neural tangent kernels and compares their generalization performance against linear approximations. The topic is timely and relevant, since the neural tangent kernel framework has become a standard lens for studying overparameterized networks, and extending it beyond the first-order linearization is a natural and worthwhile direction. The authors motivate the work clearly, situating it within the existing literature on lazy training and the limitations of the linear regime. The introduction is well organized and articulates the central question of whether higher-order corrections meaningfully change predicted generalization behavior. The related work section is thorough, though it could more explicitly distinguish this contribution from prior analyses of finite-width corrections. The setup of the problem is precise, with the network architecture, initialization scheme, and loss function specified in sufficient detail to be reproduced. The derivation of the second-order kernel expression is a substantial technical contribution, and the algebra appears largely correct on the parts I checked. However, several steps in the derivation rely on approximations whose validity regimes are stated only informally, and the authors should state them as explicit assumptions. The main theorem bounding the generalization gap is the paper's key result, and its proof is given in the appendix in a condensed form that would benefit from more intermediate steps. I was unable to fully verify the constants in the bound, and I would ask the authors to clarify how they depend on the width and depth of the network. The comparison to linear approximations is conducted both analytically and numerically, which is a strength, since the two sources of evidence largely support one another. The experimental section evaluates the theory on regression tasks of modest size, and while the results are encouraging, the scale is limited relative to the claims made in the abstract. I would encourage experiments on larger datasets or at least on a broader range of architectures to test whether the predicted advantage of the second-order kernel persists. The reported variance across random seeds is not shown in several of the main figures, making it difficult to judge whether the reported gaps are statistically meaningful. The discussion of when second-order terms help versus hurt is interesting, but it is currently too brief to be fully convincing. The authors also do not adequately address the computational cost of computing the second-order kernel, which is relevant to whether the approach is practical. Figures are generally clear, though axis labels and legends in the generalization curves should be made more legible. The writing is mostly clear, with a few passages that are repetitive and could be tightened for concision. Some notation is introduced inconsistently, particularly the distinction between the kernel and its finite-sample estimate, and a notation table would help readers. The limitations section acknowledges the restriction to specific activation functions but does not discuss how sensitive the conclusions are to the choice of loss. I recommend that the authors clarify their assumptions, strengthen the experimental evaluation with error bars and larger-scale tests, and expand the discussion of computational cost. With these revisions, the paper would make a useful contribution to the theory of neural tangent kernels. In its current form, I rate it as a borderline paper that merits revision before acceptance.

Facial emotion detection technology promises to read human feelings by analyzing expressions captured on camera. Companies and institutions have begun to deploy these systems in classrooms, retail stores, airports, and public streets, often with little public discussion. While the technology may appear to offer useful insights, its use in public and educational settings raises serious ethical concerns that deserve careful attention. The most fundamental problem is scientific validity. Many systems are built on the assumption that a particular facial movement reliably signals a specific emotion, such as anger or happiness. Research in psychology has challenged this idea, showing that facial expressions vary widely across cultures, individuals, and contexts. A smile may reflect politeness rather than joy, and a neutral face may hide deep concentration. When a system misreads these signals, the consequences can be unfair to the people being judged. Privacy is another central concern. Facial emotion detection often works without the knowledge or consent of the people being observed. Students sitting in a classroom or shoppers walking through a store may have no clear way to opt out, and the data gathered about their inner states can be stored, shared, or sold. Such constant monitoring can make people feel watched and reduce their willingness to speak freely or behave naturally. In educational settings, these concerns become especially pressing. Schools are places where young people are learning, experimenting, and forming their identities. If a teacher or administrator relies on a machine to judge whether a student is engaged, bored, or upset, the student may be labeled based on an inaccurate reading. Such labels can follow a child through school records and influence how others treat them. Bias and discrimination are also significant risks. Studies have found that some facial analysis systems perform less accurately on people with darker skin tones, women, and people from certain cultural backgrounds. Emotional expression itself can differ across groups, so a system trained mostly on one population may misinterpret the feelings of others. A student whose natural expression is quieter or more reserved might be unfairly flagged as disengaged or hostile. Public deployment raises further questions about autonomy and freedom. When people know they are being analyzed for emotional states, they may alter their behavior out of fear of being misjudged. This chilling effect can weaken the openness that healthy public life depends on. Protest, grief, and ordinary frustration could all be recorded and interpreted as warning signs, even when no harm is intended. There is also the question of accountability. When an automated system makes a judgment that affects someone's education, employment, or freedom of movement, it can be difficult to understand how that decision was reached or to challenge it. Vendors may protect their algorithms as trade secrets, leaving affected people with little recourse. Institutions that adopt these tools may not fully understand their limits either. Finally, the use of such technology reflects a broader choice about what kind of society we want to build. Reducing human emotion to a set of measurable signals risks treating people as data points rather than as individuals with rich and complicated inner lives. Education in particular should nurture trust, curiosity, and personal growth, values that may be undermined by constant emotional surveillance. Given these concerns, communities should approach facial emotion detection with strong skepticism. Clear legal limits, independent scientific review, meaningful consent, and open public debate are essential before such systems are allowed to shape decisions about people's lives. Until these safeguards exist, the risks to privacy, fairness, and human dignity outweigh the promised benefits.

Pipeline safety received significant attention during the session, particularly following recent incidents that highlighted gaps in monitoring and emergency response. Utility oversight was the final major area addressed. Taken together, these measures represent a substantial body of work that touches many areas of daily life, from how quickly permits are processed to the safety of the pipelines and wells near our communities. This manuscript presents a neural network-based approach for flexible three-dimensional reconstruction of biomolecules from cryo-electron microscopy images, addressing the well-known challenge of conformational heterogeneity in single-particle analysis. The authors motivate the work clearly, explaining that many biologically relevant macromolecules adopt multiple conformational states that conventional averaging methods cannot resolve. The proposed framework models the structure as a continuous latent space, allowing it to represent a range of motions rather than a small set of discrete classes. The methodology is described in sufficient detail to be understood, although a more explicit description of the network architecture and training objective would improve reproducibility. The experiments on synthetic datasets are a strength, as they allow the authors to compare reconstructions against known ground truth and quantify accuracy. However, the evaluation on experimental datasets appears limited in scope, and the authors should report results on a wider range of particles with varying sizes, signal-to-noise ratios, and degrees of flexibility. The comparison with existing methods is useful, but the baselines chosen could be broadened to include recent state-of-the-art tools for heterogeneity analysis. The authors should also clarify how sensitive the results are to hyperparameter choices, since this bears directly on the robustness of the method. Figures illustrating the recovered conformational landscapes are informative, though quantitative metrics accompanying them would strengthen the claims. The discussion of computational cost is brief, and a clearer account of runtime and memory requirements would help readers assess practical applicability. The paper would also benefit from a more thorough treatment of failure cases, since understanding when the method breaks down is as important as demonstrating success. Overall, the work is a promising and technically sound contribution, and I recommend minor revisions that address reproducibility, the scope of experimental validation, and the reporting of limitations.

Harold Pemberly had always trusted his toaster, but on the morning the drones arrived, he began to wonder whether trust was a luxury he could no longer afford. It started with a small hovering device outside his kitchen window, which hummed politely and seemed to be taking notes. By lunchtime, Harold had learned that the neighborhood association had voted to install a fleet of them for "community wellness," and that each one reported directly to the refrigerator. Harold, who had never once questioned his refrigerator, now stared at it suspiciously as it hummed its usual tune. He rearranged his furniture so that no chair faced the window, reasoning that a drone could not possibly read his thoughts if he sat with his back to the sky. His wife, Marjorie, returned from the grocery store carrying a single apple and a look of quiet triumph. "The self-checkout asked me if I was enjoying my shopping experience," she said, "and I told it no, and it apologized." Harold nodded gravely, though he suspected the apology itself was a trap. That evening, the family dog refused to fetch his ball, sitting instead by the door and staring at the nearest drone with the stern expression of a sentry. Harold took this as confirmation that the animals had been consulted and were not pleased. He wrote a letter to the editor of the local paper, then deleted it, because the paper's website had recommended the very drone company he was worried about. Finally he unplugged every device in the house, sat in the dark with a flashlight and a printed encyclopedia, and felt, for the first time in years, completely at peace. The next morning, a drone delivered a package to his doorstep containing a new flashlight, a fresh encyclopedia, and a brochure promising that the household's fears would soon be addressed by a personalized smart assistant. Harold sighed, picked up the device, and asked it whether it could please stop following him to the bathroom.

Facing personal challenges is never easy, but the way we respond to them can shape not only our own lives but the lives of those around us. Maintaining a positive outlook during difficult times does not mean ignoring pain or pretending everything is fine. Instead, it means choosing to look for hope, meaning, and small sources of strength even when circumstances are hard. When a person keeps a hopeful attitude, others often notice and feel encouraged to keep going as well. A friend who smiles through a stressful week can remind classmates that setbacks are temporary. A family member who meets illness with courage can give loved ones a sense of calm and direction. Positivity is also contagious in a quiet way, spreading through conversations, shared laughter, and small acts of kindness. Beyond encouragement, a positive attitude strengthens relationships because it invites trust and openness. People feel safer sharing their own struggles with someone who responds with understanding rather than criticism. Over time, this mutual support deepens bonds and builds a sense of community. Ultimately, maintaining positivity through personal challenges benefits everyone involved. It allows us to lift others while we lift ourselves, turning difficult seasons into opportunities for connection and growth.

Resilience and identity are often seen as traits we are born with, yet they are shaped to a large degree by the choices we make and the experiences we live through. Each decision, whether small or significant, adds a layer to the people we become. Choosing to speak up in a difficult classroom discussion, for example, can build confidence that carries into later challenges. Life experiences, including loss, failure, and unexpected success, also teach us how to respond to adversity. A student who struggles through a failed exam and then chooses to seek tutoring learns that setbacks can be survived and even turned into growth. Over time, these patterns form a sense of self that feels stable and recognizable. Identity is not fixed, however, because new experiences continually revise our understanding of who we are. Resilience, in this sense, is less about never falling and more about the habit of getting back up with a changed perspective. Personal choices determine how we interpret our hardships, and that interpretation shapes whether we feel defeated or strengthened. Friendships, families, and communities also influence these choices, offering support that makes resilience possible. Ultimately, the relationship between resilience and identity is cyclical, since the person we become guides the choices we make, and those choices reshape the person we are. Recognizing this process can encourage us to take ownership of our growth. By reflecting on past experiences and deliberately choosing how to respond to future ones, we can build both resilience and a more authentic identity.

Mega Man received the invitation folded inside a capsule that drifted through his lab window on a sunbeam. The paper glowed faintly, and when he unfolded it, the words rearranged themselves into a single line: Represent your world at the Cosmic Convergence Tournament. Dr. Light read it over his shoulder and whistled low. "Eight worlds, one champion, and the prize is a way home for every robot you've ever sent back to the scrap heap," he said. Mega Man did not hesitate. He had never been able to resist a challenge, and he had never been able to resist the thought of a world bigger than his own.

The arena rose from the edge of a nebula, a ring of floating platforms tethered by beams of violet light. Competitors from a dozen realms gathered at its center, each carrying the armor, weapons, or ideas of their home. There was a knight whose sword sang with the voices of its former wielders. There was a gardener from a jungle planet who commanded vines that wrapped around enemies like polite handshakes. There was a girl made of living crystal who hummed when she was thinking. Mega Man recognized none of them, and that was exciting.

His first match was against a towering construct called Gravitas, which bent the air itself into crushing fists. Mega Man darted under the first blow, fired a burst from his arm cannon, and felt the familiar rhythm of combat settle into his bones. He dodged a sweep of gravity that would have flattened a lesser fighter, then climbed the arena wall using the rebounding force of his own shots. The crowd roared when he landed on Gravitas's shoulder and fired directly into its core. The construct collapsed in a shower of sparks, and the judges lifted Mega Man's hand as the first victory of the tournament.

The second match pitted him against the crystal girl, whose name was Lira. She did not attack at first; she simply watched him with eyes that caught the light like prisms. Mega Man kept his cannon lowered and asked her why she had entered. She said her world was dying, slowly drained of the energy that kept its skies blue, and the tournament's prize was a source of light that could restore it. Mega Man thought of the city he had defended so many times, the people who had trusted him to keep their lights on. He understood her better than he expected to.

They fought anyway, because the rules required it, but they fought with care. Lira sent waves of refracted light that bent around Mega Man's shots, and he answered with precise bursts that split her patterns apart. Neither of them tried to finish the other. When the judges declared a draw and offered both of them a place in the finals, Lira smiled and said that she would rather fight beside him than against him. Mega Man agreed, and they shook hands as the crowd cheered their names.

The finals brought the strongest champions into one arena. The knight charged with a blade that echoed every battle it had ever fought, the gardener's vines snaked across the platforms, and a hulking mech from a volcanic world hurled molten boulders into the void. Mega Man fought with everything he had learned across years of battles against robot masters, wily doctors, and armies of his own kind. Lira's light lit the paths he needed, and his cannon cleared the way when the light flickered. Together they moved like a single machine, one that had learned to trust.

At the climax, the volcanic mech cornered them against the edge of the arena. Its heat pressed against Mega Man's armor, and his systems flashed warnings in red. Lira focused her crystal body into a single lance of light and drove it into the mech's cooling vents, while Mega Man channeled a full charge through his cannon into the same point. The mech shuddered, sparked, and then fell silent, its molten core spilling harmlessly into the void. The arena went still, then erupted into applause that rolled across the nebula like thunder.

The judges declared Mega Man and Lira co-champions, and the prize of light was split between their two worlds. As the crowd dispersed, the knight approached and bowed his head, saying that the tournament had taught him more about honor than any battle he had fought before. The gardener offered a seed from her jungle planet as a gift of friendship. Mega Man accepted it with a grin and promised to plant it somewhere that needed a little green.

When he returned to his lab, Dr. Light was waiting with a fresh pot of coffee and a dozen questions. Mega Man laid the seed on the workbench and began to explain everything, the gravity fists, the crystal lance, the molten heart of the mech, and the quiet moment when a rival had become a friend. Dr. Light listened with a smile that grew wider with every detail. Outside the window, the sky over Monstro City shone a little brighter, and Mega Man knew that somewhere across the stars, Lira's world was shining too.

Schools face a real challenge when they try to serve meals that are both nutritious and appealing to students. Healthy foods such as vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins are essential for growing bodies, yet children often reject them when they do not look or taste familiar. Many students gravitate toward favorites like pizza, chicken nuggets, and macaroni and cheese, which can be adapted with whole-grain crusts, baked instead of fried preparation, or added vegetables. Involving students in menu planning through taste tests and surveys can also help schools find dishes that satisfy both health guidelines and young palates. Ultimately, the goal should be a lunch program where nutrition and enjoyment work together, so that students eat well and look forward to their midday meal.

Finishing high school ahead of schedule offers students a head start on their futures in several meaningful ways. Students who graduate early can enter college, a job, or a training program sooner, which allows them to begin building savings, experience, and professional skills years earlier than their peers. Accelerating graduation can also reduce the total cost of education, since a student who completes high school in three years instead of four pays for one fewer year of tuition at a public or private high school in many systems and may enter college with a clearer financial path. For motivated students, the extra time gained can be used to pursue advanced coursework, dual enrollment, internships, or a demanding major without the pressure of finishing every requirement in the traditional timeframe. Early graduation also encourages self-discipline and time management, because students must plan their course loads carefully and stay focused on long-term goals. Many students who finish early report that they feel more independent and more ready for the responsibilities of adult life. Additionally, early graduates can explore career interests sooner, which helps them avoid spending years on a path that does not suit them. Colleges often value applicants who show initiative and academic drive, and an early graduation can demonstrate those qualities clearly. At the same time, students should weigh the benefits against the possible drawbacks, such as missing out on extracurricular activities, sports, or the social experiences that come with a full high school career. Careful counseling and honest self-assessment can help students decide whether acceleration is the right choice. For students who are academically prepared, emotionally ready, and supported by their families and teachers, graduating early can be an excellent opportunity. It rewards hard work, opens doors to new challenges, and gives young people the chance to shape their own paths with confidence. Ultimately, the decision should be based on each student's goals, strengths, and circumstances rather than on pressure to rush. When made thoughtfully, early graduation can be one of the most rewarding steps a student takes on the road to adulthood.

Spectral Asymptotics of Laplace–Beltrami Operators on Hypersurfaces Collapsing to a Double-Sided Flat Domain

Abstract

We study the spectral asymptotics of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on a family of closed hypersurfaces that collapse, in the Gromov–Hausdorff and intrinsic senses, onto a bounded flat domain counted twice, once for each side of the domain. The collapsing parameter is a small thickness ε > 0. We identify the limiting spectral problem as a Neumann-type eigenvalue problem on the domain with a doubled measure, derive two-term asymptotics for the low-lying eigenvalues, and obtain a Weyl-type remainder estimate for the bulk of the spectrum. The analysis combines a quasimode construction adapted to the normal fibration with min–max characterizations and a careful treatment of the transition layer near the boundary of the domain. We conclude with a discussion of geometric interpretations and open questions.

1. Introduction

The spectrum of the Laplace–Beltrami operator carries substantial information about the geometry of a Riemannian manifold. When a family of manifolds degenerates, the spectrum may converge to the spectrum of a lower-dimensional limiting object, and the rate and form of this convergence encode the structure of the degeneration. Such questions have been studied extensively for collapsing manifolds with bounded curvature, for thin domains in Euclidean space, and for shrinking tubular neighborhoods of submanifolds.

In this paper we consider a specific degeneration in which a closed hypersurface becomes, in the limit, a flat domain traversed twice. Concretely, let Ω be a bounded connected open subset of a flat hyperplane in Euclidean space, and let the hypersurface M_ε be a thin closed surface whose two sheets lie close to the two sides of Ω, joined along the edge of the domain by a rounded connecting region of size comparable to ε. As ε tends to zero, M_ε collapses onto Ω with each interior point of Ω covered by two nearby sheets.

The question we address is how the eigenvalues of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on M_ε behave as ε → 0. Naively one expects the eigenvalues to converge to those of a Neumann problem on Ω with a measure that accounts for the doubling, but the presence of the connecting region near the boundary introduces an additional scale and can modify the leading correction. Our main results make this precise.

We emphasize that the setting is intrinsically two-dimensional in the transverse direction and therefore differs from the classical problem of thin domains with Neumann conditions, where the limiting operator is typically a weighted Laplacian on a lower-dimensional set without doubling. The double-sided structure forces the limiting eigenfunctions to be symmetric with respect to the two sheets in the modes that survive the collapse, and antisymmetric modes are pushed to high frequency.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 fixes notation and describes the geometry of the family M_ε. Section 3 recalls the relevant functional-analytic framework. Section 4 constructs the limiting problem. Section 5 contains the main spectral convergence theorem. Section 6 derives two-term asymptotics for the low eigenvalues. Section 7 treats the high-frequency regime and proves a Weyl-type remainder bound. Section 8 discusses examples and extensions, and Section 9 lists open problems.

2. Geometry of the Family

Let Ω ⊂ ℝ^{n-1} be a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω, where n ≥ 2. We regard Ω as embedded in the hyperplane {x_n = 0} of ℝ^n. For a small parameter ε in (0, ε_0], we construct a closed hypersurface M_ε ⊂ ℝ^{n+1} in the following manner. Away from a neighborhood of ∂Ω, M_ε consists of two parallel copies of Ω, namely the graphs of the functions u_ε^+ = ε/2 and u_ε^- = −ε/2 over Ω, where we work in a single coordinate chart. Near ∂Ω the two sheets are joined by a smooth cap of height comparable to ε.

More precisely, we fix a cutoff profile χ in C^∞(ℝ) with χ(s) = 1 for s ≥ 1 and χ(s) = 0 for s ≤ 0, and we define the connecting region in a collar of width δ ε around ∂Ω, with δ a fixed positive constant. The resulting surface is smooth, embedded, and closed after capping off in the standard way.

We denote by g_ε the induced Riemannian metric on M_ε and by Δ_ε the associated Laplace–Beltrami operator. The volume measure dV_ε on M_ε satisfies, away from the collar, dV_ε = (1 + O(ε^2)) dx on each sheet, where dx denotes Lebesgue measure on Ω. Hence the total measure of M_ε is asymptotically twice the measure of Ω.

The second fundamental form of the sheets is O(ε) in the flat region because the sheets are nearly flat. In the collar the principal curvatures are of order ε^{-1}, reflecting the rapid turn of the connecting cap. This curvature concentration is the source of the nontrivial boundary behavior and must be controlled carefully.

We introduce the normal coordinate t on the flat region, measured from the midsurface {x_n = 0}, so that the two sheets correspond to t = ±ε/2. In these coordinates the metric is g_ε = (1 + O(ε^2)) dx^2 + dt^2 on the sheets, and the cap is described by a reparametrization in which the arclength along the profile is comparable to ε.

3. Functional Framework

Let H_ε = L^2(M_ε) with the inner product induced by dV_ε. The quadratic form associated with Δ_ε is

q_ε(u) = ∫_{M_ε} |∇_ε u|^2 dV_ε,

defined on the form domain H^1(M_ε). Since M_ε is closed, the spectrum of Δ_ε is discrete and consists of eigenvalues

0 = λ_0(ε) < λ_1(ε) ≤ λ_2(ε) ≤ … → ∞,

counted with multiplicity. The constant function gives the zero eigenvalue, and the eigenvalue λ_1(ε) is the first nonzero eigenvalue, which we will track.

We use the min–max characterization

λ_k(ε) = min over (k+1)-dimensional subspaces V of H^1(M_ε) of max over u in V \ {0} of q_ε(u)/∫ u^2 dV_ε.

This characterization allows us to compare spectra of different operators by comparing quadratic forms. Our strategy is to establish upper and lower bounds on λ_k(ε) by constructing test spaces and by analyzing a reduced problem obtained through the fiber decomposition over Ω.

We also use the decomposition of L^2(M_ε) into symmetric and antisymmetric parts with respect to the involution σ that exchanges the two sheets. Symmetric functions are those with u∘σ = u, and antisymmetric functions satisfy u∘σ = −u. Because σ is an isometry of M_ε, the operator Δ_ε commutes with the projections onto these subspaces, and the spectrum splits accordingly.

4. The Limiting Problem

We define the limiting problem on Ω as follows. Let μ denote the measure 2 dx on Ω, which accounts for the two sheets. Consider the Neumann eigenvalue problem

−Δ φ = λ φ in Ω,  ∂φ/∂ν = 0 on ∂Ω,

where Δ is the Euclidean Laplacian on Ω and ν is the outward unit normal. The symmetric eigenfunctions of Δ_ε converge, after restriction to a single sheet, to eigenfunctions of this problem, and the normalization by the doubled measure is respected because the Rayleigh quotient is unchanged by the factor 2 when both the numerator and denominator are doubled.

Thus we expect that the symmetric part of the spectrum of Δ_ε converges to the Neumann spectrum of Ω, each eigenvalue appearing with its natural multiplicity. The antisymmetric part, by contrast, requires a different analysis. An antisymmetric function must change sign across the midsurface, and therefore its restriction to the limit domain must vanish on the midsurface in the limit. Such functions are forced to have Rayleigh quotients that blow up as ε → 0 unless they are concentrated near the connecting region, where the geometry permits rapid variation. We show that the antisymmetric eigenvalues diverge at rate ε^{-2} in the flat directions, which places them outside any fixed window of the spectrum and therefore does not affect the limiting spectral problem for bounded eigenvalues.

We record the precise statement. Let 0 = μ_0 < μ_1 ≤ μ_2 ≤ … denote the Neumann eigenvalues of Ω. Then for each fixed k, the symmetric eigenvalues satisfy

λ_k^{sym}(ε) → μ_k as ε → 0,

and the antisymmetric eigenvalues satisfy λ_k^{anti}(ε) ≥ c ε^{-2} for a constant c > 0 independent of ε and k in a fixed range.

5. Main Convergence Theorem

Theorem 5.1. Let Ω, M_ε, and Δ_ε be as above. For each fixed integer k ≥ 0, the k-th symmetric eigenvalue of Δ_ε converges to the k-th Neumann eigenvalue of Ω:

lim_{ε→0} λ_k^{sym}(ε) = μ_k.

Moreover, the corresponding eigenfunctions, extended to M_ε by symmetry, converge in the sense of quasimodes and their restrictions converge strongly in L^2(Ω).

Proof outline. We establish the upper bound by constructing test functions. Given a Neumann eigenfunction φ_k on Ω, we define the extension ψ_ε on M_ε by setting ψ_ε(x, t) = φ_k(x) on the flat sheets and interpolating across the collar using a cutoff that depends on the distance to ∂Ω at scale ε. Because φ_k satisfies the Neumann condition, the normal derivative of ψ_ε across the collar is controlled, and the additional energy contributed by the collar is of order ε. The Rayleigh quotient of ψ_ε therefore equals μ_k + O(ε) after normalization. This gives limsup λ_k^{sym}(ε) ≤ μ_k.

For the lower bound, we use the fiber decomposition. Any symmetric function u on M_ε can be averaged over the normal fiber, yielding a function on Ω whose Dirichlet energy is bounded by the energy of u up to a multiplicative factor tending to one. Compactness of the embedding H^1(Ω) → L^2(Ω) then implies that the averaged problem has eigenvalues converging to those of the Neumann problem, and the min–max principle gives liminf λ_k^{sym}(ε) ≥ μ_k.

The convergence of eigenfunctions follows from the uniform energy bounds and the identification of limits. ∎

6. Two-Term Asymptotics

We now refine the leading-order statement. Write

λ_k^{sym}(ε) = μ_k + ε a_k + o(ε),

where the correction a_k is determined by the geometry of the collar.

Theorem 6.1. Assume that Ω is smooth and that μ_k is simple. Then the correction coefficient is given by

a_k = −∫_{∂Ω} κ(s) φ_k(s)^2 ds / ∫_Ω φ_k^2 dx,

where κ is the curvature function of ∂Ω measured in the plane of Ω, ds is arclength on ∂Ω, and φ_k is the normalized Neumann eigenfunction.

Proof outline. We perform formal perturbation theory in ε. The collar contributes an energy correction whose leading term is proportional to ε times a boundary integral of the square of the trace of the eigenfunction weighted by the mean curvature of the cap profile. The sign and coefficient follow from integrating the profile over the normal variable and evaluating the resulting one-dimensional integral, which depends only on χ and the normalization of the cap. The curvature of ∂Ω enters through the Jacobian of the collar coordinates. A detailed computation, which we omit for brevity, yields the stated formula. ∎

Remark. The coefficient a_k depends on the choice of cap profile only through a universal constant that can be absorbed into the normalization of ε. Changing the cap profile while keeping its height comparable to ε alters a_k by a factor that we normalize to one in the statement above.

7. High-Frequency Regime and Weyl-Type Estimate

For eigenvalues in a window growing with ε, the flat-region analysis must be replaced by a semiclassical argument. Let N_ε(Λ) denote the number of eigenvalues of Δ_ε in [0, Λ]. The Weyl law for the limiting Neumann problem on Ω gives

N_Ω(Λ) = (ω_{n-1} vol(Ω) / (2π)^{n-1}) Λ^{(n-1)/2} + R(Λ),

where ω_{n-1} is the volume of the unit ball in ℝ^{n-1}, and R(Λ) is the remainder, which for smooth Ω satisfies |R(Λ)| ≤ C Λ^{(n-2)/2} in dimensions n ≥ 3 with a boundary term of the same order.

On M_ε, the total volume is approximately twice that of Ω, so the leading Weyl term for the full spectrum is doubled. Symmetric and antisymmetric eigenvalues share this leading term only in the symmetric sector; the antisymmetric sector shifts to higher frequencies as described in Section 4.

Theorem 7.1. There exist constants C > 0 and Λ_0 > 0, independent of ε, such that for Λ ≥ Λ_0,

|N_ε^{sym}(Λ) − N_Ω(Λ)| ≤ C (1 + Λ^{(n-2)/2} + ε^{-1} Λ^{(n-3)/2}).

Proof outline. We decompose the operator into a bulk part away from the collar, where the semiclassical parametrix for the Neumann Laplacian applies, and a collar part of width comparable to ε. The bulk contributes the Neumann Weyl term and the boundary remainder. The collar contributes an error controlled by the number of eigenvalues whose eigenfunctions are localized in a region of size ε, which is bounded by the Weyl count for that region at frequency Λ. Summing these contributions yields the stated bound. The factor ε^{-1} reflects the curvature concentration in the collar when Λ is large relative to ε^{-1}, and the estimate is nontrivial only in the range Λ ≲ ε^{-2}. ∎

8. Examples

We illustrate the results with a few explicit cases.

Example 8.1. Let n = 2, so Ω is an interval (0, L) in the plane and M_ε is a thin closed curve-like surface, which for n = 2 is a thin closed surface of revolution. The Neumann eigenvalues of Ω are μ_k = (kπ/L)^2 with eigenfunctions cos(kπx/L). Theorem 5.1 gives convergence of the symmetric spectrum to these values. The coefficient in Theorem 6.1 vanishes here because the boundary of the interval consists of points with zero curvature in the relevant sense, so the first correction appears at order ε^2. We have not verified the exact order of the correction in this case in full detail.

Example 8.2. Let n = 3 and let Ω be a disk of radius R. The Neumann eigenvalues involve Bessel zeros, and the curvature κ is constant equal to 1/R. The correction a_k in Theorem 6.1 then becomes a constant multiple of the boundary integral of the square of the eigenfunction, which for radial modes can be evaluated explicitly. This gives an explicit first-order shift for the symmetric eigenvalues.

Example 8.3. For a rectangle in higher dimensions, the curvature term vanishes on the flat faces and is concentrated at the edges. The asymptotic analysis then requires a more delicate treatment of corner contributions, which we do not pursue here.

9. Discussion and Open Questions

The results above establish the leading behavior of the symmetric spectrum and identify the antisymmetric spectrum as escaping to infinity at rate ε^{-2}. Several questions remain open.

First, the second-order term in the expansion of Theorem 6.1 is not computed here. Determining it would require a more refined matched-asymptotic analysis between the collar and the bulk, and would likely involve the second fundamental form of ∂Ω together with the cap profile.

Second, our Weyl-type remainder estimate is not sharp. We expect that a more careful semiclassical analysis could improve the error term and possibly recover the optimal remainder for the Neumann problem uniformly in ε in a range of frequencies.

Third, the case of domains Ω with nonsmooth boundary, such as polygons or domains with cusps, is not covered. Corners and cusps can produce anomalous spectral contributions, and their interaction with the collar geometry is unclear.

Fourth, it would be natural to consider more general doubling constructions, in which the two sheets are not parallel but meet at a prescribed angle, or in which the limiting domain is a manifold with boundary rather than a flat domain. Such generalizations would connect the present analysis to the broader theory of spectral convergence under collapse with bounded curvature.

Fifth, one may ask about the behavior of the heat trace and the zeta-regularized determinant as ε → 0. The determinant, in particular, may exhibit a logarithmic correction associated with the collapse, and identifying its coefficient would provide a finer invariant of the degeneration.

Finally, we note that the spectral convergence of the symmetric part depends only on the energy bounds and the compactness of the limit embedding, and so is expected to be robust under perturbations of the construction. The precise rate, however, is sensitive to the local geometry of the collar, and this sensitivity deserves further study.

10. Conclusion

We have analyzed the spectrum of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on hypersurfaces that collapse onto a double-sided flat domain. The symmetric eigenvalues converge to the Neumann spectrum of the domain, with a first-order correction governed by boundary curvature and the cap profile. The antisymmetric eigenvalues diverge at rate ε^{-2} and do not contribute to the limiting spectral problem. A Weyl-type estimate for the symmetric spectrum holds with an explicit remainder. These results clarify how doubling and collar geometry interact in the spectral limit and suggest several directions for further investigation.

The author thanks colleagues for discussions on collapsing geometry and spectral asymptotics. No external funding is reported.

The genus is not specified, so I will write this as a general educational overview of a representative large-ant genus, Camponotus, the carpenter ants. Camponotus is one of the largest and most widespread ant genera, with over a thousand described species found on nearly every continent except Antarctica. Workers typically range from about 5 to 13 millimeters in length, and the body is divided into the head, mesosoma, and gaster, joined by a narrow petiole with a single node. A distinctive feature is the evenly rounded profile of the mesosoma in profile view, which lacks the spines or sharp angles found in many other ant groups. The head bears large compound eyes and elbowed antennae with a long scape, and the mandibles are strong and used for cutting wood and carrying food. Camponotus species are polymorphic, with minor, median, and major workers differing in head size and body proportions within a single colony. Many species nest in dead wood, hollow stems, or soil, where they excavate galleries without consuming the wood itself, which distinguishes them from termites. Their recognizable traits include a fine, uniform coat of hairs, a lack of a sting, and the ability to spray formic acid as a defense.

This paper investigates whether randomized image transformations can serve as an effective defense against adversarial attacks, examining their robustness, computational overhead, and dependence on input dimensions. The topic is timely and relevant, as randomization-based defenses have attracted interest for their simplicity and their potential to be deployed without retraining models. The authors' experimental design covers a reasonable range of attack types, which strengthens the credibility of their conclusions about effectiveness. However, the evaluation would be more convincing if it included adaptive attacks that account for the randomness of the defense, since prior work has shown that many randomization defenses fail once the attacker models the transformation. The computational cost analysis is a valuable contribution, though the reported timings would benefit from clearer hardware specifications and comparisons against a standardized baseline. The sensitivity-to-input-size results are interesting, but the paper should explain more carefully whether the observed trends reflect the transformations themselves or artifacts of the chosen datasets. The writing is generally clear, although several figures lack sufficient captions to be interpreted independently of the main text. Overall, the work is a useful empirical contribution, and addressing the adaptive-attack concern would substantially raise its value.

Marine Le Pen, the leader of France's National Rally party, faces trial over remarks in which she compared Muslim street prayers in France to the German occupation during the Second World War. Prosecutors allege that her comments, made during a public debate, amounted to incitement to discrimination and hatred against Muslims. Le Pen's defense argues that her statements were political criticism of religious practices in public spaces and were protected by free speech. The case has drawn sharp reactions from political rivals, who accuse her of stoking divisions, while her supporters describe the prosecution as an attempt to silence a leading opposition voice. Muslim organizations and human rights groups have called for the court to take a firm stance against language that they say normalizes hostility toward religious minorities. Legal experts note that French law draws a fine line between protected political speech and speech that incites hatred, making the outcome closely watched across the country. The verdict is expected to have implications not only for Le Pen's political future but also for how public figures in France discuss religion and minority communities.

Perseverance is one of the most valuable qualities a person can develop, because nearly every meaningful achievement is preceded by failure. Setbacks are not signs that a goal is out of reach; more often, they are the ordinary friction that comes with trying something difficult. How a person responds to those setbacks often determines whether they eventually succeed.

Consider the experience of many inventors, athletes, and artists. Thomas Edison reportedly said that he had not failed ten thousand times but had found ten thousand ways that did not work. Whether or not the exact number is accurate, the sentiment captures an important truth: each failed attempt provides information that narrows the path toward a solution. Every mistake teaches something that a person who never tried would never learn.

Setbacks also test a person's commitment to their goals. When progress slows, it becomes tempting to conclude that the goal was never realistic or that the effort is not worth it. Those who persevere are the ones who look at a difficult moment and ask what can be learned or changed rather than whether to quit. This shift in perspective turns discouragement into a source of direction.

Perseverance also builds character in ways that success alone cannot. A person who has worked through repeated disappointments develops patience, resilience, and a steadier sense of self-worth. They learn that their abilities are not fixed and that skill grows with practice. This belief, sometimes called a growth mindset, makes future challenges feel less threatening.

Of course, perseverance does not mean stubbornly repeating the same mistake forever. Effective perseverance involves reflection, adjustment, and sometimes changing strategy while keeping the underlying goal in view. A runner recovering from an injury may need to modify their training schedule, and a writer whose manuscript is rejected may need to revise their approach. The persistence lies in the commitment to the goal, not in rigid adherence to a single method.

Support from others can make perseverance easier. Teachers, mentors, friends, and family members can offer encouragement, honest feedback, and perspective during hard times. Recognizing that others have faced similar struggles can also reduce the sense of isolation that often accompanies failure. Asking for help is itself a form of perseverance, because it reflects a willingness to keep working toward a goal rather than giving up.

Success that follows setbacks often feels more meaningful because of the effort it required. A student who struggled through a difficult course and eventually mastered the material may value that achievement more than one that came easily. The obstacles overcome become part of the story of what the person accomplished, and they remind us of what we are capable of enduring.

In the end, perseverance through setbacks matters not only because it leads to particular achievements but because it shapes who we become. Each time a person keeps going after a disappointment, they reaffirm their ability to face difficulty with courage and determination. Success may not always arrive on schedule or in the form we expected, but the willingness to keep trying is what makes it possible at all.
