The Electoral College has been part of the American presidential system since the Constitution was ratified, yet many citizens today question whether it still serves the democratic principles the nation holds dear. Replacing it with a direct popular vote would ensure that every citizen's ballot carries equal weight, regardless of where they happen to live. Under the current system, a voter in a populous state like California or Texas has a far smaller share of influence over the outcome than a voter in a sparsely populated state like Wyoming, because each state receives electors based on its congressional representation, which gives smaller states a disproportionate voice. A direct popular vote would eliminate this imbalance and treat the vote of a Floridian and the vote of a Vermonter as equal in value. The system also produces the troubling possibility that a candidate can lose the national popular vote and still win the presidency, as occurred in 2000 and 2016. Such outcomes erode public confidence in the legitimacy of elections, and a president who lacks a majority or plurality of the nation's voters may struggle to claim a genuine mandate. Critics of the current arrangement point out that the winner-take-all method used by most states further distorts the result, since a narrow margin in a single state can award every one of its electors to a candidate who won only a slim majority there. Under a direct vote, the margin of victory in each state would no longer matter in the same way, and every vote cast nationwide would contribute to the final tally. Supporters of reform also argue that the current system concentrates campaign attention on a small number of swing states, leaving voters in safe states and many smaller communities largely ignored during presidential contests. A national popular vote would encourage candidates to speak to Americans across the entire country, addressing the concerns of rural, urban, and suburban communities alike. Moreover, a direct election would make turnout more meaningful everywhere, since voters in states that are reliably one party or another would have a reason to participate, knowing their individual ballot counts toward the national total. Defenders of the Electoral College often argue that it protects the interests of smaller states and encourages broad geographic coalitions, but a direct vote could still require candidates to secure a national plurality while maintaining the principle of one person, one vote. Some reformers propose a national popular vote with a runoff election when no candidate reaches a required threshold, which would ensure that the eventual winner commands substantial support. Concerns about recounts and close national margins could be addressed through clear federal standards for counting and certifying results. Ultimately, the nation has long embraced the idea that democratic government derives its authority from the consent of the governed. A direct popular vote would align the selection of the nation's highest office with this fundamental principle. Replacing the Electoral College would not diminish the role of states in American life, but it would affirm that the presidency belongs to the people as a whole. For these reasons, a direct popular vote deserves serious consideration as a fairer and more democratic method for choosing the president of the United States.

Community service requirements have become a common feature of high school graduation policies across the country, and they raise a question worth examining carefully: should schools require students to complete volunteer work, and should they reward those who do? Supporters argue that such requirements build civic responsibility and expose young people to problems they might otherwise never encounter. A student who tutors younger children or helps at a food pantry gains firsthand knowledge of the needs within their own community. This kind of exposure can turn abstract ideas about fairness and compassion into lived experience. Many students also discover interests and career paths through service that they would not have found in a classroom alone.

Critics, however, make a compelling case that mandatory service can undermine the very values it hopes to instill. Volunteering is defined by its voluntary nature, and when it becomes a graduation checkbox, some students may treat it as a chore to be completed rather than a commitment to be embraced. Others may choose the easiest hours available, producing service that is shallow and sometimes meaningless to both the student and the organization receiving help. There is also a fairness concern, since students with flexible schedules, transportation, and family support can accumulate hours far more easily than classmates who work part-time jobs or care for siblings.

Rewards present a related dilemma. Recognition such as certificates, scholarship consideration, or notations on transcripts can motivate students who might otherwise never volunteer. Yet when service is tied to external rewards, students may begin to focus on the reward rather than the cause, a tendency researchers sometimes describe as the overjustification effect, in which extrinsic incentives weaken intrinsic motivation. A student chasing a scholarship bonus may stop helping once the reward is secured.

A middle path may offer the best balance. Schools could encourage service through strong programming, meaningful partnerships with local organizations, and opportunities that connect to students' interests, while avoiding rigid hour requirements that reduce service to a transaction. Modest recognition, such as acknowledgment at an awards ceremony, can celebrate effort without making it the sole purpose. Schools might also ensure that students with limited time or resources have access to flexible options.

Ultimately, the goal of any service policy should be to cultivate citizens who care about their communities long after graduation. Requirements can open the door, but only genuine engagement will keep students walking through it. Schools that design their programs with this aim in mind are more likely to produce lasting civic commitment than those that simply count hours.

Joining an overseas animal-relief program offers a rare chance to combine adventure, service, and meaningful daily activity. For many students, the appeal begins with travel itself, since living in a new country exposes them to unfamiliar landscapes, languages, and traditions. Beyond sightseeing, these programs place volunteers directly in the field, where they help rescue injured animals, care for rescued dogs and cats, or support wildlife sanctuaries. Such work demands patience, observation, and quick thinking, and it teaches skills that classroom lessons rarely provide. Participants also gain a real sense of purpose, knowing that their labor helps animals recover from neglect, injury, or displacement. The service component matters just as much, because volunteers often assist local veterinarians and community members who lack the resources to address animal welfare on their own. Many programs also educate nearby residents about humane care, which can create lasting improvements long after the volunteers leave. Engaging activities such as guided treks, conservation walks, and cultural evenings keep the experience varied and energizing. Volunteers frequently return home with stronger self-reliance, since they must adapt to new routines, manage their own schedules, and communicate across cultural differences. These challenges build confidence and resilience that serve students well in future careers, whether in veterinary medicine, conservation, or any field requiring compassion and teamwork. Friendships formed during the program often last for years, as shared hard work creates bonds that run deep. The emotional rewards are also significant, since watching a frightened animal learn to trust again is a deeply moving experience. Students who participate often describe a shift in how they see the world, becoming more aware of global issues and their own capacity to make a difference. Careful research is important, so students should choose reputable organizations with transparent practices and clear safety guidelines. When chosen wisely, an animal-relief program can offer an unforgettable blend of adventure, service, and personal growth. Ultimately, the experience gives students a chance to explore the world while leaving it a little better for the animals they serve.

Community service should be a regular part of student life because it builds empathy, teaches responsibility, and connects young people to the needs of the people around them. Students who volunteer gain practical skills such as teamwork, communication, and problem-solving that are difficult to learn in a classroom alone. To make service rewarding rather than a box to check, schools can let students choose causes that genuinely interest them and reflect on their experiences in writing or discussion afterward. Pairing volunteers with mentors, celebrating their contributions publicly, and linking projects to subjects they are studying can also deepen their sense of purpose. When service feels meaningful and personal, students are far more likely to continue helping others long after graduation.

The manuscript addresses an important and technically demanding problem: imputing missing events in continuous-time point processes using particle smoothing methods. The authors frame the task clearly, noting that many real-world event datasets, such as electronic health records, financial transactions, and neural spike trains, are incomplete, and that naive imputation can bias downstream inference. The motivation is well articulated in the introduction, which situates the work within the existing literature on filtering and smoothing for latent continuous-time processes.

The central methodological contribution is a particle smoothing scheme that treats unobserved events as latent variables and propagates weighted sample paths both forward and backward in time. This is a reasonable extension of sequential Monte Carlo ideas to point process settings, where the state space includes both the intensity dynamics and the discrete event times. The authors correctly identify the difficulty of degeneracy in particle weights when the observation density is sharply peaked, and they propose a backward simulation step to mitigate it.

The derivation of the smoothing recursion is presented in a careful and mostly self-contained manner. The notation is generally consistent, although the transition from the discrete-time particle formulation to the continuous-time limit is compressed, and a reader unfamiliar with the relevant measure-theoretic background may struggle to follow it. I would encourage the authors to add an appendix that makes the limiting argument explicit, including the conditions under which the Radon-Nikodym derivatives used in the weight updates are well defined.

The theoretical analysis includes a consistency result for the particle approximation as the number of particles grows. The statement of the theorem is clear, and the proof sketch captures the main ideas, but several assumptions, particularly those controlling the boundedness of the intensity function and the mixing of the latent process, are stated without discussion of whether they are realistic in practice. A brief section on the scope of these assumptions would strengthen the paper considerably.

The experimental evaluation uses both simulated and real datasets. The simulation study is well designed: the authors generate event sequences from a Hawkes process with known parameters, randomly delete a fraction of the events, and then compare imputed sequences against the ground truth. The use of multiple deletion rates is a sensible choice, since it shows how performance degrades as missingness increases.

The results on synthetic data are encouraging. The proposed method outperforms the baselines, which include a simple linear interpolation of event counts and a Gibbs sampler for the same model, in terms of both event-time error and recovered intensity parameters. The authors report credible intervals that achieve near-nominal coverage at moderate missingness levels, which is a useful sanity check on the uncertainty quantification.

The comparison to the Gibbs sampler, however, deserves more scrutiny. The authors report wall-clock times that favor their method, but the Gibbs sampler implementation appears to use a relatively small number of iterations, and it is not clear whether it was run to convergence. Without convergence diagnostics for the baseline, the comparison of computational efficiency is difficult to interpret.

The real-data application concerns a dataset of clinical event records with substantial missingness. The authors use the imputed sequences to fit a downstream survival model and show that coefficient estimates are more stable than those obtained from complete-case analysis. This is an appealing demonstration, since it connects the methodology to a practical decision-making context. Still, the clinical interpretation is somewhat overstated, and the authors should be more cautious about causal language.

The paper would benefit from a more thorough discussion of sensitivity to the choice of particle count. The authors use a fixed number of particles across all experiments, but the performance of sequential Monte Carlo methods is known to depend strongly on this choice, especially in high-dimensional latent spaces. A sensitivity analysis varying the particle count, with corresponding effective sample size reporting, would make the results more reliable.

The paper also does not adequately address the mechanism of missingness. The entire analysis assumes that events are missing completely at random, or at least independently of the latent process. In many applications, such as clinical data, missingness is informative, since patients who are sicker may have more frequent recorded events. The authors should either extend the model to handle missing-not-at-random mechanisms or clearly state this as a limitation.

A related concern is identifiability. When events are deleted, the imputation model must distinguish between events that were truly absent and events that were simply unobserved. The authors do not discuss whether the posterior over imputed events is identifiable under their model, and a short argument or a simulation demonstrating stability would help readers judge the reliability of the imputations.

The related work section is comprehensive in its coverage of classical point process inference, but it underrepresents recent advances in neural point process models and variational approaches to imputation. Including a discussion of how the proposed method compares to these modern alternatives would position the contribution more precisely and help readers understand its relative advantages.

The authors provide code and data availability statements, which is commendable. I was able to follow the general structure of the algorithm from the pseudocode in the appendix, though the pseudocode would be easier to verify if it included explicit definitions of the proposal distribution and the weight normalization step.

The writing is generally clear, though several paragraphs in the methods section are dense and could be split for readability. Some symbols are introduced before they are defined, and there are a few inconsistencies between the notation in the text and in the figures, which should be corrected before publication.

Figure 2 is effective in showing the reduction in event-time error across deletion rates, but the error bars are not explained in the caption. The authors should specify whether they represent standard errors, standard deviations, or confidence intervals, and the number of replicates underlying them.

The discussion section appropriately acknowledges several limitations, including the computational cost of the method at large scales and its reliance on correct specification of the intensity model. However, it does not discuss what happens when the intensity model is misspecified, which is a common situation in practice. A short robustness analysis under model misspecification would substantially increase the practical value of the paper.

The paper's contribution is meaningful and the core idea is sound, but its claims about superiority over existing methods rest on a limited set of baselines and on experiments whose details are not fully reported. The theoretical results are promising but need clearer statements of assumptions and their practical relevance.

Overall, I recommend a major revision. The methodological idea is valuable and the paper is likely to interest researchers working on incomplete event data. However, the authors need to address the concerns about baseline comparisons, particle sensitivity, the missingness mechanism, and model misspecification before the conclusions can be considered fully supported.

I would be glad to review a revised version, and I believe the authors can address these points within a reasonable timeframe. With these changes, the paper could make a solid contribution to the literature on inference for continuous-time event data.

Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary: Wildlife, Habitats, Visitor Information, and Conservation History

Welcome to this introduction to Ranganathittu Bird Sanctuary, a small but richly rewarding wetland reserve in southern Karnataka. The sanctuary is made up of a cluster of islands in the Kaveri River, a river that has shaped the agriculture and culture of the region for centuries. Because the islands are small and surrounded by water, the sanctuary offers a concentrated view of river-island ecology. Visitors often describe it as one of the most accessible places in India to observe waterbirds up close. The reserve lies within easy reach of Mysuru and Bengaluru, which has helped make it a popular destination for families, students, and naturalists. This page explains what lives there, the habitats that support them, how to plan a visit, and how the sanctuary came to be protected.

The landscape of the sanctuary is defined by the river itself. The Kaveri flows around and between the islands, creating shallow channels, sandbars, and quiet backwaters. During the monsoon season the water level rises, flooding parts of the islands and changing the availability of food and nesting sites. As the water recedes in the dry months, exposed mud and sandbanks become important feeding grounds. This seasonal rhythm of flooding and drying is central to the ecology of the sanctuary. Many of the plants along the banks have adapted to periodic inundation.

The vegetation on the islands includes tall trees that provide roosting and nesting platforms, along with shrubs, grasses, and reed beds at the water's edge. Mixed riparian woodland gives shade and shelter, while open patches allow birds to dry their wings and rest. Dense thickets offer protection from predators for smaller species. The variety of plant cover is one reason the sanctuary supports such a diverse community of birds.

Birdlife is the main attraction. Visitors commonly see painted storks, spot-billed pelicans, and cormorants gathering in large numbers, especially in the breeding season. Egrets, herons, and ibises are regular sights along the water's edge. Darters, often called snake birds, can be seen perched with their wings spread to dry. Kingfishers, including the common and white-throated species, hunt from low branches and rocks. Migratory waterbirds arrive during the cooler months from distant regions, adding to the variety on display. The exact number of species recorded varies from year to year, so current checklists from the forest department or local guides are the most reliable source.

Mammals and reptiles also live in the sanctuary, though they are less conspicuous than birds. Mongooses, various rodents, and otters may occur in suitable areas, and the river supports fish, turtles, and crocodiles. Mugger crocodiles are a notable part of the riverine fauna, and visitors should respect the warnings posted near the water. Insects, including dragonflies and butterflies, are abundant in the warmer months and contribute to the food web that sustains the birds.

The sanctuary is best visited in the cooler months, roughly from November to February, when weather is pleasant and many migratory birds are present. The breeding season, typically during the monsoon and early post-monsoon period, brings colonies of nesting birds, but visitors should keep their distance to avoid disturbing them. Early mornings and late afternoons are often the most productive times for birdwatching, as birds are most active then. The sanctuary is open to visitors during daylight hours, and the forest department usually sets the operating schedule, which should be confirmed before travel.

Getting there is straightforward. The sanctuary is located near Srirangapatna, about 15 to 20 kilometres from Mysuru, and is reached by road. Boat rides on the river are a popular way to explore the islands and are usually arranged at the entry point. Boats typically operate in fixed slots, and the number of passengers and fares are regulated, so it is wise to ask at the counter. Binoculars and a camera with a good zoom lens greatly improve the experience. Comfortable walking shoes, sun protection, drinking water, and a light rain jacket are sensible additions to any day trip. Food and refreshments may be limited on the islands, so bringing snacks is helpful. Visitors are asked to avoid littering, keep noise low, and stay on designated paths and boat routes. Feeding the birds is discouraged, as it can alter their natural behaviour and harm their health.

The history of conservation in this area is closely tied to the protection of the Kaveri River and its wildlife. Before formal protection, the islands were used in ways typical of riverine communities, but the presence of nesting waterbirds drew the attention of naturalists and local authorities. Over time, the area was recognised as an important habitat that deserved legal protection. It was declared a bird sanctuary to safeguard its breeding colonies and migratory visitors from hunting and habitat loss. The exact year and legal instrument of notification should be verified with official government records, as details can differ between sources.

Management of the sanctuary has evolved over the decades. The forest department oversees the reserve, regulates visitor access, monitors bird populations, and works to maintain water quality and habitat condition. Conservation challenges include water pollution from surrounding human activity, changes in river flow due to irrigation and upstream dams, pressure from tourism, and the spread of invasive plants. Addressing these issues requires coordination between government agencies, local communities, researchers, and visitors. Many successful conservation efforts depend on sustained monitoring and public awareness, and the sanctuary has become a useful site for education and research on river ecosystems.

Community involvement has also played a role. Local residents who depend on the river for farming and fishing have a stake in its health, and their knowledge of the seasons and the river's behaviour is valuable. Boatmen and guides often have decades of experience observing the birds and can share insights that complement scientific surveys. Responsible tourism that supports local livelihoods while limiting disturbance is widely seen as the most sustainable path forward.

Education is a central purpose of the sanctuary. School groups visit to learn about food chains, migration, and the importance of wetlands. Simple lessons about why birds need clean water and undisturbed nesting sites help visitors understand the broader value of conservation. Many of the most important ecological lessons can be learned simply by sitting quietly and watching how birds use the islands through the day.

Research and monitoring continue to shape management decisions. Periodic bird counts help track changes in population size and species composition. Water quality testing reveals the health of the river, while vegetation surveys show how the islands are changing over time. Such data allow managers to respond to problems early, whether that means controlling invasive species, adjusting visitor routes, or working with upstream authorities on water management. Researchers and students are encouraged to coordinate with the forest department before conducting studies.

Looking ahead, the future of Ranganathittu depends on balancing the needs of wildlife, people, and the river. Climate variability may alter monsoon patterns and the timing of breeding seasons, making long-term monitoring more important than ever. Protecting the quality of water flowing into the sanctuary is perhaps the single most important conservation task. Continued public support, careful visitor management, and sound science will help ensure that this small river-island sanctuary remains a home for birds and a source of wonder for future generations.

For planning purposes, always check the latest visitor timings, boat fares, entry fees, and any closure notices with the Karnataka Forest Department or official tourism information before your trip, since these details can change. Respecting the rules of the sanctuary helps protect the birds and keeps the experience enjoyable for everyone.

This paper addresses an important problem in uncertainty estimation: distinguishing noisy in-domain data from genuinely out-of-distribution inputs, a distinction that many deployed systems fail to make. The authors build on Dirichlet prior networks, which predict the parameters of a distribution over class probabilities so that both data uncertainty and distributional uncertainty can be represented. The central contribution is a training objective designed to encourage the network to express high data uncertainty for noisy in-domain examples while expressing high distributional uncertainty for out-of-distribution inputs. The motivation is clearly articulated, and the authors correctly observe that standard softmax confidence conflates these two sources of uncertainty. The related work section covers the relevant lines of research on predictive uncertainty, ensembles, and prior networks, though it could more directly compare against recent Bayesian and evidential deep learning baselines. The method is described with sufficient mathematical detail to be reproduced in principle, although the derivation of the loss terms would benefit from a more intuitive explanation for readers less familiar with Dirichlet distributions. The experimental setup evaluates the approach on image classification benchmarks with synthetic label noise and standard out-of-distribution datasets, which is an appropriate testbed. The reported results show improvements in detection metrics such as AUROC over softmax-based and entropy-based baselines, and the gains are consistent across most settings. However, the paper would be stronger with error bars or results across multiple random seeds, since several reported differences are small enough that variance could plausibly account for them. The ablation study isolating each component of the training objective is valuable, though the choice of hyperparameters controlling the weighting of these terms is not justified and may have been tuned on the evaluation data. I would also ask the authors to clarify how the noise injection process was implemented, as the conclusions depend heavily on whether the noise resembles realistic labeling errors or only artificial perturbations. The discussion of computational cost is limited, and a comparison of training time and inference overhead relative to ensemble methods would help practitioners judge the trade-offs. The theoretical analysis is brief, and while it offers intuition about why the objective separates the two uncertainty types, it does not establish formal guarantees under stated assumptions. The limitations section acknowledges some restrictions but omits discussion of how sensitive the method is to the choice of out-of-distribution data used during training. Figures are generally clear, though the calibration plots would be easier to interpret with the number of samples per bin indicated. The writing is mostly precise, with a few passages in the methodology section that repeat notation without definition and could be tightened. Overall, the paper tackles a meaningful problem with a reasonable approach and sound initial evidence. I recommend a major revision that adds statistical reporting, clarifies the noise protocol, justifies hyperparameter choices, and expands the comparison to contemporary baselines. With these changes, the work would make a useful contribution to the uncertainty estimation literature.

The manuscript studies margin maximization, generalization, and convergence of gradient flow for one-hidden-layer neural networks in the mean-field regime. The authors situate their work within a growing literature that views training dynamics of wide networks through the lens of measures on parameter space rather than finite-dimensional weight vectors. The central motivation is clear and timely, since the mean-field viewpoint offers a tractable route to understanding why overparameterized networks trained by gradient descent often find solutions with good generalization. The introduction is well organized and places the contribution relative to neural tangent kernel analyses, prior margin-based generalization bounds, and earlier mean-field results. I appreciate that the authors are explicit about what their theory does and does not cover, which helps the reader calibrate expectations.

The problem formulation is set up for a binary classification task with a homogeneous activation, a logistic or exponential-type loss, and an infinite-width limit of a single hidden layer. The choice of a homogeneous activation is essential to the margin analysis, and the authors explain this reasoning in a way that is accessible. However, the assumptions on the data distribution could be stated more prominently, as some of the later results depend on separability and boundedness conditions that appear only in passing. A short summary table of assumptions, with a note on which theorems require which, would substantially improve readability.

The main theoretical contribution is a convergence result showing that the measure-valued gradient flow converges in direction toward a max-margin solution under the stated conditions. The argument proceeds through a limiting analysis of the normalized margin, and the logic is largely sound on my reading. I particularly liked the decomposition of the proof into a stage capturing the early phase of separation and a later stage capturing directional convergence. That said, several steps rely on asymptotic arguments whose uniformity in time is not fully justified, and I would ask the authors to clarify whether the constants depend on the time horizon in a way that matters for the claimed rates.

Regarding the generalization component, the authors derive a margin-based bound that scales with the inverse of the normalized margin and an appropriate complexity measure of the hidden layer. The dependence on width is handled carefully, and the authors make the nice observation that the bound does not deteriorate as the number of neurons grows, provided the normalization is chosen appropriately. This is an important point and deserves to be emphasized more in the discussion, since it distinguishes the result from classical capacity bounds that grow with parameter count. The complexity measure used is a Rademacher-type quantity over the unit ball of a reproducing space, and the authors bound it by an expression in terms of the scale of the output weights.

I would like to see a more detailed comparison with existing generalization bounds for two-layer networks, including those based on path norms and on Barron-type function spaces. The paper currently mentions these works briefly but does not provide a quantitative comparison of the bounds in a common regime. Such a comparison would clarify whether the mean-field margin bound is tighter in some regimes, looser in others, or simply different in its dependence on problem parameters. A table or a short numerical illustration would make this much more digestible.

The experimental section is modest and consists mainly of simulations on synthetic two-dimensional datasets and a small subset of a standard benchmark. The simulations are useful for visualizing the directional convergence of the normalized weights toward the max-margin direction, and the plots are clear. The benchmark experiment is less convincing, however, because the network width and training horizon used are far from the infinite-width regime that the theory addresses. The authors acknowledge this gap, which is commendable, but I would encourage either a sweep over width to show the trend toward the theoretical behavior or a more explicit statement that the experiments are illustrative rather than confirmatory.

The writing is generally precise, though some notation is overloaded. The symbol for the margin is used both for the unnormalized quantity and for its normalized counterpart in certain places, which can cause confusion when tracking the limiting arguments. Several figures lack informative captions, and the appendix proofs would benefit from brief roadmaps indicating which lemmas feed into which theorems. Minor typographical issues appear in the bibliography, including inconsistent capitalization of venue names.

The literature review is thorough in its coverage of mean-field theory, implicit bias of gradient descent, and margin theory, but it could more clearly delineate what is new. Several results in the paper overlap with prior work on the implicit bias of homogeneous networks, and the authors should state precisely which statements are extensions and which are restatements in the mean-field setting. Doing so would help the reader assess the originality of each contribution and would strengthen the paper's positioning.

The discussion section raises interesting open questions, including whether the directional convergence result extends to deeper networks and whether the margin bound can be sharpened under additional structure on the data. I found the discussion of the role of the activation function particularly thoughtful, as it points to a concrete direction for future analysis. The authors might also note that the mean-field limit presumes a particular scaling of the learning rate with width, and they should discuss how sensitive the conclusions are to departures from this scaling in finite networks.

Overall, I consider this a solid and useful contribution that connects three threads of theory in a coherent way. The main convergence result appears correct to the extent I could verify, and the generalization bound is a worthwhile addition. My principal requests are for a clearer statement of assumptions, a more careful treatment of uniformity in the limiting arguments, a quantitative comparison with existing bounds, and stronger experiments or a more cautious framing of them. I also recommend tightening notation and clarifying novelty relative to prior work on homogeneous networks.

I recommend acceptance conditional on a minor revision addressing these points. The changes requested are substantive in places but feasible within a single revision cycle, and I believe the revised version would be a valuable addition to the literature on the theory of neural network training.

Supporting a soccer team means more than cheering when the ball hits the back of the net. True loyalty is revealed in the difficult moments, when results go against the side and the stadium falls quiet. Fans who stay with their team through victories and defeats show a commitment that gives players a sense of security and purpose. Winning is exciting, but it often comes easily to fans, while losing tests whether their support is genuine. When a team concedes a late goal or suffers a humiliating loss, players feel the weight of disappointment, and a loyal crowd can lift their spirits and encourage them to keep trying. Such encouragement matters because athletes learn as much from setbacks as from triumphs, and they need supporters who believe in their growth over the long term. Defeats also offer fans lessons about patience, resilience, and fairness, reminding them that sport is a journey rather than a series of guaranteed rewards. A supporter who stays present during a losing streak helps build a culture of respect within the club, where effort is valued alongside results. This steady presence can strengthen the bond between a team and its community, creating a shared identity that survives changes in form. Clubs with devoted fans often recover from hard seasons more quickly because their players feel backed rather than abandoned. Furthermore, the atmosphere created by loyal supporters can influence the outcome of matches, as players draw energy from a crowd that keeps singing after the final whistle. In the end, supporting a team through both victories and defeats reflects maturity and a genuine love for the game. Such devotion transforms a simple spectator into a meaningful part of the team's story. It is a reminder that the true measure of a club is not only its trophies, but the people who stand behind it when times are hard.

Allowing mobile devices in classrooms is one of the most debated questions in modern education, and the answer depends heavily on how those devices are used. On one hand, phones and tablets offer students fast access to information, translation tools, interactive simulations, and digital textbooks that can make abstract ideas easier to grasp. On the other hand, the same devices carry constant notifications, social media, and games that compete for attention. Research on this topic is still developing, but several patterns have emerged that help clarify the trade-offs. The effect on focus is perhaps the most immediate concern. Studies of multitasking suggest that switching attention between a lesson and a phone reduces comprehension, and even a device sitting face down on a desk can pull attention away because students feel the pull to check it. Many teachers report that students who keep phones within reach are more likely to drift off task during lectures or discussions. Academic honesty raises a separate set of issues. Phones make it easy to look up answers during tests, share information through messaging apps, or use artificial intelligence tools to generate work that is then passed off as original. Schools that permit devices must therefore think carefully about assessment design, and many have shifted toward in-class writing, oral presentations, and supervised testing to reduce these risks. Learning outcomes are where the evidence is most mixed. When teachers deliberately design lessons that use devices for research, collaboration, or immediate feedback through polling tools, students can deepen their understanding and build digital skills they will need later. However, when devices serve mainly as entertainment or as an unstructured free-time option, learning tends to suffer. The difference lies less in the technology itself than in the purpose and planning behind its use. Equity also deserves attention. Students without reliable personal devices or internet access may fall behind when lessons assume everyone can participate digitally, while those with advanced devices may gain an advantage. Schools that allow phones should consider whether they can provide equal access so that no student is left out. Ultimately, mobile devices in classrooms are neither inherently harmful nor inherently beneficial. Clear rules, purposeful teaching, thoughtful assessment, and attention to fairness can allow schools to capture their educational value while limiting their distractions. Without these safeguards, however, the risks to focus and honesty are likely to outweigh the gains.

This paper proposes using image quality metrics as alternative energy functions to improve image generation in Boundary Equilibrium GAN (BEGAN) models, offering a fresh perspective on the training objective beyond the standard autoencoder reconstruction loss. The authors clearly motivate the problem by noting that the reconstruction-based energy used in BEGAN may not align well with perceptual image quality, which is a sensible and important question for the generative modeling community. The experimental design compares several perceptual and structural metrics as drop-in energy functions, which makes the contribution easy to understand and reproduce in principle. However, the evaluation relies heavily on a limited set of quantitative scores, and the manuscript would be considerably stronger with a broader human perceptual study to validate that metric improvements translate to visually better samples. The paper would also benefit from a more thorough ablation analysis isolating the effect of each metric, as well as clearer reporting of training stability across random seeds, since GAN results are often sensitive to initialization. The related work section is useful but somewhat selective, and a more detailed discussion of how the proposed approach relates to other energy-based and perceptual-loss formulations for GANs would help position the contribution. Some hyperparameter choices, including the weighting between the adversarial and metric-based terms, are described only briefly, and their sensitivity should be examined more carefully. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful question with a reasonable approach, and with additional validation and analysis it could make a useful contribution to the literature.

Playing sports outdoors with family and friends offers benefits that reach far beyond the playing field. Fresh air, open space, and physical activity combine to create an experience that strengthens the body, the mind, and the bonds between people. For students, these benefits are especially valuable because they help balance hours spent in classrooms and in front of screens.

The most obvious advantage is physical health. Running, throwing, kicking, and jumping build strength, endurance, and coordination in ways that are enjoyable rather than tedious. Unlike a gym workout, a game of soccer or catch in the park does not feel like a chore, so people are more likely to keep coming back to it. Regular outdoor exercise also helps lower the risk of obesity, heart disease, and other conditions linked to inactivity.

Sunlight adds another dimension to the benefits. Time outside allows the body to produce vitamin D, which supports bone strength and immune function. Many people also find that natural light helps regulate their sleep patterns, leaving them more rested and alert during the day. Fresh air, far removed from the stuffiness of indoor spaces, can make physical effort feel lighter and more refreshing.

Mental health may benefit even more than the body. Studies have suggested that spending time in green spaces can reduce stress and improve mood. Physical activity releases chemicals in the brain that are associated with feeling good, and combining exercise with nature can amplify this effect. A student who arrives home from a game of basketball in the park often feels calmer and more focused than one who has spent the same time sitting at a desk.

Playing with family and friends adds a social layer that makes the experience richer still. Sports require communication, cooperation, and trust, all of which strengthen relationships. Parents who play with their children show them that activity is worth making part of life, while siblings and cousins learn to compete fairly and celebrate one another's successes. Friendships formed or deepened on the field often last well beyond the final whistle.

Outdoor play also teaches valuable lessons that carry into other areas of life. Students learn to handle winning and losing with grace, to follow rules, and to take responsibility for their teammates. They discover how to solve problems on the spot, such as adjusting strategy when the other team changes tactics. These skills translate naturally into classrooms, workplaces, and communities.

Family sports can also create lasting memories. A family baseball game on a summer evening or a weekend hike followed by a friendly match becomes a shared story that people recall for years. These moments give young people a sense of belonging and identity, reminding them that they are part of a supportive group. Many adults look back on such experiences as some of the happiest times in their childhood.

Finally, playing sports outdoors encourages a lifelong relationship with physical activity. Children who enjoy games with their families are more likely to stay active as teenagers and adults, carrying healthy habits into the future. In a world where sedentary lifestyles are increasingly common, the simple act of stepping outside to play together offers a powerful and accessible path to well-being. Students who embrace this habit are investing in their health, their relationships, and their happiness for years to come.

The manuscript proposes an SO(3)-equivariant capsule network for point-cloud classification and pose estimation, and evaluates it across multiple rotation representations and experimental protocols. The topic is timely and well motivated, since rotation robustness remains a practical concern for point-cloud perception in robotics and 3D vision. The authors position their contribution clearly against prior equivariant point-cloud architectures, and the introduction articulates the gap in how capsule-based routing interacts with equivariance constraints. The conceptual framing of capsules as pose-carrying entities is a natural fit for pose estimation, and this alignment is one of the paper's stronger arguments. The related work section is generally thorough, although it would benefit from a more direct comparison with recent group-equivariant convolutional and transformer-based point-cloud methods. The method section describes the equivariant feature construction and the routing procedure in reasonable detail, though the derivation of the equivariance property would be easier to verify with an explicit statement of the group action on each capsule layer. The choice to compare several rotation representations, including Euler angles, quaternions, and rotation matrices, is a valuable design decision that addresses a question often left implicit in the literature. However, the paper does not fully justify why the representation should affect the learned equivariance in the way the results suggest. The experimental protocols include both canonicalized and unaligned settings, which is appropriate, but the split definitions and augmentation policies need more precise specification to allow reproduction. Reported accuracy gains on the classification benchmark are consistent across the main table, yet the margins over the strongest baselines are modest and are presented without confidence intervals or variance across random seeds. The pose estimation results are more compelling, particularly in the high-rotation regime, where the equivariant design appears to offer clear robustness benefits. The ablation study isolating the routing mechanism from the equivariant backbone is informative, but a further ablation removing capsule structure entirely would help clarify its specific contribution. Computational cost is reported only briefly, and a fuller comparison of parameter counts, training time, and inference latency would strengthen the practical claims. The authors acknowledge some limitations regarding sensitivity to point density, which is welcome, though the discussion could address how the method behaves under noisy or partial scans typical of real sensors. The qualitative visualizations of learned capsule activations are suggestive but do not yet convincingly demonstrate that capsules encode interpretable pose components. Some notation is inconsistent between the method section and the figures, particularly in the indexing of capsule layers and group elements, and this should be corrected. The writing is generally clear, though several paragraphs in the experiments section are dense and would benefit from tables summarizing protocol differences. The code availability statement is appreciated, but the authors should confirm that the released implementation includes the exact configurations used for all reported results. Overall, the paper makes a credible and useful contribution, and the rotation-representation study is a meaningful strength. I recommend a major revision addressing statistical reporting, protocol specification, and the interpretability claims, after which the work could be a valuable addition to the venue.

Tailors and seamstresses are needed in clothing shops, dry cleaners, and bridal boutiques, where precise hands and an eye for detail are highly valued. Beyond employment, sewing can also be a valuable source of independence. A person who can mend a torn seam, replace a button, or shorten a pair of pants saves money and avoids waste, which matters for families on a tight budget. In a time when clothing is often cheap and quickly discarded, the ability to repair and adjust garments extends their life and reduces the need to buy new ones. Sewing also supports people in creative and practical ways, such as making curtains, pillow covers, or bags for their home. The skill can even help in emergencies, since a quick repair to a backpack strap or a tent can make a real difference while camping or traveling. The confidence that sewing builds is just as important as the material benefits. Learning to read a pattern, measure accurately, and finish a project teaches patience and persistence. Each completed item gives the sewer a sense of accomplishment that carries over into other areas of life. Mistakes, which are inevitable, become lessons rather than failures, because a seam can be picked apart and sewn again. Over time, this process strengthens problem-solving skills and self-assurance. For students, sewing offers a meaningful way to learn these lessons while gaining skills that may someday become a profession. Whether pursued as a career, a household necessity, or a personal pastime, sewing equips people with abilities that are both practical and empowering.

Before making a significant decision, it is wise to seek out a range of viewpoints. Individuals who rely only on their own perspective risk overlooking facts, consequences, and alternatives that others would readily notice. Diverse perspectives expose the blind spots that every person carries, whether those blind spots come from experience, upbringing, or simple habit. A decision that seems obvious to one person may look questionable to someone with a different background.

Consider the history of major public policies. Many failed initiatives were designed by small groups of people who shared similar assumptions about how communities would respond. When planners later heard from residents, workers, and experts in other fields, they discovered problems that had been invisible from their original vantage point. Those lessons show that breadth of input is not a formality but a practical safeguard.

Diversity of perspective also strengthens the quality of reasoning itself. When people hold different views, they are forced to explain and defend their positions with clear evidence. Weak arguments are more easily exposed, and strong ideas are refined through challenge. The result is a decision that has been tested rather than merely accepted.

Gathering many viewpoints does not mean that every opinion carries equal weight. A thoughtful decision-maker evaluates each perspective for its reliability, relevance, and supporting evidence. Some voices will be better informed on certain questions than others, and wisdom lies in recognizing that difference. The goal is not to count votes but to understand the full shape of a problem.

There are also practical costs to ignoring other viewpoints. A business that fails to consult its customers may develop products nobody wants. A family that makes a major move without discussing it with its members may face resentment and unforeseen hardship. In each case, the missing perspective would have prevented a predictable mistake.

Diverse input can also build trust. When people feel that their concerns have been heard, they are more likely to accept a decision even if it does not match their preference. This acceptance matters, because a decision that is widely supported is more likely to be carried out effectively. Inclusion, in this sense, serves both fairness and results.

Of course, seeking many perspectives takes time and effort, and there is always a risk of delay. A decision-maker may be tempted to gather endless opinions without ever committing to a course of action. Good judgment requires knowing when enough information has been collected and when the moment has come to act. The purpose of consultation is to improve the decision, not to postpone it indefinitely.

In the end, gathering diverse perspectives reflects humility. It acknowledges that no single person, however intelligent or experienced, sees everything clearly. Seeking out other views is an admission that understanding is built collectively. Those who practice this habit tend to make wiser choices, and their choices tend to hold up better over time.

The Electoral College has been a subject of debate since the Constitutional Convention of 1787, and its fairness remains contested today. Supporters argue that it protects federalism by giving states a voice in selecting the president, rather than leaving the choice entirely to national popular vote. Under this system, each state receives electors equal to its total number of senators and representatives, which gives smaller states a weight in presidential elections that they would otherwise lack. Critics, however, point out that this arrangement can produce outcomes in which the candidate who wins the national popular vote does not win the presidency. Such results have occurred several times in American history, most recently in 2016, and they raise questions about whether the system reflects the will of the majority of voters. Defenders respond that the framers intended the Electoral College as a deliberate check on direct democracy, designed to prevent a candidate from winning through regional or demographic appeals alone. They also note that a candidate must build a broad geographic coalition across many states to win, which in their view encourages national rather than purely local campaigning. Opponents counter that the current design produces uneven attention, since a small number of closely contested swing states receive most campaign resources while many other states are largely ignored. Voters in safe states, whether Republican or Democratic, may feel that their ballots matter less, which undermines the principle of equal political participation. The distribution of electoral votes also raises concerns about representation. Because every state is guaranteed at least three electors, less populous states have proportionally more influence per resident than larger states such as California or Texas. Supporters see this as a fair reflection of the compromise that formed the Union, while critics argue it dilutes the principle of one person, one vote. The winner-take-all method used by most states compounds these effects by awarding every elector to the statewide plurality winner. This means that a candidate who wins a state by a narrow margin gains the full bloc of electoral votes, while the losing voters in that state have no direct representation in the outcome. Some states, notably Maine and Nebraska, allocate electors by congressional district, but most do not, and this variation complicates any claim that the system treats voters uniformly. Reform proposals have attempted to address these concerns in different ways. The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact would have participating states award their electors to the national popular vote winner, though it has not taken effect because it depends on states representing a majority of electoral votes. Other proposals would abolish the Electoral College and move to a direct national vote, or would require proportional allocation of electors in every state. Each approach involves trade-offs between majority rule, state influence, and the stability of the electoral process. Ultimately, whether the Electoral College fairly represents voters depends on which definition of fairness one emphasizes. If fairness means equal weight for each individual vote nationwide, the system falls short, because votes in some states carry far more influence than others. If fairness means preserving the federal character of the republic and ensuring that candidates address a broad range of states, the system has defenders who find it reasonable. Reasonable citizens may weigh these values differently, and the debate reflects deeper disagreements about the purpose of American democracy. Whatever one's position, the Electoral College remains a central feature of presidential elections, and its design continues to shape how candidates campaign and how voters understand their own influence. Understanding its strengths and weaknesses is therefore essential for any thoughtful citizen evaluating the health of the nation's democratic institutions.

Targeted Reading Support Through Neuroscience-Based Intervention

Many students who struggle with English language and reading need more than general classroom instruction. A neuroscience-based intervention draws on what researchers have learned about how the brain processes spoken and written language to design focused, effective support. Reading depends on connecting letters to sounds, sounds to meaning, and meaning to comprehension, and each link can be strengthened with structured practice. Phonological awareness, the ability to recognize and manipulate the sound units of speech, is one of the strongest predictors of early reading success. Explicit, systematic phonics instruction helps students build reliable connections between graphemes and phonemes, reducing the cognitive load of decoding. Repeated, guided reading of connected text supports fluency, allowing word recognition to become automatic so attention can shift to meaning. Vocabulary instruction is most effective when new words are taught in rich contexts and revisited across multiple sessions, which strengthens memory traces. Interventions are typically delivered in small groups or one-to-one sessions, several times per week, for a defined period. Progress is monitored with brief assessments so that instruction can be adjusted to each student's needs. Multisensory activities, such as tracing letters while saying their sounds, may engage several neural pathways at once and can aid memory for some learners. Oral language practice, including structured discussion and retelling, builds the grammatical and semantic knowledge that comprehension requires. Attention and working memory also matter, so sessions are kept short, focused, and well-paced to avoid overload. Feedback is immediate and specific, which supports learning by reinforcing correct responses and correcting errors promptly. Students are encouraged to build confidence through success, since motivation and a sense of competence influence how readily the brain engages with challenging tasks. Teachers and specialists collaborate to align the intervention with classroom instruction and to share observations about each student's progress. Families can support learning at home through shared reading, conversation, and encouragement. Research on these approaches continues to evolve, and educators should rely on evidence-based programs and ongoing professional judgment. With consistent, well-designed support, many students who once struggled gain the skills and confidence to read with independence and enjoyment.

The lawmakers stressed that the Agreement, which brought an end to decades of conflict known as the Troubles, remains a cornerstone of stability on the island of Ireland. They also condemned recent episodes of violence and intimidation, calling on all parties to reject paramilitary activity and to protect public officials and community workers. Several members said the European Union has a continuing interest in the region's peace, citing its role as a guarantor of the framework through the Withdrawal Agreement and the Northern Ireland Protocol arrangements. Officials in London and Dublin were also urged to remain engaged and to support confidence-building measures that could help break the impasse. Local political leaders have pointed to unresolved disputes over post-Brexit trade arrangements and questions of identity and governance as obstacles to progress. Critics of the current deadlock argue that repeated suspensions of the devolved assembly have left key public services without clear leadership and have weakened public trust in the political process. Supporters of the peace process, however, maintain that the institutions have survived previous crises and can do so again if the parties show political will. Community groups in both Belfast and Derry have called for renewed cross-community engagement, particularly among young people who did not experience the worst years of the conflict. The lawmakers said they would continue to monitor developments closely and offer diplomatic support to any credible initiative aimed at restoring full power-sharing. Analysts note that the coming months will be a critical test of whether the region's political leaders can move beyond short-term disputes and recommit to the principles that underpin lasting peace.

Phone use at school is a debate that touches on learning, well-being, and fairness. Many people believe that phones should be banned entirely during the school day, since they can distract students from lessons and encourage constant checking of social media. However, a complete ban may not be the best answer for every situation. Lunch time is a unique part of the school day, when students are not in class, are often tired from a morning of focused work, and need a chance to rest and recharge. During this period, allowing phones can help students stay in touch with family members, especially those who need to know that they are safe. Phones can also help students who have medical needs, such as checking blood sugar readings or contacting a parent about a health concern. Beyond safety, lunch is a social time, and some students use their phones to connect with friends who attend different schools or to share music and light entertainment that helps them relax. Allowing phones at lunch can therefore support emotional well-being as well as practical needs. At the same time, unrestricted use could lead to problems such as cyberbullying, inappropriate content, or students sitting silently in groups while staring at screens instead of talking to one another. For this reason, schools should set clear rules, such as allowing phones only in designated areas or after students finish eating. Teachers and staff should also explain why these rules matter so that students understand the reasons behind them. Trust is important here: when students are given responsibility, many will act responsibly. A balanced policy would limit phone use during class time while allowing reasonable access during lunch. This approach respects students' needs for rest and connection and still protects the learning environment. In the end, the goal should be to help students develop healthy habits with technology that they will carry into adulthood.

The basement lights hummed like insects, and Dale Wrenfield wiped his hands on a rag that had long since stopped being clean. The man tied to the chair had stopped screaming an hour ago. Now he only whimpered, a sound Dale found tedious.

He had done this for eleven years, always carefully, always alone. Tonight the silence in the room felt wrong, thick and attentive, as if the walls were listening.

Then the shadow in the corner moved against the light, though nothing cast it.

It unfolded slowly, too many joints bending in directions joints should not bend. Its face was a stretched, wet thing, eyes arranged along a seam that split when it smiled. Dale had expected terror, and he felt it briefly, but beneath the fear something older and hungrier stirred in him, and he recognized it as kinship.

"You have been practicing," the thing said. Its voice came from everywhere, a chorus of whispers beneath the floorboards.

Dale swallowed. "Who are you?"

"Call me what you like. You called me often enough in your sleep, though you never gave me a name."

The captive raised his head and begged, his voice breaking. The entity turned toward him with interest, like a connoisseur appraising a painting.

"He is tiresome," it said. "Let us make him useful."

Dale should have refused. Instead he heard himself ask what it wanted, and the answer slid into his mind smooth as oil. It wanted company. It wanted a partner for the long nights between the living and the dead, and it wanted someone who would not flinch at the things it liked to do.

"In return," it whispered, "you will never be caught. The police will look at the faces they expect and find nothing. Your hands will stay steady. Your conscience will sleep as soundly as a stone."

Dale laughed, a dry sound. He had always thought his conscience was already dead. Perhaps it had only been waiting for permission.

They worked together that night. The entity showed him techniques that no human manual had ever described, angles of pain and sequences of cruelty that bent the captive's body in ways Dale had only dreamed. He took notes in his head, delighted and sickened by his own delight.

When the man finally died, the entity sighed with pleasure and the room grew colder. Dale felt something leave him, a weight he had carried since childhood, and in its place came a hollow satisfaction.

At dawn he climbed the stairs, washed his hands, and made coffee. The entity sat across from him at the kitchen table, though no chair had been pulled out for it. Its smile stretched wider than it should.

"Tomorrow," it said, "we find the next one."

Dale nodded and drank his coffee. Outside, the morning was gray and ordinary, and no one would ever suspect a thing.

Venus is often called Earth's twin because the two planets are similar in size, mass, and composition, yet Venus has become a hostile world with surface temperatures near 465 degrees Celsius and crushing atmospheric pressure about ninety times that of Earth. Despite these dangers, exploring Venus is worth pursuing because it offers a unique window into how planets evolve. Studying why Venus developed a runaway greenhouse effect can help scientists better understand the long-term stability of Earth's own climate. Venus also holds clues about the early solar system, since its geology and atmosphere preserve records that have been erased or altered on other worlds. Recent proposals and missions, such as those studying the planet's possible volcanic activity and atmospheric chemistry, have shown that there are still major questions to answer. Robotic landers and orbiters are designed to survive harsh conditions, and advances in materials and engineering continue to make such missions more feasible. The risks of failure are real, but they are outweighed by the scientific value of the knowledge gained. Exploring Venus also pushes technological innovation, producing tools and techniques that benefit other areas of space science and industry. For these reasons, the challenges of Venus exploration are a reason to invest in it rather than a reason to abandon it.

Diligence and teamwork are two of the most powerful forces that help people reach their goals efficiently. Diligence is the steady commitment to working hard and staying focused over time, while teamwork is the ability to combine skills and effort with others. When these qualities work together, progress becomes faster, more reliable, and more rewarding. A diligent person sets clear goals and returns to them each day, even when the work becomes tedious or difficult. However, one person can only accomplish so much alone, no matter how hard they try. Teams make it possible to divide large tasks into smaller parts, so each member can focus on what they do best. Different people bring different strengths, and when they share knowledge, they often solve problems that would have stalled an individual. Diligence keeps the team moving forward, because each member takes responsibility for their own part and follows through on commitments. Regular communication within a team also prevents wasted effort, since everyone understands the shared direction and avoids duplicating work. Mistakes are also easier to catch when several people review the same task, which saves time that would otherwise be spent fixing errors later. Working together can also keep motivation high, since encouragement from others makes hard work feel more manageable. Over time, a diligent team builds trust, and that trust allows members to make decisions quickly without constant supervision. The result is a process that moves efficiently from start to finish. Many great achievements in history, from scientific discoveries to large construction projects, depended on both persistent effort and collaboration. Students can practice these habits in group projects by setting deadlines, sharing responsibilities, and checking in on each other's progress. In the end, diligence provides the determination to keep going, and teamwork provides the strength to go further together.
