Should students graduate from high school in three years, or should they take four years to prepare for the future? Three-year programs offer clear advantages. Students who finish early can save money on tuition, enter the workforce or college sooner, and avoid the boredom that some feel when they have already mastered their classes. Accelerated paths also reward motivated students who are ready to move on. However, four years give students time to explore interests, participate in sports, arts, and clubs, and develop the maturity that many young people need before facing adult responsibilities. A fourth year can also allow students to take advanced courses, earn internship experience, or recover from a difficult stretch without falling behind. Not every student learns at the same pace, and a rigid three-year timeline could push struggling students into a rush that harms their understanding. Ultimately, the best choice depends on the individual, so schools should offer both options and let students and families decide what preparation best fits their goals.

Rural women are among the most powerful agents of change in the fight against poverty and hunger, yet they often face barriers to land ownership, credit, schooling, and public decision-making. When women have equal rights to land, inheritance, and financial services, households are better able to produce food, earn income, and invest in their children's health and education. Access to education and practical training, including literacy, agricultural techniques, and business skills, enables rural women to improve crop yields, diversify livelihoods, and negotiate fairer prices for their goods. Reliable resources such as seeds, tools, savings groups, and microfinance help women weather droughts and economic shocks without falling into deeper hardship. Giving women a real voice in community decision-making, including cooperatives, water committees, and local government, ensures that programs address the needs they identify and are sustained over time. Strong legal protections against discrimination and gender-based violence are essential, since security and dignity are foundations for economic participation. Governments, NGOs, and private partners can support this work by investing in women-led initiatives and measuring progress through gender-disaggregated data. Together, these steps help build resilient rural communities where women and their families can move out of poverty and toward lasting food security.

Understanding California's Cap-and-Trade Offsets

California's cap-and-trade program is one of the most ambitious carbon pricing systems in the United States. Under the program, the state sets a limit, or cap, on greenhouse gas emissions from major polluters and issues allowances that companies must hold for each ton they emit. Companies that cut emissions below their allowances can sell the surplus, creating a market price for carbon. Alongside this system, the program allows regulated entities to use offsets, which are credits earned by projects that claim to reduce or remove greenhouse gases outside the capped sectors. Offsets are meant to lower compliance costs and reward useful climate action, but critics argue that they can weaken the program's core purpose.

The central concern is additionality. An offset is only valuable if the emissions reduction would not have happened without the credit. If a project would have proceeded anyway, because it was already profitable or required by other rules, the offset does not represent real climate benefit. Economists and environmental researchers have repeatedly raised questions about whether some forest, agricultural, and methane-capture projects meet this standard. When non-additional credits enter the market, they allow covered emitters to keep polluting while the official total appears to decline.

Measurement and verification present a second challenge. Many offset projects, especially those involving forests and soils, depend on models, baselines, and sampling methods that are difficult to check. Forests can burn, be harvested, or be damaged by disease, which threatens the permanence of stored carbon. Credits are often issued on the assumption that carbon will remain sequestered for decades, yet the actual storage may fall short. Buffer pools and insurance mechanisms exist to cover such losses, but their size and reliability are debated.

Offsets can also create a leakage problem. A project that protects one forest may simply shift logging or land clearing to a nearby area, so the net global benefit is smaller than reported. Similarly, a project that changes management practices in one location may increase emissions elsewhere. Accounting for leakage is technically complex, and imperfect estimates can overstate the climate gains from offsets.

A further concern involves the relationship between offsets and clean-energy investment. Cap-and-trade is designed to send a price signal that encourages companies to invest in cleaner technologies, such as efficient equipment, renewable power, and low-carbon fuels. If companies can meet their obligations cheaply with offsets, the incentive to make costly long-term changes may weaken. Over time, this could slow the deployment of technologies needed for deeper, lasting reductions.

The price effects are part of this debate. Abundant low-cost offsets can hold down allowance prices, which may be good for short-term affordability but reduce the signal that drives innovation. Policymakers therefore face a trade-off between keeping compliance costs modest and maintaining a price high enough to motivate real investment.

California has taken steps to address these risks. Regulators have limited the share of offsets companies may use for compliance, tightened protocols, and required certain projects to be located within the state or to deliver co-benefits to disadvantaged communities. Independent reviews have also prompted changes in how credits are validated. Supporters argue these reforms have improved integrity, while critics contend that the reforms do not go far enough.

Several questions remain open. Can offset protocols be designed to reliably detect additionality at scale? How should programs account for the long-term risk of reversal in forest and soil projects? What limit on offset use best balances cost control against the need for direct emissions cuts?

Policy design also affects the outcome. Some analysts recommend tighter caps on offset use, stronger verification, and a gradual phase-down of reliance on offsets as direct reductions become cheaper. Others propose separating funding for offsets from the compliance market, so that carbon removal and local projects can be supported without undermining the cap itself.

For students and citizens, the key lesson is that carbon markets are only as effective as the rules that govern them. A cap sets a limit, but the credibility of the limit depends on the quality of the credits allowed to count against it. Evaluating offsets requires attention to additionality, permanence, measurement, leakage, and the incentives they create for lasting investment in clean energy.

Ultimately, the debate over California's offsets reflects a broader tension in climate policy between flexibility and environmental integrity. Flexibility can lower costs and expand participation, but without strong safeguards it can allow emissions to persist behind a reassuring accounting figure. Ongoing monitoring, transparent data, and independent evaluation are essential to ensure that the program delivers the reductions it promises. Readers interested in the topic can consult publications from the California Air Resources Board, independent academic studies, and nonpartisan policy analyses to form their own assessments of how well the system is working.

The manuscript addresses weakly supervised object counting and localization, a setting in which models learn from image-level count labels rather than dense point or box annotations. The authors propose a rotation-robust regularization scheme combined with a sparsity constraint on feature maps, aiming to improve both the accuracy of predicted counts and the spatial quality of localization. The motivation is sound, since annotation cost is a major bottleneck in crowd counting, cell counting, and wildlife surveys, and the paper is well positioned within the recent literature on count-level supervision. The introduction clearly states the problem and the gap, although the claimed novelty could be sharpened by a more explicit comparison with prior rotation-equivariant and sparsity-based approaches. The related work section is thorough in covering density-map methods and weakly supervised counting, but it would benefit from discussing transformation-consistency regularizers more directly, since these are the closest conceptual relatives of the proposed rotation-robustness term. The method section describes the rotation-robust loss in reasonable detail, and the mathematical formulation of the sparse feature-map penalty is easy to follow. However, the choice of the sparsity weight and the rotation sampling strategy is not justified theoretically, and the authors should explain why these particular design decisions were preferred. The training procedure is described adequately for reproducibility at a high level, but several hyperparameters, including learning-rate schedules and augmentation parameters, are missing or only given in an appendix that was difficult to locate. The experimental setup uses standard counting benchmarks, which is appropriate, yet the paper would be stronger with evaluation on at least one dataset with substantial domain shift to test the claimed robustness. The reported results show consistent improvements in mean absolute error over the baselines the authors selected, which is encouraging. Nevertheless, some of the baselines appear to be older or re-implemented without matching training budgets, which may inflate the apparent gains. The localization evaluation relies on peak-based metrics, and the manuscript should clarify how peaks were extracted and whether the thresholds were tuned on the test data. The ablation study is useful in isolating the contributions of the rotation term and the sparsity term, but the results would be more convincing with variance estimates across multiple random seeds. The qualitative figures are informative, although the visualizations of sparse feature maps would benefit from a shared color scale across methods to allow fair comparison. The discussion of failure cases is a welcome addition, particularly the observation that heavily occluded or densely clustered objects remain challenging. The authors should expand this analysis to quantify how performance degrades as object density increases. The limitations section acknowledges the dependence on rotation-invariant object appearance, but it does not address whether the method generalizes to objects with strong orientation cues, such as vehicles or text. The conclusion summarizes the contributions accurately without overstating them, which is commendable. Overall, the paper presents a reasonable and practically relevant idea with credible but incremental improvements. Addressing the concerns about baseline fairness, statistical reporting, and domain-shift evaluation would substantially strengthen the work. I recommend a major revision before the manuscript can be considered for publication. The core contribution is promising, and with more rigorous experimentation and clearer justification of design choices, it could make a useful addition to the weakly supervised counting literature.

Working on a project alone and working with a group each offer distinct advantages and difficulties that shape the final outcome. Completing a project independently gives a student full control over the direction, pace, and quality of the work. There are no disagreements to resolve and no need to wait for others to finish their parts, so the student can follow their own ideas and develop a deeper sense of personal responsibility. Independent work also builds self-discipline and problem-solving skills, since the student must plan, research, and correct mistakes without immediate help. However, working alone can become isolating, and a single person may lack the range of knowledge needed for complex tasks. Without feedback from others, errors in reasoning can go unnoticed until late in the process. Group work, by contrast, brings together different strengths, perspectives, and skills, which often produces richer ideas and a more thorough final product. Members can divide labor, so large assignments become more manageable within a limited time. Collaboration also teaches communication, negotiation, and compromise, abilities that are valuable in nearly every professional setting. Yet group projects carry their own challenges, including unequal participation, scheduling conflicts, and disagreements over direction or credit. Some students end up doing more than their share while others contribute little, which can lead to resentment. Ultimately, the better choice depends on the nature of the task, the goals of the learner, and the willingness of the team to communicate openly. Balancing both approaches allows students to grow in independence while also learning to work well with others.

Digital tools have transformed the way people communicate, learn, entertain themselves, and solve everyday problems. In the area of communication, applications such as email, video calls, and messaging platforms allow people to stay connected with family and friends across great distances. Students can also collaborate on group projects in real time, sharing documents and ideas without meeting in person. In education, online resources give learners access to lectures, tutorials, and academic articles that were once available only in large libraries or universities. Interactive lessons and learning apps can adapt to each student's pace, making difficult subjects easier to understand. Entertainment has also been enriched by digital technology, with music, films, games, and books available instantly on many devices. These options allow people to explore new interests and enjoy creative experiences at any hour. Beyond leisure and study, digital tools help people solve everyday problems, such as using maps to navigate unfamiliar places or comparing prices before making a purchase. Calendars and reminder apps help individuals manage their time, while budgeting software supports better financial decisions. Although these tools bring many benefits, users must also learn to balance screen time and protect their privacy. When used thoughtfully, digital tools can make daily life more connected, informed, and efficient.

Scottish young people are facing widespread rejection and lengthy waits for mental health care, prompting growing calls for urgent reform from campaigners, clinicians, and families across the country.

Figures compiled from health service data and charity surveys suggest that thousands of children and young people referred for specialist support each year are turned away or placed on waiting lists that can stretch for many months. Many of those referred are assessed as needing help but do not meet the strict thresholds set by services, leaving them without support at a critical stage.

Campaigners say the situation has deteriorated in recent years, with demand rising sharply since the pandemic while staffing and funding have not kept pace. Some families report that their child's condition worsened significantly while they waited to be seen.

One parent, speaking on condition of anonymity, described months of repeated contact with health services after her daughter began experiencing severe anxiety and self-harm. She said the family was repeatedly told the case did not meet the criteria for specialist treatment, and was instead directed to general practice and online resources.

Clinicians working in the field have raised concerns about the way referrals are triaged. Some argue that rigid eligibility rules mean young people are often sent away until their difficulties become more serious, rather than being supported early when intervention is most effective.

Mental health professionals also point to shortages of trained staff, particularly child and adolescent psychiatrists and psychologists. Recruitment has proved difficult in many parts of the country, and rural areas face particular challenges in attracting and keeping specialists.

Waiting times vary considerably across Scotland's health boards. Some areas report that young people can wait well over a year for assessment, while others perform better, creating what campaigners describe as a postcode lottery in access to care.

The Scottish Government has acknowledged the pressures on services and has pointed to investment in mental health provision, including funding for school-based support and the expansion of community services. Officials have said that reducing waiting times remains a priority and that work is ongoing to improve access.

Critics, however, argue that announcements of new funding have not yet translated into meaningful change for young people on the ground. They say that without a clear and sustained plan, with measurable targets and transparent reporting, progress will remain slow.

Youth organisations have called for a more joined-up approach that brings together schools, primary care, social services, and specialist teams. They argue that young people should not have to navigate a fragmented system in which responsibility shifts between services.

Experts in youth mental health stress the importance of early intervention, noting that problems addressed in their early stages are often less severe, shorter in duration, and less costly to treat over time. They warn that rejection at the point of referral can have long-lasting consequences for education, employment, and wellbeing.

Some charities have called for the introduction of enforceable maximum waiting times for children and young people, similar to targets that exist for other parts of the health system. Supporters believe such measures would give families greater certainty and hold services to account.

Others have suggested that the thresholds for accessing specialist care should be reviewed so that young people with clear needs are not excluded on technical grounds. They argue that decisions should be guided by clinical judgement and the individual circumstances of each young person.

The issue has also drawn attention in the Scottish Parliament, where several members have raised questions about access to services and the consistency of care across regions. Some have pressed ministers for detailed data on rejection rates and the reasons behind them.

Young people themselves have spoken about the difficulty of asking for help. Several described feeling dismissed or misunderstood when they first sought support, and said that being turned away made them less willing to try again.

Youth advocates have emphasised that listening to young people must be central to any reform. They call for co-designed services that reflect the needs of those who use them, including accessible information and support that feels welcoming rather than bureaucratic.

Schools play a significant role in identifying distress, but teachers say they often lack the time, training, and resources to respond effectively. Some have called for dedicated mental health staff in every school and closer links with local specialist teams.

Primary care doctors also report feeling under pressure. Many say they are asked to manage complex cases with limited options, and that the lack of a clear route into specialist services leaves them frustrated and unable to offer the help they believe young patients need.

Financial constraints are central to the debate. Health budgets across the United Kingdom are under strain, and some economists argue that investment in youth mental health should be treated as a long-term priority, given the substantial costs of unmet need later in life.

Supporters of reform say that the cost of inaction is already visible in rising pressure on emergency departments, where young people in crisis are increasingly presenting after failing to access earlier help. They argue that prevention would ease this pressure over time.

Workforce planning is another key concern. Training more clinicians takes years, and some health leaders argue that the country must invest now to meet demand in the future. They also call for better support and career development to retain existing staff.

Digital services have been promoted as one way to widen access, and some young people have found online support helpful. However, experts caution that digital tools cannot replace face-to-face care for those with serious or complex needs, and that they should complement rather than substitute for specialist services.

Data transparency is also under scrutiny. Campaigners say that the publication of consistent, detailed statistics on referrals, rejections, and waiting times across all health boards is essential for understanding the scale of the problem and for tracking whether reforms are working.

Local communities have been affected too. Parents' groups and volunteer networks have stepped in to offer informal support, but many say they cannot replace professional care and that they are stretched by the demands placed on them.

Some families have turned to private providers, although the cost is prohibitive for most. Critics argue that this creates an unfair divide in which only those with money can secure timely help, deepening existing inequalities.

Rural and island communities face additional barriers, including travel distances and limited local services. Advocates say that any reform must address these geographical challenges and ensure that young people in remote areas receive the same standard of care.

Young people from minority ethnic backgrounds and those from deprived areas are also thought to face particular difficulties in accessing support. Researchers have called for targeted action to address these inequalities and to ensure services are culturally competent and inclusive.

Health leaders have welcomed the attention on the issue and say they share the goal of reducing waits and improving access. They point to ongoing service redesign projects and pilot programmes aimed at offering faster and more flexible routes into care.

Campaigners, however, say that pilots must be evaluated and expanded if they prove effective, rather than remaining small-scale initiatives. They warn that without national commitment, positive local examples will not help the many young people who need support now.

Looking ahead, the coming months are expected to bring further debate on how the system should change. Advocates hope that the current scrutiny will lead to concrete commitments, clear timelines, and sustained investment.

For the young people waiting for help, the stakes could not be higher. Many say they simply want to be heard, believed, and supported at the moment they reach out, and campaigners insist that this basic expectation should be met without further delay.

Wiltshire Police have launched an investigation after receiving reports of verbal approaches to schoolchildren in the Laverstock area near Salisbury. Officers were alerted to the incidents, in which children said they were spoken to by adults in a manner that made them feel uneasy. Police are appealing for anyone with information to come forward and are urging parents and carers to talk with their children about personal safety. Patrols have been increased in the area around local schools during the start and end of the school day. Detectives are reviewing any available evidence, including witness accounts and nearby CCTV footage. Police have asked the public to report any suspicious behaviour immediately by calling 999 in an emergency or 101 for non-emergencies. Anyone with information is also encouraged to contact Wiltshire Police and quote any relevant reference numbers.

Subject: Concerns Regarding Transco's Proposed Rate Increase and Disputed Return-on-Equity Analysis

Dear Colleagues,

I am writing to raise concerns about Transco's proposed rate increase and the return-on-equity analysis that supports it. The filing relies on a return-on-equity figure that several parties have challenged as higher than current market conditions and comparable pipeline returns would justify. Because the return-on-equity is a central input into the revenue requirement, even a modest change in that figure could translate into a significant difference in what ratepayers are asked to pay. The disputed methodology, including the choice of comparable companies and the treatment of capital structure, deserves close scrutiny before any rate decision is finalized. Intervenors have submitted testimony questioning these assumptions, and their arguments merit a full and transparent response from Transco. I recommend that we review the underlying workpapers and the expert testimony carefully so we can assess the strength of each position. Where the analysis appears unsupported, we should consider formally requesting additional data or an independent review. Ultimately, a fair rate outcome depends on a return-on-equity that reflects the actual risk and cost of capital, and I believe we should press for that standard. Please let me know your availability this week to discuss next steps.

Best regards,
[Your Name]

Two drivers have died in separate road accidents in Ayrshire, both involving vehicles that struck trees. Police Scotland said the first crash occurred on a rural road late on Saturday evening, when a car left the carriageway and collided with a tree, and the driver was pronounced dead at the scene. A second fatal collision took place the following morning, when another vehicle struck a tree on a separate route in the region, and the driver could not be saved despite the efforts of emergency services. Officers are appealing for witnesses and anyone with dashcam footage to come forward to help establish the circumstances of both incidents. Local residents have been urged to drive with extra care on rural roads, particularly in poor weather and at night. Next of kin have been informed, and the families have asked for privacy at this difficult time. Inquiries into the causes of both crashes are continuing.

Learning math in elementary school matters because it builds the foundation for every academic subject that follows. Young students who master counting, addition, and subtraction are better prepared to handle fractions, algebra, and eventually the complex problems they will face in high school and college. Early math skills also train the mind to think logically, break problems into smaller steps, and check whether an answer makes sense. These habits of reasoning extend far beyond arithmetic and help students in science, history, and writing as well. Mathematics teaches persistence, too, since many problems require trying different approaches before finding a solution. Students who learn to keep working through difficulty develop confidence that serves them in any challenging situation. Beyond the classroom, math appears constantly in daily life. Adults use it when they count change at a store, compare prices to find the better deal, and measure ingredients for a recipe. Budgeting a paycheck, estimating how long a trip will take, and understanding a loan or credit card statement all depend on basic number sense. Math also supports informed decision-making, because people who understand percentages and statistics are less likely to be misled by advertising or misinformation. Many careers, from nursing and engineering to retail and the skilled trades, require practical math every day. Even jobs that seem unrelated to numbers often involve scheduling, measuring, or tracking results. For these reasons, strong math instruction in the early grades gives children options and independence throughout their lives. Investing in elementary math education therefore benefits not only individual students but also their families, communities, and the wider economy.

Samsung has suspended a problematic Android update for its Galaxy S3 smartphones after a growing number of users reported serious issues following installation. Owners described rapid battery drain, apps crashing or refusing to open, and alarms that failed to sound at scheduled times, prompting concern among people who rely on their phones for daily routines. Reports began circulating on online forums and social media over the past several days, with many users saying the problems appeared shortly after the update was installed. Samsung acknowledged the complaints in a brief statement and confirmed that it had temporarily halted the rollout while its engineers investigate the cause. The company did not say how many devices were affected, though the volume of user reports suggests the problem was widespread. Affected owners were advised to avoid installing the update until a fix is available and to keep their devices charged and backed up in the meantime. Samsung also said it is reviewing its testing procedures to determine why the issues were not caught before the update reached customers. Technology analysts noted that the Galaxy S3 is an older model, and that software problems on aging hardware can be harder to resolve without compromising performance. Some users reported that rolling back to a previous software version helped restore normal function, though Samsung has not officially endorsed that approach. The company has said it will provide updates as its investigation progresses and will notify owners once a corrected version is ready for release. Customers with concerns are encouraged to contact Samsung support directly for assistance with their specific devices.

The manuscript proposes a parallel latent-variable framework for decomposing images into a shared scene background and individual object components, evaluated on Atari game frames and simulated room images. The problem is well motivated, since separating persistent background from discrete, movable objects is central to object-centric representation learning and to downstream planning and reasoning. The introduction situates the work clearly within the object-centric and slot-based literature, although it could more explicitly contrast the parallel design with sequential or recurrent alternatives such as iterative attention-based inference. The core methodological contribution, a set of parallel latent variables that jointly infer background and per-object latents without iterative refinement, is appealing because it promises computational efficiency and avoids order dependence among objects. However, the description of the generative model and its variational objective is difficult to follow in places, and the authors should provide a complete derivation of the evidence lower bound along with explicit definitions of all priors and conditional distributions. The choice of how many object slots to allocate, and how the model handles scenes with fewer objects than slots, is not adequately discussed and warrants a clear ablation. The Atari experiments are a reasonable testbed, but the paper would benefit from reporting results across a broader and more varied set of games, including those with scrolling backgrounds or heavy occlusion. The simulated-room experiments are valuable for controlled evaluation, yet the authors should specify the rendering pipeline, object distributions, and lighting variations so that the results can be reproduced. Quantitative metrics are reported for reconstruction error and segmentation quality, but the paper would be stronger with standard object-discovery measures such as adjusted mutual information and foreground adjusted Rand index, which allow direct comparison with prior work. The baseline comparisons are limited, and the omission of several recent slot-based and background-separation methods weakens the claim of improvement. The qualitative figures are informative, but several examples show objects merging or background artifacts leaking into object slots, and the authors should discuss these failure modes candidly rather than summarizing them as minor. The statistical reporting is thin: results appear to come from single training runs, and variance across seeds should be reported to support the stated differences. The discussion of limitations is brief and does not address how the approach scales to higher-resolution natural imagery or to objects that change appearance over time. The writing is generally clear at the level of high-level motivation but becomes dense in the technical sections, and a notation table would substantially aid readers. Code and trained model checkpoints are not mentioned, and releasing them would considerably increase the paper's value and reproducibility. Overall, the work offers a promising and efficient direction for scene decomposition, but the current version requires stronger baselines, multi-seed evaluation, more complete methodological detail, and a more thorough treatment of failure cases before its conclusions can be considered fully supported. My recommendation is major revision.

A rescued bull terrier has earned an award for her work as a police detection dog after a string of successful searches uncovered drugs, weapons, and hidden cash. The dog, named Bella, was surrendered to a local animal shelter two years ago after her previous owner could no longer care for her. Shelter staff noticed her high energy and intense focus during training exercises and recommended her for a canine detection program. After completing an intensive training course, Bella was partnered with Officer Mark Delaney of the city's narcotics unit. In her first year of active duty, she assisted in more than sixty searches across the county. Her finds included several kilograms of narcotics, three firearms concealed in vehicle panels, and thousands of dollars in cash hidden inside a residential wall. Police say her accuracy rate has been among the highest in the department. Last month, she received the Canine Service Award at the regional law enforcement ceremony in recognition of her contributions. Officer Delaney praised her dedication, saying she works tirelessly and never loses focus, even during long shifts. The department has also used Bella's story to encourage adoption from local shelters and to highlight the value of rescue animals in public service. Bella is expected to continue her duties for several more years, and officials say they hope her success inspires similar programs in neighboring communities.

The manuscript addresses a practically important problem: obtaining useful uncertainty estimates from neural networks without the cost of full Bayesian inference. The authors propose scalable Laplace approximations for Bayesian neural networks and position them against alternative uncertainty estimation methods, which is a relevant and timely comparison. The motivation is clearly stated, and the introduction places the work within the broader literature on approximate Bayesian inference and calibration. The central technical contribution, the scalable approximation of the posterior curvature, is described with sufficient detail to be followed, although several derivations would benefit from more explicit assumptions. The authors should state more precisely which approximation to the Hessian is used, how it scales with parameter count, and where the approximation is expected to break down. The experimental design covers standard classification benchmarks and includes out-of-distribution detection, which is appropriate for evaluating uncertainty quality. However, the comparison set would be stronger with the inclusion of deep ensembles and MC dropout trained under matched compute budgets, since these are the most common practical baselines. Reported metrics focus mainly on accuracy and negative log-likelihood, and the paper would benefit from calibration measures such as expected calibration error, along with reliability diagrams. Confidence intervals or results over multiple random seeds are not clearly reported, so it is difficult to judge whether the reported gains exceed run-to-run variance. The ablation study is informative but limited, and a sensitivity analysis over the prior precision and the choice of which layers receive the Laplace treatment would strengthen the conclusions. The runtime and memory measurements are welcome, yet they should be reported for both training and inference and across a range of model sizes to support the scalability claims. The discussion of limitations is brief and should address the dependence on a mode-finding step, the effect of underfitting or misspecification, and the known tendency of Laplace approximations to be overconfident far from the training data. The related work section is thorough on Laplace-based methods but could engage more with recent work on posterior-predictive approximations and last-layer Bayesian methods. Code availability is mentioned, which is commendable, and releasing configuration files for all experiments would aid reproducibility. The writing is generally clear, though some notation is overloaded and the definition of the predictive distribution should be stated earlier. Overall, the paper presents a useful and practical contribution, but the claims of scalability and superior uncertainty quality need more rigorous and complete empirical support. I recommend a major revision addressing the baseline comparisons, statistical reporting, and the limitations discussion before the work can be considered for acceptance.

Commander Mara Voss stood on the bridge of the *Halcyon* as the alien fleet tore open the sky above Mars. Forty-one ships had come through the rift in a single night, and every one of them was larger than the carrier that carried her. Her crew had stopped speaking an hour ago. The only sound was the low hum of the reactor and the steady countdown on the tactical display.

Earth was nine days behind the fleet, and the fleet was not slowing down.

Her weapons officer, Teodor Brankovic, looked up from his screen with bloodshot eyes. "Commander, our torpedoes are doing nothing. Their shields absorb everything we throw at them, and then they adapt. The second salvo bounces off."

"I know," Mara said. "I watched the first one bounce."

She had fought for twenty-two years, first in the Pacific patrols and then in the orbital wars that never made the news. She knew the feeling of a losing battle the way a sailor knows a coming storm. This was not a storm. This was the sea itself turning against them.

The sensor officer, a young woman named Ines Okafor, cleared her throat. "Commander, I'm picking up something odd. There's a signal, very faint, coming from beneath the surface of Phobos. Not a transmission. More like a pulse, repeating every eleven seconds."

Mara frowned. Phobos was a lump of rock, scarred and dead, and no survey had ever found anything inside it but ice and dust. "Is it natural?"

"No, ma'am. It has structure. It's mathematical."

The alien fleet began to fire. Mara watched a patrol cruiser disintegrate into a bloom of white light, and the crew inside it simply stopped existing. She made a decision she would later have trouble explaining to the admiralty.

"Get me a course to Phobos," she said. "All the power we have left. Pull everything else off the weapons."

Teodor stared at her. "Commander, we'll be dead in four minutes."

"Then we'd better go quickly."

The *Halcyon* turned, its engines screaming against the limits of their design, and slipped into the shadow of the moon while the alien ships hunted in the open. Two of them followed. Mara felt the hull shudder as their beams grazed the edge of the shields, then fell away as the moon's bulk blocked their line of sight.

The landing was rough. The ship came down on a shelf of ancient stone, and the impact threw Mara against the command chair. When she pulled herself up, the bridge windows showed not dust and black rock but a vast chamber, lit by a soft blue glow that seemed to come from the walls themselves.

They were not alone.

The figures came forward from the shadows, tall and slender, their skin the color of dusk. They did not carry weapons. One of them stepped toward the ship's airlock, and when the outer door opened, it spoke in a language that bypassed the translators entirely. Mara heard it inside her skull, clear as her own thoughts.

*You have come because the Hollowers have found you,* it said. *We have watched them for a long time. We could not stop them, and we are not able to fight them openly. But you can.*

Mara stepped down the ramp with her sidearm holstered. "Who are you?"

*We are what remains of the Seventh Concord. We left the old wars long ago and hid ourselves in the bones of the solar system. The Hollowers are a plague that consumes worlds, and every civilization that resists them is eventually eaten. We have survived only by staying small and silent.*

"Then why help us now?"

The alien paused, and its glow dimmed slightly. *Because the Hollowers are learning from you. Every battle they fight teaches them how your weapons work, how your ships move, how your people think. Soon they will know enough to hunt us, too. We cannot let them grow strong enough to find this place.*

Teodor had come down behind her, his hand on his holster. "What do you want from us?"

*A ship that can carry a seed into the heart of their fleet. Our technology, woven into the core of your reactor. It will unmake their shields, but only from the inside, and only if it is set to burn through the one thing that holds their fleet together, the mother-ship called the Anchor. It will kill the Anchor, and the fleet will fall apart.*

"And the price?" Mara asked, though she already suspected the answer.

The alien was quiet for a long moment. *The seed cannot be recovered. The ship that carries it must be destroyed when it detonates. And your reactor must be given to us, so that we may rebuild what we have lost. We will be stronger, and we will be exposed. Your world will owe us a debt for the rest of your history, and we cannot promise you will like the way we collect it.*

Mara thought of Earth, of the cities she had seen from orbit, of the children she had met on training leave and the crews she had buried. She thought of the Halcyon, the last serious warship in the Sol defense fleet, and the seventy-three people still aboard her.

She turned to Teodor and Ines, who had followed her down. "Get the crew to the escape pods," she said quietly. "Anyone who wants to leave, leave now. I'm going to need volunteers for the rest."

Ines shook her head. "Commander, I'm not leaving you."

Teodor said nothing, but he was already walking back toward the ship.

Mara turned back to the alien. "Show me how it works."

The glow of the chamber brightened, and the walls began to hum in harmony with the pulse Ines had detected. Mara felt something settle into her chest, heavy and certain, like the moment before a long fall. The price was real. She knew it would cost her the ship, her crew, and perhaps the trust of the people she had sworn to protect.

But if the Anchor fell, the fleet would scatter, and Earth would have a chance.

She reached for the console, and the light surged up around her, carrying her into a future she could not yet see.

Three days later, a single message reached the Sol defense network from the far side of Phobos. It was four words long, and it did not identify its sender. It said only: The Anchor is dead. Live well.

Should schools adopt a four-day week with longer school days in order to conserve energy and resources? This question has gained attention as districts search for ways to cut costs and reduce their environmental footprint. While the idea has real appeal, a careful look at the evidence suggests that the benefits are uneven and the trade-offs are significant.

The strongest argument for a four-day week is financial. Heating, cooling, lighting, and transportation are among the largest operating expenses for a school district. By closing buildings one day each week, a district can reduce utility bills and lower the number of bus routes it must run. Some rural districts that have made this change report meaningful savings, which can be redirected toward teacher salaries or classroom materials.

Energy conservation follows from the same logic. Fewer days of operation mean fewer hours of electricity and fuel consumption, which can translate into a smaller carbon footprint. For districts facing budget pressure and sustainability goals at the same time, a four-day schedule offers a single policy that addresses both.

However, the energy savings are not as simple as they first appear. Longer school days mean that buildings must still be heated, cooled, and lit for the same total number of hours over the year, or even more if the extended days are paired with additional activities. The reduction in energy use may therefore be smaller than expected, and in some cases the savings on one day are offset by greater use on the remaining four.

Transportation presents a similar complication. Buses still need to run on four days, and families may need to drive their children on the fifth day if they rely on childcare or after-school programs. Some parents may take additional trips by car, which could erode the environmental gains the policy was meant to achieve.

Academic concerns deserve equal weight. Students in a four-day week receive fewer total instructional days, and research on the effects of shortened weeks has produced mixed results. Some studies find little change in achievement, while others suggest that students in the lowest-performing groups may lose ground. Longer days also raise questions about student fatigue and attention, particularly for younger children.

The fifth day can also be a burden for working families. Many parents depend on schools for meals, supervision, and support services. When a school closes one day each week, families must find alternative care, which can be expensive or unavailable, and low-income students are most likely to be affected.

Teachers and staff would face their own challenges. Longer days can increase exhaustion and reduce time for planning, grading, and professional development. Some districts have addressed this by using the closed day for training, but this only shifts the burden rather than eliminating it.

Despite these concerns, a four-day week is not without merit when implemented thoughtfully. Districts that adopt it should carefully measure energy use, transportation emissions, student outcomes, and family impacts before and after the change. Such data would help determine whether the policy truly serves its goals.

Alternative strategies may achieve similar savings with fewer drawbacks. Upgrading heating and lighting systems, installing solar panels, improving insulation, optimizing bus routes, and encouraging energy-conscious habits among staff and students can all reduce consumption without shortening the school week. These measures often require upfront investment but deliver lasting benefits.

In conclusion, the four-day week offers genuine but limited advantages in cost and energy conservation. Its academic, social, and practical costs are substantial, and the environmental gains are less certain than they appear. Before adopting such a schedule, schools should consider whether more targeted efficiency measures could deliver the desired results while preserving the time students and families rely on most.

Influenza, commonly called the flu, is a contagious respiratory illness caused by influenza A and B viruses that typically spreads during the colder months. Common symptoms include sudden fever, chills, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle and body aches, headache, and fatigue, and some people may also experience nausea or vomiting, especially children. Most healthy individuals recover within one to two weeks, but the infection can lead to serious complications such as pneumonia, particularly among older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with chronic conditions. Treatment focuses on rest, fluids, and over-the-counter medicines to relieve fever and pain, while antiviral drugs such as oseltamivir may be prescribed to reduce severity and duration when started early, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset. Vaccination remains the most effective preventive measure, and in Russia annual seasonal flu vaccination campaigns are carried out each autumn, prioritizing high-risk groups, health workers, and school-age children. Virus surveillance in Russia is coordinated largely through the national influenza monitoring system, which involves sentinel clinics, laboratory testing of respiratory samples, and reporting to the Federal Service for Surveillance on Consumer Rights Protection and Human Wellbeing (Rospotrebnadzor) and the Ministry of Health. Samples are analyzed to identify circulating strains and detect antiviral resistance, and the data contribute to global surveillance networks coordinated by the World Health Organization, which informs the composition of seasonal vaccines. Anyone experiencing flu-like symptoms, especially those with breathing difficulty, persistent high fever, or worsening illness, should seek prompt medical advice.

Technology has transformed the way people shop and manage their daily lives, bringing remarkable convenience while also introducing new challenges. One of its greatest benefits is the ability to shop from almost anywhere at any time. Online stores allow consumers to compare prices, read reviews, and purchase goods without traveling to a physical location. This saves time, reduces travel costs, and gives people in rural areas access to products that might otherwise be unavailable to them. Mobile payment systems have also made transactions faster and more secure than handling cash in many situations. In everyday life, smart devices help people track their finances, manage schedules, and monitor their health. Navigation apps guide drivers through unfamiliar cities, and online banking lets individuals pay bills with a few taps. These tools make routine tasks more efficient and free up time for work, family, and leisure.

However, technology also carries significant limitations that deserve careful attention. Constant access to online shopping can encourage impulsive buying, as targeted advertisements and personalized recommendations are designed to prompt purchases. Many people find themselves spending more than they intended simply because the process is so effortless. Privacy is another concern, since retailers and apps often collect large amounts of personal data, including browsing habits, location, and payment details. Breaches of this information can expose individuals to fraud or identity theft. Technology can also widen social divides, because not everyone has reliable internet access, up-to-date devices, or the digital skills needed to use these services confidently. Older adults and low-income families may be left behind as stores and services move increasingly online. Finally, heavy reliance on screens and devices can affect attention, sleep, and face-to-face relationships.

In conclusion, technology offers substantial advantages for shopping and everyday living, from convenience and speed to greater access to goods and services. Yet these benefits come with real drawbacks, including overspending, privacy risks, digital inequality, and potential harm to well-being. The challenge for individuals and society is to use technology thoughtfully, taking advantage of its strengths while setting boundaries and protecting personal information. With mindful use and fair access, technology can serve people's needs without controlling their choices.

Our school cafeteria serves the same menu it has offered for years, and many students feel it is time for a change. The debate over whether to keep the current menu or switch to healthier lunch options touches on nutrition, student preferences, and the school's responsibility to support young people's growth. Both sides deserve a fair hearing before any decision is made.

Supporters of the current menu make a reasonable point that students should be able to choose foods they enjoy. A lunch that students eat is far more nutritious than a healthy lunch that ends up in the trash. Familiar favorites like pizza, chicken nuggets, and hamburgers are popular for good reason, and removing them could push some students to skip lunch entirely or bring less nutritious food from home. Cost is another concern, since healthier ingredients such as fresh produce and lean proteins can be more expensive, and the school budget is limited.

However, the case for healthier options is strong. Many students eat lunch at school as their main meal of the day, and the food they receive affects their concentration, energy, and long-term health. Diets heavy in fried food, refined sugar, and processed meats are linked to obesity and other health problems that begin in childhood. The school has a duty to model good habits and to offer meals that support learning rather than hinder it.

A middle path may be the most practical answer. The cafeteria could keep some favorite dishes but prepare them in healthier ways, such as baking instead of frying and using whole grain buns. Offering a wider variety of fresh fruits and vegetables would give students more choices without eliminating meals they already like. Gradual changes also give students time to adjust their tastes rather than facing a sudden shift.

Student input should guide these decisions. A survey asking what students enjoy and what they would be willing to try could reveal ideas that administrators have not considered. Involving students in menu planning can also build a sense of ownership, making them more likely to eat the food that is served.

In the end, the goal should be a cafeteria that feeds students well in every sense of the word. Healthy food matters, but so does food that students actually want to eat. By balancing nutrition with preference and cost, the school can create a lunch program that serves its students today and supports their health for years to come.

William Hill, the British bookmaker, reported a decline in profits as higher gambling taxes weighed on its earnings and the company continued to invest in its online operations. The company said the increase in duties on gambling revenue, a policy change that has squeezed margins across the UK betting sector, was the main factor behind the fall in profit. Executives acknowledged that the tax burden had made it harder to maintain previous levels of profitability while still growing the business. At the same time, William Hill has been directing funds toward its digital platforms, which it sees as central to attracting younger customers who increasingly bet on their phones. The company's spending included investment in an online lottery firm, a move intended to broaden its product range and tap into demand for lottery-style games. Analysts said the stake reflected a wider strategy of diversifying beyond traditional sports betting. Shareholders have watched the company closely as it balances short-term financial pressure with long-term growth plans. Industry observers note that other operators have faced similar challenges from the tax changes, prompting many to cut costs and reconsider marketing budgets. William Hill's management said it would continue to focus on operational efficiency while pursuing opportunities in online gaming. The company did not provide detailed forecasts for the coming year, citing ongoing uncertainty in the regulatory environment. Investors will be looking to future results to see whether the new investments can offset the impact of higher taxation. For now, the figures underline how sensitive the gambling industry remains to government policy decisions.

Tomas had grown up believing that the city's walls were the edge of the world. Every morning the loudspeakers repeated the same rules: keep your eyes on your work, speak only what is approved, and never linger near the river gates. He had obeyed them his whole life, and he had never once wondered why.

Then came the afternoon he saw Lena kneeling beside an old man who had collapsed near the bakery. The inspectors were walking past without looking. Tomas could have done the same. Instead he knelt too, and together they lifted the man onto a bench and waited for the medics, who arrived late and said nothing.

Lena looked at him with a mixture of suspicion and something softer. "You shouldn't have stopped," she said quietly. "They are watching."

"I know," Tomas answered. "I didn't like what happened when I didn't."

She almost smiled. Her name, she told him later, was spoken only in whispers in the district where she lived, because her father had written words that the authorities did not want read. She had grown up learning to be invisible, just as he had, and she was tired of it.

They began to meet in the narrow spaces the city had forgotten: the back stairwell of the library, the cold corner of the market where the vendors sold forbidden tea. They did not talk about revolution at first. They talked about small things, the color of the sky before the factory smoke rose, the songs their grandmothers had hummed, the strange silence that filled the city after dark. Each conversation felt like stepping onto ice that might crack, and each one made Tomas feel more alive than any approved sermon ever had.

Lena shared with him a folded sheet of paper, printed on a press hidden beneath a laundry house. It contained a poem her father had written before he disappeared. Tomas read it three times, and by the third reading his hands were trembling. The words described a sky without walls, a river that flowed wherever it wished, a people who spoke their own thoughts aloud.

"This is dangerous," he said.

"Yes," she replied. "So is pretending we have no thoughts at all."

The danger became real when an inspector began following Tomas home. For three nights he saw the same gray coat at the end of his street. On the fourth night, he went to the river gate alone, the place he had been warned against his entire life, and waited. The coat appeared. Tomas did not run. He stood still and let the man approach.

"You have been seen speaking with the woman from the north district," the inspector said.

Tomas felt the old fear rising in his chest, the instinct that had kept him quiet since childhood. Then he remembered the old man on the bench, the way Lena had knelt beside a stranger without hesitation, the poem describing a sky without walls.

"Yes," Tomas said. "I have spoken with her. And I will keep speaking with her, because she is kind, and because I am tired of being afraid of kindness."

The inspector's face did not change. He wrote something in his notebook, then said, "Be careful what you say next time." He turned and walked away, leaving Tomas standing alone beside the water.

Tomas did not feel safe, but he felt something he had never felt before: that his own voice belonged to him. When he returned to the stairwell that evening, Lena was waiting. He told her everything. She listened, then took his hand, and they stood together looking at the river, which moved forward without asking permission from anyone.

They did not know how the story would end. They knew only that the walls had cracks, that the cracks were growing, and that they had chosen to stand in them together. For the first time in his life, Tomas believed that freedom was not a distant promise handed down by loudspeakers, but something two people could build in the space between one honest word and the next.

I have not read the specific paper titled "A simpler Dirichlet-network loss for estimating deep learning models' uncertainty under distribution shifts," so this review is based on the title and on the general body of work on evidential and Dirichlet-based uncertainty estimation. The paper appears to address a known line of research in which neural networks output the parameters of a Dirichlet distribution over class probabilities, allowing the model to express both predictive confidence and epistemic uncertainty. The central claim, judging by the title, is that a simpler loss function can achieve reliable uncertainty estimates when test inputs differ from the training distribution. Simplicity is a worthwhile goal, since many earlier Dirichlet-network methods rely on loss terms that are sensitive to hyperparameters and can be difficult to tune. If the authors demonstrate that a streamlined objective matches or exceeds the performance of more complicated alternatives, this would be a useful practical contribution. Evaluation under distribution shift is the right setting for such a claim, because in-distribution accuracy alone says little about whether a model knows when it is being asked about unfamiliar inputs. A strong submission would therefore need to report calibration metrics such as expected calibration error, along with out-of-distribution detection measures such as AUROC on held-out shifted datasets. The manuscript should also specify which benchmarks and corruption types are used, since results on one shift family often fail to transfer to others. Comparisons should include standard baselines such as deep ensembles, Monte Carlo dropout, and the original prior-network and evidential-deep-learning losses. Reviewers should check whether the baselines were tuned with comparable effort, because an underperforming comparison method is a common way for gains to appear inflated. Ablation studies are needed to show which component of the simplified loss is responsible for the observed improvements. The theoretical motivation should be stated clearly, including what property of the loss ensures that uncertainty grows on out-of-distribution inputs. If the paper claims the loss is simpler, it should quantify this, for example through fewer hyperparameters, lower computational cost, or shorter training time. Reproducibility matters here, so the authors should release code, specify random seeds, and report variance across multiple runs rather than single results. Statistical significance should be assessed where differences between methods are small. The related work section should situate the contribution relative to recent evidential and Bayesian approaches, and it should avoid overstating novelty if the core idea is a modification of existing losses. Notation should be introduced carefully, since Dirichlet parameterizations appear in several conventions and confusion between them can obscure the method. Figures visualizing uncertainty on shifted data would help readers interpret the behavior qualitatively. Limitations deserve explicit discussion, including potential failure cases where a simpler loss might underfit or yield overconfident predictions on specific shift types. The authors should also discuss whether the approach scales to large datasets and architectures beyond the small benchmarks commonly used in this area. Claims about real-world deployment should be tempered unless supported by experiments on realistic shifts. The writing should be checked for clarity, as dense mathematical exposition without intuition can limit the paper's audience. A short summary of the algorithm in pseudocode would aid implementation. Overall, the paper's value depends on whether its empirical evidence convincingly supports the simplicity and reliability claims. If the experiments are thorough and reproducible, the work would be a helpful addition to the uncertainty estimation literature. Major revisions are advisable in areas where the comparisons, ablations, or theoretical justification are incomplete. In its current form, my recommendation would be to accept conditionally, pending these clarifications and additional experimental support. I would be glad to give a more specific review if you share the full text of the paper.

Speaking two languages is more than a useful line on a résumé; it reflects a way of thinking that employers value. A bilingual applicant has spent years moving between two systems of meaning, which builds patience, precision, and the habit of checking assumptions. These qualities matter in nearly every workplace, whether the job involves customer service, translation, teaching, healthcare, or international business.

The most visible qualification is communication. A bilingual employee can speak with customers, colleagues, or community members who might otherwise struggle to be understood. This widens the reach of an organization and builds trust with people who feel more comfortable being addressed in their own language. In many settings, a single bilingual staff member can prevent misunderstandings that would otherwise cost time, money, or goodwill.

Bilingualism also sharpens cognitive skills that carry over into professional work. Switching between languages trains the mind to focus on context, to notice subtle differences in tone, and to choose words carefully. Applicants who have done this for years tend to be strong listeners and clear writers, since they know firsthand how a single word can change a message.

Willingness to learn is equally important, and a bilingual applicant often demonstrates it already. Acquiring a second language requires sustained effort, tolerance for mistakes, and the humility to be a beginner again. Those same habits make a person adaptable when faced with new software, unfamiliar procedures, or an unfamiliar industry.

I see this in my own experience of learning a second language. Early on, I made frequent errors and felt awkward in conversations, but each mistake taught me something about how the language was structured and how native speakers actually used it. That process taught me to ask questions, accept feedback without defensiveness, and keep improving even when progress felt slow.

Employers should also consider the curiosity that bilingualism tends to foster. People who grow up or study across cultures often ask more questions about how things work and why they are done a certain way. This curiosity can lead to better problem-solving and a stronger willingness to seek out new knowledge.

For these reasons, a bilingual applicant offers far more than language ability alone. The combination of practical communication skills, sharpened thinking, and a proven commitment to growth makes such a candidate a sound investment. Any organization that values adaptability and service to a diverse public should give these qualifications serious consideration.

Sports and music are two of the most powerful ways people express themselves and find joy in everyday life. Although they seem quite different, both allow individuals to share feelings that are sometimes difficult to put into words. On the playing field, an athlete can show determination through a sprint, a leap, or a last-second shot. In the same way, a musician can communicate sorrow, excitement, or hope through the notes of a song. Each activity gives people a chance to move beyond ordinary routines and discover what they are capable of. Sports teach discipline and teamwork, while music encourages creativity and personal reflection. Many young people find their identity through a favorite team, a favorite instrument, or a favorite genre of music. These pursuits also bring people together, creating friendships that might never have formed otherwise. Fans cheer side by side in a stadium, and listeners sing along at a concert, sharing a feeling of belonging. Even those who do not play a sport or an instrument can enjoy them by watching, listening, or dancing. Such experiences offer relief from stress and remind people that life can be full of pleasure. Moreover, both sports and music have the ability to cross cultural and language barriers. A soccer match or a folk song can speak to people across the world in a way that words alone cannot. For these reasons, sports and music remain essential parts of a joyful and expressive life.

The manuscript proposes tensor-train recurrent architectures as a scalable approach for modeling long-range dependencies in temporal point processes, and the central idea is promising and timely. The authors motivate the problem clearly, noting that conventional recurrent intensity models struggle with long event histories and that parameter counts grow rapidly with the dimensionality of marks and hidden states. The use of tensor-train decomposition to compress recurrent weight matrices is a reasonable choice, since it offers a principled way to trade expressiveness against parameter efficiency. The introduction situates the work adequately within the neural temporal point process literature, though it could engage more directly with recent transformer-based and state-space alternatives that also target long-range dependencies. The problem statement is well framed, and the stated contributions are easy to identify, which I appreciate. However, the claim of scalability is the most important claim in the paper and receives the least rigorous support. The experiments are conducted on a small number of datasets, and most of them contain relatively short sequences, which does not convincingly demonstrate behavior on the long-range regimes the title emphasizes. I would like to see experiments that explicitly vary sequence length and report how training time, memory use, and predictive performance scale. The baselines are also limited; the comparison omits strong recent neural point process models and standard non-neural benchmarks such as Hawkes processes with tuned kernels. Reporting variance across random seeds is essential, as the current tables present single-run numbers whose differences are sometimes within plausible noise. The evaluation metrics, including log-likelihood and event-time prediction error, are appropriate, but the authors should clarify how these were computed for the tensor-train models, particularly regarding integration over the intensity function. The theoretical section offers a bound on approximation error induced by the tensor-train rank, which is a valuable addition. Yet the derivation relies on assumptions about the smoothness of the underlying intensity that are not verified empirically on the datasets used. A discussion of how the rank hyperparameter should be selected in practice would substantially improve the paper's usability. The ablation study is informative in showing that rank has a measurable effect on performance, but it does not isolate the contribution of the recurrent structure from that of the decomposition itself. Including a dense recurrent baseline with a matched parameter count would clarify whether the gains stem from the tensor-train parameterization or simply from reduced capacity acting as regularization. The figures are generally clear, although the learning curves would benefit from logarithmic scaling on the training-time axis and from confidence bands. Several notational choices, particularly the overloaded use of the symbol for both the rank and the dimension of the mark space, make the methods section harder to follow than necessary. The related work section is concise and accurate in most respects, but a few citations appear to describe the cited methods imprecisely. The reproducibility statement is welcome, and the authors state that code will be released, which strengthens confidence in the results. Nevertheless, the paper would benefit from specifying the optimizer, learning rate schedule, and early-stopping criteria in a single table rather than scattering them across the text. The limitations section is brief and should discuss the potential loss of interpretability introduced by the tensor-train factorization and the sensitivity of training to initialization. Ethical considerations are not discussed, which is acceptable for a methodological contribution, though a short remark on applications such as user behavior modeling would be appropriate. Overall, the paper addresses a meaningful problem with a sound and creative methodological idea. Its main weaknesses lie in the breadth of experimental validation and the strength of evidence for scalability. With additional long-sequence experiments, stronger baselines, multi-seed reporting, and a cleaner separation of the effects of factorization and recurrence, the contribution would be considerably more convincing. I recommend a major revision before the work can be considered for publication.

Optimism is more than a cheerful outlook; it is a practical habit that shapes how people approach their goals, handle setbacks, and treat the people around them. Students who expect that effort can lead to progress tend to set more ambitious goals and keep working when assignments become difficult. Rather than giving up after a poor grade, an optimistic student sees the mistake as information about what to study differently next time. This persistence often turns into real achievement over the course of a semester or a career. Optimism also builds resilience, the ability to recover from disappointment and stress. When a friendship falls apart or a project fails, an optimistic person is more likely to ask what can be learned and what steps might come next, which shortens the time spent in discouragement. Everyday challenges such as a crowded schedule or a difficult conversation become easier to face when one believes they can be managed. Optimism matters in relationships as well. People who expect good intentions from others tend to extend trust, listen more generously, and forgive small slights more readily. Their warmth is often returned, creating a cycle of cooperation and goodwill. Friends, classmates, and family members are drawn to someone who makes them feel that problems can be solved together. Of course, optimism is not the same as ignoring reality. The healthiest form of hope acknowledges difficulty while still believing that effort and support can make a difference. A student who studies for an exam, asks a teacher for help, and expects to improve is practicing this balanced kind of optimism. Over time, such small choices accumulate into greater achievement, stronger resilience, and more meaningful connections. In this way, optimism is not a gift reserved for the naturally cheerful; it is a skill that anyone can practice in daily life.
