Estimating Lead-Acid Battery Capacity from Charging and Discharging Signals Using Time-Frequency Analysis

Abstract

Accurate estimation of lead-acid battery capacity is essential for the reliable operation of uninterruptible power supplies, electric vehicle auxiliary systems, telecommunication backup systems, and renewable energy storage. Conventional capacity tests require a full discharge under controlled conditions, which is time-consuming and impractical during normal operation. This paper investigates a method for estimating battery capacity from naturally occurring charging and discharging signals using time-frequency analysis. The proposed approach treats the measured current and voltage waveforms as non-stationary signals and extracts features from their time-frequency representations. These features are then correlated with reference capacity measurements to construct an estimation model. Experimental results on a set of valve-regulated lead-acid cells across multiple aging states indicate that the method can estimate capacity with an error below a few percent under partial-cycle conditions. The study concludes with a discussion of limitations and directions for practical deployment.

1. Introduction

Lead-acid batteries remain widely used due to their low cost, high recyclability, and proven reliability. They are found in automotive starting systems, standby power installations, and off-grid energy storage. Over time, these batteries degrade through sulfation, grid corrosion, active material shedding, and electrolyte loss, leading to a gradual reduction in usable capacity. Knowledge of the present capacity is therefore central to state-of-health management, maintenance scheduling, and safety assessment.

The most direct method for determining capacity is a full discharge test at a specified rate, measuring the charge delivered before the cut-off voltage is reached. While accurate, this procedure interrupts service, consumes energy, and may stress aging cells. Consequently, considerable research has focused on indirect estimation methods that infer capacity from routine operating data. Such methods include coulomb counting with recalibration, model-based observers such as Kalman filters, impedance spectroscopy, and data-driven regression.

Coulomb counting integrates current over time to track charge throughput, but it requires a known starting state of charge and accumulates error from sensor drift. Model-based approaches depend on equivalent circuit models whose parameters vary with temperature, state of charge, and age. Impedance-based techniques require dedicated excitation hardware that may not be available in deployed systems. Data-driven methods can achieve good accuracy but often require large training datasets and may generalize poorly.

Partial charging and discharging events are common in practical systems. The current and voltage waveforms recorded during these events contain information about internal resistance, polarization effects, and the amount of charge transferred. Because these signals are non-stationary, with transient behavior at the onset of current steps and slow relaxation afterward, their information content is not fully captured by time-domain statistics alone. Time-frequency analysis provides a framework for representing such signals jointly in time and frequency, revealing how spectral energy evolves during each event.

This paper proposes and evaluates a time-frequency feature-based method for estimating lead-acid battery capacity from partial charging and discharging signals. The contributions are threefold: a feature extraction procedure based on short-time Fourier transform and continuous wavelet transform representations; a regression framework that maps these features to capacity; and an experimental validation across cells with varying degrees of degradation.

2. Background on Lead-Acid Battery Dynamics

The lead-acid electrochemical system involves reactions at lead dioxide positive plates and sponge lead negative plates in a sulfuric acid electrolyte. During discharge, both electrodes convert to lead sulfate, and the electrolyte density decreases. Charging reverses these reactions. The open-circuit voltage depends primarily on the state of charge and electrolyte concentration, while the operating voltage includes ohmic drop and polarization overpotentials.

Polarization comprises activation, concentration, and charge-transfer components, each with characteristic time constants ranging from milliseconds to hours. These time constants shape the dynamic response to current steps and provide a basis for distinguishing aging-related changes. As cells age, the active surface area of the electrodes decreases and the effective resistance increases, which alters both the amplitude and the temporal structure of the voltage response.

Capacity fade is largely attributed to loss of active material and sulfation of the negative plate, which reduces the amount of reactant available for conversion. A cell with reduced capacity reaches the cut-off voltage sooner under a given discharge profile, and its voltage curve exhibits steeper slopes in the later stages of discharge. These changes are expressed in the frequency content of the measured signals as well as in their amplitude.

3. Time-Frequency Analysis Methods

Time-frequency analysis decomposes a signal into components localized in both time and frequency. The short-time Fourier transform applies a windowed Fourier transform over successive segments, producing a spectrogram whose resolution is fixed by the window length. Shorter windows improve temporal localization at the expense of frequency resolution, and the reverse holds for longer windows.

The continuous wavelet transform uses scaled and shifted versions of a mother wavelet to achieve variable resolution, with finer time resolution at high frequencies and finer frequency resolution at low frequencies. This property suits battery signals, where fast transients at current switching are superimposed on slow electrochemical relaxation. The choice of mother wavelet affects the sensitivity of the representation to particular signal shapes; Morlet and Daubechies wavelets are commonly employed.

From the time-frequency representation, several features can be derived: the total energy in frequency bands, the spectral centroid as a function of time, the entropy of the normalized spectrum, the time-averaged dominant frequency, and the ridge trajectory of the strongest component. Features are computed over the duration of each charging or discharging event and normalized to remove dependence on current magnitude.

4. Proposed Method

The proposed method consists of four stages: signal acquisition, preprocessing, time-frequency feature extraction, and capacity regression.

In the acquisition stage, current and terminal voltage are sampled synchronously at a rate sufficient to resolve the fastest transients of interest. In this study, the sampling rate was set to 100 Hz, which captures dynamics up to 50 Hz and covers the principal electrochemical responses. Temperature was recorded alongside the electrical signals.

In the preprocessing stage, signals are filtered with a zero-phase low-pass filter to suppress measurement noise, and events are segmented based on current thresholds. Only events exceeding a minimum duration and amplitude are retained. Voltage is referenced to the pre-event rest voltage to isolate the dynamic response from the static state-of-charge contribution.

In the feature extraction stage, a spectrogram using a Hann window of 64 samples with 50 percent overlap is computed for each event. A continuous wavelet transform with a Morlet mother wavelet is computed in parallel as a cross-check. From each representation, a feature vector is formed containing band energies in six logarithmically spaced bands, spectral entropy, the mean and variance of the spectral centroid, and the integrated charge transferred during the event. Features are standardized using statistics from the training set.

In the regression stage, a set of candidate models is evaluated, including ridge regression, support vector regression with a radial basis kernel, and a shallow neural network. Model selection is performed using leave-one-cell-out cross-validation to ensure that performance is assessed on cells not seen during training.

5. Experimental Setup

The experimental dataset comprises twelve valve-regulated lead-acid cells of nominal capacity 7 Ah, rated at 12 V per module when connected in series with two cells per module. Cells were obtained from a single manufacturer and selected to cover a range of initial condition. Accelerated aging was applied through repeated deep cycling at elevated temperature, with reference capacity measured periodically by a full C/5 discharge to the manufacturer's cut-off voltage.

During the aging campaign, each cell underwent partial charging and discharging profiles representative of standby and cyclic duty. Charging used a constant-current, constant-voltage protocol at C/10 current with a voltage limit of 2.35 V per cell. Discharging used randomized current profiles with amplitudes between C/20 and C/2 and durations between five and thirty minutes. Each event was logged together with the reference capacity measured nearest in time.

The test environment was held at 25 degrees Celsius for reference measurements and monitored during aging cycles. Data acquisition used a calibrated multichannel system with a current sensor accuracy of 0.2 percent of full scale and a voltage accuracy of 1 millivolt.

6. Results

A total of 2,140 events were extracted from the dataset, with corresponding capacity labels ranging from 42 percent to 101 percent of nominal capacity. The distribution of capacities was skewed toward higher values, reflecting the aging trajectory of most cells, and the evaluation considered this imbalance.

Using leave-one-cell-out cross-validation, the support vector regression model achieved the lowest mean absolute percentage error, at 2.8 percent. The ridge regression model achieved 4.1 percent, and the neural network achieved 3.5 percent, with higher variance across folds. Performance was best for discharge events with moderate current amplitude, where the spectral features showed clear dependence on aging state.

Feature importance analysis indicated that the spectral entropy of the voltage response and the energy in the lowest-frequency band contributed most strongly to predictions. Both features increased systematically as capacity declined, consistent with increased polarization and a broader distribution of relaxation dynamics in aged cells. Features derived from the continuous wavelet transform performed comparably to those derived from the spectrogram, with a slight advantage in cases involving short events.

Estimation errors were larger for events shorter than five minutes, where the limited duration reduced the information available in the low-frequency bands. Errors were also elevated at temperatures deviating from the reference condition, suggesting that temperature compensation would be required for field deployment.

7. Discussion

The results support the premise that time-frequency representations of routine battery signals carry information about capacity that is not readily accessible through simple amplitude-based statistics. The spectral features capture the evolution of polarization dynamics during an event, which changes with aging. The relatively low estimation error achieved across a diverse set of cells suggests that the features generalize beyond the individual cells used for training.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The dataset is modest in size and derived from a single battery type and manufacturer, so the transferability of the learned models to other chemistries, formats, and manufacturers remains untested. The aging was accelerated through a specific protocol, and natural aging may produce different degradation pathways and corresponding signatures. The method also depends on the presence of sufficiently long and well-defined events, which may not occur in all applications.

Temperature dependence is a significant practical concern. Electrolyte conductivity, reaction kinetics, and diffusion rates all vary with temperature, altering the time constants observed in the signals. The present study partially addressed this through a controlled environment, but field systems experience broader thermal variation. Incorporating temperature as an explicit input feature or applying a temperature-dependent normalization is a logical next step.

Another consideration is the choice of time-frequency parameters. The window length in the spectrogram and the mother wavelet in the continuous wavelet transform influence feature quality. Optimization of these parameters was performed on the same dataset used for evaluation in the initial exploration, which may introduce optimistic bias. A more rigorous protocol would fix these parameters using an independent subset before final testing.

From a computational standpoint, the feature extraction is lightweight enough to run on embedded microcontrollers for short windows, but continuous wavelet computation on long events may require more capable hardware. The regression models are compact and could be implemented directly on the same platforms.

8. Conclusion

This paper presented a method for estimating lead-acid battery capacity from partial charging and discharging signals using time-frequency analysis. By extracting spectral features from spectrogram and wavelet representations of current and voltage events and mapping them to capacity through regression, the approach achieved a mean absolute percentage error of 2.8 percent under leave-one-cell-out validation on a set of accelerated-aged cells. The method avoids the need for dedicated full discharge tests and can be applied during normal operation.

Future work will extend the dataset to multiple manufacturers and battery formats, include natural aging trajectories, incorporate explicit temperature compensation, and evaluate the method in field installations. Investigation of deep learning architectures operating directly on time-frequency images may further improve accuracy, although interpretability and data requirements must be weighed against performance gains. The results suggest that time-frequency analysis of routine battery signals is a promising route toward practical, low-cost capacity monitoring.

Ricci Curvature Behavior of Complete Conformal Metrics in Compact Manifolds and Convex Euclidean Domains

Abstract

We study the Ricci curvature of complete conformal metrics defined on compact manifolds with boundary and on bounded convex domains in Euclidean space. The principal objects of interest are conformal deformations of a background metric whose conformal factor blows up at the boundary, producing metrics that are complete in the sense of finite-distance geodesic incompleteness being excluded. We derive formulas relating the Ricci tensor of the deformed metric to the Hessian and Laplacian of the conformal factor, analyze the sign and asymptotic behavior of the curvature near the boundary, and discuss consequences for existence, uniqueness, and rigidity. Throughout, we indicate which statements are classical, which follow from standard computations, and which we regard as conjectural or only partially verified.

1. Introduction

Conformal geometry concerns the study of Riemannian metrics up to multiplication by a positive function. Two metrics g and h on a manifold M are conformal if h = e^{2u} g for some smooth function u. Within a fixed conformal class, one seeks a representative with prescribed curvature, and among these problems the prescription of Ricci or scalar curvature has been especially fruitful. A particularly rich setting arises when the conformal factor is allowed to diverge at the boundary of a domain, so that the resulting metric is complete even though the underlying domain is bounded in the Euclidean sense.

This construction goes back to the hyperbolic metric on the unit ball, where the factor 2/(1 - |x|^2) renders the metric complete with constant negative sectional curvature. More generally, for a bounded domain Omega in R^n with smooth boundary, one may consider metrics of the form g = rho^{-2} g_0, where rho is a defining function vanishing to first order on the boundary. Such metrics are complete, and when the domain is strictly convex or the boundary has suitable pinching, their curvature exhibits controlled behavior. The Ricci tensor is of particular interest because it governs volume growth and the Einstein condition, and because its sign determines many global properties.

The purpose of this paper is to give a systematic account of the Ricci curvature of such complete conformal metrics. We treat two settings: compact Riemannian manifolds with boundary, and bounded convex domains in Euclidean space. In both cases the central question is how the Ricci curvature behaves as one approaches the boundary, and whether it can be bounded from above or below in terms of geometric data of the domain.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 fixes notation and recalls the transformation law for the Ricci tensor under conformal change. Section 3 treats the case of a compact manifold with boundary and a conformal factor defined by a boundary defining function. Section 4 specializes to convex Euclidean domains, where the Hessian of the defining function admits a convenient sign. Section 5 analyzes asymptotic expansions near the boundary. Section 6 discusses rigidity and examples. Section 7 summarizes open problems.

2. Notation and the conformal transformation law

Let (M^n, g_0) be a smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension n at least 3, and let u be a smooth real function on M. Set g = e^{2u} g_0. The Levi-Civita connections nabla and nabla^0 of g and g_0 are related by

nabla_X Y = nabla^0_X Y + X(u) Y + Y(u) X - g_0(X, Y) grad_0 u.

From this one derives the classical transformation law for the Ricci tensor,

Ric = Ric_0 - (n - 2)(Hess_0 u - du ⊗ du) - (Delta_0 u + (n - 2)|du|_0^2) g_0,

where Hess_0 u is the Hessian of u with respect to g_0, Delta_0 is the Laplace-Beltrami operator with the analyst's sign convention (so that Delta_0 u equals the trace of Hess_0 u), and |du|_0 is the norm with respect to g_0. This formula is standard and appears in most texts on conformal geometry. We use it throughout.

It is convenient to express the scalar curvature as well. Writing R and R_0 for the scalar curvatures of g and g_0, one has

R = e^{-2u} ( R_0 - 2(n - 1) Delta_0 u - (n - 2)(n - 1) |du|_0^2 ).

These two identities will be the basic tools.

3. Compact manifolds with boundary

Let (M, g_0) be a compact Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary partial M. Let rho be a boundary defining function, meaning rho is smooth and nonnegative on M, vanishes exactly on partial M, and has nonvanishing differential on partial M. We consider the conformal metric

g = rho^{-2} g_0.

In terms of the form e^{2u} g_0, we have u = -log rho. A direct substitution gives

du = -d rho / rho, and Hess_0 u = -Hess_0 rho / rho + d rho ⊗ d rho / rho^2.

Consequently Hess_0 u - du ⊗ du = -Hess_0 rho / rho, and the Ricci tensor takes the form

Ric = Ric_0 + (n - 2) Hess_0 rho / rho + (Delta_0 u + (n - 2)|du|_0^2) g_0.

Computing Delta_0 u = -Delta_0 rho / rho + |d rho|_0^2 / rho^2 and substituting, the terms involving |d rho|^2 combine to yield

Ric = Ric_0 + (n - 2) Hess_0 rho / rho + ( (n - 1)|d rho|_0^2 / rho^2 - Delta_0 rho / rho ) g_0.

This expression shows that the most singular contribution to Ric, as rho tends to zero, comes from the term proportional to |d rho|_0^2 / rho^2 multiplying g_0. Since g = rho^{-2} g_0, the ratio of the tensor g_0 to g is rho^{-2}, so in the g-norm the singular term has size of order |d rho|_0^2 rho^{-2} * rho^2 = |d rho|_0^2, which remains bounded. This is the first indication that the Ricci tensor of the complete metric is controlled near the boundary when measured in the natural norm.

Indeed, a more careful analysis in the g-orthonormal frame yields the following statement, which we regard as the central technical result of this section.

Proposition 3.1. Let rho be a boundary defining function on a compact manifold with boundary (M, g_0), and let g = rho^{-2} g_0. Suppose |d rho|_0 is bounded away from zero and infinity near the boundary. Then the Ricci tensor of g satisfies

|Ric_g|_g = (n - 1) |d rho|_0^2 - rho Delta_0 rho + (n - 2) rho |Hess_0 rho|_0 + O(1) as rho to 0 ... 

For the purposes of this exposition we record the weaker and cleaner conclusion: |Ric_g|_g is bounded near partial M, and the leading part of Ric_g in the g-norm equals the trace-type expression

(n - 1)|d rho|_0^2 - rho Delta_0 rho

together with terms that vanish at the boundary. The proof is a routine but lengthy bookkeeping exercise with the formula above, and we omit it.

The key consequence is that the metric g is asymptotically of constant Ricci curvature only in special cases. In general the Ricci tensor is bounded but not constant, and its boundary values are determined by the induced geometry of partial M together with the second fundamental form. In particular, if partial M is totally geodesic with respect to g_0 and |d rho|_0 is constant on partial M, then the boundary limit of Ric_g is a multiple of g itself, equal to -(n - 1) times the constant |d rho|_0^2 - and this is the familiar Einstein boundary behavior seen in the hyperbolic ball.

It is worth emphasizing what is not claimed here. The boundedness of Ric_g in the g-norm does not by itself imply boundedness of the sectional curvatures, which involve the full Riemann tensor rather than its trace. We address this distinction in Section 5.

4. Convex Euclidean domains

We now specialize to a bounded convex domain Omega in R^n with smooth boundary, equipped with the flat metric g_0 = delta. A natural boundary defining function is the distance to the boundary, or a smooth approximation to it. For strictly convex domains, the Hessian of such a defining function has a favorable sign, which is the source of the simplifications in this section.

Let Omega be a bounded convex domain and let rho be a defining function that is concave on Omega. Concavity means Hess rho is negative semidefinite. In the flat case Ric_0 = 0, so the formula of Section 3 reduces to

Ric_g = (n - 2) Hess rho / rho + ( (n - 1)|d rho|^2 / rho^2 - Delta rho / rho ) delta,

where all quantities are Euclidean. Because Hess rho is negative semidefinite, the first term contributes a negative semidefinite part to Ric_g. The second term has a sign governed by the competition between (n - 1)|d rho|^2 / rho^2 and Delta rho / rho.

A standard choice of rho in this setting is rho = d(x, partial Omega), which is concave whenever Omega is convex. However, distance functions are not smooth along the cut locus, so for rigorous work one often replaces it with a smooth concave defining function. Such functions exist by a standard approximation argument for bounded convex domains, and we assume one has been chosen.

Under the concavity assumption, the metric g = rho^{-2} delta is complete. Completeness follows because any curve of finite g-length must have finite rho-weighted length, and near the boundary rho tends to zero linearly in the distance to partial Omega, so the g-length of any curve approaching the boundary is infinite. This is the classical argument, and it applies verbatim to the hyperbolic metric on the ball.

We now record the sign behavior. Let lambda_1 <= ... <= lambda_n be the eigenvalues of Hess rho. Concavity gives lambda_i <= 0. The Ricci tensor of g in the g-orthonormal frame has eigenvalues determined by the same expression, and in particular the Ricci curvature in a direction e satisfies

Ric_g(e, e) = (n - 2) lambda(e) / rho + ( (n - 1)|d rho|^2 / rho^2 - Delta rho / rho ) g(e, e) * rho^2

after normalization. Since |d rho| tends to one near the boundary for the distance function, the dominant term is (n - 1) times the g-normalized quantity, which is positive. Thus, for the distance-type defining function on a convex domain, the Ricci curvature of g tends to a negative constant near the boundary, and the sign is dictated by the term (n - 1)|d rho|^2 rho^{-2} appearing in the trace.

Let us make this precise in the model case. For the unit ball B^n, take rho = (1 - |x|^2)/2. Then d rho = -x dx, |d rho|^2 = |x|^2, Hess rho = -delta, and Delta rho = -n. Substituting into the formula and using g = rho^{-2} delta, one checks that Ric_g = -(n - 1) g, which is the well-known Einstein constant of the Poincare ball model of hyperbolic space. This verifies the general formula in a case where the answer is known independently.

Proposition 4.1. Let Omega be a bounded, strictly convex domain with smooth boundary, and let rho be a smooth, strictly concave defining function satisfying |d rho| = 1 on partial Omega. Then the metric g = rho^{-2} delta on Omega is complete and satisfies

Ric_g -> -(n - 1) g

as one approaches partial Omega, in the sense that the difference Ric_g + (n - 1) g, measured in the g-norm, tends to zero at the boundary.

We sketch the argument. Near partial Omega the function rho vanishes to first order, and the identity |d rho|^2 + rho Delta rho = 1 + O(rho) can be arranged by choosing rho to be an approximate distance function with prescribed boundary behavior. Substituting into the formula for Ric_g, the singular terms cancel to leading order, leaving -(n - 1) g plus a remainder controlled by the Hessian of rho. Since Hess rho is bounded and the g-norm inflates by rho^{-2} in the tangential directions, the remainder is o(1) in the g-norm provided the Hessian of rho is O(1) as a Euclidean tensor, which holds for smooth rho. We have verified this computation in the model case and in the perturbative regime, but a fully general proof requires control of the boundary geometry that we do not carry out here.

Remark. Proposition 4.1 is consistent with the Cheng-Yau theory of complete Kähler-Einstein and Einstein metrics on bounded domains, in which the Ricci constant is forced to equal -(n - 1) by the boundary behavior. We do not reproduce that theory here.

5. Asymptotic expansions near the boundary

To understand the sectional curvatures, and not merely the Ricci tensor, one needs an expansion of the Riemann tensor of g = rho^{-2} g_0 near the boundary. The conformal change formula for the full Riemann tensor is more complicated, but the Weyl tensor is conformally invariant, so for the flat or nearly flat background one has

Rm_g = rho^{-2} ( Rm_0 - (Hessian-type terms involving rho) ) in a suitable sense.

Using the conformal invariance of the Weyl tensor, one can show that for the flat background the Weyl tensor of g vanishes identically, so g is conformally flat. This is a significant simplification: the full curvature of g is determined by its Ricci tensor, and in particular the sectional curvatures are controlled by the Ricci tensor through the Schouten decomposition.

The Schouten tensor P of g satisfies P = (1/(n - 2)) (Ric - R g/(2(n - 1))). Since g is conformally flat, the curvature tensor equals the Kulkarni-Nomizu product of P with g. Therefore sectional curvatures are bounded by a constant multiple of the norm of P. Because Ric_g is bounded near the boundary by Proposition 3.1 and its analogues, and R_g is also bounded in the setting of Proposition 4.1, the Schouten tensor is bounded, and so are all sectional curvatures.

This yields the following corollary.

Corollary 5.1. Let Omega and rho be as in Proposition 4.1. Then the metric g = rho^{-2} delta is conformally flat, and its sectional curvatures are bounded on Omega. In particular, the sectional curvatures converge to -1 as one approaches the boundary.

The claim that sectional curvatures converge to -1 follows from the constancy of the Einstein constant in the limit together with conformal flatness, since in a conformally flat Einstein metric the curvature is a constant multiple of the metric. We note that this relies on the boundary limit of the Schouten tensor being a multiple of g, which in turn uses the boundary behavior of rho. We regard this as established in the model and perturbative cases and as plausible in general.

6. Rigidity and examples

Several rigidity phenomena arise. If Omega is a bounded domain and the complete metric g = rho^{-2} delta is Einstein, then by the analysis above the Einstein constant must be -(n - 1), and by a theorem of Cheng and Yau in the complete Einstein setting the domain is forced to be projectively equivalent to the ball under suitable hypotheses. We do not state the precise hypotheses here, since the literature on this uniqueness question is extensive and the exact conditions vary between formulations.

As examples we consider the ball, the half-space model, and the simplex. The ball gives the Poincare model discussed above. The half-space H^n = {x_n > 0} with rho = x_n is not bounded, but the metric x_n^{-2} delta is the upper half-space model of hyperbolic space, complete with Ricci constant -(n - 1), providing a consistency check. For a bounded polytope the defining function cannot be smooth at the corners, and the Ricci curvature of the corresponding metric is not bounded near the vertices, which shows that smoothness of the boundary is essential for the results above.

Another example is the domain Omega = (-1, 1) times a bounded convex set in R^{n-1}. Here the product structure allows the defining function to be chosen as a function of the first coordinate alone near the flat faces, and the Ricci curvature near those faces reflects the one-dimensional behavior. We have not carried out the full computation for this example, and we flag it as an area for further work.

7. Open problems

Several questions remain open or only partially resolved in this exposition. First, the boundedness of the Ricci tensor in the g-norm is established under smoothness and nondegeneracy of rho, but a sharp characterization of the class of defining functions for which Ric_g is bounded is not given. Second, the relationship between boundary convexity and the sign of the leading Ricci term deserves a complete treatment for non-strictly convex domains, where the Hessian of the distance function may degenerate. Third, the rigidity statement in Section 6 requires a precise formulation of hypotheses, and we have not supplied one. Fourth, the extension of these results to compact manifolds with boundary of general geometry, rather than the flat or nearly flat case, requires controlling the Riemann tensor of g_0 near partial M, and the interaction between the curvature of g_0 and the boundary expansion of rho is not analyzed in detail here. Fifth, the asymptotic expansion of Ric_g to higher order in rho would give finer information about the geometry near the boundary, and we have only indicated its leading term.

We believe that a complete treatment of these questions would clarify the relationship between conformal geometry, boundary convexity, and the Einstein condition for complete metrics on domains, and we hope the framework presented here provides a useful starting point for that work.

References

The classical sources underlying this exposition include the standard texts on conformal geometry and on the Yamabe problem, the foundational work of Cheng and Yau on complete Einstein metrics on bounded domains, and the literature on the Poincare and Cayley-Klein models of hyperbolic geometry. A complete bibliography should be compiled from these sources before submission.

Vishal Sikka, the chief executive of Infosys, resigned from the Indian IT services giant on August 18, 2017, ending a turbulent tenure of just under three years at the helm.

The departure came after months of escalating tensions between Sikka and the company's founders, who had grown increasingly vocal about the direction and governance of the firm.

Sikka had joined Infosys in 2014 as the first CEO from outside the company, a move intended to usher in a new era of innovation and digital transformation.

Under his leadership, the company sought to reposition itself around artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and automation, areas he saw as essential to its future competitiveness.

His ambitious vision included a series of acquisitions aimed at bolstering Infosys's digital capabilities, which put the company on an expansive new footing.

Critics, however, questioned the cost and strategic logic of several of these deals, and some investors worried about the pace and scale of spending.

Founders such as N.R. Narayana Murthy voiced concerns about corporate governance, arguing that the board and management were not adequately accountable to shareholders.

The rift deepened as the founders pressed for greater oversight of executive compensation and the company's overall strategic choices.

Tensions also centered on a high-profile dispute over Sikka's pay package, which drew scrutiny from shareholders and proxy advisers.

Some board members and employees reportedly felt that the leadership style had grown distant from the company's long-established culture and values.

The governance debate spilled into public view, with the founders and the board trading sharp public statements over the course of several months.

Infosys's shares came under pressure during this period, reflecting investor unease about the uncertainty at the top of the organization.

Sikka, in his resignation statement, said that he had been subjected to a sustained campaign of personal attacks that made it untenable to continue leading the company effectively.

He emphasized that his decision was made to protect the company's interests and to allow it to move forward without further distraction.

The board accepted his resignation and appointed an interim leadership arrangement while it considered a longer-term successor.

Industry analysts noted that the episode raised difficult questions about how Indian companies balance the influence of founders with the expectations of professional management and institutional investors.

The leadership vacuum also prompted concern among clients, who valued continuity in large, multiyear outsourcing contracts.

Infosys had long been regarded as a model of transparent governance in India's corporate sector, making the public nature of the dispute especially striking.

Observers pointed out that the company's founders had played a central role in building the firm into a global technology services leader.

Supporters of the founders argued that their scrutiny was a necessary check on management decisions that might not serve long-term shareholder value.

Supporters of Sikka, meanwhile, contended that he had been trying to modernize a company that needed to adapt quickly to a rapidly changing technology landscape.

The company's employees, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, were watching the situation closely, as leadership uncertainty can affect morale and retention.

Market analysts said the resignation would test the resilience of Infosys's business model, which had historically proven robust through periods of change.

Regulators and corporate governance experts also weighed in, urging the company to ensure that the transition was handled transparently.

The board said it remained committed to maintaining strong governance standards and to selecting a leader capable of guiding the company through its next phase.

As Infosys prepared to name a successor, stakeholders across the industry were left to consider what the episode revealed about the challenges facing large, founder-influenced companies in a fast-evolving global market.

Sikka's exit marked a significant chapter in the history of one of India's most prominent technology firms, and its long-term consequences for the company's strategy and reputation remained to be seen.

How 20th-Century American Musicals Reflected Changing Social Attitudes and Conflicts

American musical theater in the twentieth century was more than entertainment. Its songs and stories served as a mirror and sometimes as a megaphone for the social attitudes and conflicts of its era. Shows that reached Broadway and the national stage often dramatized arguments that were unfolding in courts, factories, living rooms, and city streets.

At the start of the century, the musical was largely a form of light escapism. Operettas and revues dominated, and their plots usually centered on romance, class-crossing courtships, and comic misunderstandings. Even so, these early works reflected the assumptions of their time about marriage, wealth, and social standing.

The rise of the integrated musical marked a turning point. Oklahoma!, which opened in 1943 with music by Richard Rodgers and lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II, was a landmark because its songs and dance were woven into the story rather than serving as interruptions. Its themes of land, frontier change, and the uneasy meeting of cowboys and farmers gave audiences a version of American identity during a world war.

Show Boat, first staged in 1927 with music by Jerome Kern and a book by Hammerstein, had already tackled racial injustice in a serious way. Its portrayal of a mixed-race woman passing for white, and its depiction of anti-Black prejudice in the South, were unusually frank for the period. Its song "Ol' Man River" gave voice to the suffering of Black laborers, and the show's willingness to address these themes influenced later writers.

The Second World War and its aftermath brought new questions about freedom, identity, and belonging. Many musicals of the 1940s and 1950s explored the tension between individual desire and community expectations, reflecting a society that prized conformity while also wrestling with the ideals it had fought for abroad.

South Pacific, which premiered in 1949 with music by Rodgers and book and lyrics by Hammerstein, directly addressed racial prejudice. Its song "You've Got to Be Carefully Taught" argued that hatred is learned rather than innate, a message that was pointed for audiences living under segregation in much of the country.

The King and I, also by Rodgers and Hammerstein, explored cultural clash and the complicated relationship between Western and Eastern values. Critics have debated its portrayal of Siam and its depiction of a Western figure who imposes his worldview, and the show is now often read as both a product of its time and a site of ongoing discussion about representation.

West Side Story, staged in 1957 with music by Leonard Bernstein, lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, and a book by Arthur Laurents, transposed Romeo and Juliet onto the streets of New York. Its rival gangs, one of them made up of Puerto Rican immigrants, dramatized ethnic tensions, economic anxiety, and the difficulties newcomers faced in mid-century American cities.

Gypsy, from 1959, offered a different kind of social commentary. Its story of an aggressive stage mother and her daughters examined the commercial pressures of show business and the limited options available to women, and its frank portrait of ambition and disappointment set it apart from the more idealistic musicals of its day.

The 1960s brought the counterculture, the civil rights movement, and deepening opposition to the Vietnam War, and musicals responded with greater experimentation and sharper satire. Hair, which opened in 1968 with music by Galt MacDermot, celebrated youthful rebellion, sexual openness, and antiwar sentiment, and its nude scene and rock-inflected score signaled a break with the older Broadway tradition.

Hair's influence was considerable. It brought long hair, protest rhetoric, and rock music into a theater that had long been associated with polished pop standards, and its success demonstrated that younger audiences were eager to see their concerns onstage.

Cabaret, staged in 1966 with music by John Kander, lyrics by Fred Ebb, and a book by Joe Masteroff, used the decadence of pre-Nazi Berlin as a warning about political complacency. Its Master of Ceremonies and its dark ending left audiences uneasy, and the show's willingness to confront fascism and moral compromise made it one of the more daring works of the period.

The civil rights movement and the Black experience received musical treatment in works such as Purlie, Raisin, and Dreamgirls. Raisin, which opened in 1973 with a book by Lorraine Hansberry adapted from her play A Raisin in the Sun, explored family, aspiration, and racial discrimination in a Chicago household. Its score by Judd Woldin and Robert Brittan added warmth and musical richness to a story of ambition and dignity.

Dreamgirls, which opened in 1981 with music by Henry Krieger and lyrics by Tom Eyen, drew on the history of Motown and the Black popular music industry. Its story of a girl group navigating fame, exploitation, and commercial pressure addressed both racial and gender dynamics in the entertainment business.

Sondheim's later work brought a darker and more questioning sensibility to the stage. Company, from 1970, explored the anxieties of modern marriage and urban singleness, and its story reflected a growing public discussion about divorce, commitment, and changing expectations between men and women.

Sweeney Todd, which opened in 1979, used the grim legend of a vengeful barber to examine class exploitation and moral corruption in Victorian London. Its chilling score and unflinching plot showed how the musical could handle violence and social inequality without consolation.

Assassins, from 1990, took the unusual step of dramatizing the lives of presidential assassins and would-producers of such acts. Its presentation of American violence and the nation's fascination with celebrity and political grievance made it a provocative response to a country struggling with its own history.

The question of sexuality and gender identity gained new prominence in the later decades. Falsettos, which premiered in 1992 with music and lyrics by William Finn and a book by Finn and James Lapine, depicted a gay man's family life and the early years of the AIDS crisis, tackling a subject that had rarely appeared in mainstream musicals.

La Cage aux Folles, which opened in 1983 with music and lyrics by Jerry Herman and a book by Harvey Fierstein, featured a gay couple running a drag nightclub in Saint-Tropez. Its warmth and humor helped normalize gay characters for mainstream audiences, and its tale of a family confronting prejudice reflected the era's evolving debate about acceptance.

The Rocky Horror Show, which began in London in 1973 before reaching American audiences, provided a subversive celebration of sexual liberation and rejected conventional norms. Its cult following demonstrated that musicals could build communities around transgression and self-expression.

Rent, which opened in 1996 with music, lyrics, and book by Jonathan Larson, placed young artists in New York's East Village during the AIDS epidemic. Its contemporary rock score and its attention to poverty, illness, and queer identity spoke to a generation that saw its own struggles reflected onstage.

Musicals also engaged with women's changing roles and the feminist movement. Mame, which opened in 1966 with music and lyrics by Jerry Herman, presented a free-spirited woman who defies convention, while Hello, Dolly! had earlier offered a more traditional but still spirited portrait of an independent widow.

Women's labor and workplace discrimination were central to 9 to 5, which opened in 2009 and was adapted from the 1980 film. Its story of secretaries confronting a sexist boss gave voice to working women's frustrations and their struggle for fair treatment.

Race and identity continued to shape the musical in the late century. Miss Saigon, which opened in London in 1989 with music by Claude-Michel Schönberg and lyrics by Alain Boublil and Richard Maltby Jr., drew on the Vietnam War and its aftermath, but its casting and portrayal of Asian characters provoked widespread criticism and became a lasting example of debates about representation.

Musicals of the twentieth century also reflected economic conflicts. The Great Depression inspired shows that combined entertainment with social observation, and later works examined consumerism, corporate culture, and the American dream. How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying, which opened in 1961 with music and lyrics by Frank Loesser, satirized corporate ambition and the rise of the organization man.

Religion and morality also featured in the period. Jesus Christ Superstar, which began as a rock opera in 1971 with music by Andrew Lloyd Webber and lyrics by Tim Rice, presented Jesus through the eyes of Judas and raised questions about faith, politics, and celebrity. Its provocative take drew protests from religious groups and debate from critics.

Many musicals also reflected the tensions of the Cold War. Paradise Lost and other works of the era used satire and allegory to comment on conformity, nuclear fear, and suspicion of authority. Audiences often read these works as commentary on their own political climate.

Musical theater's engagement with social issues was not always progressive. Some shows reinforced the prejudices of their time, and revivals have often prompted fresh criticism of older portrayals of race, gender, and ethnicity. Recognizing this complexity helps readers understand how the form both challenged and reproduced social norms.

The changing audience also shaped the work. As Broadway attracted new demographics and as touring productions reached cities across the country, producers had reason to address a wider range of experiences. Commercial pressures sometimes limited bold choices, but the most successful works often found ways to speak to audiences about pressing concerns.

Television, film, and recordings expanded the reach of musicals and carried their songs into American homes. Cast recordings allowed songs such as "Ol' Man River," "Somewhere," and "Tomorrow" to circulate widely, and the social messages embedded in them could reach people who never saw the shows in person.

The relationship between musicals and their social moment was reciprocal. Shows reflected changing attitudes, but they also helped shape them by giving audiences vocabularies and emotional frameworks for thinking about difficult questions. A song could make a prejudice visible or make a marginalized person sympathetic.

Studying these works offers insight into the history of the United States. By examining the stories, songs, and staging of twentieth-century musicals, students can trace how Americans debated race, class, gender, sexuality, war, and national identity, and how art both documented and influenced those debates.

For educators and students, a few approaches can deepen the study. Comparing an early show such as Show Boat with a later work like Rent reveals how the treatment of social issues evolved. Looking at the original context of a song, the cultural assumptions it carries, and the responses it has provoked over time helps build critical thinking about the relationship between art and society.

Musicals remain a rich source for exploring American history. Their combination of drama, music, and dance made them uniquely capable of addressing sensitive subjects while also entertaining audiences, and their evolution across the twentieth century records a nation in motion.

The morning I woke up small again, I thought it was a dream, the kind where the bedroom walls seem too tall and the blanket smells of someone else's house. I reached for the glasses on the nightstand and found only a plastic cup with a cartoon fish on it. My hands were the wrong size, soft and unlined, and I could not make them stop shaking. Downstairs, a voice I had not heard in forty years called me down for breakfast, and I went because I did not yet know how to refuse my mother. At the table sat a bowl of oatmeal, and beside it, a crayon drawing I had made at six of a house with a crooked chimney. I stared at it and tried to summon the rest of me: the thirty-one years at the hospital, the daughter who now lived in another country and called on Sundays, the little garden behind our old apartment where I had grown tomatoes that won a county prize. None of it came when I reached for it. It felt like reaching into a drawer and finding only the lining. Later that afternoon, I sat under the maple tree with a library book I could not read, because the letters swam and my vocabulary had shrunk to a child's. I thought of the wedding toast I had given, the first time I held my granddaughter, the night I finished the marathon with my knees screaming. Those memories were not gone entirely, but they had gone quiet, like a radio left in another room. I grieved them the way you grieve a city you will never visit again. A neighbor boy kicked a ball toward me and laughed, and I laughed too, because that was what my body knew how to do now. Somewhere inside, the old woman I had been wept for everything she had built and everything she would never finish. I did not know if the change could be undone, or if the years I had lived would ever return to me. Night came, and my mother tucked me in, and I lay awake holding a life I could no longer hold.

Seeking advice from others is one of the most practical ways people can make safer and wiser decisions when facing difficult situations. No one sees every angle of a problem, and the pressure of a hard choice often narrows our thinking. Outside perspectives can widen that view and reveal risks, options, and consequences that we might otherwise overlook.

When we are under stress, our judgment is often clouded by emotion. Fear may push us toward rash action, while hope may make us ignore warning signs. A trusted friend, mentor, or family member can offer a calmer voice, helping us separate what we feel from what is actually happening.

Advice also protects us from blind spots rooted in our own experiences. A person who has never managed money may not realize the danger of a particular loan, while someone who has been through it can point out the traps. Hearing from people with different backgrounds gives us access to knowledge we did not have the time or chance to gain ourselves.

Consulting others also creates accountability. When we explain our plans to someone else, we often hear how they sound out loud and notice flaws we had missed. The act of putting a decision into words forces us to think it through more carefully.

Of course, not all advice is equally useful, and wisdom lies partly in knowing whom to ask. Those with relevant expertise, such as doctors for medical questions or financial advisors for money matters, usually provide more reliable guidance than people repeating rumors or offering quick opinions. Choosing advisors who are honest, thoughtful, and invested in our well-being matters as much as the act of asking.

Seeking advice does not mean surrendering responsibility for our choices. The final decision still belongs to us, and we must weigh what we hear against our own values and circumstances. The best advisors encourage us to think for ourselves rather than simply telling us what to do.

In the end, asking for guidance is a sign of strength rather than weakness. It reflects humility, the recognition that intelligence is not the same as knowing everything. By listening to others, we give ourselves the chance to act with greater care, to avoid preventable harm, and to make decisions we can stand behind in the long run.

Police are appealing for information after two men were assaulted at Haymarket railway station in Edinburgh in connection with football-related violence. The incident happened late on the evening of the match, when a group of supporters clashed on the station concourse as fans made their way home. Officers attended the scene shortly afterwards and a man in his thirties was treated for injuries to his head and face by paramedics before being taken to hospital. British Transport Police said the attack was unprovoked and that the two suspects, described as being in their twenties and wearing dark clothing, fled the scene before officers arrived. CCTV footage from the station is being reviewed, and officers are urging anyone who witnessed the incident or has mobile phone footage to come forward. Detectives are also appealing to members of the public who may recognise the men from the images being circulated. Transport police said they are working with football clubs and stewards to identify those involved and to prevent further disorder around upcoming fixtures. Anyone with information is asked to contact police directly or report it anonymously through Crimestoppers.
