This manuscript addresses a timely problem: deploying uncertainty-aware neural networks on hardware-constrained devices by combining Bayesian inference with low-precision, sign-activation architectures. The authors motivate the work clearly, noting that binary and sign-based activations reduce memory and compute costs but typically discard the calibrated uncertainty estimates that Bayesian methods provide. The proposed variational inference scheme is technically sound, and the derivation of the gradient estimator for sign activations via a straight-through surrogate is presented with reasonable care. However, the experimental section relies on a limited set of benchmarks, and the comparisons would be more convincing if they included recent quantized Bayesian baselines and reported calibration metrics such as expected calibration error alongside accuracy. The hardware efficiency claims are also underspecified: energy and latency figures should be reported on at least one concrete target platform, with the measurement methodology described in enough detail to be reproduced. I would also ask the authors to clarify how sensitive the posterior approximation is to the choice of surrogate gradient, since this could meaningfully affect both calibration and convergence. Overall, the paper makes a worthwhile contribution, and I recommend a major revision to strengthen the empirical evaluation and the hardware analysis before publication.

The morning came in pieces, like light through a broken window. Ruth opened her eyes and did not know whether it was Tuesday or the year she married Walter. The ceiling had a crack shaped like a river, and she had followed it many times, though she could not recall when she had first noticed it. A nurse moved past the doorway, her shoes squeaking, and Ruth tried to call out but the sound caught somewhere behind her teeth. She thought of the garden, of tomatoes split on the vine after a hard rain. Then she was in the garden, kneeling, and Walter was laughing at something in the kitchen window. She reached toward the sound, and her hand found only the cool rail of the bed. The clock on the wall said something, but the numbers swam like minnows and refused to hold still. Someone was holding her fingers now, a warm and steady pressure. She could not see the face, only a blur of pale hair and a voice saying her name slowly, as if reading it from a letter. Ruth wanted to say that she knew that voice, that it had been there the whole time, through the years and the long quiet afternoons. Instead she squeezed back, a small and certain pressure that she hoped would carry everything she could not say. The room grew softer at its edges. Somewhere a window was open and she could smell cut grass and rain on warm stone. She thought of the river in the ceiling, how it must flow somewhere, how all rivers do. The hand stayed where it was. Time folded over itself, and for a while there was no before or after, only the warmth and the voice and the slow rise and fall of her own breath. When she surfaced again the light had shifted, and the hand was still there. She let herself stay.

Joining a wartime livestock transport program offered young people an unusual mix of hardship, purpose, and surprising personal growth. Recruits were often assigned to move horses, mules, cattle, and sheep from farms and depots to the front lines or to ports for shipment overseas. The work demanded early mornings, long hours, and a steady hand with animals that were frightened by gunfire and unfamiliar surroundings. Yet many participants found that caring for these animals gave them a sense of responsibility that few other jobs could match. Every journey tested their patience and their ingenuity, whether they were fording a swollen river or coaxing a stubborn mule up a muddy slope. Friendships formed quickly among crews who depended on one another during long nights on the road. Travelers also saw parts of their own country, and sometimes foreign lands, that they would never have visited in peacetime. Learning to read the weather, the land, and the moods of animals gave participants practical skills that later served them in farming, veterinary work, and transport trades. The program also taught the value of discipline, since a lapse in care could cost an animal its life or delay a supply line that others were waiting on. For many, the experience built confidence that carried into adulthood. Some recalled the quiet satisfaction of arriving at a destination with every animal healthy and accounted for. Others remembered the sorrow of losses along the way, which taught them compassion and humility. Looking back, many participants believed the adventures and the lessons they gained were as important as the service they provided. In this way, the program offered a rare chance to serve a larger cause while discovering strength and character in themselves.

Summer break is often described as a time for rest, but it is also a window for growth that schools can shape in meaningful ways. A central question for educators is whether teachers should assign structured summer projects or instead let students design their own. Both approaches have real merit, and the strongest answer is that structured projects generally serve students better, especially when they are designed to leave room for personal choice.

The main argument for structured projects is that they give every student a clear starting point. Many students do not yet know how to break a large goal into manageable steps, and an open-ended assignment can leave them stuck or drifting. A well-defined project with specific deliverables, milestones, and criteria teaches planning and persistence by showing what finished work looks like.

Structure also promotes fairness. When students design their own projects, the results vary enormously in scope and quality, and grading becomes difficult to do consistently. Students from families with more resources or stronger academic support may produce impressive work, while others may produce something far less ambitious through no fault of their own. A common framework helps level the field and makes expectations transparent.

Structured projects also make it easier to build on what students learned during the school year. Teachers can connect summer work to specific skills, such as reading comprehension, scientific method, or mathematical reasoning, and can ensure that the project addresses known gaps. Self-designed projects may drift away from these goals, sometimes focusing on what is enjoyable rather than what is most useful.

Critics of structure argue that it stifles curiosity and independence, and this concern deserves to be taken seriously. Students who design their own projects often show greater ownership and intrinsic motivation, and self-direction is a valuable skill that schools should cultivate. A rigid assignment that dictates every detail may teach compliance rather than initiative.

However, the choice is not truly binary. Teachers can offer structured frameworks that still allow meaningful choice of topic, format, or method. For example, a teacher might require a research project on a community issue but let each student pick the issue and the medium of presentation. This balance preserves autonomy while providing the scaffolding that many students need.

Ultimately, structured summer projects are likely to produce better outcomes for most students, particularly those who lack experience with independent planning. The best designs combine clear expectations with room for personal interest, so that students learn both how to meet standards and how to pursue questions that matter to them. Schools that find this balance can make summer learning both productive and genuinely engaging.

Remote learning has become a powerful tool for expanding how and when students can learn, and when it is used thoughtfully, it can offer real benefits in flexibility, study environments, and access to missed lessons. One of its greatest strengths is the freedom it gives students to organize their own time. Many learners have jobs, family responsibilities, or long commutes, and online courses allow them to fit education around these obligations rather than being forced to abandon one for the other. A student who works in the morning can review recorded lectures in the evening, and a parent can study during a child's nap. This flexibility can turn education from an all-or-nothing commitment into something that adapts to real life.

Remote learning also allows students to create study environments that suit their individual needs. In a traditional classroom, every student must work at the same pace in the same noisy, shared space, regardless of whether that setup helps them concentrate. At home, a student can choose a quiet corner, adjust the lighting and temperature, or play background music if it helps them focus. Some students who feel anxious or overwhelmed in crowded classrooms find that they participate more confidently from a familiar setting. Because learning happens in a place the student controls, many feel more comfortable asking questions and taking intellectual risks.

Perhaps the most valuable advantage of remote learning is the access it provides to missed lessons. Students miss class for many reasons, including illness, injury, family emergencies, travel for sports or competitions, and religious observances. In a conventional setting, a missed lecture can leave a student confused for days or force them to rely on a classmate's incomplete notes. When lessons are recorded and posted online, students can watch the material at their own pace, pause to take notes, and rewatch difficult sections. This ensures that a single absence does not permanently disadvantage a learner.

Remote learning also supports students who need to revisit material more than once. Some learners process information more slowly or need repetition before a concept clicks, and a live lecture moves on whether or not everyone has understood. With recorded content and digital resources, a student can replay an explanation of a difficult math problem as many times as needed. This self-paced review builds confidence and mastery in a way that is difficult to achieve when the class must keep moving together.

Of course, remote learning is not without challenges, and its benefits depend on students developing strong self-discipline and reliable access to technology. Without the structure of a classroom schedule, some students struggle to stay motivated or fall behind on deadlines. Schools and teachers can address these concerns by offering clear timelines, regular check-ins, and accessible support. When these supports are in place, the flexibility of online learning becomes an asset rather than a source of stress.

In the end, remote learning offers meaningful improvements in flexibility, study environments, and access to missed lessons. It recognizes that students have different lives, needs, and learning styles, and it gives them tools to meet those differences. While it should complement rather than entirely replace in-person instruction, it represents an important step toward a more inclusive and adaptable model of education.

The manuscript addresses an important and well-motivated question: how recurrent neural networks can represent and maintain head direction by integrating angular velocity inputs, a computation thought to be carried out biologically by head direction cells in the rodent limbic system. The authors situate their work clearly within the existing literature on continuous attractor models and path integration, and the introduction makes a convincing case for why a trained network approach complements hand-designed attractor models. The central claim, that a recurrent network trained on angular velocity inputs spontaneously develops a ring-shaped attractor manifold encoding head direction, is interesting and worth publishing if it is well supported. The methods section describes the network architecture, training objective, and simulated trajectories with reasonable detail, although the authors should specify the initialization scheme, learning rate schedule, and the number of random seeds used so that readers can judge the robustness of the results. The figures showing decoded heading versus ground truth across long trajectories are persuasive at first glance, but the authors should report quantitative error metrics, such as mean absolute angular error and its growth over time, rather than relying on qualitative overlap. The analysis of the learned population activity using principal component analysis convincingly reveals a low-dimensional ring structure, yet the authors should also show that this structure is not an artifact of the chosen dimensionality reduction by presenting results from additional methods. The ablation experiments removing recurrent connections are a valuable addition, and they support the claim that recurrence is necessary for maintaining heading during periods without sensory cues. However, the manuscript would benefit from an ablation that varies the noise level in the angular velocity input, since drift under noisy integration is a key question for both biological and artificial systems. The discussion of drift accumulation is brief, and the authors should expand it to explain whether the network corrects for drift or simply degrades gracefully over time. The comparison to biological data is largely descriptive, and claims about similarity to head direction cell tuning curves would be stronger with a formal comparison, such as matching tuning width and preferred direction distribution to published recordings. The paper states that the learned representation generalizes to novel angular velocity profiles, but the test distributions appear narrow, and broader generalization tests, including unseen speeds and abrupt reversals, would substantiate this claim. Several figure legends are incomplete, failing to define axes, color scales, or the number of trials, which impedes interpretation. The related work section omits several relevant studies on learned path integration in grid-like networks, and including them would sharpen the paper's contribution. The writing is generally clear, though some sentences in the results are overly long and could be split for readability. The authors should also provide code and trained model weights to support reproducibility, which is increasingly expected in computational neuroscience. Overall, the study is promising and technically sound in its core design, but the claims about biological relevance and generalization require additional quantitative support. I recommend a major revision, with the requested analyses and clarifications addressed before the paper can be considered for acceptance.

Schools should require students to participate in extracurricular activities because these programs are a valuable part of a complete education. Classroom learning builds knowledge, but extracurricular activities build the skills and habits that students need to succeed in life. When students are required to take part in clubs, sports, music, or community service, they gain experiences that no textbook can provide.

Extracurricular activities teach teamwork in a way that group projects often cannot. On a sports team, a debate squad, or a school band, every member depends on others to succeed. Students learn to communicate, compromise, and share responsibility for a common goal. These lessons carry over into college, careers, and family life.

Participation also helps students discover their interests and strengths. Many young people do not know what they enjoy or what they are good at until they try something new. A required activity can introduce a student to photography, robotics, theater, or volunteering, and that discovery may shape their future studies and career choices.

Students who participate in extracurricular programs often develop stronger time-management skills. Balancing practice schedules, rehearsals, or meetings with homework requires planning and self-discipline. Learning to manage a full schedule prepares students for the demands of higher education and the workplace.

Extracurricular involvement can also improve academic performance. Research has suggested that students who are engaged in school activities tend to have higher attendance rates and better grades. When students feel connected to their school community, they are more motivated to attend class and complete their work.

Requiring participation also helps address social isolation. Some students are shy or struggle to find friends, and they may avoid activities on their own. A requirement gives them a structured opportunity to meet peers with similar interests, which can reduce loneliness and build a sense of belonging.

Critics argue that students should be free to choose how to spend their time and that forced participation is unfair to those with jobs or family responsibilities. These concerns deserve attention, and schools could address them by offering a wide range of options and flexible time commitments. A requirement does not need to be rigid; it can allow students to pick from many choices that fit their circumstances.

Schools also have a responsibility to prepare students for life beyond the classroom. Colleges and employers look for applicants who have shown commitment, leadership, and initiative outside of academics. By requiring participation, schools ensure that every student has the chance to develop these qualities, not just those whose families can afford private lessons or travel teams.

Equity is an important reason for requirements. Students from wealthier families often have access to enrichment programs outside school, while others do not. When schools require and provide extracurricular options at no cost, they help level the playing field so that all students can build a strong record of experience.

In conclusion, schools should require students to participate in extracurricular activities. Such requirements teach teamwork, help students discover their passions, build time-management skills, improve academic engagement, and reduce isolation. With flexible choices and strong support, these programs can benefit every student and help prepare them for the future.

This paper addresses an important and practical problem: deciding how to partition and assign the computational operations of a neural network across heterogeneous hardware devices so that inference latency is minimized. The authors propose a learning-based approach to this device placement problem, positioning it as an alternative to hand-crafted heuristics that often fail to generalize across model architectures and hardware configurations. The motivation is clearly stated and well grounded, since modern deployments routinely span CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators with differing memory capacities and communication costs. The related work section situates the contribution reasonably well, though it could engage more deeply with recent reinforcement learning and graph neural network approaches to placement. The problem formulation is described as a sequential decision process over computation graph nodes, which is a sensible framing that makes the learning objective explicit. The reward signal, based on measured or estimated execution time, is an appropriate choice, but the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of how noisy runtime measurements affect training stability. The model architecture is described in adequate detail, and the choice of encoder for capturing graph structure is justified, though the ablation supporting it is limited. The experimental setup covers several standard benchmark models, which is a strength, yet the selection of models appears to favor convolutional architectures, leaving open questions about transformer-style workloads. The baselines include expert placements and a greedy heuristic, which is appropriate, but a comparison against a stronger modern scheduling framework would make the claimed gains more convincing. Reported speedups are promising, yet the paper does not always state variance across random seeds or repeated runs, which weakens confidence in the reported numbers. The authors should clarify whether the reported latencies include communication overhead between devices, since this substantially affects real-world performance. The generalization claims are the most significant concern, as the evaluation largely concerns models and hardware seen during training, and transfer to unseen architectures is only briefly examined. Training cost is discussed but not quantified against the savings at inference time, leaving readers unable to judge the break-even point for practitioners. The writing is generally clear, though some notation for device capacity constraints is introduced inconsistently and should be unified. Figures are informative, particularly the placement visualizations, but several plots lack axis units or error bars. The discussion of limitations is brief and would be improved by addressing scalability to very large graphs and dynamic models with data-dependent control flow. Reproducibility is partially supported through the description of hyperparameters, but the absence of released code or a detailed environment specification limits independent verification. The related claim that the method is hardware-agnostic deserves more support, as the experiments use a narrow set of device types. The paper's contribution is incremental relative to prior learned placement work but is meaningful in its focus on inference rather than training, which is less explored. The conclusion accurately reflects the results but somewhat overstates the generality of the findings. Overall, the paper is a competent and useful contribution with solid motivation and promising empirical results. However, stronger baselines, variance reporting, broader model coverage, and released artifacts would considerably strengthen it. I recommend a revision addressing these points before the work can be considered for acceptance. The authors have a clear idea with practical value, and with more rigorous evaluation it could become a valuable reference for the community.

Dietary luteolin is a flavonoid found in foods such as celery, green pepper, parsley, thyme, peppermint, and chamomile tea. Research in laboratory and animal studies suggests that luteolin may help protect brain cells from oxidative stress and chronic inflammation, two processes thought to contribute to age-related memory decline. Some animal experiments have reported that luteolin can reduce markers of neuroinflammation and improve performance on memory tasks in aging or disease-model mice. Scientists have also observed that luteolin may influence signaling pathways linked to synaptic plasticity, the cellular basis of learning and memory. Limited human evidence, including some observational studies that associate higher flavonoid intake with slower cognitive decline, hints at a possible benefit, but these findings cannot prove cause and effect. Because luteolin is absorbed relatively poorly and is quickly metabolized, how much actually reaches the brain after eating these foods remains an open question. Researchers are still working to determine effective doses, the best food sources, and whether supplements offer advantages over whole foods. Most experts agree that a diet rich in vegetables, herbs, and other plant foods supports overall brain health, even if the specific role of luteolin is not yet firmly established. Anyone considering luteolin supplements, especially at high doses, should speak with a healthcare provider, since supplements can interact with medications. Future well-designed human trials will be needed to clarify whether luteolin meaningfully protects memory during aging. Until then, eating luteolin-containing foods as part of a balanced diet is a low-risk way to add beneficial plant compounds to your meals.

When people make important decisions alone, they are limited by their own experiences, assumptions, and blind spots. Consulting different people helps overcome these limits by bringing a wider range of knowledge and perspectives to the table. Each person has unique life experiences that shape how they see a problem, so a teacher, a friend, a parent, and a professional may each notice risks or opportunities that others would miss. Disagreement is also valuable, because when someone challenges our first idea, we are forced to examine our reasoning more carefully. Diverse perspectives can reveal assumptions we did not realize we were making, which often leads to more thoughtful and balanced choices. Groups with varied members also tend to avoid the trap of groupthink, where everyone agrees too quickly and important concerns go unspoken. Of course, consulting others does not mean blindly following the majority, but rather weighing different viewpoints before deciding for ourselves. In the end, listening to people who think differently from us helps us make decisions that are more informed, more fair, and more likely to succeed.

Extending the school day has become a popular proposal for improving student achievement and closing learning gaps. For students, a longer day can provide more time for core subjects, enrichment activities, and academic support, which may benefit those who fall behind. However, longer hours can also lead to fatigue, reduced time for family, sleep, and part-time jobs, and less opportunity for unstructured play and rest. Teachers may gain more time for planning, tutoring, and collaboration, yet many also face heavier workloads and longer commitments that can contribute to burnout. Schools that extend the day often find that their budgets, transportation systems, and staffing must change to accommodate the new schedule. The overall school atmosphere may become more focused and structured, but some students and staff may feel that the environment becomes more stressful or less balanced. Ultimately, the effects of a longer school day depend heavily on how it is designed, whether it includes meaningful and engaging activities, and whether it is supported with adequate resources.

The manuscript under review investigates adversarial audio perturbations capable of evading commercial copyright detection systems and seeks to expose security weaknesses in those systems. The topic is timely and of genuine practical importance, since content identification pipelines now gate large volumes of user-uploaded audio on major platforms. The authors frame their contribution as a security evaluation, which is a legitimate and valuable research direction when it is conducted responsibly. The introduction motivates the problem clearly, situating copyright fingerprinting within the broader literature on robustness of perceptual hashing and audio watermarking. The related work section is comprehensive in its coverage of adversarial examples for speech recognition and music classification, though it could engage more deeply with prior work on robust audio fingerprinting. The threat model is stated explicitly, which is commendable, and the authors specify the attacker's knowledge, capabilities, and constraints. However, the threat model would benefit from a clearer justification of why a black-box setting is realistic for the commercial systems studied. The perturbation budget is defined using a psychoacoustic masking criterion, and this choice is well motivated because it links the adversarial noise to human perceptibility. Nonetheless, the authors should report more formal perceptual evaluation, such as listening tests with a sufficient number of participants and appropriate statistical analysis. The methodology describes an optimization procedure that iteratively queries the detection system and updates the perturbation, and the algorithm is presented with reasonable clarity. The pseudocode would be more useful with explicit hyperparameter settings and stopping criteria. The experimental setup evaluates several commercial systems, but the manuscript does not always state the exact version or date of each system tested, which limits reproducibility. Because commercial systems change over time, the authors should timestamp their queries and discuss how drift may affect the results. The dataset consists of a curated collection of protected recordings, and the description of its composition, licensing, and selection criteria is adequate but could be expanded. The evaluation metrics include evasion rate, perceptual quality scores, and query efficiency, which together provide a balanced view of attack success. The reported evasion rates are high, which is significant, but the authors should include confidence intervals and variance across repeated runs. The ablation studies are informative, particularly the comparison between masking-aware and unconstrained perturbations, which demonstrates the importance of the perceptual constraint. The authors also examine transferability across systems, and the finding that some perturbations generalize partially is an interesting result that deserves further analysis. The discussion of why certain fingerprint features are more vulnerable than others is speculative and would be strengthened by targeted experiments. The manuscript acknowledges limitations related to the narrow range of audio genres tested, which is an honest and appropriate disclosure. The results would also be more convincing with evaluation on a broader range of music genres, recording conditions, and compression formats. Regarding responsible disclosure, the paper states that the authors notified the affected vendors before publication, which is an important ethical practice. However, the manuscript should describe the disclosure timeline and any vendor responses in more detail. The authors should also clarify whether they release their attack code, and if so, justify the release in light of potential misuse by parties seeking to infringe copyright. A discussion of defensive countermeasures is included and is a valuable addition, covering adversarial training, input preprocessing, and ensemble detection. The defenses section, however, evaluates only a single defense in depth, and a more comparative analysis would better inform practitioners. The writing is generally clear, though several paragraphs in the results section repeat numerical values already presented in tables, and these could be condensed. Figures are well designed, with the spectrogram comparisons being particularly effective at illustrating the imperceptibility of the perturbations. Some axis labels in the query-efficiency plot are too small to read comfortably and should be enlarged. The conclusion summarizes the findings accurately without overstating them. The authors appropriately caution that their results apply to the specific systems and configurations tested and should not be generalized to all copyright detection technology. The reference list is current and includes the most relevant recent work, although a few citations are to preprints that have since been published and should be updated. Overall, the paper makes a credible and useful contribution to the security evaluation of audio copyright detection. Its main strengths are the clear threat model, the perceptual constraint, and the honest discussion of limitations. Its main weaknesses are incomplete reproducibility details, limited statistical reporting, and a narrow evaluation scope. I recommend a minor revision, with the authors addressing the reproducibility, statistical reporting, and disclosure details. With these improvements, the manuscript would be a valuable addition to the literature on robust audio identification.

Septin-Mediated Astral Microtubule Interactions Position the Mitotic Spindle at the Yeast Bud Neck

Abstract

Accurate positioning of the mitotic spindle is essential for faithful chromosome segregation and for the spatial coordination of cytokinesis in budding yeast. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the spindle is oriented along the mother-bud axis and its midzone is placed at the bud neck, a ring of septin filaments that marks the division site. Here we review and discuss evidence that septin filaments act as cortical anchors for astral microtubule plus ends, thereby generating the pulling forces and positional cues that align and position the spindle. We outline the molecular components involved, including the septin hetero-octamers, the dynein pathway, and the kinase signaling that couples spindle position to the cell cycle. We also consider how these interactions are regulated through the cell cycle and under conditions that perturb septin organization. Finally, we identify open questions concerning the biophysical basis of the interaction and its conservation in other eukaryotes.

Introduction

The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae divides asymmetrically, producing a small daughter cell, or bud, from a larger mother cell. Because the two daughters differ in size, fate, and inheritance of organelles, the division plane must be precisely defined. The mitotic spindle must therefore be oriented along the mother-bud axis, with one spindle pole body and its associated nucleus entering the bud and the spindle midzone positioned at the constriction between mother and bud. This arrangement ensures that one complete set of chromosomes is delivered to the daughter while the spindle is correctly sited for cytokinesis.

Spindle positioning in yeast depends on the cortical interaction of astral microtubules, the microtubules that emanate from the spindle pole bodies and extend into the cytoplasm. Plus ends of these microtubules contact the cell cortex, where they are captured and pulled by force-generating machinery. The Kar9 pathway, the dynein-dynactin system, and the myosin-dependent transport of Kar9 to microtubule plus ends have each been implicated in this process. Yet the precise spatial cues that direct the capture of microtubules at the bud neck have remained incompletely defined, and this is where septins enter the picture.

Septins are a conserved family of GTP-binding proteins that assemble into heteropolymeric filaments and higher-order structures, including rings, gauzes, and cross-linked networks. In budding yeast, five septins (Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Sep7/Shs1) form a hetero-octameric rod that polymerizes into the bud neck ring during bud emergence. The septin ring is a hallmark of the bud neck and serves as a scaffold for cytokinetic machinery, including the myosin II ring and the chitin deposition apparatus. Its contribution to spindle positioning, however, has been more subtle and is the focus of this paper.

Septin Architecture and Cortical Association

The septin hetero-octamer is a rod-shaped unit with a central core formed by Cdc11 and Cdc12 at the termini and Cdc3 and Cdc10 in the interior, flanked by Shs1 or Sep7 in a configuration that supports end-to-end and lateral association. These octamers assemble into filaments that anneal into rings at the bud neck. Filament organization depends on GTP binding and hydrolysis by the septin subunits, and the transition from the early bud-tip collar to the mature neck ring is accompanied by remodeling of septin architecture.

Septins associate with the plasma membrane through interactions with phosphoinositides and with membrane-proximal proteins, which tethers the septin ring to the cortex. This anchorage is critical because it provides a stable, spatially defined platform against which microtubules may be captured. The bud neck ring is therefore well suited to act as a landmark for spindle alignment, since it occupies a fixed position relative to the mother-bud axis from bud emergence until cytokinesis.

Astral Microtubule Capture at the Bud Neck

Astral microtubules probe the cell cortex and, when their plus ends encounter a suitable cortical site, they are stabilized and pulled by dynein anchored at the cortex. In yeast, the major cortical capture factors include Kar9 and its partner Bim1, which localize to microtubule plus ends, and the cortical dynein receptor Num1 in the mother cell. Kar9 is transported along astral microtubules toward the bud, delivering a localized pulling site to the bud cortex. The presence of septins at the bud neck appears to modulate this system by concentrating cortical factors and by creating a physically defined region where microtubule ends are captured and held.

Evidence suggests that septins enhance the efficiency of microtubule capture at the bud neck. Mutations that disrupt septin organization or septin-dependent recruitment of cortical proteins produce spindle positioning defects, including misorientation and transient failure to align along the mother-bud axis. Conversely, the bud neck ring provides a reference structure that permits microtubules to engage the cortex precisely where spindle midzone placement is required. Septin-dependent capture thus contributes to the spatial precision of spindle positioning, rather than acting as a simple tether.

The mechanism by which septins promote capture likely involves local enrichment of Kar9 and other cortical determinants at the neck. Septin filaments may serve as a diffusion barrier, confining membrane proteins to the bud-neck region and preventing their dispersal into the mother or bud compartments. This compartmentalization would concentrate capture sites and reinforce the bias toward bud-neck engagement. Alternatively, septins could directly bind components of the dynein machinery or interact with the microtubule lattice through associated adaptors, although direct evidence for such interactions remains limited.

Coupling to the Cell Cycle

Spindle positioning is tightly coupled to cell cycle progression. In budding yeast, the spindle position checkpoint, mediated by the Kin4 kinase and the Bfa1-Bub2 GTPase-activating complex, delays mitotic exit until the spindle is correctly positioned across the bud neck. Kin4 is localized to the mother cell cortex and restricts the Tem1 GTPase to the bud, so that a misaligned spindle leaves the signal active and halts exit from mitosis. The septin ring contributes to the spatial organization of these checkpoint components, and septin-dependent cortical landmarks help align the readout of spindle position with the decision to exit mitosis.

The Cdc14 phosphatase is released from the nucleolus during anaphase through the mitotic exit network, and its activity is required to complete the cell cycle. Septin organization and spindle positioning are intertwined with this network, as the bud neck serves as a platform for both checkpoint signaling and the eventual localization of cytokinetic components. The timing of septin remodeling, from the hourglass to the double ring configuration after anaphase, is thought to coincide with the completion of spindle elongation into the bud and the initiation of cytokinesis.

Regulation and Perturbation

The interaction between septins and astral microtubules is regulated by the phosphorylation state of septins and their associated proteins. Cyclin-dependent kinase and polo-like kinase activities modulate septin assembly and disassembly, and the timing of these modifications may influence when microtubule capture at the neck is most effective. Perturbations that alter septin dynamics, including temperature-sensitive septin mutants and mutants in septin-associated kinases, have been used to probe the requirement for septins in spindle positioning. In such perturbations, spindle orientation is often impaired, and the frequency of spindle misalignment increases, consistent with a role for septins in promoting capture at the bud neck.

Pharmacological and genetic manipulation of microtubule dynamics also reveal how the septin contribution is balanced against other positioning mechanisms. When dynein activity is compromised, cells can still align the spindle to some extent, indicating redundancy in the system. The septin-dependent contribution appears most important under conditions where the spindle must reach the bud neck quickly or where cortical capture is otherwise limiting.

Biophysical Considerations

The forces generated during spindle positioning depend on the pulling of astral microtubules by dynein at the cortex, and these forces must be transmitted to the spindle through microtubule dynamics and motor activity. Septin filaments, being relatively stiff and anchored to the membrane, could provide a resistant platform that improves the efficiency of force transmission. The rigidity of the septin ring may also restrict lateral movement of microtubule ends, favoring their engagement at defined sites. Quantitative models of spindle positioning incorporating septin-dependent capture have suggested that such a mechanism can account for the observed alignment and stabilization of the spindle at the neck, although experimental tests of these predictions remain challenging.

Conservation and Broader Context

Septins are conserved across eukaryotes, where they contribute to cytokinesis, membrane organization, and cell polarity. In mammalian cells, septins localize to the cleavage furrow and the midbody and have been implicated in regulating microtubule organization and cortical interactions. Whether the mechanism described in yeast extends to these systems is an open question. The conservation of septin-based cortical anchoring suggests that analogous mechanisms may operate in other organisms, potentially including roles in orienting spindles in asymmetrically dividing cells.

Conclusions and Open Questions

Septins are important for positioning the mitotic spindle at the yeast bud neck, likely by concentrating cortical capture factors and by providing a stable anchorage for astral microtubule plus ends. Several questions remain. The direct molecular interactions between septin filaments and microtubule-associated proteins need to be defined structurally and biochemically. The relative contributions of septin-dependent capture and other cortical determinants under physiological conditions require quantitative assessment. The dynamic remodeling of septins during the cell cycle and its coordination with spindle movement remain to be resolved at high temporal resolution. Addressing these questions will clarify how cells integrate cytoskeletal and cell-cycle signals to achieve precise spatial control of division.

Planning and Planting Corn Plots for Winter Deer Forage

Winter is one of the most stressful seasons for wild deer, and a well-planned corn plot can provide valuable energy when natural food sources are scarce. Before planting, take time to study your property and define clear goals for the plot. Decide whether you want to supplement nutrition, attract deer for observation, or hold deer on your land during the hunting season. Choose a site that receives at least six to eight hours of direct sunlight each day, since corn needs strong light to grow well. Look for a location with good drainage, as waterlogged soil will cause poor germination and stunted plants. Ideally, place the plot near existing cover such as woodlots, thickets, or brushy edges, so deer feel secure while feeding. Avoid placing plots directly in open fields far from cover, because deer are more cautious in exposed areas and may feed mainly at night. Test your soil before planting, since pH and nutrient levels strongly affect yield. Most corn performs best in soil with a pH between 6.0 and 6.8, and a local extension office can run a test for a modest fee. Apply lime if the soil is too acidic, and follow the test recommendations for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Plan your plot size realistically; a quarter-acre to one acre is common for small properties, while larger acreage can support more extensive planting. Prepare the seedbed by tilling or disking the ground to remove weeds and loosen the soil. Weed competition in the early stages can significantly reduce corn yields, so control unwanted plants before or shortly after planting. Select a corn variety suited to your region and growing season, and prefer types recommended for wildlife or high-yield grain production. Some hybrids are bred for tall, high-tonnage growth, while others produce larger ears that remain on the stalk well into winter. Check seed labels for maturity dates and make sure the variety will mature before the first hard frost in your area. Plant in spring after the soil has warmed and the danger of severe frost has passed, typically when soil temperatures reach about 50 degrees Fahrenheit. Space seeds according to the variety's guidelines, usually planting about one to two inches deep. Fertilize according to your soil test, applying nitrogen in split applications for better efficiency. Watch the plot regularly during the growing season for insects, disease, and drought stress. Irrigation is rarely practical for small plots, so mulching and careful weed control can help conserve moisture. Many managers choose to leave standing corn in place through autumn and winter rather than harvesting it, because the stalks and ears provide food and some cover. Timing the plot's availability matters; it should be ready to provide forage by late fall, when deer begin to need extra calories. Some landowners also plant a small strip of winter wheat, clover, or brassicas nearby to extend forage availability after the corn is consumed. Be aware of local regulations, since some states and counties restrict baiting or feeding deer, and corn placement near roads or neighboring properties may be limited. Consider the ethical and ecological impacts of concentrated feeding, including the risk of disease transmission when deer congregate in large numbers. Rotate plot locations periodically to reduce soil depletion and limit the buildup of parasites and pathogens in one area. Keep records of planting dates, varieties, fertilizer use, yields, and deer activity to guide future seasons. Over time, these records will help you refine your approach and improve results on your particular property. Consulting your state wildlife agency or a local extension specialist can provide region-specific guidance on varieties, timing, and regulations. With careful planning, a well-placed corn plot can be a practical and rewarding way to support wild deer through the lean months of winter.

The advantages of in-person education over remote learning are most evident in the way students develop socially and academically. Although remote learning offered flexibility and access during difficult times, the classroom remains a uniquely powerful environment for growth. This essay argues that in-person education better supports the social skills, emotional well-being, and academic achievement that students need to thrive.

The most significant advantage of in-person schooling is the opportunity for face-to-face interaction. Students learn to read facial expressions, tone of voice, and body language, which are difficult to perceive through a screen. These nonverbal cues help young people understand how others feel and respond appropriately in conversation. Over time, this builds empathy and social awareness.

Classrooms also teach students how to work with people who are different from them. In a physical school, children share space with peers of varied backgrounds, interests, and abilities. They must negotiate disagreements, compromise on group projects, and adapt to personalities they did not choose. These experiences prepare them for the workplace and for civic life.

Friendship is another area where in-person education excels. Informal moments, such as conversations before class, shared lunches, and time on the playground, create bonds that are harder to form online. These relationships offer students a sense of belonging, which research has linked to better mental health and greater motivation to attend school.

In-person learning also provides structure and routine that many students rely on. Daily schedules, physical transitions between classes, and a clear separation between home and school help young people manage their time and attention. Remote learners, by contrast, often struggle to maintain focus when their home environment blends with their academic obligations.

Teachers play a central role in this structure. In a classroom, a teacher can observe a student's confusion, notice when someone is struggling, and adjust instruction immediately. A raised hand, a furrowed brow, or a long pause can signal a need for help that might go unnoticed during a video call. This real-time feedback supports more effective teaching and learning.

Personal attention from teachers also helps students feel known and valued. A teacher who greets students at the door, remembers their interests, and encourages them in person can make a lasting difference in their confidence. Such relationships often motivate students to take academic risks they might otherwise avoid.

Hands-on learning is far more practical in a physical setting. Science laboratories, art studios, music rooms, and physical education facilities allow students to experiment, create, and move in ways that are difficult to replicate remotely. Learning by doing deepens understanding and makes abstract ideas concrete.

Collaborative learning is also stronger in person. Group discussions, debates, and project work benefit from spontaneous exchanges of ideas, where students build on one another's thoughts in real time. Video platforms often produce awkward pauses, overlapping speech, and reluctance to speak, which can limit participation.

Access to school resources is another advantage. Libraries, computer labs, tutoring centers, and counseling offices are all available in person. Students who lack reliable internet or a quiet place to study at home can use these resources to keep pace with their peers.

In-person schooling also supports the early development of younger children. Young learners need to practice sharing, taking turns, following group rules, and managing frustration. These skills are best developed through daily physical interaction with other children and adults.

Adolescents benefit as well. Teenagers are forming their identities and learning to navigate independence. School provides a supervised but social environment where they can explore new interests, join clubs and teams, and take on leadership roles. Such activities are difficult to sustain when school is confined to a screen.

Extracurricular activities deserve special mention. Sports teams, drama productions, debate clubs, and music ensembles all depend on physical presence. They teach discipline, teamwork, and perseverance, and they give students a sense of purpose beyond the classroom.

Mental health is closely connected to social connection. Remote learning has been associated with increased feelings of isolation and loneliness for many students. In-person schools offer daily contact with supportive adults and peers, which can serve as a protective factor during stressful periods.

Schools also serve as a place where problems are identified early. Counselors, nurses, and teachers can notice signs of bullying, abuse, hunger, or emotional distress. Because they see students regularly in person, they are often the first to offer help.

Equity is an important consideration. Not every family has the technology, space, or parental support needed for effective remote learning. In-person education helps reduce gaps caused by unequal home conditions by providing a consistent environment for all students.

Concentration and attention also tend to be stronger in physical classrooms. The shared atmosphere of a room full of learners can encourage focus, while the many distractions of home, including devices, household activity, and entertainment, can pull students away from their work.

Some argue that remote learning allows greater flexibility and personalization. While these benefits are real, they do not outweigh the advantages of human connection. Personalized learning can be achieved in classrooms through small-group instruction, individual conferences, and tailored support.

Others point out that remote learning protects students from illness. Health concerns are legitimate, and schools must take reasonable precautions. However, well-designed safety measures, such as ventilation, hygiene practices, and flexible attendance policies, can address these concerns without abandoning in-person instruction.

Remote learning did reveal important lessons about technology and adaptability. Schools can continue to use digital tools to enhance instruction, such as research databases, interactive simulations, and online submission systems. Yet these tools work best as supplements to, not replacements for, physical classrooms.

The development of a student's character is also shaped by in-person experiences. Students learn responsibility by arriving on time, respecting classmates, and caring for shared spaces. They learn perseverance by facing challenges alongside peers and teachers who encourage them to keep trying.

Physical presence also teaches students how to conduct themselves in public settings. They learn to speak clearly to adults, to ask for help, to resolve conflicts, and to read social situations. These habits carry into adult life, including higher education and employment.

Communication skills improve through in-person interaction. Students practice speaking in front of groups, listening attentively, and responding thoughtfully without the buffer of a screen. These experiences build confidence that is valuable in every profession.

Cultural and community connections are also strengthened by in-person schooling. Schools host events such as science fairs, concerts, sports games, and family nights that bring communities together. These gatherings reinforce the role of education as a shared public good.

Academic achievement itself often benefits from in-person instruction. Many studies of pandemic-era learning reported learning losses, particularly among younger students and those from disadvantaged backgrounds. While many factors were involved, the reduced quality of instruction and engagement during remote learning played a significant role.

Motivation tends to be higher in the presence of peers and teachers. Students often work harder when they can see classmates engaged in the same task and when they feel accountable to a teacher who knows their name and progress.

Finally, in-person education helps students develop a sense of place and belonging in their schools and communities. Walking the halls, knowing the staff, and participating in school traditions create memories and identities that support lifelong learning.

In conclusion, in-person education offers advantages that remote learning cannot fully replicate. It fosters social skills, empathy, friendship, and emotional well-being, while also providing structure, personal attention, hands-on experiences, and stronger academic outcomes. Schools should continue to use technology thoughtfully, but the classroom remains the most effective setting for students' social and academic development.

The manuscript investigates the expressivity of tensor-train (TT) and CP tensor network decompositions as functional forms for neural architectures, with particular attention to recurrent and shallow networks. The central question, whether TT-structured models can represent a broader or more efficiently parameterized class of functions than CP-structured models, is well motivated and relevant to ongoing work on compressed neural network design. The authors situate their contribution clearly within the literature on tensor networks and expressive power, and the introduction is concise and easy to follow. The theoretical results on rank requirements and the separation between the two formats are the paper's strongest component, and the proofs appear largely sound on a first reading. However, several key lemmas rely on genericity assumptions that are stated informally, and I would ask the authors to make these conditions precise, since the claimed separations depend on them. The connection to recurrent networks is intuitive, as TT cores naturally correspond to sequential state updates, but the paper would benefit from a more formal mapping between the two, showing explicitly which recurrent architectures are captured by which TT ranks. The shallow-network implications are discussed more briefly, and the argument that TT-structured layers yield greater expressivity per parameter needs a clearer quantitative statement, ideally with bounds on the number of parameters required for a fixed approximation error. The experimental section, while supportive, is limited to small synthetic tasks, and it is unclear whether the observed advantages persist on realistic sequence modeling benchmarks. I would encourage the authors to report variance across random seeds and to include a comparison against unstructured baselines of matched parameter count. The discussion of optimization difficulties in TT-parameterized models is brief and should be expanded, since trainability may matter as much as representational capacity in practice. Some notation is inconsistent between sections, particularly the indexing of TT ranks and the definition of the mode dimensions, and a unified notation table would improve readability. The related work section omits several recent results on low-rank recurrent architectures that bear directly on the claims, and these should be discussed. Overall, the paper makes a useful theoretical contribution with a promising but preliminary empirical component. I recommend a major revision, contingent on tightening the theoretical assumptions, strengthening the experiments, and addressing the presentation issues noted above.

The manuscript addresses a practically important problem: how to assemble informative minibatches for metric learning so that training converges faster without incurring prohibitive sampling or computational overhead. The authors frame the central tension clearly, namely that hard-example mining improves gradient signal but that exhaustive pair or triplet mining is expensive, and this framing motivates the work well. The introduction situates the contribution within the existing literature on semi-hard mining, batch-hard selection, and proxy-based losses, and it correctly identifies that many prior methods trade one cost for another. The related work section is generally thorough, although it would benefit from a more explicit comparison with recent online mining strategies that operate on embedding caches. The problem statement is precise, and the stated objective of balancing sampling efficiency against computational cost is a reasonable and testable target. The proposed method constructs minibatches by combining class-aware sampling with a lightweight informativeness score computed from the previous epoch's embeddings. This design is intuitive and appears easy to implement, which is a genuine strength. However, the description of how the informativeness score is normalized across classes of very different sizes is ambiguous, and I would ask the authors to provide the exact formula along with a discussion of edge cases. The algorithm box is helpful, but it omits how the staleness of cached embeddings is handled when the model changes rapidly early in training. The theoretical analysis is limited to a bound on the variance of the minibatch gradient estimate, which is a sensible choice, yet the assumptions behind the bound, particularly the bounded-embedding-norm condition, are not justified for the architectures used in the experiments. The authors should either verify this assumption empirically or state clearly that the bound applies only under idealized conditions. The experimental setup covers three standard benchmarks for image retrieval, which is appropriate, but the choice of backbone networks is not fully justified. Using a single pretrained initialization across all baselines is commendable for fairness, yet the paper does not report whether the hyperparameters of the baselines were tuned with comparable effort. Reported gains in Recall@1 are modest, typically between one and two percentage points, and the manuscript would be stronger with confidence intervals across multiple random seeds. Presently the results appear to come from single runs, which makes it difficult to assess whether the improvements exceed run-to-run variance. The computational cost analysis is one of the more valuable parts of the paper, as it reports wall-clock time per epoch and total training time to reach a target accuracy. These measurements directly support the claim of accelerated training, and I appreciate that the authors report time as well as iteration counts. Nevertheless, the timing comparisons should specify the hardware, batch size, and whether data loading was included, since these factors can dominate the results. The ablation study isolates the contribution of the informativeness score and the class-aware sampler, which is helpful for understanding where the gains originate. The ablation does not, however, examine sensitivity to the minibatch size or the number of classes per batch, and these are the hyperparameters a practitioner would most likely need to adjust. Including such a sensitivity analysis would substantially strengthen the empirical contribution. The discussion section acknowledges some limitations, but it understates the risk that the method's benefits diminish when the training set contains heavy label noise, since informativeness scores may then prioritize mislabeled examples. I recommend the authors test this scenario explicitly, perhaps with synthetic label corruption at several noise rates. The writing is generally clear, though several figures have unlabeled axes or inconsistent legends that make comparison across methods harder than necessary. Figure 3 in particular would benefit from a consistent color scheme and error bars. Some notation is introduced inconsistently, with the same symbol used for both the embedding dimension and the number of anchors in different sections. Minor typographical errors appear throughout and should be corrected in a revision. The code availability statement is welcome, and I encourage the authors to ensure the released repository includes the exact configuration files used to produce the reported tables. Reproducibility would be further improved by documenting random seeds and the software versions employed. Overall, the paper presents a sound and practically useful idea with a reasonable experimental foundation. Its main weaknesses are the lack of statistical reporting, the untested assumptions behind the theoretical bound, and the limited robustness analysis. If the authors address these concerns, the contribution would be a valuable addition to the metric-learning literature. My recommendation is major revision.

Staying true to yourself is one of the most valuable choices a person can make. When we act according to our own values rather than bending to every expectation, we build a sense of integrity that others can trust. Honesty about who we are also frees us from the exhausting work of pretending. Yet being true to yourself does not mean ignoring others; it means letting your character guide how you treat people. Kindness is the most visible way this inner strength reaches the world. A small act of patience, a word of encouragement, or a willingness to listen can change how someone sees their own possibilities. Personal achievement matters too, because when we work hard toward goals that reflect our values, our success becomes an example. Classmates who see a peer practice discipline and persevere are often inspired to try harder themselves. The most powerful influence, however, comes from combining achievement with compassion, since success without kindness can feel distant and kindness without effort can lack direction. Together, they show that a person can be both capable and caring. Over time, these everyday choices shape a community where people feel safe being themselves. In this way, staying true to yourself becomes a gift not only to your own life but to everyone whose lives you touch.

Creativity and personal dreams are powerful forces that quietly shape the goals we set and the ways we spend our days. Many people assume that goals come only from practical needs, such as earning a living or meeting expectations, but imagination often plays a larger role than we realize. When a young person imagines becoming a architect, a musician, or a teacher, that image becomes a compass that guides choices about school, friendships, and free time. Creativity allows us to picture a life that does not yet exist, and that picture gives us something to work toward. Without it, daily routines can feel like a series of disconnected tasks with no clear direction. Dreams give those tasks meaning by linking them to a future we genuinely want. Consider a student who sketches buildings in the margins of her notebook. Her doodles may seem like a distraction, yet they reveal a vision that eventually steers her toward engineering or design. Creative habits also help us solve problems along the way. A person who dreams of opening a small bakery must invent recipes, design a storefront, and find customers, and each of these steps requires imaginative thinking. Dreams push us to experiment, and experimentation builds the confidence needed to try again after failure. Personal dreams can also shape how we spend ordinary moments. A person who longs to write a novel may read more carefully, notice details in conversations, and set aside an hour each morning to write. Small decisions, repeated over months, add up to a life that reflects what we care about most. Of course, dreams can change, and that is part of their value. As we grow, our creative interests shift, and new goals replace old ones without erasing what we learned. Even abandoned dreams leave behind skills, perspectives, and habits that influence later choices. Some people worry that chasing dreams is impractical, but a balanced approach allows both security and imagination to coexist. A person can keep a steady job while pursuing painting on weekends, letting creativity enrich a life built on responsibility. Communities benefit as well, because individuals who pursue meaningful goals often contribute new ideas, art, and solutions to shared problems. In the end, creativity and personal dreams are not luxuries reserved for the fortunate few. They are everyday tools that help us imagine who we might become and give us reasons to act on that vision. Recognizing their influence can help us make more intentional choices and live with greater purpose.

Jamie sat in the empty classroom, staring at the clock as Mr. Donnelly lectured on the offside rule for the third time that afternoon. Every sentence somehow circled back to the Premier League, and Jamie had long since stopped pretending to care about the diagrams on the whiteboard. Still, it was far better than last Tuesday, when he had spent an hour being quizzed on fractions by a tutor who sighed at every wrong answer. At least Mr. Donnelly never made him feel stupid, even if he talked about football with the intensity of a prophet. Jamie drummed his pencil against the desk and counted the minutes until the bell, grateful for small mercies. Dull as it was, detention was turning out to be the lesser of two evils.

Dutch prosecutors have opened an investigation into a former soldier who fought alongside Kurdish forces against Islamic State in Syria. The probe, confirmed by officials this week, centers on whether the man's activities abroad violated Dutch law, including rules on participation in armed conflict outside the Netherlands. Legal experts note that the Netherlands has in recent years prosecuted returning fighters under broader terrorism and war-crimes statutes, though the outcome of any case depends heavily on the specific facts. Prosecutors have not publicly named the individual or detailed the allegations, citing the ongoing nature of the inquiry. Defense representatives have said their client acted in support of a coalition effort against a group responsible for widespread atrocities, and they dispute that any offense was committed. Kurdish forces, which played a central role in the campaign to retake territory from Islamic State, were key partners of Western governments during the conflict. Human rights organizations have called for clear guidelines so that individuals who fought against the extremist group are not treated the same as those who joined it. The case has also renewed debate in Dutch politics about how the state should handle citizens who take part in foreign conflicts. Authorities said the investigation is at an early stage and that no charges have been filed. A decision on whether to prosecute is not expected for several months.
