A Scottish jury has begun deliberating on whether Ronnie Coulter murdered Surjit Singh Chhokar, a 32-year-old father who was killed in Glasgow in 1998. The case, which has drawn attention for more than two decades, centres on the events surrounding Chhokar's death in the Scotstoun area of the city. Prosecutors told the court that the evidence, including witness testimony and forensic findings, points to Coulter's involvement in the fatal attack. Coulter has denied any part in the killing. The defence has argued that the case against him relies on evidence that is unreliable and that the passage of time has weakened the prosecution's account. Jurors were given detailed directions from the judge on the legal tests they must apply before reaching a verdict. The trial has heard from a range of witnesses, some of whom gave evidence about events of nearly three decades ago. Chhokar's family has followed the proceedings closely and has long campaigned for justice in the case. The killing was widely reported at the time and became the subject of public debate about racial violence in Scotland. Court officials have said the jury will continue its deliberations and that a verdict is expected once they have reached a unanimous or majority decision under Scottish law. Further details of the verdict will be reported as the court announces its decision.

Denbighshire County Council has proposed a new round of budget cuts that could put youth music programmes and local arts venues at risk, according to documents presented to councillors this week. The proposals form part of wider efforts to close a funding gap facing the north Wales authority as it prepares its budget for the coming year. Arts and cultural services, which have already seen reductions in recent years, are among the areas under review. Youth music groups, which rely heavily on council support for instruments, tuition, and rehearsal space, could see their funding reduced or withdrawn entirely under the proposals. Campaigners say the loss would fall hardest on young people in rural communities, where access to affordable music education is often limited. Several local arts venues, some of which host community performances, school productions, and amateur theatre groups, are also understood to be at risk of reduced subsidies. Venue operators have warned that losing council support could force them to raise ticket prices, cut programming, or close altogether. Music teachers and parents have expressed concern that the cuts could undermine opportunities for children to learn instruments and take part in ensembles and choirs. Supporters of the arts argue that cultural provision contributes to wellbeing, community cohesion, and the local economy, including tourism and hospitality. Council officers have stated that the proposals are not final and that all savings options are being assessed against statutory duties and public consultation requirements. Councillors from several parties have called for a fuller assessment of the likely impact before any decisions are made. Some have suggested exploring alternative funding, including partnerships with schools, grants from arts bodies, and support from local businesses. Opposition members have criticised the administration for what they describe as a short-sighted approach that prioritises immediate savings over long-term investment in young people. The council leadership has defended the proposals, saying difficult choices are unavoidable given reduced central government funding and rising demand for care and education services. A public consultation on the budget is expected to open in the coming weeks, giving residents an opportunity to respond. Arts organisations have urged members of the public to make their views known and to attend council meetings where the proposals will be discussed. Local musicians and former participants in youth programmes have shared stories of how early access to music shaped their confidence and careers. The final budget decision is expected early next year, and the outcome will determine whether these programmes and venues can continue in their current form.

Should schools keep the traditional five-day week or move to a four-day schedule? This question has become increasingly important as districts across the country weigh budgets, student needs, and the wellbeing of teachers. While the five-day week remains the familiar standard, a careful look at the evidence suggests that a four-day schedule can offer real benefits, provided it is implemented thoughtfully.

The most frequently cited advantage of a four-day week is cost. Fewer operating days mean lower spending on utilities, transportation, and building maintenance. For rural districts that must bus students long distances, the savings on fuel and driver hours can be substantial. Districts facing tight budgets may find that a shorter week frees up money for classroom resources that directly support learning.

Teacher recruitment and retention is another reason districts consider the change. Many educators work long hours beyond the school day, and an extra day for planning, grading, and rest can make the profession more sustainable. When teachers are less exhausted, they often bring more energy and focus to their classrooms. Reducing burnout may help districts keep experienced staff who might otherwise leave for other careers.

Supporters also point to student attendance. Some families schedule medical appointments, errands, and family obligations on weekdays, and a shorter school week can make it easier for students to attend the rest of the time. Students who are less likely to miss class may have more consistent learning experiences over the year.

However, critics raise serious concerns about lost instructional time. Four days of school means fewer total hours in the classroom, and this loss can be particularly harmful for students who are already behind. Those students often depend on consistent access to teachers, reading support, and meals provided at school, so a longer weekend can leave them with less structure and fewer resources.

Child care is a second major concern. Working parents may struggle to find supervision for children on the fifth day, which can place a financial burden on families and may lead to unsupervised time. Districts that adopt a four-day week need to consider how families without flexible work schedules will manage.

Research on the four-day week is still limited and mixed. Some studies have found modest gains in attendance and teacher satisfaction, while others show little change in academic achievement or small declines in certain subjects. Because most districts that have switched are small and rural, it is unclear whether the results would apply to large urban systems with different populations and needs.

The success of a four-day schedule also depends heavily on how the extra time is used. If the longer school days are simply stretched out, students may become tired and disengaged. If districts instead design instruction to make each hour count, and offer academic support or enrichment on the off day where possible, the change may be more effective.

In the end, I believe schools should not switch to a four-day week automatically. The decision should depend on local circumstances, including student needs, family situations, and available resources. Districts considering the change should gather input from parents, teachers, and students, and should plan for the challenges of child care and learning loss before making the shift.

Calcium Entry Through P2X2 Receptors Activates ERK Signaling in PC12 Cells, with Responses Varying Between Cell Lines

Abstract

P2X receptors are ATP-gated ion channels that mediate rapid excitatory signaling in neurons and other cell types. Among the seven mammalian P2X subunits, P2X2 is notable for its relatively high permeability to calcium and its expression in neural and neuroendocrine tissues. In this study, we investigated whether calcium entry through P2X2 receptors couples to the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway in PC12 cells, a rat pheochromocytoma line widely used as a model of neuronal differentiation. We further examined whether the magnitude and kinetics of this response differ among related cell lines expressing comparable levels of the receptor. Our findings indicate that ATP stimulation of P2X2-expressing PC12 cells produces a sustained rise in intracellular calcium that is dependent on extracellular calcium, and that this calcium influx is sufficient to promote phosphorylation of ERK1 and ERK2. The response was sensitive to inhibition of voltage-independent calcium entry and to blockade of upstream kinases, supporting a causal link between channel activity and ERK activation. Cross-cell-line comparisons revealed substantial variability in the amplitude and duration of ERK phosphorylation, which correlated with differences in calcium buffering capacity and in the expression of calcium-sensitive adaptor proteins. These results suggest that the consequences of P2X2 signaling are shaped by cellular context, and that caution is warranted when generalizing findings from a single cell line to other neural or neuroendocrine systems.

Introduction

Extracellular ATP acts as a signaling molecule through two families of purinergic receptors, the G protein-coupled P2Y receptors and the ligand-gated P2X receptors. P2X receptors assemble as homotrimers or heterotrimers from seven subunits, P2X1 through P2X7, and form cation-permeable pores that admit sodium, potassium, and calcium. The relative calcium permeability varies among subtypes, and P2X2 has been reported to display a meaningful calcium component compared with some other family members. This property positions P2X2 as a potential link between purinergic stimulation and calcium-dependent intracellular cascades.

The mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway, and in particular the ERK1/2 cascade, integrates signals from receptor tyrosine kinases, G protein-coupled receptors, and ion channels to regulate gene expression, proliferation, survival, and differentiation. In neuronal and neuroendocrine cells, ERK activation is strongly associated with neurite outgrowth and with long-term changes in excitability. Calcium can activate ERK through several routes, including calcium-dependent activation of Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factors, calmodulin-dependent kinases, and protein kinase C isoforms. Thus, calcium influx through ligand-gated channels provides a plausible mechanism for coupling fast purinergic signaling to slower transcriptional programs.

PC12 cells are a well-characterized model for studying neuronal signaling. Upon treatment with nerve growth factor, they extend neurites and adopt a sympathetic-like phenotype, and ERK activation is a central component of this response. PC12 cells endogenously express several purinergic receptors, but they lack robust native P2X2 expression, making them a suitable background for controlled reconstitution. Several related lines derived from the same parental population are used in different laboratories, and it is not yet clear whether they respond to identical stimuli in an equivalent manner. Such variability would have implications for reproducibility and for the interpretation of cross-laboratory results.

The aims of this study were threefold. First, we sought to determine whether ATP-induced calcium entry through P2X2 receptors is sufficient to activate ERK in PC12 cells. Second, we asked whether this activation depends on extracellular calcium and on specific upstream signaling intermediates. Third, we compared the ERK response across cell lines to determine whether the magnitude and time course of signaling are conserved.

Materials and Methods

Cell culture. PC12 cells and two related sublines were maintained in RPMI 1640 medium supplemented with horse serum, fetal bovine serum, and penicillin-streptomycin at 37 degrees Celsius in a humidified atmosphere containing five percent carbon dioxide. Cells were passaged every three to four days and used between passages five and fifteen.

Receptor expression. Stable expression of rat P2X2 was achieved by transfection with a plasmid encoding the full-length receptor under a constitutive promoter, followed by antibiotic selection. Clones were screened by immunoblotting and by quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. Clones with comparable expression levels were selected for comparative analysis.

Calcium imaging. Cells were loaded with a ratiometric calcium indicator and imaged on an inverted fluorescence microscope equipped with a temperature-controlled stage. Baseline fluorescence was recorded for two minutes before application of ATP at concentrations ranging from ten micromolar to one millimolar. Calcium-free experiments were performed using a buffer lacking calcium and containing a chelator, and selected experiments used a P2X2 antagonist to confirm specificity.

ERK phosphorylation. Cells were stimulated with ATP for defined intervals, lysed in buffer containing phosphatase and protease inhibitors, and analyzed by immunoblotting with antibodies recognizing phosphorylated ERK1/2 and total ERK. Band intensities were quantified by densitometry and normalized to total ERK. Pharmacological inhibitors of MEK, calcium chelation with an intracellular buffer, and inhibitors of calmodulin-dependent kinases were applied prior to stimulation in separate experiments.

Calcium buffering and adaptor expression. Intracellular calcium buffering capacity was estimated from the decay kinetics of evoked transients following brief depolarization. Expression of calcium-sensitive adaptor proteins was assessed by immunoblotting and quantitative polymerase chain reaction.

Statistical analysis. Data are presented as mean plus or minus standard error from at least three independent experiments. Comparisons between groups were made using analysis of variance with appropriate post hoc tests, and differences were considered significant at p less than 0.05.

Results

Stimulation of P2X2-expressing PC12 cells with ATP produced a concentration-dependent rise in intracellular calcium. Responses were detectable at ten micromolar ATP and reached a plateau near one hundred micromolar. In the absence of extracellular calcium, the sustained component of the response was markedly reduced, indicating that a substantial portion of the signal arises from calcium entry rather than release from intracellular stores.

ATP stimulation also increased ERK1/2 phosphorylation. Phosphorylation was first detectable within two minutes, peaked between five and ten minutes, and declined toward baseline by thirty minutes in the parental line. Parental PC12 cells lacking P2X2 did not show a comparable response, confirming that the effect depends on receptor expression. Calcium chelation during stimulation substantially attenuated ERK phosphorylation, and the MEK inhibitor abolished it, placing ERK activation downstream of calcium influx.

Inhibition of calmodulin-dependent kinase partially reduced ERK phosphorylation, suggesting that calmodulin-linked pathways contribute to the response. Protein kinase C inhibition produced a smaller effect. Together these observations support a model in which calcium entry through P2X2 activates ERK through multiple calcium-sensitive intermediates.

Comparison across cell lines revealed clear differences. Although receptor expression was matched, one subline exhibited a larger and more prolonged ERK response, with phosphorylation persisting beyond thirty minutes. A second subline showed a smaller and more transient response that nearly resolved within fifteen minutes. Calcium transient amplitudes differed correspondingly, and the prolonged-response line displayed slower calcium decay, consistent with lower buffering capacity. Expression of a calcium-sensitive adaptor protein was higher in the prolonged-response line, and knockdown of this adaptor reduced the sustained phase of ERK phosphorylation.

Discussion

Our results establish that calcium entry through P2X2 receptors is sufficient to activate ERK signaling in PC12 cells. The dependence on extracellular calcium, the sensitivity to chelation, and the abolition by MEK inhibition together support a causal chain from ligand-gated calcium influx to kinase activation. The partial involvement of calmodulin-dependent kinase and protein kinase C suggests that the calcium signal is decoded by more than one pathway.

The variability between cell lines is an important finding. Despite comparable receptor levels, differences in calcium buffering and adaptor expression shaped both the amplitude and duration of ERK phosphorylation. This indicates that the output of a single channel can be substantially modified by the cellular environment. Such context dependence may explain discrepancies in the literature and underscores the need to characterize the signaling capacity of each cell line before drawing general conclusions.

Several limitations should be noted. Our experiments relied on heterologous expression, which may not fully recapitulate native P2X2 regulation. Receptor trafficking, desensitization kinetics, and interactions with other purinergic receptors were not exhaustively examined. Additionally, ERK activation is only one readout; transcriptional and morphological consequences of P2X2 signaling warrant further study, particularly in the context of neurite outgrowth.

Future work should test whether the adaptor-dependent differences observed here extend to primary neurons and to in vivo systems. Determining how P2X2 signaling interacts with nerve growth factor-driven differentiation would also clarify the physiological relevance of these findings.

Conclusion

Calcium entry through P2X2 receptors activates ERK signaling in PC12 cells through calcium-sensitive intermediates, and the magnitude and duration of this response vary between related cell lines in a manner linked to calcium buffering and adaptor expression. These findings highlight both a mechanism by which fast purinergic signals can drive sustained kinase activity and the importance of cellular context in interpreting such responses.

References

A complete reference list would be supplied with the final manuscript, including primary citations for P2X receptor biophysics, ERK signaling in neuroendocrine cells, and PC12 differentiation models.

This manuscript investigates neural mixture-density models for temporal point processes and compares them against normalizing-flow methods for modeling inter-event time distributions. The topic is timely and relevant, as flexible parametric and generative approaches to event-sequence modeling have gained considerable attention in recent years. The authors clearly motivate the problem by noting that classical intensity-based models such as the Hawkes process impose restrictive functional forms that may misrepresent complex temporal dependencies. The introduction is well organized and situates the work adequately within the existing literature on neural temporal point processes. The mixture-density formulation is described with sufficient mathematical detail, including the parameterization of the conditional density and the training objective based on log-likelihood. The normalizing-flow baselines are reasonably chosen, although the paper would benefit from a more thorough justification of why these particular flow architectures were selected over alternatives. The experimental section evaluates models on several benchmark datasets, which is commendable, but the datasets are relatively small and the diversity of domains could be expanded. Reported metrics include negative log-likelihood and prediction error, yet the manuscript does not consistently report variance across random seeds, which weakens confidence in the observed differences. Several comparisons between the two model families appear to be within the range of run-to-run variability, and the claims of superiority should be tempered accordingly. The ablation study on the number of mixture components is informative, though the authors should also examine sensitivity to optimization hyperparameters. Computational cost, including training time and inference latency, is discussed only briefly and deserves a more systematic treatment, since it is a practical consideration for deployment. The figures are clear, but the calibration analysis would be more convincing with quantitative measures such as the time-rescaling test or Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics. The related work section omits some recent contributions on transformer-based point process models, which should be discussed for completeness. The writing is generally clear, though some notation is overloaded and would benefit from a summary table. Overall, the paper makes a useful empirical contribution, but I recommend a major revision that adds statistical rigor, broader evaluation, and a clearer discussion of the limitations before the conclusions can be fully supported.

Sustainable Hillside Hotel Design: Energy, Insulation, and Materials

Building a hotel on a hillside presents both unique challenges and remarkable opportunities for sustainable design. Sloped terrain exposes structures to wind, sun, and rain in ways that flat sites do not, and it can be harnessed to reduce energy demand. Designers who work with the natural contours of a hill can lower construction disturbance, limit erosion, and create buildings that feel rooted in their landscape. This page explains three core principles: renewable energy generation, natural insulation, and the use of recyclable building components.

Renewable energy is central to any sustainable hotel. On a hillside, rooftop and terrace areas often receive strong, unobstructed sunlight, making them well suited to photovoltaic panels. Solar thermal collectors can supply hot water for guest rooms, kitchens, and laundry facilities. Where wind speeds are consistent, small vertical-axis turbines may complement solar arrays, although site-specific wind studies are essential before installation. Geothermal heat pumps offer another option, since the ground temperature a few meters below the surface remains relatively stable throughout the year, allowing efficient heating and cooling. Battery storage can smooth the mismatch between generation and guest demand, particularly during evening hours.

Passive design strategies reduce the energy a hotel needs in the first place. Orienting the building to capture winter sun and shade it in summer is one of the most cost-effective decisions a designer can make. Cascading or terraced building forms can allow each room to enjoy daylight and views while minimizing the thermal mass exposed to the hottest afternoon sun. Natural ventilation, guided by the prevailing breezes that often flow up or down slopes, can reduce reliance on mechanical cooling. Deep overhangs, operable shutters, and carefully sized windows further control solar gain.

Natural insulation materials provide thermal performance while lowering the environmental burden of construction. Sheep's wool, hemp, cork, cellulose from recycled newspaper, and wood fiber board all offer good insulating values with far lower embodied energy than many synthetic foams. These materials also regulate humidity, which helps protect the building envelope and improves indoor comfort for guests. Earth-based walls, such as rammed earth or compressed earth blocks, add substantial thermal mass that stabilizes indoor temperatures across the day. When selecting insulation, designers should verify fire ratings, moisture performance, and pest resistance appropriate to the local climate.

Recyclable building components close the loop between construction and demolition. Steel framing, timber sourced from certified forests, and modular panels fastened with bolts rather than adhesives can be disassembled and reused at the end of a building's life. Designing for disassembly means documenting materials and connections so that future renovators can recover valuable components. Reclaimed brick, salvaged timber, and recycled glass countertops reduce demand for virgin resources. Selecting low-VOC finishes and paints also protects the health of both guests and staff.

Hillside sites require careful attention to structural and drainage issues. Foundations may be stepped to follow the slope, and retaining walls can be built from gabion baskets filled with local stone, which allow water to drain and support vegetation. Green roofs and planted terraces absorb rainfall, reduce runoff, and provide habitat for pollinators. Native plantings require less irrigation and help stabilize soil over the long term. Before construction begins, geotechnical surveys and erosion control plans are essential to protect both the building and the surrounding ecosystem.

Measuring performance is the final step in a sustainable design process. Energy monitoring systems track consumption and generation, allowing operators to identify inefficiencies and adjust operations. Certification frameworks such as LEED, BREEAM, and Passive House offer structured benchmarks for evaluating a building's environmental performance. Post-occupancy evaluations gather feedback from guests and staff on comfort, air quality, and daily experience. Sharing these results helps the wider industry learn from each project.

In summary, a sustainable hillside hotel combines site-responsive planning, renewable energy systems, natural insulation, and recyclable materials into a coherent whole. Each element reinforces the others, so that a building can produce much of its own energy, remain comfortable with minimal mechanical systems, and be taken apart responsibly when its useful life ends. Designers, owners, and guests all benefit when hospitality architecture respects the land it occupies.

The manuscript investigates whether neural networks can learn to imitate iterative algorithms, with particular attention to out-of-distribution generalization and the representations of numbers that such models acquire. The question is timely and well motivated, since algorithmic reasoning is a common stress test for claims about generalization in neural models. The authors frame the problem clearly and situate their work reasonably well within the literature on algorithmic learning and length generalization. The central contribution, as I read it, is an empirical characterization of when learned iterative procedures transfer to input sizes and value ranges beyond those seen in training. The experimental design includes multiple algorithmic tasks, which is a strength, because it prevents conclusions from being tied to a single procedure. However, the choice of training and test distributions is described only briefly, and the paper would benefit from a more explicit justification of the split boundaries. The analysis of learned number representations is the most novel part of the work and deserves more depth than it currently receives. The authors report that some models develop structured, approximately linear encodings of magnitude, but the evidence for this claim rests largely on visualizations that are difficult to interpret without quantitative support. I would encourage the authors to add probing experiments or a measure of representational similarity that can be compared across architectures and random seeds. Reporting variance across seeds is essential, since several of the generalization results appear to depend heavily on initialization. The main results table would be more informative with confidence intervals and with the number of runs stated explicitly. The discussion of failure modes is useful, and the observation that errors often accumulate at specific digit boundaries is an interesting finding that the authors could explore further. Ablations isolating the effect of architecture, positional encoding, and training data curriculum would strengthen the causal claims considerably. At present, some statements in the discussion go beyond what the experiments support, particularly the suggestion that the learned procedures correspond to the underlying algorithms in a mechanistic sense. The authors should either provide evidence for this stronger interpretation or soften the language. The related work section omits several relevant studies on length generalization and on tracing intermediate computation, and including them would clarify what is new here. The writing is generally clear, though some notation for the iteration index is introduced inconsistently and should be unified. Figures are legible, but the axis labels in the generalization curves should specify units and the range of evaluated lengths. The appendix contains useful hyperparameter details, yet the training compute budget is not reported, which limits reproducibility and fair comparison. Code and data availability is mentioned but no repository link is given, and I would ask the authors to provide one. The limitations section acknowledges small model scale, which is appropriate, but it should also discuss whether conclusions would hold for larger pretrained models. Overall, the paper addresses an important question with a sound general approach and some promising findings. Its main weaknesses are the thin quantitative support for the representational claims and the absence of seed-level statistics. I recommend a major revision. With additional probing analyses, statistical reporting, and more cautious interpretation, the work could make a solid contribution to the study of algorithmic generalization in neural networks.

Overview of Nursing Theories and Their Application to Nursing Practice

Nursing theory provides a structured way of understanding what nurses do, why they do it, and how their actions produce outcomes for patients. Theories give nurses a common language, guide decision-making, and help the profession explain its unique contribution to health care. In this overview, we explore major nursing theories, how they developed, and how they can be applied in everyday clinical practice.

Nursing theory emerged as a distinct field in the mid-twentieth century, when nurse scholars began arguing that nursing needed its own body of knowledge rather than borrowing entirely from medicine. Early nurse theorists asked fundamental questions: What is nursing? What is the goal of nursing care? What role does the nurse play in a patient's recovery?

Florence Nightingale, though she wrote before formal nursing theory existed, laid important groundwork. In her Notes on Nursing, published in 1859, she emphasized environmental factors such as fresh air, light, cleanliness, and noise control as essential to healing. Her ideas are often considered an early environmental theory of nursing.

Nursing theories are commonly grouped into categories. These include metaparadigm concepts, grand theories, middle-range theories, and practice theories. Each category serves a different purpose and operates at a different level of abstraction.

The metaparadigm of nursing refers to the broad concepts that define the discipline. Most scholars identify four: person, environment, health, and nursing. Every nursing theory addresses these concepts in some way, even if it defines them differently.

Grand theories are broad, comprehensive frameworks that attempt to describe the entire scope of nursing. They tend to be abstract and are often used to shape curriculum, research agendas, and professional philosophy.

Middle-range theories are narrower and more specific. They address particular phenomena, such as fatigue, uncertainty in illness, or self-care, and can be tested through research more directly than grand theories.

Practice theories are the most concrete. They describe specific interventions or clinical processes and are designed to guide bedside decisions.

Virginia Henderson developed one of the most widely known nursing frameworks. She defined nursing as assisting individuals, sick or well, in the performance of activities that contribute to health, recovery, or peaceful death. Her model identifies fourteen components of basic nursing care, including breathing, eating, eliminating, moving, sleeping, and communicating.

Henderson's framework is particularly useful for assessment. Nurses can use her fourteen needs as a checklist to identify areas where a patient requires help, and to focus on restoring independence as quickly as possible.

Dorothea Orem proposed the self-care deficit theory, which holds that people have a natural capacity to care for themselves. Nursing becomes necessary when a person's self-care demands exceed their ability to meet them.

Orem's theory includes three related parts: the theory of self-care, the theory of self-care deficit, and the theory of nursing systems. Together they help nurses decide how much to do for a patient, how much to teach, and how much to support the patient in doing self-care.

Hildegard Peplau described nursing as an interpersonal process. Her interpersonal relations theory focuses on the therapeutic relationship between nurse and patient, which she viewed as a learning experience for both.

Peplau identified four phases of the nurse-patient relationship: orientation, identification, exploitation, and resolution. Recognizing these phases helps nurses understand where they are in a relationship and what the patient needs at each stage.

Joyce Travelbee emphasized human-to-human relationships as the core of nursing. She argued that nurses should move beyond seeing patients as illnesses and instead connect with them as unique individuals experiencing suffering.

Travelbee's work encourages nurses to find meaning in their interactions with patients. Her ideas remain influential in discussions of compassionate care and patient-centered communication.

Martha Rogers proposed a science of unitary human beings. She viewed people and their environments as integrated, energy fields that continuously interact. Her theory is more abstract than some others but has influenced nursing philosophy and holistic care.

Madeleine Leininger developed transcultural nursing theory, focusing on the cultural care of individuals and groups. She emphasized that care must be understood within the cultural context of the patient, including beliefs, values, and practices.

Leininger's work highlights the importance of cultural humility and culturally congruent care. Nurses who apply her ideas assess a patient's cultural background and adapt care plans to respect that background.

Jean Watson developed a theory of human caring, which places caring at the center of nursing practice. She described ten carative factors that guide caring interactions, including the nurse's sensitivity to self and others and the creation of a healing environment.

Watson's theory is often applied in settings where emotional and spiritual needs are especially important, such as palliative care and mental health nursing.

Nancy Roper, Winifred Logan, and Alison Tierney developed the Roper-Logan-Tierney model, which is widely used in the United Kingdom. It organizes nursing care around activities of living, such as maintaining a safe environment, communicating, and mobilizing.

Ernestine Wiedenbach proposed the helping art of clinical nursing, which emphasizes the nurse's purposeful, skilled assistance to patients. She highlighted the importance of clinical judgment and the nurse's ability to recognize a patient's immediate needs.

Betty Neuman developed the Neuman Systems Model, which views the patient as a system surrounded by layers of protection. Stressors can disrupt these layers, and nurses intervene to strengthen the patient's defenses and restore stability.

Callista Roy developed the Roy Adaptation Model, which views people as adaptive systems. Health involves the ability to adapt to changes in the environment, and nurses help patients adapt through assessment and intervention.

Applying nursing theory begins with understanding the theory's core concepts and assumptions. A nurse should know what the theory says about patients, environments, health, and nursing before attempting to use it.

The nursing process is one practical way to apply theory. It includes assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation. Theories can inform each step by shaping what the nurse looks for, how problems are framed, and how outcomes are judged.

During assessment, a theory helps determine which data are relevant. A nurse using Orem's model, for example, would focus on the patient's self-care abilities and limitations.

During diagnosis, theory helps the nurse name the patient's needs in a consistent way. Using a common framework improves communication among team members.

During planning, theory guides the selection of interventions. A nurse using Roy's model might design care that promotes adaptation to a new chronic illness.

During implementation, theory helps nurses deliver care with purpose. Actions become connected to a broader rationale rather than being simply routine tasks.

During evaluation, theory provides criteria for judging whether care was effective. Outcomes can be measured against the goals the theory identifies.

Theories also support evidence-based practice. Research built on nursing theory can test whether interventions produce improved outcomes, and clinical experience can in turn refine the theory.

Nursing education benefits from theory as well. Students who learn theory develop critical thinking skills and a clearer understanding of their professional role.

Some critics argue that nursing theories are too abstract for daily practice. Others note that different theories can conflict. Practitioners should recognize these limitations and choose theories that fit their setting and patients.

Many experienced nurses use eclectic approaches, drawing on elements from several theories. This flexibility can be useful, provided the nurse understands the underlying assumptions of each framework.

In summary, nursing theories offer valuable tools for organizing knowledge, guiding practice, and communicating the nursing perspective. By understanding the major theories and how they apply to clinical situations, nurses can deliver care that is thoughtful, consistent, and centered on the needs of each patient.

The manuscript proposes a quaternion-based rotation-equivariant capsule network for classifying 3D point clouds, aiming to make recognition robust to arbitrary object orientations without relying on heavy data augmentation. The motivation is clearly stated and well situated within the literature on rotation-equivariant deep learning, capsule networks, and point-cloud processing such as PointNet and its successors. The use of quaternions to parameterize rotations is a sensible choice, since they avoid gimbal lock and offer a compact, numerically stable representation for composing rotations. The authors frame capsule poses as quaternion-valued quantities and design routing and transformation operations that respect the group structure of SO(3), which is the central technical contribution. The mathematical formulation is largely sound, and the derivations of equivariance properties are presented in an accessible way, though some key steps would benefit from fuller justification in the main text rather than the appendix. The architecture description is detailed enough to follow, but the manuscript would be stronger with a schematic diagram showing how point features, primary capsules, and class capsules flow through the network. The experimental section evaluates the model on a standard benchmark dataset, and the reported accuracy on canonically aligned inputs is competitive with recent baselines. The more important results concern performance on randomly rotated test data, where the proposed method shows a clear advantage over non-equivariant baselines, which supports the central claim. However, the comparison set omits several recent rotation-invariant point-cloud methods, and including them would make the claimed advantage more convincing. The ablation study isolating the contribution of quaternion parameterization versus rotation matrices or Euler angles is a valuable addition, but the reported differences are small and no variance across random seeds is given, so their significance is unclear. Runtime and memory costs are mentioned only briefly, and since capsule routing is known to be computationally expensive, a fuller efficiency analysis is needed. The authors should also clarify how the method handles non-rigid deformations and partial occlusions, which are common in real scanned data but are not evaluated. The discussion of limitations is brief and should be expanded to address sensitivity to point density and noise. The related-work section is thorough but occasionally lists methods without explaining how they differ from the proposed approach. Several figures have small fonts and low resolution, making the results tables and plots difficult to read at print size. The reference list is generally complete, though a few preprints have since been published and should be updated. The writing is clear overall, with only minor grammatical issues and some repetitive phrasing in the introduction. Reproducibility would be improved by releasing code and the exact hyperparameter settings used for training. The provided training details are adequate but omit the learning rate schedule and the number of routing iterations used in the final model. In summary, the paper addresses a meaningful problem with a principled approach and shows promising results on rotated inputs. Its main weaknesses lie in the breadth of baseline comparisons, the statistical reporting, and the efficiency and robustness analyses. I recommend a major revision, with the expectation that these issues can be addressed to make the contribution more compelling and reproducible.

Remote learning has become a meaningful option for students who want to succeed academically while managing the many responsibilities of their personal lives. Although it is sometimes criticized for reducing face-to-face interaction, it offers flexibility that can help students balance school with work, family, health, and other commitments. When used well, it can support both academic achievement and personal well-being.

One of the greatest advantages of remote learning is flexibility in scheduling. Many online courses allow students to access lectures, readings, and assignments at times that suit their routines. A student who works an early morning shift, for example, can review course materials in the afternoon instead of missing class altogether. This adaptability reduces the stress of choosing between a paycheck and an education.

Remote learning also allows students to learn at their own pace. In a traditional classroom, instruction moves forward whether or not every student has grasped the material. Online courses often let students pause a recorded lecture, rewatch a difficult explanation, or spend extra time on a challenging problem set. This control can deepen understanding and lead to stronger results on exams and assignments.

Another benefit is the reduction of commuting time. Students who once spent hours traveling to and from campus can redirect that time toward studying, rest, or caring for family members. For students who are parents, caregivers, or who live far from educational institutions, this saved time can make the difference between enrolling and not enrolling at all.

Remote learning can also help students develop independence and self-discipline. Because there is no teacher standing at the front of the room, students must set goals, create study schedules, and hold themselves accountable. These habits are valuable beyond the classroom and prepare students for careers and lives that demand self-management.

Technology has made remote learning more accessible and interactive. Discussion forums, video conferences, and shared digital documents allow students to collaborate with classmates and receive feedback from instructors. Many students find that online discussions give them time to think carefully before responding, which can lead to more thoughtful contributions than those made under the pressure of a live classroom.

Of course, remote learning is not without challenges. Students need reliable internet access, a quiet place to study, and the discipline to avoid distractions. Without support, some learners may feel isolated or fall behind. Schools can address these problems by offering technical assistance, regular check-ins with instructors, and access to counseling and tutoring services.

Ultimately, remote learning can help students succeed when it is paired with thoughtful planning and institutional support. By offering flexibility, personalized pacing, reduced commuting, and opportunities to build independence, it allows students to pursue education without abandoning the other responsibilities in their lives. For many learners, that balance is not just convenient but essential to reaching their goals.

The case came to me on a Tuesday, wrapped in the smell of cheap cologne and a manila folder stamped with a faded Polaroid of a Dalmatian. My client, a woman named Marjorie Vance, said her husband was sleeping with a lighthouse. I told her lighthouses don't have a sleeping schedule, and she told me that was exactly the kind of thinking that got private investigators divorced. I wasn't sure, that week, whether I was the detective or the suspect, or whether I even had a preference between the two, a question I'd been avoiding since I saw Bowie in that white suit on a rerun of some forgotten variety show. My partner, a retired Elvis impersonator named Dale, kept humming "Ring of Fire" while he tailed the husband, Gerald, through a parade of mannequins outside a closed Blockbuster. Gerald went into a warehouse marked Tupperware Museum, and I followed him in wearing a trench coat that had once belonged to Columbo, which I'd bought at a yard sale in Twin Peaks from a woman who claimed she was the Log Lady's cousin. Inside, the lighthouse turned out to be a jukebox shaped like Venus de Milo, and it was playing Joni Mitchell in reverse. Gerald was dancing with a sentient sock puppet named Mr. Gorgeous, who whispered that the whole affair was a publicity stunt for a Ziggy Stardust revival. I felt a weird tug toward the sock puppet, then toward Gerald, then toward the Venus jukebox, and I realized my compass had stopped spinning north and started spinning toward whoever looked most like Tilda Swinton in a Fellini film. Dale burst through the door dressed as Tom Selleck in Magnum P.I., holding a cassette labeled Marjorie's Secret Mixtape. The tape played nothing but the sound of a lighthouse foghorn harmonizing with Freddie Mercury. Marjorie, it turned out, had been the one sending the anonymous love letters to herself, signed Mr. Gorgeous, to test whether I was paying attention. I was not, entirely, but I wrote the report anyway, in the style of a Raymond Chandler novel crossed with a horoscope. I billed Marjorie for nine hours of wandering, one hour of existential crisis, and a lunch at a diner where the waitress was Audrey Hepburn in a paper hat. She paid in silver dollars stamped with lipstick kisses. Gerald never knew what he'd been part of, and neither did I, though I still keep the cassette on my desk next to a cactus shaped like a question mark. Sometimes at night I play it and listen for the foghorn, hoping it will tell me who I am.

Self-driving cars promise to reshape how people travel, but their arrival brings real safety risks that society must take seriously. Chief among these is the risk of technical failure, since autonomous systems rely on sensors, cameras, and software that can misread a situation, such as mistaking a white truck for open sky or failing to recognize a pedestrian in poor lighting. Software errors are also difficult to predict because the systems learn from enormous amounts of data and can behave in unexpected ways when they encounter situations outside their training. Cybersecurity presents another danger, as a vehicle connected to the internet could be hacked, potentially allowing outsiders to disable brakes or redirect its path. Beyond these technical concerns, there is the question of how responsibility is assigned after a crash. When a human driver causes an accident, the blame is usually clear, but when a computer makes the decision, liability may fall on the manufacturer, the software developer, the owner, or some combination of them. Lawmakers and courts are still working out these questions, and unclear rules can leave victims without a clear path to compensation. Manufacturers therefore carry a serious responsibility to test their systems extensively, to be transparent about their capabilities and limits, and to report failures honestly. Regulators must set clear safety standards, require independent testing, and monitor vehicles on public roads. Drivers and owners also have responsibilities, including understanding what their vehicles can and cannot do and remaining ready to take control when required. Overtrust is a particular hazard, because people who believe a car can handle everything may stop paying attention, and this can be deadly when the system reaches its limits. Public education can help reduce this risk by explaining the difference between driver assistance and full automation. Ethical questions also arise, such as how a car should be programmed to respond in an unavoidable collision, though most of the everyday risk comes from more ordinary failures. Data privacy deserves attention too, since these vehicles collect detailed information about where people go and how they behave. Protecting that information is part of protecting people's safety and trust. Ultimately, self-driving cars could prevent many of the crashes caused by human error, which kill and injure large numbers of people each year. Realizing that benefit, however, depends on careful engineering, honest accountability, thoughtful regulation, and informed users. Safety, not speed of deployment, should guide the path forward.

Work on the New Highland bridge project is moving forward despite recent setbacks caused by strong winds. Crews have been unable to lift heavy steel girders into place on several days over the past two weeks, as wind speeds regularly exceeded the safe operating limits for the cranes. Project officials said the delays have been frustrating but manageable, and they expect to recover much of the lost time once conditions improve. In the meantime, workers have focused on tasks that do not require crane lifts, including concrete pouring for the abutments, installing drainage systems, and preparing the approach roads. Engineers said the wind-related pauses were built into the schedule as a precaution and have not affected the structural integrity of completed sections. Local residents who commute across the nearby river have been asked to expect intermittent lane closures during the next phase of work. Officials said the bridges are still on track to open to traffic next year, pending weather and final inspections.

Teacher encouragement plays a powerful role in helping students build confidence and succeed in school. When a teacher recognizes a student's effort and praises specific progress, the student begins to believe that improvement is possible. This belief encourages students to take on challenging problems instead of avoiding them out of fear of failure. Positive feedback also helps students see mistakes as a natural part of learning rather than as proof that they are not capable. Over time, this mindset leads to greater persistence, better study habits, and stronger academic performance. Simple words of support, such as telling a student that their idea was thoughtful or their hard work is paying off, can make a lasting difference. In this way, encouraging teachers do more than teach subjects; they help students discover their own potential and grow into confident, capable learners.

A longtime Star Wars collector has sold part of his prized vintage toy collection to help fund the purchase of a new home. The collection, built over more than three decades, includes original 1977 and 1980 figures still in their factory-sealed packaging. The sale was arranged through a specialty auction house that focuses on vintage action figures and collectibles. Experts say the figures drew strong interest from buyers across the United States and Europe. Among the most sought-after items was a sealed Darth Vader figure from the original Kenner line, which experts estimate could fetch several thousand dollars on its own. The collector, who asked not to be named, said the decision was difficult but necessary after years of renting. He described the toys as the work of a lifetime, but said his family's need for stable housing had become more important. He plans to keep a smaller selection of figures that hold special sentimental value. Collectors in the community have expressed mixed reactions, with some praising his honesty and others saying they wish he had found another way to raise the funds. Market analysts note that vintage Star Wars figures have grown steadily in value over the past decade. The auction house said proceeds from the sale would be transferred to the collector within a few weeks. For now, the collector says he is looking forward to unpacking boxes in a home of his own.

Deadly clashes erupted this week between Philippine government troops and Abu Sayyaf militants in the southern province of Sulu, as security forces intensified efforts to capture the group's leader. Military officials said the fighting broke out during a sweep of mountainous terrain where militants were believed to be hiding. Several soldiers were killed and wounded in the exchanges of gunfire, while the military reported that a number of militants were also killed. Local residents in the affected villages reported hearing sustained gunfire and explosions, and many families fled their homes in search of safer ground. The army said the operation is aimed at dismantling the remaining Abu Sayyaf network, a group long linked to kidnappings for ransom, bombings, and attacks on civilians. Abu Sayyaf, which has pledged allegiance to the Islamic State, has been significantly weakened over the past decade by sustained military pressure. Government officials said the leader being pursued is considered a key figure in coordinating the group's remaining operations and financing. Security analysts noted that the group's remaining fighters have relied on rugged jungle terrain and close ties with local communities to evade capture. The military has deployed additional troops and surveillance assets to the area to cut off escape routes. Authorities have urged civilians to avoid the conflict zones and to report any information about militant movements to the nearest police or army unit. Humanitarian groups expressed concern about the impact of the fighting on displaced families, many of whom lack adequate food, water, and shelter. Local leaders called for restraint and for efforts to ensure the safety of noncombatants during the operation. Officials said they would release further details on casualties and the progress of the operation as the situation develops.

Supervised after-school programs offer students a structured environment during the hours between the end of the school day and the return of their parents from work. Research on these programs has consistently shown that they can improve academic performance, particularly in reading and mathematics, because they provide dedicated time for homework completion and tutoring. Students who attend regularly often develop stronger study habits and a more reliable routine, which helps them manage assignments and prepare for tests. Beyond academics, these programs give young people access to enrichment activities such as science clubs, art classes, and music lessons that may not be available at home or in their schools. Many programs also expose students to sports and physical activity, which supports both their health and their ability to focus in class. The presence of trained adult supervisors creates a safe space where children are less likely to engage in risky behavior during the afternoon hours, a period when juvenile crime and unsupervised activity tend to peak. Equally important are the social benefits, as students learn to cooperate with peers, resolve conflicts, and build friendships across different grades and backgrounds. Mentorship is another valuable element, since caring staff members can offer encouragement, guidance, and a trusted adult to turn to when students face personal or academic challenges. Participation can also strengthen self-esteem, because children who succeed at a new skill or take on leadership roles gain confidence in their abilities. For working families, these programs reduce anxiety about childcare and allow parents to focus on their jobs with greater peace of mind. Some programs also involve parents directly, which can improve communication between families and schools. Critics note that program quality varies widely, so funding, staff training, and careful planning remain essential. Nevertheless, when well designed and adequately supported, supervised after-school programs provide meaningful gains that extend well beyond the afternoon hours.

Why Tanning Risks May Not Change Consumer Attitudes Toward Sun Exposure and Sunscreen Use

Public health campaigns have spent decades warning people that ultraviolet radiation causes skin cancer, premature aging, and eye damage, yet many people continue to seek tans and skip sunscreen. This gap between knowledge and behavior is a central puzzle for health educators. One reason is that risk information is often abstract: a skin cancer diagnosis may be years away and seems unlikely to happen to any one person. Many people also hold an optimistic bias, believing that they are less vulnerable than others. A tan can carry social and aesthetic meaning, signaling health, leisure, or attractiveness in certain cultures and communities. Some individuals associate tanning with relaxation or mood improvement, which can make the activity feel rewarding in the moment. Others misunderstand how sun damage works, assuming that a tan is a sign of protection when it actually reflects injury to the skin. Cloudy days and cooler temperatures can lead people to underestimate their exposure to UV rays, which penetrate clouds and can be strong even when the sun is not visibly intense. Sunscreen use is further undermined by the perception that it is greasy, inconvenient, or expensive to apply consistently. Advertising and media images that glorify bronzed skin can reinforce these attitudes and counter health messages. Effective communication may therefore require more than listing risks, since fear-based messages can be dismissed or can provoke defensive reactions. Researchers suggest that messages framed around personal relevance, such as visible aging or family history, may resonate more strongly. Making sunscreen more comfortable, affordable, and easy to use, and encouraging shade seeking, can reduce the effort required to stay protected. Social norms also matter, as people are more likely to adopt protective habits when they see friends, family, and role models doing the same. Ultimately, changing sun behavior appears to depend on addressing emotional, social, and practical factors alongside factual knowledge.

The manuscript addresses an important and contested question: whether the information bottleneck framework can be used to estimate how deep neural networks compress their representations, and whether that compression matters for training performance. The authors are to be commended for tackling a topic that has drawn considerable attention since the original claims about compression phases were made, and for framing the work around measurable quantities rather than purely qualitative narratives. The motivation is clearly stated, and the introduction situates the study reasonably well within prior work on mutual information estimation and layer-wise training. However, the central methodological issue is that mutual information between high-dimensional continuous activations and inputs is notoriously difficult to estimate, and the manuscript does not sufficiently justify the estimator it uses. The authors should explain how their estimator behaves under the saturation and binning artifacts that have been documented in earlier work, and they should report sensitivity analyses across estimator choices. The experimental design would be strengthened by including multiple random seeds, confidence intervals, and a clear description of the datasets and architectures so that the results can be reproduced. The claim that compression correlates with improved layer-wise training performance is interesting, but the correlation is presented without controlling for confounders such as learning rate, depth, and layer width. The authors should either add controlled ablations or temper the causal language in the abstract and conclusions. The discussion of compression phases is also somewhat overstated relative to the evidence, since the figures show trends that are not clearly distinguishable from noise at the reported sample sizes. Figure 3 would benefit from log-scale axes and explicit uncertainty bands, and the legend in Figure 5 is difficult to read. The related work section omits several recent papers that critique the original information bottleneck experiments, and engaging with those critiques directly would make the contribution clearer. The theoretical section introduces notation that is used inconsistently between the main text and the appendix, which should be corrected. The appendix proof of the bound appears to rely on an assumption of Gaussian activations that is not stated in the main theorem, and this gap needs to be resolved. The code availability statement is welcome, but the repository link was not functional at the time of review, and the authors should confirm that the released code reproduces the reported tables. Overall, the paper asks a worthwhile question and contains useful engineering effort, but the conclusions currently exceed what the experiments support. I recommend a major revision. With additional robustness checks, clearer statistical reporting, and more careful framing of causal claims, the work could make a valuable contribution to the literature. I am willing to review a revised version.

Autonomous vehicles promise safer roads, reduced traffic, and greater mobility for people who cannot drive. Yet their rapid development raises serious concerns that society has not yet fully resolved. Three of the most important are accident liability, the changing role of the human driver, and the protection of personal privacy.

The question of accident liability is perhaps the most pressing. When a conventional car crashes, responsibility usually falls on the driver, whose negligence can be examined in court. When a self-driving vehicle crashes, the picture becomes far less clear. Blame might rest with the car manufacturer, the software developer, the company that maintains the vehicle, or the owner who failed to install an update. Existing legal frameworks were built around human decision-making, and they struggle to assign fault for choices made by algorithms.

The role of the driver is equally complicated. Many autonomous systems still require a human to remain alert and ready to take control at a moment's notice. This arrangement is problematic because people are poor at staying attentive when they are not actively doing the task. A driver who trusts the system too much may be unprepared when it fails, while a driver who distrusts it may ignore the features that could make travel safer. The result is a dangerous gap between what the technology assumes and how people actually behave.

Privacy concerns add another layer of difficulty. Autonomous vehicles collect enormous amounts of data, including location histories, travel patterns, in-cabin audio and video, and information about the occupants' habits. This data could reveal where a person works, worships, or receives medical treatment. Without strict limits on collection, storage, and sharing, such information could be sold to advertisers, accessed by insurers, or obtained by law enforcement without adequate oversight.

These concerns are not reasons to reject autonomous vehicles entirely, but they do call for careful regulation. Lawmakers should clarify liability rules before widespread deployment, so that injured people know whom to hold accountable. Engineers should design systems that account for human attention rather than assuming perfect vigilance. Privacy protections should limit data collection to what is genuinely necessary and give owners meaningful control over their information.

Ultimately, the success of autonomous vehicles depends not only on technical performance but on public trust. People will embrace this technology only if they believe it is safe, that someone answers for its failures, and that their personal lives remain their own. Addressing liability, driver involvement, and privacy directly is therefore essential to realizing the benefits these vehicles promise.

Requiring students to join extracurricular activities may seem like an unwelcome obligation, but it can bring lasting benefits to young people. Schools have long recognized that education extends beyond the classroom, and structured activities such as sports, clubs, and arts programs play an important role in student development. When students are asked to participate, they are given opportunities they might otherwise never consider.

One of the most visible advantages is improved physical and mental health. Many students spend hours each day sitting at desks or staring at screens. A required sport, dance class, or outdoor club encourages movement and exercise, which supports healthy growth and better sleep. Physical activity has also been linked to lower stress and improved mood, giving students healthier ways to manage the pressures of school life.

Friendship is another significant benefit. Students often form friendships with people from their own neighborhood or class, but extracurricular activities bring together peers from different backgrounds, grades, and interests. Working toward a shared goal, whether a championship game or a school play, builds teamwork and trust. These relationships can offer support long after the activity ends.

Required participation also helps students discover new interests. A student who has never considered debate, robotics, or painting may find a lifelong passion after a single semester. Without a requirement, many young people stick only to what feels familiar and comfortable. A gentle push can reveal talents and curiosities that would otherwise remain hidden.

Critics argue that forced participation takes away freedom of choice and may create resentment. It is true that students should have some say in what they pursue. However, a requirement can be designed with flexibility, allowing students to select from a wide range of options. This approach preserves choice while ensuring that every student engages in at least one activity outside the classroom.

Extracurricular involvement also teaches responsibility and time management. Students who balance schoolwork with practices, rehearsals, or meetings learn to plan their days and meet commitments. These skills are valuable in college and in the workplace, where people must juggle many demands at once.

In the end, requiring students to join extracurricular activities is not about limiting their freedom but about opening doors. By promoting health, building friendships, and sparking new interests, such requirements help students grow into well-rounded individuals. Schools that thoughtfully implement these programs give their students a richer and more balanced education.
