Why Schools Should Not Require Students to Participate in After-School Activities

After-school activities are often praised as essential to a well-rounded education, but requiring every student to take part in them is a mistake. Students are not all the same, and a policy that treats them as if they are ignores real differences in interests, abilities, and needs. Some students thrive in clubs, sports, and music ensembles, while others find them draining or simply uninteresting. Forcing participation turns a potentially enriching experience into a chore.

Time is a precious resource for young people, and many already have demanding schedules. Students who work part-time jobs to help support their families cannot always stay late at school. Others care for younger siblings, manage long commutes, or need time to rest after a full day of classes. A mandatory requirement places an unfair burden on these students and can widen existing gaps between those who have flexible schedules and those who do not.

Mandatory activities can also undermine the very goals they are meant to serve. When participation is compulsory, students may join a club only to fulfill a rule, which often leads to low engagement and resentment. Motivation that comes from genuine interest tends to produce deeper learning and stronger commitment than motivation imposed from above. A student who chooses an activity is more likely to invest effort, build friendships, and develop real skills.

Requirements can also crowd out other valuable pursuits. Some students benefit more from independent reading, a creative project at home, volunteer work in their community, or time spent with family. Family and community responsibilities teach responsibility, empathy, and practical skills that school clubs cannot always replicate. A rigid mandate leaves no room for these alternatives and implies that only school-sponsored activities count as meaningful growth.

Finally, requiring participation places schools in the position of policing students' personal choices. Staff would need to track attendance, enforce rules, and handle exemptions, all of which consume time and resources that could be spent improving the quality of the activities themselves. Schools would do better to invest in offering a wide range of appealing options and then trusting students to choose among them.

Good after-school programs should earn students' participation through their value, not through coercion. Schools can encourage involvement by making activities welcoming, affordable, and relevant to students' interests, and by reaching out to students who might benefit. But a requirement is the wrong tool. Education should expand students' horizons and build their independence, and the best way to do that is to give them meaningful choices rather than mandates.

Argentina's long-running search for justice in the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center in Buenos Aires remains entangled with the still-unresolved death of prosecutor Alberto Nisman, who was found dead in his Puerto Madero apartment in January 2015. Nisman had spent a decade leading the investigation into the attack, which killed 85 people and remains the deadliest terrorist assault in the country's history. Just days before his death, he had filed a complaint accusing then-President Cristina Fernandez de Kirchner, Foreign Minister Hector Timerman, and others of conspiring to shield Iranian officials suspected in the bombing in exchange for oil trade deals. Iran has denied any role in the attack, and the government in Buenos Aires denied the allegations, calling the complaint politically motivated. Nisman was found with a single gunshot wound to the head, and a handgun was reportedly beside him, prompting initial reports of suicide. Prosecutors and investigators have since produced conflicting conclusions, with several forensic and judicial reviews over the years debating whether the death was suicide, homicide, or an inconclusive result. Critics of the official handling have pointed to irregularities at the crime scene, questions about the weapon, and gaps in the initial inquiry. Families of the AMIA victims have repeatedly demanded clarity, saying the twin mysteries of the bombing and Nisman's death have deprived them of accountability. In 2019 a federal court in Argentina ordered the case reopened, and proceedings have continued in fits and starts since then. Iranian suspects named in Interpol red notices have never been brought to trial, and the Argentine courts have struggled to advance the case in the face of political shifts and diplomatic constraints. The bombing itself remains officially unsolved in terms of convictions, though investigators have long attributed the attack to Iranian planning carried out with Hezbollah operatives. For many Argentines, the Nisman case has come to symbolize the difficulty of achieving transparency and justice in one of the country's most painful chapters. Observers say that until the circumstances of Nisman's death are settled and the bombing's perpetrators are tried, the issue will continue to shape public trust in Argentina's judicial and political institutions.

The Electoral College is one of the most debated features of the American political system. Designed by the Framers as a compromise between selection by Congress and direct popular vote, it allocates electors to each state according to its total number of senators and representatives. Supporters argue that this structure fairly represents voters by giving smaller states a meaningful voice in presidential elections, which might otherwise be dominated by a few large population centers. It also encourages candidates to build broad geographic coalitions rather than concentrating their efforts only in densely populated regions. Critics, however, point out that the system can produce outcomes in which the candidate who wins the national popular vote still loses the presidency, as occurred in 2000 and 2016. Because most states award all their electoral votes to the statewide winner, a voter in a safe state may feel that their ballot has little practical effect. This dynamic concentrates campaign resources in a handful of closely contested swing states, leaving many citizens with little attention from presidential candidates. Defenders respond that this focus on swing states ensures that a diverse set of issues and regional concerns receives serious consideration. Still, the unequal weight of votes across states, measured by the number of people each elector represents, raises legitimate questions about equal representation. Proposals such as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact seek to address these concerns by having participating states pledge their electors to the national popular vote winner. Opponents of such reforms argue that they would undermine federalism and the principle that states, not the national government, should structure their own elections. The debate therefore turns on how one weighs equal treatment of individual voters against the preservation of state power and regional balance. Ultimately, the Electoral College fairly represents some values, such as federalism and geographic breadth, while falling short on others, particularly equal voting power. Whether it promotes effective campaigns depends on one's view of what a successful campaign should accomplish. If the goal is to win over a broad national coalition, the system rewards strategies that target key regions. If the goal is to mobilize every voter, the system often leaves many citizens feeling overlooked. Reasonable people can disagree about which priorities matter most. Any reform should therefore be evaluated not only on its effect on election outcomes but also on how well it balances fairness, representation, and the stability of the nation's democratic institutions.

The fog lifted just enough for Tomas to see the black rocks, and then the sand, and then the shape of the island rising beyond them. He had clung to a splintered spar for two days, and now the sea had finally given him back to land.

He dragged himself onto the beach and lay there coughing up brine. The name had been painted on the sign at the harbor where his ship had departed, a warning that the sailors had laughed about over their last drinks. Graveyard Isle, they called it. No one who went there came back, the old stories said. The island was cursed, and men spoke its name in low voices.

He had not believed in curses before the storm. Now he was not sure what he believed in.

When he could stand, he limped up the path from the shore. Smoke rose from a cluster of stone cottages, and he heard voices and the clatter of pots. His legs trembled and his throat burned, but he kept walking toward the warmth.

A woman with silver braids met him at the edge of the village. She looked at his torn coat and bare feet, then at his face, and her expression softened. "You're the first in a long while," she said. "Come in before you fall down."

Inside the largest cottage, a fire crackled and a bowl of thick fish stew was pressed into his hands. Tomas ate with shaking fingers while the villagers gathered around, curious but kind. An old man with a white beard sat across from him and studied him with bright, amused eyes.

"You're wondering whether you've stumbled into a trap," the old man said.

Tomas set down his spoon. "The sailors call this place Graveyard Isle. I was told no one returns from it."

The old man laughed, a deep rumbling sound that made the others smile. "Ah. That name. We did paint that sign ourselves, you know."

Tomas stared at him. "You did?"

"Of course we did." The woman with silver braids sat down beside him, her eyes twinkling. "Do you know how many tourists come to see a cursed island? Too many. They sail in on fancy steamers, wander around with their cameras, trample the dunes, and leave their bottles and their litter behind. We wanted peace."

"So you frightened them off," Tomas said slowly.

"A little name, a few tales spread in the taverns, and the right sort of rumor carried by the right sailors," the old man said, with evident pride. "The island has ten thousand birds nesting on its cliffs, and rare orchids in the hollows. We would rather keep them than sell them."

A young boy with a gap-toothed grin piped up. "Grandfather tells the best ghost stories. He makes up the bit about the moaning wind."

"It is a very good wind," the old man said solemnly, and the room erupted in laughter again.

Tomas found himself laughing too, though it hurt his chest. The fear that had clung to him through the storm loosened its grip, slowly, like a knot undone by patient hands.

"But what about the ones who did come?" he asked. "Surely some of them were lost."

The woman's face grew serious. "A few have come, over the years. Foolish ones who did not heed the warnings, or who sailed in storms they should have avoided. We buried them with respect, and we did not hide what happened. But the curse, as you call it, is only the sea. The sea does not need our help to be dangerous."

Tomas nodded slowly. He thought of his own ship, lost to the same unforgiving water, and of the men who had not survived the night.

"You are welcome here," the woman said. "Stay as long as you need. Heal your body, and then, if you wish, we will help you find passage home. Most visitors who arrive by accident leave happier than they came, and many return on purpose once they hear the truth."

"Return on purpose?" Tomas asked, surprised.

"The birds," the old man said, winking. "And the orchids. And the stew, which is famous."

Tomas looked down at the empty bowl in his hands and felt something unfamiliar bloom in his chest. It was not quite happiness, not yet, but it was close enough to make him breathe more easily.

That night he slept in a warm bed beneath a patched quilt, listening to the wind move through the grass outside. It did moan a little, as the boy had promised. He smiled into the pillow and let himself drift off.

In the morning, the island looked different in the bright light. The cliffs glowed gold and green, and seabirds wheeled above the bay in great shimmering clouds. Children ran barefoot along the shore, shrieking with laughter as the surf chased them back.

The silver-braided woman found him on the beach, watching the waves. She handed him a cup of warm tea and stood beside him without speaking for a while.

"Do you still fear us?" she finally asked.

Tomas considered the question honestly. "No," he said. "I think I was afraid of the name more than the place."

"Names are powerful," she said. "We chose ours carefully."

He sipped the tea and watched the birds rise and fall over the water. The sea that had nearly killed him now sparkled innocently in the sunlight, and the island that had frightened him now seemed like the kindest place he had ever washed ashore.

Days later, when a fishing boat finally came to carry him home, Tomas stood at the rail and looked back at the island. The villagers waved from the shore, the boy jumping and shouting something he could not hear over the wind. The old man raised his hand in a solemn salute.

Tomas raised his own hand in return. He would tell the story to anyone who would listen, he decided, though he would take care to mention the stew first. And perhaps, one day, when the world had grown too loud and crowded, he would return to Graveyard Isle and ask for a bed, a bowl of stew, and the sound of the wind moaning through the grass.

Genetic and Environmental Influences on Young Adults' Psychological Responses to the COVID-19 Lockdown in Great Britain

Abstract

The COVID-19 pandemic and the associated lockdown measures imposed in Great Britain in 2020 represented an unprecedented social disruption, and early evidence suggested that young adults were among the groups most affected in terms of psychological wellbeing. Yet individuals exposed to the same external circumstances varied considerably in their emotional, cognitive, and behavioural responses. This paper examines the relative contributions of genetic predispositions and environmental factors to this variation among young adults aged approximately 18 to 30 living in Great Britain during the first national lockdown. Drawing on the conceptual framework of behavioural genetics, gene-environment interplay, and the diathesis-stress model, we consider how heritable traits such as neuroticism, anxiety sensitivity, and genetic liability for depression may moderate or mediate responses to lockdown stressors. We also consider environmental determinants including household composition, financial insecurity, occupational disruption, social support, access to green space, and prior adverse experiences. We argue that a full understanding of pandemic-related psychological outcomes requires an integrated approach that acknowledges both genetic susceptibility and the social conditions that shape its expression. Implications for public health planning, targeted support, and future research on population-level crises are discussed.

Introduction

The first national lockdown in the United Kingdom, which began on 23 March 2020, restricted movement, closed many workplaces and educational institutions, and sharply curtailed social contact. For young adults, these restrictions coincided with a critical developmental period characterised by transitions into higher education, early careers, independent living, and the formation of romantic and social relationships. Survey data collected during this period in Great Britain indicated elevated rates of depressive symptoms, generalised anxiety, loneliness, and sleep disturbance among people in their late teens and twenties, relative to older age groups. However, averages obscure substantial heterogeneity, and a central question for both researchers and policymakers is why some young people appeared resilient while others experienced marked and sometimes persistent psychological harm.

Psychological responses to large-scale stressors have long been understood as the product of interacting biological and environmental forces. Behavioural genetic research, including twin and family designs, has consistently found that a meaningful proportion of individual differences in depression, anxiety, and related traits are attributable to genetic factors, with heritability estimates typically falling between 30 and 50 percent for common mental health outcomes. At the same time, the environment exerts powerful effects, and much of the variance in psychological responses is non-shared, meaning it is attributable to experiences unique to individuals rather than to the family environment they share. The pandemic provided a natural context in which to examine how these two sources of variation combine.

The present paper addresses this topic by reviewing the theoretical rationale, the plausible mechanisms of genetic and environmental influence, the methodological challenges involved in studying them during an ongoing crisis, and the implications of the likely findings. Although the paper is framed as a scholarly contribution, we are explicit that the field was still developing at the time of writing, and that several conclusions remain tentative.

Theoretical Framework

The diathesis-stress model proposes that psychopathology emerges when an individual with a pre-existing vulnerability encounters sufficient environmental stress. Applied to the COVID-19 lockdown, this model predicts that young adults carrying greater genetic or dispositional vulnerability would show larger psychological deterioration when confronted with lockdown-related stressors such as isolation, uncertainty, and disrupted routines. Conversely, individuals with fewer vulnerabilities might show smaller changes or even improvements in some domains, for example where lockdown removed sources of social pressure or academic strain.

Gene-environment interplay offers a more nuanced account. Gene-environment correlation refers to the tendency for individuals' genotypes to influence the environments they select or are exposed to. Passive correlation arises within families, where parents provide both genes and environments. Evocative correlation occurs when a person's heritable characteristics elicit particular responses from others. Active correlation arises when individuals seek out environments consistent with their dispositions. Each of these processes could shape which young adults experienced greater financial hardship, more conflict at home, or fewer opportunities for social contact during lockdown, and therefore indirectly shape their psychological outcomes.

Gene-environment interaction, by contrast, describes situations in which the effect of an environmental exposure depends on an individual's genotype. Candidate gene research, much of which has since proved difficult to replicate, once focused on variants such as the serotonin transporter polymorphism as moderators of stress sensitivity. More recent work using polygenic scores, which aggregate the effects of many variants across the genome, has provided a more robust approach, though its power to detect interactions remains limited by sample size. The lockdown offered an opportunity to test whether polygenic liability for depression or anxiety predicted greater symptom change when environmental stressors intensified.

Heritable Dispositions and Vulnerability

Among the heritable characteristics most relevant to pandemic responses, neuroticism stands out. Neuroticism, a broad trait reflecting the propensity to experience negative affect, is moderately to highly heritable and is a robust predictor of depression and anxiety. Individuals high in neuroticism tend to appraise ambiguous or threatening situations as more dangerous and to have fewer resources for regulating negative emotion. The pandemic, with its uncertain health risks, shifting rules, and prolonged isolation, plausibly provided fertile ground for these tendencies to express themselves.

Anxiety sensitivity, the fear of anxiety-related sensations, is another candidate. Research suggests it is partly heritable and that it predicts the development of anxiety disorders. Given that the early pandemic was characterised by health-related anxiety, including concern about infection, bodily symptoms, and the health of relatives, individuals high in anxiety sensitivity may have been especially prone to catastrophic interpretations of ordinary physical sensations.

Genetic liability for major depression, as captured by polygenic scores derived from large genome-wide association studies, is a further consideration. Such scores explain only a small fraction of variance in any individual's depressive symptoms but are useful at the population level for identifying groups with elevated risk. It is reasonable to hypothesise that young adults with higher polygenic liability would show greater increases in depressive symptoms during lockdown, although the effect sizes are expected to be modest.

Environmental Determinants

Environmental influences during the lockdown were heterogeneous and interacted with one another. Household composition is a salient example. Young adults who lived alone reported higher levels of loneliness, while those in crowded households, or in households with conflict or domestic abuse, faced different forms of strain. Those who returned to the parental home, a common occurrence among students and early-career workers, sometimes experienced reduced autonomy and renewed family tension, which could either buffer or aggravate distress depending on the quality of family relationships.

Financial insecurity was a particularly important factor. Many young adults were employed in sectors such as hospitality, retail, and the arts, which were heavily affected by closures, and many held precarious or zero-hours contracts with limited access to statutory protection. Economic stress is well documented as a predictor of depression and anxiety, and its effects may operate through reduced control, increased worry, and the erosion of future plans.

Occupational and educational disruption also mattered. Students faced the cancellation of placements, the move to online teaching, uncertainty about examinations, and in some cases the loss of accommodation. Young workers faced furlough, redundancy, or the interruption of training. The sense of a stalled life trajectory, sometimes described as a loss of time or of developmental momentum, may have contributed to feelings of hopelessness in ways that are distinct from the immediate effects of isolation.

Social support emerged as a key buffer. Young adults who maintained contact with friends and family through digital channels, or who had access to supportive relationships in their household, tended to report better wellbeing, although the protective effect of online contact was not uniform and depended on the perceived quality of the interactions. Prior adverse experiences, including childhood maltreatment, bereavement, and previous mental health difficulties, also predicted poorer outcomes, consistent with the cumulative nature of stress exposure.

Access to green space and physical activity represents another environmental pathway. Young people living in urban areas with limited outdoor space faced particular restrictions, whereas those with gardens or access to parks were able to maintain activity and exposure to natural settings, both of which are associated with better mood. Socioeconomic status interacted with these factors, as affluent households were more likely to have outdoor space and the capacity to adapt working arrangements.

Interplay Between Genetic and Environmental Factors

The most informative account of pandemic responses is likely to involve interactions between genetic and environmental factors rather than their separate contributions. For example, a young person with high neuroticism living alone in a flat without outdoor space and facing financial insecurity may be at considerably greater risk than someone with the same genetic profile who lives with supportive family members and has access to a garden. Conversely, a young person with low genetic liability may show surprisingly large symptom increases if exposed to severe environmental adversity, such as job loss combined with bereavement.

Gene-environment correlation also complicates interpretation. If heritable traits such as sociability or conscientiousness influence the likelihood of maintaining social contact or adhering to structured routines, then part of the apparent environmental effect may itself have a genetic basis. Statistical models that fail to account for such correlations risk overestimating the independent contribution of environmental exposures, or conversely attributing to genes effects that are in fact mediated through environmental choices.

Methodological Considerations

Studying genetic and environmental influences during a crisis presents distinctive challenges. The timing of data collection relative to changing restrictions, shifts in public mood, and the availability of vaccines and treatments all introduce time-varying confounds. Longitudinal designs with pre-pandemic baseline measures are especially valuable, as they allow researchers to estimate within-person change rather than relying solely on cross-sectional comparisons, which are vulnerable to selection effects and to the problem of distinguishing between-person differences from genuine responses to the lockdown.

Sample representativeness is a persistent concern. Online surveys, which were the dominant mode of data collection, tend to over-represent certain demographic groups, including women, the highly educated, and those with pre-existing interest in the topic. Cohort studies with genotyped participants are valuable but often recruit from populations that are not fully representative of Great Britain's young adults, and ethnic diversity in genetic databases remains limited, raising questions about the generalisability of polygenic score findings.

Measurement is also difficult. Symptom questionnaires for depression and anxiety are validated but may capture different constructs in a crisis context, for example conflating normative distress with clinical symptoms. The use of ecological momentary assessment, passive smartphone data, and linked administrative records can complement self-report, but each introduces its own limitations and ethical considerations, particularly regarding consent and data protection in the handling of genetic information.

Ethical considerations extend beyond data handling. Research that identifies genetic vulnerability to psychological harm carries a risk of stigmatisation and of fostering deterministic interpretations that may discourage investment in social and economic support. Researchers should communicate findings in ways that emphasise modifiability and the role of environmental improvement, and should guard against implications that individuals with higher genetic liability are less deserving of help.

Implications for Policy and Practice

If environmental factors account for a substantial share of variation in psychological responses, then policy interventions targeting financial security, housing quality, access to green space, employment protection, and social connection are likely to yield benefits across the population, with particular value for those most exposed. Targeted support for young adults in precarious employment, those living alone, and those with prior adverse experiences would appear especially justified.

Genetic information, though not presently suitable for individual clinical prediction, may eventually inform risk stratification at the population level. Public health services could use polygenic and dispositional data, in combination with environmental indicators, to identify groups likely to need proactive outreach during future crises. Any such use would need rigorous evaluation, strong safeguards for privacy, and careful attention to equity.

Recommendations for Future Research

Future studies should prioritise longitudinal designs with pre-pandemic baselines and repeated measurement across the lockdown and recovery phases. They should incorporate larger and more diverse genetic samples to improve the accuracy and transferability of polygenic scores, and should model gene-environment correlation explicitly. Mixed-method approaches combining quantitative symptom data with qualitative accounts of lived experience would help clarify the mechanisms underlying observed associations. Finally, research should examine long-term trajectories, as the psychological consequences of the pandemic may have unfolded over years rather than months, and early patterns may not predict later outcomes.

Conclusion

Young adults in Great Britain responded to the COVID-19 lockdown in markedly different ways, and these differences reflected both inherited dispositions and the environments in which individuals were situated. A diathesis-stress and gene-environment interplay framework provides a useful lens for understanding this variation, although empirical support for specific genetic effects remains preliminary and effect sizes are modest. The strongest practical lesson is that environmental conditions, including financial security, housing, social connection, and access to meaningful activity, play a substantial role in shaping psychological outcomes, and that supportive policy can reduce harm even among those with elevated vulnerability. Continued research with rigorous designs will be needed to refine these conclusions and to inform preparedness for future crises.

Churchman's General Systems Approach to Purposeful Human Activity, Organizational Change, Management, and Value Creation

C. West Churchman (1913–2004) was an American philosopher, operations researcher, and systems thinker who spent much of his career at the University of California, Berkeley. He is best known for his writing on how systems thinking can improve human decision-making. His work bridges the gap between technical analysis and the broader questions of ethics, values, and purpose. This page introduces the core ideas of his approach and explains why they remain relevant to managers, organizations, and anyone who designs or improves human activity.

Churchman was trained in philosophy and worked in operations research during and after the Second World War. He saw that many analytical methods were powerful but often narrow, focusing on efficiency within fixed boundaries while ignoring the larger purposes a system was meant to serve. His central concern was that people could build elaborate models and still fail to address the right problem. Much of his thinking grew out of this worry. He wanted a way of thinking about systems that would keep questions of purpose and value in view at every step.

The phrase "general systems approach" refers to a family of ideas that treats systems as wholes made of interacting parts. It draws on the broader movement of general systems theory associated with thinkers such as Ludwig von Bertalanffy. Churchman adopted the general idea that complex phenomena should be understood as systems, but he went further. He argued that a system is not simply a set of components and relationships. A system is always defined relative to someone's purposes and perspective. This shift made his approach distinctive, because it placed human judgment and values at the center of systems analysis.

One of Churchman's most important claims is that every system is a human construction. The boundaries we draw around a system, the elements we include, and the outcomes we care about all reflect choices. Two people looking at the same organization may draw different boundaries and therefore see different systems. Churchman encouraged analysts to make these choices explicit rather than treating them as obvious or given. Recognizing the arbitrariness of boundaries is a first step toward more honest and inclusive analysis.

Churchman emphasized the concept of purposeful human activity. Human beings act for reasons, and their actions are directed toward goals they hold, whether individually or collectively. He argued that any serious study of systems must take these purposes seriously. Rather than asking only how a process works, one should ask what it is for and whom it serves. This emphasis distinguishes his work from purely mechanical or behavioral models that treat people as predictable components.

A key element of Churchman's thinking is the importance of multiple perspectives. Because systems are defined by viewpoints, no single viewpoint captures the whole. Different stakeholders bring different values, interests, and knowledge. Churchman believed that good systems design requires deliberately considering the views of many people, including those who are affected by a system but have no formal voice in it. He saw the inclusion of diverse viewpoints as a practical necessity and also as an ethical requirement.

Churchman's approach asks a set of guiding questions that help expose the assumptions behind any proposal. These include who the customers of a system are, what its purposes are, who the decision makers are, what resources are available, and what environment the system operates within. Asking these questions systematically helps reveal where a plan rests on unexamined assumptions. The questions are not a formula that produces answers automatically. They are prompts for disciplined reflection.

Churchman also argued that the boundaries of any analysis are never fully closed. Every system is embedded in larger systems, and those larger systems affect outcomes in ways that the analyst may not foresee. He encouraged thinking about the wider environment, including social, political, and ecological factors. A narrow focus can produce solutions that solve one problem while creating several others elsewhere. Attention to the wider context is therefore a way of guarding against unintended consequences.

Churchman distinguished between different kinds of inquiry and different ways of knowing. He was interested in how systems analysts could combine quantitative modeling with qualitative judgment, and how they could draw on different philosophical traditions. He explored the idea that different schools of inquiry, each with its own assumptions about knowledge and truth, could offer complementary insights. Rather than declaring one method superior, he sought ways to make use of several approaches while being clear about their limits.

The concept of value is central to Churchman's thought. He argued that values are not merely subjective preferences to be ignored by science and management. Values shape what counts as a good outcome, and they must therefore be part of any systematic analysis. He believed that decision makers should identify the values at stake in a situation and examine them openly. Doing so can help groups reach agreement about goals or at least understand why they disagree.

Churchman's approach has important implications for management. A manager who adopts this perspective treats management as more than the allocation of resources to achieve preset targets. Management becomes an ongoing process of defining purposes, examining assumptions, consulting diverse stakeholders, and revising goals as circumstances change. The manager is a steward of a system whose meaning must continually be reexamined.

Organizational change, in Churchman's view, is rarely a matter of simply installing a new tool or structure. Changes affect the purposes, boundaries, and perspectives that define the organization. Successful change therefore requires understanding how people within the organization see their work and what they value. Changes imposed without this understanding often fail because they conflict with the purposes that people actually hold. Churchman's approach encourages change agents to listen carefully before proposing solutions.

Churchman was interested in the relationship between analysis and action. He recognized that analysts and decision makers operate under constraints of time, information, and authority. He did not expect perfect knowledge or complete agreement. Instead, he hoped that systematic reflection would improve the quality of decisions even when certainty was unavailable. Good systems thinking, in his view, helps people act more wisely rather than promising to eliminate uncertainty.

The idea of value creation follows naturally from this perspective. Organizations create value when they serve purposes that matter to the people they affect. Churchman's approach suggests that value should be understood broadly, including economic, social, and human dimensions. A system that is efficient but serves no meaningful purpose creates little real value. Conversely, a system that clarifies purposes and involves stakeholders may create value that narrow metrics fail to capture.

Churchman was attentive to the dangers of what he sometimes called the illusion of completeness. Analysts often believe that their models capture everything important, when in fact they have simplified the situation in ways that exclude key factors. He urged humility about the limits of any model. Recognizing what a model leaves out is as important as recognizing what it includes. This humility is part of what makes systems thinking responsible rather than arrogant.

Ethics occupies a significant place in Churchman's work. He argued that systems analysts have responsibilities to the people their work affects, including people who are not present in the analysis. Decisions about system design carry moral weight because they shape the lives of others. Churchman encouraged analysts to take this responsibility seriously and to consider whether their proposals are fair, just, and humane. Ethical reflection, in his approach, is inseparable from good analysis.

His work also addressed the question of how to make systems inquiry collaborative. Churchman believed that the best understanding of a system emerges through dialogue among people with different perspectives. Structured conversation, in which participants openly examine assumptions and test ideas against one another, can produce insights that no individual would reach alone. This collaborative emphasis links his approach to later developments in participatory and dialogic methods.

Churchman often used the metaphor of inquiring systems. He described systems that learn, adapt, and reflect on their own purposes. Such systems are capable of revising their goals in light of experience and new information. Organizations can be understood as inquiring systems when they build mechanisms for reflection, feedback, and self-correction. This idea connects Churchman's thinking to the broader study of organizational learning.

Churchman distinguished between the analyst's role and the decision maker's role, but he saw the two as closely connected. The analyst provides structure and insight, while the decision maker bears responsibility for choices. Churchman believed that analysts should help decision makers see the assumptions and values underlying their options, rather than simply delivering a recommendation. This relationship is meant to be collaborative and educative.

The approach also challenges the notion that objectivity requires the removal of values. Churchman argued that a more honest form of objectivity comes from openly acknowledging the values and perspectives involved. A study that hides its assumptions is less trustworthy than one that displays them for scrutiny. In this sense, transparency about value choices is itself a form of rigor.

Churchman's writings include reflections on the nature of teams and collective decision making. He examined how groups can reason together about complex problems and how they can avoid being dominated by a single viewpoint. Effective groups, in his view, maintain a healthy tension between different perspectives and seek syntheses that respect them. This aspect of his work offers guidance for managers who lead diverse teams.

Churchman's work on the design of inquiring systems also touched on the role of information. He was interested in how information is gathered, organized, and used in decision making. He recognized that information is never neutral, because the categories used to collect it reflect the purposes and values of those who designed the system. Analysts should therefore be aware of how their information systems shape what they can see.

The approach has practical uses in planning and strategy. When organizations set out to plan for the future, Churchman's questions help them examine the purposes they serve and the assumptions they hold about their environment. Planning becomes a process of collective reflection rather than the mechanical extension of past trends. This can help organizations prepare for uncertainty and respond to changing needs.

In project management, the approach encourages attention to the purposes behind a project, not only its schedule and budget. Projects that lose sight of their purposes can complete their tasks while failing to deliver what stakeholders need. Churchman's emphasis on purpose and perspective can help project teams ask whether they are building the right thing as well as building it correctly.

For policy analysis, Churchman's approach highlights the importance of considering multiple stakeholders and long-term effects. Public policies affect diverse groups, and their consequences often extend beyond the immediate problem they address. Applying his questions to policy can reveal conflicting values and unintended impacts. This makes policy debate more transparent and potentially more constructive.

Churchman's influence can be seen in later fields such as soft systems methodology, critical systems thinking, and participatory action research. These approaches build on his recognition that systems are shaped by human purposes and values. Many of them emphasize dialogue, stakeholder involvement, and reflection on the boundaries of analysis. Churchman's ideas thus form part of a broader tradition in systems thinking.

Students of management can benefit from studying Churchman because his work challenges simple views of efficiency and control. It encourages a more reflective and ethically aware style of leadership. Reading his texts can help future managers recognize the limits of their models and the importance of listening to others. His work is also useful for anyone who wants to think more carefully about how organizations shape human lives.

There are also criticisms of Churchman's approach. Some readers find his writing abstract and difficult to apply in concrete situations. Others argue that his emphasis on multiple perspectives can make decisions slow or indecisive. Churchman himself acknowledged that his ideas required judgment and could not be reduced to a procedure. Critics and admirers alike agree that the approach demands thoughtful practice rather than mechanical application.

Applying Churchman's approach in practice typically involves several steps. First, one clarifies the purposes of the system under study. Second, one identifies the stakeholders and the range of viewpoints they hold. Third, one examines the boundaries and assumptions that define the analysis. Fourth, one considers the wider environment and possible unintended consequences. Finally, one revisits the purposes and assumptions as understanding develops. These steps are iterative rather than strictly sequential.

Clarifying purposes can be surprisingly difficult. Organizations often have stated missions that differ from what members actually pursue. Churchman's approach encourages honest examination of the gap between stated and operational purposes. Discovering this gap can be uncomfortable, but it provides valuable information for change. Purposes that are openly discussed are more likely to guide effective action.

Identifying stakeholders requires looking beyond formal authority. Some of the most affected people in a system may have little formal power. Churchman urged analysts to consider the perspectives of those who are touched by a system but excluded from decisions. Including these voices can reveal problems that powerful stakeholders have overlooked and can lead to more just outcomes.

Examining assumptions is often where the most useful insights emerge. Every analysis rests on beliefs about cause and effect, about what matters, and about what is possible. Making these beliefs explicit allows them to be tested and debated. Churchman believed that surfacing assumptions was one of the most valuable contributions that systems thinking could make.

Considering the wider environment helps analysts avoid narrowly focused solutions. Organizations interact with suppliers, customers, communities, regulators, and the natural world. Changes in one part of this web can have effects elsewhere. Churchman encouraged analysts to think expansively about these connections while accepting that no analysis can capture everything.

Revisiting purposes and assumptions acknowledges that systems and their environments change over time. A plan that made sense at one moment may become inappropriate later. Churchman's emphasis on inquiring systems suggests that organizations should build habits of periodic reflection and revision. This ongoing attention helps organizations stay aligned with the values they hold.

In summary, Churchman's general systems approach offers a way of thinking about human activity that places purpose, perspective, and value at its center. It treats systems as human constructions shaped by choices about boundaries and goals. It asks decision makers to consider multiple viewpoints, examine their assumptions, and reflect on the ethical dimensions of their work. For managers and change agents, it provides guidance for leading organizations toward meaningful and responsible outcomes. Although its application requires judgment and humility, its central insights remain valuable for anyone seeking to create lasting value through purposeful collective action.

Heightened security measures have been introduced in Calais after a series of migrant attempts to enter the United Kingdom through the Channel Tunnel caused widespread disruption to transport services this week.

Officials said the incidents, which took place near the terminal entrances and along access roads, led to temporary suspensions of Eurotunnel shuttle services. Passengers faced long delays, with some trains held for several hours while security teams searched vehicles and secured the perimeter.

Local police confirmed that dozens of individuals were detained in the area over the course of several days. Many of those detained were later released or processed under French immigration procedures, according to regional authorities.

Eurotunnel described the disruption as significant but said it was working closely with French and British authorities to restore normal operations as quickly as possible. The company advised travelers to allow extra time and to check for updates before departing.

Freight operators reported knock-on effects, with lorries queuing for long distances on routes leading to the port and terminal. Haulage companies said delays were adding costs and disrupting delivery schedules for businesses that rely on cross-Channel transport.

The Prefecture of the Pas-de-Calais announced that additional police officers and gendarmes would be deployed to the area. Security patrols, surveillance cameras and vehicle checks have been expanded at key points around the terminal.

Local residents in Calais have expressed mixed reactions. Some said they welcomed the stronger presence of security forces, while others called for more humane approaches to the situation facing the people attempting the crossings.

Humanitarian organizations working in the region warned that increased enforcement alone would not address the underlying causes of migration. They called for safe and legal routes, improved access to asylum processes and better support for vulnerable people living in informal camps.

Government representatives in both France and the United Kingdom have held talks on border cooperation in recent months. Officials said the latest incidents highlighted the need for continued coordination on intelligence sharing, patrols and the prevention of dangerous crossing attempts.

The UK Home Office said it remained committed to working with its French counterparts to tackle organized criminal networks that facilitate small boat and tunnel crossings. A spokesperson stated that people smuggling gangs put lives at risk for profit.

Police in the region said investigations were ongoing into the organizers of several recent attempts. Authorities have not yet confirmed whether the incidents were linked to a single network or multiple groups operating independently.

Transport analysts said the disruption underscored the vulnerability of cross-Channel infrastructure to security incidents. Some suggested that operators may need to invest further in detection technology and perimeter protection.

Passengers traveling through Calais this week described confusion at the terminal, with announcements sometimes delayed or unclear. Several said they were grateful for the assistance of staff who helped them rebook journeys or find alternative routes.

Eurotunnel confirmed that compensation and rebooking options were being offered to affected customers. The company asked passengers to contact customer service channels for details on eligibility.

Business groups in Kent and the surrounding region called for swift action to restore normal traffic flows. They warned that prolonged disruption could damage trade, tourism and confidence in cross-Channel travel.

The French interior ministry said the government would maintain a firm but proportionate response. Officials stressed that the rule of law must be upheld while respecting the rights of individuals in vulnerable situations.

Aid workers reported that many people attempting to cross were exhausted, cold and in need of food, medical care and shelter. They urged authorities to ensure that emergency assistance remained available alongside enforcement operations.

Local councillors have asked for a coordinated plan that addresses both security and welfare. They said communities in Calais had lived with the consequences of irregular migration for many years and needed lasting solutions.

Legal experts noted that individuals seeking asylum have the right to have their claims assessed under international and national law. They said the distinction between smuggling networks and vulnerable migrants was important in shaping policy.

Border officials on both sides of the Channel said that intelligence-led operations had led to several arrests in recent weeks. They added that new checks would be introduced to identify and deter individuals attempting to board freight vehicles illegally.

Transport unions called for the safety of staff to be prioritized. Workers at the terminal described tense situations during incidents and said they needed clear protocols and adequate protection.

Environmental groups have raised concerns about the impact of increased lighting, fencing and patrol activity on the surrounding area. They asked that any new infrastructure be designed with minimal ecological damage.

Tourism operators in the region said the uncertainty was affecting bookings for the coming months. Some hoteliers reported cancellations from travelers who were worried about delays on the route.

The incidents have also drawn attention in the political debate in both countries. Commentators said the issue remained highly sensitive, with strong views on immigration, border control and humanitarian responsibilities.

Security analysts said that deterring crossings would require sustained cooperation rather than short-term surges in policing. They pointed to the importance of tackling smuggling networks, expanding legal pathways and improving processing capacity.

Authorities said they would review the effectiveness of the current measures in the coming weeks. Officials promised that updates would be provided as the situation develops.

For now, travelers have been advised to monitor official channels for the latest information. Security checks are expected to remain in place around the terminal while investigations continue.

Residents and commuters in Calais hope that normal services can be restored soon. Many said they simply wanted a safe and predictable environment for everyone living, working and travelling through the town.

Title: Transmitter Message-Sharing and Spectral Efficiency in a Combined Point-to-Point and Multiple-Access Channel Network

Abstract

This paper investigates how sharing messages between transmitters affects spectral efficiency in a communication network that combines a point-to-point link with a multiple-access channel. Transmitter message-sharing, in which one or more transmitters obtain knowledge of messages intended for other transmitters, has been studied as a means of exploiting cooperation to improve rates. We model a two-user network in which a point-to-point link and a multiple-access channel share a common spectral resource and interfere with one another. We characterize the achievable rate region under several message-sharing configurations, including no sharing, partial sharing, and full sharing, and we analyze the resulting spectral efficiency. Our results indicate that message-sharing can increase spectral efficiency when interference is strong, but the benefit diminishes when the cost of coordination is included. We discuss the implications for network design and identify open questions for future work.

1. Introduction

Spectral efficiency is a central performance measure in wireless communication, defined as the achievable data rate per unit bandwidth. As demand for capacity grows, networks increasingly combine different communication structures within the same spectrum. Two fundamental structures are the point-to-point link, in which a single transmitter communicates with a single receiver, and the multiple-access channel, in which several transmitters communicate with a common receiver. When these structures coexist, they interact through mutual interference, and the design of the overall network becomes a coupled problem.

Information-theoretic analyses of the multiple-access channel have a long history. The capacity region of the Gaussian multiple-access channel is known and is achieved by successive decoding with an appropriate ordering of users. Point-to-point channels are comparatively simple, but their interaction with other links is not. Interference channels, in which multiple transmitter-receiver pairs share spectrum, have been studied extensively, and their capacity remains unknown in general.

Cooperation between transmitters offers a route to improved performance in interference-limited settings. In a message-sharing setting, a transmitter receives information about the messages of another transmitter, allowing the two to coordinate their signals. This idea underlies cognitive radio models, in which a secondary transmitter learns the message of a primary transmitter, and broadcast-based cooperation models, in which transmitters share a portion of their messages over a backhaul link.

Message-sharing is attractive because it can transform interference into useful signal structure. However, it also introduces costs, including the capacity consumed by the sharing link and the complexity of coordination. Whether the net effect improves spectral efficiency therefore depends on the operating regime and on how sharing is implemented. This paper addresses this question for a network that combines a point-to-point link with a multiple-access channel.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the system model. Section 3 characterizes the achievable rates under different sharing configurations. Section 4 analyzes spectral efficiency and the effect of coordination cost. Section 5 discusses implications, and Section 6 concludes.

2. System Model

We consider a network with three transmitters and two receivers operating over a common frequency band of bandwidth W. Transmitter T1 communicates with receiver R1 over a point-to-point link. Transmitters T2 and T3 communicate with receiver R2 over a Gaussian multiple-access channel. Each link experiences additive white Gaussian noise of power spectral density N0. Cross-links introduce interference, characterized by channel gains that we assume are known to all nodes.

Transmitter Ti has a message Wi drawn uniformly from a set of size 2^(nRi), where Ri denotes the rate and n the block length. Each transmitter maps its message to a codeword subject to an average power constraint P. The received signals at each receiver are the superposition of the intended and interfering transmissions plus noise.

Message-sharing is modeled by allowing a specified transmitter to know a portion of another transmitter's message. We denote by Ci→j the rate of message information shared from transmitter i to transmitter j, which is assumed to be delivered over a dedicated coordination channel with its own capacity constraint. Spectral efficiency is defined as the sum of the message rates delivered divided by the bandwidth used by the whole network, counting the bandwidth consumed by coordination where it shares the spectrum.

We assume perfect channel state information at all nodes and consider the high-SNR regime for analytical tractability, while noting where the conclusions depend on this assumption.

3. Achievable Rate Regions

We begin with the no-sharing baseline. In this case the point-to-point link and the multiple-access channel operate independently except for mutual interference. Treating interference as noise yields an achievable rate region that is generally strictly inside the capacity region, particularly when interference is strong.

Next we consider full sharing, in which T2 knows the message of T3 and the two cooperate in encoding. This turns the multiple-access channel into a configuration resembling a broadcast-plus-multiple-access structure, in which the cooperating transmitters can jointly beamform or superpose their codewords. We derive an achievable region based on superposition coding, where the common codeword carries the shared information and the private codewords carry the remaining message content.

We then consider partial sharing, in which only a fraction alpha of T3's message is shared with T2. This configuration interpolates between the no-sharing and full-sharing cases. Its achievable region is obtained by a rate-splitting argument, in which each message is divided into a common part, which is known to both cooperating transmitters, and a private part, which is not.

Across these configurations, a consistent pattern emerges. When cross-link gains are large, sharing enables the cooperating transmitters to align their interference with the intended signal, enlarging the achievable region. When cross-link gains are small, the achievable regions of all configurations nearly coincide, and sharing offers little benefit.

4. Spectral Efficiency and Coordination Cost

Spectral efficiency must account for the resources consumed by coordination. If sharing requires a separate channel, its bandwidth is subtracted from the total available for message transmission. Let eta denote the spectral efficiency, defined as the sum of delivered message rates divided by the effective bandwidth. Including the coordination cost gives eta = (R1 + R2 + R3) / (W + W_c), where W_c is the bandwidth used by the sharing link.

Under this definition, the trade-off is explicit. Sharing increases the achievable message rates in strong-interference regimes but also increases the denominator through W_c. We find that there exists a critical interference level below which sharing reduces spectral efficiency and above which it improves it. This threshold depends on the relative cost of coordination and on the fraction of the message that is shared.

When coordination is performed in-band, meaning that the shared information is carried on the same spectrum as the data, the denominator remains unchanged, but the sharing consumes part of the transmitter's rate budget. Under this alternative, the optimal sharing fraction is generally interior, neither zero nor full, reflecting a balance between cooperation gain and rate loss.

We also examine the sensitivity of these results to the power constraint. At low power, the benefit of sharing is limited because interference contributes little to the overall rate loss. At high power, interference dominates, and the potential gain from sharing is greatest, provided the coordination cost remains moderate.

5. Discussion

The results suggest that message-sharing should be applied selectively. In networks where cross-link interference is strong and coordination can be implemented at low cost, sharing can noticeably increase spectral efficiency. In networks with weak interference or expensive coordination, independent operation is preferable.

The interaction between the point-to-point link and the multiple-access channel deserves particular attention. Because the point-to-point link carries a single stream, it is affected by interference from the multiple-access transmitters but contributes less interference to them. Sharing among the multiple-access transmitters can therefore reshape the interference seen by the point-to-point receiver, and the resulting effect can be asymmetric. Designers should account for this asymmetry when allocating resources.

Practical implementations raise further considerations. Coordination links introduce latency, and the benefit of sharing may erode if the shared information becomes stale. Robustness to imperfect channel state information is also important, since the superposition and beamforming strategies underlying the achievable regions are sensitive to channel estimation errors. Our analysis assumes perfect information, and the degradation under realistic conditions remains an open question.

6. Conclusion

This paper examined how transmitter message-sharing affects spectral efficiency in a network that combines a point-to-point link with a multiple-access channel. We characterized achievable rate regions for no sharing, partial sharing, and full sharing, and we incorporated the cost of coordination into a spectral efficiency measure. Sharing improves spectral efficiency when interference is strong and coordination is inexpensive, while it offers little advantage otherwise. The optimal sharing level is generally interior, reflecting a trade-off between cooperation gain and coordination cost.

Several directions remain open. Extending the analysis to fading channels, quantifying the effect of imperfect channel state information, and developing capacity-approaching coding schemes for the shared configurations are important next steps. Establishing tighter outer bounds would also clarify how close the presented achievable regions are to optimal performance.

References

The references for this work would include foundational texts on multiple-access and interference channels, papers on cognitive radio and transmitter cooperation, and studies of rate-splitting and superposition coding. A complete bibliography should be compiled from the primary literature before submission.
