Members of Uganda's LGBTQ community gathered this week for a pride celebration despite widespread public opposition and strict legal restrictions on same-sex relations. The event, held in a discreet venue in Kampala to protect attendees from possible harassment, featured music, speeches, and displays of solidarity. Organizers said the gathering was intended to affirm the dignity and presence of queer Ugandans, many of whom live in fear of arrest, violence, or rejection by family and community. Uganda's Anti-Homosexuality Act, which was signed into law in 2023, imposes severe penalties, including life imprisonment in some cases, and has drawn sharp criticism from human rights groups and foreign governments. Several attendees described the atmosphere as cautious but hopeful, saying that simply coming together in public-facing spaces was an act of resistance. Religious and political leaders who support the law have argued that it protects traditional family values and national identity. Activists, however, warned that the legislation has already led to a rise in harassment, evictions, and the closure of health services that serve LGBTQ people. Organizers said they plan to continue holding similar events in the coming months, while acknowledging the risks involved.

The house was quiet when Daniel came home that Thursday, the kind of quiet that had settled over it since his father died. He found his mother's car still in the driveway, engine cold, and a feeling he couldn't name tightened in his chest. He called her name from the front hall and heard nothing in return. Upstairs, the bathroom door was locked, and a faint sound came through it that he would remember for the rest of his life.

He did not wait for permission or think about the right words. He put his shoulder to the door once, twice, and on the third try the frame splintered and the door swung open. His mother sat on the edge of the bathtub with an orange bottle in one hand and a glass of water in the other, her face wet and blank. She looked at him as though he were a stranger who had wandered into the wrong house.

Daniel crossed the tiny room in two steps and knelt in front of her, not touching the bottle yet. He told her he was there and that he was not going anywhere. His voice shook, and he let it shake, because he had nothing left to hide behind. She whispered that she was tired, that she had been tired for two years, that everyone would be better off without the weight of her.

He told her that he would be the one carrying the weight if she left, and that he would never set it down. He asked her to give him the bottle, and when she didn't move, he reached out slowly and placed his hand over hers. Her fingers were cold and trembling. For a long moment neither of them breathed.

Then she began to cry in earnest, the deep, broken sobs she had held back since the funeral, and the bottle slipped from her grip and clattered onto the tile. Daniel picked it up, read the label with trembling hands, and set it on the sink far out of reach. He pulled her into his arms and held her while she shook against his chest.

He called the emergency number from the floor of the bathroom while she rested her head on his shoulder. The dispatcher's voice was calm and steady, and Daniel found himself repeating her name and address over and over without realizing it. He kept one arm around his mother the whole time, afraid that if he let go she would slip away again.

The paramedics arrived within minutes, their boots loud on the stairs. They gently took over, asking questions in low, patient tones while Daniel answered as best he could. One of them put a blanket around his mother's shoulders, and another steadied Daniel by the elbow when his legs finally gave way.

At the hospital, the doctors spoke of medication, of counselors, of a long road ahead. Daniel nodded to everything they said, too exhausted to feel anything but relief. A nurse brought him coffee he didn't drink and told him he had done the right thing by acting so quickly.

Later, sitting beside his mother's bed as she slept under the fluorescent lights, Daniel thought about how close he had come to arriving too late. He thought about the hours he had spent at work that week, telling himself she was fine because she had said so. He promised himself, silently and without reservation, that he would never again mistake her silence for peace.

Weeks passed, and the healing was slow and uneven. His mother began seeing a therapist, then started attending a support group for people who had lost spouses. Some mornings she barely spoke, and some afternoons she laughed at something on the radio that made Daniel's heart ache with hope. He learned to check on her every evening, to ask the hard questions gently, and to listen without rushing to fix things.

On the first warm day of spring, she asked him to drive her to the lake where his father used to take them fishing. They sat on the dock with their feet dangling over the water, watching the light move across the surface. She reached over and squeezed his hand, and said quietly that she was glad he had come home that Thursday.

Daniel looked out at the water and felt the old tightness in his chest loosen for the first time in months. He did not say that he had been afraid every single day since, because it was enough that she was here to hear the quiet and to share it with him. The lake shimmered, the birds called from the reeds, and for one unhurried afternoon they simply sat together and let the day be what it was.

Exploring Venus presents some of the most formidable challenges in planetary science, yet it also offers rewards that justify the effort. The planet's surface temperature exceeds 460 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, and its atmosphere is crushingly dense, roughly 90 times the pressure at Earth's surface. Sulfuric acid clouds shroud the planet, blocking visual observation and corroding nearly every material engineers have tried to use. Landers such as the Soviet Venera probes survived only a few hours on the surface, and their images remain among the few ever taken there. Despite these hazards, Venus is often called Earth's twin because it is similar in size, mass, and composition, so studying it helps scientists understand how two nearly identical worlds developed such different climates. The runaway greenhouse effect that transformed Venus offers a critical warning about the limits of planetary climate stability. Missions like NASA's upcoming DAVINCI and VERITAS, along with ESA's EnVision, aim to map the surface, probe the atmosphere, and search for evidence of past oceans and geological activity. Engineers developing heat-resistant electronics and materials for these missions are also advancing technologies that may benefit other industries on Earth. Ultimately, the difficulty of reaching Venus pushes scientists and engineers to innovate, and the knowledge gained from overcoming its harsh environment deepens our understanding of planetary habitability everywhere.

The manuscript addresses the problem of testing and classifying stationary points for nonsmooth optimization problems, a topic of genuine importance because standard smooth optimality conditions do not apply directly when objective functions fail to be differentiable. The authors propose a framework that combines directional analysis, which examines the behavior of the objective along finite sets of directions, with copositive optimization, which provides a tractable route to certifying local properties through copositive and completely positive matrix formulations. The central contribution is a set of tests that can distinguish among different types of stationary points, and the classification scheme is presented as an extension of earlier work on local minimizers and saddle-type points. The introduction positions the work clearly within the literature on generalized derivatives and Clarke-type stationarity, and the motivation is convincing for practitioners who encounter piecewise-smooth or composite objectives in applications such as machine learning and control. The theoretical development is generally rigorous, with definitions stated precisely and lemmas that build logically toward the main theorems. However, several proofs rely on assumptions about the regularity of the objective near the point of interest that are stated only informally in the introduction, and I recommend that these be collected into a single, explicit hypothesis section. The connection between the directional tests and the copositive reformulation is the most novel part of the paper, yet the transition between the two is occasionally abrupt, and a short discussion explaining why copositivity is the natural certificate would greatly improve readability. The numerical section includes a small set of test problems that illustrate the classification procedure, but the benchmark is limited, and I would encourage the authors to include problems of larger dimension to demonstrate scalability. The reported computation times are useful, yet the paper does not describe the solver used for the copositive subproblems or discuss how solver tolerances affect the reliability of the classification. Comparisons with existing methods for identifying descent directions are only partially developed, and a more systematic table contrasting accuracy, cost, and assumptions would strengthen the empirical claims. The authors acknowledge that the copositive tests are computationally hard in the worst case, which is an honest and appreciated remark, but the manuscript would benefit from a clearer statement of when the proposed procedure is expected to be practical. Several notational choices, particularly the overloading of symbols for directional derivatives and generalized gradients, make some passages harder to follow than necessary. The related work section is thorough in citing foundational results on nonsmooth analysis, although a few recent contributions on second-order nonsmooth conditions appear to be missing. The discussion of limitations is brief and should be expanded to address the sensitivity of the classification to the choice of direction set. Figures are clear and well chosen, though the captions could describe the plotted quantities more fully so that the figures stand on their own. Overall the paper makes a meaningful and technically sound contribution, and I recommend a major revision addressing the assumptions, benchmarking, notation, and clarity of the copositive connection before it is suitable for publication.

Requiring every student to join an after-school activity may sound like a way to build community and discipline, but it is a poor policy that ignores the real needs of young people. The first problem is that students have very different interests, and forcing everyone into the same kind of activity rarely produces enthusiasm. A student who dislikes sports may be pushed into a team, while a student who loves painting may be stuck in a debate club, and neither experience is likely to help them grow. Mandatory participation also takes away valuable time that students could spend on homework, part-time jobs that support their families, or caring for younger siblings. Many students already juggle heavy academic loads, and an extra requirement can add stress that leads to burnout rather than balance. Some students also have health conditions, disabilities, or transportation challenges that make attending daily activities difficult, and a rigid rule would penalize them for circumstances beyond their control. Requirements can also turn activities into chores, draining the sense of choice and curiosity that makes extracurriculars meaningful in the first place. When students pick activities themselves, they are more likely to commit, form genuine friendships, and develop skills they care about. Schools that want to encourage involvement can do so by offering a wide variety of options, providing information about them, and making them easy to access. Encouragement respects students' autonomy, while compulsion treats them as obligations to be managed. A better approach is to invest in appealing programs and let students decide for themselves how to spend their time after school.

Understanding the Key Differences Between Lewy Body Dementia and Alzheimer's Disease

Lewy body dementia (LBD) and Alzheimer's disease are the two most common causes of dementia in older adults, and they are sometimes confused because they share memory loss and cognitive decline. However, they differ in their underlying biology, their early symptoms, and their treatment approaches. Alzheimer's disease is characterized by the buildup of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles in the brain, which gradually damage neurons and disrupt memory and thinking. Lewy body dementia, by contrast, is caused by abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein, which form structures known as Lewy bodies in nerve cells in areas such as the cortex and brainstem. Memory loss is typically the earliest and most prominent symptom of Alzheimer's disease, often appearing as difficulty recalling recent conversations or events. In Lewy body dementia, fluctuating attention and alertness are often among the first signs, with people experiencing periods of confusion followed by periods of clear thinking. Visual hallucinations are common in Lewy body dementia and often involve vivid, detailed images of people or animals, which are rarely a feature of Alzheimer's disease in its early stages. Many people with Lewy body dementia also develop parkinsonism, meaning slowness of movement, rigidity, tremor, and balance problems similar to those seen in Parkinson's disease. People with Lewy body dementia may experience REM sleep behavior disorder, in which they act out vivid dreams by moving or shouting during sleep, sometimes years before cognitive symptoms begin. Autonomic symptoms such as dizziness upon standing, constipation, urinary problems, and sensitivity to temperature changes are also more frequent in Lewy body dementia. Sensitivity to antipsychotic medications is a notable concern in Lewy body dementia, as some of these drugs can cause severe reactions, including worsening rigidity and confusion. Alzheimer's disease typically progresses with a steadier decline in memory, language, and reasoning, while Lewy body dementia often shows more variability from day to day. Diagnosis of both conditions relies on a combination of clinical evaluation, cognitive testing, and sometimes brain imaging, and specialists may use biomarkers or dopamine transporter scans to help distinguish between them. Treatment for Alzheimer's disease commonly includes cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, along with memorantine in moderate to severe stages. Cholinesterase inhibitors are also often used for Lewy body dementia and can help with both cognitive symptoms and hallucinations. Parkinsonism in Lewy body dementia may respond to levodopa, although the response is often less consistent than in Parkinson's disease. Melatonin or clonazepam may be prescribed for REM sleep behavior disorder, and safety around sleep and falls should be addressed with care. Because of the risk of severe reactions, clinicians generally avoid typical antipsychotics in people with Lewy body dementia, and any medication affecting dopamine should be reviewed carefully. Non-drug approaches, including structured daily routines, physical therapy, occupational therapy, and caregiver education, are important for both conditions. Supportive care focused on comfort, safety, and quality of life becomes increasingly central as either disease advances. Anyone concerned about memory, movement, or behavioral changes should consult a qualified healthcare provider, such as a neurologist or geriatrician, for a thorough evaluation.

This paper proposes using hyperdimensional computing to encode n-gram statistics for efficient text classification, and the core idea is a sound and timely one. The authors map tokens and n-grams to high-dimensional random vectors and combine them through binding and bundling operations, producing compact class prototypes that can be compared with simple similarity measures. The motivation, reducing memory and computation for resource-constrained deployment, is well stated and matches a genuine need. The introduction situates the work reasonably well within both the hyperdimensional computing literature and the broader body of bag-of-n-grams text classifiers, though it could engage more directly with recent efficient neural alternatives such as compact transformers and quantized embedding models. The methodology section describes the encoding pipeline clearly, including how positional information is preserved through permutation before binding, which is a helpful detail for reproducibility. However, the choice of vector dimensionality and the handling of hash collisions are not justified with sufficient analysis, and the authors should show how accuracy varies across a range of dimensions. The experimental setup uses several standard benchmark datasets, which is appropriate, but the paper would benefit from reporting variance across multiple random seeds, since the random item memories make results sensitive to initialization. The reported accuracy is competitive with simple linear baselines, yet the margins are small in several cases and no statistical significance testing is provided. The efficiency claims are the paper's strongest contribution, and the timing and memory measurements are informative, although the hardware description is too brief to let readers judge whether the speedups would transfer to other platforms. The comparison against a naive Bayes baseline is useful, but a comparison against a tuned logistic regression on the same n-gram features would make the case for the method more convincing. The ablation study on n-gram order is valuable and shows that higher orders provide diminishing returns, which the authors discuss thoughtfully. The discussion of limitations is brief and should be expanded to address the interpretability of the hypervector representations and their behavior on out-of-vocabulary terms. The related work section is somewhat dense and would read more clearly if organized around the specific design choices the paper makes. Figures are generally clear, though the learning curves lack error bars and the axis labels in one plot are too small to read comfortably. The writing is mostly precise, with occasional long sentences that obscure the main claims and would benefit from tightening. The code availability statement is welcome, and releasing the encoding implementation with exact hyperparameter settings would strengthen reproducibility considerably. Overall, the paper offers a clear and practically relevant contribution with promising efficiency results. Its main weaknesses lie in the lack of statistical rigor, the limited baselines, and insufficient analysis of key design parameters. I recommend a major revision addressing these points, after which the work would be a solid contribution to efficient text classification.

The homeowner, who lives in a village near Cardiff, spent several weeks decorating her front garden with hand-built wooden reindeer, glowing light tunnels, and a life-sized nativity scene. Neighbours and passersby have been queuing to see the display each evening, with many leaving donations in a collection box at the gate. The woman said she was delighted that her hobby had turned into a way to help others during the holiday season. The paper addresses an important and timely problem: producing accurate abstractive summaries of news articles with limited labeled data, by combining self-supervised pretraining on large news corpora with fine-tuning across multiple datasets. The motivation is clearly stated, and the authors make a reasonable case that news text, with its inverted-pyramid structure and lead-biased content, offers useful signals for self-supervised objectives. The introduction situates the work well within prior literature on pretrained sequence-to-sequence models and extractive baselines, though the related work section could more explicitly distinguish the proposed pretraining objective from existing gap-sentence and denoising approaches. The methodology describes the pretraining corpus, the self-supervised task, and the fine-tuning protocol in sufficient detail to follow the core pipeline, but several hyperparameters and data filtering steps are described only briefly, which limits reproducibility. The choice to fine-tune across datasets is interesting, yet the paper does not clearly explain whether the cross-dataset training uses sequential or mixed batching, nor how domain imbalance between the datasets was handled. The experimental results report ROUGE scores across several benchmarks, and the proposed method shows consistent gains over the strongest baselines on most datasets. However, ROUGE alone is a limited proxy for summary quality, and the absence of human evaluation or factuality assessment is a notable weakness given the known tendency of abstractive models to hallucinate. The ablation study is useful for isolating the contribution of pretraining scale, but it would be strengthened by a comparison that varies the fine-tuning data while holding the pretraining fixed. Statistical significance is not reported, and with differences in some cases under one ROUGE point, the claimed improvements require confidence intervals or multiple-seed results to be convincing. The analysis of failure cases is brief, and a qualitative discussion of errors such as omitted key facts or invented details would add considerable value. The paper's discussion of computational cost is also underdeveloped, since large-scale pretraining on news corpora is expensive, and readers need to know whether the gains justify the resources required. Ethical considerations, including the potential for summarization models to amplify biases present in news sources or to propagate misinformation, receive only passing mention and deserve more thorough treatment. The writing is generally clear, though some sections repeat information from the introduction and could be tightened. Figures are legible, but the architecture diagram omits details of the self-supervised objective that appear only in the text. The authors state that code will be released, which is commendable, but the current version does not include a link or repository, so this claim cannot yet be verified. The literature review would benefit from citing recent work on factuality-aware summarization, which is directly relevant to the paper's claims about summary quality. The conclusion summarizes the findings accurately but overstates generality, since the experiments cover a limited set of English-language news datasets. Future work suggestions are reasonable, particularly the extension to multilingual news, though the authors could be more specific about the obstacles involved. Overall, the paper presents a sound and incremental contribution with clear practical value, but it needs stronger evaluation, statistical rigor, and attention to factuality before its claims can be fully supported. I recommend a major revision.

The best time for students to explore career options and prepare for life after high school is during the early years of high school, when interests are still forming and there is room to experiment. Freshman and sophomore year offer the chance to take a range of classes, join clubs, and try part-time jobs or volunteer work without the pressure of making final decisions. These experiences reveal what a student enjoys and what they are good at, which makes later choices far more informed. By junior year, students should be narrowing their focus by researching colleges, trade programs, or apprenticeships that match their interests. They can attend career fairs, shadow professionals, and speak with counselors about the requirements for different paths. Standardized tests and college applications also demand early planning, so beginning the process by the start of junior year helps avoid a rushed scramble. Financial planning matters too, since scholarships, grants, and loans often have deadlines that arrive well before senior year ends. Senior year then becomes the time to finalize applications, compare offers, and make a deliberate decision about the next step. Students who start early in this way tend to enter adulthood with more confidence and fewer regrets. Ultimately, exploring options gradually across several years is more effective than waiting until the last months of high school to decide one's future.

This paper offers a least-squares interpretation of backpropagation through batch normalization and related normalization methods, providing a geometric perspective on gradients that is both novel and mathematically clean. The authors reframe the normalization step as a projection onto a constrained subspace, which makes the gradient expressions easier to understand and verify. The derivations are generally careful and well organized, and the connection drawn between the projection view and the familiar closed-form batch normalization gradient is a valuable contribution to pedagogy. The discussion extends the analysis to related methods such as layer, group, and instance normalization, showing that the same framework applies with different choices of normalization axes. However, the empirical support is limited, as the paper does not demonstrate whether the interpretation leads to any practical benefit in optimization, numerical stability, or implementation efficiency. Some notation is inconsistent between sections, and a few steps in the derivations would benefit from more explicit justification for readers less familiar with least-squares theory. The related work section could also more clearly position the contribution relative to prior analyses of normalization gradients. Overall, this is a solid theoretical contribution that would be strengthened by clearer notation, a fuller treatment of the extensions, and at least a small experimental section showing the framework's practical relevance.

Volunteering in postwar relief efforts offers communities a lifeline at a moment when institutions are fragile and needs are overwhelming. After conflict, volunteers help rebuild homes, reopen schools, and deliver food, medicine, and clean water to families who have lost nearly everything. Their presence also supports the emotional recovery of survivors, who often benefit as much from being listened to and accompanied as from any material aid. Beyond the immediate tasks, volunteers can help restore a sense of normal daily life by running youth programs, supporting local teachers, and assisting with the reunification of separated families. Their work also strengthens local capacity when it is done in partnership with community members, because it transfers skills and builds trust that outlasts any single project. For the volunteers themselves, the experience often brings a profound sense of purpose and a clearer understanding of how fortunate they are in their own lives. Many describe the friendships formed across language and cultural barriers as among the most meaningful parts of their service. Volunteers also gain practical skills in logistics, communication, and crisis response that can shape their future careers. At the same time, the experience can be emotionally demanding, and responsible programs provide training, support, and debriefing so that volunteers can cope with what they witness. Ultimately, the humanitarian impact and the personal rewards are deeply connected, since people who feel valued and useful are more likely to sustain their commitment. When volunteering is grounded in respect, humility, and genuine collaboration, it can help societies move from devastation toward dignity and lasting recovery.

Should the United States replace the Electoral College with a nationwide popular vote for president? The current system, established by the Constitution, assigns each state electors equal to its congressional delegation, and in most states the candidate who wins the statewide vote takes all of that state's electors. Supporters of a national popular vote argue that this system is fundamentally undemocratic, because it allows a candidate to win the presidency while losing the national vote, as happened in 2000 and 2016. A direct popular vote would give every citizen's ballot equal weight, regardless of where they live. It would also end the concentration of campaign attention in a handful of swing states, encouraging candidates to seek support across the entire country. Defenders of the Electoral College counter that it protects smaller states and rural regions from being ignored by candidates focused only on densely populated areas. They also argue that it promotes political stability by encouraging broad coalitions and makes a narrow recount or nationwide dispute less likely to produce a chaotic result. Critics of that position respond that the system is opaque and that the winner-take-all rule distorts representation within states as well. Ultimately, the debate turns on whether the principle of one person, one vote should outweigh the federalist structure that the framers deliberately built into the nation's government.

Summer break is often treated as a pause from learning, but it can also be a chance for students to take real ownership of their education. Allowing students to choose and plan their own summer assignments offers benefits that a fixed reading list or worksheet packet cannot easily provide. When students have a say in what they study, they tend to approach the work with greater curiosity and commitment.

The most obvious advantage is motivation. A student who selects a topic they already find interesting is far more likely to read carefully, take notes, and keep going when the work gets difficult. Assignments imposed from above can feel like chores to be completed and forgotten, while self-chosen projects feel like personal investments. This difference in attitude often determines whether learning sticks.

Choice also builds essential skills in planning and self-direction. Deciding what to study requires students to reflect on their goals, strengths, and gaps in knowledge. Once a topic is chosen, they must break it into manageable steps, set deadlines, and decide how to measure their progress. These are the same skills that college and workplace success depend on, and summer offers a low-pressure setting in which to practice them.

Ownership encourages responsibility as well. When students design their own assignments, they are accountable for the results in a way that feels personal. If a plan falls short, they must figure out why and adjust, which teaches resilience and honest self-assessment. A teacher assigning the same task to everyone rarely creates that kind of reflective learning.

Choice also allows learning to connect with the wider world. A student interested in marine biology might volunteer at an aquarium and write about conservation, while another interested in music might compose original pieces and study their structure. Assignments that grow out of real interests can bridge the gap between school and everyday life. Students begin to see that knowledge is useful beyond the classroom.

Critics sometimes worry that student-chosen work will lack rigor or that students will pick easy options. This concern is understandable, but it can be addressed through guidance rather than prohibition. Teachers and parents can help students set clear learning goals, require a written proposal, and agree on how the final product will be evaluated. With this structure, choice does not mean the absence of standards; it means students help define what meeting them looks like.

Equity is another consideration. Some families can provide travel, lessons, or materials that enrich a student's summer, while others cannot. Good planning can make choice accessible to all by offering options that require only a library card, free online resources, or time in the community. Schools can also provide suggested menus of projects so that students without outside resources still have meaningful choices.

Finally, letting students plan their own summer work respects them as capable young people. It signals that their interests matter and that they are trusted to pursue learning thoughtfully. Many students will carry this confidence into the next school year, approaching new courses with a sense that they can shape their own growth. In this way, a single summer project can become the beginning of lifelong, self-directed learning.

Making creative arts courses optional in school curricula is a question that touches on how we prioritize learning in an increasingly crowded school day. Supporters of this change argue that schools must focus limited time and funding on core subjects such as mathematics, reading, and science, which are tested and considered essential for college and career readiness. When students are given the freedom to choose, they can concentrate on the subjects that match their goals, whether that is engineering, medicine, or a trade. Optional arts courses also give students with heavy academic loads, part-time jobs, or family responsibilities more flexibility in building a schedule that works for them. Schools facing budget shortfalls may find that making arts electives optional allows them to redirect money toward tutoring, technology, or smaller class sizes in foundational subjects. However, this approach carries real risks that deserve serious attention. Many students do not yet know what they are interested in, and an optional system may mean they never discover a passion for music, drama, or visual art. Creative courses also build skills such as perseverance, collaboration, and comfort with ambiguity, which employers increasingly value. Research has suggested that arts participation can support engagement and attendance, so students who drop arts may lose a reason to stay connected to school. There is also an equity concern, since students from wealthier families often have access to arts outside school, while others may depend entirely on what the school provides. Making arts optional could therefore widen existing gaps in opportunity. A balanced solution might keep at least one arts course required while allowing students to choose among several options in later years. In this way, schools could respect student choice without abandoning the broader education that prepares young people for full and thoughtful lives. Ultimately, the decision should rest on evidence about student outcomes rather than on assumptions about which subjects matter most.

Should students be allowed to use mobile devices during class time? This question has become one of the most debated issues in modern education. Supporters of device use argue that phones and tablets are powerful learning tools that give students instant access to information, dictionaries, translation apps, and educational resources. In a world where technology shapes nearly every profession, learning to use these tools responsibly during school may prepare students for life beyond the classroom. Many teachers also report that digital polls, research tasks, and interactive apps can make lessons more engaging and help students stay involved. Allowing devices can also reduce the need for schools to provide costly materials, since students can often access textbooks and reference materials on their own phones. However, the drawbacks of unrestricted device use are significant and well documented. Phones are a constant source of distraction, with notifications, messages, and social media pulling attention away from the lesson at hand. Research on multitasking suggests that switching attention between tasks reduces comprehension and memory, meaning students who check their phones during lectures often retain less of what they hear. Devices can also enable cheating, cyberbullying, and the recording of classmates without consent, creating problems that extend well beyond individual lessons. Furthermore, not every student has equal access to technology at home, and classroom device policies can sometimes deepen these inequalities rather than close them. A balanced approach may offer the best solution. Rather than choosing between a full ban and complete freedom, schools could permit devices for specific, teacher-directed purposes while restricting them during lectures and tests. Clear expectations, consistent enforcement, and lessons on digital citizenship could help students build the self-discipline that unrestricted access requires. In the end, the goal should be to teach students not simply to avoid distraction, but to use technology with purpose. Mobile devices are neither inherently harmful nor inherently helpful, and their value depends largely on how they are used.

Florida's School Archery Program: Curriculum, Benefits, and How Schools Can Get Involved

Archery has become a popular and accessible part of physical education and extracurricular activity in many schools across Florida. Students who take part learn focus, discipline, and safe handling of equipment while building physical skills that can last a lifetime. This page explains how school archery programs in the state are typically structured, what students learn, why educators value the activity, and how a school can begin.

Most school archery programs in Florida are built around the National Archery in the Schools Program, commonly known as NASP, which provides a standardized framework used by thousands of schools nationwide. NASP-style instruction usually begins with range safety rules, equipment identification, and proper stance and grip before students shoot their first arrows. Students then progress through stance development, aiming, release technique, and scoring, with regular practice sessions that build consistency. Many programs end the year with a local or regional tournament where students can apply what they have learned under competition conditions.

The benefits of school archery extend well beyond the target. Students develop concentration and patience, since a single shot requires steady breathing, controlled movement, and a clear mind. The sport also supports hand-eye coordination, posture, and core strength, and it is low-impact, so students of many different physical abilities can participate. Archery programs often include students who may not thrive in team sports, giving them a chance to measure their own improvement and build confidence. Teachers also note that the emphasis on safety and self-control carries over into classroom behavior.

Schools that want to start an archery program generally begin by identifying a trained instructor, which may be a physical education teacher who completes a certified coaching course. The school then needs a safe, supervised range, typically an indoor gym space or outdoor area with proper backstops and clear boundaries. Equipment such as bows, arrows, targets, and protective gear must be purchased or obtained, and schools should confirm that their insurance and district policies cover the activity. Administrators can then work with the district to align the program with physical education standards and schedule regular class time.

Families and community members can also help support a school archery program through volunteer coaching, fundraising, and sponsorship of equipment. Local archery clubs, state wildlife agencies, and outdoor recreation groups are often willing to offer guidance and resources. Before launching a program, schools should review current Florida Department of Education guidelines and district requirements, as these may change over time. Starting small, with one class or a club, is a practical way to build experience and community support before expanding.

Exploring Venus is worth the risks and challenges because it offers unique scientific insight into how planets evolve. Venus is often called Earth's twin due to its similar size and mass, yet its runaway greenhouse effect has produced surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead. Studying this extreme outcome could help scientists better understand the long-term stability of Earth's own climate. The planet's dense atmosphere and crushing pressure make landing difficult, and past missions such as the Soviet Venera probes survived only a few hours on the surface. However, these hardships have driven engineers to develop stronger materials, improved heat shielding, and more creative mission designs that benefit other areas of space exploration. Orbiters and high-altitude balloon concepts could sidestep the harshest surface conditions while still gathering valuable data about clouds, winds, and volcanic activity. Recent evidence of possible phosphine in the upper atmosphere, though still debated, has also renewed interest in whether Venus's clouds could hold clues about the possibility of life beyond Earth. The cost of such missions is high, yet investments in space science have historically produced technologies and knowledge far beyond their original goals. Critics argue that funds would be better spent addressing problems on Earth, and that concern deserves serious consideration. Still, understanding Venus helps humanity recognize how fragile a habitable planet can be. For these reasons, the scientific rewards justify the difficulties, as long as missions are carefully planned and realistic about their limits.

The Chancellor is facing mounting pressure to provide relief for struggling families while holding firm to a policy of fiscal caution, a balancing act that has become more difficult as Brexit uncertainty continues to weigh on the economy. Campaigners, charities, and opposition politicians have called on the Treasury to expand support for households grappling with rising living costs, including higher energy bills, stagnant wages, and the squeeze on food and housing. Advocates argue that targeted measures, such as increased benefit payments, a freeze on fuel duty, or expanded childcare support, are needed to prevent a deepening hardship that could have lasting social consequences. Others within the governing party, however, have warned that unfunded spending commitments risk unsettling financial markets and pushing up government borrowing costs at a time when the public finances remain fragile. Officials at the Treasury have privately acknowledged the dilemma, noting that every additional pound spent on relief must be weighed against the need to maintain credibility with investors and rating agencies. Economists have offered differing views on the appropriate course, with some supporting temporary stimulus to cushion the downturn and others urging a more disciplined approach to reduce the national debt. The uncertainty surrounding Britain's trading relationships with the European Union has added a further layer of complexity, as businesses delay investment decisions and forecasters revise growth projections downward. Manufacturers in several regions have reported difficulties with supply chains, customs paperwork, and the availability of skilled workers from overseas, adding to concerns about productivity. Against this backdrop, the debate over infrastructure spending has taken on new urgency, with proponents arguing that investment in transport, housing, and broadband could boost long-term growth and create jobs. Critics counter that large capital projects often run over budget and that the returns on such spending can take many years to materialise. Regional leaders have pressed for a greater share of planned investment to be directed toward towns and cities outside the capital, citing persistent gaps in living standards and connectivity. Transport groups have called for accelerated funding for rail upgrades and road maintenance, warning that delays are already increasing costs. The construction industry has welcomed the prospect of new contracts but has urged the government to provide clearer and more stable long-term commitments so firms can plan their workforce and equipment needs. Environmental organisations have raised questions about the carbon impact of some proposed schemes and have urged that any investment be aligned with climate targets. Many families, meanwhile, say they are less concerned with the technical details of the debate than with whether their household budgets will be able to withstand the coming months. Food bank operators report rising demand, particularly from working households who had previously managed without assistance. Local councils have reported strain on services, with some warning that they may need to cut back on support for vulnerable residents if central funding does not increase. Trade unions have argued that public sector pay must keep pace with inflation, and several strikes have been called in recent weeks. The Chancellor is expected to set out detailed proposals in the coming weeks, and the government has indicated that it will seek to reassure markets while acknowledging the hardship facing many households. Opposition parties have said the government's approach lacks ambition and that bolder action is needed to address the cost of living. Ministers have responded that responsible management of the economy is the best way to protect families over the long term, arguing that stability and low inflation are prerequisites for sustained improvements in living standards. Whether the Chancellor can reconcile these competing demands will likely shape public confidence in the government heading into the next electoral cycle. Analysts say the coming budget will be a critical test of the government's priorities and its ability to deliver both relief and restraint.

Optimism is often described as a simple attitude, yet its influence on personal growth and success runs deeper than a cheerful outlook. At its core, optimism is the belief that effort can lead to positive outcomes, and this belief shapes how people approach challenges. When individuals expect that their actions matter, they are more willing to try difficult tasks and persist when progress is slow. Setbacks, which are inevitable in any meaningful pursuit, become temporary obstacles rather than proof of failure. Psychologists who study resilience have found that optimistic people tend to recover more quickly from disappointment because they interpret negative events as specific and changeable rather than permanent. This interpretation encourages them to learn from mistakes instead of withdrawing from them. Over time, that willingness to learn compounds into skill, knowledge, and experience. Optimism also strengthens relationships, since hopeful people are often more open, generous, and inviting to others. Such connections provide support, mentorship, and opportunities that can be decisive in a person's development. Furthermore, optimism supports better health, as individuals with a positive outlook often manage stress more effectively and maintain healthier habits. Physical and mental well-being, in turn, give people the energy needed to pursue long-term goals. It is important to recognize, however, that optimism is not the same as denying reality. Blind confidence can lead to poor planning, while realistic optimism acknowledges risks while still believing in the possibility of success. The most effective people combine hope with preparation, setting clear goals and taking practical steps toward them. In this balanced form, optimism becomes a powerful engine for growth. Ultimately, the role of optimism lies in its ability to turn intention into action and action into achievement. Cultivating a hopeful yet grounded mindset can therefore be one of the most valuable investments a person can make in their own future.

Detective Anna Reyes had been certain for three weeks that Samuel Hart killed the bookkeeper, Mara Collins, in the rain-soaked alley behind the Bell Street bakery. The evidence seemed to point straight at him: a torn coat button, a hotel receipt from the night of the murder, and a record of old debts that read like a motive. She drove to the hospice on a grey Tuesday to confront him before his heart gave out for good. Samuel lay propped against white pillows, breathing in thin, careful pulls, and he watched her without speaking. She laid the button on his blanket and told him what she knew, her voice hard with the satisfaction of a case about to close. He looked at the button for a long moment, then asked her, very softly, whether anyone had ever checked where he had been that night. Anna said it didn't matter, that his past spoke for him. Samuel told her about the sick daughter he had sat with in a city hospital, the debts he had taken on to pay for her care, and the hotel receipt that proved he had been there, holding a child's hand, not standing in an alley. Anna felt the floor shift beneath her, and she reached for the file she had built so confidently. She found the hospital's visitor log in a folder she had never opened, and it bore his name and the exact hours he had signed in. Samuel had already closed his eyes when she looked up, and his breathing had grown slower. He died two days later, before she could bring herself to apologize. Anna kept the torn button in her desk drawer for years afterward, and she never again let a suspect's history stand in for the truth.

Persistence and consistent effort are essential for achieving personal goals and overcoming challenges. Many people dream of accomplishing great things, yet only a few follow through on those dreams. The difference often lies not in talent or luck but in the willingness to keep working when progress feels slow. Every worthwhile goal demands time, and that time is filled with obstacles, setbacks, and moments of doubt. Those who succeed understand that failure is not the end but a part of the process. Consistent effort builds skills gradually, so that what seemed impossible at the start becomes manageable through steady practice. Consider a student learning a difficult language. In the first weeks, the grammar seems confusing and the vocabulary slips away from memory. A student who studies for only one intense weekend will likely forget most of it by Monday. However, a student who practices fifteen minutes each day will slowly notice improvement, and within months, conversations become possible. Persistence transforms small daily actions into remarkable results. Challenges also test character in ways that easy victories never can. When a runner training for a marathon faces an injury, the decision to rest, recover, and return to training reveals the strength of their commitment. When a writer receives rejection letters, the choice to revise the manuscript and submit it again shows the determination that separates published authors from abandoned drafts. These moments teach that obstacles are not permanent walls but invitations to adapt. Consistency also matters because motivation is unreliable. Feelings of excitement fade, and enthusiasm often disappears after the first few weeks of any new project. People who depend solely on inspiration will struggle, while those who build habits can keep moving forward even on difficult days. Routines, schedules, and small commitments create a structure that carries us through periods when our energy runs low. Over time, the habit itself becomes a source of strength. Persistence does not mean ignoring problems or refusing to change direction. Sometimes a goal needs to be reconsidered, and wise people adjust their methods when experience shows that a different approach would work better. The key is to keep showing up, learning, and trying again rather than giving up at the first sign of difficulty. Effort guided by reflection is far more powerful than effort without thought. The rewards of persistence extend beyond the final achievement. Along the way, people develop discipline, patience, resilience, and self-trust. They learn that they are capable of more than they once believed. These qualities help in every area of life, from careers and relationships to personal health and creative pursuits. Therefore, persistence is not merely a means to an end but a valuable way of becoming a stronger person. In conclusion, personal goals and the ability to overcome challenges depend heavily on persistence and consistent effort. Talent may open doors, but steady work keeps us moving through them. Those who commit to their goals, even when progress is slow, discover that small steps taken every day eventually lead to meaningful success.

Venus is often called Earth's twin because the two planets are similar in size, mass, and composition, yet they have developed in dramatically different ways. Its surface is hidden beneath a thick cloud deck of sulfuric acid droplets, and its atmosphere is roughly ninety times denser than Earth's. The surface temperature reaches about 465 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead, and the pressure there is comparable to that found nearly a kilometer beneath the ocean on Earth. These extreme conditions have made Venus one of the most difficult destinations in the Solar System to study, and they present the first major challenge to any human effort to explore it.

Robotic missions have shown what a surface lander must survive. The Soviet Venera landers of the 1970s and 1980s transmitted images and data for only short periods, often less than two hours, before their electronics failed under the heat and pressure. Engineers have since learned that materials, electronics, batteries, and seals must all be redesigned to function in such an environment, and progress in high-temperature electronics made from silicon carbide and gallium nitride offers a promising path forward. Even so, a long-duration surface mission remains technically demanding and expensive.

Atmospheric exploration offers a more realistic near-term alternative. At altitudes of roughly 50 to 60 kilometers above the surface, the pressure and temperature are similar to conditions on Earth, and the upper cloud layers receive ample sunlight. This region has inspired proposals for crewed airships or floating platforms that could carry scientists and instruments while avoiding the crushing conditions below. Such a platform would need to manage the corrosive sulfuric acid clouds, which pose a serious threat to any exposed material.

Scientific interest in Venus remains strong. Its runaway greenhouse effect is a powerful natural experiment in how planetary climates can change, and understanding it may help researchers better evaluate climate processes on Earth. Questions also persist about whether Venus once had oceans, how its volcanism has shaped its surface, and whether any unusual chemical signatures in its clouds, such as the disputed detection of phosphine, might point to unknown processes. Answering these questions requires sustained observation and direct sampling.

Looking ahead, several missions have been proposed or approved by space agencies, including orbiters and atmospheric probes intended to study the planet's chemistry, geology, and climate history. These missions will provide data that could guide later decisions about more ambitious plans. Whether humans will ever live on Venus remains uncertain, but its challenges are increasingly becoming problems that engineering and science can address. Venus, once considered a hostile and mysterious neighbor, may yet become a valuable frontier for discovery.

Theo woke to the gray light of morning seeping through the blinds, his head thick with sleep. For a moment he couldn't feel his arms at all, just a dull pressure where they had been pinned beneath him all night. He flexed his fingers slowly, waiting for the prickling pins and needles to climb back into his hands. They came in a rush, stinging and warm, and he groaned as he sat up.

He rubbed his face and stumbled toward the kitchen, where the coffee maker had already been set to brew the night before. The smell hit him first, bitter and comforting. He poured a mug, burned his tongue on the first sip, and carried it back down the hallway.

His desk sat in the corner of the spare room, cluttered with yesterday's notes and a half-eaten granola bar. He pushed the clutter aside, dropped into the chair, and nudged the mouse. The screen flickered to life, showing the document he had abandoned at midnight.

He read the last sentence twice, then began to type. His fingers were still clumsy, and he made a few errors, but the words came more easily as the caffeine kicked in. Outside, a car door slammed and a dog barked somewhere down the street.

By the time the sun cleared the rooftops, Theo had filled two pages and lost track of the empty mug at his elbow. He leaned back, stretched his arms overhead, and felt the blood flow freely through them. It was a good start, he decided, and he pulled the chair closer to the desk.

Subject: Fantasy League Trade Rules and Deadlines for Player Transactions

Dear League Members,

I am writing to outline the trade rules and deadlines that will govern player transactions for the remainder of the season. Please read this carefully so that everyone is working from the same understanding.

Trades are permitted at any point between the opening of the regular season and the official trade deadline. Once the trade deadline passes, no player trades may be processed until the start of the next season, with the exception of commissioner-approved corrections.

The official trade deadline for this season is Monday at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time. Any trade proposal not accepted and processed by that time will be considered void.

All trade proposals must be submitted through the league platform. Verbal agreements, text messages, and social media offers do not count as valid trades and will not be enforced by the commissioner.

Each proposal must clearly list the players and draft picks being exchanged, and must identify both the proposing team and the receiving team.

A trade proposal remains open for acceptance for 48 hours after it is submitted. If the receiving manager does not respond within that window, the proposal will automatically expire.

Managers may withdraw their own trade proposals at any time before they are accepted by the other party.

Once a trade is accepted by the receiving manager, it will be reviewed by the commissioner for compliance with league rules. Most reviews are completed within 24 hours.

The commissioner reserves the right to veto any trade that appears collusive, unbalanced to a degree that suggests manipulation, or otherwise contrary to the spirit of fair play. Vetoes will be communicated to both managers involved, along with a brief explanation.

Managers may propose trades involving two-for-one or three-for-one exchanges, but roster limits must be respected at all times. A team that would exceed its maximum roster size after a trade must release players before the trade can be processed.

Players who are currently injured may be traded, but managers are responsible for evaluating the health status of any player they acquire. The league does not offer refunds or reversals for trades based on injuries that occur after the transaction is complete.

Draft picks may be traded for players or other picks, provided the picks are for the current or upcoming season and have not already been used. Future picks beyond the next season are not tradable in this league.

Each team may make up to five trades during the regular season. Trades that are vetoed by the commissioner do not count toward this limit.

Trade proposals must be submitted with enough time to be accepted before the deadline. The league platform cannot guarantee processing for proposals submitted in the final hour before the deadline.

Players acquired in a trade are locked to their new team for a period of 24 hours, meaning they cannot be traded again during that window.

Managers may not trade a player on the same day that player is scheduled to play, if the game has already started. Lineup changes made after a game begins will follow the standard lineup lock policy.

Waiver claims are processed separately from trades. A player who is placed on waivers may not be traded until the waiver period has concluded.

Any manager who wishes to dispute a trade decision may contact the commissioner within 24 hours of the decision. Disputes submitted after that window will not be considered.

The commissioner's decisions on trade disputes are final for this season.

Managers who fail to maintain a legal roster after a trade will receive a warning on the first offense. Repeated violations may result in a forfeited transaction or a penalty to the team's standings.

Please remember that trades are intended to improve competition and enjoyment for everyone. Attempts to exploit loopholes or engage in deals designed to unfairly strengthen one team at another's expense will not be tolerated.

League members are encouraged to communicate openly about trade interests, but all official negotiations should be finalized through the platform to ensure a clear record.

If you have questions about any of these rules, please contact the commissioner before submitting a proposal. It is much easier to resolve uncertainty in advance than after a trade has been processed.

The trade rules listed above will be posted in the league rules section of the platform for easy reference throughout the season.

Thank you for your cooperation in keeping our league fair and competitive. We look forward to an exciting remainder of the season.

Best regards,

The League Commissioner

Subject: Requested Revisions to Draft Gas Supply Agreements for Public Service Company of Colorado and Cheyenne Light, Fuel & Power

Dear Team,

Thank you for providing the draft gas supply agreements for Public Service Company of Colorado and Cheyenne Light, Fuel & Power for our review. We have now completed our initial assessment of both documents and wanted to share our requested revisions in one consolidated message so that we can move toward finalization efficiently. Our comments are organized by topic, and where a revision applies to both agreements, we have noted that explicitly to avoid duplicative discussion. We appreciate the care that went into the drafts and recognize that the underlying structure is sound in many respects. The revisions below are intended to clarify obligations, align terms with our operational requirements, and reduce the risk of disputes during the life of the contracts.

First, we request clarification of the definition of Gas Day and the associated nomination deadlines. The current language refers to nominations being due by a time that does not clearly align with the timing of the pipeline's own scheduling cycles. We propose that the agreements specify the nomination windows by reference to the applicable interstate pipeline tariff, with a fallback provision for intraday changes. This change applies to both agreements.

Second, we ask that the agreements include an explicit description of the measurement standards to be used for determining delivered volumes. We recommend that volumes be measured in accordance with the applicable American Gas Association standards and that the measurement points be identified by name and location in an exhibit. Discrepancies between metered and nominated volumes should be resolved according to a defined procedure rather than left to ongoing negotiation.

Third, regarding the quantity provisions, we request that the daily contract quantity and any seasonal or monthly maximum quantities be stated in a single schedule for ease of reference. We also ask that the tolerance band for daily variances be made symmetrical, so that over-deliveries and under-deliveries are subject to comparable treatment. The current draft contains asymmetric imbalance charges that we believe should be revisited.

Fourth, we propose revisions to the balancing provisions. Specifically, we request that cumulative imbalances be cleared on a monthly basis rather than at the end of the contract year, which will reduce the accumulation of large imbalances and the associated financial exposure. We also request a cap on any cash-out pricing applied to imbalances and a clear statement of the index that will be used to determine the cash-out price.

Fifth, we ask for clearer language on force majeure. The current draft lists events that would excuse performance but does not address how notice must be given, how long the excuse may continue, or whether the affected party must make reasonable efforts to resume performance. We propose adding a notice requirement of no more than two business days, a requirement to mitigate, and a termination right if the force majeure event continues beyond a specified period. This revision applies to both agreements.

Sixth, we request that the pricing provisions be restated with greater precision. The reference to the index price should identify the specific publication, the trading location, and the pricing period. Where a fixed fee component applies, its amount and the escalation mechanism should appear in the body of the agreement rather than only in an attachment.

Seventh, regarding invoicing and payment, we ask that invoices be issued within a defined period after the close of each billing month and that payment terms be stated as a specific number of days from receipt of a correct invoice. We further request a dispute procedure that permits the undisputed portion of an invoice to be paid on time, with disputed amounts resolved under the agreed process.

Eighth, we propose adding a late payment provision that sets the interest rate by reference to a recognized published rate, and that limits the application of interest to undisputed amounts that remain unpaid after the due date and a short cure period.

Ninth, we request revisions to the credit support provisions. The draft requires security in an amount that we consider higher than necessary given the volumes and payment history involved. We propose that the security requirement be tied to a defined exposure calculation, that it be reviewed quarterly, and that it may be satisfied by a letter of credit, a parent guarantee, or cash deposit at our election.

Tenth, we ask that the agreements specify the conditions under which a party may suspend deliveries or receipts for nonpayment. We recommend a notice period, a cure opportunity, and a clear statement that suspension does not relieve either party of its other obligations under the agreement.

Eleventh, regarding default and termination, we request that the cross-default provisions be narrowed so that a default under an unrelated agreement does not automatically trigger a default here unless it exceeds a specified threshold. We also ask for a defined cure period for each category of default and a mutual termination right for prolonged force majeure.

Twelfth, we propose revisions to the limitation of liability section. We request that consequential, indirect, and punitive damages be expressly excluded for both parties, subject to a carve-out for indemnification obligations relating to third-party claims. We also ask that the liability cap be stated in a specific dollar amount or as a multiple of annual contract value.

Thirteenth, we request that the indemnification clause be made reciprocal. The current draft places a broader indemnity obligation on our side than on the counterparty, and we do not believe that allocation reflects the respective responsibilities of the parties with respect to title, custody, and operation of facilities.

Fourteenth, regarding title and risk of loss, we ask that the agreements state that title and risk of loss pass at the agreed custody transfer point and that the point be described with reference to an exhibit. This will remove any ambiguity about responsibility for gas in transit.

Fifteenth, we propose clarifying the warranty provisions. Specifically, we request that the seller warrant good title, the right to sell, and that the gas meets the applicable quality specifications. We ask that the quality specifications be attached as an exhibit and that any remedy for off-specification gas be defined.

Sixteenth, regarding regulatory changes, we request a change-in-law provision that allows either party to seek renegotiation if a change in law or regulation materially affects the economics or legality of performance. We further ask that the parties agree to cooperate in good faith to preserve the original intent of the agreement to the extent permitted by law.

Seventeenth, we ask that the agreements address the treatment of Commission-approved tariffs and rates. Where the agreement incorporates regulated rates, we request that it expressly state that such rates control in the event of a conflict and that the agreement will be reformed as necessary to comply with any future regulatory order.

Eighteenth, we propose adding a confidentiality provision that protects commercially sensitive information, including pricing and volume data, while permitting disclosure to regulators, auditors, financing parties, and affiliates on a need-to-know basis. This provision should survive termination for a stated period.

Nineteenth, we request a dispute resolution clause that begins with escalation to senior management, followed by non-binding mediation, and only then arbitration or litigation in a specified forum. We ask that the governing law and venue be identified explicitly.

Twentieth, regarding assignment, we request that neither party may assign the agreement without the other party's consent, except to an affiliate with comparable creditworthiness or to a successor by merger or sale of substantially all assets, provided written notice is given in advance.

Twenty-first, we ask that the notice provisions specify addresses, email contacts, and deemed receipt rules for each party, and that a designated representative be named for operational communications separate from contract administration.

Twenty-second, we propose that the agreements include a term and renewal provision that states the initial term, the notice period for non-renewal, and the process for extending the agreement on mutually acceptable terms.

Twenty-third, we request that the agreements contain a most-favored-nation or similar review clause only if it is mutually agreed, and that any price review mechanism be clearly defined with specific triggers and timelines.

Twenty-fourth, regarding operational coordination, we ask that the parties commit to share forecasts of demand and supply on a defined schedule and to notify each other promptly of any event that is expected to affect deliveries.

Twenty-fifth, we request that the agreements address pipeline capacity, specifying which party holds the capacity, how it is to be used, and how any release or recall of capacity will be handled in connection with the gas supply obligations.

Twenty-sixth, we ask that operational flow orders and similar directives from the pipeline be expressly addressed, with a statement that each party will comply with such orders and that costs resulting from non-compliance will be allocated to the responsible party.

Twenty-seventh, regarding emergencies, we propose a provision that addresses curtailment priorities consistent with applicable regulations and that allocates responsibility for curtailment decisions and their costs.

Twenty-eighth, we request that the agreements contain a clear statement of the reporting obligations each party has to the other, including any information needed for regulatory filings, and a reasonable timetable for delivering that information.

Twenty-ninth, we ask that the audit rights be defined, including the frequency of audits, the notice required, the scope of records available, and the allocation of audit costs.

Thirtieth, we propose that the agreements address record retention, requiring each party to maintain relevant records for a stated period after the end of the contract term.

Thirty-first, we request that the agreements include a representation regarding compliance with applicable laws, sanctions, and anti-corruption requirements, with a corresponding covenant from each party.

Thirty-second, regarding insurance, we ask that the required coverages, minimum limits, and certificate delivery requirements be stated in the agreement, and that each party maintain its coverage during the term.

Thirty-third, we propose that the agreements expressly address environmental responsibilities, including allocation of responsibility for emissions, methane reporting, and any compliance costs arising from changes in environmental requirements.

Thirty-fourth, we request that the agreements address safety obligations, including compliance with applicable pipeline safety standards and a requirement to notify the other party promptly of any incident affecting deliveries or facilities.

Thirty-fifth, we ask that the agreements state which party is responsible for obtaining permits and approvals necessary for its performance and for any facilities it owns or operates.

Thirty-sixth, regarding taxes, we request that the agreements allocate responsibility for applicable taxes and fees, with a statement that each party will bear taxes imposed on its own income and that any new taxes will be passed through as appropriate.

Thirty-seventh, we propose a provision on gas quality testing and reporting, including the frequency of testing, the laboratory or method to be used, and the procedure for resolving disputed test results.

Thirty-eighth, we ask that the agreements address the treatment of gas losses and fuel use, specifying how these will be measured and allocated between the parties.

Thirty-ninth, we request that the agreements contain a clear statement of the relationship between the parties, confirming that they are independent contractors and that nothing in the agreement creates a partnership, joint venture, or agency relationship.

Fortieth, we propose adding a waiver clause stating that a failure to enforce any provision does not constitute a waiver of that provision or of future enforcement rights.

Forty-first, we ask that the severability clause be retained and strengthened so that if any provision is held invalid, the remainder of the agreement continues in effect and the parties negotiate a valid substitute that reflects the original intent.

Forty-second, we request that the entire agreement clause be reviewed to confirm that it supersedes prior understandings, while preserving any confidentiality or other obligations that were intended to survive.

Forty-third, we propose that amendments be valid only if made in writing and signed by authorized representatives of both parties, and we ask that the agreements specify the authority levels required for execution.

Forty-fourth, regarding counterparts and electronic signatures, we request that the agreements expressly permit execution in counterparts and by electronic signature, with each counterpart considered an original.

Forty-fifth, we ask that the agreements include a survival clause identifying which obligations continue after termination, including payment, indemnification, confidentiality, audit, and limitation of liability provisions.

Forty-sixth, we propose that the exhibits be finalized and attached before execution, and that any exhibit that refers to a future index, tariff, or specification include a clear method for updating it.

Forty-seventh, we request that the agreements define key terms consistently throughout, and that a defined terms section be added at the beginning of each agreement to reduce ambiguity.

Forty-eighth, we ask that the agreements include a cross-reference table linking the operational provisions to the applicable tariff sections, so that the relationship between the contract and the regulated framework is easy to follow.

Forty-ninth, we propose that the parties agree on a joint implementation schedule that identifies the steps needed before the agreements take effect, including system setup, nomination testing, and communications protocols.

Fiftieth, we request that a pilot period or transition arrangement be considered for the first months of the term, during which the parties can test operational procedures and identify any practical issues before full reliance on the contract terms.

Fifty-first, we ask that the agreements specify the process for resolving operational disagreements on a day-to-day basis, distinct from the formal dispute resolution process, so that routine matters do not escalate unnecessarily.

Fifty-second, we propose that the parties establish a governance committee with representatives from each side that meets on a regular schedule to review performance, address emerging issues, and recommend amendments where appropriate.

Fifty-third, we request that the agreements address performance metrics, including delivery reliability and response times, and that any remedies or incentives tied to those metrics be clearly defined.

Fifty-fifth, we propose that the agreements clarify the treatment of gas purchased in replacement, including the pricing reference and the documentation required to support any claim.
